Step two: research the product's competitors — collect their ads, landing pages and targeting signals, then write down explicitly what they are not doing: which customer type, life circumstance or outcome they never mention.
Look for angles that are visibly rare in the ad set rather than completely absent, since a small amount of validation reduces the risk of an angle nobody wants.
Position your whole campaign on the gap — avatar, hook, imagery, proof — rather than adding it as a secondary message.
Repeat the audit whenever entering a new category; the source frames this as thinking rather than automating, and argues most dropshippers do not do it.
caveats: 'Do something nobody's doing' is the source's maxim and a direction of travel, not evidence that any untaken angle will convert.
Competitor ad libraries only show what is currently running, so recently paused tests can be invisible.
cards.source_name: Full Product Research Course for Dropshipping (Find Winning Products FAST).docx

cards.title: Judging product quality: real value versus viral junk
cards.summary: Distinguish products that solve a durable human problem and hold margin from cheap trend items that rely on novelty and have no utility.
cards.use_when: Rejecting candidates during any research method, or deciding whether a trending item deserves a test.
steps: Ask whether the product changes the customer's day-to-day life: relieving pain, enabling home workouts, improving hygiene. The source's contrast is a $25 hand massager sold at $80 for daily pain relief versus a music-projector vibe product.
Check the margin math, not the trend: the source rejects products that are cheap with no room for a $30–$40+ markup.
Be sceptical of products whose appeal is purely the trend itself — the source says these come and go and have no real usage.
Remember that passing this filter is necessary but not sufficient: the source notes that even genuinely good products in crowded niches will fail without a differentiation plan.
Use this test during Reels and ad-library scrolling to keep the feed trained on higher-quality candidates.
caveats: Value judgements about what 'helps people' come from the presenter and are subjective; some novelty products do sustain profitable campaigns.
The source's own Pilates and hand-massager examples are his successes and should not be read as typical outcomes.
cards.source_name: Full Product Research Course for Dropshipping (Find Winning Products FAST).docx

cards.title: What a trained Instagram Reels feed yields and how to read it
cards.summary: Practical expectations for the Reels method: a mix of junk and winners, and a qualification step on AliExpress before logging a product.
cards.use_when: Running the Reels discovery loop and deciding which of the surfaced products to keep.
steps: Expect roughly three categories in the feed: no-value plastic trend junk (discard), quirky but plausible problem solvers (evaluate), and high-value life-improving products (prioritise).
When a plausible product appears — for example a lower-back pain device or a travel suitcase organiser — reinforce it with a like so the feed serves more of that type.
Take the product to AliExpress to establish the real sourcing cost: the source's example is a period-cramp belt at $17 sourced and priced at $59 on the store.
Confirm the margin, the problem solved and that the ad footage is usable before adding it to your sheet.
Keep scrolling in short sessions rather than long ones; the source frames this as something you do continuously, even idly, rather than as a single research block.
caveats: The period-belt pricing is one observed example; sourcing prices and viable retail prices vary by product and market.
Discarding 'junk' too aggressively can filter out categories your audience actually buys, so keep a written rationale rather than gut feel alone.
cards.source_name: Full Product Research Course for Dropshipping (Find Winning Products FAST).docx

cards.title: Target Massive Stagnant Categories Instead of Educating Consumers
cards.summary: Pick huge existing commodity categories with a 'sea of sameness' so you skip consumer education and compete on differentiation rather than category creation.
cards.use_when: Choosing which product category to enter or reinvent, especially when deciding between a novel category and an established commodity.
steps: Scan for categories that are already massive and well-understood so you never have to teach the customer what the product is or why they need it.
Within those categories, hunt for a 'sea of sameness' — every incumbent uses near-identical packaging, color, form and voice, and the category takes itself too seriously.
Eric Ryan's examples: dish soap where everything is green and framed as toxic, and vitamins that are all round and pseudo-scientific.
Treat sameness as the opportunity: incumbents have trained the consumer on function but left the emotional and aesthetic space empty.
Tie the entry decision to your ability to visibly break that pattern rather than to incremental function claims.
caveats: Choosing a huge category means competing against entrenched brands and shelf space; the framework says nothing about distribution or capital requirements, which sit outside product-research scope.
A 'sea of sameness' observation is qualitative; validate consumer boredom or dissatisfaction before committing.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Force-Apply Outside Cultural Shifts to Create Creative Tension
cards.summary: Identify a macro cultural trend from a different domain and bolt it onto the stagnant category to produce an 'intersection of familiar and novel'.
cards.use_when: Developing the core concept or brand world for a commodity product that needs to feel culturally current rather than functionally new.
steps: Map macro shifts happening outside your category — behaviors, values and rituals consumers already care about. Ryan's example is boutique fitness being treated as a spiritual pursuit.
Take one of those shifts and force-apply it to the dormant category — e.g., bring that fitness-as-spirituality energy into daily vitamins.
Aim for the 'intersection of familiar and novel': the product's function stays instantly recognizable while the cultural framing is new.
Score the concept by how much tension it creates between what the category expects and what you present.
Use the shift to write the brand's belief and language, not just the packaging — the tension should be legible across the whole experience.
caveats: The source presents this as a qualitative creative device, not a tested growth lever; no performance benchmark is claimed.
Tension that is too strong drifts into novelty for its own sake — pairing this with the one-iteration rule keeps adoption viable.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: The One Iteration Rule: Change Exactly One Product Variable
cards.summary: Limit reinvention to one major variable from the category's core expectation, because changing two or more makes the product too novel for adoption.
cards.use_when: Deciding how far to deviate from a familiar product format, scent, form, function or price point during concept design.
steps: List the core expectations the category has trained consumers on — form factor, function, color, scent, ritual, packaging format.
Choose exactly ONE of those to break, and keep everything else within expectation.
Ryan's rule: if you change two or three variables simultaneously, the product becomes 'too novel' and breaks consumer adoption.
Treat additional changes as a roadmap for later iterations rather than launch features.
When testing the concept, check whether the single change reads as surprising-but-legible; if consumers cannot quickly place it, reduce novelty further.
caveats: This is a cognitive-adoption heuristic attributed to Eric Ryan, not an experimentally derived threshold; some categories and audiences tolerate more change.
What counts as 'one' variable is subjective — form and packaging can be perceived as one aesthetic change or two.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Cross-Industry Aesthetic Theft to Force Differentiation
cards.summary: Borrow design architecture from a completely unrelated industry — the further apart the dots, the more powerful the differentiation.
cards.use_when: Generating packaging and brand-visual direction for a category where all incumbents share the same visual language.
steps: Define the visual clichés of your category so you know exactly what to avoid.
Deliberately source aesthetic references from industries with no adjacency — Ryan's example is stealing high-end houseware vase shapes and applying them to dish soap packaging.
Prioritize references further from your category; the source claims the further apart the dots, the more powerful the idea.
Apply the stolen architecture to structure, silhouette and materials, not just surface graphics, so the difference survives at shelf and in thumbnails.
Check that the borrowed language still communicates the category function at a glance; theft should shift perception, not obscure what the product is.
caveats: Distant references must be translated, not copied, to avoid looking mismatched or derivative of the borrowed industry.
The 'further apart is stronger' claim is the source's creative heuristic, not a measured result.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Naming Architecture from a Single Jumping-Off Word
cards.summary: Derive brand names from one emotional 'jumping-off word' tied to the product's ultimate goal, with the holy grail being one word and four letters.
cards.use_when: Running a brand naming process for a reinvented commodity product where the name must carry the new positioning.
steps: Identify the product's ultimate goal in emotional rather than functional terms — Ryan uses 'technique' for cleaning, which produced Method, and 'friendly' for vitamins, which produced Olly.
Base the entire naming search on that single feeling word rather than on category vocabulary.
Keep constraints tight: the stated holy grail is one word, four letters.
Generate candidates that could only belong to this brand world; reject names that sound like the incumbents you are escaping.
Stress-test the winner for shelf readability, spoken clarity and whether it still evokes the jumping-off word after repeated exposure.
caveats: The four-letter, one-word target is a stated ideal, not a requirement — Method succeeds at six letters.
This is a creative starting constraint; legal availability and trademark clearance are separate processes not covered here.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Iterate One Variable on a Proven Category
cards.summary: Enter large existing categories and change exactly one major variable to stay familiar-but-novel.
cards.use_when: Choosing which product or category to build in, or deciding how bold a repositioning should be
steps: Target well-established, easy-to-understand categories rather than inventing a category from scratch: you avoid driving consumer education for something wildly new.
Run the 'one iteration' rule: change exactly ONE major variable from the core product expectation (e.g., package shape OR benefit framing OR format).
Avoid changing two or three things at once — that pushes the product into 'too novel,' breaking consumer adoption.
Diagnose failed launches by counting changes: serial founder Eric Ryan says he fails more often from being too novel than too familiar.

For an underperforming pitch or launch, strip it to the single most convincing differentiator instead of stacking four; audiences drop multiple simultaneous changes the way they drop multiple thrown eggs.
caveats: Ryan applies this beyond consumer goods (even B2B), but notes he knows consumer better; treat cross-domain claims as his opinion.
One-variable discipline is a probability argument, not a guarantee.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Hunt for Cultural Shifts a Category Has Missed
cards.summary: The opportunity sits between a macro cultural shift and a stagnant category that hasn't absorbed it yet.
cards.use_when: Scanning a stuck or commoditized aisle for a repositioning opportunity
steps: Walk the retail aisle physically and look for a 'sea of sameness' — near-identical packaging, colors and claims.

Identify a cultural shift already visible in another category the target category has missed (Method: 'lifestyling of the home' plus health/sustainability; the home-care aisle still equated cleaning with poison).
Frame the business as the gap between that trend and where the category currently sits.
Ask whether the category has made something unnecessarily complicated, or takes itself too seriously — Ryan reads both as signals of insecurity hiding in the category.
Bring a childlike or playful angle into a self-serious category (gummy vitamins for adults, patterned bandages).
caveats: Ryan's read is that over-complication or self-seriousness signals insecurity — his interpretation, not a proven law.
The shift must already be visible elsewhere; you are connecting existing dots, not predicting a market.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Cross-Industry Theft to Create Creative Tension
cards.summary: Steal aesthetics and mechanics from far-away industries; the further apart the dots, the more powerful the idea.
cards.use_when: Generating distinct product, packaging or brand directions in a saturated category
steps: Steal from as far away as possible rather than copying competitors — from personal care into home care, or housewares into dish soap.
Ask the core question 'what if this, but for that?' to bridge two disparate domains.

Apply the mechanic to concrete cases: vase shapes became Method bottles; a Tokyo building's pillowed skin texture became a handwash design; a Norwegian camping-fuel bottle's shoulders became the original Method bottle.
Design everything as an object of desire, not a package — if a product is meant to sit on a counter, you look at it more than you use it.
Note that the strongest ideas pair two opposing concepts (eco + chic) to create creative tension, which Ryan argues deepens the experience and loyalty.
caveats: Distant combinations 'are not always going to work' — failure rate rises with novelty.
Ryan built the first Method bottle this way partly because a designer was unaffordable; theft-by-riffing suited the constraint.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Design for the Familiar-Novel Intersection
cards.summary: Land products at the intersection of familiar and novel: too familiar loses differentiation, too novel kills trial.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether a concept is differentiated enough to matter yet easy enough to adopt
steps: Test the concept on two axes: if it's too familiar it lacks differentiation; if it's too novel it feels foreign and is harder to get someone to try.
Aim for enough familiarity to give consumers a jumping-off point and enough novelty to make it a new experience.
Use familiarity anchors consumers already trust — e.g., fiber as a benefit people already believe is good for them — and add novelty at the brand/product level.
Accept that finding the intersection is 'easy to say, hard to find' — it is the art of the process, so generate several candidate bridges rather than assuming the first works.
caveats: No numeric ratio of familiar to novel is given; it is a judgment call.
Consumer-education burden is the practical cost of drifting toward novel.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Simplify Instead of Demonstrating Sophistication
cards.summary: Best entrepreneurs simplify complex ideas; over-complication is often ego and weakens the pitch.
cards.use_when: Tightening a pitch, product story, or positioning that sounds impressive but isn't landing
steps: Assume the category or pitch has been made unnecessarily complicated; ask how to simplify it back for the consumer.

Cut to one convincing reason to switch, not a list. In one growth call, an AI company kept saying 'we're better' in many ways but could not name the single biggest one — they forgot to say how they're different.
Substitute a concrete scenario: 'for this person, here's the problem with your current tool, and here's how we do it instead.'
Watch for ego-driven complexity — Ryan sees founders overcomplicating to signal specialness or justify valuation.
Treat simplification as transferable: it helps consumers get it and teams execute it.
caveats: The AI-company example is an anecdote, not a measured result.
This is Ryan's opinion; some categories (technical B2B) may legitimately need more explanation.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Brand Naming Constraints: One Word, Four Letters
cards.summary: Start naming from a core feeling word tied to the product's goal, aiming for one word and four letters.
cards.use_when: Naming a new brand or product line
steps: Identify a 'jumping-off word' derived from the product's ultimate goal or feeling — 'technique' for cleaning pointed toward Method; 'friendly' for vitamins pointed toward Olly.
Run the naming search purely on that feeling rather than on descriptive or functional terms.
Treat the holy grail as one word, four letters, which tends to be short, memorable and ownable.
Check the name against the category's existing associations: a name evoking illness or bureaucracy (e.g., legacy fiber brand names) reinforces the outdated positioning you're trying to escape.
caveats: Four letters/one word is a target, not a requirement — Method is six letters.
No naming-availability or trademark process is described here.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Reimagine the Aisle as the Consumer's Experience
cards.summary: Walk the actual aisle and study shopper behavior to find the real pain the category ignores.
cards.use_when: Doing first-hand category research before defining a product concept
steps: Physically stand in the vitamin aisle (or equivalent) and watch shoppers — Ryan observed people visibly stressed trying to choose something healthy, asking strangers what magnesium is for.
Note the practical failures: hard to shop, uninspiring brands, poor packaging — this is the signal to dig.
Identify the big cultural shift the category missed (millennials treating health and wellness as a lifestyle pursuit, visible in how SoulCycle reframed fitness as almost spiritual).
Translate the shift into a design question: 'what would the Soul Cycle of vitamins look like?'
Design the product as a lifestyle object — a counter-worthy jar with the cap doubling as the logo — so it has intrinsic value and gets used.
caveats: Single-category observation is a source of hypotheses, not a validated finding.
Ryan's SoulCycle/wellness framing is his interpretation of millennial behavior.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Translate Benefits on Packaging, Not Features
cards.summary: Sell the outcome word ('sleep', 'beauty') instead of the ingredient name consumers can't decode.
cards.use_when: Writing product-page, packaging or shelf copy for a technical or unfamiliar product
steps: Observe the inference gap: legacy vitamins listed ingredients like vitamin D or melatonin, forcing shoppers to already know what each does.
Rewrite the label or page as the benefit — 'sleep' instead of melatonin, 'beauty' instead of biotin, 'immunity' instead of a nutrient name.
Pair benefit naming with unique blends positioned around the outcome, not the molecule.
Apply the same logic online: headline the job to be done, and let the ingredient detail live lower on the page for those who want to verify.
caveats: Regulatory rules for supplement claims vary by market and were not covered; verify before publishing benefit claims.
Benefit-first naming works best when the underlying benefit is already believed (e.g., fiber is good for you).
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Look at What Everybody Else Does and Do the Opposite
cards.summary: A single structural contrast — like everyone is round, so we go square — can be the whole differentiator.
cards.use_when: Designing packaging or page layout in a visually homogeneous category
steps: Survey the category's physical or visual conventions (in vitamins, every jar was round; in dish soap, every bottle looked alike).
Choose the simplest structural inversion: square jar with a white cap, or a bottle shape borrowed from another industry.
Make the contrast the icon — one 'single stroke that cuts through the noise' rather than many small differences.
Verify the contrast is the kind of change that can be defended and repeated consistently across range extensions.
Keep the rest familiar so the inversion reads as novel rather than confusing.
caveats: The source presents 'square' as an example of the one-variable rule, not a formula to copy literally.
A visual contrast is not sufficient on its own; Method and Olly also changed positioning and naming.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Run Trend Trips with a 24-Hour Make Cycle
cards.summary: Kick off a trend trip with macro trends, assign in-field scavenger hunts, and turn findings into presented concepts within 24 hours.
cards.use_when: Planning a trend or inspiration trip intended to produce sellable concepts, not a photo library
steps: Kick off with the big macro trends to ground the group before going into the field.
Hire someone on the ground for the region (Asia, Europe) and visit the most influential retail in that market.
Give everyone an assignment/scavenger hunt: by the 5pm happy hour, each person must bring multiple ideas they're excited about, then the group picks a few.
At dinner, call the brief in to the in-house creative team in San Francisco (their morning), who work on it all day and send it back at end of day.
Present near-polished concepts at breakfast — so you can sell in new products before the flight home.
caveats: The speed is deliberate: two weeks later the emotion and wow factor are gone, per the source.
Depends on having a creative team in a distant time zone and on-the-ground local support.
Trend trips commonly fail because attendees return to overflowing inboxes; the deadline structure is what prevents that.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Pitch Buyers to Improve, Not to Prove
cards.summary: Bring concepts to retailers asking for feedback, not approval — especially for early product direction.
cards.use_when: Preparing to show a concept to retail buyers or partners
steps: Shift the framing from 'I'm here to prove myself' to 'I'm here to improve myself.'
Do not ask buyers to choose A versus B; invite their reaction into the process.
Bring more than a slide: bring the concept as close to real as possible so the reaction is to the work, not the deck.
Use the same fast-turnaround discipline: showing up with near-finished concepts quickly is the wow factor, since emotion fades over weeks.
caveats: This is Ryan's practice, not a rule buyers expect; some buyers will still want a straight pitch.
Ryan built an unusually close early relationship with Target, which is not available to every brand.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Solve the Work in the Creative Before Research
cards.summary: Resolve concept direction by making it, then use qualitative feedback and retailer reaction to guide the choice.
cards.use_when: Choosing between two or three distinct concept directions
steps: Take the candidate directions and have a designer and creative team bring each fully to life before deciding.
Ask first which one you personally are most excited about — this is the energy test.
Share with friends and family: if they don't like it, why would anybody else?
Run 'consumer auditions' — qualitative focus groups — not to let consumers pick A versus B, but to hear feedback that guides your own decision.
Also put the concepts in front of retailers for their input.
Prepare to run two very different concepts (e.g., a blunt comedian-led version and an elevated beauty-style version) rather than splitting the difference.
caveats: Consumer auditions are qualitative guidance, not a vote or a validated preference test.
The energy/enthusiasm test is subjective and may mislead when founders are too close to the idea.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Use 'If It's Hard, It's Probably Wrong' as a Signal
cards.summary: Treat friction and lack of flow as diagnostic signals, though genuine breakthroughs can require an uphill phase first.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to keep pushing a concept or change direction
steps: Track energy flow: if working on something gives energy back, it's a sign it's right.
If you're 'pushing water uphill' for months with pain and no traction, treat that as a warning rather than a badge of effort.
Watch for the break point: once insight starts unlocking the next insight and the narrative comes together, momentum accelerates sharply.
Do not equate effort with value — Ryan warns against assuming a billion-dollar outcome requires visibly billion-dollar amounts of struggle.
Caveat the rule with Ryan's own experience: he pushed uphill for roughly six months on a current concept before it broke.
caveats: Ryan states this as a heuristic, not a law; the source itself describes a months-long uphill phase before a concept worked.
Energy-flow judgments are personal and can be rationalized either way.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Build as an Artisan Operator
cards.summary: Combine creative imagination with predictable operating discipline — supply chain, finance, controls — rather than choosing one.
cards.use_when: Building the team, culture or operating model for a consumer brand
steps: Adopt Ryan's 'artisan operator' philosophy: companies that both innovate imaginatively and run predictable businesses.
Invest deliberately in operating infrastructure — supply chain, finance, controls — alongside creative capability.
Note the scarcity Ryan cites: few companies do both well at scale (he names Apple and Nike).
Protect a small, agile make-focused team; Ryan argues builders and doers thrive in a state of make while managers 'just get in the way' (a deliberately provocative framing).
caveats: 'Managers get in the way' is Ryan's strong opinion, not an operating rule to adopt universally.
The Apple/Nike comparison is illustrative, not evidence of a required model.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Treat Selling as Transfer of Emotion and Energy
cards.summary: Early retail wins came from persistence and contagious belief, not from buyers believing in the product first.
cards.use_when: Selling into independent retailers, distributors or any gatekeeper as an unknown brand
steps: Recognize the realistic window: showing up at 6am to a local grocery store manager gave roughly three minutes to pitch a new premium cleaning brand.
Accept that the buyer may never believe in the product — aim to get them to believe in you, and to believe you'll keep showing up until they say yes.
Find genuine love and energy for what you're building first, so the emotion is real and transferable.
Pair that with the serial-founder pattern Ryan describes: being top 20% at two unrelated things (design plus hustle) rather than top 1% at one.
Be willing to do sample handouts and repeat visits past the point most people quit.
caveats: This describes early-stage, founder-led selling into local accounts; it does not map directly to online acquisition.
Persistence can tip into sunk cost; the source pairs it with the energy-flow test.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Time to Fun (TTF): the onboarding metric that predicts retention
cards.summary: Measure how long it takes a first-time user to reach a moment of genuine fun or value, and ruthlessly cut that time.
cards.use_when: Designing onboarding, first session, registration flow, or first-purchase experience for a product or store.
steps: Define the earliest moment a new customer genuinely experiences the product's core pleasure. In mobile games this is called TTF (time to fun) — the gap between tapping to open the app and the first moment of delight.

Audit your current flow and count every step between arrival and that moment: registration, email capture, phone number, push-notification opt-in, tutorials. The source's example: a game that demanded sign-up and permissions before the player had tried anything had effectively no time to fun at all.

Compress the path so the core pleasure arrives first and the data collection or account creation comes after. Mario's first 15 seconds teach all the controls, let you defeat the easiest enemy, earn a coin, and grow bigger — no tutorial.

Map the concept to your own channel: for ecommerce the equivalent moment might be seeing a hero product in use, receiving a sample, or landing on a page that immediately communicates the product's payoff.
Set a target TTF and treat every element that doesn't shorten it as a candidate for removal or deferral.
Recognize that reducing TTF changes perceived wait time as well as actual wait time — a small early payoff makes a long experience feel shorter.
caveats: The source is a podcast conversation, not a tested ecommerce benchmark; it offers no numeric target for TTF in commerce.
Removing registration friction must be balanced against whatever data the business genuinely needs — the claim is that fun should come first, not that accounts never matter.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Borrow low-TTF tactics from restaurants, samples and arrival rituals
cards.summary: Small, immediate sensory payoffs at the start of an experience lower perceived wait and raise engagement.
cards.use_when: Designing the first minutes of an in-person experience, or translating those mechanics to a digital first impression.
steps: Identify the dead time between arrival and the main payoff. The source's diner example: 22 minutes from sitting down to anything on the table, which reads as a TTF problem.
Insert a small, instant taste of the payoff during that gap — a munchkin, smoothie shot, or free sample so customers get a piece of the experience immediately rather than all of it at the end.
Use more than one sense when possible: the diner riff combined a smell cue with a small taste, and Costco's entry sample (a cracker) gave kids a reason to like the place instantly.

Consider a ritual at arrival that makes the experience feel welcoming and distinctive — the source cites the sushi-restaurant custom of the whole kitchen shouting a welcome when the door chime sounds, and the Hawaiian lei handed out right as you exit the airport.
Keep the payoff small. The intent is to take the edge off the wait and hook the customer, not to deliver the full product for free.
caveats: These are improvised ideas in a brainstorming conversation, not measured experiments; the diner, Costco, Five Guys peanut barrel and hotel-lei examples are illustrations, not verified results.
The speakers note the risk of over-engineering: adding sound effects or extra mechanics to an already-good idea can make it worse.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: White-space scan: look for a category with no brand anyone can name
cards.summary: Walk the aisles or the market looking for high-frequency purchase categories where customers cannot name a single brand — that absence is an opening.
cards.use_when: Sourcing new product or brand ideas in consumer categories.
steps: Define your filters before you look: everyday product, repeat purchase, bought by everyone, and no brand anyone has a favorite in.

Test the category by asking people to name their top three brands in it. In the source's chicken example, none of the participants could name a favorite packaged-chicken brand, and the product itself was literally called 'medium brown egg' in sterile packaging.

Confirm the delta by comparing the commodity shelf to the artisanal version of the same category. Fine cheese has an artisanal counter where sellers 'romance' the product like wine, while packaged cheese is unchanged cheddar and mozzarella — a visible gap between the two.

Look at what already broke the sameness and how: the source cites dinosaur-shaped breaded nuggets, Chick-fil-A sandwiches, and Vital Farms' illustrated cartons as cases where branding, shape, or story created identity in a commodity.
When you find the gap, the job is not to invent a new product but to attach story, identity and design to a familiar one — the 'familiar and novel' combination.
caveats: The absence of a beloved brand is a hypothesis, not proof of demand; the source treats it as an opening to brainstorm, and none of the example ventures were validated.
Some white space is white space because the economics are bad — the source's own jewelry retail attempt failed despite strong consumer response.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Sell the farm, not the chicken: origin story as differentiation
cards.summary: For commodity products, build the brand around the origin story and the life behind the product rather than the product specification.
cards.use_when: Differentiating a commodity or unbranded product where the physical product is hard to distinguish.
steps: Recognize the psychological problem: customers don't want to think about the chicken because it was killed, so give them a story that makes them feel good about the quality and the animal's short life. In the source's framing, the brand is built around a 'heavenly farm' for chickens.
Build the story into the iconography — in the riff, the farm workers become heroes in the brand's illustrated world, borrowing from children's-book storytelling ('Old McDonald had a farm').

Consider starting the brand in social media before the product: the proposal was to build an aesthetic farm account that people love first, so that buying chicken from your favorite farm becomes the natural next step.
Think of this as a narrative wrapper on a white-labeled product, which the source explicitly acknowledges is a form of constructed authenticity.

Pair the story with a concrete quality signal where you can: the source describes a real venture putting RFID tags in cows and chickens so consumers can scan and see how far the animals actually roamed, testing whether 'free range' was truthful.
caveats: The source flags the inauthenticity risk directly — a fictional farm marketed as real is a constructed story, and the speaker names that tension rather than resolving it.
The RFID traceability example is someone else's in-development business, mentioned secondhand; treat it as an idea, not a proven model.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Altruism plus narcissism: the two-sided consumer brand framework
cards.summary: A durable consumer brand delivers a self-interested benefit and a feel-good benefit at the same time.
cards.use_when: Positioning a new consumer brand or reframing an existing product's benefits.
steps: Identify the narcissistic reason the customer buys: the fragrance they love, the design they want on the counter, the taste, the convenience. In the source's Method example, people bought it because they liked how it looked and smelled.

Identify the altruistic reason they come back: it's better for the planet, better for the animal, better for them. The combination is what the source calls the intersection of altruism and narcissism.

Test your positioning by asking whether either half stands alone. A product that is only virtuous tends to lose to one that is also pleasurable; a product that is only pleasurable has no reason to stay chosen.

Apply the frame to a commodity example: the chicken brand in the source's brainstorm would sell the narcissism of the most organic, best-tasting chicken and the altruism that the bird had a good life.
Use this as a positioning checklist for every brand in a portfolio, as the source says he does.
caveats: This is a practitioner's heuristic from an interview, not a measured model, and the source gives no data on how much each half contributes.
The altruism claim has to be substantiated where it touches regulated or verifiable claims; the source does not address compliance.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Jumping-off words: a repeatable naming method for brands
cards.summary: Start naming from a single word that captures what the brand must represent, then generate names from it.
cards.use_when: Naming a brand, product line or sub-brand and you need a starting constraint rather than a blank page.
steps: Choose one jumping-off word that represents the core idea. For Method, the word was 'technique' — the idea of getting force through good technique, because the product cleaned without force.

Generate candidate names against that word rather than against a list of liked sounds. The Method name came out of a co-founder conversation while brushing teeth; the reaction was immediate recognition rather than deliberation.

For each category, identify what every existing name does and deliberately choose the opposite register. In the supplements category, names were either pseudo-science (Centrum) or folksy (Nature's Garden), so the goal was a name that simply sounded friendly — which produced Olly, after Alan Dye of Apple suggested 'Olly Slate' and the team realized it could secure 'Olly' alone.
For a healthcare-adjacent brand, the source wanted a caring icon and arrived at Nightingale as a jumping-off concept; an agency turned that into Wellie.
Treat the final test as instant, no-debate recognition — in the source's experience, every name that worked produced an immediate 'that's it.'
caveats: The source says naming is the hardest part of a startup and that everything is taken; expect legal and availability work even after you fall for a name.
He describes himself as good at spotting a name rather than generating one, and used agencies or collaborators for several of them.

A lawyer initially said 'Method' was too generic to secure; the source asked the lawyer what he'd do if the name were critical, got 'go for it,' and it worked — an anecdote, not a legal clearance process.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Change of presentation: reframe a rejection instead of accepting it
cards.summary: When a customer rejects a product, change how it is presented before concluding they don't like it.
cards.use_when: You see low trial, low repeat or flat engagement and are tempted to conclude the product or audience is wrong.
steps: Adopt the reframe: it is not a question of whether the customer likes it, but what change of presentation would get them to try it. The source credits the phrase to his mother-in-law, who got a milk-refusing toddler to drink by pouring milk into the cap as a tiny cup.
Look for format and portion changes first — a smaller single-serve vessel, a different container, a shape, a ritual.

Apply it to packaging decisions. Babybel's wax-wrapped single serve works because it is grab-and-go, pocketable, and the peeling ritual is oddly satisfying; the source describes its time-to-fun as about three seconds.

Consider packaging mechanics that feel delightful and repeatable — the source compares the way the wax splits into two halves to opening an oyster, and cites the redesigned Coke cap that stays attached to the bottle as another satisfying, recyclable mechanism.

Test the presentation change with a specific audience before scaling. The proposed gourmet-cheese line takes a kid's format and elevates it for adults with different flavor profiles and slightly larger size.
caveats: The source's own co-host pushes back that adding a toy or tool to the product may not be scalable and that the presentation-shift insight is stronger than that specific application.
The source also warns that over-innovating a good idea can ruin it — he says he was 'making a good idea bad' by adding a sound effect to the wax peel.
The milk and bread examples are family anecdotes, not consumer research.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Familiar plus novel: how to reposition a commodity format
cards.summary: Take a recognized product or format and add one clear element of novelty rather than inventing from scratch.
cards.use_when: Developing a new product in a crowded commodity category.
steps: Start from what people already know and buy — sliced cheese, single-serve wax-wrapped cheese, chicken — rather than a new category requiring education.

Add novelty in one dimension: shape, format, flavor profile, size, or the ritual of use. Dinosaur-shaped breaded nuggets and restaurant-served chicken sandwiches are the source's examples of familiar chicken made novel by form and context.

Look for formats that already have emotional attachment and increase their appeal for a new audience. Babybel's wax form is a children's product; the pitch is to make a gourmet version for adults with more sophisticated flavor profiles, slightly bigger, in different colors.

Ask whether the novelty creates an annuity — a consumable that people rebuy — rather than a one-time novelty purchase. The source notes a shape-stamper toy risks being a durable good rather than a repeat purchase.
Keep the number of innovations small: one iteration on the familiar product, not several stacked at once.
caveats: The cheese concepts in the source were brainstormed live and not tested; the participants disagree about whether the stamper idea is scalable.
Novelty formats can be copied easily, and the source gives no evidence on defensibility.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: When a hard business is the wrong business: recognize capital intensity
cards.summary: The source's rule of thumb is that if it's hard, it may be wrong — distinguish difficulty you can iterate out of from structural economics you can't.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to keep funding a venture, particularly retail, physical or capital-intensive consumer concepts.
steps: Diagnose whether the difficulty is operational or structural. The source's jewelry retail brand had strong consumer response, celebrity exposure and a Nordstrom partnership with capital, but was so capital intensive that a path to profitability and raising capital in that market were both extremely difficult.
Check the inputs you cannot control. In that case, gold pricing was spiking, diamond pricing was crashing, and A-class leases were being eaten up by LVMH, making expansion economics untenable.
Look for the structural ceiling before you scale: in the source's words, it was like a plane made of gold — no matter how fast it went down the runway, it could not get airborne.
Give it real effort before quitting — the source worked on the jewelry business from launch to dead, roughly three to four years.

Change tables rather than grinding at a table where the economics can't work. The source cites Tony Hsieh's advice that sometimes you have to move poker tables, and interprets his own situation as sitting at the wrong table.
caveats: 'If it's hard, it's wrong' is the source's opinion and a retrospective framing; many viable businesses are simply hard.
Strong consumer traction, press and partnerships did not save this business, so those signals alone should not be read as validation of the unit economics.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Incubator model: build the concept, hire a CEO, then step back
cards.summary: Create the idea, assemble the team and capital, then bring in an operator — and expect the handoff to be the hardest part.
cards.use_when: Founders who want to keep originating ideas without running the company long term.
steps: Define the division of labor: the source wants to create the concept and pull together the team and capital, hire a CEO, and work alongside that team rather than leading it.

Understand what the operator actually needs to do: in a startup, the plan is iterative — you try things, they work or they don't, and you keep making adjustments. The person running it must live in that uncertainty without panicking, keep the team confident and bring people along.

Screen for that tolerance, not just for accomplishment. The source found a recurring failure pattern: highly accomplished hires whose careers had been linear — good grades unlock a good college, which unlocks the next step — struggled badly when things started going wrong, as they always do in a startup.
Expect the transfer of your own idea and energy into another person to be genuinely difficult, and treat finding leaders as the main constraint on the model.
Consider pairing the incubator with a fund or coaching role, as the source did by joining a consumer-brands fund to work with entrepreneurs.
caveats: The source states plainly that finding those leaders has been really hard and is the hardest part of this model.
The linear-career generalization is his observation from his own hires, not a validated screening criterion.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Inverse international expansion sequence to dodge US ad auction saturation
cards.summary: Enter secondary English-speaking markets in the order Australia, UK, Europe, Canada, then US to build dominant share before competitors saturate Meta auctions.
cards.use_when: Planning geographic expansion for an established ecommerce brand that has product-market fit in one market and is deciding which country to enter next.
steps: Sequence entry as Australia, then UK, then Europe, then Canada, and only then the US. The point of going in reverse order of market size is to accumulate revenue, data and brand proof in less contested channels before the largest, most expensive auction.
Treat the US last because its Meta ad auctions are the most competitive and expensive; a brand entering cold faces established incumbents bidding up the same audiences.
Use the earlier markets as proving grounds: each launch should produce conversion data, creative learnings and social proof that makes the eventual US entry stronger.

Confirm the strategy is viable for your situation before committing: this sequence assumes sufficient capital to run several launches and a product that travels across English-speaking markets with minimal localisation.
Validate demand independently in each new market rather than assuming spillover from the previous one; auction dynamics, competitors and buyer behaviour differ by country.
caveats: This is one operator's stated sequence from a podcast interview, not a universal rule; the source qualifies it as conditional on brand state and available capital.
Deferring the US can mean leaving the largest revenue pool to competitors who arrive first; the trade-off is market share versus total addressable revenue.
The source's broader context was a founder interview including dropshipping anecdotes and mental-health discussion; only the geographic expansion model is transferable.
Do not score markets on ad demand alone via ad-library scrapers; that approach has different economics and failure modes from a brand expansion.
cards.source_name: How to Build an Billion Dollar E-Commerce Empire.docx

cards.title: Why secondary English-speaking markets are cheaper to win first
cards.summary: Entering Australia, UK, Canada and Europe before the US exploits lower auction competition and English-language reuse while the US remains saturated.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether to launch in a smaller English-speaking market first instead of the US, or comparing cost of entry across candidate countries.
steps: Identify candidate markets that share a language with your current store so creative, copy, reviews and customer support can be reused with little rework; English-speaking markets are the source's example.
Compare auction competitiveness rather than population: a smaller country with fewer established bidders can produce cheaper customer acquisition than a large saturated one.
Assess whether you can establish dominant share in the secondary market; the source's claim is first-mover position is achievable there in a way it is not in the US.
Model the capital required for a launch in each market including local logistics, payment methods and any regulatory or tax registration, before treating the market as a low-cost test.
Stack the launches in sequence so learnings from earlier markets feed the next rather than running all geographies simultaneously.
caveats: Lower auction competition is an inference from the source's stated strategy, not a benchmark with numbers; verify current costs in your own account.
Language reuse only holds if the product, sizing, compliance and returns policy work in the target country.
First-mover advantage is not guaranteed and depends on the category's competitive density.
cards.source_name: How to Build an Billion Dollar E-Commerce Empire.docx

cards.title: Product Selection Over Brand: The Fast Ecommerce Play
cards.summary: Prioritise finding a trending product in an under-served market over building a brand if your goal is fast ecommerce growth.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest in brand building or rapid product acquisition for a new ecommerce venture.
steps: Accept that speed to $10M in year one comes from aggressive acquisition and riding a trend wave, not from brand building — the source states he could not even define a brand when scaling to $10M.
Find a market that sells a trending product but lacks brand awareness: people are problem-aware and product-aware but not brand-aware, so you do not have to warm them up.
Boost an engagement post as a paid ad to test the product; the source recalls a simple photo of his mother in the product returning 12x ROAS.
Use the initial cash to build the team and operations, then layer brand and secondary products for sustainability.
Recognise that a founder who excels at brand may not achieve $10M in year one, and a founder who achieves $10M in year one may not understand brand — identify your skill gaps and close them.
caveats: Not practical if you want a durable, long-lasting business from the start; the source lost his first three big brands after failing to build brand, systems and teams.
Works best when you are first or early to a market with a trending product.
cards.source_name: How to Build an Billion Dollar E-Commerce Empire.docx

cards.title: Inverse Geographic Market Entry Sequence
cards.summary: Enter secondary English-speaking markets before the US to secure first-mover advantage and avoid saturated Meta ad auctions.
cards.use_when: Planning international expansion for an ecommerce brand and deciding which market to enter first.
steps: Reverse the conventional US-first sequence: launch in Australia, then the UK, then Europe, then Canada, and finally the US.
Use this sequence to be first to market in each region before competitors arrive and before the US auction becomes saturated.
Accept that the US may remain your smallest market — the source's US market is currently his smallest — because the point is first-mover advantage, not market size.
Note that this model is conditional on your brand state and available capital; it is not a universal rule.
After establishing the product, build out the team and brand on that product layer, then add evergreen secondary products.
caveats: A saturated US ad auction with multiple competitors for the same product drives up CPMs and changes unit economics.
This method assumes you have a product or brand proven in at least one market already.
cards.source_name: How to Build an Billion Dollar E-Commerce Empire.docx

cards.title: Trend Spotting Through Deliberate Observation
cards.summary: Identify tipping trends by paying close attention to repeated signals and asking follow-up questions instead of dismissing them.
cards.use_when: Searching for a new product or market opportunity and needing a repeatable way to spot emerging trends.
steps: Practise being highly observant: the best trend spotters notice a throwaway comment or a niche obsession that others dismiss.
When you hear about something new — e.g. Bitcoin at a conference or a US cookie a kid is obsessed with on social media — ask the person to explain it again instead of moving on.
Treat the opportunity as early rather than complete: many AI companies are only months old, and the source views this as inning 0.1 of AI.

Recognise that people using AI as an excuse not to enter a field (e.g. 'why become a copywriter if AI will replace it') are making a mistake — the disruption levels the playing field and rewards those who adopt the tools.
Look for arbitrage where you can apply a cutting-edge tool to a traditional market that does not know it exists.
caveats: Trend spotting is a learned skill, not a guaranteed formula — the source notes it requires the ability to judge which trends will tip and be profitable for you.
Trends can fatigue and reverse quickly; what goes up fast can come down fast.
cards.source_name: How to Build an Billion Dollar E-Commerce Empire.docx

cards.title: Using the Facebook Ads Library to Find Positioning Gaps
cards.summary: Scrape the Facebook ads library to find a trending product, map all its use cases, then target an unserved avatar with unique positioning.
cards.use_when: Sourcing products and developing unique positioning from existing market activity.
steps: Use tools such as Trend Rocket, Exploding Topics, or Mania (which scrapes ad libraries) to find trending products; you can also use the free Facebook Ads Library to see what is scaling.
Identify a product and write down all its current use cases — the source's example is a TENS device marketed for period pain.
Spot an avatar not being served by the existing positioning — e.g. ultramarathon runners needing muscle recovery.
Use that gap to create unique positioning with a unique product for an unserved market, which lets you scale aggressively.

Launch a generic store and test multiple creative angles simultaneously — one for muscle cramps, one for period pain, one for ultramarathon runners — then scale the landing pages and build the brand around whichever avatar takes off.
caveats: Tool names and interfaces change; verify current availability before relying on them.
The source filmed an 11-hour course on this topic on his YouTube channel, so this card is a starting point, not a complete method.
cards.source_name: How to Build an Billion Dollar E-Commerce Empire.docx

cards.title: Riding a Trend Wave to Build a Sustainable Business
cards.summary: Use a trending hero product to generate cash, then build brand and add evergreen secondary products before the trend declines.
cards.use_when: Managing a fast-growing ecommerce brand that depends on a trend-driven hero product.
steps: Maximise the trend while it lasts: get the product, ride the wave, capture the cash and focus on product and brand.
Build the brand around the function the hero product serves — for a hoodie it is comfort — so the brand outlives the trend.
Add secondary products that are evergreen; the source's secondary sleep-tee, dressing gown and bath hoodie range is growing 20% year consistently for three to four years.

Expect the hero product to decline: the source's wearable blanket is declining faster than the secondary products are growing, and he is extrapolating the 20% secondary growth to rebalance the business.
Accept that the overall business may still decline in the transition period even with a good strategy.
caveats: 'What goes up fast must come down fast' — the source attributes his decline to trend fatigue, competition and COVID mean reversion, not solely to his exit from the CEO role.
Secondary products may not fully offset hero-product decline for several years; patience is required.
cards.source_name: How to Build an Billion Dollar E-Commerce Empire.docx

cards.title: Competition and CPM Dynamics in Facebook Ad Auctions
cards.summary: Understand that Facebook is an auction where a second or third competitor for the same product grossly increases CPMs and changes the business.
cards.use_when: Assessing the long-term viability of a product niche or deciding when to pivot.
steps: Recognise that Facebook finds the users for you, but as soon as two or three competitors sell the identical product, CPMs rise sharply.
Target underserved niches and pockets where there is little competition, because that is where the crazy initial results come from.
Enter a product that does well in a different market, bring it to a market that does not have it, and run it for as long as it is not overcrowded.
Monitor competitive density as a leading indicator for when the business model will need to change.
caveats: Competition is not the only factor in decline; the source also cites trend fatigue and mean reversion after COVID acceleration.
CPM increases are described from the source's experience, not as a fixed numerical benchmark.
cards.source_name: How to Build an Billion Dollar E-Commerce Empire.docx

cards.title: Skill Gaps as the Constraint on Sustainable Growth
cards.summary: Identify and close the specific skill gaps that prevent your ecommerce business from scaling beyond its initial product success.
cards.use_when: A brand has achieved rapid product-led growth but is now plateauing or declining due to founder limitations.
steps: List the variables you need to commit to beyond product and acquisition: leading teams, building systems, removing yourself from operations, building culture, creating secondary products, and creating a brand.
Recognise that the founder who achieves fast growth is often the one least equipped to sustain it — the source scaled to $200M annually but could not lead teams or build systems.
Use pattern recognition of your blind spots; the source's mentor immediately identified that ecommerce people cannot do sales calls because they have never had to — closing it all on Shopify.
Identify skill gaps and close them as quickly as possible rather than staying attached to the dopamine of launching new products.
Accept that successful long-lasting businesses have founders with a broad range of skills, but they were not always that way.
caveats: The source learned this through failure: he launched 10-12 ecommerce businesses after his initial successes and they all failed.
This is a founder-level diagnosis, not a quick operational fix.
cards.source_name: How to Build an Billion Dollar E-Commerce Empire.docx

cards.title: Hiring a Replacement CEO: Archetype and Retention
cards.summary: Define the exact archetype the business needs before hiring a replacement CEO, and trial candidates for six months if possible.
cards.use_when: Stepping back from the CEO role of an ecommerce brand you founded.
steps: Define the exact archetype the business needs, rather than defaulting to the traits you personally lack.
Avoid the main mistake of hiring someone too opposite to you: the business reached its size because of your traits, so sacrificing them can harm the business.
Choose between an internal hire (lower risk because you know the person), an external hire (use a recruiter), or someone you know well such as a friend.
Trial the candidate for six months where possible before committing.
Put the team and systems in place to make the business run without you before you step back.
caveats: The source found his replacement via a hire he acknowledged he 'lucked out' on — she was operational but also strong at marketing — so he did not fully follow his own archetype checklist.
Even a good CEO may not reverse a decline caused by trend fatigue and legacy issues.
cards.source_name: How to Build an Billion Dollar E-Commerce Empire.docx

cards.title: Exposure Therapy for Founder Anxiety and Panic
cards.summary: Face anxiety-triggering opportunities deliberately rather than avoiding them, and give yourself permission to make mistakes.
cards.use_when: A founder is experiencing anxiety or panic attacks and is considering declining a significant opportunity because of them.
steps: Recognise that avoidance reinforces anxiety; the source chose to say yes to becoming a Shark Tank judge despite a recent panic attack period.
Use exposure therapy: put yourself in the triggering situation and realise it will not be the end of the world.

Separate the fear of the trigger from the trigger itself — the source discovered his panic attacks occurred in elevators with people present, not when alone, because the fear was of having an attack in front of others.
Give yourself permission to make the mistake; on recorded TV, a panic attack is cut and is not a big deal.

Seek and accept help: the source's psychiatrist told him to stop working, which cured his anxiety temporarily, and he also used extreme diet (carnivore for six to twelve months helped) and meditation.
Understand that recovery takes years — the source says 10 years of intense behaviour cannot be reversed in two years.
caveats: The source notes medication did not work for him but may work for others.
This is the source's personal experience and coping strategy, not clinical advice; consult a professional.
cards.source_name: How to Build an Billion Dollar E-Commerce Empire.docx

cards.title: Motivation Shift from External to Internal Drivers
cards.summary: Recognise when your drive shifts from proving others wrong to intrinsic purpose, and choose your peer group accordingly.
cards.use_when: Reflecting on what actually motivates you and managing competitive impulses as a founder.
steps: Acknowledge that early-stage founder drive is often about proving others wrong or proving a decision was correct, which powers insane work hours.
Expect the driver to shift over time from external reward to mission-based intrinsic reward — the source describes this as his current transition.
Manage your susceptibility to your peer group: the source considers himself a very susceptible person who could be convinced into a driven state by who he is around.
Choose to spend time with mindful, balanced people whose values align with the life you want, or with money-driven people if more money would genuinely make you happier.
Accept that exceptional outcomes typically require roughly five years to get good at something and five years to get the reward from it.
caveats: The source does not present this as a universal rule; he states everyone is different and the right peer group depends on your own definition of happiness.
Intense competitive drive can be productive but also contributed to the source's burnout and panic attacks.
cards.source_name: How to Build an Billion Dollar E-Commerce Empire.docx

cards.title: Ecommerce Exit Multiples and Timing
cards.summary: Understand the valuation ranges for different ecommerce business models and the importance of market timing when selling.
cards.use_when: Planning to sell an ecommerce brand or assessing what your business might be worth.
steps: Recognise the rough range: a dropshipping brand might get one to two times EBITDA, while an ecommerce brand with replenishable or subscription products like beauty or supplements might get three to six times EBITDA.
Exceptional outlier businesses with retail distribution, a clear product flywheel and a strong brand following may reach three to five times revenue or thirty times EBITDA.
Do not assume you have an outlier business just because outliers exist.

Consider market timing: the source sold his agency in 2021 at eleven times profit, which he describes as absurd for an agency, because luxury clients, 90% retained revenue and COVID growth inflated the multiple.
Accept that listed ecommerce brands mostly declined, dragging down sale multiples for private ecommerce sellers.
caveats: These multiples are the source's generalisations, not fixed rules — the agency comparison (normally around six times) shows sector and timing matter enormously.
Exit processes can fail: the source had a $130M offer collapse after a 4PL failed to sign a piece of paperwork and goods were seized on Black Friday.
cards.source_name: How to Build an Billion Dollar E-Commerce Empire.docx

cards.title: Protecting Black Friday Trade After Logistics Failures
cards.summary: Do not let logistics and compliance failures cost you Black Friday, which the source says generates around 80% of his profits in two months.
cards.use_when: Managing ecommerce operations and third-party logistics ahead of peak trading periods.
steps: Treat Black Friday as the period where the vast majority of profit is made — the source states roughly 80% of profits come in those two months.
Verify that your 4PL or logistics partner has signed all required paperwork for every region; one missing piece of paperwork led to all goods being seized on Black Friday and collapsed a $130M sale.
Build redundancy and check compliance well before peak season, because two consecutive Black Fridays were disrupted in the source's case.
Recognise that Black Friday logistics failures have knock-on effects beyond lost revenue, including derailing acquisition deals.
caveats: The specific 80% profit figure is the source's own business, not a universal benchmark.
The source notes he never had a proper trade period during those years, so the full impact is hard to isolate.
cards.source_name: How to Build an Billion Dollar E-Commerce Empire.docx

cards.title: Retail-Distributed Brands Command Higher Exit Valuations
cards.summary: Target niche product categories with retail exposure to access higher exit valuations and more stable business economics.
cards.use_when: Choosing a product category or planning a brand that could attract acquisition interest.
steps: Prioritise niches with proven high exit valuations — the source cites kids' shampoo as one such category.
Aim to build both ecommerce and retail distribution; the source's invested kids' shampoo brand already had retail exposure in addition to reaching 150k per month in its first two months on ecommerce.
Expect ecommerce brand-building to take time: the source says five to seven years is normal and some exits may take nine years.
Use the Shark Tank example of the dress-glue brand, which raised at a $10M valuation shortly after appearing, as an illustration of how fast a well-positioned niche brand can attract capital.
caveats: The kids' shampoo and dress-glue results are individual case-study outcomes, not promises of similar results.
The source notes the dress-glue founder won the deal but did not take his investment because she raised at five times the on-show valuation.
cards.source_name: How to Build an Billion Dollar E-Commerce Empire.docx

cards.title: Building an AI-Era Service Arbitrage
cards.summary: Sell AI-enabled services to traditional businesses that do not understand the tools, creating an information arbitrage.
cards.use_when: A beginner wanting to reach a first $10,000 per month without building a full product business.
steps: Pick a traditional business niche you can get access to — the source suggests dentistry as an example — and knock on those doors.
Sell AI services to them: copywriting, design, or other outputs produced with AI tools.
Use the information gap: the client will not know whether you or the cutting edge of the market produced the work, creating arbitrage.
Once embedded and providing services, look for a better product or tool built around the same niche.
Apply the same logic to product development: build a layer on top of ChatGPT rather than building your own AI, just as ecommerce brands layer on top of Shopify.
caveats: This is the source's suggested path for beginners, not a guaranteed route to income.
AI tool interfaces and capabilities change quickly; verify current options and pricing.
cards.source_name: How to Build an Billion Dollar E-Commerce Empire.docx

cards.title: When to Focus on the Main Business vs. Saving Side Projects
cards.summary: Resist diverting attention to failing side businesses when your main brand needs you; the source calls his diversion a stupid use of time.
cards.use_when: A founder is spreading attention across multiple businesses and one main brand is struggling.
steps: Recognise the pattern: the source launched 10-12 ecommerce businesses after his initial successes and all failed, partly because he was chasing the dopamine of a new product launch.
Cut the distraction: the source spent only about two hours a day on his main brand while focusing on YouTube and other businesses trying to save them.
Step down as CEO if you cannot give the main business the focus it needs, and put a replacement in place.
Focus your highest-leverage effort on the business with the most potential rather than on projects that are already failing.
caveats: The source did not follow this advice at the time — he admits he should have focused on the main thing.
Stepping down as CEO does not guarantee the business will recover; the source's main brand still declined due to competition, trend fatigue and market mean reversion.
cards.source_name: How to Build an Billion Dollar E-Commerce Empire.docx

cards.title: The Founder Trait Trap in Hiring and Business Design
cards.summary: Avoid hiring people who are the opposite of you, and avoid abandoning the traits that made the business successful.
cards.use_when: Hiring senior leaders or scaling an ecommerce business past founder-led operations.
steps: Recognise that founders are often attracted to the traits they do not have — the source describes this as a potential cancer for the business.
Understand that the business got to its current size because of your traits, so sacrificing them to compensate for perceived weaknesses can undermine what worked.
When hiring, list the exact archetype the business needs and check whether your attraction to a candidate is based on complementing or erasing your strengths.
Trial candidates for six months where possible before committing to a permanent hire.
Use internal, external, or known candidates depending on risk tolerance — external hires benefit from a recruiter.
caveats: The source acknowledges he did not fully follow this principle and lucks played a role in his replacement hire.
Complementary skills are still needed; the point is not to avoid all differences but to avoid sacrificing the strengths that built the business.
cards.source_name: How to Build an Billion Dollar E-Commerce Empire.docx

cards.title: Brand as a Defensive Moat for Ecommerce
cards.summary: Build a brand layer on top of a trending product to survive competitors entering and the power law of competition.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much to invest in brand building relative to aggressive acquisition.
steps: Accept the power law: if you do anything well enough, others will enter, so a winning product alone is not durable.
Recognise that many dropshippers launch a product, do well briefly, then lose out because they never build the brand.
Build a brand around the product's function — comfort for a hoodie — and add secondary evergreen products.
Balance acquisition and brand investment: a brand-focused founder may grow more slowly, while an acquisition-focused founder may not understand brand at all.
Close the skill gap of whichever side you are missing, because long-lasting businesses are built by founders with a broad skill range.
caveats: The source openly states he could not define a brand while doing $10M per year, so fast acquisition does not require brand understanding at the start.
The source's own brands were all lost after his fast-growth phase, which he partly attributes to failing to build brand and secondary products.
cards.source_name: How to Build an Billion Dollar E-Commerce Empire.docx

cards.title: Losing a Shark Tank Deal to a Higher Valuation
cards.summary: A strong Shark Tank pitch can attract outside capital at a higher valuation than the on-show offer, so investors may be outbid.
cards.use_when: Preparing for a pitch or evaluating whether a TV pitch is your best fundraising route.
steps: Understand that a good pitch can generate competing offers: the dress-glue founder who stopped women's dresses falling down raised at a $10M valuation shortly after the show, because she had already secured distribution in service stations and pharmacies.
Note that the founder asked for the perfect amount of money, which led to multiple sharks fighting over the deal.
Accept that a shark's investment offer is not binding if the founder raises at a higher valuation elsewhere — the source was an investor in that deal but the founder did not take his investment.
Prepare for the pitch process: the source describes a week of 12-hour days and about 12 pitches before the sharks found their rhythm, and by week two they were working well together.
Give yourself permission to be terrible at first; early pitches are rough and the sharks had to learn when to jump in and how to pull out the story.
caveats: Case-study outcomes are examples, not promises of similar fundraising results.
The source notes most pitches are founders who do not know what they are doing, so the exceptional pitch is rare.
cards.source_name: How to Build an Billion Dollar E-Commerce Empire.docx

cards.title: Why a Founder Should Not Judge Pitches Too Harshly
cards.summary: Most early-stage pitches are rough, and the founder's job is to identify potential rather than dismiss founders for lack of polish.
cards.use_when: Evaluating early-stage businesses or preparing for your own first pitch.
steps: Recognise that the vast majority of pitches involve founders who do not truly know what they are doing yet but have something there.
Avoid judging harshly, because the source says he and his co-hosts were in exactly that position when they started.
Look for the components that can be worked on — the product, the market, the founder's ability to learn — rather than expecting a finished pitch.

Use the example of the AI school software pitch, where the founder's pitch was too complex and Robert Herjavec stood up and re-pitched the business clearly; the lesson is that clarity of positioning matters more than technical depth.
Accept that even a strong business may take years to pay off — the source says five to seven years is normal and some may take nine.
caveats: The source notes the bad pitches are the most memorable, which biases recollection.
This card reflects the source's personal experience as an investor, not a formal investment framework.
cards.source_name: How to Build an Billion Dollar E-Commerce Empire.docx

cards.title: Agency exit multiples: what drives valuation
cards.summary: An agency owner breaks down the factors behind exit multiples, from client quality to retention and growth trajectory.
cards.use_when: Evaluating an agency or service business for sale, or planning an exit strategy for a services firm.
steps: Recognize that a small design/build web or app agency might command 3–5x profit, but recurring or retained revenue pushes the multiplier up.
Lock in long-term contracts: predictable revenue 9 months out increases the multiple because buyers can forecast cash flow.
Build a roster of hard-to-get, prestigious clients — the difficulty of replicating those relationships raises enterprise value.
Demonstrate strong retention (e.g., 90% retained revenue) and consistent growth in the years before exit; the source grew the business 2.5x from COVID to 18 months post-COVID and secured 11x profit.
Aim for scale or a strategic acquirer who can open doors to much larger contracts, as happened in the earnout year when individual contracts exceeded the entire previous agency revenue.
Time the market: the source sold in 2021, described as an ideal seller's market, though timing is not fully controllable.
caveats: Multiples are highly situational; 11x is described as absurdly high for an agency and not a target.
Shouldn't think about exit multiples as a beginner — focus on creating cash flow and learning lessons first.
cards.source_name: How to Build an Billion Dollar E-Commerce Empire.docx

cards.title: Compounding returns of long-term specialization
cards.summary: A strategy for maximizing wealth: do what you're good at for an extremely long period to become world-class, rather than chasing fast money.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to allocate time and energy across ventures, especially when tempted by quick-return opportunities like crypto or speculative investing.
steps: Identify the activity you're already good at and commit to doing it for an 'insane period of time' — the source's agency took 10 years (age 21 to 30) to build.
Expect that the real payoff is not a short spike but a prolonged compound effect; the source warns that private-equity-style fast wealth is a trap that distracts from your core work.
Avoid getting seduced by crypto, meme coins, or investment schemes; the source notes these take your eye off the ball and require different, equally difficult skills.
If you get bored and want fulfillment outside of money, deliberately pivot — but recognize that big money and big fulfillment may pull in different directions.
Focus on continuous learning through direct conversations with people who have walked the path; the source credits talking to experienced people as the most important learning method.
caveats: The 'do it for an insane period' advice is aimed at maximizing money; the source explicitly says if you want fulfillment, do something else.
Survivorship bias is real — for every Doc Martens-style scaled success, there are many bad stories.
cards.source_name: How to Build an Billion Dollar E-Commerce Empire.docx

cards.title: Build in public: how a speech impediment became a YouTube presence
cards.summary: A creator's method for overcoming public-speaking anxiety by starting on camera, then translating that to live leadership.
cards.use_when: Founders or operators who struggle with public speaking, video content, or addressing teams and need a desensitization approach.
steps: Force exposure to the medium you fear: the source had a speech impediment and made himself get in front of a camera, even getting drunk for his first video.
Use a low-stakes format like YouTube or Zoom to build fluency before attempting live audiences; the source initially addressed his company only via Zoom with the camera off.
Seek out people who uplift you in the specific area you're weak in; the source credits two weeks with an experienced presenter who reframed nerves as unnecessary comparison.
After internalizing the reframe ('I have my own great story'), seize the next natural moment to perform live — the source addressed 40 people the day after a flight, without prior rehearsal.
