Notice the environment effect: being around someone who makes you feel capable raises your performance, while critics make you retreat; choose your circle deliberately.
caveats: The source's first video method (drinking to speak) is a personal anecdote, not a recommended tactic for others.
Public-speaking progress was gradual and situational, not a one-off fix.
cards.source_name: How to Build an Billion Dollar E-Commerce Empire.docx

cards.title: Do what you're good at, not what you're passionate about (early on)
cards.summary: A reframe of the 'follow your passion' advice: build competency and profit first, then pursue passion once financially free.
cards.use_when: Giving or receiving career advice for young people or early-stage founders, especially when choosing between a passion project and a practical income path.
steps: Recognize that billionaires who say 'follow your passion' already have the financial liberty to do so; their advice isn't practical for beginners.
If you follow your passion before achieving success, you'll likely fail and lose the ability to continue that passion — it becomes unsustainable.
Instead, deliberately become passionate about success metrics: the first sale, the first profit, the first cash flow.
Use that momentum to build a stable financial base, after which you can pursue whatever you want because money is no longer the constraint.
Apply the same logic to business choices: prioritize opportunities based on learning speed and cash flow over personal interest when starting out.
caveats: This is presented as advice for making money; if fulfillment is your goal, the source says to do something else.
Not a universal rule — some people may thrive by pursuing passion directly, though the source argues against it for young people.
cards.source_name: How to Build an Billion Dollar E-Commerce Empire.docx

cards.title: Billionaire habits: the one common denominator
cards.summary: Observing that sustained, long-term ambition to create money is the only consistent trait among billionaires; other factors vary widely.
cards.use_when: Analyzing high-net-worth individuals or deciding whether extreme wealth accumulation is the right goal for you.
steps: Look past product genius, work hours, or biohacking routines — the source found these differ greatly among billionaires.
Identify the common thread: they have all been doing it for a very long time and have never relented in their ambition to create money.
Accept that this single-minded pursuit may be 'boring' and not necessarily appealing if you value other things like family, hobbies, or a relaxed lifestyle.
Recognize that for those with massive wealth, the driver is often ego and curiosity rather than money itself, so more wealth doesn't change behavior.
Use this to self-assess: if you aren't willing to chase money relentlessly for decades, you likely won't become a billionaire — and that may be fine.
caveats: Based on the source's personal observation of billionaires, not a controlled study.
The source acknowledges he could be a billionaire but chooses not to, implying the trait is necessary but not sufficient.
cards.source_name: How to Build an Billion Dollar E-Commerce Empire.docx

cards.title: Fake it till you make it: situational and growth-oriented
cards.summary: A nuanced take on imposter syndrome and exaggeration: useful when non-malicious and directed toward building real capability.
cards.use_when: When feeling insecure in a new role or venture, or when assessing whether to project confidence you don't yet feel.
steps: Acknowledge that many successful entrepreneurs exhibited some exaggeration when growing up — to win clients, build an audience, or close deals.
Use self-talk or external projection as a temporary state to reduce anxiety and enter a more confident frame, as the source does by reminding himself of past achievements.
Ensure the exaggeration isn't malicious or a zero-sum exploitation of others; it should be about stretching into a future self.
Often you end up growing into the claim or surpassing it, so the gap closes over time.
Shift your focus: consciously care about different things, and the need to fake it diminishes.
caveats: The source draws a line at malicious or exploitative deception.
The source also notes he has moved toward 100% truthfulness and confronting why he cares what others think as a better long-term approach.
cards.source_name: How to Build an Billion Dollar E-Commerce Empire.docx

cards.title: Two foundations for reduced anxiety: truthfulness and confronting approval-seeking
cards.summary: The source's personal practices for greater peace: living 100% truthfully and examining why you care about others' opinions.
cards.use_when: Founders or high-performers experiencing anxiety, insecurity, or people-pleasing that affects decision-making.
steps: Commit to telling the truth 100% of the time; you may annoy people, but you'll never have to worry about what you said or keep track of lies.
Regularly ask yourself why you care what other people think, and interrogate the answer — you often find the reason is irrelevant or unhelpful.
When anxious, use deliberate self-affirmation ('you've done this, you're great') to shift state, but recognize these are thoughts, not beliefs, if you still feel insecure.
Eliminate 'fake it till you make it' as a default mode as you mature; the source moved from faking to truthfulness as a source of stability.
caveats: These are personal practices from the source's experience, not clinical advice.
Truthfulness may have social costs; the source accepts that trade-off.
cards.source_name: How to Build an Billion Dollar E-Commerce Empire.docx

cards.title: Spot product gaps by pairing search volume with a weak average rating
cards.summary: Use trend data to find sub-niches with high demand but poor existing product execution, flagged by a low average Amazon rating.
cards.use_when: Screening a product category or sub-niche for a viable entry point before committing to sourcing.
steps: Pull trend data that shows search volume against sales count for the category so you can see whether interest is stable or only spiking. Stable demand with reasonable sales is safer than a volatile surge.

Read past the aggregate trend to the specific product variations the tool surfaces (for example convertible cribs with specific certifications, or smart-feature variations) rather than stopping at the top-level category.
Check the average Amazon rating for the sub-niche. The source treats a sub-niche averaging around 3.8 or below as a structural gap: demand exists but current sellers are not satisfying buyers.
Mine the positive and negative review tags attached to those listings to see why ratings are low, which points at the specific attribute to improve rather than a generic 'better product'.
Cross-check the underlying sources before acting; the source notes you can verify claims in a separate research tool.
caveats: The 3.8 threshold is the presenter's heuristic, not a validated benchmark; use it as a prompt to investigate, not a rule.
AI-summarised trend and rating data should be verified against the actual Amazon listings.
cards.source_name: Making $$ with Alibaba's NEW AI Agent (Full Demo).docx

cards.title: Run an agent prompt that extracts and ranks unmet pain points
cards.summary: Prompt the AI agent to pull customer complaints from reviews, forums and Amazon Q&A, cluster them by theme and rank by urgency and willingness to pay.
cards.use_when: You have picked a category and need a defensible list of what customers actually want fixed before designing a product.
steps: Write the prompt with explicit scope, sources and required output structure, e.g. 'Analyze [product category] and list the top 10 unmet customer pain points with proof from reviews, forums, and Amazon Q&A. Cluster them by theme and rank by urgency and willingness to pay.'
Name the forums that matter for that niche, not just Amazon. The source example used Reddit and Geekhack for mechanical keyboards because the enthusiast discussion lives there.
Let the agent plan its own searches, then inspect the sources it cites to check the evidence is real and specific rather than generic.
Insist on the willingness-to-pay dimension: the agent may run extra searches for user statements about paying extra for a specific feature. Without that instruction the ranking is only urgency-based.
Use the resulting ranked pain points as the brief for the product concept, so the design decisions trace back to evidence rather than intuition.
Expect the output as a clustered chart or table; check whether items are genuinely distinct complaints before treating them as separate features.
caveats: Clustering and ranking are AI judgements; the willingness-to-pay scores are inferred from forum chatter, not from primary pricing research.
Pain points from enthusiast forums may not represent the mass market you intend to sell to.
cards.source_name: Making $$ with Alibaba's NEW AI Agent (Full Demo).docx

cards.title: Translate consumer language into manufacturing terminology before contacting suppliers
cards.summary: Use the AI agent to convert consumer-desired outcomes into precise manufacturing terms so supplier quotes reflect real specifications.
cards.use_when: Drafting a request for quote or first supplier message for a product whose quality depends on process details.
steps: Feed the agent the pain points and the desired sensory or functional outcome, not just the product name.

Ask it to express the requirement in manufacturing vocabulary. The source examples: request 'e-coating' rather than 'matte paint', and a '5-layer internal dampening structure' rather than a vague 'quiet keyboard'.
Verify the term is actually used in that industry before sending; the value comes from suppliers recognising the specification, so a wrong term undermines the point.
Watch for adjacent details the agent flags, such as matching a plastic keycap colour to a CNC case colour for a seamless monochrome aesthetic, which you would likely not have specified yourself.
Keep the translated terms in your RFQ template so every supplier quote can be compared against the same specification.
caveats: The presenter's claim that correct jargon prevents inflated quotes or being taken advantage of is his opinion, not a tested result.
Confirm industry terminology with a knowledgeable contact, since AI-generated terms can be plausible but wrong.
cards.source_name: Making $$ with Alibaba's NEW AI Agent (Full Demo).docx

cards.title: Filter suppliers with a structured sourcing prompt
cards.summary: Specify OEM service, private label, MOQ ceiling and certifications in one prompt to get a shortlist instead of an overwhelming marketplace search.
cards.use_when: You have a validated product concept and need candidate manufacturers rather than browsing Alibaba manually.
steps: Write a single sourcing prompt naming the product and the commercial requirements, e.g. 'Find manufacturers that offer high quality [product] with OEM service, private label available, MOQ under 500, official certifications, and strong reviews.'
Set the MOQ ceiling to what you can actually fund for a first order. The source's example used MOQ under 500 and advised buying roughly 50 units initially rather than 5,000.
Review the returned supplier profiles, including reorder rate and why each was matched (for example, the supplier offers screen printing and embroidery).
Use the match reasoning to separate suppliers who genuinely fit the product requirements from those who merely match the category.
Where the platform supports it, send the inquiry directly; otherwise export the shortlist into your own outreach process.
caveats: Supplier ratings and match reasoning are not a substitute for due diligence; the source explicitly says to call suppliers, form your own judgement and start with a small order.
MOQ, certification and pricing details change, so re-verify current terms with the supplier.
cards.source_name: Making $$ with Alibaba's NEW AI Agent (Full Demo).docx

cards.title: Score opportunities on wholesale-to-retail margin before designing
cards.summary: The sourcing tool reports wholesale cost, target retail price and gross margin percentage so you can compare product ideas on economics, not just demand.
cards.use_when: Choosing between several validated product ideas, or sanity-checking that a category can support the ad and fulfilment costs of ecommerce.
steps: For each candidate product, record wholesale cost, target retail price, MOQ range and the reported gross margin percentage.

Compare across products on margin as well as demand. The source's example showed hoodies at roughly 200-300% margin while phone cases were cited at 300-400%, with a $6.71 wholesale hoodie as a concrete figure.
Where margins depend on licensing, treat the licence cost as a separate line before deciding; the source flags licensing as a requirement for the branded example.
Treat margin percentage as covering product cost only. It does not include freight, platform fees, returns or paid acquisition, so model those separately before committing.
caveats: Margin and wholesale figures from the tool are estimates and vary by supplier and order size; confirm with actual quotes.
A high margin category may still be unviable once acquisition cost and returns are included.
cards.source_name: Making $$ with Alibaba's NEW AI Agent (Full Demo).docx

cards.title: Generate visual product concepts for a specific sub-demographic
cards.summary: Prompt the AI for brand identity, product line and visual mockups aimed at a narrow audience to test positioning before any manufacturing spend.
cards.use_when: You have a validated niche and a rough audience but no concrete product concept or brand direction.
steps: Name both the product category and a narrow audience plus a trend, for example 'a mechanical keyboard for Gen Z women with a cozy gaming aesthetic' or 'Squid Game inspired products'.
Ask for a brand identity, a product concept and a preliminary roadmap so the output is a coherent direction rather than isolated images.

Read the output as creative stimulus, not a finished design. The source is explicit that the mockups are not production-ready and are meant to get ideas flowing and to be iterated with other design tools.
Use the generated concepts to write the specification you take to suppliers, combining them with the ranked pain points from review mining.
Keep the audience definition narrow enough to drive concrete choices (materials, colourways, form factor) rather than generic aesthetics.
caveats: Generated visuals are concept imagery; they do not confirm manufacturability, tooling cost or regulatory compliance.
Trend-driven concepts based on current media (for example a popular series) may carry IP or licensing risk.
cards.source_name: Making $$ with Alibaba's NEW AI Agent (Full Demo).docx

cards.title: Vet shortlisted suppliers with three technical questions before ordering
cards.summary: Ask a small number of verification questions that expose whether a supplier can actually meet the differentiating specification.
cards.use_when: You have an AI-generated supplier shortlist and are about to contact them for the first time.
steps: Pick the two or three features that define the product's differentiation, not a long checklist. The source example used finish (ceramic versus anodisation), sound profile (can they support a 5-layer internal dampening structure) and colour matching (plastic keycap colour matched to the CNC case colour).
Phrase each as a capability question the supplier must answer specifically, so a vague reply is itself informative.
Contact suppliers directly by phone or call, not only through the platform. The source stresses that a high platform rating does not guarantee your experience will be good.
Start with a small trial order, around 50 units in the source's example, rather than thousands, and let that order validate quality before scaling.
Build relationships with the supplier rather than treating the transaction as anonymous.
caveats: This verification approach is the presenter's practical advice from running the demo, not a documented outcome.
Specifications and supplier capabilities should be reconfirmed at the time of ordering.
cards.source_name: Making $$ with Alibaba's NEW AI Agent (Full Demo).docx

cards.title: Use agentic research to move from trend to concept, but keep human verification in the loop
cards.summary: AI agents compress market analysis, pain-point extraction and concept generation into one workflow, while sourcing decisions still require human checks.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much of an ecommerce product research workflow to delegate to an AI agent and where to intervene.
steps: Use the agent for the research-heavy stages: scanning trends, mining reviews and forums, clustering pain points and generating a first-pass concept with sourcing options.
Inspect its work in progress; the source notes you can open the sources it consulted during a task to check the evidence.
Keep the decision stages human: deciding whether the concept is worth building, vetting suppliers by call, and choosing order size.
Use the agent's structured output (ranked pain points, specification terms, supplier shortlist) as input to your own judgement rather than as a final answer.
Re-run research periodically, since agent capabilities and platform features in this space change quickly and any workflow documented today may not match the current interface.
caveats: The presenter has no affiliation with the tool and is describing a live demo, not a measured business outcome.
Multi-million-dollar opportunity claims are promotional framing; treat generated opportunities as hypotheses to test.
cards.source_name: Making $$ with Alibaba's NEW AI Agent (Full Demo).docx

cards.title: Private supplier vs. AliExpress: understand the middleman model
cards.summary: A private supplier is a middleman who sources from Chinese factories/1688, routes goods through their own warehouse, then ships to your customer with better speed and pricing than public marketplaces.
cards.use_when: Deciding which fulfillment route to use for a dropshipping store, or explaining supply-chain options before sourcing a product
steps: Define the chain: your supplier's agent buys from a network of Chinese warehouses (including 1688, described as the Chinese equivalent of Alibaba/AliExpress), receives goods at their own warehouse in about 2-3 days, then dispatches to your customer.

Note that most Chinese warehouses are 'general' (hundreds of products) while some are niche-specific (toys, supplements, clothing) — a good supplier knows which warehouse makes the best version of a given product.
Expect the supplier to negotiate both price and shipping line on your behalf, since they do not manufacture — their value is warehouse network access and negotiation.

Compare against AliExpress/Alibaba: typically 10-15 day delivery, limited or no branding, and (per the source) weaker customer support; AliExpress faster options exist but at much higher product cost.
Treat this as a working relationship: suppliers lower your quoted cost as they see consistent daily order volume.
caveats: This is a dropshipping-specific supply model; if you hold inventory or manufacture, the tradeoffs differ.
Supplier quality varies — the source warns a bad supplier means poor product quality, refunds and chargebacks.
Warehouse counts, delivery-day ranges and marketplace speed claims are the source's general figures, not guarantees for a specific supplier.
cards.source_name: The Best Supplier For Branded Dropshipping in 2026 (It's Free!).docx

cards.title: Request the right shipping line to balance cost and speed
cards.summary: Choose a premium shipping line that keeps delivery inside roughly 6-10 days without overpaying, because slow delivery drives chargebacks.
cards.use_when: Configuring fulfillment with a private supplier or 3PL, or evaluating whether a quoted shipping cost is acceptable
steps: Ask your supplier for a premium fast line rather than the default; the source names Uni Express as its preferred line for the best cost-to-speed balance after testing many lines.

Use the supplier's product view to compare lines: for one US-bound product the default line showed 8-15 days, while switching to the faster line (named 'Yune' in the demo, likely the same family) gave 5-8 day shipping for about $3 more per unit added to COGS.

Judge the upgrade against your economics: the source argues roughly 8-15 days (about a week to a week and a half) is acceptable for beginners, and 5-8 days is 'a little overkill' unless margins or AOV/bundling can absorb the extra $3.
Check destination sensitivity: the same product shipping to the UK was notably cheaper and faster than to the US — US from China is typically the most expensive route.
Note that China has 10+ shipping lines with a general pattern: slower lines (10-15 days) cost less, faster lines (6-10 days) cost more.
caveats: Line names and per-unit surcharges are illustrative examples from the source and will change — re-quote before committing.
The source's opinion is that 14-day delivery is no longer acceptable to customers; treat it as the presenter's positioning, not an industry rule.
The $3 upgrade math only works if your AOV or bundle price supports it.
cards.source_name: The Best Supplier For Branded Dropshipping in 2026 (It's Free!).docx

cards.title: Get the product quote low enough that retail pricing stays viable
cards.summary: COGS is a primary lever on net margin — negotiate supplier quotes down and track how small per-unit savings compound across order volume.
cards.use_when: Quoting a product with a supplier, setting retail price, or reviewing net margin after a test
steps: Separate the two components you actually pay: product cost plus shipping to the customer. Nothing else is owed under a free fulfillment platform.
Get an initial quote as a new seller: the source's wallet example was about $7 per unit with no order history — realistic for a beginner, not a blocker.
Ask again once you are moving volume: the same wallet can drop to about $5.50. The $1.50 difference is about $5,000 extra profit across 1,000 orders.
Check whether your supplier lowers the price automatically as order volume grows; the source says a good one will, but you should still ask periodically.
Sanity-check the retail implication: high COGS forces a higher customer price and reduces purchase conversion, so a cheap quote makes profitable ad spend easier to achieve.
Keep net margin (what you actually take home after ads and COGS) as the headline metric rather than revenue.
caveats: The $7/$5.50/$1.50 numbers are the source's illustration, not a benchmark you can assume.
The source attributes its own high-margin screenshots to its private supplier; those income figures are promotional and should not be treated as expected results.
Volume tiers and negotiation leverage depend on the individual supplier.
cards.source_name: The Best Supplier For Branded Dropshipping in 2026 (It's Free!).docx

cards.title: Add branded packaging once a product is proven
cards.summary: Custom logos, mailers and thank-you inserts turn a commodity dropship item into a defensible brand and reduce undercutting.
cards.use_when: A product has validated sales and you want to protect margin from copycat competitors
steps: Wait until the product is proven profitable before spending on branding — the source stresses this is a post-validation upgrade, not a launch step.
Instruct the supplier to add a custom logo on the product, branded mailer packaging and an internal thank-you card.
Use the fulfillment platform's packaging section to select mailer type and then connect that packaging to the specific product, so all future orders use it automatically.
Treat the goal as building a real brand rather than repeatedly flipping and restarting stores every few months.
Expect branding to make it harder for generic competitors to undercut your exact offer, since they cannot replicate the unboxing experience.
caveats: Branding adds cost and complexity per order; the source explicitly ties it to validated demand.
Custom packaging cannot be done through plain AliExpress/Alibaba marketplace orders according to the source, so it requires a private supplier or agent.
cards.source_name: The Best Supplier For Branded Dropshipping in 2026 (It's Free!).docx

cards.title: Add your fulfillment app as a Shopify location or checkout breaks
cards.summary: After installing a 3PL app you must manually register it as a Shopify fulfillment location, otherwise the storefront shows out-of-stock or add-to-cart failures.
cards.use_when: Setting up a new fulfillment/3PL integration on Shopify
steps: Sign up for the fulfillment platform using the same email as your Shopify account, then click 'add store' / 'authorize store' and follow the prompts to install the app on your Shopify dashboard.
After authorizing, open Shopify Settings → Shipping and Delivery.
Click the fulfillment locations icon and add the fulfillment app explicitly as a location (e.g. add 'Team Drop'), then save.
Confirm the app can both see your products/orders and act as a recognized fulfillment location — the app connection alone is not sufficient.
Troubleshoot by symptom: if a product shows 'out of stock' or customers cannot add to cart, the missing fulfillment location is the likely cause.
Note the fulfilment app is free with no monthly fee (contrasted with AutoDS and Zendrop subscriptions), so you only pay COGS.
Verify the current Shopify and app interface steps yourself — menu names and app screens change over time.
caveats: Exact Shopify menu naming and app screens may differ from the source's walkthrough; verify before relying on it.
Pricing and 'free' claims about any platform should be re-checked at signup.
cards.source_name: The Best Supplier For Branded Dropshipping in 2026 (It's Free!).docx

cards.title: Pre-fund a 3PL wallet so orders fulfill automatically
cards.summary: Fulfillment networks debit a pre-funded balance as Shopify orders arrive, removing manual order entry; top up by bank transfer/wire.
cards.use_when: Automating order fulfillment after connecting a private supplier or 3PL to Shopify
steps: Understand the model: orders sync from Shopify automatically, and the platform debits your wallet for product + shipping as each order comes in.
Open the platform's top-up/billing section, choose an amount, and submit.
Fund via the provided bank transfer/wire details (the source calls wire the easiest option); platform-received funds then cover COGS.
Expect payment processing to occur within roughly 24 hours and orders to move from 'awaiting payment' to 'awaiting collection' once purchased from the source warehouse.

Track order states in the orders/purchase-order dashboard: awaiting payment, awaiting collection (order placed with warehouse, in transit to supplier's warehouse), shipped, delivered, completed, and a separate canceled tab.
Keep the balance topped up — a low balance stalls fulfillment and creates delays.
caveats: Bank/wire top-ups can add friction and transfer time; plan for a buffer balance before scaling ad spend.
Processing-time and status-label details are platform-specific and may change.
cards.source_name: The Best Supplier For Branded Dropshipping in 2026 (It's Free!).docx

cards.title: Source products through an agent on WhatsApp
cards.summary: A dedicated agent can source a product from a photo or marketplace link and return a quote, giving beginners support that public marketplaces lack.
cards.use_when: You have identified a product to sell but need a supplier quote, or you need help resolving a fulfillment issue
steps: Contact the assigned agent via the platform's WhatsApp button (the source says every signup gets a dedicated agent at no extra cost).
Send a picture of the product; if you have an AliExpress or Alibaba link, include it to speed up the search.

Wait for the quote and confirm the shipping line, then list the product on your Shopify store — either through the platform's 'list to store' flow or by creating it directly in Shopify and linking it.
If listing inside the platform, choose your store ID, enter product info and images; you can edit the listing in Shopify afterward and the link stays intact.
Use the agent for post-purchase problems too, e.g. 'tracking says delivered but the customer can't find it' — a supplier can trace it and send a replacement unit.
Consider buying a sample first; the source highlights sample purchase as an option it had not seen on competing platforms.
caveats: Agent quality varies, and the source frames supplier support as a key differentiator of private suppliers versus raw marketplaces.
Response speed from an agent is not guaranteed.
cards.source_name: The Best Supplier For Branded Dropshipping in 2026 (It's Free!).docx

cards.title: Why the source rejects subscription fulfillment platforms and raw marketplaces
cards.summary: The presenter argues AliExpress/Alibaba and paid tools like AutoDS/Zendrop are poor options vs. a free private-supplier platform, on grounds of speed, branding, support and monthly fees.
cards.use_when: Choosing between marketplace dropshipping, paid fulfillment SaaS, and a private supplier/agent
steps: Evaluate marketplaces on four axes the source calls out: shipping time (10-15 days typical), ability to brand, cost of faster options (a wallet example jumped to ~$40 for an 8-day AliExpress shipment), and customer support.

Evaluate paid platforms on the subscription question: the source argues it should not cost a monthly fee to have orders fulfilled and shipped, and dislikes paying for sourcing on top of a subscription.

Weigh the source's counter-position that a free private-supplier platform plus agent is more beginner-friendly, since beginners may not have a validated product yet and extra fees compound risk early.
Check that a candidate free platform provides the features you need before switching: supplier network, shipping-line choice, branding options, agent/WhatsApp support, and profile/store integration.
Verify the current fee structure and features directly with each provider — pricing and terms change.
caveats: This is a presenter's opinion delivered while promoting one platform; treat the 'never use these' framing as positioning, not neutral advice.
Competing platforms (AutoDS, Zendrop) offer features not discussed here — evaluate against your own needs.
The source receives signup bonuses/coupons for its recommended platform, so its comparison is not disinterested.
cards.source_name: The Best Supplier For Branded Dropshipping in 2026 (It's Free!).docx

cards.title: Judge net margin and refunds as the real supply-chain KPI
cards.summary: Low COGS plus reliable, traceable delivery protects net margin and prevents revenue loss to refunds and chargebacks.
cards.use_when: Reviewing whether a supplier or shipping line is worth keeping
steps: Track net margin — the share of revenue you actually keep — with ads and COGS as the two biggest expense lines the source names.
Treat product quality as a supply-chain variable, since multiple warehouses make the same item and a bad pick causes refunds and chargebacks.
Recognize the escalation the source warns about: enough chargebacks can lead to withheld payments or loss of the Shopify account.
Give customers tracking numbers so they can follow delivery — the source treats this as part of the standard service level, not a nice-to-have.
Use delivery speed as a chargeback-reduction tool: 6-10 days was cited as the target window, with roughly a week being acceptable.
Re-quote and re-check the supplier relationship periodically rather than assuming the initial terms hold.
caveats: Chargeback and account-closure outcomes depend on processor and platform policies; the source states them as a risk, not a certainty.
The source's own margin screenshots are promotional and are not evidence of typical results.
cards.source_name: The Best Supplier For Branded Dropshipping in 2026 (It's Free!).docx

cards.title: Competitor profit as the primary product-viability filter
cards.summary: Treat active, profitable competitors as proof of concept rather than a disqualifying sign of saturation.
cards.use_when: Choosing whether to pursue a product or brushing off one because 'everyone is selling it'.
steps: Before anything else, require evidence that at least one other seller is moving this product and making money. The presenter argues this matters more than abstract criteria like 'solves a problem' or 'is in demand'.

Reframe saturation: there are too many people online to reach everyone with one product, so big competitors do not mean no room; the presenter points to continual new entrants in heavily-marketed categories like teeth-whitening pens.

When a niche looks saturated, look for an untapped angle rather than abandoning the niche — e.g. a clothing brand targeting only girlfriends of boyfriends 5'8" and under, which hooks attention and speaks to a very narrow demographic.
Confirm the product is either problem-solving or serves a passionate community, then validate there are multiple competitors doing well before committing.
caveats: This is the presenter's opinion and it runs against the common 'pick an unsaturated niche' advice; treat both as situational.
Saturation can still make paid acquisition more expensive; the angle trick is not a guarantee, only a way to differentiate.
cards.source_name: The Only Product Research Video You Need to Start Dropshipping.docx

cards.title: Separating evergreen and trending products and the results each should deliver
cards.summary: Classify candidate products as evergreen (brand, slower start) or trending (fast cash, weeks-long window) because expectations and effort differ.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much testing budget and patience a product deserves before launching.
steps: Sort each candidate into evergreen (sellable year-round, can build a brand around it for years) or trending (seasonal or culturally viral: Christmas, Mother's Day, pop-culture moments).

For evergreen products, expect a slower start and budget for more ad testing and iteration; the presenter says these take more time and money to find the winning angle but produce a sustainable business.
For trending products, expect fast money that will likely be gone in a few weeks; an example given is a Kendrick-vs-Drake rap-beef t-shirt capitalizing on news of the moment.
A seasonal hybrid example: a portable ice-air cooler is only useful in summer and reads as oversaturated, but still works as a quick trending test because there is so much competitor proof.
Match your goal: test-and-flip products for immediate cash velocity versus long-horizon catalog pieces for brand equity.
caveats: The 2–4 week trending lifespan is the presenter's rough estimate and depends on the trend; verify current demand before buying inventory.
Trending products carry risk of inventory left when demand disappears.
cards.source_name: The Only Product Research Video You Need to Start Dropshipping.docx

cards.title: Training a TikTok feed to surface dropshipping products
cards.summary: Use a fresh TikTok account, engage with blatant product-selling videos, and mine the feed for product candidates.
cards.use_when: You want low-cost product discovery from organic social rather than paid databases.
steps: Create a new TikTok account dedicated to product research.
Engage (watch, like, follow patterns) with every dropshipping-style video you see — blatant direct product pitches are the signal.
Keep scrolling until the algorithm feeds you more of the same; the presenter notes these videos reuse the same sounds and hooks, which makes them recognizable.
When a product catches your eye and it fits the criteria (problem-solving or passionate community), immediately pivot to competitor validation instead of stopping at the video.
Use this as a fast screen: the presenter found one candidate within ~40 seconds of scrolling.
caveats: Feed training takes time and gets polluted by other content; keep the account activity focused on product content.
Organic virality alone is not proof of sales — validate with ad-library and revenue tools.
cards.source_name: The Only Product Research Video You Need to Start Dropshipping.docx

cards.title: One-hit-wonder check on a creator's profile
cards.summary: Before trusting a viral product video, audit the creator's profile for multiple high-view videos.
cards.use_when: A single viral video makes a product look promising and you need to know if it is repeatable or luck.
steps: Find the viral product video and open the creator's profile.
Count videos above 1,000,000 views.
Require at least three videos with over 1,000,000 views to conclude the product or account has consistent viral potential, not a one-off fluke.
If it passes, treat it as a candidate and move to sourcing, competitor counts and revenue validation; if it fails, keep scrolling.
caveats: The three-videos-over-1M threshold is the presenter's personal heuristic, not a measured benchmark.
High views on the account could reflect the creator's personality rather than the product's market.
cards.source_name: The Only Product Research Video You Need to Start Dropshipping.docx

cards.title: PP Ads filter workflow: longest-running ads first
cards.summary: Reverse-engineer winning products from ad-spy tools by sorting for the longest-running creatives and excluding mega-brands.
cards.use_when: You want a repeatable pipeline of candidate products from paid ad intelligence.
steps: In PP Ads, set the filter you prefer, then sort by 'Days running' with the longest-running ads first — long runtimes are the presenter's proxy for baseline profitability.
Set results to 500 per page so you can scan broadly per sort.
Scan the list and skip heavily branded, established mega-corporations; look for generic, adaptable products that a new seller could source and rebrand.

When something interesting appears, open the advertiser's website to check whether they look like a dropshipper or an established brand, and search the product image on AliExpress to get raw cost and margin floor (example: a travel bag sourced around $16 and sold for $98).
Inside the ad records, sort by ad impressions to find the top-performing creative, then study the exact target audience, ad copy and number of creative variants to inspire your own angle.
caveats: PP Ads is a paid third-party tool; interfaces and filters change, so verify the current UI and filters.
Long runtime suggests the ad is working, not that the product will work for you at your cost and angle.
cards.source_name: The Only Product Research Video You Need to Start Dropshipping.docx

cards.title: Estimating competitor revenue with a spy tool
cards.summary: Use a revenue estimator such as ShopHunter to confirm a product's sales before committing.
cards.use_when: You have a candidate product and want evidence that views or ads translate into actual sales.
steps: Take a competitor's store URL (found from TikTok, PP Ads or the Facebook Ad Library) and enter it into a revenue-estimation tool such as ShopHunter.
Read the estimated monthly sales/revenue figure as a directional confirmation — the presenter cites one account at roughly $90,000 in the prior month.
Use the same tool's search to find additional stores selling the same or similar products and compare their estimated volumes.
Cross-check with the Facebook Ad Library: a competitor running a high volume of simultaneous ads suggests the product is profitable at scale.
Only proceed once you have competitor proof, demand signals and a workable sourcing price.
caveats: Estimates are third-party approximations, not verified sales data; treat them as rough ranges.
One strong month is a snapshot; seasonality and ad spend spikes can distort it.
cards.source_name: The Only Product Research Video You Need to Start Dropshipping.docx

cards.title: Facebook Ad Library keyword hunting for dropshippers
cards.summary: Find ecommerce advertisers and their products by searching generic direct-response keywords in the Facebook Ad Library.
cards.use_when: You want an unlimited free source of live competitor ads and product ideas.
steps: Open the Facebook Ad Library and search generic direct-response phrases such as '50% off' or 'shop now'.
Review the advertisers that surface; these are most likely dropshippers or direct-response ecommerce brands.
Inspect what products they sell, what their ads look like, and how many ads they are running.
Treat a high number of simultaneous active ads as a sign the product is doing well, and use those ads as inspiration for your own creative approach.
Optionally search a specific competitor's name directly to see their full active ad set.
caveats: Ad volume is a proxy for spend and testing, not guaranteed profitability.
Free library data is less filterable than paid ad-spy tools.
cards.source_name: The Only Product Research Video You Need to Start Dropshipping.docx

cards.title: Reverse-sourcing a competitor product image to AliExpress
cards.summary: Use Google reverse image search on a competitor's product photo to find the raw supplier and margin floor.
cards.use_when: You have a validated product candidate and need to check sourcing cost and margin before committing.
steps: Right-click the competitor's product image on their site or ad.
Run a Google reverse image search (Search by Image).
Scroll results until an AliExpress or similar supplier link appears; the same or near-identical product usually shows up quickly.
Read the raw unit price as your margin floor — the presenter found an anime katana sold for about $75 and sourced for around $40 on the first listing found, noting it can likely be found cheaper.
If the margin holds, message suppliers about customization or bulk pricing, as the presenter describes brands doing after they start placing bulk orders.
caveats: The listing found may differ in quality, size or specification from the competitor's version.
Shipping time and supplier reliability matter as much as unit cost; verify before ordering.
cards.source_name: The Only Product Research Video You Need to Start Dropshipping.docx

cards.title: Anime katana worked example: validating a passionate-community product
cards.summary: A full walk-through of validating a non-problem-solving product because it serves a passionate niche community.
cards.use_when: A product does not solve a problem but clearly has an intense fan base; you need a validation sequence to follow.
steps: Start from an organic TikTok find — the presenter spotted anime katanas as the second video on a fresh feed.
Accept it despite not solving a problem, because the anime community is highly passionate and therefore buys fandom goods.
Audit the creator's profile: confirm at least three videos with over 1,000,000 views, ruling out a one-hit wonder.
Check the store price (about $75) and reverse-image search to AliExpress (about $40 on the first listing found, likely cheaper elsewhere).

Search TikTok and competitor stores for other sellers of the same product (found one with 2.8 million likes), then confirm sales with a revenue estimator — one account estimated around $90,000 for the month.
Conclude the product has potential because there are competitors, demand signals and workable sourcing, then proceed to test.
caveats: Results like $90,000/month are a single case example, not a promise.
Fandom products can carry IP or trademark risk; the presenter does not address licensing.
cards.source_name: The Only Product Research Video You Need to Start Dropshipping.docx

cards.title: Customization products as a TikTok-friendly product class
cards.summary: Prefer customizable products because personalized items perform well in short-form product advertising.
cards.use_when: Scanning candidate lists and deciding which product types to shortlist for organic or paid testing.
steps: While scanning ad-spy results, flag products where the buyer personalizes the item — examples given are a phone case that scans an object and prints it on the case, and a vintage-looking crystal frame holding a custom image.
Treat customization as a demand signal: the presenter says people love custom items and they advertise well on TikTok.
Run the same validation stack on them: competitor count, ad volume, revenue estimate and sourcing check.
Consider how the customization step fits your fulfillment before committing, since it adds production handling.
caveats: Customization can complicate fulfillment, lead times and returns; the source only covers the discovery angle.
The presenter's 'people love custom items' is a general observation, not a tested benchmark.
cards.source_name: The Only Product Research Video You Need to Start Dropshipping.docx

cards.title: Deploying a saturated seasonal product with proven demand
cards.summary: When a product is heavily sold but repeatedly proves out, a short seasonal test can still be worthwhile even if it will not become a brand.
cards.use_when: You see the same product sold by many accounts and want a fast, low-ambition test rather than a long-term brand.
steps: Recognize the signal: if you scroll for a few days and see at least 10 different accounts selling the exact same product, it is heavily saturated but repeatedly validated.
Check whether it is time-sensitive — the portable ice-cube AC only works in summer, which is why so many entrants chase it each year.
Judge brand potential honestly: the presenter says this product does not look like a strong long-term brand, but its repeated proof of concept makes it a reasonable short test.
Make simple product videos while the season is active and see how far you can push it, accepting a short lifespan.
Do not overbuild around it; use it as a cash-flow test rather than a foundation.
caveats: Seasonal windows close fast; late entry means competing for limited remaining demand.
Heavy saturation usually raises ad costs.
cards.source_name: The Only Product Research Video You Need to Start Dropshipping.docx

cards.title: Auxiliary product-discovery sources worth sampling
cards.summary: Supplementary channels — Twitter/X practitioners and trend sites — for finding product ideas, with quality caveats.
cards.use_when: Your main TikTok and ad-spy pipelines feel exhausted and you want additional idea inputs.
steps: Follow dropshipping and ecommerce operators on Twitter/X; the presenter says good gems surface if you follow the right people, while warning that much of the content is cringe.
Check trend-discovery sites such as Exploding Topics to see what is rising right now and translate that into product ideas.
Treat every idea from these sources as a lead, not a conclusion — run it through the same competitor, demand, revenue and sourcing checks.
Combine sources rather than relying on one; the presenter presents TikTok and PP Ads as the primary methods and these as extras.
caveats: The source only mentions Exploding Topics and Twitter gurus in passing; it does not provide detailed execution steps for them.
Commentary accounts may be promotional or unverified.
cards.source_name: The Only Product Research Video You Need to Start Dropshipping.docx

cards.title: The validation checklist applied to every product before selling
cards.summary: A repeatable gate: proof of competitors making money, demand signals, sourcing price and fulfillment readiness.
cards.use_when: Right before committing money or building a store around a product.
steps: Confirm competitors exist and are making money with the product — the core criterion from the start of the workflow.
Confirm the product either solves a problem or serves a passionate community.
Confirm demand through repeated viral evidence, multiple competitors, or high active ad volume in the Facebook Ad Library.
Confirm sourcing: reverse-image search the product to find supplier cost and a margin floor, and check shipping speed.
Confirm the marketing angle you would use is not already fully occupied — look for a specific sub-demographic or creative angle competitors have not tapped.
Only then move to store build, creative production and testing; the presenter says once you see what works for competitors there is no need to reinvent the wheel, just adapt it.
caveats: This is a screening framework from a practitioner, not a statistical model; each signal can be wrong in isolation.
Fulfillment tooling (e.g. sourcing/3PL apps) is out of scope for this workflow and should be verified separately as interfaces change.
cards.source_name: The Only Product Research Video You Need to Start Dropshipping.docx

cards.title: Kalodata baseline filter settings for early-breakout products
cards.summary: Configuring the Kalodata/Shop Plus product screen (timeframe, revenue band, video-only attribution, ascending sort) to surface untapped TikTok Shop winners instead of saturated giants.
cards.use_when: Starting a product hunt in Kalodata or Shop Plus (accessed via Spy Crew) and needing a repeatable first-pass filter before graph analysis.
steps: Set the timeframe to Last 30 Days so you are reading current momentum, not lifetime totals.

Set the revenue range to $33,000–$97,000 per month. The upper bound exists to filter out $300k+/month products that already attract heavy competitor attention; the lower bound keeps enough baseline demand to prove the product sells.
Restrict revenue source to Video only and exclude Live stream revenue. Live revenue is not replicable with paid static/UGC video ads, so it distorts what you can actually copy.

Restrict categories to: Health, Beauty & Personal Care, Women's Wear/Underwear, Men's Wear/Underwear, Home Improvement. (These are the source's chosen hunting grounds; the mechanics apply to other categories if you prefer.)
Sort revenue from Lowest to Highest within the filtered range. The products near the bottom of the band are the earliest breakouts — higher in the band means more competition already in.
Open each candidate and proceed to 30-day and 180-day graph analysis rather than trusting the list number alone.
caveats: Spy-tool interfaces, revenue bands and category menus change frequently — verify the current Kalodata/Shop Plus UI before acting.
The $33k–$97k band is a heuristic from one operator, not a validated benchmark; adjust to your own capital and margin profile.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Validate a product's growth curve with 30-day and 180-day graphs
cards.summary: Reading the 30-day upward tilt, then immediately checking the 180-day view to reject products that peaked months ago and are now dying.
cards.use_when: After a Kalodata/Shop Plus candidate passes the revenue-band filter, to decide whether it is genuinely climbing or a dead product attempting a revival.
steps: Open the 30-day revenue graph and look for a clear upward tilt at the end of the window — ideally stabilization followed by an upward turn, not a spike-and-drop or a flat line.
Immediately switch to the 180-day view. This is the step that separates early breakouts from zombies.
Discard the product if the 180-day graph shows it peaked months ago and is currently flatlining or trending down. A product whose best days were months back has already been mined by other sellers.
Discard flatlines outright — no trajectory, no reason to expect your ad spend will change the curve.
Discard any product trending straight down, even if the last few days tick up; one small bump inside a downtrend is not a trend.
Only advance products that show a rising trajectory across both windows, meaning the recent uptick sits on a still-living, non-faded base.
caveats: Graph reads are subjective; a short-lived spike can look like an uptrend in the 30-day view, which is why the 180-day check is mandatory rather than optional.
Trend-tool data lags and can be revised, so treat the graph as one signal, not proof.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Check revenue distribution across recent videos, not one old viral hit
cards.summary: Inspecting a product's top videos to confirm revenue comes from multiple recent creatives rather than a single aged anomaly that will not repeat.
cards.use_when: When a Kalodata/Shop Plus product looks promising on the graph and you need to verify the revenue is repeatable with new creative.
steps: Click into the product's video list and look at the top-performing videos and their posting dates.
Confirm the highest-revenue video was posted within the last 7 to 14 days. An old top video means the momentum has passed.
Discard the product if roughly 90–95% of revenue is carried by a single old video — for example a six-month-old viral hit. That is an anomaly, not a repeatable demand signal.
Require a healthy spread: revenue distributed across at least 3 to 5 recent videos. Multiple recent sellers succeeding suggests the product's demand is broad enough for a new entrant.
Sanity-check the count of creators running ads on the product in Facebook Ad Library (search the product name) to gauge how crowded the space already is.
caveats: A product with strongly distributed recent revenue is also a product others have noticed; distribution and competition rise together.
Before sourcing, also discard ~$9.99 TikTok Shop products — the source treats that price point as lacking the margin to survive Meta ad acquisition costs.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Cross-reference TikTok demand with Google Trends and Meta Ad Library
cards.summary: Validating a TikTok Shop candidate off-platform by searching the exact sub-niche in Google Trends and counting competitors running Meta ads.
cards.use_when: Before committing to sourcing or a paid test, to confirm demand is not confined to TikTok's algorithmic bubble.
steps: Open Google Trends and search the exact product variation, not the broad parent category. The source's example: search "GLP-1 patches" rather than just "GLP-1".
Read the 12-month graph and require an active, current upward trajectory. A sub-niche already declining or spiking-and-fading on search interest is a weaker bet even if TikTok revenue looks fine.

Go to Facebook Ad Library and search the product name to see how many advertisers are currently running ads on it. Zero to few advertisers on a validated product can indicate an open lane; a crowded library means the window is closing.
Treat the two checks as tension tests: rising search interest plus a thin advertiser pool is the most attractive combination; rising interest plus dozens of advertisers means you are late.
If the product also shows a renewable/subscription angle (e.g. patches, refills), weigh that favorably — the source prefers repeat-purchase products for MRR, though it is optional.
caveats: Google Trends is relative, not absolute volume, and can be skewed by news spikes; match the term precisely or the read is meaningless.
Ad Library coverage and search behavior change often; verify current tool behavior.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: The sourcing criteria stack: problem-solving, English ads, renewable demand
cards.summary: The qualitative screen applied alongside Kalodata's numeric filters — problem/insecurity angle, English-language creative, repeat-purchase potential, and margin-friendly pricing.
cards.use_when: Choosing between several candidates that already pass the revenue, graph and video-distribution filters.
steps: Prefer products that solve a problem or address an insecurity. Problem-driven and insecurity-driven products give you a clear hook and a reason for the viewer to stop scrolling.
Restrict to English-speaking ads only (exclude Spanish-language creative in the source's filter). You want to be able to read and adapt the winning angles yourself.

Favor a renewable product if possible — something customers rebuy or subscribe to — because it supports subscription MRR rather than one-off purchases. The source marks this as optional but preferred, so do not discard a strong one-off solely for failing it.
Reject products priced around $9.99 on TikTok Shop. At that price the sale is a cheap impulse buy and there is no margin left for Meta acquisition costs.
Score candidates on all criteria together rather than letting any single metric dominate; the numeric filters prove demand, the qualitative criteria predict whether you can profitably acquire buyers.
caveats: The renewable-product preference is an operator's stated preference, not a rule; some winners are purely one-off purchases.
Price thresholds are illustrative — run your own margin math against your expected CPA rather than copying a number.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Mix-and-match sourcing: borrow a viral TikTok hook, attach your own UGC body
cards.summary: A testing setup that takes a proven native TikTok hook from a top video and stitches it to a longer convincing UGC body for Meta ads.
cards.use_when: Once a product has passed sourcing validation and you are preparing the first Meta test creative.
steps: From the product's validated top videos, identify the hook — the opening seconds that clearly drove the native TikTok performance. Treat it as a controllable variable separate from the rest of the ad.
Take that proven hook and stitch it onto a longer, convincing UGC video body of your own. The hypothesis is that the borrowed hook carries attention and the UGC body carries persuasion.
Keep the creative work in your ad-creative process, not your sourcing process — sourcing ends at product selection; the splice is a creative decision.
Check on-platform validation first: if the hook came from a video posted within the last 7–14 days on a product with distributed revenue, it is the most defensible piece to reuse.
Use the resulting mix as the test asset in a short paid-media validation phase; do not let testing mechanics crowd out the product-selection decision.
caveats: Do not reproduce competitors' creative wholesale; adapt hooks rather than copying full videos.
The source presents stitching as its standard testing setup, not a guarantee of Meta performance — test it against your own controls.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Keep sourcing, creative, media buying and storefront as separate decisions
cards.summary: Drawing scope boundaries so the product-research phase stays about trend and demand validation rather than drifting into ad editing, campaign setup or store design.
cards.use_when: Running or delegating a TikTok Shop product hunt and needing to know where the sourcing job ends.
steps: Scope the hunt to active sourcing using TikTok Shop intelligence tools (Kalodata / Shop Plus): filtering mechanics, graph analysis, video-age verification and cross-platform trend validation.
Stop sourcing work at a validated product and validated demand signals. Do not fold in the editing of spliced hook-plus-UGC creatives — that is a creative-strategy task.
Do not fold in launching the two-to-three-day Meta ads testing phase or any media-buying execution — that is paid-media work.
Do not fold in designing the branded storefront — that is a storefront-architecture task.

Practically: keep one document or kanban column for candidate products with their graph/video/trend evidence, and hand off the product with the evidence attached so downstream creative and media decisions start from validated demand.
caveats: The boundary mapping is a workflow convention from the source's system, not an industry standard; adapt it to your team's real handoffs.
Sourcing tools and validation signals are fast-decaying, so re-verify mechanics before each hunt.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: TikTok Shop product screening criteria (Baseline)
cards.summary: A seven-point filter for screening TikTok Shop products for dropshipping tests, including renewable potential, problem-solving angle, ad age, revenue trend and range, and English-speaking market.
cards.use_when: Screening a raw list of TikTok Shop products in a research tool (Kalodata/Shop Plus) before committing budget to a test.
steps: Check if the product is renewable — can you build a subscription or repeat-purchase offer around it? This is optional, not a dealbreaker, but the source prioritizes it because it enables long-term brand building and recurring revenue.

Confirm it solves a real problem or insecurity. The source claims many beginner picks fail because the perceived problem is too small; winning products often converge on the same desires (anti-bloat, slimming, energy, looking/feeling better) with different marketing angles and ingredients.
Verify the ad creatives are new to the market, not just that revenue exists. Look at the videos actually promoting the product, not only the revenue figure.
Require a strong upward revenue trend, not a flat or declining one.
Keep revenue moderate: the source's target is roughly $33K–$97K in the last 30 days. Products doing $300K–$1M+/month signal heavy competition rather than opportunity.
Prefer English-speaking products; the source discards products whose ads are entirely in Spanish because they succeed by selling to Latin American buyers, not the US market.
Treat this as a blueprint, not a hard rulebook — the source explicitly warns beginners against turning criteria into a 'bible' and says conviction can justify breaking filters.
caveats: The revenue range and thresholds are the source's personal working numbers, not validated benchmarks.
The criteria are explicitly described as flexible; strict adherence can cause missed winners.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Reading 30-day vs 180-day revenue graphs in Kalodata
cards.summary: How to use the 30-day graph to spot uptrends, then immediately switch to 180-day data to reject products that peaked months ago.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a product's visible growth in the default research-tool view is real momentum or a dying product that only looks alive in a short window.
steps: In the product list, ignore the product images on first pass — the source covers them with a hand and looks only at the graph shape. Look for a graph that is flat or tilting upward, not one pointing to the sky.
Click a product whose 30-day graph looks slightly upward, then immediately switch to the 180-day view to get the full picture.
In the 180-day view, reject the product if it was selling months ago and is now flatlining near the bottom — e.g. previously hitting highs of ~1K/day and now doing roughly one sale per day.
Watch for the pattern where a product dipped and is now climbing back up; the source finds this interesting enough to investigate further, whereas a straight downtrend is an immediate skip.
Treat a product only recently launched with a steeply rising 180-day curve (e.g. 2K → 16K → 21K → 20K over successive periods) as a strong green flag for early entry.
caveats: Switching back to the 180-day view can completely reverse a 30-day impression; the source calls this 'getting the full picture' and says it prevents wasted testing spend.
Products on a straight vertical graph have no downside data, so sustainability is unknown — the source calls these 'gamble products'.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Video age and revenue distribution checks
cards.summary: Validate a product by requiring a top-performing video posted in the last 7–14 days and revenue spread across at least three to five recent videos rather than one old hero video.
cards.use_when: After a product passes the revenue-graph screen, before deciding whether you have enough proven creative to build an ad test.
steps: Open the product's video tab and check the posting dates of the top-performing videos. The highest-revenue video must have been posted within the last 7 to 14 days.
Reject products where an old video (months old) is still carrying revenue — an old ad running with an ad symbol can indicate a brand trying to revive a dead product rather than fresh momentum.
Check revenue distribution across the top videos. Discard products where 90%+ of revenue comes from a single old video.
Require at least 3–5 recent videos contributing meaningful revenue so you have multiple proven creatives to work with.

Use the 7-day view in addition to the 180-day view: the top ad in the recent window can differ from the top ad historically, and the most recent proven creative is the one most likely to transfer to your own Meta test.

Exception the source allows: if the product's recent revenue is large enough (e.g. ~60K in 7 days), a top video with 58K versus a second video at 600 is acceptable, because conviction from overall validation outweighs the distribution rule — you can pair the winning hook with other weaker clips.
caveats: A single dominant creative means you lack proven assets for your own campaign, raising execution risk even if the product concept is strong.
The source's own exception (high recent revenue justifies a lopsided distribution) is a judgment call, not a rule.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Filtering out live-sales and cheap-impulse products
cards.summary: Reject TikTok Shop products whose revenue comes primarily from live streams or whose price point depends on cheap impulse buying.
cards.use_when: Screening candidate products in Kalodata and interpreting price and revenue-source data.
steps: Check the revenue source breakdown. The source sets 'video' as the required revenue source, because it wants video/UGC creatives, not live-stream sales.
Get off the product immediately if live revenue is around 25K or higher — that indicates success driven by live streams rather than transferable video ads.
Reject products selling at roughly $9.99. The source treats this as a major red flag because cheap impulse buys rarely carry enough margin to survive Meta acquisition costs.
Apply these as filters alongside the graph checks, not in isolation — a strong graph with a cheap price is still a skip.
caveats: Live-commerce can be a legitimate channel in other contexts; this filter is specific to dropshippers whose model depends on video ads and Meta traffic.
The 25K live-revenue threshold and $9.99 rejection are the source's heuristics, not measured breakpoints.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Using revenue filters and the law of diminishing returns
cards.summary: How to set and adjust the revenue range filter based on whether previous tests produced profitable or unprofitable sales.
cards.use_when: Setting the revenue range in Kalodata and iterating on it after a test result.
steps: The source treats the revenue range as a lenient, changeable filter — the specific numbers used (e.g. 55K–97K) were chosen arbitrarily, and the source says any nearby value would work the same.

Evaluate results before adjusting: if a product did a lot of sales but was highly unprofitable and had been doing ~20K/month in revenue, raise the range on the next hunt (e.g. to 40K) and test again to see if profitability improves.
Be aware of diminishing returns: pushing the range to 200K–300K brings you into the most competitive space, which is 'playing with fire' rather than a shortcut to profitability.
Remember the source's rationale: TikTok Shop customer demand translates over to Meta, so TikTok revenue level is usable as a proxy for market demand when setting the filter.
Set revenue source to 'video' and avoid using the 'growing' trend filter — the source says selecting it makes Kalodata hide many good products.
caveats: The relationship between higher TikTok revenue and Meta profitability is not guaranteed; the source frames it as something to test empirically.
Very high revenue products come with heavy competition, not just validation.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Validating a sub-niche trend on Google Trends
cards.summary: Validate that the exact product variation — not the broad category — has an active 12-month upward trajectory on Google Trends.
cards.use_when: After a specific product passes tool screening and you want trend confirmation before testing, especially for emerging formats like patches.
steps: Search the exact variation, not the parent keyword. Example: search 'GLP-1 patches' rather than just 'GLP-1'.
Check the 12-month graph. It must show an active, current upward trajectory — not a peak that has already flattened.

Use the comparison insightfully: in the source's example, the broad 'GLP-1' term was at an all-time high (index 100, rare on Google Trends) while the 'GLP-1 patches' variation was on its own rising uptrend — indicating an early sub-niche with room to grow.
Treat this step as optional. The source skips it when conviction is already high and goes straight to testing, calling the Google Trends check a sidetrack when he is convinced.
caveats: The source explicitly marks this step optional and says it can slow down execution.
Google Trends measures search interest, not purchase intent.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Competition assessment via Facebook Ad Library and Page Transparency
cards.summary: Assess how many direct competitors are running the product, how long they've been running, and whether their stores and offers look beatable.
cards.use_when: Validating saturation and competitive positioning right before you decide to buy or build the store.
steps: Search the product term in Facebook Ad Library. Assess the whole niche first (e.g. all GLP products: gummies, liquids, pills, powders), then narrow to your exact variation (e.g. GLP patches).
Open the page for each competitor, go to About → Page Transparency, confirm whether the page is currently running ads, then open their ad library to see every active ad.

Note how long they have been running. A competitor running ads for only nine hours has no spend history, so their ads validate nothing yet — the source says to bookmark them and watch rather than infer a winner.
Check whether they run video or image ads and what language they target. A competitor running Spanish-only image ads, for example, is not a direct competitor in the US English market.

Evaluate their store and offer. The source rejects a competitor's store as 'completely trash' — minimal template, wrong product imagery — and notes a stronger brand presentation plus subscription option as a differentiator he could use.

Expect more competitors to appear over time; finding three already means the product is moving. Speed matters — a competitor found the same product 24 hours earlier, which the source treats as a meaningful head start.
caveats: Ad Library shows ads, not spend, so you cannot tell if a competitor's campaign is profitable.
Page Transparency and Ad Library interfaces change; verify current navigation in the tool.
New competitors with hours of runtime provide no validation either way.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Spy Crew as a budget alternative to full-price research tools
cards.summary: Use Spy Crew's bundled browser and tool access to get Kalodata, Shop Plus, PP Spy and other research utilities at a lower monthly cost than subscribing separately.
cards.use_when: Setting up a research stack when Kalodata's standalone price is the constraint.
steps: Recognize the cost problem the source is solving: Kalodata alone is $80/month.
Use Spy Crew's Pro plan at roughly $49/month, which the source says includes Kalodata access plus a customized browser environment.

Exploit the browser structure: every new tab opens Spy Crew's dashboard with a tool directory, including Runway ML, Tikstar, Playbook, Helium 10, Drop Spy, Future Live, cutout.pro, Shop Plus, Kalodata, PP Spy, Canva and PP Ads.
Use Shop Plus as a Kalodata 'dupe' for a second data angle, and PP Spy (Chrome extension) to check whether a competitor store has recently added new products.
Also keep free standalone tabs open for the core validation loop: Facebook Ad Library, Google Trends, Amazon, and Google search.
caveats: The source states he would not do product research the way he does without Spy Crew; this is a tool-access argument, not an endorsement of outcomes.
Tool bundles and pricing change — verify current plans and included tools before subscribing.
The video also contains promotional segments for the presenter's paid mentorship, which are not part of this method.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Searching for the most untapped products: sort and ignore images
cards.summary: In the product list, sort revenue lowest to highest and screen on graph shape first, using product images only to spot known-saturated items.
cards.use_when: Starting a live hunt in Kalodata and deciding which rows to click into.
steps: Filter down to one niche at a time rather than flooding the page with all categories. The source uses the last-30-days date range and only the products tab, ignoring the other top tabs.
Change the default sort from highest revenue to lowest revenue. The source's stated reason is that this surfaces the most untapped products.

On the list, ignore product images as a first screen. Don't even look at them — evaluate the graph shape, looking for a line that is not going down (flat or slightly uptrending is enough; it does not need to shoot to the moon).

Treat the image as a second, quick saturation check: if you recognize a long-established, heavily sold product (the source's example is moringa, seen multiple times in the same list and known to be widely run by friends and others on Facebook), skip it regardless of graph.
Use pattern recognition from daily hunting: seeing the same category repeatedly (e.g. GLP products everywhere on TikTok Shop) is itself a signal that a niche is hot.
caveats: The source admits he sometimes glances at the image anyway when the graph excites him; the primary screen remains the graph.
Niche familiarity is required for the image-based saturation check — beginners will not recognize long-running products.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Reading stacked hooks that introduce a novel ingredient or format
cards.summary: How branded ingredient or unusual format claims (liposomal, NAD, patches) create perceived sophistication and a reason to click.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether a supplement or wellness product has a defensible angle beyond a commodity ingredient.
steps: Look at the label copy in the product image and product title for a branded or technical ingredient signal — the source points to 'liposomal' or 'NAD' as examples that sound sophisticated and differentiate a commodity.
Recognize that the ingredient itself does not need to be new; introducing a specific-sounding ingredient to the customer's mind as the solution is what the source says drives performance.

Check for format novelty within a known niche. The source maps six supplement formats — patches, consumables/pills, powders, liquids, resins, gummies — and treats a format not yet saturated in a hot niche as an opening; GLP patches were his example against abundant GLP pills and powders.
Combine ingredient/format novelty with the trend check: novelty explains why it is working now, Google Trends confirms the variation is still rising.
Reject pH products unless the company is introducing something new — a new angle or new ingredient — because the source knows how many pH products already exist.
caveats: 'Sophisticated-sounding ingredient' is a persuasion judgment, not a clinical claim; do not treat it as efficacy evidence.
Commodity supplements are a highly competitive niche in the source's view, even though they are the most profitable because they enable renewability.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Translating a TikTok-native creative into a Meta ad (mix-match)
cards.summary: Combine a validated short TikTok hook with a longer, more convincing creator body to produce a Meta-optimized ad.
cards.use_when: Building your first ad set after buying a validated product, especially when the top TikTok video is a very short viral clip.
steps: Take the validated short hook — the source's example is a 5-second clip opening with 'your insurance doesn't cover Zepbound, but GLP patches exist' — and use its first ~3 seconds as your hook.
Cut at roughly the 3-second mark into a longer creator video (the source uses a ~1 minute 10 second creator explaining her experience and answering comments) so the viewer gets depth and proof.

Apply the source's stated ad principles: lowest CPC and shortest/most fun videos are typically not the highest converters on Meta; the highest converters are the most convincing, and convincing takes time.
Use the TikTok-native short as the attention device and the Facebook-native long creator clip as the argument — the source notes the long clip would outperform the short one on Meta for that reason.
Do not simply rip one ad wholesale. The source warns that ripped ads make you indistinguishable from competitors — everyone can rip the same creative; editing your own is the differentiator.
Plan to make 5–8 ads when testing a product, per the source's testing practice.
caveats: The source's own scope note says to ignore instructions on editing mix-match creatives in this particular video; the concept appears here but is not developed as step-by-step editing instruction.
Hooks and clips should be validated by their own performance data, not copied blindly.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Acting on brand-new videos to get ahead of a spike
cards.summary: Use very recent video posting dates and rapid view velocity as an early-entry signal before a product saturates, and accept the gamble that comes with it.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to move immediately on a product whose graph is rising steeply and whose top videos were posted days ago.
steps: Check the posting date of the top video against today's date. In the source's example, a video posted June 5 had 8.39 million views by June 11 — six days — which he treats as an exceptional green flag.

Run rough arithmetic on recent units to estimate trajectory: a video posted four days earlier that already sold 45 units implies roughly 3,000 units/month if the pace holds, approaching the revenue of the current top video.

Interpret the timing advantage: getting in before the product is widely found lets you hold Facebook ad placements and bid ahead of later entrants, and the source says Meta favors advertisers with longer histories on a product (a 'legacy' advantage).
Verify the recency of multiple top videos, not just one — the source checks each and finds all were posted within days.
