Accept the trade-off: a steeply rising product with no prior decline has no sustainability data. The source calls it a gamble — it can keep climbing or drop to zero and wipe out early advertisers along with everyone else.

Compare against established products that show a range of lows and highs over time (e.g. lows around a few hundred dollars/day with an overall uptrend), which the source calls a healthier signal even if less explosive.
caveats: The source states plainly that he cannot know whether the example product kept rising or collapsed by publication time.
Meta's favor toward earlier advertisers is presented as the source's belief, not a documented platform rule.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Pricing and offer strategy when translating a cheap TikTok product to Meta
cards.summary: Raise price and build an offer structure on your own store because Meta audiences respond to longer, more convincing ad-to-site experiences.
cards.use_when: You have validated a low-priced TikTok Shop product (e.g. $15) and need a viable offer for a Meta funnel.
steps: Accept that a $9.99 TikTok price is not a viable Meta price — the source rejects sub-$10 products because cheap impulse pricing leaves no margin for acquisition costs.

Reposition the product at a higher price on your own store. In the source's example, a $15 TikTok product could be sold around $29.99 with a buy-one-get-one-free offer, and shipping of $4–$5 can be charged.
Anchor the higher price to perceived value: the source argues people will pay more because Meta ads are longer and more convincing and the website looks better than a TikTok Shop listing.

Build in renewability where the product supports it — the source cites a subscription product generating over $5,000/month recurring, with a 33% subscription rate (1 in 3 customers), and describes that as the path to a durable brand.
Use a no-subscription high-volume product as a valid alternative: the source's own $1.5M store had zero subscribers.
caveats: The $29.99/BOGO and shipping numbers are the source's illustration, not a tested benchmark for every product.
A 33% subscription rate is one brand's reported result, not a promise.
The source notes supplements are highly competitive even though they are the most profitable because of renewability.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Choosing a niche based on business model
cards.summary: Pick your research category according to whether you want recurring revenue or high-volume one-off sales.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to hunt in Kalodata's category filter before starting a product search.
steps: If you want MRR and subscription revenue, hunt in the health niche, because it lends itself to reusable products and subscription offers.

If you want high-volume, no-subscription ecommerce volume, the source points to beauty and personal care, women's wear and underwear, men's wear and underwear, home improvement, and jewelry and accessories.

Use the source's own contrast as the decision frame: his $1.5M store had no subscribers, while a separate product generated $5K/month recurring revenue with a 33% subscription rate — different models from the same system.
Filter one niche at a time in the tool rather than mixing categories on a single search, and only use the product tab plus the last-30-days range the source works with.
Treat category choice as a strategic decision made before you start hunting, not something to resolve by picking whatever appears on the first page.
caveats: The category list reflects the source's own experience, not a ranked study of niche profitability.
Supplements inside the health niche are noted as the most profitable but also very competitive.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Read short-term spikes as gambling products
cards.summary: Distinguish 'gamble' products that blow up just recently from products with sustained revenue history.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a product whose revenue graph shows a recent sharp spike, before committing to test it.
steps: Switch the dashboard to the 180-day view rather than judging from a 7- or 30-day window.
Look for sustained performance, e.g. a product running at ~$2K days since early in the year while also trending up recently: that is much healthier than one that only jumped in the last few days.

If a product was doing lows of a few hundred dollars per day and is essentially spiking now, treat it as a 'gamble product'. The source still tests these sometimes, but frames them as gambles, not validated winners.
Check whether the spike coincides with one very recent piece of content or an older piece that suddenly resurfaced; the latter is a weaker signal.
caveats: A gamble product is a judgment call, not a rule; the presenter explicitly says the risk is his own preference.
Recent spikes can be real demand or a single lucky video; the dashboard alone cannot tell which.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Lower revenue filters to cut competitive products
cards.summary: Narrowing the revenue band to roughly $36K-$70K surfaces less saturated products than a $70K+ band.
cards.use_when: The product list is full of products you've seen advertised many times, or you want less competitive candidates.
steps: Start with a wider revenue range, then notice when results are dominated by products you recognize from being advertised everywhere.
Reduce the band to about $36,000 low and $70,000 high to see far fewer competitors.
Treat the lower band as a healthier hunting ground, but accept smaller upside: a validated product in a less crowded band may scale less than a big branded one.
Verify current dashboard filter behavior before relying on exact thresholds; interfaces change.
caveats: The exact numbers are this presenter's live example, not a universal benchmark.
Low-revenue products can be low-revenue because demand is genuinely small, not only because competition is low.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Screen out non-English creatives before testing
cards.summary: Products whose winning content is in Spanish are a hard skip because they don't transfer to English-speaking audiences.
cards.use_when: Checking a product's top-performing videos during research.
steps: Open the product's last-7-days videos and identify the language of the top creative.
If the best-performing video is in Spanish, disqualify the product for an English-language test — the source has found these do not replicate for English speakers.
Apply the same screen to Spanish-language ads found later in the feed even when the revenue graph looks good.
Also check that live selling has not overtaken the revenue; if a large share comes from live streams rather than regular ads, the ad data is less usable.
caveats: This is the presenter's tested heuristic for English-speaking markets; it says nothing about success when targeting Spanish-speaking audiences.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Check how concentrated the winning videos are
cards.summary: Revenue spread across several videos is healthier than one dominant winning video.
cards.use_when: Judging whether a candidate product's recent sales are repeatable across creative.
steps: Review the individual videos driving the past 7 days of revenue.
Look for distribution like $2K, $1.8K, $1.4K across three different videos: this indicates multiple creatives are working, which is a strong sign.
If a single winning video carries most of the revenue, treat it as more fragile — one video can be luck or an outlier.
Then check the winning video's post date: a video posted a couple of weeks ago that is still scaling is a mild red flag; content posted this week and already performing well is the stronger signal.
caveats: One dominant video can still be a real winner; even revenue spread does not guarantee performance when you test your own offer.
Post dates only tell you about the observed creative, not about the product's long-term demand.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Competitor-set your niche, not just your product
cards.summary: When you sell a variant format you still compete with every other format of the same ingredient or niche.
cards.use_when: Assessing saturation for supplement-style or format-substitution products.
steps: Identify the underlying ingredient or niche (e.g. GLP), not just the exact product (e.g. patches).
Recognize that even if nobody else sells the patch version, you are competing for the same customers who know the powder, gummies, resin, or pills.
Add competitor checks against the niches you compete in as a whole, in addition to the specific product keywords.
Use this to decide whether a healthy-looking graph is actually in a crowded customer pool.
caveats: A niche-wide competitor set will always look large; the point is to price your differentiation, not to avoid the category entirely.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Pressure-test the offer before you sell the same product
cards.summary: Competitor offers often bundle a commodity product into a branded kit; copyable offer structure matters as much as the product.
cards.use_when: You found a product with an appealing graph but generic positioning, and need a differentiation angle.
steps: Click into a competitor's store from the Facebook Ad Library result and inspect the offer page.
Note the structure rather than the product: e.g. a 'youth reset kit' on top of NAD patches, buy-one-get-one-free, plus a free ebook and an eye mask. The presenter rates this structure as strong.

Look for ingredient-level specificity over adjectives: 'youthful' is a vague adjective, while naming an active ingredient (e.g. bee venom, known to the target female audience) tells the customer why the product works.
Use that specificity — plus your own offer stack — as the reason your variant of the same product could still win.
caveats: Strong offers still face the niche-wide competition described elsewhere.
Verify current ad library navigation before assuming a given layout.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Skip products with low perceived-value pricing
cards.summary: Under-$10 price points force matching price and usually fail the perceived-value test.
cards.use_when: A researched product shows a good graph but sells cheaply.
steps: Check the store's selling price, e.g. a bug-bite suction device at $9.99.
If the price is low like that, recognize you will be forced to run the same low-price play, which caps margins and ad economics.
Prefer products with higher perceived value that can support a healthy price band, like the skin-tag removal cream the presenter flagged as well-priced.
Treat low price as a structural constraint on the funnel, not just a number to edit on a test.
caveats: Low-price products can work in volume models; this is the presenter's preference for his drop-shipping tests, not a universal rule.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Use the shape of the 180-day graph as a fast filter
cards.summary: Up-down-up with an overall uptrend is healthy; a graph already in the gutter or on a downtrend is not worth testing.
cards.use_when: Scanning many products and deciding which ones deserve a closer look.
steps: Open the 180-day view first and read the overall trend rather than the last blip.

Screen out graphs that are clearly declining — the presenter rejected a tinted lip serum doing $40K in 30 days because the 180-day graph was 'in the gutter', and rejected several others as downtrends.
Keep the products whose graph oscillates but trends up overall.
Only then spend time on videos, competitor lookup and trend checks for the survivors.
caveats: Graph reading is a screening step, not proof of demand transfer to your own store.
Tools, ranges and labels change; confirm what the chart shows in your tool's current version.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Research candidates against Facebook Ad Library and Google Trends
cards.summary: A product counts as validated when it survives both a competitor search and a trend check.
cards.use_when: You have a candidate with a good graph and need a go/no-go before testing.
steps: Search the product keyword in the Facebook Ad Library to gauge how many advertisers are running it right now.
Look for signals like a competitor who launched an ad only hours ago — that shows the space is live and being contested.
Search the product on Google Trends to see whether search interest is building rather than decaying.
Test only if the product looks validated across both checks; if no competition is findable at all, judge whether the trend and recency justify a speculative test.
caveats: Keyword selection is the hard part: for unfamiliar products like gut-cleansing protocols or fulvic acid blends, the obvious terms may surface nothing even when competitors exist.
Absence of visible competitors is ambiguous, not automatically good.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Switch filter categories to find cross-listed winners
cards.summary: A product can appear under a different dashboard category than the niche it truly belongs to, so loosen category filters.
cards.use_when: You are searching a niche and the category filter may be hiding relevant products.
steps: Don't treat the dashboard category as truth: an arnica removal cream can sit under beauty and personal care while functionally being a supplement-driven health product.
When a promising product is not showing in your main category, widen or change the category filter so it can appear.
Once found, evaluate it on the same criteria as everything else: 7-day revenue (~$8K in the example), distribution across videos, price band and untapped feel.
Confirm the product actually has a mechanism story (e.g. removing skin tags) rather than being a random listing.
caveats: Category filters are tool-specific and can change; verify how the platform you use organizes categories today.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Choose niches by competition level, not popularity
cards.summary: Beauty and personal care equals health in potential but also in competition; less-hyped niches like home, tools and appliances often have lower competition.
cards.use_when: Deciding which niche to hunt in before opening the product dashboard.
steps: Treat beauty and personal care as equally viable to the health niche, with the same caveat of being equally competitive.
Also consider women's wear and underwear, men's wear and underwear, home supplies, tools and hardware, home improvement and household appliances — niches the presenter says have low competition.
Recognize that not hearing about a niche is the point: few sellers are in it, so a product with real revenue behind it is close to a validated winner.
Expect fewer candidates per session in these niches because the option pool is smaller, and sift routinely rather than expecting every product to be good.
caveats: The presenter also notes these niches can attract passionate buyers and more product options, but quality still varies product by product.
Low competition is not the same as proven demand; the revenue graph still has to be there.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Beware recognizable products and brands
cards.summary: If you've seen the product or brand many times — in ads or as an established retailer — pass on it.
cards.use_when: A candidate looks familiar or comes from a long-established brand.
steps: During scanning, treat your own familiarity as a red flag: the presenter skipped a known natural shampoo brand because it has been around a long time and isn't worth testing.
Do the same for products you've personally seen advertised before (e.g. a deworming protocol ad the presenter recalled), since many other advertisers are likely running them too.

Confirm with the competitor check: a shilajit-and-collagen bundle graph looked healthy, but the presenter rejected it because he knows the product and expects heavy competition in Facebook Ad Library.
Keep scanning rather than trying to out-execute a saturated, well-known product.
caveats: Familiarity is a heuristic for saturation, not proof; a familiar category can still contain an untapped variant.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Decide whether to keep hunting or switch niches
cards.summary: If pages of results are duds, adjust filters or switch niche rather than quitting early.
cards.use_when: You have scrolled several result pages without a candidate worth testing.
steps: Check how deep you actually are: the presenter refused to give up at page five of a many-page list.
If duds dominate while your filters look reasonable, widen or change the category filter rather than assuming the whole niche is dead.
Only switch niche after adjusting filters and still finding nothing — the presenter did this after the health niche run.
Remember speed compounds: as you repeat this, you will no longer need a walkthrough video, and a single session can plausibly surface two or three strong candidates.
caveats: There is no fixed number of pages that means 'give up'; the source only warns against quitting too early.
Sessions can produce zero winners, and that is a normal research outcome, not a failure of the method.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Accept that validated products can still fail your test
cards.summary: Testing a validated product on Meta with your own ads and offer is a new experiment, not a guaranteed win.
cards.use_when: Planning a product test after research signals look strong.
steps: Recognize the gap: the product was validated on its own store with its own content, while you test on Meta with more edited ads and a different offer.
Treat research as generating candidates worth a test, not as evidence of certain success.
If the test fails, reuse the same research method to find the next candidate rather than abandoning the process.
Run the test for about 2-3 days on Meta, then assess and move on to the next product if it did badly.
caveats: The 2-3 day assessment window is the presenter's own practice for drop-shipping tests, not a universal statistical standard.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Run a 16-question validation pass before sourcing any physical product
cards.summary: A structured 16-point checklist that screens a product idea across market, competition, economics, logistics and retention before you spend on inventory.
cards.use_when: You have a physical product idea and want an objective go/no-go screen before committing time, sourcing spend or manufacturing.
steps: Split the checklist into two blocks: market-level questions (demand size, competitor landscape, trend direction, local availability, target customer) and product-level questions (selling price, markup, SKU count, subscription fit, size/weight, durability, seasonality, pain vs passion, consumability, perishability, restrictions).
Work market questions first: they can kill an idea before you spend effort on unit economics.
Score each question as pass, caution or red flag rather than a binary yes/no. The source stresses that not every box will be checked.

At the end, write an explicit list of highlights and concerns for the idea. In the source's coconut hair mask example, highlights were low startup cost, strong search demand, upward trend and rankable keywords; concerns were the low price point and fragmented competition.
Only proceed when the concerns look fixable through branding, differentiation or positioning rather than through hoping the numbers change.
caveats: This is a baseline screening framework, not a guarantee of demand. The source explicitly says search volume and social mentions are a 'vote of confidence' in interest, not proof of buyers.
Validator work does not replace supplier negotiation, sourcing or storefront build, which sit in other workflows.
cards.source_name: Transcript of How To Find And Validate WINNING PRODUCTS_ The 16 Step Product Research Guide.docx

cards.title: Size demand with Keyword Planner search volume plus social mention volume
cards.summary: Use free search-volume and social-listening tools to estimate whether enough people are actively looking for the product before investing.
cards.use_when: You need a first quantitative read on demand for a product concept and have not yet chosen suppliers.
steps: Open Google Keyword Planner (free) and query the core keywords and close variants that describe your product idea, e.g. 'coconut oil hair mask'.
Record the combined monthly search volume. In the source example, related terms returned roughly 73,000 searches per month.
Use a social listening tool such as BuzzSumo to count how many people mention the main keywords per day. The example found around 150 tweets per day.
Read the two numbers together as a demand signal, not a forecast: high search volume plus steady social chatter indicates live interest.
Cross-check the keyword direction in Google Trends (see the trend-direction card) because a large but shrinking search base can still be a bad bet.
caveats: Keyword Planner volume is an estimate and can be inflated by broad-match terms; the source treats it as directional.
Social mentions include people discussing, not buying. High chatter with no commercial intent language is weaker evidence.
cards.source_name: Transcript of How To Find And Validate WINNING PRODUCTS_ The 16 Step Product Research Guide.docx

cards.title: Classify the market direction: growing, flat, fad or declining
cards.summary: Use Google Trends and trend research to separate a durable upward category from a passing fad or a market you have already missed.
cards.use_when: Demand volume looks acceptable and you need to judge whether the category will still exist in two to three years.
steps: Plot the main and adjacent keywords in Google Trends over the longest available window and look at the trajectory, not a single month.
Label the pattern: consistently rising, flat, spiking and collapsing (fad), or declining.

Research why the trend is moving. In the source example, coconut oil interest had grown over several years, but the presenter notes that the beauty industry rotates new 'breakthrough' ingredients, so an ingredient trend can eventually die.
Use trend-hunting resources or your own category intuition when the data is ambiguous; the source notes many entrepreneurs rely on gut instinct for trend timing.
Treat a rising trend as a green light for entry but plan for it to flatten, and avoid building the whole business around a single fashionable ingredient or format.
caveats: The source's own case study shows a rising trend that may still decline, so treat trend direction as a risk factor rather than an anchor.
Trend tools are external services whose interfaces and output change; verify current functionality before relying on them.
cards.source_name: Transcript of How To Find And Validate WINNING PRODUCTS_ The 16 Step Product Research Guide.docx

cards.title: Map competitors, including free and DIY substitutes
cards.summary: Research the competitive landscape in your target markets, treating grocery-store alternatives and homemade substitutes as real competitors.
cards.use_when: You are validating a product category and want to know whether there is room for a new entrant.
steps: Search Google in each country you intend to sell in, using the language customers would use, not your internal product name.

List every credible substitute, not just branded products. In the source example three competitive areas emerged: pure coconut oil sold in grocery stores, DIY recipes, and commercial products from large businesses.

Note whether the market is dominated by a recognizable leader or is fragmented among many manufacturers and retailers. The source treats a fragmented market with no true market leaders as a possible opportunity signal.
Check offline availability directly. If the product is easy to buy at a local store, online viability drops because there is one less reason to order online; scarcity offline is a positive sign.
Fold the result into your overall concern list rather than declaring victory: fragmentation can mean opportunity or simply that nobody has made the category work online.
caveats: Fragmentation is ambiguous: the source calls it a possible opportunity, not proof of a viable gap.
A market with major incumbents is harder to read; the source suggests using traffic and demographic estimates on incumbent sites to learn about the buyer.
cards.source_name: Transcript of How To Find And Validate WINNING PRODUCTS_ The 16 Step Product Research Guide.docx

cards.title: Profile target customers before committing to a product
cards.summary: Estimate who the buyers are, where they live and whether they buy online, so you do not discover unshippable or unreachable demand too late.
cards.use_when: You need to confirm the product's audience is reachable and in a country you can ship to and advertise in.
steps: If major competitors have websites, use audience-estimation tools to read the demographics of their traffic as a proxy for the category's buyers.
If the market is too fragmented for that, sample social platforms directly: read posts and profiles that use your keywords and infer gender and age range.
In the source example, the people tweeting about coconut hair masks were mostly female, with an inferred average age of 18 to 35.
Use Google Trends region data to see which countries dominate the interest. The example showed the US and Canada.
Check that the demographic is comfortable buying online and that shipping to the identified countries is feasible; the source treats the ability to reach the audience easily as a strong positive.
Capture this profile now, because it feeds creative, channel choice and pricing later.
caveats: Profile-image and tweet-based demographic inference is a rough estimate. The source presents it as a feel for the audience when no incumbent data exists.
Trend region data shows where search happens, not where people are willing to pay international shipping.
cards.source_name: Transcript of How To Find And Validate WINNING PRODUCTS_ The 16 Step Product Research Guide.docx

cards.title: Target the $50–$150 retail price band for paid-acquisition economics
cards.summary: A commonly cited sweet spot where a product carries enough margin to fund paid ads but is not so expensive that buyers expect premium service.
cards.use_when: You are choosing between product concepts or setting an initial retail price for a product you intend to acquire customers for with paid ads.
steps: Price-check comparable products from at least a couple of dozen brands to establish the category's realistic band. In the source example about two dozen comparable hair masks implied roughly $9–$20 for 120ml.
Compare that band against the widely cited $50–$150 sweet spot used by many ecommerce operators.
Reason about both ends: below the band, per-unit profit is too thin to absorb paid advertising; above it, customers hesitate online and expect premium service such as phone support.
If your product's realistic price sits below the band, treat it as a red flag for a paid-traffic-first business rather than an automatic reject, as the source does with the hair mask example.
Flag low-price products as candidates for organic traffic, bundles, larger sizes or a higher-value-positioned formulation instead of a straight paid-ads launch.
caveats: The $50–$150 range is described in the source as generally accepted by many top ecommerce entrepreneurs, not a proven law; it may not apply to categories with strong repeat purchase or cheap organic acquisition.
The source's own case study sat at $9–$20 and was flagged as a margin risk, showing low price is a caution rather than a disqualifier.
cards.source_name: Transcript of How To Find And Validate WINNING PRODUCTS_ The 16 Step Product Research Guide.docx

cards.title: Model markup at low and high price points, including future bulk costing
cards.summary: Estimate cost per unit and profit per unit across the plausible price range so a single bad price assumption does not sink the business.
cards.use_when: You have a rough price band and a first cost estimate and need to see whether the product can carry your expenses.
steps: Estimate all-in cost of goods for an initial small run: ingredients or components, packaging, and any assembly. In the source example producing 100 units cost about $583, i.e. roughly $5.83 per unit.
Compute markup at the bottom and the top of your realistic price band, not just the middle. At $9 the source's example markup was a concern; at $20 it was healthy.
List what markup must cover: operating expenses, marketing and profit.
Model how cost changes as order volume grows, since bulk pricing lowers unit cost and increases the leftover margin as you scale.
If markup only works at the top of the band, verify that buyers will actually pay the top price before sourcing.
caveats: The source's $583 per 100 units is a case-study figure, not a benchmark for any other product.
Early cost estimates often omit inbound freight, duties, payment fees and returns; treat this as a first-pass screen.
cards.source_name: Transcript of How To Find And Validate WINNING PRODUCTS_ The 16 Step Product Research Guide.docx

cards.title: Launch with exactly one SKU and treat extra variants as complexity debt
cards.summary: Minimize SKUs at launch because each variant adds inventory capital, storage cost and shipping-error risk.
cards.use_when: You are deciding how many sizes, colors or formulations to launch with.
steps: Default the launch to a single SKU. The source calls a one-SKU product a bonus.
Treat each additional SKU as three costs: more inventory capital tied up, more storage cost, and a higher chance of picking and shipping the wrong item.

Use the single SKU as the starting wedge, then expand into a line only after the core product proves out. The source notes that a one-SKU concept can later extend into a full line, which opens opportunities down the road.
If the category demands variants (e.g. sizes), pick the single best-selling configuration first and let demand data justify the next one.
caveats: A single SKU limits the baskets you can build from the start; the source presents it as a risk-minimization trade-off, not a permanent rule.
Some categories cannot compete credibly without shade or size ranges.
cards.source_name: Transcript of How To Find And Validate WINNING PRODUCTS_ The 16 Step Product Research Guide.docx

cards.title: Judge subscription fit by real consumption rate, not category type
cards.summary: Subscriptions are desirable but only work when the customer genuinely repurchases often enough to justify the cadence.
cards.use_when: You are evaluating whether a product can support recurring revenue and lower blended acquisition cost.
steps: Check the product's fundamental nature first: consumable and disposable products such as supplements, cosmetics, foods and cleaning products create natural repeat purchase.

Then estimate real consumption. In the source example the hair mask was consumable, but a customer would likely use only a couple per year, so any subscription plan would have to reflect that slow cadence.
Set the replenishment interval from observed usage rather than an aggressive default; a mismatched cadence produces churn and refunds.
Note that subscription capability is desirable but not required: the source explicitly says subscriptions are not necessary to build a successful online business.
If repeat purchase is slow, model retention value from consumable resale and bundles rather than a monthly plan.
caveats: Slow-consumption products still help retention but cannot support high-frequency subscription billing.
The source treats subscription potential as a positive attribute, not a pass/fail criterion.
cards.source_name: Transcript of How To Find And Validate WINNING PRODUCTS_ The 16 Step Product Research Guide.docx

cards.title: Screen size, weight and shipping cost before you commit
cards.summary: Oversized or heavy products create shipping costs that deter buyers or eat margin, so estimate carrier costs on rough dimensions early.
cards.use_when: You are comparing product concepts and shipping economics matter to your margin.
steps: Measure or estimate the packed size and weight of the product as it would ship, not just the raw item.
Go to your carrier's website and price a rough shipment using those numbers to get a feel for real cost before sourcing.
Compare the result against your markup. If shipping consumes a large share of the spread between cost and price, the product needs a higher price point or a smaller format.
Prefer small and light formats. In the source example the hair mask was classified by most shippers as a small package in both weight and size, which kept shipping manageable.
Recheck shipping assumptions for the destinations your customer profile points to, since cross-border rates differ.
caveats: Carrier pricing and dimensional rules change over time; verify current rates before building them into a cost model.
Shipping cost estimates do not include inbound freight, packaging materials or returns.
cards.source_name: Transcript of How To Find And Validate WINNING PRODUCTS_ The 16 Step Product Research Guide.docx

cards.title: Design for durability to cut returns, breakage and refunds
cards.summary: Durability covers both packaging and product formulation, and directly reduces returns and in-transit damage.
cards.use_when: You are choosing materials, packaging or formulation for a shippable physical product.
steps: Assess the failure mode that would generate a return or refund, then design against it.
Choose packaging that survives parcel handling. The source's example prefers a plastic container over glass because it is cheaper and more reliable in transit.
Verify the product itself will not degrade, leak or separate during shipping and storage.
Consider ingredient or component quality as part of durability: the source argues for effective, safe ingredients so the product also holds up on performance, not just in transit.
Think about durability holistically across packaging and product; both drive returns and reviews.
caveats: Cheaper durable packaging can conflict with premium positioning; the source frames plastic as a practical margin decision, not a universal aesthetic rule.
Regulated categories may constrain packaging material choices.
cards.source_name: Transcript of How To Find And Validate WINNING PRODUCTS_ The 16 Step Product Research Guide.docx

cards.title: Map seasonality to protect cash flow
cards.summary: Identifying seasonal demand swings with Google Trends lets you plan inventory buys and marketing calendar around cash flow.
cards.use_when: You are validating a product whose demand may cluster in specific months, or planning inventory and ad budgets.
steps: Plot the core keywords in Google Trends across multiple years, looking for recurring monthly spikes.
Label the pattern: extreme seasonality (the source uses Christmas trees, almost all bought in November and December), mild seasonality, or year-round demand.
If seasonality exists, plan cash flow around it: inventory must be paid for before the spike, and off-season months still carry storage and overhead.
Use the seasonal pattern in marketing too. In the source example subtle January search spikes were interpreted as cold-weather hair rescue demand and noted for winter marketing.
Do not confuse mild seasonal variation with a fad; check whether the spikes repeat each year before treating them as predictable.
caveats: A mildly seasonal product can still be a strong business; the source keeps the data for campaign timing rather than rejecting the product.
Strong seasonality concentrates both revenue and risk, and complicates launching a new brand from zero.
cards.source_name: Transcript of How To Find And Validate WINNING PRODUCTS_ The 16 Step Product Research Guide.docx

cards.title: Prioritize products that solve a pain or serve a passion
cards.summary: Products tied to a real problem or an active hobby make customer acquisition easier than nice-to-have items.
cards.use_when: You are ranking several viable product ideas and want a qualitative tiebreaker on marketability.
steps: Classify each idea as solving a pain point, serving a passion, or merely nice to have.
Deprioritize nice-to-have products, which the source says are tougher to sell because the buyer has no urgency or identity stake.
Note that a product can do both. In the source example the hair mask treats dry or brittle hair (pain) while also serving people invested in keeping their hair healthy (passion).
Use the classification to shape positioning: pain-led products sell relief and outcomes, passion-led products sell identity, community and enthusiasm.
Combine with consumability (see the repeat-purchase card) because pain or passion plus repeat use compounds acquisition efficiency.
caveats: This is a qualitative judgement, not a measured threshold; the source treats it as one input among sixteen.
A pain-solving product in a crowded category can still fail on price and differentiation.
cards.source_name: Transcript of How To Find And Validate WINNING PRODUCTS_ The 16 Step Product Research Guide.docx

cards.title: Favor consumable and disposable formats for repeat business
cards.summary: Consumable products naturally generate repeat purchase and open the door to subscriptions and better lifetime value.
cards.use_when: Choosing between otherwise comparable product ideas, or building a retention plan.
steps: Prefer products the customer must rebuy: food, cleaning products and personal care such as the source's hair mask example.
Treat repeat purchase as a business advantage that improves the economics of acquiring a customer once.
Pair consumability with an honest replenishment cadence so repeat orders actually happen (see the subscription card).
Where the product is not inherently consumable, look for recurring add-ons, refills or accessories to create a repeat path.
Combine consumability with pain/passion positioning for the strongest retention profile.
caveats: Consumability does not guarantee repeat purchase: a bad first experience kills the second order.
Slow-consumption consumables produce weaker repeat frequency than daily-use products.
cards.source_name: Transcript of How To Find And Validate WINNING PRODUCTS_ The 16 Step Product Research Guide.docx

cards.title: Check shelf life and perishability before stocking inventory
cards.summary: Perishable goods risk dead stock and write-offs if sales are slow, so verify shelf life against your realistic sell-through window.
cards.use_when: You are evaluating food, cosmetics or any product with an expiry or degradation risk.
steps: Establish the product's shelf life in the condition it will be stored and shipped.

Compare that window against the time you need to build a marketing plan, generate sales and get the product in front of buyers. The source's example product had a shelf life of roughly three years or more, which it judged more than enough runway.
Also account for how long the customer takes to consume the product once delivered; a long customer-use window reduces pressure on the next order cycle.
If shelf life is short, plan smaller inventory buys and faster turns, and expect higher storage and waste cost.
Reject or redesign any perishable concept whose sell-through window is shorter than your realistic launch and ramp timeline.
caveats: The three-year shelf life is a case-study figure for coconut oil, not a general requirement.
Perishability risk rises sharply if your forecasts are optimistic or if shipping delays extend transit time.
cards.source_name: Transcript of How To Find And Validate WINNING PRODUCTS_ The 16 Step Product Research Guide.docx

cards.title: Research regulations and restrictions before investing in a category
cards.summary: Food, cosmetics, baby products and similar categories carry compliance requirements that should be identified before you spend on sourcing.
cards.use_when: Your product idea touches regulated categories or you are unsure whether claims, labelling or testing rules apply.
steps: Identify which regime your product falls into. The source names food, cosmetics and baby toys as categories that clearly require upfront research.
Check requirements for every country you plan to sell in, since labelling and ingredient rules differ by market.
Find out what the rules mean for your marketing claims, packaging copy and any testing or documentation obligations.
Do the research before investment, not after, because discovering a compliance blocker late wastes both time and money.
Record any restrictions as explicit concerns in your validation summary so the go/no-go decision accounts for them.
caveats: The source's example product had few restrictions, which is category-specific and not a general finding.
This card flags the need for research; it does not substitute for qualified regulatory or legal advice.
cards.source_name: Transcript of How To Find And Validate WINNING PRODUCTS_ The 16 Step Product Research Guide.docx

cards.title: Close validation with a written highlights-and-concerns summary
cards.summary: End the framework by stating what is working and what is not, so the decision to proceed is explicit rather than assumed.
cards.use_when: You have completed the sixteen validation questions and need to make a go/no-go call or justify one to a partner.
steps: List the highlights. In the source example they were low cost to start, strong search demand, a positive trend trajectory and rankable keywords.
List the concerns. The same example flagged the low price point and the competitive landscape.

Decide whether each concern can be answered by something under your control. The source says much of the potential success comes from building a strong brand around the product and from making the product more effective than the raw commodity alternative, such as plain coconut oil.
If concerns depend on market forces changing, treat the idea as a weaker bet than one whose concerns are fixable through branding, formulation or positioning.
Proceed when the concerns have a plausible plan, and revisit the summary after launch to check which assumptions held.
caveats: The source does not provide a scoring formula; it deliberately accepts unresolved red flags and relies on the operator's judgement.
A strong brand plan does not fix fundamentally thin unit economics in paid acquisition.
cards.source_name: Transcript of How To Find And Validate WINNING PRODUCTS_ The 16 Step Product Research Guide.docx

cards.title: Filter Ad Spy Tools for Proven, Facebook-Scaled Winners
cards.summary: Exact Get Hooked filter stack for surfacing validated, older-demographic Facebook winners.
cards.use_when: Configuring an ad-spy tool such as Get Hooked to find products that already have proven spend and scale behind them.
steps: Set Location to USA.
Turn on 'Top performing' only, so you see proven winners rather than speculative tests.
Cap results to a maximum of four ads per brand to reduce noise from one advertiser flooding the feed.
Set Format to Video.
Set Status to 'Currently running' so you only see live, funded campaigns.
Set Minimum Runtime to 14 days — the source treats this as the proof of baseline profitability.
Set Channel to Facebook, because the source argues Facebook skews to older, easier-to-convert buyers.
Set Brand Active Ads to greater than 50, indicating high scale and budget.
Try a niche category first; if results are junk or repetitive, turn the niche off and search manual keywords instead (e.g., a specific symptom or condition), because categories misclassify some ads.
Expect this to require hours of scrolling, not a quick pass; the source frames persistence as the actual work.
caveats: Tool interfaces and filter names change; verify the current Get Hooked layout before relying on exact labels.
The 14-day runtime and 50-active-ads thresholds are the presenter's heuristics, not guarantees of profitability.
Niche categories under-include relevant health ads, so manual keyword search is often necessary.
cards.source_name: Transcript of the product research method that made me $670k.docx

cards.title: Product Criteria: Daily Problem Plus Retail Absence
cards.summary: Two baseline criteria — a problem that recurs daily and no big-box retail availability — for screening product ideas.
cards.use_when: Screening candidate products before spending on creative, site build or inventory, especially in health and wellness.
steps: Check that the product solves a real problem, either a deep emotional problem/desire or a physical problem the buyer feels every single day.
Use the source's example: foot pain — felt every time the person walks — so they will buy almost anything if the copy is good.
Confirm the product is not available in big-box retail stores; retail absence protects margin and ad-driven demand.
Prefer problems with high daily frequency and strong aversion (chronic pain, child sleep disruption, incontinence) because urgency shortens the buying decision.

Assess 'deeply annoying daily problem' as a better signal than 'cool product' — the source explicitly rates a boring problem like tinnitus higher than a gimmicky pillow because of the ongoing irritation.
caveats: Applies to physical problem-solution goods aimed at older buyers; not a universal test for all ecommerce categories.
Retail absence is a margin/protection heuristic, not proof of demand — validate separately with ad intelligence.
The source presents these as his screen, not an empirically benchmarked rule.
cards.source_name: Transcript of the product research method that made me $670k.docx

cards.title: Native Ad Scouting on News Publisher Widgets
cards.summary: Use paid-content widgets on weather and news sites to surface recurring, older-demographic health offers.
cards.use_when: Sourcing product ideas and native-ad angles aimed at a 60+ audience outside of ad spy tools.
steps: Open a news or weather site with a paid content / sponsored widget block — the source names weather.com and CNN.
Repeatedly refresh the widget to rotate through a new batch of paid placements; the same few offers recurring across refreshes is the signal.
Log the health and wellness categories that keep appearing — the source repeatedly sees neuropathy, tinnitus, bladder control, hearing aids, snoring/sleep apnea, neck pain, hip and knee pain.
Treat candidates that are new stores (little or no visit data shown) as under-advertised opportunities rather than reasons to skip.
Evaluate the problem's severity and privacy sensitivity: the source rates female 60+ bladder incontinence as a strong problem because sufferers strongly want to stop it.
Choose an angle against the problem type, not just the product: for tinnitus, the source argues a supplement could beat an existing pillow offer by going after the underlying irritation.
caveats: Works specifically because older audiences dominate these sites — it is a demographic-targeting tactic, not a general trend feed.
Traffic-estimate tools may show nothing for new or low-traffic stores; absence of data is not absence of demand but also not validation.
Many widgets show low-quality or repeated offers; expect to filter heavily.
cards.source_name: Transcript of the product research method that made me $670k.docx

cards.title: Cross-Validate With the Free Facebook Ad Library
cards.summary: Use Ad Library image filtering and run-time checks as a free substitute for a paid ad spy tool before committing.
cards.use_when: Validating a shortlisted product and checking whether competitors are already running native-style image ads.
steps: Set the Ad Library country filter to the target market (the source uses USA) and search the product keyword, e.g. 'sleep patch'.
Switch the media filter to Images to surface native-style static ads rather than video.
Confirm the ads have been active for more than about one week; that run time is the source's signal that the offer is converting.

Read the pattern, not one ad: for the child sleep patch example the source found image ads running but judged that almost nobody was actually running native for it, concluding it was an open opportunity.
Treat Ad Library as the free equivalent of Get Hooked — useful when you do not pay for an ad spy subscription, but it requires manual keyword hunting (e.g., 'health', 'pain').
caveats: Ad Library does not expose the performance or engagement metrics a paid spy tool provides; run time is a proxy, not proof.
One week of activity is the presenter's heuristic.
Searching vague keywords produces a lot of irrelevant results and takes longer than filtered spy tools.
cards.source_name: Transcript of the product research method that made me $670k.docx

cards.title: Mine the Longest-Running Ad for the Winning Angle
cards.summary: Extract the marketing avatar and message from a validated product's longest-running creative and reuse that angle.
cards.use_when: You have a validated product with a history of running ads and need a starting creative angle before building your own.
steps: Open the advertiser's full Facebook page profile for the validated product.
Sort or locate the longest-running ads on that page — persistence is treated as the strongest available evidence of what converts.
Identify the specific avatar being spoken to (e.g., a mother worn down by a four-year-old's bedtime battles) and the exact message framing used in that ad.
Duplicate that avatar and angle when building your own native ad for the same problem.
Use a better-executed version of the same angle rather than inventing a new one, and go deeper on research than the competition when entering a contested problem like neuropathy.
caveats: This is angle mining, not permission to copy creative assets; the source describes replicating the angle and avatar, not the production.
Longest-running ads may still be unprofitable — run time only proves continued spend, not positive ROAS.
In saturated categories (the source names neuropathy), the same angle alone may not be enough; deeper copy research is his stated edge.
cards.source_name: Transcript of the product research method that made me $670k.docx

cards.title: Prioritize Facebook Over TikTok/Instagram Burner Scouting
cards.summary: Deprioritize TikTok and Instagram burner-account scouting in favor of Facebook-based and tool-based research.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to spend product-research hours, particularly as a beginner without a trained dropshipping eye.
steps: Treat TikTok and Instagram burner-account scrolling as outdated and ineffective for finding winners, per the source.

Recognize that burner methods work only with a trained 'dropshipping eye', which the source says takes 3–6 months to develop, and that Instagram burners largely repost content from TikTok or AliExpress.
If you still want a burner method, use a Facebook burner account: the source says it surfaces the older demographic and is a decent research surface.
Replace burner scrolling with the three 2026 methods: native scouting, a paid ad spy tool (Get Hooked), and the free Ad Library.
Avoid ripping a product from a crowded sourcing feed: the source argues you learn no skill, cannot replicate the win, and face high CPMs/CPCs because 'thousands' of people work the same feed daily.
caveats: This is the presenter's opinion and is tied to his stated 2026 timeframe; platform behavior changes.
The criticism applies to learning quality and saturation, not to whether winning products exist on those platforms at all.
A trained eye is presented as a prerequisite for burner methods, so beginners are the group most disadvantaged by them.
cards.source_name: Transcript of the product research method that made me $670k.docx

cards.title: Market-First Product Research Hierarchy
cards.summary: Choose a passionate market and an emotional problem before picking a product, because market and problem drive sales more than the product itself.
cards.use_when: Starting a new ecommerce product search, or when a previous product test failed and you're tempted to jump straight to product hunting.
steps: Start with market research, not product research. The presenter argues the market influences success far beyond the product, using the analogy of selling umbrellas in a thunderstorm versus on a sunny day: same product, very different sales volume.

Pick from markets known for passion and emotion: pets, weight loss, hair growth, cosmetics/skincare (anything with a clear before-and-after transformation), supplements, beauty, health and wellness. The presenter says these markets are broad enough that the market itself won't be the reason for failure.
Narrow to an emotional problem inside that market before choosing the physical product. Examples given: lower back stiffness, neck and shoulder tension, plantar fasciitis, migraines.

Keep the problem broad enough to support many products. One winning problem (e.g. migraines) can be solved by supplements, a head band, a massage gun, a neck traction device, or a clinic visit — so you have many product options and room to test.
Only then select the actual product that solves the chosen problem.
Don't overthink market selection — pick one and move on. The presenter explicitly frames this as the easiest, most spoonfed part of the process.
caveats: 'Market first' is the presenter's opinion and framework, not a proven law; it does not remove the need for validation and a solid funnel.
The listed markets are his examples, not a guaranteed set — supplements in particular he calls challenging despite long-term potential.
cards.source_name: _asked claude to find me a $1k_day product (it worked).docx

cards.title: Use Claude to Generate Winning Emotional Sub-Niches
cards.summary: Prompt Claude (Opus or Sonnet) to produce a list of emotional sub-niches downstream from your chosen market, then pick five to research further.
cards.use_when: You have picked a market and want a fast list of specific emotional problems to build products and offers around.
steps: Open Claude directly — the presenter used Opus (he says Sonnet would likely be fine) and states no other tool (e.g. Fable) is needed for this step.
Paste a large structured prompt asking for a list of emotional sub-niches for a DTC beginner brand in your chosen market. The output shown in the video was a list of 30 sub-niches.

Review the list for problems with demonstrated commercial history — his examples: lower back stiffness, neck and shoulder tension, plantar fasciitis. He claims each of these has multiple seven- and eight-figure businesses inside it.
Select five sub-niches you like most. These five become the search scope you feed into the next step (ad-spy tool via MCP).
Treat the AI output as candidate problems, not validated winners — the validation step with real competitor traffic data comes later.
caveats: The exact models, prompt text and list quality decay quickly; verify what the current Claude interface and models actually produce.
The presenter's claim that each sub-niche contains multiple seven/eight-figure businesses is his assertion, not measured evidence.
cards.source_name: _asked claude to find me a $1k_day product (it worked).docx

cards.title: Connect Get Hooked to Claude via MCP for Ad-Library Sourcing
cards.summary: Wire the Get Hooked ad-aggregator MCP server into Claude as a custom connector so the AI can pull live competitor brand and ad data.
cards.use_when: You want Claude to research real competitor brands, active ads, angles and funnels instead of relying on its training data alone.
steps: Create an account (the presenter used a free trial) at get hooked.ai.
In Get Hooked, open your account menu (bottom-left), then select 'AI and MCP'.
Scroll past the API section to the 'Connect to AI agent' / MCP section.
Copy the MCP server URL and the OAuth Client ID shown there.
In Claude, go to the left-hand sidebar, select 'Customize', then 'Connectors', then the plus icon, then 'Add custom connector'.
Name it (e.g. 'Get Hooked'), paste the MCP server URL, then paste the OAuth Client ID into the corresponding field, and click Add.
You now effectively have Claude plus a large Facebook/Meta ad library in one interface. Verify the current menu labels and flow, since MCP connectors and UIs change quickly.
caveats: Exact UI paths and field names are high-decay — confirm them in both tools before relying on this sequence.
Get Hooked is described as a free trial; pricing and access may change.
cards.source_name: _asked claude to find me a $1k_day product (it worked).docx

cards.title: Run the MCP Product-Sourcing Prompt Over Your Five Sub-Niches
cards.summary: Feed the MCP-connected Claude a prompt with MCP usage instructions plus your five chosen sub-niches to return qualifying brands, pain points, ad patterns and funnels.
cards.use_when: Claude is connected to the Get Hooked MCP and you have narrowed to five emotional sub-niches.
steps: Write one prompt that includes (a) information about the MCP and how to use it, (b) the research process Claude should follow, and (c) the five sub-niches you selected earlier.
Submit and let it run — the presenter says this takes a few minutes.

Read the output: qualifying brands that are running enough active ads and fit your input sub-niches. For each, the output shown included the product, the pain point, the ad pattern typically used, the funnel architecture (e.g. driving to a PDP vs. an advertorial), and a top-performing ad.
Use the funnel-architecture field as competitive intelligence, not just the product name — it tells you where competitors send traffic.
The presenter's example find: a Facebook page 'Fall Prevention Tips' running 232 active ads across a few subdomains, selling wide toe box barefoot shoes with a foot-pain angle.
The presenter claims this makes product selection achievable in about an hour with the right tools.
caveats: The hour-long claim is the presenter's experience, not a benchmark.
Qualifying criteria come from active ad volume, which can reflect budget or testing rather than proven profitability — validate separately.
The exact prompt contents are not fully reproduced in the source; reconstruct to fit your own sub-niches.
cards.source_name: _asked claude to find me a $1k_day product (it worked).docx

cards.title: Estimate Competitor Revenue with the SimilarWeb Formula
cards.summary: Reverse-engineer a competitor's monthly revenue floor as monthly visits × estimated conversion rate × estimated AOV, and require roughly $200k–$300k+/month before treating them as proof of a winning product.
cards.use_when: Validating whether brands surfaced by your ad-spy research are actually selling at scale.
steps: Install the SimilarWeb extension and open the competitor's store page with it enabled to read estimated monthly visits. The presenter notes about three free searches per day.
Estimate a conversion rate. He uses a baseline of 2% and typically ranges 1.5%–3.5%; he says the more expensive the product, the lower the rate tends to be (e.g. ~1.5% for high-ticket).
Estimate an AOV conservatively, using the visible offer stack as a guide. In his example the store sold shoes at $70/pair and he estimated AOV around $90, using $90 as a conservative figure.
Multiply: monthly visits × conversion rate = monthly orders; then × estimated AOV = estimated monthly revenue.
Example from the video: 1.5 million visits (conservative, actual ~2M) × 2% = ~30,000 orders; × $90 AOV = ~$2.7M/month.
Set a floor: the presenter says he only wants to see candidates above roughly $200k–$300k/month in estimated revenue.
caveats: These are rough estimates, not financials — the presenter states plainly he cannot calculate exact revenue.
Both conversion rate and AOV are assumptions; conservative inputs make the floor more trustworthy than an optimistic guess.
SimilarWeb visit figures are estimates and free-tier search limits apply.
cards.source_name: _asked claude to find me a $1k_day product (it worked).docx

cards.title: The Two Golden Margin Rules: 3x COGS and $30 Gross Margin
cards.summary: Require at least 3x cost of goods sold at retail price and at least $30 of gross margin per unit so the product can absorb rising Meta ad costs.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a sourced product can support paid acquisition before committing to a test.
steps: Rule one: price at minimum 3x your landed cost of goods sold (sourced plus shipped). If it costs $15 landed, sell at $45 or more.
Rule two: keep at least $30 of gross profit per unit. The presenter says he used to use $20 and raised it because Facebook ad costs keep increasing.
Check both rules at once. Example: source for $15, sell for $50 gives a $35 gross margin — this satisfies both the 3x multiplier and the $30 floor.
Account for the fact that established competitors have negotiated better supplier rates than a new dropshipping brand, so do not assume you can match their cost base.
caveats: These are the presenter's rules of thumb for a specific ad-cost environment, not universal economics.
3x COGS with a $30 floor can conflict at low price points — a $12 product gives 3.6x but only ~$36 margin, while a $10 product at 3x yields only $20 margin and fails rule two.
Margins must also cover shipping, payment fees and refunds; the rules as stated only address ad costs.
cards.source_name: _asked claude to find me a $1k_day product (it worked).docx

cards.title: Diagnose a Failed Product Test: Ads Problem or Funnel Problem
cards.summary: After a failed test, ask 'why' and split the cause into ad-related issues (CPC/CTR/CPM) or funnel-related issues (ATC, checkout completion, AOV) before abandoning the product.
cards.use_when: A product test underperforms and you're deciding whether to kill the product, fix creatives, or fix the funnel.
steps: Run the full process — market, problem, product selection, validation, then a sales game plan — before concluding the method failed. The presenter stresses that people often test with no plan and quit at the first unprofitable day.
Recognize that the product is rarely the issue. The presenter says top six-, seven- and eight-figure brands sell nothing especially remarkable; they have ads and funnel dialed in.
Ask which bucket the failure falls into: ad-related (creatives not good enough) or funnel-related (store, advertorial or checkout not good enough).
If concrete funnel KPI checks surface a checkout or payment-processing problem, fix that before touching the product.
The presenter claims roughly 90% of the failures he sees are ad-related, usually because sellers believe their ads are good when they aren't.
caveats: The 90% figure is the presenter's observation, not a measured statistic.
This is in scope as test-triage, but optimizing the ads themselves belongs to creative and media-buying work, and fixing the checkout belongs to storefront work.
cards.source_name: _asked claude to find me a $1k_day product (it worked).docx

cards.title: Ad Failure KPIs: CPC, CTR and CPM Thresholds
cards.summary: Use link CPC above $1.50, CTR below 3%, and CPM above $80 as indicators that a failed test is an advertising problem, usually a creative problem.
cards.use_when: A US product test is unprofitable and you need to determine whether the ads, not the offer or product, are the constraint.
steps: Read link CPC first: target roughly $1.50 for US targeting. If it's elevated — $2, $3, $4 — treat it as a check-engine light: it signals something is wrong but not what.
Check CTR next: aim for a 3% minimum, and the presenter prefers closer to 4%. A sub-3% CTR means a serious creative problem — weak hooks or copy.
If CTR is healthy (4–5%) but CPC is still elevated, look at CPM. He offers no strict CPM KPI and calls it niche- and location-dependent, but says above roughly $80 CPM in the US is on the high end.
Note the feedback loop: poor creatives both lower CTR and raise CPM because the platform penalizes low-engagement ads, producing a high CPC.
Resist maxing CTR for vanity. High-CTR curiosity/native creatives that don't convert mean you forgot to sell — balance engagement with conversion intent.
caveats: Thresholds are US-specific and will decay as ad costs change; treat them as directional.
The presenter explicitly says CPM targets are relative and have no fixed KPI — the $80 line is his rough guide, not a rule.
cards.source_name: _asked claude to find me a $1k_day product (it worked).docx

cards.title: Funnel Failure KPIs: ATC Ratio, Checkout Completion and AOV
cards.summary: Use landing-page-to-add-to-cart below 10%, ATC-to-purchase below 30%, and AOV under a 20–40% markup over base price as indicators that the failed test is a funnel problem.
cards.use_when: Ad metrics look acceptable but the product still isn't converting, or you need to locate friction between click and purchase.
steps: Add-to-cart ratio: of everyone who lands on the first page (advertorial, pre-sell page, or PDP), at least 10% should add to cart. This is somewhat price-dependent — for more expensive products 8–9% can be acceptable. Below that, the funnel or the traffic quality is failing.

ATC-to-purchase ratio: aim for 30% completion, so 3 of every 10 add-to-carts purchase. Below 30% points to friction between cart and purchase — check payment-processor approval rates and simplify the checkout. The presenter favors removing steps over adding conversion bumpers.

AOV: on a straight Shopify setup, target AOV 20–40% above the base selling price (he suggests pushing even 50% above for a one-product store). A low AOV usually means missing upsells or downsells on the first purchase.
LTV: for subscription or retention-heavy models, LTV should be substantially higher than AOV. A low LTV means you acquire customers reasonably well but don't earn enough from them over time.
caveats: These are the presenter's working benchmarks, not validated universal thresholds; they vary with price point and model.
ATC and checkout figures can be distorted by bot traffic or by traffic quality from the ad itself, so read the ad and funnel metrics together.
cards.source_name: _asked claude to find me a $1k_day product (it worked).docx

cards.title: Keep AI Sourcing and Ad Execution in Separate Ownership
cards.summary: AI-assisted sourcing ends at a validated, margin-checked product; creative, media buying and storefront work are separate disciplines that determine whether the product actually succeeds.
cards.use_when: Scoping a product-research sprint, or setting expectations that finding the product is only one part of a profitable launch.
steps: Delimit the sourcing workflow to: market selection, emotional problem identification, product selection via AI plus ad-spy data, competitor revenue validation, margin checks, and a basic test-triage game plan.
Route creative writing and ad design to your creative process — the sourcing workflow does not produce winning ads.
Route bid management and CPC/CPM optimization to paid-media execution.
Route checkout-flow and landing-page layout changes to storefront work.
Treat the KPI thresholds in this method as validation and triage signals for a product test, not as a substitute for media-buying or funnel-building skills.
Use this split when briefing a team or reviewing a failed test, so you don't replace a creative or checkout fix with another product search.
caveats: The source maps these boundaries as a module taxonomy; it does not argue paid media or creative are unimportant — the reverse.
cards.source_name: _asked claude to find me a $1k_day product (it worked).docx

cards.title: A job is progress in a circumstance, not a customer type
cards.summary: Define jobs as the functional, social and emotional progress someone seeks in a specific circumstance, rather than as demographic segments.
cards.use_when: Starting any avatar or customer-research effort and deciding what unit of analysis to research and record.
steps: State the job as progress-in-a-circumstance: 'when [situation], I want to [progress], so I can [outcome]'.
Include all three dimensions: what the person is trying to accomplish functionally, how they want to be seen (social), and how they want to feel (emotional).
Reject substitutes that are demographics-only: age, gender, income or a stock-photo persona with no causal mechanism does not define who buys or why.
Treat the circumstance as the driver of the decision; the same person can hire different solutions in different situations.
Test the definition by asking whether it explains why a real customer chose this and not an alternative in that moment.
caveats: Demographics can still be used for media buying or reach planning, but they do not explain the choice and should not be the avatar's core.
A job statement without a circumstance usually collapses back into a generic persona.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Mine five sources for undiscovered jobs
cards.summary: Find jobs by looking in personal life, nonconsumption, workarounds, negative jobs and unusual uses rather than asking customers for feature ideas.
cards.use_when: When you need new job candidates rather than validation of existing assumptions or feature wishlists.
steps: Personal life: look outside the product category at routines and struggles in everyday life that your product could serve.
Nonconsumption: study people who currently buy nothing in the category and find out what they do instead.
Workarounds and compensating behaviors: watch for duct-tape solutions, spreadsheets, manual steps and homemade fixes that reveal an unmet job.
Negative jobs: identify tasks people hate doing or dread and would gladly hand off.
Unusual uses: examine off-label and edge-case uses of the product; they often expose a job the product was not designed for.
For each candidate, record quoted evidence from the person and the trigger circumstance, not just the inferred need.
caveats: Feature-request surveys and focus groups asking what to add produce wishlists, not jobs; they miss the context that causes purchase.
Off-label use signals a possible job, but confirm it recurs before treating it as a segment.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Prioritize passive struggle data over active operational data
cards.summary: Favor observations of customer struggle over sales and customer-attribute reports, which are easier to collect but describe outcomes rather than causes.
cards.use_when: When choosing what evidence to gather and when a data-driven team wants to substitute reports for direct research.
steps: Recognize the fallacy of active data: sales figures, CRM fields and customer characteristics are readily available and tend to crowd out the harder-to-get data about why people acted.
Treat sales and attribute data as outcome evidence: useful for sizing and segmentation, but not for explaining the causal mechanism of choice.
Collect passive data of struggle: what the customer tried, what frustrated them, what they rigged up, and what finally triggered the switch.
Record the struggle in the customer's own words so the avatar rests on quoted evidence.
Use quantitative data afterward to check whether the discovered job is common enough to matter.
caveats: This is not a rejection of analytics; it is a warning about using convenient operational data to answer causal questions.
Small qualitative samples can reveal a job but cannot establish its prevalence without follow-up measurement.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Map the forces: push and pull versus habits and anxieties
cards.summary: A purchase happens when the push of the struggle and the pull of the new solution outweigh the habits of the present and the anxiety of the new.
cards.use_when: When diagnosing why prospects stall or abandon, or when building objection-handling into an avatar record.
steps: Identify the push: the frustration or triggering event that makes the current situation untenable.
Identify the pull: the attractiveness of the new solution and the progress it promises.
Identify the habits of the present: routines, sunk costs and defaults that keep the customer using the old approach.
Identify the anxieties of the new: fear of the unknown, risk of looking foolish, switching cost, data-migration worry, uncertainty that it will work.
Judge relative magnitude: if pull is weak or anxiety and habit are strong, the purchase does not happen even when the customer wants the outcome.
Record opposing forces as objections to address later in page or offer design; the avatar's job is to name them, not resolve them here.
caveats: Addressing objections on the page belongs to landing-page and offer work; this section only discovers and documents them.
Strong anxiety is not the same as low desire; a customer can want the progress and still not switch.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Interview by reconstructing the purchase timeline
cards.summary: Interview technique that traces the chain of triggers and events leading to a decision instead of asking about product attributes or satisfaction.
cards.use_when: Running customer interviews to uncover the job and the trigger moment behind a purchase.
steps: Ask the customer to tell the story of how they came to buy, starting before they knew your product existed.
Track the timeline: the first thought something had to change, the events in between, and the moment of decision.
Probe for the trigger event: what specifically happened that made the status quo unacceptable that week or that day.
Ask what they tried before, what they almost bought, and what they turned down, to surface competing solutions.
Avoid attribute questions such as 'which feature did you like' or hypotheticals such as 'would you buy this'; they generate rationalizations rather than stories.
Capture verbatim quotes at each stage so the avatar record carries evidence rather than summary.
caveats: Retrospective accounts are imperfect; ask for concrete events and sequences to reduce post-hoc rationalization.
Do not lead the customer toward the answer you want; let the timeline reveal the cause.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Distinguish the Big Hire from the Little Hire
cards.summary: Separate the purchase decision from the actual use and repeat-use decision, because a good job on the buying side does not guarantee retention.
cards.use_when: When diagnosing whether problems sit in acquisition or in onboarding, activation and repeat usage.
steps: Define the Big Hire as the moment of purchase or signup: what triggered it, what was compared, what anxiety was overcome.
Define the Little Hire as each subsequent decision to actually use and keep using the product.
Interview separately for each: the Big Hire timeline often differs from the Little Hire experience.
Look for mismatch: a customer may buy enthusiastically and then never activate, signalling the job promised at purchase was not the job they experienced.
Record both in the avatar: the buying job and the using job, with their distinct triggers and obstacles.
caveats: Confusing the two produces avatars that explain acquisition but not retention, or vice versa.
A strong Big Hire can mask a broken Little Hire for months before churn shows up.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Build the job spec: tradeoffs, competition and obstacles
cards.summary: A job spec is the résumé of experiences a solution must deliver, defining which tradeoffs the customer accepts, what alternatives must be beaten, and what obstacles must be removed.
cards.use_when: After a job is identified, when translating it into requirements for product, offer or messaging.
steps: List the tradeoffs the customer is willing to make, and those they are not; these bound acceptable solutions.
Identify the competing solutions that must be beaten in the customer's mind, including doing nothing, workarounds and adjacent products.
List the obstacles that must be removed before the customer can make progress, both practical and emotional.
Express the spec as the sequence of experiences the customer expects, in the order they encounter them.
Use the spec as the yardstick for product, offer and message decisions rather than adding features by request.
caveats: A spec describes experiences, not a feature list; converting it into features is product work that follows.
The spec changes when the circumstance changes, so re-check it against new interview evidence.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Storyboard the customer's struggle
cards.summary: Visualize the sequence of a customer's struggle and choices to expose where the current situation breaks down and where your solution enters.
cards.use_when: Synthesizing interview material into a shared internal view of the job before writing avatar records or messaging.
steps: Lay out the timeline as scenes: first thought of change, search, consideration, purchase, first use, repeat use.
At each scene, note what the customer did, felt, said and worried about.
Mark the trigger moment where the status quo became unacceptable.
Mark the points of anxiety and the moments of habit that nearly stopped the decision.
Mark where competing solutions, including doing nothing, appeared.
Use the storyboard to check that your avatar record, offer and messaging address the actual sequence rather than an assumed funnel.
caveats: The storyboard is a synthesis artifact, not a substitute for raw quotes and evidence.
Resist smoothing the story into a tidy funnel; the messy path is where the insight lives.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Give every avatar quoted evidence
cards.summary: A non-negotiable baseline for avatar records: direct quotes from research that support the job, the trigger and the objections.
cards.use_when: Writing or reviewing avatar records, especially when tempted to summarize without evidence.
steps: Attach at least one verbatim quote to each key claim: the job, the circumstance, the trigger and the opposing forces.
Keep quotes specific and contextual; a quote about a feeling or a workaround is more useful than a quote about liking the brand.
Note the source of each quote, such as an interview or an observation, so the record can be traced.
