Remove or flag claims with no supporting quote rather than smoothing them into confident prose.
Use the quotes in downstream messaging as raw language the market actually uses.
caveats: Quotes can be edited for clarity but not for meaning; preserving the customer's phrasing is much of the value.
A single quote illustrates a job; it does not prove prevalence.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Inventory candidates before fixing the number of avatars
cards.summary: Research should produce a discovered set of jobs from interviews and observations rather than a predetermined count of personas.
cards.use_when: Planning avatar research and deciding how many distinct avatars to maintain.
steps: Collect job candidates from the five mining sources: personal life, nonconsumption, workarounds, negative jobs and unusual uses.
Cluster candidates by the circumstance and progress sought, not by demographics.
Merge clusters that differ only superficially; keep clusters that involve genuinely different tradeoffs, triggers or obstacles.
Keep the volume of avatars in a sensible operating range so the library stays usable rather than becoming a folder of near-duplicates.
Revisit the set as new interview evidence arrives; avatars can be added, split or retired.
caveats: No fixed number of avatars is universal; the right count depends on how many distinct jobs exist in your market.
Each retained avatar should carry the same evidence standard, so the set stays comparable.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Use negative jobs as an opportunity lens
cards.summary: Tasks people dread doing are strong job candidates because removing an unpleasant obligation is a clear progress worth paying for.
cards.use_when: When hunting for new offers or messaging angles, especially in categories where customers complain about the process rather than the product.
steps: Ask what part of the process customers visibly procrastinate over, complain about or delegate whenever possible.
Distinguish dread from mere inconvenience: a negative job involves reluctance and avoidance, not just time cost.
Find the workaround people use to avoid the task, such as paying someone else, batching it, or ignoring it entirely.
Test whether removing that task is the real promise: 'you never have to do X' may beat feature comparisons.
Record the negative job with a quote describing the dread in the customer's own words.
caveats: Negative jobs still require a trigger to activate the purchase; discomfort alone does not cause switching.
Removing a task can reduce perceived value for some buyers who take pride in doing it themselves.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Diagnose a stalled decision with the competing-solutions list
cards.summary: Identify every alternative the customer weighed, including doing nothing and DIY fixes, to find which one actually wins and why.
cards.use_when: When conversion is weak or customers describe long deliberation before buying.
steps: Ask the customer what they almost bought or did instead, and what made them hesitate.
Include non-obvious competitors: doing nothing, a spreadsheet, an intern, an agency, a template, a friend's advice, or a different category entirely.
For each alternative, record the advantage the customer saw in it, such as price, familiarity or lower risk.
Identify the specific advantage your solution must have to beat the winning alternative.
Feed the resulting comparison into the avatar record as evidence of the real competitive set.
caveats: The customer's mental competitive set often differs from the industry's own competitive map.
Doing nothing is frequently the strongest competitor and is easy to overlook.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Capture trigger moments as discrete, datable events
cards.summary: A trigger is a specific event that made the status quo unacceptable, and pinpointing it beats recording vague motivations.
cards.use_when: When your avatar or messaging lacks urgency and prospects agree with the message but never act.
steps: Ask what changed in the week or month before the purchase: a move, a hire, a failed task, a deadline, an incident.
Write the trigger as a concrete event with a rough date rather than a general condition such as 'wanted to grow'.
Check how much time elapsed between trigger and purchase; a long gap suggests unresolved anxiety or habit.
Use the trigger to time messaging and offers rather than presenting always-on urgency that means nothing.
Record the trigger in the avatar as part of the job statement's circumstance.
caveats: Some categories have recurring triggers rather than one dramatic event; record the pattern, not a fabricated story.
Correlation between an event and purchase in one interview does not establish it as the general trigger.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Treat habits of the present as the silent competitor
cards.summary: The customer's existing routine and defaults block change even when the new solution is clearly better, so map the habit before assuming desire is enough.
cards.use_when: When prospects acknowledge the problem and the solution yet fail to switch.
steps: Identify what the customer currently does and what makes it easy, such as existing workflow, learned skill or a sunk-cost tool.
Ask what would have to change in their routine for adoption, and who else would be affected.
Look for frictionless switch mechanisms: import tools, migration help, templates, guided onboarding, a service that does the setup.
Estimate the strength of the habit against the strength of the push; if habit is strong, reduce friction rather than amplify messaging.
Record the habit in the avatar as an obstacle to be removed, not an objection to be argued away.
caveats: More persuasive claims do not overcome a strong habit; friction removal usually matters more.
Some habits represent genuine preference and should be respected rather than attacked.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Study nonconsumption to find latent demand
cards.summary: People who buy nothing in the category are a rich source of jobs because their current coping mechanisms reveal unmet progress.
cards.use_when: When the existing market is crowded and growth requires serving buyers the category has never reached.
steps: Define nonconsumers as people with the struggle who currently purchase no solution, including those who have never bought in the category.
Interview them about how they cope: manual methods, avoidance, borrowing from friends, or living with the problem.
Identify why the category is invisible or unacceptable to them: price, complexity, distrust, or identity.
Find the progress they want that no current product frames itself around.
Record the nonconsumption job separately from existing-customer jobs, since triggers and objections differ.
caveats: Nonconsumers may be hard to recruit through normal customer channels; use referrals and community contexts.
Serving nonconsumers often requires rethinking the offer and the entry point, not just the message.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Use unusual uses as a research probe, not an instant segment
cards.summary: Off-label and edge-case uses point to jobs the product was not designed for; validate the recurring pattern before acting on it.
cards.use_when: When reviewing support tickets, reviews or usage data and finding customers using the product in unexpected ways.
steps: Scan reviews, support conversations and community posts for uses outside the intended purpose.
Ask those customers what they were trying to accomplish and what triggered the need for the workaround use.
Check how many other customers show the same pattern before promoting it to a job or avatar.
Assess whether serving the pattern requires product change or only clearer framing and positioning.
If the pattern recurs, record it as a job with quotes and triggers like any other avatar.
caveats: One creative customer is an anecdote, not a market; recurrence is the test.
Pursuing every unusual use fragments focus and can dilute the core job.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Avoid persona theater: no demographic avatars without a job
cards.summary: Avatars built from demographic fields or fictional characters with stock photos do not explain behavior and should not be produced.
cards.use_when: When reviewing existing persona documents or when a stakeholder asks for an age-and-income-based avatar template.
steps: Check whether the avatar defines a circumstance and progress sought; if it only lists age, gender and income, it is not usable for decision-making.
Replace demographic descriptors with the job statement and the quotes supporting it.
If demographics are retained for media targeting, keep them in a separate layer, clearly marked as reach criteria rather than motivation.
Test the avatar by asking whether it predicts what a customer will do next and what they will object to.
Retire avatar documents that cannot answer those questions.
caveats: Demographic data still has legitimate uses in media buying, audience sizing and compliance; the objection is to using it as the causal explanation.
Fictional characters can be useful for communication and empathy, but only when built on real evidence rather than invented.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Ask what the customer fired, not only what they hired
cards.summary: The job includes what the customer stopped using, and knowing what got dismissed shows the tradeoffs and loyalties at stake.
cards.use_when: When mapping the competitive set and understanding what switching away from a solution really costs the customer.
steps: Ask what they were using before and what finally made them abandon it.
Probe for emotional and social cost of switching, such as embarrassment about the old choice or reluctance to let a relationship go.
Note whether the fired solution was a product, a person, a service or a habit.
Identify what would make the customer fire your product next; that is your retention risk.
Record both the hire and the fire in the avatar so downstream offers reflect the real tradeoff.
caveats: Customers may underreport what they fire out of politeness or loyalty; cross-check with the timeline.
In B2B contexts, firing a solution can involve relationships and politics beyond the product.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Jobs Theory: Innovation Built on Causality, Not Correlation
cards.summary: Christensen's core argument that customers 'hire' products to make progress in a specific circumstance, and that this causal job — not demographics or product attributes — predicts innovation success.
cards.use_when: Framing an innovation or product strategy, or when your team's data is descriptive (who buys, what they look like) but cannot predict which new offer will succeed.
steps: Reframe the innovation question from 'how do we make our product better, more profitable, or more differentiated?' to 'what job did the customer hire this product to do?' (Christensen's central question).
Treat buying as hiring and quitting as firing: when a product does the job, it gets re-hired in the same circumstance; when it does the job badly, the customer fires it and looks for a replacement.

Accept that customer attributes (age, ZIP code, income, shoe size — Christensen's own example is that his height, age and shoe size never caused him to buy the New York Times) are not causal. Correlations can help describe a market but cannot reveal why a purchase happened.

Look for the circumstance, not the customer: a job arises from a situation ('long boring commute', 'want to say yes to my kid once this week'), and the same person can hire the same product for entirely different jobs at different times of day.

Use the job to redefine the competitive set. If margarine is hired to moisten bread so it's easier to chew, its competitors may be cream cheese, olive oil and mayonnaise; if hired to keep food from burning in a pan, competitors are Teflon and cooking spray in a different aisle.
Recognize that a market defined by internal category language ('yellow fats', 'spreads') is not how customers shop — they arrive with a specific job.
Expect the payoff to be predictability, not just post-hoc storytelling: the value of the theory is in predicting new successes, not celebrating past ones.
caveats: Jobs Theory tells you why customers make choices and what to build; it does not tell you whether a job is ethical to serve (Christensen notes cigarettes can be hired to satisfy jobs but harm the customer — ethical judgment is separate).
A job is a highly specific construct, not a catchphrase for something a customer wants or needs; the loose use of 'jobs' as a buzzword defeats the purpose.
Christensen claims the odds of creating exactly the right product even when a firm intends to disrupt are probably less than 25% 'if that' — presented as his estimate, not a measured benchmark.
Identifying the job is only the beginning; you still need to design the accompanying experiences and integrate internal capabilities, or the insight does not convert to advantage.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: The Milk Shake Study: Circumstance Interviews Beat Attribute Surveys
cards.summary: How a fast-food chain discovered two different jobs for the same milk shake by observing buyers and probing what else they hired instead, and why asking customers to improve the product produced zero sales change.
cards.use_when: Designing customer research for a product with flat or declining sales, or when survey feedback ('cheaper, chunkier, chewier') is producing changes that don't move the number.
steps: Run the conventional effort first if you must, to see its limits: the chain surveyed target-profile customers with 'How can we improve our milk shakes so you'd buy more? Do you want it cheaper? Chunkier? Chewier? Chocolatier?' and acted on the answers. Within months, sales of the category were unchanged.

Then observe instead of asking. The team stood in a restaurant for eighteen hours watching: what time people bought, what they wore, whether they were alone, whether they bought other food, and whether they stayed or drove off.
Note the pattern that emerged: a surprising share of shakes sold before 9 a.m. to solo customers who bought nothing else and left with it in the car.

Interview those buyers about the job, opening with an admission that you are puzzled ('What job were you trying to do that caused you to come here and hire that milk shake?'). Customers often cannot answer directly, so probe on what else they sometimes hired instead.

Collect the substitute set and each substitute's failure mode: bananas 'gone too quickly', doughnuts too crumbly and sticky on fingers and steering wheel, bagels dry and requiring two hands to spread, a Snickers bar that created guilt about candy for breakfast.

Identify the winning job statement in the customer's own terms: help me stay awake and occupied and make the morning commute more fun, while heading off mid-morning hunger. The thick shake through a thin straw took ~20 minutes and fit the cup holder.

Serve each job with its own design: for the commute job, a thicker shake (fruit or chocolate bits as surprise, for interest, not health) plus faster self-serve dispensing at the front counter with a swipe card; for the afternoon parent job, half sizes that finish quickly and reduce dad's guilt.
Note that the same product was competing against different things in each job — morning against bagels, bars and juice; afternoon against stopping at the toy store or a later game of catch.
Do not average the two jobs into one product. Christensen's explicit warning: averaging dad and commuter responses yields a one-size-fits-none shake that does neither job well.
caveats: This is a case study of one chain's discovery, not a promised sales outcome.
Demographics did not separate the morning buyers — what they shared was a job, not a profile.
The afternoon job is inferred from Christensen's own experience as a father in line; it illustrates the reasoning rather than reporting measured sales.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Jobs Interviews: Track the Timeline of Triggers, Not Product Attributes
cards.summary: The interview method for surfacing a job: reconstruct the causal timeline of what happened before a purchase and avoid questions about the product's features.
cards.use_when: Building avatars, running win/loss or purchase interviews, or briefing an agency or researcher before qualitative fieldwork.
steps: Reconstruct the timeline of events and thoughts that led to the decision, in order, rather than asking for opinions about the product.
Do not focus on product attributes; the goal is the causal story of the choice, not feature preferences.
If the customer struggles to answer directly, ask what else they considered or sometimes hired instead of this product — substitutes expose the real competition and the real job.

Capture the language in the customer's own words, since the job statement should reflect their framing ('I'm full all morning', 'it fits right here in my cup holder') rather than the company's category vocabulary.
Treat the interview output as evidence: each avatar should carry quoted evidence plus the trigger moment and a job statement.
caveats: Attribute-focused interviews and direct feature requests are the failure mode this method is designed to replace — they tell you what people say they want, not why they chose.
A trigger moment and a job statement are presented as the minimum baseline for any avatar; how many avatars you end up with is not fixed by the method.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Push, Pull, Anxiety and Habit: The Forces Behind a Purchase Decision
cards.summary: A decision to change happens when the push of frustration plus the pull of the new solution outweighs the anxiety about the new and the habit of the present — useful as the diagnostic frame for avatar research.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why prospects stall mid-funnel, or structuring interview notes and avatar definitions around what actually triggered and blocked a switch.
steps: Map the push: the magnitude of the frustration in the current situation that makes the customer want to change at all.
Map the pull: the attraction of the new solution relative to the alternatives available for the same job.
Map the anxiety: the fears and uncertainties about adopting the new solution.
Map the habit: the inertia of the present behaviour that must be overcome for the switch to happen.
Treat the job spec as the output of this analysis: the tradeoffs the customer is willing to make, the competing solutions that must be beaten, and the obstacles that must be removed.
Use the balance to explain timing — a job sitting under strong habit and anxiety will not convert, however good the pull.
caveats: The four forces are a diagnostic frame for the decision, not a scoring model with published weights.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: What to Skip: Demographic Personas and Feature-Wish Surveys
cards.summary: Christensen's explicit list of research artefacts the jobs method rejects, and what to do instead.
cards.use_when: Auditing an existing avatar or persona deck, or approving a research brief, to check it is built on causal evidence rather than demographics.
steps: Skip persona templates that carry demographic fields and no job — anything that produces a fictional character with a stock photo.
Skip segmentation based on age, gender or income when it does not define the underlying causal mechanism.
Skip focus group data or surveys that simply ask customers what features they want added, without understanding the context of the job.
Avoid the Fallacy of Active Data: do not prioritise operations-related data (sales, customer characteristics) over the passive data of customer struggle.
Replace all of the above with the baseline: every avatar must contain quoted evidence, a trigger moment and a job statement.
Keep demographic facts only as context on the person, never as the explanatory mechanism for the choice.
caveats: The method is presented as universal, so the minimum requirements (evidence, trigger, job statement) apply to any avatar set; the number of avatars is explicitly not universal.
Christensen's own illustration: his age, height, shoe size and suburb did not cause him to buy the New York Times. Attributes can correlate with purchase propensity without causing it.
Correlation-based data is comfortable and makes managers sleep at night, which is why the fallacy is hard to shake — knowing it is a fallacy is not the same as acting on the difference.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Why Big Data and Customer Satisfaction Metrics Miss the Point
cards.summary: Data that groups customers by similarity or reports satisfaction cannot explain why a purchase happened, and assuming it can leads to churning out mediocrity.
cards.use_when: When a dashboard of demographics, market share and CSAT is being used as the basis for a product or growth decision.
steps: Recognise the shape of the data most companies hold: 'this customer looks like that one', 'this product has similar attributes to that one', 'these people behaved the same way in the past', or a preference split like '68% of customers say they prefer version A over version B'. None of it states why the choice was made.

Keep the correlation-versus-causation distinction operational, not decorative. Christensen cites Nate Silver: ice cream sales and forest fires correlate because both rise in summer heat, but buying a pint of Häagen-Dazs does not set the Montana brush on fire.

Watch for processes that operationalise a belief in randomness: if you believe innovation is unknowable and messy, you design a process that perfectly delivers messy, unknowable results. As Deming put it, every process is perfectly designed to deliver the results it gets.
Treat customer satisfaction metrics with suspicion for innovation purposes: they tell you whether a customer is happy, not how to do the job better — yet they are how most companies track success.
Ask better questions instead. Deming: if you do not know how to ask the right question, you discover nothing.

Beware stage-gates, six-sigma-style precision and rapid iteration applied to the wrong question: all that activity can give the illusion of progress without causing it, with R&D spend rising while breakthrough innovation is missed.
caveats: Christensen's framing of the data problem is an argument about explanatory power for innovation, not a claim that operations data has no value for running the business.
The 'less than 25%' odds figure is his estimate for hitting the right product, not a documented statistic from the sources cited.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Avoid Innovating Toward 'Average': The Jagged-Profile Lesson
cards.summary: The US Air Force cockpit case, retold by Christensen, shows that a design fitted to the average user fits nobody — a direct argument against averaging segment needs into one solution.
cards.use_when: When a roadmap item or landing page is being designed to 'work for everyone', or when multiple jobs are being averaged into a single offer.
steps: Recall the sequence: the Air Force assumed pilot control problems were training or pilot error, then found a cockpit designed around the 1920s average pilot.

They measured over four thousand pilots on nearly a dozen dimensions of size to update the average — then found that none of the pilots actually fell within the definition of average; every pilot had a jagged profile (some long legs, others long arms, height not corresponding to chest or head size).
The revised cockpits designed for everyone fit no one; the fix came only when baseline assumptions were swept aside and the adjustable seat was invented.

Apply the same logic to a jobs analysis: if morning commuters need a thick, slow shake and afternoon parents need a small, quickly finished one, do not design the average shake — design for each job or pick one deliberately.
In practice this argues for adjustability or genuinely distinct variants rather than one compromise offer.
caveats: This is an analogy from military procurement borrowed from Todd Rose's The End of Average; it is illustrative, not an ecommerce experiment.
It does not follow that every product must be customised — the lesson is against averaging incompatible jobs, not against standardisation.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Rewrite the Competitive Set as a Résumé of Alternatives
cards.summary: For any job, list every product the customer might hire and what each is good at, including items in entirely different aisles or categories, to see the real market size.
cards.use_when: Doing competitive analysis, sizing an opportunity, or repositioning a product that looks like a commodity inside its own category.
steps: State the job precisely first, because the competitor set changes with it. 'Moisten the crust on my bread so it's easier to chew' brings in butter, cream cheese, olive oil and mayonnaise. 'Keep my food from burning while cooking' brings in Teflon and nonstick spray, none of which sit in the cold foods aisle.
Write a résumé for each competing product: what job it gets hired for, in what circumstance, and where it falls short.
Accept that the same product can be hired for different jobs at different points in a customer's life, so one product may appear on several résumés.
Use the resumé lens to expose growth you cannot see through market share: Unilever held about 70% of US margarine, but no customer walks in asking for 'something in the yellow fats category'.

Check whether your differentiation is competing on an attribute irrelevant to the job — the twenty-one margarine SKUs differentiated on fat percentage, an attribute that did not map to any job Christensen and his daughter could observe.
Treat the competitive set as the design brief: the product must beat every alternative on the specific job, or the customer keeps hiring the substitute.
caveats: Christensen admits he and his daughter may not have identified all the substitutes correctly that day — the exercise is directional.

The Unilever episode is a negative case: the executives present were not moved by the reframe and the firm continued differentiating in traditional ways, with margarine later declining in US households amid trans-fat health concerns. The outcome is presented as an outsider's observation about a counterfactual, not proof that this lens would have saved the business.
Jobs Theory clarifies why customers choose, not whether the solution is good for them — trans-fat and ethical questions sit outside the theory.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: From Broken Category Assumptions to Growth: Disruption vs Jobs
cards.summary: Disruption explains how incumbents respond to threats but does not say where to look for growth; Jobs Theory is offered as the offensive complement.
cards.use_when: Choosing the strategic frame for an innovation programme, or when a disruption lens has identified a threat but produced no product roadmap.
steps: Use disruption for what it does: it explains and predicts incumbent behaviour in the face of a threat and helps incumbents judge which innovations on the horizon are the greatest disruptive threats.

Do not use disruption as an opportunity map. Christensen is explicit that it does not tell you where to look, how to undermine established leaders, where to create new markets, or which new products will succeed.
Be careful with the term itself: over two decades it has been stretched to mean anything clever, new and ambitious, which drains it of predictive power.
Use Jobs Theory for the offensive question — what causes customers to pull a product into their lives — since that is the causal mechanism behind successful innovation.

Apply this to ecommerce positioning: leaders often come close to the right idea and miss — AT&T showed a picture phone decades before the iPhone, major yogurt makers understood demand for Greek yogurt before Chobani's founder built a ~$1bn business. Knowing the demand exists is not the same as resolving the job, or the incumbent's constraints.
Expect different competitors, different priorities and different results once you adopt the jobs lens.
caveats: Christensen's claim that a well-defined job was implicitly at the core of most historic innovation successes is his belief, and he warns against relying on retrospective explanation — the value is in prediction.
This is theory framing from a 2016 book; treat the named company trajectories as examples at a point in time.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Why Smart Managers Fail: Processes Perfectly Designed for Mediocrity
cards.summary: Great managers following all the best advice can still lead firms to the top and off a cliff, and the 'stupid manager' explanation collapses when a whole industry falls at once.
cards.use_when: Post-mortems where leadership failure is the assumed explanation, or when building an innovation process that you expect to produce breakthroughs.
steps: Distrust the management-quality narrative. Digital Equipment Corporation's success was attributed to the brilliance of its management and its collapse to the ineptitude of the same people — Christensen asks how smart people get so stupid so fast.
Test the individual-blame hypothesis against the industry: almost every minicomputer company in the world collapsed in unison, which points to something structural rather than a few bad leaders.

Accept that disciplined processes can be the problem. Careful stage-gates, rapid iteration, checks and balances, calculated risks and six-sigma-derived requirements give the appearance of a mastered scientific process while innovation stays hit or miss.

Notice the evidence of wasted effort: 84% of global executives in a McKinsey poll said innovation was extremely important, 94% were unsatisfied with their own innovation performance, and one thousand publicly held companies spent $680bn on R&D in 2015, up 5.1% — more activity and more data without more breakthroughs.
Diagnose your own process for whether it is designed around a belief that innovation is random; if so, it will keep delivering randomness even with better talent and bigger budgets.
caveats: The poll, spend and satisfaction figures are cited from period sources (McKinsey; strategy+business, 2015) and describe that period, not current benchmarks.
The DEC 'stupid manager' critique is an argument about structural causes, not a denial that management matters.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Recognising a Job: Little and Big, Predictable and Sudden
cards.summary: Jobs arise from situations; classifying them by size and predictability helps a team notice which jobs its product could plausibly be hired for.
cards.use_when: Generating job hypotheses in a workshop before doing timeline interviews, or mapping where an offer might fit into a customer's day.
steps: Start from the premise that every day things happen to us and jobs arise that need to be done; when a job arises, the customer reaches out and pulls something into their life to get it done.
Sort candidates by scale: little jobs such as 'pass the time while waiting in line', big jobs such as 'find a more fulfilling career'.

Sort by predictability: some jobs surface unpredictably, like dressing for an out-of-town meeting after the airline loses your suitcase; others are regular, like packing a healthy, tasty lunch for a daughter to take to school.

Use the classification to see how the same product can be pulled in for different reasons — the New York Times might be hired to fill waiting-room time, to serve March Madness basketball interest, or to be delivered to the door so neighbours see you as informed.
Note that no ZIP code or median household income figure would reveal the last of those reasons, which is why circumstance beats demographic inference.
caveats: These are illustrative examples from the book, not a taxonomy with operational thresholds.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: It's Not Just About Jobs: Experiences and Integration Create the Moat
cards.summary: Identifying the job is only the start; competitors can copy products but not well-integrated experiences, which is where sustained advantage sits.
cards.use_when: Planning what happens after a jobs insight is validated — turning it into a blueprint, an experience and internal process change.
steps: Translate the job insight into a blueprint that guides development of the product or service and, crucially, the set of experiences that accompany it in solving the job.
Then integrate the company's internal capabilities and processes so the job is nailed consistently, rather than solved well once.
Treat integration as the defensible part: Christensen notes it may be easy for competitors to copy products but difficult to copy experiences integrated into your processes.
Expect the effort to be holistic — from the original insight through to the product reaching the consumer, involving decisions and influence from virtually everyone in the company.

Protect against internal drift: return on net assets pressures, well-intentioned efficiency drives and everyday frontline decisions can quietly break the delivery of a solution you already understood correctly.
Note the payoff asymmetry: even innovators clear about the jobs their products are hired for can lose their way, so the theory is not self-executing.
caveats: Presented as the authors' framework across chapters 6 to 8; the specifics of implementation are not detailed in this section.
Christensen's claim that experiences are harder to copy than products is a strategic argument, not an experimental result.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Define a job as progress in a circumstance
cards.summary: Jobs Theory defines the unit of innovation as the progress a person seeks in a specific circumstance, not a product category or customer type.
cards.use_when: When framing a new product, offer or campaign and you need to state clearly what the customer is actually trying to accomplish rather than describing features or audience demographics.
steps: Write the job as a sentence about progress: 'I want to ___ in this situation.' Avoid naming your product or 'I need ___'.

Specify the circumstance: where, when, with whom, while doing what, and what happens before and after. Circumstance is the unit of analysis because the same person wants different things in different situations.
Describe the functional, social and emotional dimensions of the progress. Social and emotional needs can outweigh functional ones (e.g. trusting someone with your children).
Treat the job as ongoing and recurring rather than a single event; people re-hire solutions whenever the circumstance recurs.
Check it is a job, not a 'need' or a life theme. 'I need to eat' and 'I want to be a good dad' are too general to guide a specific product choice.
caveats: A job is discovered, not created; the underlying job endures even as solutions change.
Jobs are fragile, story-like insights: breaking them into binary segments (male/female, new/existing) destroys meaning.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Film the mini-documentary to characterise a job
cards.summary: Five prompts turn a vague customer struggle into a fully specified Job to Be Done by imagining a filmed episode of the customer's struggle.
cards.use_when: When you need to flesh out a job for messaging, product design or an interview guide and the usual demographic or needs-based descriptions feel empty.
steps: State the progress the person is trying to achieve: what would 'better' look like for them.
Capture the circumstances: who, when, where, while doing what. Example from the source: a manager wants their sales force better equipped so churn falls.
List the obstacles in the way: failed attempts, frustrations, dead ends ('I've tried whitening toothpastes and they don't really work').
Identify compensating behaviour: are they using an imperfect product, cobbling together a workaround, or doing nothing? All three are signals of a live job.
Ask how they would define 'quality' in a better solution and which tradeoffs they would accept (e.g. professional-level whitening without the cost and inconvenience of a dentist visit).
caveats: The answers are rich in context and resist spreadsheet breakdown; cluster them into a coherent story rather than segmenting further.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Use jobs theory to redraw your competitive landscape
cards.summary: Competition should be defined by everything the customer could hire in the same circumstance, not by products the industry buckets together.
cards.use_when: When assessing competitors, setting positioning, or feeling that your market is a zero-sum fight among near-identical products.
steps: Ask what else the customer could 'hire' to get the same progress in that circumstance, including non-consumption (doing nothing).
Expect non-obvious competitors: Netflix's Reed Hastings said it competes with everything you do to relax, including video games and a bottle of wine.
Look at substitutions across categories: a smoker taking a break for calm, a social moment and a work escape may be served by cigarettes or by Facebook.

Benchmark outside your category once the true job is identified - BMW, after reframing its job as mobility, found itself competing with Tesla, Uber, Zipcar and self-driving projects, and launched BMW i and DriveNow.
Redraw the market size: SNHU's online division was not really fighting local colleges but competing against adults choosing non-consumption, which is a far larger opportunity.
caveats: Working out the true job can take sustained effort and goes against habits built around product-attribute or demographic framing.
Do not assume the new framing makes you win; it only reveals who you must beat.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Diagnose why needs- and trends-based innovation fails
cards.summary: Needs, trends and guiding principles are too general to predict a purchase; jobs are specific enough to build an innovation blueprint.
cards.use_when: When a product or campaign built around an important-sounding need or a trend has stalled, or when reviewing an innovation brief that lacks circumstantial detail.
steps: Check whether your framing is a need ('I need to eat', 'I need personal transportation'), a trend, or a life theme ('I want to be a good dad'). These are directionally useful but cannot tell you what someone will choose or whether they will act at all.
Note that needs don't explain behaviour: people eat when not hungry, skip meals, and act for reasons unrelated to the need.
Replace the general statement with the job: the progress sought in a particular circumstance, with its functional, social and emotional dimensions and the tradeoffs the customer will make.
Use the Segway as a cautionary example: it was built around 'more efficient personal transportation' without answering whose need, when and in what circumstances.
Forecast the conversion effect: a specific job gives you the criteria for what is essential versus extraneous in the offer, while a need does not.
caveats: Needs and trends are not wrong, just insufficient for predicting choice on their own.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Ask 'what has to prove true' before committing resources
cards.summary: Discovery-driven planning forces teams to surface and test the assumptions behind a new initiative before large investment locks them in.
cards.use_when: When approving a new product, channel or market entry, or when projections look attractive but rest on untested beliefs.
steps: Write down every assumption that must be true for the strategy to succeed - the source calls this discovery-driven planning (MacMillan and McGrath).
Rank assumptions by importance and by how uncertain they are.
Test the most critical, least certain assumptions cheaply and early, before assigning significant money, time and headcount.
Do not adjust projections after the fact to match what is actually happening; treat each assumption as something to be proven or falsified.
Watch for the failure pattern: projects get approved on incorrect guesses, the team becomes 100 percent committed, and nobody wants to tell management the original assumptions were wrong.
caveats: The source presents this as a complement to Jobs Theory, not a replacement for having a causal theory of customer choice.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Apply Jobs Theory only where a real struggle exists
cards.summary: Jobs Theory is not universal; it stops being useful when existing solutions are good enough or the decision is purely rational and calculable.
cards.use_when: When deciding whether to run a jobs-based research project or whether another method (efficiency analysis, price modelling) is the better tool.
steps: Confirm there is a genuine struggle for progress; if existing solutions are good enough, jobs research has little to explain.

Check whether the purchase decision is largely mathematical, such as commodity trading or straightforward cost and efficiency comparisons; there the source says jobs theory is not useful because there is no complex bundle of social, emotional and functional needs.
Treat theory as if-then propositions: a good theory says when it applies and when it does not, and telling you when it fails is itself valuable.
Use anomalies as opportunities to sharpen the theory rather than discarding it wholesale.
caveats: Cost or efficiency is explicitly not a core element of a job, so don't force a jobs frame onto a purely economic decision.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Use theory as a causal lens, not a formula
cards.summary: Good theory tells you how to think about causes and produces if-then predictions you can test, unlike borrowed best practices.
cards.use_when: When diagnosing an innovation problem, teaching a team to reason about customer choice, or when results from industry best practices are inconsistent.
steps: Ask the causal question first: what actually causes a customer to purchase and use this product or service?
Apply a theory like a lens: use it to explain why past problems and opportunities emerged, then to predict what is likely next and what actions will be needed.
Prefer theories that dispense advice as if-then statements over probabilistic tools, hunches or tips that worked for other companies.
Remember Pasteur: identifying the causal mechanism (germs) enabled prevention and vaccines, while correlation (Snow's water pump) only improved the situation without explaining it.
Recognise that theories are not right or wrong but more or less accurate predictions given the circumstances you are in.
caveats: This is a management-practice argument from the source; theory still needs testing and refinement in your own context.
Prioritise different theories by the problem at hand rather than applying jobs theory to everything.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Look outside the four habitual innovation lenses
cards.summary: Most managers organise innovation around product attributes, customer characteristics, trends or competitive response - all insufficient for predicting behaviour.
cards.use_when: When reviewing an innovation or marketing brief and deciding whether the framing is likely to predict customer choice.
steps: Audit the brief for the four default organising principles named in the source: product attributes, customer characteristics, trends, and competitive response.
Note these are not wrong, just insufficient: they describe who or what rather than why a choice happens.
Adding jobs as a lens means centring the circumstance rather than the customer segment or product category.
Rewrite your problem statement in terms of progress sought and obstacles faced, then check whether your existing data can answer it.
Use the answer to set the tradeoffs: which benefits are essential and which are extraneous to the new offering.
caveats: Jobs theory does not replace segmentation for execution purposes; it changes what the primary unit of innovation work is.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Learn from Toyota: design defects out with if-then process tests
cards.summary: Treating each defect as an anomaly to be root-caused and designed out of the process beat the Detroit approach of inspecting and reworking.
cards.use_when: When a repeatable process (fulfilment, creative production, onboarding) keeps producing errors that get patched rather than prevented.
steps: Stop defaulting to added inspection, inventory and rework, which the source says ballooned cost and complexity while leaving the root cause untouched.
Treat each defect as a scientist treats an anomaly: find its specific cause, then change the process so the error cannot recur.
Standardise each value-adding step: do it the same way every time, so that managers know whether the next step works with it.
See each standardised repetition as a test of the if-then statement: 'if we do this, then that will be the result.'
Accept that complexity (thousands of parts, hundreds of suppliers, many countries) does not make errors inevitable if the process focuses on identifying and removing causes.
caveats: The automotive quality story is used here as an analogy for innovation, not as an ecommerce case with measured results.
The source explicitly says innovation is still in a 'pre-quality revolution' state, so do not overstate how far this transfers.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Recognise the legacy process that produces what you don't want
cards.summary: US automakers unwittingly designed a process highly effective at producing costly, inconsistent cars - a warning about the systems behind your outcomes.
cards.use_when: When outcomes are consistently poor or unpredictable and the reflex is to add patching steps rather than redesign the process.
steps: Inventory the patches currently in place - extra checks, buffers, rework stages - and ask what problem each is mitigating rather than solving.
Ask what the current process is actually designed to produce, and whether that matches what you want customers to experience.
Reframe 'inherent randomness' as an untested assumption: the Japanese manufacturers showed that specific causes of defects existed and could be removed.
Shift investment from correction after the fact to prevention inside the process.
Expect quality and cost to improve together once root causes are removed, as happened with Japanese manufacturers in the 1970s and 1980s.
caveats: The historical account is descriptive; it does not guarantee the same cost trajectory in other industries.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Reframe a market by serving non-consumption
cards.summary: SNHU found its biggest opportunity not by beating local colleges but by serving adults who otherwise would have done nothing.
cards.use_when: When your category looks saturated and growth has stalled under a one-size-fits-all offer aimed at the 'average' customer.
steps: Identify the distinct jobs different groups hire you for, even when they look identical on paper (e.g. the same accounting degree for an 18-year-old and a 35-year-old).
For SNHU's coming-of-age students, the job centred on experiences - sports teams, climbing walls, long conversations with faculty - while parents asked about academics and financial aid.

For online adult learners, the job was different in kind: convenience, customer service, credentials and speedy completion, in the circumstance of juggling work and family with unfinished credits and debt.
Notice that the second group was also competing with non-consumption - doing nothing about their education - which makes the addressable market far larger than a local applicant pool.
Align policies, structures and service levels to the actual job; SNHU's financial-aid process was designed around a leisurely, low-urgency conversation that did not fit adult learners' needs.
caveats: SNHU's revenue growth figures (about $535m by fiscal 2016; 34% compounded annual growth over six years) are case results, not promises.
The source notes the online division earned a modest $32m before the reframing and succeeded somewhat despite, not because of, existing processes.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Use a jobs lens to separate functional from experience-based buying
cards.summary: Prospects may ask about practical features while actually hiring you for a social and emotional experience, and the two require different offers.
cards.use_when: When designing a landing page, tour or sales conversation and deciding which elements actually drive the decision.
steps: Look at who asks which questions: in SNHU's case parents asked about academics and aid while prospective students asked about experiences.
Decide which dimension your core segment is really buying against, and build the offer and proof around it.
If the buying dimension is experiential, the functional questions still need answering but are not the primary persuasive content.
Consider serving both dimensions with differentiated journeys rather than one generic pitch for the 'average' customer.
Treat a generic message as a warning sign that you have not distinguished the jobs your different customers are hiring you for.
caveats: This is a qualitative read from one university example; verify with your own prospect conversations before rebuilding a funnel.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Map competition as a shifted landscape, not a finite share fight
cards.summary: Seeing competition through jobs changes who you benchmark and how you innovate, from supply-side selling to demand-side responding.
cards.use_when: When your strategic plan assumes growth must come from taking share from direct rivals in a fixed market.
steps: List every alternative a customer might choose for the job, including products from other categories and doing nothing.
Accept that some competitors are invisible at first: Reid Hoffman's point that 'sometimes it's a job you can't currently see.'
Watch for incumbents redefining themselves around jobs, as Ford described itself as a mobility company and GM invested in Lyft and launched Maven.
Shift from a supply-side view (what we make, dealers as customers) to a demand-side view (what job the buyer is trying to get done).
Expect competitive advantage to go to whoever understands and best solves the job, including the surrounding experiences and removing roadblocks to progress.
caveats: Strategic repositioning examples from BMW, Ford and GM are illustrations from the source, not verified outcomes for ecommerce.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Accept that the job endures while solutions change
cards.summary: Jobs are discovered, not created, and the underlying job stays stable even as the way people solve it changes dramatically.
cards.use_when: When evaluating a new technology or channel and wondering whether it changes the customer's need or just the means of solving it.
steps: Ask what enduring job your category solves - sharing information across distances persisted from Pony Express to email.
Teenagers' job of communicating without parental oversight persisted from passing notes to Snapchat, which solved it with disappearing messages.
Focus on understanding the underlying job rather than falling in love with your current solution, because a better solution can always displace yours.

Keep improving your understanding of the complex social, emotional and functional needs in each circumstance - the source says Snapchat itself remains vulnerable to someone with a better understanding.
caveats: Don't read this as an argument to ignore new technology; the source says new technology can improve how a job is solved.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Convert jobs insight into experience and process requirements
cards.summary: A layered job usually cannot be satisfied by a product alone; it demands a bundle of integrated experiences, which is where defensibility comes from.
cards.use_when: When moving from research findings to designing the full customer experience, including post-purchase and service layers.
steps: List every dimension of the job - functional, social and emotional - and the tradeoffs the customer said they would make.
Design an experience that addresses each dimension, not just the core functional transaction.
Integrate those experiences into company processes so they are delivered consistently rather than as isolated campaigns.
Treat the integration as the moat: the source argues that when you have done this well it is almost impossible for competitors to copy.
Test each element against the job rather than against competitor feature lists.
caveats: This is a claim about defensibility from the authors; it assumes deep integration, not a single added feature.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Run leadership questions to test customer understanding
cards.summary: A short question set checks whether you actually know why customers choose you and who you are really competing with.
cards.use_when: When preparing a strategy review, onboarding a team, or stress-testing a positioning statement.
steps: Ask: do you understand the real reason customers choose your product, or why they choose something else instead?
Ask how your product helps customers make progress and in which circumstances they are trying to make it.
Break the progress into functional, emotional and social dimensions and record what you know versus what you are assuming.
Ask what else is competing for that job, including options outside the traditional view of your industry and non-consumption.
Close the gaps with direct customer research where answers are weak or generic.
caveats: These are diagnostic prompts, not a measurement instrument; pair them with evidence from customers.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: One-size-fits-none: segment by job, not by customer category
cards.summary: Serving distinct job-based segments with a single averaged solution fails everyone; separate them and rebuild each journey.
cards.use_when: You have multiple customer types (e.g., first-time buyers vs. repeat bulk buyers) receiving the same onboarding, offers or support flow and growth has stalled.
steps: Identify the distinct jobs held by different groups using your product. Example: SNHU's traditional-age students hired the university for a coming-of-age experience where financial aid mattered to parents; adult online learners hired it to gain credentials that improve professional prospects fast, making cost and speed central.
Map the full journey for each job from first inquiry to first purchase (and beyond) on one board, then mark every point where your process adds friction, delay or irrelevance for that job.

Remove or replace each friction point with an experience that fits the job. SNHU replaced a generic 24-hour email with a phone call in under 10 minutes, resolved aid and credit-transfer decisions in days instead of weeks, and gave each online student a personal adviser who checks in when assignments or tests go badly.

Accept that this can mean 'pretty much everything' changes, including org structure, budget priority and physical separation of the team serving the new job — SNHU moved its online team to separate offices so traditional university policies wouldn't constrain it.

Track whether the job is actually delivered, not just enrollment: SNHU treats a student as fired if it fails to deliver the credential outcome, and dials back recruiting when internal support systems can't keep up.
caveats: SNHU's growth (75,000+ online students, 10% surpluses, no tuition increases in four years) is a case example, not a benchmark you can copy.
Serving one job well may require deliberate de-prioritization of another segment — a strategic trade-off, not a free win.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Job-hunting method 1: mine your own life for jobs
cards.summary: Unresolved jobs in your own daily life are legitimate innovation territory; your life is articulate data.
cards.use_when: You need an innovation hypothesis and have no budget for formal research, or you're a founder/operator building for a market you personally belong to.
steps: Look for a recurring struggle in your own routine — a task you dread, a workaround you've built, or a desire for progress you can't satisfy with existing products.

Treat your own frustration as a hypothesis, not proof. Khan's math videos for his cousin and Marcelo's child-care search both started as personal jobs; the videos were technically inferior to existing tutorials but were fun and conceptually clear, which is what the cousin was hiring them to do.

Note the functional, emotional and social dimensions of your job, since those often differ from what competitors optimize. Khan's cousin wanted to feel successful and low-stakes learning; Khan wanted family connection and to share his love of learning.

Validate against actual users before scaling. Sony's Morita ignored market research that said consumers wouldn't buy a non-recording tape player with earphones, and the Walkman sold 330 million-plus units — but this is an illustration of one leader's conviction, not a rule to skip research.
caveats: The Walkman example is retrospective and often cited selectively; ignoring research is survivorship-biased and not a recommended default.
A job that matters to you may still be too niche to build a business on without testing demand.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Job-hunting method 2: hunt nonconsumption, not competitor share
cards.summary: People who use no solution at all — not competitors' customers — often hold the largest growth opportunity.
cards.use_when: Your category looks mature, saturated or price-competitive, and you suspect existing market-size data can't see untapped demand.
steps: Look for people who would benefit but buy nothing, or rely on homemade substitutes, rather than only studying customers of competing brands.

Quantify the gap if you can. Kimberly-Clark found roughly 40% of adults over 50 suffer incontinence and about one in three women over 18 experience some issue, yet only a small percentage use any incontinence product; many suffer up to two years before buying.

Diagnose why they abstain. Depend's problem was stigma: pack size and shape resembled children's diapers, and it looked bulky, white and crinkly — so people used feminine pads, avoided travel and restaurants, or disengaged socially instead.

Redesign the whole product and purchase experience around the job 'help me reclaim my life,' which meant inventing new materials so briefs looked and felt like underwear and packaging that looked like ordinary underwear with a transparent window.
Check whether you're cannibalizing yourself. The relaunch generated about $60 million in year one and 30% growth in year two without harming the existing line.
caveats: Nonconsumption is invisible in current sales data; you must deliberately look for it.
The Depend figures are the company's own research and a single launch's results, not a general benchmark.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Job-hunting method 3: read workarounds as demand signals
cards.summary: Compensating behaviors show customers who want a job solved badly enough to build their own solution.
cards.use_when: You're scanning for unmet needs and notice customers jury-rigging spreadsheets, manual processes or odd substitutes.
steps: Immerse yourself in the customer's context; workarounds are hard to see from a distance. Look for cobbled-together substitutes, manual steps and time-consuming rituals.

Examples to pattern-match: small businesses using personal finance software as de facto bookkeeping; a parent running a household 'bank' to teach compound interest; calling restaurants and friends repeatedly to coordinate a dinner.
Translate the workaround into the underlying job — often the job is what people don't want to do (learn formal accounting, deal with bank minimums, coordinate scheduling) rather than what they want.

Design a solution that absorbs the complexity in the background, as QuickBooks did: it offered half the functionality of sophisticated accounting software at twice the price, and became the market leader by hiding journal entries and accounting language.
Remember the real competitor set expands to include the workaround itself: doing it yourself, hiring a person, spreadsheets, or a literal shoebox of receipts.
caveats: Workarounds don't guarantee willingness to buy — validate that customers will pay for removed effort or anxiety.
QuickBooks' pricing/feature trade-off is a specific case, not a formula for pricing.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Job-hunting method 4: negative jobs — what customers don't want to do
cards.summary: Jobs framed as 'I don't want to X' are often the richest opportunities, especially where the alternative is time-consuming and anxiety-laden.
cards.use_when: You're evaluating service design, flow simplification or any category where customers tolerate a painful routine.
steps: List disliked routines in your category. Example: 'I don't want to see the doctor' for a likely strep throat — the parent wants quick relief without an unscheduled appointment, a long wait and a pharmacy delay.

Ask whether the job can be satisfied by removing the dreaded step rather than improving it. QuickMedx, the forerunner of CVS MinuteClinics, offered instant walk-in care with nurse practitioners prescribing for routine ailments like conjunctivitis, ear infections and strep throat.
Note the scale this validated: more than a thousand MinuteClinic locations inside CVS pharmacy stores across 33 states.

In ecommerce terms: negative jobs surface as 'I don't want to create an account,' 'I don't want to call support,' 'I don't want to compare 40 SKUs.' Each is a candidate for removing a step rather than adding a feature.
Pair each negative job with willingness-to-pay testing — relief from dread is often worth paying for, but you must confirm it.
caveats: Negative jobs in regulated categories (health, finance) may require new operational or legal structures, not just UX changes.
The MinuteClinic growth figures are a case illustration, not a forecast.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Job-hunting method 5: unusual uses reveal hidden jobs
cards.summary: Customers using your product off-label are showing you jobs your category doesn't acknowledge — and new revenue lines.
cards.use_when: You have a long-established product, flat growth, and suspect you're defined by a category rather than by what customers are doing with it.
steps: Observe actual use, not intended use. Church & Dwight noticed consumers adding Arm & Hammer baking soda to laundry detergent, mixing it into toothpaste, sprinkling it on carpets and leaving an open box in the fridge.

Convert each observation into a job statement. The brand now maps products to jobs like 'help my mouth feel fresh,' 'deodorize my refrigerator,' 'clean and freshen my carpets,' 'deodorize that stinky cat litter' and 'remove shower stain and mildew.'

Build or reposition products against those jobs. Arm & Hammer's original orange-box baking soda is now under 7% of its consumer revenue, meaning most of the business came from jobs discovered off-label.
Apply elsewhere: NyQuil users were taking it to sleep when not sick, so ZzzQuil stripped out the cold ingredients and sold the good night's sleep alone.
Check reviews, support tickets and search queries for off-label language; that's where unusual uses show up in ecommerce.
caveats: Non-medical off-label use can carry regulatory and safety risk; ZzzQuil required reformulating, not just marketing.
Single-brand revenue split figures are illustrative, not a target.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Sell the outcome, not the course catalog: B2B job alignment
cards.summary: When the buyer's job is to matter internally, sell subscriptions and owned outcomes around their business goals rather than discrete products.
cards.use_when: You sell to a functional buyer (HR, L&D, IT, marketing ops) whose internal credibility depends on connecting your product to executive priorities.
steps: Probe past the transaction to the buyer's real job. FranklinCovey's CEO visited nearly 400 customers before seeing the pattern: HR and learning leaders were hiring training products partly to be seen as vital contributors to company priorities like customer loyalty and growth — and products couldn't deliver that on their own.

Restructure the offer around arising jobs, not SKUs. FranklinCovey moved from selling individual courses to subscriptions giving near-unlimited access to all content, deliverable as full courses, bite-size modules or single-point lessons for a staff meeting.

Own outcomes, not just delivery. For one IT equipment client, FranklinCovey stationed a full-time coach at headquarters to enforce process improvements on every sales opportunity above $500 million — 'our deliverable is really a process, not a product,' with measurable ROI.

Use job definition to find uncontested positioning: FranklinCovey says it aims at jobs that don't have competitors — strategy-setting still goes to consulting firms, but strategy implementation and behavior change is a lane with few rivals.
Expect adjacent players to become lead sources rather than pure competitors; consulting firms now refer implementation work.
caveats: FranklinCovey's revenue path ($589M peak in 2000, $130M in 2009, $220M in 2015) is a turnaround case example, not a template.
Owning outcomes requires delivery capacity; a subscription model fails if the customer's arising job isn't actually served.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Excavate the job with timeline interviews, not feature wish lists
cards.summary: Asking recent buyers to draw their decision timeline surfaces the emotional obstacle that features and surveys miss.
cards.use_when: You have traffic but poor conversion, or focus groups keep returning feature requests that don't move sales.
steps: Interview people who already bought, and ask them to draw a timeline of how they got there rather than to rate features.

Look for what does NOT predict purchase. Moesta found no clear demographic or psychographic profile among downsizers, and none of the luxury features (squeakless floors, granite counters, 30 pages of customization options) tipped the decision — the customization checklist was actually an obstacle.

Search for the emotional blocker hiding in the details. The clue was repeated anxiety about the dining room table — a symbol of family life that made the move feel like discarding memories; one buyer needed days and multiple boxes of tissues to clear one closet.

Redesign around removing that blocker alongside the functional job. The builder shrank second bedrooms 20% to fit a classic dining table, provided moving services and two years of storage, and added an on-site sorting room for unhurried decisions.
Simplify choice architecture: replacing 30 pages of options with three finished-unit variations cut cold-feet cancellations from five or six a month to one.
Re-price to cover the added services — they raised the price $3,500 profitably, and grew 25% in 2007 while the market fell 49%.
caveats: Growth and cancellation figures come from one Detroit-area builder in a distressed market; treat as a case example.
Timeline interviews require interpretation; a single dramatic quote is not proof of the pattern.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Use Jobs Theory as an integration tool for fragmented research
cards.summary: Jobs Theory tells you which pieces of existing research matter and how they fit together, without discarding your data.
cards.use_when: You already have personas, focus groups, panels and competitive analysis but they don't produce clear innovation direction.
steps: Keep your existing inputs — personas, ethnographic research, focus groups, customer panels, competitive analysis — but change the lens you view them through.

For each job, build a full narrative of the customer's circumstances, functional, social and emotional dimensions, obstacles removed and experiences sought. The book's framing: a comprehensive narrative versus a few scattered random frames of a movie.
Use the job to determine which information is needed and how it relates, so the causal mechanism of choice becomes visible.

Apply it as a leadership heuristic. LeBlanc said Jobs to Be Done 'gave us the language' for the leadership team and campus to discuss what had to change — the value was shared vocabulary and prioritization, not a research artifact.

Recheck the market-sizing implication: because jobs cut across product and customer categories, the addressable market (including nonconsumers and workaround users) can be far larger than category sales suggest.
caveats: Jobs-based segments often don't align with your existing reporting segments, which creates internal friction.
The approach doesn't supply validated market size on its own; existing data may still miss nonconsumption.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Five recurring questions to audit every offer
cards.summary: A reusable audit checklist drawn from the jobs framework to test whether your offer is built around a real job.
cards.use_when: Running a positioning, offer or roadmap review and needing a structured set of challenge questions.
steps: Ask what jobs customers are hiring your product or service to get done — in their words and circumstances, not your category label.
Ask whether distinct job-based segments exist that you are inadequately serving with a one-size-fits-none solution, and whether a segment is absorbing a compromise designed for someone else.
Ask whether your product — or a competitor's — is overshooting what customers are willing to pay for, i.e., adding features on dimensions that don't cause customers to buy.
Ask what experiences customers seek in order to make progress and what obstacles must be removed for them to succeed, mapping the whole find-purchase-use journey.

Ask what your understanding of the job reveals about your real competition — often not the brands in your category leaderboard but doing nothing, workarounds, spreadsheets, hiring a person or a household ritual.
Recruit nonconsumers, not just existing customers, into the evidence base; they see a different part of the job.
caveats: These questions surface hypotheses; each still needs testing with real customers and purchase behavior.
The nonconsumption framing is the authors' theory, and job-based segmentation may conflict with how your business is currently organized and measured.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Define the Market by Job, Not Product or Customer Category
cards.summary: Re-framing the market around the customer's Job to Be Done reveals growth where product- or demographic-based categories show none.
cards.use_when: You are sizing a market, prioritizing a roadmap, or suspect your category definition is hiding demand (e.g., an ecommerce brand defining itself by product type instead of the progress customers want).
steps: List the product or customer categories your business currently uses to describe its market (e.g., 'mattresses', 'women 25-40').
For each, restate it as the progress a customer is trying to make in a circumstance (e.g., 'help me wake up without pain so I can be productive as a parent and worker').
Look at who solves that job today — including products in other categories, workarounds, and doing nothing — because those are your real competitors.

Re-estimate the market from this job perspective; the addressable set often looks very different. The book's example: P&G assumed low-cost diapers would sell to millions of non-diaper-using Chinese parents, but the functional 'containment device' framing missed the emotional/social job of a baby sleeping through the night.
caveats: Reframing does not guarantee a large market; the job must have enough magnitude to change behavior.
The Pampers China outcome (approx. $1.6B and ~30% share by 2013) is a reported case result, not a benchmark.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Drill Deep and Look Wide: Functional, Emotional, Social Dimensions
cards.summary: A job has functional, emotional and social dimensions; innovations that only address the functional miss context and fail.
cards.use_when: You are defining requirements for a product, page, or experience and want to avoid the common trap of solving only the functional dimension.
steps: For a promising job, write out the functional dimension (what task it performs), the social dimension (how the customer wants to be seen by others), and the emotional dimension (how they want to feel).
Treat all three as potentially equal in weight; do not assume emotional/social are secondary to functional.

In the book's Intermountain example, clinicians were given state-of-the-art diagnostic software but chose paper and pen because typing broke eye contact during a diagnosis — the emotional job of reassuring an anxious patient beat the functional tool.
Audit your own offering the same way: what functional problem does it solve, and what emotional/social reassurance is either helped or harmed at that moment?
caveats: The source attributes the 'don't separate the three dimensions' insight to P&G's David Goulait; it is presented as his conversion, not a universal law.
Emotional/social weight varies by circumstance; don't assume it always dominates.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Don't Do Design Requirements in a Conference Room — Go Into the Wild
cards.summary: Asking experts what they want in a conference room misses the real job; observe people in the actual circumstances where they use the product.
cards.use_when: You are gathering requirements from internal stakeholders, power users, or customers via interviews and need to validate that stated needs match real behavior.
steps: Note the trap: asking people what they need and building exactly that, based on the assumption that they can explain their own job accurately.
Actually watch the product being used in its real context (the clinic, the kitchen, the checkout flow) before finalizing requirements.

Look for the gap between what people say they do and what they do — Intermountain found clinicians' stated needs didn't match what they actually wanted in practice, and they had missed a whole customer: the patient.
Maintain a 'beginner's mind'; the source's goal is to observe the job, not just catalog behavior sequence ('what happened first, second').
caveats: This is the source's opinion (voiced via Intermountain's Todd Dunn) that 'you can't do design requirements in a conference room.' Apply with judgment for your context.
For ecommerce, transfer the technique as observing real browsing/checkout behavior and customer support context rather than assuming stated preferences.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Study Nonconsumers and Workarounds for High-Potential Jobs
cards.summary: People who buy nothing (not even from competitors) and people inventing workarounds often reveal the richest unmet jobs.
cards.use_when: Your growth has plateaued with current customers and you want to find new demand outside your existing base.
steps: Identify nonconsumers: people who aren't buying your product or anyone else's for this job.
Ask what makes nonconsumers' jobs different from current customers' jobs, and what's blocking them from using any solution.
Watch for 'compensating behavior' — people rigging their own workaround. The source treats this as a strong clue that the job is important and the person is frustrated enough to invent a solution.
For ecommerce, look at searchers who bounce, abandoned carts, and people using spreadsheets/manual processes instead of buying a tool.
caveats: The book states most companies over-invest in studying current customers; nonconsumers are the underused source, not a replacement.
Workarounds signal opportunity but not guaranteed willingness to switch.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Distinguish the Big Hire from the Little Hire
