cards.summary: Most data tracks the purchase (Big Hire) but ignores the moment of consumption (Little Hire), which determines whether the product really solves the job.
cards.use_when: You are measuring product-market fit, retention, or why downloads/purchases don't translate into repeat use.
steps: Define the Big Hire: the purchase moment (e.g., app download, first order).
Define the Little Hire: the moment the product is actually brought into the customer's life and used (the dress tag comes off, the app opens again).
Measure the Little Hire, not just the Big Hire; a product that truly solves the job gets hired again and again.
Classic example: many downloaded apps are never reopened — tracking downloads alone tells you nothing about whether the job is being done.
For ecommerce, track repeat purchase and consumption behavior, not just first-order conversion.
caveats: Sales/marketing data commonly reflects only the Big Hire; supplement with consumption data.
Whether a product is 'doing a good job' depends on the customer's ongoing behavior, which single-point data can't show.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Map the Four Forces: Push, Pull, Inertia, Anxiety
cards.summary: Two forces drive change (the push of the situation and the pull of the new solution) and two block it (habits of the present and anxiety about the new); all four must be understood.
cards.use_when: You are designing for conversion or adoption and want to reduce friction, not just add appeal.
steps: Identify the push: the frustration or problem substantial enough to trigger action (a merely annoying problem may not qualify).
Identify the pull: how the new solution makes progress that improves the customer's life.
Identify inertia: 'habits of the present' — the comfort of the current workaround, even an imperfect one.

Identify anxiety: fear of the new — cost, learning curve, the unknown. The source cites Kahneman and Tversky that loss aversion is roughly twice as psychologically powerful as the allure of gains (their finding).
Design so the pull clearly exceeds the sum of inertia plus anxiety. Address anxiety explicitly with reassurance.
caveats: Loss aversion 'twice as powerful' is attributed to Kahneman and Tversky, not this book's original claim.
The formula 'pull > inertia + anxiety' is a conceptual model, not a measurable equation.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Reduce Switching Anxiety, Not Just Increase Appeal
cards.summary: Innovators over-focus on making the new solution attractive and under-focus on the anxieties that block people from switching.
cards.use_when: You have a strong offer but adoption/checkout is stalling, or you are launching a new or trust-sensitive product type.
steps: Enumerate the customer's specific anxieties: cost, learning something new, fear the new solution fails, fear of needing a backup, fear it's not better.

Design reassurance directly against each: e.g., ING Direct opened physical cafés (you can't do teller cash transactions there) primarily to signal it is a 'real' bank; SNHU's not-for-profit status and real campus reduce fear that online education is a scam.
Remove structural anxiety sources: health clubs using annual contracts reportedly created so much anxiety it prevented people from joining at all.
For ecommerce, translate this into trust signals, easy returns, money-back guarantees, and transparent pricing on the checkout page.
caveats: These are the source's illustrations; the 'annual contracts prevent joining' point is framed as the industry 'coming around to the idea,' i.e., an evolving view.
Reassurance must be credible; a physical café that can't do banking is a brand signal, not a service.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Identify What Must Be Fired for Your Product to Be Hired
cards.summary: Every hire requires firing the current solution — including doing nothing; companies under-consider what their product replaces.
cards.use_when: You are launching or repositioning and need to understand the real competition and switching cost.
steps: List all current solutions for the job, including the solution of doing nothing and any workaround.
Explain how much friction there is in firing each: functional-only solutions are easy to fire, but solutions with emotional and social dimensions are far harder to let go.
Recognize the decision to fire/hire begins long before the customer enters the store or site.

Design messaging and offers that lower the cost of firing: e.g., mobile phones displaced wristwatches; catch-up TV replaced a weekly magazine subscription; anti-incontinence products let people leave home instead of staying in.
caveats: Customers are reluctant to fire anything until sure something is better, even when firing an imperfect solution.
Applies in B2B too — the source notes procurement decisions still carry emotional/social weight (e.g., a plant manager's career anxiety, a project manager's need to look competent).
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Storyboard the Customer's Struggle to Reveal Competing Forces
cards.summary: Sketch the customer's struggle as a narrative (Pixar-style beats) to surface pushes, pulls, anxieties and context.
cards.use_when: You need to convert interview or observation notes into a structured narrative of a decision, or design an onboarding/purchase experience around real moments.
steps: Use the narrative beats: 'Once upon a time... Every day... One day... Because of that we did this... Because of this we did that... Finally I did...'
Talk to consumers as if building a documentary, capturing their struggle to storyboard later.

For each beat, ask about the specific details (who, where, tired or not, how many bags) — Airbnb's founders storyboarded 45 emotional moments for hosts and guests, down to how a guest is greeted on arrival.
Use the storyboard to design moments that match the customer's vision of what they hired you to do — including the first 'Little Hire' moment.
caveats: The Airbnb 45-storyboards detail is a reported example, not a required number.
Storyboarding is a tool to organize the struggle; it is not itself the research.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Run a Documentary-Style Job Interview on Circumstances, Not Features
cards.summary: A JTBD interview reconstructs a timeline of the purchase decision from the first thought, focusing on circumstances, not product features.
cards.use_when: You are interviewing recent buyers/purchasers to understand why they really chose you, and standard feature-preference surveys aren't giving usable answers.
steps: Frame it as filming a documentary: you want all details from when they first started thinking about the purchase, to the decision, to first use.
Reconstruct a timeline with granular, sometimes seemingly irrelevant, probe questions: exact date, weekday/weekend, where, who was with them, what else was in the cart, how they felt.
Do not lead with feature probes ('soft enough? right support? price important?') — the source warns these miss the real story.
Ask about the roles of others in purchase and use, friction points, alternatives considered, and unusual or non-use moments.
Sample size of one: treat each interview as a rich narrative, then cluster stories to find patterns rather than bucketing answers into categories.
caveats: The mattress transcript is explicitly NOT a prototype for all customer-research interviews; it is one illustration of depth.
The ambling, painstaking deficit-gathering is intentional but not suitable as a universal template.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Read the Mattress Case: Clues in Circumstances, Not Features
cards.summary: In the Mattress Agenda interview, the real story was pain, spousal conflict, warranty frustration, and store anxiety — not coil count or firmness.
cards.use_when: You want a concrete model of how an apparently simple, impulse-looking purchase conceals a long, complex job when you gather circumstances.
steps: Note the surface story: Brian Walker bought a $699 memory-foam mattress at Costco on a weekend, seemingly on impulse.

The reconstructed story: it followed four years of back/neck/headaches, a $2,000 pillow-top that sank, a failed Macy's warranty claim (needed 1.5-inch sinkage; a relative sold it to him), spousal sleep conflict, a chaotic Costco trip with kids, and ~3 months of online research.
Extract the job dimension: it was about a good night's sleep and being productive as a business owner, dad, and husband — not coils vs. foam.

Note the firing/anti-anxiety drivers: he feared online/Groupon purchase because of his earlier bad in-store experience; Costco's local presence and easy return lowered that anxiety, and he chose the priciest of two options.
caveats: This is a single retrospective interview; treat as an illustrative pattern, not statistical evidence.
The transcript is edited for length; details may be incomplete.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Watch for Unusual Product Use as a Job Clue
cards.summary: How customers use your product — especially in unexpected or unusual ways — reveals the real job better than their stated preferences.
cards.use_when: You are mining customer behavior or support data and want to spot jobs you aren't currently designing for.
steps: Observe the circumstances in which customers use the product, not just what they say about it.
Flag unusual or unexpected uses and ask what job that behavior is trying to complete.
Look for products used in moments you'd expect them not to be, or not used in moments you'd expect them to be — the source lists both as clue-generating questions.
Cross-check against compensating behavior (see nonconsumer card) to distinguish a true unmet job from noise.
caveats: Unusual use can also indicate misuse or a different segment; investigate before designing for it.
The source frames this as a source of insight, not a proven method with fixed steps.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Use Your Own Life as a Legitimate Source of Job Insights
cards.summary: The book's takeaways include that personal experience is a valid, rich source of JTBD insights — many successful innovations came from introspection.
cards.use_when: You are stuck for insight or want a low-cost way to start identifying jobs without launching a full research program.
steps: Ask: what are the important, unsatisfied jobs in your own life and the lives of those closest to you?
Flesh out the circumstances and the functional, emotional and social dimensions of the progress you're trying to make.
If you consume your own product, ask which jobs you use it for and where it falls short — and why.

Be mindful of the pitfall the source names: don't start from your existing product and ask how to tweak it (faster? more colors? cheaper?), and don't rely on industry category definitions — you may have already missed the job.
caveats: Personal insight is a starting point; the source still recommends observation of others and nonconsumers.
The trap of only tweaking an existing product is a caution, not a prohibition.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Focus on Cause, Not Luck, in Innovation
cards.summary: The JTBD lens treats innovation as a search for cause — asking what will cause what — so breakthroughs don't depend on lucky accidents.
cards.use_when: You are framing an innovation or experimentation program and want to argue for hypothesis-driven search over hoping for a lucky find.
steps: Explicitly frame the work as discovering what causes a customer to hire your solution in a given circumstance.
Note that the lens lets you look at the same things everyone else sees but 'see differently' — the advantage is in what you look for, not privileged data.
Remember the source's stance: there is no one special method; what matters is the questions you ask and how you piece the resulting information together.
Treat the 'fracking' for jobs metaphor as the mindset: drill deep, then explore widely around a found vein.
caveats: This is the author's framing/opinion, not an empirically proven law.
The book claims no black box, but the cases it cites are selected successes and may suffer survivorship bias.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Signal 'This Is Not for You' to Avoid Alienating Wrong-Fit Buyers
cards.summary: If a customer hires your product for reasons other than its intended job, they may later call it a bad product; signaling who it's not for protects you.
cards.use_when: You have a strong niche offer and are tempted to broaden messaging to grab more buyers, or you're getting mismatched customers who churn or complain.
steps: Identify the job your product is actually solving and what the buyer should expect.
Explicitly signal 'this product is not for you' where the mismatch risk is high, rather than chasing any buyer.
The source's rationale: if a consumer doesn't see their job in your product it's 'game over', and if they hire it for the wrong job and it fails to solve that, they may be alienated permanently.
For ecommerce, translate this into clear product descriptions and expectation-setting to lower returns and bad reviews from mismatched buyers.
caveats: This is the source's opinion and depends on having a defined target job.
Over-signaling can unnecessarily shrink your market; calibrate to where mismatched hires cause real harm.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: B2B Jobs Still Carry Emotional and Social Weight
cards.summary: Even constrained B2B procurement decisions involve anxiety, reputation, career risk and habits of the present.
cards.use_when: You sell to businesses/teams and are tempted to treat the purchase as purely rational or functional.
steps: Identify the personal stakes for the buyer: reputation with peers and managers, being seen as prepared and competent, avoiding sleepless nights or career anxiety.
Design reassurance for the social/emotional job as well as the functional one.

Mercer example: for pension-plan buyouts, clients (HR/CFO) wanted to be seen as careful, competent and having left no stone unturned; Mercer built a Pension Risk Exchange with real-time trading and a modeling/monitoring module so clients could model options before committing — an 'anxiety-reducing practice run.'
Reduce the time and opacity of the process, which the source identifies as core sources of anxiety.
caveats: The Mercer Pension Risk Exchange results (launched in US, UK, Canada; part of growth strategy) are reported case outcomes, not guarantees.
Transfer this reasoning to ecommerce only where you sell to professional buyers who carry personal accountability (e.g., B2B wholesale, team tools).
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Reframe 'Good Enough' as a Jobs Question, Not an Opinion
cards.summary: Judgments of whether a product is good enough are unresolvable without a Job to Be Done to anchor them.
cards.use_when: Your team is stuck arguing whether a feature, page, or offer is 'good enough' and the debate keeps cycling.
steps: Stop asking 'Is it good enough?' — the source says this produces opinions and never-ending arguments.
Reframe: 'Is it good enough to help a consumer make this kind of progress in this kind of situation?'
Anchor the answer to the specific circumstance of progress, which the source calls critical to understanding causality.
Use the job definition to make the debate decidable rather than a matter of taste.
caveats: The reframing is attributed to Chris Spiek of the Re-Wired Group, and is presented as his approach/knowledge.
Still requires a well-defined job; without one the reframed question is equally vague.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Big Hire vs Little Hire: Separating Purchase from Continued Use
cards.summary: Distinguish the moment a customer buys a product (Big Hire) from the repeated moments they actually use it (Little Hire), and treat both as separate jobs to be won.
cards.use_when: Evaluating why a product sells but churns, or why purchase data looks healthy while usage or retention lags
steps: Define the Big Hire for your product: the moment and circumstance in which a customer commits to buy. Track where, when and with whom that decision happens, not just the conversion rate.
Define the Little Hire: the recurring act of using or re-using the product in the customer's life. Ask whether the product is actually satisfying the job each time it is used.
Recognise that Big Hire data alone is misleading: a sale does not prove the job was solved. Only a consistent series of Little Hires confirms it.
Investigate what the customer had to fire, stop using or abandon in order to hire yours. Something always needs to get fired before something is hired.

Look for the failing Little Hires of the current solution: repeated daily frustration with an old product can be the strongest driver of a new purchase (illustrated by the mattress buyer who finally bought after a year of poor sleep).
Map barriers separately on each side: what stops the Big Hire (e.g. anxiety, spousal agreement, payment) and what makes the Little Hire hard (e.g. difficult setup, poor fit, disposal of old product).
Use the two-hire distinction in onboarding and post-purchase flows to diagnose where customers drop their new habit, not just where they fail to check out.
caveats: Based on a single customer interview in the source; the authors explicitly say jobs discovery is about clustering insights, not one eureka.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Storyboarding the Switch: Push, Pull, Inertia and Anxiety
cards.summary: Build a rich storyboard of the customer's circumstances and struggles, capturing the four forces that push customers toward or hold them back from a new solution.
cards.use_when: Designing qualitative customer research, mapping a purchase journey or choosing which friction to remove first
steps: Assemble a storyboard for one real customer that describes, in sequence: the circumstance of struggle, the moments of imperfect experience, the frustrations, and the final decision.
Name the two forces that compel change: the push of the unsatisfied job (present pain with the current solution) and the pull of the new solution (the attraction of a better outcome).
Name the two forces that oppose change: the inertia of current habits and the anxiety about the new (will I like it, will my partner criticise it, can I get rid of the old one).
Look for workarounds the customer already uses to cope (in the mattress case, painkillers and energy drinks were effective competitors). These reveal the real competitive set and unmet job.

Turn each opposing force into a design question: what experience could reduce this anxiety or habit lock-in? Examples raised in the source include free removal of the old product, immediate delivery, a no-questions trial period and engaging couples together.
Reconstruct the ending only after the story is complete; the authors argue only a full narrative allows you to change how the story ends.
Prioritise the force that appears strongest in interviews for your market, rather than assuming every category faces the same barrier profile.
caveats: The four-force framing is the authors' Jobs Theory model, not a validated scoring system.
Barrier examples come from a single mattress interview and are hypotheses to test, not proven levers.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Depth over Breadth: Why Fewer, Richer Interviews Beat Large Samples
cards.summary: Collect many data points per person from a small sample instead of a few data points from a huge sample, because innovation insight comes from depth rather than breadth.
cards.use_when: Designing qualitative research, deciding between a survey and interviews, or when quantitative data shows patterns without explaining them
steps: Choose a small sample of customers who have recently made a real purchase decision, rather than a large random sample of the general market.

Interview each person for a long, unscripted session covering the full story of the decision: where they were, what they were feeling, what they had tried before, who was present, what almost stopped them.
Keep a beginner's mind during interviews. The source warns that pre-existing assumptions can filter out critical information before you notice it.
Resist stopping at the first coherent explanation. Keep probing the emotional and social dimensions alongside the functional one.
Treat each single interview as a source of hypotheses, not conclusions. Look for what recurs across a cluster of interviews before acting.
Compare what people say they want with what they actually did, as the source notes these often diverge.
Use the resulting storyboards as the raw material for a job spec, not as statistically representative findings.
caveats: Qualitative depth does not replace statistical validation of a hypothesis once it is formed.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Writing a Job Spec: From Customer Job to Design Blueprint
cards.summary: Translate a multifaceted customer job into an innovator-side spec covering functional, emotional and social dimensions, tradeoffs, competitors and obstacles.
cards.use_when: Moving from customer research to product, offer or experience design for a new or repositioned product
steps: Start from the customer-side job statement: the circumstance and the progress the customer is trying to make.
Write the spec from the innovator's point of view, answering: what must I design, develop and deliver so this job is solved well?

Include the functional dimension (what the product must do), the emotional dimension (how the customer wants to feel) and the social dimension (how they want to be seen, e.g. as a good spouse or parent).
State the tradeoffs the customer is willing to make, such as accepting assembly, delay or higher price in exchange for speed, control or certainty.
List the full set of competing solutions that must be beaten, including non-obvious alternatives (for the mattress buyer, painkillers and energy drinks counted as competition).
List the obstacles and anxieties that must be overcome, and pair each with a planned experience that surmounts it.

Use the spec as the blueprint for purchase and use experiences. The source argues that without a clear job spec, even advanced products are likely to fail because there are too many details to guess right.
caveats: The source presents this as a framework, not a template with fixed fields; adapt the dimensions to the category.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Competing with Nonconsumption and Unlikely Alternatives
cards.summary: Identify the real competitive set by looking at what customers hire instead of your product, including workarounds, adjacent categories and doing nothing.
cards.use_when: Doing competitive analysis, category positioning or identifying barriers to adoption in a low-penetration market
steps: List obvious competitors, then deliberately add: workaround behaviours, product substitutes, borrowing, postponement and nonconsumption.
In the mattress example, the effective competitors included painkillers, energy drinks and the old mattress itself, not just rival mattress brands.

In the Medtronic India pacemaker case, the team visited hospitals and care facilities and interviewed over a hundred physicians, nurses, administrators and patients, and identified four barriers: lack of patient awareness, lack of proper diagnostics, inability to navigate the care pathway, and affordability.
Treat the largest barrier as the biggest competitor. Medtronic's main competition in India was nonconsumption, because patients could not complete the pathway to treatment.

Design the offer to remove those barriers, as Medtronic did with screening clinics, a loan programme approved within two days with minimum paperwork and no asset mortgage, and patient counsellor ('Sherpa') roles to help patients navigate hospital bureaucracy.

Test assumptions about what customers want with actual customers: Medtronic initially assumed patients wanted loans forgiven at death, then learned families often preferred to rally funds, making a bridge loan the better fit.
Where a partner capability removes a barrier (financing, logistics, counselling), build the relationship rather than assuming your product alone must solve everything.
caveats: Medtronic's results are a case example, not a promise; the source reports screening, counselling and treatment counts under one programme.
Barrier sets are market-specific and must be re-researched for each geography.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Selling Experiences, Not Features: The Resume That Gets You Hired
cards.summary: Create the right set of purchase and use experiences around a clearly defined job so the product's 'resume' earns the hire, which is harder for competitors to copy than features.
cards.use_when: Differentiating in a category where features are easily copied, or justifying a premium price
steps: Accept the source's claim that new products succeed because of the experiences they enable, not the features they offer.
Design the full experience chain around the job: discovery, purchase, delivery, setup, first use, repeat use and any post-purchase service.

Reduce friction at every step where the customer could stumble: examples from the source include child-care areas, flat-pack cartons that fit in a car, a single included tool stored inside the packaging, and a café or ice-cream reward at the end of the trip.

Examine small packaging details for experiential value: American Girl deliberately kept a belly band and tissue paper that added about two cents and twenty-seven seconds per box, because the small delay of opening made the moment more exciting.

Map where customers currently pay a premium because they are trapped or interdependent (printer ink, chargers) versus where they are grateful to pay; the source distinguishes resentment pricing from genuine premium pricing for a solved job.
Use the experience set to organise company processes, not just marketing, since the source argues integration around the job is what produces durable advantage.
Test whether the experience is repeatable enough to be woven into customers' lives; the reward for nailing a job is not brand fame but being hired and hired again.
caveats: The premium-price argument is the authors' interpretation, illustrated with cases such as IKEA, Uber and American Girl; it is not a tested formula for any specific category.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Structuring the Business Around Jobs Instead of Demographics
cards.summary: Organise products, stores and processes around a shared job rather than a demographic segment, which produces experiences competitors cannot easily reverse-engineer.
cards.use_when: Reconsidering audience segmentation, store or site structure, or how to defend against copycat competitors
steps: Identify the shared circumstance-based job that spans demographics rather than defining the target by age, income or gender. IKEA serves anyone furnishing a place fast, such as a student moving to a new city for a doctoral programme.
Accept that competitors can copy products, prices and store layouts, but the experience set built around the job is much harder to replicate.

Design operational choices directly from the job: furnish-the-place-today implies immediate availability, cartons that fit in a car, simple assembly with one included tool, and a way to occupy children during the trip.

Evaluate the tradeoffs customers will accept in exchange for speed and certainty, since the source argues the full cost of a failed solution (wasted time, frustration, repeated spending) makes a premium look small.
Recognise that disruptive entrants usually do not have a better sense of the job; they see only the product. This is why the experience layer is a defensible advantage.
Apply the same logic online: structure navigation, bundles and content around jobs and circumstances rather than around demographic cohorts or internal product categories.
Re-examine existing merchandising that assumes impulse behaviour; the source cautions that a Costco mattress purchase looked impulsive but followed a year of deliberation.
caveats: Job-based reorganisation is a strategic claim from the authors, illustrated with IKEA and American Girl, not a repeatable step-by-step process.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Designing Against Anxiety: Anticipating Objections Before the Purchase
cards.summary: Actively design experiences that defuse the anxieties blocking a purchase, especially spouse approval, disposal of the old product and fear of choosing wrong.
cards.use_when: Reducing pre-purchase hesitation on considered purchases such as furniture, mattresses or high-ticket items
steps: Identify the specific anxieties named by customers in interviews rather than general low-intent signals. In the mattress case these were: fear of store salespeople, fear the spouse would criticise the choice, uncertainty about getting rid of the old mattress, and worry that the new one might not suit.

Where the product is shared by a household, design for the decision being made with another person present or absent. The source asks whether stores should handle the case where only one spouse is in the store, and suggests engaging couples differently.
Give the accompanying decision-maker a direct experience: in the example, the wife could touch the mattress and give her blessing, which removed a major anxiety.
Reduce trial risk with mechanisms such as a ninety-day free trial with no questions asked, immediate delivery, or free removal of the old product.
Use return policies as explicit anxiety-reducing signals; Costco's easy returns were named as the final barrier removed before purchase.
Consider bundles and partnerships that remove adjacent friction, such as pairing with local movers so the move and the furniture happen together.

Test whether staff should be repositioned around the customer's outcome (for example sleep experts rather than mattress-feature experts), which the source raises as a hypothesis affecting hiring, training and compensation.
caveats: These are hypotheses generated from a single interview in the source, not validated programme results.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Reviews as Job-Matching Evidence
cards.summary: Understand that online reviews work by letting buyers find reviewers who share their job, and manage reviews as a two-sided asset that also tells wrong-fit customers not to buy.
cards.use_when: Optimising product pages, managing marketplace reputation, or deciding what review content to surface
steps: Recognise that buyers often skip the feature spec and go straight to review counts and answered questions to judge whether the product fits their job.
Surface reviews by use case, not just average rating: the source's example is wanting to know whether a toaster oven heats a frozen pizza, not whether it browns toast evenly.

Encourage and highlight reviews from verified purchasers and those voted helpful, and account for recency; Amazon introduced automated weighting for newer reviews, verified purchases and helpful votes in 2015.
Treat negative reviews as a fit signal to manage. The source argues reviews are the first era in which a business must communicate who should not hire its product.

Set expectations honestly in listings so wrong-fit buyers self-select out. Airbnb advises hosts to describe neighbourhood character, quietness or centrality accurately, because overselling quickly produces poor reviews.

Use post-purchase follow-up to resolve problems before they become reviews; sellers on Amazon routinely email buyers shortly after delivery and use no-hassle refunds or replacements to preempt public complaints.

Note the source's cited figures that up to 95 percent of consumers use reviews and 86 percent call them essential, with nearly a third of consumers under forty-five consulting them for every purchase. Verify with your own market data before relying on them.
caveats: The 95/86/one-third figures are cited from external research in the source and are dated; validate against current data for your category.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Building a Purpose Brand Around One Job
cards.summary: Aim for a purpose brand that becomes synonymous with a specific job, which produces price premiums, recall without heavy advertising, and protection from disruption.
cards.use_when: Developing brand positioning, naming a product line, or deciding whether to extend a brand into new categories
steps: Define the job your brand should own in the customer's mind and check it against the examples the source cites as purpose brands, such as Uber, TurboTax, FedEx, OnStar and IKEA.

Design the product and experience to do that job repeatedly and well, since the source argues purpose brands are built by being hired successfully, not primarily through advertising. FedEx became a verb through repeated successful hires.

Use distinct product names tied to specific jobs where the parent brand is generic: Milwaukee's Sawzall and HOLE HAWG own their job markets and have held over 80 percent share for decades, while the Milwaukee name alone does not.
Be wary of adding features and benefits purely for marketplace news or price justification, which the source says erodes a purpose brand; it cites Volvo as a cautionary example.
Where a brand lacks a job anchor, expect category-placeholder status and price competition alongside look-alike rivals, such as airlines, automakers and car-rental firms.
Check whether the brand helps the customer stop searching ('Your search is over, pick me') rather than merely being recognisable.
caveats: Purpose-brand claims and the 80 percent share figure for Milwaukee are presented by the authors and are not independently evidenced in the text.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Avoiding Feature-Only Research: What Traditional Panels Miss
cards.summary: Traditional panel and survey research reveals functional preferences but misses the experiences and obstacles that determine whether customers actually adopt a solution.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a research plan that relies mainly on doctor or expert panels, feature-preference surveys or disease/behaviour statistics
steps: Recognise the limitation the source describes: Medtronic was good at understanding functional jobs, and ran physician panels plus quantitative surveys to validate new pacemaker features, yet the products did not sell as hoped in India.

Add research with the broader stakeholder set, not only the purchasing expert (doctors) or the end user. The Medtronic team interviewed physicians, nurses, hospital administrators and patients across India.
Look for experience barriers that feature research cannot reveal, such as a thirty-second GP visit, symptom ambiguity, an unfamiliar referral system, and out-of-pocket costs.
Check whether the product's advocates and end users differ; in ecommerce terms, the person who compares features may not be the person who decides or the person who must be persuaded after purchase.
Reframe the research question from 'what features do you want' to 'why would you want to hire this and what gets in the way'.
Use qualitative findings to define the barrier list, then use later quantitative work to size and prioritise the barriers rather than to generate them.
caveats: Based on a medical-device case; principles transfer to considered ecommerce purchases but specific numbers do not.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Recognising an Insight: It Feels True on Conception
cards.summary: A genuine jobs insight lands as intuitively true and is contrarian, seeing something others have missed; in hindsight it seems obvious, but it rarely was.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a research finding is a real insight worth building on or just an interesting data point
steps: Apply the source's test, attributed to Gerald Zaltman: an insight is a thought experienced as true on conception, requiring no self-persuasion about its importance.

Check for contrarianism: if the finding simply confirms the category's conventional wisdom, it is unlikely to be a breakthrough. The mattress buyer looked like an impulse purchase but had deliberated for a year.
Expect hindsight bias. The source notes breakthrough insights look obvious once found, which is why they are easy for competitors to dismiss afterwards.
Design a solution that exceeds what customers themselves could articulate they wanted; the source argues customers often cannot describe what they want, and their actions may contradict their words.

Use insights to build the narrative and storyboard, then continue into experience design and organisational integration. The source stresses that uncovering the job is only the first step and that you are selling progress, not products.
caveats: Feeling true is a subjective signal, not validation; the source pairs it with continued research and clustered interviews.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Using Job Research to Generate Retail and Marketing Hypotheses
cards.summary: Convert depth interviews into testable hypotheses about store staffing, couple engagement, partnerships and advertising rather than jumping to conclusions from one interview.
cards.use_when: Turning qualitative job research into a prioritised roadmap of experiments for a retailer or brand
steps: Be explicit that a single interview supports hypotheses only; the authors caution that jobs discovery is about clustering insights, not one eureka.

Form hypotheses from the observed tension. From the mattress interview, examples include: salespeople focus on features and price when the job is sleep; the ideal store experience may need sleep experts rather than mattress experts, with effects on hiring, training and compensation.
Add hypotheses about shared decisions: when couples will both use the product, how should the experience change when only one spouse is present?

Add hypotheses about adjacent friction, such as partnering with local movers to bundle a deal with the move, offering immediate delivery, free removal of the old product, or a ninety-day no-questions trial.

Add hypotheses about demand generation for the manufacturer: if success depends on the in-store experience, advertising should communicate the benefits that actually drive store visits and sales, not just product performance.
Prioritise further interviews to fill gaps in the storyboard rather than running a large survey immediately.
Track which hypotheses survive subsequent interviews before committing major investment.
caveats: All hypotheses in the source derive from one interview and are explicitly framed as starting points.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Jobs Theory and Design Thinking as Complementary Approaches
cards.summary: Jobs Theory supplies the causal explanation and language for customer insight, which complements design thinking's emphasis on empathy, divergent thinking and rapid iteration.
cards.use_when: Reconciling an existing design-thinking or human-centred design process with jobs-based research
steps: Note the common ground the source identifies: design thinking prioritises users' experiences over product attributes, which aligns with jobs thinking.
Use jobs language to explain why customers will embrace some innovations and not others, giving the design process a causal frame rather than only an empathic one.
Feed job specs and storyboards into divergent ideation so concepts are generated against a defined job rather than against product attributes.
Check that the resulting experiences address the functional, emotional and social dimensions identified in the job research before iterating on form and features.
Treat the two approaches as compatible rather than competing, and pick the framing that produces clearer specifications for your team.
caveats: This is a positioning observation by the authors about their own theory, not an empirical comparison of methods.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Purpose brand: own a job, not a category
cards.summary: Integrate the brand around one clear Job to Be Done so customers think of you automatically, instead of becoming a price-competing category placeholder.
cards.use_when: Deciding brand positioning or evaluating whether feature/benefit expansion is diluting what the brand stands for
steps: Identify the specific job the brand is associated with and check whether it has become the default answer in customers' minds (the source notes strong brands like Google and Starbucks became verbs for their job and were built with minimal advertising).

Recognize the failure mode: brands that don't integrate around a job become category placeholders forced to compete on price with look-alike competitors (source cites airlines, automakers, business hotel chains, rental cars, PC clones).
Use the purpose brand as an internal filter: a clear job makes explicit which features and improvements are relevant and which are irrelevant, guiding product, marketing and advertising decisions.
Treat it as an economic asset: the source argues purpose brands create differentiation, premium pricing and growth potential.
Watch for erosion when the company chases 'news' or price justification through added benefits rather than deepening the job.
caveats: Brand status is hard to regain once lost; the source treats Volvo's post-1999 shift toward flashier cars as a cautionary case where a safety purpose brand weakened and recovery was slow.
The 'ultimate competitive advantage' framing is the source's strong claim, not a guaranteed outcome.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Write a job spec before designing the solution
cards.summary: Capture the full richness of the customer's job in a job spec covering functional, emotional and social dimensions, tradeoffs, competitors and anxieties, then use it as the innovation blueprint.
cards.use_when: After customer research has surfaced a job and you need to translate it into requirements for a product, service or experience
steps: Document the functional, emotional and social dimensions that define the desired progress the customer wants.
Record the tradeoffs the customer is willing to make (what they will accept or give up to get the job done).
List the full set of competing solutions that must be beaten, not just direct product competitors.
Identify the obstacles and anxieties that must be overcome for the customer to switch or to succeed with the solution.
Treat the job spec as the blueprint for innovation: it should be detailed enough to guide design of the product and of the purchase and use experiences.
caveats: A job is rich and complex; a thin or purely functional spec will produce a solution that misses what customers actually need.
The source insists solutions must be complete, meaning core product plus purchase and use experiences; a good product alone is not enough.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Treat every complete solution as a service
cards.summary: Even product companies must design the full experience of purchase and use, because a complete solution to a job always functions like a service.
cards.use_when: When your product is strong but customers still struggle to buy, onboard or get value from it
steps: Map the customer's end-to-end experience of buying and using your offering, not just the product itself.
Identify obstacles or anxieties at each step that could stop the customer from hiring you or from firing their current solution.
Design deliberate experiences that remove those obstacles, since the source argues all successful job solutions ultimately behave like services even for product companies.
Check for misalignment: the purchase and use experience must match what the job spec requires, not what is convenient for internal functions.
caveats: This is a design principle, not a claim that every company must literally sell a subscription or service.
The source's examples come from healthcare, automotive and education; the transfer to ecommerce is that checkout, delivery, onboarding and support all count as part of the solution.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Integrate processes around the job, not the org chart
cards.summary: Competitive advantage comes from proprietary cross-functional processes that deliver the customer's job, and large reorganizations usually fail to create that value.
cards.use_when: When restructuring seems like the answer to growth or execution problems, or when functions deliver in silos
steps: Before reorganizing, ask how different parts of the organization interact to systematically deliver the offering that performs the customer's job; that is what matters more than reporting lines.
Note the source's evidence: a 2010 Bain study found fewer than one-third of major reorganizations delivered material improvement, and many destroyed value.
Look for the missing role: in most companies nobody owns understanding and delivering the customer's job, so assign stewardship of the job.
Deliberately define new processes and coordination mechanisms where functions are usually siloed.
Accept that traditional structures and functions will persist, so move toward job-centricity through processes, metrics and culture rather than a single sweeping reorg.
caveats: The source explicitly says large-scale reorgs are usually not practical and traditional structures have value; this is not a call to abolish functions.
Building job-centered processes is described as very hard and slow, not a quick fix.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Shift complexity from the customer to your processes
cards.summary: Job-aligned processes should absorb the nuisance work customers would otherwise do themselves, leaving them with positive experience and progress.
cards.use_when: When customers abandon or stall because of friction such as paperwork, coordination or repeated follow-up
steps: Identify the steps where the customer currently carries complexity (finding information, chasing documents, coordinating multiple parties, navigating policies).
Redesign internal processes so the vendor takes on that work instead of the customer.

Use SNHU as the example: it moved from mailing packages and waiting weeks for the prospect to follow up, to tracking response time in minutes with a goal of calling back in under ten minutes, asking permission on the call to chase transcripts, and paying the transcript fee itself.
Measure the outcome the customer cares about (how quickly they get a decision and complete information) rather than the volume of internal activity like packages sent.
caveats: The SNHU results are a case example, not a guaranteed return for other businesses.
Removing customer complexity usually raises internal cost and process intensity; the source argues this pays off through acquisition and premium pricing, but that tradeoff should be tested.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Measure customer-benefit metrics, not internal activity
cards.summary: Replace internal financial and activity metrics with externally relevant measures of whether the customer's job got done.
cards.use_when: When dashboards full of conversion, retention or cost metrics don't explain whether customers are actually succeeding
steps: Define metrics that track the customer benefit tied to the specific job, and use them to steer processes.

Use the source's examples as patterns: SNHU tracks minutes to respond to an inquiry; Amazon tracks when orders are delivered, not when they are shipped; Intuit builds a unique metric set per product tied to the specific benefit delivered.
Ask questions like: how much time did we save this customer, did we spare them work they didn't want to do, did we improve their cash flow.
Recognize that the right metrics often don't fall out of existing systems; Intuit reports interpolating survey and server data to estimate things like labor hours avoided.
Treat the right job spec as the origin of the right processes, which in turn generate the right data for judging performance.
caveats: Internal revenue metrics can mislead: the source describes Intuit forcing trial users to register by phone to enable upsells, which created friction and focused people on revenue rather than the customer benefit.
Customer-benefit measurement is described as genuinely hard and not automatically available from systems.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Process optimization needs a job-alignment factor
cards.summary: Efficiency alone can make you better at the wrong things; optimize processes for efficiency and alignment with the customer's job.
cards.use_when: When process improvement, automation or cost reduction is underway and you need a criterion beyond throughput
steps: Add an explicit job-alignment check to any optimization effort: does this change improve delivery of the customer's job?
Remember the source's warning that optimizing an unaligned process means getting better and better at doing the wrong thing.
Use Amazon as the pattern: it starts from the customer and the metrics that matter for the customer, and works backward to processes for vast selection, low prices and fast delivery.
Accept ambidexterity: processes should be both efficient and flexible, because how you solve a job changes over time even though the job itself is stable.
Stay attached to the job, not to today's solution, so you don't bend the definition of the job to fit the process.
caveats: The source's point is that textbook process optimization is insufficient, not that efficiency is unimportant.
Flexibility has costs; the claim is that job attachment justifies them when the job is well understood.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Use subroutines to make process reuse deliberate
cards.summary: Instead of informally sharing best practices, identify repeatable process modules that can be reused wherever the same operation is needed.
cards.use_when: When scaling operations across regions, product lines or channels and each team reinvents the same steps
steps: For each process step, ask whether this process or subroutine is likely to be needed in other activities.
Treat the organization as a collection of processes, each a string of subroutines, some custom and some modular imports, aligned to the customer's job.
Keep some pieces persistent and let others change over time, mirroring the programming use of subroutines that reduce development and maintenance cost while improving quality and reliability.
Use the Amazon model of shared platform, technology and guiding principles across businesses so teams can move fast.
caveats: The source presents this as a principle imported from software engineering, illustrated by Amazon, not as a universal implementation recipe.
Modular reuse can conflict with local adaptation; the alignment with the job is the tie-breaker.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Start every innovation from the job-spec press release
cards.summary: Frame a new offering by writing the customer-facing announcement first, so experience and process decisions derive from the job it will be hired to do.
cards.use_when: Kicking off a new product, feature or service, especially when engineering or channel ownership is fragmented
steps: Write a mock press release describing what the customer will be able to accomplish and the job the product is hired for.
Present it to everyone whose work will contribute to fulfilling that job, including engineers, analysts and marketing, not just the product owner.
Derive all experiences and processes from the clarity of that stated job, and keep the group aligned even if different people own different pieces of the product.
Treat Amazon's use of this practice as the source's example of starting from the customer and designing backward.
caveats: The press release is a framing device, not a substitute for customer research into the job.
The source does not describe the full Amazon document or approval process; treat details beyond the framing as outside the source.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Give the customer's job an internal owner
cards.summary: Assign stewardship of end-to-end job delivery, because functions and product lines rarely have anyone accountable for the customer's job.
cards.use_when: When customers experience a broken journey across handoffs and each function believes it is doing its job
steps: Check whether any role is responsible for understanding and consistently delivering the customer's job across functions.
Use the intensive care example: post-surgical patients died because the critical-care job had no owner in any existing medical function, until Dwight Harken created the concept and the ICU.

Empower a process owner over a job-facing sequence, following the Mayo Clinic pattern where one person takes charge of coordinating specialties, data and sequencing for the visit, with specialists keeping open slots for real-time needs.
Ask the diagnostic question Harken asked: everyone is doing what they are supposed to and all processes work as designed, so why is the customer outcome still failing?
caveats: This does not require a full reorganization; the source says stewardship can be achieved through processes, metrics and culture.
The Mayo and ICU cases are healthcare examples; in ecommerce the transferable idea is owning the end-to-end job journey across teams.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Run meetings focused on the job to avoid politics
cards.summary: A recurring cross-functional forum centered on the customer's job gives diverse specialists a shared language and prevents debate from collapsing into opinions and turf.
cards.use_when: When cross-functional teams argue from their own professional backgrounds instead of solving the customer's problem
steps: Convene senior staff from across the organization regularly, as the source describes the CFPB's policy committee doing weekly for two hours.
Direct the entire conversation to one job to be done and what tools will be used over time to address it.
Invite each participant to bring their expertise and opinions on solving that job, rather than defending their function's mission.

Design the organization so groups with potentially conflicting past-focused and future-focused missions share a division and a job, as the source describes merging enforcement with supervision, and research with markets and regulation.
Use the job as the rallying cause: if you don't focus on a job, the source says people focus on their scars and politics.
caveats: This is drawn from the CFPB setup under Elizabeth Warren, a regulatory context; the transferable mechanism is the job-focused meeting, not the specific divisional structure.
The source warns of a typical DC paralysis risk that the job focus was designed to avoid.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Beware stack fallacy when moving into adjacent solutions
cards.summary: Technical strength in your layer does not mean you understand the customer one level up, so moving up the stack requires first-hand empathy for that customer's context.
cards.use_when: When considering a product extension or new service built on your existing technology or supply strength
steps: Check whether you have first-hand understanding of what customers one level above your current offering actually want and the context in which they use it.
Watch for the tendency to dismiss the downstream application as trivial, which the source calls stack fallacy.

Note the cautionary case: Ford and Qualcomm had deep technical capability but Wingcast, announced in 2000 for a 2003 launch, was scrapped two years later, while OnStar succeeded by focusing on the job rather than the product spec.
Import the principle outside tech: growing herbs and cooking for yourself does not prepare you to run a restaurant, and the source notes eight out of ten restaurants fail within five years.
caveats: The restaurant failure figure is the source's illustration, not a claim about your market.
The source frames stack fallacy as highlighting the same hazard as Jobs Theory, not as a rigorous predictive model.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Find the job in moments of struggle, not feature lists
cards.summary: OnStar initially bundled cool features as brochure ware, but the real job emerged only when the team listened to actual customer calls at moments of crisis.
cards.use_when: When your product has many features but customers churn because they don't need most of them
steps: Note the initial failure pattern: OnStar was a bundle of novelty features, fun at first but treated as a toy, and customers canceled because the concierge features were nice but not necessary.
Have the whole team listen directly to real customer interactions; the source describes requiring all 300 OnStar staff to spend an hour on live call-center calls.
Identify the circumstances of struggle that reveal the job: accidents, cars still moving, people screaming, and later late-night driving in unfamiliar places.

Reframe features around the job: directions became less about finding a restaurant and more about being routed through safe streets; diagnostics became about deciding what to do right now when the check-engine light comes on at 2 a.m.
Let the job explain surprising data: Chevy buyers subscribed at the same rate as Cadillac buyers because peace of mind is essential, not a luxury upgrade.
caveats: The source attributes OnStar's ultimate success to this job focus and to process innovation, not to the features it launched with.
Listening to calls is described as revealing and uncomfortable work, not a one-off survey.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Repeat time-consuming research at each execution stage
cards.summary: Features and collateral are not enough when a growing team loses touch with customer reality; direct exposure to real interactions must be repeated as the company scales.
cards.use_when: When a growing organization is making decisions from data and internal assumptions rather than customer contact
steps: Embed recurring direct customer exposure into how teams work, rather than treating it as a one-time study.

Design products and stages so internal rewards don't distort activity: the source notes that features and collateral that kept staff busy for a year didn't stop the team from lacking strong product choices at execution stage.
Notice when success in one phase (planning, collateral, sales materials) masks weakness in the next (actual product, execution).
Use the principle that understanding moments of struggle changes not only design but also how you interact with customers in those situations.
caveats: The source does not prescribe a research cadence or sample size; it argues for repeated direct exposure as the company grows.
Attribution here is the source's interpretation; it is not an experimentally validated rule.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Build process flexibility to match faster technology cycles
cards.summary: When your delivery technology iterates much faster than your host industry's validation cycle, create deliberate mid-cycle processes or you will ship outdated versions.
cards.use_when: When your product depends on rapidly improving technology embedded in a slow-moving hardware, channel or regulatory environment
steps: Diagnose the cycle mismatch: automotive development took three to five years with cars staying on the market up to ten years, while wireless technology improved faster.
Decide explicitly whether to enter at all if the standard validation rules cannot be suspended; the OnStar CEO said otherwise they'd sell eight-track tapes while others sold CDs.
Create your own mid-cycle processes and tests in cooperation with the existing validation teams, using your own staff expertise to meet the parent organization's overall quality standards.
Test across every plausible combination: different car models, windows down, pouring rain, CD player on, airbag deployed.
Recognize that even when competitors buy your technology, their slower processes may leave them a generation behind.
caveats: This required going outside the normal approval and validation sequence, described as very hard in an established organization.
The competitive advantage came from the process set as much as the product; simply owning the technology was not sufficient.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Make channel incentives a process design problem
cards.summary: A dealer or partner whose economics don't reward selling your offering can quietly kill it, so design the channel process and incentive around the job.
cards.use_when: When a partner or channel is the front line of purchase and your offering is a small share of their revenue
steps: Quantify what the partner actually earns: the source notes a dealership got a 20 percent cut of ten dollars in monthly OnStar fees, trivial compared with adding heated seats to a sale.
Expect that sales staff will avoid offerings with complicated value explanations and low commissions, so build simple explanations and account for their economics.

Anticipate the questions that derail a sale, such as whether the service is satellite or cell-phone based, whether someone always knows the driver's location, and whether someone can eavesdrop, and prepare clear answers.
Improve processes iteratively based on what you learn in the channel, rather than assuming the first design is right.
Treat service as an integrated product carried through the channel, not an add-on feature on a spec sheet.
caveats: The specific 20 percent and ten-dollar figures are from the source's OnStar example, not a general benchmark.
Channel incentives differ by market and contract structure; verify your own economics rather than copying these numbers.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Take responsibility for customer business outcomes
cards.summary: Shift from selling training modules or tools to owning the customer's transformation, and spend R&D on process innovation that shifts complexity away from the client.
cards.use_when: When your category is vulnerable to budget cuts because clients see it as a discretionary product purchase
steps: Identify the critical jobs to be done for customers, such as sales transformation rather than sales training supply.
Take responsibility for helping customers achieve their business goals, as FranklinCovey did when it moved from selling its own products to optimizing customer outcomes.
Direct R&D toward process innovation: the source reports FranklinCovey spends two-thirds of its R&D budget on process innovation to make rollout cheaper, faster and easier.

Address customer capacity constraints: Marriott could dedicate nearly ten full-time staff to a program, but most customers cannot, so designing for lighter-touch implementation becomes part of the offering.
Set expectations correctly; the source warns it is no good if clients sign up for an exercise class and discover they must climb Mount Everest.
caveats: The source reports FranklinCovey doubled revenue and increased profit tenfold over six years, but this is a case example, not a forecast for other firms.
Taking responsibility for outcomes increases scope and risk compared with selling a bounded product.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Diagnose your organization's immune system
cards.summary: Unchanged processes and local resource-allocation habits can reject a validated idea before it ships; treating process change as an immune response helps you plan for it.
cards.use_when: When a research-backed improvement keeps dying in implementation despite good evidence
steps: Trace where the idea stops: the source describes the fast-food company rejecting changes recommended to boost milkshake sales because local managers judged changes to routine processes and resource allocations too difficult.
Recognize that absence of a process is still a process; things get done chaotically and that is a warning sign, not a neutral state.
Expect that new processes introduced into an established organization are very hard, and that solutions may look impractical financially or cumbersome culturally.
Prepare for the gravitational pull of existing processes by planning coordination mechanisms, incentives and metrics before rollout.
Use jobs alignment as the criterion for whether a process should persist or change.
caveats: The milkshake example ended in a quiet death of the idea; the source uses it to show how internal forces defeat good ideas, not to claim all process changes fail.
Deming's line that if you can't describe what you are doing as a process then you don't know what you are doing is the source's framing, not an operational rule.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Use the job spec to review experiences and obstacles
cards.summary: The source's leader questions turn a job spec into an audit of whether current solutions address every detail, obstacle and stage of the customer's experience.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a product line, customer journey or growth plan against the job you believe you are hired for
steps: List the most critical details that must be included in the job spec for your target job.
Identify the obstacles that currently get in customers' way while they try to make progress.
Check whether current solutions address every one of those details, not just the functional core.
Map the experiences of purchase and use customers actually have and compare them with what the job spec requires.
Define where to improve, and ask how the organization ensures the customer's job guides product development, marketing and customer service decisions.
Check whether the functions involved in the customer's experience support the job in a coordinated way or whether they conflict.
caveats: These are diagnostic questions from the source, not a validated scoring instrument.
Answers will be organization-specific; the exercise is meant to surface misalignment, not produce a benchmark.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: The Three Fallacies of Innovation Data
cards.summary: Growing companies drift from customer jobs because operators fall for three data traps: active-vs-passive data, surface growth, and conforming data.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why a once jobs-focused ecommerce brand now chases product lines, channel metrics or exec pet projects instead of customer progress.
steps: Name the three fallacies explicitly in a leadership review so the team has shared language: (1) Active versus Passive Data — after launch, spreadsheets about sales, customers, assets and competitors crowd out the messy context-of-struggle data that revealed the job. (2) Surface Growth — sunk investment in customer relationships creates incentive to sell more products to existing customers or solve more jobs, rather than solving the core job better. (3) Conforming Data — data gets shaped to support the preexisting business model and the functional agenda of whoever presents it.

For each, ask what evidence would show you are in it: are decisions driven mainly by product-mix and channel dashboards? Is the catalog or SKU count growing faster than clarity about who each item is for? Does each function bring data that conveniently supports its own plan?
Treat awareness as only the first step — chronic exposure requires ongoing vigilance, a named owner and intervention, not a one-off workshop.
Keep the reference to Levitt/Drucker: customers buy the quarter-inch hole, not the drill; product-defined self-image is the root cause of the drift.
caveats: The fallacies describe tendencies in the authors' research and experience, not a measured law; treat as diagnostic lenses.
The V8 case (sales quadrupled in under a year after re-framing against vegetables) is a single anecdote, not a benchmark or promise.

Reorganizations are usually impractical; the authors recommend embedding jobs focus in processes, metrics and culture over time rather than large reorgs. A cited 2010 Bain study of 57 major reorganizations found fewer than one-third produced meaningful performance improvement.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Passive Data Needs Active Management
cards.summary: The context-rich signal that reveals a job has no voice, structure or champion, so leaders must deliberately give it a standing role in decisions.
cards.use_when: Setting up research cadence and decision rights so customer-job evidence survives contact with the operating dashboard.
steps: Recognize that passive data — the unfiltered context of customers' struggles, frustrations, workarounds and undesirable tradeoffs — is always present but never loud, and has no champion or agenda.

Because the job itself does not change much while operations data changes constantly, managers naturally respond to the loud operations signal; install a counterweight rather than relying on good intentions.
Assign a specific person or forum to own and present job evidence in innovation and investment decisions, so it competes on equal footing with product, sales and finance data.

In early-stage or new-opportunity work, act as a puzzle solver rather than a number cruncher: seek out nonconsumption and workarounds, assemble the narrative of the struggle, and relentlessly ask why.
Design processes to be flexible so the way you solve the job can adapt as circumstances change, instead of freezing one interpretation of the job into policy.
caveats: Passive data is qualitative and context-dependent; it is directionally helpful, not objective reality, and will not survive being reduced to a single KPI.
The authors' argument that no customer has a job called 'I need to spend a couple of hours at the store' is an assertion about retail, not a general law.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Surface Growth vs. Solving the Core Job Better
cards.summary: Copying competitors' products or piling new jobs onto the same customers grows revenue on paper while diluting the job that won the customer.
cards.use_when: Evaluating catalog expansion, brand extension, line extensions or acquisition of adjacent product lines before committing.
steps: Flag surface growth when the logic for a new product is 'our existing customers could also buy this' or 'competitors sell it, so we can too' rather than 'this solves the same job better.'

Consider the DeWalt pattern: a brand built on a stellar radial arm saw expanded into aisles of imitative drills and clamps, often outsourced for cheap production; the authors argue that stealing revenue with lower-quality imitations is not a growth plan to count on.

Consider the New York Times pattern: serving many jobs for the same readers (unwind, stay current, feel informed, fill time productively) exposes you to a focused competitor for each job — The Economist for weekly briefing, TV for unwinding, free commuter papers for filling time.
Keep the job spec as the screen for expansion: if the new offer cannot be tied to the core job, expect customer confusion about what the brand is for and firing of the wrong product.
Watch the 'sweat the assets' pressure from sunk investment in production, IP and talent, especially under short-horizon shareholders — it is the mechanism that converts small add-ons into drift.
caveats: This does not forbid any expansion; it warns that expansion without a job rationale confuses customers and invites focused disrupters.

The V8 line proliferation (Spicy Hot, Lemon, Picante, Roasted Chicken, Low-sodium, Organic, Splash, V-Fusion + Tea) is the authors' illustrative example of lost clarity, not a measured failure of any specific flavor.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Conforming Data: Why You Miss the Obvious
cards.summary: Each function brings data that supports its own incentives, and decision 'leaps' are often pre-skewed before the meeting starts.
cards.use_when: Running innovation, range or investment reviews where sales, marketing, product and finance all present supporting numbers.
steps: Expect predictable positions: sales claims to know customer needs from constant contact; marketing proposes brand-leverage variants (new versions, flavors, colors, offers); product/R&D pushes features and technology; the business head pushes whatever can hit the P&L this year. Each arrives with carefully constructed supporting data.
Accept that none of these views is wrong but none is objective, and none models the customer's job — so a decision cannot be made simply by weighing the decks.

Counteract confirmation bias with Nate Silver's point: prediction failures cluster where we focus on signals that tell the story we want, not the story that is; and Holmes's 'nothing is more deceptive than the obvious fact.'

Apply Gerald Zaltman's cautions: decisions often 'happen' rather than get made, and a common error is treating facts as insights and leaping from data straight to action — data should fuel imaginative insight, not prove a point.
Before the meeting, publicly ask what data should be created and which dimensions should be ignored; senior leaders should invest as much in designing measurement as in analyzing it.
If a decision looks like A-vs-B, audit the layers beneath it to see whether the data was already skewed toward A before the leader entered.
caveats: This is a critique of decision process, not a claim that quantitative data is worthless — the point is that all data is man-made and embeds choices.
Psychological dissonance-avoidance is offered as an explanation of the pattern, not a tested organizational law.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: All Data Is Made by Someone with an Agenda
cards.summary: Numerical precision hides judgment: financials, big-data models and surveys all embed human choices about what to count.
cards.use_when: Choosing or defending a data source for a positioning or product decision, or when a team treats dashboards as ground truth.
steps: Stop privileging quantitative over qualitative on the assumption that only numbers are objective; both are abstractions from a more complex reality, and qualitative subjectivity is at least visible while numeric bias hides behind precision.

Recognize that financial-statement revenues, costs and profits result from estimation, negotiation, debate and politics in allocating overhead — Johnson and Kaplan showed these can grossly misstate true cost and profit.

Use the Google Flu Trends parable as the cautionary case: 50 million search terms matched against 1,152 data points overestimated US flu cases for more than two years; the Science analysis blamed 'algorithmic dynamics' and 'big data hubris' rooted in engineers' modeling choices. Just because search behavior can be computed does not make it valid data.
Ask who created this data, what they chose to collect, organize and present, and what meaning they inferred — data carries the agenda of its creator whether intended or not.
Keep Tom Monahan's 'Museum of False Precision' joke as a cultural shorthand for humility about dashboards.
caveats: The authors still call search-trend data directionally helpful; the objection is to treating it as objective reality, not to using it at all.
The Bobby Kennedy GNP passage and the author's son's HBS section-leader story are illustrative arguments about unmeasured value, not research findings.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Jobs as the Unit of Analysis: TurboTax's Shift from Interview to Done
cards.summary: Reframing from the product's internal component to the customer's desired outcome unlocks creativity and a clearer roadmap.
cards.use_when: When feature requests and backlog items pile up but no one can say which ones matter, or a core product step has become the optimization target itself.
steps: Notice the flawed unit of analysis: Intuit's team spent years perfecting the TurboTax interview (questions, data entry, accuracy) because that was the visible product surface.
Recognize that customers were not hiring TurboTax to get a better interview — they hired it to get their taxes done, and did not want to answer questions or enter data at all.

Reframe the goal to 'taxes are done' and let that drive the roadmap, even if the full vision takes a decade; Sasan Goodarzi's reframing produced an immediate burst of creativity once the team focused on the job.
