Pursue interim steps that reduce work for the customer, not just polish the existing flow: with permission, prefill data such as W-2 information pulled from payroll providers like ADP.

Use the 2015 experiment as the pattern: preloading data in just one 'chapter' of the questionnaire (there are roughly four to forty chapters depending on the taxpayer) produced a noticeable uptick in interview completion, even though customers still had to correct some auto-filled data.
Treat survey wish lists (customers asking for 150 features) as unusable without a job definition: Scott Cook's view is that feature requests without a job are 'like navigating without a compass.'
caveats: The chapter-prefill result is a company experiment, not a published benchmark or guaranteed lift.
Full 'no interview' TurboTax is described as years away; interim progress is still meaningful but incomplete.
Scott Cook frames the challenge of sustaining focus as an open question — 'the sixty-four-billion-dollar question' — rather than a solved management problem.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Four Organizational Benefits of a Jobs Focus
cards.summary: Jobs clarity pays off in decision autonomy, resource allocation, culture and measurement — four distinct levers, not one vague morale boost.
cards.use_when: Making the internal business case for adopting jobs-based language, or auditing which of the four benefits is actually missing.
steps: Distributed decision making with clarity of purpose: when the job is understood, employees at all levels can make good jobs-aligned decisions autonomously and innovate without escalation.
Align resources against what matters most — and free resources from what does not; jobs clarity makes it easier to decide what does and does not belong in the offer.
Inspire people and unify culture around what customers care about most, so individual workstreams have evident meaning.
Measure what matters most: customer progress, employee contributions and incentives — not only product and channel metrics.

Use the job as 'commander's intent': a well-articulated job spec lets people balance necessary tradeoffs without being told each time what to prioritize (what is most important, what cannot be compromised, what the ultimate goal is, what their role is).
Expect this to build over time through shared learning; a culture that forms around the job becomes self-managing and does not require rule enforcement.
caveats: The four categories are drawn from CEOs the authors interviewed, not from controlled study.
The authors acknowledge unanswered questions about how to keep teams consistently rallying around a hard goal; treat this as direction, not a complete operating system.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Why Mission Statements Fail as Daily Guides
cards.summary: Generic mission statements inspire but cannot arbitrate daily tradeoffs; a specific job spec can.
cards.use_when: When a company has a mission or purpose statement that nobody can translate into product, service or merchandising decisions.
steps: Test the mission against daily use: examples like 'to help all people live healthy lives,' 'to be the most respected financial services firm in the world' or 'to realize the tremendous potential of the railway' are too high-level and generic to guide action, decision making and innovation.

Keep the mission if it works as a theme, but do not mistake it for an operating guide — the authors compare mission statements to life themes like 'I want to be a good parent,' useful but not actionable alone.

Nest a job under the mission. Unilever's Lifebuoy kept the mission of helping children in emerging markets live to five, then specified the job: make handwashing actually happen in real circumstances.

Anchor the job in circumstances and thresholds: experts say thirty seconds of vigorous washing with soap and hot water eliminates germs, yet most people wash about seven seconds and rarely more than fifteen, and children hurry more; in India nearly 400,000 children under five died from diarrheal disease in a year at the time described — over a thousand deaths a day.

Design to the real circumstance, not the ideal one: color-changing soap signals when ten seconds is reached (sufficient with Unilever's special formula) and makes it more fun for children to stay with it.
Generalize the lesson: the more precisely you understand the job, the more it can connect internally and the more innovation it can drive.
caveats: The Lifebuoy outcome is a company success story (one of the fastest-growing brands in the period described), not a controlled trial of the job-framing method.
Health behavior thresholds cited are as reported by the source; do not restate them as current medical guidance outside that context.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Two-Sided Compass: Using the Job to Decide What Not to Do
cards.summary: A clear job definition narrows options productively — deciding what does not belong as much as what does — and speeds crisis decisions.
cards.use_when: Prioritizing a service, feature or benefit roadmap where everything looks technically feasible and marketable.
steps: Shift focus from cool 'brochure ware' features to benefits aligned with the job; OnStar's clarity that customers hired it for peace of mind while driving let the team judge what belonged in the suite and what did not.
Accept that narrowing feels limiting but provides clarity: less time and energy is spent evaluating options, and technical priorities become easier to rank.

Use the job as a compass heading for unanticipated events: when Hurricanes Katrina and Rita hit the Gulf Coast less than a month apart in 2005, OnStar's call center was flooded with panicked callers, some of whom were told mid-evacuation that real-time directions required a plan upgrade.

Decide by the job, not by the upsell opportunity: by Rita's approach the team treated these as regional crisis events, and the employee responsible for that business simply decided to give anyone calling from a crisis area all OnStar services immediately without requiring an upgrade — the founding CEO describes it as about a fifteen-second conversation.

Execute even when systems resist: OnStar had to build workarounds ('duct tape and Velcro') to detect calls from a crisis region and route them to a specialized team with evacuation routes and weather information.
Embed this in the team's instincts: when something clearly intersects the compass heading, people get on it rather than resisting 'one more thing'; clarity of purpose motivates the best work.
caveats: The fifteen-second decision was fast, but implementation was not — the source distinguishes deciding from executing and acknowledges imperfect workarounds.
OnStar's founding-CEO account is a single-company narrative, not evidence that any organization can replicate the autonomy.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Make Jobs the Common Language Across Functions
cards.summary: A one-syllable phrase gives marketing, engineering, sales and service a shared reference point instead of talking past each other.
cards.use_when: Cross-functional planning sessions where each department optimizes its own metrics and meetings end without alignment.
steps: Adopt jobs language as the integration layer: marketers, engineers, salespeople and customer service can communicate through it rather than through their own functional models.
Keep the articulation simple and unengineered — Jobs To Be Done is one-syllable words, and, as Mercer's Jacques Goulet puts it, its simplicity is what focuses the mind.
Expect strategy to be formed in everyday choices about resources, processes and priorities; jobs clarity is the 'intuitive playbook' employees draw on when no instruction exists.
Note the caveat that getting jobs-based goals right is hard — jobs are complex and nuanced and require deep understanding of the progress a customer is trying to make.
When done well, expect a productivity effect: clarity lets a much greater share of human capital be deployed with the right balance of autonomy and alignment.
caveats: The claimed productivity impact is a leadership observation from the authors' interviews, not a measured effect size.
Simple language does not mean simple analysis; the difficulty of defining jobs accurately is stated explicitly.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Leader Questions to Audit Jobs-Centeredness
cards.summary: A reusable question set reveals whether the customer's job is genuinely guiding product, marketing, service and investment decisions.
cards.use_when: Running a quarterly strategy or innovation review, or onboarding a new functional leader, to test alignment around customer progress.
steps: Ask whether the customer's job guides all critical decisions in product development, marketing and customer service.
Ask whether the functions that shape the customer experience (product, service, marketing, sales, after-sale service) support nailing the job in a coordinated way or are in conflict.
Ask what new processes could ensure more integrated delivery of the experiences the job requires.
Ask which elements of the end-to-end experience are most critical to perfectly solving the job, and what metrics would track performance against those elements.
Ask how people would characterize the fundamental business: in terms of solving an important job in customers' lives, or in terms of the products and services offered.

Ask what data drives innovation and investment decisions and how closely it connects to customers' jobs; probe specifically for surface growth — extra products sold to existing customers without understanding the progress customers seek.
Ask what mechanisms ensure the data presented reveals what you need to see rather than what is comfortable to believe, and how the job has a voice in resource allocation.

Follow the authors' process advice rather than restructuring: carefully set up and integrate the right processes, measure the right things, and over time embed jobs centricity in culture, building in flexibility so solutions can adapt.
caveats: These are the authors' diagnostic prompts, not a validated assessment instrument.
The process-over-reorg recommendation is a general argument; it does not guarantee culture change without sustained leadership attention.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Levitt and Drucker: The Drill-vs-Hole Disconnect
cards.summary: Customers buy solutions to problems, yet company behavior usually reveals a product-defined self-image — the core gap Jobs Theory addresses.
cards.use_when: Teaching or re-anchoring a team on customer-centric framing before writing positioning, roadmaps or campaign briefs.
steps: State the premise plainly: people do not want a quarter-inch drill, they want a quarter-inch hole; customers do not want products, they want solutions to their problems. The authors attribute the popularization to Ted Levitt, who in The Marketing Imagination credited Leo McGinneva.
Use Drucker's parallel warning that the customer rarely buys what the company thinks it is selling to frame the company-customer disconnect.

Expect company drift after success: most successful organizations were de facto founded on an identified job, but after launch the job gets lost and the company defines itself by products — this is a common pattern even among the best companies.

Apply the railroad lesson: the railroad industry declined not because transportation demand fell (it grew) but because cars, trucks, planes and telephones did the job better; as Levitt wrote in 1960, railroads assumed they were in the railroad business rather than the transportation business.

Note the self-defining market frame: no customer has a job called 'I need to spend a couple of hours going to the store,' so brick-and-mortar-organized retailers tend to play defense; OpenTable, Salesforce.com, Airbnb, craigslist and IKEA are cited as businesses organized around a distinct job with minimal competition.

For startups, treat the founder's own struggle as a research asset: the Netflix origin story began with an entrepreneur in a circumstance with no clear solution saying 'I'm going to fix this,' collapsing the distance between innovator and customer job.
caveats: The 'no customer job to go to the store' claim is illustrative of the authors' framework, not an empirical finding about all retail.
The listed successes are examples chosen to illustrate job-centered organizing; their outcomes are not attributed to this framework alone.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Use a Job Statement as an Alignment Compass
cards.summary: A clearly articulated job statement acts as a two-sided compass: it aligns both the customer's problem and the internal job spec, enabling autonomous employee decisions.
cards.use_when: When an ecommerce team's roadmap or feature debates lack a shared anchor, or when employees need to make day-to-day tradeoffs without escalation.
steps: Write the job your customers are hiring you to solve as a short statement in verbs and nouns (not adjectives).
Treat the statement as a two-sided compass: one side points to deeper understanding of the customer's job, the other to the job spec (features, processes) that must align with it.
When an unplanned issue or opportunity surfaces, test it against the compass heading: if it clearly intersects the job, let people act without asking permission.
Expect energized, self-directed action rather than 'don't give me one more thing' resistance — the source reports this pattern at OnStar, Intuit and SNHU.
Revisit the statement periodically so the job spec side keeps up with the evolving customer side.
caveats: The source presents this as observed pattern across several organizations, not a guaranteed outcome.
A vague job statement in adjectives ('be convenient') fails as a compass.
People whose work doesn't align with the job may need to be restructured or counseled out, per the Deseret News example.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Jobs Focus Produces Four Organizational Benefits
cards.summary: An organization explicitly focused on a well-defined job enjoys distributed decision making, resource optimization, inspiration, and better measurement.
cards.use_when: When making the business case for job-based positioning, or when restructuring teams, budgets or KPIs around customer jobs.
steps: Distributed decision making: empower employees throughout the organization to make decisions that align with the job, so they can be autonomous and innovative without waiting for top-down direction.
Resource optimization: audit where resources are currently allocated against what matters most to the job; rebalance toward job-critical work and away from misaligned activities.

Inspiration: connect work to how it lets real people make progress in their lives — the source reports engineers working hard because they knew lives were at stake, not because they were told to work nights and weekends.
Better measurement: let a job focus pull the team toward more customer-centric metrics rather than only easy-to-capture internal numbers.
Articulate the job in mission and communications, and drive it deeply into culture over time — the source says this is difficult, takes real work, but pays off.
caveats: The source describes these as benefits observed across successful organizations, not a guaranteed sequence.
Embedding jobs in culture is described as slow and effortful; expect resistance from parts of the organization.
Operational efficiency still matters — the source argues it is only value-creating when it serves a high-priority job.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Culture Built on the Job Enables Unprompted Action
cards.summary: When employees deeply understand the job, they clear roadblocks on their own; the leader's role is to build structures that let those choices happen.
cards.use_when: When designing customer-service or support empowerment policies, or when deciding how much discretion front-line staff should have.
steps: Make the job explicit enough that staff can judge whether an action serves it.
Give front-line employees authority to act on that judgment without approval — SNHU advisers independently arranged grocery gift cards and a hospital diploma presentation for students in need.
Treat those unprompted actions as consistent with the job, not as policy violations.
As leader, focus on creating structures and culture that make the right choices natural, rather than scripting every case.
Use job clarity as the mechanism for waste reduction: once everyone is aligned, wasted time, energy and resources are minimized systematically (the 'lean' effect LeBlanc describes).
caveats: Examples are drawn from higher education (SNHU), not ecommerce; the transferable mechanism is discretion bounded by job clarity.
Unbounded discretion is not the claim — actions were still consistent with an explicit job.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Replace Generic Mission Statements with Job Statements
cards.summary: A well-crafted statement of the jobs a company exists to solve can be both inspiring and practical, unlike generic mission statements.
cards.use_when: When rewriting a company mission, vision or internal rallying cry so it actually guides decisions.
steps: Identify the most important job or jobs your organization exists to solve for customers.
Express the statement in verbs and nouns describing customer progress, not abstract aspirations like 'be more honest' or 'deliver convenience'.
Use the jobs statement rather than a generic mission statement as the rallying cry that aligns individuals across functions.
Check breadth of understanding: ask whether the jobs are understood across the organization and reflected in leadership and corporate communications.
Reinforce it as an enduring innovation North Star in leadership communications and culture.
Use shorthand phrases to keep the standard honest — American Girl used 'story, not stuff'; Deseret News used 'we are not the Sacramento Bee'.
caveats: The source warns against generic mission statements but still says articulation requires real work and deep cultural embedding.
Shorthand rallying cries only work when the underlying job is genuinely understood.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Measure What Improves Customers' Lives, Not Just What's Easy
cards.summary: Companies tend to measure easily captured data and miss whether they are improving customers' lives; measure the job-relevant outcome instead.
cards.use_when: When choosing KPIs or analytics dashboards for an ecommerce business, or when data is abundant but feels disconnected from customer value.
steps: Audit current metrics: identify which ones exist mainly because they roll off servers easily (traffic, screens, frequency, conversion rates).
Identify what outcome the customer is actually hiring you for — Intuit's accountants hire software to save time on tax returns so they can take more clients or gain free time.
Ask directly whether the product is helping customers achieve that outcome, even when the outcome is hard to measure.
Add job-relevant measures alongside efficiency measures rather than replacing them — measure what matters while still improving efficiency.

Pressure-test with a single customer-centric question if needed: SNHU keeps 'would graduates do it all over again?' front and center (95% said yes as of early 2016) while still tracking reams of micro-level data.
Watch for internal filters (business units, segments) that build data models which rarely map to customer jobs.
caveats: The source argues data reflects the biases of whoever chose what to collect and discard; treat internal metrics as models, not reality.
Hard-to-measure outcomes still matter profoundly; the 95% figure is an example from SNHU, not a benchmark.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Amazon-Style Job Metrics with Automatic Price Adjustment
cards.summary: Amazon anchors its retail business on three customer job measures — vast selection, low prices, fast delivery — monitored minute by minute and treated as defect-free requirements.
cards.use_when: When designing monitoring and enforcement systems for a core customer promise such as price competitiveness or delivery speed.
steps: Define the small set of promises that matter in your retail business, as Amazon did with selection, price and delivery speed.
Build automation that enforces the promise continuously — Amazon's shopping robot scours prices of hundreds of benchmark products twice daily and automatically lowers its price to beat competitors.
Expect visible consequences: a lower price can appear while an item sits in a customer's cart.
Set a gross-margin threshold below which the automatic price change triggers human review rather than proceeding silently.
Treat delays or misses in the promise as defects to be eradicated, not accidents or ordinary underperformance.
Keep the system efficiency-focused but aimed squarely at the job customers hire you to do.
caveats: This describes Amazon's system as reported by the authors; your margins, product set and competitor set differ — don't copy the threshold.
Requires reliable benchmark price data and automation; manual equivalents may not keep pace.
Check your local pricing and competition regulations before implementing automatic undercutting.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Separate the Distinct Jobs a Product Is Hired For
cards.summary: Traditional products often bundle several different customer jobs and do none well, hiding what people actually hire them to do.
cards.use_when: When an established product or channel is losing ground and you need to decide which jobs to double down on and which to abandon.
steps: List the distinct jobs your product or channel has historically been hired for (for newspapers: breaking news, classified employment and low-cost item ads, opinion alignment).
Ask whether each job is now better served by other solutions — the Boston Marathon bombing showed print was beaten on breaking news by TV, live blogs and Twitter.
Without the jobs lens, teams muddle all jobs together and can't tell which solution remains distinctive.
Choose the job(s) where you can still be distinctive and stop spending resources on jobs for which you are no longer relevant.
Use the job definition to filter coverage and scope: Deseret News covered 5 family-relevant legislative issues rather than all thirty bills on the A1 page.
Expect a realignment cost: some staff won't accept the focus and may need restructuring or counseling out.
caveats: This is a strategic triage process, not a quick optimization; the Deseret News example took years and organizational change.
Abandoning a job can mean losing customers and staff who valued the old bundle.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Use Functional, Emotional and Social Lenses on the Job
cards.summary: Define a job through its functional, emotional and social dimensions, since customers often hire a solution for the emotional payoff on top of a functional task.
cards.use_when: When writing positioning or creative strategy and the functional benefit alone doesn't explain customer attachment.
steps: State the functional job plainly: Deseret News readers needed deeper analysis after an event was already reported — 'Perspective, Insight, Context and Analysis' (PICA).
Layer the emotional dimension: readers wanted to be well-informed, confident in their knowledge, and true to their beliefs so they could make a difference at home and in their community.
Identify the social dimension: connecting with like-minded readers and community members.
Check whether your current solution serves only the functional layer while competitors or adjacent products supply the emotional payoff.

Build content, community and distribution around the emotional benefit rather than around the product format — Deseret built Facebook communities around faith and family themes, saying social strategy around the job opened a much broader audience than the newspaper product ever could have.
caveats: The Deseret News social growth figures (low millions to over 100 million followers through its FamilyShare Network) come from one organization's reported results and should be treated as an example, not a benchmark.
Emotional framing that doesn't match a real job is positioning decoration, not Jobs Theory.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Segment by Job, Not Demographics
cards.summary: A segment can be large, distinct and underserved yet invisible to demographic and psychographic segmentation because it is defined by a shared job.
cards.use_when: When demographic or psychographic segments aren't producing differentiated messaging, or when a promising audience seems 'unfindable' by standard targeting.
steps: Start with a suspected demographic segment and then test whether a job explains behavior better — Deseret's process began as demographic segmentation and became jobs-based segmentation.
Define the job in customer terms: 'I want to be well-informed, feel more confident in my knowledge, and still be true to my beliefs so I can make a difference in my home and community.'
Map subgroups that share the job even when their surface attributes differ — Deseret grouped tolerant believers, devoted denominationalists and strugglers as 'like-minded believers'.
Check size and saturation: the source reports this group was nearly 56% of American news consumers and felt massively underserved.
Verify the job's emotional tension — Deseret readers consumed both the New York Times and Sean Hannity and hated both, wanting rigor without disconnect from their values and values without polemic.
Build message and offering to the job rather than the demographic profile.
caveats: The 56% figure is one research finding about American news consumers, not a general benchmark.
Job-based segments may be invisible to standard ad targeting; you may need to reach them through behavior or interest signals instead.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Watch for Organizational Drift Away from the Job
cards.summary: As companies grow, the organizing unit shifts from the customer's job to internal processes, products, competitors and investors, creating an edited view of the customer.
cards.use_when: When a scaling ecommerce business's processes, org chart or reporting feel increasingly detached from what customers want.
steps: Recognize the baseline: successful start-ups are organized around the customer's job — small teams wearing multiple hats who share an understanding of what enables customer progress.

Recognize the drift: growth requires layers of management and defined processes, and the organizing unit moves to focus on customers-as-data, products, competitors and investors, with less focus on the job.
Notice the specific risk: managers frame their task as efficiently executing internal processes rather than effectively resolving customers' jobs.
Counter it by keeping managers close to the customer context; distance makes it easier to adopt a highly edited view of the external world.
Audit 'competencies' that were once job-serving but are now just internally benchmarked capabilities being optimized for their own sake.
Keep operational efficiency, but require it to create customer value by fulfilling a high-priority job.

Use one simple unifying question in disputes: 'What are our customers hiring us to do?' — the source reports that internal disagreement about spreadsheets or campaigns is fine, but nobody should be debating the job.
caveats: Efficiency and process discipline are not the enemy — the source says functional oversight is a requirement of competitive markets.
This is a persistent structural drift, not a one-time fix; expect to re-audit as you grow.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Validate a Job Statement by Abstraction Level
cards.summary: A valid job statement is expressed in verbs and nouns and can be solved by candidates from multiple, different product categories.
cards.use_when: When checking whether a job statement is genuinely a job, or when a team's 'job' is really a preference, a spec or an aspiration.
steps: Reject job statements made of adjectives and adverbs. 'Convenience' is not a job — it may be an experience that causes a customer to choose you, but it isn't the job.
Express the job in verbs and nouns, e.g. 'I need to write books verbally, obviating the need to type or edit by hand.'
Apply the category test: if the architecture of the product or system can only be met by products within the same product class, you haven't found a job.

Move up one level of abstraction until candidates come from different categories. 'A 12-ounce chocolate milkshake in a disposable container' is not a job; 'keep me occupied with what's happening on the road while I drive and fill me up so I'm not hungry during a 10am meeting' is, because a banana, doughnuts, bagels, a Snickers or coffee could all be hired.

Distinguish technical specifications from jobs: a spec such as a thin sheet with a high coefficient of friction and low thermal conduction is not a job; the underlying job is keeping the family warm and dry through Boston winters and summers while minimizing heating and cooling costs — which wood pulp, fiberglass, Tyvek, dehumidifiers and fans or even relocating could all serve.
Do this work seriously — the source insists calling something a job should not roll off the tongue with minimal thought.
caveats: Setting the right level of abstraction is described as more art than science; expect iteration.
Jobs theory is bounded — applying 'job' to every human motivation dilutes its clarity and predictability.
The theory was built inductively and its author explicitly says anomalies are useful signals of its boundaries, not disproof.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Demand Matrix: Classify an Idea by Price vs. Customer Volume
cards.summary: Back-of-napkin framework that sorts a product idea into high-end, golden goose, mass market, or the unprofitable labor-of-love quadrant.
cards.use_when: You have a rough product or offer idea and need a fast sanity check on whether it can be profitable before investing in research or creation.
steps: Draw two axes: price (low to high) and number of customers (few to many).

Place the idea into one of four quadrants. High-end = high price, few customers (examples given: Rolls-Royce, Bentley, Prada, Leica). Golden goose = high price, many customers (source's example: iPhone). Mass market = low price, many customers (source's examples: McDonald's, Starbucks). Labor of love = low price, few customers.
Discard labor-of-love ideas immediately per the source: you may love it, but there is little or no demand. Use the presenter's habanero-salsa teaching dream as the cautionary illustration.
Estimate rather than agonize over precision. This is a back-of-the-napkin exercise; the source stresses there is no definitively right answer.

Recognize that the same core idea can land in different quadrants depending on refinement. The source's fat-loss-for-men example could be high-end (personal coaching wealthy time-poor clients), golden goose, or mass market (a book).
Note adjacent examples from the source: personal finance has many potential customers but typically low prices for a book or product.
Use the quadrant you chose to guide how you refine the idea — it is a positioning decision, not just a label.
caveats: Company examples are the presenter's illustrations, not benchmarks.
The matrix is an estimation tool, not a demand-measurement instrument; quantitative search volume validation lives elsewhere.
cards.source_name: EXACTLY how I do market research for new products.docx

cards.title: Google Competitor Scan to Index Sub-Markets and Framing
cards.summary: Use basic Google searches on problem keywords to catalog competitor sites and read their imagery, tone, and headlines for distinct sub-niches.
cards.use_when: You are starting qualitative research on a new niche and need to see who already sells to this market and how they frame themselves.
steps: Search natural-language problem phrases, not just keywords — e.g. 'how to burn fat and gain confidence for men', 'fat burning advice for men in their 20s', 'men gain confidence by going to the gym'.
Record every notable site in your research doc as you go.

Read each site's imagery, tone, and headline to infer the specific sub-market it addresses. The source's example: an aggressive, testosterone-focused site attracts a different man than a site for normal out-of-shape guys who just want to lose weight for a regular life.

Look for narrow identity calls. One headline explicitly named 'nerds, misfits and mutants' with self-deprecating, fun tone; another addressed 'skinny fat guys' and explicitly distinguished them from regular guys.
Treat specificity as instructive: the source highlights a course on handstands aimed at video-game nerds as an example of how narrow an audience can be.
Capture each distinct sub-market in your notes with the positioning that defines it (aggressive, self-deprecating, time-starved, beginner, advanced).
Use this scan to generate candidate avatars, not to copy a competitor's exact message.
caveats: This is a qualitative framing scan; it does not measure demand or traffic.
A competitor's existence and polish are signals to study, not proof you can win the same segment.
cards.source_name: EXACTLY how I do market research for new products.docx

cards.title: Read Competitor Headlines for Pain, Constraints and Promise
cards.summary: Extract the buyer constraints and desired speed of results encoded in competitor promises ('25 minutes for an hour's results').
cards.use_when: Analyzing competitor landing pages or sales copy to infer what kind of buyer each promise is written for.
steps: Take the headline literally and ask what constraint or desire it implies. 'Get an hour's worth of results in just 25 minutes' implies buyers who lack time or believe they lack it — possibly busy professionals or parents.

Note the emotional reward the promise implies. 'Short, intense, results ridiculous' suggests buyers who enjoy being challenged and may even prefer hard if it is fast (source's read: ambitious, want results fast).

Separate promise-driven framing from identity-driven framing. The mass-market example promised 'feel better look better fast' and named no specific type of person; the skinny-fat example called out exactly who it was for.

For each competitor, note the offer format and price so you can see where it sits in the demand matrix: the source's example was a 14-week DVD program with workouts, nutrition plan and bonuses at about $60 total (mass market).
Check whether the site looks like a serious business making money. The source argues profitable competitors are a good sign for the market; if none make money, that hurts your case too.
Use the extracted pain/constraint/promise pattern as raw material for your own positioning and headline tests.
caveats: The source's inference about a given buyer's psychology is interpretation of copy, not verified data.
A $60 price point and DVD format are examples from one case, not benchmarks to copy.
cards.source_name: EXACTLY how I do market research for new products.docx

cards.title: Amazon 3-Star Review Mining for Structural Gaps
cards.summary: Filter to middle reviews to find recurring product criticisms and structural gaps rather than emotional buying triggers.
cards.use_when: You want to know what a category's existing books or products fail to deliver, so you can design around known shortcomings.
steps: Go to Amazon and identify the top 5–10 books or products in the category.
Read the 5-star reviews first for what people genuinely liked.
Then read the 2- to 4-star reviews for criticisms. The source specifically treats 3-star reviews as the most representative source of structural complaints.

Look for recurring phrasing across reviews. In the source's example, multiple 3-star reviews of one fitness book said 'good for beginners, but oversimplified' — a signal about level and pacing, not just taste.

Read comments as market-level evidence about content depth. If beginners are the target, the criticism suggests studying how a beginner book speaks to the market; if you serve more advanced buyers, add depth rather than oversimplifying.
Capture other concrete gaps, such as a review complaining the diet is too expensive with under $50 a week for food. The source reads that as an opportunity for budget meal-planning content.
Write the pattern down as a design constraint for your product.
caveats: Reviews reflect a self-selected sample of buyers; the source also warns that some commenters are 'keyboard warriors' who consume programs without applying them.
Do not treat a single critical review as a mandate to change direction — the source says you cannot respond to every piece of feedback.
cards.source_name: EXACTLY how I do market research for new products.docx

cards.title: Mine 1- and 5-Star Reviews for the Failed-Solution Buyer
cards.summary: Identify buyers who already spent money on solutions that did not work — the source's definition of a best prospect.
cards.use_when: You are hunting for high-intent, self-aware prospects and want pain-point language they will recognize instantly.
steps: Scan 1-star and 5-star reviews for variations of 'I spent thousands of dollars and it didn't work' — e.g. the source's example of a reviewer who hired many personal trainers across a variety of exercises and was never satisfied.

Treat these buyers as your strongest prospects for two reasons the source gives: they already recognize the problem enough to have spent time and money, and they have not gotten results, so they are still hunting for a better solution.
Do not waste messaging convincing these people the problem exists; lead instead with a better solution and the reasons previous attempts failed.
Apply the same signal in customer interviews: when someone says 'I already tried X and it didn't do Y', lean in and ask more. The source flags this as your potential best customer.
Capture their exact vocabulary for later use in copy, since they describe the failed-solution cycle in their own words.
Separate this from beginner prospects who have never tried anything — they need education about the problem first.
caveats: A 100% never-tried-anything list is not necessarily worse; the source's claim is that failed-solution buyers are among the best, not the only good segment.
You still have to solve their actual problem; the source does not suggest exploiting past frustration.
cards.source_name: EXACTLY how I do market research for new products.docx

cards.title: Reddit for Emotional Mechanics, Quora for Tactics
cards.summary: Split forum research by platform: use Reddit for raw feelings and barriers, avoid Quora when you need emotional pain points.
cards.use_when: You are choosing where to dig for psychological hurdles rather than tactical how-to answers.
steps: Search Google with site-relevant queries like 'reddit fitness confidence men' or 'reddit why don't you go to the gym' to surface relevant threads.

On Reddit, harvest emotional mechanics. The source's examples: 'what did working out do to your confidence', answers about feeling at ease talking to people, recovering from embarrassment, becoming focused and goal-oriented, and being treated with more respect.

Search explicit barrier phrases: [niche] + [fear/barrier]. Direct quotes the source collected include 'I feel like it's always look at the new fat guy that doesn't know how to do anything', 'I feel watched', 'too far and too expensive', and 'I feel like people are judging me'.
Note patterns across many answers rather than isolated ones — the source saw a recurring pattern of people who want to get fit but are not ready to go to the gym.

Explicitly avoid Quora for emotional pain-point mining. The source finds Quora heavily skewed to long-form tactical how-to answers, as in a 'fitness plan for someone extremely busy' thread full of long instructional posts.
Treat both platforms as places to understand the problem before offering a solution; the source stresses staying in problem-discovery mode at this stage.

Expect both honesty and performative answers — the source warns people give answers they think others want to hear, even anonymously, so look for recurring nuggets rather than trusting any single comment.
caveats: The source's Reddit-versus-Quora split is the presenter's experience, not a platform rule; verify per category.
Online answers cannot be verified for identity or truthfulness; the source finds this limitation significant enough to justify primary interviews.
cards.source_name: EXACTLY how I do market research for new products.docx

cards.title: Track Repeated Words and Counterintuitive Benefit Connections
cards.summary: Use word frequency and surprising link patterns in forum threads to surface emotional benefits beyond the obvious outcome.
cards.use_when: You have a pile of forum answers and need to convert them into avatar language and benefit angles.
steps: Scan threads for words that recur across answers. The source's example: the word 'motivation' appeared over and over, so he searched 'how do you find the motivation to exercise' and 'how do you find motivation to work out after long hours at work' to see how people talk about it.
Record the mindset anecdotes people use rather than only the tactical advice — the source describes these threads as full of short anecdotes about mindsets that keep people working out.
Look for counterintuitive connections between the outcome and unexpected benefits. Example from the source: losing weight linked to improved focus, which he flags as worth writing down.

Build a benefits list that goes beyond appearance: feeling at ease talking to people, recovering from embarrassment, gaining focus and goal orientation, being treated with more respect, increased dating attention.
Keep the exact wording of each benefit so copy can echo the avatar's own vocabulary.
Map each benefit to the sub-avatar most likely to feel it (e.g. social anxiety relief for gym-reluctant beginners, focus and goal orientation for ambitious time-poor professionals).
Use these benefit connections to test headline angles later, not as finished claims.
caveats: Quoted benefits come from a fitness example; transfer the method, not the specific claims, to other categories.
Word frequency reflects who happens to post, not the whole market.
cards.source_name: EXACTLY how I do market research for new products.docx

cards.title: Run Primary Customer Interviews With a Lateral Question Approach
cards.summary: Go beyond online reading by talking to real people, using indirect questions that surface context rather than pitching your idea.
cards.use_when: You have desk research and want to validate and deepen it with real conversations before building.
steps: Treat online research as incomplete on its own — the source cites not knowing who is honest as a core limitation and says talking to real people has set his products apart from competitors.

Choose broad sources of interviewees: email readers, phone calls, lunches. The source describes reading every email, replying to hundreds, and putting customer-research calls on the calendar for himself and his team.

Ask lateral questions rather than head-on ones. Source examples: 'Have you thought about XYZ? Is this something that's on your mind? How do you think about it? Who else do you know that's done this? Why did they do it?'
Listen for the failed-solution signal during interviews and follow up when you hear it — the source treats this as a green light.
Schedule at least one conversation this week rather than waiting for a perfect sample; the source suggests putting an hour on the calendar and pushing yourself to talk to someone.
Keep a research document open during and after calls and paste exact quotes into it.
caveats: The source's volume claim (thousands of emails, hundreds of replies) is his scale, not a required benchmark.
Interviews and forum posts can both contain socially desirable answers; look for repeated patterns to reduce noise.
cards.source_name: EXACTLY how I do market research for new products.docx

cards.title: Keep Qualitative Research Manual and Quote-Based
cards.summary: Deliberate ban on automating review and forum parsing so you absorb emotional nuance and exact vocabulary.
cards.use_when: You are mining reviews or forum threads and feel tempted to script, scrape, or summarize with an algorithm.
steps: Do the reading yourself. The source states the point is not to do it efficiently but effectively: read through the comments and let it take time.
Manually copy and paste exact quotes into your research document so you remember precisely what people said.
Do not use scripts, algorithms or AI to parse reviews at this stage — the source argues that destroys the emotional nuance and vocabulary of the avatar.
Accept the mess. The source stresses there is no Minority Report-style dashboard: multiple documents open, headline drafts, moving pieces around.
Define a short goal before each session: collect and absorb everything, not to produce an output artifact.

Use the accumulated notes to inductively derive sub-avatars (busy people, people without money, people who want scientific proof, skinny-fat guy, nerd gamer) along with their pain points, hopes and obstacles.
Treat this as a concentrated time investment — the source reports spending 60–80% of new-product development time on this research phase and says getting this step right makes the rest easier.
caveats: The 60–80% figure is the presenter's personal time allocation, not a universal rule.
Manual reading does not scale; the source accepts that trade-off deliberately and others may choose differently.
cards.source_name: EXACTLY how I do market research for new products.docx

cards.title: Don't Chase Every Piece of Feedback
cards.summary: Reconcile contradictory reviews before changing your product or positioning.
cards.use_when: You are reading critical reviews and trying to decide which complaints to act on.
steps: Expect contradictions. In the source's example, one 3-star reviewer of a fitness book wanted more scientific proof and step-by-step plans based on studies, while another said the material was too technical and over one's head.
Recognize that reacting to every complaint pulls you in a million directions; the source says it is your job to weigh the notes and decide where to go.
Sometimes conclude the market is simply not that reviewer. The source's imagined response as the author: people come to my book because I am the human guinea pig; you are not the market I want.
Other times, file the feedback away as a future idea rather than acting now — the source's phrase is to listen and think about it.

Look for a resolution that satisfies both sides when possible. Example: provide solid scientific information in a way that stays easy to read, with references in an appendix for the small minority who want them — simple enough for laypeople, deep enough for the one percent.
Use recurring patterns across many reviews as the trigger for change, not single voices.
caveats: The book and review details are illustrative examples, not proof that science depth causes purchase or non-purchase.
Choosing to ignore feedback can be wrong if the complaint is repeated across the target segment.
cards.source_name: EXACTLY how I do market research for new products.docx

cards.title: Use Economic Signals to Gauge Whether a Market Supports Your Idea
cards.summary: Study whether competitors look like serious, profitable businesses before committing to a niche.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether a niche has commercial backing for a paid product or offer.
steps: Assess competitor presentation quality. The source flags look and professionalism — the 'feel better look better fast' example had polished pages, indicating a serious business behind it.
Draw the inference the source draws: profitable competitors are a good sign, because if nobody were making money the market would not support your idea either.

Place competitor offers and price points into the demand matrix so you can see which quadrant they occupy. The source's example: a 14-week DVD program with videos, nutrition plan and bonuses priced around $60 sits in mass market.

Use the offer mix, formats and price points you observe to generate your own offer options — coaching, PDF packages, DVD/video programs, forum and call access were all present in the source's examples.

Treat sub-market diversity as evidence of a deep market. The same broad niche hosted aggressive testosterone branding, self-deprecating nerd branding, skinny-fat identity branding, and time-compressed challenge branding.
Remember this whole phase costs little; the source presents it as a low-cost alternative to ad testing for early idea validation.
caveats: Competitor profitability is inferred from appearance in this method, not verified; treat it as a directional signal.
Price examples from the source are case illustrations, not recommended pricing.
cards.source_name: EXACTLY how I do market research for new products.docx

cards.title: Avatar vs. Demographic: The Empty-Nester Test
cards.summary: Why 'women 45+' is a demographic, not an avatar, and the specific-context standard that separates them.
cards.use_when: You are about to write ad copy, a VSL or a landing page and want to check whether you actually know who you are writing to.
steps: Test your avatar by pausing and riffing for 30 seconds on: exactly who they are, their hopes and dreams, their current situation, the problem they face, and what they would wish for if they could snap their fingers. If you cannot do this, do more research before writing.

Treat age and gender as a starting demographic only, not an avatar. The source's example: 'women 45 and up with cats' is a gender and an age; it says nothing about fears, dreams or how they describe the problem to a friend at 2 a.m.

Build a specific person carrying situational and emotional context. The source's model avatar is Margaret, 55, on her third cat, an empty nester after her husband passed and her kids moved 2,000 miles away; she has already lost two cats to chronic kidney disease, has tried fountains, different water bowls and adding water to food, and is anxious and paranoid about losing the third.

Include what the avatar has tried and what fails. The source argues struggling ads usually trace back to not understanding the avatar well enough, so unanswered failed-solution history is a signal to keep researching.
Every avatar in your library should carry quoted evidence, a trigger moment and a job statement before you use it for creative work.
caveats: The source's $10k/day framing comes from a paid-community marketer selling a drop-shipping course; treat scale claims as his positioning, not a benchmark.
Translating avatar language into hooks and scripts belongs in a later creative module; this card is only about the avatar definition.
cards.source_name: How I Find Avatars That Scale Facebook Ads to $10k_day.docx

cards.title: 60-Minute Manual Research Sprint: 80/20 Reddit and Amazon
cards.summary: The source's one-hour protocol: 30 minutes on public forums and 30 minutes on Amazon reviews, manually copying verbatim text.
cards.use_when: You have picked a demographic and need to build a real avatar without defaulting to AI-generated personas.
steps: Pick the starting demographic from the top customer demographic of your largest competitor, using tools like SimilarWeb, another spy tool, or asking a chatbot, so research is aimed at a plausible buyer profile.

Block 60 minutes total. Spend roughly 80% on public discussion forums (Reddit and niche forums) and 20% on Amazon reviews. The source says Reddit is the largest public discussion library for understanding an avatar.

For the 30 forum minutes, adopt the avatar's mind state: literally sit as that person and search the problem in their words, e.g. 'my cat won't drink water Reddit' or 'hair loss making me less attractive Reddit'.
Open a Google Doc as your research library. Copy-paste whole comments and posts, then bold or underline emotional language, failed solutions, situational details and repeated phrases.
Read the comment sections, not just the original posts; the source finds the strongest material in replies and in confession-oriented subreddits where people admit insecurities.
Repeat for 30 minutes on Amazon reviews of competing products, harvesting the same categories: fears, desired outcomes, emotional mind states and previously tried solutions.
If you cannot spare an hour in one sitting, spread it across multiple days, but complete the hour before writing copy.
caveats: This is a manual-first protocol; the source still says AI tools like Gemini or Claude have unmatched efficiency and detail once you already understand your avatar.
The method is universal but the 80/20 forum-to-review split is the presenter's recommendation, not a measured law.
cards.source_name: How I Find Avatars That Scale Facebook Ads to $10k_day.docx

cards.title: Search Query Craft for Avatar Research
cards.summary: How to write search queries as the avatar to surface the rawest forum threads on their problem.
cards.use_when: You are starting the forum half of a manual research sprint and need to find threads worth mining.
steps: Write queries as the avatar searching for help, not as a marketer searching for topics. Examples from the source: 'my cat won't drink water please help Reddit', 'how do I get my cat to drink more water Reddit', 'my cat refuses to drink water'.
Include the problem's emotional phrasing when relevant, e.g. 'straight up hair loss making me less attractive Reddit'.
Add demographic or identity qualifiers to sharpen the avatar, e.g. adding 'men' or 'ask men over 30' when researching men 30-50 with hair loss.
Read threads word for word within a timed block and let the vocabulary guide the next query; one thread usually reveals adjacent phrasings and subreddits worth searching.
Prioritise confession-heavy communities such as 'off my chest' where people describe the problem in extreme emotional detail, since these give the rawest mind-state language.
caveats: The source's specific example queries are for a cat kidney product and a hair-restoration product; substitute your own category's problem statements rather than copying them.
Search-engine behaviour and subreddit availability change, so verify what surfaces for your niche rather than assuming these exact queries still return the same threads.
cards.source_name: How I Find Avatars That Scale Facebook Ads to $10k_day.docx

cards.title: Copy Verbatim and Bold: Building the Language Library
cards.summary: The mechanical habit of pasting raw quotes into a doc and marking emotional language, failed solutions and situational context.
cards.use_when: You are in a research session and need a repeatable way to capture material you can actually write from.
steps: Paste whole posts and comments rather than paraphrasing; the source says there is no real structure to the doc, just copy-paste with spacing between entries.
Bold or underline phrases and keywords that stand out: emotional language, named failed solutions, demographic detail and self-descriptions.
Screenshots are acceptable and often efficient when a post is dense with material, but bold or underline text when you want it findable later.

Preserve exact wording including harsh or self-deprecating phrasing. The source's example: write 'do you hate and feel like your balding is making you look uglier', not a sanitised 'are you tired of looking worse'.
Tag each pasted block implicitly by where it came from, so you can return to the thread later for comments you skipped.
Run this continuously while the timer runs; the point is volume of authentic language, and after 30 focused minutes the source claims copy starts to write itself.
caveats: The source's advice to use the avatar's own words including insults is about authenticity, not about harassing customers; use judgement on what is ethical to reflect back.
Do not attribute a single Reddit comment to your whole audience; it is one data point, and the method relies on repetition across many threads.
cards.source_name: How I Find Avatars That Scale Facebook Ads to $10k_day.docx

cards.title: Emotional Mind States: Frustration vs. Fear
cards.summary: Identify the dominant emotion behind the problem because each mind state needs different copy.
cards.use_when: You have raw research and need to decide the emotional register your ads should use.
steps: While researching, explicitly log whether the avatar feels guilt, embarrassment, shame, frustration, fear, anxiety or depression about the situation.

Ask which emotion dominates for this avatar. The source contrasts drop shippers hitting failed tests, whose primary emotion is frustration, with an empty nester protecting a pet, whose primary emotion is fear, anxiety and possibly depression.
Adapt the copy register to the emotion: frustration copy can call out wasted effort and broken promises, while fear copy should speak to loss, worst-case outcomes and protection.

Use the documented worst-case moment as your emotional anchor. In the hair-loss example the source singles out one man's account of a friend pointing out his hair loss condescendingly in a room full of staring people while he was already depressed, and says he would write ad copy from that one instance alone.
Re-check your current ads against the logged mind state and cut copy that addresses a different emotion than the one the research shows.
caveats: Emotional register and claims must stay within ad-platform policies and honest representation; the source's vivid fear framing is a copy technique, not permission to exaggerate outcomes.
The source is describing a marketing course audience and a pet supplement example; verify the dominant emotion in your own niche rather than assuming it transfers.
cards.source_name: How I Find Avatars That Scale Facebook Ads to $10k_day.docx

cards.title: Mine Named Failed Solutions, Not Generic Categories
cards.summary: Extract the exact products and procedures the avatar already tried so copy can name them specifically.
cards.use_when: You are writing hooks or objection-handling copy and want to reference failed prior attempts credibly.
steps: While reading forums and reviews, capture every named product, drug, procedure or workaround the avatar mentions failing with.
Replace generic categories with specific names in copy. The source's example from hair loss: do not write 'have you tried hair supplements or drugs', write 'have you tried minoxidil'.

Capture the cost and extensiveness of failed solutions. In the hair-loss research, a forum user described spending $6,500 on Neograft for the front and $5,000 for the crown with a rebuild-per-section process, framing it as roughly $300 a month.
For low-cost workarounds like cat hydration, capture the specific variants tried, e.g. fountains, different water bowls and adding water to food.
Use the named failures to position the offer against what the avatar has already rejected, since the source treats failed-solution history as part of the avatar record.
caveats: Named competitor or medical solutions should be referenced factually; do not invent efficacy comparisons the research does not support.
Price figures quoted by forum users are anecdotes, not verified market pricing.
cards.source_name: How I Find Avatars That Scale Facebook Ads to $10k_day.docx

cards.title: Understanding Before Curiosity: How to Build a Hook
cards.summary: Curiosity-driven hooks fail alone; pair deep understanding of the avatar's situation with attention-grabbing phrasing.
cards.use_when: You are writing hook lines and want to avoid clever-but-empty angles that make the avatar roll their eyes.
steps: Diagnose the common beginner trap: turning a claim into a curiosity hook and assuming it converts. The source's example 'the easiest way to drop ship is not what you think' drives curiosity but fails to make the avatar feel understood, so the target audience rolls their eyes.

Start from the current situation and deepest fear, then add curiosity mechanics on top. The cat example: 'Two women whose cats don't drink water. It seems innocent but could be the reason you lose your last companion a few years too early.'

Identify the situational call-out ('two women whose cats don't drink water'), the curiosity element ('it seems innocent'), the deepest fear (losing the companion early) and the identity-specific language ('last companion' signalling empty nesters).
Replace generic pain-point hooks such as 'are you tired of this pain point' plus a product claim with copy that articulates the avatar's situation in their own words.
Ground the hook in specific mechanics your audience actually recognises. The source's own course example cites '$200 CPMs and $5 CPCs on launch day' rather than the vague 'my product test failed'.
caveats: The source's framing 'people buy when they feel understood' is his opinion, supported by example, not a measured conversion law.
Hook creation and script writing belong downstream in a creative module; this card covers only the understanding required before writing them.
cards.source_name: How I Find Avatars That Scale Facebook Ads to $10k_day.docx

cards.title: Use AI as a Supplement, Not a Substitute for Research
cards.summary: The source's argument for manual research first: AI is efficient but becomes a crutch when you do not know what you are looking for.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to run deep-research prompts instead of doing forum and review mining yourself.
steps: Acknowledge the tool's real strength: the source explicitly says AI tools such as Gemini, ChatGPT and Claude have unmatched efficiency and level of detail.

Delay heavy AI use while you are still learning what to look for. The source says if you are just starting out, do not use it yet, because you will mistake polished output for genuine avatar understanding.
Avoid the trap of running a deep-research prompt and assuming you now understand the avatar. The source compares it to answering emails and feeling productive without moving the needle.
Do a manual research sprint first, then use AI to accelerate work you can already evaluate, since an LLM is only as good as the inputs the operator provides.

Audit current AI-written copy against your manual research. The source claims you will find lines that are off-base: not what the customer wants, not how they describe the problem, not the emotions they feel.
caveats: This is a strong opinion from a marketer who sells community access, and it is framed as a starting-out rule; experienced operators may get value from AI-assisted research with strong inputs.
The source does not claim manual research is superior to AI in efficiency or detail, only in building genuine understanding.
cards.source_name: How I Find Avatars That Scale Facebook Ads to $10k_day.docx

cards.title: Avatar Record Requirements: Quotes, Trigger, Job
cards.summary: The minimum contents any avatar must have in your library before it is usable for creative work.
cards.use_when: You are cataloguing research into avatar records or auditing whether an existing avatar is complete.
steps: Include quoted evidence from real sources so the avatar is traceable to what people actually wrote, not to your paraphrase.
Record a trigger moment: the specific situation that starts the search or purchase, such as a friend's comment about hair loss in front of others, or a cat refusing water.
Write a job statement capturing what progress the avatar wants, not just the demographic fields.
Capture specific situational context rather than broad life stages, e.g. the source's example of a 55-year-old empty nester with her third cat rather than 'women 45 and up'.

Capture procedural and category vocabulary exactly: 'Neograft rebuilding the front and crown' and 'minoxidil' rather than 'transplants and drugs', or 'fountains and water bowls' rather than 'hydration products'.
Note vernacular differences between avatars, since the source's method hinges on exact phrasing rather than a generic persona template.
caveats: The source warns against persona templates with demographic fields and no job, such as '30+ year old woman with knee pain'; those should not count as avatars.
A quoted line from one forum user may not represent the whole demographic; consolidate multiple sources into the record.
cards.source_name: How I Find Avatars That Scale Facebook Ads to $10k_day.docx

cards.title: Research Before Scaling: The $10k-Day Premise and Its Limits
cards.summary: The source's argument that avatar clarity gates scaling, framed with its commercial context and limitations.
cards.use_when: You are deciding how much research effort to invest before spending on ads or scaling a proven offer.
steps: Accept the source's premise that if you struggle to write winning ads, it is likely because you do not know and understand your avatar well enough.
Set research intensity against ambition: the source says a $1k day still requires an avatar, but claims a shot at $10,000 days requires knowing the avatar deeply.
Apply the research to the formats you actually run. The source connects manual avatar research to his long-form Facebook ad copy with native images, and says the same applies to VSLs.
Run the comparison test: after a manual research sprint, read your current copy and look for lines that miss what the customer wants, how they describe the problem, or what they actually feel.
Use the gaps found in that comparison as the improvement list for your next tests, then judge the method by your own testing and scaling results.
caveats: The presenter is selling a drop-shipping course and community and uses $10,000 days as marketing framing; results are his example, not a promise for your account.
No specific spend, testing budget, timeframe or statistical benchmark is given, so do not treat the scale claims as a forecast.
cards.source_name: How I Find Avatars That Scale Facebook Ads to $10k_day.docx

cards.title: Pre-Existing Insecurity Changes How You Write
cards.summary: Segment avatars by whether the problem stacks on top of existing confidence issues, because the copy register differs.
cards.use_when: You are drafting copy for a problem where some buyers are already confident and others are not.
steps: Look for self-descriptions in the research that reveal baseline confidence. The source's hair-loss example quotes a man turning 31, single, a bit chubby, with self-confidence and self-esteem issues who says his hair gives him a confidence boost.
Treat the compounding case differently: for someone already unconfident, hair loss stacks on top of existing insecurity rather than being a standalone problem.
Write differently to the already-confident avatar, who has life 'put together' and starts balding, versus the unconfident avatar for whom the loss accelerates an existing struggle.

Capture repeated preference statements that reveal the comparison the avatar makes. In the source's research, multiple forum participants said it is better to be bald than balding, i.e. avoid 'no man's land'.
Use the avatar's own framing of how others perceive them, e.g. worry that receding hairlines look unappealing to women 25 and older, rather than abstract attractiveness claims.
caveats: These are quotes from individual forum users in one niche; verify that the same stacking dynamic exists in your category before building a segment around it.
Sensitive appearance and dating insecurities require careful, non-exploitative creative; the source's technique is about authenticity, not amplifying shame.
cards.source_name: How I Find Avatars That Scale Facebook Ads to $10k_day.docx

cards.title: Replace Demographic Profiles With Situational Avatars
cards.summary: Why broad demographic targeting fails and how to build avatars around trigger moments, failed solutions, and identity loss instead.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why creatives or offers aren't differentiating, or when starting avatar research from scratch.
steps: Recognize the failure mode: a demographic like '30+ year old women with knee pain' is not an avatar. The source's test is that a million other products and creatives target the same label, so nothing about yours stands out and there's no leverage against billion-dollar competitors.

Test any avatar you have by asking: what do they vent to a friend about? What products have they already tried? What promises are they sick of hearing? If you can't answer, you don't understand the customer, which is why ad concepts feel like brainstorming instead of problem-solving.
Build the avatar around a specific scenario, e.g. a knee-surgery patient whose physical therapy didn't work and who now wants a holistic solution fitting her daily life.

Anchor the avatar in four layers: the pain, the failed attempts, what they actually want, and day-to-day struggles, including restricted identity activities (e.g. can no longer ice skate with friends).
Note the source's claim: if you don't have a genuinely superior product, niching down on the avatar is the only remaining way to win; the strongest case is to have both.
The source's stated end goal: make the target feel the offer is 'one of one and bespoke to them' even when the underlying product is generic.
caveats: The source treats this as a universal baseline (every avatar needs quoted evidence, a trigger moment, and a job statement), but only claims broad avatars hurt you when you lack a superior product, not as an absolute law.
The number of avatars is not universal; how many you need depends on your business.
cards.source_name: How I find Avatars that Scale Facebook Creatives to 100k_Day.docx

cards.title: Mine Competitor 1-Star Reviews for Failure and Trust Markers
cards.summary: Extracting explicit mechanical flaws, trust breaks, and repeated claims from 1-star competitor reviews to feed ad hooks and objections.
cards.use_when: Sourcing granular complaints, objections, and physical product friction before writing creatives or landing pages.
steps: Search Amazon (and wherever else your category is reviewed) for 1-star reviews on competitor listings.

Catalog explicit failure points and mechanical friction verbatim, e.g. 'I was in serious pain and couldn't get the brace off my knee fast enough' — the source treats this kind of complaint as ad-ready material.
Log broken trust markers: things customers say they no longer believe, and repeated product claims that have become exhausted through overuse.
Log recurring venting topics and objections; the source argues these are typically skipped and then reinvented from scratch by marketers.
Look for language patterns that reveal an angle most competitors aren't targeting, e.g. reviews mentioning post-knee-surgery use as an underexploited hook.
Feed the collected phrases into the pre-lander, landing page, and creative so the messaging mirrors what buyers already said rather than what you brainstormed.
caveats: Reviews reveal prior-product failures and objections, not necessarily your own product's performance; don't present competitor flaws as proven claims about you.
The source gives one illustration ('couldn't get the brace off fast enough'), not a guaranteed winning hook — treat it as evidence of a pattern to verify in your own category.
cards.source_name: How I find Avatars that Scale Facebook Creatives to 100k_Day.docx

cards.title: Run Direct Phone Calls and Post-Purchase Surveys at Scale
cards.summary: The source's core sourcing routine: continuous outbound contact with existing buyers plus an automated Shopify survey to surface unvarnished lifestyle limitations.
cards.use_when: When you have buyers and need primary evidence of day-to-day friction, concerns, and language you can't get from reviews alone.
steps: Set up a post-purchase survey on Shopify that fires after someone buys (the source also mentions email follow-up).
Do continuous phone outreach to existing buyers rather than a one-off study; the source cites a nine-figure friend whose whole team still calls customers just to ask how everything is going.
DM buyers and ask directly what their concerns are; the source calls this underrated and specifically notes to ask what surprises them.
Ask about day-to-day lifestyle limitations, such as being unable to participate in a defining hobby or sport, not just symptoms.
Watch for patterns across responses: recurring frustrations, specific phrases, broken trust markers, and product claims people no longer believe.
Treat call and survey output as the substrate for messaging across creatives, offer, and landing page — the source's framing is that this intel is the alternative to running on assumptions.
caveats: The nine-figure team call routine is an example of a practice at scale, not a guaranteed conversion result.
Phone and DM research requires buyer volume and staff time; the source ties the payoff to how deep you're willing to go relative to competitors using generic phrasing.
cards.source_name: How I find Avatars that Scale Facebook Creatives to 100k_Day.docx

cards.title: Mine Condition-Specific Reddit Forums and Niche Groups
cards.summary: Using community forums as a source of clinical vocabulary, condition-specific pain points, and untapped angles.
cards.use_when: Researching a health, hobby, or subculture niche where customers congregate and describe their situation in their own terms.
steps: Identify condition-specific or problem-specific forums (Reddit is the example given) rather than generic social feeds.
Read what people actually discuss, e.g. 'post-op knees hurt', and log the phrasing as candidate creative copy.
Segment further by which condition or which life consequence to target: inability to do the job versus inability to play sports are described as very different avatars.

Harvest specialized procedural vocabulary, e.g. 'patellar tendon graft'. The source's claim is that a person who has that exact procedure will feel instantly seen by the term, while a general audience won't.
Use forum-level specificity to test narrow angles, e.g. post-knee-surgery recovery for knee braces.
Layer forum research with other sources (Amazon reviews, Google searches, social platforms) rather than relying on one community.
caveats: The source advises researching as many places as possible, not just one; a single forum risks an unrepresentative slice.
Specialized terms only work when your target actually uses them — verify the term's prevalence in the community before building a hook on it.
cards.source_name: How I find Avatars that Scale Facebook Creatives to 100k_Day.docx

cards.title: Match Phrasing to the Age Cohort and Platform
cards.summary: Same condition, different cohort, different words: catalog exact vernacular differences so ads sound like the customer, not the marketer.
cards.use_when: Writing ad copy and choosing channels for a specific cohort you're targeting.
steps: Accept that a 20-year-old and a 50-year-old with the same knee problem are different avatars with different day-to-day scenarios and different phrasing.
For the younger cohort, the motive may be competitive running; for the older cohort, running for fun — map the desire, not just the diagnosis.

Collect the sentences people actually form in the places they spend time: for 50-plus, look at Facebook groups or Amazon; for younger audiences, look at TikTok-specific phrasing. The source warns against using TikTok phrasing for a 50-plus audience.
Record exact phrasing, syntax, and terminology from customer vents rather than inventing copy in a brainstorming session.
Build an avatar record that includes age-cohort language, restricted lifestyle activities, and procedural vocabulary, so anyone writing copy can sound like the buyer.
Cross-check your drafts against the verbatim quotes before shipping.
caveats: The channel mapping (Facebook groups for older, TikTok for younger) is the source's illustrative example, not a validated demographic rule — verify against your own buyer data.
Copying a phrase out of context can misfire; the source's point is congruence with the lived experience, not keyword stuffing.
cards.source_name: How I find Avatars that Scale Facebook Creatives to 100k_Day.docx

cards.title: Build Belief Through the Avatar's Sequence of Failed Attempts
cards.summary: Structuring creative and landing-page narratives from the buyer's own journey: problem, past failure, why it failed, then the new mechanism.
cards.use_when: Writing ads or landing pages for a researched avatar and converting objections into hooks.
steps: Open by calling out the avatars precisely, e.g. 'do you have a patellar tendon graft / post-op knee?' — the source calls this the hook that stops the scroll.
Move immediately into scenarios they've lived through, including failed solutions such as physical therapy, and name the failure.
Briefly explain why the previous solution failed (for example, that it doesn't address the core problem), which is where your mechanism becomes credible.
Show, don't just tell: the source insists that what the buyer has failed with (PT, other experts) must be depicted congruently, not just asserted.

Keep creative, pre-lander, and landing page congruent on the same condition and the same journey — the source's example: if the creative targets a patellar tendon issue, the landing page can't switch to arthritis, a totally different condition.

Reuse the same objection-to-hook conversion in everything: a strong pattern is naming the prospect in the hook (the source retells Hormozi-style 'are you a gym owner?' hooks) before delivering the value.
caveats: The source defers hook-writing and script mechanics to a separate topic/module; this card covers the belief sequence, not hook formulas.
Congruence is described as improving conversion, not guaranteeing it; test the sequence rather than assuming a template will scale.
cards.source_name: How I find Avatars that Scale Facebook Creatives to 100k_Day.docx

cards.title: Let Avatar Research Make the Offer Feel Bespoke
cards.summary: Reframing: the offer is not just the bundle and price but the expectations and language set through deep avatar understanding.
cards.use_when: Positioning a commodity product against identical competitors, or when testing offers and framing.
