steps: Understand that buyers compare against familiarity: if your ad names their exact day-to-day struggle in the moment of need — the source's vivid test is an ad that says 'just got out of the shower?' — it feels like a far better fit than a generic pitch.
Treat the offer as including the framing and expectations, not just the price/promo: the source states the offer is not just '2x2 free one'.
Shift the framed outcome from the condition to the restored identity: instead of 'knee pain', the promise becomes enjoying your youth and running again — a very different desire.
Use the avatar's specific language to position your generic product as one of one and bespoke, so the same product as competitors reads differently.
Run this as a competitive move: competitors use generic phrasing; specificity is the leverage.
Feed avatar research into creative strategy, CRO, offers, and retention — the source argues the gap between your assumed customer and the real one bleeds into everything.
caveats: This is the source's positioning opinion, not a universal law: it explicitly notes a genuinely superior product also wins, so you don't have to rely on avatar niche alone.
Framing cannot rescue a product that fails the stated job; the approach is about congruence and specificity, not manufactured claims.
cards.source_name: How I find Avatars that Scale Facebook Creatives to 100k_Day.docx

cards.title: Set the Universal Avatar Baseline: Quotes, Trigger, Job
cards.summary: A minimum evidence standard for every avatar record so personas don't drift back into demographic fields with no job.
cards.use_when: Creating or auditing avatar documents, and onboarding writers or media buyers to them.
steps: Require quoted evidence for each avatar: verbatim language drawn from reviews, forums, surveys, calls, or DMs.
Require a trigger moment: the situation in which the person enters the market (the source's example is post-knee-surgery, when PT failed).
Require a job statement: what progress the person is trying to make in their day-to-day life, including restored identity markers such as a sport or hobby.
Reject persona templates that contain only demographics and no job, and reject broad segmentation without situational context or failed past attempts.
Follow the source's stated baseline: quoted evidence, a trigger moment, and a job statement for every avatar — this part is universal, while the number of avatars is not.
Keep the record usable by writers: store the phrasing, the restricted activities, and the specific terminology so copy can be built directly from it.
caveats: The source presents this baseline as its own standard, not a measured benchmark; treat it as a discipline for research quality.
Avatar-count guidance is explicitly not universal in the source — don't force one uniform number across markets.
cards.source_name: How I find Avatars that Scale Facebook Creatives to 100k_Day.docx

cards.title: 5W Avatar Framework for Ecommerce Market Research
cards.summary: A five-question framework (Who, What, When, Where, Why) for defining an ecommerce customer avatar before writing marketing copy or building offers.
cards.use_when: Starting a new business, launching a new offer, or entering a new niche and you need a structured avatar before producing marketing assets.
steps: Who: capture three layers — demographics (age, gender, income, occupation), geographics (city, state, province, country), and psychographics (values, attitudes, beliefs, lifestyles).

What: separate 'miracles' (wants, dreams, goals, desired outcomes) from 'miseries' (fears, frustrations, pains, problems). Write these as two distinct lists because they feed different marketing angles.

When: identify life events that shift buying decisions (marriage, divorce, new child, new job, moving) and daily schedules that affect consumption timing (traditional 9-5 vs. stay-at-home parent vs. home entrepreneur).

Where: locate where the avatar is present online and offline — which platforms they read, watch and socialize on. A quick search for 'social media demographics' shows which platforms skew to which groups.
Why: dig into the deeper motivations behind wanting the benefits — why those benefits matter to them personally.
If launching to an existing market, identify your top 20% of customers and look for shared patterns across demographics, geographics and psychographics rather than working from assumptions.
caveats: The framework is a baseline research structure, not a validation method on its own — pair it with the intent-mining methods to confirm real demand.
The source notes it wrote a 'jingle' as a memory aid; the framework itself, not the mnemonic, is the substance.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx

cards.title: Avoid Focus Groups and Leading Surveys for Market Research
cards.summary: Traditional market research methods such as focus groups, badly worded surveys, and academic white papers are flagged as expensive, biased or outdated compared with direct intent mining.
cards.use_when: Choosing which research method to invest time and budget in, or deciding whether a proposed focus group or survey is worth running.
steps: Treat focus groups as low priority: the source calls them expensive, hard to get in-depth data from, and prone to moderator bias, where the person running the group injects opinions and sways direction through how questions are framed.

Treat surveys as fragile: rephrasing a question from positive to negative can change results, leading questions skew responses before the respondent thinks, and question order plus the survey's own description can prime answers.
Treat academic white papers and research reports as often too academic or theoretical for real-world use, and potentially outdated the moment they are published, especially in fast-moving industries.
Substitute direct behaviour data: mine what people actually search (Google), what they actually buy (Amazon), and what competitors actually spend on (Meta Ad Library).
If you must use a survey, expect to invest heavily in neutral wording and careful interpretation rather than treating results as clean data.
caveats: These are the presenter's strong opinions about method trade-offs, not a universal rule; focus groups and surveys can still be appropriate where qualitative depth or statistically representative samples are genuinely required.
The critique applies to poorly constructed versions specifically — the source cites leading questions, framing effects and moderator bias as the failure modes.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx

cards.title: Google Autocomplete to Map Search Intent
cards.summary: Use Google's autocomplete suggestions to enumerate long-tail search intent around a core niche keyword before sizing volume.
cards.use_when: Early niche or offer research when you need to discover the language and sub-topics your market actually searches for.
steps: Type your main niche keyword into Google without pressing enter and read the autocomplete suggestions that appear after it.

Work through the suggestions that look relevant to your business, then keep typing a promising stem to surface deeper suggestions (e.g. typing a seed phrase yields further suggestions like 'for beginners', a file format, or a tool type).
Record the relevant suggestions as candidate topics or sub-niches; relevance depends on whether your business is product- or service-based, so filter accordingly.
Evaluate each promising term for overall search volume — the source uses Google Ads Keyword Planner for this, but verify the current interface and workflow in Google Ads before relying on it.
The source chose a deliberately obscure example niche to show the method works for almost anything, so do not skip this step just because your niche feels too niche.
caveats: Autocomplete shows what people type, not how many people type it — you need a volume tool to judge size.
Search volume reflects stated intent, not purchase behaviour; pair with purchase intent data before committing.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx

cards.title: Size Niche Keywords and Spot Seasonality in Keyword Planner
cards.summary: Use Google Ads Keyword Planner's 'discover new keywords' flow to pull keyword ideas with volume, competition and trend data for a target geography.
cards.use_when: After autocomplete mining, when you need to size demand, compare sub-topics, or check whether a niche has seasonal patterns.
steps: Log into Google Ads, open Keyword Planner, and choose the option to discover new keywords (verify the current label and location in the present Google Ads interface, as menus change).
Enter your seed search term and select the geographic pool you want to research — the source used US and Canada as an example.
Review the returned list of keyword ideas, which the source describes as over a thousand for a single seed term, along with search volume and competition.
Use the data to check overall competition in the niche, spot trends and seasonality, and decide which sub-topics are worth building content or offers around.
Sort and prioritise terms, but keep judgment: volume and competition are inputs, not a mandate to target every high-volume term.
caveats: Volume ranges in Keyword Planner are estimates and should be treated as directional, not exact.
The source found its example niche surprisingly competitive once volume was checked — expect your assumptions about a niche's size to be corrected.
Tool navigation is version-dependent; confirm current steps in Google Ads.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx

cards.title: Amazon Autocomplete and Book Titles for Purchase Intent
cards.summary: Amazon surfaces what people actually buy via autocomplete, optimized book titles/subtitles, and listing copy that reflects real market language.
cards.use_when: Validating that a niche has real buyers and harvesting market-tested language, after search-intent research on Google.
steps: Search your main keyword on Amazon and read the autocomplete suggestions; the source notes they often look similar to Google's but reflect shopping behaviour rather than information seeking.

Hit enter and study the book titles and subtitles in the niche — because books take far longer to produce than a blog or social post, authors spend significant effort optimizing titles, subtitles and descriptions to appeal to the exact target demographic.
Treat that book copy as pre-optimized marketing language you can mine for headline and offer phrasing.
Check the products and categories returned to see what formats the market actually pays for.
If your niche has no meaningful book presence, adapt the same logic to the most heavily optimized listings in the category.
caveats: Book title language is optimized for a publishing market, which may not map perfectly onto your product category.
Amazon search results are a snapshot of current listings; check whether the niche's book presence is genuine rather than incidental.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx

cards.title: Amazon Review Mining and Review-Count Sales Estimation
cards.summary: Read Amazon reviews to extract what buyers liked and disliked, and use review counts as a rough proxy for sales velocity.
cards.use_when: Estimating demand and gathering voice-of-customer language for a specific product or niche on Amazon.
steps: Open listings in your niche and read the reviews for what buyers specifically liked and did not like about what they bought — this is the primary data source.
Use those likes and dislikes to shape product angles, objection handling and copy themes.
Estimate relative sales volume by comparing the number of reviews a listing has received; the source presents this as a rough guess, since exact units sold are not visible.
Compare review counts across competing listings to rank which products are moving.
Feed the extracted language into your marketing angle alongside the avatar's miracles and miseries.
caveats: Review counts are only a rough proxy for sales — they depend on review rates, listing age and seller practices, so do not treat them as precise sales figures.
The source explicitly frames this as a guess, not a measurement.
Review sentiment can be gamed or skewed by a small number of vocal buyers.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx

cards.title: Facebook Ad Library to Identify Profitable Competitor Angles
cards.summary: Use Meta's Ad Library via a competitor's Page Transparency to find which ad angles have run longest, as duration is treated as a proxy for profitability.
cards.use_when: Researching competitor messaging and offer angles in industries with active Meta advertising, after you have defined your avatar.
steps: Go to Facebook, search for your industry or a specific competitor's page, and open that page.
Scroll to the 'Page Transparency' section and click to see all details.
If the page is running ads, click through to the Ad Library so all of their ads appear.
Study each ad, paying special attention to ads that appear repeatedly and to those closest to the bottom of the feed, which indicates they have run the longest.
Treat long-running ads as the most likely to be profitable relative to the others, then adapt the underlying angle rather than copying the creative.
Repeat across as many competitors as possible who advertise on Facebook or Instagram.
caveats: The source states that longer-running generally means more profitable, but adds that this is not always the case — do due diligence before assuming.
Some industries (the source contrasts a niche craft example with health and fitness) have far fewer competitor ads available to study.
Requires ads to be publicly visible in the library; ad library coverage and interface details change and should be verified.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx

cards.title: Separate What Customers Say From What They Buy
cards.summary: Stated wants (search behaviour) and actual purchases (retail behaviour) are two different datasets and both are required for useful market research.
cards.use_when: Designing a research plan or deciding how much weight to give survey-style stated preferences versus behavioural evidence.
steps: Capture what people say they want using search engines — the source treats search queries as the best available proxy for stated desire, mined via Google autocomplete and Keyword Planner.
Capture what people actually buy using Amazon — autocomplete, optimized book titles, and review data reflecting completed purchases.
Treat the two as complementary: stated wants shape marketing language and campaign copy; actual purchases confirm real demand.
Apply the principle that talk is cheap — asking whether someone would buy something is different from putting the product in front of them and asking for payment.
When the two datasets disagree, weight behavioural evidence more heavily for offer and product decisions, and stated language for messaging.
caveats: Search intent still over-represents researchers versus buyers; it is an indication, not a guarantee of purchase.
The source's core claim is that stated-vs-actual must be distinguished, not that either dataset is sufficient alone.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx

cards.title: Miracles and Miseries Extraction for Marketing Angles
cards.summary: Convert avatar research into two concrete lists — desired outcomes and pains — and turn them into marketing angles.
cards.use_when: Moving from raw avatar research into copy themes, ad angles and offer framing.
steps: List 'miracles': all of the wants, dreams, goals and desires the avatar is hoping to obtain.
List 'miseries': all of the fears, frustrations, pains and problems they are trying to get away from.
Keep the lists explicit and specific rather than summarising them into generic categories, because the specific items become the angles.
Use miracles to write aspirational messaging and offer promises.
Use miseries to write problem-agitation messaging and objection handling.
Cross-check the lists against what you found in purchase intent data so angles are grounded in real buying behaviour, not assumption.
caveats: This is qualitative synthesis; the source does not provide thresholds or weighting for how many items are enough.
Miseries stated in research can be exaggerated or socially shaped — validate against purchase behaviour before building a whole campaign on one.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx

cards.title: Research Top 20% of Existing Customers for a New Offer
cards.summary: When launching a new offer to an existing audience, base the avatar on your top 20% of customers rather than on imagined demographics.
cards.use_when: You already have a customer base and are preparing a new offer, upsell or product line for that same market.
steps: Identify your top 20% of customers — the segment the source treats as the highest-value reference group.

Look for shared patterns across three categories: demographics (age, gender, income, occupation), geographics (city, state, province, country), and psychographics (values, attitudes, beliefs, lifestyles).
Cross-reference those patterns with the miracles and miseries lists to understand what this segment is buying and avoiding.
Use the resulting shared profile to shape the new offer's positioning rather than reusing a generic avatar from a previous launch.
If the offer is genuinely new to a new market instead, switch to studying competitors' ads and targeting to infer the audience.
caveats: The 'top 20%' figure is the source's framing without a stated method for ranking customers — define your own ranking metric (revenue, repeat purchase, margin) and document it.
Survivorship bias applies: your existing best customers may not represent the wider addressable market for a new offer.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx

cards.title: Social Media Demographics Search for Platform Placement
cards.summary: A quick search for platform demographic data tells you which groups use which social channels, informing where to place content.
cards.use_when: Deciding which platforms to prioritise for content and campaigns based on your avatar's actual presence.
steps: Complete the 'Where' step of the avatar framework first by noting where your audience reads, watches, socialises and engages online and offline.
Run a quick search for a term like 'social media demographics' to find which kinds of people use which platforms.
Match your avatar's demographic and psychographic profile against those platform skews.
Prioritise content production on the platforms where your avatar is actually active, then expand once you have evidence.
Use this as an input to the creative and distribution brief rather than running ads directly from this step.
caveats: Demographic data sources vary in methodology and are usually revised; confirm figures from a current, credible source rather than relying on a single page.
Platform demographics describe averages, not your specific niche — validate against your own audience data where available.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx

cards.title: Life Events and Daily Schedules as Buying Triggers
cards.summary: The 'When' lens targets moments in the customer's life and day that change buying behaviour and content consumption.
cards.use_when: Planning campaign timing, seasonal pushes, or content scheduling around your avatar's routines and transitions.
steps: Scan for life events that alter or influence buying decisions — the source lists marriage, divorce, a new child, a new job, and moving to a new city as examples.
Map how each event changes needs and what the avatar is looking for immediately after it.
Examine day-to-day schedules to determine when and where they consume content or make buying decisions.
Contrast schedule types explicitly — the source distinguishes a traditional 9-5 worker from a stay-at-home parent or home entrepreneur, treating them as materially different buying contexts.
Use the timing findings to schedule sends, posts and ad flights to match when the avatar is actually reachable.
caveats: Life-event research identifies correlation with buying windows, not proof that the event caused a purchase.
No specific timing benchmarks are given, so test scheduling assumptions rather than assuming them.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx

cards.title: Demographic, Geographic and Psychographic Layering for Ecommerce Avatars
cards.summary: Build the 'Who' layer as three stacked dimensions — demographics, geographics and psychographics — rather than demographics alone.
cards.use_when: Constructing an avatar document that will be handed to copywriters, media buyers or creative teams.
steps: Demographic details: age, gender, income, occupation.
Geographic details: city, state or province, country — relevant for shipping, regional language and channel selection.
Psychographic details: values, attitudes, beliefs and lifestyles.
When basing the avatar on an existing customer base, compare these three categories across your top customers to find shared traits rather than listing every variation.
When the offer is new, infer the three categories from competitors' ads and targeting instead of guessing.
Keep all three layers visible when writing copy — demographics alone produce generic messaging.
caveats: Psychographics are inferred from behaviour and interviews, so they are less reliable than demographic fields.
Geographic segmentation matters less for purely digital delivery but still affects channel and language choices.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx

cards.title: Boundary Between Research, Creative, Media and Web Work
cards.summary: Market research and avatar work sits upstream of ad production, media buying and landing-page implementation and should hand off cleanly.
cards.use_when: Scoping who does what when planning a launch so research outputs are not confused with execution deliverables.
steps: Keep in the research phase: baseline qualitative and quantitative frameworks for defining avatars, extracting pain points, and validating demand via search intent, purchase intent and competitor ad libraries.
Hand off copywriting and creative asset production to the creative function rather than doing it during research.
Hand off launching and managing paid media campaigns to the media execution function.
Hand off implementing the messaging on landing pages to the storefront/site function.
Deliver research outputs as inputs — avatar profile, miracles and miseries lists, keyword map, competitor angle list — and let downstream owners apply them.
caveats: These boundaries come from one internal operating model and may need adapting to small teams where one person covers several stages.
The research phase produces direction, not finished copy or media plans.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx

cards.title: Judge Whether an Ad's Longevity Signals Profitability
cards.summary: Ad duration is a usable but imperfect proxy for profitability; apply informed judgment and corroborate before treating a long-running ad as proven.
cards.use_when: Screening competitor ads in the Meta Ad Library and deciding which angles to model or test.
steps: Sort attention to ads at the bottom of the competitor's ad library feed, since these have run the longest.
Also note ads that recur repeatedly across your scan — repetition is treated as a second signal.
Interpret duration as an indication that the advertiser keeps paying for it, which suggests it is producing better results than their alternatives.
Corroborate before acting: the source explicitly says running longest is not always the same as most profitable, so do due diligence rather than copying on duration alone.
Combine the surviving angles with your own miracles/miseries research and keyword data to build a test slate.
caveats: Duration can also reflect campaigns left running by neglect, always-on brand ads, or ads with low spend — the underlying assumption is the presenter's, not a measured fact.
Ad Library visibility and sorting behaviour can change; verify the current interface.
Only applies where competitors actually run ads on Meta.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx

cards.title: Why Deeper Motivation Belongs in the Avatar
cards.summary: The 'Why' step converts features and benefits into motivation, telling you which benefits to lead with.
cards.use_when: Writing the value proposition or offer copy after the Who, What, When and Where steps are complete.
steps: For each benefit your offer provides, ask why that benefit matters to the avatar personally.
Check whether the customer would actually benefit from your specific offer, not just from the generic category.
Record the chain from feature to benefit to underlying motivation so copywriters can pick the right lead.
Cross-check the motivation against the miracles list — the stated desire and the underlying driver should align or the discrepancy should be noted.
Use the deeper driver to decide which benefit gets headline placement versus supporting copy.
caveats: Why-level motivations are interpretive and can be wrong; validate with purchase behaviour and customer conversations where possible.
The source offers no method for ranking motivations against each other — prioritise by evidence from your own customers.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx

cards.title: Differentiate a saturated product with a new avatar instead of a new mechanism
cards.summary: When your product has no genuine mechanical or visual differentiation, compete by finding an unserved buyer group rather than fighting incumbents head-on.
cards.use_when: You are sourcing or marketing a saturated dropshipping product (e.g., an AB stimulator) and deciding how to enter a market dominated by 7-figure brands.
steps: Identify the problem your product solves and the mainstream avatar competitors already target.
Recognise that competing for the same avatar means fighting a bigger budget, better creative, better offers and higher tolerated CPA — the source says you may only get 'scraps'.

Assess whether you have a genuinely new mechanism: something visually, mechanically or functionally different that promises to solve the existing problem in a new way. The source argues most AliExpress dropshipping products do not offer this.
If you lack a new mechanism, pursue a new avatar: a group that wants the product's outcome but is not being marketed to, so there is little or no paid competition.
Prioritise differentiation above all else when choosing between candidate avatars; overwhelming evidence of an unserved group struggling with the problem is the source's stated selection criterion.
caveats: The source attributes much of the differentiation advantage to a new avatar, but a truly new product mechanism can also work — this is a situational alternative, not an absolute rule.
The '100K/month' framing is the source's own goal and case example, not a guaranteed outcome.
cards.source_name: How To Scale Facebook Creatives To $100k_mo With _Untapped Avatars_.docx

cards.title: Use Facebook Ad Library to map and exclude the mainstream avatar
cards.summary: Scan competitor creatives in the Ad Library to build a psychographic profile of the avatar you must avoid competing against.
cards.use_when: You need to know which demographics and desires incumbents already own before choosing an untapped avatar.
steps: Open Facebook Ad Library and search your product keyword (e.g., 'ab stimulator').
Identify the brands that appear to be scaling — repeated creatives, many variations, professional production.
Play video ads and note visible people: approximate age, gender and body type (the source estimated middle-aged men roughly early 40s to mid-60s).
Record what desires and USPs the creative appeals to (e.g., defined abs, hands-free use while working).
Note whether messaging assumes product awareness — speaking to people who know the category but need convincing why yours is better.
Repeat across as many successful competitors as you can until the mainstream avatar picture is stable.
caveats: Access to tools that estimate ad spend or traffic (such as third-party ad spy software) can speed this up; verify current functionality before relying on it.
Avatar inference from creatives is approximate — the source calls his own age read a 'spitball' estimate.
cards.source_name: How To Scale Facebook Creatives To $100k_mo With _Untapped Avatars_.docx

cards.title: Mine Amazon reviews for outlier buyer stories
cards.summary: Long Amazon reviews that narrate a buyer's life reveal alternative avatars distinct from the mainstream target.
cards.use_when: After mapping the incumbent avatar, you want candidate buyer segments your product already serves but competitors ignore.
steps: Go to the highest-review-count listing in your general category — it need not be the exact product.
Sort reviews by 'Top reviews'; filter to reviews containing images or videos, and consider scanning positive reviews for life-story detail.
Prioritise reviews where people describe their whole situation (weight history, surgery, stress, age, physical limitations) — these are the 'gold mines'.
Skip short generic reviews; they rarely reveal usable avatar information.
Record each distinct profile as a candidate avatar numbered in a document (e.g., 'Avatar 1: postpartum woman with C-section pooch').
Aim to leave the session with three to four different potential avatar ideas before deep-diving any one.
caveats: Store only the profile insight, not identifiable personal details from reviewers — the source explicitly flags this ethical concern.
Review visibility and sorting options on Amazon change over time; confirm the current interface.
cards.source_name: How To Scale Facebook Creatives To $100k_mo With _Untapped Avatars_.docx

cards.title: Validate avatar market size and problem severity on Reddit
cards.summary: Search Reddit threads to confirm a candidate avatar is a real, recurring, emotionally acute problem with enough people to scale against.
cards.use_when: You have a candidate avatar from review mining and need evidence it is large and painful enough to justify a campaign.
steps: Turn the review detail into a search query (e.g., 'post C-section weight gain Reddit') and review the resulting threads.
Check volume and recency of threads: many active discussions indicate a prominent, recurring problem rather than a one-off.
Read threads for how people describe the problem in their own words, how it makes them feel, their existing beliefs and their failed solutions.
Capture verbatim vocabulary (e.g., 'C-section pooch'), beliefs (e.g., 'surgery is the only way to get a flat stomach') and emotional states (self-image, body confidence).
Confirm the product's outcome directly addresses the pain — e.g., a stimulator promising a tighter midsection for a woman who desperately wants one.
caveats: The source requires a 'heavy burden of proof' that the avatar genuinely struggles with the problem and that enough such people exist before committing.
The source calls weight-loss fitness evergreen, but this is his assertion, not a guarantee for every niche.
cards.source_name: How To Scale Facebook Creatives To $100k_mo With _Untapped Avatars_.docx

cards.title: Assemble a raw avatar profile before deep research
cards.summary: Compile the observational evidence from ads and reviews into a bare-bones avatar sketch that deep research can later expand.
cards.use_when: You are between discovery and deep research and need a structured starting input for an AI prompt or manual research.
steps: Write a rough demographic band from Ad Library observations (e.g., men early 40s–mid-60s; or women late 20s–early 40s postpartum).
State the core problem in the avatar's own language (e.g., 'C-section pooch', flabbiness around the midsection).
List desires and valued USPs competitors emphasise (e.g., hands-free, use while working or cooking).
Record known beliefs and failed solutions (e.g., believes surgery is the only path; has tried cheap knockoff devices).
Mark this document as preliminary — the source stresses it is not yet a real avatar, only a general profile.
Repeat for each candidate avatar so you have several to test.
caveats: Do not mistake the preliminary sketch for a finished avatar record; the value comes from the subsequent deep research.
cards.source_name: How To Scale Facebook Creatives To $100k_mo With _Untapped Avatars_.docx

cards.title: Run an AI deep-research prompt to produce a full avatar report
cards.summary: Feed a preliminary avatar sketch to ChatGPT or Gemini in deep-research mode to synthesise psychology, beliefs and verbatim language from public sources into a long report.
cards.use_when: You have prioritised one avatar and need comprehensive psychological and situational detail before writing copy.
steps: Enable deep research in ChatGPT or Gemini (the source notes deep research alone was sufficient, search did not need to be separate).
Paste your prompt template and replace only the placeholder with the specific avatar — keep the rest identical for comparability.
Include the avatar name/identifier and the raw profile: demographics, problem, desires, known beliefs, failed solutions.

Instruct the model to cover: demographics and identity, avatar synopsis, day-to-day life struggles, how the problem makes them feel, how they describe it in their own words, prior failed solutions, limiting beliefs, existing beliefs about solutions (surgery, competing products), core identity beliefs, attitudes, hopes and dreams.
Wait for completion — the source's run took roughly 22 minutes and produced a 30+ page report.
Expect each claim to be backed by cited evidence and specific quotes from discussion forums, Reddit, social comments and other public sources.
Read the output manually, then click through to the cited sources line by line yourself.
caveats: The source found Gemini wider in depth of sources while ChatGPT was slightly less deep in his one comparison — this is a single-run observation, not a stable benchmark.
Do not paste outputs straight into ads; use them as research that you personally verify.
cards.source_name: How To Scale Facebook Creatives To $100k_mo With _Untapped Avatars_.docx

cards.title: Prioritise avatars with zero paid competition over better-known segments
cards.summary: Choose the avatar that appears completely isolated from existing advertising, provided the burden of proof on size and pain is met.
cards.use_when: You have two or three candidate avatars and must pick one to build a campaign around.
steps: Rank candidates primarily by differentiation: which group is currently unserved by Facebook advertisers.
A totally unmarketed avatar that wants your product's outcome is the source's stated 'gold mine' because there is no competition.
Before committing, verify three things: the avatar genuinely struggles with the problem, enough such people exist, and they desperately want what the product does.
Consider adjacent unserved pockets from the same reviews — e.g., seniors with pre-existing conditions who cannot easily get to a gym and still want abs.
If a group has overwhelming evidence and an obvious fit, that is the one to take into deep research first.
caveats: An isolated avatar can be commercially thin; the source pairs this with a heavy proof requirement for exactly that reason.
Do not choose solely on novelty if the avatar lacks urgency or buying desire.
cards.source_name: How To Scale Facebook Creatives To $100k_mo With _Untapped Avatars_.docx

cards.title: Turn the avatar record into copy-ready psychological inputs
cards.summary: A complete avatar record should contain the specific categories of insight that feed long-form ad copy and creative.
cards.use_when: You are finalising research to hand off to copywriting or creative development (the source routes writing to a separate copy module).
steps: Capture demographics and identity: who the person is and what defines them.
Document day-to-day life struggles and how the problem manifests in daily life.
Record how the problem makes them feel and the exact words they use to describe it.
List everything they have tried before and why it failed, if applicable.
Extract limiting beliefs (e.g., 'surgery is the only way to get a flat stomach') and existing beliefs about solutions in the category.
Note attitudes, hopes, dreams and beliefs that hold them back.
Use these categories directly as the raw material for advertising copy and creative angles.
caveats: Avatar work is deliberately separated from media buying, landing pages and product engineering — keep those decisions out of this record.
cards.source_name: How To Scale Facebook Creatives To $100k_mo With _Untapped Avatars_.docx

cards.title: Match the differentiation route to the product's actual state
cards.summary: If you have a genuinely different product, compete on a new mechanism; if it is the same commodity item, compete on a new avatar.
cards.use_when: Deciding strategy at the start of marketing a product in a saturated or dropshipped category.
steps: Audit the product for real differentiation: is it visually, mechanically or functionally unique versus the standard listing?
If yes, build a new mechanism narrative — a new cause of the problem and a new promised solution the audience has not heard.
If no, accept that a new mechanism is not credible (the source argues most AliExpress products lack this) and pursue a new avatar instead.
Recognise that a new mechanism often performs best when you are actually creating something new, not reskinning an existing item with a fresh claim.
Choose the route first, because avatar discovery, creative and offer all flow from it.
caveats: The source's preference for avatar over mechanism is opinion tied to commodity dropshipping, not a universal law.
Claiming a new mechanism without real product difference risks the audience disbelieving you.
cards.source_name: How To Scale Facebook Creatives To $100k_mo With _Untapped Avatars_.docx

cards.title: Three-tier audience taxonomy: TAM, ICP and persona
cards.summary: Separate total addressable market, fit-based ICP and buying-committee personas to plan reach, campaigns and metric vocabulary.
cards.use_when: You or a colleague keep conflating TAM, ICP and persona, or campaign briefs lack a clear audience boundary before content planning.
steps: Define TAM as the broadest layer: everyone who could be interested in the product. Use it for overall business planning and sizing the opportunity.

Narrow to ICP (ideal customer profile), which the source frames mainly for B2B: the target firmographic profile you want to sell into, plus the department-level decision maker. Example: director of marketing at a mid-market manufacturing company in the Northeast.

Narrow further to persona: the individual stakeholder inside that account's buying committee (e.g., director of marketing, head of IT, head of sales). Each has different daily tasks, career goals, pain points and measurement vocabulary.
Size and characterize each layer: note how many people/accounts fall into TAM, ICP and each persona, then use that to prioritize what work you do.
Match message vocabulary to the persona's role: marketers respond to CPL and ROAS; sellers to quota, pipeline and president's club.
Use the three layers to decide campaigns, channels, content topics and the specific individual you are communicating with.
caveats: The source presents the taxonomy as foundational work to do up front, not an ongoing growth motion.
ICP criteria lean B2B/firmographic in this discussion; adapt the layers differently for B2C contexts.
cards.source_name: How to Define Your Ideal Customer Profile (ICP).docx

cards.title: Run five 30-minute qualitative customer interviews
cards.summary: A quick, low-cost interview protocol: pick your top five customers and ask for 30 minutes each to capture language and situation.
cards.use_when: You lack a documented ICP or persona and need raw customer language fast, or want the qualitative layer that surveys and CRM fields cannot provide.
steps: Pick your top five customers.
Ask each if you can spend 30 minutes going through what is going on for them. The source reports customers want to get on the phone and share what they are going through.
On the call, capture the conversation as an auto-generated transcript if the customer is open to being recorded/transcribed.
Keep the format conversational rather than a rigid survey; the goal is unstructured language, not clean responses.
Treat interviews as one of the easier and quicker qualitative starting points, even though the volume of work can sound long and hard before you begin.
caveats: Five interviews is framed as a rapid starting point, not statistical validation.
Get consent before recording or transcribing calls.
The transcript is raw input; it still has to be synthesized before it becomes a usable profile.
cards.source_name: How to Define Your Ideal Customer Profile (ICP).docx

cards.title: Source data externally and pull CRM firmographics
cards.summary: Combine external research (surveys, interviews, social mining) with internal CRM fields to assemble the ICP data picture.
cards.use_when: You are assembling ICP data and trying to work out where the evidence should come from for a specific company size.
steps: Gather external data: customer surveys, direct customer conversations and social platforms such as LinkedIn, Reddit and Instagram where prospects discuss pain points and solution needs.
Improve your collection prompt for communities: ask what pain points people have, or what they would want if you were designing a solution for their industry.
Pull internal data: industry, company size, location, seniority and job profile already in your CRM or database.
Mine sales and support calls for recurring pain points, company types and who on the buying side seeks information.

If you lack a CRM, use LinkedIn to research target accounts in your market, and use sales/call transcripts if you have them; the source jokes you could simply get a CRM, so treat tooling as a sourcing decision, not a blocker.
Package everything together into the data layer you will use to define ICP or persona.
caveats: Which data you can access depends on company size and existing tooling.
No CRM and no transcripts means leaning more heavily on community mining and direct conversations.
The source notes only 48% of over 300 surveyed marketers had a clear, well-documented ICP, so starting from thin data is common.
cards.source_name: How to Define Your Ideal Customer Profile (ICP).docx

cards.title: Synthesize unstructured transcripts into an ICP with an LLM
cards.summary: Feed call transcripts, survey data, CRM firmographics and content performance into an LLM and ask it to define the ICP and surface themes.
cards.use_when: You have raw qualitative data and need to turn it into a tangible ICP or persona document for the team and tools.
steps: Collect the inputs: AI transcripts from the five customer calls, customer survey results and CRM firmographic data.
Include your own content performance data so the model can see what resonates with the audience.

Upload everything into a dedicated project/knowledge base in a tool such as ChatGPT or Claude, which the source treats as context for the LLM. Verify the current interface for creating and sharing a project before instructing a team.
Ask direct questions: who am I speaking to, what are their pain points, what do they care about most, what themes keep recurring.
Ask the model to define an ICP from the supplied demographics and qualitative learning, then turn it into something tangible you can use or share with the team.
Also load information about your own company, products, features and pricing so the model can connect what you offer with what the audience needs.
caveats: This is intended to compress hours or weeks of team synthesis, not to replace the raw data; output quality depends on input quality.
Review the output against source transcripts before treating it as the documented ICP.
Tool project features change; confirm current behavior in the LLM you use.
cards.source_name: How to Define Your Ideal Customer Profile (ICP).docx

cards.title: Use a live LLM persona as an on-demand focus group
cards.summary: Keep the ICP or persona in an interactive LLM project so marketers can test whether copy, campaigns and positioning will resonate before publishing.
cards.use_when: Your persona lives in a PDF nobody opens, or marketers need a fast way to stress-test messaging, positioning and content ideas.
steps: Create a dedicated LLM project containing the persona/ICP knowledge base and use it for every new project rather than sharing a static document.
Have marketers ask the project questions: would this resonate with this ICP, will she hate it, how should I position this, what words should I use.
Treat the answers as a directional check, not binary: ask how to tweak the message to make it as impactful as possible, not only whether it works.
Where your publishing platform supports saving a persona, save it so new content gets automatic QA signals against that ICP. Check your platform's current capabilities.
Use the project as an alignment mechanism for new hires and long-tenured staff, so everyone agrees who we are talking to and what that person cares about.
caveats: The source calls this an on-demand free focus group; it is a messaging QA aid, not a substitute for real customer validation.
Automatic QA checks and persona saving depend on the platform's current features.
The source's working example persona (Growth Gabby) is internally specific and is not a universal template.
cards.source_name: How to Define Your Ideal Customer Profile (ICP).docx

cards.title: Set content altitude by persona seniority
cards.summary: Use the persona to decide whether a topic is covered at the introductory 101 level or the advanced 301 level.
cards.use_when: You are planning content topics and there is disagreement about how deep or advanced the coverage should be.
steps: Work from the persona's experience and daily tasks rather than a generic content calendar.

Example: an experienced marketing leader persona has already set up many Facebook pages and is generating leads and revenue from Meta ads, so they need more advanced content; a 101 piece on setting up a Facebook page answers a question they are not asking.
Call this the altitude decision: 101 versus 301, per topic and per audience.

Do not treat covering multiple audiences or topic levels as a mistake; the source says there is nothing wrong with covering different topics or audiences, but doing the up-front work lets you get specific about which channel and content are for whom.
Feed audience context and your own content-performance data into the LLM task so altitude decisions are grounded in what already resonates.
caveats: The Growth Gabby example is the source's internal persona, not a proven benchmark for other businesses.
The source presents altitude as a persona-driven content planning decision, not a universal rule about always going advanced.
cards.source_name: How to Define Your Ideal Customer Profile (ICP).docx

cards.title: Separate ICP data layer from persona scope: firmographics vs committee roles
cards.summary: Keep firmographic target-account data at the ICP level and role-specific tasks, goals and metric vocabulary at the persona level.
cards.use_when: You are building the ICP record and need to decide which fields belong to the account profile versus each buying-committee member.
steps: For the ICP layer, collect firmographic features: industry, location, company size, seniority and job profile. For example, director of marketing at a manufacturing company in the Northeast.
Identify the decision-making department you want to talk to; for marketing software this is often the director or head of marketing.
For the persona layer, model each individual in the buying committee separately, including roles outside your primary buyer such as head of IT or head of sales.
Capture for each persona: daily tasks, career goals, pain points and the specific vocabulary they use for success.
Use that difference to drive campaigns and content strategy per role rather than one blended message to the whole account.
Size each layer (TAM, ICP, each persona) to prioritize where to spend effort.
caveats: The buying-committee framing is presented as primarily B2B; B2C needs adaptation.
The source positions persona work down here as a growth capability, while the TAM/ICP/persona taxonomy and interview method are baseline.
cards.source_name: How to Define Your Ideal Customer Profile (ICP).docx

cards.title: Use social communities when CRM and transcripts are missing
cards.summary: Mine Reddit, LinkedIn and Instagram pain-point threads when you have no CRM data or call transcripts to start from.
cards.use_when: You are starting from zero data and cannot yet run customer interviews or pull CRM records.
steps: Search Reddit and similar communities for people asking about pain points in your industry, or prompt the community with what they would want from a solution.
Search LinkedIn for target companies and job profiles in your market to build a picture of the target account set.
Consider Instagram and other social platforms where your audience discusses the problem.
You can also ask an LLM to help you understand market trends and the most common personas or ICP profiles in the space, and adapt the answer to whether it is B2B or B2C.
See this as a temporary data layer, not the destination: the source's recommendation for the highest-quality layer is to get on the phone with someone and capture a transcript.
caveats: Community mining is external, self-selected and lower confidence than direct customer conversations.
LLM answers about market trends are not a substitute for your own customer data.
cards.source_name: How to Define Your Ideal Customer Profile (ICP).docx

cards.title: Avatar discovery via review mining
cards.summary: Mine competitor, marketplace and own-product reviews for identity phrases to uncover hidden buyer segments.
cards.use_when: You are picking a product to sell or launching a brand and need to identify which distinct buyer groups already buy something like it.
steps: Identify comparable products: if selling generic running shoes, look at reviews for Nike, Reebok, Under Armour and On Cloud because they sell into the same category.
Read reviews on generic marketplaces (e.g. AliExpress), competitor sites, and your own product reviews.

Scan for identity-marking phrases such as 'I am a…', 'As a…', or any phrasing where the reviewer explains who they are. Examples: 'I am a nurse, I'm on my feet all day and these On Clouds are amazing' or 'As a registered dietitian for the last 20 years I'm on my feet all day talking to patients'.
Tally recurring roles: a repeated 'as a nurse' pattern is a signal that a distinct avatar exists and is buying.
Use the discovered role as the basis for tailoring creative, product copy and product page later; note that downstream application happens in other modules.
caveats: Works best when there is enough review volume; a brand-new product with no reviews must rely on competitor and marketplace reviews.
Do not present the source's anecdotal volume claims as benchmarks.
cards.source_name: How to create avatars that scale Facebook Ads to $30k days.docx

cards.title: Survey existing buyers to name your avatar
cards.summary: Use a free form and email to ask customers how they describe themselves, their situation and how the product helps.
cards.use_when: You have an existing customer list and want to turn implicit buyer segments into explicitly named avatars.
steps: Create a free Google Forms survey (verify current free limits and question types in the tool).
Send it to existing customers through whatever email software you already use.
Ask how they would describe themselves — role, job, family role (husband, father, wife) — and their specific job title.
Ask what specifically about the product works for them and what their unique situation is.
Look for answers that pair an identity with a mechanism, e.g. 'I'm a nurse, I'm on my feet all day, so these shoes work really well.'
Aggregate recurring identity-plus-situation pairs and treat those as avatar candidates.
caveats: The source positions this as baseline avatar discovery rather than an advanced method.
Self-reported descriptions can be aspirational; prefer patterns repeated across many respondents.
cards.source_name: How to create avatars that scale Facebook Ads to $30k days.docx

cards.title: Talk to customers directly to detect your dominant avatar
cards.summary: One-on-one and group conversations reveal which avatar actually dominates your customer base.
cards.use_when: You already sell to a mixed audience and want to know which single avatar deserves concentrated messaging.
steps: Hold one-on-one and group calls with customers, as the source does inside a mentorship community.
Note the identity customers use when describing themselves, such as 'ecom brand owner'.
If roughly 95% of people in your program say they are ecom brand owners, treat ecom as the dominant avatar.
Point all outward content — Instagram, YouTube, landing page VSL, group call recordings — at that dominant avatar.
Re-run this periodically; if the mix shifts, the avatar the content should target shifts with it.
caveats: The 95% figure is the source's own program, not a general benchmark.
A dominant avatar in your existing base does not guarantee it is the largest available market; combine with review and trend research.
cards.source_name: How to create avatars that scale Facebook Ads to $30k days.docx

cards.title: Market sophistication forces broad markets to fracture into sub-avatars
cards.summary: As buyers try and fail with generic offers, they demand specialists, creating niche avatar opportunities.
cards.use_when: You are choosing whether to address a whole market or a specialist slice of it, and need a reason to niche down.
steps: Recognise the sophistication curve: early buyers accept generic providers ('you run Facebook ads? run mine'), later buyers ask 'have you done this before?' and then 'I want someone who only works with my type of business'.

Note that this shift happened in agency markets around 2017–2018 when specialists for chiropractors, lawyers, dentists and roofers emerged after those buyers had already failed with generalist agencies.
Treat the resulting specialist niche as the avatar: a dialed-in subset of the broad market.

Accept that a niche can still be large enough to build a substantial business — the source cites a client agency serving only financial advisors that sold for roughly $3 million, though this is one example, not a target.
Prefer being narrow and deep over broad and shallow: with one avatar, systems, marketing and advertising can be fine-tuned and the message sharpened.
caveats: Not every market has reached this sophistication stage; specialisation is the growth move gated by market maturity.
The agency-sale figure is an anecdote, not a valuation benchmark for ecommerce.
cards.source_name: How to create avatars that scale Facebook Ads to $30k days.docx

cards.title: Test whether a niche is big enough before specialising
cards.summary: Sub-niches can be too small to sustain a business, so check the size of the parent market before niching down.
cards.use_when: You have identified a sub-avatar and must decide whether to build a brand or offer exclusively for it.
steps: Estimate the size of the parent market first; the source notes gym-goers alone may exceed 100 million people worldwide, leaving room for many sub-niches.
Then estimate the sub-avatar. If the parent market is only around 20,000 people, a further sub-niche could contain just 100–1,000 people, which may be too small to promote into.

Check trend signals before committing: the founder of Gym Shark reportedly observed growing workout content online, then flew creators to an expo and sponsored them with clothing, which helped establish the gym-clothing niche.
Choose the depth of niching based on both the size of the parent market and the level of market sophistication.
caveats: Population estimates in the source are illustrative, not measured data.
The Gym Shark example is a case study, not a repeatable guarantee.
cards.source_name: How to create avatars that scale Facebook Ads to $30k days.docx

cards.title: Map sub-avatars through social content
cards.summary: Watch how general niches split into distinct subcultures on TikTok and similar platforms.
cards.use_when: You want to find or anticipate emergent buyer subcultures inside a category you already understand.
steps: Search broad category terms on social platforms — e.g. bodybuilding, CrossFit, or gym clothing — and study the distinct groups posting.
Trace the nesting-doll split: mass athletic apparel (Reebok, Under Armour) served all sports and general gym-goers; Gym Shark then specialised in gym wear; further brands each claimed a sub-avatar.

Identify what distinguishes each sub-avatar, e.g. Anaka Power described as alternative, trend-resistant 'misfits'; Alphalite oriented around entrepreneur/learn-more-be-more values; Buff Bunny exclusively female; Young LA the 'broccoli-haired' gym-bench-scroll crowd.
Note the mechanisms brands use to signal the avatar: creatives, product design, branding, and which people they 'uplift' by featuring and sponsoring them.
Pick a sub-avatar whose identity you can signal consistently across all of these.
caveats: Brand characterisations reflect the source's own reading of these brands; verify current positioning before borrowing it.
Requires ongoing monitoring, since sub-avatars keep splitting.
cards.source_name: How to create avatars that scale Facebook Ads to $30k days.docx

cards.title: Define an avatar by growth signals, not a definition
cards.summary: Treat an avatar as a group that is measurably growing in your reviews, customer base or community.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether an observed segment is a real avatar worth building around or just noise.
steps: Look for repetition: many reviews saying 'as a nurse' repeatedly, or many program joiners saying they are ecom owners.
Go one level deeper when a pattern holds — e.g. ecom owners who all do at least $100k a month, not just ecom owners.
Treat a rising count of people self-identifying the same way as the signal that the avatar is forming and growing.
Recognise the window: once a collective group gathers, they are waiting for someone to sell them something, so being first to serve them matters.
Keep re-checking; nested sub-avatars keep emerging, as the source says is currently happening with perimenopausal and postmenopausal weight-loss audiences spawning further subsets.
caveats: The source explicitly says there is no single-word definition of an avatar.
The $100k/month and menopause examples are the source's illustrations of the depth rule, not fixed thresholds.
cards.source_name: How to create avatars that scale Facebook Ads to $30k days.docx

cards.title: Enter emerging trends as the first dedicated brand
cards.summary: When a new pastime takes off, sell into it as the first brand dedicated to participants rather than competing on the core equipment.
cards.use_when: You spot a fast-growing recreational trend and want a lower-competition entry point than the obvious product category.
steps: Identify an emerging trend or sport — the source uses cornhole becoming a mainstream sport in the USA.
Avoid the crowded core: do not try to compete with every cornhole board manufacturer.
Instead become the first dedicated brand for cornhole participants in an adjacent category: clothing, supplements, or an energy drink for cornhole players.
You can start from products that already exist in other niches and rebrand them as specifically for that avatar, with all marketing and advertising created only for that group.
Move early, since the advantage comes from being first to serve the newly forming avatar.
caveats: The cornhole example is the source's hypothetical illustration, not a documented launch result.
Emerging trends can fade; the source offers no validation criteria beyond early adoption.
cards.source_name: How to create avatars that scale Facebook Ads to $30k days.docx

cards.title: How deep niching fits ecommerce and dropshipping
cards.summary: The same avatar structure translates from agency niches to ecom brands by pointing a mass-market play at one sub-avatar.
cards.use_when: You are an ecommerce or dropshipping operator considering whether avatar specialisation applies to your model.
steps: Start with a mass-market product already proven by other ecom brands in a category.
Study the working ads of the mass-market brands and note what they claim and show.
Rework that same material for a single specific avatar instead of the whole market.
Tailor the primary text, the creative itself, the landing or product page, and even the way you name the business.
Only show results or case studies belonging to that avatar; generic proof undermines the fit.

The source describes a student who launched with a 5x ROAS on day one, then found the main buyers in his niche and copied competitors' mass-market ads while showing the result only for that avatar — an example, not a promised outcome.
caveats: The 5x-ROAS launch is a single anecdote and should not be treated as an expectation.
Copying competitor ads is only the starting point; the avatar-specific adaptation is the actual work.
cards.source_name: How to create avatars that scale Facebook Ads to $30k days.docx

cards.title: Tailor the whole funnel to one avatar, not just the hook
cards.summary: Avatar fit must run through creative, primary text, page, proof and sales conversation — putting the avatar only in the hook is the common mistake.
cards.use_when: You have chosen an avatar and are rebuilding ads and landing/product pages to match it.
steps: Take the mass-market version of the message and adapt every layer: 'how to scale Facebook ads' becomes 'how to scale Facebook ads for roofers'.
Change the creative setting to match the avatar's world — the source's example goes from an office to standing on a roof.
Replace generic case studies on the landing page with only case studies belonging to that avatar (roofing results, not mixed results).
Adapt the sales conversation so it speaks to how the offer is tailored to that avatar's business.
Extend the same tailoring to product photos and every claim on the product page, framed by what that avatar wants.

The test: if someone outside the avatar lands in the funnel, they should feel they are in the wrong place. The source's analogy is ordering McDonald's and arriving at Chick-fil-A — the wrong-fit buyer should leave.
caveats: Deliberately repelling non-avatar traffic is the source's opinion, presented as a trade-off against trying to reach everyone.
It still runs on broad targeting; the creative, not the targeting settings, does the filtering.
Paid targeting structure belongs to a separate advertising module.
cards.source_name: How to create avatars that scale Facebook Ads to $30k days.docx

cards.title: Keep broad targeting while narrowing the avatar
cards.summary: Pair avatar-specific creative with broad targeting and let Facebook's algorithm locate the matching audience.
cards.use_when: You are running Meta ads for a niche avatar and deciding whether to narrow the audience settings.
steps: Keep broad targeting even after niching down; the source states this is still what he does.
Let the platform do the audience-finding work based on which creatives perform.
Because the algorithm relies on the creative to find the right people, the creatives must be tightly dialed to the avatar.
Treat avatar-specific creative as the replacement for narrow audience settings, not an addition to them.
caveats: This is the source's stated practice; account structure and targeting settings are covered in another module and platform behaviour may change — verify current ad platform guidance.
Weak or generic creative under broad targeting gives the algorithm no avatar signal to work with.
cards.source_name: How to create avatars that scale Facebook Ads to $30k days.docx

cards.title: Rebrand existing products for a single avatar
cards.summary: Take products that already exist in other niches and market them exclusively to one avatar.
cards.use_when: You want to serve a newly forming avatar without developing new products from scratch.
steps: Identify the avatar first through reviews, customer conversations or emerging trend signals.
Source or reuse products already sold in other niches rather than inventing new ones.
Reposition them as exclusively for that avatar through branding and naming.
Create advertising and marketing only for that avatar, consistent with the rest of the funnel being tailored to it.
The source's example: rather than competing on cornhole boards, be the first cornhole clothing, supplement or energy brand.
caveats: Exclusivity claims should be truthful relative to the actual product.
The source presents this as a strategic approach, not a demonstrated performance result.
cards.source_name: How to create avatars that scale Facebook Ads to $30k days.docx

cards.title: Four-pronged buyer research methodology
cards.summary: Combine qualitative customer conversations, quantitative surveys, digital intelligence tools and social listening to answer who your buyers are, how they behave and why.
cards.use_when: You need to build or rebuild buyer personas and want evidence-based insights rather than assumptions or template personas.
steps: Run qualitative customer conversations first (about 20 x 30-minute calls) to surface the buyer's why, trigger moment, journey, pain points and emotional drivers.
Design a quantitative survey to verify the interview trends at scale and to collect data-centric attributes that are easier to capture in a form (role, company size, years in role).

Use digital intelligence tools (for the source: SparkToro, Audience, IBM Watson-based data) to see how the wider audience actually behaves: platforms they use, influencers who shape buying decisions, and buying mindset (e.g. move fast vs needs a sales team, risk-taker vs conservative, self-serve vs wants support).
Run social listening (source used Brand24) to track topics and pain points people discuss, not to monitor your own brand mentions.
Compile all four data sets, then segment the personas by jobs to be done rather than by age, gender or job title.
Use the digital data for how people behave and the conversations for why they behave that way; cross-check what people say against what the tools show they do.
caveats: The four-prong framework is universal in the source's view, but the number of personas and specific data points gathered are not universal and should match the business.
Digital tools show behavior but never explain motivation; conversations explain motivation but can be inaccurate about behavior.
cards.source_name: _Adrienne Barnes on Best Buyer Personas, Marketing & Motherhood.docx

cards.title: Run 30-minute discovery calls, not sales calls
cards.summary: Frame customer interviews explicitly as exploratory conversations about the buyer's experience to fill your calendar and avoid the demo/upsell fear.
cards.use_when: Recruiting and conducting customer interviews to extract buyer insights for personas, messaging or product decisions.
steps: State clearly up front (in the scheduling email and at the start of the call) that you are not a product expert, cannot solve their problem, and are not there to demo or upsell.
Tell them exactly what the call is about and how much time you need (source uses 30 minutes) so there is no confusion or concern about a hidden sales motive.
Ask about their full customer journey: how they found the product, why they use it, their experience and emotions around it.
Aim for about 20 conversations; the source cites Nielsen/company research (via Deploy Empathy by Michele Hansen) that 20 conversations yield about 97% sentiment coverage of the audience.
Expect customers who love or hate the product to want to talk; if few people will book, that itself signals weak feeling toward the product.
caveats: The 97% figure is a cited research claim, not a guarantee for every audience.
Fear of bothering customers or triggering cancellations is largely unfounded per the source's experience, but interviews should still be handled with care.
cards.source_name: _Adrienne Barnes on Best Buyer Personas, Marketing & Motherhood.docx

cards.title: Incentivize hard-to-reach interview participants
cards.summary: Match the incentive to the participant's status: product perks for normal customers, charitable donations for busy executives.
cards.use_when: Recruiting interviews with customers who are hard to book, especially senior or high-earning buyers.
steps: For regular customers, offer low-cost brand-relevant perks: a company t-shirt for signing up, or early/beta access to a new tool (source example: three months of beta access).
For busy founders, CEOs or difficult audiences, donate a set amount to a charity of their choice in their name rather than paying them (source used $30 for 30 minutes).
Avoid offering cash to people whose time is worth far more than the amount; it creates an awkward business transaction and cheapens the ask.
Use the charitable framing as a favor exchange that attracts the right caliber of participant without quantifying their time.
caveats: Incentive type and amount are examples, not benchmarks; calibrate to the audience.
Confirm any tool or platform perks are still offered before promising them.
cards.source_name: _Adrienne Barnes on Best Buyer Personas, Marketing & Motherhood.docx

cards.title: Segment personas by jobs to be done, not demographics
cards.summary: Group buyers by the job they are trying to accomplish and the trigger that makes them buy, which produces stronger segmentation than age, gender or job title.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to structure buyer personas or audience segments for campaigns, product and strategy.
steps: Reject purely demographic groupings (age, gender, favorite color, grocery store) because they do not help you write copy or make product decisions.
Identify the job the buyer is trying to get done and the trigger moment that causes them to start looking for a solution.
Group people who share the same job and trigger into one persona, even if their titles or demographics differ.
Write the persona so it can serve marketing, product, sales and customer success, not just one campaign.
Every persona should contain evidence, trigger moments and a job statement.
caveats: The number of personas is not universal; scope varies by business.
Some marketers insist a persona must follow the traditional named/acronym format; the source treats naming as optional and argues the job-based insight matters more.
cards.source_name: _Adrienne Barnes on Best Buyer Personas, Marketing & Motherhood.docx

cards.title: Avoid the dusty, unused persona trap
cards.summary: Most marketers create personas but never use them; build documentation that is actually referenced for campaigns, product and strategy.
cards.use_when: Auditing or replacing an existing persona doc that is not used in go-to-market work.
steps: Check whether the current persona is referenced in campaign launches, product launches, copy or strategy; if not, treat it as a check-the-box artifact.
Replace fluff (fictional names, stock photos, lifestyle details like shops at Trader Joe's) with buyer insights: concerns, product-related jobs, objections and trigger moments.
Call the output whatever the team will accept (buyer persona, buyer insights, buyer documentation) as long as the content is useful.
Distribute the persona across marketing, product, sales and customer success so the research investment pays off in multiple functions.
caveats: Citing the source's survey via Audience: roughly 90%+ of marketers create personas, but about 77% never use them for a launch or copy; these are reported figures, not guarantees.
Naming conventions are contentious; do not force one if it blocks adoption.
cards.source_name: _Adrienne Barnes on Best Buyer Personas, Marketing & Motherhood.docx

cards.title: Use surveys to verify interviews and capture data-centric attributes
cards.summary: Design a survey after interviews to confirm trends at scale and collect structured facts that work better in a form than in conversation.
cards.use_when: You have preliminary interview insights and want to validate them across a larger audience.
steps: Develop the survey questions after analyzing interview themes, focusing on what needs verification at scale.
Include structured, factual items that are easier to answer in a form: role, tenure with the company, number of employees, buying authority, and similar data-centric fields.
Use the survey to confirm or challenge the qualitative trends rather than to discover entirely new motivations.
Combine survey results with conversations, digital intelligence and social listening before forming personas.
caveats: Surveys are better for facts and scale than for uncovering deep motivation; keep them complementary to interviews.
Question and sample design still affect validity; do not treat survey output as automatically representative.
cards.source_name: _Adrienne Barnes on Best Buyer Personas, Marketing & Motherhood.docx

cards.title: Social listening for pain-point topics, not brand mentions
cards.summary: Track what people say about problems and frustrations rather than your brand so personas reflect real language and concerns.
cards.use_when: Adding a social listening layer to persona research or messaging development.
steps: Set up a listening tool (source used Brand24; verify current alternatives and interfaces).
Monitor the topics and pain points relevant to your category, not brand handles or mentions, because the goal is audience context rather than community management.
Capture how people describe frustrations and objections in their own words for use in copy and messaging.
Use listening data to fact-check interview themes and to gauge whether interviewees' descriptions match broader public conversation.
caveats: Listening provides background and validation, not the why behind individual behavior; that still comes from conversations.
Tool capabilities and pricing change; confirm before committing.
cards.source_name: _Adrienne Barnes on Best Buyer Personas, Marketing & Motherhood.docx

cards.title: Use digital intelligence to see how buyers actually behave
cards.summary: Digital intelligence tools reveal platforms, influencers and buying mindsets of the wider audience, filling in behavior that interviews cannot reliably capture.
cards.use_when: You need audience behavior, channel and buying-mindset data to complement interviews and surveys.
steps: Use audience research tools (source used SparkToro and Audience) to see where the broader audience spends time and which platforms they use most.
Identify influencers who shape their decisions, both on social media and in buying contexts.
Assess buying mindset: do they purchase quickly, prefer self-serve, or require a sales team; are they risk-takers or conservative; do they want help or figure it out alone.
Layer in psychographic or socio-emotional data where available (source cites IBM Watson-based data) to understand risk tolerance and support preferences.
Combine these behavioral signals with conversation insights to complete the picture.
caveats: Behaviors seen in tools can be wrong or incomplete; treat them as directional.
Tool availability and data sources change; verify current capabilities.
cards.source_name: _Adrienne Barnes on Best Buyer Personas, Marketing & Motherhood.docx

cards.title: Ask churned customers why they left
cards.summary: Direct outreach to churning customers reveals fixable reasons and can be acted on quickly, as in the subscription chicken-box example.
cards.use_when: Retention is slipping or cancellation rates are rising, especially when paid acquisition is getting harder.
steps: Identify customers who are leaving or have recently cancelled.
Ask them directly why they are leaving instead of inferring from usage data alone.
Act on the specific reported reasons (the source's example: a live chat option on the site).
Keep this as an ongoing practice, not a one-time investigation.
caveats: The chicken-box example is anecdotal and illustrative, not a benchmark.
Some reasons will be outside your control; separate fixable from non-fixable causes.
cards.source_name: _Adrienne Barnes on Best Buyer Personas, Marketing & Motherhood.docx

cards.title: Talk to first customers and keep it in your culture
cards.summary: Regardless of business type, understand what you solve for customers and keep talking to buyers from day one instead of stopping after launch.
cards.use_when: Starting or scaling any business and deciding whether to institutionalize customer conversations.
steps: Figure out exactly why customers purchase; do not assume you already know.
Talk to your very first buyers and treat the conversations as exploratory, not as demos or upgrades.
Make customer conversations a permanent part of company culture rather than a one-time research phase.
Push different functions (marketing, support, sales) into customer calls so they understand what is being solved and can feed insight back into the business.
caveats: The source frames this as universally applicable (plumber, farm, B2B SaaS, DTC), but execution details differ by business.
Do not let the practice become a disguised sales call, which defeats the purpose.
cards.source_name: _Adrienne Barnes on Best Buyer Personas, Marketing & Motherhood.docx

cards.title: Cross-check what people say against what they do
cards.summary: Conversations reveal the why of behavior but people can misreport what they do; digital intelligence and listening data show actual behavior.
cards.use_when: Reconciling conflicting evidence between interviews and analytics/listening data, or designing research to minimize blind spots.
steps: Get motivation and the why from conversations, since digital tools will never explain motivation.
Get how people actually behave from digital intelligence, since people can misreport their own behavior.
Triangulate across all four data sources (conversations, surveys, digital intelligence, social listening) before committing to persona conclusions.
Expect mismatch between stated and observed behavior and treat it as signal rather than error.
caveats: No single data source is authoritative; triangulation is the point.
Source frames this as a cognitive bias problem: people describe what they think they do.
cards.source_name: _Adrienne Barnes on Best Buyer Personas, Marketing & Motherhood.docx

cards.title: Apply jobs-to-be-done using the milkshake story
cards.summary: The milkshake case is a compact way to explain JTBD to clients and teams before applying it to their business.
cards.use_when: Introducing jobs-to-be-done to a client or internal team that has not encountered it.
steps: Tell the milkshake example: intuition says people buy milkshakes for a sweet tooth, but the job was a clean, easy on-the-go snack.
