Pillars interact: belonging without ritual or symbols tends to produce passive affinity rather than repeat purchase.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Build Somatic Markers, Not Feature Lists
cards.summary: Consumers choose brands via unconscious somatic markers — emotional brain shortcuts formed from past reward/punishment — so build associations rather than arguing features.
cards.use_when: Writing PDP copy, category-page merchandising or ad creative and choosing what claim or image should dominate.
steps: Accept the source's claim that many purchase decisions are fast, emotional shortcuts, not slow rational comparisons — Lindstrom cites Gruppe Nymphenberg finding over 50% of in-store purchasing decisions are made spontaneously at point of sale. Treat that as the presenter's cited study, not a universal law.

For your product, write out the rational internal monologue a shopper could have (price suspicion, 'generic brand', past disappointment, childhood memories) — the Jif vs. organic peanut butter example shows buyers weighing trust, nostalgia, price and 'you get what you pay for' in seconds.

Identify which single concept you want linked to your brand (e.g. 'German engineering' for Audi) and repeat that link consistently across packaging, name, price signal and imagery so the association compounds.
Make associations concrete and sensory where possible: the Andrex puppy links to softness, growing young families and even toilet training without ever being a feature claim.

Audit whether your current creative produces a distinct, memorable marker or is interchangeable with competitors — Michelin tires all look the same; the Michelin Man, baby and Guides are what create preference.

Reinforce existing positive links instead of replacing them; the GaJol lozenge campaign worked only because it borrowed an existing nationwide emotion (Pavarotti's canceled concert) and attached the brand to it within hours.
caveats: Somatic-marker theory is presented as neuroscience-backed but the specific percentages are cited studies, not benchmarks you should promise in a plan.
Incongruous or negative associations can also stick permanently — associations are hard to erase once formed.
This is a brand-association strategy; it explains preference, not a guaranteed lift in conversion.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Use Shock and Incongruity to Make Creative Memorable
cards.summary: Because somatic markers bond two incompatible elements, deliberately surprising or shocking juxtapositions are more memorable than smooth, expected brand messages.
cards.use_when: Planning acquisition creative, social video, or a launch stunt where the goal is recall rather than immediate purchase.
steps: Design one unexpected pairing rather than a list of benefits: Blendtec's 'Will it blend?' puts a kitchen blender against iPhones, hockey pucks and garden hoses, and Sony put a urinal seven feet up in a cinema restroom to promote Spider-Man 3.
Keep the shock tied to the product's core promise so the marker reinforces it — Blendtec's pulverizing residue links back to blending power; the Sony stunt links to an upcoming film.
Consider humor-based anthropomorphizing where the category is unglamorous — the Lamisil gremlin living under a toenail links the brand to germ-fighting in a memorable way.
For ecommerce, translate stunts into PDP hero video, UGC-style demonstration content, or a landing-page hook that shows the extreme use case, then link it directly to the buy button.
Track whether the startling image is being recalled and attributed to your brand; a marker that is memorable but unattributed wastes the spend.
caveats: Shock that is unrelated to the product is a risk; the source's examples all keep a product link.
Stunts can misfire with audiences — the source records the San Francisco 'Got Milk?' cookie-scented bus shelters being scrapped after 36 hours when commuters reported allergic reactions.
No conversion benchmark is established; these are illustrative cases, not promised results.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Fear-Based Positioning and Its Limits
cards.summary: Fear creates powerful markers but should be used sparingly and honestly — the source shows fear saturation across categories and warns it may spread further.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to lead with a risk-avoidance message on a PDP, ad or email, e.g. gum disease, hair loss, device failure.
steps: Recognise the mechanism: No More Tears shampoo sells by evoking the fear it prevents; Colgate's ad linked gum disease to heart disease, diabetes and stroke; ADD medicine ads walk parents through a chain ending in jail.
If you use fear, name the specific consequence and pair it with a clear, credible remedy in the same asset so the shopper isn't left with only anxiety.
Prefer prevention framing around an existing, personally-felt pain over inventing unlikely catastrophes — Lindstrom notes practically every category plays on fear, directly or indirectly.
Test fear-led creative against benefit-led or identity-led creative; the source predicts fear-based advertising will increase, which is an opinion, not a finding.
In regulated categories (health, supplements, finance), verify current claims rules before running a disease-link message.
caveats: The source explicitly notes that overt or manipulated fear can be counterproductive and ethically fraught.
The disease-linkage example is a specific ad claim; do not repeat health claims without substantiation.
Fear appeals vary by audience and category; no universal uplift is claimed.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Avoid Overt Religion and Belief-Specific Campaigns
cards.summary: Explicit religious symbolism in ecommerce campaigns risks alienating large segments — the source's Lego advent-calendar case shows an inexpensive idea causing global backlash.
cards.use_when: Planning seasonal campaigns, calendars, gift guides or packaging around holidays with religious roots.
steps: Before shipping a religiously-coded mechanic, ask which beliefs it encodes — the source's virtual advent calendar was Christian-specific and Lego was quickly perceived as promoting a religious agenda.
Check timezone and locale mechanics: the Lego campaign needed a per-country script because Australian and New Zealand users couldn't open doors on the right day.
Prefer implicit or suggestive seasonal cues (winter, cosiness, family, counting down) over explicit religious iconography when you sell to a global audience.
If you must localise religious content, segment by market and permission rather than shipping one mechanic worldwide.
Plan the support load for backlash — the source describes thousands of angry emails landing on one person's desk.
caveats: The source's conclusion is that covert use of religion often doesn't work and can harm a brand; it also notes some companies may use religious elements quietly without admitting it.
Regional norms differ — Vodafone's Pope-quote text service and saint-of-the-day messages were planned for Italy, a market with different expectations.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Choose Fragrance That Is Congruent With the Product
cards.summary: Odour can activate the same brain regions as product imagery, but only when scent and image match — incongruent pairings trigger aversion and are forgotten.
cards.use_when: Designing unboxing, store or packaging scent experiences, or choosing whether to add a signature scent to a product or mailing.
steps: Decide the emotional target first, then pick a scent that plausibly belongs to that product — Dr Calvert's lab found image+fragrance ratings dropped sharply when a Dove soap image was paired with scorched canola oil, and rose when a fish-filet image was paired with a lemon note.
Use the scent as a memory cue for the product not an unrelated mood: smelling doughnut is claimed to make people picture Dunkin' or Krispy Kreme branding.

For packaging, engineer scent release at the moment of opening — the source cites Nescafé and peanut butter jars designed to release maximum fragrance when the lid comes off (freeze-dried coffee needed reformulating since it barely smells).
For mailers, consider microencapsulated scent released on opening, as Royal Mail and BRAND sense developed for shampoo flyers.
Consider the category's own conventions: vanilla is cited as the most popular US scent and appears in Coca-Cola Vanilla variants and other products because of early childhood associations.
caveats: Scent preferences vary by culture and generation — sandalwood is cited as popular in India, and the source notes birth-cohort differences (fresh-mown grass and horses for pre-1930, synthetic Play-Doh and Sweet Tarts for later cohorts).
Scent experiments can backfire on sensitive customers; the 'Got Milk?' bus shelter case had to be removed within 36 hours.
The claimed purchase effects come from cited studies (e.g. floral-scented Nike rooms in Dr Hirsch's experiment) rather than verified ecommerce results.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Use Ambient Scent to Shift In-Store Behaviour
cards.summary: Subtle ambient scents measurably shift behaviour without shoppers noticing, which matters for retail spaces but has implications for pop-ups and packaging.
cards.use_when: Planning a pop-up, showroom or event, or deciding whether to include scent in physical packaging and samples.
steps: Anchor scent near the entry or point of decision: supermarkets put bakeries by the entrance because baking-bread aroma is claimed to increase spending across bread, butter and jam and to make shoppers abandon lists.

Match scent to the target behaviour — a barely detectable lemon cleaning scent raised the share of people who wrote cleaning activities on their to-do list from 11% to 36%, and those in the scented room made less mess eating a crumbly cookie.

Test whether scent changes evaluation metrics, not just mood: in Hirsch's Nike experiment, 84% of volunteers preferred the shoes in the florally scented room and estimated them roughly $10 higher, and a freshly-cut-grass scent in a German home-improvement store led 49% of surveyed customers to say staff seemed more knowledgeable.
Keep concentrations low: in these studies subjects were unaware of the scent and it appears the effect depends on non-conscious exposure.
For ecommerce, treat scent as an offline/UGC asset — include scented inserts or samples where a smell can cue the product experience, and capture the moment in video for the PDP.
caveats: All results are cited studies, not benchmarks; effect sizes vary by setting.
Some customers are sensitive or allergic to fragrance, so scent should be optional or absent in shared spaces.
The source does not show that ambient scent raises online conversion.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Treat Sound as a Branded Asset, Not Decoration
cards.summary: Signature sounds work like auditory logos and can steer product choice — the Leicester wine study showed shoppers were 3–4 times more likely to pick wine matching the overhead music.
cards.use_when: Choosing background music for a store, pop-up or video, or designing notification, unboxing and jingle sounds.
steps: Decide the association you want and pick music that carries it: on French accordion days 77% of shoppers bought French wine, while on Bierkeller brass days most bought German wine, and only one of 44 interviewed customers mentioned the music as a reason.
Build sounds into product moments where they will be repeated — the GE three-chime, the iPod wheel tick, the Kellogg's engineered crunch and Ford's vault-like door latch.

Engineer sounds at the point of opening or use to signal freshness or quality — the source describes the engineered sound of a coffee jar or Pringles can opening, and the beep of a McDonald's fry machine.

Use music with a behavioural purpose where relevant: classical music in London Underground locations was reported to be associated with a 33% drop in robberies, 25% fewer assaults on staff and 37% less vandalism (cited figures, not a proven causal ecommerce result).
For online acquisition, design audio into video ads and ensure the sound carries the brand cue even when heard alone.
caveats: The wine study is a cited field experiment; treat the multiplier as an example.
Signature sounds can become irritating with overexposure — Nokia's default ring tone is the source's central case of a beloved brand damaged by its own ubiquity.
Music affects different audiences differently; no universal genre works.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Weight, Touch and Packaging Shape Quality Perception
cards.summary: How a product feels in hand — weight, texture, shape — drives perceived quality independently of actual performance.
cards.use_when: Choosing packaging materials, device weight, garment presentation or sample format so the physical feel matches the intended price tier.
steps: Test the weight of your packaging against your price point — the source's Bang & Olufsen test gave 100 consumers identical-function remotes with and without a useless aluminium insert; without it, users said 'it's broken' even when told it worked.

Do not assume lighter is always better: electronics buyers often read small and light as advanced (per Underhill's observation that shoppers touch clothing before buying, and the source's note on slim gadgets), but premium categories can rely on heft.
Match form to buyer body image where relevant — in the French diet-mayonnaise test, all diet-conscious women chose the bottle with a narrow waist over the genie-bottle shape before tasting either.
Design packaging to invite touch: open tables, swatch samples, unboxing steps that require handling the product.
For Duracell-style weight cueing, note the source's caution that adding weight can reduce actual performance while increasing perceived power — decide which signal you're buying.
caveats: These are experiments with small samples, described by the author; they are illustrative, not universal rules.
Weight expectations differ by category — a heavy phone may read as dated to some buyers.
The Duracell bullet-battery concept never reached the market, so treat it as an anecdote.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Use Colour Deliberately to Signal Brand Meaning
cards.summary: Colour carries strong emotional associations and appears to raise attention and recognition, so treat colour choice as a strategic branding decision rather than a palette preference.
cards.use_when: Choosing a brand palette, packaging colour, product variant colours or a category-disrupting visual identity — including for banks, apps or supplements.
steps: Pick a colour that carries the association you want: the source describes women's heart rates rising 20% on receiving a blue Tiffany box with no logo visible, and pink carrying luxury, sensuality and femininity associations.

Consider deliberate category incongruity to earn attention: the source advised a bank CEO to paint branches, cars, uniforms and his tie pink; after roughly three months, he reported the highest brand awareness of any bank in the country and marketing costs halved. Treat this as one anecdote, not a formula.

Remember colour also shapes packaging perception and product variants — Heinz EZ Squirt green ketchup sold over 10 million bottles in its first seven months, the brand's biggest sales spike, and Apple's candy-coloured iMacs were preordered heavily.

Test attention and recognition effects: cited studies include coloured phone-directory ads holding attention two seconds or more against under one second for black-and-white, Seoul International Color Expo's claim that colour can raise brand recognition up to 80%, and 84.7% of respondents saying colour was more than half their brand-choice criterion.
In fast-scrolling commerce, treat colour as your thumbnail's primary attention device — the source cites that products have roughly one-twentieth of a second to grab attention.
caveats: These figures are from cited studies and one anecdote; they are not guarantees and should be verified for your category and market.
The pink-bank example includes a period where customers hated the change before it became accepted — expect an adjustment period if you take a disruptive colour route.
Colour meanings differ by culture and demography.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Design Yolk, Surface and Substrate Cues for Food Products
cards.summary: For food products, colour of the visible product — not just packaging — drives selection, and growers and brands can shape it legitimately.
cards.use_when: Sourcing, photographing or commissioning food products where appearance signals quality: eggs, produce, baked goods, sauces.
steps: Identify the instinctive quality cue in your category: the source notes the egg industry's rule of thumb that more yellow yolks appeal more, likely an evolved signal that kept ancestors from eating bad eggs.

Decide whether to shift the cue through diet or inputs — egg farmers add colouring to grain to deepen yolk colour, and the source identified a vitamin mix as a less artificial route, producing a spectrum from light to deep yellow.
Apply the same logic to your imagery and specification: how the product looks on the plate or in the jar should match the cue shoppers already use to judge quality.
Note that appearance preferences shift over time with no clear cause — white eggs were once associated with cleanliness and hygiene before brown eggs came to be read as more organic and natural.
Treat this as expectation-setting: egg colour itself is an unreliable quality indicator, so pair the visual cue with honest product information.
caveats: Preferences such as white vs brown eggs and yolk depth vary by market and change over time.
Adding colouring to feed raises ethical questions; the source declined artificial colouring for that reason.
Do not claim the colour cue proves nutritional quality.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Reinforce Brand Cues Without Redesigning Them
cards.summary: Signature fragrances and sensory identifiers are easy to lose and hard to recreate, so protect and document them as brand assets.
cards.use_when: Planning a reformulation, rebrand, packaging refresh or outsourcing of any sensory element (scent, crunch, sound, colour).
steps: Document the exact formulation or asset before any change — the source reports Johnson & Johnson and Play-Doh altered their fragrances so much that competitors' scents now smell closer to the original than their own.
Consider that a reformulated sensory asset may never be recovered: the source says Play-Doh has never fully replicated its original smell, estimating it is only about 80% there.
Guard against accidental erosion from patchwork changes — small tweaks compound into a different signature.
When you must reformulate (regulation, supply, cost), test whether existing customers still recognise and prefer it before switching, and treat recognisability as a KPI.
Apply the same discipline to signature sounds, colours and packaging shapes so a refresh does not silently retire the marker that drives repeat purchase.
caveats: The Johnson & Johnson and Play-Doh examples are the author's firsthand accounts; exact percentages of scent fidelity are the company's own estimate.
Some reformulation is unavoidable for legal or supply reasons — the aim is deliberate management, not freezing the asset forever.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Recognise That Overexposure Can Turn a Signature Asset Against You
cards.summary: A highly recognisable brand sound or cue can become hated through ubiquity, which is a maintenance risk for brands whose identity relies on one repeated element.
cards.use_when: Deciding how often to repeat a sonic logo, notification sound, ad jingle or packaging cue across the customer journey.
steps: Monitor whether your signature cue is becoming irritating rather than reassuring — the source notes Nokia's default ring tone was kept by 20% of subscribers, 41% of UK subscribers could recall or hum it, and yet it drove many users mad through constant overexposure.
Where a cue is unavoidable, offer control: ring tones, notification sounds and autoplay audio can be muted or varied by the user.
Track sentiment separately from recognition — high recall is not the same as positive association.
For ecommerce, apply this to email notification sounds, autoplay video and repeated audio in ads: recognition without goodwill can trigger unsubscribes.
If a signature asset is tainted, create a new one rather than trying to talk customers out of the irritation.
caveats: This is a qualitative argument illustrated with Nokia data; the source does not establish a threshold at which a sound becomes net-negative.
A loud minority complaining does not prove brand damage — pair sentiment tracking with behavioural data.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Stack Senses Rather Than Relying on Visuals Alone
cards.summary: Combining congruent sensory cues in one asset produces stronger appeal, memory and — in the cited cases — attention than visuals alone.
cards.use_when: Briefing video ads, PDP media, in-game or streaming placements, or designing sensory touchpoints for a store or pop-up.
steps: Assume visual saturation reduces the attention any single logo or banner can win — Neuroco's study for 20th Century Fox placed ads in a video game but found visual saturation produced glazed eyes rather than attention.

Pair images with matching sound or scent rather than adding either alone: Dr Calvert's experiment showed image-plus-fragrance combinations were rated more pleasant than either element on its own when they matched.
Where possible add a third channel: the source cites a Diet Pepsi magazine ad with sound, taste and pop-up features achieving 100% reader awareness in People, the magazine's first such result.
Choose only cues that make sense for the product — incongruence drives aversion and poorer recall.
Measure combined-asset recall and preference against visual-only controls instead of assuming a single logo will carry the message.
caveats: The 100% awareness figure is a cited, single-issue result and should not be promised.
Added sensory elements raise production cost and can be blocked by platforms (autoplay, audio) — check current ad policies before committing.
The Fox study's conclusion is that generic visual saturation fails, not that all visual advertising is useless.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Pair Signature Sound With Logo to Boost Liking and Recall
cards.summary: Simultaneous congruent audio plus logo increases attention, pleasantness and long-term memory encoding versus either alone.
cards.use_when: Designing brand assets for a PDP, video ad, unboxing page or app: deciding whether to add a sonic signature, jingle or branded audio cue alongside your logo.
steps: Have one distinctive branded sound (jingle, sting, sonic logo) and one highly recognizable visual mark, then always present them together rather than separately.

In video and animated PDP media, time the sound to land exactly on the logo reveal so eyes and ears fire simultaneously; simultaneous pairing outperformed sound-only or image-only in Lindstrom's fMRI study.
Check congruence: the sound's mood must match the product category and imagery, since the positive results held when sound and vision were combined in a congruent way.

Test the pairing, not just the assets: measure whether the combined unit is liked and remembered, because a sound that is liked in isolation can still suppress feeling for the logo (the Nokia result).
For audio-only channels where a logo cannot appear, expect weaker liking and recall than the paired version and compensate with repetition or an additional visual cue elsewhere.
caveats: Findings come from a small lab fMRI study of four brands; three of four benefited from pairing, so treat it as a directional principle, not a guaranteed lift.
This is preference, emotional engagement and memory encoding data, not measured purchase lift.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Audit Your Signature Sound for Negative Somatic Associations
cards.summary: A famous, ubiquitous brand sound can become a negative somatic marker that suppresses positive feeling for the visual brand.
cards.use_when: Reviewing an existing sonic identity, notification sound, hold music or app alert that has been in market for years and may now be associated with interruption.
steps: Recognize the Nokia pattern: the ring was among the most successfully branded tunes ever, yet when paired with Nokia imagery it produced across-the-board negative emotional response and dragged down preference for the phones themselves.
Investigate the context of exposure, not the melody. Negative associations came from where the sound was heard: a phone interrupting dinner, a movie, a yoga class, a call from the boss.
Watch for a tell in your own team: Lindstrom noticed an 'uncomfortable yikes feeling' when his own phone rang. Ask internal staff and customer-facing teams what feeling your sound triggers.

If the cue is a functional alert (order shipped, someone joined a call, doorbell, message), separate the functional alert from the branded marketing sound so the brand is not attached to interruption.
Test preference for your imagery with and without your signature sound. If the sound suppresses feeling for the logo, replace or retire it even if recall of the sound is high.
caveats: Source opinion: Lindstrom judged the Nokia tone was 'killing the brand' based on fMRI and rating data from his own study, not a sales regression.
Familiarity alone is not evidence of brand equity; high recall can coexist with negative affect.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Multi-Sensory Congruence: Design Beyond Sight
cards.summary: Senses are intertwined in the brain, so the right pairing of smell, sound and touch with visuals makes a brand more engaging than visual-only design.
cards.use_when: Planning retail interiors, packaging, unboxing experience, brand film or event activation where you can add a non-visual cue on top of the visual identity.
steps: Pick the sense that carries the meaning you want, not just the loudest one. Lindstrom's vision of future retail links a lemon scent to sneakers, fresh orange to sporting goods, perfume to a hotel entrance.
Choose a congruent sensory note rather than a random pleasant one, since the benefit came from the right pairing of sensory inputs.

Build the cue into the physical product where it can carry association: GSK's Alli used vivid red, blue, yellow and green on white plus a uniquely shaped, portable 'shuttle' pill carrier with a gentle bubbled texture to evoke partnership and a journey together.
Repeat the cue across channels (packaging, store, site video, ad) so the sensory signal becomes a recognizable asset rather than a one-off stunt.
Track emotional engagement and recall in tests, not just stated liking, because stated preference diverges from measured response.
caveats: The Times Square smell-and-sound scenario is Lindstrom's prediction, not a documented result.
Scent and sound in ecommerce are largely limited to video, packaging and physical retail; browser-based scent is not a practical channel today.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Test Congruent Cue Combinations, Not Single Cues
cards.summary: Sound-plus-image combinations were rated more favorably and left more impression than either element alone, but one brand's cue actively harmed the pairing.
cards.use_when: Setting up creative testing for ad or PDP assets where you plan to combine a logo, a jingle, a face, a color or a spokesperson.
steps: Structure the test as three arms minimum: cue A alone, cue B alone, and the combination, so you can see whether the pairing is additive, neutral or destructive.
Follow Lindstrom's run design: present the sound alone, then the image alone, then both simultaneously, and repeat the sequence to capture stable responses.
Include a neutral benchmark in each category (a generic ring tone, an unrelated image) because Nokia's ring made subjects prefer unrelated benchmark images over Nokia phones.

Interpret combination results in context, not in isolation: Microsoft's logo tested less positive than its sound, yet the joint presentation of logo and melody raised preference slightly, so combining can rescue a weaker element.
Decide the go/no-go on the combined asset's emotional engagement and long-term memory encoding if you have access to those measures, otherwise on recall and preference for the pair.
caveats: This is fMRI lab methodology; most ecommerce teams can only approximate it with survey-based recall and preference tests.
Results varied by brand, so a positive category-level pattern does not guarantee your pairing will be additive.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Treat Stated Buy Intent as Unreliable for Launch Decisions
cards.summary: Questionnaire responses often do not match behavioral outcomes, so stated liking is a weak predictor of product or content success.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to launch a new product, SKU, bundle, landing page concept or ad campaign based on survey, focus group or concept-test feedback.
steps: Compare stated preference to a harder measure before committing budget. In Lindstrom's TV study, How Clean Is Your House? was a proven hit and The Swan a proven flop, yet the two scored neck and neck on viewers' stated likelihood to watch.
Collection note: the source text contains a corrupted character (a single letter) where one of the two scores would appear, so only the neck-and-neck conclusion is reliable.

Look for the divergence pattern: Quizmania was rated the show viewers would least likely watch, yet brain engagement landed between the flop and the hit, and it subsequently performed as the scans predicted in the U.K.

Use non-verbal or behavioral proxies available to an ecommerce team: actual click-through and add-to-cart for creative variants, or the eye-tracking-style attention data below, rather than stated intent alone.
Keep the benchmark logic: predict relative rank against known successes and known failures rather than an absolute pass/fail.
caveats: The brain-engagement method is not available to most merchants; the transferable lesson is skepticism toward stated intent, not the specific prediction method.
The 99 percent statistical certainty in the source refers to that study's confidence, not to any product launch prediction you make.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Vampire Effect: Titillating Creative Steals Attention From the Brand
cards.summary: Sexual imagery draws gaze to itself and away from the brand name, reducing brand recall versus neutral creative.
cards.use_when: Reviewing acquisition creative, hero images, model photography or landing page visuals that are suggestive but may not be carrying your logo, product name or offer.
steps: Check what the image is actually competing with: MediaAnalyzer's eye-movement test found men spent inordinate time on breasts and largely bypassed brand name, logo and body text.

Compare recall numbers to decide whether the creative earns its place: brand recall was about 9.8 percent for men viewing sexual ads versus almost 20 percent for nonsexual ads, and about 10.85 percent versus 22.3 percent for women.

Reduce the problem by physically separating the provocative element from the information: keep logo, product name and price in a zone the eye must land on, or overlay the brand mark on or near the focal point.
Avoid stacking sexual creative on top of already sexual context, since viewers of Sex and the City had worse ad recall than viewers of a non-erotic sitcom, as the show's own content eclipsed the ads.
Measure brand recall, not just CTR, when testing this category of creative: a suggestive image may win clicks and still fail to lodge the brand.
caveats: The Eye-movement and recall studies used print ads and young adult samples, so figures are study-specific and not benchmarks for your store.
The conclusion attributed to Parker and Furnham is that sex 'does not sell anything other than itself', which is a strong generalization from their recall study.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Choose Controversy Over Titillation When You Want Attention
cards.summary: Evidence points to controversy, not sexual content per se, being the more potent driver of attention and purchase influence.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a provocative campaign, limited drop or naming choice is worth the risk to brand perception.
steps: Separate the two levers in your planning: sexual content draws the eyes to itself (Vampire Effect), while controversy generates publicity and news coverage around the brand.

Consider the Calvin Klein pattern as a case study, not a playbook: the 1980 Brooke Shields campaign was reported to drive jeans sales up to roughly two million pairs a month, and by 1984 the business was worth nearly a billion dollars a year — but the source also notes sales have declined, the brand was sold to Phillips Van Heusen in 2002, and the same provocative ads these shoppers saw also drew boycotts, TV network refusals and a Justice Department investigation.

Weigh the reversibility of brand damage: pull ads generated fresh publicity (the pattern Lindstrom describes as a deliberate PR maneuver), but some brands suffered — the source says Dolce & Gabbana was hurt after a gang-rape-look ad was pulled under protest.
Decide the message in advance: an ad needs attention, the name in memory, and consistency. Nike's ad worked because the image pointed to product performance and brand, not to an unrelated sight gag.
Watch the boundary: controversy may drive short-term customers away while making the ad more memorable, so it is a trade, not a free win.
caveats: Controversy-driven growth claims are historical case observations, not controlled tests, and the source explicitly says the mechanism is unproven.
Boycotts and retailer refusals are real costs the source documents alongside the sales gains.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Keep Sex and Attention-Getters Pointing at the Product
cards.summary: Attention-grabbing devices work when they direct attention to the product and misfire when they merely grab attention for themselves.
cards.use_when: Judging hero imagery, spokesperson choice, humour or shock value in an ad or PDP before committing spend.
steps: Ask what the viewer will look at and remember: if it is the joke, the model or the controversy rather than the product, the creative fails the Vampire Effect test.

Contrast pairs: the source presents a sexualized image of a dominatrix holding a vacuum cleaner, a suggestive toilet-paper image and a suggestive car ad as examples where the relevant connection is weak or absurd, while Nike's product-performance-toned campaign is presented as a case where the provocative image pointed straight at the product.

For ecommerce applications, adapt this to PDP video and social creative: the eye-catching element should be the product in use, or a demonstration of the claim, rather than a model or gag unrelated to it.

Check the exception: for fashion categories with a natural link between body and product (lingerie, fragrance, swimwear), the productive path is to keep the presentation on the product and its wearer, as the source argues Calvin Klein does.
If your only aim is clicks and the product link is weak, expect a short-lived spike and measure post-click quality (add-to-cart, return rate) rather than click volume.
caveats: The comparison set is Lindstrom's editorial selection of ads he saw, not a controlled experiment.
The source's own viewpoint is that most sexual advertising is 'harder to swallow', so treat the sex-versus-controversy distinction as his interpretation.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Measure Before Believing: Human Responses Don't Match Stated Intent
cards.summary: People misreport why they say they can't wait to buy, because conscious and unconscious processes differ.
cards.use_when: Designing post-purchase surveys, NPS follow-ups, ad recall questions or any research meant to predict which product, offer or campaign will actually sell.
steps: Treat stated intent as a hypothesis to verify, not a finding: how we say we feel about a product cannot truly predict how we behave.
Design questions around past behaviour (what did you buy, when) — memory of actual past behaviour is more reliable than prediction of future behaviour.

Where possible, measure emotional response alongside rational response; in Lindstrom's TV study the brain data matched the show's real performance while the questionnaire did not match either show's real performance.
Keep a benchmark: include a product or campaign with known outcomes when testing new concepts so you can see whether the test can separate winners from losers at all.
Watch for the novelty effect: Lindstrom's team gave viewers the DVDs to watch and 'sleep on it' before scanning, to reduce the inflated response first-time viewing produces.
caveats: The source's own confidence is high, but the technique under test in his book is not considered settled science.
Some of the source's claims about fMRI methodology exceeding research capability are carried over from the research team, not independently proved.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Run Quarterly NPS and Segment by Historical Value
cards.summary: NPS combines a simple recommendation question with open comments, and its business insight comes from linking responses to historical customer value and behaviour.
cards.use_when: Setting up recurring customer feedback for a store and deciding where to spend service, range, price and convenience effort.
steps: Ask the recommend question on a 0-10 scale repeatedly and consistently so you can track trend rather than one-off scores.

Do not collapse feedback into the score: read the comments for category-specific issues that word clouds hide, such as store cleanliness, staff attitude, price and range in the source's grocery example.

Link scores to historical transaction data: the source reports that for one business the most valuable customer segments were measurably more likely to be promoters, and that senior store managers whose locations scored well on service were more likely to exceed profit plans.
Use the feedback for budget decisions: the source describes how the NPS result redirected investment away from long-underfunded service areas toward store-level improvements.
Set an internal threshold for action and follow the score over time so you can tell whether a change moved the needle, rather than chasing a single survey cycle.
caveats: The source reports some of these findings as its own consulting analysis rather than as independently published results.
NPS is a public-domain measure with contested academic support, so treat it as one input alongside behavioural metrics.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Use Recurring Research With Complaining and Non-Complaining Customers
cards.summary: Reichheld's approach pairs a simple recommendation survey with follow-up on the people who do not complain, then links answers to spending and retention.
cards.use_when: Building a customer research cadence for an ecommerce brand and deciding which responses should trigger a follow-up or win-back action.
steps: Ask a short, repeatable recommendation question with an open comment box.
Do not rely on complaints alone: the source's view is that unhappy customers who never complain are a hidden cost because the company believes they are satisfied.
Read comments at category level and watch for the gap between what leadership assumes and what the free text actually says, as the source describes for store cleanliness and staff attitude.

Use the closed-loop follow-up as the mechanism: Lindstrom describes a chief executive who called customers personally because 'that is how I learn', which is the spirit of following up rather than only scoring.
Tie results to spend behaviour where you can, since the source connects promoter likelihood to higher historical customer value and to store-level performance.
caveats: The 85 percent threshold for successful promoters and the segment-level comparisons in the source are reported as one consultancy's proprietary results, not independently verified.
A single survey cannot tell you why a customer behaves as they do; pair it with transaction data.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Move Research Out of the Building to See Real Behaviour
cards.summary: Reichheld argues that companies spend too much time in internal meetings and not enough observing customers and front-line operations directly.
cards.use_when: Planning a product, pricing or merchandising decision and deciding how much effort to spend on direct customer contact versus internal deck reviews.
steps: Build direct observation into the calendar the way Lindstrom describes: personally working the front line and calling users is the version of 'getting out of the building' the source recommends.
Attend the touchpoints where your customers actually make decisions — search and product pages for a store, aisles and tills for physical locations — rather than reviewing reports about them.
Capture questions customers ask and objections they raise on the call, at the till, or in chats, and use them verbatim as inputs to copy and FAQ.
Push the observation habit down to senior managers so store-level or channel-level decisions are informed by their own observations, not just from reporting.
Reserve time for this every quarter; the source's criticism is that leaders drift toward internal meetings as the default.
caveats: This is executive practice guidance from the source, not a controlled study.
Direct observation is qualitative and should not replace measurement of conversion, retention and margin.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Design Products That Fit the Way the Brain Works
cards.summary: Reichheld's closing argument is that product design should follow how the brain actually works rather than force people to think in a new way.
cards.use_when: Deciding on navigation, checkout flow, packaging format or subscription mechanics where users must learn a new pattern.
steps: Prefer the pattern that feels natural: the source's example is Amazon's Simple Storage Service, which won because it was simple, and TiVo, which lost because it left the user in no-man's-land between recording and watching television.

When you invent a new model, test whether users can predict what happens next: the failure mode in the TiVo example is that the software divided the mind and required the user to deal with a newly present and equal-demanding dual entity.
Apply this to subscription and replenishment design: keep control and expectations explicit so customers can see what will happen, when and how to change it.
Apply it to the site or app: use familiar, logical navigation and visible indicators (progress, stock, delivery estimates) so the user's mental model matches the interface.
Treat category-leading functionality as insufficient: the source argues that superior products can still fail on usability and that better understanding of the brain improves both design and service.
caveats: TiVo and Amazon are Lindstrom's chosen examples of design principles, not tested experiments in the book.
Underestimating the next big idea is a risk the source also acknowledges; simplicity should not be read as 'never innovate'.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Assume ~90% of Buying Is Unconscious — Fix Self-Report Research
cards.summary: Lindstrom argues most purchase behaviour is unconscious, so stated-reason research must be supplemented with behavioural observation for product and offer decisions.
cards.use_when: Designing customer research before a product launch, repositioning, or pricing change, and deciding how much weight to put on surveys, reviews and interview answers.
steps: Accept the source's framing that roughly 90% of consumer buying behaviour is unconscious, meaning 'why did you buy this?' answers capture only a thin slice of the real drivers.
Keep surveys, NPS and exit polls for what they are good at: stated preference, feature comprehension, price expectation ranges and open complaints.
Add observational evidence — session recordings, heatmaps, click/scroll data, search-term mining, cart-abandon reason coding, unboxing and shelf footage — for anything about attention and impulse.
Test at the behaviour level instead of asking: run A/B tests on headline, hero image, price framing, bundle composition and page order, and let measured add-to-cart and purchase conversion decide.
Treat stated preference as directional only for expensive qualitative decisions such as new brand names or category entry, and confirm with small live experiments on traffic you already own.
Record which findings came from stated versus observed data so later analysis does not treat opinions as measurements.
caveats: The 90% figure is the author's summary of the neuromarketing field, not a store-measurable benchmark; do not quote it as an internal KPI.
Small-n lab studies (some cited experiments used ten to twenty volunteers) are illustrative, not predictive of your traffic.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Price and Product Story Shape Perceived Enjoyment
cards.summary: Brain-imaging work cited by Lindstrom shows higher prices and branded framing increase reported and neural pleasure, while discounts can raise reward and lower purchase conflict.
cards.use_when: Setting price positioning, discount depth and PDP copy for premium or gift-oriented products where perceived quality drives purchase.
steps: Decide deliberately whether the product is sold as a premium or a value item before writing copy, because the source's wine and luxury studies suggest price itself feeds perceived pleasantness.
For premium positioning, avoid habitual discounting on the same PDP: the same item shown heavily discounted changes the reward/conflict balance and can flatten the quality story you paid to build.
Support the price with concrete provenance, materials, origin, certification or craft detail (see the Seki saba brand case, where certification and handling rules justified a large price rise).
For value positioning, make the saving explicit and immediate so reward rises while purchase conflict falls — bundle value, quantity breaks, or clear comparison framing.
Test price-anchoring variants (bundle vs single, gift vs refill) as experiments rather than assuming your audience matches the study populations.
Do not run both stories on the same page: pick the premium narrative or the discount narrative per SKU and per landing page.
caveats: The luxury and wine findings come from small fMRI studies with students and volunteers; treat them as hypotheses about framing, not proof your customers will pay more.
Discounts may be necessary for liquidation, seasonality or competitive reasons — the point is not to discount reflexively alongside premium positioning.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Branding Turns Commodities into Premium SKUs
cards.summary: Using the Seki saba mackerel case, Lindstrom shows how naming, rules and certification raised a commodity's price by roughly 600% by making it perceptibly special.
cards.use_when: Differentiating commodity or undifferentiated products — own-label food, staples, unbranded accessories — to escape price comparison.
steps: Name the product with a specific origin, method or maker rather than a generic descriptor, so buyers can reference it and repeat it.
Write explicit inclusion rules: what qualifies as the genuine product and what does not (the source's example required rod-caught fish, a specific bleeding technique, and no weighing or measuring).
Publish the standard visibly on the PDP, packaging or certificate so the rules become a trust signal rather than internal trivia.
Remove or rename near-identical variants that dilute the special-name claim, as confusion with lookalike items erased the price premium in the source case.
Build scarcity and inspection rituals into the buying process where relevant to your category — limited batches, sealed packaging, hand-checked grading.
Check that the differentiated SKU's margin actually absorbs the added process cost; the branding premium only pays if the operations behind it are real.
caveats: The 600% price rise is a case-study outcome from a regulated, region-specific fishery and an official government certificate; your category may have no equivalent certification lever.
Fabricated provenance is a legal and reputational risk — only claim standards you can document.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Escalate Fear-Based Messaging Carefully on PDPs and Ads
cards.summary: The Super Bowl fMRI study found fear-inducing ads triggered amygdala activity and left viewers anxious, but the author argues fear works when it targets personal insecurity rather than general dread.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to lead acquisition creative or PDP copy with risk, loss, or self-doubt framing for problem-solving products (skincare, insurance, security, health).
steps: Classify the fear you plan to use: generalised anxiety (economy, job loss, vague doom) versus specific personal insecurity your product resolves (bad skin, dull hair, missed protection).
Prefer insecurity-with-solution framing over ambient fear, because the cited brain scans showed generalised dread produced anxiety without moving viewers toward the brand.
Pair every fear cue with a clear, credible solution on the same screen — product, claim and next step — so the negative emotion has an exit.
Balance fear assets with reassurance assets: reviews, guarantees, demonstrations, before/after, expert endorsement or certification.
Test fear-led versus benefit-led creatives against purchase conversion, not just click-through, since anxious viewers may click out of discomfort.
Recheck tone on retention surfaces: the same fear messaging that works on cold acquisition can damage repeat-purchase and subscription renewal rates.
caveats: The amygdala findings come from ten volunteers viewing two Super Bowl ads — strong directional evidence, not a rule about your audience.
The author openly predicts more fear-based marketing will appear; that is a prediction and endorsement of effectiveness, not proof of ethics or long-term brand safety.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Cognitive Dissonance as a Post-Purchase Retention Tool
cards.summary: The source's naming of 'somatic markers' and dissonance research implies buyers rationalise expensive choices after the fact, giving operators a lever at the confirmation stage.
cards.use_when: Designing post-purchase email flows, thank-you pages, unboxing inserts and review requests for high-consideration or high-price purchases.
steps: Identify where a buyer is most likely to regret an expensive or unfamiliar purchase: right after checkout, at first-use, and at renewal.

On the thank-you page and confirmation email, immediately reinforce the reason for the choice with proof — the guarantee, the ingredient, the certification, the review — so the buyer can defend the decision to themselves and others.
Time a follow-up message to arrive before the first use or unboxing, offering setup help, care instructions or a first-win tip so the product delivers the promised benefit early.
Ask for a review or testimonial only after the customer has had a positive use experience, not at delivery, so the rationalisation is anchored in a real outcome.
For subscription or consumable products, resurface the original choice rationale in the pre-renewal email to reduce quiet churn.
Track refund/return rate and second-purchase rate as the outcome measures, not open rates.
caveats: Lindstrom summarises Damasio's somatic-marker work rather than running store-level retention tests; the mechanism is well-supported but the retail tactics here are an adaptation.
Aggressive post-purchase upselling can undermine the reassurance the tactic depends on.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Ritual Attachment Builds Repeat Purchase Habits
cards.summary: Lindstrom's ritual evidence (Mallomars, Guinness, Got Milk) shows repeat behaviour is often tied to seasonal or habitual rituals, not rational preference.
cards.use_when: Planning replenishment cadence, seasonal drops, subscription timing or loyalty programmes for consumables and repeat-purchase categories.
steps: Map the real-world occasions when your customers already use the product — morning routine, weekend treat, holiday, sports night, back-to-school — by interviewing buyers about the moment, not the product.
Design packaging, comms and product formats around one existing occasion rather than inventing a new behaviour; attach the brand to a ritual already happening.
Time restock and reminder emails to the customer's own cadence (measured from reorder intervals) rather than a fixed calendar.
Where a seasonal ritual exists, make the product's availability part of it — limited windows, announcement dates, collector variants.
Give the ritual a small repeatable step customers perform (a serving method, a storage habit, a pairing) and document it on the PDP and packaging.
Measure success by repeat-purchase rate and orders per customer per year, not by campaign engagement.
caveats: The rituals cited are drawn from established consumer culture and folklore; a new brand cannot manufacture a ritual instantly and should borrow rather than invent.
Over-instrumenting a ritual (aggressive reminders, gamified streaks) can turn a pleasant habit into an annoyance.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Use Mirror-Neuron Logic to Make Social Proof Believable
cards.summary: Lindstrom's mirror-neuron chapter argues we simulate observed actions and emotions, so seeing real users act on a product is more persuasive than reading claims.
cards.use_when: Producing PDP imagery, UGC, video testimonials and acquisition creative for products where usage needs demonstrating.
steps: Show people actually using the product in the exact context of the intended buyer, so viewers can simulate the action rather than interpret a written claim.
Prefer unpolished, real-user footage over studio comps where authenticity drives trust; the source's examples lean on observed behaviour, not scripts.
For complex products, demonstrate the physical step sequence — unbox, install, apply, prepare — because mirroring a clear action reduces perceived effort and returns.
Use reviewers' own photos and video in reviews to extend the mirroring effect beyond your own assets.
A/B test demonstration-led hero assets against benefit-copy heroes on add-to-cart rate.
Keep demonstrations honest: a mirrored action that fails on delivery triggers returns, which the same mechanism predicts.
caveats: The mirror-neuron research Lindstrom cites comes from lab studies on imitation; the retail applications are reasonable adaptations, not tested store tactics.
High-production gloss is not automatically wrong — categories such as luxury may need it; test rather than assume.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Sensory Branding Extends Beyond the Screen
cards.summary: From the BRAND sense work Lindstrom references, multisensory cues — scent, sound, texture — can anchor brand recall and affect product perception at physical or unboxing touchpoints.
cards.use_when: Designing packaging, unboxing experience, in-store or pop-up environments, and audio cues for apps or physical retail.
steps: List the senses your customer actually encounters at each touchpoint — packaging smell and feel, delivery box sound, tonal signature on app or ad — then decide which one to own.
Choose one distinctive sensory signature the brand can repeat consistently (a scent, a sound, a texture) rather than decorating every touchpoint.
Ensure the sensory cue is tied to a benefit or memory: scent triggering cleanliness in a cleaning product, or a sound tied to your app's core action.
For ecommerce specifically, invest first in tactile and olfactory unboxing quality, since it is the closest analogue to the multisensory brand experience the source describes.
Test whether the cue improves repeat purchase, not just pleasant comments in reviews.
Audit for sensory noise: competing scents, harsh packaging, jarring ad audio can distort or contradict the branded cue.
caveats: Sensory-branding payoffs in the source are drawn from established brands with large budgets; small stores should prioritise unboxing and packaging before scent machines or bespoke audio.
Scented or textured packaging may raise shipping cost and complicate returns — model that before committing.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Human and Founder Brands Increase Attention
cards.summary: Lindstrom predicts more '24-hour human brands' as founders and personalities become the most visible, always-on expression of a company's identity.
cards.use_when: Deciding how visible a founder or named expert should be in acquisition creative, PDP trust blocks and social content.
steps: Decide whether a real, named person is the credible voice for the product — a chef for food, a formulator for skincare, a maker for crafts — and feature them where trust is needed.
Put the human story on the PDP trust block, about page and ad creative consistently, rather than letting brand and person run conflicting narratives.
Give the persona a reason to be visible beyond promotion: process stories, failures, sourcing trips, decisions — content that generates attention on its own.
Prepare a contingency plan for when a human brand misbehaves or leaves, since the source materials warn of the reputational risk of tying corporate value to one person's behaviour.
Measure whether founder-led creative moves purchase conversion versus anonymous brand creative before scaling spend.
Keep founder content clearly separate from endorsed claims subject to advertising rules.
caveats: The source's examples — Paris Hilton, Richard Branson — are large public personas; scaling this tactic in a small store means a lot of founder time for uncertain returns.
Attribution is uncertain: increased attention from a personality does not automatically translate into purchase conversion or repeat orders.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Superstition and Lucky Charm Opportunities in Merchandising
cards.summary: Lindstrom's chapter on magic and superstition documents consumer attachment to lucky tokens, collector items and symbolic objects as purchase drivers.
cards.use_when: Planning limited-edition drops, keyrings, charms, collector packs and seasonal gift SKUs that lean on symbolic value.
steps: Look for an existing symbolic meaning in your category (tradition, fortune, protection, celebration) and attach a product to it rather than inventing one.
Use limited runs, numbered items or seasonal symbols to make the object feel singular; the source's Berlin Wall rock and moon rock examples show value comes from claimed uniqueness.
Bundle a small symbolic token with a functional product to add gift appeal without changing the core SKU.
Present the story of the token clearly on the PDP — origin, meaning and reason for the limited run — so it does not read as filler.
Run a limited drop and watch sell-through rate and time-to-sell-out as the measure, rather than the size of the launch campaign.
caveats: Superstition-driven buying is culturally specific and varies by market; test rather than generalise the source's Japanese and US examples to your customer base.
Limited tokens must be genuinely limited to preserve the effect — repeat 'limited' runs erode the symbolic premium.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Reapply Neuroscience Methods Ethically to Store Research
cards.summary: Lindstrom's appendix documents the ethics and practical process of brain-imaging studies — volunteer briefing, consent, oversight — a model for how to run any consumer research store-side.
cards.use_when: Commissioning customer research studies, usability sessions, or eye-tracking and biometric tests for ecommerce decision-making.
steps: Write the hypothesis first (for example, 'our hero banner drives attention away from the buy button') before choosing a tool.
Choose the cheapest method that can test the hypothesis — session replay and A/B tests for behaviour, interviews for language, biometric or eye-tracking only where inference of attention matters.
Brief participants clearly on what will be recorded and how data will be used, and obtain explicit written consent before any session.
Allow participants to stop at any point without penalty and never make participation dependent on continuing a session.
Keep records of what was tested, on whom, and with what method so results are not retrofitted into general truths.
Apply results to decisions with the smallest relevant sample: repeat promising findings with a live A/B test before rolling out.
caveats: Lindstrom's studies used independent ethics committees and paid volunteers; small ecommerce teams have no such infrastructure but still need consent and privacy compliance.
Biometric and neuromarketing vendors vary in methodology — verify methods, sample sizes and claims before paying for them.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Tell Your Own Stories to Keep Teams Engaged
cards.summary: The Sydney Harbour Bridge guide case shows that teams who build their own stories about the product remain engaged and convincing far longer than those reciting scripts.
cards.use_when: Training product, support and content teams; building brand storytelling for the website and acquisition creative.
steps: Give sales, support and content staff time to research their own material — interviewing makers, long-time customers, logistics partners, engineers — rather than handing them a script.
Encourage each team member to develop a version of the product story that is authentically theirs, drawn from that research.
Surface the resulting stories on the PDP, help centre and social channels as real accounts, not as generic copy.
Use the source's training analogy: allocating a substantial share of onboarding time to story-building rather than procedures can improve retention and customer interactions.
Review outcomes as repeat engagement, support ticket tone and customer feedback — not script adherence.
caveats: This is an analogy from a tourist guide training programme, not an ecommerce study; the transferable point is investment in story depth, not a specific time allocation.
Unmanaged storytelling can drift from verified claims — keep a fact sheet of approved product truths for people to build from.
cards.source_name: BUYOLOGY MARTIN LINDSTROM (1).docx

cards.title: Run a Rebrand as a Decision About What to Keep, Not Just What to Change
cards.summary: Use an explicit keep/change inventory to justify a rebrand and protect existing brand equity
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to rebrand an existing store or product line that already sells, or scoping what a redesign should touch
steps: State why you are changing anything: the source's framing is that even a healthy business updates its brand because its opinions, values, and market understanding have sharpened over time, not because growth stalled. Write down the questions driving your review, e.g. where have we been, what is our vision, how do we stand out, what is worth keeping, what must change to grow. ['Where have we been in the last five years, and what's our vision for the future?', 'How might we position our brand and products to be distinct in the marketplace?', 'What's worth keeping and what needs to change for our business to grow?']

Treat the brand as the customer's gut feeling about you, shaped by every touchpoint, rather than as logo, colors and typefaces. Checklist what each touchpoint currently communicates before redesigning any of them, so visual changes stay connected to perception.

Run the work through the Double Diamond: Discover (research and data gathering), Define (synthesize into a clear design challenge), Develop (explore directions, e.g. stylescapes), Deliver (refine and roll out). In the source's case study, this ran several weeks for strategy and roughly four months before rollout began, with rollout continuing for months after.

Explicitly audit brand equity before replacing assets. In the Mode case study, the logo was kept and only slightly refined because it worked and equity had been built around it; the emphasis went to usage detail rather than replacement. Apply the same test to your own logo, product names, and packaging: keep what carries recognition, change what blocks your goal.

Expect revamping to include catalog decisions. The source's Define phase resulted in discontinuing certain products to sharpen focus on better ones — treat assortment as part of the brand decision, not a separate merchandising task.
caveats: This is one company's documented process (Mode, 2025, several weeks of strategy work), not a benchmark for timeline or outcome.
A rebrand is not a guaranteed revenue driver; the source explicitly notes impact takes time to see.
cards.source_name: Building a Brand – Redesigning a Business Start to Finish.docx

cards.title: XY Competitive Mapping to Find Crowded Pools and Open Space
cards.summary: Plot competitors and out-of-industry brands on opposing-qualities axes to locate an ownable position
cards.use_when: Positioning a store or product line against competitors, or refreshing an existing position that feels undifferentiated
steps: Define the brand's attributes first (values and beliefs, features and benefits, voice and tone, look and feel) using focused prompts and free brainstorming; group similar ideas into word clusters and prioritize what resonates most with the team.

Describe positioning as the space the brand occupies in the hearts and minds of customers relative to competitors, then build an X/Y map with opposing brand qualities on each axis. Voice examples from the source: understated vs. outspoken, opaque company vs. transparent and human. Aesthetic examples: warm and inviting vs. stark and industrial, highly curated vs. raw and unedited, premium vs. budget or standard.
Plot both direct competitors and brands from other industries on the grid. The out-of-category brands reveal visual and tonal space that keyboard- or category-only comparison hides.

Read the map for crowded pools — the source found Mode was swimming in a crowded pool in some areas with little to set it apart, which triggered the questions of how to carve out unique space and what must change to create distinction. Use those two questions as the output of the exercise.

Translate the resulting open space into one or two concrete positioning themes, e.g. the source's 'Warm Tech' (making technology feel human and inviting) and 'creating joy in everyday experiences'. Carry these forward as filters for later visual and messaging decisions rather than as slogans.
caveats: Axis choice is subjective; the map is a discussion and alignment tool, not a quantitative scoring model.
Brands from other industries are plot references for contrast, not direct competitors to benchmark against.
cards.source_name: Building a Brand – Redesigning a Business Start to Finish.docx

cards.title: Build Three Stylescapes Before Commissioning Custom Design
cards.summary: Use three wide-layout curated mood boards to preview a brand across touchpoints before investing in design work
cards.use_when: Choosing a visual direction for a store, packaging or campaign when the strategy is agreed but the look is not
steps: Identify the key themes from your discovery and definition work, then gather visual references that match each theme. Adjust the references so they sit together in harmony rather than reading as a random collection.

Arrange each direction on a wide layout that previews the brand across multiple touchpoints — packaging through digital screens — so the team sees application, not just a mood. This is the source's definition of a stylescape and its purpose: exploring directions quickly before paying for custom design.

Produce three distinct directions, each with a name and a clear personality. The Mode case study used 'Serious Fun' (clean, curated, colorful), 'Crafted Narrative' (editorial-inspired with rich contrasting colors), and 'Bits of Joy' (bright and fun, nostalgic lo-fi graphics). Name yours so feedback can be referenced by direction instead of by vague preference.

Present and evaluate against two tests: what resonates with the team, and how well each direction matches the previously defined brand values. Explicitly ask which elements people want borrowed across directions.

Combine winners into a final stylescape rather than treating the three as finalists to eliminate. In the case study, 'Crafted Narrative' was most popular for its dark green palette and typography, but bitmap typefaces from 'Bits of Joy' and illustrations from 'Serious Fun' were merged into a final direction named 'The Story of Craft', which then became the foundation for the full visual identity.
caveats: Stylescapes are exploration artifacts, not production design; expect and plan for the merge step.
Presenter opinion: the source treats three directions as the working number, not a measured optimum.
cards.source_name: Building a Brand – Redesigning a Business Start to Finish.docx

cards.title: Assign Typography by Job, Not by Taste
cards.summary: Mix serif, sans-serif, monospace and bitmap typefaces by the function each piece of copy performs
cards.use_when: Specifying a type system for a product page, packaging, or brand refresh where technical and emotional copy coexist
steps: Split your copy into jobs first — headers, body, technical or specification copy, and any historical or personality-driven moments — then pick typefaces that fit each job rather than choosing one family for everything.

In the Mode case study the allocation was: serif and sans-serif for header and body copy, a monospace font specifically for technical copy to highlight engineering, and selective bitmap-style typefaces as a nod to the history of computing and mechanical keyboards. Apply the same mapping to an ecommerce context: product spec tables and compatibility notes alongside expressive headline and body type.

Test combinations in a type specimen, then look at them in context on sample pages before committing. The source explicitly uses sample webpages for this, because a pairing that works in a specimen can fail against layout, image and button styles.
Keep specialty typefaces selective — the source describes bitmap as 'selective use' and a 'fun nod', not as a workhorse. Overuse dilutes the contrast that makes the specialty face meaningful.

Verify legibility and rendering across your actual surfaces (packaging print vs. screen) when choosing final pairings, since the source chose a palette and type system that had to work across physical and digital collateral.
caveats: The specific fonts chosen for Mode are case-study specifics, not a recommended stack for other brands.
Bitmap and highly stylized faces are risky for long copy and accessibility; the source only assigns them decorative and referential roles.
cards.source_name: Building a Brand – Redesigning a Business Start to Finish.docx

cards.title: Anchor a Brand Palette with One Core Color and Supporting Accents
cards.summary: Choose one memorable anchor color plus a manageable set of accent colors that work across print and screen
cards.use_when: Establishing or refreshing the color system for a store, packaging, and acquisition creative that must stay consistent everywhere
steps: Start from the brand themes rather than from trending colors. In the Mode case study the anchor was a deep green chosen because it felt bold yet calming through its tie to nature, which directly expressed the 'Warm Tech' positioning.
Select a small set of secondary colors explicitly designated as accents. The source's structure is one anchor color with supporting accent colors, not a flat palette of equals.

Review swatches and combinations in multiple dedicated sessions and check them across every surface you ship: physical packaging and on-screen website at minimum. The source calls this one of the most intense parts of the process because color affects so much of the brand and business.

Where the palette feels unresolved, allow the merge behavior seen with stylescapes: in the case study the dark green palette from one direction was the reason that direction was preferred, and it survived the merge into the final direction.

Specify usage in your brand guidelines once decided — which color carries backgrounds, which marks actions and highlights — so future merchandising and ad creative stays consistent without re-deciding.
caveats: The source gives no contrast or accessibility thresholds; test legibility yourself for text on every chosen color.
Screen and print reproduction differ; a swatch review on one medium is not sufficient validation.
cards.source_name: Building a Brand – Redesigning a Business Start to Finish.docx

cards.title: Set Photography Rules as Explicit Constraints
cards.summary: Define a short list of photographic constraints so product imagery stays cohesive across vendors and channels
cards.use_when: Briefing product photography or UGC for a store, packaging, or social creative where images currently look inconsistent
steps: Write down the principles rather than collecting loose references. The Mode principles were: strong directional lighting; warm and natural tones with subtle film grain; scenes that feel lived-in but not messy; and people featured in a way that does not detract from the product.

Pair each rule with reference images that best capture that quality, so the brief is both verbal and visual. The source explicitly pairs rules with references to give the internal team enough guidance to capture photos and videos in the new direction.

Apply the rules to the decision of whether people appear in a shot. The rule that people must not detract from the product implies a merchandising constraint — human presence is context, not the subject, so the product remains the focus of a PDP image.

Institutionalize the rules in your brand guidelines and set up a capture environment for them. Mode's team built a dedicated studio setup to shoot photos and video that roll out on the site and in content, which is how the rules actually get followed at volume.
Use the same constraints for third-party and user content selection: lived-in but not messy is a usable inclusion filter for curated UGC on product pages.
caveats: These four rules are this brand's chosen style, not a universal best practice; a clinical or high-tech brand might deliberately choose the opposite.
Film grain and warm grading can misrepresent product color; test against accuracy requirements before adopting.
cards.source_name: Building a Brand – Redesigning a Business Start to Finish.docx

cards.title: Strip Technical Jargon from Product and Marketing Copy
cards.summary: Write a brand voice that is human, confident and clear even in a technical product category
cards.use_when: Writing product descriptions, specs pages, emails or ads for a technically complex product where copy has drifted into insider language
steps: Set the target balance explicitly. The source's stated goal was professional but not corporate, friendly but not fake, and it describes this as a difficult balance to strike — write the two poles down as a copy review test.

Assume your buyer is not a specialist. Even though the keyboard world is full of technical jargon, the source makes a conscious effort to use clear, simple language anyone can understand, on the reasoning that newcomers and enthusiasts both need to buy.

Draft core messages collaboratively in a shared document and refine them over multiple passes. Mode used a Notion document to write and refine core messages so word choices felt authentic rather than imposed.

Ban marketing buzzwords and favor honest, straightforward communication. Keep the emotional promise concrete — the source's themes were 'making technology feel more human and inviting' and 'creating joy in everyday experiences', expressed plainly rather than as abstract brandspeak.

Produce messaging samples attached to specific placements (website, marketing) rather than a general tone document, and keep a separate set of thought-starter 'brand expressions' showing the voice applied across physical and digital surfaces for future launches and events.
caveats: Voice work was done by an internal team with an outside facilitator; a solo operator should expect more drafting rounds to reach the same clarity.
Simplifying does not mean removing necessary specs — the source keeps deep technical information available for research-heavy buyers and reserves simple language for messaging.
cards.source_name: Building a Brand – Redesigning a Business Start to Finish.docx

cards.title: Segment Buyers by Behavior, Not Just Demographics
cards.summary: Build contrasting personas whose buying behavior demands different marketing and site treatments
cards.use_when: Deciding how to structure a product page, catalog, or campaign when the audience ranges from expert hobbyists to busy first-time buyers
steps: Gather qualitative input specifically about why people buy or pass. The source combined website traffic and sales data analysis, customer surveys in the community, and in-depth video interviews with specific community members.

Build personas with names, constraints, desires and stories, and make sure at least two of them require entirely different treatments. The Mode examples: Tim, an experienced UX design manager in Austin who researches extensively, values quality and community, knows the people behind brands, and would enjoy building keyboard kits; versus Jay, a young software engineer in San Francisco seeking a workspace upgrade, who is busy, relies on influencer and publication recommendations, and wants a simple purchase process and ready-to-use products.

Derive concrete site requirements from each persona's behavior rather than stopping at description. For the researcher persona the conclusion is detailed product information plus visible community; for the busy persona it is a simple purchase path with clear guidance and pre-built options.

Concentrate exercise time on customers you do not already understand. Mode knew many current customers by name, so the segmentation work focused on attracting new ones — apply the same rule when your repeat base is already well understood.
