cards.summary: After a successful positioning campaign, keep the same position for years instead of drifting into aspiration or new campaigns that abandon what worked.
cards.use_when: Reviewing brand messaging, campaign themes, or homepage copy that has accumulated multiple taglines over time.
steps: Audit how many different themes your brand has run; the source notes that despite Avis's many campaigns, the one theme people remember is the original 'No. 2' idea.
Identify the single concept you actually own in the customer's mind and make it the consistent spine of your messaging.
Don't advertise aspirations that contradict your position (Avis's 'Avis is going to be No. 1' abandoned the underdog sympathy and No. 2 relationship that was working).
Reuse the same position across campaigns, product pages, and ads rather than rotating fresh taglines for novelty.
Accept that a strong position may cap some ambitions — if you can't exploit a real leader weakness, the source says you're not destined to be No. 1 just by wishing it.
caveats: The source treats consistency as the core positioning discipline; it doesn't argue you can never launch new products, only that the owned position shouldn't be abandoned.
Failing to hold your position risks being passed by a competitor, as the source warns about Avis and National.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Check whether you can even 'get there from here'
cards.summary: Before pouring budget into a category push, honestly assess whether your current position makes the goal achievable at all, since effort cannot overcome a structurally hopeless position.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to enter a new product category, compete with a dominant platform, or fund an aggressive growth goal.
steps: Identify the entrenched leader and its share (the source cites IBM's 70% of the mainframe business): head-on attacks against a mental leader have no hope of progress.
Do not mimic the leader's approach — acting like IBM in the source's example is the most common and fatal mistake of bigger challengers.

Instead, relate your existing owned position to the new category: the source suggested RCA (a communications leader) should position computers around communications, and GE around its time-sharing strength; NCR progressed by focusing on retail data-entry (computerized cash registers).
Where the situation is genuinely hopeless, redirect resources to areas of your business where you do hold a position; the source argues outright failure is often preferable to mediocre success.
Distinguish strategic positions where extra effort early builds leadership from ones where no amount of money or can-do spirit closes the gap.
caveats: The RCA and GE computer outcomes are historical case examples, not predictions about your market; treat them as illustrations of a rule about head-on competition.
The source also says extra effort is valuable when applied early to establish leadership — timing matters, so 'can't get there' applies mainly to late, head-on moves.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Avoid the everybody trap and commit to a specific niche
cards.summary: In a crowded market, appeal to everyone dilutes your position; carve out a specific slot even if you lose some customers doing so.
cards.use_when: Writing category, homepage, or brand copy and choosing whether to keep broad, inclusive messaging or commit to a defined customer segment.
steps: Accept that being all things to all people can keep an established brand afloat but is deadly when building a position from nothing.
Choose a specific position along a real dimension (use case, price tier, customer segment, ingredient stance) and state it unambiguously, as Volkswagen did with 'Think small.'
Accept that taking a strong position makes some enemies or excludes some buyers — the source argues you can't win by stepping on no one's toes.
Avoid multiple vague value claims competing for space on the same page; one clear position beats a list of universal benefits.
Recognize the volume of competing messages customers face — the source compares sorting product names to a vocabulary problem, so a single claim is what can register.
caveats: This is the source's advice for brands trying to build a position; it concedes a broad, already-dominant brand may survive without a sharp niche.
The source's argument rests on the overcommunicated-market premise, not on measured conversion data.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Make the product name do positioning work
cards.summary: The name is the hook that hangs a brand on the ladder in the customer's mind, and the source calls it the single most important marketing decision.
cards.use_when: Naming a new product, private label, or sub-brand, or diagnosing why a well-positioned offer underperforms.
steps: Choose a name that supports the intended position rather than contradicting it — the source argues Scope's repositioning of Listerine was partly undone because 'Scope' sounds like a board game, not a good-tasting mouthwash.
Avoid house-name extensions for genuinely new concepts, since they trade a quick share of market for a diluted position.
Prefer names that reinforce the positioning angle, such as Luke's masculine name or 'Old Milwaukee' for a low-priced beer versus the owner's own name on the cheapest brand.

Remember the source's claim about sensory expectations: people 'taste what they expect to taste,' so a name and copy implying artificiality can make the product itself seem worse (the Pringle's ingredient-list backlash).
Test the name against the mind's existing associations, not just internal brand logic.
caveats: The naming failures cited (Scope, Max Factor's 'Just Call Me Maxi') are historical anecdotes presented as illustrations, not controlled evidence.
The source treats the name as critical but does not claim a name alone fixes a product with no position.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Race on launch speed and budget, not late 'better'
cards.summary: Most me-too products fail because they spend time improving the product while a competitor establishes leadership first; speed, launch budget, and a good name beat incremental superiority.
cards.use_when: Planning a product or category launch, deciding launch timing, naming, and marketing spend against an incumbent.
steps: Prioritize being first to establish the position over making a marginally better version; the source says accent should be on speed, not 'better.'
Give the launch a substantial budget — the source warns the opposite happens: me-too brands waste time, then launch with a smaller budget than the leader's.
Give the new product its own name rather than the house name, since house names are the easy way to get quick share but a positioning trap.
If you're late and can't be first, use a follower strategy (alternative position or repositioning the leader) rather than a better-me-too claim.
Weigh timing explicitly, as the source does when describing Lorillard's late masculine cigarette brand 'Luke' failing about 20 years after Marlboro claimed masculinity.
caveats: The source's claim about 'first gets twice the long-term share' is presented as a general historical pattern, not a formula or a guaranteed benchmark for your category.
This reflects the source's view that first-mover advantage dominates; a truly differentiated late entry can still win, but not by fighting the leader head-on.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Turn sensory expectation into a merchandising and copy lever
cards.summary: Customers taste and judge what they expect to taste, so ingredient and description language on the page shapes perceived product quality.
cards.use_when: Writing product page copy, ingredient lists, or label descriptions for food, supplements, or any product judged by sensory quality.
steps: Recognize that consumer taste is partly mental: the source notes Pringle's common complaint was 'tastes like cardboard' after rivals read its industrial-sounding ingredient list on TV.
Keep ingredient and process copy human and concrete; long chemical names invite negative perception even when the product is fine.
Use the water-vs-'dihydrogen oxide' example as the principle: identical substances can be perceived differently based on the words used.
When a competitor's formulation is technically fine but sounds unappealing, you can reposition it honestly by focusing attention on what it contains, as Borden's Wise did comparing ingredient lists.
Pair sensory-expectation copy with the actual product experience so expectations don't outrun reality.
caveats: The Pringle's outcome is a historical case, not a controlled test; use as illustration, not a guaranteed result.
Once a product is widely perceived as a 'loser,' the source says recovering is very hard, so this lever works better ahead of negative perception than after.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Competitive ads vs. repositioning ads: know the difference
cards.summary: Most comparative advertising fails because it benchmarks against the leader instead of changing the customer's view of that leader's product.
cards.use_when: Planning comparison content, 'us vs. them' pages, or competitor-focused acquisition creative.
steps: Avoid the 'we're better than X, Y, Z' structure; the prospect reacts with 'then why aren't you the leader?', and you're saying what they already expect you to say.

Instead, state something about the competitor's product that changes the customer's understanding: Tylenol on aspirin's risks, Royal Doulton on Lenox's American origin, Stolichnaya on rivals' US production.
Run the competitor-framing portion first and in real detail before mentioning your own product — the source notes Tylenol's roughly 60 words of aspirin copy before naming itself.
Be factually accurate to keep the tactic honest and defensible; the source cites these as verifiable claims, not invented ones.

Keep in mind that such claims are legally permitted in many markets (the source traces US TV comparative-ad acceptance to FTC pressure in the 1970s), but verify current rules and platform policies for your market.
caveats: Repositioning draws ethical objections, which the source acknowledges while defending it as more effective than brag-and-boast.
Comparative claims carry legal and platform risk; the source's regulatory timeline is historical and specific rules should be verified with counsel.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Treat equality between top brands as unstable
cards.summary: When two brands run neck and neck, the category is unstable and one will usually pull ahead; that's when extra effort pays off most.
cards.use_when: Timing a promotional push or brand investment in a category where you're roughly tied with a rival for the top spot.
steps: Watch for a genuine dead heat at the top of a category — the source argues it's inherently unstable and typically resolves to a lasting lead (citing Hertz/Avis, Harvard/Yale, and the Ford/Chevrolet race resolved by Chevrolet in 1931).
Concentrate extra marketing effort during that period of doubt rather than spreading it evenly, since the source says the time for extra effort is when neither side has clear superiority.
Expect a near-term win to lock in a long-term advantage; the source says winning sales leadership in a single year often clinches victory for decades.

Recognize leader advantages beyond sales — preferential retail stocking, better hiring, and customer default repurchase habits (buying the same brand as last time) — and account for them in your plan.
Once ahead, shift from fight to defense: use short-term flexibility to protect the long-term position rather than continuing to spend as if tied.
caveats: These patterns come from historical consumer-goods and auto examples; the source presents them as general positioning rules, not modern measured benchmarks.
The 'twice the long-term share' figure is a source heuristics claim, not a calculation to plan against literally.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Position by a category dimension before rivals do
cards.summary: Sex, age, time of day, distribution channel, and usage intensity are all positionable dimensions — first to claim them wins, latecomers fail.
cards.use_when: Choosing an angle for a new product, line, or landing-page narrative in a mature category where broad claims are taken.
steps: Survey the category for unclaimed dimensions: gender coding (Marlboro's masculinity, Virginia Slims' femininity), age (Geritol for older customers, Aim toothpaste for children), time of day (Nyquil as the first night-time cold remedy), distribution (L'eggs in supermarkets), and heavy-user framing (Schaefer for the frequent beer drinker).
Pick a dimension you can be first to own; the source emphasizes timing is critical and cites late me-toos like Eve and Luke as failures against earlier claimants.
Consider the counterintuitive direction: the source notes the largest perfume became Charlie, the first brand to use a masculine name with pantsuit advertising, even though most brands were feminine.
If a rival already owns the dimension, don't copy it — a me-too naming and ad campaign on the same axis tends to fail.
Translate the chosen dimension into a specific, single-minded claim in the product page headline and imagery.
caveats: Numeric share claims like Aim's '10 percent of the toothpaste market' are historical examples, not targets.
The source's timing claims are anecdotal case comparisons, not controlled tests, so validate demand for the dimension with customers before building around it.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Name as the Core Positioning Decision
cards.summary: The product or brand name is the single most important marketing decision because it is the hook that hangs the brand on a ladder in the prospect's mind.
cards.use_when: Naming a new product, brand, SKU or storefront, or deciding whether to rename an existing product line.
steps: Treat the name as the first positioning act, not a cosmetic label. The source (Ries & Trout) argues that in an overcommunicated market the name is the single most important marketing decision, because the mind stores a product by its name.
Choose a name that begins the positioning process: pick a name that telegraphs the product's major benefit, in the way Head & Shoulders signals dandruff care and DieHard signals long battery life.
For ecommerce listings, aim for a name that makes the benefit legible in the search result, the cart line and the ad headline — where you have seconds, not a salesperson.
Avoid names that are lazy, do-nothing or purely internal (project codes, initials, founder surnames) unless the brand is already first and famous in the category.
Remember that Shakespeare was wrong according to the source: a rose by any other name would not smell as sweet, because people see and smell what they expect to.
Run a sounding test before committing to a name you plan to say in video, podcast ads or voice search.
caveats: The source is opinionated and dated; the core claim is a positioning argument, not a measured benchmark.
Benefit-led names risk becoming generic if too close to the category (see separate card on that trap).
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Descriptive Names Beat Coined Names — Unless You're First
cards.summary: Pick a name that nearly describes the benefit rather than a meaningless coined word, because only a genuine first mover can afford an empty name.
cards.use_when: Deciding between a descriptive name (e.g. Soy Butter, Spray 'n Wash) and a coined or abstract brand name for a new product or store line.
steps: Prefer common descriptive words that say what the product does, in the tradition of Spray 'n Wash and DieHard; these block me-too competitors from muscling into your territory.
Reserve coined, meaningless names (the source's examples: Kodak, Keds, Kleenex) for the case where you are first into the mind with an absolutely new product that millions will want.

Understand that Coca-Cola, Kodak and Xerox succeeded because they were first in their categories, not because the names were invented; the source calls this the Charles Lindbergh syndrome — get in first and any name works.

For an ecommerce store launching a familiar category (supplements, cookware, apparel basics), use a benefit-descriptive naming pattern rather than abstract invented words, since you are not likely to be first.
Check letter-frequency as a rough guide: the most common English initial letters are S, C, P, A and T, and the least common are X, Z, Y, Q and K — a name starting with X is far harder to recall.
caveats: The source's claim that only first-movers can afford coined names is a heuristic, not a tested rule.
Descriptive names invite trademark trouble and category substitution (Lite problem).
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Don't Let a Name Become Generic
cards.summary: A name should point to your benefit without sliding all the way into a generic category word, or you lose exclusive rights to it.
cards.use_when: Naming or trademarking a launch SKU, deciding whether to coin a new word for a new product format, or reviewing a product name that has become a category catch-all.
steps: Aim for a name that is almost-but-not-quite generic, the way the source describes choosing like driving a racing car — you must take chances and occasionally spin out.

Watch the cautionary case of 'Lite beer from Miller': the press and public shortened it to 'Miller Lite,' and Miller lost exclusive rights to 'light' or its phonetic equivalent as a trademark for beer.

If your name is already a category word (e.g. a store brand literally called 'Vitamin C'), the source's warning applies at scale: you have made it easy for competitors to sell under the same literal label.
When a coined name is genuinely warranted, keep it distinguishable: a strong, generic-like but not-generic name blocks me-too competitors, according to the source.
Consult trademark counsel before launch on any name that reads as a category description; the source notes trademark lawyers prefer coined marks like Kodak and Xerox.
caveats: Choice of name is a trade-off: too abstract and the prospect learns nothing; too descriptive and you lose the mark.
Legal standards vary by jurisdiction and category; get current local advice.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Audit Existing Names for Obsolescence and Confusion
cards.summary: Names decay as products and markets change; audit the ladder to spot names that mislead or overlap with competitors.
cards.use_when: Portfolio review: assessing whether a legacy brand or product name still communicates the current offer, or whether a rename is warranted.
steps: Check the ladder position, not the aesthetics. The source's Eastern Airlines case: a regional name placed Eastern in the same mental bracket as Piedmont and Ozark, not the national carriers.
Look for names that no longer match what the product does: United Shoe Machinery, RCA and Esquire all outgrew or lost the thing their name meant.

Watch for name confusion with a larger competitor. In the source's famous case, B. F. Goodrich was the first to market steel-belted radials in the U.S., yet 56% of buyers named Goodyear (which didn't make them domestically) versus 47% who named Goodrich.
Check the Toledo triplet / Continental confusion problem: when multiple brands share a common word, prospect research cannot distinguish them; use a name test to measure misattribution.

Recall that names can carry hidden devalued meaning (the source's example of 'margarine' hiding its soy origin), so test whether the current name withholds or misrepresents what the product actually is.

Assess whether a rename will actually help. The source says most companies refuse to change because they believe 'our customers and employees would never accept a new name' — but cites Uniroyal, Eaton, Mobil and Exxon as successful renames.
caveats: Rename case studies are retrospective examples, not guarantees of improved sales.
Goodrich opted to keep the name and effectively told customers it was their problem to remember it — a defensible but expensive choice.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Test Names and Headlines for Sound, Not Just Look
cards.summary: The mind processes words aurally, so evaluate names, slogans and headlines by how they sound, especially for future voice and podcast channels.
cards.use_when: Choosing a store or product name, writing ad headlines or slogans, or preparing a brand name for voice search and audio advertising.
steps: Read names and headlines aloud before committing; if a name sounds bad, it will feel bad even in print, because the brain translates letters into sound.
Apply the phonetic shorthand test: RCA (3 syllables) works versus Radio Corporation of America (12); GE works versus General Electric (6); but Ford is rarely FM because Ford is already one syllable.
For ecommerce, test the name in spoken contexts — audio ads, video UGC, voice search queries — not just in a logo lockup, since ads are increasingly heard.
Design ad copy for 'radio first' as the source suggests, then adapt to print and display, because the primal medium is sound.
Watch name collisions that only appear in written form: USM's 'US' doesn't stand for anything, so it sorts into the phone-book front matter where no one looks.
caveats: Phonetic shorthand rules were developed in an era dominated by radio and print; streaming and app search change the retrieval rules but not the value of a pronounceable name.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Initials and Acronyms Are a Shortcut Trap
cards.summary: Companies copy IBM's initials and mistake cause for effect — initials work only after a name is already famous.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to brand a new store line, private label or acquisition sub-brand with initials or an acronym, or reviewing a corporate rebrand.
steps: Apply the cause-and-effect test: the source argues that IBM got rich and famous first (the cause), which made its initials widely understood (the effect). Reversing the sequence does not work.

Take the source's measured example with caution: a Business Week subscriber survey found average awareness of 'initial' companies at 49% versus 68% for a matched group of 'name' companies, a 19-point gap.
If you inherit an initial name, verify there is a buried, well-known original name for the initials to trigger; otherwise the mind gets nothing back when it reads the letters.
Check the telephone-directory (or search-results) behavior of an initial name: MCI sorts 48 pages away from where customers look, and competes with several other MCI-containing companies.

Prefer a shortened name with phonetic gain over initials. The source contrasts Pan Am (2 syllables, better than PAA) with TWA, where 'Trans World' (2 syllables) is shorter and clearer than the T-Double-U-A it uses.
Reserve initials for brands that are already household-level famous; even the source concedes ITT and NCR work only because they were well known before they went initial.
caveats: The 49%/68% awareness survey is a single source study and should be read as illustrative, not a benchmark for your category.
Some acronyms are deliberate and work as names (CARE, MADD, Fiat, Sabena), so the rule is 'do the initials add phonetic or mnemonic value?' not 'never abbreviate'.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Line Extension Blurs a Hard-Won Position
cards.summary: Hanging a known name on a new category fails because the brand name is a surrogate for the original product in the prospect's mind.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to launch a new product or category under the existing hero brand name versus creating a new brand or sub-brand, e.g. an existing supplement brand moving into skincare.
steps: Apply the teeter-totter principle: one name cannot stand for two distinctly different products; when one goes up, the other goes down.

Recall the source's Bayer case: 'Bayer nonaspirin' never took more than a tiny share of the acetaminophen market, and each extension — Bayer timed-release aspirin, Bayer decongestant cold tablets — undercut the core aspirin position.
Recall Dial: a large share of the soap market and a very small share of the deodorant market after extending the Dial name.
Recall Protein 21: from a 13% share of shampoo to 2% after launching hairspray, conditioner and Protein 29 for men.
For ecommerce, decide pre-launch whether a new product requires a new mental ladder. If the source's logic holds, a genuinely new product needs a new ladder and therefore a new name.
Weigh the inside-out argument ('our customers know us, they'll accept it, we'll save marketing dollars') against the outside-in view (the prospect thinks in products, not companies).
caveats: The source argues that Procter & Gamble's no-house-name strategy beat Colgate-Palmolive (roughly twice the business and five times the profit) — a historical comparison, not a guaranteed operating rule.
There are exceptions: some brands extend successfully when the new product is genuinely within the same ladder. Run a name-fit test before launching.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Use a Distinctly Named Hero SKU to Hold a Feature
cards.summary: Give a product a name that carries the benefit, so the customer has a hook to hang attributes on.
cards.use_when: Naming a flagship SKU or private-label item where you want one benefit to be remembered, e.g. an extended-life battery, a durability claim, or a specific food benefit.
steps: Name the product for the benefit, not the retailer. In the source's example, the DieHard battery gave the buyer a mental hook for 'long-lasting', while the JCPenney battery gave a weak hook for the 'never needs water' feature.

Accept the trade-off: the DieHard name makes it hard to remember it is only sold at Sears, but the source argues it is better to establish the position in the prospect's mind first and solve the retail connection later.
For a store brand, consider whether your retail name is strong enough to hold a functional claim, or whether a differentiated product brand fits the ladder better.
When naming a bundle or kit, choose a name that conveys the primary benefit rather than a house name that simply identifies who made it.
Recognize that 'the obvious name is not always the best name'; the source warns that obvious, internal-logic names are a barrier to success.
caveats: Sears' retail-connection problem is real; a great name cannot fix distribution customers cannot easily reach.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: New Product, New Ladder, New Name
cards.summary: A truly new product cannot live on a famous name because the famous name occupies a sharply defined rung of a different ladder.
cards.use_when: Launching a new product line in a new category under a company that already owns a position in another category.
steps: Ask what the existing brand name stands for in the prospect's mind. If the answer is a specific product (Xerox means copier), the name cannot also mean a new category.

Recall the Xerox experiment: Xerox bought Scientific Data Systems and renamed it Xerox Data Systems; the ad line 'This Xerox machine can't make a copy' signals the trap, and the company folded the computer operation with an additional $84.4 million write-off.
Also recall Heinz: it made Heinz mean ketchup, gaining the No. 1 ketchup position, while losing pickle leadership to Vlasic — the other end of the teeter-totter.
Before launch, ask whether you are prepared to make the hero name mean the new thing. If the answer is no, launch under a new dedicated name.
Be honest about the corporate-ego problem: the source observes that telling GE not to put GE on a new product is very difficult, which is exactly why the wrong decisions get made.
caveats: This is the source's opinion, illustrated through historical cases; not every extension fails.
Sub-brand naming can capture some, but not all, of the separation benefits described.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Use Negative Names to Polarize Instead of Hide
cards.summary: When a product's origin is hidden, prospects suspect a problem; a proudly descriptive name builds 'pride of origin' and a long-term positioning campaign.
cards.use_when: Naming or renaming a product whose origin or formulation is unfamiliar to buyers — alternative ingredients, plant-based or lab-made goods, or a product seen as an imitation.
steps: Bring the product out of the closet by deliberately naming the origin, as in the source's prescription that margarine should have been called 'soy butter' rather than hiding its source.

The source's logic: because the origin of margarine is hidden, the prospect assumes something is wrong with it; a name that names the source allows a long-term program selling the advantages of soy butter versus cow butter.

Apply the same principle to corn sweeteners, which the source says were hampered by names like 'high-fructose corn syrup'; renaming to 'corn sugars' let corn stand on equal footing with cane and beet.
For an ecommerce store selling a product category that suffers from an imitation perception, build the origin into the brand name and the PDP headline rather than burying it in the 'About' section.

When fighting an entrenched competitor term (the source cites 'fair trade' laws), do not try to rename the competition — that only confuses the audience. Turn the name around: 'Fair to the trade, but unfair to the consumer.'
caveats: Renaming an entrenched concept early — before the powerful name takes root — is much more effective than late; the source notes 'price maintenance' as a blocking strategy would probably have worked only early.
Some origin words carry stigma the brand may not be able to neutralize; validate with real customer language before committing.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Protect a Position You Already Own
cards.summary: A brand that owns a category position (Kleenex, Hertz, Cadillac, Xerox) holds enormous long-term value; do not spend it on a different category.
cards.use_when: Portfolio and pricing decisions when a hero brand or hero SKU is being considered as a vehicle for a new offer, bundle or adjacent category.
steps: Identify the position the name actually owns — the generic substitute customers use in speech ('hand me a Kleenex', 'get me a Xerox copy').
Note that generic-strong brands can promote the category, not the brand ('Coffee keeps you awake? Drink Sanka'), which is an efficiency advantage worth protecting.
Beware of teaching the prospect that your brand is 'nothing but a brand name'. Each line extension, according to the source, destroys the illusion that the brand is a superior form of the product.
For subscription and replenishment stores, keep the hero position on the hero product and avoid using it as a banner for consumables of a different job-to-be-done.
If you must grow into a new category, create a new brand or an explicitly distinct sub-brand rather than diluting the core name.
caveats: The source is strongly anti-extension; some brands do extend profitably, so treat this as a risk framework rather than an absolute ban.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Spend Publicity Like a Budget, Not a Habit
cards.summary: Anonymity is an easily squandered resource; a lesser-known product gains far more from publicity than a famous one does.
cards.use_when: Planning a PR push, press outreach or influencer campaign for a new store, brand or hero product, and deciding when to use your best story.
steps: Conserve anonymity until you are ready to spend it, then spend it big, keeping the objective on a position in the prospect's mind rather than on coverage for its own sake.
Recognize that media hunger is for the new and fresh face; an unknown company with an unknown product has more to gain from publicity than a well-known company with an established product.
Note the source's caution that nothing kills the publicity potential of a product quite as much as a cover story in a national magazine — repeated exposure without a purpose burns the asset.
For an ecommerce launch, time the one big reveal around the moment a purchase decision is actually possible (site live, inventory ready), not months before.
Use the momentum of a media moment to convert — landing page, offer and stock — rather than treating coverage as the goal.
caveats: The source treats publicity as finite, which may understate the compounding effect of a well-run content channel.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Use House Names and Separate Names According to Provenance
cards.summary: How a product was created (internal development vs. acquisition) historically drives naming strategy, but the prospect's mind should be the deciding factor.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether an acquired brand or a newly developed product should carry the parent store/brand name, after an acquisition or a category expansion.
steps: Know the pattern the source describes: internally developed products usually get the corporate name (General Electric computers), while acquired products usually keep their name (Hertz under RCA, Avis under ITT) — though Xerox broke the pattern by renaming Scientific Data Systems.
Treat the pattern as a default born of corporate ego, not as a decision rule derived from the customer's mind.
For an ecommerce operator buying a DTC brand, do not automatically rename the acquired brand to the parent; consider whether the acquired name holds a distinct position the parent name cannot serve.
If the parent name clearly dominates in search, subscription recognition or ad efficiency, weigh a deliberate rename against the position the acquired name already owns.
Account for conglomerate logic honestly: the source credits conglomerates with funding competition, but that business benefit does not by itself justify a naming decision.
caveats: The source's naming analysis is drawn from large industrial and packaged-goods history; small ecommerce portfolios may have different trade-offs.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Position Against the Future, Not the Past, When Renaming
cards.summary: When a name is obsolete, a foot-in-the-past abbreviation freezes it; a clean new name can reposition the whole company.
cards.use_when: Renaming a store, a legacy product line, or a brand after a pivot, product obsolescence or a merger.
steps: Diagnose the obsolescence honestly: U.S. Rubber sold many non-rubber products, Eaton Yale & Towne was a merger with a complicated name, and Socony-Mobil was saddled with a Standard Oil legacy name.
Do not take the easy abbreviation route; the source calls USR Corporation, EY&T Company and SM Inc. three marketing monstrosities.
Adopt a clean new name rather than initials. Uniroyal, Eaton and Mobil came from 'forgetting the past' and positioning against the future.
Expect a transitional cost but note the source's claim that there is only negative equity in a bad name — when the name is bad, things tend to get worse.
Ask the same question about a store that started in one category: is the store name now a USM-style liability, and would a name change produce a cleaner position?
caveats: Renaming is rare in practice because companies believe they have too much equity in the current name; the source counter-cites Olin, Mobil, Uniroyal, Xerox and Exxon as companies that made the change work.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Use the Shopping List Test to Diagnose Brand Dilution
cards.summary: A quick test for whether your brand name means one thing or many, by asking what a spouse would bring back from a written shopping list.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to launch a new product category, sub-brand, or SKU under your existing store/brand name, or evaluating whether an existing catalog is already diluted.
steps: Write down your brand name alone on a list, the way a customer would. Ask: if someone read just this name, is there exactly one product they would return with?

Contrast with strong names: 'Kleenex', 'Bayer', and 'Dial' pass because they map to one product each. 'Heinz', 'Scott', and 'Kraft' fail because the reader cannot tell whether they mean ketchup, pickles, or baby food.
Apply this to your own catalog: list your brand plus each category you sell under that same name. If customers cannot predict the product from the name alone, the name has no independent position.

Note the source's claim that the damage is slow and cumulative — the brand becomes a 'burned-out hulk' over years, not quarters, so a single successful quarter of extension sales does not disprove the problem.
Treat 'what's a [brand]?' as the diagnostic question: if the answer is 'it's everything and nothing', you have a positioning problem to fix before extending further.
caveats: The source is a 1980s packaged-goods argument; its share-loss examples are illustrative, not benchmarks for your store.
A broad house name works fine for low-involvement commodity items where shoppers have no going-in preference — the test matters most where you want to own a category.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Line Extension's Short-Term Sales Illusion
cards.summary: New line extensions create an instant recognition flash and pipeline sales that look strong for months, then fade when reorders do not come.
cards.use_when: Interpreting early sales data after launching a new SKU under an existing brand name, or setting expectations with a founder before a sub-brand launch.
steps: Recognize that a name related to the original ('Diet Coca-Cola', 'Alka-Seltzer Plus') produces an instant flash of understanding and an instant flash of sales.

Separate pipeline from demand: retail buyers stocking the new SKU produce good numbers in the first months regardless of consumer pull. The source notes that booking $1 million only requires $35 of stocking per supermarket.
Watch the reorder curve as the real signal. When reorders do not arrive, the source says things turn dark quickly.
Expect the extended name to be forgettable because it has no independent position — the source calls such names satellites to the original, contributing only blur.
For an online store, the analog is a variant or bundle launched under a hero product's name: check repeat purchase and direct search for the new item, not just launch-week sell-through.
caveats: The '$35 per supermarket' figure is the source's illustrative arithmetic for physical retail distribution, not a benchmark for ecommerce.
Anti-extension argument, not a blanket ban; the source explicitly allows extension when there is no competition and no intention to build a position.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Bayer and Protein 21: How Sub-Brands Undercut the Parent
cards.summary: Every extension hung on a strong brand erodes the parent's meaning, shown in falling share for Bayer analgesics and Protein 21 shampoo.
cards.use_when: Considering whether to attach your main brand name to an adjacent product line, ingredient variant, or differently-positioned version.
steps: Apply the contradiction test: if the brand means aspirin, 'Bayer nonaspirin' cannot logically exist in the customer's mind. Each extension — timed-release, decongestant, nonaspirin — undercuts the aspirin position.
Track the share consequence the source reports: Bayer's total analgesic share kept falling as the line extended.

Use Protein 21 as the cautionary arc: a shampoo/conditioner that reached a 13% share of the shampoo market, then extended into hairspray, conditioner, concentrate, and Protein 29 for men, and fell to 2%.
Translate to a store: if your brand means one ingredient or one job, do not put that name on a product with a contradictory job. Give the new job a new name.
Treat the share declines as the source's historical examples, and check your own category data before concluding extension caused it.
caveats: Share figures are historical packaged-goods examples from the source, not predictive benchmarks.
The source also warns the decline is 'bound to continue' — an opinion about trajectory, worth testing rather than assuming.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Broadening the Base: Reverse Line Extension
cards.summary: Same product, same package, same name — only the use occasion changes, which is how Johnson's baby shampoo became an adult brand.
cards.use_when: Looking for growth from an existing hero product without launching a new SKU, or planning messaging and landing-page angles for a narrowly perceived product.
steps: Identify a product whose current perception limits its audience but whose actual attributes fit a bigger one. Johnson's baby shampoo was promoted for its mildness to the adult market and became a leading adult shampoo.
Keep product, package, and label unchanged. The source states that a separate 'Johnson's adult shampoo' extension would not have been nearly as successful.

Find the sole unclaimed usage claim, as Blue Nun did by advertising a white wine as good with meat as well as fish. The source argues these work because each is the first and only brand making that claim.
Apply to ecommerce: rewrite PDP copy, ad creative, and use-case imagery to promote the additional occasion or audience for the same SKU, rather than creating a duplicate listing under a new name.
Check that no competitor already owns the broadened claim before investing; the source attributes the success partly to being first with it.
caveats: Source's examples are beverages and personal care; the mechanism (usage broadening) transfers, the results do not.
Advertising-intensive: the source ties these wins to sustained promotion, so a silent PDP edit alone is unlikely to shift perception.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: The Bartender Test for Step-Up and Step-Down Products
cards.summary: Premium and entry-price variants built on a value name create confusion and weak sales at the premium end except when the buyer can name them without the parent.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a premium tier or a cheaper entry model should carry your existing brand name, and how to name tiers in a catalog or subscription ladder.
steps: Run the bartender test on your own brand: order it the way a customer would. 'J&B on the rocks' reliably gets scotch; 'Chivas' reliably gets the premium version. 'Cutty' does not tell the bartender whether you mean Cutty Sark or Cutty 12.

For step-up products, the source observes they usually produce anemic sales at the higher price — buyers do not want to pay premium prices for a low-price name. Chivas Regal outsold the earlier Johnnie Walker Black Label.

For step-down products, the source observes near-instant success followed by a hangover: Packard's inexpensive Clipper was its best-selling car and destroyed the prestige position that kept the company alive.

The exception: Vaseline Intensive Care works because customers simply call the product 'Intensive Care' — in the mind, Vaseline is petroleum jelly and Intensive Care is hand lotion. A separate name in the customer's mouth is what saves it.
Store application: name premium tiers so customers can say the tier name alone, and avoid slapping the hero brand on a cheap entry SKU that pays the bills short-term but erodes pricing power.
caveats: The step-up and step-down patterns are the source's observations from liquor and autos, stated as tendencies, not laws.
The Vaseline case shows extension can survive when the extension name is what people actually say — verify this through customer language, not internal naming documents.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: When to Use the House Name: Five Rules of the Road
cards.summary: The source's five criteria for deciding whether a new product should carry the existing house brand or get its own name.
cards.use_when: Deciding naming and brand architecture for a new product launch, collection, or private-label item in a multi-product catalog.
steps: Expected volume: potential winners should not bear the house name; small-volume products should.
Competition: in a vacuum a brand should not bear the house name; in a crowded field it should.
Advertising support: big-budget brands should not bear the house name; small-budget brands should.
Significance: breakthrough products should not bear the house name; commodity products such as chemicals should.
Distribution: off-the-shelf items should not bear the house name; items sold by sales reps should.

Note the underlying reasoning: products with no going-in preference in the shopper's mind will do better under any known name than an unknown one, and companies with thousands of small-volume products cannot afford a new name for each.
Store translation: a flagship, ad-supported, differentiated hero SKU likely earns its own name; a long-tail commodity SKU can ride the house name.
caveats: These are the source's stated heuristics, framed as 'an economics call as much as a judgment call' — apply with your own volume and margin data.
The rules assume a world where advertising budget and distribution channel differ by product; re-derive them for your channel mix.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: First-Mover Position and the 100mm Cigarette
cards.summary: Being first into a new product concept is worthless if the name does not claim the concept — a competitor with a clearer name can preempt the position.
cards.use_when: You are early into a new product category, format, or claim and choosing how to name and describe it in your store and ads.
steps: Identify whether you are genuinely first with a new concept, format, or benefit, as Pall Mall Gold was the first 100mm cigarette and Mazola was the first corn-oil margarine.

Do not dilute the first-mover claim by attaching the incumbent house name to it. The source argues Pall Mall's line-extension thinking let Benson & Hedges preempt the long-cigarette position, and Fleischmann's now leads corn-oil margarine.

Name the new concept so the name itself carries the idea. Taster's Choice beat Maxim 2-to-1 even though General Foods invented freeze-dried coffee, partly because 'Maxim' connoted nothing and 'Taster's Choice' plus 'tastes like ground roast' related the product to a standard of excellence.
Apply the same to a store: a genuinely new format or benefit deserves a distinct, benefit-connoting name and copy, not a variant SKU of a legacy bestseller.
Watch the share trajectory after extending: Pall Mall went from No. 1 in 1964 with 14.4% share to 3.8%, per the source, following its first extension in 1965.
caveats: All share figures are the source's historical examples, not forecasts for your category.
The source acknowledges that leading brands like Marlboro and Winston also extended — it frames the outcome as a tendency, not an inevitability.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: The Three-Act Pattern of a Positioned Brand's Decline
cards.summary: A breakthrough brand often loses its position by extending into adjacent models, as Volkswagen fell from first to fourth among imports.
cards.use_when: Reviewing an expanding product line or variant count, or planning a range extension for a category-leading product.
steps: Act One: a big breakthrough from finding a wide-open slot and exploiting it — Volkswagen with 'Think small' and the small-car position. The source notes the brand rose above name to become a lifestyle statement for a practical, no-nonsense buyer.
Act Two: greed and visions of unending success lead to extending the same reliability and quality to bigger, more expensive cars, buses, and jeep-type vehicles.
Act Three: the reversal. The source reports Volkswagen fell from first among imported cars to fourth, behind Toyota, Datsun, and Honda.
Diagnose your own line: count the models or variants carrying the hero name. The source asks whether eight models can sell as well as one — and answers that in this case they did not.
Use 'what's a [brand]?' on your own expanded line. If the answer is 'a big, small, cheap, expensive car' (the source's Chevrolet critique), the range has entered the everybody trap.
If breadth is needed, the source's alternative is a new concept with a new position and a new name.
caveats: The Volkswagen decline is the source's example, with its own era's competitive context, not a general law about range width.
Range breadth can be right for some retailers; the source's argument targets brands attempting to own a position in the customer's mind.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Name as Rubber Band: How Far to Stretch
cards.summary: A brand name stretches only so far before weakening, so decide extension scope by category economics and by whether a focused competitor can out-position you.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many product categories one brand name should cover, versus launching a separate brand or holding a category-specific name.
steps: Accept that the stretch limit is an economics question, not purely a judgment call: putting a separate name on peas, corn, and string beans would not be economical, so Del Monte using one name across canned fruits and vegetables is probably right.
Watch for the focused attacker. Dole versus Del Monte in canned pineapple is, in the source's words, 'no contest' — the specialist wins.
Run the teeter-totter check: if Dole makes the name mean bananas, what happens to the pineapple franchise? Extending one meaning trades against another.

Decide consciously whether you want full-line supplier status or a category franchise. The source says Dole can become full-line only at the expense of its valuable pineapple franchise, and with the added disadvantage of being the last to extend.
For a store: if a category has a credible specialist competitor, holding a category-specific name or sub-brand for that category protects the position better than folding it into a general brand.
caveats: Del Monte and Dole conclusions are the source's market observations, not universal rules.
The source explicitly tolerates broad names for commodities with no meaningful brand preference.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Diagnose Star Products Whose Sales Outrun Their Position
cards.summary: A product can lead a market it does not own in the customer's mind — Jergens Extra Dry lost to Intensive Care because the name did not convey the difference.
cards.use_when: Reviewing whether a category-leading SKU in your catalog actually owns a distinct claim, or launching an innovation that looks like a variant of an existing product.
steps: Separate market share from share of mind, as the source does for Scott: leading the paper-products market did not mean owning a position, and Charmin eventually displaced ScotTissue.
Test whether the customer can name which product does which job: the source asks which brand is engineered for the nose, Scotties or ScotTissue — the answer is unclear, so the name sits in limbo.

When you have a real innovation hidden inside a familiar name, rename it. Jergens Extra Dry was a creamlike lotion in an era of liquid lotions, but the similar name meant prospects did not recognize the difference; Chesebrough-Pond's Intensive Care named and positioned it clearly and took the lead.

Watch for the specialist's opening: if a competitor clearly names and positions the difference you buried, the source says the marketing victory goes to them, and a late counter-brand (Direct Aid) may be too little, too late.
Even a line-extended winner here is called by its extension name — customers say 'Intensive Care', not 'Vaseline' — so check what customers actually call your product.
caveats: History is the source's packaged-goods examples, not a measured forecast.
The lesson is about distinct position, not merely renaming: a rename without a real, communicated difference will not carry the position.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Position the Destination, Not the Vehicle (Country and Company Positioning)
cards.summary: Sabena could not sell flights to a country nobody wanted to visit, so the productive move was positioning Belgium as a destination first.
cards.use_when: Marketing a marketplace, region, or store category where demand must be grown before your own product can sell, including multi-seller marketplace or regional seller positioning.
steps: Find the destination-level problem before optimizing your own offer. Sabena sold food and service while only one in fifty North Atlantic passengers flew to Belgium at all; the source argues no amount of food advertising induces a flight to somewhere the traveler does not want to go.
Do what KLM had done for Amsterdam: make the place a destination people want to spend time in, rather than a place they pass through.
Build the position on a perception already in the prospect's mind. The 'three-star cities of beautiful Belgium' campaign anchored to Amsterdam, which travelers already knew.
Borrow credibility from an authority already trusted. The source credits the Michelin Guide (which rated five Belgian cities three-star 'worth a special journey') with making the claim believable.

Make the offer sufficient for a multi-day decision. The source notes nobody treats Monaco as a destination because Monte Carlo can be seen in an evening — five cities made Belgium a bona fide destination.
For a store: if your category requires a habit or occasion the customer does not yet have, market the occasion, then your product as the best execution of it.
caveats: The Belgium program, per the source, was not ultimately executed because new management did not commit — the source treats that as its own lesson about long-term commitment.
This is an agency case from the source's era; the transferable mechanism is anchoring to existing perceptions, not the specific media plan.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Avoid Cliché Visuals That Blur Your Category
cards.summary: Beaches-and-palms visuals for every Caribbean island get dumped in one mental slot, so use a distinctive visual device tied to your specific position.
cards.use_when: Planning ad creative, PDP imagery, or a landing-page hero where your category's visuals look identical to competitors'.
steps: Audit your category's standard imagery. The source notes the couple on the beach under palms is a visual cliché for the Caribbean, and asks whether a customer can keep Nassau, the Virgin Islands, and Barbados separate in mind. If not, the mind files them under 'islands' and tunes out.
Break with the cliché using something already meaningful, as Jamaica's neighbor Bermuda did with motorbikes beside pink sand — an enduring, effective visual.
Design a distinctive device that carries your position's meaning. For Belgium, Michelin stars were used as if they were church bells ringing as they were superimposed on city scenes.

Reach for moving image when the position is visual: the source says television drives pictures of a place into the mind faster than print. Adapt for ecommerce by using video where the position is pictorial.
Warn against the same blur in other formats: quaint European villages or smiling residents waving mugs of beer fail for the same reason as the palms.
caveats: The Bermuda visual is cited as effective and long-running, not as a measured lift.
The Belgium television work is described by the source as generating substantial response, but the program was not fully deployed — treat response as directional.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Positioning Must Be Sustained by Committed Management
cards.summary: A positioning program lives or dies on a long-term commitment from the people in charge, not on the quality of the concept alone.
cards.use_when: Setting positioning or rebranding direction for a store and deciding how to protect it through team, agency, or platform changes.
steps: Treat positioning as a multi-year commitment. The source's Belgium program failed not because the concept was weak but because new management arrived uncommitted and headquarters changed strategy.
Write the position down with the reasoning and the evidence (the shopping-list test result, the anchor perception, the credibility source) so a successor inherits the argument, not just the slogan.
Note the source's own framing: whether it's a corporation, a church, an airline, or a country, a successful positioning program requires major long-term commitment by the people in charge.
Build in a re-check rather than a rewrite: the source says you must constantly keep your position targeted to today's problems and today's markets, which is different from abandoning it for fashion.
For an ecommerce operator with high founder or agency turnover, document the position in the brand guide and tie creative, naming, and range decisions to it.
caveats: The source's evidence is a case study where the program was abandoned; it demonstrates the risk, not a measured effect of commitment.
The source acknowledges this is difficult in a constantly changing political environment — the same applies to fast-changing platform and marketing environments.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Third-Leg Strategy: Grow From the Position You Own
cards.summary: Rather than fighting a leader on their turf, Xerox's opportunity was to extend its copier position into the adjacent output lane it already owned.
cards.use_when: Deciding which adjacent category, product line, or feature set to enter when your store already owns one strong position and a bigger competitor owns the adjacent one.
steps: Map the market as legs. The office had three: telephones (AT&T), typewriters/computers (IBM), and copiers (Xerox). Ask which leg you currently own and whether new technology has changed what that leg means.
Do not attack the leg you do not own. The source notes Xerox failed at computers, workstations, and local area networks (IBM's leg), and IBM failed at copiers (Xerox's leg).
Find what your own leg has become. The copier leg of the future is the output leg: printers, scanners, storage devices.

Look for a technology that has already earned credibility elsewhere to attach to that leg — the laser, in the source's account, had proven itself in communication, medicine, retail checkout, and consumer disk players.

Name the new capability so it connects to your existing meaning: 'lasography' sounds new and different, sounds related to xerography, and uses a leading-edge technology, so it broadens the existing position instead of abandoning it.

For a store: extend from your owned position outward (e.g., from one category you genuinely own into adjacent formats for the same job), not into a category where a dominant specialist already owns the customer's mind.
caveats: Xerox's attempts are recounted as failures by the source; this is a strategic proposal made at the time, not a documented success.
The leg framework reflects that era's office market; the reasoning about avoiding the leader's turf transfers, the specific technologies do not.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Corporate Clarity: What Does Your Company Name Stand For?
cards.summary: A company name should stand for something specific inside its industry, since diversification and 'our people' are weak corporate positioning platforms.
cards.use_when: Positioning your store or company as a whole — for recruiting, supplier relationships, or investor conversations— rather than positioning one product.
steps: Check whether your name locks you to a past reputation. The source notes Pullman is barely a factor in railroad cars and Greyhound's buses keep it perceptually stuck despite millions telling the financial community it is 'more than a bus company'. If you want a broader meaning, the source argues you need a new name, not corporate advertising against the existing one.
Pick a quality that cuts across all your offerings, as Ford settled on 'innovation' ('Ford has a better idea') since it builds all types and sizes.

Avoid a people-based platform. The source argues most people assume bigger, more successful companies have better people, so claiming better people from a non-top position creates an inconsistency the prospect resolves against you.

Avoid 'diversification' as the theme. The source states positions are built on major achievements, not broad product lines, and cites GE as known for electrical manufacturing rather than diversified goods — plus stock markets undervaluing conglomerates.

Beware positions so broad they are meaningless: the source cites a company describing itself as 'a developer and supplier of information systems for work, education, and entertainment' — Bell & Howell.
Apply to a store: if you cannot state what your company name means in one specific way inside your category, tighten it before recruiting or supplier campaigns.
caveats: These are the source's observations about corporate advertising platforms, offered as strong opinions ('diversification is not the answer').
The Pullman and Greyhound examples are historical; verify current brand facts before citing them.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Find the Mental Postcard Before Shooting New Imagery
cards.summary: If one image perfectly captured your product's essence, someone would already have used it — so search for the existing perception rather than hunting a new shot.
cards.use_when: Planning brand photography, a category hero image, or creative territory for a store whose category visuals are interchangeable with competitors'.
steps: Start from perceptions already in the prospect's mind, not from a blank creative brief. In the travel case, countries are stored as mental picture postcards — England as pageantry and Big Ben, Amsterdam as tulips and canals, New York as a skyline.

Do not begin by sorting existing imagery for the one perfect picture. The source's reasoning is decisive: if one image captured the essence of the island, someone would have noticed and used it, meaning an image would already be burned into some minds.
Do not begin by shooting hundreds or thousands of new photos either. In the Jamaica case, the source reports that nothing totally right turned up from that approach.
Instead, locate the strongest existing perception or authority claim and build the visual system around it — as the Belgium work anchored to Amsterdam and borrowed Michelin's stars.

For a store: before commissioning a shoot, ask which image your customers already associate with your product's job, then produce imagery that sharpens that association rather than a generic category shot.
caveats: The Jamaica passage is where the source's extract ends; the resolution of that search is not stated here.
The insight is about search method (existing perception first), not proof that new photography can never work.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Reverse engineer positioning from the prospect's mind, not the destination/product
cards.summary: Tourism and product brands should hunt for the postcard or image already inside the prospect's head rather than inventing or photographing a new one.
cards.use_when: Deciding brand positioning for a store, destination, or product when you are tempted to shoot new creative or write new copy about your own features.
steps: Start from the mind, not the product: the source's Jamaica case tried three approaches — hunting existing postcards, commissioning new photography, then finally looking inside the prospect's mind. Only the third worked because the first two assume no image exists yet.
Ask what mental picture or verbal essence already lives in the customer's head about your category (Hawaii = big green volcanic mountains meeting blue sea).
Select one existing image you can tie your brand to rather than trying to build a fresh mental image from scratch; this saves the time and money of creating an image over years.

Reinforce the chosen analogy with supporting facts the prospect can verify — Jamaica's Blue Mountain at 7,402 feet is higher than any point east of the Mississippi, and the island is far larger than competitors.
Repeat the borrowed-image tactic at the metaphor's suggestion: the source proposes copying Hawaii's airport flower greeting to add a 'friendly' dimension to the beauty claim.
Use the analogy to differentiate against named competitors explicitly (a scale-drawn map showing Bermuda as tiny), and as a platform for adjacent markets (Europe, where Hawaii is far away).
caveats: Borrowing another destination's imagery risks looking derivative if the analogy is not backed by verifiable substance.
The source attributes Jamaica's inaction to politics, not positioning failure — execution depends on decision-makers, not the strategy alone.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Look in the prospect's mind, not the product, to solve a positioning problem
cards.summary: Milk Duds was repositioned as the long-lasting alternative to the candy bar, found by studying what candy buyers already think, not by inventing a new product claim.
cards.use_when: Choosing positioning for a slow-moving SKU or category where your brand has little advertising budget and competitors dominate the mental category.
steps: Identify who the real prospect is with research, not assumption: for Milk Duds the buyer was not a naive child but an experienced 10-year-old 'sophisticated candy buyer' who has been in candy stores hundreds of times and watches for value.
List what the prospect already thinks when the category is mentioned — for Milk Duds, the mind conjures candy bars (Hershey, Nestlé, Mounds, Almond Joy, Reese's, Snickers, Milky Way), not Milk Duds.

If you cannot afford to build a separate identity, reposition the category instead: set your brand as the alternative to the dominant form rather than adding another name to an overloaded mental list.

Find the visible weakness of the leader. The source's example: a Hershey bar is gone in 2.3 seconds and shrinking, producing documented dissatisfaction ('my allowance doesn't last long', 'candy bars are getting smaller').
Translate your product's real structure into that weakness — 15 individually wrapped slow-eating caramels in a box versus one fast bar — and name the position plainly: 'the long-lasting alternative.'

Sugarcoat the position in the prospect's own language in creative (kid with a giant mouth, candy bars disappearing, Milk Duds rolling one by one) and repeat it for years. The source notes the company had never used the long-lasting idea in 15 years of TV.
caveats: The Milk Duds sales result (reverse of a downward trend, record volume) is a case example, not a promised outcome.
Self-cannibalization objections may be raised by internal teams, as with Mailgram; expect to defend the strategic logic.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Position a service against the familiar mental anchor, then test low-cost vs high-speed claims
cards.summary: Mailgram was positioned as 'impact of a Telegram at a fraction of the cost' rather than as a high-speed letter, and the low-cost frame more than doubled awareness in test markets.
cards.use_when: Introducing a new service or subscription tier and deciding which existing behavior or alternative to contrast it against in messaging.
steps: Resist leading with technical sophistication. The source notes the traditional approach would have sold Mailgram as a 'new automated computerized electronic communication service,' which relates to nothing in the prospect's mind.
Find the existing mental anchor your brand name or category already triggers: 'Western Union' conjures the yellow Telegram, and the '-gram' in Mailgram reinforces it.
Quote the concrete difference the prospect can verify — the Telegram costs about three times a Mailgram and both use the same telegraphic format and demand immediate attention.

Consider the alternative anchor before committing: Mailgram could instead have been framed against first-class mail (68 billion letters, 815 per household per year), a much larger pool than telegrams.

Test both frames in real matched markets rather than deciding by judgment alone; the source used six large communication centers over a 13-week program and measured volume and awareness before and after.

Compare awareness change, not just volume: low-cost Telegram cities moved from 23% to 47% awareness while high-speed letter cities slipped from 27% to 25%, suggesting the low-cost frame had more long-term potential.
Expect internal objections about cannibalizing the existing service; in this case Telegram volume held stable and the source argues the campaign helped rather than hurt it.
caveats: Awareness and volume figures are a specific test-market case, not a benchmark for other services.
The source says the company later switched strategy to 'next-day delivery' and volume declined — an example, not proof that strategy changes always cause decline.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Map the prospect's mind with semantic differential research before choosing a position
cards.summary: Semantic differential research scored banks on attributes from 1 to 10, revealing that Long Island Trust was rated last on traditional banking attributes but first on loyalty to Long Island.
cards.use_when: Choosing a positioning territory for a local retailer, bank, or store facing larger outside competitors, when internal consensus is weak.
steps: Select attributes that matter to the category. For banking, price perception is nearly absent, so the study used six: many branches, full range of services, quality of service, large capital, helps Long Island residents, and helps the Long Island economy.
Have prospects rank each competitor on each attribute on a 1-to-10 scale and tabulate the results.
Read the pattern: Long Island Trust ranked last on all four traditional attributes but first on both Long Island attributes — a position created largely by the power of its name.
Ignore conventional wisdom that says accept your strengths and fix your weaknesses; the source's positioning theory says start with what the prospect is already willing to give you.
Turn the attribute where you lead into the campaign theme and name the enemy: 'Why send your money to the city if you live on the Island?' contrasted with city banks' Nassau and Cayman branches.

Re-run the same research after the campaign to confirm movement. Fifteen months later Long Island Trust moved from last to first on both 'many branches' and 'large capital' despite a competitor having more than twice as many actual Long Island branches.
caveats: The source says formal research is often not needed when the insight is intuitive (Western Union/Telegram), but it is useful for building strategy and selling it to top management.
Perception shifts in research do not guarantee real-world branch or financial results.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Position a local business against the giant's size weakness, then make operations match the promise
cards.summary: United Jersey became the 'fast-moving bank' by exploiting big New York banks' slow service and backing the ad promise with seven concrete operational commitments.
cards.use_when: Positioning a smaller store or local brand against a large national competitor whose weakness is slowness or bureaucracy.
steps: Study the competition, not yourself, to find the position, as Tylenol did by studying aspirin's problems rather than its own product.

Target the competitors who actually occupy the prospect's mind, not smaller rivals nobody thinks about — the source chose the big New York banks because 'positioning is always a question of dealing with what's in the mind.'
Name the leader's real weakness: large size means slow reaction time, similar to the Avis 'shorter line' claim.

Before advertising the promise, change operations to deliver it. United Jersey made seven commitments: decentralized decisions (a lending team can approve a $10 million loan, meeting daily), cross-training staff so questions aren't referred elsewhere, statewide ATM commitment, six-times-daily lock box pickups, FACT terminals for fast merchant approvals, responsiveness on rates and products, and a Princeton headquarters central to all customers.

Only then run the promise-based advertising. TV spots contrasted United Jersey bankers with the fictional 'Lethargic National Bank,' and print used headlines like 'Haste makes money' and 'Banks shouldn't hold up people.'
Reinforce internally with 'Time Is Money' desk signs for officers.

Track awareness and attitude, not just sales. The source reports unaided awareness nearly tripled in just over a year and one officer noted line officers were visibly striving to live up to the promise.
caveats: The reported earnings increase of $30 million (26%) is a specific case result, not a general expectation.
The source's essence criterion is that a good position transcends every aspect of the company — if operations can't match the ad, the strategy fails.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Use 'top 10' list authority to justify a premium or longer journey
cards.summary: Stowe positioned itself as the only Eastern resort among the world's top 10 ski resorts, borrowing a trusted authority's list to justify the extra drive from New York.
cards.use_when: Selling a product or store that is farther, pricier, or less convenient than alternatives and needs a reason the customer will accept.
steps: Identify the disadvantage you must overcome: Stowe is one to two hours farther from New York City than Stratton, Sugarbush, Big Bromley, and Mt. Snow.

Find an independent authority rather than claiming superiority yourself. The source used ski and travel writer Abby Rand in Harper's Bazaar selecting the top 10 ski resorts in the world, with Stowe as the only Eastern one.
Present the list visually and explicitly: shoulder patches for each resort with the line 'Of the world's top 10 ski resorts, only one is in the East.'
Frame the reward for the customer's extra effort or spend — the ad promised a ski vacation of a lifetime without going to the Alps, Andes, or Rockies.
Keep the list strategy running indefinitely; the source notes there is no reason to change a position built on a recognized list.

Rely on the human tendency to defer to authority: the source cites Candid Camera creator Allen Funt's observation that people obey even minimal signs of authority, asking 'Is Jersey open?' when told 'Delaware Closed Today.'
caveats: The source presents the defer-to-authority tendency as a dark side of human nature; using it manipulatively can erode trust if the list is self-serving or fabricated.
The Stowe response — thousands of brochure requests and record attendance — is a case result, not a benchmark.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Reposition by retracing the organization's original business and stating it simply
cards.summary: The Catholic Church's identity crisis was traced to losing its clear position; retracing Scripture produced 'teacher of the word' as the simple repositioning answer.
cards.use_when: When a brand or store has changed format, ownership, or assortment and customers no longer know what it stands for.
steps: Recognize the symptoms of lost position: after Vatican II the Church's clear 'teacher of the law' position blurred, Mass attendance fell below 50% (a 20% drop while Protestant attendance stayed stable), and vocations dropped 60%.
Audit communication for a central theme; the source found haphazard programs with no central theme or continuity, like General Motors with no corporate advertising and only local dealers speaking.
Retrace the organization's steps to find its basic business, as corporate identity programs pore over old plans and annual reports — here going back 2,000 years to Scripture.

Extract the simplest single expression of the role: the Gospels (Matt. 17:23 and 28:19) point to the Church as teacher of the word, keeping Christ alive in each new generation and relating his word to current problems.

Accept that the obvious is hardest to sell internally; the source says the human mind admires the complicated and dismisses the obvious, and the clergy preferred a theologian's six-role answer over a single clear position.

Implement the position through concrete capabilities that serve the theme — pulpit training for better sermons and an introductory film to dramatize the new direction — because a position sets the direction for all organizational activities.
caveats: The source states the program was never implemented; the bishops resisted lay people telling them how to run the Church and found the solution too obvious. The card describes the method, not a proven outcome.
The attendance, vocation, and executive-ranking statistics are source-reported context from the book's era, not current data.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Define a single personal position and build a career strategy around it
