Invite the person who produced the rejected idea to solve the constraint (cost, legal availability) rather than dropping the idea.
caveats: These are the source's management prescriptions and personal practice, not measured team-performance results.
Small teams may not be able to isolate phases in separate people; they still need to isolate them in time.
cards.source_name: We named a billion dollar “startup” with the guy that named BlackBerry, Febreeze and Swiffer.docx

cards.title: Use an Inconvenient Outside Source to Force New Connections
cards.summary: Spend 30 minutes in unfamiliar material and deliberately look for transferable connections before finalizing creative work.
cards.use_when: A headline, PDP narrative, campaign angle or product story feels like generic category copy and you need a genuinely different perspective.
steps: Choose genuinely unfamiliar material for the category — a couple of magazines you never read, or a book on a subject unrelated to your product such as Thomas Edison.
Spend about 30 minutes reading only for connections that could move into the piece, suspending logic and evaluation during that window.
The source's claim, from his own practice, is that roughly 30% of the time this yields a new perspective, spin or insight for the work — treat that as his experience, not a measured rate.

This supports the source's broader principle of synchronicity: creativity comes from connecting seemingly irrelevant things. Impossible Burger is the cited case — deliberately not a natural-foods-style name that would blend into the Whole Foods shelf.

Extend the same move to the natural world, which the source sometimes uses as a direct source: for 'lightness' he looked at what makes an airplane lift, and at Greek roots and expressions for feeling light.

Ecommerce application: before finalizing a product narrative or ad hook, read one industry-adjacent and one completely unrelated publication or community, and mine them for a metaphor or angle you can justify with your real product facts.
Make the borrowed angle serve the product truth, not replace it — a clever reference that overstates the product breaks believability.
caveats: The 30% hit rate is the source's own estimate from practice.
Borrowed metaphors must be checked against what your product actually does before use in claims.
cards.source_name: We named a billion dollar “startup” with the guy that named BlackBerry, Febreeze and Swiffer.docx

cards.title: Judging names is the scarce skill, not generating them
cards.summary: AI can mass-produce name candidates, so the durable advantage shifts to your ability to judge which names are right versus merely okay.
cards.use_when: When naming a new product, brand line, or store, or when you have a longlist of candidates and need to pick the one to launch with.
steps: Generate a wide longlist of candidate names with AI or a group brainstorm; the naming expert behind BlackBerry, Febreze and Swiffer notes that anyone can now generate 200-300 names with AI tools, so generation is no longer the bottleneck.

Instead of spending your time generating more, invest it in building a judgment framework: define what 'right' means for this product before you evaluate, so the criteria are not reverse-engineered from whichever names you happen to like.
Score each candidate against that framework rather than arguing pairwise. The source's point is that separating the right names from the good and the okay names is where the value now sits.
Apply the same judgment to each candidate: does it fit the product category, the positioning line you intend, and the customer's vocabulary?
Keep the rejected-but-good names in a file; they may suit a future SKU or sub-brand.
caveats: The source runs a naming firm whose competitive advantage is proprietary data and software integrated with AI; a small brand will not replicate that dataset, so allocate more weight to your own category and customer knowledge.
cards.source_name: We named a billion dollar “startup” with the guy that named BlackBerry, Febreeze and Swiffer.docx

cards.title: Budget and scope for professional naming work
cards.summary: Name-development projects from an established naming firm typically run roughly $75k to $150k, with large corporate programs reaching about $200k, and usually include more than just the name.
cards.use_when: When planning budget, scope, or an in-house vs agency decision for a new brand, product line, or flagship SKU.
steps: Treat these numbers as a directional benchmark from one firm, not a market rate. The source describes most projects landing between a low of about $75k and a high of about $150k, with big corporate work up to roughly $200k.
Expect the deliverable to extend beyond the name: the source describes helping with nomenclature (how the product is defined), a positioning line, and a short brand story.
Ask about tracking research: the firm runs small quantitative studies monitoring how the name lands over roughly 90-120 days after launch.
If your budget cannot support this tier, decide explicitly which parts you can do yourself (name generation, positioning line) and where you will buy expertise (qualitative validation, tracking).
Convert the fee into a per-year cost if the name will be used for years, and compare it against the cost of a later rename: packaging, listings, domain, ad creative, and accumulated search equity.
caveats: These are one firm's 2026-era numbers for consulting projects; costs vary widely by region, scope and firm size.
Small ecommerce brands rarely need this spend for every SKU; reserve it for the flagship or umbrella brand.
cards.source_name: We named a billion dollar “startup” with the guy that named BlackBerry, Febreeze and Swiffer.docx

cards.title: Name launches usually include a post-launch tracking study
cards.summary: After delivering a name, naming firms often run small quantitative tracking research over 90-120 days to see how the name is landing with the market.
cards.use_when: When you have just launched or rebranded and want to know whether the new name is gaining traction before locking in packaging, listings and ad spend.
steps: Define a small set of measurable signals before launch: unaided and aided recall of the name, correct association with the product category, and how easily it is repeated or spelled when someone hears it.
Run a lightweight survey at launch and again at roughly 90-120 days; the source describes exactly this cadence as typical tracking research.
Include a practical commerce signal: can people find the store by searching the name, and does the paid-search auction for the name show rising volume?
Watch for name-specific failure modes: misspellings in search queries, voice-assistant mishearing, and people confusing the name with an existing brand.
Decide in advance what result triggers action: if recall and category association do not improve materially by the second wave, weigh the cost of a repositioning line versus a full rename.
Feed findings back into the positioning line and short brand story rather than changing the name reflexively.
caveats: The source describes the practice but gives no numeric thresholds; choose your own meaningful improvement level.
Small samples can be noisy, so treat the second wave as directional.
cards.source_name: We named a billion dollar “startup” with the guy that named BlackBerry, Febreeze and Swiffer.docx

cards.title: Use 'approximate thinking' to unlock team creativity
cards.summary: Draw a line with bizarre/absurd/illegal ideas on one end and safe workable ideas on the other, put 'approximate thinking' in the middle, and explicitly give people permission to stop there instead of jumping straight to safe answers.
cards.use_when: When briefing your team or an agency on ad creative, product naming, landing-page concepts, or any ideation session where output has become predictable.
steps: Draw the spectrum: on one end bizarre, absurd or even illegal ideas; on the other, safe workable ideas. Write 'approximate thinking' in the middle and show it to your team.
Explain the rule: you may move from bizarre through approximate, then stop there. Do not force the jump to finished, safe ideas.
Present the approximate set deliberately unfinished: not baked out, not full, possibly bad. The source states that giving people permission to work at this stage makes creativity spike.
As the operator, resist killing an idea because it is not yet a campaign. Ask instead: what would have to be true for this to work?
Select a small number of approximate ideas to develop further into ads, PDP copy, or bundles, and keep the bizarre end visible so the safe end does not become the whole range.
Repeat the exercise each time the output gets stale rather than only once.
caveats: This is the source's own coaching device for creative teams, not a documented experiment; expect to sift a lot of unusable material.
Not every category can absorb a bizarre concept, and in regulated categories legal review still applies.
cards.source_name: We named a billion dollar “startup” with the guy that named BlackBerry, Febreeze and Swiffer.docx

cards.title: Give AI the generation work, keep the judgment in-house
cards.summary: Integrating AI into a naming process took one firm about 16 months and shifted its edge from producing names to judging them against proprietary data.
cards.use_when: When deciding how far to automate naming, product-copy generation, or creative concepts, and what capability to keep human.
steps: Use AI to widen the funnel cheaply: the source notes anyone can now generate 200-300 names with assistants such as ChatGPT or Claude. Treat that output as raw material, not decisions.
Build the judgment layer yourself: define the criteria, the category conventions, and the customer vocabulary that a name or concept must satisfy.

Invest in the data that makes judgment repeatable: the source firm spent about 16 months integrating AI into a database it had already invested in. For a retailer, that may be search-query logs, review language and returns reasons rather than a naming database.
Note the source's observation that six of roughly twelve or thirteen active projects were AI-driven, i.e. even an established naming practice is restructuring around the technology.
Assign a single owner to final judgment so AI output does not get adopted by whoever generated the most options.
caveats: The 16-month integration and the project mix are one firm's experience, not a productivity benchmark.
AI output may reproduce existing or trademarked names; run clearance checks before committing to anything.
cards.source_name: We named a billion dollar “startup” with the guy that named BlackBerry, Febreeze and Swiffer.docx

cards.title: The Daily 3: Cut to Three Needle-Movers
cards.summary: Each day pick only the top 3 tasks that move the store forward and say no to the other 97%.
cards.use_when: Weekly planning for a lean ecommerce team or solo operator overwhelmed by merchandising, marketing, and ops tasks.
steps: Each morning (or the night before), list everything you could do across your store — product pages, ads, inventory, email, support.
Force-rank and select only 3 tasks that most move the needle (e.g. fix the top PDP, launch the restock email, resolve a checkout drop-off).
Work top to bottom through those 3 before touching anything else.
Say no to the other 97% deliberately; defer, delegate, or delete them.
Review the pattern over weeks so recurring 'yes' items reflect your real priorities, not noise.
caveats: Source is the presenter's personal operating rule, not a proven system for all teams.
Some urgent ops issues (stockouts, payment failures) may need same-day handling outside the 3.
cards.source_name: the psychology of building a brand everyone loves.docx

cards.title: "Audience Comes Last": Build to Your Taste, Not Market Guessing
cards.summary: Ignore surveys and focus groups during the creative act; rely on personal intuition and taste, then test in market.
cards.use_when: Designing brand identity, packaging, creative direction, or new products where you're tempted to poll customers first.
steps: Separate the creation phase from the validation phase: block the audience out while conceiving the brand, product, or creative.
Lean on your own taste, intuition, and judgment as the core input rather than surveys or focus groups (the Rick Rubin / Steve Jobs principle the presenter cites).
Trust the signal from your inner voice to distill to one simple idea.
After creating, take it to market where real behavior (clicks, add-to-cart, repeat orders) is the test.
Note the source's framing: the audience only knows what has come before, so customers tend to ask for a faster horse rather than something genuinely new.
caveats: This concerns the creative act; it is not a license to skip customer research, pricing tests, or post-launch data.
The presenter attributes this to Rubin and Jobs — treat as their philosophy, not a validated universal method.
cards.source_name: the psychology of building a brand everyone loves.docx

cards.title: Let Weirdness Become the Brand's Authentic Edge
cards.summary: Digging into your own quirks and 'woo woo' interests produces authentic differentiation competitors don't copy.
cards.use_when: Positioning a store in a crowded category where every brand sounds and looks the same.
steps: Identify the beliefs, niche interests, or approaches you hold that others in your category call odd or dismiss.
Ignore critics who say it's too niche or nobody cares; the source kept his 'soulful' angle despite pushback.
Lean that unfair advantage into brand voice, product curation, and creative instead of flattening to category norms.
Use the search through your own weirdness to find what is genuinely you — the presenter says authenticity comes from that exploration.
Express it consistently across PDP copy, packaging, and social so it reads as a coherent brand, not a gimmick.
caveats: Distinctiveness can narrow appeal; ensure the core offer still solves a clear customer problem.
Authenticity claims are the presenter's philosophy, not a measured conversion driver.
cards.source_name: the psychology of building a brand everyone loves.docx

cards.title: Obsess Over the Craft, Not the Metrics
cards.summary: Betting maximum effort on the craft every time compounds exponentially, and obsession becomes contagious to an audience.
cards.use_when: Allocating effort between chasing metrics (views, follower counts) versus improving the actual product, photos, or content quality.
steps: Redirect effort from metric-chasing to mastering the craft: cinematography, lighting, copy, product quality.
Go all-in on each project rather than spreading thin — the source cites Mr. Beast 'betting the farm' each video.
Aim to solve the problem three times deeper than competitors; different solutions follow from deeper work.
Pick a single format on a single platform and try to make it best-in-world rather than dabbling across all of them (the presenter says dabbling gets lost in the noise).
Example cited: hand-drawing concept images on LinkedIn out of genuine obsession led to ~110,000 followers in a month — treat this as an anecdote, not a target.
caveats: Obsession compounding is the presenter's analogy, not a linear formula with verified numbers.
The Mr. Beast and LinkedIn follower results are case examples, not promises.
cards.source_name: the psychology of building a brand everyone loves.docx

cards.title: Insanely Simple: Strip to One Idea
cards.summary: Relentlessly simplify products, UX, and messaging to one clear thing, on the Henry Ford principle that people don't know what they want.
cards.use_when: Simplifying a cluttered PDP, navigation, product line, or ad concept that has too many competing messages.
steps: Iterate toward fewer elements: the source recounts iPhone prototypes going from three buttons to one to a buttonless interface under Jobs.
Apply the same to messaging — Apple's ads made a simple, memorable comparison rather than an exhaustive feature list.
Distill your product or store down to one simple thing customers can remember.
Cut feature creep and competing CTAs; each extra element dilutes the signal.
Note the Ford framing: customers didn't ask for a car, they asked for a faster horse — so simplicity often means leading, not polling.
caveats: Simplification can strip genuinely useful features; test whether customers still complete the task.
The Apple/Jobs story is illustrative, not a documented playbook you can copy directly.
cards.source_name: the psychology of building a brand everyone loves.docx

cards.title: Choose One Format on One Platform
cards.summary: Dabbling across platforms gets lost in the noise; obsessing over a single format on a single platform sets you apart.
cards.use_when: Deciding which organic channel to build for a store instead of posting thinly across X, LinkedIn, YouTube, and Instagram.
steps: Pick one platform and one format (e.g. a weekly founder video, a daily concept image, one recurring email).
Commit to making that single format the best in the world rather than spreading effort.
Refuse to treat it as a side hobby or something to dabble in — the presenter says that path gets lost in the noise.
Obsess over the format's craft, not the follower count.
Let the format compound: the source's hand-drawn concept images shared thousands of times and grew LinkedIn by ~110k in a month (an anecdote, not a benchmark).
caveats: Single-platform focus trades reach for depth; revisit the choice only after sufficient reps.
The follower-growth example is a case result, not a repeatable promise.
cards.source_name: the psychology of building a brand everyone loves.docx

cards.title: Go Deep, Not Wide: Shape the Company's Character
cards.summary: Iconic brands go deep rather than wide, and deliberately training through 'pain and suffering' refines a company's character.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to broaden a product line or deepen an existing category and internal standard of quality.
steps: Bias toward depth: improve the core product, sourcing, or experience rather than adding categories.
Adopt the source's framing of using 'pain and suffering' deliberately — i.e. embrace hard refinements that train the character of the company.
Treat the goal as building an icon over decades, not chasing the next product launch.
Apply the principle to team standards: obsess over craft quality so the brand's depth shows in every touchpoint.
Remember the closing line: icons aren't born, they're built.
caveats: Depth can mean slower diversification; weigh against the realities of your category and cash flow.
The 'pain and suffering' language is the presenter's rhetorical framing, not an operating metric.
cards.source_name: the psychology of building a brand everyone loves.docx

cards.title: Inject custom Liquid sections into a Shopify theme via Edit Code
cards.summary: Click path for creating a reusable custom section file in a Shopify theme by pasting external HTML/Liquid through the Edit Code interface.
cards.use_when: You need a custom PDP, landing page, or storefront section (founder block, ingredient panel, size chart) that Shopify's default page builder sections cannot produce, and want it reusable across templates.
steps: Keep the current theme available for rollback and preview the complete purchase journey before publishing any edited theme.
From the Shopify admin go to Online Store, then open the Themes page.
Duplicate the current theme and work on the unpublished copy; click its actions menu, and choose Edit Code to open the code editor.
In the left file tree, open the Sections folder.
Use Add a new section, give the file a descriptive name that ends in .liquid (for example wle_hair_nectar_gg.liquid), and create it.
Paste your prepared HTML/Liquid code into the new file and Save.
The section now appears in the theme customizer's Add Section picker, where you can place it and edit its schema settings.
To update the section later, reopen Edit Code, paste the new code over the old, Save, and preview the draft page on desktop and mobile to confirm the change rendered.
caveats: Sections live inside the theme, so changes are lost or overwritten if the theme is replaced or updated without carrying the file forward — keep a copy of the Liquid code outside Shopify.
Shopify's Edit Code interface labels and menu positions change; verify the current click path in your admin before following these steps literally.
Verify the section has valid theme-compatible schema and any preset needed for the Add Section picker; pasted HTML alone does not guarantee a configurable section.
cards.source_name: Claude & Shopify Built $750k_m Ai Powered Ecom Brand.docx

cards.title: Assign a product to a custom page template
cards.summary: Click path for building a custom Shopify product template that hides default sections and populates your custom Liquid section with a specific product.
cards.use_when: Merchandising a hero or specialty product on a bespoke PDP layout, or building a landing page where you want your custom section to render that product's data.
steps: Create the product first: Products, Add product, upload the images you want the custom section to display, and set the price.
Open Online Store, then Customize Theme to enter the theme editor.
In the template selector at the top, create a new template for the product (for example name it hair_nectar_gg) rather than editing the default product template.
Hide or remove the default sections so only your intended layout shows.
Use Add Section and select the custom Liquid file you created (for example wle_hair_nectar_gg) to place it on the template.
Assign the specific product to the template so the custom section's product object references it and populates correctly.
Preview the template with that product assigned to confirm images, price and section content all render.
caveats: A custom product template only applies to products you assign to it; leaving a product on the default template means the custom layout will not appear.
If the custom section references product objects, it will render empty or broken on products that have no such data assigned.
cards.source_name: Claude & Shopify Built $750k_m Ai Powered Ecom Brand.docx

cards.title: Make a product buyable with inventory set before launch
cards.summary: Ensuring a freshly added Shopify product can actually be added to cart by editing the product and setting available inventory.
cards.use_when: After adding a product through Products, Add product, before driving any traffic — you need to confirm the product is not showing as sold out or unavailable at checkout.
steps: Go to Products in the Shopify admin and open the product you just added.
Set the price and make sure the product is set to Active so it is published to the storefront.
Set available inventory for the variant (the source example uses 10,000 units) and Save.
Open the live storefront product page in a fresh session and confirm the add-to-cart button is enabled rather than showing Sold out.
Add the product to cart and reach the checkout start to verify it is genuinely purchasable end to end.
caveats: The 10,000 figure is just an example from the source, not a recommended stock level — set inventory to match your real replenishment plan.
Inventory can be tracked or untracked per variant; a product with inventory tracking on and zero available will display as sold out even if the page looks correct.
cards.source_name: Claude & Shopify Built $750k_m Ai Powered Ecom Brand.docx

cards.title: Verify each store-setup step on the live storefront
cards.summary: Adding a verification step after every mechanical store configuration task so a click path that 'looked done' is proven to actually work.
cards.use_when: Any time you complete a store setup task — theme code, product, payment, shipping profile or tax — before moving to the next setup item.
steps: After each setup task, define the observable behaviour that proves it worked (product adds to cart, page shows the new section, order can complete).
Open the live storefront in a private/incognito window or offline-test mode so admin-session caching does not mask problems.
Exercise the exact customer action tied to that task — add to cart, reach checkout, submit a test order where your payment settings allow it.
If you edited Liquid, hard-refresh the live page rather than trusting the theme editor preview, which can show unsaved or cached states.
Record the setup item as verified only after the live behaviour matches, then move on.
caveats: Preferences and interfaces vary; the specific test steps depend on your payment, shipping and tax configuration, so adapt the verification to each item.
Test orders and payment gateways may need test mode or refunding, which is outside the scope of the pure click path.
cards.source_name: Claude & Shopify Built $750k_m Ai Powered Ecom Brand.docx

cards.title: Inject custom Liquid sections into a Shopify theme
cards.summary: Mechanical click path for adding a custom Liquid section file to a Shopify theme so a bespoke product page can be built manually.
cards.use_when: You need to build a custom PDP section or page by hand in Shopify (no page builder), e.g. a branded product template for a new SKU.
steps: In Shopify admin go to Online Store, then Edit Code to open the theme code editor.
Open the Sections folder and choose Add a new section; name the file with a clear convention (in the source example: a product-specific name like [brand]_[product]_gg.liquid).
Paste your HTML/Liquid code into the new section file and Save.
To revise later, return to Edit Code, paste the new code over the old code, Save, then refresh the live page to confirm the change rendered.
Verify the current Shopify admin labels and menus yourself — theme editor layout changes over time.
caveats: Section code lives in the theme; theme updates or switching themes can drop or conflict with custom files.
Only edit code in a duplicated/published-safe theme if you cannot afford downtime.
cards.source_name: Claude & Shopify Built $750k_m Ai Powered Ecom Brand.docx

cards.title: Assign a custom page template to a specific product
cards.summary: Click path for creating a product-specific template in the theme customizer and pointing one product at it so it renders a custom Liquid section.
cards.use_when: You want one hero/paid-traffic product to have a unique PDP layout while all other products keep the default template.
steps: Create the product first: Products, Add product, upload images, set price, and Save.
Go to Online Store, then Customize Theme and create a new template for the product (name it per product, e.g. hair_nectar_gg).
Inside that template, hide the default sections you do not want, then Add Section and select the custom Liquid file you created earlier.
Assign the specific product to the template so it populates the section.
Confirm the product page renders the custom layout and that the default template is untouched for other products.
Verify current Shopify template-assignment UI before relying on this path.
caveats: Template names are arbitrary but must match what you assign in the product; mismatches silently fall back to the default template.
Hiding default sections is not deletion — you can restore them if the layout breaks.
cards.source_name: Claude & Shopify Built $750k_m Ai Powered Ecom Brand.docx

cards.title: Make a product actually buyable before launch
cards.summary: The minimum product-admin steps to stop a new product from showing sold out or unaddable-to-cart at launch.
cards.use_when: Immediately before driving paid traffic or launch content to a new product, to avoid wasting spend on an unbuyable PDP.
steps: Go to Products, Edit product on the SKU you are launching.
Set Available inventory (the source example used a large number like 10,000 for a launch SKU) and Save.
If drop shipping, confirm the fulfillment app or supplier actually holds that stock — Shopify inventory is only a number and does not create real stock.
After saving, add the product to cart yourself on the live store to confirm it is purchasable and the variant/price is correct.
caveats: Setting a large inventory number on a drop-ship SKU does not guarantee fulfillment; keep it aligned with real supplier stock.
If you later toggle inventory tracking, re-check the PDP still allows purchase.
cards.source_name: Claude & Shopify Built $750k_m Ai Powered Ecom Brand.docx

cards.title: Reverse-engineer a validated product via a challenger angle
cards.summary: Score a candidate product across demand, ad momentum, store-level and competition signals, then only pursue it with a differentiating brand/content angle rather than a clone.
cards.use_when: Product selection: deciding whether to base a new store on a proven seller you found in ad libraries.
steps: Pick a product from a brand already scaling with active ads; treat sustained active-ad counts as the strongest ad-momentum indicator (source treats growing active ads as the key signal).
Score the opportunity across demand, ad momentum, store-level revenue/trust signals (e.g. Trustpilot), competition/concentration of top-spending ads, and Facebook/Meta ad-fit.
Check for a moat: if the winning tier is crowded and the moat is brand- and content-driven, a clone will lose — you must bring a sharp angle.
Check policies and ad-language compliance before committing, since category language can gate scaling.
If the score is high but the moat is brand-driven, plan for serious content and influencer support, not just a better product.
Treat the source's 7.95/10 'go with conditions' verdict as a heuristic example, not a benchmark threshold.
caveats: Scores combine one tool's ad-library data plus web research; without ad-library access expect materially less data (source cites roughly 55% of its data set).
Source opinion: a product can be validated yet still fail if you clone the incumbent instead of out-branding it.
cards.source_name: Claude & Shopify Built $750k_m Ai Powered Ecom Brand.docx

cards.title: Capture competitor pages and ads as structured research inputs
cards.summary: Use screenshots of a proven competitor page as the seed input to product validation, branding, mockups and page-mirroring workflows.
cards.use_when: Starting any reverse-engineering workflow (validation, branding, product mockup, page clone) and needing a clean source image of the target brand page.
steps: Open the competitor's store page in the browser.
Use a full-page capture browser extension to screenshot the entire page, then download it.
Feed the screenshot into the research/branding tool as the reference brand you are modeling.
Note what is copied versus elevated: the source explicitly says it models what works but intends to improve pages, branding and voice rather than clone.
If visual references are needed, a page-image extraction extension lists every image on the page and lets you download them individually for use as inspiration inputs.
caveats: Downloading a competitor's imagery is for research/inspiration; do not ship their copyrighted assets as your own.
Screenshots are reference inputs, not validated product data — pair with ad-library and store-level signals.
cards.source_name: Claude & Shopify Built $750k_m Ai Powered Ecom Brand.docx

cards.title: Build the brand kit before the store: intake, positioning and naming
cards.summary: Sequence for generating a usable brand system (strategy, voice, palette, logo, name) from a modeled competitor using an AI branding workflow.
cards.use_when: Building a new store's brand from scratch when you already have a validated product and a competitor to model.
steps: Run a branding intake with: specific product, business name, target market, price position, competitors, existing assets, and launch channel (the source used a US target market and a Shopify store).

Set brand-voice sliders (playful vs. serious, bold vs. soft), then answer the positioning prompts — source cites the 'dinner party test', '3-second feeling', and naming the territory/instinct questions.
Generate a brand strategy snapshot: colors, motif, product names.
Generate candidate names, then critique them against the actual customer; the source rejected names that felt disconnected and asked for names with 'hair' in them, which produced usable options.
Check domain availability and pick alternates (.co, .shop prefix, 'co' suffix) if the .com is taken.
Lock the name before generating assets so everything downstream stays consistent.
caveats: First-round AI names can miss the customer; plan to give corrective feedback rather than accepting the first list.
The source's chosen name and domain alternatives are examples, not recommendations for your category.
cards.source_name: Claude & Shopify Built $750k_m Ai Powered Ecom Brand.docx

cards.title: Generate a brand board, then lock it for production consistency
cards.summary: Use a generative image tool to explore a brand board, then move it into a precise design tool to freeze logo and palette for suppliers and print.
cards.use_when: Preparing brand assets before sending a logo or packaging to a supplier or designer, or building landing-page visuals on-brand.
steps: Prompt a text-to-image tool to generate a brand board: logo, signature palette, pattern, headline treatment, element style and social vibe (the source used a poster-style brand board and preferred the most visual output over the most technical one).
Feed your accepted brand board back so the brand strategy can be finalized.
Generate logo concepts at a square (1:1) aspect ratio and pick one; the source generated four options and chose manually.
Move the chosen logo and palette into a precision design tool to recreate them exactly — generative tools approximate logos, which is unsafe for supplier files.
Export pixel-accurate PNGs of the logo in its variants and the exact color palette, so the mark never drifts across assets.
caveats: Generative image outputs are approximations — never send a generated logo to a supplier without recreating it precisely.
The source preferred one specific visual style/tool, which is a taste preference, not a universal rule.
cards.source_name: Claude & Shopify Built $750k_m Ai Powered Ecom Brand.docx

cards.title: Write a brand reference guide for every downstream asset creator
cards.summary: Produce a short written brand description so mockups, product photography prompts and any hired creator can stay on-brand.
cards.use_when: Briefing product mockup generation, a photographer/videographer, or a designer and needing one consistent description of what the brand stands for.
steps: From your branding exercise, request a written description covering: what the brand is, what it stands for, its personality, and its unique identity.
Format it as a reference usable by a photographer, videographer or any asset creator.
Reuse the same guide as an input to product mockup and image generation so visuals stay consistent with the positioning.
Update the guide if the brand positioning shifts, so old asset prompts do not pull in stale mood.
caveats: The guide is only useful if it is actually pasted into every asset workflow; a file nobody opens changes nothing.
Keep it descriptive and specific — generic adjectives produce generic imagery.
cards.source_name: Claude & Shopify Built $750k_m Ai Powered Ecom Brand.docx

cards.title: Draft the product mockup before contacting any supplier
cards.summary: Sequence for producing approved bottle and packaging mockups plus a clean pack shot from a competitor photo, logo, brand board and brand guide.
cards.use_when: Product sourcing and packaging prep: you need a visual target to send a supplier and to populate PDP imagery.
steps: Start with a competitor product photo so the tool understands the physical product you are making.
Add your logo, brand board, and written brand guide as inputs, then confirm the generated brand snapshot.
Name the first product with a consumer-friendly name (the source used a fun name instead of an ingredient name) and approve a bottle concept, e.g. a 'nectar window' label style.
Generate the base product image in the image tool at a print-friendly ratio (source used 3:4, 2K, medium) and generate multiple variations to choose from.
For image two, use your approved mockup plus your logo to generate lifestyle/setting shots; for image three, generate a clean pack shot.
Feed the approved images into a packaging brief to produce front/hero and back-panel packaging art, then send the product image and packaging spec together to the supplier.
caveats: Suppliers can improve on your spec — treat it as a direction, not a final print file.
Generated mockups are concepts; verify dimensions and label legal/ingredient copy before production.
cards.source_name: Claude & Shopify Built $750k_m Ai Powered Ecom Brand.docx

cards.title: Create on-brand lifestyle imagery from competitor inspiration
cards.summary: Adapt competitor lifestyle shot compositions into your own branded images by pairing an inspiration image with your product reference and a written prompt.
cards.use_when: Building PDP, landing-page and ad creative imagery that looks on-brand without a photoshoot.
steps: Collect inspiration images from the competitor page (a page-image downloader extension speeds this up).
Pair each inspiration image (composition/lighting reference) with an image of your own product (identity reference).
Rewrite the scene for your formulation: the source swapped competitor props (e.g. white ice, oranges, lavender) for props matching its own ingredients (rosemary, cucumber, honey, avocado).
Generate at a usable resolution and iterate by swapping only the inspiration image while keeping the brand reference constant.
Use these images for the store, supplier presentations, influencer briefs and investor/pitch visuals.
caveats: Output quality tracks prompt quality — the source states images are only as good as the prompts.
Reusing a competitor's exact composition may risk looking derivative; change props, setting and brand cues.
cards.source_name: Claude & Shopify Built $750k_m Ai Powered Ecom Brand.docx

cards.title: Sequence sourcing modes: dropship, then faster fulfillment, then private label
cards.summary: A staged sourcing recommendation: start dropshipping to test demand, upgrade fulfillment for speed, then move to private-label inventory as volume proves out.
cards.use_when: Choosing fulfillment/sourcing model for a new store built around a validated product, especially when launch capital is limited.
steps: Build the sourcing report for the product: supplier options by model, unit costs and margins, ETA and trust signals for each.
Launch on dropshipping first to take orders without inventory risk, using supplier product images for your store's product visuals.
Once orders are coming, move to a faster/domestic delivery option (source names ZenDrop/Spocket) to cut delivery time.
Once sales justify it, move into private labeling: order inventory, send your branding, have labels printed and the product prepared by the supplier.

If branded packaging is not yet affordable ($500–$1,000 stock example in the source), keep dropshipping and apply branding on the website and brand pages rather than the product — avoid showing branded product photos that mismatch the unbranded item the customer receives.
Do branding first anyway, as a target vision, even while shipping unbranded stock.
caveats: The source's model sequence (dropship → ZenDrop/Spocket → private label) is a recommendation, not a proven mandatory path.
A branded PDP with an unbranded shipped product creates a visible mismatch — the source explicitly warns against this; reconcile imagery with what actually ships.
cards.source_name: Claude & Shopify Built $750k_m Ai Powered Ecom Brand.docx

cards.title: Mirror a proven competitor page into your brand as a starting structure
cards.summary: Use a page-mirroring tool to replicate a high-performing competitor page's section structure, then rebrand it to your palette and logo.
cards.use_when: Building a homepage, collection page or PDP for a new brand when you have a proven competitor page to model and no page-builder available.
steps: Open the proven competitor page and run the mirror tool to crawl and capture the page's full section structure.
Name the mirrored product/page and declare whether the page is transactional (customers buy on it) — checkout needs differ for buy-on-page vs. browse-only pages.

Watch the section-by-section build to confirm the tool captured the right structure; compare against the original section by section (hero media, description, video grid, reviews, FAQs, testimonials, footer).
Upload your logo and color palette and generate theme variants, then pick one that matches your brand.
Export/save your work (download the HTML) and re-upload to resume later — the source warns to always save before exiting.
caveats: Tool names, plans and buttons in the source are vendor-specific and may change — verify the current interface.
Mirroring produces a neutral structural template; you still need to rebrand copy and imagery or the result reads as a clone.
cards.source_name: Claude & Shopify Built $750k_m Ai Powered Ecom Brand.docx

cards.title: Score and upgrade a mirrored page section-by-section
cards.summary: Audit a page against a scoring model, then add the missing sections it recommends rather than shipping the mirrored structure unchanged.
cards.use_when: Pre-launch page review: improving a PDP or homepage before spending on acquisition.
steps: Run the page score calculation so the tool evaluates existing sections and outputs a score plus specific missing-section recommendations.
Treat the score as a comparative heuristic, not an absolute benchmark: the source's mirrored page scored 55/100 and it added every recommended section.
Add recommended sections (the source suggested adding all of them), then manually reorder, hide, or add sections as needed for your offer.
Rewrite copy with AI as a separate pass rather than accepting mirrored copy.
Re-score after edits and compare before/after so the upgrade is measurable within the tool's model.
caveats: The 55/100 figure and 'add all sections' advice are the source's tool and opinion, not a published standard — judge whether each section fits your offer.
Adding sections can lengthen the page; do not add a block that has no real content behind it.
cards.source_name: Claude & Shopify Built $750k_m Ai Powered Ecom Brand.docx

cards.title: Score a Product Page Against a High-Converting Template and Fill the Gaps
cards.summary: Use an AI page scorer to grade a PDP out of 100, then auto-inject the missing sections a proven high-converting page would have.
cards.use_when: Auditing an existing product page or deciding which sections a new PDP needs before launch.
steps: Enter the product page into a scoring tool that compares it to a modeled library of high-performing pages and returns a 0-100 score with a list of missing sections.

Treat the score as a directional checklist, not a guaranteed conversion forecast: the source's model was trained on 'thousands of pages,' so the bands are a heuristic for layout completeness, not a formula.
Review the flagged gaps and prioritise the ones tied to buyer objections: risk reversal (guarantee), how it works, us-versus-them comparison, and founder/brand credibility.
Add or generate each missing block, keeping the tool's suggested ordering as a starting point since it places sections based on where high-performing pages typically put them.
Re-score after adding the sections to confirm the page is structurally complete before moving on to copy and imagery.

In the source example, a page moved from 55 to 92 after adding guarantee, how-it-works, us-versus-them, and founder-credibility sections — treat that jump as an illustration of the method, not a benchmark you should expect.
caveats: A high structural score does not guarantee sales; copy, offer, traffic and price still drive results.
Do not chase a perfect score at the expense of clarity or brand fit.
cards.source_name: Claude & Shopify Built $750k_m Ai Powered Ecom Brand.docx

cards.title: The Four Objection-Covering Sections Every PDP Should Consider
cards.summary: Guarantee, how-it-works, us-versus-them, and founder-credibility sections each answer a specific reason shoppers hesitate.
cards.use_when: Deciding what content blocks to add to a product page that feels thin or isn't converting.
steps: Add a risk-reversal / guarantee block near the top or after the price: state the guarantee and the exact number of days (e.g. '90-day promise'), because 'nobody knows if it's 100% risk-free' and that uncertainty stops purchases.
Add a how-it-works block as 3 numbered steps showing the mechanism by which the product achieves the customer's goal, so the buyer understands the path from use to result.
Add an 'us versus them' comparison that states why the buyer should choose this product over alternatives, so differentiation is explicit rather than assumed.
Add a founder / brand credibility block that answers 'who is this coming from and why should I trust you', which is especially valuable for newer or unbranded stores.
Keep the wording tied to the actual product claim; in the source example the founder note and guarantee coexist with testimonials and an FAQ section.
caveats: The exact mix should match the product's price point and buyer skepticism; not every section is mandatory for every SKU.
A guarantee must reflect a policy you will actually honour at scale.
cards.source_name: Claude & Shopify Built $750k_m Ai Powered Ecom Brand.docx

cards.title: Feed the Copywriter Raw Product Data for Better PDP Copy
cards.summary: AI PDP copy quality scales with the amount and specificity of product input you paste in, not with prompt cleverness.
cards.use_when: Generating product descriptions, benefit copy, FAQ text, or section headings for a new or refreshed product page.
steps: Open your supplier page or spec sheet in a separate tab and collect ingredients, materials, mechanism details, sizing, and genuine customer review language.
Paste that raw material into the copy tool along with the product name and brand name so the model has concrete nouns and claims to work from.
Generate the copy and treat it as a first draft: the source calls it 'a really good standard to start with' rather than a finished asset.
Edit aggressively for accuracy and voice — in the source build the operator manually corrected text colours and wording after generation.
Keep review quotes intact where they read like real customer language, since testimonial phrasing (e.g. shedding, scalp comfort, hair looking younger) carries credibility that invented copy lacks.
After copy is in place, replace placeholder or oversized images so layout and load stay clean.
caveats: Do not publish generated claims (health, efficacy, or timeframe) without verifying they match your product and comply with advertising rules.
More input improves output but never removes the need for human editing.
cards.source_name: Claude & Shopify Built $750k_m Ai Powered Ecom Brand.docx

cards.title: Publish a Custom PDP into Shopify as a Reusable Section
cards.summary: Ship a designed product page into Shopify by pasting the generated code as a Liquid section file, then adding it to a product template.
cards.use_when: Moving a page built in an external page designer into a live Shopify store.
steps: In Shopify admin go to Online Store, then edit the theme code, and create a new section file with a clear naming convention (source used a WLE/brand/product prefix plus the .liquid extension).
Paste the generated page code into that section file and save; the file is then stored permanently in the store and can be deleted later if needed.

Create the product in Products, upload images, set the selling price (source used the supplier's recommended price of 21.50), and confirm inventory is not zero — the source set available units to 10,000 so the page would not show 'sold out'.
Under the theme's product templates, create a new template for this product and hide the default theme sections you do not want.
Add a section and select your custom section from the list; the whole page loads in.
In the section settings, explicitly select the product — the source says this is 'the biggest thing' to do — which then populates images and price automatically.
Reorder, show or hide individual blocks within the section to match your preferred merchandising.
Verify the current Shopify theme editor steps in your admin, as menus and labels change.
caveats: Custom Liquid sections need maintenance when the theme updates.
Bundles and subscription options are configured separately in the product area, not inside the page section.
cards.source_name: Claude & Shopify Built $750k_m Ai Powered Ecom Brand.docx

cards.title: Update a Live Shopify Section Without Rebuilding the Page
cards.summary: Re-publish just the changed section code and paste it back into the existing Liquid file to push edits live.
cards.use_when: Fixing or improving one block (e.g. a broken accordion) on an already-published PDP.
steps: Keep the page designer open alongside Shopify so you can edit a single section rather than the whole page.
Select the block you want to change; in the source tool you can click a section to change layout, design, or rebuild it directly.

When a block misbehaves because it was generated as placeholder code (source example: an accordion that did not open), request a rebuild specifying the behaviour — e.g. 'clicking the plus button should open the accordion'.
Re-publish to Shopify and download or copy the regenerated code.
Return to the theme code editor, open the existing section file, paste the new code over it, and save — do not create a second section file, or you will end up with duplicates.
Refresh the live site to confirm the change appears, then edit the text/descriptions inside the block as needed.
Verify current publish/export labels in the page tool, since these interfaces change.
caveats: Placeholder-generated interactive elements (accordions, sliders) often need an explicit rebuild instruction to function.
Overwriting the wrong file or creating duplicates can break the page layout.
cards.source_name: Claude & Shopify Built $750k_m Ai Powered Ecom Brand.docx

cards.title: Generate On-Brand Product and Lifestyle Images with AI Assistants
cards.summary: Use specialised AI image workflows — brand-styled mimicry, prompt generation, and customer-experience scenes — to build a full PDP asset set.
cards.use_when: Producing hero images, ingredient/lifestyle shots, and customer-use imagery for a product page or ad creative.
steps: Use a branding/design assistant to develop image prompts that stay inside your brand's visual system before generating anything.
Use an image-mirroring workflow that takes a competitor's visual and recreates it in your own brand style — useful for referencing a proven composition without copying assets.
Use a customer-experience workflow to generate images of people using your product, filling the testimonial and lifestyle blocks on the PDP.
Match asset dimensions to the section before upload: the source build looked broken because images were uploaded at very large sizes, which was fixed by using normally sized images.
Sort product-page images and choose the hero/first image deliberately, since it sets expectations and drives click-through from collection pages.
For video, use equivalent AI workflows to produce testimonial and product-use clips if video blocks are on the page.
caveats: Generated images must be checked for accuracy against the real product — never show a product or result the customer won't receive.
Oversized uploads hurt layout and load time regardless of generator quality.
cards.source_name: Claude & Shopify Built $750k_m Ai Powered Ecom Brand.docx

cards.title: Product Page Template Standardisation as an Output, Not the Goal
cards.summary: The section-based approach trades some design uniqueness for speed and repeatability across many products.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to build each PDP from scratch or reuse a section library for a multi-SKU store or a white-label brand launch.
steps: Build the first PDP as modular sections (guarantee, how-it-works, comparison, founder, testimonials, FAQ) so subsequent products can reuse the same structure.
Store the page as a section file so it can be added to any product template in the store.
Swap the logo, copy, imagery and product selection to relabel the same structure for a different brand or product — the source describes this as the white-label launch path from zero to live quickly.
Customise per product only where the buyer's objections differ; keep the objection-covering blocks consistent.
Compare against a chosen reference brand's page to sanity-check that your page covers everything theirs does and, per the source's intent, adds sections theirs is missing.
caveats: Reusing one structure across many products can make a store feel generic if copy and imagery aren't genuinely differentiated.
The source's claim that the rebuilt page often looks better than the original is the presenter's opinion from a single build, not a measured result.
cards.source_name: Claude & Shopify Built $750k_m Ai Powered Ecom Brand.docx

cards.title: Use a Competitor PDP as the Reference Target for a New Build
cards.summary: Anchor your page spec to the sections, flow and proof a proven competitor page already uses, then fill the gaps they miss.
cards.use_when: Planning a PDP for a new product where you lack your own conversion data.
steps: Pick a competitor or reference brand that is already selling a comparable product at volume and open its PDP for study.
Inventory every block on their page: hero, ingredients, how-it-works, testimonials with specifics, comparison, FAQ, guarantee, founder note.
Map your design so that everything they have is covered as a baseline.
Then add the sections the source's audit flags as commonly missing — risk reversal, mechanism explanation, us-versus-them, founder credibility — so you exceed the reference rather than match it.

Adapt their subscription/purchase structure decisions: the source's reference brand only offered one-time purchase and subscribe-and-save, so no extra bundle logic was built; replicate only what fits your economics.
Record their pricing and selling units, and set your own price against your costs rather than copying theirs.
caveats: Studying structure is not the same as copying copy or assets — produce your own.
A competitor's page may be optimised for a different traffic source and buyer awareness level.
cards.source_name: Claude & Shopify Built $750k_m Ai Powered Ecom Brand.docx

cards.title: Configure Purchase Options and Inventory So the Page Can Actually Sell
cards.summary: Subscription, bundle and inventory settings on the product decide what the PDP offers and whether it renders as purchasable.
cards.use_when: Finalising a new product listing before launching traffic to the PDP.
steps: Set the selling price from your cost structure and a reference point; the source used the supplier's recommended single-unit price rather than inventing one.

Decide the purchase structure explicitly: if you want buy-one-get-one or multi-unit bundles, add them as bundle options on the product; if you are matching a reference brand that only runs one-time and subscribe-and-save, you may not need bundle logic at all.
Check inventory quantity is non-zero, otherwise the theme shows 'sold out' and blocks purchase — the source set a high available count to guarantee purchasability.
Verify that the custom section displays the right product by selecting it in the section settings, which pulls images, price and variants automatically.
Re-check the live page in an incognito window with no admin branding so you see exactly what a shopper sees before spending on traffic.
caveats: Inventory counts, currency and variant setup can override what the section displays; test an actual add-to-cart.
Bundles and subscriptions need separate app or platform configuration beyond the page section.
cards.source_name: Claude & Shopify Built $750k_m Ai Powered Ecom Brand.docx

cards.title: Inspect the Guest-View Page Before Launching Traffic
cards.summary: Load the finished PDP in an incognito window to see the unbranded, logged-out experience your visitors will get.
cards.use_when: Final QA pass on a PDP, landing page or store before running ads or sending traffic.
steps: Open the product URL in a private/incognito browser window so Shopify or admin toolbars don't appear.
Walk the page top to bottom and confirm every section renders: hero, ingredients, mechanism, testimonial grid, FAQ accordion, guarantee, founder note, footer.
Confirm interactive elements actually work — click every accordion, tab and slider; the source found accordions that did not open because the code was a placeholder.
Check images are correctly sized and not oversized, and that all links and menus connect to a real destination.
Confirm the product is purchasable: price shows, no 'sold out' state, variants selectable.
Compare against the reference competitor page one final time and fix anything missing before launch.
caveats: Incognito hides logged-in state and admin tools but won't simulate every device or slow connection.
Do a separate mobile check — the source demo was desktop-focused.
cards.source_name: Claude & Shopify Built $750k_m Ai Powered Ecom Brand.docx

cards.title: Set Up a Local AI Coding Environment for Shopify Theme Edits
cards.summary: Prepare an AI coding workspace for Shopify theme work, checking current tool access and editing an unpublished theme copy.
cards.use_when: You want to make custom theme or product-page edits (new blocks, modified cart, custom templates) without hiring a developer or adding apps.
steps: Verify current Claude Code access, authentication and billing options before buying a plan. The tutorial used a paid Claude plan; its plan-access claim is point-in-time.
Download and install Visual Studio Code (free).
In VS Code, use File > Open Folder to create and open an empty directory named something like 'Shopify editor'; this folder becomes the environment where theme files and connections live.
Open the Extensions panel, search 'Claude', and install the extension published by Anthropic (ignore other similarly named extensions).
Click the Claude button in the top-right to open the Claude chat panel inside VS Code; the left sidebar shows your files, the chat panel is the main work area.
Verify the current Claude/VS Code extension interface and menu locations at install time, since extension UI and plan names change.
caveats: Install only the Anthropic-published extension among the many search results.
This sets up the tooling; it does not guarantee conversion improvements on its own.
Use an unpublished theme copy and preview changes before making them live.
cards.source_name: Claude Just Changed Shopify Forever.docx

cards.title: Connect Shopify CLI and Authenticate Your Store
cards.summary: Have Claude install the Shopify CLI (NPM version) and authenticate your store so it can list and pull themes.
cards.use_when: Your local Claude/VS Code environment is set up but not yet connected to your Shopify store, so you need it to see and pull themes.
steps: Prompt Claude to install the Shopify CLI (command line interface) — this is the tool that lets Claude talk to your store.
When asked how to install, choose the NPM version. The presenter reports the Homebrew version failed for them; treat this as a situational preference, not a universal rule.
Approve the installation prompts as they appear, checking each one before allowing.
Prompt Claude to 'connect to my Shopify store and give me a list of the themes' — this triggers authentication.
Provide the store URL when asked, then copy the authentication command Claude gives you (e.g. 'shopify auth login') into a new VS Code terminal and run it.
Choose the correct account in the terminal prompt; a browser authentication screen may appear on some setups.
Once authenticated, confirm Claude can list your themes (the presenter's store showed 13).
Verify current CLI install options and login command in the Shopify CLI docs, since these change.
caveats: Claude cannot authenticate on your behalf for security reasons; you complete login manually in the terminal.
Ask for the theme list first to confirm the connection before editing anything.
cards.source_name: Claude Just Changed Shopify Forever.docx

cards.title: Duplicate the Live Theme Before Any AI Editing
cards.summary: Create a copy of the live theme and confine all edits to that copy to avoid breaking the storefront.
cards.use_when: You are about to make any AI-driven theme change and need a safe staging environment.
steps: After connecting, prompt Claude to 'duplicate the live theme' — the presenter's result was called 'copy of horizon'.
Immediately instruct Claude to 'continue to work just on that theme' so every subsequent edit targets the copy.
Confirm the duplicated theme appears under Online Store > Themes in Shopify (the copy is created on the store as well as pulled locally).
Verify all theme files are now pulled into your local folder so edits happen against the copy's code.
Treat the live theme as untouchable until the edited copy is validated and published.
caveats: Editing a live theme risks breaking the entire storefront if something goes wrong.
Do not skip the 'work only on that theme' instruction — otherwise Claude may target the wrong theme.
cards.source_name: Claude Just Changed Shopify Forever.docx

cards.title: Inject an Editable Objection-Busting Trust Block Under Add to Cart
cards.summary: Prompt Claude to add a reusable theme-editor block of trust icons and text directly below the buy buttons.
cards.use_when: Your product page lacks shipping, guarantee and returns reassurance near the add-to-cart button and you want it editable without an app.
steps: Identify the template to edit (e.g. the default product template) in the theme editor.

Prompt Claude with specifics, e.g.: 'In the product page default template, underneath the add-to-cart button, add three icons and text I can edit in the theme editor — one for shipping, one for guarantees, one for returns.'
Optionally approve all edits for the session to avoid confirming each change individually.
Wait for Claude to report what it built (the example produced delivery truck, shield and refresh-arrow icons).
In the theme editor, refresh the template and confirm a new block (named something like 'Product Trust Buttons') appears, is movable/reorderable, and its icons and text are editable.
Replicate the pattern for other repeated reassurance needs (payment icons, sizing notes).
caveats: This is more capable than Shopify's Sidekick, which the presenter says can essentially only generate sections — Claude Code can add editable blocks and templates.
Build time in the example was roughly one to two minutes; longer prompts or many instructions can fail (see the one-change-at-a-time caveat).
cards.source_name: Claude Just Changed Shopify Forever.docx

cards.title: Generate a Full High-Converting Product Template from a Framework Document
cards.summary: Upload a product-page framework to Claude and have it code an entire reusable template with standard conversion sections.
cards.use_when: You want a structured, reusable PDP template beyond what your default theme ships with, and you already have a page anatomy/framework to follow.
steps: Have your product-page framework document ready (the presenter uses a 'Perfect Product Page' framework covering hero, trust badges, benefits grid, outcome, image+text, feature highlight and social proof).
Prompt Claude: 'Create a brand new product template in this theme using the attached framework,' and upload the document.
Let Claude analyze the framework and generate the template; the example took a couple of minutes.
In Shopify, refresh and confirm a new template (labeled e.g. 'PPP') exists on the duplicate theme.
Treat the generated template as a baseline outline to refine: toggle sections on/off, resize icons, remove duplicated elements (the presenter hid a redundant benefits grid).
Use the theme editor's section settings (badge position, swatch style, etc.) to configure the template per product.
Assign the template to products where it fits, or duplicate it for testing.
caveats: The generated layout is a starting outline, not a finished page — expect to edit and remove redundant sections.
Don't assume the framework itself will translate into conversion gains without testing.
cards.source_name: Claude Just Changed Shopify Forever.docx

cards.title: Clone a Competitor Design Element via Screenshot
cards.summary: Paste a screenshot of a competitor feature into Claude and have it build a matching, customizable component on your store.
cards.use_when: You spot a specific high-performing UI element (e.g. a 'Top Seller' badge on a swatch) on a competitor's store and want an equivalent on your PDP.
steps: Find the element on the competitor's site (the example is True Classic's 'Top Seller' heart badge on a variant swatch).
Screenshot or copy that section.

Attach the image to Claude with a prompt like: 'Using the attached reference image, add a similar badge... to my swatches on my product page. I need to add an icon, change the text and color, but the styling must look exactly the same as the reference image.'
Let Claude build the component; it will return setup instructions (the example added a 'Swatch label' block with an emoji/icon and color options).
Apply it in the theme editor: click Add block > Swatch label, and set the option/option value to match the variant name exactly.
Customize the icon, text and color to fit your brand.
caveats: Match the swatch label to the exact option value, or the badge won't bind to the variant.
Copy the styling pattern, not the competitor's trademark or content — avoid using their brand assets.
This copies a design element, not proven conversion results; test it on your own store.
cards.source_name: Claude Just Changed Shopify Forever.docx

cards.title: Make Global Theme Edits (Cart Icon and Notification Bubble)
cards.summary: Prompt Claude to change sitewide theme utilities like the cart icon style, add a selection of preset icons, and customize the cart count bubble.
cards.use_when: You want storewide cosmetic/UX changes (cart icon, cart count color, add-to-cart feedback) that aren't exposed as template-level settings.
steps: Prompt with a clear scope, e.g.: 'Change the shopping cart icon and let me pick from pre-selected icons like cart, bag, trolley. Add a small animation when something is added to cart, and let me change the color of the number notification on the cart.'
Wait for Claude to report where the new controls live (the example placed them under Header > Utilities).
In the theme editor, go to the reported location and select the new icon style and set the cart count background and number colors.
Test add-to-cart feedback on the storefront.
caveats: The presenter's bundle of instructions produced the icons and colors but failed to implement the requested add-to-cart animation — too many instructions at once is the suggested cause.
If a requested feature doesn't appear, break it into a single focused follow-up prompt rather than assuming it worked.
cards.source_name: Claude Just Changed Shopify Forever.docx

cards.title: Give Claude One Change at a Time, Not a Bundle
cards.summary: Split AI theme requests into single focused prompts, because bundling several changes risks partial or failed implementation.
cards.use_when: You are planning a series of theme or PDP edits and deciding how to sequence prompts.
steps: Decide the single change you want (e.g. change the cart icon only).
Write a prompt scoped to that one change.
Verify the result in the theme editor before moving on.
If a bundled prompt (like the cart icon + animation + count color request) partially fails, re-run the missing piece as its own prompt.
Track which changes succeeded so you can re-issue the failed ones.
caveats: This is the presenter's observed lesson from a request that partially failed, not a hard rule — a clearly related bundle can still work but is riskier.
cards.source_name: Claude Just Changed Shopify Forever.docx

cards.title: Manage Claude Usage Limits During Heavy Theme Coding
cards.summary: Plan for hitting Claude's usage limit and cooldown when running many theme edits.
cards.use_when: You are doing multi-hour AI theme work and want to avoid running out mid-task.
steps: Watch for the usage-limit warning (the example reported '90% of your limit used').
When you hit the limit, pause theme coding — the source states it resets in about an hour.
Use the cooldown to plan the next changes or review already-generated output.
Batch your most important edits earlier in a session before the limit approaches.
caveats: The reset window (about an hour) and limit percentage are the source's observation and may change with Claude's plans — verify current limits.
cards.source_name: Claude Just Changed Shopify Forever.docx

cards.title: Publish a Claude-Edited Theme and Maintain an Up-to-Date Working Copy
cards.summary: Publish your edited duplicate safely, then re-duplicate the live theme for the next round of edits.
cards.use_when: Your AI-edited theme or template is validated and you are ready to push it live.
steps: In Shopify, confirm the duplicate theme looks correct before publishing.
Click Publish on the edited theme; the previously live theme moves to unpublished.
Treat theme file edits as saved automatically in the theme files — only in-editor content/setting changes need saving.
For the next round of work, duplicate the now-live theme so your working copy is the most current, then edit and republish that.
caveats: Publishing is the riskiest step — the source calls it the scariest part of the process.
Skipping the re-duplicate step means you could edit a stale copy and overwrite newer live changes.
cards.source_name: Claude Just Changed Shopify Forever.docx

cards.title: Clean a Fresh WordPress/WooCommerce Install
cards.summary: Remove identified demo content and unnecessary bundled plugins from a fresh store, then confirm its identity and timezone.
cards.use_when: Setting up a brand-new WooCommerce store on Hostinger and needing a clean baseline before adding products, pages or shipping rules.
steps: Review the bundled plugins individually and remove only confirmed unused demo or promotional plugins. Keep WooCommerce and required payment, security, backup and hosting integrations; test the storefront after changes.
Go to Pages and move every Hello-World style placeholder page to Trash (select all, Bulk Actions > Move to Trash). Empty the trash so dead pages don't get indexed later.

Go to Settings > General and change the Site Title from 'My WordPress Website' to a phrase matching your search intent and market. The source's example is 'Prima Sofas for USA and Canada' rather than a generic default - this title appears in browser tabs and search results.
Set the Timezone in Settings > General to your operating region so order timestamps and scheduled tasks align with your customers and bookkeeping.
Verify the WordPress address and site URL still point to the domain you configured during the Hostinger onboarding, then load the storefront once to confirm it renders.
caveats: Menu labels and plugin bundles vary by host and WordPress version - verify the current admin interface before following click paths.
The 'Prima Sofas' title is an illustrative naming pattern, not a keyword recommendation for your niche.
This cleanup is for a fresh installation. On an existing store, use a backup and staging site and preserve cart, checkout, account, product and order data.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Pick the Right WooCommerce Product Type for Each Item
cards.summary: Map each catalog item to the correct WooCommerce product type - simple, variable, service, downloadable or affiliate - so inventory, pricing and checkout behave correctly.
cards.use_when: Adding products to a new WooCommerce store and choosing which product type template fits each item.
steps: For an item with one option that ships physically (one SKU, one price), use the Simple product type and set price, stock and shipping weight.

For an item sold in multiple options (size, color, material), use the Variable product type. Install a variation swatches plugin so buyers can pick attributes visually, then generate variations and assign each one its own price and inventory count.
For a booking, repair, installation or consulting offer with no physical shipment, create a Simple product and mark it Virtual so no shipping is charged.
For digital goods (ebooks, templates, files), create a Simple product, mark it Virtual and Downloadable, then attach the file URL so buyers receive the download after purchase.
For products you promote but fulfil elsewhere, use the External/Affiliate product type and supply the destination link and button text.
Audit the catalog afterward: a wrongly typed product (e.g. physical item marked downloadable) breaks shipping and tax calculations.
caveats: Variable products require attributes and generated variations; if you never generate variations the product shows no selectable options.
External/affiliate products leave your checkout entirely, so your payment, tax and shipping rules do not apply to them.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Connect Stripe and PayPal with Test Mode First
cards.summary: Install the official Stripe and PayPal plugins, connect via API credentials, run sandbox transactions, and choose where express checkout buttons appear on the store.
cards.use_when: Enabling payment collection on a new WooCommerce store and deciding where Apple Pay / Google Pay buttons show.
steps: Install the official WooCommerce Stripe and PayPal plugins from the plugin directory so payments sync cleanly with WooCommerce orders.
In each plugin's settings, connect your account through the API keys (or the plugin's connect flow for Stripe). Keep Test Mode / sandbox enabled for your first transactions.

Place a live test order using the provider's test card while in sandbox mode, then confirm the order appears in WooCommerce with the correct status and the payment records correctly on the provider dashboard.

Decide express checkout placement: enable Apple Pay / Google Pay buttons either on product pages (faster impulse purchase) or restrict them to the checkout page (less premature checkout, cleaner product page). The plugin toggles control this.
Once sandbox orders succeed, switch to live mode, re-enter live API credentials and place a small real order to verify.
caveats: API key locations and toggle names change across plugin versions and provider dashboards - verify the current interface.
Express buttons appearing on product pages can create a separate checkout path that bypasses some cart logic; test both placements before committing.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Set Up Flexible Table-Rate Shipping by Order Value
cards.summary: Use a table-rate shipping plugin to charge tiered flat rates based on cart price brackets and to unlock free shipping above a threshold, encouraging larger baskets.
cards.use_when: Configuring shipping charges and free-shipping thresholds in a new WooCommerce store, especially when rate should depend on order value rather than just weight.
steps: Install the 'Table Rate Flexible Shipping' plugin (or an equivalent table-rate plugin) and add a shipping zone covering the regions you sell to.
Create a flat-rate method inside the zone and add conditional rules. The source's example: charge a flat $4.99 when the cart total is below $200, and set free shipping above $200.
Use bracket-based conditions for finer tiers. The source's example brackets: $0-$90 costs $6.99; $20-$49 costs $8.99 - demonstrating that the plugin charges shipping based on cart price brackets.
Stack conditions with care: if brackets overlap or leave gaps, some carts will have no available method and checkout will fail. Order your rules so each cart falls into exactly one bracket.
Add weight-based conditions where physical shipping cost is driven by mass, and test multiple example carts near each bracket boundary to confirm the correct rate appears.
Publish the free-shipping threshold on the site (announcement bar or cart) so customers know how much more to spend to earn free shipping.
caveats: The dollar figures here are the source's examples, not benchmarks - set brackets from your own margin and carrier costs.
Rule priority and overlap behaviour is plugin-specific; verify how your installed version resolves conflicting conditions.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Configure Standard, Reduced and Zero Tax Rates
cards.summary: Assign products the correct tax class and set the store's price display so tax is shown consistently with your customer type.
cards.use_when: Setting up tax classes and price display in WooCommerce, particularly when you sell a mix of physical goods, reduced-rate items and digital products.
steps: Decide the tax class for each product: Standard for most physical goods, Reduced for items taxed at a lower statutory rate (the source's example is books), and Zero for digital products where no tax applies.
Assign the correct tax class on each product or variation rather than relying on a blanket default, since digital goods and books often differ from the rest of the catalog.
Turn on tax calculations in WooCommerce settings so prices and cart totals reflect the class and rate applied.

Consider the B2B/B2C hybrid display option: the source describes displaying prices exclusive of tax in the shop but inclusive of tax at checkout, which lets buyers see net prices while still showing the final gross amount before paying.
After configuring classes and display, place test orders for one product of each class and confirm the tax shown matches expectations.
caveats: Tax law and rates vary by jurisdiction and change over time - confirm rates with a current authority or calculation service; this source only shows the mechanism, not current rates.
The exclusive-in-shop / inclusive-at-checkout display is a specific setting choice, not a universal best practice; it can confuse some consumer audiences.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Manually Configure US State Tax Rates in WooCommerce
cards.summary: Enter per-state standard tax rates manually in WooCommerce, using state codes and precise percentages sourced from a calculation service.
cards.use_when: Setting up tax collection in WooCommerce for US states where you need state-specific rates without an automated tax service.
steps: Determine the exact combined percentage you should charge for the target state using a tax calculation service (the source uses TaxJar).
In WooCommerce, go to Tax > Standard Rates.
Click Insert Row to add a rate. Set the Country Code to US, then the State Code (e.g. CA for California or NV for Nevada).
Enter the exact percentage using four decimals (the source's example is 7.2500) rather than rounding, so the amount matches the service's figure.
