Repeat the insert for each state you are required to collect in. Add a row per state rather than trying to approximate with a single rate.
Place a test order to a destination in each configured state and verify the tax line matches the rate you entered.
caveats: Rates change; a manually entered rate will silently become wrong - schedule a periodic review or move to an automated service.
Nexus rules determine which states you should collect in, and this source does not cover nexus analysis - get tax advice for your specific obligations.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Create Legal Pages and Place Them in a Footer Menu
cards.summary: Generate Privacy Policy and Terms & Conditions copy, publish them as WordPress pages, build a dedicated Legal menu and attach it to the footer.
cards.use_when: Publishing a new ecommerce store and needing Privacy Policy and Terms & Conditions pages linked from every page for trust and compliance.
steps: Draft the Privacy Policy and Terms & Conditions content (the source suggests generating a first draft with ChatGPT). Use it as a starting point to speed up the first version rather than as final legal advice.
Create two WordPress pages and paste the respective content into each, with clear titles such as 'Privacy Policy' and 'Terms & Conditions'.
Go to Appearance > Menus and create a dedicated menu - the source names it 'Legal' - containing only those legal page links, separate from your primary navigation.
Open the WordPress customizer and assign the Legal menu to the footer menu location so it is reachable from every page without cluttering the main header navigation.
Load the storefront and confirm the footer links resolve to the correct pages on both desktop and mobile widths.
caveats: AI-generated legal text is a draft; review it against the regulations that apply to your business and jurisdiction before publishing - this source only describes the mechanics.
Customizer menu locations differ by theme (the source uses Blocksy), so verify where footer menus are assigned in your theme.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Set Up Free Hosting, Domain and WordPress for a WooCommerce Store
cards.summary: End-to-end baseline setup: buy shared hosting, claim the free domain, install WordPress and pick the server region closest to your buying audience.
cards.use_when: Launching a brand-new store from scratch and you need hosting, a domain and WordPress installed before any product work can start.
steps: Buy a hosting plan that includes a free domain for the first year and free domain privacy; the source's example tier allowed roughly 50 sites on NVMe storage with daily backups at a promotional rate when paid for a long term (the presenter notes longer terms lower the monthly price, and later upgrades are always possible).
Register with an email and password, complete billing, and pay with whatever local method is offered; corporate/company billing fields may remove VAT charges depending on your country.
In the hosting onboarding choose: website for yourself or your business → create a new website → WordPress → set your admin email and password → create a blank website (skip AI/theme preview).
Claim the free domain at the checkout step (choose .com or a local extension), complete registrant details, and confirm via the verification email.
When asked for the target audience location, choose the server region closest to your focused buyers; the source still notes CDN keeps load times fast globally.

Expect the real domain to activate in ~10 minutes (rarely up to 24 hours); meanwhile the site loads on a temporary domain. Once active, log into the WordPress dashboard (backend) and view the front end.
caveats: Exact plan names, prices, promo codes and storage figures change; verify the current hosting interface before buying.
Domain privacy and free-domain-for-a-year offers are provider-specific, not universal.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Clean a Fresh WordPress Install Before Building the Store
cards.summary: Remove default plugins, pages, posts and themes so the dashboard stays uncluttered and only the tools you actually need remain.
cards.use_when: Right after a fresh WordPress install, before installing WooCommerce, themes or page builders.
steps: Dismiss the dashboard welcome notice and open Screen Options to switch off the widget panels you don't use, so the dashboard is scannable.
Go to Plugins, select all, Bulk Actions → Deactivate, apply, then select all again → Delete, apply; this removes preinstalled tools such as caching plugins you may not need.
Go to Pages, select all, Move to Trash, then empty the trash; do the same for the default post under Posts.
Go to Appearance → Themes, open Theme Details on every inactive theme and Delete it, leaving exactly one theme.

Edit your profile: set first name, last name and nickname, choose the display name shown publicly on posts, pick an admin color scheme, and set the admin color scheme/display name — this is what shows as 'Howdy [name]' and authors blog posts.
Optionally register the profile email at Gravatar (free) so an avatar appears next to your author name site-wide.
Under Settings → General set site language, time zone, date format, time format and first day of week, then save.
caveats: Deleting default plugins can remove a built-in caching layer; add a caching plugin later if you need one.
Profile display name becomes public author byline — choose it deliberately.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Write a Site Title That Matches What Buyers Search
cards.summary: Name the store around the products and markets people actually search for, not around a generic welcome phrase.
cards.use_when: Setting the WordPress site title and tagline for a new store, or rewriting them when organic/paid traffic lands on generic pages.
steps: Never use a generic site title like 'my website' or a welcome phrase; customers search for the thing they want to buy, not for your store's existence.

Check what competitors in your niche put in their titles and descriptions (e.g. searching 'buy PS5 online' surfaces titles like 'PlayStation 5, PS5, buy online'), then describe your store the same concrete way.
Optionally prompt an AI assistant with a plain description ('my website is about selling furniture, mostly sofas, in the USA and Canada — write me a great site title') and adapt the output.
Order the words so the searchable product/category terms come first and your brand name last.
Use the tagline to state a concrete service promise (the source's example: 'we deliver in the USA and Canada'), keeping it consistent with the title.
caveats: The source treats title wording as a discoverability aid, not a ranking guarantee; rankings depend on far more than the title.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Install a Free Store Theme and Import a Starter Site
cards.summary: Use a free multipurpose theme with importable ecommerce starter sites to get product pages, categories and pages styled in minutes.
cards.use_when: Choosing the visual foundation of a new WooCommerce store when you want a working layout fast instead of designing pages from scratch.
steps: Install a free theme from Appearance → Themes → Add New by name (the source uses Blocksy), then activate it and install its companion plugin when prompted.
Delete the previously active default theme afterwards to keep the theme list to one.
Open the theme's starter-sites screen, filter to Free plans, then filter category to e-commerce.
Preview each candidate template (open several, review them, then close the ones you reject) and pick one whose product presentation you actually like.

Import it: choose the editor variant offered (the source supports Gutenberg and Elementor but notes some front-end effects such as hover zoom are missing in the Elementor variant) and select Gutenberg if you want the full set.
If WooCommerce is not yet installed it will be installed by the import; otherwise it is greyed out. Finish the import and view the site.
Inspect a demo product page: breadcrumb, title, price, short description, add-to-cart, additional information tab, and related products should already be in place.
caveats: Imported demo content includes placeholder products, images and copy — you must replace all of it before launch.
Elementor vs Gutenberg variants differ in available features; decide before importing.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Install WooCommerce Manually and Complete the Setup Wizard
cards.summary: Add WooCommerce from the plugin repository and answer the onboarding questions so currency, industry and store address are correct.
cards.use_when: Building the store without importing a starter site, or when you need to re-run the WooCommerce setup wizard after import.
steps: Go to Plugins → Add New, search WooCommerce, install and activate; the source notes it has millions of active installs, recent updates and is maintained by the WordPress makers.
Check the 'set up my store' box after activation to enter the onboarding wizard.
Choose 'I'm just starting my business' (or the appropriate alternative) and continue.
Select your industry and the store's physical location; the country selection sets the store currency (choosing United States gives dollars).
Enter your email address, continue, and skip steps you can configure later.
Afterwards, verify the front end now shows Cart, Checkout, My Account and Shop pages — note WooCommerce places the store in 'coming soon' mode by default.
Clean the dashboard of the leftover WooCommerce setup panel via Screen Options once done.
caveats: Changing store country later affects currency, tax and shipping defaults; set it correctly up front.
The wizard wording and steps change between WooCommerce versions — verify the current wizard.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Apply Global Brand Colors and a Logo Through the Customizer
cards.summary: Change the palette once in global color settings and have it propagate across the whole storefront, instead of editing each page.
cards.use_when: Rebranding an imported store template, adjusting colors for a client, or setting a logo/favicon before content launch.
steps: Open Appearance → Customize and locate the theme's global color settings; the source's theme exposes six palette slots used consistently across the site.
Set slot 1 (the primary/accent color used in buttons and highlights) to your brand color and watch every instance update live — this replaces manual per-element edits.
Fill the remaining slots with derived tints/shades of the same family (paste a color, drag the slider for a lighter or darker tint) so hover states and backgrounds stay coherent.

For the logo: upload an SVG where possible for sharpness and small file size (the source's example logo was about 4 KB), then set logo height (around 35 px in the example) and add the alt text and description.
Set the site icon (favicon) under Site Identity: a square image with transparent background, uploaded and cropped as needed — this shows in browser tabs and helps visitors recognise the site.

Publish and check the front end; if a section background looks off (e.g. mismatched grey vs the new accent), open the page in the block editor, select the block, and set the background to the global color or to a custom color.
caveats: Global palette slots and their names are theme-specific; a different theme may not expose the same six colors.
The source recommends SVG logos but some themes/headers may not accept SVG — test before committing.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Shape the Header and Main Menu for Store Navigation
cards.summary: Trim and reorder the main menu, remove redundant entries, and style it to keep the sticky header usable on any page.
cards.use_when: Configuring site navigation right after importing a theme, especially before adding many product categories.
steps: Open Appearance → Customize → Menus → Main Menu and delete entries that don't belong, e.g. a 'Home' item, because the logo already links home (this mirrors how large retailer sites behave).
Drag items to reorder; drag an item slightly to the right to nest it as a sub-item under its parent (so hovering 'Products' reveals children).
Choose the menu style variant that fits (the source preferred a simple hover colour-change style over more elaborate animated styles).
Reduce excessive spacing between menu items, roughly 30 px in the source's example, to keep the header compact.
Set the menu link font colour to a darker palette slot and the hover colour to your accent slot; do the same for the header search icon and other header icons.

In header settings, choose the icon set, optionally give the header a background colour, reduce header height, and enable 'sticky' if you want the header to remain visible while scrolling (transparency is also available).
Set the header defined as the global header so the same header appears on every page; publish and verify.
caveats: Sticky headers consume vertical space on mobile; test on a phone before keeping it.
Menu style names (Type 1–4) are theme-specific.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Standardise Layout Widths for Store and Product Pages
cards.summary: Set a container width and a narrow single-product layout so product pages read comfortably on desktop.
cards.use_when: Imported template pages feel too wide or cramped and you want a consistent grid across shop, category and product pages.
steps: In the customizer, open the global Layout section and set the site container width to about 1120 px — the source calls this a reliable default for most sites.
Then open the WooCommerce → Single Product section in the customizer and switch the single product layout to the narrower width.
Close the customizer and inspect a live product page: images, add-to-cart and description should no longer stretch edge to edge.
Re-check the shop archive and category pages to confirm the grid still looks balanced at the new container width.
caveats: 1120 px is a source-specific heuristic, not a benchmark; very image-heavy or editorial stores may need a wider container.
Option names vary by theme.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Create a Simple Product with Price, Sale Price, Stock and Categories
cards.summary: Configure a single-option product fully: description, short description, pricing, SKU, inventory, back-order policy, purchase note, images, categories and tags.
cards.use_when: Adding a physical product that has no size/colour variants — e.g. a couch, glasses, a cap — and you need the PDP to be complete before launch.
steps: Create the product with just a name and publish to see the bare PDP, then go back and fill it in progressively.
Add a long description (appears below the fold) and a short description (appears next to the price) — they serve different positions on the product page.
Under Product data keep type 'Simple'; leave Virtual and Downloadable unchecked for physical goods.

Set the regular price and, if running a promotion, a sale price; enter sale dates so the regular price returns automatically after the end date (the source sets a sale ending the last day of the month).

Under Inventory set a SKU (useful to search stock across variants), enable stock management, enter quantity, and choose the back-order policy: disallow (safest), allow but notify customers when restocked, or allow silently — the source warns silent back-orders only work if you can restock fast.
Set a low-stock threshold (e.g. notify at two remaining) and optionally enable 'sold individually' to cap one unit per order.
Under Advanced set a purchase note shown after purchase (e.g. instructions or a scheduling link for services).
Upload a featured product image (this is the thumbnail on archives) and additional gallery images; copy the title into alt text and description for each.
Assign a category (parent or sub-category, e.g. Furniture → Sofas) and tags (material, colour, style) so the breadcrumb and related filters work.
caveats: Sale prices without an end date stay discounted until you remove them — set an end date if the promotion is time-limited.
Allowing back-orders without reliable restocking creates unhappy customers.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Build Variable Products with Attributes, Swatches and Generated Variations
cards.summary: Define size/colour attributes once, generate every combination as a variation, then bulk-edit price and stock and set per-variation images.
cards.use_when: Listing apparel or any product with multiple sizes/colours and you want customers to select options visually on the product page.
steps: Install a variation-swatches plugin (the source uses the one from Brainstorm Force) from Plugins → Add New and activate it.

Create global attributes under WooCommerce → Attributes: define one attribute per option type (e.g. Size with type 'Label', Color with type 'Color'), each with a shape (e.g. circle) and size (e.g. 36 px).

Populate each attribute's terms: for Size add XS, S, M, L, XL, 2XL, 3XL and reorder them because new terms may be added in reverse; for Color add each colour name and pick its swatch colour (you can paste an exact hex).

Create a new product, set Product data type to 'Variable', and under Attributes add each global attribute and tick only the values this product actually has (e.g. XS, M, L, XL and black, white, navy — not all terms).
Save attributes, then click 'Generate variations': the number of variations equals the product of the selected values (4 sizes × 3 colours = 12).

Use bulk actions on the variations list to toggle manage stock across all, then set a base regular price (e.g. 19.99) and adjust outliers individually (e.g. XL at 24.99) — the PDP then shows a price range.
Override stock per variation where demand differs (XS black at 3 units, L black at 10).
Assign a featured image and gallery, then open each variation and assign its own image so switching colour changes the displayed photo; the source notes this is done once and then runs automatically.
Optionally set default form values (e.g. large + navy) and, via the swatches plugin's global styling, thicken swatch borders and centre-align swatches.
caveats: With many attribute combinations the variation list becomes long and manual per-variation images are time-consuming — budget for it.
The default-selected variation should be one you actually stock and want to feature.
Swatch styling options and centring may require extra CSS depending on theme; the source uses additional CSS for centring.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Create a Downloadable Digital Product with Unlimited Delivery
cards.summary: Sell a file (ebook, template, software) once and deliver it automatically an unlimited number of times to each buyer.
cards.use_when: Listing any non-physical deliverable where the same file serves every customer.
steps: Create a product, set type Simple, and tick both Virtual and Downloadable.
Set a regular price (the source uses 14.99 for an ebook) — for a fixed-price digital item a sale price isn't required.
In the Downloadable files section add the file: either upload it via the media library and copy the file URL into the Downloadable files field, or select an existing media item.
Set the download expiry — leave blank/never-expiring in the source's example, or set a day limit such as 365 days if you want to limit access.
Add a short description and long description, assign a category (e.g. eBooks), and publish.
Optionally enable 'Sold individually' under Inventory so one buyer cannot purchase the same download twice in one order.
Test the purchase flow end to end to confirm the delivery link works after payment.
caveats: Uploaded media URLs are guessable if unprotected — consider a download-protection setup if the file is valuable.
The source presents unlimited downloads as a benefit, but some sellers prefer expiry windows for licensing reasons.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: List an Affiliate/External Product Without Shipping or Inventory
cards.summary: Promote a third-party product through your affiliate link by using the External/Affiliate product type, so the store shows it but checkout happens on the partner's site.
cards.use_when: Monetising storefront traffic with tools, themes or services you resell via an affiliate programme.
steps: Copy your affiliate link for the partner product.
Create a new product, give it the partner's product name, and upload a product image (the source recommends fixing odd aspect ratios, e.g. resizing to a square canvas, before uploading).
Change Product data type to 'External/Affiliate' — this removes inventory and shipping fields.
Paste the affiliate link into the product URL field and set the button text (e.g. 'Buy now', 'More information', 'See plans') to match the destination's call to action.
Enter the price context (the source shows a 'from $5 per month' style price) so shoppers know the commitment before clicking.
Write a short and long description covering what the tool does and why you recommend it, assign a category (e.g. Tools), and publish.
Open the live product page and click the button to confirm the affiliate link and tracking parameters survive the round trip.
caveats: Revenue depends on the partner's commission terms and cookie window, which the store owner does not control.
The source recommends checking the image dimensions first because external products are often displayed cropped.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Configure Currency and Store Locale in WooCommerce
cards.summary: Set currency, formatting and separators so all prices display correctly for the store's market.
cards.use_when: Right after setting the store's country, or when the store sells to a different market than its setup country.
steps: Go to WooCommerce → Settings → General.
Set the store's country selection first, because it determines the default currency (choosing United States sets dollars).
Choose the currency symbol, then the currency position (before or after the amount).
Set the thousand separator and decimal separator per your market's convention so large prices read naturally (e.g. a $1,999 couch should not appear as 1.999).
Set the number of decimal places — the source uses two.
Save and inspect a product page and a cart page to confirm prices render across the PDP, cart, checkout and any price ranges on variable products.
caveats: Changing the currency after publishing products does not convert existing prices; you must update each price manually.
Separator and decimal settings are market conventions, not universal — match your buyer's locale.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Use the Contrast Trick to Fix Mismatched Block Backgrounds
cards.summary: When a page section's background doesn't match the surrounding design, sample the correct colour and apply it in the block editor styles panel.
cards.use_when: After importing a template, a section on the homepage or landing page has a slightly-off background that breaks visual consistency.
steps: Install/use a browser colour-picker extension (the source uses a Chrome colour picker) to sample the exact colour of the surrounding area you want to match.
Copy the hex value.
Open the page you want to change via Edit Page (the source uses the Gutenberg block editor).
Select the section/block, open the Styles panel on the right, and choose Background.
Either pick one of the theme's global colour variations or choose Custom colour and paste the sampled hex.
Consider leaving the section transparent instead of filling it, which the source found looked better in their example.
Save and compare the rendered page against the adjacent sections.
caveats: Only applies to editors that expose a styles/background panel (e.g. Gutenberg); block or theme differences may move the option.
Sampling the wrong region compounds the mismatch — sample from the area you want to match, not from the broken section.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Set Up Manual US State Tax Rates with Inclusive/Exclusive Display
cards.summary: Enter per-state tax percentages manually and decide whether shop prices show excluding tax while checkout shows tax inclusive.
cards.use_when: Selling to US customers where you must charge state-level sales tax, especially in a B2B/B2C hybrid store.
steps: Research the correct state and local rate for each destination you charge (the source derives exact rates, e.g. 7.2500, from TaxJar).
In WooCommerce, go to Tax → Standard Rates and insert a new row per jurisdiction.
Set the country code (e.g. US) and the state code (e.g. CA, NV) for each row, then enter the rate to four decimal places (e.g. 7.2500).
Repeat for each state you ship to, rather than applying one blanket rate.
Decide whether standard, reduced and zero rates are needed — reduced for categories like books, zero for digital products.

For hybrid B2B/B2C stores, configure prices to display excluding tax in the shop/catalogue but inclusive at checkout so B2B buyers can see the net figure while consumers see the final amount they pay.
Test the cart and checkout with an address in each configured state to confirm the rate applies and the display mode behaves as intended.
caveats: The source notes exact US state rates should come from a tax service rather than being guessed — many states have local district taxes on top of the state rate.
Displaying net prices in the shop while charging gross at checkout can surprise consumers; check this matches your market's legal expectations.
Tax rules and WooCommerce tax screens have changed across versions — verify the current settings UI.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Set Shipping Cost Brackets and a Free-Shipping Threshold in WooCommerce
cards.summary: Use a shipping plugin's conditions to charge by cart-price bracket and unlock free shipping above a threshold.
cards.use_when: Configuring shipping zones and rates for a physical-goods store where you want shipping cost to scale with order value.
steps: Install a WooCommerce shipping plugin that supports conditions based on cart totals or price brackets.
Define brackets mapping cart value to cost — the source's examples include $0–$90 costing $6.99 and a $20–$49 bracket costing $8.99.
Add a free-shipping condition for carts above your chosen threshold (the source uses $200).
Review the brackets for gaps or overlaps before saving; a customer's cart value must land in exactly one bracket.
Test the cart at several price points — just under and just over the free-shipping threshold, and inside each bracket — to confirm the correct rate appears.
Check that variable and sale-priced products still produce the same bracket logic at checkout.
caveats: Bracket values and the free-shipping threshold are source-specific examples, not recommended numbers — set them from your own margin analysis.
Plugin conditions vary: some evaluate cart subtotal before tax/discounts, others after, which changes which bracket applies.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Create WooCommerce affiliate products with external/affiliate product type
cards.summary: Set up an affiliate product in WooCommerce by switching product type to external/affiliate, adding your affiliate link and price label, so you earn commission without holding inventory.
cards.use_when: Merchandising: you want to add a partner tool, brand or recommended gear to your catalog and earn affiliate commission on click-through rather than selling stocked goods.
steps: Create a new product and switch the product type dropdown to 'External/Affiliate product' in the linked product data area.
Paste your affiliate link into the product URL field and set the button text (e.g. 'More information' or 'See plans') in the button text field.
Enter the starting price (e.g. '$5 per month') and add a short description of the partner product.
Assign a relevant category (e.g. 'tools').
Fix cropped product images: open the image in an editor, expand the canvas to a square (e.g. 1000x1000 px) and re-upload so the tile displays correctly on the shop archive.
Publish and view the product; confirm the button links out through your affiliate URL.
caveats: Affiliate products do not use your checkout or inventory — the transaction happens on the partner site, so you cannot offer your own coupons or control the post-purchase experience.
If no related-product block appears, that is expected until you add upsells/cross-sells manually.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Add WooCommerce upsells (product page) vs cross-sells (cart)
cards.summary: Configure upsells to appear on a product page and cross-sells in the cart, and understand that cross-sells are only triggered by the specific product in the cart.
cards.use_when: Merchandising / AOV: you want to lift average order value by recommending complementary products at the product page or in the cart.
steps: Open the product, go to the 'Linked products' section in product data.
Add one or more products to the 'Upsells' field — these display on the product page (theme-dependent, often as 'You may also like').
Add one or more products to the 'Cross-sells' field — these display in the cart below the cart line items.
Update the product and verify by viewing the product page (upsells) and adding the product to the cart (cross-sells).
Test remove: if you empty the triggering product from the cart, the cross-sells disappear because they are tied to that specific product.
caveats: Cross-sells only show when a matching product is in the cart, so they will not surface for unrelated carts.
Upsell placement and label text depend on the active theme.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Customize shop look with fonts, spacing and archive layout
cards.summary: Use the WordPress customizer typography and WooCommerce product archive settings to control fonts, product card layout, spacing and colors, especially to lift the heavy title area above the product grid.
cards.use_when: PDP/landing page and storefront design: your product archive looks cluttered or off-brand and you want to tighten the top area and standardize typography before running traffic.
steps: Pick fonts on fonts.google.com (filter by category, e.g. sans-serif). Use one font for headings and another for body text for contrast.
In the customizer's typography settings, set the base font (e.g. Open Sans) and set the heading/title font (e.g. Nunito Sans).
Under the appearance menu, set the menu font to the heading font; adjust capitalisation, letter spacing (e.g. 0.05) and size.
On the product archive, reduce or remove the big page title area so products appear higher; toggle the display type to control whether pricing shows.
Turn on 'add to cart and price' cart options if you want those on the archive, or use a variation layout (e.g. variation type 1) with image, title, price ordering.
Drag archive element order (image, title, price, rating, taxonomies) to rearrange; set image border radius (1em ≈ 16px) and confirm a hover zoom if desired.
Match colors (price, taxonomies, buttons) to your brand palette; add custom CSS (e.g. rounded buttons) under Additional CSS and publish.
caveats: Exact settings, labels and preview behavior depend on the active theme (shown here with a free theme).
If you want a test order flow, remember to disable 'coming soon' maintenance mode first.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Sell to specific countries and set flexible table-rate shipping by price tiers
cards.summary: Restrict selling/shipping to specific countries and configure the Flexible Shipping (table-rate) plugin to charge shipping based on cart price tiers, with a free-shipping threshold.
cards.use_when: Fulfillment / pricing: you ship to a limited set of countries and want shipping cost that scales with order value instead of a flat rate.
steps: Go to WooCommerce → Settings → General, set Selling locations to 'Sell to specific countries' (or all except some) and list the target countries.
Remove the default free-shipping method in WooCommerce → Settings → Shipping → Shipping zones.
Install and activate a table-rate plugin (e.g. 'Flexible Shipping' from Octolize) from the plugin repository; keep it updated.
Add a shipping method to each zone, name the carrier (e.g. UPS), and set a free-shipping minimum order value (e.g. $200).
Build price-based rules, e.g. $0–$99.99 = $6.99, $20–$49.99 = $8.99 (adjust band edges to be non-overlapping), $50–$99.99 = $12.99, $100–$199.99 = $14.99.
If your band edges overlap, items get placed in the widest matching region — review band boundaries carefully.
Alternatively switch the rule basis to weight; set product weights/dimensions and adjust weight/length units in WooCommerce → Settings → Products.
Repeat the whole method for each additional country zone (e.g. Canada with FedEx and a different free-shipping threshold).
caveats: The example price tiers and free-shipping thresholds are the presenter's own setup, not universal rules — set your own based on margins.
Table-rate plugins and their settings screens change over time; verify the current interface.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Configure tax rates by country, state and product class
cards.summary: Enable WooCommerce taxes, build standard/reduced/zero rate classes, assign product tax classes, and choose whether displayed prices include tax — matching the whole customer journey.
cards.use_when: Pricing/checkout: you sell physical, book/reduced and digital products across multiple countries and need tax to calculate correctly and display consistently.
steps: Ensure the store address is filled in, then enable taxes in WooCommerce → Settings → General; the Tax tab appears.
Understand the three classes: standard (normal physical products), reduced (e.g. books), zero (e.g. digital in the US). Add custom classes if needed.
In Standard rates, add per-region rows: e.g. US 20%, Canada 30% (fill in real rates for your business).
In Reduced/Zero rates, set the appropriate percentages per country.
To decide whether tax is added on shipping, turn it on if you sell to companies.
Assign a product's Tax class (standard/reduced/zero) on the product's General tab — this changes the tax applied at cart/checkout.

Choose how prices display: enter prices inclusive or exclusive of tax, and set whether prices in shop / cart / checkout display including tax. Aim for a consistent number across product page → cart → checkout.
To calculate taxes per US state, look up state rates (e.g. California 7.25%, Nevada 6.85%) and add each state row, checking the correct state code.
Alternatively use WooCommerce automated taxes (paid add-on) via the plugin search to avoid manual state-by-state entry.
caveats: The example percentages used in the tutorial are illustrative, not real tax advice — apply your own jurisdiction's rules.
Display price inclusive vs exclusive changes the cart line maths; mixing shop-inclusive with checkout-exclusive causes confusing prices.
Automated tax is a paid tool; whether it is worth it depends on your volume.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Generate legal pages content and add them to the footer menu
cards.summary: Draft the legal pages you need (privacy, terms, returns, etc.) with an AI assistant and publish them into a footer legal menu so they are linked from every page.
cards.use_when: Store setup: you are preparing to launch and need compliant legal pages without paying for legal drafting, and want them discoverable sitewide.
steps: Ask an AI assistant: 'I sell [category] in [countries]. Which legal pages do I need? Create the content, and tell me what info you need from my company.'
Provide your legal company name, business address and product category so the drafts are specific.
In the customizer's menus, create a new menu (e.g. 'Legal') and add pages: Privacy Policy, Terms and Conditions, and any additional required policies.
Paste the generated content into each page and publish.
Edit the footer, remove any placeholder info, and add the Legal menu so it appears sitewide.
Save and preview each legal page from the live site to confirm content and links render.
caveats: AI-drafted legal text is a starting point, not legal advice — have it reviewed for your jurisdiction and business model.
Requirements differ by country and product type (e.g. subscription, digital, furniture), so verify what applies to you.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Enable card, PayPal and wallet payments (Stripe + PayPal) and test the flow
cards.summary: Install the WooCommerce Stripe gateway to accept cards and wallets, add PayPal as a secondary method, run a test-mode order, then flip to live and simplify the checkout fields.
cards.use_when: Checkout: you are launching a store and need working card, PayPal and wallet payment methods before sending real traffic.
steps: Install 'WooCommerce Stripe Payment Gateway' from the plugin directory and click activate.
Connect your Stripe account via the on-screen flow (returning redirects to WooCommerce).
In Stripe settings, enable test mode first; create/connect a test account to generate the webhook so payouts and webhook status show enabled.
Optionally turn on Apple Pay / Google Pay in the payment settings and hide them on product pages if you don't want express buttons there.
Install 'WooCommerce PayPal Payments' and connect your business PayPal account; enable it and set your preferred payment method order (drag card above PayPal, or vice versa).
Place a test order to confirm the buyer confirmation email and the seller new-order email both fire.
When ready, uncheck test mode on Stripe so live payments are enabled, then place a live test order.

In the customizer's WooCommerce → Checkout page settings, hide unnecessary fields (company name, second address line) and make phone optional if you don't need it, then link the Privacy Policy and Terms pages so buyers must agree before ordering.
caveats: Live mode uses real cards and real charges — verify amounts before finalising.
Plugin settings, webhook naming and account-connection steps change over time; confirm the current interface before following screenshots.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Handle incoming orders and manage WooCommerce order statuses
cards.summary: Use order statuses to move an order from Processing to Completed when physical goods ship, or to Cancelled/Refunded as needed, which triggers the appropriate customer emails.
cards.use_when: Fulfillment: you have live orders and need a repeatable process for processing, shipping, completing or refunding them.
steps: Go to WooCommerce → Orders and open an order.
For paid physical orders the status starts as Processing (the buyer receives 'we received your order and it's now being processed').
After shipping, change the status to Completed and update — the buyer then receives the completed-order email (e.g. 'good things are heading your way').
Use Cancelled or Refunded statuses when the order doesn't proceed.

Because products, shipping, taxes and payments are already configured, the only manual step for physical goods is dispatching the shipment — digital products and services need no manual shipping step.
caveats: Status-to-email mapping depends on your WooCommerce email settings; verify which emails are sent to customer vs admin.
Automated flows cover the order lifecycle but physical fulfilment still requires you (or your 3PL) to ship.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Brand transactional order emails (colors, logo, copy)
cards.summary: Style and edit WooCommerce customer emails — colors, logo, headings and body copy — so transactional messages match the store's branding and read clearly.
cards.use_when: Retention / post-purchase: your order confirmation emails look generic and you want them consistent with your brand and better worded.
steps: Go to WooCommerce → Settings → Emails to see the list of customer and admin emails; each shows a preview of the email it corresponds to.
Copy the site's primary color from the customizer's colors section and paste it into the email style color field so the buttons/accents match.
Upload your logo, set the logo size (e.g. 120) and alignment, and confirm site title / store address text lower in the email.
Edit the processing email's heading (e.g. 'your order at [store].com has been received') and additional content (e.g. a help/contact line).

To change hard-coded template strings, copy the WooCommerce email template file to the theme (Appearance → Theme File Editor → WooCommerce → emails) and edit the PHP text, or copy the template into your child theme first.
Set the From name (e.g. 'Ferdy from SofaSupa') and From address so replies route correctly, then send a test email or place a test order.
caveats: Editing theme PHP directly means theme updates can overwrite your changes — the tutorial explicitly notes making a copy; use a child theme in practice.
Changing wording in the settings only covers the fields exposed there; deeper copy lives in template files.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Connect OmniSend to WooCommerce and brand the account
cards.summary: Install the OmniSend plugin to sync a WooCommerce store with an email platform so you can build lists, send campaigns and track email-attributed revenue.
cards.use_when: Retention/acquisition: you want an email list and marketing automation tied to your store, plus revenue attribution from email.
steps: Sign up at OmniSend via email (business email), verify via the link sent to that inbox.
Enter store details (name, URL), platform (WooCommerce) and current provider (or 'none'), business address and time zone.
Install the OmniSend plugin from the plugin uploader (download the connect plugin, then upload → install → activate).
Click 'connect your store' and approve the required permissions; OmniSend will attempt to grab your branding colors automatically.
Set brand assets: accent/dark/light colors from the customizer, upload a logo PNG, choose heading fonts, add social links if wanted, then save brand assets.
Note whether you migrated from another provider — OmniSend offers a migration service via a form (claimed completion within five business days).
Track email-attributed revenue in the OmniSend dashboard once sending begins.
caveats: The free tier has a monthly sending cap (500 emails/month shown) and displays OmniSend branding; paid tiers remove branding and raise limits.
Automated migration timing is the vendor's claim, not a guarantee.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Build a discount opt-in pop-up to grow the email list
cards.summary: Create an OmniSend opt-in form that offers a first-order discount in exchange for name and email, control when it triggers, and match it to the store's styling.
cards.use_when: Acquisition/retention: you want to capture emails on-site by offering a discount pop-up instead of relying only on paid traffic.
steps: In OmniSend, go to Forms and pick a template (e.g. a simple pop-up offering 'get 10% off your first order').
Edit the heading and copy, then add a first-name field and remove its label so it reads 'enter your first name'.
Match the store style: set button corner radius, field radius, fonts and colors to the site's existing look, and make the success message in capital letters/style consistent.

Set display rules: trigger after a time on site (e.g. 3–10 seconds), after scrolling a percentage (e.g. 30%) or on exit intent; set the frequency so it reappears e.g. once per day after being dismissed.
Choose display type (pop-up, flyout, landing page or embed) and device targeting.
Enable the form so it goes live on the store — the connected store means enabling it triggers the pop-up on-site.
Optionally include a phone field only if you plan to send SMS, otherwise remove it to reduce friction.
caveats: In the free tier the form shows OmniSend branding/badge; remove it only by upgrading.
Trigger and frequency settings are the tutorial's preferences — test them against your own traffic.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Set up a welcome automation with a unique per-person discount code
cards.summary: Build an OmniSend welcome workflow triggered by the signup form that sends a sequence of emails containing a unique single-use discount code, and reuse that same code across the sequence.
cards.use_when: Retention: after a visitor subscribes, you want an automated welcome sequence that delivers a personal discount and nudges a first purchase.
steps: On the form, copy its name so you can match the form to the workflow.
In OmniSend Automation, choose a welcome workflow template (e.g. three-email version).
Set the trigger to 'subscribed via a signup form' and add a filter so only subscribers from this specific form (e.g. the 10% discount pop-up) enter — prevents cross-contamination between forms.
Adjust the wait nodes: remove or shorten the default wait if you want the first email to send immediately.

In the email, add a 'unique discount code' element; choose percent (e.g. 10%) or fixed amount, set the expiry (e.g. 7 days), and check 'reuse the unique discount code in this workflow' so the same code appears in later emails.
Personalise the subject line and body with a first-name variable, and note the discount expiry is calculated once and reused automatically — do not re-set it per email.
Style the email (rounded buttons, colors) to match the site, then finish editing and start the workflow to make it live.
Edit the follow-up emails (e.g. day 1 and day 4) to include the reused unique discount element and the same button.
caveats: The 10% discount, 7-day expiry and 1-day/4-day sends are the presenter's example values — pick numbers that protect your margin.
Workflows made with email-dependent code generation require the connected store; verify the discount element works before launching widely.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Welcome Email Series with Unique Per-Subscriber Coupon Codes
cards.summary: Build a multi-email welcome automation where each subscriber receives a personally generated single-use discount code.
cards.use_when: You are setting up the opt-in to first-purchase email flow and want a personal, trackable discount instead of one shared public code.
steps: Create the opt-in form on the site (name + email) and connect it to an email platform automation workflow.
In the workflow builder, add an email step and insert the 'unique discount code' element so the platform generates a one-code-per-contact coupon, not a static code.
Set the coupon expiry once in the workflow settings; it is calculated automatically per recipient, so you should NOT adjust the expiry date per individual email.
Personalize the copy with the subscriber's first name, and include a redeemable copy button plus a link that applies the code at cart/checkout.
Add a second email with a different angle or urgency, then a third, so the sequence continues beyond the first message (e.g., day 1, then day 4).
Remove any leftover block or element not needed in the follow-up emails before publishing.
Publish and finish the workflow, then test the full path: sign up with a real or test email, receive the code, add a product, apply the coupon at cart, and check out.
Verify in the store's coupon list that a unique coupon was created and is restricted to a single use for that contact.
caveats: The unique discount code feature is platform-specific; verify the current element name and location in your email tool's interface.
Confirm that coupon usage limits and expiry are actually enforced by your store coupon settings after the code is generated.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Split Testing Email Subject Lines and Content to Lift Revenue
cards.summary: Use drag-and-drop A/B split testing on emails to find subject lines and content that increase opens and sales.
cards.use_when: You have an established email flow or campaign and want to improve open rates or revenue per send.
steps: In your email platform's workflow or campaign builder, locate the split/A-B testing element and drag it into the flow.
Duplicate the email into two branches and change one variable at a time, e.g., change only the subject line to 'last chance' vs. the original.
Assign a portion of the list to each variant so results are comparable rather than sending different messages sequentially.
Publish and let the test run long enough to collect meaningful data before declaring a winner (two-day tests are too short for strong conclusions).
Compare open rate first, then clicks and sales, and keep the winning version as the standard for that send.
Repeat tests on other emails in the sequence so improvements accumulate across the whole flow.
caveats: The presenter claims A/B testing can 'increase revenue big time' — treat that as a general argument for testing, not a guaranteed result.
Short tests (e.g., a day) give unreliable winners; avoid acting on tiny sample sizes.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Abandoned Cart Email Triggered by Cart Inactivity
cards.summary: Set up an automation that emails shoppers who add an item to cart but do not purchase within a defined inactivity window.
cards.use_when: You want to recover checkout/cart abandonment without manual outreach.
steps: Create a new workflow in your email platform and select the abandoned cart trigger.
Set the trigger to fire on cart inactivity after a realistic window (the tutorial uses one hour in production; one minute was used only for demo purposes).
Build the email with a subject line that creates urgency (e.g., 'items in your cart are selling out fast').
Dynamically insert the actual cart contents so the recipient sees the specific product(s) and a link back to buy.
Activate the workflow so it runs automatically as soon as shoppers opt in and leave items in the cart.
Test end-to-end: add a product, stop activity, confirm the email arrives and the product link resolves correctly.
caveats: The one-minute delay was only for demonstration — production delays should reflect real shopping behavior, typically at least one hour.
This flow depends on the visitor being identifiable (e.g., opted in or logged in) for the email address to be captured.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Behavioral and Value-Based Subscriber Segments Feeding Targeted Automations
cards.summary: Create segments from email engagement, purchase behavior, region, and value, then trigger tailored workflows when contacts enter a segment.
cards.use_when: You want to send different offers to different customer groups automatically rather than one list-wide campaign.
steps: Go to the audience segments area and use AI creation or the pre-built segment templates to define groups.

Build segments such as: active email subscribers, birthdays, inactive subscribers (no opens or purchases across recent weeks/months or last ~20 emails), geographically grouped (e.g., Europe), recent buyers, and high-value subscribers (active openers who purchase).
Create a new workflow from scratch and select 'entered a segment' as the trigger, then choose the specific segment.
Add an appropriate delay (e.g., 10 days for a high-value segment) before sending.
Send a segment-specific message, e.g., a 15% extra discount for three days to customers who spent over $1,000, or a 'we miss you' offer (e.g., 50% off for two days) to inactive subscribers.
Activate each workflow so offers fire automatically as contacts qualify for or move between segments.
Review segment membership periodically to ensure the criteria still match your intent.
caveats: The 'bought more than $1,000' and discount levels (15%, 50%) are illustrative examples from the tutorial, not recommended thresholds.
Confirm the actual segment criteria options in your email platform's interface before building, as names and logic may change.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Custom Branded Order Confirmation Email Replacing the Default
cards.summary: Create a styled order confirmation workflow so customers receive a better-looking confirmation than the default store email.
cards.use_when: Your default WooCommerce order confirmation looks generic and you want a branded post-purchase touchpoint.
steps: In your email platform, create a new workflow and select the order confirmation trigger (search 'confirmation' if needed).
Edit the email content and maintain consistent styling, including button settings (e.g., primary button color/style) to match your brand.
Finish editing and start the workflow.
Test by placing a real or test order through checkout, and confirm that the customer receives the branded email (you as the shop owner will still see the WooCommerce order notification).
Decide whether to use the platform's version instead of the default store confirmation going forward.
caveats: The default WooCommerce confirmation still fires by default; manage messaging to avoid customers receiving confusing duplicates if both are active.
Verify current trigger names and settings in the email platform, as interfaces change.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Revenue Attribution: Separating Platform-Driven Sales from Total Store Revenue
cards.summary: Use your email/automation platform's tracking to see how much revenue is directly driven by automations versus the store as a whole.
cards.use_when: You want to judge whether your email automations and opt-in offers are actually driving revenue before investing further.
steps: Connect your email platform to your store so it can track sales originating from its automations (the tutorial shows the platform distinguishing WooCommerce-driven vs. platform-driven sales).
In the platform dashboard, compare total store revenue against the revenue attributed to automations.
Use campaign-level reporting to see how many sales came from a specific broadcast to the whole list.
Use this split to decide where to invest: more automation, better flows, or list-building campaigns.
Re-measure after each significant change to see whether attributed revenue moves.
caveats: Attribution logic is platform-dependent and can overlap; treat platform-attributed revenue as directional, not exact.
The tutorial's figures ($1,991 total, $900 from automations) are one example, not a benchmark.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Swap Shared Discount Codes for Unique, Single-Use, Time-Limited Codes
cards.summary: Use per-contact, expiry-limited, single-use coupon codes so discounts can be tracked to individuals and cannot be reused.
cards.use_when: You are designing an opt-in incentive and want protection against code sharing and clearer attribution.
steps: Use an automation element that generates a unique coupon code per subscriber rather than publishing one universal discount code.
Set an expiry window (the tutorial used seven days) so urgency is created and liability is limited.
Enforce single use so the code cannot be redeemed again once used.
Confirm in your store's coupon list that the code appears, is limited to one use, and carries the intended expiry date.
Deliver the code so the shopper can copy it and apply it at cart.
Test applying the code yourself, then verify that it is marked used and cannot be reused.
caveats: Confirm your store's coupon settings actually enforce single-use and expiry after the platform generates the code.
Manage the operational burden of many coupon records as your list grows.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Editing Homepage Content, Product Blocks and Prices in the Site Editor
cards.summary: Directly edit homepage text, images, product references, prices and styling in the WordPress block editor by clicking and adjusting right-side settings.
cards.use_when: You need to update your store homepage hero, featured product blocks, or promotional text without a developer.
steps: Open the page for editing and triple-click (or click into) a text block to change copy directly.

For a button: open the style tab to set hover behavior (e.g., darken or scale) and the borders/shadows settings to adjust border radius; in the details panel, set the link and type the target product/page name so the editor auto-suggests matching products, pages and posts.
For a featured product image: select the image block, choose select image, and replace it with the product photo.
Update the price text manually to the new value (e.g., $90.99); if the text is too large, adjust size under typography.
Repeat for a second featured product block the same way.
For icons, click the icon block and search for a replacement icon.
Dynamic sections like 'Arrivals' are auto-fetched from the store, so verify they reflect the intended products rather than editing them by hand.
For background images: open style > background and choose a new image; for text color, open style > typography and set the color (e.g., white) per text block.
To add new page areas, click and add a block (or type '/' to pick a block type).
caveats: Manually edited prices can drift out of sync with actual product prices — update both when you change pricing.
Exact block names and panels vary by theme/editor version; verify against your current WordPress editor.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Making the Header, Menu and Off-Canvas Mobile View Responsive
cards.summary: Use the editor's tablet/mobile preview to fix header, menu, logo and icon styling so the site works on all devices.
cards.use_when: Your site looks broken on tablet or mobile and you need to correct layout and styling for smaller screens.
steps: Open the header/footer builder and switch to the tablet/mobile view.
Check how elements render on the smaller breakpoint and identify what looks wrong or misaligned.
In the design settings, set the background (e.g., light), swap the logo for the appropriate version, and confirm it updates.
Select the main menu, go to design, set text color (e.g., dark) and the hover color (e.g., orange); adjust fonts as needed.
Add or adjust the location/HTML block with matching dark-text and orange-hover styling.
Switch to mobile view, open the off-canvas menu area, and under design set the icon color (e.g., dark) so the X/close control is visible.
Publish and re-check both tablet and mobile to confirm the header, menu and off-canvas behavior are correct.
caveats: The specific settings paths depend on your builder/theme; verify the current options in your editor.
Always preview on desktop, tablet and mobile after changes before publishing.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Optional Channels: Texts and Push Notifications Alongside Email
cards.summary: Extend your automation workflows to SMS and push notifications when you have the subscriber's contact details.
cards.use_when: Your list includes phone numbers or app/device access and you want to reach people beyond the inbox.
steps: If you collect phone numbers, add an SMS step in the workflow (additional to the email steps).
If push notifications are available, add a push step so subscribers see the message on their device.
Use timing/delay controls so channels do not fire simultaneously and overwhelm the contact.
Use tags for context so a step only sends when a contact has a specific tag (e.g., only send this offer to a particular group).
Test each channel separately to confirm delivery before activating.
caveats: SMS requires collecting phone numbers and appropriate consent; only send where you have permission.
Channel availability depends on your platform and integrations — verify current support.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Using Tags to Conditionally Gate Automation Emails
cards.summary: Apply tags to contacts and use them as conditions so emails only send to appropriately grouped people.
cards.use_when: You want certain workflow emails to fire only for a subsection of subscribers (e.g., a specific offer or cohort).
steps: Assign meaningful tags to contacts based on behavior or source (e.g., a tag identifying a specific interest or purchase context).
In the workflow, add a condition/tag step that checks whether the contact has the required tag.
Place the conditional email after the tag check so only tagged contacts proceed.
Use delays before or after the tag condition to control timing.
Test with a tagged and an untagged contact to confirm the email only reaches the intended group.
caveats: Tag hygiene matters — a bloated or inconsistent tag scheme causes misfires.
Conditional logic naming and placement differ by platform; verify the current interface.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Prioritizing Your Next Store Improvements: SEO and Email First
cards.summary: The presenter ranks learning SEO (via a rank-tracking plugin) and email marketing as the highest-value follow-on skills for a WooCommerce store.
cards.use_when: You have a functioning store and are deciding which growth skill or project to invest in next.
steps: If your store lacks organic discovery, prioritize learning search optimization and using a rank-tracking plugin to be found in search results.
If you already have traffic but weak repeat revenue, prioritize deepening your email list and automation setup.
Treat affiliate marketing as an optional, separate monetization path (promoting other people's products) rather than a core store requirement.
Pick one priority at a time and implement it fully before moving on.
caveats: This is the presenter's stated opinion on prioritization, not a proven universal rule; your store's bottleneck should drive the choice.
The presenter's affiliate earnings figure is a personal example, not a promise of results.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Install Node, Git and Shopify CLI before AI-assisted theme work
cards.summary: Set up the local toolchain (Node.js, Git, Shopify CLI) that lets Claude Code read and edit a live Shopify theme.
cards.use_when: You are preparing a machine to build or modify a Shopify theme with an AI coding agent rather than in the theme editor.
steps: Install Node.js from nodejs.org using the pre-built installer for your OS; accept defaults. On the 'Tools for native modules' screen leave the box unchecked — the presenter says it is not needed for this setup.
Install Git from git-scm.com (needed as a helper for the Shopify CLI).
Open PowerShell (Windows) or Terminal (Mac) and run npm install -g @shopify/cli@latest on a single line.
Verify with shopify version. A version number means it installed; lines of install output are normal, not errors.
Install Claude Code separately: on Windows run irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex, then restart the terminal and type claude to authenticate.
Log in with the Claude account that has the Pro subscription, since Pro is what includes Claude Code.
Verify current install URLs and commands in the official docs before running them — these interfaces change.
caveats: The presenter's exact install commands and pricing are point-in-time and should be re-verified.
Native modules were left unchecked specifically for this workflow; other Node projects may need them.
cards.source_name: How to Build a Full Shopify Store using AI (Claude Code).docx

cards.title: Pull the live theme locally so the AI can edit real code
cards.summary: Use shopify theme pull to copy the store's current live theme into a clean project folder, giving the AI agent read/write access to actual theme files.
cards.use_when: You are about to have an AI agent customise a Shopify theme and need the live theme files on your machine first.
steps: Exit any running Claude Code session with /exit to return to a plain terminal.
Create and enter a fresh project folder: mkdir my-store-build then cd my-store-build.
Copy your store domain from Shopify admin > Settings (top of the page).
Run shopify theme pull --store [your-store-domain] --live.
Complete the browser login prompt; the code shown in the terminal confirms you are logging into the correct device.
Wait for the 'pulled successfully' message, which means the theme is now local and editable by the agent.
caveats: Pulling --live copies the live theme; changes are made locally first and are not live until you push and publish.
The store password and account password are different things — see the preview card.
cards.source_name: How to Build a Full Shopify Store using AI (Claude Code).docx

cards.title: Add products and collections before generating the store
cards.summary: Seed the store with real products first so the AI designs the homepage and PDPs around actual catalog data rather than placeholders.
cards.use_when: You are starting an AI-assisted store build and need something for the design to be built around.
steps: In Shopify admin go to Products > Add product.

Draft the title and description yourself or ask a chat AI for a short, clean title and description, dragging the product image into the prompt for context; iterate with feedback if the first version misses.
Upload product photos in the Media section — own photos, AI-generated, or stock (the presenter used Pexels stock).
Set price, inventory quantity and shipping per product; enable variants (e.g. Size: S/M/L/XL) and set per-variant price, inventory and variant-specific images where relevant.
Create a manual collection (e.g. 'T-Shirts') for each product type and assign the product, optionally with a collection image, then save.
Repeat for every product; collections make the catalog easier to organise as it grows.
caveats: Category metafields and SEO fields were left at defaults in the walkthrough — not required for a first build.
Shipping is configured later at the store level, not fully per product.
cards.source_name: How to Build a Full Shopify Store using AI (Claude Code).docx

cards.title: Organise a local asset folder as the AI's design brief
cards.summary: Compile screenshots of desired theme sections plus your own logos, product photos and lifestyle images into one folder the AI reads as visual constraints.
cards.use_when: You are briefing an AI agent to build a homepage or theme and need it to match a specific look instead of guessing.
steps: Browse the Shopify theme store demo pages and screenshot the specific sections you like — hero, product display, collection page, product page, reviews, story — mixing and matching across themes.
Create folders for product photos, store inspiration screenshots, logo (including transparent dark and light versions), and homepage lifestyle images.
Generate a logo if needed (the presenter used Canva) and source lifestyle images from stock sites, AI generation or your own photography.
Inside your project folder run mkdir inspiration, then 'explorer .' (Windows) to open the folder and paste all assets in.
Start the agent with the project open so it can see the inspiration directory before it writes any code.
caveats: Folder structure does not have to match the presenter's exactly; the point is that every reference asset is reachable in one place.
Screenshots of third-party themes are references, not licensed assets to copy wholesale.
cards.source_name: How to Build a Full Shopify Store using AI (Claude Code).docx

cards.title: Prompt the AI to interview you before it builds
cards.summary: Kick off a theme build with a prompt that makes the agent explore the theme and assets, ask about brand direction, and propose a plan instead of generating everything at once.
cards.use_when: You are starting a store build or major redesign and want controlled, reviewable output rather than a single giant generation.
steps: Write an initial prompt that gives the agent a few instructions and guidelines, and swap in your real brand name (the guide's version uses a placeholder).
Let it first read the theme and the inspiration folder to understand the starting point.
Answer its questions: choose the visual direction (e.g. loud/blue-yellow inspiration vs clean and neutral matching your logo and photography), select homepage sections, and pick fonts.
Expect a plan confirmation request including your Shopify URL; approve building only the first section.
Approve command-permission prompts as they appear (choose 'yes, and don't ask again' for repeat permissions) and use plain English to correct anything that diverges.
caveats: The presenter frames this as working like a real designer — the interview step is what stops mismatched output, so do not skip to 'build the whole store'.
Approving commands blindly is risky; read what the agent is about to run.
cards.source_name: How to Build a Full Shopify Store using AI (Claude Code).docx

cards.title: Build the homepage section by section in plain English
cards.summary: Have the AI generate one homepage section at a time, review it in a private preview, request plain-English tweaks, then explicitly move to the next section.
cards.use_when: You are generating or redesigning a homepage and want to catch layout and content problems before they compound.
steps: Order sections deliberately, e.g. Hero, Shop by Category, Featured Products, Customer Reviews, Our Story.
After each section, refresh the local preview, judge it, and describe changes conversationally ('the icons don't match the category — quality check this section').
When the Featured Products section comes up, explicitly instruct the agent to use the real products already in the store: 'my store already has three products — use the real products.'
Approve the section verbally ('looks great') and then explicitly tell it to build the next section in the same style.
Once every section exists, run a final quality pass prompt asking it to catch anything missed and improve polish.
Optionally batch small remaining fixes (product pages, header with logo, footer with policy links, rest of the store) into one prompt.
caveats: Placeholder review names, text and images will need real replacement later.
Section prompts assume the store already has products — add them first or the featured section has nothing to reference.
cards.source_name: How to Build a Full Shopify Store using AI (Claude Code).docx

cards.title: Preview changes privately on a local dev server
cards.summary: Run a private local preview of the AI-built theme, using the store's Shopify-generated password, so you can review each section before anything goes public.
cards.use_when: You are iterating on theme code and need to see changes live without exposing them to customers.
steps: Pick 'local dev server' when the agent asks how to preview sections — it is a private live preview running on your machine that updates as the agent writes.
Open a second terminal, cd into the project folder, and paste the preview command the agent prints.
When asked for a store password, use the Shopify admin Online Store password (Online Store > Edit password), not your account password.
Open the resulting link in a browser and refresh after each change to see updates.
Request adjustments in plain English — e.g. ask for easing animations on load and fade-in on scroll, then refine speed and stagger timing.
caveats: This is the presenter's recommended preview mode; unpublished preview theme and static mockups were the other options offered.
After the initial easing request the presenter found the result improved but noted timing may need further refinement.
cards.source_name: How to Build a Full Shopify Store using AI (Claude Code).docx

cards.title: Use easing and scroll animations to soften load friction
cards.summary: Ask the agent to add entry and scroll animations so sections fade in rather than snapping onto the screen.
cards.use_when: A page feels harsh or unpolished because everything renders instantly on load.
steps: Review the first load: if all text and images appear at once, request a clean easing animation for elements as they appear.
Also request that subsequent sections fade in as the visitor scrolls.
Phrase it in plain English to the coding agent, describing the desired feel rather than the implementation.
After the change, refresh the preview and judge it; if needed, ask to tune the animation speed and stagger timing.
Confirm the effect on both desktop and mobile before moving on.
caveats: This is the presenter's taste judgement, not a measured conversion claim.
Animation is a polish step, not a substitute for content or offer quality.
cards.source_name: How to Build a Full Shopify Store using AI (Claude Code).docx

cards.title: Push the AI-built theme, then keep editing it in Shopify
cards.summary: Upload the finished theme to Shopify unpublised, verify it in the theme editor and on mobile, and keep using Shopify's native editor for manual changes.
cards.use_when: Your AI-assisted theme build is done and you need to review, adjust and prepare it for publishing.
steps: Tell the agent you are ready to publish to the live theme; it will return a command for your preview terminal.
In the preview terminal press Ctrl+C, paste the upload command and run it — the theme uploads to Shopify without being published.
In Shopify admin go to Online Store and click Edit theme on the uploaded theme.
Manually edit text and images by clicking sections, reorder sections by dragging them in the left panel, add sections with the plus button, and undo from the top right.
Use the mobile-phone icon in the editor to check every page and section on mobile as well as desktop, then save.
Only after manual review, publish.
caveats: Anything you change in the visual editor works the same as any other Shopify theme — building with AI does not lock you into code-only edits.
Reordering sections changes the homepage format; review after each move.
cards.source_name: How to Build a Full Shopify Store using AI (Claude Code).docx

cards.title: Configure shipping zones, free-shipping thresholds and taxes
cards.summary: Set up Shopify Payments, a single free-shipping zone with an order minimum and transit time, delete unwanted zones, and confirm tax regions.
cards.use_when: You are finishing back-office configuration before taking orders.
steps: In Settings > Payments, complete Shopify Payments setup so you can be paid.
In Settings > Shipping and delivery, open your shipping profile; the presenter recommends simply offering free shipping for most stores.
Delete the express option if unused, then edit the standard rate: rename to 'Free Shipping', turn on the offer-free-shipping toggle, and set the minimum order amount (e.g. $10).
Set the transit time you will actually honour (the example used 5–8 business days) and save.
For international zones, configure them deliberately or delete the zone entirely if you do not ship internationally (the example kept only US free shipping).
In Settings > Taxes and duties, confirm the Shopify tax service and the regions where you collect tax — in the example, only the US.
caveats: The $10 free-shipping minimum and 5–8 day transit are the presenter's examples, not benchmarks; choose based on your margins and carrier reality.
The presenter advises consulting a tax professional if unsure.
cards.source_name: How to Build a Full Shopify Store using AI (Claude Code).docx

cards.title: Generate policy pages from templates and AI, then publish
cards.summary: Fill in Refund, Privacy and Terms policies using Shopify templates, write a custom shipping policy with AI, and publish them so footer links appear.
cards.use_when: You need the legal pages that checkout and the theme footer link to before you remove the store password.
steps: In Settings > Policies, open each policy and use the Insert template option where offered.
Scan the template for placeholders — e.g. delete 'insert return address' and enter your real return address — before publishing.
Publish each policy after reviewing it.
Write your own shipping policy if no template exists, using an AI with your exact shipping rules and regions, then paste and publish.
Skip the legal notice only if it genuinely does not apply; the presenter says to consult a professional if unsure.
Recheck the store footer afterwards: the presenter's build only showed policy links once policies existed in admin.
caveats: Templates are a starting point, not legal advice.
AI-written policies should be reviewed for accuracy against your actual operations.
cards.source_name: How to Build a Full Shopify Store using AI (Claude Code).docx

cards.title: Connect a custom domain and go live
cards.summary: Replace the default myshopify.com domain with a purchased .com, then publish the theme and remove the store password.
cards.use_when: You are finalising the store for public launch.
steps: In Settings > Domains, choose Connect existing domain or Buy new domain (the example priced a .com at about $16/year).
The presenter recommends a .com for a professional store rather than staying on the Shopify subdomain long term.
Once products, theme, shipping, taxes and policies are done, go to Online Store, open the theme, click Publish and confirm.
Click Remove password to open the store to everyone.
Use View store to confirm the published theme transferred correctly.
