caveats: Domain pricing is point-in-time and varies by registrar/TLD.
The presenter treats the default Shopify domain as a long-term liability for professionalism, but it works for testing.
cards.source_name: How to Build a Full Shopify Store using AI (Claude Code).docx

cards.title: WordPress + WooCommerce baseline stack with Astra and Elementor
cards.summary: Set up a new WooCommerce store on WordPress using the Astra theme and Elementor page builder instead of the default block editor.
cards.use_when: Standing up a brand-new store from scratch and choosing your theme and page builder before building any pages or products.
steps: Install WordPress on your chosen host first, then install WooCommerce to create the store foundation.
Install the Astra theme via Appearance > Themes > Add Theme, then activate it.
Install and activate the Astra Starter Templates plugin to get prebuilt site designs.

When prompted to choose a page builder during Starter Template import, explicitly select Elementor rather than the WordPress block editor — this decision locks in which editor you will use for later page edits.

Because WordPress, Elementor and Astra interfaces change frequently, verify current menu names and click paths against live documentation before following any step-by-step tutorial, and avoid tutorials older than roughly 18 months.
caveats: The source is a walkthrough for a specific version of the tools; menu locations may have moved.
Hosting affiliate pitches and domain/server definitions in the source are not part of the setup procedure and can be skipped.
cards.source_name: How to Create an Ecommerce Website with WordPress 2026 (step by step).docx

cards.title: Creating mobile-specific layouts with Elementor responsive toggles
cards.summary: Build separate mobile and desktop section layouts by duplicating containers and using Elementor's Hide on mobile/tablet/desktop toggles.
cards.use_when: Merchandising a homepage or landing page where the desktop layout (e.g. wide hero with side-by-side blocks) would break or read poorly on phones.
steps: Build the primary section or container for desktop first, e.g. a wide hero with two columns.
Duplicate the entire container so you have an identical copy to modify.
On the duplicate, restyle it for mobile — stack elements, enlarge tap targets, simplify content.
Open the duplicate's Advanced > Responsive settings.
Use the 'Hide on tablet' and 'Hide on desktop' toggles on the mobile version, and the 'Hide on mobile' toggle on the original desktop version, so only one version renders per device.
Preview each breakpoint in Elementor to confirm the correct variant appears and no duplicate content shows.
Because the Elementor interface changes, verify the current location of the Responsive toggles in your installed version.
caveats: Duplicating full sections doubles maintenance: a content change must be made in both the desktop and mobile copies.
Device-specific hiding is a layout tool, not a substitute for genuinely responsive design — overuse creates divergent content across devices.
cards.source_name: How to Create an Ecommerce Website with WordPress 2026 (step by step).docx

cards.title: Building WooCommerce variable products with color/size variations
cards.summary: Configure a variable product so each variation (e.g. per color) has its own SKU, stock level and price.
cards.use_when: Listing a product that comes in multiple colors, sizes or options where each variant needs separate inventory and pricing.
steps: Create or edit the product, then change Product type to 'Variable product'.
Go to the Attributes tab, add an attribute such as Color, and enter its values separated by the | symbol (for example Red | Blue | Green).
Check 'Use for variations' for that attribute so WooCommerce treats it as a variation axis, then save the attribute.
Open the Variations tab and click 'Generate variations' to build a row for every combination of attribute values.
Edit each generated variation individually to set its SKU, stock quantity and price.
Save the product and preview it on the front end to confirm the variation dropdown shows all options and updates price/availability correctly.
Verify current menu labels in your WooCommerce version, as admin screens shift between releases.
caveats: Every variation generated must be manually configured — generated rows start blank, so unedited variations can ship with missing prices or SKUs.
Attribute values typed with the | separator must match exactly across the attribute definition and variation rows.
cards.source_name: How to Create an Ecommerce Website with WordPress 2026 (step by step).docx

cards.title: Connecting Stripe and PayPal payments in WooCommerce
cards.summary: Install the Stripe and PayPal WooCommerce gateway plugins, connect the accounts, run the connection test, and switch from Test to Live mode.
cards.use_when: Enabling card and PayPal checkout on a new store before going live.
steps: Install the WooCommerce Stripe payment gateway plugin and the WooCommerce PayPal payment gateway plugin (the source names 'Payment Plugins for Stripe WooCommerce' and 'Payment Plugins for PayPal WooCommerce').
Open each plugin's settings and connect it to your Stripe and PayPal merchant accounts.
Run the built-in connection test each plugin provides to confirm the handshake works.
Place a test order using each gateway while still in Test mode to verify the full checkout and confirmation flow.
Explicitly switch each gateway's mode setting from 'Test' to 'Live' — orders will not actually charge cards while Test mode is active.
Re-verify in the live dashboard that the mode indicator reads Live after switching.
Plugin names and settings screens change; confirm the current plugin and mode toggle before relying on these steps.
caveats: Forgetting to flip from Test to Live mode is a common silent failure — checkout appears to work but no money is collected.
The specific plugin vendors named may be replaced or renamed; verify you are installing the current, maintained integration.
cards.source_name: How to Create an Ecommerce Website with WordPress 2026 (step by step).docx

cards.title: Configuring shipping zones with flat rate vs free-shipping thresholds
cards.summary: Set up WooCommerce shipping zones and choose between a flat rate and a free-shipping minimum to shape buyer incentive.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to charge for shipping and whether to offer a free-shipping threshold to lift average order value.
steps: Create Shipping Zones in WooCommerce for the regions you actually ship to (e.g. domestic, specific countries).
Within each zone, add the shipping method you want to offer.
Choose between a flat rate — a fixed charge per order regardless of basket size — and a free-shipping method conditioned on a minimum spend.
If using free shipping, set a threshold amount (the source uses $100 as an example) above which shipping becomes free.
Verify the threshold math in cart: confirm orders below the minimum are charged and orders at/above it show free shipping.

Consider whether the threshold is set below, at, or above your typical basket size — a threshold just above average order value is what encourages an add-on. The $100 figure is the source's example, not a universal benchmark.
caveats: A free-shipping threshold below typical basket size gives away margin without changing behavior.
Flat rate and free-shipping-threshold models are situational alternatives, not a single correct answer.
cards.source_name: How to Create an Ecommerce Website with WordPress 2026 (step by step).docx

cards.title: Setting up a first-purchase welcome coupon with usage controls
cards.summary: Create a one-per-customer discount coupon to drive first orders while limiting abuse.
cards.use_when: Launching a store or running an acquisition push where you want a first-purchase incentive without unlimited reuse.
steps: Create a new coupon in WooCommerce and give it a recognizable code.
Set the discount type to 'Percentage discount' with the rate you intend.
Set 'Usage limit per user' to 1 so each customer can redeem it only once.
Optionally set an overall usage limit and an expiry date to bound total liability.
Test the coupon at checkout: confirm it applies, respects the one-per-user rule, and produces the expected order total.
Confirm the discount is factored into your effective margin before promoting it widely.
caveats: A percentage discount applied without a usage limit per user can be stacked repeatedly by the same buyer.
Coupon abuse controls depend on customer account or email matching — guests may still work around limits.
cards.source_name: How to Create an Ecommerce Website with WordPress 2026 (step by step).docx

cards.title: Set up WooCommerce variable products with generated variations
cards.summary: Configure a variable product end-to-end: attributes, generated variations, per-variation SKU, price, stock and thumbnail.
cards.use_when: Adding a product that comes in multiple colors, sizes or other options on a WooCommerce store.
steps: Create the product and change Product type to 'Variable product' before saving.
In the Attributes tab add an attribute (e.g. Color), enter values separated by the pipe | symbol (white|blue|pink), tick 'Use for variations', and save attributes.
Open the Variations tab and click 'Generate variations' to auto-create one row per combination instead of adding them manually.
Edit each variation individually to set its own SKU (e.g. kova-echo-white), regular price, sale price, thumbnail and, if you manage stock per variation, stock quantity and low stock threshold.
Set the main Product image (the image shown before a shopper picks a variation) and add extra gallery images for the default color.
Publish, then preview the storefront and click through each option to confirm the image and price swap correctly per variation.
caveats: The specific button labels live in the WooCommerce product editor and can move between versions; verify the current interface.
Separate variations add admin overhead — don't generate variations for attributes that are purely descriptive.
cards.source_name: How to Create an Ecommerce Website with WordPress 2026 (step by step).docx

cards.title: Product data fields that drive PDP content: SKU, stock, weight
cards.summary: Fill WooCommerce Product Data tabs so stock messaging, shipping and descriptions match what the shopper sees.
cards.use_when: Creating or auditing a physical product listing on WooCommerce before it goes live.
steps: Set the SKU (your own stock-keeping code) and, if you have a real barcode, a UPC/GTIN. Skip barcodes for placeholder or made-up products.
Tick 'Track stock quantity' and enter the units on hand; set backorders to 'Do not allow' if you don't want to sell what you can't ship.
Set a low stock threshold (e.g. 10) so the product page can show 'low stock, order soon' messaging.
In the Shipping tab enter the weight and dimensions of the entire package — this is what shipping rates and label calculations use.
Write two descriptions: the long product description (the full sales story) and the short description (the summary that appears near the price/button).
Use the product image as the default PDP visual, a gallery for supporting shots, and category/tags so the item surfaces in on-site search and category browsing.
For downloadable or service products select Virtual/Downloadable instead of shipping fields.
caveats: Weight/dimensions are per package, not per item, when items ship together.
Low-stock and stock-count messages only show if you actually track inventory.
cards.source_name: How to Create an Ecommerce Website with WordPress 2026 (step by step).docx

cards.title: Configure Stripe and PayPal for WooCommerce and switch to live
cards.summary: Install payment plugins, connect accounts, run the connection test and flip the mode from Test to Live before launch.
cards.use_when: Enabling credit card and PayPal checkout on a WooCommerce store.
steps: Install and activate the Stripe and PayPal WooCommerce payment plugins from Plugins > Add New (search by name).
Open WooCommerce settings for Stripe, connect your Stripe account (business details, bank account, statement descriptor) and agree/submit.
With the account connected, change mode from Test to Live, run the connection test, and save.
Repeat the connection flow for PayPal, then go to WooCommerce > Settings > Payments and enable the PayPal gateway (it may be inactive by default).
Verify by adding a product to the cart, proceeding to checkout, and confirming both the card fields and the PayPal option appear.
caveats: Plugin names and settings screens change; verify current onboarding flow.
Do a live-mode test transaction before launch — the connection test confirms the link, not that checkout charges correctly.
The presenter is compensated via a hosting affiliate link; treat host recommendations as opinion.
cards.source_name: How to Create an Ecommerce Website with WordPress 2026 (step by step).docx

cards.title: Shipping zones, flat rate and free-shipping thresholds
cards.summary: Build shipping zones with a flat rate plus a free-shipping method gated by an order minimum, ordered so free shipping wins.
cards.use_when: Setting up shipping charges and a free-shipping minimum for an online store.
steps: In WooCommerce > Settings > Shipping create a zone per region (e.g. United States) and assign zone regions.
Add a Flat rate method: give it a name like 'Standard rate', set taxable status as appropriate, and enter a cost (example used: $10).
Add a Free shipping method and set its requirement to Minimum order amount (example threshold: $100). The operator can use any threshold; it must be chosen so shipping cost is covered.
Leave 'Apply minimum order rule before coupon' unchecked if the free-shipping threshold should be judged after coupons reduce the total.
Drag Free shipping above the flat rate inside the zone so qualifying carts get it automatically.
Save changes and test with a cart just above and just below the threshold.
caveats: The $100 threshold and $10 rate are the tutorial's examples, not benchmarks — margin and average order value should set your own numbers.
Local pickup is listed as rarely used; judge by whether customers can collect.
cards.source_name: How to Create an Ecommerce Website with WordPress 2026 (step by step).docx

cards.title: Welcome coupon setup: percentage, usage limits, exclusions
cards.summary: Create a first-order welcome coupon with a percentage discount and a one-use-per-customer limit.
cards.use_when: Launching a store or promo and you need a discount code that can't be abused.
steps: Go to WooCommerce > Marketing > Coupons and create a coupon with a simple code (e.g. welcome10).
Set discount type to Percentage and enter the value (example: 10).
Optionally tick 'free shipping' to bundle shipping into the coupon; skip it for the welcome case in the tutorial.
Set an expiration date, then under Usage restriction set minimum/maximum spend, prevent coupon stacking, exclude sale items, and scope to products/categories/brands if needed.
Under Usage limits set the per-user limit (example: 1) so each shopper can use it once, and optionally a total usage cap.
Publish, then test on the storefront by adding a product, applying the code in the cart, and confirming the discount amount.
caveats: Discount depth is a margin decision — the 10% example is illustrative, not a recommended rate.
Limits only work as configured; verify the per-user rule actually blocks a second redemption.
cards.source_name: How to Create an Ecommerce Website with WordPress 2026 (step by step).docx

cards.title: Use a starter template, then customize instead of building from scratch
cards.summary: Install a theme plus starter templates and Elementor so a full store layout exists before you customize.
cards.use_when: Building a new WordPress/WooCommerce storefront and you want a working layout fast.
steps: Install and activate a lightweight theme (Astra is used in the tutorial), then launch its starter-templates plugin.
When choosing templates, click back before proceeding and explicitly select Elementor as the page builder — the tutorial warns against the block editor for this workflow.
Filter templates by Ecommerce, pick a free one (premium tags are paid), and let the importer install the pages, Elementor and WooCommerce.
Logo, font and color choices at import are placeholders — the presenter says they get replaced later, so don't over-invest there.
After import, use 'Edit with Elementor' on the homepage and replace text, images and backgrounds section by section rather than rebuilding.
caveats: Imported templates include demo products and categories (e.g. 'Indoor plants') that must be deleted.
Template import writes many pages/settings; check for leftover demo content before launch.
cards.source_name: How to Create an Ecommerce Website with WordPress 2026 (step by step).docx

cards.title: Elementor structure: sections, containers and widgets
cards.summary: Understand the three-level Elementor hierarchy and how to build a hero section from an empty canvas.
cards.use_when: Editing the homepage or a landing page in Elementor and you need to control layout and positioning.
steps: Treat the page as sections (full-width background bands, shown by the pink outline), containers inside them (gray dashed boxes), and widgets/elements inside containers.
Add a section with the plus button, pick Flexbox, and choose a column/container arrangement; templates or AI-generated layouts are alternative starting points.
To make a section fill the screen, select the container's six-dot handle, change minimum height units to VH and drag the slider to 100.
Drag widgets in from the element panel (Heading, Text Editor, Divider, Button, Image, Icon Box) and edit text either in the sidebar field or directly on canvas.
Center content vertically with the container's Justify Content setting.
Reorder by dragging sections on canvas or by dragging entries in the structure/layers panel.
Preview without editing outlines using the preview arrow, then publish to save.
caveats: Newer Elementor versions default to containers rather than the older section/column model; verify the current editor.
Two-height, viewport-sized sections can behave differently on mobile until you set responsive padding.
cards.source_name: How to Create an Ecommerce Website with WordPress 2026 (step by step).docx

cards.title: Style buttons for visibility: normal vs hover states, padding, radius
cards.summary: Configure button normal and hover states, padding and border radius so the CTA stands out on the page.
cards.use_when: Designing add-to-cart or buy-now buttons on a homepage, landing page or product page.
steps: Select the button widget and open Style; note there are separate Normal and Hover tabs — set both.
Set text color and background (classic solid color or gradient) for Normal; set a clearly different text and background for Hover so the change is obvious to shoppers.
Optionally apply a hover animation such as 'Grow' to draw attention to the CTA.
Control shape with Border Radius: 0 gives a square button, higher values approach a circle; the tutorial lands mid-range (~15).
Control size with Padding; unlink the four values when you want wide but not tall buttons (example: 32 left/right, 15 top/bottom).
Keep button padding and label short enough that the button doesn't read as a large box on mobile.
caveats: These are styling levers, not proven conversion lifts — validate any change against your own analytics.
Hover states don't exist on touch devices, so don't rely on hover alone to signal interactivity.
cards.source_name: How to Create an Ecommerce Website with WordPress 2026 (step by step).docx

cards.title: Video and image hero sections on the homepage
cards.summary: Use an Elementor section with a video or gradient background, then fix contrast so overlaid text stays readable.
cards.use_when: Building or replacing the homepage hero that showcases a top product.
steps: Select the hero section's six-dot handle, open Style > Background, and choose Classic (solid), Gradient, or the Video tab.
For video, host it (the tutorial uses an unlisted YouTube video) and paste the link into the video URL field.
Add a subtle gradient overlay or choose text colors that contrast with the moving background.
After adding the video, change text to white (or a contrasting color) in Style > Text Color for each heading and paragraph, since overlaying copy on video can obscure it.
Swap individual elements freely: duplicate a heading to create a subheading, adjust typography weight and size, and add a Divider at reduced width to separate content.
Use an Image widget for product visuals where video is not appropriate.
caveats: Background video typically will not autoplay on mobile and can look broken — plan a mobile-specific alternative (see responsive card).
Only use media you have the rights to host.
cards.source_name: How to Create an Ecommerce Website with WordPress 2026 (step by step).docx

cards.title: Header and footer are theme settings, not Elementor
cards.summary: Edit the Astra header via Customize (logo, menu, transparent header) while page content stays in Elementor.
cards.use_when: Changing the store logo, navigation menu or header background color.
steps: Open Customize from the admin bar — this controls the theme header and footer, which Elementor does not manage.
Replace the logo: untoggle the separate transparent logo option so one logo is used sitewide, then upload a transparent PNG and set the logo width (skip cropping so the image isn't cut).
Set the site title, which is what appears in the browser tab.
Enable a transparent header on the complete website, and uncheck it for WooCommerce product pages if you want the same header on PDPs.
Adjust header background under Design > Primary Header: choose a color (e.g. black) and reduce the slider to about half opacity for a translucent header.

Edit the navigation menu via the pencil icon > Configure Menu > Primary Menu: add Pages, Custom Links, Posts, Products or product categories, and drag items sideways under another item to create dropdown sub-items.
Set menu text/link color and hover color under Transparent Header > Design to match the site's palette.
Publish.
caveats: Theme options and labels shift between Astra versions; verify the current Customizer panels.
Changing header colors may require updating body-section text colors for contrast.
cards.source_name: How to Create an Ecommerce Website with WordPress 2026 (step by step).docx

cards.title: Organize the catalog with product categories and parent/child structure
cards.summary: Create product categories (and parents) so shoppers can sort and categories surface on the homepage.
cards.use_when: Organizing a WooCommerce product catalog into navigable categories and subcategories before building collection menus and homepage sections.
steps: Go to Products > Categories and delete demo categories that shipped with the template (e.g. 'Indoor plants').
Add a new category with a clear name, a simple lowercase slug for the URL, and optionally a parent category.
Use parent categories to group variants, e.g. put 'Wireless headphones' and 'Earbuds' under a parent 'Headphones'.
Skip thumbnail/description for now if they aren't ready — they can be added later.
Assign each product to the right category in the product editor (and uncheck Uncategorized) so it appears in that category's listings and the homepage sections that pull from it.
Add tags to products to help on-site search, using your own brand or product name as tags.
caveats: Categories are what on-site browsing and menu dropdowns rely on; tags help search but shouldn't replace categories.
A flat, one-level category set is fine for small catalogs — the tutorial starts that way.
cards.source_name: How to Create an Ecommerce Website with WordPress 2026 (step by step).docx

cards.title: Upsells and cross-sells in WooCommerce linked products
cards.summary: Use WooCommerce Linked Products so shoppers see an upgrade on the product page and add-ons in the cart.
cards.use_when: Setting product recommendations on a PDP and in the cart to raise average order value.
steps: In the product editor's Linked Products tab, add Upsells — these show on the product page as an upgraded or higher-priced alternative to the item being viewed.
Add Cross-sells — these appear in the cart when the shopper is close to checking out.
Search for the products by name in each field; the targets must already exist as products in the store.
Keep the relationship relevant (related product, not a random item) so the recommendation makes sense.
Review on the storefront: open a PDP to see upsells and add an item to cart to see cross-sells render.
caveats: Recommending unrelated items can distract from checkout; the tutorial's example pairs a cheaper headphone with a nicer one, not an arbitrary product.
Cross-sells add cart steps — measure whether they help or hurt checkout completion.
cards.source_name: How to Create an Ecommerce Website with WordPress 2026 (step by step).docx

cards.title: Clean up demo products before adding your own catalog
cards.summary: Delete template products and their trash, then replicate a configured product for the rest of the catalog instead of rebuilding each one.
cards.use_when: Starting a store from an imported template and needing to replace placeholder products.
steps: Go to Products > All Products, select all demo products, apply the 'Move to trash' bulk action, then empty the trash.
With an empty catalog, the 'Add product' flow prompts for product type: Physical (shipped), Variable (has variations like color/size), Grouped (a bundle sold as one).
Reuse the structure: duplicate an existing configured product and edit it for the next item rather than repeating every field from scratch.
Confirm new items appear in the homepage product sections that reference the catalog, and assign each to its category and price.
If product thumbnails look grainy in grids, change the product image size in Customizer to e.g. 900x600 and republish.
caveats: Duplicating carries over old images, descriptions and variations — scrub those before publishing.
Image-size values are examples from the tutorial, not measured optimal sizes.
cards.source_name: How to Create an Ecommerce Website with WordPress 2026 (step by step).docx

cards.title: Responsive design: serve different sections per device in Elementor
cards.summary: Duplicate a desktop section and use Elementor's responsive controls to show a simplified version only on mobile.
cards.use_when: Fixing the homepage on mobile/tablet, e.g. a background video that doesn't play on phones.
steps: Switch to the phone/tablet icon in Elementor's responsive preview and inspect the section — video backgrounds often render as a gray gap on mobile.
Duplicate the desktop hero section so you have two copies.
On the duplicate meant for mobile, open Advanced > Responsive and hide it on tablet and desktop, leaving mobile enabled.
On the original desktop section, hide it on mobile and leave tablet/desktop enabled, so each device sees one clean version.
In the mobile section, remove the video link (or leave it blank), set the background to a gradient, and add a product Image widget instead.
Use Advanced > Padding with the mobile-only indicator to space the section and keep content clear of the header; adjust per-element mobile settings like button position.
Preview each device view before publishing.
caveats: Duplicated sections multiply maintenance — update both when content changes.
Pixel values shown are illustrative; check across real devices.
cards.source_name: How to Create an Ecommerce Website with WordPress 2026 (step by step).docx

cards.title: Single product page spacing and button styling via Customize
cards.summary: Fix PDP padding and recolor add-to-cart buttons in the Customizer rather than in Elementor.
cards.use_when: Adjusting layout and colors on the WooCommerce product page so content clears the header and CTAs match the brand.
steps: Open the single product page and click Customize to reach the WooCommerce Single Product settings (these are theme options, not Elementor).
Under Single Product > Design, unlink the padding values and set top padding (example: 120px) so the content clears the sticky header.
Change the sticky add-to-cart button colors (background and hover) under the same Design panel; a page refresh may be needed for updates to show.
Change global button background/hover under Global > Buttons, then publish and refresh to confirm.
Edit the shipping-note text on the PDP (e.g. 'free shipping') under General > Single Product if your shipping terms differ.
Add a purchase note under the product's Advanced tab for a custom post-purchase message, and keep menu order at 0 unless you need manual sorting.
caveats: Setting padding without checking the responsive views can push content off small screens.
Customizer labels vary by theme version.
cards.source_name: How to Create an Ecommerce Website with WordPress 2026 (step by step).docx

cards.title: Edit Elementor sections with device-specific padding
cards.summary: Use Elementor's per-device padding controls and the mobile-only icon indicator to fix section spacing differently on mobile, tablet and desktop.
cards.use_when: Tuning store homepage, PDP or landing-page section spacing in Elementor so content isn't cut off or crammed on mobile while staying correct on desktop.
steps: Select the section by clicking its six-dot handle, then open the Advanced tab to reach padding controls.
Watch for the small device icon next to a control: if the icon is present the change applies only to that device; if it is absent the change is global across all breakpoints.
Add padding around the section, unlink the values, and push extra padding to the top to move content down away from the header.
Switch the editor viewport (desktop / tablet / mobile) and repeat the adjustment for each device that needs different spacing.
Also edit individual widgets per device — buttons, headings and image widgets each have their own responsive controls.
Click Publish to save, then use the preview (eyeball) icon to check the live rendering before moving on.
caveats: Remember the device icon rule: a global edit will overwrite the value on every breakpoint, so make global changes first and device-specific ones after.
If a section is disabled for desktop it won't render there at all — verify the correct breakpoint before assuming a layout is broken.
cards.source_name: How to Create an Ecommerce Website with WordPress 2026 (step by step).docx

cards.title: Center misaligned Elementor widgets per breakpoint
cards.summary: Fix widgets that sit off to the left on mobile by setting their Style > Position to center within the mobile-only viewport.
cards.use_when: Correcting a call-to-action button, heading or image on a store landing page that looks left-aligned or off-center on phones after template import.
steps: Switch the Elementor viewport to the device you want to fix (start with mobile).
Click the widget (for example the button) and open the Style tab, then find the Position setting.
Confirm the mobile device icon is showing next to the control before changing it, so the edit is scoped to that breakpoint only.
Set the position to center.
Switch back to desktop view — the widget automatically returns to its original alignment (for example left) because the change was mobile-scoped.
Repeat the same operation in tablet view, then Publish and preview.
caveats: If the device icon is not present, the alignment change will apply to all breakpoints — check before saving.
Responsive overrides only behave as expected if the original desktop layout was left intact.
cards.source_name: How to Create an Ecommerce Website with WordPress 2026 (step by step).docx

cards.title: Launch a WooCommerce store by switching from coming-soon to live
cards.summary: Take the WordPress/WooCommerce site out of store-coming-soon mode and save changes so shoppers can actually buy.
cards.use_when: Final go-live step after building and previewing a WooCommerce store, when checkout and product pages need to be publicly reachable.
steps: Finish all page building, responsive edits and content replacement, and Publish your work in the builder.
Preview the site with the eyeball icon to confirm layout, images, copy and store pages look correct on desktop and mobile.
Locate the store's coming-soon indicator/notice and click it to open the setting.
Change the status from Coming Soon to Live.
Save changes.
Verify on a logged-out browser or incognito window that product pages and checkout are reachable to the public.
caveats: Don't switch to Live before testing checkout, payments and shipping settings — going live exposes the store immediately.
Preview inside the editor is not the same as a public visit; confirm from an incognito session.
cards.source_name: How to Create an Ecommerce Website with WordPress 2026 (step by step).docx

cards.title: Customise an imported template by replacing images, colours and text
cards.summary: Build a store page faster by starting from a template and swapping images, text and colours rather than designing from scratch.
cards.use_when: Building a store homepage, category page or landing page quickly when a template already provides the section structure.
steps: Add or open the desired section and drop in an Image widget via the Add Element panel.
Replace the placeholder image by selecting the image control and choosing the desired file from the media library.
Overwrite placeholder copy with your own product, category or brand text.
Change the template's accent colours in Style settings so the page matches your brand palette.
Adjust spacing and alignment per device (see responsive padding/position cards) after swapping content, because template spacing rarely fits your assets.
Publish and preview to confirm the swapped assets render correctly.
caveats: Template images and copy may carry licensing/branding constraints — replace them before going live.
Swapping content often breaks the original spacing, so always re-check padding and alignment afterwards.
cards.source_name: How to Create an Ecommerce Website with WordPress 2026 (step by step).docx

cards.title: Claim the $1/month trial link before the 3-day window closes
cards.summary: Sequence Shopify account creation so the extended promotional trial price is secured before the free trial expires.
cards.use_when: Opening a new Shopify account for a store build and choosing which plan to start on.
steps: Start at Shopify's official site, enter email, click start free trial, create a password and complete signup. Shopify then redirects to a promotional offer (source describes 3 months at $1/month, roughly 96% off).
Activate the discounted plan immediately, or complete the short business setup questions first — the source says they take about 20 seconds and you still land on the dashboard afterward.
If you skipped the offer in the signup flow, the source says it can still be claimed from the lower-left corner of the dashboard, but only before the initial 3-day free trial expires.
Pick the Basic plan for a first store: it covers launching, accepting payments and running a functional store, and you can upgrade later.
Verify the current plan names, trial length and offer terms in your own admin before assuming the promotional pricing still exists.
caveats: Plan names, trial lengths and promotional pricing change; the source's figures are as-described at recording time.
The source explicitly skips promotional pitches — treat the offer as a billing detail, not the point of the build.
cards.source_name: Shopify Store Setup Full Tutorial 2026_ Step by Step.docx

cards.title: Know which three Shopify admin areas actually run the store
cards.summary: Reduce admin overwhelm to Products, Online Store and Settings, the three sections that control selling, appearance and configuration.
cards.use_when: Orienting yourself in a new Shopify admin before adding products, designing the storefront or configuring checkout.
steps: Treat the admin as the store's control center: Orders, Products, Customers, Marketing, Discounts, Content, Markets, Analytics all live in one menu.
Prioritize Products — this is where you add and manage the items you sell, including titles, descriptions, images, pricing, inventory and variants.
Then Online Store — where you select and edit themes, build pages and manage navigation and the visual front end.
Then Settings — where payments, shipping, taxes and store-wide configuration live.
The source claims these three areas cover almost everything that matters; use them as the map, not as a reason to ignore Orders, discounts or analytics once you are live.
Also note the source's framing: your store is technically already live at signup but password-protected, so you are optimizing an existing shell rather than starting from zero.
caveats: Admin layout and menu labels change between Shopify releases; verify the current interface rather than hunting for exact labels.
cards.source_name: Shopify Store Setup Full Tutorial 2026_ Step by Step.docx

cards.title: Choose a clean, brandable domain instead of an over-thought one
cards.summary: Domain naming criteria that protect trust and ad click-through, plus an AI ideation method to avoid blank-page stalls.
cards.use_when: Selecting the store domain before running ads, email or packaging that will display the URL.
steps: Run a quick ideation pass with a text AI — e.g. "generate 20 brandable domain names for a fitness apparel store" — to produce short variations instead of starting from nothing.

Apply the source's filter: one or two words at most; no hyphens or numbers (buyers mis-type them and forget whether numbers are spelled out); no unusual spellings that force double-checking; brandable rather than generic. The source contrasts generic descriptors unfavorably with names like Gymshark, Allbirds or Glossier.
Remember the impression cost: a myshopify.com URL or a long messy address appearing in an ad, email or packaging can create hesitation before a visitor reads a single product description.
The source frames the goal as clarity, not perfection — easy to spell and easy to pronounce if heard once.
Confirm availability and purchase inside Shopify where possible, so DNS connects automatically.
caveats: Brand examples are the source's illustrations, not verified performance data.
Perfectionism is explicitly called out as the failure mode; do not stall the build searching for an unused, flawless name.
cards.source_name: Shopify Store Setup Full Tutorial 2026_ Step by Step.docx

cards.title: Buy the domain inside Shopify vs. connecting an existing third-party domain
cards.summary: Two connection paths with different effort levels, plus the propagation window to plan your launch around.
cards.use_when: Setting up or migrating the store's domain before launch and before printing or advertising the URL.
steps: Fast path (buy new): go to Settings > Domains, click buy new domain, search the name, purchase if available. The source says it connects automatically with no manual DNS configuration.
Migration path (existing domain, e.g. from GoDaddy): go to Settings > Domains > connect existing domain. Copy the DNS records Shopify provides, paste them into the registrar's DNS settings, save.
Expect propagation to take a few hours; status may read as pending during that window. Do not treat pending as failure.
The source flags a trade-off on third-party registrars: lower first-year pricing but often higher renewals. Buying through Shopify is described as the smoother route for beginners.
Confirm the domain shows as connected before publishing, since launching on a broken domain creates immediate trust problems.
caveats: DNS record names and screens differ by registrar and Shopify release; verify against the current Shopify domain instructions.
The source's preference for buying through Shopify is a simplicity recommendation, not a cost guarantee.
cards.source_name: Shopify Store Setup Full Tutorial 2026_ Step by Step.docx

cards.title: Pick and publish a lightweight free Shopify theme before customizing
cards.summary: Theme selection criteria and the preview-then-publish habit that prevents installing a look you have not seen.
cards.use_when: Choosing the storefront theme (fashion, beauty, large-catalog or general store) before any design work.
steps: Go to Online Store > Themes and scroll to explore free themes. The source names Dawn (minimal, versatile — suits fashion, beauty and general stores), Horizon (modern, bold — for stronger visual impact) and Trade (built for larger catalogs with many products).
Always click the theme and choose view demo before installing. Preview first rather than installing blind.
If it matches your brand direction, click add to theme library, then publish; the storefront updates within seconds.

Weigh paid themes carefully: the source cites $200–$400 with extra built-in features, and argues most beginners do not need them because free themes now offer clean layouts, strong mobile optimization and fast loading. Speed matters because visitors abandon slow pages, especially on mobile.
Do not over-analyze: the source says you can switch themes later, so pick one matching your niche and catalog size and move on.
caveats: Theme names, features and paid pricing change; verify in the current theme store.
Theme choice is not a permanent decision — treat it as reversible.
cards.source_name: Shopify Store Setup Full Tutorial 2026_ Step by Step.docx

cards.title: Turn a default theme into a brand with global settings and a transparent logo
cards.summary: The fast foundational pass — hero H1, colors, typography, logo — that makes a template feel intentional before deeper section work.
cards.use_when: Customizing a freshly published theme so it stops looking generic and starts reading as a real brand.
steps: Open Edit theme. The left panel lists sections; the right panel is a live preview you refresh as you change things.
Start with the header structure and alignment even if your logo is not ready yet.
Go to Theme settings > Colors: set the primary brand color and keep the background white. The source argues white backgrounds generally convert better because products stand out on them.

Go to typography settings and choose simple, readable fonts (the source names Montserrat and Source Sans Pro). Decorative fonts are explicitly called a clarity risk — if customers struggle to read, they leave.

Generate a minimal logo with an AI image tool or free logo tools; text-based logos work well. Then use a background remover such as remove.bg to export a transparent PNG — the source calls messy logo backgrounds a common beginner mistake that instantly lowers perceived quality.
Upload via the header/theme settings and adjust size so it looks balanced, not oversized or tiny.
Optionally build a cohesive palette by asking an AI for a primary, secondary and accent hex set, then paste the primary hex into the color field and keep contrast high so text stays legible.
Optionally use the theme editor's AI section recommendations: describe your brand in a few sentences and it generates layout suggestions for your niche.
caveats: AI-generated palettes and sections are starting points; you still apply and review them inside the theme editor.
White background and font choices are the source's conversion-oriented opinions, not tested rules for every brand.
cards.source_name: Shopify Store Setup Full Tutorial 2026_ Step by Step.docx

cards.title: Structure header, menu style and announcement bar for product count
cards.summary: Match navigation pattern to catalog size and use a benefit-driven announcement bar to guide first actions.
cards.use_when: Configuring the storefront header, menus and announcement bar before driving traffic to the store.
steps: In the theme editor, click header and review layout options — logo left or centered, depending on the aesthetic you want.
Choose the menu style by catalog size: a drawer menu for stores with heavy mobile traffic, a dropdown menu for smaller catalogs, a mega menu for large stores with many categories.
Keep the menu short. The source's reasoning: too many items create confusion and confused buyers rarely complete purchases.
Enable the announcement bar and write a benefit-led prompt, e.g. free shipping on orders over $50 or a limited-time launch sale. The source frames these as small urgency cues that guide action.
Refresh the preview and check the header/announcement combination doesn't crowd the top of the page, then re-check in mobile view.
caveats: Menu-style suitability is the source's rule of thumb; test what fits your own traffic mix.
Urgency prompts should reflect real terms — do not advertise a threshold or sale you will not honor.
cards.source_name: Shopify Store Setup Full Tutorial 2026_ Step by Step.docx

cards.title: Build a hero banner that communicates one clear benefit
cards.summary: Hero image, headline, subtext and CTA decisions with a mobile contrast check.
cards.use_when: Designing or refining the homepage hero section — the first thing visitors see from ads or social traffic.
steps: Source the image direction first: prompt an AI with something like "produce a hero banner image that matches this brand" to get a concept aligned to your niche and positioning.

Then use Shopify's built-in image library: click the hero section, select image, explore free images, and search niche keywords (fitness, skincare, jewelry). Choose high-resolution files only — a blurry banner immediately hurts credibility.
Set a headline that communicates a benefit or outcome rather than a product name; the source's example is "confidence starts with skin."

Add one short subtext sentence supporting the message, then a clear CTA button such as Shop now or Explore collection. The source says never leave a banner without a button because buttons drive the next click.
Set the main homepage hero heading to an H1 tag so search engines can read the page structure.
Preview on mobile: confirm the headline is readable and does not blend into the image. If contrast is weak, add a subtle overlay behind the text.
caveats: Free stock imagery can look generic; the source treats image direction and resolution as the quality levers, not the source.
H1 placement is a structural SEO practice the source asserts, not a ranking guarantee.
cards.source_name: Shopify Store Setup Full Tutorial 2026_ Step by Step.docx

cards.title: Generate policies from Shopify templates and customize every detail
cards.summary: Use built-in policy templates, then edit shipping and refund specifics so disputes and chargebacks are reduced.
cards.use_when: Setting up privacy, terms, shipping and refund policies before the store accepts public orders.
steps: Go to Settings > Policies. Shopify provides templates for Privacy Policy, Terms of Service, Shipping Policy and Refund Policy; click create from template for each.
Read through each generated policy and confirm it matches your actual business rather than publishing the default text unchanged.

Draft shipping terms you will actually honor: delivery windows, handling time and conditions. The source notes that ignoring shipping details is a common beginner mistake that leads to disputes and unnecessary refunds.
For the refund policy, decide the return window in days and who pays return shipping. The source ties clarity here directly to fewer chargebacks.

If drafting is slow, prompt an AI (e.g. "write a simple shipping policy for this brand") for a starting draft, then replace every placeholder with your real terms — the source warns never to copy blindly.
Save and confirm Shopify places the policies in the footer automatically.
caveats: Templates are a starting point, not legal advice; the source repeatedly instructs reviewing and customizing them.
Policy content must reflect what you actually do, or the mismatch creates the disputes it was meant to prevent.
cards.source_name: Shopify Store Setup Full Tutorial 2026_ Step by Step.docx

cards.title: Write a product page by describing the product, then generating and rewriting the copy
cards.summary: Replace supplier text with benefit-led descriptions using Shopify's AI writing assistant plus short paragraphs and a brand-voice edit.
cards.use_when: Adding a product to the catalog and building the PDP copy that will carry conversion.
steps: Go to Products > Add product. Write a simple, specific title so customers immediately know what the item is without guessing.
Avoid copying supplier descriptions — the source says generic supplier text lowers trust because it reads overused.
Write to benefits, not just features: explain how the product helps, improves or solves a problem, in short paragraphs that scan easily.
To move faster, click the sparkle icon in the description box, briefly describe the product and let Shopify generate a draft — then edit it to match your brand voice.
Keep formatting clean; better readability supports conversion.
Also enable Track quantity and enter your available stock so you cannot oversell. The source notes dropshippers may disable tracking, but says tracking helps prevent order issues.
Set the search engine listing preview: include your main keyword in the page title and write a concise meta description explaining what the product is.
caveats: AI drafts are editing starting points, not finished copy.
The track-quantity advice is framed with a legitimate dropshipping exception, so it is a situational default.
cards.source_name: Shopify Store Setup Full Tutorial 2026_ Step by Step.docx

cards.title: Use compare-at pricing, variants and 1000px+ images on the product page
cards.summary: Pricing display, product options and image quality checks that shape perceived value and reduce refunds.
cards.use_when: Completing the pricing, options and imagery fields for each new product listing.
steps: Fill in both price and compare at price. The source's example: if the product sells for $49, set compare-at to $79 and Shopify displays the higher price struck through, creating perceived value. Keep the discount realistic — the source says overstated discounts reduce credibility.
If the product has options like size or color, click add options and create variants (for example small, medium, large). Clear options smooth the buying process.
Configure physical package dimensions in the product details so shipping calculations have accurate inputs.
Upload bright, clear photos at least 1000x1000 pixels. Zoom in and check for blur; replace anything low quality. Sharper images build confidence and the source links this to fewer refund requests.
Add product tags so the item can be grouped and found by your collections and internal search.
Order the images so the first shot reads as the clearest representation of the product.
caveats: Compare-at pricing only reads as credible when the original price is genuine; the source warns that exaggerated discounts backfire.
The 1000x1000 pixel figure is the source's minimum guidance, not a platform requirement.
cards.source_name: Shopify Store Setup Full Tutorial 2026_ Step by Step.docx

cards.title: Choose manual vs. automatic collections and surface them on the homepage
cards.summary: Collection type decision by catalog growth, plus the homepage section that gets products out of the backend.
cards.use_when: Organizing the catalog into browsable categories and featuring them on the homepage.
steps: Go to Products > Collections > Create collection and name it clearly so customers know exactly what is inside.

Choose manual collections to hand-pick individual products; choose automatic (smart) collections to group products by rules. The source's reasoning: automatic collections save time as the store grows.
Add a collection image and a short description explaining what the category includes — this is what makes the browse step feel intentional rather than random.
Return to the homepage in the theme editor, add a section that features your collection and select the correct category from the section settings.
Preview the page and confirm products are now visible in the storefront rather than hidden in the backend.
Use product tags consistently at the product level if you rely on smart collections, since rule-based grouping depends on those fields.
caveats: Smart collection behavior depends on the rules and tags you configure; a mistagged product silently lands in the wrong collection.
Collection image and description quality is what the source credits for perceived structure, not the collection type itself.
cards.source_name: Shopify Store Setup Full Tutorial 2026_ Step by Step.docx

cards.title: Prune and rebuild the main menu around collections, then test it on mobile
cards.summary: Navigation hygiene as a conversion issue: remove defaults, add collections, verify on a phone.
cards.use_when: Cleaning up store navigation before launch so customers can actually find products.
steps: Go to Online Store > Navigation and open your main menu. Remove default links such as home, catalog and contact that add no shopping path. The source's claim: cleaner menus convert better because they reduce decision fatigue.
Click add menu item, name it clearly, click link, choose collections, select the matching collection and save. Repeat for your main categories.
Limit the number of links — the source argues more options make customers hesitate.

Open the theme preview and switch to the mobile view. Review spacing, test dropdown behavior and check the menu does not feel crowded; most buyers shop on their phone, so the layout must be thumb-friendly.
Click every link, submenu and collection to confirm there are no broken paths or dead ends.
Confirm your policies and support pages are reachable from the footer.
caveats: Menu naming and link-picking flows change between Shopify versions; verify the current admin.
The 'fewer menu items convert better' position is the source's stated rationale, not a measured benchmark.
cards.source_name: Shopify Store Setup Full Tutorial 2026_ Step by Step.docx

cards.title: Order the homepage: hero, collections, featured products, then trust blocks
cards.summary: Sequence homepage sections so the page reads as guided rather than random, adding testimonials and an FAQ.
cards.use_when: Arranging or auditing homepage sections after products and collections exist.
steps: Open the homepage in the theme editor and use Add section.
Add a testimonials section. Even a few short quotes raise credibility; the source says pre-launch feedback from friends or early testers is acceptable when you have no buyers yet.
Add an FAQ section covering the questions customers actually ask — shipping times, return policy, sizing. The source ties FAQs to reduced hesitation and fewer support emails.

Review the whole page top to bottom and check the order: hero, then collections, then featured products, then trust elements like testimonials and FAQs. When it flows in that order the homepage feels guided rather than random.
Look for anything that feels cluttered; the source compares the homepage to a storefront window where a random layout sends visitors away quickly.
Re-check the same sequence in mobile view.
caveats: Testimonials must be genuine; the source allows early tester feedback but misrepresenting reviews undermines the trust the section exists to build.
Section names and availability vary by theme.
cards.source_name: Shopify Store Setup Full Tutorial 2026_ Step by Step.docx

cards.title: Activate Shopify Payments plus at least one alternative gateway
cards.summary: Payment setup that connects payouts and adds a familiar fallback option for hesitant and international buyers.
cards.use_when: Enabling payment methods before taking the store off password protection.
steps: In admin, find Shopify Payments, click choose a provider, select it and complete setup — this connects payouts directly to your bank account and enables major card brands without separate integrations.
Add at least one alternative method. The source calls activating only one method a common beginner mistake because it limits flexibility and can reduce trust.
Enable PayPal: it is often already linked to your account email; otherwise click activate PayPal, log in and grant permissions — the source estimates about a minute.
Consider that PayPal is familiar to international customers and may increase their comfort at checkout.
Check what gateways are actually available in your region; the source notes some countries require specific providers.
Reason from the source's principle: the smoother the checkout path, the less friction stands between a ready buyer and a completed order.
caveats: Gateway availability and setup flows vary by country and change over time — verify what your region supports.
Identity or document verification may be required and can delay payouts.
cards.source_name: Shopify Store Setup Full Tutorial 2026_ Step by Step.docx

cards.title: Define shipping zones, rates and a free-shipping threshold
cards.summary: Zone, rate-model and threshold decisions that keep delivery expectations clear and lift average order value.
cards.use_when: Configuring shipping and delivery settings before launch, including whether to ship internationally.
steps: Go to Settings > Shipping and delivery, open your primary zone and define the countries you actually ship to. Decide deliberately between domestic-only and worldwide — the source notes global shipping adds complexity and starting simple is usually better.

Pick a pricing model. Flat rate means a single fixed charge customers understand; dynamic rates calculate in real time by weight and carrier. The source says flat rate is often easier for beginners to manage and avoids confusion.
Consider a free shipping threshold — the source's example is free over $75 — because customers respond strongly to free shipping and will add items to qualify, which lifts average order value.
If you ship internationally, create separate zones and set higher flat rates or calculated rates for them.
Add a handling buffer where it applies; the source describes adding around $5 to cover handling.
State delivery times clearly everywhere shipping is mentioned. The source links long shipping without clear expectations to complaints.
caveats: The $75 threshold and $5 handling buffer are the source's illustrative examples, not benchmarks for your margins — model them against your own cost structure.
Carrier-calculated rates depend on accurate product weights and package dimensions.
cards.source_name: Shopify Store Setup Full Tutorial 2026_ Step by Step.docx

cards.title: Configure taxes by verifying your own obligations first
cards.summary: Use Shopify's automatic tax tools, but establish nexus or VAT registration requirements before relying on them.
cards.use_when: Setting up tax collection for a store selling domestically or across borders.
steps: Go to Settings > Taxes and duties. The source's starting point: requirements depend entirely on your location, so verify your obligations under local law rather than guessing.
Enable automatic tax collection, which calculates based on the customer's location, and review the rates configured for your region to confirm they align.
If registered in the United States, review your state nexus rules to determine whether you must collect sales tax.
If operating in the European Union, check VAT requirements and registration thresholds.
Consult a tax professional if obligations are unclear — the source says mistakes here become expensive quickly.
Once configured correctly, Shopify handles the calculations in the background.
caveats: The source explicitly defers to local law and professionals; do not treat Shopify's defaults as compliance.
Nexus and VAT rules change; re-verify as you add markets.
cards.source_name: Shopify Store Setup Full Tutorial 2026_ Step by Step.docx

cards.title: Install three apps, not ten — reviews, email, tracking
cards.summary: A lean app stack with a review tool chosen for free-plan strength versus photo-centric reviews.
cards.use_when: Adding apps to a new store without degrading page speed before launch.
steps: Go to Apps, open the Shopify app store and search only for essential tools. The source says most new stores need three things: a review app, an email app and a tracking/analytics app.

Prioritize the review app because the source says reviews increase conversions almost immediately. Two named options are Judge.me and Loox: Judge.me is described as stronger on its free plan, Loox as focused on photo-based reviews.
Enable automatic review requests so customers receive follow-up emails after purchase.
Install a tracking/analytics app so you can see traffic sources, best-performing products and where people drop off. The source's framing: guessing is not a strategy.
Resist installing many apps at once — the source says every added app adds weight and site speed affects conversion. Start lean and expand only when the business needs more.
Review pricing and features before installing each app, especially as a store scales past the free tier.
caveats: App features and free-tier limits change; the source's app comparisons reflect its recording time.
Review apps may require configuration to avoid sending requests that look spammy or mistimed.
cards.source_name: Shopify Store Setup Full Tutorial 2026_ Step by Step.docx

cards.title: Run the pre-launch checklist: store details, domain, test order, mobile, policies, links
cards.summary: The final verification pass that catches small errors before the store goes public.
cards.use_when: The last step before removing password protection and making the store publicly accessible.
steps: Verify store details: Settings > Store details — business name correct, email accurate, and store currency matching your target market. The source warns the wrong currency can confuse buyers and cause checkout abandonment.
Check the domain: Settings > Domains should show Connected. If it still shows pending, allow a few hours for DNS propagation rather than launching on a broken domain.

Test payments: enable test mode in payment settings, place a test order yourself, walk through the full checkout and confirm the order confirmation email actually arrives. Then disable test mode before launch.
Review the store on your phone: scroll slowly, tap every button, add a product to the cart and complete checkout. Most customers shop on mobile, so the experience must feel smooth.
Open every policy page from the footer and read the first paragraph — confirm your business name appears correctly and no placeholder or incomplete text remains.
Click every menu item, submenu and collection to confirm no link leads to an empty or broken page.
caveats: The source frames these as low-effort checks that prevent large post-launch problems; skipping the payment test is called out as risky because failed payments damage trust quickly.
Test mode must be turned back off — launching with it active blocks real orders.
cards.source_name: Shopify Store Setup Full Tutorial 2026_ Step by Step.docx

cards.title: Remove password protection and verify the live store as a customer
cards.summary: The publishing step plus a first-visitor walkthrough of the live domain.
cards.use_when: Taking the store public for the first time, immediately before sharing the link on social or with testers.
steps: Go to Online Store and click remove password. The source describes this as the single step that makes the store publicly accessible — no preview mode, no restriction.
Confirm the correct theme is live: go to Online Store > Themes and check your current theme shows as live. If it does not, click publish and confirm.
Open a new browser tab, manually type your domain, and browse as a first-time visitor would: homepage, open a product, add it to cart, walk through checkout.
Then start distributing the link — social bios, messages, a friend — and collect feedback rather than continuing to polish.
The source's closing framing: the goal is progress, not perfection; keep improving and testing after launch.
Also enable the email and SMS marketing opt-in checkboxes at the checkout/sign-in step so buyer consent is captured directly.
caveats: Launching before collecting feedback is preferable to endless pre-launch tweaking, per the source; but re-run the checklist if any admin changes were made after the test order.
Marketing opt-ins must match the consent rules in your jurisdiction.
cards.source_name: Shopify Store Setup Full Tutorial 2026_ Step by Step.docx

cards.title: Shopify backend launch order
cards.summary: Sequence the pre-launch Shopify backend tasks in the order that prevents rework: general settings, payments, shipping, policies, domain, then remove the storefront password.
cards.use_when: Preparing a newly built Shopify store to go live (final backend pass before publishing).
steps: In Settings > General, confirm store name, billing address, currency and default units. Getting these wrong affects order records later.

Settings > Payments: activate Shopify Payments and connect the bank account. Have an ID document (driver's licence or passport) ready — identity verification is part of activation. Optionally add extra methods (e.g. crypto) via Add payment method; availability varies by region.
Settings > Shipping and delivery: define zones and rates (details in the shipping card).
Settings > Policies: generate refund, privacy, terms and contact templates; write a custom shipping policy (no template).
Settings > Domains: connect an existing domain or buy one (the tutorial quotes roughly $16/year; verify current pricing).
Online store: click Remove password — the store is inaccessible to customers until this is done.
caveats: The presenter skips Shopify's onboarding questionnaire, noting it does not change what you get in the backend; skipping is fine but you must supply business details from your own records.
Domain pricing and payment-method availability change over time — verify the current Shopify interface.
Tax setup is jurisdiction-specific; consult a tax professional.
cards.source_name: Shopify Tutorial for Beginners 2026 - Full Store Setup Guide.docx

cards.title: Adding product variants for size and colour
cards.summary: Use Shopify's variant section to sell size/colour combinations, setting per-variant prices where larger sizes or colours should cost more.
cards.use_when: Product setup for an apparel store where one listing must cover multiple sizes or colours.
steps: Open the variant section while editing a product and add options such as size and colour.
Add each option value so Shopify creates the variant grid.

Set a distinct price per variant where justified (e.g. larger sizes or premium colours). In the tutorial's example the base product is $49 and variants are left at the default, but Shopify supports different prices per variant.
Check inventory per variant after saving so each size/colour tracks separately.
Save and confirm the variants appear on the product page and are selectable.
caveats: Variant-level pricing is supported but the tutorial does not test it here; verify on your own listing.
Skipping variants entirely means one price and one stock count for the whole product.
cards.source_name: Shopify Tutorial for Beginners 2026 - Full Store Setup Guide.docx

cards.title: Compare-at price strike-through
cards.summary: Enter a higher 'compare at' price so the product page shows the current price as a discount off a struck-through original.
cards.use_when: Pricing a product on its Shopify product page when you want visible discount framing.
steps: While editing a product, set the Price field to the actual selling price (e.g. $49 in the tutorial).
Fill the Compare at price field with the higher reference price. Shopify renders it as a strikethrough next to the live price.
Save and preview the product page to check the discount reads clearly and the reference price is credible.
caveats: The source presents this purely as a visual discount effect; it does not validate the fairness or legality of the reference price.
Displaying a permanently raised compare-at price undermines trust if customers see the 'discount' never ends.
cards.source_name: Shopify Tutorial for Beginners 2026 - Full Store Setup Guide.docx

cards.title: Inventory tracking and out-of-stock behaviour
cards.summary: Decide whether an item shows 'sold out' or keeps selling when inventory hits zero, based on whether you can actually restock on demand.
cards.use_when: Backend inventory setup for a store deciding how to handle a product running out.
steps: Under Inventory, enter the current stock count; Shopify decrements it automatically on each sale.
Leave 'continue selling when out of stock' off if you want the storefront to show a sold-out state when the count reaches zero.
Turn it on if the product can be sourced after the sale (e.g. dropshipping) so checkout is not blocked.
When new stock arrives, manually update the count.
If you enable continued selling, watch that you can genuinely fulfil those orders or your refund/dispute rate will suffer.
caveats: The source frames this as 'up to you' with no single rule; it notes manually adjusting the number when restocking.
cards.source_name: Shopify Tutorial for Beginners 2026 - Full Store Setup Guide.docx

cards.title: Manual collections: build category pages from a product list
cards.summary: Create manual collections so the storefront can show category pages (e.g. Shirts) and home-page grids built from hand-picked products.
cards.use_when: Organising products into shoppable categories for navigation and the home page.
steps: Go to Products > Collections and add a collection.
Give it a clear category title and upload a collection image — the image appears in collection lists and grids.
Keep the collection type as Manual so you control membership.
Under Products, click Browse, select the products for this collection and add them, then Save.
Repeat for each category and for any curated set (the tutorial also builds a 'New arrivals' collection for home-page featuring).
If Shopify pre-creates collections you do not want (e.g. a default Home page collection), delete it to keep the list clean.
caveats: Manual collections do not auto-update as new products are added — you maintain them by hand, so revisit them when you add products.
Collection images interact with the storefront layout (grids and lists) so choose crops that read at thumbnail size.
cards.source_name: Shopify Tutorial for Beginners 2026 - Full Store Setup Guide.docx

cards.title: Delete default shipping zones before adding your own
cards.summary: Remove Shopify's default weight-based US zone and rates, then build your own zone and flat rates so pricing reflects your actual fulfilment.
cards.use_when: Shipping configuration on a new store where default rates do not match your shipping plan.
steps: Settings > Shipping and delivery shows a profile for all products (one profile is fine for a simple store).
Inspect the default zone: domestic shipping with weight-based rates and a free-shipping threshold ($50 and up in the tutorial).
Delete the default zone via the three-dot menu > Delete — the source stresses this as a necessary step before adding your own.
Click Add shipping zone, type the region (e.g. US), select it and Click done.
Click Add rate, choose Flat rate (or dynamic rates by weight/volume/carrier), pick the shipping type (Standard, Express, Economy) and set the price — the tutorial uses Standard $6 and Express $15.
Save and confirm the buyer-facing options at checkout.
caveats: The transcript's 'Add rate' menu offers flat, dynamic and carrier-based rates; use flat only if you are not metering weight or volume.
The $6/$15 figures are the source's example prices, not a benchmark — set rates to match your real costs.
cards.source_name: Shopify Tutorial for Beginners 2026 - Full Store Setup Guide.docx

cards.title: Product shipping weight and box volume
cards.summary: Fill shipping weight and volume on products only if you intend to charge weight- or volume-based rates; flat-rate shippers can skip them.
cards.use_when: Product setup where you are deciding whether to populate shipping dimensions.
steps: Under the product's Shipping section, enter the weight of the product and the volume of the box you ship it in.
Use these fields only if your shipping rates are calculated by weight or volume.
If you charge a flat rate, leave them blank — the tutorial deliberately skips them because it uses flat rates.
caveats: Weight/volume only affects pricing if the matching rate type is active in shipping settings; filling fields without a dynamic rate does nothing.
Accurate numbers matter later if you switch to dynamic rates; loose estimates produce wrong charges.
cards.source_name: Shopify Tutorial for Beginners 2026 - Full Store Setup Guide.docx

cards.title: Product description and imagery for the PDP
cards.summary: Write the title and description first, then add high-quality images and choose which one leads on the product page.
cards.use_when: Adding or improving a product listing on a Shopify store.
steps: Enter the product title, then the description; if stuck, use Shopify's built-in AI description helper (source offers this without judging quality).
Drag several high-quality product images in, showing the product in its best light.
Rearrange the image order because the first image is the one customers see on product and collection pages.
Optionally complete the search-engine listing section of the product to control how the item appears in search results (the source leaves it default here).
Save and preview on desktop and mobile.
caveats: The source notes you should use high-quality images but offers no pixel or count guidance; decide based on your product.
AI-written descriptions are offered as a convenience, not vetted for accuracy or brand voice.
cards.source_name: Shopify Tutorial for Beginners 2026 - Full Store Setup Guide.docx

cards.title: Pre-launch asset preparation checklist
cards.summary: Prepare logo, favicon, colors, fonts and product/collection assets before touching the Shopify theme to avoid rework.
cards.use_when: You are about to build or rebuild a Shopify storefront and need to decide what to gather before starting theme customization.
steps: Prepare a logo as a transparent-background PNG (remove background with Canva, CapCut, or an AI background remover if you only have a colored-background version).
Prepare a square favicon - the small icon shown in the browser tab; a single brand letter is enough, keep it simple.

Lock a palette of four or five hex colors containing both dark and light values so you have contrast flexibility later in design; choose colors that make sense for the niche (blues for water-related products, greens for nature-related ones).

Choose one or two fonts supported by the selected theme, and check matching fonts are available for other brand assets. Custom fonts may require theme configuration or code; verify the chosen theme rather than assuming a hired developer is mandatory.
Prepare product list, collection list, product photos, lifestyle photos, and the About Us copy before building, since having them ready makes store work substantially easier.
caveats: The source presents the four-to-five-color rule as a working habit, not an enforced standard.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Choosing a Shopify plan by card rate and staff seats
cards.summary: Compare Basic, Grow and Advanced on card rates, staff seats and global/market features, and check legacy accounts separately.
cards.use_when: You are deciding which Shopify plan to subscribe to, or whether upgrading will pay for itself at your current sales volume.
steps: Compare the card rates the source cites: Basic 1.5%, Grow 1.3%, Advanced 1.1% on store payments - the main difference between tiers in this account.
Estimate your monthly processed sales and check whether the rate saving on the higher tier exceeds the price difference before upgrading purely for rates.
Check staff seats: Basic allows roughly one to two users, Grow up to five, Advanced up to 15; if multiple people must manage orders or the storefront, factor that in.
Check whether you sell into multiple markets or need global settings; the source says market/global features differ by tier, so international sellers may need Grow or Advanced.
Treat Shopify Plus separately: it is the only plan that allows customizing the Shopify checkout page, and the source cites roughly $2,000-$2,300/month - relevant only at an advanced stage.

If your store is old, open Settings and audit which features you actually have: the source reports legacy accounts were migrated with varying entitlements, so an old Grow account may or may not include global settings.
Verify plan pricing, card rates and seat limits in the current Shopify admin before committing, since these change.
caveats: The 1.5/1.3/1.1% card rates are the source's figures at recording time; verify current rates.
Plan names, seat counts and Plus pricing are the source's account and may have since changed.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Store details, currency, and order numbering configuration
cards.summary: Set store name, contact email, billing region, currency and order ID settings so customer-facing notifications and localization are correct.
cards.use_when: You are in Shopify Settings > General during initial store setup and need to configure identity, currency and order numbering.
steps: Under General > Store details, set the store name exactly as you want customers to see it - it appears on order confirmation emails - and use a frequently-checked email for the store email address, ideally a branded one (e.g. hello@yourstore.com).
Set the billing/legal business address to the region where the business is registered; the source says this drives which payment and shipping options, plus market behavior, Shopify offers you.

Under Store defaults, set the store currency to your business region (e.g. EUR for a France-registered business) and change currency formatting there; per-market display currencies are managed under Markets and depend on payment gateway availability.
Set the backup region, which is where customers outside your defined markets land by default.
Choose the unit system you personally understand (e.g. kilograms).

If you do not want customers inferring your order volume from order numbers (relevant during large launches), add a prefix or extra digits in the order ID settings so numbers are longer and harder to guess.
caveats: Multi-currency display for foreign customers requires a suitable payment gateway such as Shopify Payments; availability depends on the country where the business is registered (the source notes limitations in some Middle East markets).
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Registering Shopify with your own owner email
cards.summary: Sign up with an email you control so you remain the store owner, then complete payment and business details in one pass.
cards.use_when: You are creating a new Shopify account, possibly with help from an agency or freelancer.
steps: Sign up using your own email, not a contractor's or agency's address; the source stresses that only the store owner can change currencies, delete the store and similar critical actions.
You can start on a personal Gmail, but plan to create a branded email later and use it for customer-facing communication to look more professional.
