Complete the payment method step (credit card or PayPal) to start the trial; the source describes Shopify commonly offering something like a short free trial then a heavily discounted first three months.
Fill in business information properly at signup even though it can be edited later - under General settings this drives payment, shipping and market options.
Set your store name when prompted; it can be changed afterward but appears in customer notifications, so choose deliberately.
caveats: Trial length and introductory pricing vary; the source describes seeing seven-day and 14-day trials and roughly three months at $1 in different periods - confirm the current offer.
Business-location restrictions mean some payment features (e.g. Shopify Payments) may not be available in your country.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Using role-based staff permissions instead of blanket access
cards.summary: Add staff users with custom roles scoped to exactly the admin areas they need, and use collaborator access as a cheaper workaround.
cards.use_when: You need to give an employee, contractor or agency access to your Shopify admin without exposing sales figures or settings.
steps: Upgrade to a plan with enough staff seats (the source moved to Grow to add users beyond the Basic limit).
In Settings > Users, add the person's email; they receive a staff invitation to accept.
Instead of a default role, create a custom role: name it, describe it, then tick exact permissions per admin area (home, products, orders, markets, etc.).
Be deliberate about orders access - the source warns that order permissions let the person see your sales numbers, so grant it only where operationally necessary.

If you cannot add a user on your plan, use collaborator access instead: share your myshopify.com domain and collaboration code so the developer or app requests access, then approve them as a collaborator.
Remove access at any time as the store owner.
caveats: Collaborator access is a workaround for the user-seat limit, not a full substitute - the source says at some point most stores genuinely need a paid staff seat, e.g. an order manager.
Admin navigation and permission labels may change; verify in the current Shopify interface.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Connecting a custom domain and handling DNS records
cards.summary: Buy a .com domain early, connect it to Shopify, and learn to add DNS records yourself because future apps will require it.
cards.use_when: You are moving from the default myshopify.com URL to a branded customer-facing domain, or an app asks you to edit DNS records.
steps: Check domain availability when you first choose your brand name - the source warns that later, taken or premium names can be expensive or unavailable.
Prefer the .com for customer familiarity and cross-market recognition; consider also buying other extensions (.co, .au, .de) defensively so nobody else registers your brand name.
Buy either directly through Shopify (simplest, auto-linked to the store) or through a registrar like GoDaddy and use Settings > Domains > Connect existing to link it.
Note that your myshopify.com domain remains important internally - apps and support may ask for it - even though customers should never see it.

If automatic linking is unavailable, log into your registrar, open the domain's Manage DNS section, and add the records the requesting tool specifies: it usually provides type, name and value; the source says most tools require about three records.
Save the records and allow propagation time before testing.
Apply the same DNS-record workflow later for sender emails (Klaviyo, Omnisend) and review apps.
caveats: The source notes it is not certain every registrar behaves identically to GoDaddy; consult the specific provider's DNS interface.
Each DNS tool supplies its own record set - do not copy records between tools.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Setting up store policies and return rules
cards.summary: Generate and customize privacy, terms, shipping, return/refund and contact policies, enable native return rules, and link them in the footer.
cards.use_when: You are preparing to launch or run ads and need legally presentable store policies plus a workable returns process.
steps: In Settings > Policies, use Shopify's insert-template option for each policy (privacy, terms of service, shipping, contact information, terms of sale, legal notice) and then edit the template to match your actual business rather than publishing it untouched.
Configure return rules so customers can initiate returns from their customer account; set the return window and shipping rates in the manage settings.
Keep the shipping policy distinct from actual checkout shipping rates - the source notes rates are configured elsewhere, while the policy communicates how you manage shipping generally.
Link shipping and return/refund policies in the product page where relevant, and all policies in the footer at minimum; the source treats this as required for running ads and for legal coverage.
For contact information, review the auto-filled template - it pulls from your general business details - and edit anything you do not want published (e.g. a personal address).
caveats: The source recommends double-checking policies with a lawyer or legal advisor, especially for the EU and UAE; it flags the UK privacy policy as having different rules.
Shopify's default templates are described as generally good but needing tweaking.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Choosing customer support tooling by catalog complexity
cards.summary: Start with the free Shopify Inbox and migrate to AI-assisted support once your catalog or product education demands scale.
cards.use_when: You are deciding how customers will ask pre-purchase questions and how you will answer them at launch versus at scale.
steps: For a new or simple store, install Shopify Inbox: the source describes it as free, with a phone app and a view of each customer's order history so you can reply with context rather than cold.

For large catalogs or education-heavy niches (cosmetics, skincare, electronics) where customers ask many product questions, plan to move to a tool with AI reply features; the source names Gorgias and Tidio as examples.
Use the customer's order and browsing history visible in the inbox to tailor the answer - the source explicitly contrasts context-based replies with random ones.
Before launch, check that contact information is complete in your policies so the support channel is discoverable.
caveats: The source describes the AI option as what you may need later, not a launch requirement; a simple business can run on Shopify Inbox.
Tool names and feature sets change - verify current capabilities and pricing in each tool.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Adding a product: title, description and image ratios
cards.summary: Fill product title/URL, keep the inline description short, and upload all images at one consistent ratio.
cards.use_when: You are creating a product record in Shopify before or alongside PDP design.
steps: Enter the product title. Decide per brand whether to use a clear SEO-friendly name or a branded product name - the source presents both as valid choices.
Save, then check the auto-generated URL at the bottom of the editor; if you later rename the product, return and update the URL handle.

Write a short, simple inline description. Treat it as the text appearing beside the product photos rather than as the whole sales argument - the source says complicated, education-heavy products should get their additional information in a properly structured product page below the fold instead.

Upload all product images in one batch, and keep every image in the same dimensions and ratio across the catalog. The source prefers square because squares cannot mismatch, preventing weird cropping and misalignment.
Keep final image sourcing consistent with the variants you will create (e.g. one set per color).
caveats: Shopify's built-in AI description generator exists in the editor, but the source prefers writing descriptions with ChatGPT; use whichever produces on-brand copy.
The source's short-inline-description guidance is a recommendation, not a hard rule - what determines length is product complexity.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Configuring product type, vendor, tags and category
cards.summary: Set type and tags with your future collection filters in mind, and pick a precise Shopify category to unlock extra metafields.
cards.use_when: You are adding products and want collections, filters and product attributes to work without rework.
steps: Set the product Type to the closest descriptive term (e.g. legging, bra, jumpsuit, accessory) - the source notes type feeds collection filters, so specificity now saves cleanup later.
Set the Vendor to the brand name of the item; use the actual third-party brand if you resell other labels.

Use tags as product properties for collection rules, not as social-media-style hashtags. The source's method: decide which collections you intend to build (e.g. 'leggings', 'black leggings') and add tags matching them, because tag-based collection rules are hard to get wrong.

Choose the most precise Shopify product Category via the suggested category. The source shows that a specific category (legging) unlocks an extra attribute section - colors, activewear/clothing features - whereas an uncategorized product shows nothing extra.
Review the auto-detected attribute values (e.g. colors) Shopify pre-fills, then decide which to accept; the source accepted all and noted accuracy was close but not perfect.
Optionally add the product to a collection manually; Shopify places new products in the homepage collection by default and the source considers keeping that acceptable.
caveats: Metafields unlocked by category are not mandatory to fill.
The source describes the category feature as relatively new at recording time; the available attributes per category may have expanded.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Pricing fields: compare-at and cost of goods
cards.summary: Use price, compare-at price and cost per item correctly so discount display works and margin calculations are possible later.
cards.use_when: You are setting product pricing or running a sale and want correct strikethrough display and usable cost data.
steps: In the Pricing section, enter the Price as the amount the customer actually pays today.

To show a sale, enter the original higher amount in Compare at price and the current amount in Price; the source describes the customer seeing the compare-at figure struck through next to the current price.

Enter the per-unit Cost of goods - what you pay for the item itself, not all other expenses. The source cites the example of a €60 selling price with a €20 cost, and stresses that recording cost makes later margin, audit and profitability calculations easier.
Use the 'sell by unit' option only where it applies to your product (the source does not use it for apparel).
caveats: Cost of goods in the source's example excludes other business costs; do not treat it as full landed cost unless you include those.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Independent inventory, SKUs and warehouse coordination
cards.summary: Track inventory in Shopify with SKUs/barcodes so warehouses can match orders accurately, and understand available vs committed vs unavailable.
cards.use_when: You are setting stock levels and identifiers on a product, or preparing to hand fulfillment to a warehouse.
steps: Turn on inventory tracking rather than managing stock only outside Shopify; the source questions the value of switching it off.
Enter the on-hand quantity. Here 'available' is what you can sell; when an order comes in, 'committed' rises and available drops (100 in stock, first order shows committed 1 and available 99).
Use the 'unavailable' quantity field for stock you hold back - damaged items or inventory you do not want publicly sellable - so it is not lost from your records.

Enter at least one of SKU or barcode; the source says most warehouses work adequately with either, and suggests you can even use the same value in both fields. This is how the warehouse identifies what the customer bought and keeps order processing accurate.
If you operate multiple warehouses/locations, each location shows its own quantity field so you can allocate stock per location.
Decide deliberately whether to continue selling when out of stock, based on how quickly you can restock.
caveats: The source describes SKU/barcode importance mainly in the context of third-party warehouse fulfillment.
Inventory location behavior assumes locations are configured; the source covers that setup separately.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Product weight, shipping profile and variants
cards.summary: Record a physical weight so Shopify does not treat the item as digital, and create variants for the option axes customers choose.
cards.use_when: You are completing the shipping section of a product and setting up size/color options for apparel or similar catalog.
steps: In the Shipping section, switch weight on and enter the product weight (the source uses 0.25 in a chosen unit). The source states that leaving weight off makes Shopify treat the item as a digital product, so physical goods need it.
Record weight even if you do not bill shipping by weight: the source notes some warehouses need product weight regardless of your shipping rate method.
Use the customs/duties fields if you ship internationally.
To create variants, click Add options and define the axes; the source's activewear example uses Size (small, medium, large shown, with more needed) and Colour (navy and red).
Expect variants to drive separate media associations and per-variant inventory/pricing where relevant.
caveats: The source's size list in the example is deliberately incomplete for a legging range - build the full size run your catalog needs.
Weight units and the physical/digital determination should be verified in the current Shopify product editor.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Defining brand assets in Shopify settings
cards.summary: Load logo, square logo, colors, cover image, slogan and social links into Store assets so the theme inherits them automatically.
cards.use_when: You are in Settings > General > Store assets and want theme customization to pull consistent branding without manual re-entry.
steps: Upload the rectangular brand logo, then upload a square logo - the source reuses the favicon here because a favicon is square.

Add brand colors by clicking plus and pasting each hex code; define a primary color, a contrasting color chosen to be light against the dark primary for contrast, and secondary colors. The source says brands typically use four to five colors.
Optionally upload a cover image and add a slogan and short business description.
Add social links - at minimum Instagram, TikTok and Facebook. The source observes that people landing on a new brand often check its Instagram next, so missing links cost credibility.
Save. The source emphasizes that defining assets here makes later theme customization easier because the theme draws on these values.
caveats: Cover image, slogan and description are optional in the source's walkthrough.
This step only pays off if your theme is configured to use the store's brand assets; verify in your theme.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Orienting yourself in the Shopify admin navigation
cards.summary: Learn the left-hand admin map so you can find product, order, market and analytics functions without hunting.
cards.use_when: You are new to Shopify admin or onboarding a staff member and need to know where each store operation lives.
steps: Home: Shopify communications and later a sales summary.
Orders: incoming orders and their management.
Products: the product list, plus sub-items for Collections, Inventory, Purchase orders, Transfers and Gift cards.
Customers and Segments: everyone who bought or merely signed up, with segmentation available.
Marketing: campaigns and automations; Discounts sits alongside it.
Content: uploaded files, Menus, Blog posts and Metaobjects (the source flags metaobjects as relevant when creating colour swatches).
Markets: selling internationally to different countries or regions.
Finance and Analytics: analytics becomes important once you have data; the source defers deep coverage to the end of the course.
Sales channels: where you sell; Online Store by default, plus Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and Shop once connected.
Apps: third-party apps; and Settings in the corner for all business configuration.
caveats: Admin labels and grouping can change between Shopify releases; verify current navigation.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Create Physical Products with Weight to Enable Shipping
cards.summary: Turning on product weight is required so Shopify treats an item as physical and offers shipping rates.
cards.use_when: Adding a new physical product in Shopify admin and configuring shipping eligibility.
steps: When creating the product, enable the weight field; otherwise Shopify treats the product as digital and will not present shipping options.
Enter the product weight (e.g. 0.25) and change the unit as needed to match your warehouse and carrier conventions.
Optional: add customs/duties-related information for cross-border shipping from the same area.
Save, then verify the weight by checking the product in the Shipping settings or by previewing checkout rates for a destination.
caveats: Applies to physical goods; digital products intentionally skip weight.
Weight units affect calculated carrier rates — keep them consistent across the catalog.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Set Up Product Variants for Size and Color
cards.summary: Add variant options so one product listing offers all sizes and colors with per-variant pricing, stock, and images.
cards.use_when: Listing apparel or any product that comes in multiple sizes, colors, or materials.
steps: In the product editor, scroll to Variants and click Add options; add the first option such as Size and list values (Small, Medium, Large), then Done.
Add a second option such as Color; Shopify links variant colors to the product's category meta fields automatically.
Assign an image to each variant so shoppers see the right photo when they select a combination.
Edit price and quantity per variant (e.g. 100 units each) if they differ; confirm quantities are accurate before saving.
Click Save; if you use exotic colors or patterns, plan to set up color swatches later rather than relying on default names.
caveats: Variant options are limited by Shopify's maximum option/combination constraints — verify current limit in the admin.
Multiple images per single variant requires specific (often paid) themes.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Build Manual vs Smart Collections
cards.summary: Smart collections auto-populate by rules like tags, vendor, price, or inventory, and the type is locked once created.
cards.use_when: Organizing a catalog into collections that stay current as products are added.
steps: Go to Products > Collections and click Add collection.
Name the collection and optionally add a description and image.
Choose Manual (hand-pick products) or Smart (rule-based); once saved the type cannot be switched, so decide with future catalog growth in mind.
For Smart collections, set a condition such as product tag equals 'leggings' so any tagged product joins automatically.
Alternative rules include product type, category, vendor (e.g. Adidas), weight, or inventory stock (e.g. only items with 10 units left).
Save and confirm the collection's condition displays correctly in the collections list.
caveats: You cannot convert manual to smart or vice versa after creation — plan ahead for large catalogs.
Tag-based collections require consistent tag spelling across products or items will not appear.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Tag Products Consistently for Smart Collections
cards.summary: Standardized product tags drive reliable smart collections, and inconsistent spelling silently excludes products.
cards.use_when: Assigning tags to products so collections, filters, and navigation stay organized.
steps: Decide on a small, consistent tag vocabulary (e.g. leggings, bras, accessories, overalls) before tagging.
In each product, add the exact tag text — copy and paste to avoid typos like 'bras' vs 'bra'.
Build smart collections with conditions matching those tags (tag equals leggings, tag equals accessories).
After saving, refresh the collections view; updates can take a few seconds to propagate.
If a product is missing, verify its tag spelling and re-save.
Only tag products with the category they are sold under to keep collections clean.
caveats: Smart collections depend on exact tag matching; small typos break the rule silently.
Tags can be edited later, but bulk changes may need third-party apps when Shopify's bulk editor is limited.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Use Bulk Edit for Prices, Quantities, and Tags
cards.summary: Shopify's spreadsheet-style bulk editor updates many products at once but has limits that may require a third-party app.
cards.use_when: Cleaning up prices, stock levels, or tags across a large product catalog.
steps: Go to Products, select products, and click Bulk edit to open the spreadsheet-style view.
Use Columns to choose which fields are visible (e.g. price, inventory, tags).
Fill in missing prices or quantities; drag values down across rows like a spreadsheet.
For inventory, confirm 'track quantity' status per product and set quantities (e.g. 100) where missing.
For tags, add consistent values such as 'accessories' or 'leggings' so future smart collections catch them.
Save and re-verify in the products list and collections.
caveats: Bulk edit has limitations; complex changes may require a dedicated bulk-editing third-party app.
Tag changes propagate to smart collections only after a short delay or refresh.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Edit Product Images In-Shopify: Crop, Resize, Remove Background
cards.summary: Shopify's built-in image tools handle cropping, resizing, background removal, and background generation at the product level.
cards.use_when: Fixing inconsistent product photos or making PDP images match your visual standards without external tools.
steps: Open a product, click an image, and use the built-in tools.
Crop to a fixed ratio (e.g. square) when images are inconsistent.
Rotate, flip, or resize to a specific pixel size.
Use background removal to strip the background and apply a solid color like white for consistent PDP backgrounds.
Optionally use the AI background generator with a text prompt (e.g. 'outdoor garden') to place the product in a scene, but expect occasional failures.
Choose Save in place or Save as new; saving as new keeps the original and adds the edited image to the product.
caveats: The built-in AI background generator can fail or produce mediocre results; dedicated tools like Canva may be stronger for complex edits.
AI-generated backgrounds may not match brand aesthetics — review before saving to the live PDP.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Generate Product Images with Sidekick AI
cards.summary: Shopify's Sidekick can generate lifestyle product images from a product photo and a prompt, iterating conversationally.
cards.use_when: Creating lifestyle or contextual imagery for product pages or ads when you lack photoshoots.
steps: From the Shopify dashboard, click the Sidekick icon to open the AI assistant.
Upload or paste your product image into the Sidekick conversation.
Write a simple prompt describing the scene you want (e.g. 'show someone drinking this coffee in an office').
If the first result is illogical, refine the prompt (e.g. 'show someone holding the coffee in their hands') and regenerate.
Save the resulting image file from the Sidekick chat and upload it to the product or page.
Verify the current interface, as Sidekick's capabilities and access change with Shopify releases.
caveats: Access to Sidekick and its image generation may vary by store and Shopify plan; the interface has changed in recent editions.
AI images can look unrealistic for some niches — review against brand standards before publishing.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Configure Variant Color Swatches with Hex or Pattern Images
cards.summary: Shopify assigns default variant colors from category meta fields; you can override with exact hex codes or pattern images.
cards.use_when: Setting up color swatches for a product where default swatch colors are inaccurate or you sell patterns/textures.
steps: In the product editor, look under the linked category meta field for colors.
Replace default color names by editing entries; add new entries like 'dark blue' or 'dark green' via Add new entry.
Provide an exact hex code (search Google for the color hex if needed) so the swatch matches the real product color.
For patterns, textures, or uncertain colors (e.g. lip butter texture), upload a label image instead of a hex code.
Save and assign variant images for each color.
Note: showing only selected-variant images on the PDP requires theme support — often paid themes, not free ones.
caveats: Default Shopify color extraction is not accurate — always verify or override.
Some themes (usually paid) support variant-specific image display; free themes often do not, and setup differs per theme.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Set Up Storefront Filters with the Search and Discovery App
cards.summary: Shopify's free Search and Discovery app controls which filters (price, availability, category meta fields, or custom) appear on collection pages.
cards.use_when: Adding filterable navigation to a collection page so shoppers can narrow a large catalog by attributes.
steps: Install the free Shopify Search and Discovery app.
Open Filters; Shopify starts with availability and price — remove those that don't fit your catalog.
Click Add filter and pick a source: category meta fields, standard fields like vendor/brand, or your own product meta fields.
Save and verify on the storefront that the right filter values exist for products in the collection.
To check which categories a meta field applies to, go to Settings > Custom data > Products > Assigned to categories.
Filter options to consider: brand, color, size, availability, sport type, waist style, length — driven by what shoppers actually search for.
caveats: Filters only appear if the underlying meta field values are populated on products.
The app's UI and available sources change with Shopify updates — verify the current interface.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Create Custom Product Filters When Category Meta Fields Fall Short
cards.summary: Custom product meta fields let you add filters beyond Shopify's category defaults and apply them across all products.
cards.use_when: Adding a filter attribute your niche needs that isn't in the default category meta fields.
steps: Go to Settings > Custom data (meta fields and meta objects) > Products, then Add definition.
Name it (e.g. 'trial filter') and choose a type; 'list of values' lets one product appear under multiple values (e.g. gold and white gold).
Set the input type (e.g. single line text) and assign it to categories or leave it open for all products.
Save, then fill the meta field per product (or bulk edit across products).
Return to the Search and Discovery app, Add filter, and choose the new product meta field as the source.
Verify on the collection page after saving.
caveats: If left unassigned to categories, the field appears on all products — which may add confusion for categories where it doesn't apply.
Values must be populated per product or the filter shows empty.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Choose Filters from Customer Search Language
cards.summary: Filters should reflect how shoppers search and what competitors in the niche expose, not every attribute you have.
cards.use_when: Deciding which filters to expose on category pages for a new or existing store.
steps: Review your product categories in Shopify to see default meta fields Shopify pre-assigns (e.g. yoga mats get color, material).
Study competitors and large stores in your niche to see which filters they surface.
List questions customers commonly ask and the ways they describe products (e.g. 'cotton leggings', 'ankle length', 'black leggings').
Select only filters that map to real search intent — don't include every available attribute.
For stores with large catalogs, plan filters early so the catalog stays organized as it grows.
caveats: This is the presenter's recommended approach, not a universal rule; small catalogs may need fewer filters.
Over-filtering with rarely used attributes clutters collection pages and can hurt navigation.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Filter Shopify Themes by Industry, Catalog Size, and Required Features
cards.summary: Use Shopify theme store filters to narrow hundreds of themes down to a shortlist matching your niche, catalog size, and required sections.
cards.use_when: Shortlisting candidate Shopify themes before committing to a design foundation.
steps: In the theme store, filter by Industry to see demo themes closest to your niche (e.g. Beauty).
Filter by Catalog size: modest catalogs (roughly 11–100 products) differ from large (500+) stores, which need heavier search and navigation.
Filter by Features: e.g. before/after slider for cosmetics, color swatches, combined listing, age verifier for regulated goods.
Prioritize paid themes ($100–$400 one-time) when the source's experience suggests free themes often lack features and polish; the source's opinion, not a universal rule.
Open the demo store, check the PDP layout and section list, and read the reviews.
Inspect the developer: click through to their profile, check how many themes they publish, and search the company on Google to gauge legitimacy.
caveats: Filters may over-narrow results (e.g. only 20 themes for combined listing) — relax filters if the shortlist is too small.
The source's preference for paid themes is a personal opinion; free themes can work for simple stores.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Preview Mobile and Desktop Before Buying a Theme
cards.summary: Always check a theme's mobile demo since most traffic is mobile, and shortlist only themes whose mobile experience holds up.
cards.use_when: Evaluating theme candidates before purchase or trial installation.
steps: On the theme's page, click View demo to open the full desktop storefront.
Scroll through home and PDP sections to evaluate layout, social proof placement (UGC video, before/after), and section variety.
Check the mobile preview or open the demo URL on a phone; mobile is where most shoppers land.
Note which sections exist in any demo preset of the same theme — features seen in one preset apply across the theme.
Keep only themes whose mobile layout meets your standard; discard the rest.
caveats: Demo stores may use different presets; confirm the feature you want actually exists in the theme settings.
This is preparatory research, not a substitute for testing the theme with your own catalog.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Trial a Theme Before Buying to Preserve Work
cards.summary: Shopify lets you install a full theme trial, customize it, and buy later without losing changes.
cards.use_when: Deciding between finalist themes before committing to a purchase.
steps: Confirm you are signed into the correct Shopify store.
Click Try theme on the theme's store page; Shopify adds a full trial version you can edit but not publish.
Open the theme editor and build out key sections (home, PDP, coming soon page) to test fit.
If satisfied, click Buy; all your changes are preserved and the theme becomes publishable.
Optional: before upgrading, duplicate the theme via the three-dot menu to back it up (or use a backup app).
caveats: Some features — e.g. editing theme code or using product page templates — may require purchase first; verify current limitations.
Trial versions cannot be published to customers.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Duplicate Your Theme as a Backup Before Big Changes
cards.summary: Duplicating the theme creates a safe restore point before customizations or updates.
cards.use_when: Before large theme edits, version pushes, or any risky change to a live storefront.
steps: Go to Online Store > Themes.
Click the three dots next to the theme and choose Duplicate.
Rename the duplicate clearly (e.g. 'backup pre-update').
Use third-party theme backup apps if you need scheduled or versioned backups that Shopify's built-in duplication doesn't cover.
Verify the duplicate appears in the theme list before proceeding with the risky change.
caveats: Built-in duplication gives a snapshot, not automated version history; apps provide more robust backups.
Duplicating is not a substitute for testing changes in a trial or unpublished theme first.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Set Up a Password-Protected Coming Soon Page
cards.summary: Every Shopify store is password-locked by default and the 'password' theme controls what visitors see pre-launch.
cards.use_when: Preparing to launch a store or keep a site private while building it.
steps: By default the store is protected; visitors see the coming soon (password) page instead of the storefront.
Go to Online Store > Themes > Password theme and start customizing — it works like any other theme page.
To preview what customers see, open your store's domain in an incognito window (avoid the logged-in admin view).
The password required to unlock the store is set under Settings > Preferences (or the account's password page settings) — share it only with intended viewers.
Remove the lock when the store is ready to launch.
caveats: Forgetting the store password or leaving the lock on post-launch blocks all customer traffic.
The exact settings path may shift with Shopify releases — verify in your admin.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Reject One-Click AI Whole-Store Theming; Design for Conversion
cards.summary: Shopify's instant AI store generator may shortchange the conversion-focused design work that a curated theme delivers.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to launch with an auto-generated theme or to design the storefront deliberately.
steps: Optional test: run Shopify's AI theme generator (e.g. with a prompt like 'active wear brand') to see the generated layout.
Treat the output as a starting idea, not a final storefront — the source is not a fan of the feature and prefers building step-by-step.
Design for conversion, not only aesthetics: make information legible, products easy to explore, and social proof visible.
Aim to convert visitors into first-time buyers and repeat customers, not just to look polished.
If the theme lacks needed sections, consider a paid theme or theme AI editor tools rather than forcing the auto-generated layout.
caveats: Availability of the AI theme generator varies by store and Shopify plan.
This is the presenter's opinion; some merchants may find the generated themes a useful starting point.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Plan Theme Around Site Structure and Future Catalog
cards.summary: Theme choice is a multi-year decision — pick based on the features, sections, and catalog growth you expect, not just today's look.
cards.use_when: Committing to a theme for a store you plan to grow over years.
steps: Before browsing themes, list the features/sections you want (visual effects, product recommendations, comparison tables, ingredient panels, UGC, before/after sliders).
Do competitor research and note the sections and layouts you want to emulate.
Accept that the theme is a one-time, multi-year choice — changing later means redoing setup and settings across the store.
Prefer themes from proven developers when planning to stay on the theme for years, since they maintain updates.
Use the theme store's filters and the demo browser to shortlist and compare candidate themes.
Keep in mind that the Shopify editor's logic applies across themes even if exact settings differ — you are learning the process, not one theme's menu.
caveats: Theme migration later is possible but time-consuming; the presenter treats this as a major commitment.
The theme's AI section-building tools are described as glitchy and inconsistent — don't rely on them as the primary customization method.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Lock the store with password during setup and use it for early access
cards.summary: Every new Shopify store is password-protected by default; keep the lock until launch, or use it deliberately to give waitlist customers early access before the public launch.
cards.use_when: Launching or pre-launching your store, or running an early-access drop for waitlist subscribers.
steps: Understand the default: every new Shopify store is locked with a password set by Shopify automatically, found under Preferences in the Shopify admin.
Verify the lock by copying your store's domain and loading it in an incognito/private browser window (so you're not signed in); you should see only a 'coming soon' page with a password field.
Before you go live, return to Preferences and turn the password protection off, or customers will keep seeing the coming soon page instead of your store.

For a launch tactic: give your waitlist email subscribers the password a few hours before the public launch so they get first access to the products. This mirrors an approach the presenter used with a client's early-access launch, not a guaranteed outcome.
Consider how long you leave the store locked; the longer it stays locked, the longer you delay any organic discovery or ads traffic actually seeing products.
Confirm the current location of the password setting in your admin, as Shopify's interface changes over time.
caveats: The default password and location of the Preferences setting may differ by Shopify plan and admin version; verify in your own store.
Keeping the store locked means ad or SEO traffic cannot see products until you unlock it.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Edit products, collections and pages inside the theme editor
cards.summary: Modern Shopify lets you modify product, collection and page content from within the theme editor itself instead of bouncing back to the admin backend.
cards.use_when: Eyeballing a section and wanting to tweak the linked product, collection title/description or page content while you stay in visual edit mode.
steps: Open the theme editor and click the section whose underlying data you want to change (for example a Featured Collection section pointing at your active wear collection).
Click the edit pencil/button on the setting; the collection editor popup appears directly in front of you, so you can change the collection's rules, title or description without leaving the editor.
Apply the same logic to products and pages: click the setting that references the product or page and edit it in the popup.
Use this when merchandising sections quickly, e.g. swapping which collection a homepage section shows or fixing a collection title you noticed looks wrong in the preview.
Still go back to the Shopify backend for things the editor doesn't handle: adding richer product information, creating menus, and other admin-level tasks.
Confirm these inline edit affordances exist in your current theme and Shopify version before relying on them.
caveats: This inline editing capability is tied to recent Shopify updates and may not cover every field or every theme setting.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Navigate the theme editor: locations, pages, inspector and view modes
cards.summary: Orient within the Shopify theme editor—store location selector, page selector, inspector toggle, desktop/mobile/fullscreen views and undo/redo/save.
cards.use_when: Setting up your store theme and figuring out where to make changes and which page or market you're editing.
steps: Check the location selector: at the start you must be editing Store Default; later you can customize per-market or per-country (for example a French banner for France, a German flag banner for Germany).

Know the plan limitation: per-market customization is not available on the basic Shopify plan; if you plan to sell worldwide with per-market changes, you need to upgrade. Verify current plan features.
Check the page selector: the editor always opens on the Homepage, but you can switch to Products (default product template), collections, pages, etc.
Use the Sidekick button (Shopify's AI) for quick data questions—e.g. asking how many units of a specific product have sold instead of digging through analytics reports.
Toggle the Inspector: hovering over store elements turns them blue so you can click them to open and add sections; turn it off to navigate from the sidebar instead.
Switch between desktop, mobile and full-screen views; treat mobile view as accurate but not 100% accurate—always preview the real link on a phone before finishing.
Use the three dots menu for preview, theme documentation and keyboard shortcuts; undo, redo and save control your edits in the sidebar.
caveats: Mobile in-editor preview is not exactly the live mobile rendering.
Per-market customization is plan-gated; check your Shopify plan before planning localized banners.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Get a shareable preview link for draft and published themes
cards.summary: Draft themes expose a copyable preview link directly, but published themes require right-click-copy-link on the preview to share a mobile-testable URL.
cards.use_when: Testing your store on a real phone, or sending a work-in-progress theme to a client or teammate for review.
steps: For a non-published (draft) theme: click the three dots, click Preview, then use the bar that appears and click Copy preview link—share that URL freely.
For the published theme: the preview doesn't behave the same way. Click the three dots, click Preview, then right-click and choose Copy link address to obtain the shareable preview URL.
Open the copied link in an incognito/private window or on a phone to check real mobile rendering, since the in-editor mobile view isn't exact.
Use this before finalizing merchandising changes on mobile-first shoppers, especially for product card layout and menu behavior.
Re-verify the three-dot menu options and preview bar behavior in your Shopify version, as the UI changes.
caveats: The published-theme copy method depends on browser right-click behavior and may shift with theme/Shopify updates.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Set brand colors once and connect theme colors to them via dynamic sources
cards.summary: Define a small palette in Shopify brand settings, then link theme color fields to those brand colors with dynamic sources so a palette change updates the whole theme at once.
cards.use_when: Setting up theme colors before launch, or rebranding, so a palette swap doesn't require hunting through every color field.
steps: Go to Shopify general settings and define your brand colors first (primary, accent, contrasting/secondary, light page, etc.).

In the theme editor's Colors settings, click the dynamic-source icon on a color field (the icon that connects to a metafield) and pick from your saved brand colors instead of typing hex codes each time.
Map the palette purposefully: text and headings to the primary brand color, links to an accent/contrasting color, product card sale badge to the accent color so it stands out.
Set product card states: 'sale', 'sold out' and 'pre-order' badge colors should be chosen deliberately—if you don't need a given state (e.g. low inventory), skip changing it to save time.
When you later change a brand color once at the brand-assets level, every theme field linked to it updates automatically—no field-by-field editing.
Decide colors iteratively: it's hard to judge colors before seeing them on real content, so return to Colors settings after uploading images and sections; stay within your brand palette.
caveats: The number and naming of color options varies by theme; more professional themes typically expose more options, some themes push choices down to section level instead.
Dynamic source linking requires brand colors to be defined first.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Configure buttons, background, header and section color schemes
cards.summary: Set primary/secondary button styling, overall background, header colors and a small set of reusable section color schemes so sections can alternate backgrounds without a boring look.
cards.use_when: Merchandising your storefront design, and planning how homepage sections will visually alternate (light/dark backgrounds) across the store.
steps: Define the primary button: choose background, hover background and text colors. This button appears across the store (e.g. Add to cart, checkout). Then define the secondary button (often white background with a border).
Set the background: choose the full-store background color; keep it white for the shopper's ease of reading. Using an image as background is not recommended (you'd control repeat/tile options).
Set header colors: background, text, main menu link color, hover color and the featured link color; you can also add a menu background color.
Use image overlays (a transparent black layer over hero images) at adjustable opacity to make overlaid text pop; tune this after you upload real images rather than during initial setup.

Build section color schemes: a scheme is a predefined combination of your brand colors (background, heading, text, links, plus primary/secondary button variations) so you can alternate between sections without re-picking colors.
Create at least two schemes (e.g. white background with primary text; a bold/beige background with dark-blue text) and apply them to alternating sections so the design doesn't feel monotonous.
Pick colors you can live with, then adjust after previewing; if you don't use a feature (e.g. low-inventory label), don't spend time styling it.
caveats: Color schemes are theme-dependent; some themes don't offer them and only expose colors at the section or theme-settings level.
Overlay opacity and scheme choices should be judged against actual imagery, not the placeholder content.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Set typography, sizes and button shapes from theme settings
cards.summary: Configure heading/text/navigation fonts, font sizes and button rounding in one place, choosing fonts from Shopify's library to avoid custom coding.
cards.use_when: Setting up theme typography and button styling before launch, or tuning readability after seeing the store on desktop and mobile.
steps: Choose fonts from Shopify's font library so your font is guaranteed available without custom coding; this is the recommended approach over uploading custom fonts.
Set the heading font (with options like all-caps and heading letter spacing), then text/button text, navigation text and store-name text separately.
After selecting a font, check the style dropdown for available weights/styles and pick the one you want.
Use the Sizes settings to adjust heading size, base size, navigation size and store-name size to get a readable hierarchy.
Choose button text case (normal or all caps) and corner rounding (slightly rounded to fully rounded) if the theme exposes it—nicer than custom CSS to achieve rounded buttons.
Verify typography and button choices on mobile preview and a real phone, since sizes read differently at small widths.
Expect these settings to differ per theme but follow the same logic; search for the relevant setting if it isn't where expected.
caveats: Available typography and button-shape options vary by theme; some require custom CSS.
Custom-code solutions carry more risk than the built-in settings.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Customize product cards: image shape, cropping, alignment and mobile per-row count
cards.summary: Control how product cards display—image aspect/crop behavior, alignment, text alignment, hover image, labels and mobile products per row—to keep product listings consistent.
cards.use_when: Setting up how products appear on homepage and collection listings; fixing a listing where mixed square/portrait product images look inconsistent.
steps: Decide image shape (portrait, square, landscape). If you upload images pre-sized to the shape you want, the card looks clean; if you mix square and portrait/landscape images, most themes will crop to fill the required shape, which can cut products awkwardly.

If the theme offers a 'don't crop' option, you can avoid cropping, but it's usually not practical because card sizes become mismatched; the better fix is uploading correctly sized images from the start.
When cropping, set the image alignment (top/middle/bottom) to control which part of the image is retained—useful when a crop cuts off the product.
Set image alignment (for example top) and text alignment (left/center/right) for the card text; center is a common choice.
Keep mobile products per row at two for a more user-friendly browse experience; one per row is an option but less efficient.
Enable additional images on hover where the theme supports it—a nice way to show a second shot without clicking.

Choose quick-buy behavior: as a button or 'whole product' (clicking the card opens the product so customers can buy there); optionally allow app blocks (e.g. review ratings) and subscription options inside quick buy.
Set overlay label position (top-right/left recommended) and show the sale reduction by percent or value; these options vary by theme.
caveats: Cropping behavior and the availability of a 'no crop' option vary by theme; many themes crop automatically without offering a choice.
Some card features (subtitles, swatches, app blocks in quick buy) depend on theme and installed apps.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Set up header: announcement bar, sticky header and menus
cards.summary: Configure the header group—announcements with optional countdown and country/language selectors, logo sizing, sticky behavior and the main menu—while keeping it simple.
cards.use_when: Building the site-wide header that shoppers see on every page, including promo messaging and navigation.
steps: Announcement bar: add up to about three announcements (typically the theme limit). Type plain messages like free shipping, optionally link them (e.g. to your shipping policy) and add a countdown timer with an end date for promos.

Use section-level vs block-level settings correctly: clicking the section changes section settings; clicking a block changes that block's settings. Style individual messages or let them inherit the section style.

Add a country/region selector if you sell in multiple markets so shoppers can switch location and see products/pricing/shipping for their region; add a language selector if you offer multiple languages.
Header: set logo width and mobile logo dimensions, and enable a sticky header so navigation follows as shoppers scroll (recommended).
Optionally enable a transparent header (useful over a hero image) with a separate logo for the transparent state, but decide based on whether your first image suits it.

Create the menu in the Shopify backend under Content > Menus, then link it in the header's Navigation setting; understand that a '#' prefix makes an item non-clickable, while linking to Products makes it link to all products.
Keep the header simple: adding sections in the header group makes them appear on every page, which clutters navigation. Use Section settings to fine-tune.
caveats: Announcement count is theme-limited (commonly three).
Country/language selector usefulness depends on markets/languages actually configured.
Sticky and transparent header options vary by theme.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Build multi-level and mega menus that mirror how shoppers think
cards.summary: Structure multi-level and mega menus so the same product can be reached from multiple mental models (product type, activity, gender, etc.), matching how a reference retailer organizes navigation.
cards.use_when: Designing site navigation and collection hierarchy to help different shopper intents find products quickly.
steps: Decide your top-level split by mental model. For activewear, a layered structure could be Shop > Clothes (with leggings, bras, jumpsuits) and Shop > Accessories (with bottle, mat), plus a second angle like Shop by Activity (yoga, pilates).

Deliberately allow the same products to appear in multiple collections, because different shoppers search differently: some look for 'yoga leggings' specifically; others just want general activewear. Give each intent a path.
Draw structure from a reference site's navigation (the presenter cites Lululemon): sports-based browsing, plus Men/Women browsing, so shoppers can enter from whichever angle fits them.

Make second- and third-level items non-clickable if you don't yet have a collection for them, or make them clickable by creating a collection that includes all relevant products (e.g. a 'clothes' collection containing all clothes sub-collections).
Feature a specific link (e.g. Leggings, or a sale/outlet collection) with a distinct featured color to highlight it—useful for promotions.

Optionally use a different, simpler menu for mobile, and add theme-specific menu promotions (wide or small) with images and a call to action; helpful for luxury niches. Avoid adding header sections beyond navigation and maybe a slim store-message bar.
When done, link the new menu in the theme editor Navigation setting; the header updates.
caveats: Menu promotion blocks and featured-link coloring are theme-dependent (Symmetry-specific in the example).
Deep multi-level menus can complicate mobile navigation; consider a simplified mobile menu.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Configure cart behavior: drawer vs page and free shipping bar
cards.summary: Choose whether Add to cart opens a cart drawer or navigates to the cart page, and whether to add a free shipping bar, since it affects how easily shoppers keep browsing.
cards.use_when: Setting up cart experience before launch, and optimizing how customers proceed from product to checkout.
steps: In theme settings' Cart options, choose between 'drawer' and 'page'. Drawer opens a popup overlay; page sends the shopper to the cart page.

Prefer the drawer: the presenter argues page cart forces shoppers to click back to keep browsing, making it worse for browsing flow. Confirm this against your own store's data rather than treating it as universal.
Optionally add a free shipping bar in the cart drawer and customize its colors, so shoppers see progress toward free shipping.
Test the actual add-to-cart flow via quick buy and normal product page to confirm the drawer/page setting applies consistently in your theme.
Review cart-related theme settings for anything else (e.g. cart notes, upsell blocks) that the theme exposes, and skip settings you won't use.
caveats: Drawer vs page preference is a stated opinion; some stores/traffic convert better on the cart page. Test rather than assume.
Available cart settings vary by theme.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Use currency formats, advanced settings and custom CSS carefully
cards.summary: Adjust price display via currency formats, review advanced filter/link options, and use theme-level custom CSS only to override display without touching theme files.
cards.use_when: Tweaking minor store display details (price formatting, filter and link behavior) or applying small display overrides without editing theme code.
steps: Currency formats: adjust how prices appear on the store if needed; keep defaults if you're happy with standard formatting.
Advanced settings: review options related to filters and links; defaults are generally fine and many themes won't expose these settings.

Custom CSS at the theme level: use it to change the display of the store globally (font styles, sizes, etc.) rather than editing theme base files—this is lighter-weight than editing theme files and lower risk because the editor CSS overrides theme code.
Note there is also custom CSS at the section level for per-section overrides; choose the right scope for your change.
If you're not familiar with CSS, skip this section—it's optional and everything works without it.
caveats: Custom CSS is for those comfortable with it; misuse can produce broken displays.
Pricing changes and formatting can have tax/legal implications depending on your markets—confirm before pushing live.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Use theme style presets as a starting point
cards.summary: Theme 'style' presets let you pick a pre-built demo layout as a starting base instead of building every section from scratch.
cards.use_when: Starting a new theme setup when you want a faster starting point and are willing to replace most section content anyway.
steps: In the theme editor, open the Theme style settings, which lets you switch between different pre-built demo styles.
Review the demos and pick the one whose layout most resembles what you want your store to look like.
Use it as a starting point, then customize sections and content as usual.
Note that if you plan to replace most sections and content anyway, switching styles may not save much—many users keep the style they started with.
After applying, review your color schemes and typography settings since presets can set defaults there.
caveats: Switching styles affects many theme settings; verify your brand colors and typography survive the switch.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Build the footer with link lists, blocks and policies
cards.summary: The footer is common across all pages; set its colors in theme settings, then add blocks such as text/logo, link lists and newsletter—linking to policies you generate in the backend.
cards.use_when: Building site-wide secondary navigation and policy links at launch, and deciding whether to include a newsletter signup in the footer.
steps: Set footer background and text/heading colors in the theme settings' Colors section first; footer colors are global.
In the Footer group, click the footer section to see its settings, then add blocks: Text (with logo), Link list and Newsletter.
For each link list, create the menu in the Shopify backend under Content > Menus (e.g. Quick Links, Customer Support) and link it here; you can have multiple footer menus for different purposes.

Generate your store policies in Settings > Policies (e.g. Terms of Service, Shipping Policy) using the provided templates, then link to those pages from a footer link list; read over any generated template before publishing.
Consider hiding the footer newsletter block if you already capture emails via popups, or keep it if you want the footer as an additional capture point.

Avoid adding unnecessary sections (like a scrolling banner) inside the footer group, since anything in header/footer/overlay groups appears on every page—keep the footer focused on links and policies.
caveats: Footer blocks available vary by theme.
Newsletter in footer may be redundant if you use popups—decide based on your email capture strategy.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Build footer policy and support menus before linking them in the theme
cards.summary: Create Shopify policies and an About page first, then assemble two or three footer link menus and attach them as footer link-list blocks.
cards.use_when: Setting up the store footer so policy, contact and support pages are reachable from every page of the storefront.
steps: Generate every required policy in the Shopify admin under Settings > Policies (terms of service, refund, privacy, shipping). Insert the template for each, review and edit the text so it matches your store, then click Publish — unpublished policies have no URL to link to.

Create the pages you want to link: go to Online Store > Pages and add at least an About Us page (and a contact/support page if the theme's default contact page isn't enough). Save without styling; edit the copy later.

Go to Online Store > Navigation > Menus and create separate menus rather than one long list: for example 'Helpful Links' containing all policies, and 'Quick Links' containing About Us, Contact and support pages. This mirrors how larger retailers split footer navigation into services / help / about columns.

Return to the theme editor, open the footer section, and point each Links block at one of the menus you created. Use the plus between footer blocks to add additional link-list blocks, then rename each block heading (e.g. 'Support') so customers can scan them.
Optionally hide the newsletter block in the footer since popups already capture signups; keep it if the footer is your only email capture point.
caveats: Menu contents are shared across all pages, so any change to a footer menu updates sitewide — double-check links after editing.
The available footer blocks and their naming differ by theme; check the block types your theme actually exposes.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Choose theme sections by first checking the available section library
cards.summary: Inspect the theme's full section library and confirm niche-critical sections exist before committing to a theme.
cards.use_when: Selecting or trialling a Shopify theme, or planning which homepage/PDP/collection sections your store will need.
steps: In the theme editor, hover between two existing sections, click the plus icon and browse the complete list of available sections, grouped by type (banners, collections, forms, info, product lists, etc.).
Note that the default homepage sections a theme ships with are only a subset — you can remove them and add any other available section to any page.

Map your niche requirements against that list before buying the theme. Example: a cosmetics brand needing a before/after gallery must verify the theme offers such a section, since it can't be added later if it doesn't exist.

Confirm which section types are universal vs theme-specific: banners, collection list and featured collection are near-universal, while logo list, multicolumn, testimonials and subcollection blocks vary by theme.
If the exact section is missing, look for generic substitutes — a multicolumn or column block that supports an image, text and link can stand in for a logo list.
caveats: Reconciling this check against the theme store preview is faster than rebuilding later; section availability is a hard constraint, not a styling preference.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Assemble the homepage in a deliberate section order
cards.summary: Build the homepage one section at a time in a sequence that moves from brand message to proof to bestsellers to story, removing theme defaults you don't need.
cards.use_when: Designing or rebuilding the store homepage structure after the header and footer are set.
steps: Start with a slideshow or background video as the first banner. Use it to state what you sell, announce a new collection or drop, and link the image or button directly to that collection — this is the source's recommended way to open a homepage.

Keep the hero simple: one image or video, or at most two to three slides. Use a landscape image for desktop, and upload a separate mobile image if the theme allows it rather than accepting a bad crop.
Follow the hero with a USP or logo-list section: each logo block carries one unique selling proposition (image, title, link). The same section type can show certifications or press logos.
Add a featured-collection section for your bestsellers. The source's stated position is that bestsellers are bestsellers for a reason, so showing them on the homepage is always recommended.
Continue with collection list, image-with-text linking to the About page, and a testimonial section populated with the strongest real reviews and optional customer photos.
Add remaining sections only as needed (blog, rich text) and delete the theme's default filler — a shorter, intentional homepage is preferred over keeping everything the theme shipped.
caveats: The recommended section sequence is the presenter's design opinion, not a tested universal rule; adapt to your catalogue and traffic source.
Testimonial sections can also come from an app via app blocks; the theme's built-in section just avoids the dependency.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Set hero slideshow height and focal point to prevent bad crops
cards.summary: Control slideshow height, per-device images and image focal points so the hero looks intentional on desktop and mobile.
cards.use_when: Configuring a homepage hero slideshow or banner section where images crop awkwardly across devices.
steps: Click the slideshow section (not the individual slide) to reach its general settings, then choose a height mode: full screen, adapt to first image, or fixed height.
Prefer 'adapt to first image' if you uploaded images at the correct dimensions — this shows the full image without cropping.

If you need a consistent band instead, use fixed height. The source's working example used around 600px on both desktop and mobile; treat that number as a starting point, not a benchmark, and check both viewports.
For images that still crop badly, open the image in the editor and set the focal point on the part that must survive cropping (e.g. a model's face). The theme then crops around that point.
Set a separate mobile image where the theme supports it, and give each slide a full-slide link as an alternative to a button if you don't want a visible CTA.
Check the mobile preview after each change; text-below-image on mobile is discouraged when a dedicated mobile image is available.
caveats: Fixed-height values and the availability of mobile-specific images, focal points and text-below settings vary by theme; verify in your theme's editor.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Use duplicate and copy-paste to build section sets quickly and consistently
cards.summary: Duplicate blocks to inherit identical dimensions, and copy entire sections between pages so shared layouts stay consistent.
cards.use_when: Building repetitive section structures such as logo lists, USP rows or cross-page content bands in the theme editor.
steps: Set the first block up completely — including image width — then use Duplicate to create siblings. Duplicated blocks inherit the same dimensions, so you only swap the image/text instead of resizing each one; the source explicitly regrets resizing every logo individually.
Reorder blocks or sections by hovering and dragging them to the new position, including dragging a section to a different point in the page.
To move a section to another page, select it and use Copy, then navigate to the target page and use Paste (or Paste after) — copied sections can be pasted on any Shopify page.
Blocks can only be pasted into a section type that supports that block type, so keep whole reusable layouts at section level.
Edit block text either through the settings panel or by turning on direct editing and double-clicking the text on the canvas.
caveats: Section copy/paste between pages is a newer Shopify editor capability; interface details may change, so verify it exists in your editor version.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Create a bestsellers collection with tags and feature it
cards.summary: Tag chosen products, build an automated tag-based bestsellers collection, and render it via a featured-collection section.
cards.use_when: Adding a bestsellers or curated homepage product row when the store has no existing bestsellers collection.
steps: Decide which products to feature, then tag them (e.g. tag equal to 'bestsellers') using Select all > Bulk edit > add tag in the products list.
Go to Products > Collections and create a collection named 'bestsellers' with an automated condition of tag equals bestsellers, then save.

In the theme editor, add a Featured Collection section and select the bestsellers collection. Some themes let you select individual products instead of a collection; this workflow assumes collection-only selection.
Where the theme supports it, change the section's colour scheme to differentiate the band from adjacent sections and check badge styling in each scheme.
Later, maintain the tag as your real bestsellers change — the section updates automatically because the collection is condition-based.
caveats: The source recommends showing bestsellers on the homepage; if you have little or no sales data, define 'bestseller' by your own judgement or omit the label rather than implying sales volume you don't have.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Build automated collections with AND-style tag conditions
cards.summary: Create one collection from multiple tag conditions so products tagged with any of several values all appear in a single category.
cards.use_when: Building a parent category (e.g. all activewear) that should gather several product types tagged separately.
steps: In Products > Collections, create a new collection and choose automated conditions rather than manual selection.

Decide whether products must match ALL conditions or ANY condition. To pool leggings, bras and overalls into one activewear collection, set 'any condition' with separate rules: tag equals leggings, tag equals bra, tag equals overall.
Save and verify the product count matches expectations; the collection updates automatically as tags change.
Keep tag values consistent in the product data or products will silently fall out of the collection.
caveats: Using 'any condition' is the opposite of what you'd want for narrowing rules; mixing ALL and ANY logic carelessly produces either over-broad or empty collections.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Configure collection filters using Shopify Search & Discovery
cards.summary: Add product-type, size, colour and other filters via the Search & Discovery app, then make sure the underlying product data is populated.
cards.use_when: Setting up collection page filtering so shoppers can narrow a large catalogue by type, size, colour or price.
steps: In Shopify admin, open the Search & Discovery app > Filters and add the filters you want (standard fields such as product type and size, plus custom ones like fabric or colour).

Fill in the underlying product data for filters to return results. A filter with only one value in the admin usually means you haven't entered product type (or the relevant field) on the other products — bulk-edit products to populate it.
Write values consistently: 'legging' and 'leggings' create two separate filter options, so standardise the wording across products.
Order filters in the app (e.g. product type before fabric, size where it fits logically) and save; order is controlled from the app, not the theme.
In the theme editor's collection template, review theme-level filter settings — some themes render certain filters as buttons (e.g. sizes) and may support colour swatches natively.
caveats: Filter display options vary by theme; the app determines which filters exist and their order, the theme determines how they render.
Price is available as a filter but the source's example set also leaned on product data quality, which is the usual failure point.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Turn on colour swatches with defined colours or variant images
cards.summary: Expose variant colours on collection product cards using either named colour swatches with hex values or automatically pulled variant images.
cards.use_when: Collection-page merchandising when products come in multiple colours but the cards show no colour indication.
steps: In the theme editor, open the product card/swatch settings inside the collection template (or theme settings > swatches) and enable swatches.

For hex-based swatches: select the colour-list option, then define each variant colour name and its hex code (look the code up by searching e.g. 'red hex'). The swatch appears once the name matches the variant value.
For image swatches: select the variant-image option so the theme pulls the actual variant image, which the source preferred for its store.

For custom swatch graphics (e.g. patterns rather than flat colours), upload an image named exactly after the variant value with the correct extension (e.g. red.png) and the theme will use it in place of the colour.
Save and open the live/collection preview to confirm swatches appear under the product cards.
caveats: Swatch configuration differs across themes, though all common themes support swatches; if they don't show, a setting is usually unset rather than unsupported.
Variant naming must match swatch names exactly for the association to work.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Work on the default collection template first, then branch to custom templates
cards.summary: Set universal collection settings once in the default template, then create named templates for collections that need extra sections.
cards.use_when: Deciding between editing the shared default collection layout and creating per-collection layouts.
steps: Open the theme editor's Collections section; the Default collection template applies to every collection assigned to it (the source observed six collections sharing one template).

Configure the shared settings there: show/hide collection title and image, heading image height, overlay style, show/hide description, products per page, products per row, and whether to show vendor and product count.
Add the description and collection image if you care about SEO, since these feed the collection page content.
Set the default sort (bestselling, alphabetical, price low to high) in the collection section settings.
Where a collection needs different content or extra sections, click Create template in the Collections area, name it after the collection (e.g. 'activewear'), and build its sections.
Assign the template per collection in the admin; if the theme isn't published yet, template assignment may not be visible, so plan to assign after publishing.
caveats: Changes to the default template affect every collection assigned to it — a common source of unintended sitewide edits.
Template assignment options depend on whether the theme is published.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Add a visual subcollection row with a multicolumn section
cards.summary: Simulate subcollection navigation by duplicating a multicolumn block per subcollection, each with image and link, at the top of a custom collection template.
cards.use_when: Large catalogues where a parent collection needs to route shoppers into leggings/bras/overalls-style subsections.
steps: Create a dedicated collection template for the parent collection and preview that collection against it.
Add a multicolumn section above the product grid, delete all but one block, then fully configure the first: image, title (e.g. Leggings) and a link to that subcollection.
Set the media width to a consistent, small size on the first block, then Duplicate it for each remaining subcollection and swap the image, title and link — duplicating preserves the dimensions.
Hide the parent collection's own title and product count in the template settings so the subcollection row reads as the page's primary navigation.
Optionally add a rich-text section above the row with an instruction such as 'select by product type' and its own heading removed, to avoid repeating the collection title.
Use product images with transparent backgrounds where possible for a cleaner subcollection row, as seen on reference stores using the same theme.
caveats: Native subcollection blocks exist in some themes but not all; the multicolumn approach is the portable fallback.
This template must then be assigned to the specific collection in the admin once the theme is published.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Use collection metafields to vary content inside a shared collection template
cards.summary: Define collection metafields for image, title, text and link, then connect section fields to dynamic sources so one layout shows different promotional content per collection.
