caveats: Posting cadence of 3–4 times per week is the source's recommendation, not a validated performance benchmark.
Get permission before reposting customer testimonials or user-generated content.
Organic content builds long-term demand; for immediate new-store traffic the source points to paid ads.
cards.source_name: The OFFICIAL Shopify 2026 Tutorial.docx

cards.title: Vet Shopify apps before installing
cards.summary: Screen apps by rating, review count, recency of reviews, developer track record and Built for Shopify badge, and install one at a time.
cards.use_when: Adding any app — email/SMS, reviews, pop-ups, referrals — to your store and deciding which one to trust.
steps: Check the app rating and review count: look for 4+ stars, ideally 4.5 or higher, and at least 100+ reviews as a reliability sign.
Read recent reviews, not just the top ones, and look for patterns in complaints.
Verify the developer by clicking the developer name to see their other apps; established developers usually have multiple apps or a strong track record.
Look for the Built for Shopify badge — these apps meet Shopify's highest quality standards.
In the beginning install one app at a time as an actual need arises, not a full stack upfront.
Browse by category via Settings, Apps, Shopify App Store, filtering by rating, free-to-paid and category; or ask Sidekick for recommendations.
caveats: Rating and review thresholds are the source's heuristics, not guaranteed quality measures.
App features, free tiers and pricing change; recheck before committing.
Every app adds code that loads, so app count directly affects speed.
cards.source_name: The OFFICIAL Shopify 2026 Tutorial.docx

cards.title: Match app choices to the marketing job you need done
cards.summary: Pick apps by the specific gap — email scale, SMS, reviews, pop-ups, referrals — and avoid overlapping tools.
cards.use_when: You have outgrown built-in Shopify messaging or need SMS, review collection, pop-up capture or a referral program.
steps: Email beyond basics: if sending more than 10,000 emails a month, paid platforms become more competitive; the source names Klaviyo for advanced automations across email, SMS, WhatsApp and push, AI tools and support, noting a steeper learning curve.

SMS: apps such as Postscript and Attentive send opted-in promotional texts; the source cites texts as strong for time-sensitive offers, flash sales, abandoned cart recovery and urgent updates, and quotes a 98% open rate with reads typically within minutes.

Reviews/social proof: Judge.me and Loox automatically gather ratings with photos and videos, provide customizable widgets, sync to Google Shopping and the Shop app, offer discount incentives and allow importing reviews; the source calls Judge.me a good starting point and Loox a fit for consistent volume with more AI features.

Pop-ups: Privy is positioned as an all-in-one with pop-ups plus email and SMS; Justuno focuses purely on advanced pop-up conversion, which the source suggests if you already use a platform like Klaviyo and don't want duplicate email tools.
Referrals: Referral Candy runs referral and affiliate programs and integrates with themes and other apps.
Check whether a listed SMS feature is available in your market before choosing an SMS app, since Shopify's own SMS support is limited to select markets.
caveats: App names, pricing and features change; verify current capabilities and costs.
The cited 98% SMS open rate is the presenter's figure, not a store-specific result.
Avoid stacking overlapping tools (e.g. two email platforms) because of cost and complexity.
cards.source_name: The OFFICIAL Shopify 2026 Tutorial.docx

cards.title: Find your largest funnel drop-off with the conversion rate breakdown report
cards.summary: Use Shopify's conversion rate breakdown to locate the biggest leak between sessions, add-to-cart, checkout and purchase.
cards.use_when: Traffic is steady but purchases are low and you need to know which funnel stage to fix first.
steps: Go to Analytics, select Reports, open the category filter and choose Behavior.
Open the conversion rate breakdown report.
Read the chart on the right: sessions, sessions with cart additions, sessions that reached checkout, sessions that completed checkout.

Identify the largest proportional drop. Example from the source: out of 100 sessions, 5 added to cart while 95 left without adding — the drop is before cart, so the leak is on product pages and merchandising, not checkout.
Fix the stage with the biggest drop first; different stages call for different work (product page visuals/copy vs checkout friction).
Ask Sidekick targeted questions such as 'Why is my product page conversion rate low?' — it surfaces common causes and suggested fixes you can act on.
Optimization is continuous: recheck the funnel after changes because what works now can change in months.
caveats: Stage comparisons are your own data, not industry benchmarks; read proportions within your funnel rather than comparing to another store's numbers.
Sidekick insight cards and report locations shift between Shopify releases — verify the current interface.
cards.source_name: The OFFICIAL Shopify 2026 Tutorial.docx

cards.title: Fix product pages: visuals, descriptions, trust signals and CTA
cards.summary: Address the common conversion killers on product pages — weak images, generic descriptions, mismatched price-to-value, missing reviews or murky returns — with specific fixes.
cards.use_when: Your biggest funnel drop is before add-to-cart, or product pages get traffic but don't convert.
steps: Visuals: add at least 3–5 real images showing multiple angles with working zoom so buyers can see texture and stitching. Consider a product video or 3D model, which Shopify supports free alongside photos. Example from the source: footwear brand Vessi uses four images per product covering all angles, one lifestyle shot in a puddle, plus a 360-degree video. For anything where size or fit matters, include a scale-reference photo.

Descriptions: lead with benefits and support with features ('so soft you'll forget you're wearing it' over 'made with organic cotton'), include sizing and fit information where relevant, and avoid generic copy with no story.
Trust: install a review app (the source names Judge.me, Loox and Yotpo) and push for user-generated photos; a murky return policy removes trust — make it clear.
Price vs perceived value: if the drop sits here, either strengthen value presentation or reconsider the price, since misalignment is one of the three named conversion killers.
CTA: make Add to cart impossible to miss with high contrast and clear text, and test a sticky add-to-cart button that stays visible as mobile shoppers scroll through description and reviews.
Consider showing inventory levels when stock is low — 'only three left' creates genuine urgency that can prompt buying now rather than bookmarking.
Ask Sidekick: 'Analyze my top product page and suggest improvements' to get recommendations based on your actual content.
caveats: The claim that product pages cause 60–70% of conversion killers is the presenter's framing, not a measured benchmark.
Low-stock urgency only works if stock levels are genuine.
Review and UGC use requires customer permission where applicable.
cards.source_name: The OFFICIAL Shopify 2026 Tutorial.docx

cards.title: Reduce navigation friction with click depth, clear categories and mega menus
cards.summary: Keep products reachable in 2–3 clicks, name categories in plain language, and use mega menus and breadcrumbs on larger catalogs.
cards.use_when: Shoppers can't find products, bounce out of category pages, or you're structuring a menu for a growing catalog.
steps: Count clicks from the homepage to products; the source's rule is any product should be reachable in two to three clicks maximum. Ask Sidekick to 'show my current navigation menu structure and identify how many clicks it takes to reach products' to get a click-depth analysis and feedback.

Replace vague category names like 'products', 'shop', or 'items' with plain, descriptive names — 'Women's apparel' tells shoppers what's inside; 'The collection' doesn't. Ask Sidekick to review category names and suggest clearer alternatives for your store's theme.

For large catalogs, use a mega menu — a large hover drop-down showing multiple categories and featured products at once. Ask Sidekick whether your theme supports mega menus and how to set one up, then preview via the eye icon next to Online Store.

Add breadcrumb navigation on product and category pages so shoppers see where they are (Home > Women's > Dresses > Summer) and can move back up without the back button; many modern themes include them — check with Sidekick or use a free app such as Breadcrumbs Uncomplicated.
On mobile, make the search bar prominent by switching the theme editor to mobile view and moving search placement to the top of the header if it isn't already, then save.
caveats: The two-to-three-click rule is the source's heuristic, not a universal law.
Theme capabilities for mega menus and breadcrumbs vary; confirm support before promising the feature.
cards.source_name: The OFFICIAL Shopify 2026 Tutorial.docx

cards.title: Improve site search with predictive text and synonyms
cards.summary: Enable predictive search and add synonyms for misspellings and alternative terms so shoppers find products using their own words.
cards.use_when: Shoppers search and get no results, or you sell products with regional/alternative names (e.g. sneakers vs trainers).
steps: Check whether predictive text is already active by going to your live store view and typing in the search bar — predictive text shows related products as the customer types (typing 'cocoa' surfaces coconut matcha).
Some themes include it automatically (the source names Horizon); if not, install the free Shopify-made Search and Discovery app and enable custom search suggestions and predictive search.
Add search synonyms for common misspellings and alternative terms: if you sell sneakers, shoppers searching 'trainers' or 'tennis shoes' should still find the products.
On mobile, keep the search icon visible in the header — phone shoppers prefer to search rather than browse nested menus.
Ask Sidekick how to improve navigation on mobile if you're not sure where shoppers are getting lost.
caveats: Search and Discovery app features and availability vary; confirm in the current app store listing.
Synonym lists need maintenance as your catalog and customer vocabulary change.
cards.source_name: The OFFICIAL Shopify 2026 Tutorial.docx

cards.title: Diagnose and reduce site speed problems
cards.summary: Use bounce rate and PageSpeed Insights to find speed problems, then cut unused apps, compress images and replace heavy theme elements.
cards.use_when: Your bounce rate looks high, mobile pages load slowly, or conversions feel capped despite traffic.
steps: Check the signal first: under Analytics and Reports, open Bounce rate over time; the source treats above 60% as a likely speed problem.
Test specific pages with Google's free PageSpeed Insights tool to get detailed performance metrics.

Cut apps: in Apps, Installed apps, audit what is actively used and uninstall disabled or dormant apps (that popup app you tried months ago, the never-activated currency converter). If unsure, ask Sidekick to 'audit my installed apps and identify which ones are slowing down my store' and which to remove or replace.
Optimize images before uploading: compress with free tools like TinyPNG or Squoosh, keep each image under 200 KB, use JPEG for product photos and PNG for graphics with transparency like logos.
Handle video carefully: avoid autoplay on the homepage, especially on mobile; make video click-to-play.

Check your theme: older themes can be replaced with ones built on Shopify's modern theme architecture (the source names the Horizon theme foundation), which use Shopify's CDN to serve images from servers near customers. Check load speed under Online Store, Themes, where Shopify reports milliseconds and a green/yellow/red rating.
Optimize every element not rated green.
caveats: The 'every 1 second delay costs around 7% in conversions' figure is cited by the source from studies — treat it as an illustrative estimate, not a guarantee. The source's own $10,000/month example is arithmetic on that assumption.
The 60% bounce rate threshold is a heuristic for flagging a possible speed issue, not proof of one.
PageSpeed tool output changes over time; interpret scores in context of your own pages.
cards.source_name: The OFFICIAL Shopify 2026 Tutorial.docx

cards.title: Cut checkout friction: payment options, forms and cost transparency
cards.summary: Reduce the checkout drop by enabling accelerated payments, guest checkout, minimal form fields and early shipping cost visibility.
cards.use_when: The largest funnel drop is between cart/checkout and completed purchase, or abandoned cart rates look high.
steps: Enable accelerated checkout options — Shop Pay, Apple Pay, Google Pay — in payment settings via Manage payment methods (these auto-fill customer info so buyers check out in seconds). The source calls Shop Pay a standout because returning customers can check out in one click.

Keep guest checkout on — forcing account creation before purchase kills conversions; the source suggests asking for an account after the purchase instead. Guest checkout is enabled by default in Shopify.

Minimize form fields: go to Settings, Checkout and ask for only one of email or phone rather than both, and make company name, address line 2, and shipping phone optional. Every extra field is another chance for the buyer to leave.
Show shipping costs early — surprise costs at the last step kill checkouts. If possible show estimated shipping on product pages or at least in the cart.

Use the announcement bar to communicate thresholds upfront; in the theme editor, hover the announcement bar, click 'ask for changes' and enter something like 'Add free shipping over $75 to this announcement bar' (a Sidekick-assisted edit).
If unsure where to focus, ask Sidekick to analyze checkout abandonment and suggest improvements, then review checkout abandonment analytics for specific problems.
caveats: The ~70% average cart abandonment rate the source cites is an industry-wide figure; much abandonment is normal comparison shopping, not fixable friction.
Accelerated payment availability depends on plan, region and buyer device.
Free-shipping thresholds are a merchandising choice; the $75 example is illustrative.
cards.source_name: The OFFICIAL Shopify 2026 Tutorial.docx

cards.title: Build checkout trust with badges and concrete delivery dates
cards.summary: Add secure-checkout signals and specific delivery estimates to reduce last-step hesitation.
cards.use_when: Checkout is where buyers hesitate, or you want clearer expectations to reduce 'where is my order' friction and abandonment.
steps: Payment logos and SSL padlock appear automatically in the checkout footer once payment methods are enabled, so enabling methods is the first trust step.

Consider trust-badge apps from the Shopify app store (the source names Essential Trust Badges and Icons, Conversion Bear Trust Badges, Super Trust Badges and Icons) and pick the one that fits your look.
Add estimated delivery dates: 'Arrives by Thursday' is more compelling than 'standard shipping 5–7 business days' because it is concrete and confident.

On a professional plan, turn on automated delivery dates via Settings, Shipping and Delivery, Estimated Delivery Dates, selecting Automated, and setting your fulfillment time — Shopify then estimates delivery from carrier transit times.
For more control, set manual delivery dates by adjusting processing times, transit times on flat-rate shipping, or by using carrier-calculated rates.
The goal is removing uncertainty so checkout feels easy, clear and trustworthy.
caveats: Automated delivery dates require specific plans/features; check your plan before promising the feature.
Delivery estimates depend on accurate fulfillment and transit settings — wrong estimates create worse post-purchase problems.
cards.source_name: The OFFICIAL Shopify 2026 Tutorial.docx

cards.title: Set up abandoned cart and abandonment recovery flows
cards.summary: Recover lost buyers with a default abandoned checkout email, a cart-abandonment automation, and optional WhatsApp recovery for higher-value carts.
cards.use_when: Customers add to cart or reach checkout then leave without buying, and you want automated recovery without manual outreach.
steps: Go to Marketing, Automations and confirm 'Recover abandoned checkout' is enabled — Shopify creates the email automatically. Review the design, messaging and recipient list.
That email typically sends a few hours after abandonment and links directly back to the cart so the buyer can finish in one click; customize content and timing to match your brand.

Also use the cart-abandonment automation, which fires when a customer adds at least one item and leaves without continuing to checkout. It automatically excludes anyone who received an abandoned checkout or product browse email in the last 14 days, preventing over-emailing the same person.
Preview each template, edit the messaging and design to match your brand, then turn on the automation.

For higher-value carts, layer WhatsApp recovery via Shopify Flow: install Flow if needed, browse templates, search for sending a WhatsApp message to recover abandoned checkout, install and turn on the workflow.
If unsure where to focus, ask Sidekick to analyze checkout abandonment and suggest improvements, then use the abandonment analytics it points to.
caveats: Automation emails generally go only to customers subscribed to marketing.
The 14-day exclusion window is Shopify's default behavior, not a universal rule; review whether it fits your send cadence.
Abandoned checkout emails are free under Shopify Messaging even though other campaigns count toward the monthly allowance.
WhatsApp recovery involves external apps and regional availability.
cards.source_name: The OFFICIAL Shopify 2026 Tutorial.docx

cards.title: Run a VIP campaign using top products, a segment and an exclusive code
cards.summary: Personalize offers to loyal customers instead of discounting the whole list, using a repeatable workflow of bestsellers, a VIP segment and a targeted code.
cards.use_when: You want to reward repeat buyers and protect margin instead of sending a blanket discount to everyone.
steps: Identify bestselling products via Analytics, Reports, Sales by product, or ask Sidekick to 'show me my top five bestselling products'.

Create a collection for the campaign — ask Sidekick to create an automated collection called Best Sellers VIP with those top products, review the collection details form, adjust title, description or products, preview, then save.
Define VIPs in Customers, Segments using behavior such as two or more orders or total spend over a threshold like $200.

Create a discount for the segment — for example ask Sidekick to create a 10% code called VIP10 for orders over $50; under eligibility choose the specific VIP segment; set usage limits (total or one per customer) and the active start and end dates; save.

Draft the campaign email asking Sidekick to write a subject line and body promoting the VIP collection with the code; review and refine with follow-up prompts like 'make it shorter' or 'add more urgency'.
Create the email campaign, choose a template, paste the copy, select the VIP segment from step three, review, then send or schedule.
caveats: The source's reasoning is that blanket discounts give money to buyers who would have paid full price — that's a margin argument, not a measured result.
VIP thresholds like two orders or $200 spend are examples; set the ones that match your order economics.
Segments, discounts and campaigns depend on having enough identified repeat customers.
cards.source_name: The OFFICIAL Shopify 2026 Tutorial.docx

cards.title: Test one variable at a time and watch real behavior with heat maps
cards.summary: Run simple A/B tests on single elements and use heat maps to see where visitors click, scroll and ignore.
cards.use_when: You want to improve conversion scientifically rather than guessing, and need to prioritize which element to change first.
steps: Show half your visitors version A and half version B, then compare performance.
Test only one element at a time — changing headline, images and button color together means you won't know which change made the difference.
Worth-testing candidates named by the source: product page layouts, headline copy, add-to-cart button text (e.g. 'Add to cart' vs 'Buy now' vs 'Get yours'), and homepage hero images.
Run tests for at least two weeks before drawing conclusions, so you have enough data to be confident the result isn't random variation.

Consider a heat map app such as Lucky Orange or Hotjar to see where visitors click, how far they scroll and what they ignore — this reveals behavior you wouldn't guess and helps prioritize what to optimize next.
Treat optimization as continuous: what works now can change in a few months, so re-test after meaningful changes.
caveats: The two-week minimum is a rule of thumb; low-traffic stores need longer to reach confidence.
Heat map tools add scripts that can affect speed — weigh the insight against load cost.
cards.source_name: The OFFICIAL Shopify 2026 Tutorial.docx

cards.title: Keep a weekly marketing routine of one email, your post goal, one data-driven change
cards.summary: A simple repeating checklist prevents burnout and builds momentum: send an email, hit your social goal, check the dashboard, adjust one thing.
cards.use_when: You're managing marketing alongside everything else and need a sustainable weekly cadence rather than launching five strategies at once.
steps: Send one email per week — an offer, update or story.
Meet your social media post goal (one to two, or three to four posts, depending on the cadence you set).
Check the marketing dashboard inside Shopify admin and review: which channel drove the most sessions, which brought sales, and what your conversion rate is.
Adjust one thing based on that data rather than changing everything.
Use Sidekick for ideas, summaries, suggestions and pulling reports so the routine isn't entirely manual.
If you're tempted to start multiple new strategies, start with one, build the habit, then layer in more as you learn what works.
caveats: This is the presenter's recommended cadence, not a proven universal optimum.
Consistency and small tweaks are the stated goal; intensity is explicitly discouraged because of burnout risk.
cards.source_name: The OFFICIAL Shopify 2026 Tutorial.docx

cards.title: Use Sidekick across setup, analysis and creative tasks
cards.summary: Route recurring store questions and tasks — attribution advice, menu audits, app auditing, copy, segments and campaigns — through Sidekick instead of digging through admin manually.
cards.use_when: You need a quick answer or action in Shopify admin without knowing where to click, or you want to move faster on setup, optimization and content.
steps: Ask plain questions like 'Which attribution should I use for my store?' — the source says Sidekick suggests a model and explains what each measures (awareness, full journey, last touch).
Delegate analysis: request a marketing section report at the top of the day, ask why product page conversion is low, or ask it to analyze top product pages and suggest improvements.
Delegate build tasks: creating automated collections, discount codes for segments, subject lines and preview text, or a full VIP campaign email draft.

Use it for store structure questions: menu structure and click-depth analysis, category naming suggestions, whether your theme supports mega menus or breadcrumbs, and how to improve mobile navigation.
Use it for app and speed work: audit installed apps and identify which to remove or replace to improve speed and conversions.
Use it as a setup guide for new features — it will either do the task or walk you through the steps in real time.
Review anything Sidekick drafts or changes before sending or saving.
caveats: Sidekick's capabilities, prompts and interface change across Shopify releases; verify the current behavior.
AI-generated copy, collections and discounts still need human review for brand voice, accuracy and pricing logic.
cards.source_name: The OFFICIAL Shopify 2026 Tutorial.docx

cards.title: Optimize WordPress permalinks and strip default plugins after install
cards.summary: Configure clean post-name URLs and deactivate bundled plugins before building a WooCommerce store, so product URLs stay readable and the site isn't bloated.
cards.use_when: You've just installed WordPress and WooCommerce on your host and need to lock down URL structure and plugin bloat before adding products.
steps: Go to Settings > Permalinks and select 'Post name' so product and page URLs read as /product-name/ rather than /?p=123. This matters for SEO and for customers sharing product links.

Go to the Plugins screen and use bulk actions to deactivate and delete default plugins that ship with the host's WordPress install and aren't needed (e.g., sample/hello-world plugins, bundled marketing or AI plugins you won't use).
After permalink changes, verify a product page and a category page load correctly, because some hosts need a .htaccess or server rewrite refresh.
Confirm your SSL is active before launching checkout, since permalink and rewrites interact with HTTPS redirects on most hosts.
caveats: The exact plugin names bundled by a host vary; verify which plugins are truly safe to delete before bulk-deleting.
Some managed hosts force a permalink structure or manage rewrites themselves.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Set origin-based vs destination-based tax correctly per state
cards.summary: Cross-reference TaxJar to determine whether each state taxes by shop base address or customer shipping address, then enter rates with four decimal places in WooCommerce.
cards.use_when: You're configuring WooCommerce tax rates and need to decide which address WooCommerce should use as the tax basis for each state you sell into.
steps: Use TaxJar (or a similar reference) to look up each state's tax rule and confirm whether the state is origin-based or destination-based.

In WooCommerce, go to WooCommerce > Settings > Tax and choose the 'Calculate tax based on' option. For origin-based states, select 'Shop base address' so tax is computed from where your business is. For destination-based states, select 'Customer shipping address' so tax follows the buyer's location.
Add tax rates with four decimal places (e.g., 7.2500), matching how WooCommerce expects rate entry.
Test a cart with a shipping address in each type of state to confirm the tax line matches your expectation.
For multi-state selling, use tax tables/rates per state rather than a single blanket rate.
caveats: WooCommerce's setting is global; if you ship to both origin- and destination-based states, you need per-state rate tables plus rules, not just one setting.
TaxJar data and state rules change; re-verify rates periodically or use an automated tax service for accuracy.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Charge flat-rate shipping per item instead of per order
cards.summary: Use the [qty] shortcode in WooCommerce's flat-rate cost field to multiply a dollar amount by the number of items in the cart.
cards.use_when: You want shipping priced per unit (e.g., heavy or bulky goods) rather than a flat charge for the whole order.
steps: In WooCommerce, go to Settings > Shipping, create or edit a shipping zone, and add a Flat Rate method.
In the Flat Rate cost field, enter a formula such as [qty] * 10 where 10 is your per-item dollar amount, so each item adds $10 to shipping.
Save and test with a two-item and three-item cart to confirm the shipping line scales as expected.
Combine with shipping classes if different product types need different per-item amounts.
caveats: [qty] counts total cart quantity; if you need per-weight or per-dimension pricing, use weight/dimension-based rules instead.
Free-shipping thresholds or coupons can interact with flat-rate formulas; test combinations.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Install Stripe and PayPal via dedicated third-party plugins, not defaults
cards.summary: The source recommends skipping WooCommerce's bundled payment plugins and installing 'Payment Plugins for Stripe WooCommerce' and 'Payment Plugins for PayPal WooCommerce' for API-key setup.
cards.use_when: You're connecting card and PayPal payments and deciding which gateway plugin to install and how to enter API credentials.
steps: In WordPress, go to Plugins > Add New and search for 'Payment Plugins for Stripe WooCommerce'; install and activate it. Repeat for 'Payment Plugins for PayPal WooCommerce'.

For Stripe: obtain your Publishable Key and Secret Key from your Stripe dashboard, then in the plugin go to Stripe API Settings, paste the Publishable Key, paste the Secret Key, and run the provided Connection Test.
Confirm the connection test passes before going live; a failed test usually means a wrong key or a test/live key mismatch.
Repeat the analogous API-key flow in the PayPal plugin, using your PayPal app credentials.
Place a live test transaction (small amount) and refund it to confirm the full capture and refund path works before launch.
caveats: This is the presenter's recommendation; default WooCommerce gateway plugins also exist and may suit simpler setups.
Plugin interfaces and menu names change — verify the current settings paths in your installed version.
Never paste live secret keys into a shared or test environment you don't control.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Create global product attributes before building variable products
cards.summary: For variable products, define attributes globally first, then attach them to the product and generate variations with individual SKUs, images, prices and stock.
cards.use_when: You're creating a variable product (e.g., apparel with sizes and colors) and need a repeatable, correctly ordered workflow.
steps: Go to Products > Attributes and create global attributes (e.g., Weight, Toy Option, Size, Color) with their terms. Do this globally rather than only at the product level so attributes can be reused across the catalog.
Open the product and set Product data to 'Variable product'.
Add the existing global attributes on the Attributes tab and check 'Used for variations' for each one you want to generate combinations from.
Click 'Generate variations' to create the full combination set, then assign each variation its own SKU, image, price and stock.
Ensure every variation has a price, because a variation with no price is not purchasable.
Save and check the product page to confirm all desired variations appear and are selectable.
caveats: Generating all combinations can create many variations for multi-attribute products; prune unused combinations.
Global attributes are the recommended pattern, but product-level (custom) attributes still exist and may be fine for one-off products.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Build a Variable Product with Global Attributes
cards.summary: Correct order of operations for creating purchasable WooCommerce variable products with global attributes and generated variations.
cards.use_when: Adding a product to the catalog that comes in multiple sizes, weights, colors or option types and must be purchasable per variation.
steps: Create attributes globally first: go to Products > Attributes (not the product-level custom attribute field) and define each attribute such as Weight or Toy Option. Global attributes are reusable across the whole catalog and keep naming consistent, which matters once you have dozens of products.
Create the product and set its type to Variable product.
In the Attributes tab, add the existing global attributes, then tick 'Used for variations' on each one. An attribute not marked for variations cannot be used to generate variants.
Click 'Generate variations' to create the child rows, then assign each variation its own SKU, image and price.
Verify every variation you want sold has a price; a variation without a price is not purchasable, so it will silently fail at add-to-cart.
Set stock, weight and dimensions per variation if they differ, then save and test add-to-cart for at least two variations on the front end.
caveats: Building attributes at product level instead of globally forces you to re-enter them for every new product and causes inconsistent filter/attribute listings later.
The product type must be set to Variable before the Attributes tab offers the variation options.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Install Payment Gateways for Stripe and PayPal
cards.summary: Skip default payment plugins and wire dedicated Stripe/PayPal gateway plugins so customers can pay on-site without third-party redirects.
cards.use_when: Preparing a store checkout to accept card and PayPal payments directly on your own domain instead of sending buyers off-site.
steps: Decide the principle first: the goal is payment processed inside your store. The source recommends not relying on the default WooCommerce payment options and instead installing dedicated gateway plugins — specifically 'Payment Plugins for Stripe WooCommerce' and 'Payment Plugins for PayPal WooCommerce'.
Install and activate both plugins from Plugins > Add New, searching the exact plugin names.
Open the Stripe settings and enter credentials in this order: Stripe API Settings, paste the Publishable Key, paste the Secret Key, then run the Connection Test.
Only move on to checkout testing after the connection test passes; a failed test means keys were mistyped or copied from the wrong Stripe mode (test vs live).
Repeat for PayPal with its own credentials, then place a real low-value test order to confirm the charge goes through and the order status updates.
Keep an offline method (e.g. cash on delivery) enabled if you serve local buyers, and enable local/regional gateways per the store's market.
caveats: Plugin names, settings paths and key labels change between versions — verify the current plugin interface before following a click path.
Never publish or share secret keys; rotate them if they are exposed.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Set Store Address, Selling and Shipping Locations
cards.summary: Configure WooCommerce General settings so tax, currency and shipping only apply to the markets you actually serve.
cards.use_when: Setting up or restricting which countries and regions your store sells and ships to before launching products.
steps: Go to WooCommerce > Settings > General and set the store address (use your business base if you have no physical store), city, state and postcode. This address feeds tax and shipping logic.
Under Selling location, choose one of three modes: sell to all countries; sell to specific countries (a whitelist — select each country you serve); or sell to all countries except (a blacklist).

Pick the shipping location mode. If you sell physical goods, keep 'ship to all countries you sell to' so shipping mirrors your selling whitelist. If the store sells only virtual goods (gift cards, ebooks, digital downloads), choose 'disable shipping and shipping calculations' instead.
Enable taxes if you will calculate tax rates, and enable coupons if you plan to run discount codes; both add settings tabs you will need afterwards.
Set the store currency (e.g. USD) — this is the currency all product prices are entered in.
Save changes, then re-open the settings to confirm the new Taxes/Coupons tabs appeared as expected.
caveats: Mismatched selling and shipping rules cause checkout errors for valid customers, so review both before launch.
The disable-shipping option only makes sense when nothing physical is shipped.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Set a Catalog Placeholder Image
cards.summary: Upload a branded placeholder image so products with missing or broken images still look intentional in the shop grid.
cards.use_when: Launching a shop catalog where image uploads may fail or products may lack images, and you do not want empty grey boxes in the grid.
steps: Upload your desired placeholder graphic to WordPress Media Library (a simple branded tile works).
Click the image and copy its File URL — this is what WooCommerce needs, an attachment ID or URL.
Go to WooCommerce > Settings > Products and paste the URL into the Placeholder image field, replacing the default numeric value.
Save changes, then view the shop page and confirm the placeholder renders wherever a product image fails to load.
caveats: The placeholder is global: it appears for any product whose image is missing or fails to load, so it should look neutral rather than product-specific.
This does not fix the underlying missing image — flag products lacking real imagery separately.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Choose Tax-Inclusive or Tax-Exclusive Product Pricing
cards.summary: Decide whether your entered product prices include tax, since this changes what shoppers see on the shop page versus checkout.
cards.use_when: Configuring store tax settings before entering product prices, especially for multi-state or multi-country tax rules.
steps: Open WooCommerce > Settings > Taxes and pick between 'Yes, I will enter prices inclusive of tax' and 'No, I will enter prices exclusive of tax'.

Understand the consequence with an example: if the intended all-in price is $100 and tax is 5%, inclusive mode means you type 105 as the product price; exclusive mode means you type 100 and the 5% is added at checkout.
Consider what the shop page shows: inclusive mode displays the tax-included number to shoppers; exclusive mode displays the base price and adds tax later based on the buyer's location.
Note that the customer's final total is effectively the same either way; only the display and the number you type differ.
The source prefers exclusive pricing so the store page shows the base price and tax appears at checkout — but this is a presentation choice, so match it to your market convention.
Set 'calculate tax based on customer shipping address' (the default) if tax should follow where the order ships, then save.
caveats: Once you have entered many products, switching modes means re-checking every price.
Tax display conventions differ by country; what looks correct in one market can look misleading in another.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Build Location-Based Tax Rates with State Rows
cards.summary: Create per-state tax rules so US customers are charged the correct rate for where they are, with a country-level fallback.
cards.use_when: Selling into the US (or any region with sub-region tax rates) and needing checkout to apply the right percentage automatically.
steps: Look up accurate current rates from a sales-tax reference (the source uses TaxJar's sales tax by state page) rather than guessing — for example California 7.25%, New York 4%, Washington 6.5%.
In WooCommerce > Settings > Taxes, either use the standard rate table or create a new tax class by typing a name into the additional tax classes field and saving; the new tab appears for editing.

In the rate table, insert rows: enter the country code (US), then the state code (CA, NY), leave postcode and city blank for a whole-state rule, and enter the rate with four decimal places — write 7.25 as 7.2500 and 4 as 4.0000.
Give each row a tax name (e.g. Tax) and keep priority at 1 unless you need to stack rules.
Toggle the shipping option per row: enable it if that state taxes shipping, disable it if not — this varies by state, so decide per rule.

Add a country-level fallback row with country code US and state code left empty (e.g. 5.0000) so customers in states you have not listed still get taxed; save and test checkout with California and a non-listed state address.
caveats: Rules can overlap — a California customer matches both the CA row and any US-wide row, so understand priority rather than assuming one silently wins.
Rates change; verify against a current source before relying on any number.
This covers tax configuration only, not full compliance obligations.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Set Weight and Dimension Units Before Adding Products
cards.summary: Choose store-wide weight and dimension units early so product data and shipping calculations are entered consistently.
cards.use_when: Configuring a store that ships physical goods and will rely on weight/dimension data for shipping rates.
steps: Go to WooCommerce > Settings > Products > Measurements.
Pick a weight unit (kilogram, gram, lbs, oz) — the source chose gram — and a dimension unit (meter, centimeter, millimeter, inches), choosing inches in the example.
Save changes before creating products; units are store-wide, so changing later means re-entering or converting every product's numeric data.
When creating products, enter weight and dimensions in these units only, and be consistent across the catalog so shipping rules compute correctly.
caveats: Mixed units across products silently produce wrong shipping calculations.
Product-level weight/dimensions won't matter until you configure shipping methods that use them.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Enable Customer Registration with Subscriber Role
cards.summary: Allow shoppers to create accounts on the store while keeping their permissions limited to subscriber level.
cards.use_when: Setting up account-based features such as order history, saved addresses, wishlists and logged-in checkout.
steps: In WordPress Settings > General, tick 'Anyone can register' so shoppers can create accounts.
Set 'New user default role' to Subscriber, not Administrator, Editor, Author or Contributor. You remain the Administrator; everyone who self-registers gets only subscriber capabilities.
Save changes, then test by registering a new account and confirming it lands as a subscriber.
Expect WooCommerce to supply the customer-facing pages — My Account, Cart, Checkout, Shop, Wishlist — after activation; you will customise them rather than build from scratch.
caveats: Leaving the default role above subscriber is a real security risk — self-registered users could edit or publish content.
Some stores deliberately allow guest checkout instead of forcing accounts; this setting enables registration but does not obligate it.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Set Post Name Permalinks for Clean Product and Page URLs
cards.summary: Switch WordPress permalinks to post name so shop, product and post URLs are readable for shoppers and search engines.
cards.use_when: Immediately after installing WordPress and before creating shop, product or blog pages that should rank and be shareable.
steps: Go to Settings > Permalinks and review the default structures (plain, day and name, month and name, numeric, or post name).
Understand the difference: plain produces URLs with random numbers and characters; day-and-name embeds the publish date; post name produces short readable slugs such as domain.com/shop.
Select 'Post name' and save changes.

Do this early — the source's recommendation is strong on post name because readable URLs look better to shoppers and support search ranking, but changing structure later can break existing links, so pair it with redirects if you switch after launch.
caveats: Post name is a general good practice rather than a guaranteed ranking factor; content and site structure still drive SEO.
Changing permalink structure on a live store requires maintaining redirects so old indexed URLs don't 404.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Configure Site Title and Tagline as Positioning Statements
cards.summary: Use the WordPress site title and tagline to state clearly what the store sells and where, instead of leaving a generic name.
cards.use_when: Setting up a new store and choosing the wording that appears in the browser tab, search results and site header.
steps: Go to Settings > General and set the Site Title to your store or brand name — it updates the header instantly.
Write a tagline that is specific and market-facing rather than generic. The source's example: 'best pet food online store in California' — naming the category and the geography.
Rationale: a specific phrase matches how a shopper might actually search, so the store has a chance of appearing for that kind of query.
Keep the tagline meaningful and descriptive; avoid filler that says nothing about what you sell or who you serve.
Save and check the front end to confirm the title and tagline read correctly in the header and title bar.
caveats: The tagline is a positioning aid, not a guaranteed ranking mechanism — the source frames it as increasing the chance of appearing, not securing a position.
Keep it short enough to display cleanly in headers and search snippets.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Choose a Lightweight Ecommerce Theme and Build with a Page Builder
cards.summary: Use a lightweight WooCommerce-supporting theme plus a page builder instead of a heavy pre-designed theme for full design control.
cards.use_when: Deciding the design stack for a new storefront before you build the homepage, shop and product pages.
steps: Recognise the trade-off: themes change the whole look-and-feel with one activation but constrain design, while a page builder gives control over every element — the source chose the builder route and built from scratch rather than using a template.

Install a lightweight theme that still brings ecommerce structure. The source used the free Wooify theme, which provides an ecommerce-friendly sidebar for shop widgets and store customisation options.

Install the page builder (Elementor) plus supporting add-on plugins for extra widgets and forms (the source added Elements Kit and MetForm), a wishlist plugin (MC Wish List / MoreConvert), a variation swatches plugin, and Classic Widgets for widget areas.
Activate plugins in the correct order: WooCommerce first, then the variation swatches plugin that depends on it. WooCommerce being inactive blocks dependent plugins from activating.
Expect WooCommerce to auto-create Cart, Checkout, My Account, Shop and Wishlist pages on activation — these are the pages you will design and configure, not replace.
caveats: A page builder adds weight and its own update surface; the free version omits the theme builder, popups and form widgets that the pro tiers include.
Plugin slugs and names shift between releases — confirm you are installing the current, actively maintained plugin.
Build on staging or take a backup before swapping themes on a live store.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Back Up and Clean a Fresh WordPress Install
cards.summary: Remove default plugins and dashboard clutter and confirm backups exist before building the store.
cards.use_when: Right after installing WordPress and before installing store plugins, to start from a clean, secure base.
steps: Close the welcome popup and either dismiss dashboard widgets individually or use Screen Options to deselect every panel you do not need.
Go to Plugins, select all default plugins, choose Deactivate from Bulk actions and apply, then select all again and choose Delete — the source deletes the stock plugins as a matter of course.
Note it is safer to take a backup before bulk deletions; on the recommended hosting plan daily backups are included, so confirm backups are running before you delete.
Deactivate before deleting — deleting active plugins directly can leave orphaned settings or errors.
Verify that HTTPS is enforced (Force HTTPS enabled in the hosting panel) so the store serves the secure padlock buyers and search engines expect.
After installing your store plugin set, reactivate in dependency order, starting with WooCommerce.
caveats: Some default plugins may be required by the host or by a specific theme; check before deleting.
Do not delete plugins you have not identified — the source's approach is bulk deletion of known stock plugins, not indiscriminate removal.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Verify Hosting, Domain and SSL Before Building
cards.summary: Claim the domain, verify email and enable HTTPS so checkout runs on a secure, controllable foundation.
cards.use_when: Commissioning hosting and the domain for a new store, prior to installing WordPress and WooCommerce.
steps: Purchase hosting and claim the included free first-year domain. Choose a term based on budget: the source notes longer terms give bigger discounts and recommends the 48-month lock-in if affordable, but 12 months is fine to start small.
Register the hosting account with an email you check regularly, because verification codes and domain notices go there.
Verify the email address for the hosting account and again for the domain registration — the source stresses verification is required to complete domain registration.
Choose the .com extension for professionalism, checking availability before committing.
Select the data centre region nearest your target audience when prompted (e.g. a US region for US customers) since this affects site speed for those shoppers.
Enable Force HTTPS in the hosting panel after WordPress is installed, then log into WordPress admin via the hosting dashboard or by appending /wp-admin to your domain.
caveats: Term lengths, plan prices and onboarding flows vary and change frequently — treat specific prices or plan names as examples, and verify current terms.
Rather than relying on an onboarding wizard's layout, the source goes through the host admin panel so the steps remain findable even when onboarding changes.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Build Store Front-End Structure That Mirrors Top Ecommerce Sites
cards.summary: Lay out the storefront with the standard components shoppers expect on the homepage, shop and product pages.
cards.use_when: Planning homepage and shop-page sections for a new store, so shoppers can search, browse and buy without friction.
steps: Header: logo left, navigation menu centre, and search, account and cart buttons right. Make the cart a mini-cart drawer that opens from the side and links to the full cart page.
My Account should let customers manage orders, delivery addresses and account details so they self-serve instead of contacting you.

Homepage order used in the build: banner, call-to-action, best-selling products with add-to-cart, a category section, latest products with a countdown offer, testimonials for trust, blog posts, and a footer.
Shop page: product grid with add-to-cart and wishlist heart buttons, plus sidebar widgets — product search, price filter, recently viewed products, and category/tag filters.

Product page: name, description, images, variations, a stock progress bar showing remaining stock, quantity selector, add-to-cart, full description, additional information, reviews and related products.

Cart and checkout: allow removing items and editing quantities in the cart, then checkout with contact details, billing address, payment method choice, a coupon field that discounts automatically, an order summary showing tax, discount, subtotal and total, and a thank-you page after the order is placed.
caveats: This is a conventional structure the source copied from large marketplaces, not a validated conversion benchmark — treat each section as a hypothesis to test for your catalog.
A stock progress bar can create urgency or backfire by discouraging purchase when stock looks low; test it.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Set State and Country Tax Rates with Priority Rules
cards.summary: Create WooCommerce tax rate rows for specific states, whole countries and fallback rates, then use priority numbers to resolve overlapping rules.
cards.use_when: Configuring tax tables for a store that ships to multiple US states or countries and you need correct rates at checkout.
steps: Open WooCommerce > Settings > Tax (verify current label) and create rate rows. Enter a two-letter country code and, for state-level rules, the two-letter state code; leave state empty for a country-wide fallback rule.
Enter rates in four-decimal format, e.g. California 7.2500 or a source-quoted New York 4.0000, so rounding behaves predictably.
Build a hierarchy: state-specific rows for states with known rates, plus one country-wide row (e.g. US at 5.0000) as a catch-all.

Resolve overlap with priority: when a California customer matches both a California row and the US row, the lower priority number wins. The source set California to priority 1 and the country fallback to priority 2, so California paid 7.25%.
Turn off the shipping-tax flag on rows where you do not want tax charged on shipping cost, then save changes.
Verify at checkout with a test address in each state before launch, and keep the rate table updated as jurisdictions change.
caveats: Source caution: lower number = higher priority; getting this backwards silently charges the wrong rate.
Use your jurisdiction's official rates; the quoted 7.25% California, 4% New York and 5% placeholder are examples, not current guidance.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Use Shipping Zones to Localize Fulfillment Offers
cards.summary: WooCommerce shipping zones let you scope free-shipping and flat-rate rules to a country or a single state.
cards.use_when: Deciding what shipping to offer for a whole country versus a specific state or region, and wanting region-specific perks.
steps: Go to WooCommerce > Settings > Shipping and click Add Zone (verify current interface).
Name the zone (e.g. 'Whole USA') and search the region list for the country; for a state-level zone search and select the state entry, e.g. California, United States.
Add a shipping method to the zone and click Continue; repeat per method.
For a national zone, add a flat rate covering all states. For a narrower zone like California, add a different method such as free shipping with a requirement.
Attach requirements to free shipping: a valid free-shipping coupon or a minimum order amount. The source example granted California free shipping only above a $400 order.
Stack zones deliberately: general rules in the country zone, localized perks in the state zone, so a customer sees both applicable options at checkout.
caveats: The $400 free-shipping threshold is the presenter's example setup, not a recommended benchmark.
Zone and method names may differ in your WooCommerce version; confirm labels in the current UI.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Choose Per-Order or Per-Item Flat Rate Shipping
cards.summary: Flat-rate shipping can be charged once per order or multiplied by quantity using a formula, and heavy goods usually need the per-item version.
cards.use_when: Setting the delivery cost for a physical product line where shipping multiple units would otherwise be unprofitable.
steps: In the zone's flat-rate method settings, enter the base cost as a number with two decimals, e.g. 10.00. By default this charges $10 per order regardless of quantity.
Test the math: with per-order pricing, 10 units still cost $10 total.

To charge per unit, write the cost as a formula using the quantity placeholder: a bracket-wrapped QTY token, a space, an asterisk, then the unit price. The source used [qty] * 10, so 1 unit = $10, 3 units = $30, 10 units = $100.

Decide by product economics: bulky or high-cube goods like furniture should use per-item pricing because one bed pack cannot cost the same to ship as three; low-cost repeat-purchase goods like pet food packets can use per-order pricing to make bulk buys attractive.
Set taxable/none on shipping to match your tax decisions, then save.
caveats: The formula syntax and placeholder tokens can vary by shipping method and version; verify in your settings before relying on it.
Mixing per-order simplicity with heavy goods can erode margin on large orders.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Create Shipping Classes for Heavy or Premium Packaging
cards.summary: Shipping classes let one zone charge a different rate for special packaging while keeping a normal default cost for everything else.
cards.use_when: Storing products whose packaging weight or cost differs materially from the standard packaging, e.g. premium or heavy packs.
steps: In WooCommerce > Settings > Shipping > Classes, click Add Shipping Class (verify current labels).
Name it for the customer-facing consequence (e.g. Premium Shipping), give it a unique slug, and describe what it covers, such as heavy packages.
Return to the zone and edit the flat-rate method; a shipping-class cost field appears alongside a no-shipping-class cost.
Enter the premium class price (source example: $20) and the default no-class price (source example: $10), so products without a class fall back to $10.
Assign the class per product later on the product's Shipping tab, or assign it to a whole variable product so all variations inherit it.
Review margins: raising a class rate is the lever for heavy packaging; keeping a low default keeps light goods competitive.
caveats: The $10/$20 figures are the presenter's illustrative numbers; price from your own carrier rates.
Only one class applies per product, so plan classes around your main cost drivers.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Enable Cod and Verify Stripe and PayPal Setup
cards.summary: Add cash on delivery plus Stripe and PayPal so customers can pay on-site, and test connections before switching to live.
cards.use_when: Turning on payment methods in a new store and connecting gateway accounts safely.
steps: In WooCommerce > Settings > Payments, enable offline methods such as direct bank transfer, check payments and cash on delivery; the source treated COD as a popular, easy win.
Install and activate a Stripe plugin and a PayPal plugin from the plugin repository (the source chose the 'payment plugins' vendor versions; verify current vendor and compatibility).
For Stripe: log into the Stripe dashboard, open Developers > API keys, copy the publishable key and secret key, paste them into the plugin's API settings, then run the connection test.
While testing, stay in test mode and confirm a successful connection message before touching live keys.
For go-live, switch the Stripe account to live mode, complete identity/bank verification, select live mode in the plugin too, and replace keys with live ones.

For PayPal: use API settings with production (not sandbox) environment and paste production client ID and secret, or use Connect to PayPal and log in to link automatically; confirm the status reads connected.
caveats: Plugin menu names and OAuth flows change; verify the current steps in the plugin UI. Never paste live keys while the plugin is still in test mode, and vice versa.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Configure Accounts and Checkout Login Options
cards.summary: Guest checkout plus optional account creation reduces checkout friction while still building a customer list.
cards.use_when: Setting account and checkout behaviour for a new store to balance frictionless purchase against account-based retention.
steps: Open WooCommerce > Settings > Accounts and Privacy (verify label).
Enable guest checkout so buyers can complete an order without registering; the source calls this recommended.
Enable login during checkout so returning customers can sign in from the cart/checkout flow.
Allow account creation during checkout and on the My Account page so new buyers can register in one step rather than after the fact.
Leave remaining defaults unless you have a specific need; the source kept them as-is.
Save changes and test the whole path: add to cart as a guest, checkout, then confirm the account was created so order history, downloads and addresses are available.
caveats: Guest checkout trades some account data capture for higher completion; if subscriptions or repeat purchases dominate, weigh whether requiring an account is worth the friction.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Turn On Transactional Email Notifications Per Event
cards.summary: WooCommerce emails are per-event and many are off by default, so enable and edit each one you actually want sent.
cards.use_when: After orders start flowing, when customers report missing confirmations or you want branded status emails.
steps: Open WooCommerce > Settings > Emails and review each event: new order, cancelled, failed, on hold, processing, completed, refunded, and customer-facing copies.
Identify the recipient for each: admin events go to your store email address, customer events go to the buyer.
Enable each notification you want by opening Manage and using its enable toggle, then save; the source noted disabled notifications simply never send.
Edit the recipient address, subject line, heading, and additional content to match your brand tone; the source edited a cancellation email's heading and closing line.
Adjust the email colour palette so the template matches your store branding.
Confirm both sides of a two-step flow, e.g. an order cancellation first notifies the admin and then, once confirmed, notifies the customer.
caveats: Email delivery depends on your host or SMTP provider; if mail lands in spam, fix sending infrastructure rather than the templates.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Keep the Store in Coming Soon Until Catalogs and Pages Are Ready
cards.summary: Site visibility is a launch switch; keep the store hidden while building, then go live deliberately.
cards.use_when: Building a store before launch and deciding when customers should be able to reach it.
steps: Find the visibility setting (the source used WooCommerce > Settings > Site Visibility; verify current location) and confirm it currently reads Coming Soon.
While in Coming Soon, build the tax, shipping, payment, product and design work with real settings and products.
Before switching to Live, complete a full purchase test: add to cart, checkout with each payment method, apply a coupon, confirm emails and download links arrive.
Set a static homepage and confirm navigation, cart, checkout and My Account pages all resolve.
Switch visibility to Live and save; the dashboard status should change to show the store is live.
Treat launch as the last step, not a first one: the source deliberately published products, tested purchase flow, then went live.
caveats: Coming Soon blocks search-engine and customer access, so switch it off only when products, pages and payments are verified.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Fill Store Details and Page Assignments in Settings
cards.summary: Store name, address, policies and page assignments power invoices, emails and checkout links, so set them rather than relying on placeholders.
cards.use_when: Finalizing store identity and confirming the cart, checkout, account and policy pages WooCommerce uses.
steps: In the point-of-sale/store settings area, replace the default store name with your brand name.
Add the physical store address, phone number and email if you operate a physical location; these feed documents and contact details.
Paste your refund and return policy text in the provided field so it can surface where policies are referenced.
Under Advanced > Page Setup, verify the Cart, Checkout and My Account pages are assigned; the source kept WooCommerce defaults because they worked and looked fine.
Assign a Terms and Conditions page; until you write one, the source temporarily selected the privacy policy page and planned to swap it once the real page existed.
Save and click through each assigned page on the front end to confirm it loads and behaves.
caveats: Do not leave a borrowed policy page as your terms permanently; replace it with accurate terms before launch.
Interface labels for store details and page setup can move between versions.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Create a Simple Physical Product With Pricing, SKU and Stock
cards.summary: The simple product flow covers name, description, price/sale price, SKU, stock, shipping dimensions and categories.
cards.use_when: Adding standard physical products to the catalog at initial setup.
steps: Go to Products > Add New, enter the product name and edit the auto-generated permalink slug only if needed.
Write the rich-text description (headings, bold, lists) that appears in the product's main description area.
In Product Data choose Simple. Set regular price and sale price with two decimals; the sale price displays as the active price with the original struck through.
Set tax status to taxable and pick the tax class you built earlier so the product inherits your state/country rate logic.
Add a unique SKU: the source built it from the title, lowercased, spaces replaced with hyphens, plus a sequence number (e.g. canine-crunch-01) so later variants become 02, 03.
Enable stock management and enter quantity so the product page shows e.g. 10 in stock.
On the Shipping tab enter weight in grams and length/width/height of the full package, not the bare product, then attach a shipping class or leave none for the default rate.
Assign categories and tags for on-site search, set the thumbnail and gallery images, add a short description, and publish; then view /shop to confirm it appears.
caveats: Measure the shipped package, not the item, or carrier rates will be wrong.
SKU conventions are the presenter's suggestion; any unique, consistent scheme works.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Build Variable Products from Global Attributes
cards.summary: Create attributes once at the global level, then generate all variation combinations and price each one individually.
cards.use_when: Selling a product in multiple sizes, weights or bundle options where price and stock differ per option.
steps: Create attributes globally under Products > Attributes so they are reusable across products; the source created a Weight attribute with button type and terms 200g, 400g, 600g, and a Toy attribute with radio type and terms with-toy/without-toy.
On the product, choose Variable, then use Add Existing to attach attributes and select their values, saving attributes each time.
Click Generate Variations to auto-create every combination (two attributes with 3 and 2 values produced 6 variations).
Open each variation and set its thumbnail, unique SKU, price, weight, shipping class and tax class; class and tax class set at the top level apply to all variations unless you override.
Price by value logic: the source charged less for without-toy and more for larger weights, illustrating that option differences should be reflected in price.

Set the parent product's short description, thumbnail, gallery, categories and tags, publish, then check the product page shows Select Options, the price range (e.g. $37–$68) and that switching options updates price.
caveats: The source's per-variation pricing accidentally inverted the with-toy/without-toy logic, showing that option-price mapping must be reviewed.
Many attributes multiply variation count quickly; too many combinations make maintenance heavy.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Create Virtual Downloadable Products for Digital Goods
cards.summary: Marking a product virtual removes shipping; making it downloadable attaches files customers receive after purchase.
cards.use_when: Selling ebooks, guides, templates or other digital files in the store.
steps: Add a new product and keep it Simple, then tick Virtual: the shipping fields disappear because nothing ships.
Tick Downloadable and add files either by pasting a URL or choosing a file from the media library; the source inserted a PDF and attached its file URL.
Set regular and sale price as for a physical product, and assign the appropriate tax class.
Decide download limits and expiry: the source left downloads unlimited and expiry at never; if you want controlled access, set a limit or day count.
Skip stock management because digital goods do not deplete; give the product a SKU such as ebook-01.
Link the digital product to other products as upsells/cross-sells, add a short description, thumbnail, tags and publish.
After a test purchase, verify the order confirmation page exposes the download button and the file opens.
caveats: Unlimited downloads and no expiry make sharing easy; if piracy matters, set limits and expiry or use protected delivery.
File hosting and link stability affect delivery; host files somewhere durable.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: List Affiliate Products as External Products
cards.summary: External/affiliate product type sends buyers to a partner URL with custom button text while keeping the listing on your store.
cards.use_when: Monetizing affiliate programs by merchandising partner goods without fulfillment responsibility.
steps: Add a new product and choose External/Affiliate in Product Data.
Paste your affiliate product URL in the product URL field; this is where the purchase button sends visitors.
Set the button text to set expectations, e.g. 'Buy from Amazon'; the source used exactly that phrasing.
Enter the partner's displayed price so listings look comparable, and skip tax status/class because the transaction occurs off-site.
Add a description, short description, a product image you are allowed to use, and categories/tags, then publish.
On the front end, confirm the button reads as intended and opens the partner page in the expected way.
caveats: Commission is earned only when the tracked link converts; the source frames this as an example, not a guaranteed revenue channel.
Check partner program terms for image and price display rules.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Use Upsells and Cross-Sells to Raise Cart Value
cards.summary: Upsells appear as upgrade suggestions on the product/cart, while cross-sells appear as complementary recommendations.
cards.use_when: Configuring related-product recommendations on product pages and in the cart.
steps: On the product's Linked Products tab, add products to Upsells; the source says these surface in the cart as 'you may be interested in' suggestions tied to the viewed product.
Add products to Cross-Sells; these render as 'you may also like' style recommendations connected to the cart contents.
Build the catalog first: the source could not demonstrate upsells/cross-sells on the first product because no other products existed yet.
Add complementary logic, not duplicates: pair the ebook guide with food, or an accessory with the main item, so the suggestion is relevant.
After publishing, buy-through once to confirm both recommendation blocks appear in the cart and product page.
caveats: Recommendations only work once there are other published products to select.
The source notes upsell/cross-sell placements are tied to how WooCommerce renders them, which theme customization can change.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Configure Coupon Type, Restrictions and Usage Limits
cards.summary: Coupons combine a discount type with spend thresholds, product/category restrictions and per-user or per-coupon caps.
cards.use_when: Running a promotional discount and controlling who can use it, on what, and how often.
steps: Go to Marketing > Coupons > Add New and set the customer-facing code (e.g. JFD20) plus an internal description.
Pick a discount type: Percentage Discount applies a percent of order or product value (20% of $100 = $20), while Fixed Cart/Fixed Product Discount subtract a flat amount regardless of price.
Optionally set an expiry date so the promotion ends automatically.

Use usage restrictions to steer behaviour: minimum spend (e.g. $200) makes the coupon unusable below the threshold; maximum spend (e.g. $500) switches it off above a ceiling because a large percentage becomes expensive; the source left both off.
Include specific products/categories to target the offer, or exclude products/categories to protect low-margin lines.
Set usage limit per coupon (total redemptions, source example 10) and usage limit per user (source example 10 per customer), then publish.
Verify in checkout by applying the code and confirming the discount line and new total update.
caveats: High percentages plus no maximum spend can gut margin on large carts; maximum-spend ceilings exist for that reason.
Limits and thresholds shown are the presenter's examples, not recommended defaults.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Run an End-to-End Purchase and Order Management Test
cards.summary: Testing the full buyer journey and then processing the order from admin verifies setup before launch.
cards.use_when: Before going live, and whenever payments, tax, shipping or emails change.
steps: As a shopper, add several product types: a simple product, a downloadable product and a variable product with a chosen option; manage quantities from the mini-cart and full cart.
Open the cart page and read the totals breakdown: subtotal, shipping (flat rate), tax and estimated total, confirming each reflects your settings.
Proceed to checkout, enter contact and shipping details, choose the shipping method, select a payment method (cash on delivery, Stripe card or PayPal), and optionally add an order note.
Apply the coupon in the order summary and confirm the discount and new total, e.g. a 20% code reducing the total.
Place the order and inspect the thank-you page for order details and, for digital products, the download button.

As admin, go to WooCommerce > Orders, open the order, review items and prices, then set status (pending, on hold, completed, cancelled, refunded, failed) and update; shipping happens before marking completed, and the customer is notified.
Check the My Account area for order history, downloads, addresses and payment methods as the customer sees it.
caveats: Test mode payments do not move real money; repeat key checks with live credentials before relying on the flow.
Order status wording and available statuses may vary with installed extensions.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Set a Static Homepage Before Building the Storefront
cards.summary: WordPress serves posts on the root URL by default; assigning a static page makes your designed homepage reachable at the domain.
cards.use_when: After creating the homepage page and before designing it in a page builder.
steps: Go to Pages > Add New, title it Home and publish; it can be empty at first.
Open Settings > Reading and under homepage display change from latest posts to a static page, then select the new Home page as the homepage.
Save changes and visit the bare domain to confirm the Home page loads instead of a blog roll.
Then open the page with the Elementor editor (or your page builder) to design it.
Note that default WooCommerce pages such as cart, checkout and my account already exist; leave them assigned and do not overwrite them with the homepage.
caveats: Changing homepage display later requires re-selecting the page; if the root looks empty, check this setting first.
Page-builder menu names and locations shift across versions.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Know Free Page Builder Versus Pro Widget Boundaries
cards.summary: Elementor's free widgets cover layout, headings, images, text, video and buttons, while advanced widgets such as posts, portfolio, loop and carousel require the pro tier or add-on plugins.
cards.use_when: Planning how to build product and homepage sections without buying pro, and deciding whether add-on widget plugins are needed.
steps: In the editor sidebar, inventory the free widgets: containers, grid, heading, image, text editor, video, button and similar basics.
Scroll to the pro group to see advanced widgets like search, posts, portfolio, gallery, loop and carousel; these will not be available on the free tier.
Plan sections using free equivalents: build image grids and headings manually rather than expecting a loop or portfolio widget.
Consider add-on widget plugins such as the source's Elementskit to expand available widgets if the free set is insufficient.
Check compatibility and performance before stacking multiple widget plugins, since each adds weight and update risk.
caveats: Feature tiers and widget lists change; verify what your installed version includes.
The source mentions a paid template marketplace; evaluate whether templates or building from scratch fits your time budget.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Build a WooCommerce Homepage Banner in Elementor with Containers
cards.summary: Step-by-step Elementor container setup for a conversion-focused store homepage banner with heading, CTA button, and social proof counter.
cards.use_when: Building or rebuilding the hero/banner section of a WooCommerce storefront homepage in Elementor, or deciding how to structure the top-of-page offer area.
steps: Start from an empty Elementor canvas: add a container, rename it 'banner section' (renaming is organisational only, it has no functional effect but keeps structure navigable).
Set the banner container to content width 'boxed' at 1240px, gaps 0, background color classic (e.g. a beige #FFF8F0), and padding of 20px left/right and ~132px bottom to create breathing room.
Nest a 'top area' container inside it, set direction row, width 100%, padding-top ~34px, padding-bottom ~104px.

Split the top area into three inner containers: left (~32.6% width, holds product imagery), middle (~31.5% width, holds headline copy and button), right (~31.2% width, justify-content end, holds visual accents).
