For the headline use a Heading widget with a heavy weight (source used 96px size, 800 weight, tight line-height ~108px and negative letter spacing for a compact editorial look) so the store's value proposition reads as the dominant page element.

Add a CTA Button widget linking to the shop page (type 'shop' in the link field and select the suggested page). Add an SVG icon via Upload SVG with ~12px icon spacing, 50px border radius for a pill shape, and brand background colour.

Add a social-proof cluster: image + Counter widget (source showed '40k+' regular customers). Use number suffix for 'k+' and style the label separately. This is a trust element placed inside the hero, not a separate section.

If the section doesn't span the viewport, fix it with Page Settings > Page Layout > Elementor Full Width, and set a global page background colour under Page Settings > Style so individual sections don't each need their own fill.
Use position:absolute on decorative images (Advanced tab > Position) with horizontal/vertical offsets — e.g. right/-15, top/-15 — so they overlay without consuming layout space.
Set the outer bottom area container to direction row, justify-content space-between, align-items center for a balanced footer strip within the banner.
caveats: The specific pixel values (1240px, 96px type, 132px padding) are the presenter's chosen design values for one project, not performance-proven numbers — adjust to your brand and test on real devices.
The source used Elementor v3.33.6 for stability; the newest version at time of recording (4.0.1) was considered unstable, so pin to a known stable version during build.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Roll Back Elementor to a Stable Version Before Building
cards.summary: Safely freeze a page builder at a known stable release via Elementor's version control to avoid mid-build incompatibilities.
cards.use_when: Before starting or resuming a storefront build when a page builder has just released a major version and layouts, widgets, or third-party add-ons may break.
steps: Confirm your builder version: open the editor, click the Elementor logo and read the version indicator in the panel.

Exit to the WordPress dashboard via the logo menu, and hover over Elementor > Tools (this is where version control lives in the interface at time of recording — verify the current location as Elementor's menu can change).
Open Version Control, choose 'Rollback Version', select the specific version you want (source used 3.33.6), and click Reinstall, then Continue.
Close and reopen the editor tab, refresh, and confirm the older version is active before you build anything.
Complete the whole build on the stable version; you can update to the newest release afterward once it settles.
Publish frequently during the build so a refresh, browser crash, or closed tab doesn't cost you design work.
caveats: Version numbers cited (3.33.6 stable, 4.0.1 unstable) are from the recording date; check the current release status yourself before pinning.
The exact menu path (Elementor > Tools > Version Control) is UI-dependent and should be verified in your current installation.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Speed Up Store Builds with Elementor Global Colors and Global Fonts
cards.summary: Configure global brand colours, fonts, container width, and zero default padding/gaps once so every new section inherits the store's design system.
cards.use_when: When first configuring a WooCommerce theme/page builder so that every subsequent product section, category block, or landing page is faster to build and visually consistent.
steps: Open the editor's site settings (Elementor > Site Settings > Global Colors) and reassign the defaults: put your most-used brand colour into Primary, your accent/CTA colour into Secondary, paragraph colour into Text, and the accent colour you reuse most into Accent.

Under Global Fonts, set all four typography slots (Primary, Secondary, Text, Accent) to your brand typeface so new headings and paragraphs pick it up automatically instead of you re-selecting fonts each time.

Under Site Settings > Layout, set Content Width to your design width (source used 1240px from a 1140px default), set default container padding to 0 and default gaps to 0 so each new container starts clean.
Save changes, close the panel, then Publish and refresh the page — global settings don't apply to the already-loaded editor until you reload.
After reload, add a new container and confirm the width and zero-gap defaults are inherited; this is the fastest ongoing check.
Create reusable global colours inside the individual typography/colour pickers (the plus icon) for any brand tone you use repeatedly, e.g. a named 'black' text colour and 'orange' CTA colour.
caveats: Global settings only take effect after a page refresh; forgetting to publish first risks losing unsaved work.
Some widget typography fields (e.g. the countdown widget in the source) don't inherit the global font family by default and require selecting a custom/global font manually.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Use Position Absolute + Offsets to Place Decorative Store Images Precisely
cards.summary: Take hero and section images out of normal flow with absolute positioning and numeric offsets for pixel-accurate layering.
cards.use_when: Layering product photos, badges, paw prints, or accent graphics over a hero, category block, or promo box where images must overlap copy or each other at exact coordinates.
steps: Add the image widget where it belongs in the structure, then open Advanced > Positioning and set Position to Absolute.

Set Horizontal Orientation (left/right/center) plus an offset in px, and Vertical Orientation (top/bottom/center) plus an offset. Example from source: right/-15 horizontally and top/-15 vertically to overlap a corner.

Instead of offsets, you can also drag the image by hand once it is absolute — useful for eyeballing decorative placements, but switch to numeric offsets for values you want to reuse across breakpoints.

For images that sit over a solid or branded section, use Style > CSS Filters to recolour them without a new asset: setting Contrast to 0 makes the image grey, and lowering Opacity (source used 0.7) softens it against the background.
Give absolutely-positioned decorative images explicit Custom width/height in px (e.g. 96px, 49px, 52px) so they scale predictably.
To stack avatars/thumbnails in a row, apply a negative margin (source used -35px) to pull the overlapping image over its neighbour.
Set a text caption or label over an image by making the Heading widget absolute as well (source used right offset 28, top offset 56) rather than adding a background layer.
caveats: Absolute positioning removes the element from layout flow, so sibling containers won't reserve space for it — verify each breakpoint separately or decoratives will overlap badly on mobile.
Drag-and-drop positioning is not remembered per breakpoint; only numeric offsets are reliable across desktop/tablet/mobile.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Embed Best-Selling and Latest WooCommerce Products via Shortcode
cards.summary: Pull live WooCommerce product collections into builder sections using the official WooCommerce product shortcodes.
cards.use_when: Adding a best-sellers or new-arrivals rail to a homepage, landing page, or category page without hand-picking products that go stale.
steps: Add a Shortcode widget inside a container on your page.

Get the shortcode code from the WooCommerce documentation (source showed 'product shortcode for best selling product' and 'for latest product' as distinct copy-paste lines — verify the current shortcode names and arguments in WooCommerce docs, as they can change).
Paste the full shortcode line into the widget's shortcode field and the products load automatically from your catalogue.
If product images render doubled/tall in the editor, ignore it — the source notes this is an editor display glitch that resolves on the published front end.
Leave default shortcode styling for now; the raw output looks unfinished and is meant to be styled via WooCommerce/theme customization once you move to dashboard styling.

For a 'latest products' rail, use the latest-products shortcode; for best sellers, use the best-selling one — don't manually reorder products to fake 'latest' since a real shortcode keeps the rail current as new items publish.
caveats: Shortcode names, parameters, and styling behaviour are WooCommerce/plugin dependent and can change between versions — confirm in current docs.
Default shortcode output is unstyled and will look broken until product title, price, and card layout are customized.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Import a Prebuilt Elementor Template (e.g. Reviews Section) Instead of Building From Scratch
cards.summary: Upload a saved Elementor JSON template and insert it as a section, then customize its widgets rather than reconstructing the layout.
cards.use_when: Adding a common but tedious store section such as testimonials/reviews, contact, or FAQ where you already have a saved design file.
steps: Click the folder/Add Template icon in the Elementor panel, then use the Upload Template option and drag in your saved template JSON files.
If a template fails to appear after a batch upload, re-upload the missing one individually (source had to re-upload the review section).
Click Insert to drop the template in as a new section.
Expect it to look messy in the editor — the source says evaluate it on the front end, where the layout resolves correctly.

Customize editorial copy by selecting the text elements directly, and customize the testimonial widget via its Style tab (column gap, background colour, active background colour) and Content tab (description text, typography, text colour).
Treat the imported template as fully yours — every element remains editable, so adapt spacing and colours to your globals rather than leaving template defaults.
caveats: Templates carry their own typography and colour values, so you will need to re-map them to your global colours/fonts for brand consistency.
The upload interface and icon location are Elementor-version dependent — verify in your version.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Build a Countdown-Timer Promo Box for Offers and Drops
cards.summary: Set up a styled countdown widget inside a promo box to create urgency for a sale, launch, or limited drop.
cards.use_when: Running a time-limited promotion, flash sale, or product drop on a homepage or campaign landing page where urgency is part of the offer.
steps: Create a box container with a brand background colour (source used #F0D8B2) and a border radius (16px) so it reads as a distinct promo unit; give it balanced padding (source used 55/36/55/36).
Add a Heading (offer title), a subheading (terms/description), the Countdown widget, and a Button inside the box.
In the Countdown timer settings, set the exact expiration date and time. The widget counts down from now until that moment; on expiry the Expire Action shows a custom title and message you write.
Customize the unit labels (days/hours/minutes/seconds) if your audience needs different wording, though the defaults are usually clear.
For a flat look, remove the widget's background by setting the background type to classic and the colour to fully transparent (source did this so the timer matched the promo box).

Style the digit and label separately: source set digits ~36px/700 weight/48px line height, labels ~20px/500 weight/30px line height, and saved these as typography presets so each of the four units could be restyled in one click.
Set a top margin (~40px) to separate the timer from copy, and add a CTA button (source reused the hero button via copy/paste then centred it).
caveats: The countdown widget in the source came from a third-party plugin (Elements Kit), not Elementor core — availability and settings depend on which add-on you install.
Saved typography presets are what make the four-unit styling fast; without them, each unit must be styled manually.
Urgency timers should only flag genuine deadlines; resetting a timer arbitrarily undermines the trust the offer depends on.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Build a Category Showcase Section with Floating Badges
cards.summary: Lay out category tiles as clickable images with overlaid, rounded category-name badges that double as navigation.
cards.use_when: Building a homepage or landing page category block that routes shoppers into top-level product categories (e.g. dog food, cat food).
steps: Create a section container with generous padding (source used 132/20/68/20) and add floating decorative images using absolute positioning (e.g. left -41/top 90; left 40/top 70; right -140/bottom 40) — they can sit outside the visible flow and settle into place once content is added.
Inside, make a row container with justify-content center to hold the category tiles.
For each tile: add a category image, then a Heading widget for the category name. Use a BR tag in the heading text to force a deliberate line break rather than letting it wrap arbitrarily.

Style the heading with centre alignment and a bold weight (source used 36px/700, tight line-height 45px, negative letter spacing -2.52px) then make it absolute with right/bottom offsets so it sits on the image as a badge.

Give the badge a coloured, rounded background: background type classic with your secondary/brand colour, then a border radius of 50% for a pill/circle shape. Give it padding (source used 41px top/bottom) and a set pixel width (~172px).

Duplicate the whole group to create additional tiles, then just swap the image and the heading text and change the badge colour — this is the fastest way to keep badge sizing consistent across categories.
caveats: Badges depend on precise absolute offsets; changing tile image aspect ratios later will require re-tuning those offsets.
Keeping the badge text short matters — long category names will overflow the fixed-width pill.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Make Elementor Store Sections Responsive Without Breaking Desktop
cards.summary: Fix tablets and mobile using per-breakpoint container widths, reduced typography, per-breakpoint padding, and Order instead of physically moving elements.
cards.use_when: After building a desktop store homepage/section, when it breaks on tablet or mobile and you need to correct it without regressing the desktop layout.
steps: Switch the editor to Tablet or Mobile mode at the bottom of the panel — edits you make in a breakpoint apply only to that breakpoint and below.
Adjust outer section padding per breakpoint: source changed the banner's bottom padding from 104px to 90px on tablet, then set all-round padding to roughly 20/70/20 on mobile.
Reduce hero typography on smaller screens: the source dropped the main heading from 96px to 72px (line-height 86px) on tablet, then to 64px (line-height 72px) on mobile.
Fix multi-column rankings by changing each container's width per breakpoint (source: three hero columns 30%/32%/24% on tablet, then 48%+48% on mobile so two items share a row).

When a block needs to move position on mobile only, DO NOT drag it — dragging changes the desktop order too. Instead, open Advanced > Order and set it to 'end' (or a number) so it reorders only for that breakpoint.
Add breakpoint-specific spacing with margin (source added 30px bottom margin on mobile to push the second hero block down).
Use per-breakpoint image controls (width slider) to reposition decorative images like paw graphics so they land sensibly at mobile widths.
caveats: Edits made while in a smaller breakpoint cascade downward, so always check mobile after changing tablet.
Drag-and-drop reordering inside a breakpoint is a common mistake the source warns against — use the Order property instead.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Set a Global Page Background and Full-Width Layout Once Per Page
cards.summary: Use Page Settings to apply a single background colour and full-width canvas instead of styling every section individually.
cards.use_when: When a store homepage or landing page needs a consistent background and its sections must span the full browser width.
steps: Open Page Settings (the gear/editor settings) and go to the Layout section.
Under Page Layout, change from 'Default' to 'Elementor Full Width' so sections stretch edge-to-edge; the source used this to remove leftover side gutters.
Go to the Style tab of Page Settings and set a global page background colour (the source used a soft cream) so you don't have to add a background to every section.
Because the global page background gives the base colour, sections then only need their own distinct background where the design calls for a different tone (e.g. a pink promo band or beige hero).
Apply these page-level settings once per page and build sections on top; this keeps the page background consistent even as you add, delete, and duplicate sections.
caveats: Full-width layout changes how the 1240px content-width containers render, so verify hero spacing after switching.
A global page background overrides the visual expectation of an empty section — sections intended to look 'plain' will now be cream, not white.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Use Negatives Margins and Order to Control Store Section Spacing
cards.summary: Fine-tune spacing between hero copy, buttons, and grouped elements with margins, negative margins, and container order rather than adding empty blocks.
cards.use_when: Tightening or separating elements within a product hero, promo box, or footer strip where default gaps look wrong.
steps: Use the Advanced > Margin control (unlink it) for element-level spacing: the source added 100px top / 50px bottom margin to a button to pull it away from surrounding content.
Use padding on the parent container to create interior breathing room around a group, and keep child margins for finer control within the group.
Use negative margins to overlap elements deliberately, e.g. -35px to pull one avatar/thumbnail onto the previous one for a stacked look.
To reorder items on one breakpoint only, use Advanced > Order; to reorder across all breakpoints, physically drag the widget in the Structure tree.

Check the Structure panel to confirm nesting is correct before styling — many spacing problems are caused by a widget being nested one level too deep (the source repeatedly moved widgets out of the wrong parent container).
Name containers ('banner section', 'top area', 'title', 'count') so you can find and adjust the right one quickly during spacing passes.
caveats: Negative margins can cause overlap on breakpoints the designer didn't check; verify on mobile and tablet.
The editor's drag-and-drop can place a new container inside an existing one by accident — drag outside first, then position, or use 'Add to Container' to place it as a sibling.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Create Global Font and Colour Shortcuts Inside Widget Settings
cards.summary: Save frequently used fonts and colours as named global presets from within any typography/colour picker to avoid re-selecting them repeatedly.
cards.use_when: When building a store page and you find yourself re-applying the same font family, size/weight combination, or brand colour on every heading and button.
steps: In any typography panel, click the plus icon next to the font family field to create a global font (source created one named after the brand font, e.g. 'Nito').
A small globe/earth icon then appears wherever typography is set — click it to select the saved global font rather than browsing the font list again.
Likewise, in any colour picker click the plus to create a named global colour (source created 'black' for the primary text tone and an 'orange' for the CTA colour).

For fonts used at different sizes across many widgets (the source found this necessary in the countdown widget), save typography presets for each role, e.g. a 'digit' preset for countdown numbers and a 'label' preset for their captions.
When you duplicate a widget (e.g. for the four countdown units or duplicated category tiles), apply the saved presets so every instance stays consistent and future brand changes propagate.
Use these presets alongside the Site Settings global colours/fonts to keep section-level styling fast without re-inventing the palette on each section.
caveats: Saved typography presets are widget/site specific — verify they appear in the typography popup as expected, since some widgets (like countdown) don't inherit site-wide fonts and need a custom selection.
Naming presets by role ('digit', 'label', 'black', 'orange') rather than by value keeps them maintainable when the brand palette changes.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Plan for a Blog Section by Deferring Styling Until Posts Exist
cards.summary: Add the blog/latest-posts block to the homepage structurally, but wait to style it until real blog content exists so the design preview isn't misleading.
cards.use_when: Building a store homepage in a builder where a blog/news section is planned but no real posts have been published yet.
steps: Add a container for the blog section (source used 132/20/132/20 padding) and a centred section heading (source used 72px/600 weight, 80px line height, in the brand colour).
Add the Blog Posts / Posts widget; it will pull from your site's existing posts.
If only the default 'Hello World' post exists, the widget will show a single item — the source deliberately leaves it unstyled at this stage.
Proceed to build the rest of the homepage, then return to style this block once you've created and published real posts from the dashboard and can judge the layout with representative content.
When you come back, style the post archive on the front end with the same typography and spacing conventions as the rest of the page.
caveats: Styling an archive section with only placeholder content often leads to incorrect decisions — the source explicitly recommends deferring this work.
Blog Posts widget availability and options depend on Elementor Pro or a third-party add-on; verify which widget you actually have.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Fix the SVG Icon Upload 'Only One Image Shows' Bug
cards.summary: Recover missing SVG icons in the media library by publishing and refreshing the editor, then re-opening the uploader.
cards.use_when: When uploading a batch of SVG icons (for store badges, payment icons, CTA arrows) and only one appears in the media library.
steps: Batch-select all your SVG files and drag them into the media library upload area as normal.
If only one (or a few) show up after upload, don't re-upload repeatedly first — publish the page so you don't lose design work.
Refresh the editor page.
Select the widget using the SVG (e.g. the button), open Upload SVG again, and all uploaded icons should now be visible and selectable.
For SVG icons to appear at all, the site must have SVG uploads enabled — the source enabled this ('click Enable') when first attempting an SVG upload.
After inserting an icon, control its relationship to the text with the Icon Spacing control (source used 12px) and style the button icon separately from the label if needed.
caveats: The source mentions the button icon can look small relative to the text and planned to fix that with custom CSS later.
SVG upload is a security-sensitive capability on some hosts; enabling it is a site configuration decision, not just a UI toggle.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Renaming and the Structure Panel Keep Complex Store Builds Sane
cards.summary: Double-click to rename containers and use the Structure tree to navigate, select, and reorder deeply nested store sections.
cards.use_when: Managing a multi-section store homepage where containers are nested several levels deep and selecting the right one in the canvas is slow or error-prone.
steps: Double-click a container's label to rename it with a functional name (e.g. 'banner section', 'top area', 'title', 'product section', 'testimonials section'); renaming has no functional effect but makes the build navigable.
Use the Structure panel (the tree icon) to see the exact nesting: open a container there and you'll see its children listed, which is how the source diagnosed misplaced widgets.

Reorder or move a widget by dragging it within the Structure tree, or use right-click > Add to Container to insert a new container as a sibling (source used this to add a container 'beside' rather than 'inside' the selected one).
Delete example/placeholder content by right-clicking the container in Structure and choosing Delete, which removes the container and everything inside it cleanly.
Rename sections as you go (source renamed a generic 'product section' to 'product section two' and a section to 'testimonials section') so later customisation passes and handoff are unambiguous.
caveats: Renaming is organisation only — it does not affect rendering, so don't expect it to change spacing or layout.
The exact Structure panel location and right-click options are version dependent; verify in your Elementor version.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Choose the Right Text Widget for Store Copy
cards.summary: Use Heading for large display text and Text Editor for paragraphs, because they offer different styling control.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to add hero headlines, product descriptions, or mixed-format body copy to a store page in a visual builder.
steps: For large display text (hero headlines, section titles, price callouts) use the Heading widget, which is designed for a single line of prominent text and gives clean control over alignment, typography, size, weight, line height, letter spacing, and text colour.

For paragraphs and body copy use the Text Editor widget, which provides a rich inline editor (like a word processor) so you can style individual words within one block — e.g. colour just the words 'premium shop' in a different tone while the rest of the sentence stays black.
Use inline styling sparingly and deliberately: it is powerful for emphasising a phrase inside a paragraph, but it creates inconsistency if overused.
Apply global styling (alignment, font family, size, weight, colour) at the widget level using the Style tab so the whole block stays coherent, layering inline styles only on top.

Remember both widgets respect your saved global fonts and colours, so the fastest path is to set the font role globally first and then only adjust size, weight, line height, and letter spacing per instance.
caveats: Inline rich-text styling lives inside the widget content, not the global style, so it will not update automatically if you change brand colours later.
Mixing many one-off inline colours across a page is hard to maintain; keep the palette to your global colours where possible.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Building a responsive homepage in Elementor (tablet/mobile pass)
cards.summary: Method for making an Elementor page builder homepage banner, product and category sections responsive across tablet and mobile by adjusting padding, direction, width and gaps.
cards.use_when: You are laying out a WooCommerce store homepage in Elementor and it looks broken on tablet or mobile breakpoints.
steps: Work section by section: select the section, open Advanced, and reduce padding (e.g. top 90, sides 20, bottom 60–90) so content isn't cramped on narrow screens.
When a banner's big heading is too large, select the text directly and lower font size (e.g. 60–64 on tablet, 36 on mobile) and line height (72 tablet, 48 mobile) separately.
For two side-by-side items that should stack, set each container width to 100% and change the parent's layout direction to column.
Add vertical breathing room with margin (e.g. margin-bottom 30 on tablet, 20 on mobile) rather than reordering widgets.
For image/illustration widgets, set a custom width (e.g. 115px, 120px, 150px) and use offset values (horizontal/vertical) instead of drag to place decorations precisely.
Adjust column gaps on the container's layout tab (e.g. gaps column 40 on tablet, gaps row 30 on mobile) to space repeated items.
caveats: Exact pixel values in the source are one designer's choices, not universal; match them to your own type scale and grid.
Gap settings sometimes don't fix a leftover gap — style the widget's margin instead (e.g. margin-right 20).
Elementor's exact panel names change between versions; verify the current interface.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Adding more pages before theme customization
cards.summary: Create a contact page and a blog list page as standalone WordPress pages, then finish them alongside theme customization so site-wide settings apply everywhere.
cards.use_when: You have published a store homepage and now need additional pages such as contact and blog before doing global theme setup.
steps: From the WordPress dashboard go to Pages → Add New, title the page (e.g. 'Contact'), and publish.
Open the page with the page builder (Elementor) to design it.
Keep a separate 'Blogs' page as an empty placeholder: publish it, then set it under Settings → Reading as the Posts page so the theme auto-populates it with all blog posts.
Return to the homepage afterward to wire widgets (like a blog post widget) that depend on posts existing.
Expect the product grid, header and footer to remain incomplete until theme customization; treat those as the last pass.
caveats: An empty Blogs page shows content only after real posts exist.
Theme and builder menus labels may shift with updates — verify current paths.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Designing a contact page banner and contact-detail cards
cards.summary: Create a styled contact page top banner and reusable contact-detail cards (phone, email, address) using containers and icon widgets.
cards.use_when: You are building or polishing the contact page of a WooCommerce store and want it visually consistent with the brand.
steps: Add a container, rename it 'page banner', give it a background color, and set padding (e.g. 122 top/bottom, 0 sides).
Add a heading ('Contact Us'), center it, specify a large size (e.g. 72), weight 800, line height 82 and slight negative letter spacing; add a secondary intro heading below it.
If you constrain the intro text with a custom width, set align-self to center so it stays centered.
Add decorative images as absolutely positioned widgets with offset values (e.g. left 72, bottom 0) and control stacking with width and transform flip if needed.
Build contact detail 'cards' as containers: background color, border radius 12, padding 40/30. Duplicate the card three times for phone, email and shop address.
Inside each card add an icon widget (upload SVG, set view to stacked and shape to circle), then a label heading and the actual value. Reuse cards by copy/paste and only swap the icon and text.
caveats: Absolute-positioned decorative images need manual offset tweaks per breakpoint or they overlap text on mobile.
SVG upload support depends on your WordPress/plugin configuration.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Building a contact form with MetForm in Elementor
cards.summary: Assemble a styled contact form (name, email, message, submit) using the MetForm widget, then wire admin notifications.
cards.use_when: Your store contact page needs a functional form that emails submissions to you.
steps: Add the MetForm widget to the page, click Edit Form, create a new form and name it.
Inside the form builder add a container, then rows: make each row direction 'row' for side-by-side fields and adjust the column gap (e.g. 10–20px).

Add an MF Text widget for first name; turn off 'Show Label' and set the placeholder. Style padding (e.g. 17/16/17/20), text color, white background, 1px solid border, border radius ~100 for a pill shape, and set placeholder typography.
Duplicate the field for last name. Use 'Paste Style' to copy styling onto new inputs instead of restyling each.

Add an MF Email field with 'Required' enabled so the form cannot submit without it; set its width to 100%. Add an MF Text Area for message and paste the style, but reduce border radius (~20) because the large radius looks wrong on a tall box.
Add the submit widget, relabel it (e.g. 'Send Message'), align left, style padding, uppercase, accent background, radius 50%, and set box-shadow color transparent to remove default shadow.
In Form Settings → Notifications, enable admin notification, set subject, and add one or more recipient addresses separated by comma-space; save the form then update the page.
caveats: MetForm's interface differs by version; verify current label names.
Requiring email improves data quality but adds friction — consider which fields truly need to be mandatory.
Deliverability of form email depends on your host/SMTP setup.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Embedding a store location map widget
cards.summary: Add a Google Maps widget focused on your shop location by feeding the map the exact place title plus store name.
cards.use_when: Your store's contact page or footer should show where customers can find you physically.
steps: Add a Google Maps widget into a container on the contact page.
Search your shop address in Google Maps on a separate tab and copy the exact place title shown.
In the widget's location field, paste that exact title followed by a comma and your store name so the pin resolves to the right place.
Set the zoom (e.g. 13–15) so the surrounding area is visible, and set the map height (e.g. 500) to match your layout.
Add a 1px solid border with a partially transparent color and a border radius (e.g. 12) to match other cards.
On tablet/mobile, reduce the map height so it doesn't dominate the viewport.
caveats: The map only resolves correctly if the place title text matches Google's data.
A live embedded map may require an API key on some setups; confirm your configuration.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Writing and publishing store blog posts
cards.summary: Create blog posts in the WordPress block/rich-text editor with featured image, categories and tags, then surface them via a dedicated posts page.
cards.use_when: You want content marketing or SEO articles attached to your store and discoverable by visitors.
steps: From the dashboard go to Posts; trash the default 'Hello World' post and click Add Post.
Write the body in the rich text editor; use the plus icon to insert headings, lists, images, galleries, video and prebuilt patterns.
Set a Featured Image in the right-side panel — it becomes the post thumbnail wherever the post is listed.
Set the author, assign or create a Category, and add Tags.
Publish, then verify with 'View Post'.
Ensure a Blogs page exists and is assigned under Settings → Reading as the Posts page so visitors can browse all posts.
caveats: Without the Posts-page setting, visitors cannot find posts through navigation.
Comment functionality is on by default; decide whether to keep it for your store.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Configuring the blog post widget on the homepage
cards.summary: Style the Elementor blog-posts widget into a clean grid of image, metadata and title for a storefront homepage blog section.
cards.use_when: You want to surface recent articles on the homepage and control exactly what each card shows.
steps: Select the blog posts widget, set the layout style to 'Grid with Thumb' and set the featured image size to full so images show at full resolution.
Turn off 'Show Content' and 'Read More' if you only want image + title cards; open Query and set number of posts shown (e.g. 3) and order by (category or recent).
Enable meta data, set position to 'Before Title', then add the meta items you want (date, author) and delete the unwanted icons.
In Style: set background type classic, make card backgrounds transparent, set box-shadow color fully transparent, and zero out radius/widths.
Style the featured image: border radius ~12, margin-bottom ~15, padding 0, and set the image to cover so corners round correctly.

Style meta typography (e.g. 14/500, line height 20) and set item margin (e.g. 10 right/bottom) with zero item padding and icon spacing; style the title (e.g. 24/600, line height 32) in your primary color.
caveats: The source notes some card layouts still need custom CSS to look right — expect to revisit.
Number of posts shown is a design choice, not a performance rule.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Setting site identity: logo, title, tagline and favicon
cards.summary: Configure WordPress site identity so the header logo, browser tab icon, site title and tagline reflect the store brand.
cards.use_when: You are doing the global brand pass on a new store and the header still shows a default site title instead of a logo.
steps: Go to Appearance → Customize → Site Identity and select your logo; choose 'Skip Cropping' to keep the full image.
Use the logo size slider (e.g. 185px) to fit the header; optionally set a retina logo for high-density screens and a separate smaller mobile logo.
Edit the site title so it describes the store (it appears in the browser tab and search results).
Write a tagline that reinforces what the store sells.
Set the site icon (favicon) and publish.
Verify the header updates immediately with the logo.
caveats: Logo dimensions vary by theme; adjust the slider until the header looks balanced rather than using a fixed number.
Retina and mobile logos are optional but help sharpness and layout on small screens.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Setting global theme layout, colors and scroll-to-top
cards.summary: Use the theme customizer's Layout and Colors panels to set a site-wide background, container width, header color, footer columns, copyright text and scroll-to-top button.
cards.use_when: You want store-wide consistency instead of fixing colors and spacing page by page.
steps: In Customize → Layout → Site Container, set the main background color every page inherits (e.g. a beige FFF0E0-type tone) and set the content width (e.g. 1240px).
Set the header background color to your accent color in the header design panel.
For blog settings, choose the blog list structure and limit how many posts load per page (source kept 20; adjust to taste).
For blog single, reorder or hide elements (title, featured image, meta) in the order you want readers to see them.
Choose where sidebars appear: e.g. sidebar on blog single and shop archive (left), but none on the blog list if you prefer a cleaner archive.

In Footer settings, set the number of widget columns (e.g. 4) and edit the copyright text; the theme supports dynamic tags like current year and site title, so remove any parts (e.g. theme author) you don't want.
Configure the scroll-to-top button: which devices show it, position (left/right), background color, icon size and border radius.
In Colors, verify theme/text/accent/link-hover colors — these propagate to buttons and many components.
caveats: Changing global theme colors affects many elements at once; preview before publishing.
Theme customizer option names vary between themes — verify in your current theme.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Configuring WooCommerce catalog and product display settings
cards.summary: Tune the WooCommerce customizer panels so shop pages show the right number of products, consistent image sizes, hover behavior, sale tags and add-to-cart style.
cards.use_when: You are finishing the shop archive and need catalog, image and product-card behavior set up correctly.
steps: In Customize → WooCommerce → Site Notice, replace the default demo-store notice text or clear it once the store is live.
Under Product Catalog, set products per page (e.g. 12) — pagination appears after that count.
Under Product Images, keep the thumbnail width and cropping/aspect ratio and, most importantly, upload product images at the same width and height so cards align.
In Shop Archive → Product Content, choose what the card shows (title, rating, price) and alignment (e.g. center).
Set the product image hover effect — the source switched from gallery-image swap to zoom because the swap 'looked bad'.
For the sale tag, choose whether to show a percentage or custom text and set its background color to match your palette.
For the add-to-cart button, choose the style; the source preferred the hidden variant that appears on hover.
On Product Single, set content background, gallery layout option, and reorder description/reviews sections.
caveats: Same-size product images is a presentation rule, not a hard WooCommerce requirement, but misaligned cards hurt trust.
Hover effects and card options differ by theme/plugin version.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Creating header and footer nav menus in WordPress
cards.summary: Build the primary header menu and multiple footer menus so visitors can actually navigate the store.
cards.use_when: Your store pages are published but there is no working navigation in the header or footer.
steps: In Appearance → Menus, create a new menu (e.g. 'Main Menu') and assign it to the primary/header location.
Use 'Add Items' to pull in published pages (home, shop, blog, contact); reorder them logically (e.g. shop right after home).
For the footer, create additional menus (e.g. 'Footer Menu 1' for quick links like blog/contact/shop/account) and assign them to footer locations.
Create a legal/utility footer menu (e.g. 'Footer Menu 2') with custom links for privacy policy, terms and disclaimer; use '#' as a placeholder URL until those pages exist.
Ensure each menu is assigned to a theme location, then save.
Verify navigation works from the live site, not only the dashboard.
caveats: Custom links with '#' placeholders go nowhere until you create the target pages — don't forget to fill them in.
Menu locations available depend on the active theme.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Building footer widget columns with logo, menus and contact info
cards.summary: Populate theme footer widget areas with a logo block, descriptive text, navigation menu blocks and contact details.
cards.use_when: The footer area is empty and you want quick links, brand identity and contact details there.
steps: Go to Appearance → Widgets and add a Columns block (one column) into the footer widget area.
Add an Image block for the store logo; in the block's settings set a width (e.g. 200px) so it isn't oversized.
Add a Paragraph block after the image with a short brand description.
In the next footer column add a Navigation Menu block, give it a title (e.g. 'Quick Links') and select the corresponding footer menu.
Repeat for additional footer menus (e.g. a 'Website' column for legal links).
Add a Heading block ('Contact Us') plus contact detail blocks in a final column.
Because the footer column count is set in the theme customizer (e.g. 4 columns), match the number of widget columns you populate.
caveats: Footer widget areas must be registered by your theme; missing areas mean you must use a footer builder instead.
Block editor vs widget editor differences will shift some labels — verify in your WordPress version.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Catching left-over homepage sections and finishing the pass
cards.summary: Recognize which homepage sections (e.g. blog grid, product grids) remain incomplete and defer them until their dependent content or global setup exists.
cards.use_when: You are finishing a store homepage and some sections look broken or empty.
steps: Identify sections that depend on content not yet created — a blog section is empty until posts exist and a posts page is set.
Identify sections that depend on global customization — product grids and button styles may be fixed via theme-level CSS or customizer settings rather than per-widget tweaks.
After creating the missing content, refresh the page and re-select the widget to surface its settings.
Log the remaining fixes (header setup, footer setup, product settings) and address them in the customization phase rather than forcing them early.
Publish and re-check the homepage end to end.
caveats: The source explicitly defers some visual fixes to custom CSS in the customization phase; don't assume every issue is a widget setting.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Build a multi-column footer with navigation menus and contact details
cards.summary: Assemble a four-column footer (logo/description, quick links, website links, contact info) in a block-based theme editor, then fix column layout problems.
cards.use_when: Setting up or fixing a store footer in a block-based theme (e.g., WooCommerce block theme) so navigation, contact details and copyright display correctly.
steps: Add blocks sequentially in a footer column using the block inserter. For the first column, add an image (logo/site icon), then a paragraph block after it for a short store description.

For the second column, add a Navigation Menu block, set its title (e.g. 'Quick Links') and select the footer menu assigned to it. You can rename the menu title (e.g. change to 'Shop') without changing the underlying menu.
Repeat the Navigation Menu block in the third column, rename the title (e.g. 'Website') and select a second footer menu.
For the contact column, add a Heading block ('Contact Us'), then add paragraph blocks after it for email, phone and address, adding each with the 'add after' option.

If content spreads across the whole footer instead of staying in one column, insert a Columns block with a single column and drag each block into it one by one until all footer content sits in a single vertical column.
Publish, then check the footer preview. If extra menus appear that you don't want, return to Appearance > Menus, open the relevant footer menu, deselect its footer menu location, save, and reload.
Verify the current block inserter and menu-location interface in your WordPress/WooCommerce version, as labels may change.
caveats: Menu location assignment must match the Navigation Menu block's selected menu, or the wrong links appear in the footer.
Deselecting a menu's footer location removes it from the footer entirely, including any copyright or other links built into that menu.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Apply a curated custom-CSS set to polish theme design elements
cards.summary: Use a provided sequence of custom CSS snippets (buttons, headings, counters, product cards, blog images, cart/checkout) to unify a store's visuals beyond default theme styling.
cards.use_when: When default theme styling makes product grids, buttons, counters, blog images or cart/checkout pages look unpolished and you want consistent store-wide design quickly.
steps: Go to Appearance > Customize > Additional CSS (or the theme's Additional CSS panel) and paste each snippet in order after the previous one, leaving spacing between blocks.
Start with the site default style snippet to establish baseline typography and element styling.
Add the homepage button style snippet — verify buttons and their icons become larger and more consistent.
Add the product heading snippet for homepage section headings.

Add the counter style snippet to fix counter/countdown widgets that break at tablet and smaller widths. After pasting, add the documented class name to the countdown widget's Advanced > Additional CSS Class field, publish, and resize the browser to confirm it holds at all widths.
Add the blog post image snippet, then add the documented class name to the blog post widget's Advanced > Additional CSS Class field and refresh to confirm images are no longer distorted.

Add the page header, product card, blog post and cart/checkout snippets. The product card snippet is the one that restyles product archives/shop grids; the cart/checkout snippet only takes effect once the WooCommerce shortcodes are placed on those pages.
Publish/update and refresh the relevant pages after each batch to confirm the change applied.
caveats: CSS snippets are theme/plugin-specific — they assume the same starter theme, widgets and class names. Adapt before assuming they transfer.
Class names referenced by the CSS must be added to the specific widget's Advanced > CSS Classes field, or the styling silently does nothing.
Layering many snippets makes future theme updates or redesigns harder to unpick; keep snippets commented.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Replace default cart and checkout widgets with WooCommerce shortcodes
cards.summary: Swap bloated default cart/checkout widget layouts for WooCommerce shortcodes to get cleaner, theme-matching cart and checkout pages.
cards.use_when: When cart or checkout pages use default template/widget layouts that look inconsistent with the rest of the store, and you want a simpler page structure.
steps: Look up the current WooCommerce shortcodes list in the official WooCommerce documentation (verify the exact shortcode names for your version rather than relying on copied text).
Open Pages > Cart, edit it, select the existing cart container/blocks, delete them, and paste the cart shortcode. Save.
Open Pages > Checkout, delete the default checkout widgets/blocks and paste the checkout shortcode. Save.
Refresh both pages to confirm the shortcode-rendered layout appears and matches the theme.

If the shortcode layout looks worse than the default, revert: open the page, remove the shortcode, insert the default Cart block/widget (search 'cart' in the block inserter) and re-add default structure.
Optionally apply custom CSS after placing shortcodes, since cart/checkout styling snippets only affect shortcode-rendered pages.
caveats: Deleting the default cart/checkout blocks removes the layout you may want to fall back to — note or screenshot before deleting.
Shortcode output and available attributes change between WooCommerce versions; always check current documentation.
The source presenter preferred the default widget layout for checkout with their theme but chose to showcase shortcode layout for cart — treat as a style preference, not a fixed rule.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Enable and style a page header banner with breadcrumbs
cards.summary: Turn on the theme's Page Header template part to add a branded title banner with breadcrumbs to shop, blog, cart and other pages.
cards.use_when: When non-homepage store pages (shop, blog, cart, contact) start abruptly with no header context and you want a consistent branded banner with breadcrumbs.
steps: Go to Appearance > Customize > Layout > Page Header (naming varies by theme) and turn on 'Page Header Display'.
Enable display of the page title and the breadcrumb trail so each page shows its name and navigation path.
In the Page Header design settings, set the background color to a brand or theme color consistent with the site palette.
Set padding-top and padding-bottom to roughly 112px each to give the banner breathing room (source used 112 top and 112 bottom), and keep margin-bottom around 68px to space content below.
Publish and visit representative pages (shop, blog, cart, contact) to confirm the banner and breadcrumbs render consistently.
Note the blog/page header CSS snippet works together with this setting — the banner may need the CSS present and the correct page settings enabled.
caveats: Page Header is a template part; enabling it affects all pages that use the header, so verify it doesn't clash with pages that already have a custom hero.
The exact menu path and setting labels differ across themes; locate the equivalent setting in your theme's customizer or site editor.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Change the blog author display name store-wide
cards.summary: Edit the WordPress user profile so blog posts show a chosen full display name instead of a username.
cards.use_when: When blog posts on the store's content section show a generic or blank author name and you want a personal or brand author name to appear.
steps: Go to Dashboard > Users and open the relevant user profile.
Enter First Name and Last Name. WordPress will generate display-name variants from these fields.
Choose the preferred Display Name from the dropdown (e.g., full name or first+last).
Click Update Profile.
Visit a published blog post to confirm the author name now reflects the chosen display name across all posts.
If the theme hides author names, check the single-post template settings for an author/byline toggle.
caveats: For guest authorship or a brand author, a role and capability review is often needed — simply changing display name keeps the account's publishing permissions.
Changing the display name updates the byline everywhere that user is the author; verify it doesn't break any author archive links you rely on.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: Verify storefront pages end-to-end after setup
cards.summary: Run a structured walkthrough of all key storefront pages (shop, product, blog, contact, account, cart) after design and configuration to confirm functionality and appearance.
cards.use_when: After completing theme setup, CSS, footer and shortcode work, before handing off or launching an ecommerce store.
steps: Check top navigation: confirm Home, Shop, Blog, Contact and other key links route to the right pages.
Visit Shop: confirm product grid, sidebar search, price filter, category and attribute filters all render and return results.
Open a product: verify gallery images, variation selector (sizes/options), description, related products and add-to-cart all work.
Open the Blog listing and a single post: confirm title, featured image and related posts display, and that blog image/title CSS applied.
Open the Contact page: confirm store details, the working contact form and the embedded map point to the real business location.
Test search: find a product by keyword. Test the user account dashboard: wishlist (even empty), orders with details and mini-cart behavior.
Close the loop by fixing anything visually broken (CSS class missing, wrong block in a column) and re-verify.
caveats: The source walkthrough is a visual/functional sweep, not a payment or fulfillment test — actually place a test order separately.
Wishlist and account features depend on installed plugins; confirm those are active before testing.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial 2026_ Complete MasterClass for Beginners.docx

cards.title: WooCommerce Setup Order: From Blank to Sellable Store
cards.summary: A sequenced checklist for standing up a WooCommerce store: domain, WordPress, theme and builder, payments, shipping, taxes, then products.
cards.use_when: You are launching a new WooCommerce store from nothing and need the correct build order so later steps (payments, shipping, taxes) have products and addresses to bind to.
steps: Start with domain and hosting, then install WordPress — this is the foundation everything else attaches to.
Install the Blocksy theme (Appearance > Themes > Add Theme), then activate the Blocksy Companion plugin.
Import a Starter Site template (Starter Sites > filter builder = Elementor > import, e.g. the 'Garter Robe' template) to get a working page structure fast.
In Elementor settings, disable the Atomic Editor while you are learning — the source recommends this for beginners to avoid an extra editing paradigm.
Configure store address and currency (this address drives tax origin rules, so do it before taxes).
Create at least one Simple Product so you have something to test checkout with.
Connect payments last-but-one: install Stripe and PayPal plugins, link accounts via API, run the connection test, and leave them in Test mode.
Set up Shipping Zones and Tax, then run a full test order (test card, test address) before switching payments to Live.
caveats: Tool menus and plugin names change between versions — verify the current click paths in your own WordPress admin.
Starter Site templates bring demo content and styling you will need to strip out.
Do not go Live on payments until a test order completes end-to-end.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: Installing and Importing a Blocksy + Elementor Starter Site
cards.summary: Click path to get Blocksy theme, Blocksy Companion, and an Elementor-built starter template onto a fresh WordPress install.
cards.use_when: You are on a fresh WordPress install and want a styled, editable storefront skeleton without designing every page from scratch.
steps: Install the Blocksy theme via Appearance > Themes > Add Theme, then activate it.
Install and activate the Blocksy Companion plugin — it unlocks the Starter Sites importer and Blocksy's extra options.
Open Starter Sites, filter by builder = Elementor so the imported pages are editable in Elementor rather than another builder.
Import a template that matches your niche (the source uses 'Garter Robe' as the worked example).
Go into Elementor settings and turn off the Atomic Editor if you are a beginner — the source says it is recommended for beginners to reduce confusion.
After import, replace demo copy, imagery and links with your own before going live.
caveats: Imported templates ship with placeholder products and imagery that must be replaced.
The Atomic Editor recommendation is the source's opinion aimed at beginners, not a universal rule.
Verify current plugin and menu names — WordPress admin labels change between versions.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: Creating a Simple Product in WooCommerce
cards.summary: The field-by-field path for adding a single-option product: pricing, inventory, shipping dimensions, category and image.
cards.use_when: You are listing a product with no size/color variants and need it purchasable, stocked correctly, and shipping-ready.
steps: Go to Products > Add New.
Enter a clear product title and write the description (and short description for listing/above-the-fold placement).
Set Product Type = Simple Product.
Enter regular price and, if discounting, the sale price — WooCommerce applies the sale price automatically during the sale window.
Manage inventory: enable stock management and set the stock quantity and low-stock threshold so you get warned before you sell out.
Enter shipping weight and dimensions — these feed weight-based and class-based shipping rates, so missing them can break calculated shipping.
Assign product categories and upload the featured image before publishing.
caveats: Without weight/dimensions filled in, weight-based shipping rules will not calculate correctly.
Skipping the low-stock threshold means you only find out you are out of stock from customers.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: Creating a Variable Product with Attributes and Generated Variations
cards.summary: How to build size/color variants in WooCommerce using an attribute list, then generate each combination and price it individually.
cards.use_when: You sell a product in multiple sizes, colors or materials and need each combination to have its own SKU, stock and price.
steps: Create the product (Products > Add New) and change Product Type to Variable product.
Open the Attributes tab. Create or select an attribute (e.g. Size, Color) and enter its values separated by the pipe symbol, e.g. 8 | 9 | 10 | 11.
Tick 'Use for variations' — without this tick the values will not become selectable buying options.
Save the attributes.
Open the Variations tab and click 'Generate variations' (or 'Generate all variations') — WooCommerce creates one row per combination, e.g. Size 10 / Red.
For each variation, set an SKU, its own price, and its own stock level. A variation with no price set is not purchasable.
Add variation images if buyers need to see each colorway, then publish and test every combination in the shop.
caveats: A variation with no price will not be buyable — check every generated combination, not just the first.
Generated variations can leave orphan rows when you later remove an attribute value; prune them.
Verify current tab names in your WooCommerce version.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: Connecting Stripe and PayPal via Payment Plugins
cards.summary: Install the Stripe/PayPal WooCommerce plugins, link accounts by API, run the connection test, and stay in test mode until verified.
cards.use_when: You are turning on card and wallet payments for a WooCommerce store and want to confirm the connection before taking real money.
steps: Install 'Payment Plugins for Stripe WooCommerce' and 'Payment Plugins for PayPal WooCommerce' (or your chosen WooCommerce payment extensions).
Open the plugin settings and connect each account by entering the API keys/credentials from your Stripe and PayPal dashboards.
Run the plugin's built-in connection test to confirm the credentials work.
Set both plugins to Test mode first, then place a real test order using test card numbers.
Confirm the order status changes correctly, the customer receives the confirmation email, and a refund path exists in the dashboard.
Only switch to Live mode after the test order completes cleanly.
caveats: API key fields and test-mode toggles differ between plugin versions — verify against the current plugin docs.
Test-mode and live-mode credentials are different keys; swapping them is a common launch error.
Payment plugin availability and interface may change over time.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: Shipping Zones, Flat Rate vs Free-Over-Threshold, and Shipping Classes
cards.summary: Structure shipping by zone, decide between flat-rate and a free-shipping minimum, and use Shipping Classes to charge more for heavy or bulky items.
cards.use_when: You are setting shipping charges for a WooCommerce store and need to handle multi-region rates plus oversized/heavy products without losing margin.
steps: Create Shipping Zones for each region you sell into (e.g. United States, EU).
Inside each zone, add Shipping Methods — a flat rate for standard orders and/or a free shipping method.
Configure free shipping with a minimum-order threshold (the source uses $100 as an example) so free shipping rewards larger baskets instead of eroding every order's margin.
Create Shipping Classes (e.g. 'Heavy') for oversized or weighty products.
Assign the Heavy class to the relevant products, then add a Shipping Class cost to the zone's flat-rate method so those items carry a higher per-item charge.
Place test orders with light-only, heavy-only, and mixed carts to confirm the rates combine the way you intend.
caveats: The $100 free-shipping figure is the source's illustrative example, not a recommended benchmark — set yours from your own margins and AOV.
Shipping Class costs are typically applied per item, so a cart of multiple heavy items can stack charges unexpectedly.
Verify current WooCommerce shipping UI labels in your version.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: Automated Sales Tax with WooCommerce Tax
cards.summary: Enable WooCommerce Tax (powered by TaxJar), set the store address, pick origin- vs destination-based calculation, and add reduced/zero rates per category.
cards.use_when: You need correct sales tax across US states or other jurisdictions without hand-maintaining every rate table, or you sell goods with special tax treatment.
steps: Install and connect the 'WooCommerce Tax' plugin (by WooCommerce/Automattic, powered by TaxJar).
Set your store address accurately — it determines whether origin-based or destination-based tax rules apply.
Choose the calculation method that matches how your jurisdiction's law works (origin-based vs destination-based) rather than guessing.
Enable automated calculation so rates update when jurisdictions change.
For special categories — e.g. digital goods, or goods that are tax-exempt locally — configure reduced or zero tax rates tied to those product categories instead of a blanket rate.
Run a test order to a few different addresses to confirm the tax lines look right before launch.
caveats: Tax law varies by state and jurisdiction; automated tools assist but do not replace confirming your obligations with a tax professional.
Correct store address is a prerequisite — a wrong address produces wrong tax.
Plugin name, pricing and connection flow may change; verify the current interface.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: Elementor Responsive Controls for Product and Landing Pages
cards.summary: Use Elementor flexbox container settings and device toggles to hide, realign, or swap background images per viewport instead of shipping one desktop layout to mobile shoppers.
cards.use_when: Your store pages look fine on desktop but cramped, overlapped or unreadable on mobile/tablet, and you need a mobile merchandising fix inside the builder.
steps: Open the section/container in Elementor and switch to Mobile or Tablet preview using the responsive device icons at the bottom of the panel.
Use the device-specific toggle next to any setting (the little screen icon) so a change applies only to that viewport — this is how you adjust alignment, spacing and sizing per device.
Use Advanced > Responsive to hide elements that do not belong on a given device (decorative graphics, wide comparison tables, dense desktop nav).
Replace or reposition background images per device so hero imagery stays legible on narrow screens rather than cropping awkwardly.
Preview on the actual device or a narrow browser window, not just the builder's preview, before publishing.
caveats: Hiding content on mobile means that content is gone for mobile buyers — do not hide something they need to make a purchase decision.
Per-device overrides multiply settings; document what you changed so later edits do not silently revert.
Elementor's panel layout and icon placement change between versions — verify in your current build.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: Pre-Launch Store Configuration Checklist (Topic Map)
cards.summary: A four-part coverage map for a WooCommerce build — domain/email, store configuration, payments/tax, and shipping profiles — to verify nothing was skipped before launch.
cards.use_when: You are auditing a WooCommerce store before going live and want to confirm each configuration area is actually done rather than assumed.
steps: Domain and email: confirm the store's domain resolves and transactional email (order confirmations, password resets) actually sends and lands in inboxes — not just spam.
Store configuration: WordPress installed, theme (e.g. Blocksy) active, page builder (e.g. Elementor) working, store address and currency set correctly.
Products: at least one Simple Product and one Variable Product published, with prices, stock thresholds, weights/dimensions, and categories assigned.
Payments and tax: Stripe and PayPal connected and connection-tested, tax plugin configured against the correct store address and calculation basis, test order completed.
Shipping profiles: zones created for each region, flat vs free-shipping thresholds set deliberately, Shipping Classes assigned to heavy/oversized items and costed.
Mobile: check key pages on a phone viewport and fix with Elementor responsive toggles.
Finish with a full test purchase in Test mode before flipping payments to Live.
caveats: This is a coverage map for baseline configuration — page copy, analytic accuracy, and ongoing speed work belong to separate disciplines and are not covered here.
Do not treat 'plugin installed' as 'plugin configured'; the test order is the real verification.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: WooCommerce baseline store configuration order
cards.summary: Sequence for standing up a WooCommerce store: deactivate/delete default plugins, set profile, disable comments, install an ecommerce theme with starter site, then configure products, payments, shipping and tax.
cards.use_when: Launching a new WooCommerce store or deciding what to configure first before adding real products and taking live payments.
steps: Deactivate and delete the plugins pre-installed by the host (keeping only the caching plugin, e.g. LiteSpeed Cache) — the source notes leftover plugins can conflict with demo/starter-site imports; they can be reinstalled later.

Set store-owner basics in Users > Profile (color scheme, contact email, password) and disable comments in Settings > Discussion by unchecking comment options and the 'email me whenever' boxes to block spam on a store that does not use blogging.

Install an ecommerce theme (the tutorial uses Bloxy) plus its companion plugin, then import a free starter site using the Elementor builder with a selected set of pages and plugins: theme options, widgets, content, standard plugins and WooCommerce.
Create products: at minimum learn the simple product (single price, no options) and the variable product (size/color combinations) — the source calls these the two most common types.
Connect payments with the Stripe and PayPal WooCommerce plugins, add API credentials, run the connection test, and leave gateways in Test mode until verification succeeds.

Configure shipping as zones (e.g. United States) with flat-rate vs free-shipping minimum thresholds (example: $100) and Shipping Classes such as 'Heavy' to charge per-item rates for oversized products.

Configure tax with the WooCommerce Tax plugin (automatic calculation), the store address, and the origin- vs destination-based method required by the relevant state law; set reduced or zero rates for categories like digital goods.
caveats: Host onboarding screens change frequently; treat the host's exact click path and plan names as of the recording date and verify the current interface.
Free-shipping thresholds and tax methods depend on your jurisdiction and margins — the $100 and US example are illustrations, not benchmarks.
Payment plugins and tax plugins are third-party; confirm current setup steps in their own docs.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: Simple product configuration in WooCommerce
cards.summary: Field-by-field setup of a WooCommerce simple product, including pricing, sale schedule, inventory rules, shipping dimensions, upsells/cross-sells and category/brand assignment.
cards.use_when: Adding a single-SKU product to a WooCommerce catalog, or auditing an existing product page for missing inventory, shipping or cross-sell data.
steps: Name the product and fill the long description with spec-style content (origin, technicals) that appears below the product; reserve selling copy for the short description, which is the text shoppers see first.
Under Product data choose Simple product; optionally mark Virtual or Downloadable and add files for digital goods.
Set Regular price and Sale price, and use Sale schedule to bound a promotion by date (example in the source: a $100 shirt on sale for $50 from the 6th to the 31st).

Enter the SKU, enable stock management if you want quantities shown on the storefront, set the quantity (example: 10), decide on backorders (example: allow but notify the customer) and set a low-stock threshold (example: 3) so you are alerted before running out.
Add weight and dimensions so shipping rates by weight or size calculate correctly.
Attach an Upsell (shown on this product page, e.g. a matching cap) and a Cross-sell (offered further down the funnel at cart/checkout) — the source distinguishes the two by placement.
Set the main product image and gallery images, assign a product category (creating a new one if needed, e.g. 'Daryl shirts') and add tags or brands.
Publish and view the product page to confirm the price, sale badge, stock count, images, description, additional information and the 'You may also like' upsell block all render.
caveats: Backorder choice is a policy decision: allowing backorders but promising notification means you must fulfil the notification.
The source flags the short description as the most important text because it is what the customer reads first — do not bury key selling points in the long description.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: Variable product setup for size and color options
cards.summary: How to build a WooCommerce variable product so shoppers can select attributes such as color and size, with per-variation price, stock and image.
cards.use_when: Adding apparel, footwear or any product sold in multiple sizes, colors or materials, or when shoppers cannot currently select a variant on the PDP.
steps: Create the product as normal, then under Product data select Variable product instead of Simple.
Define attributes (e.g. Color, Size) and the values for each attribute; the source demonstrates this style of selection against a real store selling multiple colors and sizes.
Generate variations from those attributes and edit each one individually.
Set stock level, price and (where the option is offered) a variant-specific image for every combination, e.g. Size 10 / Red.
Enforce the rule that a price must be set for each variation — otherwise that combination is not purchasable and the shopper hits a dead option.
Preview the product page and click through each attribute combination to confirm prices, stock and images update as expected.
caveats: Variation count multiplies quickly; every attribute combination is a row to price and stock, so keep attribute lists to what you actually sell.
The source notes attributes only apply to variable products, so do not populate them on simple products.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: Upsell vs cross-sell placement in WooCommerce
cards.summary: Distinguish WooCommerce upsells (on the current product page) from cross-sells (offered at cart/checkout) and pick which products to place where.
cards.use_when: Merchandising a product page or cart to raise average order value with complementary items.
steps: Treat an Upsell as a recommendation shown while the shopper is viewing the current product — it appears at the bottom of that product page in a 'You may also like' style block.
Treat a Cross-sell as a recommendation shown at checkout/cart after the item is added — used to attach lower-priced or complementary items to an existing basket.
Populate both fields from the product edit screen when creating the product; the source demonstrates an upsell with a snapback cap on a t-shirt product.

Choose the relationship deliberately: on the PDP, offer a comparable or upgraded item (the source's example pairs the shirt with a cap); at cart/checkout, offer additions that complement what is already in the basket.
Verify on the live product page and cart that the correct products surface in each slot.
caveats: The source illustrates the mechanism but gives no AOV results; treat uplift from upsells/cross-sells as something to test on your own catalog rather than an assumed gain.
Adding too many recommendations can clutter the PDP or checkout — the source shows a single slot in each location.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: Elementor container and flexbox layout for ecommerce pages
cards.summary: Using Elementor containers with flexbox direction, justify-content and per-column width to build clean product and landing layouts that adapt across devices.
cards.use_when: Building or fixing a homepage, category or landing page layout in Elementor — e.g. getting two buttons to sit side by side or making an image column narrower than a text column.
steps: Add a container (click plus) and choose Flexbox rather than Grid — the source calls flexbox easier and the common choice.

Drag elements into the container; note that plain elements such as two buttons stack vertically with no control, so wrap side-by-side items (e.g. 'Shop now' + 'Contact us') inside their own container.
On the container, switch the flex Direction to Horizontal to place children side by side, or Vertical to stack them; use reversed direction to swap order.
Use Justify content to position children — center, start, end, space-between, space-around, space-evenly — rather than adding manual padding.
Adjust per-column Width when one column should be smaller (e.g. an image column narrower than the text column).
For a full-height hero, set the container's Minimum height to 100VH on the section rather than the inner container — the interface itself labels this as the way to achieve full-height containers.
Editing each element exposes three tabs: Content (the text/media itself), Style (typography, colors, sizes) and Advanced (padding/margins and motion effects such as entrance animations).

Use the responsive breakpoints (desktop, tablet portrait, mobile portrait) to re-apply flex settings per device — centering, changing a background image, resizing type or hiding elements only on that device.
caveats: Do not put too many items horizontal in a narrow box: the source shows elements render badly when there is not enough space and recommends vertical plus centered instead.
The source opinion that Gutenberg 'is terrible' and Elementor is the number-one builder is a presenter preference; if you already have a working builder stack, changing it is optional.
Elementor has released 'Atomic Elements' aimed at developers; the tutorial recommends deactivating them while building a store and notes the interface may change.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: Starter-site import and why to remove conflicting plugins
cards.summary: Importing an ecommerce starter template (theme options, widgets, content and plugins) to get a functioning store skeleton fast, and cleaning up pre-installed plugins first to avoid broken imports.
