cards.use_when: Setting up a new store quickly and needing a working shop layout — header, hero, category blocks, product grid — before replacing demo content with real products.
steps: In the theme's dashboard, open Starter Sites, filter to Free plans and select the Elementor builder.
Pick a template and click Import; choose Elementor when prompted for a page builder.
Keep the import options for theme options, widgets and content selected, and confirm it is a clean install so the demo imports without leftovers.
Keep the plugin list selected on the next step — typically the page builder, a contact-form plugin and WooCommerce (the shopping-cart integration) — then click install and wait roughly a minute.

After import, view the site: the starter provides a menu, hero landing section, trust badges (free delivery, 30-day returns, secure payment), dummy products, category blocks (jackets, sweaters, accessories), a popular-products section and a shop page with a filterable sidebar gallery.
Delete or trash demo products afterwards (Products > select all > bulk actions > Move to trash, recoverable from Trash) and replace images and copy with your own.
Import demo pages (shop, services, about us) and adapt them rather than building every page from scratch.
caveats: Delete pre-installed host plugins before importing — the source says they can conflict with the demo import.
The imported content is demo data: replace dummy products, images and text before launch so the storefront is not visibly a template.
Starter-site availability and the import wizard change over time; verify the current flow in your theme.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: Header settings that block page building and product imagery
cards.summary: Two theme-customizer header toggles — sticky header and transparent header — that interfere with page building and hero images, and when to switch them off.
cards.use_when: Troubleshooting an Elementor editing experience where the menu collides with the builder, or a hero image pushing up under the menu and hiding content.
steps: Open the theme customizer (Websites > Customize) and go to Header > Global Header.
Turn off the sticky-header option if the fixed menu blocks or collides with the builder while you are working — the source disables it purely to remove that friction during building.
Turn off transparent header if the starter template uses one: a transparent header forces page content up under the menu, cuts access to those areas and can push hero imagery into the navigation.
After changing header settings, publish and refresh the Elementor editor to confirm the page now starts below the header and you have space to add sections.
Re-enable sticky header after the build if you want the persistent navigation for shoppers — the source's reason for disabling it was editorial convenience, not a storefront recommendation.

While a hero is being styled, remove any custom position on the background first and set display size to Cover, then pick a focal position (center right vs center center etc.) so subjects are not cropped out.
caveats: These are theme-specific settings; the exact labels live under the theme customizer and may differ by theme.
Disabling sticky or transparent headers changes shopper-facing navigation behavior — decide the final setting on user experience, not just build convenience.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: Responsive optimization pass across desktop, tablet and mobile
cards.summary: Per-device layout review in Elementor: centering flex content, swapping background images, applying overlays for text contrast, resizing text and hiding elements that break small screens.
cards.use_when: Doing the mobile/tablet pass on a store homepage, category page or landing page before launch, or fixing text that is illegible over an image on small screens.
steps: Switch the editor to each device view (desktop, tablet portrait, mobile portrait) — settings changed while a device view is active are saved scoped to that device.
Center stacked content per device: select the flexbox container and set justify-content to center for tablet and mobile instead of leaving left-aligned rows.
Change background images per device where the desktop crop does not work on mobile — Elementor stores a separate image for the tablet or mobile breakpoint.
Add a background overlay with a darker color and increased opacity when light imagery makes overlaid text unreadable, and scope the overlay to the device that needs it.
Adjust typography size per device for text that reads too small or too large (e.g. enlarge a heading only on tablet portrait).
Hide elements that do not fit small screens: open the element's Advanced settings, find Responsive, and hide it on tablet/mobile — the same controls work for sections and columns.
Re-check the default auto-generated sections; the source notes WooCommerce product displays are automatically responsive, but manual sections and footers still need review.
caveats: Changing a background per device makes maintenance heavier — keep one image across devices unless the desktop crop genuinely fails.
Hiding elements removes information for that audience; check the hidden element is not a required CTA or price.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: Elementor element editing, copy-paste style and AI page drafts
cards.summary: Working efficiently inside Elementor: the content/style/advanced tab model, duplicating elements and columns, copying style between same-type elements, and using Elementor AI to draft a page quickly.
cards.use_when: Building a reusable store page (About, Team, landing section) and needing to keep typography, colors and spacing consistent without restyling each element by hand.
steps: Select any element to get three tabs: Content for the text, image or link; Style for typography, colors and size; Advanced for padding/margins and motion effects such as entrance animations.
Right-click an element or container to Duplicate or Delete; duplicating a container clones a whole column so you can build repeated card rows quickly.
Configure one element fully, then right-click it and Copy, and on each matching element use Paste style — the source notes this works between the same element type and keeps a page consistent.
For the button link field, type the page name and the builder resolves the page URL automatically, so 'shop now' can be pointed at the Shop page without copying a URL.
For a quick page draft, use Elementor AI: prompt it for a layout (e.g. a three-column row) and click Use layouts, then clean up the result.
Treat AI-generated pages as a starting point: the source's own test requested three columns and got four, so delete extra sections and replace placeholder images and names before publishing.
caveats: The source explicitly rates Elementor's AI builder as 'not the best' but occasionally useful — do not ship its output unchecked.
The demo used a specific font choice (Poppins bold) as a personal preference, not a conversion recommendation; pick one brand font family and apply it consistently.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: Creating pages, menus and dropdown navigation for a store
cards.summary: Adding WooCommerce pages such as About/Team, assigning them to the site menu, building dropdown submenus and adding external custom links (e.g. a community URL).
cards.use_when: Building out an online store's site structure — adding an Our Team or Services page, organizing the navigation under shop and contact, or linking to an off-site channel.
steps: In Pages > Add Page, create the new page, publish it, then open the Elementor builder to design it (the source drafts a Team page with a three-column layout of images, names and roles).
Go to Appearance > Menus — the menu created at import holds the starter item structure.
Under Pages click View all, tick the new page (e.g. Our Team) and click Add to menu.
Drag the item to the desired position; nest it under a parent (e.g. under Services) to create a dropdown that appears on hover.

To link off-site destinations (a Facebook group or school), use the Custom Links section: paste the URL, give it a label, click Add to menu, then position it (e.g. under a Contact item) and click Save menu.
Visit the live site to confirm the dropdown opens on hover and the custom link resolves to the right destination.
caveats: Menu structure is theme-driven; the dropdown behavior and depth limits come from the theme.
Custom links point off-site, so they take shoppers away from checkout — place them where abandonment risk is low.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: WooCommerce admin surfaces for running the store after launch
cards.summary: Which WooCommerce admin screens exist and what each one answers for a store operator: orders, customers, coupons, reports and the upgraded analytics view.
cards.use_when: Setting up the operational side of a WooCommerce store — reviewing orders, tracking customers, issuing coupons and checking sales reporting after launch.
steps: Use Orders to review everything customers have purchased; each order appears here as it is placed.
Use Customers to see everyone who has purchased, with username and email, so you can identify repeat buyers or export a list for retention work.
Use Coupons to create and manage discount codes applied on the storefront.
Use Reports for the legacy sales report listing.
Use WooCommerce Analytics for the upgraded view showing total sales, net sales, orders, products sold and related metrics — the source treats this as the primary reporting surface.
Use Settings as the central configuration screen for the store (the source flags it as the most important section, covering the store-level configuration used for payments, shipping and tax).
caveats: The source admits to skipping many WooCommerce options as unnecessary for a basic store; the depth you configure should match your sales volume and tax/shipping complexity.
Metric definitions in Reports vs Analytics differ (total vs net sales) — confirm which figure you are quoting before acting on it.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: Create variable products with size/color attributes and variation images
cards.summary: Build a variable product by defining attributes first, generating variations, then assigning per-variation image and price so the PDP swaps visuals by customer selection.
cards.use_when: Setting up a product with multiple options (sizes, colors) on the PDP so customers see the correct image and price per choice.
steps: Create the product and set Product Data to 'Variable product'.

Open the Attributes tab and add your first attribute (e.g. 'Size'), entering each term (e.g. 10, 11, 12). To enter multiple terms in the field, hold Shift and press the key above your keyboard's Enter key to separate values. Click Save attributes.
Add a second attribute (e.g. 'Color' with gray, red, beige), save attributes again.
Open the Variations tab and click Generate variations — WooCommerce combines every term of both attributes (size 10 gray, size 10 red, size 11 gray, etc.).
Edit each variation individually: assign the matching image, set the price, and optionally weight. This is the tedious part but you must do it per variation.
Set the product short description, then set the main Product image and Default form values (default size and color) so the default selection matches the default image shown.
Publish. Confirm the storefront displays a price range (e.g. $50–$80) and that selecting a different combination swaps the image and price.
caveats: Every variation must have a price — a variation without a price cannot be added to the cart.
Attribute term entry, the generate-variations button and default-form-values labels can shift between WooCommerce versions; verify the current interface.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: Configure selling locations, shipping locations and customer location sensibly
cards.summary: Restrict selling to your actual markets and base the default customer location on the shop address rather than geolocation.
cards.use_when: Configuring store-wide General settings on a new store so checkout country fields and shipping match where you actually do business.
steps: Enter the store address first — it drives tax and shipping calculations.

Under General > Selling locations choose 'Sell to specific countries' and select only the countries you actually serve (e.g. United States and Canada). This is the most commonly used setting in the source's web-design experience.
Set shipping location to the countries you sell to rather than all countries, so you only ship where you do business.
Set the default customer location to Shop country rather than Geolocate — the source recommends this because many customers use VPNs, so geolocation is unreliable.
Skip address autocomplete unless you are willing to add the third-party plugin it requires.
Enable taxes and enable the use of coupons, check the remaining boxes, and choose your store currency. Save.
caveats: The source's preference for shop-country default over geolocation is a practitioner recommendation, not a rule — test it against your actual buyer mix.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: Decide add-to-cart redirect behavior and product review permissions
cards.summary: Configure whether adding to cart diverts users to the cart page and whether reviews require a verified purchase or allow open reviews.
cards.use_when: Setting up Products settings on a multi-product store to reduce cart-page bounce and choose a review policy.
steps: In WooCommerce > Settings > Products, review the 'Add to cart behavior' option. The source advises against redirecting to the cart page when you have multiple products, because users get pulled away from browsing every time they add something.
Choose measurement and dimension units matching your market (pounds/ounces for the US; kilograms/grams for Europe; inches or centimeters for dimensions).
Under Reviews, decide whether to enable reviews at all, and whether to only allow reviews from customers who actually purchased. Star ratings can be enabled independently.
Save changes.
Optionally visit Inventory settings to enable stock management, and the Downloadable products settings if you sell digital goods.
caveats: The source's own store leaves verified-purchase-only reviews unchecked; treat this as a policy choice, not a recommendation.
The no-redirect advice is attributed to the source and suits catalog browsing; a single-product store may reasonably differ.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: Set tax calculation basis correctly by origin vs destination state
cards.summary: Choose shop-base address vs customer shipping address for tax calculation depending on whether your state is an origin-based sales-tax state.
cards.use_when: Configuring WooCommerce tax settings before going live in the US, to avoid collecting tax on the wrong basis.
steps: In WooCommerce > Settings > Tax, keep 'Prices entered with tax' unchecked so product prices display without tax, which the source says is what most stores do.

Set 'Calculate tax based on' to the correct basis: a handful of states (the source names Arizona, California, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Tennessee as examples) are origin-based, meaning you charge tax based on where you are physically located — use Shop base address. For most other states, use Customer shipping address.
Verify your own state's status with a current tax reference (the source cites taxjar.com's map and state lists) rather than relying on the example list.
Leave 'Shipping tax class' based on cart items unless you charge a single flat rate, in which case select Standard.

Set rounding and rate naming as you prefer, and save — then add rates under Standard rates by inserting a row with country code (US), state code (CA), postcode, rate (e.g. 7.25), a tax name, priority for competing rates, whether the rate compounds, and whether shipping is taxable in that state.
caveats: Origin-state lists and rates change over time — confirm with a current tax source; the source's list is illustrative, not authoritative.
Enabled taxes are required before any of these settings matter.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: Use reduced tax rates for special product classes
cards.summary: Create a reduced tax class (e.g. 0% for digital goods) and assign it to specific products so mixed catalogs are taxed correctly.
cards.use_when: Selling a catalog mixing physical and digital (or otherwise differently taxed) items on one store.
steps: Under Tax > Reduced rates, insert rows for special rates — for example in California, digital products carry no sales tax, so enter a 0% rate named 'Digital'. Save.
Edit the affected product and open the General tab under Product data.
Set Tax status and change Tax class from Standard to your reduced class (e.g. 'Reduced rate'). Update the product.
Result: standard products use your general rate (e.g. 7.25%) while the digital product is charged at 0%.
Confirm with a test checkout that the correct rate applies to each product type.
caveats: Rate treatment per category varies by state/country — verify the actual taxability of digital goods where you are registered.
Reduced-rate handling and labels may differ in current WooCommerce versions; check the interface.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: Automate tax rates with the WooCommerce Tax plugin
cards.summary: Install and connect the official WooCommerce Tax plugin to pull calculated rates from a live tax service instead of maintaining rows manually.
cards.use_when: You want hands-off sales-tax rates across many jurisdictions instead of hand-building standard and reduced rate rows.
steps: Go to Plugins > Add new, search for 'WooCommerce Tax', install and activate the plugin published by WooCommerce.
Click Connect and create/authorize a free WordPress.com account when prompted — this uses the WordPress.com API.
When connected, return to WooCommerce > Settings > Tax and enable automated taxes, then save.
Rates are drawn from the connected tax service (the source cites TaxJar) which WooCommerce partners with, so they stay current.
If you prefer full manual control, you can still maintain Standard and Reduced rate rows instead of enabling automation.
caveats: Requires a WordPress.com connection and a live service; plugin name, connection flow and settings screens may change — verify in the current interface.
Automation may not cover every edge case (mixed digital/physical rules), so spot-check representative products.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: Build shipping zones with free shipping, flat rate and local pickup
cards.summary: Create a shipping zone, then layer free-shipping thresholds, a flat rate and local pickup as selectable methods at checkout.
cards.use_when: Setting up shipping options for a store that ships to specific countries or regions.
steps: Go to WooCommerce > Shipping and click Add shipping zone; name it (e.g. 'United States').
Set zone regions to 'Everywhere' if the zone name already reflects your selling countries and you ship to all of them, or restrict to specific states/regions if you only ship to some.

Add a shipping method: choose Free shipping, then set its requirement — the options are no requirement, a valid free-shipping coupon, a minimum order amount, or a combination. The source uses a $100 minimum order amount as the free-shipping threshold.
Add a second method: Flat rate, and enter a default rate (the source uses $5) for orders that don't qualify for free shipping.
Add a third method: Local pickup, typically with a zero fee, and mark it not taxable.
Save each method; the storefront cart then offers these options to the customer.
caveats: All three methods being offered together assumes you accept pickup — omit it if you only ship.
Zone and method labels differ slightly between WooCommerce versions; verify the current interface.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: Charge per-product shipping with shipping classes and per-class calculation
cards.summary: Create shipping classes for bulky or heavy items and set the flat-rate method to charge per class so large items cost more to ship.
cards.use_when: Your catalog contains items with very different shipping costs (small apparel vs heavy/bulky goods) and you need item-level pricing.
steps: Go to WooCommerce > Shipping > Shipping classes and add a class (e.g. 'Heavy' / heavy packages) and create it.
Return to the shipping zone's Flat rate method and edit it. Keep the default flat rate (e.g. $5) for normal products, then add a per-class cost row for your heavy class (e.g. $10).

Set Calculation type to 'Per class' rather than 'Per order'. Per class charges the rate for each item in the cart; per order applies only the most expensive shipping class across the cart, which undercharges mixed carts.
Save the method.
Edit each product that should use the class, open the Shipping tab under Product data, set its Shipping class to the heavy class, and update.
Test with a cart containing both a normal and a heavy item to confirm both class rates apply as expected.
caveats: Per-class is the source's recommendation for accuracy; per-order is a simpler but less precise alternative.
The example rates ($5 default, $10 heavy) are illustrative — set your own based on real carrier costs.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: Connect Stripe and PayPal payment gateways
cards.summary: Add card and PayPal payments by installing the recommended gateway plugins, creating the merchant accounts, and connecting them to the store.
cards.use_when: Enabling card and PayPal checkout on a new WooCommerce store.
steps: In Plugins > Add new, search for the Stripe plugin from the 'payment plugins' developer. The source specifically does not recommend the official Stripe plugin, stating it malfunctions often; the third-party plugin is described as an official Stripe partner and shows high ratings. Install and activate it.
Likewise install and activate the payment-plugins PayPal extension when prompted.

Create a free Stripe account — the source notes Stripe has no setup cost, no credit check and no monthly fee, only a per-transaction fee. Connect it from the plugin's settings, login in the browser, select the business, and connect; leave it in Test mode until ready for real payments.
Create a PayPal Business account (a personal account will not sync with the site) and use the plugin's click-to-connect flow.
Save changes; a card field and PayPal option then appear at checkout.
caveats: The anti-official-Stripe-plugin opinion is the presenter's from his own experience — re-evaluate current plugin quality and Stripe's own recommended integrations before choosing.
Fees, onboarding and whether a personal PayPal account works can change; verify current terms and interface.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: Run a test order to verify shipping, tax and checkout end to end
cards.summary: Place a live checkout with test card details to confirm free-shipping thresholds, taxes and gateway behavior before launch.
cards.use_when: Pre-launch QA of checkout, shipping options and tax configuration in a new store.
steps: Add a product to the cart and view the cart: confirm the flat rate (e.g. $5) and local pickup appear and choose as appropriate.
Increase quantity until the cart passes the free-shipping threshold (the source uses $100) and click Update; confirm free shipping becomes selectable, then proceed to checkout.
Fill in billing details: confirm the country dropdown only lists your configured selling countries (e.g. US and Canada).
Uncheck 'ship to a different address' if shipping to the billing address, or enter an alternate shipping address to verify separate shipping fields.
With Stripe in test mode, enter test card number 4242 across the card field and any future expiry/CVC, then place the order.
Confirm the order appears under WooCommerce > Orders with totals, line items, billing and shipping addresses — and that the My Account page shows the order for the customer.
caveats: The 4242 test card only works while Stripe is in test mode; switch to live mode for real transactions.
Tax shown depends on your origin/destination configuration — confirm it matches your intended rule.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: Manage and fulfill orders, issue refunds, and understand the customer My Account page
cards.summary: Locate orders, mark them complete to notify the customer, process refunds from the order screen, and confirm what customers can self-serve.
cards.use_when: Post-purchase operations: fulfilling orders, handling refund requests, and supporting customer self-service.
steps: Go to WooCommerce > Orders and open an order to see status, order details, and billing/shipping addresses.

Change the status to Completed and click Update, which notifies the customer that the order is done and shipping. (The source notes auto-fulfillment is an option you can configure, but by default orders sit as 'Processing'.)
To refund, scroll to the bottom of the order and use the Refund action, entering the refund amount and confirming; test orders show $0 because no real funds exist.
Direct customers to the automatically created My Account page, where they can view their past orders and totals, update addresses, update payment methods, and log in or out.
Optionally offer social-login via a third-party WordPress plugin to simplify customer sign-in.
caveats: Refund amounts on test orders will read $0 by design; real refunds require live payments.
Status names and available actions may vary by WooCommerce version and installed extensions.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: Organize product categories and handle undeletable defaults
cards.summary: Clean up imported categories, keep only what you need, and repurpose the undeletable default category instead of leaving it unused.
cards.use_when: Tidying catalog navigation and category structure after a theme import on a new store.
steps: Go to Products > Categories in the dashboard. Themes often import categories you don't need.
Select the unwanted categories and delete them.
Note that one default category cannot be deleted. The source's workaround is to rename and repurpose it as a real category (e.g. rename it to your brand gear such as 'Daryl's Gear') and update it.
Use that repurposed category as a legitimate part of your navigation, and make sure any products that land in it intentionally belong there.
caveats: If you create categories, the source advises using the existing undeletable category as one of yours rather than fighting it.
Category labels and the delete/rename flow may differ slightly by WooCommerce version.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: Check email deliverability and customize transactional emails
cards.summary: Ensure customer order emails actually send by configuring SMTP, and optionally customize email templates with a free builder plugin.
cards.use_when: After store setup, before launch, and when customers report missing order emails.
steps: Recognize that on a brand-new WooCommerce install, emails to customers often fail to send — plan to fix this before launch rather than after complaints.
Configure SMTP settings (the source points to a separate free-plugin walkthrough) so order emails reliably reach customers.
Review email recipients in WooCommerce > Settings > Emails: new-order notifications go to you, while processing/on-hold and similar status emails go to customers.
Leave the default subject lines and headings as-is — the source recommends defaults for simplicity.
If you want branded emails, install a free drag-and-drop email builder plugin and design templates visually, since the built-in email cannot be edited directly.
caveats: The source warns plugin pop-ups and marketing nags appear in the WordPress admin; expect and dismiss them.
Specific SMTP plugin and email-builder names are not given in this source — verify current options.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: Tune coupon and review settings for a workable default configuration
cards.summary: Enable coupons, set measurement units and review permissions so the store behaves correctly from day one.
cards.use_when: Final pass through WooCommerce Products and General settings before launch.
steps: In General settings, enable coupons alongside taxes so coupon functionality is available for promotions.
In Products settings, set weight and dimension units matching your market so shipping calculations and product details are correct.
Decide the review policy: leave reviews open, or require a verified purchase, and independently enable star ratings.
Leave the remaining product settings at their defaults unless you sell inventory-tracked or downloadable goods, then visit Inventory or Downloadable products settings accordingly.
Revisit General > Accounts and privacy: the source calls disabling guest checkout 'a terrible idea' and treats the default account/privacy options as standard for ecommerce.
caveats: The guest-checkout opinion is attributed to the source and reflects his experience; evaluate against your own conversion and account strategy.
Default labels and option placement vary between WooCommerce versions.
cards.source_name: WooCommerce Tutorial for Beginners 2026.docx

cards.title: What the Meta Conversions API Gateway actually is
cards.summary: A hybrid setup where the client-side pixel fires as usual and also relays the same event to a first-party subdomain gateway that forwards it to Meta's Conversions API.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to add server-side conversion tracking to an ecommerce store when you have no developer resources and are considering the Meta CAPI Gateway instead of a full server-side tag manager.
steps: Understand the topology: the existing browser pixel continues sending events directly to Meta, and simultaneously sends a copy of each event to a custom subdomain (e.g. cpg.yourdomain.com) that runs only a forwarding server for Meta events.
Recognize this is a 'gateway', not a general-purpose server container: it accepts Meta events and passes them on; it is not a GTM server-side environment you can extend with other tags.

Know the intended audience: merchants who lack the skills/resources for true server-side tagging, want a low-effort accuracy bump, and are not already on a plugin that auto-installs both the pixel and Conversions API.
Decide deliberately: choose the gateway only as a quick stopgap; treat full server-side tagging as the target state if deduplication and cookie control matter.
If you proceed, verify on a live page in DevTools Network tab that both the direct Meta request and a request to your gateway subdomain carry the same event ID.
caveats: The vendor claims (e.g. average cost-per-result improvements up to 13% and ~7% more conversions) are vendor-reported figures, not guarantees; the source argues real-world results are lower because of the architecture.
This is one practitioner's opinion (Analytics Mania); treat the recommendation against the gateway as a situational judgment, not a universal rule.
cards.source_name: Facebook Conversions API gateway tutorial (FB CAPI Gateway a.k.a. Meta CAPI gateway).docx

cards.title: Why the CAPI Gateway fails against ad blockers
cards.summary: Because the gateway call is triggered by the client-side pixel, anything that blocks the pixel also blocks the server-side relay, defeating the main reason to adopt server-side tracking.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether the Meta CAPI Gateway will recover conversions lost to ad blockers and browser privacy extensions on your storefront before you invest in it.
steps: Accept the dependency: the request to the gateway subdomain is initiated by the browser pixel, so the gateway is not an independent, server-originated data path.
Test it yourself: install an aggressive blocker (the source used Ghostery) in a clean browser, reload a product or checkout page, and filter the Network tab for 'facebook'.
Expected observation: with the blocker active, the pixel request never loads, and therefore no request to the gateway subdomain is made either.

Conclude that 'bypassing ad blockers' — the primary value proposition of server-side tracking — is largely unachieved here; the source estimates the realistic improvement from this gateway at best 1–2%, versus the vendor's promotional numbers.
If blocker resilience is your actual goal, plan for a genuinely independent server-side setup instead of a client-triggered gateway.
caveats: The 1–2% figure is the presenter's estimate, not a measured benchmark.
Blocker behavior changes over time; retest rather than relying on any fixed number.
cards.source_name: Facebook Conversions API gateway tutorial (FB CAPI Gateway a.k.a. Meta CAPI gateway).docx

cards.title: Deduplicating pixel and Conversions API events with matching IDs
cards.summary: The gateway auto-attaches the same event ID to both the browser pixel event and the server-side event so Meta can deduplicate the pair.
cards.use_when: Verifying your conversion tracking after installing the CAPI Gateway, or diagnosing double-counted purchases and inflated conversion counts.
steps: After connecting your pixel to the gateway, open the Meta Pixel Helper on a live page and confirm an event ID is now present on the pixel event.
Open DevTools Network, filter for 'facebook', and locate the request going to your gateway subdomain.
Inspect that request's payload and confirm the same event ID appears that you saw in the Pixel Helper.
Confirm the event IDs match for each event type (page view, AddToCart, Purchase, etc.); mismatched or missing IDs mean deduplication will fail and conversions may be double counted.
Monitor Events Manager after a few days for duplicate-event warnings or unexpected conversion volume jumps from dedup failures.
caveats: Deduplication ID handling is automatic with the gateway; if you build custom server-side tagging you must manage event IDs yourself.
Meta's interface and deduplication diagnostics change over time — verify current behavior in Events Manager.
cards.source_name: Facebook Conversions API gateway tutorial (FB CAPI Gateway a.k.a. Meta CAPI gateway).docx

cards.title: Setting up the gateway via Stape: pricing and subdomain mapping
cards.summary: A cheaper third-party host (Stape) provisions the Meta CAPI gateway, but the real setup step is mapping a dedicated CNAME subdomain so the pixel has a first-party endpoint.
cards.use_when: Provisioning the Meta CAPI Gateway for a store and mapping a first-party subdomain as a low-cost alternative to Meta's own gateway hosting.
steps: Create the gateway with a third-party host: the source used Stape, where a Meta CAPI gateway costs about $10/month per pixel (price per pixel drops as you add more); Meta's own Events Manager-hosted option starts around $30 because it uses Amazon servers. Verify current pricing before buying.
Sign up (7-day trial available in the source's example), name the gateway after the store, choose a location, confirm email, and set a password.
In the gateway interface, click 'add data source', select Facebook login, confirm identity, choose the business account, then select the pixel installed on the site.
Configure DNS: pick a subdomain used by nothing else (e.g. cpg for cpg.yourdomain.com) — if the site is www.example.com, enter the root domain and the subdomain separately.
Create a CNAME record at your DNS provider: type CNAME, name = your subdomain, target = the host-provided domain, and disable proxying.
Wait for propagation — the source saw 5–10 minutes with Cloudflare, but it can take up to an hour — then confirm the setup shows 'optimized' with a green check.
Note that the subdomain change does not take effect immediately; allow time before re-checking Network requests.
caveats: DNS propagation time depends on your DNS vendor and is outside your control.
Interface steps and pricing change; verify in the current Stape and Meta UIs.
Disabling proxy at the DNS layer matters for the CNAME to resolve correctly.
cards.source_name: Facebook Conversions API gateway tutorial (FB CAPI Gateway a.k.a. Meta CAPI gateway).docx

cards.title: What true server-side tagging buys over the gateway
cards.summary: A full server-side setup can rewrite request URLs via a custom loader for higher delivery rates and can extend cookie lifetime, which the gateway does not do.
cards.use_when: Choosing between the Meta CAPI Gateway and a full server-side (e.g. GTM server container) setup for a store that needs durable attribution and cookie longevity.
steps: Assess the gateway's gaps: it does not let you modify the request URL sent to your server, and it does not extend cookie lifetime.
Consider a custom loader approach (the source cites Stape's) that rewrites the entire request URL to your server, which raises the odds the data reaches the server before being forwarded to Meta.
If longer attribution windows matter — e.g. considered purchases with multi-day research before checkout — evaluate server-side cookie lifetime extension, which the gateway cannot do.
Weigh effort against gain: proper server-side tagging takes more configuration, but the source argues the results are meaningfully better than the gateway.
Plan the migration path: start on the gateway to get Conversions API going quickly, then move to a server container when you have developer capacity.
caveats: The source's claim that server-side 'results are much better' is a practitioner opinion; the gain varies by site, traffic mix, and blocker exposure.
Custom loader and cookie-extension features depend on the host platform and must be verified as currently available.
cards.source_name: Facebook Conversions API gateway tutorial (FB CAPI Gateway a.k.a. Meta CAPI gateway).docx

cards.title: Measure purchase conversion rate, not raw key event rate
cards.summary: GA4's 'key events' bundle purchases with other actions, so you must manually filter to the purchase event before reading any conversion rate.
cards.use_when: Judging whether your store's or a channel's conversion rate is healthy before making merchandising or media-spend decisions.
steps: Understand the trap: in GA4, key events are not only purchase events; page views, add-to-carts and other actions can be marked as key events.
When you add the 'session key event rate' metric to any report, drill into the metric and set the event filter explicitly to 'purchase'.
Only then read the percentage as your conversion rate.
Sanity-check the result against total revenue in the same table so you are not reading a rate built on the wrong event set.
Re-check this filter after any GA4 configuration change, since the key-event set can drift over time.
caveats: The source's own store showed ~1.7% conversion rate after filtering to purchase; treat that as an example, not a benchmark.
GA4's interface changes over time, so verify the current click path before relying on it.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 For eCommerce 2025 ( Perfect for beginners).docx

cards.title: Find conversion rate by traffic channel
cards.summary: Customize the Traffic Acquisition report to add session key event rate filtered to purchase so you can compare conversion performance across organic, CPC and email.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to shift acquisition budget or fix a channel that drives traffic but no sales.
steps: Go to Reports -> Life Cycle -> Traffic Acquisition.
Click 'Customize report', then under Metrics add 'Session key event rate'.
Filter that metric to the purchase event only, as raw key events overstate conversion.
Optionally add the 'medium' dimension to split further, e.g. distinguishing organic from CPC and identifying specific senders like an email platform.
Save the customized report so you can return to it without redoing the setup.
Compare conversion rate across channels: a channel with strong sessions but weak purchase rate is a targeting or landing-page problem, not a volume problem.
caveats: Channel grouping depends on correct UTM tagging; untagged campaigns will fall into the wrong bucket and distort the comparison.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 For eCommerce 2025 ( Perfect for beginners).docx

cards.title: Read engaged sessions as a traffic-relevance signal
cards.summary: GA4 counts a session as engaged when it lasts longer than 10 seconds, making it a quick relevance check on the traffic you are buying or earning.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing whether paid or organic traffic is actually reaching a page that matches the visitor's intent.
steps: Open the Traffic Acquisition report and read engaged sessions, engagement rate and average engagement time by channel.
Treat a very low engaged-session count on a channel as a signal that visitors are not finding what they searched for or that the landing page does not match the query.
Cross-reference with the Landing Pages report to see whether specific entry pages are dragging the channel's engagement down.
If paid traffic shows low engagement, check ad-to-landing-page message match before increasing spend.
If organic shows low engagement, review whether the ranking page's content and product selection match the search intent.
caveats: The 10-second threshold is GA4's definition of an engaged session, not a performance target you must hit.
Low engagement can also come from bot traffic or mis-tagged campaigns, so rule those out first.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 For eCommerce 2025 ( Perfect for beginners).docx

cards.title: Compare product-page conversion rates in the Landing Pages report
cards.summary: Add the purchase-filtered session key event rate to the Landing Pages report to see which product pages convert and which are leaking.
cards.use_when: Deciding which product pages need new copy, photography or price tests, or whether a page's traffic is simply mismatched.
steps: Go to Reports -> Engagement -> Landing Pages.
Click to edit the report and add the 'session key event rate' metric.
Filter the metric to the purchase event so the rate reflects buyers, not all key events.
Compare rates across your top product pages, looking for outliers far above or far below the others.
Interpret a low outlier as one of three causes: wrong traffic being sent to that page, a page that needs more work, or a product that is simply less appealing.
Investigate the cause before rewriting the page, since a traffic mismatch will not be fixed by design changes.
caveats: Small traffic volumes produce noisy rates; a page with a handful of sessions can look dramatically better or worse than it is.
Shopify's native analytics does not expose this page-level conversion rate, which is why the GA4 setup matters.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 For eCommerce 2025 ( Perfect for beginners).docx

cards.title: Diagnose funnel drop-off with the Purchase Journey report
cards.summary: The Monetization -> Purchase Journey report shows drop-off between session start, product view, add to cart, checkout and purchase so you can localise friction.
cards.use_when: Investigating where shoppers abandon so you can decide whether to fix navigation, cart, pricing or checkout trust.
steps: Go to Reports -> Monetization -> Purchase Journey and set your date range.
Read the step-by-step progression: session started, viewed product, added to cart, began checkout, purchased.
Treat the drop between session started and viewed product as largely normal—many visitors are just browsing.
Focus on the drops between add to cart, checkout and purchase, which are the diagnostically meaningful ones.
If many sessions never view a product, question collection clarity, navigation and search rather than the product pages themselves.
If shoppers drop between add to cart and checkout, suspect the cart page; if they drop between checkout and purchase, suspect shipping cost, trust or checkout process friction.
caveats: In the source example, roughly half of sessions viewed a product, most viewers added to cart, 63% of those began checkout and 50% of those purchased—these are illustrative, not targets.
Funnel steps depend on correct event tracking; missing add-to-cart or checkout events will show fake drop-offs.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 For eCommerce 2025 ( Perfect for beginners).docx

cards.title: Segment traffic by channel and medium together
cards.summary: Adding the medium dimension to the Traffic Acquisition report gives a second layer of detail, separating CPC from paid social and identifying specific senders like your email platform.
cards.use_when: Working out which specific paid or owned channel is producing sessions, before shifting budget or cadence.
steps: Open Traffic Acquisition and customize the report to display the medium dimension alongside session primary channel group.
Read the resulting rows to separate, for example, CPC campaigns from paid social placements and email sends.
Use the split to spot channels that consume budget or send volume without contributing purchases.
Combine with the purchase-filtered session key event rate to rank mediums by conversion, not just volume.
Save the view and re-check on a regular cadence rather than a single snapshot.
caveats: Medium values come from UTM parameters, so discipline in tagging determines whether this view is trustworthy.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 For eCommerce 2025 ( Perfect for beginners).docx

cards.title: Customize and save GA4 reports instead of reading defaults
cards.summary: Default GA4 tables omit the metrics you actually need; adding metrics under Customize Report -> Metrics and saving the view is the core workflow.
cards.use_when: Setting up a repeatable weekly reporting routine you do not want to rebuild each time.
steps: Open the report you want to change (Traffic Acquisition or Landing Pages are the reported starting points).
Click 'Customize report', then under Metrics add the fields you care about—session key event rate, engagement rate, average engagement time, total revenue.
Apply the metric, then set any event filters (notably purchase) so the numbers mean what you think they mean.
Save the customized report so it persists for future sessions.
Use the Library section to add or remove report elements if the default navigation is distracting, but keeping defaults is also a valid choice.
caveats: The source explicitly warns that key events include more than purchases, so any added key-event-based metric must be filtered before interpretation.
GA4's customization interface is subject to change; confirm current labels before writing internal documentation.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 For eCommerce 2025 ( Perfect for beginners).docx

cards.title: Use GA4 to fill gaps Shopify analytics leaves
cards.summary: GA4's traffic-source and per-page detail exceeds what the Shopify dashboard reports, so treat GA4 as the channel and page diagnostic layer and Shopify as the order-level view.
cards.use_when: Deciding which analytics tool to check for a given question about traffic or page performance.
steps: Keep the GA4 home dashboard for a quick overview only; the source notes most of those numbers duplicate Shopify.
Use GA4 Reports for channel-level traffic detail, engagement quality and per-landing-page conversion, which Shopify does not provide at this granularity.
Use Shopify for order and product sales totals, and GA4's e-commerce purchases report to explore product-level purchase behaviour.
If you run Google Ads, link GA4 to Google Ads and to your store through the Shopify integration so advertising results surface inside GA4.
Walk the Life Cycle report set in GA4 as a standing review habit rather than relying on the default home screen.
caveats: Numbers will differ between GA4 and Shopify due to different attribution and session definitions; decide which system is your source of truth per question.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 For eCommerce 2025 ( Perfect for beginners).docx

cards.title: Read GA4's AI Insights for quick answers, not deep analysis
cards.summary: The Insights tool offers predefined suggested questions and short answers, useful for fast orientation when you are new to the platform.
cards.use_when: Getting a fast orientation answer such as which countries your visitors come from, before digging into a full report.
steps: Open the Insights tool from the GA4 home area and browse the suggested questions.
Pick a question relevant to the decision at hand—for example demographics or country distribution.
Read the short answer as a starting pointer, then verify in the underlying report before acting on it.
Do not treat the predefined question list as comprehensive; it is limited by what GA4 offers.
caveats: The question set is limited and predefined by GA4; it cannot answer arbitrary business questions.
The source treats this as a convenience only, not a substitute for the Traffic Acquisition and Landing Pages reports.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 For eCommerce 2025 ( Perfect for beginners).docx

cards.title: GA4 data retention: switch from 2 months to 14 months
cards.summary: Choose a suitable retention window for ecommerce explorations; standard aggregated reports are unaffected.
cards.use_when: Setting up a fresh GA4 property or auditing an existing one before relying on it for year-over-year ecommerce reporting.
steps: Open the correct GA4 property and review its Data Retention settings.
Where available and appropriate for the store, select 14 months for seasonal explorations. Verify property eligibility and required retention policy.
An increase preserves previously collected data that still exists; it cannot restore already deleted data.
caveats: Retention affects explorations and funnel reports, not standard aggregated reports. Large-property limits and some data categories have separate rules.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Prevent fragmented sessions by extending GA4 session timeout
cards.summary: GA4's default 30-minute session timeout can split a single shopping journey into multiple sessions, distorting engagement and conversion metrics.
cards.use_when: Configuring a new GA4 property or investigating why session counts and conversion rates look inflated or fragmented for a store with long browse-to-purchase lag.
steps: Open GA4 Admin > Data Streams > select the stream > Configure Tag Settings (or the data stream's session settings depending on current UI).
Locate the session timeout setting, which defaults to 30 minutes.
Increase it toward the allowed maximum (the source cites up to 7 hours and 55 minutes) when customers commonly leave and return within a browsing session on the same device.
Weigh the tradeoff: a longer timeout keeps a single journey intact but can merge genuinely separate visits into one session, lowering apparent per-session conversion rate.
Re-check the resulting session and conversion-rate reports after the change to confirm the shift matches the store's real buying behavior.
caveats: Choosing the maximum is not automatically correct; the source presents extending the timeout as a fix for fragmented sessions, not a universal requirement. Test against the store's actual purchase lag.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Configure cross-domain tracking for checkout on a separate domain
cards.summary: If any step of a purchase journey crosses domains (e.g., a third-party checkout), analytics without cross-domain tracking will attribute the sale to a new session and lose the true source.
cards.use_when: Setting up analytics for a store whose checkout, cart, or landing flow uses a different domain than the main site — common with hosted checkouts and upsell tools.
steps: Map the full customer journey and list every domain a single visitor touches between landing and purchase.
Decide whether to use one GA4 property spanning all of them; the source recommends a single property with cross-domain tracking when visitors jump between domains in one journey.
In GA4 Admin, open the data stream's Configure Tag Settings and add the additional domains under 'Configure your domains'.
Verify by running through a full purchase journey and confirming it appears as one session with the original acquisition source intact, not as a referral from your own checkout domain.
Also exclude internal/office IP traffic so staff testing the checkout don't pollute conversion data.
caveats: Cross-domain tracking around third-party checkout systems can be limited by how that vendor handles redirects and iframes; confirm compatibility with the checkout provider. Verify current GA4 cross-domain setup steps in the interface.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Filter internal office IP traffic out of GA4
cards.summary: Office and testing traffic inflates sessions and distorts conversion metrics, so define and exclude it during setup.
cards.use_when: New GA4 setup or ongoing data-quality audit for a store where staff frequently visit the site to test products, pricing, or checkout.
steps: Find the public IP address(es) of the office or any location where staff browse and test the store.
In GA4 Admin > Data Streams > Configure Tag Settings > Define Internal Traffic, add a rule matching those IP addresses.
Create or activate an 'Internal Traffic' exclusion filter (data filter) at the property level, using the internal-traffic rule and setting it to exclude.
Confirm the filter is active rather than in testing mode before relying on the data.
Re-test with a request from the office network and confirm it does not appear in real-time reports.
caveats: Home-office and VPN traffic uses changing IPs and is not fully filtered by this method. GA4 filters can take effect going forward only and may not restate past data.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Create custom GA4 events via GTM with triggers and parameters
cards.summary: Track meaningful on-page interactions (like menu link clicks) as custom GA4 events by configuring them in Google Tag Manager with precise triggers and parameters.
cards.use_when: Building out analytics for a store where default GA4 events don't capture the interactions that matter for merchandising or navigation decisions.
steps: In GTM, create a new Tag using the 'GA4 Event' tag type and give the event a name using only lowercase letters and underscores (GA4 naming convention) — e.g., menu_link_click.
Create a Trigger for the interaction, using conditions such as 'Click Classes' contains a specific class or 'Click Element' matching a selector, so the trigger fires only on the intended clicks.
Map custom parameters in the tag — for example menu_item_name and menu_item_url — using GTM variables to pull the clicked item's text or href.
Use GTM Preview mode to connect to the site, trigger the interaction, and confirm the tag fired.
Use GA4 DebugView to confirm the event and its parameters were actually received by GA4 before publishing the container.
caveats: Custom parameters will not appear in GA4 standard reports until you register them as Custom Dimensions in the GA4 admin panel and data finishes processing.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Register GTM custom parameters as GA4 Custom Dimensions
cards.summary: Custom event parameters you send through GTM are invisible in GA4 reports until you register them as Custom Dimensions.
cards.use_when: After setting up a custom event (e.g., menu link clicks) and finding its parameters are not available for reporting or explorations.
steps: Confirm the parameter is already being sent, verified via DebugView.
In GA4 Admin > Custom Definitions > Custom Dimensions, create a new dimension.
Set the Dimension Name (a friendly label for reports) and the Event Parameter (the exact parameter key sent in the tag, e.g., menu_item_name), matching case exactly.
Choose the correct scope (Event scope for event parameters).
Allow 24 to 48 hours for GA4 to process the data before the dimension appears populated in standard reports.
caveats: GA4 processing lag means newly registered dimensions won't show data immediately; don't assume the setup failed. Also, GTM preview and DebugView are more reliable for verifying parameters than standard reports right after configuration.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Test GA4/GTM event setup before publishing the container
cards.summary: Verify every new tracking tag in GTM Preview and GA4 DebugView before publishing, so broken tracking doesn't silently corrupt data.
cards.use_when: Any time you add or change a tracking tag for a store, before pushing the change live to all users.
steps: Open GTM Preview mode and connect to the site.
Perform the real interaction you want to track (click, add-to-cart, etc.).
In GTM Preview, confirm the correct trigger fired and the tag executed.
Open GA4 DebugView (via Admin > DebugView, or with the Stream URL) and confirm the event name and all parameters arrived with the correct values.
Only after both GTM and DebugView confirm success, publish the GTM container version.
Allow 24 to 48 hours for GA4 to process event data before expecting it in standard reports.
caveats: The source warns GA4 takes 24 to 48 hours to fully process events, so new tags won't appear in reports instantly. DebugView is temporary and only shows a recent window of debug events.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Use a single GA4 property across domains in one journey
cards.summary: When a single customer journey crosses multiple domains, the source recommends one GA4 property with cross-domain tracking rather than separate properties.
cards.use_when: Deciding property architecture for a store that uses a main site plus a separate checkout, landing, or app domain.
steps: Trace the visitor journey and identify all domains involved.
If visitors jump between domains within a single purchase journey, configure one single GA4 property rather than splitting them.
Enable cross-domain tracking in the data stream by listing all involved domains under 'Configure your domains'.
Test a full journey to confirm it resolves to a single session with the original source, not self-referrals.
Keep the acquisition and monetization data unified so attribution and conversion counts stay accurate.
caveats: This is the source's recommendation for multi-domain journeys; a single-property setup can complicate administration if the domains serve genuinely separate businesses with different owners or reporting needs.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Reverse-engineer the purchase path with Path Exploration
cards.summary: GA4 Path Exploration lets you start from a purchase event and work backward to see the sequence of pages and events preceding conversions.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing where buyers drop off or what pages precede a purchase, to inform merchandising and PDP/checkout improvements.
steps: Open GA4 Explore and create a Path Exploration.
Set the end-point (or starting-point) node to the Purchase event and work backward to see the common preceding steps.
Alternatively, start from a high-traffic landing page and forward-track where users go next.
Identify the most common paths to purchase and the points where users exit or stall — these are friction candidates.
Translate the top friction points into testable changes (e.g., PDP layout, add-to-cart placement, cart-step clarity) rather than guessing.
caveats: Explorations are subject to sampling and data thresholds, and require enough traffic volume to be reliable. Path exploration reflects correlation of sequences, not proof of causation.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Build Free Form tables in GA4 Explorations
cards.summary: Free Form analysis in GA4 lets you build custom cross-tabulated tables of dimensions and metrics to answer specific store questions beyond standard reports.
cards.use_when: When a store question (e.g., which products convert best by traffic source, or how a specific landing page performs) is not answerable from GA4's standard reports.
steps: Open GA4 Explore and create a Blank or Free Form exploration.
Drag in Dimensions (e.g., landing page, session source/medium, device category) as rows or columns.
Add Metrics (e.g., sessions, conversions, revenue, engagement rate) as values.
Apply filters or segments to isolate the question, such as a single campaign or product category.
Interpret with caution due to data thresholds and sampling on smaller segments, and export or screenshot before the exploration expires.
caveats: Explorations are not saved indefinitely the way standard reports are; heavier filtering increases sampling and thresholding, which can hide data on low-traffic segments.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Extend the engaged-session threshold above the 10-second default
cards.summary: GA4's default engaged-session threshold of 10 seconds understates meaningful engagement, so the source recommends raising it to at least 30 seconds.
cards.use_when: Configuring GA4 settings for a store where you want engagement metrics to reflect genuine browsing rather than momentary visits.
steps: Locate the engaged-session definitions in GA4 configuration (Admin > Data Streams > Configure Tag Settings or session settings depending on current UI).
Note that GA4's default treats a session as engaged at 10 seconds.
Adjust the threshold to at least 30 seconds per the source's recommendation.
Revisit engagement-rate reporting to confirm it now better reflects real browsing behavior rather than brief visits.
Use the adjusted metric when comparing landing pages or traffic sources for engagement quality.
caveats: The 30-second figure is the source's recommendation, not an industry standard; choose a threshold matching your product's consideration time. Changing definitions affects comparability with historical data.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Enable Google Signals for demographic audience data
cards.summary: Google Signals provides demographic reporting (age, gender, interests) and enables cross-device information in GA4.
cards.use_when: When you want demographic or interest data to guide ad targeting, creative strategy, or audience definitions for a store.
steps: In GA4 Admin > Data Settings > Data Collection, enable Google Signals under Data Collection and Modification.
Review what has changed in current GA4 versions — the data collection toggle and privacy controls have shifted over time, so verify the current interface.
Once enabled and after data accumulates, review demographic reports to understand the age/gender/interest composition of converting vs. non-converting segments.
Apply insights to ad audience selection and creative strategy rather than to individual-level targeting decisions.
Confirm consent/privacy compliance for your regions before enabling, since Signals uses Google's signed-in user data.
caveats: Enabling Google Signals requires a privacy/compliance review; it involves Google-signed-in user data and can be restricted in some jurisdictions. The source lists it as one of five mandatory settings but also the availability and behavior can vary by region.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Apply GA4 naming conventions to custom events
cards.summary: Use lowercase letters and underscores for GA4 event names to keep tracking consistent and avoid downstream reporting breaks.
cards.use_when: Creating any custom event in GA4/GTM for a store, or standardizing event names across teams and tools.
steps: When naming a custom event, restrict it to lowercase letters and underscores — e.g., cart_add_item, menu_link_click.
Avoid spaces, camelCase, or mixed case in event names, which the source warns against for GA4.
Keep naming consistent across tags so reports aggregate properly rather than splitting the same action across variants.
Document event names so future team members use the same conventions.
Note that GA4 has reserved/automatic event names; avoid colliding with them.
caveats: The source specifically states the lowercase-and-underscore requirement for GA4 event names; verify against current GA4 documentation since accepted conventions can evolve.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Treat GA4 setup as a five-setting baseline for ecommerce accuracy
cards.summary: The source identifies five mandatory GA4 admin configurations to make ecommerce data trustworthy before you rely on it.
cards.use_when: Onboarding a new GA4 property or auditing an established store analytics setup before making merchandising or marketing decisions from it.
steps: 1) Extend data retention from the 2-month default to 14 months.
2) Configure cross-domain tracking if the journey spans domains.
3) Define and filter internal office/office IP traffic.
4) Extend the default 30-minute session timeout toward the allowed maximum to avoid fragmented sessions.
5) Enable Google Signals for demographic data (subject to privacy review).
Verify each setting is active and not just staged, then re-test a purchase journey end-to-end before trusting the numbers.
caveats: These are the source's prescribed baseline settings, some of which (maximum session timeout, Signals) carry tradeoffs or compliance considerations. Treat them as a starting checklist, not universal rules; verify current GA4 interface behavior.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Do not rely on AI chat assistants for GA4 technical configuration
cards.summary: The source warns that an AI analytics chat assistant hallucinated incorrect technical advice about GA4, so verify AI-generated setup guidance against GA4's actual interface.
cards.use_when: When seeking quick answers on GA4 setup or landing-page attribution issues, before applying AI-generated configuration advice to a live store property.
steps: Treat AI-suggested GA4 configuration steps as hypotheses, not instructions.
Verify any claim (e.g., how 'not set' landing pages work) against GA4's official documentation or the interface itself.
Where AI advice conflicts with observed DebugView/Preview behavior, trust the observed data.
Keep a record of what actually works in your property for future reference.
Avoid applying AI-suggested changes to a production container without the GTM Preview/DebugView verification step.
caveats: This reflects the source's experience with a specific AI assistant; it's a caution about verification, not a claim that all AI tools are useless.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Structure a GA4 account for an ecommerce store
cards.summary: Decide account, property and data stream structure based on whether your storefront, checkout and subdomains form one user journey.
cards.use_when: Setting up GA4 for a store that spans several domains (e.g. main shop domain plus a separate checkout or landing domains) and you need to decide how many properties and streams to create.
steps: Treat the GA4 account as the organization: for a single business, one account is usually enough.

Create one property per distinct user journey you want measured together. If a shopper moves from your main site to a dedicated checkout domain and then purchases, use ONE property for both so the journey is visible in one place.
If your sites are separate business lines whose data you never want combined (e.g. two unrelated product ranges), give each its own property so data is not mixed.
Inside a property, use one web data stream even for multiple websites — Google recommends one web stream across sites rather than a stream per domain.
Which domain you type when creating the web stream is not critical; the stream still works for the other domains in the property.
When multiple domains are in one property, configure cross-domain tracking in the data stream settings so sessions are not split when visitors jump domains.
Select reporting time zone and currency at property creation — these match where the business is, not the individual shopper.
Choose business objectives at setup; they only change which report collections are unlocked. The presenter prefers the older report layout, so pick objectives you'll actually use or select 'other'.
Verify the current interface wording in the GA4 admin panel before following these steps, as Google changes report collection names.
caveats: Report collection names differ depending on the business objectives selected and change over time; content is similar but labels vary.
GA4 takes roughly 24–48 hours to fully process data, so a fresh property or new custom dimensions will not appear in standard reports immediately.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Install the GA4 tag: CMS, hardcode, or GTM
cards.summary: Choose between a CMS tracking-ID field, developer-installed code, or Google Tag Manager for deploying GA4 on an ecommerce site.
cards.use_when: Choosing how to deploy GA4 (and later ecommerce event tags) on your storefront, especially when you lack developer time or need to add vendor tags.
steps: Option 1 — built-in integration: many ecommerce platforms have a field for the measurement ID (starts with 'G-'). Find it in GA4 under Admin > Data Streams > your web stream > Measurement ID, paste it into the platform field, and the platform installs GA4 for you.
Option 2 — custom site: hand the Google tag snippet to a developer to add to every page. Google recommends the <head> section; the <body> also works if the head is not feasible.

Option 3 — Google Tag Manager: create a container at tagmanager.google.com, install the first GTM container code on all pages (the second snippet can be ignored), then add a Google tag with your measurement ID inside GTM.
A container needs its code on every page for the Google tag to activate everywhere, so this is the critical developer handoff.
GTM's main advantage is managing many tags (GA4, Meta pixel, LinkedIn insight tag) without repeated developer involvement — useful when you need to iterate on ecommerce event tracking.
After publishing in GTM, GA4 starts collecting data; allow 24–48 hours before trusting new reports.
caveats: GTM has a learning curve; the presenter's stated preference for GTM is his opinion, not a universal requirement.
Exact GTM and GA4 button labels change; verify the current interface before instructing a developer.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Test a GA4 tag with GTM Preview and DebugView
cards.summary: Run the GTM preview → DebugView sequence to confirm a tag fires and GA4 receives the event and its parameters before publishing.
cards.use_when: Validating any new GA4 tracking tag (ecommerce events, custom events) on your store before publishing it to live shoppers.
steps: In GTM click Preview, enter the store URL, and click Connect; the site opens in a new tab with tag assistant connected.
Trigger the action you want to measure if needed (for a page-load tag, just visiting is enough) and inspect the event in the preview panel — confirm your tag fired.
Open GA4 in another tab: Admin > Debug View. Confirm the events arrive (e.g. page_view, scroll, session_start) and that parameters such as page location and URL match.
For custom events, click into the event in DebugView and verify the custom parameters you attached (e.g. menu item name/URL) are present, not just the default ones.
Only after both GTM preview and DebugView confirm receipt, go back to GTM and Submit / Publish the container version.
Re-enable Preview each time you restart a GTM session if the preview disconnects.
caveats: A preview-mode 'unknown tag type' warning can be a preview bug — tags can still work correctly.
Newly published events and custom dimensions can take 24–48 hours to surface in standard GA4 reports, so DebugView is the fast check, not the report.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Read acquisition reports: first touch vs session
cards.summary: Distinguish user acquisition (first source ever) from traffic acquisition (per session) to answer the right question about store traffic.
cards.use_when: Deciding which channel or campaign drove purchases and revenue for your store, and avoiding misreading first-touch attribution as current-session attribution.
steps: Use User Acquisition to see the FIRST source that ever acquired a visitor — a user acquired months ago by organic search stays in the organic row for all later sessions.
Use Traffic Acquisition for per-session data, which most marketers actually want: group traffic sources, then drill into Session source/medium.
Add sessions, then revenue, as metrics and sort by the metric you care about — e.g. sort by revenue to see which sources actually paid off, not just which drove volume.
Add Session campaign name via the plus button (dimension) to break revenue down by individual campaign, e.g. to find which email newsletter generated the most revenue.

Use quick filters to isolate a channel: filter Session medium exactly matches email, or combine Session medium = cpc with Session source contains facebook.com to see paid social campaigns and their revenue.
Change chart granularity (day vs week) and the date range to read trends; clearing rows can blank a chart, so reselect rows or click plot rows to restore data.
caveats: Assertion that 'most marketers want traffic acquisition' is the presenter's opinion.
The default chart shows only the top five sources; deselect or plot specific rows to see others.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Use the ecommerce purchases report for product decisions
cards.summary: Read item views, add-to-carts, purchases and item revenue per product to find merchandising winners and drop-off points.
cards.use_when: Merchandising and product-selection decisions — spotting products with strong views but weak add-to-cart or purchase rates, or identifying top revenue items.
steps: Open the Monetization report (might be labeled revenue in your layout) and go to E-commerce purchases.
Read the columns per item: how often the product was viewed, added to cart, purchased, and item revenue. Sorting by item revenue surfaces top performers (e.g. a best-selling sweater).
Use gaps between view → add-to-cart → purchase as a signal: a product viewed a lot but rarely bought may have pricing, imagery, or PDP-copy issues worth testing.
Treat this data as available ONLY if you or your platform sends view_item / add_to_cart / purchase events with product and revenue parameters — GA4 does not track this out of the box.
If the data is missing, either ask your platform about its GA4 ecommerce integration or have a developer/GTM send the events, then allow 24–48 hours for processing.
caveats: Out-of-the-box GA4 does not send ecommerce events; without configuration this report is empty or partial.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Diagnose checkout drop-off by device or browser
cards.summary: Use the checkout journey report with breakdown dimensions to find where and on which devices/browsers shoppers abandon checkout.
cards.use_when: Optimizing the cart and checkout flow — locating funnel steps that lose the most shoppers and checking whether a specific browser/device has a technical problem.
steps: Open the checkout journey report to see drop-off between steps: users who started checkout, added shipping info, added payment info, then purchased.
Change the breakdown dimension to Device category to compare completion rates across desktop, mobile and tablet.
Switch the breakdown to Browser and scan for a step where one browser drops off significantly more — that pattern suggests a technical bug rather than a UX preference.
Investigate the suspect step in that browser (e.g. reproduce the failing checkout) before assuming it is a design issue.
Repeat across steps to prioritise which fix affects the most lost orders.
caveats: Requires ecommerce events (begin_checkout, add_shipping_info, add_payment_info, purchase) to be configured; GA4 does not collect these automatically.
A higher drop-off for one browser is a hypothesis pointing to a bug, not proof.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Landing page vs pages and screens report
cards.summary: Use the landing-page report for session entry pages and pages-and-screens for total page views, and understand why revenue in the pages report can mislead.
cards.use_when: Evaluating which entry pages (homepage, collections, checkout URL) start sessions and drive revenue, versus measuring overall page popularity.
steps: Use the Landing page report to see the FIRST page of each session and revenue attributed to those entry sessions — useful for judging which entry points (homepage, new arrivals, clearance) actually produce revenue.
Use Pages and screens for total page views regardless of position in the session, plus users and active users per page.

Sort Pages and screens by views or users to find the most-visited pages; be aware revenue in this report is attributed to the page where the conversion occurred, so almost all revenue lands on checkout — the presenter considers revenue unhelpful here.
Interpret 'active users': a user who spent at least 10 seconds, converted (a key event), viewed 2+ pages in a session, or is a new user.

Expect checkout URLs to appear as landing pages when a session expires mid-purchase — a visitor who leaves after adding to cart and returns later can start a new session with checkout as the landing page.
To reduce that false signal, consider raising the default session timeout (see the session-timeout card).
