caveats: Revenue in the pages-and-screens report is attributed to the conversion page, making it near-useless for judging page value.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Mark key events and pick the right conversion metric
cards.summary: Distinguish plain events from key events (purchase, signup) and use them in acquisition and exploration reports to count real business outcomes.
cards.use_when: Deciding which ecommerce actions (purchase, newsletter signup, account creation) should count as conversions and where to read them by traffic source.
steps: Treat every interaction GA4 records as an event; mark business-critical ones (purchase, signup) as key events.
In acquisition reports, use the event-count selector to count a specific event (e.g. purchase) by traffic source, and use the key-events section for events you have promoted.
Remember User Acquisition counts key events on a first-touch basis, so a repeat buyer counts under the original acquisition source.
When building explorations, filter by event name (exactly matches purchase) to isolate the action and avoid mixing in irrelevant events.
Only mark as key the actions that map to revenue or clear value — over-marking dilutes the signal.
caveats: Key events are only available once the underlying event is actually being sent; GA4 does not detect purchases without configuration.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Build a free-form exploration for product/device decisions
cards.summary: Create free-form explorations with dimensions as rows/columns and metrics as values to cross-tab store performance, e.g. revenue by country and device.
cards.use_when: Answering a specific merchandising or targeting question — e.g. which countries or device categories generate the most purchase revenue — beyond what standard reports allow.
steps: Open Explore, choose Free form (blank), and note the three-pane layout: Variables (dimensions, metrics, segments), Settings, and the output table.
Add dimensions you will use (e.g. Device category, Country) and metrics (e.g. purchase revenue) via the plus buttons, then confirm.
Drag dimensions into Rows and Columns, and the metric into Values; double-clicking a dimension also adds it.
Read the resulting table, e.g. revenue by country split into desktop/mobile/tablet, then switch visualization between bar chart, heat map (darker = higher), and plain table.
Share a finished exploration via the share icon so other property users can see it.
caveats: Explorations are private to their creator by default; sharing is view-only — others must copy and modify their own version to change it.
Exploration data is limited by the property's data retention window (default 2 months).
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Mine site-search terms to find assortment gaps
cards.summary: Build a free-form exploration of site search terms and event counts to see what shoppers ask for and whether your catalogue answers it.
cards.use_when: Product selection and assortment planning — spotting search terms with high demand but no matching products, or reframing how products are named/merchandised.
steps: Open Explore, add a new free-form tab.
Add dimensions Event name and Search term, and metric Event count.
Put Search term in Rows and Event count in Values.

Filter Event name exactly matches the search-results event (the presenter's demo uses 'view search results') so the report stops mixing search with all other events — without the filter you get a large blank row aggregating everything.
Read the top keywords; terms searched often with no matching product point to assortment gaps or merchandising/labeling improvements.
caveats: The site-search event name depends on your setup; the exact name 'view search results' is specific to the demo property.
Requires the site-search event parameters to be captured and, if you want them in standard reports, registered as custom dimensions.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Funnel exploration: build an ecommerce funnel with breakdowns
cards.summary: Define ordered steps (view_item → add_to_cart → begin_checkout → purchase) in a funnel exploration and break them down by device to find where completion drops.
cards.use_when: Pinpointing the biggest conversion leak in your purchase path and checking whether it differs by device category.
steps: Open Explore, add a Funnel exploration, and click the pencil to edit Steps.
Define each step as an event condition: step 1 view_item, step 2 add_to_cart, step 3 begin_checkout, step 4 purchase (use your platform's actual event names).
Optional: narrow a step with a parameter (e.g. item ID) to funnel only a specific product, or by page host name/location.
Apply and read the counts of users reaching each step and the drop-off between them.
Add a breakdown dimension such as Device category to compare completion rates — the demo shows desktop completing better, hinting mobile UX is worth investigating.
Only treat ecommerce events as available if you or your platform send them; GA4 does not collect them out of the box.
caveats: Requires configured ecommerce events; absent them the funnel will have no steps to match.
Higher desktop completion is a signal to investigate, not proof of a mobile defect.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Path exploration: work backward from purchase or checkout events
cards.summary: Set the ending point to purchase or begin_checkout and read backward to reveal looping or confusing paths before conversion.
cards.use_when: Investigating why shoppers abandon checkout (e.g. logging in and out repeatedly) or what pages precede a purchase.
steps: Open Explore, add a Path exploration.
Click Start over and choose the ENDING point — e.g. event name purchase — to see what happened before the conversion.
Switch the dimension to Page path and expand backward; expect checkout pages adjacent to purchase, then keep expanding until non-checkout pages appear for useful context.
Alternatively set the starting point to begin_checkout and expand forward to watch where shoppers go; the demo shows users bouncing to account/login and back to checkout.
Interpret looping between checkout and account pages as a possible UX or login-friction problem worth testing.
caveats: Looping patterns indicate a hypothesis to investigate, not a proven cause.
Path explorations are private by default, like all explorations.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Create and register custom events and dimensions in GA4 via GTM
cards.summary: Send a custom event (e.g. menu-link click) with parameters from GTM, then register those parameters as custom dimensions to use them in reports.
cards.use_when: Tracking a store interaction GA4 does not collect automatically — e.g. clicks on a homepage banner, nav menu, or a category tile you want to evaluate.
steps: In GTM create a trigger (e.g. Just Links) and use Preview to identify the click; inspect the Variables panel for click text, click URL and click classes.
If click-related variables are missing, enable them under Variables > Configure > Click variables.
Narrow the trigger with click classes contains a class value that identifies the element (e.g. nav link) — inspect your own site's classes since these differ by site.
Create a tag: Google Analytics > GA4 event, paste the measurement ID, name the event in lowercase with underscores (GA4 event names must be lowercase, no spaces).
Add event parameters (e.g. menu_item_name = click text, menu_item_url = click URL) using GTM variables.
Attach the tag to the trigger, name and save it, then test through GTM Preview and GA4 DebugView before publishing.
In GA4, register each custom parameter as a custom dimension (Admin > Custom definitions > Create custom dimension) with scope Event so it appears in reports and explorations.
Publish the GTM container after successful testing.
caveats: Custom dimensions only appear in standard reports after the event is sent and data has processed (roughly 24–48 hours).
Parameter and event names are case-sensitive and must match exactly between GTM, GA4 registration and filters.
Verify current GTM/GA4 menus, which change over time.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Configure five settings in every new GA4 property
cards.summary: Day-one GA4 configuration: event data retention to 14 months, cross-domain tracking, session timeout, engaged-session threshold, and internal traffic exclusions.
cards.use_when: Setting up a new store property or fixing a recently created one where exploration history is short or sessions split unnaturally.
steps: 1. Data retention: Admin > Data retention, change event data retention from the default 2 months to 14 months (Premium can go longer). Explorations only see data within the retention window, so set this at property creation.

2. Multiple domains: if one property covers several domains, tell GA4 which domains belong to your business and configure cross-domain tracking in the data stream settings so sessions join across domains.
3. Session timeout: extend the default session duration (the demo property is 30 minutes) if leaving-mid-checkout breaks sessions into a new session with checkout as the landing page.
4. Engaged sessions: the presenter recommends raising the default 10-second engaged-session threshold to at least 30 seconds to better reflect real store engagement.
5. Internal traffic: exclude your own/team IP addresses so staff visits and test orders do not pollute revenue and conversion data.
caveats: Thresholds (10s default, 30s recommendation, 30-minute session timeout) are the presenter's guidance, not absolutes; choose values that fit how your shoppers buy.
Premium (360) allows longer retention; the standard limit is 14 months.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Use Analytics Advisor cautiously for quick questions
cards.summary: The Gemini-powered Analytics Advisor answers natural-language questions about your GA4 data, but hallucinates on technical causes.
cards.use_when: Getting a fast number from your own GA4 property (e.g. purchases from organic search last week) without building an exploration.
steps: Open the Analytics Advisor icon in the GA4 interface and type a question, e.g. 'How many purchases came from organic search in the last week?'
Verify the answer against the source report it references (e.g. the traffic acquisition report) and check the date range it applied matches your question.
Rely on it for simple numeric lookups where you can independently confirm the result.

Do NOT trust its explanations of why data looks a certain way — the demo shows it asserting a myth that firing a custom event before page_view causes 'not set' landing pages (the presenter's testing shows this is false).
caveats: Feature is in beta and powered by Gemini; it can hallucinate, cite wrong sources and opens reports with incorrect date ranges.
Useful for experienced users as a time-saver; the presenter warns it can mislead complete beginners.
Verify the current interface and beta status before relying on it.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Demographics, tech and region reports for audience context
cards.summary: Use user attributes and tech detail reports to see where shoppers are and what they browse on, treating demographics as directional.
cards.use_when: Shaping merchandising, shipping or site-experience decisions — e.g. localising assortment by region or prioritising mobile experience.
steps: In User attributes > Demographic details, view country, region or city of shoppers to spot core markets.
If Google signals is enabled you may also see age, gender and interests — treat these three as imprecise and directional only.
In Tech > Tech details, view browser performance and switch the dimension to operating system or device category.
Cross-check device/tech findings against the checkout journey and funnel reports to confirm whether a given device or browser truly under-converts.
caveats: Demographic dimensions (age/gender/interests) are not highly accurate and require Google signals.
Report collection names vary by the business objectives chosen at setup.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Set GA4 event data retention to 14 months at property creation
cards.summary: Choose a suitable retention window for ecommerce explorations; standard aggregated reports are unaffected.
cards.use_when: Setting up a new GA4 property for an ecommerce store, or auditing an existing property before doing seasonal/year-over-year merchandising and product performance analysis.
steps: Open the correct GA4 property and review its Data Retention settings.
Where available and appropriate for the store, select 14 months for seasonal explorations. Verify property eligibility and required retention policy.
An increase preserves previously collected data that still exists; it cannot restore already deleted data.
caveats: Retention affects explorations and funnel reports, not standard aggregated reports. Large-property limits and some data categories have separate rules.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Register all business domains for cross-domain tracking in GA4
cards.summary: List every domain your store uses in GA4 domain configuration so sessions spanning multiple properties are attributed correctly.
cards.use_when: When your ecommerce operation runs across multiple domains or subdomains (e.g., main store and a separate checkout or regional domain) and you need accurate session and conversion attribution.
steps: Go to Admin > Data Streams and select your website data stream.
Scroll to Configure tag settings and open Configure your domains.
Add each domain your business uses that is tracked by the same GA4 property (e.g., example.com and another-website.com).
Enter the root domain only; entering example.com automatically covers all of its subdomains, so subdomains do not need separate entries.
If five domains are tracked by one property, add all five, then Save.
Confirm the setting afterward by testing a journey that crosses domains and checking that it stays in one session.
caveats: This setting is specifically about cross-domain tracking; it does not by itself fix other attribution gaps.
Only relevant if you actually track multiple domains with the same property.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Exclude internal (employee) traffic from GA4 reports
cards.summary: Define internal traffic rules by IP and activate the data filter so staff visits do not pollute ecommerce metrics.
cards.use_when: When employees work from an office or have static IPs and you are making decisions from conversion rate, session, or product-performance reports that staff browsing would distort.
steps: In Admin, go to the tag settings area and click Show more, then Define internal traffic.
Click Create and add a rule naming the traffic (e.g., 'office IP') and a condition such as IP address equals your office IP.
Add multiple conditions if needed, but ensure the relevant IP addresses are included.
Go to Data Collection > Data Filters and find the internal traffic filter, which starts in testing mode.
Activate the filter so employee traffic is excluded going forward.
Re-check after activation that sessions drop to expected levels.
caveats: Works only where IPs are static; remote or dynamic-IP staff will not be covered reliably.
Activation excludes traffic from that point forward; it does not clean historical data.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Extend GA4 session timeout and engagement timer (source opinion)
cards.summary: The presenter recommends raising the default 30-minute session timeout and the engaged-session timer, accepting fewer but longer sessions in exchange for cleaner landing-page data.
cards.use_when: When reviewing landing-page and acquisition reports and seeing many 'not set' landing pages or sessions that break up a single shopping visit.
steps: Go to Data Streams, select your website data stream, then Configure tag settings and Show more.
Open Adjust session timeout. Default is 30 minutes; the presenter usually sets at least 4 hours and often the maximum of 7 hours and 55 minutes.
Open the engaged-session timer setting and raise it from the default; the presenter considers 10 seconds too short and sets at least 30 seconds or more.
Save your changes.
Be aware of the trade-off the source states: longer timeouts can merge multiple daily visits into one session, reducing total session count, while reducing 'not set' landing pages.
caveats: This is explicitly the presenter's personal recommendation, and he notes some people disagree.
Merged sessions can understate visit frequency, which affects frequency-based retention analysis.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Enable Google Signals to populate demographics and interests
cards.summary: Turn on Google Signals in GA4 so age, gender, and interest dimensions stop being empty, weighing advertising-feature and privacy implications first.
cards.use_when: When you want demographic or interest data to segment ecommerce audiences (e.g., which age bands drive purchases) but your reports currently show no data for those dimensions.
steps: Go to the GA Admin panel, then Data Collection, then Google Signals data collection.
Toggle the setting on; demographics like age, gender, and interest will begin populating after activation.
Expect a delay — the source notes it can take weeks for data to appear.
Before enabling, consider that turning it on activates certain Google advertising features; if your company is strict about legal requirements, consult the legal team first.
caveats: Requires user consent/data-collection eligibility; data may remain sparse if consent rates are low.
Enabling it links GA data to Google advertising features, so privacy/legal review is advised.
Population is not instant.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Configure five foundational GA4 settings in the correct order
cards.summary: A starting checklist for a new GA4 property: data retention, domain configuration, internal traffic exclusion, session timing, and Google Signals.
cards.use_when: When onboarding a new ecommerce GA4 property or auditing an existing one before trusting its conversion and product reports.
steps: Use the Admin panel — most settings live at property level, though some exist at account level.
1) Data retention: raise from 2 months to 14 months and save immediately.
2) Domains: if tracking multiple sites in one property, register all root domains under Configure your domains.
3) Internal traffic: define employee IPs and activate the data filter so staff traffic is excluded.
4) Session timing (presenter's recommendation): extend session timeout and the engaged-session timer.
5) Google Signals: enable it if you want demographic/interest data, subject to legal review.
Treat this as a minimum baseline to consider, not a complete implementation; the source notes it only scratches the surface of GA4 setup.
caveats: Some steps (session timeout, Google Signals) are source opinions or carry privacy trade-offs, not universal mandates.
Menu paths and defaults can change across GA4 versions; verify the current interface.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Structure a GA4 account and property for your store
cards.summary: Set up one GA4 account per business with a property that holds your website data, named and configured to match your store.
cards.use_when: You're creating GA4 for your first ecommerce store or onboarding a new store/brand into your existing Google setup.
steps: Sign in at marketingplatform.google.com with the Google account that will own the store's analytics.
Go to Admin > Create > Account for each distinct business. Accounts organize properties; keep one account per business.
Create a property inside that account as the container where your store's data actually lives and reports render. One property can collect from a single site or from multiple sites and apps.
Name the account and property after the store/brand so future you can tell them apart in the property switcher.

Set the reporting time zone carefully: changing it later produces a gap or overlap in data. Set the currency to the primary currency you actually sell in, since GA4 auto-converts values sent in other currencies.
Choose 'Other Business Objectives' as the objective — the source recommends it because it loads the fullest set of pre-configured reports, effectively including the other four options.
Create a Web data stream for the store domain. This is the pipeline that sends data into the property.
caveats: Changing reporting time zone later causes data gaps or overlaps — decide before you collect.
The 'Other Business Objectives' recommendation is the presenter's opinion, not a GA4 requirement.
Interface may change; verify current click paths.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics Tutorial For Beginners (2026 Update).docx

cards.title: Review enhanced measurement instead of accepting defaults
cards.summary: GA4 auto-tracks page views, scrolls, outbound clicks, site search, forms, video and file downloads — audit these against what your store actually needs.
cards.use_when: You're finalizing the data stream for a store and deciding which automatic events should feed your reports.
steps: When creating the data stream, open the enhanced measurement settings gear rather than clicking through.
Confirm which events fire without code: page_views plus scrolls, outbound link clicks, site search, form interactions, embedded YouTube views, and file downloads.
Disable any event that misrepresents your store's intent. Example: if you don't want form engagement counted, switch forms off and Save.

Think about store consequences — scroll events are useful engagement signals, but a form-interaction event on every newsletter field blur may inflate engagement metrics you later compare against purchases.
After creation, note the measurement ID shown top-right of the stream: it's what routes data into your property.
caveats: Enhanced measurement is on by default and is a good starting point but is not tailored to your store.
Standard reports can take 12–24 hours to reflect new events.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics Tutorial For Beginners (2026 Update).docx

cards.title: Create a thank-you-page event as a purchase-adjacent key event
cards.summary: Turn a confirmation/thank-you URL into a distinct key event without touching code, using GA4's Create Event.
cards.use_when: You want to count store conversions like completed lead forms or a thank-you page that isn't already covered by a purchase event.
steps: Go to Admin > Events > Create Event (requires marketer, editor, or admin access).
Name the new event, e.g. generate_lead for a thank-you page.
Enable 'Mark as key event' so it counts as a conversion, and optionally set a default dollar value to represent what the action is worth.
Leave counting at 'Once per event' unless you deliberately want repeated counts.
Keep 'Create without code' selected and base it on the page_view event, then set the URL condition to match your confirmation page (e.g. URL contains 'thank-you').
Click Create. The event appears in Realtime immediately; standard reports lag 12–24 hours.
Note: enabling page_view itself as a key event would count every page view as a conversion — use the dedicated URL event instead.
caveats: Requires at least marketer-level access; demo properties won't allow it.
Many stores should rely on the standard purchase ecommerce event instead of a thank-you page event; this is a fallback for non-purchase conversions.
Verify current GA4 UI paths.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics Tutorial For Beginners (2026 Update).docx

cards.title: Deploy the GA4 tag via Google Tag Manager
cards.summary: Install GA4 on your store with a GTM Google Tag, a Constant variable for the Measurement ID, and an Initialization trigger.
cards.use_when: You're installing or re-installing GA4 tracking on a store site and want flexibility to add more tags later.
steps: Get your measurement ID from Admin > Data Collection and Modification > Data Streams, then click your stream and copy the ID from the top right.
In GTM, create a new tag named something like 'Google Tag GA4 Page View' and choose 'Google Tag' as the tag type.
Create a GTM Variable named 'GA4 Measurement ID' of type Constant and paste the ID as its value so you can reuse it across tags.
Set the trigger to 'Initialization - All Pages' so it fires on every page before other tags.
Save, then use Preview with your store URL to test, confirming the tag fires in Tag Assistant.
In GA4, open DebugView to confirm events are arriving from the test session.
Submit and Publish the GTM version to route live store traffic into GA4.
The source prefers GTM over the plain Google tag because GTM can manage many tags and track other site actions, not just GA4.
caveats: Preview/DebugView confirms implementation, not data quality — check for duplicate or missing events over the following day.
GTM interface and GA4 DebugView location may change; verify.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics Tutorial For Beginners (2026 Update).docx

cards.title: Use Explore funnels for checkout drop-off analysis
cards.summary: Build a Funnel Exploration on begin_checkout → add_payment_info → purchase to see where shoppers abandon.
cards.use_when: You need to diagnose cart/checkout abandonment and pinpoint the step where shoppers drop out.
steps: Go to Explore > blank report and set the technique to Funnel Exploration.
Click the pencil to define steps. Add 'Begin Checkout' with condition begin_checkout.
Add 'Add Payment Info' with condition add_payment_info.
Add 'Purchase' with condition purchase.

Choose between 'indirectly followed by' (users can view other pages between steps) and 'directly followed by' (excludes anyone who views another page first). The presenter leaves the default indirect unless he specifically wants to exclude off-path behavior.
Optionally set a time limit per step so slow shoppers don't count.
Apply and read the visualization: users through each step and drop-off below.
Enable Make Open Funnel to let users enter at any step, or use Trended Funnel to see the shape over the date range.
caveats: Requires the ecommerce events to be implemented on the site — the funnel reflects the events received, not intent.
The direct/indirect choice materially changes the numbers; pick based on the question you're asking.
This source attributes the technique to GA4 Explore; the specific step band is one example, not a benchmark.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics Tutorial For Beginners (2026 Update).docx

cards.title: Filter campaign rows out of a Free Form Explore report
cards.summary: Use the regex filter ^\(.*\)$ with 'Does Not Match Regex' to strip organic, direct and not-set rows so only named campaigns remain.
cards.use_when: You want an exploration report that shows only traffic from named UTM campaigns, without generic default-channel rows muddying the table.
steps: Build a Free Form report with Session Campaign as the row dimension, and metrics like Sessions, Active Users and Key Events.
Scroll to Filters in the second column and choose Session Campaign.
Pick 'Does Not Match Regex' and enter ^\(.*\)$ — this excludes anything that starts and ends with a parenthesis.
That removes rows like (organic), (direct) and (not set), leaving only named campaigns.
Apply the filter and verify the table now lists your campaign names.
caveats: This is a GA4 exploration report, not a fixed report; the filter regex is specific to this report's purposes.
It excludes campaigns whose names literally contain parenthetical wrapping — unlikely but possible with odd UTM naming.
Copy the regex if it's unfamiliar; the presenter explicitly says not to memorize it.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics Tutorial For Beginners (2026 Update).docx

cards.title: Choose User Acquisition vs Traffic Acquisition for the question at hand
cards.summary: User Acquisition attributes to the first source a user ever arrived from; Traffic Acquisition attributes to the session's most recent source.
cards.use_when: You're reporting on acquisition performance and need to decide whether you're evaluating first-touch brand discovery or per-session channel mix.
steps: Open Reports > Acquisition > User Acquisition to see how people first found the store, with metrics broken down by first-user dimension.
Switch to Traffic Acquisition to see how people found the store at the start of each session, with session-based metrics.

Use the dimension dropdown to change what you're looking at (Channel Group, Medium, Source, etc.), and add a second dimension like Landing Page to see whether a specific paid page is pulling in the sessions.
Apply this when evaluating store channel decisions: first-touch is the right lens for brand and lifetime-value discussions, last-touch/session for campaign and budget performance.
caveats: Neither report tells you incrementality — they are attribution slices, not causal measurement.
Attribution windows and model settings elsewhere in the property affect these reports.
The default channel groupings can be redefined (Admin > Channel Groups), which changes what you're comparing.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics Tutorial For Beginners (2026 Update).docx

cards.title: Read the Monetization reports for purchase revenue, items, and list/promotion breakdowns
cards.summary: Use GA4 ecommerce reports to see purchase revenue, purchasers, items bought, list membership, promotions and coupon revenue.
cards.use_when: You're reviewing store revenue performance in GA4 and want to break down purchases by product, list placement or promotion code.
steps: Open Monetization > Overview: Total Revenue is the value from all events; Purchase Revenue is transaction revenue only. They match unless you've assigned dollar values to non-purchase events.
Note which metrics are user-based (purchasers, first-time purchasers) versus event-based (purchase revenue).
Check the top items card for the products selling most.
Scroll to the item list, promotion and coupon code cards to see which collections, promotions and discount codes are driving purchases — these depend on that data being sent to GA4.
Open Ecommerce Purchases for a more granular item-level table; change the dimension dropdown to slice differently.
Use the Purchase Journey and Checkout Journey reports for the funnel views, and transaction-ID reports for reconciliation with your platform.
caveats: Coupon, promotion and list reporting only works if those parameters are implemented on your store's events.
Revenue metrics depend on correct value/currency parameters being sent, not on GA4 inferring them.
For attribution of purchased revenue across campaigns, use the Advertising reports rather than the Monetization reports.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics Tutorial For Beginners (2026 Update).docx

cards.title: Analyze landing page performance with the Landing Page report
cards.summary: See which pages are your top entry points and how many key events occur after users land on each one.
cards.use_when: You're deciding which entry pages to invest in, cross-promote or optimize for conversions.
steps: Open Engagement > Landing Page to see the first page people viewed when starting a session.
Sort or scan the table to identify the top entry points to your store — these are the pages paid and organic traffic lands on.
Look at the key events column to see what happens after people land on each page, not just how many arrive.
Cross-reference with cross-promotion needs: pages with high entrances but low key events are candidates for merchandising or content changes.
caveats: Counts key events that occur after landing, not strictly on that page — the attribution is landing-page-based.
Requires key events to be configured; otherwise this column is empty.
The report shows page paths (URLs); naming conventions in URLs affect readability.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics Tutorial For Beginners (2026 Update).docx

cards.title: Compare Last Click and Data Driven attribution for channel decisions
cards.summary: The Key Event Attribution Models report shows each channel's key events and revenue under both Last Click and Data Driven models, plus the gap between them.
cards.use_when: You're deciding where to shift budget and need to see which channels last-click undervalues or overvalues.
steps: Open the Key Event Attribution Models report in the Advertising section.
Read the first set of metrics under Last Click attribution and the second under Data Driven.
Look at the difference column at the right to see percentage increases and decreases per channel.

Use the gap as a signal, not a verdict — a channel that receives far more credit under Data Driven than Last Click is being undervalued by the simpler model, which matters when reallocating store acquisition budget.
Optionally open the Key Event Attribution Paths report to see the touchpoint combinations that lead to a conversion.
caveats: These reports require key events to be configured; without them they show nothing useful.
The presenter describes the reports as helping you understand relationships — he does not claim any model is ground truth.
Attribution models are descriptive, not incremental; budget decisions based on model shifts should be complemented by holdout or incrementality testing where feasible.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics Tutorial For Beginners (2026 Update).docx

cards.title: Enable Google Signals and extend data retention
cards.summary: Turn on Google Signals for demographics and Google Ads audience use, and extend GA4 data retention from the 2-month default to 14 months.
cards.use_when: You're configuring GA4 property settings and want richer audience reporting plus longer lookback in Explore reports.
steps: Go to Admin > Data Collection and Modification > Data Collection and enable Google Signals. Without it, age, gender and interests are missing from User Attributes reports, and audiences cannot be used in linked Google Ads accounts.
In Data Retention, change the retention period from the default 2 months to 14 months so historical data remains available in Explore reports.
In Data Filters, configure a filter to exclude internal/employee traffic via IP address so store performance isn't diluted by your own visits.
Check Consent Settings to confirm consent mode is set up if you serve EU users and want their data usable for Google Ads targeting.
Link Google Ads and Google Search Console under Product Links for additional reports and insights.
caveats: Data retention only offers 2 or 14 months depending on the plan setting; the presenter recommends 14 but the choice is yours.
Enabling Google Signals has privacy implications for user data — check your consent obligations before turning on.
Consent mode is required for EU data to be used for remarketing; without it, audiences won't be usable for those users.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics Tutorial For Beginners (2026 Update).docx

cards.title: Build audiences in GA4 for retention and remarketing segmentation
cards.summary: Create custom audiences (e.g. users who haven't triggered a lead event) for reporting and for remarketing in linked Google Ads.
cards.use_when: You want to group users such as repeat purchasers or unconverted visitors for reporting, retargeting or lifecycle campaigns.
steps: Go to Admin > Data Display > Audiences. Note the two predefined audiences: All Users and Purchases (the latter is empty if purchase events aren't being sent).
Click New Audience and choose Create a Custom Audience to build your own.
For an unconverted-visitor audience, name it clearly (e.g. 'Haven't Generated Lead'), start with the default Include Users When condition, then click 'Add Group to Exclude'.
Set the exclusion to your conversion event (e.g. generate_lead). Since the event was created recently, it might not be listed — search for it and choose 'Create Event' to add it as a new condition.
Save. The audience now contains users who did not trigger the event.
Use it two ways: for reporting to study how that group behaves, and as a targeting source in a linked Google Ads account for remarketing.
Remember audiences are useful even without Google Ads linkage — you can use them purely as reporting segments.
caveats: Audiences based on events you just created may take time to populate.
Audiences must reach minimum list sizes for remarketing use in Google Ads.
The presenter notes remarketing also requires Google Signals and appropriate consent for EU users.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics Tutorial For Beginners (2026 Update).docx

cards.title: Use GA4's realtime reports to sanity-check store launches and campaigns
cards.summary: Realtime Reports show pages, sources and events within seconds of arrival, useful for verifying a launch or campaign is landing correctly.
cards.use_when: You've just pushed a campaign email, ad or store change and want immediate confirmation that traffic is landing where you expect.
steps: Open Reports > Realtime. The overview shows users in the last 30 minutes (and last 5 minutes).
Read the bar chart right-to-left: the rightmost bar is the current minute, each bar leftward is an earlier minute in the last 30.
Check the geography map to confirm the right regions are arriving.
Scroll to see where people found the site, whether users are matched to audiences, which pages they're viewing, and which events are being collected.
For a focused view, open Realtime Pages to see the individual pages currently being viewed.
Use this immediately after sending a campaign email to confirm click-throughs are landing on the expected pages.
caveats: Realtime data may not persist into standard reports identically due to processing delays (standard reports typically lag 12–24 hours).
Realtime is a diagnostic, not a performance analysis tool — use Explore and Reports for deeper questions.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics Tutorial For Beginners (2026 Update).docx

cards.title: Use Reports for monitoring and Explore for specific store questions
cards.summary: GA4 Reports are for ongoing monitoring of standard patterns; Explore is for answering a single analytical question with a custom view.
cards.use_when: You're deciding which part of GA4 to open for a given store question — a routine check or a diagnostic analysis.
steps: When monitoring week-to-week store performance, use Reports: Reports snapshot, Acquisition, Engagement, Monetization, User Attributes, Tech and Advertising.

When you have a specific question — 'which campaigns drove key events?', 'where in checkout do users drop off?', 'how do users' paths diverge before purchase?' — open Explore and choose the technique that matches.

Available Explore techniques include Free Form (tables/charts), Funnel Exploration (sequential steps), Path Exploration (journeys), Segment Overlap, Cohort Exploration, User Lifetime and User Exploration (own property only).
Use the compare option in reports to compare current to previous periods, and the predefined/custom date-range selector to frame the analysis.
In your own property, use Library to customize the reporting menu if you have editor or admin access.
caveats: Explore reports require you to configure dimensions, metrics and filters yourself — they aren't pre-answered.
Some techniques (like User Exploration) are only available in your own property, not the demo property.
The presenter's framing (monitoring vs question-answering) is a mental model, not a GA4 restriction.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics Tutorial For Beginners (2026 Update).docx

cards.title: Distinguish Key Events in GA4 from Conversions in Google Ads
cards.summary: Advertising reports show both: Key Events are GA4 important actions, while Conversions are Google Ads conversion actions including imported GA4 events.
cards.use_when: You're reviewing advertising performance and trying to reconcile numbers between GA4 and Google Ads.
steps: In the Advertising reports, note there are two separate metrics: Key events (GA4's important actions) and Conversions (Google Ads conversion actions).
Conversions in the Advertising reports include GA4 key events that were imported into Google Ads, plus any conversion actions created directly inside Google Ads.
Open Conversion Management to see the full list of conversions configured across GA4 and linked Google Ads accounts, and compare settings between the platforms.
Use this when comparing paid channel performance in GA4 against what Google Ads optimizes on — the numbers won't necessarily match, and the difference is what's included in each definition.
caveats: This duplication is a GA4/Google Ads convention, not an error.
If conversions in Google Ads include additional actions not present as key events in GA4, the Advertising reports will not reconcile simply.
Requires Google Ads to be linked and conversion tracking to be configured.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics Tutorial For Beginners (2026 Update).docx

cards.title: Check audience size and budget projections in the Advertising reports
cards.summary: Advertising Segments shows how many users are available for targeting; Budgeting tools forecast conversions and spend under different budgets.
cards.use_when: You're planning paid acquisition spend and verifying remarketing audiences are large enough to be usable.
steps: Open Advertising > Advertising Segments to see the number of users available for targeting in Google Ads — use this to check whether an audience meets minimum list sizes for a remarketing campaign.
Open Advertising > Budgeting > Overview, Projection and Scenario Planner to see forecasts for paid advertising and how budget changes could affect conversions and spend.
Use these together before committing spend to a channel that depends on a segment that may be too small.
caveats: Budgeting tools require Google Ads to be linked and may depend on sufficient historical conversion data to forecast meaningfully.
Forecasts are estimates based on historical patterns, not guarantees of performance.
Small audiences may not meet remarketing minimums; check before designing a campaign that relies on them.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics Tutorial For Beginners (2026 Update).docx

cards.title: Use DebugView to test store event implementation
cards.summary: DebugView shows a live feed of events as they're triggered from your site, letting you verify implementation before publishing changes.
cards.use_when: You've added or changed event tracking on your store and need to confirm events fire correctly before relying on them.
steps: In GTM, click Preview, enter your store URL and Connect to open Tag Assistant.
Navigate through your store and perform the actions you're tracking (add to cart, begin checkout, complete purchase).
In the Tag Assistant tab, confirm the tags you expected actually fired.
In GA4, open Admin > DebugView to see the live stream of events arriving from the test session.
Once you're satisfied, return to GTM, click Submit, name the version and Publish so live traffic collects the same events.
caveats: DebugView tests that events arrive, not that parameters (value, item name, currency) are correct — inspect event parameters if you depend on them.
Debug sessions may appear in data if left open; standard reports can lag 12–24 hours.
GTM Preview and DebugView interfaces may change; verify.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics Tutorial For Beginners (2026 Update).docx

cards.title: Register custom dimensions and metrics for store-specific reporting
cards.summary: Custom Definitions let you surface parameters sent with events as usable dimensions or metrics in your GA4 reports.
cards.use_when: You're sending store-specific event parameters (e.g. membership tier, loyalty status) and want to slice reports by them.
steps: Go to Admin > Data Display > Custom Definitions.
Decide which parameters sent with your store's events you want to appear as dimensions or metrics.
Register each parameter as a custom dimension (text) or custom metric (number) depending on the parameter's nature.
Once registered, the custom definition becomes available in the standard Reports and Explore dimensions/metrics pickers.
Use this when the default GA4 dimensions don't capture something that matters to your store, like whether a purchase came from a loyalty member.
caveats: Only parameters being sent with events can be registered — without the parameter, the definition will be empty.
Registration limits apply per property (verify current GA4 limits).
The presenter does not recommend creating custom definitions indiscriminately; add only what you'll report on.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics Tutorial For Beginners (2026 Update).docx

cards.title: Create and use Comparisons as segment overlays on Reports
cards.summary: Comparisons are segments you apply to standard reports to compare user groups side by side.
cards.use_when: You want to see how one store segment performs against another within the same report, e.g. mobile vs desktop conversions.
steps: Open any standard report and use the Comparisons feature (below the report menu).
Use a pre-configured comparison or create your own.
Apply it to the report — GA4 will show the metric broken out for each comparison group.
Use this to isolate the effect of a variable (device, geography, channel) rather than switching between separate reports.
caveats: Comparisons apply as an overlay on standard reports, not on Explore reports — for Explore you configure segments directly.
Creating a comparison does not persist as a saved view by default; recreate as needed or use Explore for reusable segmentation.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics Tutorial For Beginners (2026 Update).docx

cards.title: Use AI-driven insights and Analytics Advisor as starting points
cards.summary: GA4 surfaces automated insights on unusual changes and offers an AI chat interface to query the property's data.
cards.use_when: You've opened a store report and want a starting point for what's changed, or want a quick answer without building a report.
steps: On Home, note automated insights that flag unusual changes or trends — these differ per property.
On reports like Events, the same style of automated insight appears at the top.
Optionally configure custom insights on metrics/conditions you care about rather than relying entirely on Google's default picks.
For ad hoc questions, use Analytics Advisor via the icon in the top-right and ask a plain-language question (e.g. 'How is the website performing year on year?').
Treat the answers as a starting point for further investigation rather than a final analysis.
caveats: The presenter describes Analytics Advisor as a generic query interface; he does not present it as a substitute for structured reports.
Automated insights depend on the data available in the property and can miss context you'd recognize.
AI answers should be verified against the underlying reports before acting on store decisions.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics Tutorial For Beginners (2026 Update).docx

cards.title: Check data freshness expectations before acting on GA4 numbers
cards.summary: Realtime reports update within seconds, but standard reports can take 12–24 hours — set expectations on when store changes will be visible.
cards.use_when: You've just launched a campaign or event and are checking whether GA4 reports already reflect it.
steps: Verify immediate events in Realtime — data appears within seconds of arrival.
Do not expect standard reports (Events, Acquisition, Monetization) to update instantly; the presenter states data can take 12 to 24 hours to appear.
When validating a thank-you-page event in your own property, check Realtime today and re-check the standard events report tomorrow.
Use this cadence when making changes: it's normal for a new event to be invisible in standard reports for the rest of the day.
caveats: 12–24 hours is the source's described latency; actual latency may vary by property and volume.
Attribution and aggregation in standard reports will also affect final numbers versus realtime.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics Tutorial For Beginners (2026 Update).docx

cards.title: Verify the Platform dimension when blending web and app data
cards.summary: The Platform dimension shows whether each user came from the Web or App data stream — useful when a store runs both.
cards.use_when: Your store has both a website and a mobile app feeding the same property and you need to separate their metrics.
steps: In the Tech Overview report, locate the Platform dimension.
A web-only property will show 100% Web here; a web-plus-app property will show both.
Use Platform as a filter or breakdown when you report on behavior so web and app users aren't merged without you knowing.
Where relevant, add Platform as a secondary dimension in Explore reports to distinguish behavior.
caveats: The Platform dimension only appears meaningfully when more than one data stream type is configured.
App-only reports can appear blank in a web-only property (as happened in the demo).
Verify current GA4 dimension naming; the presenter notes Platform shows data-stream type.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics Tutorial For Beginners (2026 Update).docx

cards.title: Use User Attributes reports and treat 'not set' as unknown
cards.summary: User Attributes and Demographic Details expose country, city, gender, interests, age and language — with 'not set' meaning the value is unknown.
cards.use_when: You're profiling your store's audience for merchandising, content or campaign targeting decisions.
steps: Open Reports > User Attributes > Overview to see top-level geographic, gender, interests, age and language summaries.
Open Demographic Details to change the dimension (e.g. Country to City) and see granular breakdowns.
When you see 'not set' in a row, read it as 'unknown' — GA4 collected data about the user but can't provide the specific value.
If age, gender and interests are missing entirely, enable Google Signals in property settings; without it these fields won't populate.
Use the language dimension as device-based, not as a declared preference, when reasoning about localisation.
caveats: Demographic data depends on Google Signals being enabled.
Language in the report reflects the device setting, not a user-declared preference.
'not set' rows are real and should not be treated as an error.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics Tutorial For Beginners (2026 Update).docx

cards.title: Forecast with Analytics Advisor only as a first-pass input
cards.summary: The presenter demonstrates Analytics Advisor answering year-on-year performance questions from GA4 data.
cards.use_when: You need a quick baseline on store performance trends without building a report, e.g. before a monthly review.
steps: Open Analytics Advisor via the icon top-right of the GA4 interface.
Ask a natural language question about your store, e.g. how the website is performing year on year.
Analytics Advisor analyses the available data in the property and returns a summary — this can take a few moments.
Use the answer as a starting point for a proper report or Explore investigation rather than as a final answer.
caveats: The presenter explicitly frames this as a generic query interface and does not present it as an authoritative analysis.
Accuracy depends on data available in the property and on how the question is phrased.
Do not base pricing, assortment or budget decisions on an AI summary alone — validate in reports.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics Tutorial For Beginners (2026 Update).docx

cards.title: Redundant Meta Ads tracking: browser pixel plus server Conversions API
cards.summary: Meta's recommended setup fires the same event twice — once from the browser pixel and once from the server-side Conversions API — then merges them with deduplication.
cards.use_when: Planning or auditing the tracking architecture that feeds Meta Ads purchase and lead optimization for your store, e.g. after iOS/ad-blocker signal loss hurts reported ROAS.
steps: Keep the standard Facebook/Meta pixel firing client-side from your normal GTM container, and add server-side tags that send the same events to the Conversions API from a server-side GTM container.
Treat the result as two streams for the same event: the presenter shows this as the setup Meta recommends, framed as a redundant setup where the same event is tracked twice.
Verify in Meta Events Manager that each event appears once from the browser and once from the server (the presenter demos a PageView and a Contact event showing both sources).
Do not stop at 'both are firing' — without deduplication Meta would count the event twice, so pair this with matching Event IDs on both streams.
Note the server event often arrives later than the browser event, so check again a moment after the browser event appears before concluding the server tag failed.
In the server container's preview mode confirm each Meta tag reports 'succeeded'; a failed/succeeded=false result usually points to a wrong or malformed API access token.
caveats: Redundancy without deduplication means double counting; the two parts must ship together.
Setup depends on an existing server-side GTM container and consent mode configuration; the presenter treats this as a follow-on to those tutorials.
cards.source_name: Install Facebook (Meta Ads) Conversion API with server-side GTM.docx

cards.title: Get the two credentials the Conversions API setup requires
cards.summary: Meta Conversions API setup needs exactly two credentials from Events Manager: the pixel/dataset ID and a Conversions API access token.
cards.use_when: Starting a store's Meta Conversions API implementation and you need the identifiers to paste into GTM variables.
steps: Open Meta Events Manager, go to Data Sources, and copy the pixel ID — in the current interface the presenter finds it labelled as the dataset ID.
Still under Data Sources, open Settings and scroll to the Conversions API section, then press 'Generate access token' to produce the token.
Save both values where you can reference them repeatedly (the presenter keeps a text file and uses GTM constant variables rather than pasting raw values into tags).
If the generate-token button is greyed out, you cannot create it yourself — ask whoever administers the Meta account to generate it and send it to you.
In GTM, create a constant variable for the pixel ID and a constant variable for the token in each container so tags reference one place rather than duplicated literals.
Verify the current Events Manager label and button names before following — Meta's interface changes over time.
caveats: Token generation is permission-gated; do not assume your role can create it.
Each GTM container needs its own copy of the constant variable — server and client containers do not share variables.
cards.source_name: Install Facebook (Meta Ads) Conversion API with server-side GTM.docx

cards.title: Consent-gate the client-side Meta pixel so it fires on the same page as opt-in
cards.summary: Require marketing/storage consent on the pixel tag and trigger it on the cookie-consent-update event so opt-in is recorded on the first page view rather than only on the next page.
cards.use_when: Formatting the client-side pixel tag in GTM for a store with a cookie banner, where you need Meta to receive the event on the page where the shopper actually consents.
steps: Create the pixel tag (in the presenter's naming habit, something like 'meta ads page view') and choose the Facebook pixel template from the Community Template Gallery, adding it to the workspace.
In the tag's event name field enter the standard 'PageView' event.
Under Advanced Settings > Consent Settings, select 'Require additional consent for tag to fire' and require 'ad_storage' so the tag only loads when the user granted marketing permission.

Do not use the Initialization – All Pages trigger for this: the presenter demonstrates that when a visitor accepts cookies, the initialization trigger has already run and the tag is blocked, so the pixel only fires on the following page.
Change the trigger to the cookie consent update dataLayer event instead, so the pixel fires on the same first page load once consent is granted.
Test with preview: with consent denied the tag shows as blocked by consent settings; after clicking 'Allow all', the pixel fires immediately on the same page.
caveats: Correct behaviour depends on your consent-mode implementation being in place first.
The consent variable naming and structure come from the presenter's earlier consent-mode tutorial; adapt to your own consent setup.
cards.source_name: Install Facebook (Meta Ads) Conversion API with server-side GTM.docx

cards.title: Send Meta store events server-side with the Conversions API template
cards.summary: Configure server-side GTM tags with the Facebook Conversions API template, overriding event names, wiring token and pixel variables, and gating on consent.
cards.use_when: Building the server-side half of a store's Meta tracking, for example sending PageView and a form/purchase-style conversion event through the Conversions API.
steps: In the server container create a new tag, pick the Facebook Conversions API template from the Community Template Gallery, and add it to the workspace.
For Event Name Setup Method choose Override rather than inheriting from the client — the presenter prefers explicit control so you can name exactly which event is sent.
Set Action Source to Website.
Reference your constant variable for the API access token, and create a second constant variable for the pixel ID inside this container (variables are not shared across containers).
Create a trigger for all pages that passes a consent condition — the presenter uses a consent-mode variable requiring consent granted, so nothing is transmitted to Meta without permission.

For conversion events (e.g. contact form submit), build a custom-event trigger whose event name exactly matches the event name arriving in the server container's preview, and attach the same consent condition.
Test by submitting the form and confirming the event arrives in the server container preview and the Meta tag reports success.
caveats: Only send data to Meta when consent is given — the presenter stresses this repeatedly.
The custom event name must match exactly or the trigger will never fire.
cards.source_name: Install Facebook (Meta Ads) Conversion API with server-side GTM.docx

cards.title: Automate the Meta test event ID with a Debug Mode lookup table
cards.summary: A GTM lookup table keyed on Debug Mode supplies the Meta test event code only in preview, so a forgotten test ID can never leak into production and suppress live conversion data.
cards.use_when: Testing Meta Conversions API tags in a live store, where forgetting to remove a hard-coded test event code would silently divert real conversions into the test screen.
steps: In Meta Events Manager open the Test Events tab and copy the test event code it displays.
In GTM create a variable named for the Meta test ID and set it as a Lookup Table rather than a constant.
Choose Debug Mode as the input variable (it is a built-in variable, found under built-in variables).
Leave the default value empty so that outside preview the tag sends no test ID at all.
Add one output row: when Debug Mode equals true, output the test event code you copied.
Reference this variable in the Test ID field of every Meta tag that has one (the presenter wires it into both the page view and contact tags).
Inspect the outgoing request or Events Manager to confirm that in preview the test ID is attached, and that a normal visit contains no test ID.
If the test code has changed between sessions, update the lookup table's output value manually.
caveats: The presenter notes the test event code can change day to day, so the stored output may need refreshing before a new test session.
Test events do not count in the real data — they appear in the test screen only.
cards.source_name: Install Facebook (Meta Ads) Conversion API with server-side GTM.docx

cards.title: Deduplicate Meta events by passing one Event ID into both streams
cards.summary: The Conversions API and the browser pixel only merge when both carry the identical Event ID, which Meta uses to collapse the duplicate into one event.
cards.use_when: Finishing a redundant Meta tracking setup on a store so that each page view and conversion is counted once, not twice.
steps: In the client container, install an Event ID variable from the Community Template Gallery (the presenter uses one by Markus Baersch; Stape's is also noted as good) — it has no settings to configure.
Open the client-side Meta pixel tag, go to More Settings, and set its Event ID field to that variable; repeat for every pixel tag (the presenter does it for both page view and contact).

For the server side, send the same Event ID through your GA4 events, because those events ultimately trigger the Meta Ads tags: add an event parameter with the name 'event ID' and the Event ID variable as its value.
Apply that event parameter to every GA4 tag that drives a Meta event (the presenter does it for the page view tag and the contact form submit tag).
The Meta tag recognises the 'event ID' key and forwards the same ID into the outgoing Conversions API request automatically — inspect the outgoing request to confirm the field is present.

Prove deduplication by copying an Event ID from the browser event and searching for it in Events Manager: the browser event and server event should both carry the same ID and appear as one deduplicated event.
Re-check after each change; the presenter notes the forwarding does not always work, so the copy-and-search test is the real verification.
caveats: The site's GA4 event naming and parameter conventions must be consistent for the 'event ID' parameter to propagate.
Deduplication depends on identical IDs — any divergence reintroduces double counting.
cards.source_name: Install Facebook (Meta Ads) Conversion API with server-side GTM.docx

cards.title: Verification checks that both Meta tracking streams land and merge
cards.summary: A three-place check — server container preview, tag success status, and Events Manager — confirms the Conversions API is correctly receiving deduplicated events.
cards.use_when: After deploying or editing Meta tracking tags for a store, before trusting the reported conversion counts.
steps: Load a page and confirm in the server-side container's preview that a page view event arrives from the client container.
Check that the Meta tag in that preview reports succeeded; a failure usually means a bad pixel ID or API access token, so re-check the values entered.
In Meta Events Manager (Test Events tab when using a test ID) confirm that you see two entries — one browser, one server — for the same event.
Repeat the flow for a real conversion action (the presenter submits a contact form) and confirm both a browser and a server conversion appear.
Where a test ID is configured, run everything under preview so the checks stay out of production data; when finished, normal visits should show no test ID.
Once deduplication is added, look up a single Event ID in Events Manager to confirm the two entries now sit under the same ID rather than counting separately.
caveats: Server events can lag behind browser events, so allow time before diagnosing a failure.
The presenter's tested events are page views and contact submissions; substitute your store's own conversion event names.
cards.source_name: Install Facebook (Meta Ads) Conversion API with server-side GTM.docx

cards.title: Separate sales-based marketing revenue from actual cash receipts
cards.summary: Label the source revenue proxy clearly and reconcile actual receipts separately.
cards.use_when: Reconciling revenue for marketing spend decisions or profit calculations on your Shopify store.
steps: If using the source Net Sales plus Shipping proxy, label it a sales-based metric, not cash collected or profit.
Net sales deducts discounts and sales reversals; sales reports may include unpaid orders. Use payments finance reports for payment and refund transactions.
Show refund timing separately for cohort analysis rather than adding refunds back and calling the result cash.
caveats: Sales, receipts and profit measure different things. This corrects the source label rather than endorsing it as an accounting definition.
cards.source_name: What Metrics Matter In The Shopify Analytics Dashboard.docx

cards.title: Revenue Troubleshooting Framework: Sessions x Conversion Rate x AOV
cards.summary: Use the decomposition Total Sales = Sessions x Conversion Rate x AOV to diagnose the root cause of any revenue dip in your Shopify store.
cards.use_when: When revenue drops or spikes unexpectedly, to pinpoint the specific metric causing the change.
steps: Pull the three metrics: Sessions, Conversion Rate, and Average Order Value for the period in question.
Calculate Total Sales (or Net Sales + Shipping) as Sessions × Conversion Rate × AOV.
If Sales decreased, check which of the three metrics dropped (or if all dropped). It's mathematically impossible for sales to fall if all three are stable or up, except due to returns.

Investigate each metric: AOV drop may indicate a shift to lower-priced products; Conversion Rate drop may be seasonal or due to a site issue; Sessions drop often correlates with paid media spend or CPC changes.
For small single-digit percentage dips across metrics, consider them natural fluctuation and avoid overreacting unless the overall impact is significant.
Also use this framework when sales increase to understand which lever drove growth.
caveats: Returns processed later can cause sales to dip even if the metrics are stable; treat returns as an exception.
Single-digit variations may compound into larger top-line changes; evaluate in context of business goals.
cards.source_name: What Metrics Matter In The Shopify Analytics Dashboard.docx

cards.title: Cross-check Shopify attribution before reallocating spend
cards.summary: Treat the presenter's skepticism as a prompt to triangulate channel evidence, not a blanket instruction to discard Shopify reports.
cards.use_when: When analyzing marketing channel performance or deciding where to allocate ad spend.
steps: Compare attribution windows, channel definitions, consent coverage and other evidence before acting on a reported channel difference. Do not treat any one view as causal proof.
Identify and ignore the following sections in Shopify Analytics: 'Total sales by social referral', 'Sessions by social referral', 'Top referrals by session', 'Sales attributed to marketing'.
Do not base marketing budget or channel optimization on these metrics.
Use third-party attribution tools or UTM parameters with a dedicated analytics platform for more reliable channel performance data.
If you need to understand referral traffic quality, cross-reference with Google Analytics 4 or another platform that better filters bot traffic.
caveats: The source's recommendation to ignore these metrics is a practitioner opinion, not a universal rule.
Use attribution as one input alongside customer research and incrementality tests where feasible.
cards.source_name: What Metrics Matter In The Shopify Analytics Dashboard.docx

cards.title: Use Cohort Analysis Instead of Shopify's Returning Customer Rate
cards.summary: Shopify's 'Returning Customer Rate' is misleading for gauging loyalty; use cohort analysis for accurate retention and lifetime value insights.
cards.use_when: When evaluating customer loyalty, retention, or predicting long-term revenue from a cohort.
steps: Do not interpret Returning Customer Rate as the percentage of customers who repurchase; it's the ratio of returning orders to total orders in a period, skewed by new customer acquisition spikes.
Access Shopify's cohort analysis report: Analytics > Reports > Cohort analysis. Click into it to view the detailed table.
Analyze cohorts by month to see repeat purchase behavior over time. This shows actual retention and helps forecast LTV.
Use the cohort data to inform retention strategies such as email flows, loyalty programs, or replenishment reminders.
caveats: The default cohort analysis in Shopify is rudimentary; the source notes custom models may be better.
Cohort analysis can be complex; seek tutorials to interpret it correctly.
cards.source_name: What Metrics Matter In The Shopify Analytics Dashboard.docx

cards.title: Funnel Drop-off Ratios: 4:2:1 and 2:1:1
cards.summary: Analyze Shopify's funnel breakdown (Add to Cart, Reach Checkout, Purchase) against benchmark ratios to identify conversion optimization opportunities.
cards.use_when: When optimizing checkout flow or diagnosing where customers abandon the purchase process.
steps: Go to Shopify Analytics > Reports > Funnel breakdown (or similar).
Compare your ratio of Add to Carts : Reach Checkout : Purchases. A common average is 4:2:1 (e.g., 400 ATC, 200 Reach Checkout, 100 Purchases).
Aim for a 2:1:1 ratio for low-ticket or FMCG brands, where drop-off between checkout and purchase is minimal.

If drop-off is high after Add to Cart, investigate product page clarity, cart visibility, or unexpected costs. If high after Reach Checkout, check checkout page friction, payment options, or shipping fees.
Fix identified issues quickly; the source claims conversion rate increases of 40-50% overnight are possible from such fixes.
caveats: Ratios are benchmarks, not universal; industry and price point affect expectations.
Source's claimed 40-50% lift is anecdotal from their experience, not a guaranteed result.
cards.source_name: What Metrics Matter In The Shopify Analytics Dashboard.docx

cards.title: Average Order Value: Context and Limitations
cards.summary: Shopify's AOV metric excludes shipping charges and is a mean, not median; use it as a top-line indicator but dig deeper before making changes.
cards.use_when: When assessing pricing, bundling, or upsell strategies, or when AOV appears in revenue troubleshooting.
steps: Understand that Shopify calculates AOV as (Gross Sales - Discounts) / Orders, excluding shipping charges. If you collect significant shipping, your true AOV is higher.
Manually add shipping charges to AOV for a more accurate picture, especially if shipping is a notable revenue component.
Recognize that AOV is a mean; the distribution matters. Analyze AOV by new vs. returning customers, product categories, and order pathways.
Avoid making business decisions based on the single AOV number alone. Instead, use it as a starting point to investigate underlying drivers.
Consider running AOV improvement initiatives like bundles, upsells, or free shipping thresholds, but measure their impact with more granular data.
caveats: Shopify's AOV may not reflect actual cash collected due to excluded shipping; adjust manually if needed.
The source warns against acting on AOV in isolation without distribution and segment analysis.
cards.source_name: What Metrics Matter In The Shopify Analytics Dashboard.docx

cards.title: Sessions Discrepancy: Shopify vs. Google Analytics 4
cards.summary: Shopify's session count often includes bot traffic, inflating numbers compared to GA4; cross-reference both for accurate traffic and conversion rate analysis.
cards.use_when: When analyzing traffic trends or calculating conversion rates, especially if you suspect bot traffic or see unexplained dips.
steps: Compare Shopify's 'Sessions over time' with Google Analytics 4's session count for the same period. GA4 typically filters bots better, so its number is often lower.
If Shopify shows a spike or dip not reflected in GA4, it may be bot traffic. Use GA4 as a more reliable source for session trends.
For conversion rate calculations, use GA4 sessions as the denominator for a more accurate rate, or at least validate Shopify's conversion rate against GA4-derived data.
Check 'Sessions by location' in Shopify: sort by city to spot unusual spikes that may indicate bot servers. If found, consider filtering that traffic in your analytics.
caveats: No analytics platform is perfect; both have limitations. Use multiple sources for validation.
Bot traffic can also affect other metrics; be cautious with any single-source data.
cards.source_name: What Metrics Matter In The Shopify Analytics Dashboard.docx

cards.title: Product Sell-Through Rate for Inventory Planning
cards.summary: Track sell-through rate at product and category levels to optimize inventory, cash flow, and sustainable growth.
cards.use_when: When planning inventory purchases, managing cash conversion cycle, or deciding which products to reorder or discontinue.
steps: Access Shopify Analytics > Reports > Products by sell-through rate (or similar report at the bottom of the dashboard).
Calculate sell-through rate as units sold divided by units received over a period.
Monitor sell-through by product and category to identify fast vs. slow movers. High sell-through means you can reorder more frequently and reduce stockouts; low sell-through ties up cash.
Use sell-through insights to adjust purchasing quantities and timing, aiming to reduce excess inventory and improve cash flow.
Link sell-through to your net profit margin and cash conversion cycle: higher sell-through allows faster reinvestment and growth.
caveats: Sell-through alone doesn't account for profitability; combine with margin analysis.
The source notes this is often overlooked by new brands but is critical for scaling.
cards.source_name: What Metrics Matter In The Shopify Analytics Dashboard.docx

cards.title: Customizing the Shopify Analytics Dashboard
cards.summary: The default Shopify Analytics dashboard contains many misleading or unhelpful metrics; customize it to focus on actionable data.
cards.use_when: When setting up your Shopify analytics for the first time or when overwhelmed by irrelevant metrics.
steps: Click the 'Customize' button in the top right corner of the Analytics dashboard.
Remove or reposition cards that are not useful for your business, such as attribution reports, returning customer rate, and social referral sections.
Prioritize adding cards for Net Sales, Shipping Charges, Sessions, Conversion Rate, Average Order Value, and Funnel Breakdown.
Save your customized layout so you see the most relevant metrics at a glance.
Regularly review and adjust as your business needs change.
caveats: Customization options may vary by Shopify plan and interface updates; verify current capabilities.
Some reports (like cohort analysis) require clicking into them for full detail; the dashboard snapshot may not suffice.
cards.source_name: What Metrics Matter In The Shopify Analytics Dashboard.docx

cards.title: Identifying Bot Traffic via Location Report
cards.summary: Use Shopify's 'Sessions by location' report to detect bot traffic spikes from specific cities, which can skew session and conversion metrics.
cards.use_when: When you suspect inflated sessions or unexplained conversion rate changes, especially if traffic sources seem off.
steps: Go to Shopify Analytics > Reports > Sessions by location.
Click into the report and sort by individual cities to see session counts.
Look for unusual spikes from a single city or region that don't align with your target market. This may indicate bot traffic hitting your site.
If you identify bot traffic, consider excluding those sessions in Google Analytics or using a bot filtering tool to get cleaner data.
Cross-reference with GA4 to confirm the anomaly is not present there, as GA4 often filters bots.
caveats: Bot traffic patterns can change; periodic checks are needed.
Filtering bots in Shopify is not straightforward; you may need third-party tools.
cards.source_name: What Metrics Matter In The Shopify Analytics Dashboard.docx

cards.title: Orders vs. Orders Fulfilled for Operational Health
cards.summary: Monitor the gap between orders and orders fulfilled to track unshipped orders and fulfillment efficiency.
cards.use_when: When assessing fulfillment operations, identifying backlog, or communicating with customers about shipping delays.
steps: In Shopify Analytics, compare 'Orders' and 'Orders Fulfilled' for a given period.
The difference represents orders not yet shipped. A large gap may indicate fulfillment bottlenecks or high order volume.
Investigate causes: insufficient staff, inventory issues, or delayed processing.
Use this metric to set operational targets and improve fulfillment speed, which affects customer satisfaction and repeat purchase.
For subscription or replenishment models, ensure fulfillment keeps pace to avoid churn.
caveats: Seasonal spikes may naturally increase the gap; interpret in context.
This metric doesn't capture partial fulfillments or backorders.
cards.source_name: What Metrics Matter In The Shopify Analytics Dashboard.docx

cards.title: Sales Channel Breakdown for Accountability
cards.summary: Use Shopify's 'Sales by channel' report to separate online store revenue from other channels like POS or Shop app.
cards.use_when: When managing multi-channel sales or holding marketing partners accountable for online store performance.
steps: Navigate to Shopify Analytics > Reports > Sales by channel.
Identify revenue from Online Store, POS, Shop app, draft orders, etc.
If your primary paid media drives online store sales, filter all reports to 'Online Store' channel for accurate performance evaluation.
Use this breakdown to allocate resources appropriately and measure channel-specific ROI.
For ecommerce partners, ensure they are optimizing for the correct channel; misalignment can lead to wasted ad spend.
caveats: Attribution across channels can be complex; this report is descriptive, not causal.
For stores selling primarily through one channel, this may be less critical.
cards.source_name: What Metrics Matter In The Shopify Analytics Dashboard.docx

cards.title: Zero-party vs first-party vs third-party data
cards.summary: Define the three data tiers and recognize that first-party tracking often misattributes the true source of a conversion.
cards.use_when: When deciding which customer data to collect and trust for store merchandising, acquisition channel decisions, or attribution reporting.
