Recognize that most people only think about the visual, which is why they miss easy performance gains.
Test the source's example: a hook performing okay, then adding exaggerated on-screen copy (e.g., 'this transformed my life') doubled hook rate and performance.
When diagnosing a flat hook, ask which of the three is the weakest link, then change only that element.
For the visual element: consider camera movement, dynamic cuts, and pacing.
For copy: decide whether you're just captioning the spoken audio or writing a distinct overlay headline that pulls attention.
Use the three-way split to multiply variation: changing visual, audio, and copy independently lets you create 20–30 hook variations from one concept.
caveats: Copy here means text appearing on the creative (overlay or captions), which may overlap with but is not the same as the ad's primary text.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ad Hooks That Scale.docx

cards.title: Plug-and-play hook template: Persona + Problem + Pattern Interrupt + Promise
cards.summary: A four-part hook structure that filters the audience, agitates the problem, retains attention, and gives a reason to keep watching.
cards.use_when: Writing a first draft hook for an ecommerce ad from scratch, or briefing an LLM or creator to generate hook copy at volume.
steps: Persona: open by naming who the ad is for — this immediately filters out anyone who isn't the target buyer.
Problem: agitate the pain within the first ~2 seconds, before viewers decide they're watching an ad.
Pattern interrupt: insert something unexpected at this point because you'll lose people once they sense a pitch is coming.
Promise: give a reason to keep watching through the rest of the video.
Example structure: 'If you're [persona] and you have [pain point], you're probably doing [common approach] right now. That's why you're getting [bad outcome]. Here's the better method.'
Apply to ecommerce by replacing persona and pain with the specific buyer type and specific problem the product solves.

Maintain continuity: the person speaking in the ad must plausibly be the persona being called out. A mismatched speaker breaks trust and relevance (the source's example: a 50-year-old mom delivering a hook aimed at 20-year-old guys).
To scale: paste the template sentence into an LLM with your website and product context and generate many variations.
caveats: The source likes this template as a starting point but recommends moving away from frameworks as you mature, because everyone uses them and they become generic.
Adapt speaker and persona together — a template with mismatched speaker/persona will underperform.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ad Hooks That Scale.docx

cards.title: Common hook types and when to use each
cards.summary: A working set of hook categories — contrarian truth, specific proof, common mistakes, high-stakes warning, curiosity gap, tactical promise, mythbusting objection — with notes on ecommerce fit.
cards.use_when: Choosing an angle for a new ecommerce ad, or generating a set of hook variations to test against a control.
steps: Contrarian truth: 'The advice everyone follows is backwards because…' followed by an educational payoff. Works well in paid and organic.
Specific proof: 'We did X and got Y in Z days. Here's what actually caused it.' Cited as a strong performer.
Common mistakes: 'The number one mistake brands make when scaling.' The source uses it but warns it is heavily overused and has lost weight with audiences.

High-stakes warning: 'If you're using protein powder, you're slowly destroying your gut.' The source uses this frequently in ecommerce and notes it lets you swap the warning to resonate with different audience pools.

Curiosity gap: create an information gap in the hook and even in the thumbnail/copy. For statics, infomercial-style images that explain nothing (e.g., a symptom with no explanation) can produce very high CTR.
Tactical promise: 'In 90 seconds I'll give you the exact checklist…' — the source notes this suits service businesses more than ecom.
Mythbusting objection: 'If you think X, you're not wrong. Here's how to tell if yours is the exception.' Adapts to ecommerce by busting myths about your product category.
caveats: Most common does not mean best — if competitors saturate a hook type, look for white space, though doubling down on what competitors do can also work.

Curiosity-gap statics can attract junk clickthroughs from people not primed to buy; the source says they require dropping traffic onto a long educational/listical landing page that sells only at the end.
Numeric claims in example hooks (days, percentages) are illustrative, not validated benchmarks.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ad Hooks That Scale.docx

cards.title: Grade hooks on clarity, relevance, novelty — then specificity, credibility
cards.summary: A five-criteria scoring rubric in order of importance for judging whether a hook is worth running.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a batch of ecommerce ad hooks before production, or deciding which of several hook concepts to put spend behind.
steps: Score clarity first: can a stranger understand what the product is and what is happening within the creative?
Score relevance second: is the pain point obvious, and can the viewer directly relate the product to themselves?
Score novelty third: is there a twist, new angle, or new format that demonstrates white space?
Score specificity fourth (secondary): are you calling out something concrete?

Score credibility last (secondary): is there proof or a reason to believe? The source says this is hard to fit into a 3–4 second hook and not a priority; you can get it for free by using a known influencer or person.
Use the rubric to find the lowest-scoring criterion and fix just that element rather than rewriting the whole hook.
Apply the result: a hook that is clear and relevant but low novelty may still run; a hook low on clarity and relevance will not filter for buyers regardless of how entertaining it is.
caveats: Order of importance is the source's ranking; specificity and credibility are explicitly second-tier for hooks.
Rubric is a judgment aid, not a numeric benchmark — the source provides no thresholds.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ad Hooks That Scale.docx

cards.title: Diagnosing a failing hook: the case of the audio-only jerky hook
cards.summary: A worked example showing how a scroll-stopping curiosity gap can fail because it doesn't attract the right audience or convey clarity and relevance.
cards.use_when: Auditing a live ecommerce ad hook that is getting views but not converting, and deciding whether to rewrite the angle entirely.
steps: Use the example: a jerky ad opens at a fast cut with the product being eaten and a brief audio line — an audio hook with a curiosity gap, no clear copy.

Run the hook through the rubric: clarity fails (a stranger can't tell what the product is), relevance fails (no obvious pain point or self-relation), novelty is potential (an unusual format), specificity fails, credibility fails.
Recognize the core failure: the hook attracts anyone curious about 'what are they eating?' — including people who don't like jerky — so spending optimizes toward non-buyers.
Read the body for context: the ad then lists value propositions ('no processed ingredients, grass-fed beef, herbs and spices') with no emotion attached.

Rewrite the hook by picking a stronger type. Examples given: 'If most jerky is either dry as cardboard or loaded with rubbish ingredients, we fix both — I'll show you how' (problem + promise); 'If you're still eating protein snacks that are basically sugar, stop — here's the 3-second label check before you buy jerky' (high-stakes warning into education).
Note how the rewritten hooks avoid selling: they go straight into an educational piece and don't reveal the ad for the first seconds.
caveats: Rewrites shown are the source's live examples for one product category, not validated results.
The source stresses a rewritten hook script alone will not fix performance — the visual must also be rebuilt.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ad Hooks That Scale.docx

cards.title: Specificity in the hook: 'two problems' beats 'some problems'
cards.summary: Concrete numbers and constraints in the hook increase trust and hold viewers longer than generic phrasing.
cards.use_when: Writing or editing ecommerce hook copy where a claim could be made more specific — e.g., number of problems, reasons, steps or results.
steps: Take the example: 'We taste tested the bestselling jerkys and found the same two problems in almost all of them.'
Compare to 'we found the same problems in all of them' — the source argues the generic version has a worse hook rate because it feels like a setup for a pitch.
Explain why 'two' works: it feels small enough to sit through and specific enough to be credible, and it raises the question of which two problems.
Apply the principle to your own hooks: replace vague quantifiers with a concrete, verifiable-sounding number or constraint wherever it is truthful.
Consider dropping the selling sentence entirely when the specificity plus curiosity gap is already strong enough to carry the hook.
Pair the specific claim with a visual that proves it (the source suggests showing 10–20 jerky packages on screen as the hook's visual).
caveats: The specificity gain is the source's stated reasoning, not a measured A/B result.
Do not invent numbers that the product cannot substantiate — the source does not address claim substantiation here.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ad Hooks That Scale.docx

cards.title: Turning one hook script into dozens of variations via visual and copy swaps
cards.summary: Vary visual and overlay copy independently to multiply hook variants and discover which combination performs.
cards.use_when: Running creative testing on an ecommerce video ad when the audio script is working but hook rate is flat, or when you need volume of hook variations cheaply.
steps: Write a strong audio hook first (e.g., the jerky 'two problems' line delivered by a UGC creator).

Generate variants by changing only the visual: one version with a talking head versus one where the creator cuts away at ~1 second to a pan shot of someone grabbing jerky off supermarket shelves, through checkout, then back to the creator pulling out a whiteboard with '1' and '2' blacked out.
Recognize the source's argument: the fast-paced, relevant visual version should be more compelling and retain more viewers through the hook than a plain talking head — but you must test to see.

Change the overlay copy independently: try bold headlines over the top that speak to a specific viewer pool (the source's electrolyte example lists headlines such as 'thought I had a testosterone issue' or 'how I doubled my strength', with a caution to check health-claim rules).
Change the audio independently as well to produce new combinations — the source says changing all three elements can yield 20–30 distinct hooks from one concept.
Note that visual options can be simple: a 1–2 second AI or practical B-roll of jerky cracking like cardboard, a pan through competitor ingredient labels, or throwing competitor products in the bin.
caveats: Specific visual performance claims are the source's expectations, not measured results — test before assuming.
Health-claim overlays in supplement categories must be checked against ad policy; the source explicitly flags this for the electrolyte example.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ad Hooks That Scale.docx

cards.title: The product awareness curve: keep awareness near zero through the hook and let it rise slowly
cards.summary: Map how aware the viewer is that they're being sold to, and keep it low through the hook, gently rising toward the CTA.
cards.use_when: Structuring the full script of an ecommerce video ad — particularly deciding when the product should first appear on screen.
steps: On a graph with time on the X-axis and product awareness on the Y-axis, target a line that stays near zero through the hook, slowly creeps up across the body, and reaches its highest point only at the CTA.

Watch the counterexample: an electrolyte ad opens with a workout line and the product poured into a bottle and names the product in the first sentence. This produces an immediate product-awareness spike right after the hook, causing drop-off.
Note the source's other failing pattern: stepstoning straight to a sales pitch at each transition instead of letting awareness build continuously.

Apply the target shape: education first, product introduced briefly, back to education, product reintroduced — the source says a small bump plus a return to education is acceptable, as in the Hyro example.
For your own scripts, ask at each second: does the viewer know yet that this is an ad for a specific product? If yes before the CTA, dial the selling back and return to teaching.
caveats: The curve is the speaker's mental model, not a measured retention metric.
Some minor early product mention can be tolerable; a small bump followed by more education is not treated as a failure.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ad Hooks That Scale.docx

cards.title: Bridging the hook into the body: do not spike into a pitch
cards.summary: The transition from hook to body is where good ads often lose viewers; educate smoothly and embed the product gradually.
cards.use_when: Editing or writing the first 5–15 seconds after the hook of a video ad, and diagnosing retention curve drop-offs.
steps: After the hook, do not immediately sell. The source's example of a bad bridge: 'If you think agencies can't be trusted, you're not wrong. Here's how to tell if yours is the exception. Book below and talk to me' — straight from hook into offer.
Instead, bridge as smoothly as possible into education: teach something the viewer actually values before making any product claim.
Introduce the product briefly and then immediately return to education, so viewers sense an ad may be coming without being sold to outright.
Keep the bridge visually engaging as well — the source points to the electrolyte example where the speaker keeps moving a sponge with no functional reason, purely as a visual cue to hold attention.

Watch for the specific failure pattern: a good hook plus a good body but a bad bridge right before the CTA — the source says strong creative often flops here because viewers have no reason to move from education into buying.
Diagnose on your retention curve: if the drop is right after the hook or right before the CTA, the bridge, not the hook, is the problem.
caveats: Bridge construction in static ads differs from video — the source says the curve model applies most cleanly to video assets.
Bridge quality is the source's stated common mistake among otherwise strong ad makers; it's an observation, not a benchmarked rule.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ad Hooks That Scale.docx

cards.title: Rewriting a generic product-first hook into a persona-led educational hook
cards.summary: Take a weak product-led hook and rebuild it around the buyer's pain, common failed attempts, and an educational payoff.
cards.use_when: Reworking an ecommerce ad whose hook shows the product immediately and leads with brand claims rather than a customer problem.
steps: Start from the weak example: an electrolyte ad opens with 'just finished my workout' and the product being poured into a bottle, with the product named in the first sentence and on-screen copy just captioning the spoken words.
Diagnose: no audience filtering, no visual attention trigger, and immediate product awareness — it violates all three hook elements plus the awareness curve.

Rewrite the audio using the Persona + Problem + Pattern Interrupt + Promise structure: name the persona (people who love the gym whose workouts keep getting shorter), agitate the problem (less motivation, tried testosterone boosters and eating more), insert education as the interrupt (dehydration and sodium imbalance), and promise the explanation.
Keep the product out of the visuals through the hook — the source says to use a talking head or dynamic B-roll of the person feeling bad rather than pouring the product.
Bring the product in late in the body after trying (and rejecting) alternatives, then move into the offer/CTA.
Consider overlay headline options that speak to a specific worry to pull a distinct audience pool — the source suggests testing different severity levels while checking health-claim rules.
caveats: The rewritten script is the source's live example, not a tested result.
Supplement and health ads require checking claim rules; the source explicitly warns about how far you can go with overlays like 'how I doubled my strength' when the product is only loosely related.
The source notes the reframing logic (fixing tiredness enabled gym progress, so the ad pushes strength) is a messaging angle, not a causal product claim.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ad Hooks That Scale.docx

cards.title: Frameworks as a starting point, not an end state
cards.summary: Use templates to get your first hooks written, then move off them to find white space competitors can't copy.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to lean on hook templates or invest in original hook development for an ecommerce brand's ad library.
steps: If you can't yet tell a good hook from a bad one, grab templates and frameworks — the source says this is a good way to get one foot in front of the other.

Recognize the downside: when everyone uses the same templates, hooks become generic and feel like everyone else's. The source points to 'the number one mistake' hook as an example that has lost its substance through overuse.
Move toward writing hooks from scratch so you can innovate on the format and find white space against competitors.
Combine both motions: identify white space, but also double down on what competitors are doing when it's working.

Use the case study pattern as a model: the source works through a live bad hook, scores it on the rubric, picks a hook type, then rewrites the audio, then separately plans the visual and overlay copy.
caveats: The source notes almost everything stated has roughly a 1–2% exception for specific niches.
No universal rule is intended — a saturated hook type can still be worth testing alongside differentiated angles.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ad Hooks That Scale.docx

cards.title: Start creative with a customer problem, not a format
cards.summary: Before choosing UGC, static or carousel, mine customer research to find one problem, then let the problem dictate the format.
cards.use_when: Kicking off a new paid-social creative round for a product and you don't yet know which angle or format to produce.
steps: Mine sources that already contain customer language: existing product reviews, comments under your own ads and social posts, support tickets, post-purchase survey responses, Reddit discussion, and competitor reviews and ad comments.

From those sources, extract three things: what the customer wants, what is stopping them from getting it, and what they have already tried (which reveals failed alternatives you can position against).

Example: for a compact walking pad sold to work-from-home buyers, reviews surface 'I sit at my desk 8 hours and barely move', 'I want a treadmill but don't have space', and 'I can't have something loud while I'm on calls'. Each is a ready-made ad angle.

Only after you have the problem do you choose a format. If the value is simple and instantly understood, a static image can carry it; if the value requires seeing it fold open, slide under a desk, or be used in real life, you need video.

Competitor reviews are especially valuable because they surface what rivals are failing at, giving you an objection to counter inside your ad and a differentiation angle beyond 'we have this and it's good'.
caveats: The source says it looks at these sources usually; treat it as a research menu, not a mandatory checklist.
Avoid starting the conversation from 'should we make UGC or a static' — the source calls that thinking backwards.
cards.source_name: How to create killer ad creatives (to blow up your business).docx

cards.title: Build one ad around one argument, not ten selling points
cards.summary: Packing every selling point into a single ad produces a confusing infomercial; instead pick the single argument for the persona and prove it.
cards.use_when: Writing the script or storyboard for a cold-traffic ad and the draft is accumulating warranty, returns, dimensions, motor speed and every other feature.
steps: Write the angle as a single sentence that states one argument for one persona, e.g. 'Get more steps while you work without a giant treadmill taking precious space.'

Make every element inside the ad support that sentence. If the ad is about space and portability, show the room still having space, show the pad sliding under the desk, show it folding or being moved to a closet.
Deliberately withhold logistics like the 30-day return, warranty and guarantee — the source notes the customer will learn all of that later on the landing page.

If the product is genuinely quiet enough for calls, a strong execution is a video of someone on an important call or interview, then the camera zooms out to reveal they are getting steps in — painting the value without talking about the treadmill itself.
Contrast this with a white-background product shot labelled 'at home treadmill': it shows the metal rectangle rather than the reason to buy.
caveats: A plain product rectangle image can still work for high-intent audiences who are already sold and are only deciding who to buy from and when; it is cold traffic that needs the picture painted.
One product can have ten reasons someone buys it and therefore ten angles — but that becomes ten separate creatives, budget permitting, not one giant ad.
cards.source_name: How to create killer ad creatives (to blow up your business).docx

cards.title: Match every product claim with visual proof
cards.summary: Any claim made in an ad script needs a corresponding on-screen demonstration, because audiences no longer trust bare assertions.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a finished creative before launch to check whether the claims in the voiceover or copy are actually demonstrated on screen.
steps: List every product claim in the ad, then for each one ask 'how can I prove this visually?'

If you say it's compact, show how small it actually is; if you say it fits under a desk, film it under a desk; if you say it stores easily, show someone putting it in an apartment closet or moving it, and consider showing an older (55+) user doing it to signal ease.
If a product claim is quantifiable and the brand has data to support it, show the actual number rather than the adjective.

Treat visual proof as the main selling mechanism: the source argues anyone can say 'this product changed my life' and that audiences, especially with widespread AI-generated copy, no longer trust it. The creative should do as much selling as possible visually.

This is also what separates an ad that gets clicks from one that gets buying behaviour: in the source's example, a 'routine / before-and-after / application' video explained what was being sold and produced website buying behaviour, while a visually stimulating but unexplained ad did not.
caveats: Only show a quantified number if the brand actually has the data to back it; otherwise it's an unsupported claim.
Do not confuse a visually proven ad with a highly engaging one — an ad that proves nothing can still rack up a very high CTR.
cards.source_name: How to create killer ad creatives (to blow up your business).docx

cards.title: Write hooks directly from the stated customer problem
cards.summary: Turn the researched customer complaint into the first line of the ad so the right viewer self-selects and keeps listening.
cards.use_when: Drafting hooks and opening seconds for a cold-traffic video ad after you have selected one customer problem.
steps: Convert the problem into a direct, qualifying hook, e.g. 'If you work from home and somehow finish the day with 800 steps when your goal was 10,000, keep listening.'
Follow with the solution in plain terms: the pad fits under a standing desk, lets you get steps in while working, and can be put away afterwards.

For video, show the whole process on screen: someone working at the desk, the pad underneath, them on a call, then putting it away. The source notes this sequence can carry the ad on its own without heavy text overlay.

Optimize for comprehension and self-recognition rather than cleverness: if the ad resonates with the viewer's life it clicks subconsciously, and hearing 'this solves my exact problem' is more powerful than making a cinematic ad that appeals to everyone.
Reuse the customer's own words from reviews and support tickets where possible, since those phrases are the ones that trigger recognition.
caveats: A direct problem-statement hook trades broad appeal for resonance; that is the intended trade-off for cold traffic, not a way to appeal to a general audience.
The source explicitly is not trying to be super clever — don't optimize hooks for wit at the expense of clarity.
cards.source_name: How to create killer ad creatives (to blow up your business).docx

cards.title: Generate more angles from consistently repeated review themes
cards.summary: Segmenting reviews by use case can multiply a single generic creative into several distinct, proven ad angles.
cards.use_when: A brand has one generic creative and wants more angles without inventing new positioning from scratch.
steps: Read reviews looking for clusters — the same use case or same job-to-be-done appearing repeatedly rather than one-off mentions.
In the source's blackout blinds example, reviews repeatedly showed nursery use, RV use, and truck drivers using them in their trucks.
Build separate creatives around each consistently mentioned use case rather than producing more variations of the generic blackout blind ad.
Prioritize which segments to produce first based on how often the theme appears and how well it lines up with the audience you can actually reach affordably.
caveats: The blinds example is illustrative of the method, not a guaranteed result; the value comes from the repeated pattern in your own reviews.
The source notes you need budget to afford building out multiple angles — it recommends building one angle to profitability first, then using side budget to test others.
cards.source_name: How to create killer ad creatives (to blow up your business).docx

cards.title: Match creative testing volume to your daily ad spend
cards.summary: Launching dozens of ads on a small budget means most never get distribution, so 'it didn't work' is not a real finding.
cards.use_when: Planning how many new creatives to launch this month given your current daily spend.
steps: Before producing or launching a batch, check daily spend. The source's rule of thumb: at 30, 50 or 100 dollars a day you cannot feed an unlimited number of ads enough spend to learn anything.

Launch a focused batch instead and give the platform enough opportunity to distribute spend and return a signal, so the next round of creative is based on real customer response rather than guesswork.

In the source's $30/day account example, 13 ads were launched and the impression limit was initially set to 1,000, then lowered to 800 because CPMs were averaging $50–70 and the test needed to finish efficiently without burning budget.
Aim to find winners within the first week to two weeks rather than waiting indefinitely for under-spent ads to prove themselves.
If most of a large batch never received spend, do not record them as failures — record the test as inconclusive and re-run fewer creatives with adequate distribution.
caveats: The 1,000 and 800 impression limits and the $50–70 CPM are the source's specific example from one newer account with a pixel that lacked data; your CPMs and therefore practical limits will differ.
The exact interface for setting impression limits and viewing distribution changes over time — verify the current ad platform controls.
cards.source_name: How to create killer ad creatives (to blow up your business).docx

cards.title: Don't crown the ad the platform spent the most on
cards.summary: An ad that receives the bulk of spend naturally drives the most sales, so 'winner' must be judged on supporting metrics, not volume.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a creative test where one ad has taken most of the spend and you are about to declare it the winner and scale it.
steps: Check whether the other ads genuinely received distribution. The source describes brands with small budgets launching 30 ads, declaring failure two days later, when in reality all spend kept going to the same single ad.

Recognize that the platform snowballs spend on an ad with a strong CTR, good link click-through rate and lower-than-average CPM, and will keep pushing it to $150, $200 or $400 — but that decision is the platform reacting to engagement, not proof of buying intent.
Instead of taking engagement at face value, watch the ad and understand why it is working, then check whether that reason relates to the product and its value.
Judge ads on the full supporting metric set, never on CPA or ROAS alone, so you can distinguish a genuinely scalable creative from one that merely had the most volume behind it.
Also ask whether the ad can hold spend at larger scale, because an ad that looks great at $30/day can fall apart as budget rises.
caveats: A good CPA does not automatically mean a good top-of-funnel ad — it may only work at low spend, or it may be better deployed as a retargeting creative.
The source states its opinion that CPA/ROAS alone is insufficient reasoning; treat this as its stated position rather than a universal platform rule.
cards.source_name: How to create killer ad creatives (to blow up your business).docx

cards.title: Read CTR and link CTR together to spot empty attention
cards.summary: A high CTR with a large CTR-to-link-CTR drop signals an ad that entertains but fails to explain the product.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing whether a high-CTR creative is actually driving qualified buying traffic or just capturing attention.
steps: Compare CTR against link click-through rate. The source's anchor example: an ad with a 10.9% CTR (described as very high for ecommerce) lost over 3% between CTR and link CTR, while a lower-CTR ad (6.3%) lost less than 2%.
Interpret a large CTR-to-link-CTR gap as people engaging with the video but not being primed enough to want to visit the site — the creative did not explain the product or its value.
Check post-click behaviour as well, including conversion rate, add-to-carts, checkouts, drop-off percentages and on-site behaviour, to confirm whether the traffic had buying intent.

Watch the ad itself to explain the numbers: the source's high-CTR example was visually stimulating (calming, cutting-style footage) but the viewer never learned what was being sold, while the lower-CTR ad showed the routine, the before-and-after, the application and what you actually buy.
Note that a viewer may not even be a potential customer for that product category — attention and purchase intent are different things.
caveats: Do not treat the 10.9% / 6.3% CTRs or the 3% vs 2% drop as benchmarks; they come from one account and one pair of ads.
Lower CTR with strong post-click behaviour can be the better ad; the conclusion is about the whole metric pattern, not CTR in isolation.
cards.source_name: How to create killer ad creatives (to blow up your business).docx

cards.title: Run single-variable creative tests within the same angle
cards.summary: Vary only the delivery format while holding angle and product constant so you can attribute the result to something specific.
cards.use_when: You have a promising angle and want to learn something rather than randomly produce new ads.
steps: Take one validated angle — e.g. 'get your steps in while you work without needing a giant treadmill' — and produce two versions that share the same product and argument.
Example pairing from the source: version one as a UGC video, version two as a carousel where the slides tell the story, with a different opening format but the same underlying angle.
Run them in an apples-to-apples environment where each gets equal visibility, then read the data to identify why one was better.
Never change the hook, angle, audience, landing page, offer, campaign and creative simultaneously — the source's point is that if performance changes you will have no idea which change caused it.

After isolating the winner, cut the weaker version and carry the learning into the next brief, focusing on how to make a better version of what worked (the source suggests more before-and-after and routine footage as a next step in its example).
caveats: The source acknowledges that video versus carousel is a large format difference; the principle is to control as much as possible, not that all format comparisons are perfectly clean.
Format is only a variable to test once the angle itself is defined — the source explicitly de-prioritizes starting from format.
cards.source_name: How to create killer ad creatives (to blow up your business).docx

cards.title: Diagnose creative through the attention-to-purchase journey
cards.summary: Trace each metric stage — stop, click, post-click behaviour — to locate where the ad or the site is actually failing.
cards.use_when: An ad is underperforming and you need to decide whether to rebuild the creative, the landing page or something else.
steps: First ask: did we get their attention? If nobody stops, the hook may be too weak or the visual itself is not interesting.

Second ask: did they click to the site? If people watch but nobody clicks, the creative may be entertaining but the product and its value are not compelling or not being communicated — possibly they don't understand why they need the product.

Third ask: what happened after the click? If an ad gets lots of quality clicks but nobody buys, do not blame the creative immediately — it may be a good ad acting as the vehicle to the website, with the problem sitting in landing page load speed or quality.
When investigating post-click problems, review conversion rate, add-to-carts, checkouts, offer, pricing, shipping and website experience.

Frame the whole system as a two-piece puzzle: the cost to acquire attention and the conversion rate. The source's illustration: sending a million people to a site converting at 0.5% can never be profitable because the cost of that traffic is too high.
caveats: The 0.5% figure is an illustrative example used to make the arithmetic point, not a benchmark or threshold.
Use the diagnostic order as a way to assign blame, not as a claim that only one stage can be at fault.
cards.source_name: How to create killer ad creatives (to blow up your business).docx

cards.title: Use each creative test as the brief for the next round
cards.summary: Every test result should specify what to produce next — more of a winning angle, more of a winning hook, or more of a winning format.
cards.use_when: Scheduling the next creative production round and deciding what the team should actually make.
steps: After each test, read the result as a production instruction rather than a score. If an angle worked, make more creatives around that angle; if one hook crushed the others, keep that hook and write three different video bodies after it.
If a format underperformed, follow the evidence — e.g. if review-style UGC lost but a simple product demonstration worked, explore more product demonstration creatives.

Feed competitor weaknesses into the brief: if competitor reviews show they handle something poorly, build an ad that counters that objection, giving you differentiation beyond 'we have this and it's really good'.

Use the source's closing formula for each round: choose one customer problem, write the angle in a single sentence, and make every line of the ad prove that sentence, then change one meaningful thing at a time.

Replace the vague weekly question 'can we get AI to make more static images?' — which the source says yielded no results over two weeks — with 'what did customers respond to last week and what should we make from it?'
caveats: This is the source's stated operating philosophy from managing paid ads across many brands, not a guarantee of results in any particular account.
The Monday cadence is the source's example of how to structure the review; the essential part is that the test output drives the next brief.
cards.source_name: How to create killer ad creatives (to blow up your business).docx

cards.title: Handpick ads into funnel positions based on supporting metrics
cards.summary: Individual winners serve different funnel roles, and the combination of metrics tells you whether an ad belongs at top, middle or bottom of funnel.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to deploy each winning creative — prospecting versus retargeting — and what budget structure to give it.
steps: Judge ads on the combined evidence of CTR, link click-through rate, CPA, post-click behaviour and whether the ad can hold spend at larger scale — no single metric assigns a funnel role.
Recognize that a strong CPA might simply mean an ad works at low spend, and that such an ad may be a strong retargeting candidate rather than a scalable prospecting ad.
Place each handpicked ad into the funnel position its metric pattern supports, then build the account structure around those placements so you get the result you want.
Continue watching whether promising ads hold up as budget increases, since an ad that performs at $30/day can fall apart on scale.
Where you don't yet have enough budget to place a full set into each position, prioritize the angle that pays for itself, then use side budget to test the remaining angles.
caveats: The source notes these decisions are made in its own service by refusing to take platform engagement at face value; the general principle is that funnel role is inferred from combined metrics, not from one number.
Metric thresholds vary by account; the source does not give universal funnel-placement cutoffs.
cards.source_name: How to create killer ad creatives (to blow up your business).docx

cards.title: Four psychological pillars of scroll-stopping Meta ads
cards.summary: Every strong ad must earn attention, open a curiosity gap, trigger an emotion, and signal connection to a specific buyer.
cards.use_when: Drafting or reviewing a new paid social creative for a product launch or existing SKU on Meta.
steps: Before writing anything, walk your concept through the four pillars: (1) Attention — grab it in the first half-second, not the widely cited three seconds; scrolling users leave faster than a second. (2) Curiosity — open a gap, especially if the ad routes to a quiz, listicle, or solid landing page that finishes the sell. You do not need to close the sale inside the ad. (3) Emotion — pick one core feeling (fear, insecurity, excitement, humor) matched to where the buyer is emotionally. (4) Connection — use the ICP's own language, slang, and in-jokes so it reads as 'made for me'.

Treat the pillars as a checklist, not a sequence: ads can lean hard on curiosity/emotion (dark problem-solving brands) or on attention/connection (light, meme-style product ads) — neither is universally correct.
Verify pillar fit by asking whether your ICP would stop on this ad versus scrolling past in two seconds; wrong-ICP ads fail regardless of production quality.
caveats: The 'half-second attention' claim is the presenter's opinion, not a benchmark; treat it as a directional push toward faster hooks rather than a measured threshold.
cards.source_name: How to make Meta Ad Creatives (in 2026).docx

cards.title: Match ad type to whether the funnel finishes the sale
cards.summary: Problem-heavy, curiosity-driven ads work when a quiz or landing page continues the sell; simple product ads should instead win on attention and shareability.
cards.use_when: Choosing the creative style (dark problem-solving vs. light meme) for a given product and funnel type.
steps: Decide whether your ad must fully sell or only earn a click. If the ad routes to a quiz, consumption funnel, or strong landing page, the ad only needs to spark curiosity and emotion — do not force a full pitch.

For products with a large emotional problem (e.g., fertility, appearance), lead with the ICP's private fear or self-blame and offer a quiz or next step. Example: 'Stop blaming yourself… take the quiz and see what's stopping you' hits attention, curiosity, emotion, and connection at once.

For lighter, low-emotion products (golf accessories, dip cups, novelty items), win on fast attention and connection: meme formats, jokes, and humor. Example: 'Made for spitters, not quitters' works because it is funny and shareable.
Assess emotion on both ends of the spectrum — positive (humor, laughter) and negative (fear, insecurity) — and pick the one most likely to move your specific buyer, based on your ICP research.
caveats: Examples are the presenter's own client work for DTC brands, not guaranteed results; copy the underlying logic, not the exact lines.
cards.source_name: How to make Meta Ad Creatives (in 2026).docx

cards.title: Design shareable meme ads that raise AOV
cards.summary: Funny, shareable ad creative lets buyers spread the product and can lift average order value by encouraging friend-to-friend sends.
cards.use_when: Creating acquisition creative for a light-resonance product where you want organic shares or higher basket value.
steps: Identify the in-group identity your buyer wants to signal. For Gen Z / millennial golfers, that meant ads that feel like being 'one of the boys' rather than appealing to the traditional older golfer.
Write in meme language and joke-format copy so the ad itself becomes something the buyer would send to friends. Example: 'the foresome experience you dream about' for golf accessories.
Note the AOV angle: if the ad is shareable and funny, a buyer may forward it, which the presenter ties to increased average order value — treat this as an observed logic, not a guaranteed lift.
Confirm the humor lands with the exact ICP: the same ad should make the target laugh and make an off-target viewer scroll past. Use that two-second test to validate fit before spending.
caveats: The AOV increase is the presenter's observation, not a documented benchmark; test it rather than assuming it.
cards.source_name: How to make Meta Ad Creatives (in 2026).docx

cards.title: Do days of manual creative research before writing ads
cards.summary: Build a handwritten research document from Reddit, reviews, and comments instead of trusting a five-minute AI research prompt.
cards.use_when: Starting creative production for a new product, niche, or category where you lack buyer language.
steps: Block out three to four consecutive days for manual research on the niche and product before making any ad.
Spend that time inside your customers' real words: Reddit threads, competitor-site reviews, Amazon reviews, TikTok comments, and ad comments.
Build a dedicated research document by manually copying and pasting quotes, reviews, and comments, and taking screenshots — capture raw language, not cleaned-up summaries.
Do not outsource the judgment to AI. As the presenter stresses, a chatbot will not write a funny golf or dipping joke for you; you must find the humor and phrasing yourself from real material.
Use this document as the source of truth for briefs and copy, so ads echo the customer's own voice and in-group slang rather than generic claims.
caveats: The '3–4 days' figure is the presenter's recommendation, scale it to how unfamiliar the niche is; AI can assist in selecting candidates if reviewed by a human.
cards.source_name: How to make Meta Ad Creatives (in 2026).docx

cards.title: Write creative briefs with six mandatory fields before producing ads
cards.summary: A structured brief (concept, creative type, angle, headline, CTA, visual direction) prevents making 100 copies of one ad.
cards.use_when: Handing off a static ad to a designer or producing it yourself in Canva.
steps: After research, write a brief per ad. Include these fields: (1) Concept, (2) Creative type — curiosity static, us-versus-them, USP callout, social-proof/review, etc. (3) Angle — what you are actually doing and who you are selling to. (4) Headline. (5) CTA. (6) Visual direction.
Always name the creative type explicitly so your set stays diverse and you do not make one hundred near-identical variants.
Use the brief as the production spec: ship it to a designer's attention or review your own brief and build the ad in Canva.
Treat each field as a decision to make deliberately — a missing creative-type or angle field is the fastest route to a monotone, undifferentiated set of ads.
caveats: This is the presenter's own briefing framework; adapt the field list to your team's handoff format.
cards.source_name: How to make Meta Ad Creatives (in 2026).docx

cards.title: Test ad concepts against a four-question 'made for me' scorecard
cards.summary: A quick checklist confirms an ad speaks to the ICP, opens a curiosity gap, triggers emotion, and shows a path to a solution.
cards.use_when: Pre-launch review of a new creative before you commit spend on Meta.
steps: Score the ad on four points: does it speak directly to the ICP? Does it create a curiosity gap? Does it trigger an emotional response? Does it provide a clear path to a solution?
Use the scorecard to make the viewer feel the ad was made specifically for them — the emotional 'this hits me' reaction, rather than a polished but generic ad.
Kill or rework any ad that looks like everyone else's generic ad or that shows product-spec details nobody cares about, such as t-shirt weight or GSM.
Also test the offer layer alongside the psychology: the presenter admits he often buys purely on a strong offer he cannot refuse — so pair good ad psychology with a compelling offer.
Apply the scorecard before large spend and consider a systematic creative test rather than a single ad slam-dunk.
caveats: The scorecard is a qualitative heuristic from the presenter, not a validated measurement instrument.
cards.source_name: How to make Meta Ad Creatives (in 2026).docx

cards.title: Live Auction Show Planning: Schedule Early, Promote Hard
cards.summary: Schedule live auction shows at least a week ahead and promote across channels to maximize bookmarks, which drives viewer turnout and higher average selling price.
cards.use_when: Planning a live-stream selling event (Whatnot or similar live auction) and deciding how far in advance to schedule and how to promote it.
steps: Schedule the show at least one week ahead, and two to three weeks out if possible, so the platform can remind bookmarked users when you go live.
Advertise the scheduled show on every channel you have: personal Facebook page, reseller Facebook groups, Instagram stories, and your YouTube videos.
Post promotion multiple times with escalating urgency: roughly one week before, two to three days before, and a few hours before the show.
Center the pre-show message on the quality of inventory and a reason to show up (for example 'high-quality inventory, all starting at $1'), not just the date.
Track bookmarks and max concurrent viewers as your feedback signal — the source's 530 max concurrent viewers (top-10 show in three years) was attributed to this multi-channel promotion.
caveats: The source's link between bookmarks and higher ASP is the seller's own experience, not a platform benchmark.
The presenter acknowledges their existing YouTube following helped; they also state sellers with no prior social following can grow purely inside the app.
cards.source_name: Our Secret Strategies to Making $975_Hour on Whatnot!.docx

cards.title: Thumbnail Design: Value Callouts and Brand Recognition
cards.summary: Build the show thumbnail in a free tool like Canva with the biggest incentive and recognizable brand names to win attention while viewers scroll.
cards.use_when: Creating the static thumbnail image for a live auction show listing on a platform where buyers scroll past many shows.
steps: Use a free design tool (the source used Canva) to make a simple static thumbnail.
Put the single biggest viewer incentive in large text — in the source's case 'Free iPad'.
List recognizable brand names of items being sold alongside their starting price, e.g. brands that would resell for $50–$150 on eBay, all starting at $1.
Keep the message consistent with your ad posts so anyone who saw the promo recognizes the show instantly.
Treat the thumbnail as a low-cost supporting asset: the source is unsure how much the thumbnail alone matters but argues it's worth making since you're already promoting heavily.
caveats: The source explicitly says they are not sure whether the thumbnail is 'super important' — treat it as a cheap complement to promotion, not a proven driver.
cards.source_name: Our Secret Strategies to Making $975_Hour on Whatnot!.docx

cards.title: Anchor High-Ticket Items Early to Shape Price Perception
cards.summary: Borrow Costco's front-of-store $5,000 TV logic: show your most expensive items first so everything after feels cheap and buyers bid more freely.
cards.use_when: Sequencing items during a live auction show or ordering products on a storefront/landing page to influence perceived value.
steps: Identify your highest-priced, most impressive items before the show starts.
Run or display those high-ticket anchor items early, mirroring how Costco puts the $5,000 flat-screen right at the entrance.
Let the rest of the catalog be perceived as comparatively affordable, which the source argues leads buyers to purchase more.
Segment the catalog: the source's show had ~50 high-value items ($50–$150 resale) meant to create excitement, and ~200 lower-cost items that carried the actual profit.
Accept that some anchor items may sell below eBay market value — that's the cost of the excitement they generate.
caveats: This is the presenter's analogy to observed retail practice, not a tested auction result.
You may lose money or margin on anchor items; plan the rest of the catalog's profitability accordingly.
cards.source_name: Our Secret Strategies to Making $975_Hour on Whatnot!.docx

cards.title: Use Loss Leaders and Freebies to Pull Buyers Toward Profitable Inventory
cards.summary: Make your money on the 80% of cheap, high-margin items while using giveaway-grade high-value items as the draw.
cards.use_when: Building a product mix for a live sale or promotion where you need traffic and engagement but profit comes from lower-cost goods.
steps: Identify a small share of your inventory that will be exciting but likely unprofitable (source: ~50 of 250 items, worth $50–$150, expected to sell below market).
Fill the majority of the show with low-cost goods you can buy cheaply and triple your money on — the source's normal shows buy at Goodwill bins or flea markets for $0.25–$5 and sell for $8–$15.
Use the loss-leader items purely as the hook that brings people in and keeps the room full; the source calls the leftover, already-paid-off inventory effectively 'free' cost of goods.
Recover the cost of a paid loss leader across the volume of the show: e.g., a $250 iPad is covered if each of ~250 items earns just one extra bid dollar.
caveats: The 'one extra dollar per item covers the iPad' arithmetic is the presenter's own framing example, not a guaranteed outcome.
Loss leaders can sell for far below market — the source saw this with Nike sneakers and motocross boots.
cards.source_name: Our Secret Strategies to Making $975_Hour on Whatnot!.docx

cards.title: Buyer Giveaway Mechanics: Reward Buyers, Incentivize Bids
cards.summary: Gate a giveaway to customers only (a 'buyer's giveaway') so it rewards purchases and nudges non-buyers to bid at least once.
cards.use_when: Designing a giveaway or incentive for a live-stream sale or event to convert viewers into buyers and lift purchase volume.
steps: Choose a giveaway prize large enough to motivate action — the source gave away an iPad, roughly $250.
Make the giveaway a 'buyer's giveaway': only people who made a purchase during the show can enter.
Run a small second giveaway early in the show (the source used Hello Kitty earrings) to spark engagement from the start, and save the bigger prize for the end.
Announce the giveaway in pre-show advertising so it also drives bookmarks.
Frame the math: if the prize makes each of N items earn an extra small bid, the prize pays for itself — the source felt their iPad did.
caveats: Whether the giveaway truly paid for itself is the presenter's own belief ('I think it worked'), not measured.
Prize cost is real cash outlay and must be included in your show's break-even calculation.
cards.source_name: Our Secret Strategies to Making $975_Hour on Whatnot!.docx

cards.title: Starting Bids at $1: When It Works and When It Doesn't
cards.summary: $1 starts create excitement only when the room is full; the source says most sellers should not use them.
cards.use_when: Deciding starting bid prices for auction inventory in a live-stream show.
steps: Reserve $1 starting bids for high-quality, recognizable items ($50–$150 resale value) — buyers ignore $1 starts on $5–$10 junk.
Only start at $1 if you expect a large, excited room; the source describes success with 300–500 concurrent viewers.
Publicize '$1 starts' in your advertising because it is a strong hook that drives bookmarks.
Accept the unpredictability: some $1-start items will sell below market and some far above; the source calls this the inherent nature of $1 auctions.
For normal shows without a big promoted audience, start higher — the source explicitly does not recommend $1 starts for most sellers.
caveats: The recommendation to avoid $1 starts for most sellers is the presenter's opinion, tied to room size.
No guaranteed price floor exists; losses on individual items are expected.
cards.source_name: Our Secret Strategies to Making $975_Hour on Whatnot!.docx

cards.title: Entertainment as Conversion: Costumes, Music, Energy
cards.summary: If viewers have fun they become buyers, and if buyers have fun they become repeat buyers — so build small bits into every show.
cards.use_when: Hosting a live-stream sale and trying to hold viewers, increase engagement, and improve conversion to purchase.
steps: Wear something visually distinct (a silly hat, viking helmet, shark costume); the source reports it becomes the main topic of chat every time and stands out while viewers scroll.
Play background music at low volume — not to entertain viewers but to make it easier for the seller to talk continuously and fill dead air.
Avoid silence: the source says doing literally nothing is the one thing to never do; dance, chat, or keep energy up.
Talk directly to new viewers in chat (ask first-timers to say hello) to make them feel included and more likely to buy.
Find a style that fits you — the source warns that forced comedy that the chat doesn't enjoy reads as 'cringe,' so play with it and adjust.
caveats: The source stresses entertainment style is highly individual; there is no universal script.
The buyer/repeat-buyer chain is the presenter's causal claim, not a measured funnel.
cards.source_name: Our Secret Strategies to Making $975_Hour on Whatnot!.docx

cards.title: Pacing a High-Volume Auction Show
cards.summary: Budget ~45 seconds to 1 minute per item and expect a 250-item show to run close to 4 hours.
cards.use_when: Planning show length, item count, and staffing for a live auction event.
steps: Estimate time per lot: the source's 252 items took 3 hours 57 minutes, roughly 45 seconds to 1 minute each.
Set a minimum countdown (their auctions start at 15 seconds) but let bids extend the timer when bidding continues.
Account for your own talking time — the source's show ran longer than planned (2.5–3 hours expected, ~4 actual) because of extended commentary and 'soap boxes'.
Plan capacity accordingly: staff shipping/replenishment so orders from a big show can be processed afterward (their helper took ~2 days, 6–7 paid hours at $25/hour).
Use the time-per-item figure to sanity-check whether a target item count is realistic for your show length.
caveats: Time per item is the source's own observed average, not a platform standard.
Sellers who talk more or less will see different totals.
cards.source_name: Our Secret Strategies to Making $975_Hour on Whatnot!.docx

cards.title: Calculate Show Profitability: Gross Sales, Fees, COGS
cards.summary: Track gross sales, platform fees and adjustments, inventory cost, and giveaway cost to get true show profit.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether a live-stream sale was actually profitable and planning break-even for the next show.
steps: Record gross sales for the show — the source's example: 252 items, $5,565 gross, ASP ~$22 (versus ~$9.85 in normal shows).
Subtract platform fees, shipping adjustments, and coupon/points redemptions to get actual payout — the source's example netted $4,006 from $5,565 gross.
Total your cost of goods: inventory purchases, the cost of any giveaway prize (iPad ~$250), and any included leftover stock you'd already paid off.
Add labor: the source counted ~6–7 hours of a helper at $25/hour for shipping, reducing profit from ~$3,900 to ~$3,750.
Set your break-even point: with ~$1,000 of inventory in, break-even was ~$1,000 in sales; everything above that was profit.
Win the show on a higher average selling price, not just item count — doubling ASP from ~$9.85 to ~$22 was the biggest single lever.
caveats: All figures are one seller's single show, not benchmarks or promises.
Fees, shipping adjustments and rewards deductions vary by platform and change over time — verify current fee structures.
cards.source_name: Our Secret Strategies to Making $975_Hour on Whatnot!.docx

cards.title: Read Show Health Metrics: Buyers, New Buyers, Concurrents
cards.summary: Use buyers-per-item, first-time buyers, max concurrent viewers, and total unique viewers to judge whether promotion worked.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a completed live sale to diagnose whether your promotion and show design succeeded and what to change next time.
steps: Count total buyers versus items sold to see repeat purchasing — the source sold 250 items to 153 buyers, indicating many multi-item buyers.
Track first-time buyers as a signal that promotion reached new audiences — 49 of the 153 were first-time buyers on the platform.
Track max concurrent viewers to gauge the peak of your audience — the source hit 530, among their top 10 shows in three years.
Track total unique viewers across the show — the source reached 6,158 people over ~4 hours, showing the platform's audience size.
Compare all of these against your normal, non-promoted shows to quantify the effect of the extra advertising effort.
caveats: These are the source's own single-show numbers, not benchmarks to target.
First-time buyer counts depend on platform tracking; verify how your platform reports them.
cards.source_name: Our Secret Strategies to Making $975_Hour on Whatnot!.docx

cards.title: Build Inventory Cheap to Protect Auction Margins
cards.summary: Source product from thrift bins, flea markets, and lot deals to keep COGS low enough that even $8–$15 sales are profitable.
cards.use_when: Sourcing inventory for a live auction or resale channel where per-item prices are low and volume is high.
steps: Buy from low-cost sources: thrift-store bins, flea markets, and bulk lots; the source buys at $0.25–$5 per item.
Look for bulk lot opportunities from other sellers — the source's friend offered 67 Funko Pops for $250 (~$4 per pop), which they considered a good deal.
Reuse already-paid-off inventory from previous events as effectively free cost of goods for the next show.
Aim for a consistent multiplier: the source targets roughly tripling money on low-cost items ($2 in, ~$8+ out) and relies on volume (about 150 items a week) for profitability.
Keep the show's total inventory cost low enough that break-even comes early — the source's $1,000-in / $1,000-out break-even for a 250-item show.
caveats: Low-cost sourcing is labor-intensive and depends on local supply; margins on tiny items are thin until moved at volume.
The source's sourcing channels (Goodwill bins, flea markets) are their own; other sources may yield different costs.
cards.source_name: Our Secret Strategies to Making $975_Hour on Whatnot!.docx

cards.title: Large Show vs. Routine Show: Match Format to Goal
cards.summary: Run small frequent shows for baseline cash and occasional big promoted shows with better inventory to lift ASP and reach new buyers.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to run a normal weekly live sale or invest in a larger, promoted event.
steps: In routine mode, run frequent smaller shows (the source does 2–3 per week with 30–50 items) as reliable baseline revenue.
In event mode, run a larger show (the source's 252 items) with higher-quality inventory and heavier promotion, accepting more planning and inventory outlay.
Use the event show to lift average selling price — the source went from ~$9.85 to ~$22 by combining better inventory, promotion, and excitement.
Accept more variability in a large show: some items sell below market and some above; the source says you 'never really know' with $1 starts.
Use the event to acquire new buyers who become followers for future routine shows.
caveats: Event shows demand more inventory capital, planning, and post-show shipping labor than routine shows.
The source notes not every seller can execute this format — it needs a full room and heavy promotion.
cards.source_name: Our Secret Strategies to Making $975_Hour on Whatnot!.docx

cards.title: Grow a Following Inside the Platform Without Off-Platform Audiences
cards.summary: A pre-existing social following helps but is not required — sellers can build audience directly on the selling platform.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest time in off-platform promotion or in-platform audience growth for a live-selling channel.
steps: Invest in the platform's own discovery tools: schedule shows, use strong thumbnails, promote within the app, and engage chat consistently.
Post show-to-show so repeat buyers keep coming back — the source credits the fun-buyer-repeat-buyer loop for channel growth.
Recognize that some highly successful sellers have no social media following and build entirely on-platform (the source cites sellers doing high volumes weekly with no external audience).
If you do have an off-platform following, use it as a multiplier for big events (the source attributes a top-10 show partly to YouTube and Instagram promotion).
Set expectations by category: routine small-show revenue versus large event revenue differ greatly — measure your own numbers rather than aiming at someone else's.
caveats: The source explicitly acknowledges their own YouTube following aided their results, so their outcomes are not directly reproducible without one.
High-revenue examples from other sellers are cited by the presenter as anecdotes, not audited figures.
cards.source_name: Our Secret Strategies to Making $975_Hour on Whatnot!.docx

cards.title: Decide if your product needs a VSL ad before producing one
cards.summary: Use the three qualifying conditions—complex product, low-trust category, or new-to-market category—to decide whether a long educational video ad is worth the production cost.
cards.use_when: Choosing an acquisition creative format for a complicated, distrusted, or brand-new product category, versus running standard short ads.
steps: Qualify your product against the three VSL use cases: (1) complicated products that are hard to explain in a short ad, (2) low-trust categories where the buyer assumes the seller is sketchy, and (3) new categories or new ingredients nobody has heard of.

Check whether your top-of-funnel conversion is capped because customers don't understand the product. If yes, you must educate either in the ad or on the landing page—if not the landing page, then the ad, and the source argues VSLs are the best vehicle for that.
Recognize the production tradeoff: longer VSLs cost more to produce, so start short, learn, then extend. The source warns against jumping straight into a 60-minute script.
If you do not need heavy education to convert, a VSL is not your format—do not adopt it just because it worked for a supplement brand.
Pair the ad with a contextually matched landing page (advertorial or dedicated page), since the source's referenced accounts drove every VSL to a different landing page rather than a generic PDP.
caveats: Qualification is based on the source's stated use cases, not a tested benchmark; the 150% profit lift and low frequency figures are one Australian supplement account's example, not a promise.
Source opinion: VSLs perform better with older demographics, so they may fit your audience differently than a younger one.
cards.source_name: The 7-Part VSL Framework for eCommerce (With Examples).docx

cards.title: The seven-part VSL scripting framework
cards.summary: A repeatable order for scripting a long-form video sales letter: Hook, Problem, Mechanism, Objection Handling, Proof, Risk Reversal, CTA.
cards.use_when: Writing a full VSL ad script for a complex product or low-trust category where doubt must be removed before purchase.
steps: Hook: open with something relevant to the viewer's problem, not a brand introduction.
Problem: state the problem in the customer's own words so the viewer recognizes themselves.
Mechanism: explain why your solution works—in CPG/supplements this is the specific ingredient or technology, not just a claim.
Objection Handling: name the other things the customer tried and explain why those failed, so they don't assume your product will fail the same way.
Proof: product-level evidence (UGC, testimonial, customer count).
Risk Reversal: reduce purchase risk (e.g., a money-back window) before asking for the sale.
CTA: a simple, clear closing ask.
Treat the order as a starting point, not a fixed rule—the source says you don't always script it this way and that the sequence can be reordered.
caveats: Source frames this as a good starting point rather than a universal sequence; it explicitly notes some VSLs work with reordered sections.
A VSL is not a long video for its own sake—the source stresses it's a sales argument that removes doubt in a specific order, and good ones can be as short as 90 seconds.
cards.source_name: The 7-Part VSL Framework for eCommerce (With Examples).docx

cards.title: Hook is the highest-leverage test in a VSL
cards.summary: Because roughly 80% of viewers drop off before the body script starts, test 3–6 hook variations against a fixed body and CTA rather than rewriting everything.
cards.use_when: Improving performance of an already-produced VSL, or structuring a paid social test plan for a long-form video ad.
steps: Build the body of the VSL (problem, mechanism, proof, CTA) first, then produce 3–6 competing hooks against that same body.
Test the hooks as the primary variable rather than rewriting the entire script each time.

Do not bridge immediately into brand or product after the hook—transition into the Problem phase with educational problem-agitation (e.g., explain the biological cause of tooth decay) so viewers stay engaged and don't realize early that it's an ad.

Match hook relevance to audience: the source's strong examples open with content specific to who has the problem (e.g., 'people with tonsil stones'), which filters in the right viewer and lets others self-select out.
Keep the CTA on the main asset if this is your first VSL rather than splitting it into a separate retargeting asset.
caveats: The 80% drop-off figure is the source's stated figure, not a measured benchmark.
The source says many VSLs perform better with older demographics, so readable, large text matters—unreadable text is an editor-level failure it calls out.
cards.source_name: The 7-Part VSL Framework for eCommerce (With Examples).docx

cards.title: Mine real customer data for the objection-handling section
cards.summary: Populate the VSL objection section with verbatim customer reasons for almost-not-buying, drawn from reviews, support tickets, post-purchase surveys, and call recordings.
cards.use_when: Writing the objection-handling portion of a VSL script for a product where buyers considered alternatives or hesitated before purchase.
steps: Pull from reviews, support tickets, post-purchase surveys, and call recordings the reasons people almost didn't buy or what they had already tried.

Map each reason to the script's objection-handling section: name the thing they tried and explain why it didn't work (e.g., gargling only rinses the surface and can't reach the deep biofilm where bacteria live).
Sequence this so the customer feels understood before you introduce the mechanism and product.
Use this miner approach rather than guessing at objections from internal assumptions.
caveats: Source frames this as its own recommended method; it does not provide a validated benchmark for how much objection handling lifts performance.
cards.source_name: The 7-Part VSL Framework for eCommerce (With Examples).docx

cards.title: Use modular editing to cheaply generate VSL variants
cards.summary: Because VSLs are long, you can move whole sections around and cut multiple durations from one asset to produce more creative tests without new shoots.
cards.use_when: Generating multiple creative variations from a single long-form VSL to test on paid social.
steps: After building the full VSL, test reordering sections—e.g., lead with the mechanism before the problem, or pull objection handling earlier. The source reports seeing success moving sections around.
Cut a range of lengths from one script: the source says a 6–10 minute asset can typically be chopped into a 2–3 minute version and a 45-second version by an editor.
Treat length as a variation source rather than the driver of performance—the source believes scripting matters more than length.
Source says length does not have a massive impact on actual performance, so do not over-index on it.
Given a warm viewer who made it through deep ingredient education, push them to a matching landing page rather than a generic PDP.
caveats: Source opinion: length is not the main driver; this is the presenter's view, not a tested law.
Longer production raises cost, so the source recommends starting small.
cards.source_name: The 7-Part VSL Framework for eCommerce (With Examples).docx

cards.title: Bridge from education to product without a premature pitch
cards.summary: Avoid the common mistake of pivoting straight from the intro to a brand/CTA pitch; earn the right to sell by first building the problem and mechanism.
cards.use_when: Drafting the transition from VSL education into the product introduction so viewers don't disengage early.
steps: After the hook, do not cut to a brand or product pitch. Instead move into problem education (e.g., the biological cause of the problem).
Build substantial educational content on the mechanism (in the source's dental example, roughly 30 seconds explaining ingredients and why they work) before presenting the product.
Present the product as the consolidated solution once education has landed—e.g., 'you don't have to source all these ingredients separately; this brand combined them into one.'
Avoid the mistake of stacking claims with no mechanism: too much 'what it is' and not enough 'why it matters' is a listed common failure.
Keep the ad as an educational piece so it doesn't feel like an ad until late in the sequence.
caveats: Source notes some viewers won't tolerate extended mechanism education; it recommends testing a faster version of the same section.
The specific 30-second education length is from one example ad, not a universal target.
cards.source_name: The 7-Part VSL Framework for eCommerce (With Examples).docx

cards.title: Avoid the six common VSL scripting mistakes
cards.summary: A checklist of recurring VSL failures: brand-story hook, claims without mechanism, weak proof, vague offer or missing CTA, and slow pacing or unreadable text.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a drafted VSL script or an underperforming VSL before briefing an editor or relaunching.
steps: Check the hook: a brand story can work as an ad, but source says a VSL is not a brand-story ad—hook with something relevant to the viewer's problem instead. You can weave the founder story into social proof or objection handling later.
Check for mechanism: don't just list what the product does; explain why it works. Claims without mechanism is a listed common mistake.
Check proof: weak or buried proof is a common, easy-to-fix cause of underperformance—surface UGC, testimonials, and customer counts.
Check the offer and CTA: make the offer clear and convincing and include a CTA. The source recommends always including one.
Check pacing and text legibility: slow pacing and small/hard-to-read text are editor-level issues the source says you must be able to spot, especially given VSLs skew toward older viewers.
Add a risk reversal if it's missing—the source criticizes VSLs that skip it.
caveats: Source opinion: 'I recommend you have a CTA'—it is a recommendation, not a proven rule, and the source acknowledges some VSLs run without one.
The source notes an example ad that performed very well despite missing objection handling, so these mistakes are patterns rather than absolute ceilings.
cards.source_name: The 7-Part VSL Framework for eCommerce (With Examples).docx

cards.title: Why some VSLs omit the CTA (and when that's acceptable)
cards.summary: An asset without a CTA is usually an error, but can be deliberate when it feeds an Amazon funnel or a retargeting campaign that handles the close.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to include a CTA on a VSL or whether to run it as top-of-funnel only with a separate retargeting close.
steps: Include a CTA on your primary VSL asset if this is your first—the source recommends it.

If a VSL runs with no CTA, check whether it's pushing traffic to a separate high-converting marketplace (source cites US patterns of running ads or organic content that push people to Amazon, which the source says converts higher than a website landing page).

Or check whether it's a pure top-of-funnel educational asset with retargeting for anyone who watches past a threshold (the source cites retargeting viewers past 25% video views with a hard close), plus natural platform retargeting.
Do not split the CTA out of the VSL on a first attempt—the source says not to complicate the retargeting structure and instead to include the CTA directly.
caveats: The source is explicit that this is its recommendation for beginners, not a universal rule.
The Amazon-funnel and retargeting interpretations are the source's hypotheses for why an example ad lacked a CTA, not confirmed facts about that advertiser.
cards.source_name: The 7-Part VSL Framework for eCommerce (With Examples).docx

cards.title: Pair each VSL with a matching educational landing page
cards.summary: The VSL narrative must continue onto a contextually relevant advertorial or dedicated landing page—dropping to a generic product page breaks continuity and undercuts the ad.
cards.use_when: Setting up the post-click destination for a VSL campaign or running an advertorial/landing page test.
steps: Do not send VSL traffic to a standard PDP with no continuity to what the ad communicated. The source says the VSL won't work if the landing page isn't contextually relevant.
Create a custom landing page (advertorial or dedicated page) per message/angle; the referenced supplement account tied every VSL to a different landing page.
Mirror the ad's mechanism and education on the page so viewers who arrive pre-sold see the story continue rather than restarting.
Make the landing page itself strong, since the source stresses both ad and page quality matter to hold spend.
caveats: Source's account results (aggregated millions, one VSL at ~$360k spend, ROAS ~2.5–3) are examples, not guarantees.
That account made most of its money on second and third purchases (source cites ~150% profit lift after year one), so the VSL's economics depend on your retention, not just first-order ROAS.
cards.source_name: The 7-Part VSL Framework for eCommerce (With Examples).docx

cards.title: Combine UGC, AI animation, and real footage to build VSL B-roll
cards.summary: VSLs stitch together AI UGC, real UGC, and animated motion graphics to explain complex mechanisms without a dedicated shoot.
cards.use_when: Planning the visual production and B-roll sourcing for a long-form educational VSL ad.
steps: Pull together whatever footage and animation ties the story together so you can sustain a long ad without a full shoot.

Use AI video to animate static imagery (e.g., animating a still image of an anatomical process) to create motion graphics for hard-to-shoot technical explanation—the source says this is a very easy way to get B-roll on complex topics.
Mix formats deliberately: the source notes VSLs typically switch between AI UGC, real UGC, and heavy animation.

Watch for stylistic inconsistency—the source criticizes one ad for being too aggressive in using any footage available, coming across as scammy; it recommends keeping branding more consistent (more UGC and less animation, or going all-in on animation).
caveats: The source's 'comes across a little scammy' reaction is a subjective judgment on one ad, not a measured outcome.
Do not read this as an endorsement that more animation always performs—the source pushes for consistency.
cards.source_name: The 7-Part VSL Framework for eCommerce (With Examples).docx

cards.title: Read performance signals: likes, launch age, and frequency
cards.summary: Use public engagement and launch age as rough signals of a VSL's spend level, and frequency as a rough indicator of how cold an ad still is.
cards.use_when: Sourcing winning VSL examples for creative inspiration or assessing whether an ad is still reaching new audiences.
steps: Treat like count and launch age as a rough proxy for lifetime spend—the source cites an ad with ~25,000 likes launched roughly 2 months prior as having spent at least $100k.
Track frequency as an indicator of how cold the ad is and how well it is moving into new audiences, especially in the current platform era the source calls 'post-Andromeda.'

Contextualize frequency against market size: holding large spend at very low frequency in a small market (the source cites Australia) is notable, while the US can support similar spend at lower frequency because the population is far larger.
Remember the source's point that a low first-order ROAS (~2.5–3) can still be highly profitable when retention drives most of the revenue on later purchases.
caveats: These are rough heuristics from public ad observations, not verified spend data or benchmarks.
The source explicitly says ROAS and scaling rules belong in analytics/performance, not creative—use these signals for creative sourcing, not as performance targets.
cards.source_name: The 7-Part VSL Framework for eCommerce (With Examples).docx

cards.title: Recognize when a VSL script can reorder its sections
cards.summary: The seven-part order is a template, not a fixed sequence—the source's working example moves problem before hook education and mechanism after objection handling.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to keep or reorder the standard VSL section flow when scripting a new creative.
steps: Use the standard order (Hook → Problem → Mechanism → Objection Handling → Proof → Risk Reversal → CTA) as a default starting point.
