Consider reordering if it serves the audience: the source's tonsil-stone example ran Hook → Problem → Objection Handling → Mechanism, and the source calls this valid rather than wrong.
Consider pulling problem agitation forward if the hook is ingredient-heavy—the source says it would test moving the agitation earlier in the dental example.
Test reordered versions as modular variations of the same asset rather than writing entirely new scripts.
Keep the elements intact even when reordering: the dental example skipped objection handling and the source flagged that gap as something to add in future versions.
caveats: The source says reordering is situational and the default order is a starting point, not a universal requirement.
Reordering evidence in the source is observational (the source's own notes on ads it reviewed), not a controlled test result.
cards.source_name: The 7-Part VSL Framework for eCommerce (With Examples).docx

cards.title: AI Ads: Use Context, Not Volume
cards.summary: Most AI ad generation fails because it produces high-volume generic 'slop' instead of ads built on proven angles and specific customer avatars.
cards.use_when: You are deciding how to deploy AI tools for paid social ad production and are tempted to bulk-generate ads quickly.
steps: Treat AI as an accelerant layered on top of an existing creative strategy, not as a standalone strategy. The source argues brands winning with AI are the ones who already have strategy and use AI to speed execution.

Before generating anything, feed the tool deep context: your brand URL, a defined list of competitors, and your product catalog. A tool that scrapes your site can build a brand book (do's, don'ts, must-haves) that improves every future output.
Research recurring competitor angles as inspiration, then test original concepts for the store. Public ad-library presence does not prove an ad is profitable.
Expect losers even with good context. The presenter describes roughly 50% usable output as an excellent result when context is strong—not 100%.
Keep producing your own human creative alongside AI output; AI is explicitly framed as not a total replacement for creative production.
caveats: Source is a sponsored-feeling walkthrough of one specific AI tool; verify current tool features and pricing before committing.
The ~50% usable-output figure is the presenter's stated personal expectation, not a measured benchmark.
Accessing exact incremental revenue/ROAS per ad requires connecting your ad account, not just the public ad library.
cards.source_name: The Best AI Ad Creative Strategy for 2026.docx

cards.title: Avatar + Template = Ad Concept (Creative as Targeting)
cards.summary: Shift from building ads for manual audiences to building ad concepts from an avatar plus a template, letting Meta's algorithm use the creative messaging to find the audience.
cards.use_when: You are structuring new ad concepts and deciding how to organize targeting, ad sets, and messaging intent in your prospecting campaign.
steps: Define the specific buyer avatar first (e.g., hair-loss buyer vs. weight-loss buyer). The presenters' 'new way' is: avatars create audiences.
Pair that avatar with a creative template (format/angle) to produce a single ad concept. Example formats cited: 'GLP-1's New Bestie,' iPhone Notes, '60 ingredients, one gummy.'
Let the messaging in the creative do the audience targeting on Meta's algorithm rather than relying primarily on manual backend audience selection.
Group ads strictly by avatar inside a campaign. Do not mix, for example, hair ads and weight-loss ads in the same ad set, because that muddies the messaging intent the algorithm reads.
When generating with AI, include the avatar and the borrowed template explicitly so the output stays on-message.
caveats: This is the presenter's stated 'new way' opinion for 2026 Meta advertising; results depend on account, offer, and creative quality.
Template/angle inspiration drawn from competitor ads should be adapted, not copied verbatim.
cards.source_name: The Best AI Ad Creative Strategy for 2026.docx

cards.title: Pack-Based Modular Creative Testing Structure
cards.summary: Launch each new round of creatives as a 'pack' ad set grouped by avatar, sized 4–8 ads, inside the prospecting campaign.
cards.use_when: You are setting up prospecting campaign structure and deciding how to organize and isolate new creative rounds.
steps: Keep a simple two-campaign structure: a prospecting campaign and a retention campaign. Focus testing inside prospecting.
Every time you launch a new round of creative, create a new 'pack' ad set (e.g., broad pack one, broad pack two). New ads = new pack; new concept = new pack.
Group packs by avatar: keep different avatars' ads in separate ad sets even when they sit in the same campaign.
Size a pack between 2 and 10 creatives, with 4–8 ads as the stated sweet spot—enough angles to test without diluting spend across too many angles.
Pause, keep, or modify packs over time; the structure is meant to be modular and evolving as you run more rounds.
caveats: Pack counts scale with account size (one pack today could be many later); no fixed universal number.
Grouping by avatar assumes you have clearly distinct avatars; overlapping avatars may warrant different grouping.
cards.source_name: The Best AI Ad Creative Strategy for 2026.docx

cards.title: Seven-Day Minimum Budget Constraint to Force Creative Testing
cards.summary: Set an ad-set minimum spend equal to 1x target CPA for 7 days to force the algorithm to test new creatives, then remove it to let winners scale.
cards.use_when: You are launching new creative packs and need to guarantee they get a fair chance at spend rather than being starved by the algorithm.
steps: Go to the ad set (your 'pack') budget section and find ad set spending limits.
Set the daily minimum dollar value to 1x your cost-per-acquisition (CPA) target. If target CPA is $50, enter $50.
If that figure equals too large a share of your budget, cap it at 20% of the daily budget maximum.
Apply this as a 7-day minimum so new ads are tested at your target CPA; if they perform, they spend above the minimum; if not, they fade and scale down.
After 7 days, remove the minimum constraint and let the pack run freely so the best ads scale naturally.
caveats: The 7-day and 1x-CPA figures are the source's recommended heuristics, not a proven universal benchmark.
The 20% cap is the presenter's suggested safeguard for smaller budgets; verify current Ads Manager budget-limit interface before setting.
cards.source_name: The Best AI Ad Creative Strategy for 2026.docx

cards.title: Iteration Engine: Scale Winners from Incremental Revenue Data
cards.summary: Find top ads by incremental revenue and incremental ROAS, then produce meaningful variations—not word-level tweaks—of those winning concepts.
cards.use_when: You have winning ads in the account and want to systematically expand them into new iterations for continued prospecting.
steps: In the main prospecting campaign, open all ads and go to the column set, selecting the attribution comparison for incremental attribution.
Sort ads by incremental revenue and incremental ROAS to surface ads that drove revenue that wouldn't have occurred without the ad.
Take the top ads and produce variations—either by re-generating with an AI tool using the winning ad as input, or by manually tweaking them.
Make iterations a 'decent swing': in the presenter's framing, an iteration today would have qualified as a wholly new ad in old-school Facebook—not just changing one word in the headline.
Feed each new iteration round into the pack-based testing structure as a new pack.
caveats: Incremental attribution requires proper account setup and interpretation; verify current column-set options in Ads Manager.
Incremental ROAS is more reliable than relevance scores or impressions from the public ad library.
cards.source_name: The Best AI Ad Creative Strategy for 2026.docx

cards.title: What 'Good' AI Ad Output Looks Like
cards.summary: Judge AI ad output by whether it maps to a named, proven angle or format—not by raw volume produced.
cards.use_when: You are reviewing a batch of AI-generated static or video ad concepts and deciding which to run and which to discard.
steps: Check each output for an explicit concept/angle label and an 'inspired by' reference to a proven competitor or your own winning ad.
Flag outputs you personally dislike (the presenter skipped a generic 'lifestyle in kitchen' concept) and either discard them or regenerate variants.
Reformat as needed: a 4x5 concept can be regenerated to 9x16 with one click in the cited tool.
Prefer concepts tied to demonstrated winners—e.g., formats proven in the brand's own ad account or widely used across the niche (GLP-1 'New Bestie,' iPhone Notes, '60 ingredients, one gummy').
Use a starter prompt library ('expert library' prompts like 'winning ad iteration' or 'top of funnel creative testing') to standardize high-quality inputs across the team.
caveats: Specific formats named are examples from the source's niche (supplements), not universal winners; adapt angle to your category.
Tool prompt libraries and format-conversion buttons are tool-specific; verify they exist in your current tool.
cards.source_name: The Best AI Ad Creative Strategy for 2026.docx

cards.title: Source winning ad concepts from competitors' longest-running ads
cards.summary: Find proven creative concepts by scanning the Facebook Ad Library or a tool like Magic Brief for competitors' longest-running, highest-spend ads.
cards.use_when: You need new ad concepts to test for your store and are deciding where to source creative inspiration.
steps: Open Facebook Ad Library, click 'All Ads,' and search each of your most relevant competitors by page name. Set active status to 'All' so paused ads also appear, since some competitors run ads across multiple pages.

Identify ads that have been live the longest or spent the most. Source advice: avoid anything marked 'low impression count' since that signals it is not performing, and scroll to ads that have run for the longest time period.

Optionally use a paid tool like Magic Brief (verify current name/interface) to view an aggregate of a competitor's active ads across pages and to filter more easily. The free Ad Library route requires searching each page separately.
Treat each long-running ad as a distinct concept, not a template to copy identically. Note it and plan to extrapolate dozens of variations for your own products.
Build a collection spanning formats — videos, statics, GIFs, carousels — and look for common threads that repeat across multiple competitors in your category.
Pick comparison brands one or two steps above your own size (e.g., if you do $1M, study a $10M brand), not category giants, so their concepts are achievable for your budget and catalog.
caveats: The source says not to compare a small brand to Lululemon or Nike; oversized benchmarks distort what is realistic.
Ad Library may split a competitor's activity across several pages, so results can be incomplete.
Longevity and spend are proxies for performance, not proof of profitability.
cards.source_name: The Best Facebook Ad Creative Strategy for 2026.docx

cards.title: Recreate competitor concepts as your own catalog variations
cards.summary: Turn a competitor's winning concept into a large batch of on-brand iterations across your own products rather than a single copy.
cards.use_when: You have identified a competitor ad that has run a long time and want to convert it into testable creative for your store's catalog.
steps: Take the winning competitor concept and re-shoot or re-design it with your product and brand assets — do not reuse their files.

If it is a proven concept, rebuild it for every applicable product in your catalog, not just one SKU. The source example: recreate a Lululemon carousel for a competing athleisure brand for each product.

Produce dozens of distinct variations per concept rather than copying your own best-performing ad. The source stresses new concepts, iterations, and variations as three different things, matching current Meta/Andromeda algorithmic behavior.
Spread the variations across formats the competitor used (video, static, GIF, carousel) to test concept and format simultaneously.
Keep a running concept library so each new ad maps to a known concept rather than being ad-hoc.
caveats: The source frames this as increasing win rate versus mass-producing low-quality UGC; volume alone is not the goal.
Copying creative too literally risks brand and legal issues — treat competitor ads as inspiration for the concept, not assets to clone.
Source advice is presenter opinion on how current Meta delivery works and may change with platform updates.
cards.source_name: The Best Facebook Ad Creative Strategy for 2026.docx

cards.title: Launch new ads as isolated 'packs' inside a prospecting CBO campaign
cards.summary: Group each batch of new creatives into its own ad set in a CBO prospecting campaign so new concepts compete with each other on the same budget.
cards.use_when: You are setting up campaign structure to test a new batch of creative concepts and deciding how to organize ad sets.
steps: Run all new creative inside one prospecting CBO (campaign budget optimization) campaign so the algorithm allocates across ad sets.
Every time you have a batch of new creatives, put them into a brand-new ad set — a 'pack' — rather than adding them to an existing ad set.
Batch 4 to 8 creatives per pack as the source's stated sweet spot, though anywhere from 1 to 15 is workable. Keep it simple rather than over-engineering.
Expect many ad sets over time — the source example shows a brand running past 'Broadpack 76' after continuous testing.
Do not treat the pack structure as fixed forever; the source notes nuances exist depending on product, category, and business setup.
caveats: The source is describing Meta's CBO prospecting setup as of this recording; verify current campaign options in Ads Manager.
Grouping by product or category instead of all-at-once is presented as a legitimate alternative, not an error.
cards.source_name: The Best Facebook Ad Creative Strategy for 2026.docx

cards.title: Force early spend on new ads with a 1x-CPA ad set minimum
cards.summary: Set an ad set minimum daily spend equal to 1x your target CPA for 7 days to prevent new creatives from starving behind older winning ads.
cards.use_when: New ad sets are getting almost no delivery because older ads hog the budget, and you need to test them quickly.
steps: In Ads Manager, go to the ad set's Budget & Schedule section and click 'Ad set spending limits.'
Choose 'Set a minimum or maximum,' switch the percent value to a dollar value, and enter an average daily minimum equal to 1x your target cost per acquisition (e.g., target CPA of $50 → $50 minimum).
Keep the minimum on for a maximum of 7 days at a time. Set a calendar reminder or alarm so you actually return to review it — the source says these never stay on longer than 7 days.

After 7 days, decide per ad set: if the creative is spending above the minimum, leave it running (a winner will keep spending above the floor even if you remove it); if it is only spending at the floor, remove the minimum so it drops spend, or kill it.
Reassess and reapply for the next pack of new creatives.
caveats: The 1x-CPA and 7-day limits are the source's specific heuristics, not platform-enforced rules or universal benchmarks.
If you keep the minimum on a losing ad set it will continue spending at that level — most cases the source advises against keeping it.
This forces spend; it does not guarantee the correct audience or creative quality.
cards.source_name: The Best Facebook Ad Creative Strategy for 2026.docx

cards.title: Analyze winners with incremental attribution and a spend/ROAS threshold
cards.summary: Review ad performance using incremental attribution, sort by spend, and flag high-spend ads that beat your brand's ROAS threshold as iteration candidates.
cards.use_when: You are running the analysis step of a creative testing cycle and deciding which ads to iterate or scale.
steps: In the prospecting campaign, open the column set, go to Compare Attribution Settings, and select incremental attribution.
Sort the account by highest spend to lowest spend. The source notes you may instead break the view into groups by product or category depending on your business.

Identify ads that are simultaneously high-spend, above your brand's incremental ROAS threshold, and showing outsized results on that spend. The example brand required an incremental ROAS above ~1.1 for new customers; a standout ad spent $26k (over 25% of campaign spend) at 1.46.
Do not touch ads sitting right at the threshold (e.g., 1.13–1.16 in the example) — leave them for now.
Take the true standouts and feed them back into the flywheel as concepts to duplicate, vary, and iterate.
Set your threshold from your own economics — the source explicitly notes low threshold figures sound crazy but reflect what that brand can function at.
caveats: The 1.1 threshold, $26k spend, and 1.46 ROAS are one brand's example, not a benchmark to copy.
Incremental attribution differs from standard reported ROAS; compare like-for-like before judging.
Source is presenter opinion on how analysis should work under current Meta reporting.
cards.source_name: The Best Facebook Ad Creative Strategy for 2026.docx

cards.title: Iterate off your own winners to complete the creative flywheel
cards.summary: Duplicate, vary, and merge your best-performing ads the same way you do competitors, feeding results back into continuous testing.
cards.use_when: You have identified high-spend, above-threshold winning ads and want to extend their life and solidify core concepts.
steps: Take each winning ad and create duplicates, variants, and new iterations, exactly as you would when mining competitor concepts.
Create merged concepts by combining two proven concepts (the source example: concept A + concept B → concept C).
Build variant families: reuse one winning concept across collections, swapping products, model shots, or the in-between repeated shots while keeping the simple headline structure.
Run the loop continuously: source concepts → launch packs → wait → analyze incremental performance → iterate winners → source again.
As the account grows, do not fear increasing spend or re-entering the learning phase — the source frames this system as a growth engine, not a maintenance system.
caveats: Iterating indefinitely on one concept can saturate over time; the flywheel is meant to keep new concepts entering alongside iterations.
The source's examples (brand 'Talentless' running a concept for a year) are illustrations, not guaranteed outcomes.
cards.source_name: The Best Facebook Ad Creative Strategy for 2026.docx

cards.title: Judge ads by total profit across concepts, not a single top ROAS
cards.summary: Run a portfolio of concepts where profitable high-spend and lower-spend winners coexist, rather than chasing only the highest ROAS ad.
cards.use_when: You are deciding which ad concepts to keep, scale, or cut based on ROAS versus spend capacity.
steps: Map each concept's return rate against how much it can actually spend — a target 2x ROAS concept might spend $10k, a 3x concept $3k, a 10x concept only $500, and a 2.2x concept $50k.

Instead of running only the highest-ROAS ad (the source calls this 'old school' thinking versus current Meta behavior), keep every concept that is profitable at its spend level, because each adds profit.
Prioritize total contribution to your bank account over the headline ROAS number — the source argues you should care less about a 5x versus a 2x as long as the 2x is profitable.
Match each concept to the audiences it performs with best; concepts perform at different rates per audience.
Use this view when allocating budget across packs and deciding which concepts to iterate further.
caveats: Profitability depends on your true margins and costs, not on the ROAS the ad platform reports.
The specific 2x/3x/10x/$500/$50k figures are illustrative examples from the source, not benchmarks.
Presenter opinion: the 'focus on all profitable concepts' stance is current as of this recording and may shift with Meta delivery changes.
cards.source_name: The Best Facebook Ad Creative Strategy for 2026.docx

cards.title: Build a predictable creative machine instead of duplicating old ads
cards.summary: Replace ad-hoc creative production (duplicate winners or mass-produce UGC) with a repeatable system that raises the win rate of new concepts.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to keep pumping out volume-based creative or invest in a structured creative production and testing workflow.
steps: Move away from the legacy workflow of thinking of an idea, making ads similar to past ones, uploading as single image or video, and manually writing primary text, headlines, and descriptions each time.
Define the flywheel as four linked stages: source new concepts (mostly from competitors), launch new ads in isolated packs, wait through the forced-spend window, analyze incremental performance.
Feed winning ads back as new concepts to iterate, keeping concepts, iterations, and variations as distinct outputs.
Use creator, in-house or AI-assisted production to execute researched concepts; do not substitute invented customer experiences for genuine UGC.
Treat creative iteration and testing as a standing capability the account runs continuously, similar to how the source says its team runs it across 100+ brands.
caveats: The source's results across its brand roster are its own, not a promised outcome.
System requires sustained iteration and monitoring; it is not a one-time launch.
Promotional content about the source's paid community is excluded from this card.
cards.source_name: The Best Facebook Ad Creative Strategy for 2026.docx

cards.title: The 33% Rule for Creative Sourcing
cards.summary: Split ad creative production roughly into thirds across in-house, UGC creator army, and AI so volume, authenticity and control are all covered.
cards.use_when: Planning monthly creative production volume for a Meta ad account and deciding where the next batch of ads should come from.
steps: Allocate about one third of creatives to in-house content: self-filmed and self-designed videos and statics explaining the product, founder story, or brand point of view. Fast to control, typically ~30 minutes per asset, but not infinitely scalable.

Allocate about one third to UGC from a creator army: mass-seeded creators producing authentic testimonial, unboxing, review and problem-solution videos. High volume and trust, but 1-4 weeks lead time per batch due to shipping, creator schedules and posting.

Allocate about one third to AI-generated creatives (tools like Higgsfield, Imaginative, Foreplay to clone or produce statics). Source describes costs of a few dollars per creative and minutes of production time, making it the fastest lever for testing angles — but weaker on trust if the audience detects AI.
Do not run only one pillar. The source's stated reason to run all three is that each contributes a different job (testing speed, volume/authenticity, brand trust) and any single pillar leaves a gap.
Track which pillar each asset came from so you can see which format or angle source is actually producing winners and shift sample budget accordingly.
caveats: The 33/33/33 split is the source's recommendation (credited to one advertiser's $600M+ spend experience), not a measured optimum — treat as a starting heuristic.
AI creative costs and tool capabilities change quickly; verify current pricing and output quality before budgeting.
AI-generated UGC is described as not cost-efficient enough to replace real creator trust.
cards.source_name: The Best Facebook Ad Creative Strategy for 2027.docx

cards.title: Creator Army Sourcing Workflow (Sample Seeding to Ad Account)
cards.summary: Send mass creator invites, ship product samples, and require 2-3 videos per sample so you build an always-on pool of UGC for TikTok and Meta.
cards.use_when: Building or replenishing UGC ad supply for Meta and TikTok, or resetting creative volume after a launch or offer change.
steps: Send automated mass invites to TikTok creators using a seeding/automation tool. The source cites one case of 100,000 invites over 60 days leading to 6,000 onboarded creators and ~5,800 videos.
Approve interested creators and ship product samples. Note the lead time: shipping ~7 days, creator hold time, then posting — expect roughly 1-4 weeks before creatives land.
Require 2-3 videos back per sample shipped so a single product spend yields multiple assets. Source frames it as 2-3x the video-to-product ratio.
Run the videos on TikTok GMBB Max campaigns first, then migrate the winners to Meta so TikTok spend also functions as a creative testing ground.
Keep the army warm after the first wave: source describes it as a standing 'salesforce' you can re-ping for any new product launch or offer to get thousands of assets in weeks.
Operate the community on a dedicated tool (Tribe, Yuko cited) or free on Discord, with VIP incentives, to educate creators on what's working.
caveats: Creator videos may never ship; source says some creators sit on product or never post, so plan for partial return rate.
The 100k invites/6,000 creators/5,800 videos figure is one agency case study, not a benchmark.
Tribe, Yuko and similar seeding tools change frequently — verify current capabilities before committing.
cards.source_name: The Best Facebook Ad Creative Strategy for 2027.docx

cards.title: Brief Creators Wide vs Specific to Steer Winning Formats
cards.summary: Use open-ended briefs to surface new angles and specific briefs pointing at proven top ads to multiply winners you already know.
cards.use_when: Onboarding a creator army or a new batch of UGC creators and deciding what instructions to give them.
steps: Send wide briefs (product-first only) to a portion of creators. Let them interpret the product through their own story so you can discover angles you would never have scripted.

Send specific briefs to other creators: point them at your top-performing ads with real numbers (e.g., 'this ad did a 7x ROAS and $10k spend, go make ads like this') so the winning format gets reproduced.
Use a community tool (Tribe cited) to publish what's working to the whole creator base so the volume shifts toward proven formats without you managing each creator individually.

Watch for the creative signal you didn't expect. The source's ingredient-label example: a UGC creator led with a simple-ingredient-label angle the in-house team had never tested, and the client reported account ROAS moving from 1.7x to 4x — not a guaranteed result, but the reason to leave room for creator freedom.
When a UGC angle overperforms, hand it back to the in-house and AI pillars to produce more variants of that exact angle.
caveats: Outsized results like the 1.7x-to-4x case are examples from one brand's account, not typical or promised outcomes.
Over-specifying all briefs removes the discovery value of the UGC pillar.
cards.source_name: The Best Facebook Ad Creative Strategy for 2027.docx

cards.title: Map Ad Creatives to Buyer Awareness Stages
cards.summary: Break creatives into unaware, problem, solution, product and most-aware formats so Meta's algorithm can serve the right message at the right moment.
cards.use_when: Building a new ad set or auditing an existing one to see whether the creative mix covers the full buyer journey.
steps: Unaware: educational stats or founder-story hooks that name a problem the buyer hasn't recognized (e.g., a bold prevalence stat like '74% of people suffer from gut issues', or an unknown downside of a product they already use).
Problem aware: before/afters and 'did you know' feature/benefit call-outs showing what life looks like after the problem is solved, plus three-reasons-why framings.
Solution aware: us-versus-competitor comparisons and social proof (reviews, quotes, testimonial UGC) to frame your product as the pick among alternatives.
Product aware: limited-time offers, bundles, buy-one deals, and more testimonial UGC for people who have visited the site or added to cart but haven't purchased.
Most aware: very direct calls to buy, abandoned-cart reminders, final-offer framing driving straight to checkout.
Place all stages in the same ad set rather than targeting awareness stages with separate audiences — the source says Meta's Andromeda update favors this and will allocate impressions by stage.
caveats: The source attributes this structure to Meta's algorithm behavior; platform behavior changes and should be re-validated in your own account.
Some stages (like unaware educational ads) may look weak on direct ROAS but still hold a place in the funnel — the source says not to switch them off just for that.
cards.source_name: The Best Facebook Ad Creative Strategy for 2027.docx

cards.title: Test a broader creative portfolio when one format dominates spend
cards.summary: The source recommends distinct formats and angles to reduce dependence on a few winners; validate with store economics.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to iterate on a single winning ad or invest in new formats, or diagnosing sudden ROAS decay after scaling.
steps: Recognize the old pattern (source labels it '2026 strategy'): find one winning ad, then produce minor variants (new background, same format) and scale. Result per the source: nearly all spend concentrates in 1-2 creatives and, when that format fatigues, the account crashes because nothing else can absorb the budget.

Adopt the newer approach: maintain 10-15 distinct formats and angles running simultaneously — e.g., three-reasons-why, before/after, try-on videos, comparison ads, ingredient breakdowns, educational breakdowns.
Inspect spend concentration as a portfolio diagnostic, then judge purchases and contribution margin; evenly distributed spend alone is not success.
Do not immediately kill a low-ROAS creative that occupies a valid funnel stage — per the source, it still has a role in moving people down the funnel.
Recheck after scale increases. In the 2026 pattern the source describes ROAS dropping as spend rose and only holding temporarily until fatigue hit.
caveats: This is one advertiser's strategic opinion (backed by claimed 2x-10x cases, not benchmarks) — test against your own account dynamics.
The 10-15 format count and the 'spend spread' success signal are source-specific heuristics, not calculation-based thresholds.
Maintaining 10-15 distinct formats is production-intensive; do not attempt without the 33% sourcing pipeline in place.
Year labels are the source framing, not a verified platform transition or a requirement to stop hook iteration.
cards.source_name: The Best Facebook Ad Creative Strategy for 2027.docx

cards.title: Diagnosing Creative Fatigue Across the Lifetime of a Winning Ad
cards.summary: Map how ROAS responds to rising spend — variant-only campaigns decay in cycles; distinct-format portfolios hold longer.
cards.use_when: Interpreting an account whose ROAS declined after a spend increase, or forecasting whether a current creative set can absorb planned scale.
steps: Plot spend versus ROAS over time. Variant-based accounts (per the source's illustration) show ROAS falling as spend rises, briefly recovering when a fresh batch of variants launches, then dropping once the single format fatigues — a repeating cycle.
Audit the dominant creative format. If most spend sits in one or two creatives or one format family, the account has no cushion when that format expires.
Rebuild the portfolio with new, distinct formats spanning the full awareness range rather than more variants of the current winner.
Evaluate the portfolio's stability as spend increases: the source claims diversified format sets hold ROAS as spend scales, but this is a heuristic illustration, not an account-specific benchmark.
Watch for creative fatigue speed — the source claims variant-only accounts hit fatigue faster than portfolios of 10-15 distinct creatives; treat as directional, not measured.
caveats: The two curves described are conceptual diagrams from the source, not tested values; verify against your own weekly account data.
Creative fatigue depends on audience size, frequency and budget — factors the source does not quantify.
cards.source_name: The Best Facebook Ad Creative Strategy for 2027.docx

cards.title: Ad Creative Flywheel
cards.summary: Loop UGC sourcing, creator briefing, winner identification, static/AI derivation and in-house production so new creatives feed continuously into the ad account.
cards.use_when: Designing a repeatable monthly creative workflow instead of one-off creative pushes before a launch.
steps: Automate UGC sourcing: send invites, ship samples, collect videos per the creator-army workflow.
Brief creators on the script styles you need (wide briefs for discovery, specific briefs pointing to proven winners).
Wait for videos, then identify which angles and formats are actually winning by spend and results.
Tell the creator community which videos won so they can produce more like them, compounding your best formats.
Derive static and AI-generated creatives from winning UGC concepts so the winning angle multiplies across formats.
Keep the in-house pillar producing in parallel so brand-controlled assets (founder story, product film) are always entering the mix — the source positions this as the trust anchor of the loop.
Repeat as a perpetual cycle rather than a one-time campaign burst; the source's stated goal is a perpetual supply of fresh creatives for the account.
caveats: The source presents this as a strategy recommendation from an advertiser claiming 2x-10x client results — treat those as case examples, not predicted returns.
Requires real production capacity across three sources; a solo operator may only be able to run one loop at a time.
cards.source_name: The Best Facebook Ad Creative Strategy for 2027.docx

cards.title: In-House and Founder Story Creatives as the Trust Pillar
cards.summary: Keep producing self-made and founder-led video ads because they carry authenticity and brand trust the other two pillars can't, but plan for their limited scalability.
cards.use_when: Allocating production time between team-made content and creator/AI output, or deciding whether to keep running founder-story ads.
steps: Film founder and team content yourself: how the brand started, problems you had with the product or supplier, comparisons of your product versus alternatives.

Keep founder videos in rotation even if the conventional wisdom you're hearing says to lead with a brand-only account — the source explicitly disagrees with that advice and argues relatable founder stories help buyers empathize.
Use behind-the-scenes and warehouse footage that UGC and AI cannot produce, to differentiate your brand trust from competitors.

Budget for the constraint: the source notes in-house is the least scalable pillar because you or the team must personally produce each asset (roughly 30 minutes per creative on average, more with research).
Because these assets are easiest for competitors to copy, treat them as one part of the mix rather than the whole account.
caveats: The claim that founder stories are a 'greatest way to scale' is the presenter's opinion — the source says many experts advise the opposite, so treat as a situational choice.
Founder videos consume founder time; do not overcommit to a cadence you can't sustain.
cards.source_name: The Best Facebook Ad Creative Strategy for 2027.docx

cards.title: AI Creatives for Fast, Cheap Angle Testing
cards.summary: Use AI-generated statics and ads to clone proven formats and test new angles in minutes and low cost, then feed winners into the other pillars.
cards.use_when: Rapidly filling gaps in a creative format matrix or testing a batch of new angles before committing creator or in-house production time.
steps: Pick a proven or competitor static and reproduce it with an AI creative tool (sources cite Higgsfield, Imaginative, Foreplay) so you get a launch-ready asset fast.
Use AI as the discovery layer: produce many angle variants cheaply (source says a few dollars per creative) to find which hooks and claims resonate.
Use AI to fill format gaps you'd otherwise wait weeks for UGC to cover — examples the source names include three-reasons-why, educational breakdowns and ingredient breakdowns.
Recognize what AI does not replace: authentic UGC trust and founder/in-house trust. The source says audiences may detect AI and discount authenticity.
Feed AI winners back into the flywheel so in-house and creator pillars produce more of the winning angle in higher-trust formats.
caveats: AI outputs and tool capabilities change rapidly; verify current tools, costs and licensing before relying on any named product.
AI UGC video generation is described as less cost-efficient than real creator UGC in the source.
Do not rely on AI as your only pillar — the source explicitly says it lacks the trust of the other two.
cards.source_name: The Best Facebook Ad Creative Strategy for 2027.docx

cards.title: Personification: Scaling by Adding New Avatars and Use Cases
cards.summary: Once spend plateaus on one avatar, unlock new audience pockets by creating ads for entirely different buyers and use cases of the same product.
cards.use_when: High-spend accounts (source cites thousands to $10k+/day) that have saturated their primary audience and need a new scaling lever.
steps: Identify the current primary avatar (e.g., 'people who struggle to fall asleep' for a sleep gummy).
List other distinct avatars the same product solves for — e.g., people who sleep but wake up groggy; people who fall asleep fast but wake up repeatedly or to use the restroom.
Confirm each avatar is a genuinely different problem, not a rewording of the first, so creative and copy can speak to a distinct person.
Produce new ad creatives and copy for each avatar, using the awareness-stage framework within each one rather than assuming the same message works across avatars.

For products with multiple benefits, list lifestyle identities too (source cites IM8 Health examples: athletes, everyday moms who work out three days a week, busy professionals, constant travelers, gifts for a nutritionist friend).
Deploy personified creatives to expand reach once the original avatar's impressions have driven spend to a plateau.
caveats: The source frames personification as most relevant at high daily spend and notes it's a common reason brands fail to reach large scale — not a first step for small budgets.
Avatar examples and the IM8 reference are illustrative; adapt to your own product's real benefits rather than copying them.
cards.source_name: The Best Facebook Ad Creative Strategy for 2027.docx

cards.title: Awareness-Stage Ad Set Structure: Why It Belongs Inside One Ad Set
cards.summary: Place unaware, problem, solution, product and most-aware creatives in the same ad set to let Meta's algorithm match message to buyer stage rather than forcing manual stage-based targeting.
cards.use_when: Setting up or restructuring ad sets before a launch, or deciding whether to split creative formats across separate audiences.
steps: Build individual creatives, each mapped to one awareness stage per the awareness-stage card (educational/unaware, before-after/problem, comparison/solution, offer/product, direct/most-aware).
Load all of these creatives into a single ad set rather than separating them into stage-specific audiences.
Rely on the platform's algorithm (the source attributes this to Meta's Andromeda update) to serve each creative to people at the appropriate stage.
Evaluate success by whether spend is distributed across creatives of all stages; the source treats skewed spend as a signal the structure is being used incorrectly.
When adding new distinct formats, add them to the same ad set so the stage coverage stays intact.
caveats: Meta's algorithm behavior and features change — the source's claim about Andromeda favoring this structure should be validated in your own account as of your current setup.
Source does not quantify how much creative volume per ad set is optimal, nor how long to let it run before judging.
cards.source_name: The Best Facebook Ad Creative Strategy for 2027.docx

cards.title: Pillar Speeds: Turnaround Times and Why the Mix Matters
cards.summary: Each creative pillar has a different production speed and control level — AI is minutes/fast, in-house is controlled but capacity-bound, UGC is high-volume but slow to arrive.
cards.use_when: Planning in-app launch dates, accelerating creative testing, or diagnosing why creative supply can't keep up with scale.
steps: AI pillar: fastest for launching and cloning ads (source describes minutes per asset), best for covering missing formats and rapidly testing angles; least trust-bearing.

In-house pillar: roughly 30 minutes on average per creative (source notes it varies from 15-20 minutes to a few hours depending on research), gives complete control over script and message with no drift from creators or AI.
UGC pillar: 1-4 weeks per batch due to ~7 day shipping, creator hold time, and whether the creator posts at all — but yields massive volume because many creators contribute rather than a single team.
Match your launch calendar to these speeds: use AI to fill testing slots immediately, in-house for controlled brand messages, and pre-seed UGC weeks before you need it.
Treat the mix as a portfolio: each pillar's trade-off (speed, volume, trust, control) is why the source recommends running all three rather than optimising for one.
caveats: The 30-minute in-house average and 1-4 week UGC window are the source's stated estimates, not measured benchmarks.
UGC volume is variable — some creators never post, so plan for less than full expected return.
cards.source_name: The Best Facebook Ad Creative Strategy for 2027.docx

cards.title: Why Platform-First Variant Testing Forces a Find-Replace Cycle
cards.summary: Optimising solely on a single winning format creates a dependency on that creative; the source argues this forces endless re-discovery instead of durable scale.
cards.use_when: Reviewing performance data with a plan to trim creatives, or deciding whether to keep spending on non-top-performing ad formats.
steps: Audit whether creative decisions are being driven by ranking creatives by ROAS and cutting the losers — the source calls this the outdated mindset.
Check the concentration of spend: if nearly all budget sits on one or two creatives, the account is exposed when that format fatigues.
Replace the pattern: keep creatives that cover valid awareness stages even if they aren't top ROAS, because they move buyers through the funnel.
Introduce new distinct formats rather than new visual variants of the current winner.
Re-evaluate success on distribution across creatives plus overall account stability rather than simply the highest-performing single ad.
caveats: The source does not give numeric kill or keep thresholds — deciding when a low-ROAS creative is genuinely dead rather than stage-supporting requires your own account data.

Cutting non-Roas winners is often correct at the level of a specific placement or budget constraint; the source's point is specifically about preservation for funnel coverage, not never cutting anything.
cards.source_name: The Best Facebook Ad Creative Strategy for 2027.docx

cards.title: Ad Creative Funnel Stages with Concrete Format Examples
cards.summary: Use specific creative formats to move buyers from unaware through most-aware, covering education, proof, offers and direct CTAs.
cards.use_when: Writing the creative brief list for a new campaign or filling gaps in an existing funnel format matrix.
steps: Unaware: educational stats ('74% of people suffer from gut issues'), founder origin stories, and reframing down-sides of things buyers already do (e.g., GLP-1 side effects).
Problem: before/after imagery showing the after-state, feature call-outs ('this gummy supports glow, healthier skin, fixes gut issues'), three-reasons-why framings.
Solution: us-versus-them comparison ads, quote-based social proof, testimonial-based UGC from creators who have used the product over time.
Product: limited-time offers, buy-one offers, bundle offers, plus further testimonial UGC to convert site visitors and cart abandoners.
Most aware: direct response ads ('you left this in your cart, here's the final offer, buy now') sending viewers straight to checkout.
Brief these formats distinctly — do not just restyle one winning ad across all stages.
caveats: The example stats, product types and formats are illustrative from the source; substitute your own product facts rather than copying claims.
The list is not exhaustive — creators should be free to propose new formats the source doesn't mention.
cards.source_name: The Best Facebook Ad Creative Strategy for 2027.docx

cards.title: Evaluating Whether a Creative Portfolio Is Structurally Healthy
cards.summary: Read spend distribution across creatives as the health signal for portfolio-based creative strategy, and correct structure when spend skews to one or two assets.
cards.use_when: Weekly creative review in a scaling ad account to decide whether to cut, keep or add creatives.
steps: Pull spend by creative and check whether budget is levelled across many creatives or concentrated in one to three — the former is the source's stated sign that the structure is working.
If skewed, don't jump to killing the non-spenders: check whether each format covers a distinct awareness stage and whether the skew is caused by trimming/iteration decisions.
Add distinct new formats when creative types overlap, since the source attributes over-concentration to too many variants of one format.
Keep low-ROAS stage-supporting creatives in place unless they demonstrably contribute nothing across multiple reporting windows — the source claims every creative has a place in the funnel.
Scale spend only after spend distribution is levelled; source claims spread-heavy accounts hold ROAS as budget grows and spread-thin accounts don't.
caveats: 'Levelled spend' is not accompanied by a numeric threshold — the source gives it as a qualitative signal, so use your own judgment on acceptable concentration.
Some accounts legitimately concentrate spend because of narrow targeting or product-stage — check before restructuring.
cards.source_name: The Best Facebook Ad Creative Strategy for 2027.docx

cards.title: Use clear product personas and angles as creative targeting hypotheses
cards.summary: The source prioritizes creative relevance over granular audience work; test this emphasis against store results.
cards.use_when: Planning a Meta ad account structure and deciding how much effort to put into interest/lookalike targeting versus creative production.
steps: State the intended shopper, product need and buying angle in the creative brief so copy and visuals send a coherent message.
Test broader targeting against the account baseline when appropriate; do not discard useful audience controls solely on the source algorithm description.
Instead, encode your target persona and angle directly into the creative concept so the algorithm has explicit signals for who should receive the ad.
Audit your existing adsets to confirm each one carries a clear, consistent audience signal rather than relying on a manually configured interest selection.
Reallocate planning time from audience-list building toward producing more distinct creative concepts, since creative now drives audience selection and reach.
caveats: This reflects the source's description of Meta's Andromeda behavior; verify current platform mechanics as they change.
The source account of internal algorithm behavior is not independently verified here and does not establish that interests or lookalikes are obsolete.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Creative Similarity Score and Its Reach Penalty
cards.summary: Andromeda bundles visually or thematically similar creatives under one entity ID, forcing them to compete for the same audience and inflating frequency while depressing ROAS.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing rising frequency, flat or falling ROAS, and shrinking unique reach across a Meta ad account.
steps: Recognize that when creatives look or feel similar, Andromeda groups them under a single entity ID and serves them to the same audience cluster.
Treat clustered creatives as a red flag: they restrict unique reach, drive frequency up, and degrade ROAS as the same people see near-identical ads.
When you see frequency climbing and unique reach stalling, assume creative similarity is the cause before blaming audiences or budget.
Deliberately diversify visual style, concept, angle, and format across ads to reduce similarity, rather than producing iterative variations of one winner.
Periodically review your ad library as a whole and ask whether a machine could easily tell your ads apart; if not, force more conceptual distance between them.
caveats: The 'Creative Similarity Score' is the source's characterization of Meta's behavior, not a metric you can directly read in Ads Manager.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Architect Adsets by Concept, Not by Arbitrary Traits
cards.summary: Consolidate creative variations into concept-specific adsets built on Persona plus Angle plus Offer to feed the algorithm clean learning signals.
cards.use_when: Setting up or restructuring Meta ad account adsets before scaling spend.
steps: Define each adset around a single coherent concept expressed as Persona + Angle + Offer, so the algorithm receives one clear signal per adset.
Do not segment adsets by arbitrary traits such as launch dates, which fragment learning without meaning.
Do not mix conflicting personas (for example men and women) inside the same adset, since conflicting signals confuse the machine learning targeting models.
Group all creative variations that share the same persona, angle, and offer into one adset rather than splitting them by minor visual differences.
Review your account's adsets for any that combine inconsistent audiences or offers and consolidate or split them so each adset carries one signal.
caveats: Some deliberate multi-persona testing structures exist; the source's rule specifically warns against mixing conflicting personas within a single adset.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Amount Spent as the Creative Performance Proxy
cards.summary: Because Meta optimizes for multi-click and view-through journeys, amount spent is a more reliable ad-level proxy for creative performance than last-click ROAS.
cards.use_when: Evaluating which top-of-funnel Meta creatives to keep, cut, or scale.
steps: Recognize that Meta optimizes ad delivery for multi-click and view-through journeys, so in-platform ad-level last-click ROAS is highly unreliable for top-of-funnel creative.
Use Amount Spent as the most reliable proxy metric for creative performance at the ad level, since Meta allocates budget toward ads it believes perform in the multi-touch sequence.
Do not kill a top-of-funnel creative solely because its ad-level last-click ROAS looks weak; correlate performance at the adset or account level instead.
Combine amount spent with your own incrementality or blended measurement to validate creative impact, rather than trusting platform-reported last-click numbers.
Apply this especially when judging prospecting creative that by design will not show strong direct last-click returns.
caveats: This distinguishes ad-level last-click ROAS from blended or incrementality-based measurement; do not read it as saying ROAS is meaningless in aggregate.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Track KPIs at Adset Level to Avoid Last-Click Flaws
cards.summary: Adset-level KPI tracking is more reliable than ad-level for creative decisions because the algorithm optimizes multi-touch paths.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to structure reporting and which creative to cut during active Meta campaigns.
steps: Set your primary creative-evaluation reporting at the adset level rather than the individual ad level.
Understand that ad-level metrics are distorted by Meta's multi-touch and view-through optimization, which credits and routes budget across a sequence rather than a single click.
Use adset-level performance to make keep-cut-scale decisions, comparing concept-level (Persona + Angle + Offer) results rather than individual ad ROAS.
Use ad-level Amount Spent as a directional signal of which creative the algorithm is favoring, not as a profit verdict.
Pair platform adset metrics with a blended or third-party measurement layer to confirm true incremental value.
caveats: Adset-level tracking still inherits platform attribution limitations; it reduces noise rather than eliminating it.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Avoid the DPA Death Spiral Masking Weak Prospecting
cards.summary: Dynamic Product Ads can inflate bottom-of-funnel retargeting ROAS while hiding poor top-of-funnel performance.
cards.use_when: Reviewing retargeting or catalog campaigns when overall performance looks strong but new-customer growth is weak.
steps: Recognize that DPAs (Dynamic Product Ads) frequently deliver high retargeting ROAS by re-engaging people already close to purchase.
Watch for the 'death spiral': strong DPA retargeting numbers masking poor top-of-funnel prospecting performance.
Separate prospecting and retargeting reporting so DPA-driven bottom-of-funnel ROAS cannot cover for weak top-of-funnel results.
Evaluate DPAs on new-customer or incremental metrics, not just blended ROAS, to see whether they are truly adding revenue or just harvesting existing demand.
If top-of-funnel acquisition is weak, fix creative and prospecting rather than leaning harder on DPAs for headline ROAS.
caveats: DPAs are not inherently bad; the risk is using them to mask weak prospecting in blended reporting.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Portfolio Scaling to Avoid Hero-Ad Dependence
cards.summary: Rely on a portfolio of recognizable creative concepts rather than a single hero ad that will hit its spend ceiling and fatigue.
cards.use_when: Scaling Meta spend and deciding whether to concentrate budget on one winner or distribute across a roster.
steps: Reject the single 'hero ad' strategy: any one ad eventually reaches its maximum daily spend capacity and fatigues.
Build a portfolio of distinct creative concepts so spend can shift as individual ads plateau.
Track which concepts are absorbing budget and continuously introduce new ones to replace fatiguing winners.
Maintain production volume high enough that new creative is always available to feed the portfolio, since scaling depends on supply of fresh concepts.
When an ad nears its ceiling, shift incremental budget to other proven concepts rather than only forcing spend into the fatiguing one.
caveats: Portfolio approaches require more creative production capacity and budget than a single-winner strategy.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: CBO and the 4/64 Pareto Spend Pattern
cards.summary: Campaign Budget Optimization exploits Pareto concentration where roughly 4% of ads command about 64% of spend, but over-concentration creates revenue risk.
cards.use_when: Setting budget distribution rules for Meta campaigns and deciding how much to let the algorithm concentrate spend.
steps: Use Campaign Budget Optimization (CBO) to let the algorithm route budget toward the best-performing ads efficiently.
Expect strong concentration: per the source's Pareto observation, roughly 4% of ads command about 64% of spend, so a small set of ads will carry most delivery.
Monitor for over-concentration, since depending on a tiny number of ads exposes the business to sudden revenue drops if those ads fatigue or break.
Keep a pipeline of back-up concepts ready so that when the top ads decline, replacements already have delivery history.
Balance CBO efficiency against risk by setting guardrails that ensure not all budget is hostage to a few ads.
caveats: The 4%/64% figure is the source's heuristic observation of spend distribution, not a guaranteed ratio.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Allocate 10-25% of Media Budget to Creative Production
cards.summary: Reserve a meaningful share of media spend for creative production, scaled to the brand's spend level, to sustain the volume needed to combat fatigue.
cards.use_when: Setting the creative production budget for a Meta advertising program.
steps: Commit a minimum allocation of 10% to 25% of total media budget directly to creative production.
Scale the percentage to spend level: per the source, allocate around 25% of media spend for brands spending $30K-$100K per month.
For brands spending over $100K per month, the source suggests scaling the creative allocation down toward 10%.
Treat the creative budget as a volume requirement, not a nice-to-have: sustained ad volume is what keeps fatigue from eroding performance.
Review creative output against this budget regularly to confirm production volume is actually matching the pace of fatigue.
caveats: The 25% and 10% figures are the source's recommended benchmarks tied to specific spend bands, not universal rules; adjust for your production model.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Sequence Ads for Multi-Click and View-Through Journeys
cards.summary: Meta optimizes for multi-touch journeys, so plan ad sequencing and evaluate performance across the journey rather than on isolated clicks.
cards.use_when: Planning ad sequencing and measuring a multi-stage Meta funnel from prospecting to conversion.
steps: Recognize that Meta's algorithm optimizes for multi-click and view-through journeys, not single-click attribution.
Plan ad sequencing so prospects see coherent messaging across exposures rather than unrelated one-off ads.
Interpret performance across the journey: an ad that generates views and later clicks may look weak at the ad level but perform in sequence.
Do not over-optimize early-funnel ads for last-click results, since that misaligns with how the algorithm sequences delivery.
Use journey-aware reporting (blended or incrementality measures) to judge whether the sequence as a whole is driving conversion.
caveats: View-through and multi-click attribution can overstate causal impact if used alone; pair with incrementality testing.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Creative-as-Targeting: Structuring Meta Ad Sets by Concept
cards.summary: Under Meta's Andromeda system the creative itself does the targeting, so each ad set should hold one concept (persona + angle + offer) rather than a mix.
cards.use_when: Setting up or restructuring Meta ad campaigns and deciding what goes inside each ad set.
steps: Accept the mechanical shift the source describes: pre-Andromeda you picked interests and loaded creatives underneath them; post-Andromeda you load creatives with broad (or no) targeting and Meta reads transcripts, copy and visuals to decide who to show them to. The creative is the targeting.

Because targeting largely lives at the ad set level, put only one concept per ad set. A concept = persona + angle + offer. If you bundle several concepts into one ad set, the ad set cannot resolve who it is for and performance degrades.
Define each ad set so its ads all call out the same kind of person, agitate the same problem and present the same argument.
Diversify across ad sets instead of within them: three ads in one ad set should talk to three different people (different concepts), not three near-identical edits of the same shoot.
Reason the source gives: unique concepts reach their own audiences, so frequency stays low on cold traffic and you can scale into colder audiences without efficiency collapsing.
Verify the current Ads Manager interface and any similarity/bundling reporting available to your account before restructuring, since Meta's tooling changes.
caveats: The source describes Andromeda behavior as of the recording; Meta's algorithm and interface change, so re-verify.
Some ad-level audience siloing exists, but the presenter argues most targeting still sits at the ad set level.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Diagnose Frequency Above 2 on Cold Ads as a Fatigue Red Flag
cards.summary: Cold-traffic ads should rarely exceed frequency 2; if they do you likely lack creative diversity or volume rather than needing a media-buying fix.
cards.use_when: Weekly or monthly ad account health check, deciding whether to produce more creative or change campaign setup.
steps: Pull the account to the ad level and filter to cold/prospecting campaigns over the last 30–60 days.
Look at frequency per cold ad. The source's rule of thumb: cold ads should almost never show frequency above 2. If they do, treat it as a red flag, not a normal condition.

If frequency is high, diagnose it as insufficient concept diversity and volume, not as a bidding or targeting problem to fix with media-buying levers. The fix is new concepts and formats entering the account.

Support the diagnosis with the source's citation of a Meta article (roughly four to five years old at time of recording) stating the probability of purchase falls sharply after about two impressions of an identical creative, but stays high when a novel creative is introduced instead.
Act by adding differentiated concepts at the ad set level and new formats, then re-check frequency after the new assets have had time to run.
caveats: The frequency-2 threshold is the presenter's heuristic for cold campaigns, not a universal rule for all account types or warm/retargeting audiences.
The referenced Meta article's exact wording and current availability should be verified.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Creative Portfolio Model: Avoid Over-Levering Into One or Two Ads
cards.summary: Spread spend across many ads rather than one or two heroes, because every creative eventually fatigues and no single ad holds unlimited spend.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much of total spend to concentrate in top-performing ads and whether to keep funding creative production.
steps: Frame the account as two scenarios at the same $1,000/day and same blended 4x: one creative holding the entire budget versus three creatives splitting it. The source prefers the three-creative version because any one ad can fatigue while the others absorb spend and maintain efficiency.
Accept the premise that every creative eventually fatigues and has a maximum spend threshold, so concentration is a delayed liability, not a win.

Watch for the pattern the source describes from client experience: brands built eight-figure businesses on a handful of creatives that held large spend, stopped producing, then faced 40%+ year-over-year declines in new customer acquisition when those ads fatigued. The source says this is typically fixable 6–8 months earlier, not at the moment of decline.
Set the operating goal as many ads holding as much spend as possible, and keep feeding the portfolio even when current winners are hitting KPI.
Allocate budget to creative production as a revenue driver, not a cost center — the source treats the creative, not the platform, as the engine and Meta as distribution.
caveats: The 4x and $1,000/day figures are illustrative, not benchmarks.
The 40% decline and 6–8 month window are case-study observations from the presenter's clients, not measured averages.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Use Amount Spent as the Ad-Level Proxy for Creative Performance
cards.summary: At the ad level judge creatives by how much spend Meta allocates to them, because in-platform ROAS at the ad level is distorted by last-click attribution.
cards.use_when: Reviewing the ad-level table in Ads Manager to decide which creatives are working.
steps: Understand that Meta optimizes distribution using multi-touch sequencing (multi-click and view), but reports ROAS on last-click. So the ad that gets credited with the purchase may only be the closer, while earlier ads did the persuasion work.

Read the ad-level ROAS column with skepticism. A 6x closer ad does not mean the 1.4x opener ad is useless — the source says turning off the low-ROAS opener destroys performance when the sequence was working.
Treat Amount Spent as the better ad-level signal: if Meta is allocating spend to a creative, it is because the system believes that creative contributes to conversions across the sequence.
Use this to avoid the mistake of killing 'underperforming' ads that are actually doing top-of-funnel work.
Verify the current Ads Manager columns and any multi-touch reporting options available, since these change.
caveats: Amount Spent is a proxy, not proof of incrementality. The source says there is no direct visibility into Meta's multi-touch sequencing.
Ad-level ROAS is not useless when you have no better data; it just should not be the primary decision metric for creative sequencing.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Measure ROAS at Ad Set and Campaign Level, Not the Ad Level
cards.summary: Reliability of ROAS improves as you move up the account structure from ad to ad set to campaign, so make optimisation decisions higher up.
cards.use_when: Deciding which level of the account to base budget and creative decisions on.
steps: Rank reliability: ad-level ROAS is the least trustworthy because of last-click attribution and multi-touch journeys; ad-set-level ROAS groups the sequenced ads and is more reliable for evaluating a concept; campaign-level ROAS on 7-day click (with existing customers excluded) is the most reliable and tends to be congruent with the P&L.
Use the ad set as your concept-level scorecard. If one concept per ad set is working at the ad-set level, you can confidently say the concept works and make more like it.

Note the caveat the source flags: some cross-ad-set serving still occurs, so one ad set can pick up bottom-of-funnel conversions generated by another. Keep concepts diversified across ad sets, and measure the overlap, to reduce this.
Make structuring and creative-introduction decisions using ad-set and campaign numbers, and use ad-level numbers only as secondary context.
caveats: Campaign-level reliability depends on 7-day click attribution and excluding existing customers; other settings change the interpretation.
Cross-ad-set overlap is possible and can make individual ad sets look better than they are.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: The Concept Framework: Persona, Angle, Offer (and Format)
cards.summary: A concept is a persona, an angle, and an offer; changing any one of the three produces genuinely different targeting.
cards.use_when: Ideating the next batch of ads or auditing whether recent ads were actually different from each other.
steps: Define concept as persona + angle + offer. Two ads only count as different concepts if at least one of these three changes.
Persona: think about who you are talking to AND who is in the ad. A 60-year-old woman in the ad versus a 20-year-old woman will reach different people even with the same product.
Angle: the problem you agitate and the argument you make. Skincare agitating wrinkles versus agitating hormonal acne reaches two different audiences with the same product.
Offer: the product itself and how value is framed (bundles, gifts with purchase, subscriptions, tiered discounts).

Add format as a fourth, weaker variable: with the same persona, angle and offer, changing format can reach some new people (e.g. people who never click UGC), but it hits largely the same audience. Rank it last.
Naming convention and ideation sheets should encode persona/angle/offer so you can see at a glance whether new ads are genuinely new concepts.
caveats: Format is the source's lowest-priority lever for novelty; do not treat a format swap as a new concept.
Some brands can make very broad unaware ads work, but the source says that requires high skill and is not needed for most accounts.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Testing Priority Order: Angle First, Then Offer, Persona, Format
cards.summary: When creative isn't working, fix angle first, then offer, then persona, and test format last.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why ads are underperforming and deciding what variable to test next.
steps: Rank the four levers in the source's order: (1) angle, (2) offer, (3) persona, (4) format. The source says most teams invert this and spend all their time testing formats.
Angle first: if you are targeting personas who already purchase from you, and they still aren't buying, the problem is message or argument. Rotate and improve the angle.

Offer second: it may be the single most important variable, but flexibility is limited. With one or two products you cannot change the product, and offer variants (bundles, gift with purchase, tiered discounts, subscriptions) eventually run out. The source warns against solving this with heavy discounts that eat margin and create discount dependence.
Persona third: it is mainly what gives you breadth and volume once angle and offer are dialled in.
Format last: 'UGC doesn't work' is the wrong lesson — the script, persona, angle and offer inside the format are what work. Same for professional photo shoots.
caveats: The source treats the ranking as a practical heuristic, not an absolute law, and notes offer is arguably the most important variable in theory.
The claim that most accounts do not need broad-audience unaware ads is the presenter's opinion based on their client experience.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Build Sharp Personas From Problems, Not Demographics
cards.summary: Use specific problem-defined archetypes rather than age/gender bands, because broad personas produce forgettable, unscalable creative.
cards.use_when: Writing creative briefs and deciding who each new ad is speaking to.
steps: Define personas as archetypes defined by problems, desires and buying triggers — not as demographics. Reject 'women 25–45' or 'busy professional' as too broad.

Sharpen to a concrete situation. Fashion example: not 'busy professional' but 'a consultant who flies twice a week and needs a carry-on wardrobe that works for boardrooms and bars'. Supplement example: not 'health-conscious parent' but 'a mom who's tried six different supplements because her toddler won't eat vegetables'.
For each persona, capture the pains, the language used to talk to them, and the proof they need. These three things determine the brief, the script, the casting and the visuals.
Expect breadth from depth: the source argues five ads for one sharp persona will beat five ads for a broad audience until you are a large eight-figure brand with the skill to run broad unaware ads.

Use age/gender only as a starting split, then immediately subdivide by the underlying problem. Acne at 20-25, acne at 30-35 (possibly hormonal) and acne at 40-45 are three distinct problems and three distinct personas.
caveats: Fair, the source is presenter opinion based on client work, not measured lift.
Ultra-broad unaware ads can work for large brands — that is a different, higher-skill play, not a contradiction.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Scale Persona Ideation Manually, Then Use LLMs to Expand
cards.summary: Do 20–40 sharp personas manually first, then use an LLM with heavy context to expand, and curate the output back down.
cards.use_when: Building a persona library for creative ideation.
steps: Spend focused manual time (the source suggests ~20 minutes of hard thinking) listing personas and the problems/desires/triggers behind each.
Take the manually built list (20–40 personas) and give it to an LLM along with as much business and target-demographic context as possible. Ask for 20–30 more.
The source warns LLMs default to averages: if you only give it three or four personas plus your website, you get a mean-reverting, generic list that everyone else also gets.
Curate the LLM output. Of ~20 generated personas, keep the four or five strongest and feed those back with a request for 10–20 more. Use this loop to roughly double the library.
Reject any persona on the list that is broad (e.g. 'women 25–45') — broad personas produce mediocre creative.
caveats: LLM persona output is starting material, not finished work; the source says curation is mandatory.
The 20–40 and 20–30 figures are the source's suggested working amounts, not measured benchmarks.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Angle Playbook: Problem Agitation, Contrarian Truth, Curiosity Gap, Proof, Comparison, Transformation
cards.summary: Assemble angles from a known set of persuasive components rather than defaulting to product features.
cards.use_when: Writing ad scripts or deciding what the next angle variant should be.
steps: Lead with pain where possible: make the viewer feel the problem and feel heard before introducing the solution. The source notes you cannot problem-agitate someone who isn't problem-aware, so this is not universal.
Contrarian truth: challenge a common belief to reframe, e.g. 'everything you've been told about X is wrong', then educate.

Curiosity gap: open with an information gap (e.g. 'here's what the top 1% of millionaires know about saving money that they don't want you to know') and delay the answer, holding attention through problem agitation and story before paying it off.

Social proof and domain authority: use proof specific to the persona and the domain — a marathon runner for a running product, a clinical study for a creatine energy claim aimed at 40–45-year-old women.
Comparison and objection handling: acknowledge what the viewer has already tried and why this works differently. UGC scripts often narrate 'I tried X, it didn't work, then I tried this'.
Transformation / before-after: the source calls it the best-performing component but the least compliant; it must be worked in so the platform doesn't flag it.
Simplify the angle into a one-sentence claim (persona → product → argument), then expand it into a script.
caveats: Before-after ads are called out as non-compliant; the source describes sneaking them in, which carries platform and policy risk — treat compliance as your responsibility.
The source says not every angle needs every component; choose elements that fit the persona's awareness level.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Write Hooks That Call Out a Real Persona With a Real Pain
cards.summary: Hooks drive persona targeting on Meta, so a badly aimed call-out pushes your ad to irrelevant people.
cards.use_when: Producing hooks and opening seconds for video ads.
steps: Understand that Meta auto-transcribes every ad and uses transcript content to find the audience. A hook that says 'if you're a business owner doing over $5M a year' will make the system hunt for that audience.
Check your hook actually matches your buyer. If the call-out names a persona that is not your audience, you have pushed distribution toward irrelevant people.
Pair the persona call-out with problem agitation. The source's most common criticism is creators call out a persona without agitating the problem, producing a weak hook.
Keep the call-out specific (see the persona card) so the system has a clear signal about who to find.
Treat hooks as one of the highest-leverage creative elements under Andromeda, alongside volume and concept diversity.
caveats: The transcription-and-targeting mechanism is the source's explanation of Andromeda behaviour and may change; verify current behaviour.
'Most ads I see are not good' is the presenter's qualitative opinion, not a measured failure rate.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Stop Confusing Creative Activity for Creative Strategy
cards.summary: Launching thousands of ads a month without quality and a point of view wastes budget and signals a misdiagnosed bottleneck.
cards.use_when: Reviewing monthly creative production volume and output quality.
steps: Check whether volume is producing scale. The source describes two accounts launching 2,000+ new ads per month that could barely hold $4M/month in spend and were unprofitable — evidence the constraint was not volume.

Diagnose which bottleneck is actually limiting you before adding more ads. Candidate creative bottlenecks the source lists: creative quality, format diversification, insufficient top-of-funnel/awareness assets, and failure to use partnership ads or other distribution unlocks.

Fix the diagnosed bottleneck rather than adding activity to a constraint you have not identified. The source's example: increasing sheer volume when the real problem was quality or funnel-stage mix does nothing.
Set a quality bar alongside volume. The source supports launching as many ads as possible but only with a quality standard and a strategy behind the batch.
caveats: The 2,000 ads/month and $4M/month figures are specific case examples, not benchmarks.
The source does not give a numeric ads-per-month target — it explicitly rejects a simple volume formula.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Include Creative Production in the Media Budget at 10–25%
cards.summary: The source recommends dedicating roughly 10–25% of media spend to creative production to sustain the volume needed against fatigue.
cards.use_when: Setting or defending the creative production budget for the coming quarter.
steps: Decide creative production as a percentage of media spend rather than a flat fee. The source's stated benchmark: about 25% of media spend for brands spending $30K–$100K per month, scaling down to about 10% for brands spending over $100K per month.
Also hold a minimum allocation of 10–25% of total media budget to creative production so you can maintain the volume required to combat ad fatigue.

Treat this as an investment in the revenue driver, not a cost to minimise. The source's argument: the creative is what drives revenue; Meta and other platforms only drive distribution, and the same creative can also earn free distribution organically.
Compare your current production spend against this band to see if you are under- or over-investing.
caveats: These percentages are the source's recommended benchmarks, not measured results; they should be adjusted to category, margin and asset types.
The bands ($30K–$100K, over $100K) are the source's stated spend brackets, not derived from an audited study.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Do Not Switch Off a Creative That Is Hitting Ad Set KPI
cards.summary: Meta sequences creatives across a purchase journey and optimises on multi-touch, so low ad-level ROAS can be the opener doing the work.
