cards.use_when: Deciding whether to pause the 'underperforming' ads in a working ad set.
steps: Before pausing, look at the ad set level. If the ad set is hitting your overall performance goal, the source says leave the creatives alone.

If you can read the creatives, infer the likely sequence: an unaware top-of-funnel asset usually opens, a product-aware asset sits in the middle, and a very bottom-of-funnel asset closes. The closer often shows the highest ad-level ROAS while the opener shows the lowest.
Recognise that Meta's optimisation is multi-click and view based, so it allocates spend to the opener knowing it contributed, while reporting all revenue to the closer under last-click.
Avoid the trap of turning off the opener because its ad-level ROAS looks weak — the source says this destroys performance.
If you cannot read the sequence from the assets, rely on the ad-set-level number rather than ad-level ROAS.
caveats: Attribution visibility into Meta's multi-touch sequencing is not available in Ads Manager, so this relies on trusting the system.
The 6x/2x/1.4x figures are illustrative examples from the source, not benchmarks.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Creative Fatigue Is Structural: Build for Obsolescence From Day One
cards.summary: Every creative has a maximum spend ceiling and will fatigue, so plan replacement before decline rather than after.
cards.use_when: Planning the creative roadmap for a scaling account and deciding how far ahead to produce.
steps: Accept as a planning premise that every creative fatigues and every creative has a maximum spend threshold — there is no permanent winner.
Treat a drop in a previously strong ad as expected, not as an anomaly, and have replacement concepts already in the account or pipeline.

Watch the failure pattern the source describes: brands hit by year-over-year new-customer declines of around 40% after building on a small number of high-spend creatives, arriving when corrective work is already 6–8 months late.
Use the portfolio approach (many ads holding spend) and the 10–25% creative production budget as the structural defences.
Benchmark per-ad spend capacity. The source cites mean ad spend per ad unit landing around $700–$1,500 depending on the account, meaning volume is needed to carry the total budget.
caveats: The $700–$1,500 average ad spend figure is the source's observation across accounts, not a universal benchmark; it will differ by account and objective.
The 40% decline and 6–8 month window are case-study observations.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Format Diversity Is Needed to Reach People Meta Won't Show Certain Formats
cards.summary: Meta suppresses formats a user does not engage with, so a single-format account cannot reach everyone.
cards.use_when: Deciding the format mix for a new batch of ads or auditing why reach has plateaued.
steps: Assume Meta learns individual format preferences and stops serving formats people do not click. The source's personal example: he never sees UGC or dynamic product ads (DPAs) in his feed because he does not click them.
If your account runs only UGC, or only UGC plus DPA, you are invisible to users like him regardless of how good the persona and angle are.
Build format variety into the account so the same concept can be delivered to people who respond to different formats.
Expect only incremental new reach from a format swap, not a breakthrough. The source ranks format fourth in the testing priority order because it does not change who the message is for.
Audit reach and frequency by format, and check the current Meta reporting interface for available format breakdowns.
caveats: The presenter's own feed experience is an anecdote, not a measured audience study.
Meta's format-serving behaviour and any DPA/format reporting change over time; verify before making firm conclusions.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Escape Interest Targeting Without Lobbing Everyone Into One Broad Bucket
cards.summary: Broad targeting works because the creative does the targeting, but weak or generic creative then gets pushed to the whole population.
cards.use_when: Setting audience targeting in Meta and writing the call-outs that steer it.
steps: Run broadly for the vast majority of accounts — the source recommends roughly 99% of people run broad, and says interest targeting has been effectively dead in their accounts for around two years.
Understand why: labelling people with an interest and serving all creatives to that label ignores the age, psychographic and behavioural nuance that actually predicts purchase.
Recognise the downside of vague creative under broad targeting. If every ad says 'hey everyone, look at this', Meta has no subset to aim at and may serve across the whole population.
Give the algorithm a clear persona signal in the creative so broad targeting still resolves to a defined audience.
Keep one concept per ad set so the ad set is not asked to serve multiple contradictory personas.
caveats: Interest targeting can still make sense in narrow situations; the source's recommendation is directional, and '99%' is the presenter's estimate.
Verify current Meta targeting options before changing account structure.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Structure Ad Sets by Concept, Not Mixed Formats
cards.summary: Build Meta campaigns with one persona-angle-offer concept per ad set so you get a real learning feedback loop instead of guesswork.
cards.use_when: When structuring a paid social account and deciding what goes in each ad set for a product launch or scaling push.
steps: Define a concept as the combination of persona, angle and offer (for example: casual male runner training sub-4-hour marathon + creatine improves long-run recovery + buy-two-get-one-free gummies).
Place all ads derived from one concept into a single ad set so that performance differences can be attributed to creative execution rather than concept confusion.
Mix and match one variable at a time across ad sets (swap the persona, then the angle, then the offer) to reach new audiences from the same core concept.
Accept that when concepts are scrambled at ad set level you cannot reliably draw conclusions from ROAS at ad level; the source states this removes any genuine learning loop.
Use the four variables (persona, angle, offer, format) as the dials you rotate to build new ad sets once a concept is validated.
caveats: The source describes this as a general structure for small-to-midsize businesses; account complexity should scale with business complexity, so large multi-SKU retailers may need more.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Write the Persona-Angle-Offer Brief Before Any Format
cards.summary: Document a detailed persona, a tailored angle and a value-framed offer as the required foundation before choosing creative formats.
cards.use_when: When briefing new ad creative and deciding what to make, before any format or production decision.
steps: Write the persona with specifics: goal (sub-4-hour marathon), gender, adjacent behavior (gym-goer), influencers they follow, and income (~$70K/yr).

Set the angle to speak directly to that persona's situation, for example creatine improves recovery specifically for long runs, which enables a 5-minute marathon-time improvement rather than a generic recovery claim.

Choose the offer against the persona's income and price perception; the source picked buy-two-get-one-free for creatine gummies partly because creatine brands are generally expensive and perceived value needed raising.
Only after persona, angle and offer are locked, select formats; the source explicitly says format is the last step, not the starting point.
Keep the brief as the reusable template so variants (different persona or angle) can be spun out without re-doing strategy.
caveats: The specific creatine example is illustrative; the source does not claim any measured result from it.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Treat the Hook as a Relevancy Promise
cards.summary: The hook's job is to promise relevance to the right viewer, not to trick anyone into watching with bait.
cards.use_when: When scripting or reviewing the first three seconds of any video ad for a product.
steps: Understand that the hook is a play towards relevancy: it tells the viewer what they are about to watch is contextual to them.
Avoid meme or bait hooks that inflate hook rate but do not convert; the source notes the source optimizes the wrong metric when doing this.
Use the three layers of the hook simultaneously: visual (what is on screen), audio (the underlying sound/voice), and copy (on-screen text or primary ad text).
Because the source cites that 80% of people never watch past the hook, treat the first three seconds as the highest-value real estate in the asset.
For ecommerce PDP/creative work, make sure the hook names the problem the product solves rather than who the viewer is.
caveats: The 80% figure is the source's stated figure for video assets, not a universal benchmark; treat as a heuristic.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Allocate Time to More Hooks, Not More Bodies
cards.summary: Spend equal production time producing more hook variations rather than more body variations because the performance delta is larger in hooks.
cards.use_when: When budgeting creative production time for a batch of video ads and deciding how many hooks versus bodies to shoot.
steps: Compare two options: one hour making two hooks and five bodies, versus one hour making two bodies and fifteen hooks.
Choose the higher-hook option, based on the source's view that the available performance delta is normally larger in the hook than the body, assuming good scripting on the bodies.
When recording, shoot the same body once but record the hook six (or more) times; the extra time is a few minutes.
Apply the same logic to existing winners: re-record new hooks onto an already-performing body rather than rebuilding the whole asset.
Only lean into hook volume once script quality on the body is genuinely good, otherwise a lucky body script will distort your read on what actually worked.
caveats: The source explicitly qualifies this: if scripting quality is poor, one good body script can misrepresent the true impact of the hook.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Grade a Hook on Five Criteria
cards.summary: Score hooks on clarity, relevance, novelty, specificity and credibility, needing only a few done well rather than all five.
cards.use_when: When reviewing or approving a batch of ad hooks before launching them.
steps: Clarity: can a stranger understand what you're talking about within the first three seconds? Avoid confusion-as-hook tactics.

Relevance: make the problem agitation relevant to the viewer rather than using persona call-outs; the source states persona call-outs are overrated because people don't want to hear themselves called out.
Novelty: ask 'has this hook been done a million times?' If yes, don't do it; use novelty to create white space, though it is not a requirement.
Specificity: use numbers, names, or quantified outcomes early (e.g. a percentage, a timeframe) to build authority.
Credibility: usually delivered through the visual (a trusted figure or contextually relevant person appearing at the start), not through copy or audio.
Accept hooks scoring well on just a couple of these as viable; the source says you don't need 10/10 on all.
caveats: The source's claim that persona call-outs underperform is stated as personal experience and opinion, not a measured benchmark.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Nine Practitioner Hook Types to Deploy on Ecommerce Ads
cards.summary: A menu of hook archetypes to rotate into product ad creative, each with its awareness-stage fit.
cards.use_when: When generating hook concepts for a product's ad batch and needing variety that still converts.
steps: Problem agitation: lead with the pain the viewer already feels (e.g. 'are you struggling with back pain from desk work?'); works only on problem-aware audiences, not above that stage.
Contrarian truth: challenge a common assumption (e.g. 'everything you've been told about protein timing is wrong'); works across awareness levels and in organic and paid.
Specific proof: lead with a measurable outcome, number or timeframe to build authority.
Curiosity gap: create an information gap only closed by watching; the source notes this hook held average view time over 45 seconds in their organic content.

Truth bomb: lead with an uncomfortable truth about price, ingredients or industry (e.g. 'this product costs $120... it's our best seller'); works well for premium or high-AOV products where price is the main objection.
Psychological confrontation: direct, pattern-interrupting statement that feels like a friend calling you out.
Texture/ASMR hook: 2-3 seconds of fabric handled, product squeezed, liquid poured or packaging opened, no words needed; reportedly strong in fashion.
Founder's letter: open with the founder's origin story and real stakes (e.g. remortgaged and put $300,000 into first inventory); only real circumstances work.
Social proof: lead with a credibility marker (e.g. '90% of customers saw results in 30 days').
caveats: The source says roughly seven of the nine usually apply to any given brand; pick the ones that fit.
Curiosity-gap and founder-stakes effectiveness are the source's stated experience, not universal benchmarks.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Bridge Smoothly from Hook to Body
cards.summary: The transition between hook, body and CTA must blend product introduction, not jump abruptly, or the whole asset fails.
cards.use_when: When scripting the segues in a video ad between the opening, the education and the call to action.
steps: Identify the two critical bridges: hook-to-body and body-to-CTA.
Avoid the abrupt version: hooking with a problem then jumping straight to 'well, [brand]'s product is your solution'. The source states this ad won't perform.
Blend product introduction progressively so viewers slowly become aware they're being sold to, rather than a step-change from education to sales pitch.
Move the viewer through awareness stages across the asset (unaware → problem-aware → solution-aware → product-aware) so the transition feels earned.
Apply this on PDP/landing-page video too: don't introduce the product in the first beat before the problem is established.
caveats: The source calls this largely intuitive; it gives the principle rather than a formula.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Introduce the Product Late in Top-of-Funnel Assets
cards.summary: Delaying product introduction and CTA produces higher-intent, higher-converting viewers even though fewer reach that point.
cards.use_when: When scripting a VSL-style or long-form video ad and deciding where to place the product reveal and CTA.
steps: Move people through awareness stages before introducing the product: hook the unaware, then problem-aware, then solution-aware, then product-aware.
Resist the temptation to introduce the product before the 90-second mark just because most viewers drop off early; the source argues this logic is wrong.
Recognize that introducing earlier means more total people see the product, but they are lower intent, so total purchase volume can still be worse.
Use VSL (video sales letter) formats for products requiring education, since their length allows you to teach through the asset.
On a static ad with long-form copy, use the copy to pull readers through the same awareness stages, ending at the product.
caveats: The source frames this as a general principle for top-of-funnel unaware ads; the exact placement is context-dependent.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Hook Testing Still Works Post-Andromeda
cards.summary: Test new openings as low-cost refinements of existing product-ad concepts and measure their purchase impact.
cards.use_when: When deciding whether to invest in hook variation under Meta's Andromeda-era diversity expectations.
steps: Create hook variants while keeping the body stable. A changed opening does not by itself prove that delivery will reach a new audience.
Accept overlap risk: because most of the body is identical, the concept is the same, so treat hook swaps as refinements of one concept, not new concepts.
Do it because the effort is nearly free: recording hooks six times takes minutes.

Revive fatigued winners: the source reports ads that spent $50,000-$100,000 then fatigued, and rotating 50 new hooks yielded another $100,000 of spend at the same efficiency from roughly one hour of shooting.
Revive losers with a bad hook rate by fixing only the hook, keeping the rest of the asset.
Treat hooks as the highest-leverage point across video, organic and YouTube, per the source.
caveats: The $50k-$100k figures are the source's own case examples, not guaranteed results.
Andromeda behavior may change; verify current platform behavior.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Five Questions Before Choosing an Ad Format
cards.summary: Decide format last, after concept, education needs, single-frame communicability, demo needs and awareness stage.
cards.use_when: When selecting whether a concept becomes a static, carousel, UGC video or long-form asset.
steps: Define the concept first (persona, angle, offer) and only then pick the format; the source states format is the last step, never the starting point.
Ask whether the concept requires education: if yes, lean to a longer-form asset that can teach.
Ask whether the value proposition can be communicated in a single frame: if yes, prefer statics, carousels or other cheap-to-produce assets.
Ask whether the product needs a demo: if yes, that pushes toward video unless you have a strong designer.
Match format to awareness stage: higher awareness often needs a longer teaching format; lower awareness can use DPAs and statics with bottom-of-funnel ads.
Rebuttal the belief that statics are only bottom-of-funnel; the source states top-of-funnel statics are possible and that the belief is a skill issue.
caveats: The source's claims about statics doing top-of-funnel are its own position, not a platform guarantee.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Use Cost of Production Versus Contribution Margin to Choose Statics or Video
cards.summary: Compare per-ad production cost against expected contribution margin to decide how heavily to invest in statics versus video.
cards.use_when: When budgeting creative production across image and video formats for an ad account.
steps: Calculate average revenue per ad put into the account; the source cites roughly $2,000 as typical for many accounts.
Convert this to contribution margin per ad unit by subtracting gross profit and the cost of serving the ad (the source's example: ~$350 per ad unit).
Compare against the cost of producing each ad; if production cost exceeds contribution margin, the equation doesn't work.

Delineate by format: e.g. images costing ~$50 to produce earning ~$300, versus video costing ~$500 earning ~$400, meaning images have a better cost-to-contribution ratio even though videos may perform better in absolute terms.
If statics win on this ratio, double down on them; the source states some operators run $200,000/day on AI images alone.
Use statics both to test angles/concepts for fast feedback and as a scalable format in their own right.
caveats: Figures are the source's illustrative examples, not universal benchmarks; recalculate with your own margin and production costs.
The $200,000/day AI-image example is a stated example, not a promise.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Use Long-Form-Copy Static Ads for Older Audiences
cards.summary: Long-form-copy statics move unaware viewers through awareness stages and reportedly perform well for 50+ audiences.
cards.use_when: When targeting a 50+ demographic on Facebook feeds and creative needs to educate an unaware audience.
steps: Write a long-form story that starts with the unaware audience and pulls them into problem-aware, solution-aware, then product-aware.
Keep the copy emotionally attuned to the specific target demographic; the source warns that AI assistance alone won't work without copywriting fundamentals.
Consider the 'advertorial' static structure: problem agitation targeting a very wide symptom set (e.g. dry eyes, low energy, bad skin, bleeding gums), then education on the cause, then product.
Reinforce the organic feel by running through a non-brand profile (whitelisting/partnership-style) so viewers don't immediately recognize it as an ad.
If using an advertorial funnel, educate heavily on the landing page or in the primary text to make the format work.
caveats: Optimize placement for older demographics on Facebook feeds; this format is the source's stated fit, not a rule for all audiences.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Build Advertorials With Ranked Lists and a Funnel
cards.summary: An advertorial static driving to a ranked-review article with an only-clickable winner can convert cold traffic via quiz funnel.
cards.use_when: When designing an educational landing funnel that feels like third-party editorial rather than an ad.
steps: Frame the headline around a list (e.g. 'the best hair growth products of 2025 and the ones to avoid') to signal education, not sales.
Run it through an authoritative profile (e.g. a dermatologist's page) and open with the author's authority and mission.
Rank multiple products with reasoning, but make only the chosen product clickable; the others either aren't clickable or route to affiliate links.
Route the clickable product to a custom landing page that pushes into a quiz funnel, then to conversion.
Use checkmark comparisons (mostly green ticks, one/differentiation negative) to reinforce the recommended product.
Only make this work if you can genuinely write emotionally attuned copy that pulls people through awareness stages; the source warns this is where copywriting skill matters most.
caveats: Requires genuine copywriting skill; AI assistance alone is described as insufficient.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Use VSSLs for Education-Heavy Products
cards.summary: Video sales letters educate through the full awareness ladder and reportedly pair well with AI-assisted production for cold audiences.
cards.use_when: When a product requires significant education before purchase and you're building a top-of-funnel video asset.
steps: Open with a persona call-out or objection-handling UGC to hook (the source notes one VSSL ad running 3-4 years with 25M views).
Handle the common objection or 'usual fix' first, then agitate the problem and open a curiosity gap.
Educate step by step: explain the mechanism, then introduce the product as the solution containing those mechanisms.
Avoid contrast negation scripting ('it's not X, it's Y'); the source flags it as an AI-script tell and says to cut it.
Add social proof (e.g. clinical trial stat) toward the end.
Consider AI VSSLs end-to-end; the source states they can perform well and some hold hundreds of thousands in spend.
If bridging from education to product too abruptly, extend by ~15 seconds to educate on the ingredients/mechanism before naming the product.
caveats: The 25M views / 3-4 years and 'hundreds of thousands in spend' figures are the source's cited examples, not guarantees.
Source says the VSSL format fits older demographics; not universal.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Understand Incremental Attribution Before Trusting DPA ROAS
cards.summary: Meta's incremental attribution reveals that DPA ROAS is often much lower on new audiences than the platform default shows.
cards.use_when: When evaluating DPA (dynamic product ad) performance and deciding whether to scale or pull budget.
steps: Recognize that dynamic product ads dynamically pull products the user has already visited, so default ROAS is heavily inflated by existing-customer retargeting.
Delineate existing customers out of the ROAS figure first; the source states it drops precipitously.
In Meta, use the columns button, switch attribution settings to incremental attribution, and review the incremental ROAS split.

Understand the mechanism: Meta holds out ~10% of users daily as a control group, compares conversion rates (e.g. 1% control vs 2% treated) and applies a difference-in-difference calculation, yielding the true incremental lift (1%).
Apply this to any high-ROAS DPA figure; the source gives an example where a 5 ROAS DPA should be adjusted down by ~50% to 2.5 incremental.
Conclude that DPA is generally not a highly scalable cold-audience type; the source says it can spend $1,000/day in some accounts, but not $50,000/day on cold audiences.
caveats: The 10% holdout and the difference-in-difference figures are the source's simplified explanation; actual platform mechanics may vary.
Source says it has never seen an account where DPA is a great scalable cold-audience ad type — this is its observation, not a universal law.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Budget by Creative Volume: 70-90% Top of Funnel
cards.summary: Allocate creative production toward top-of-funnel assets because modern consolidation means budget follows asset volume.
cards.use_when: When deciding how many top- versus bottom-of-funnel assets to produce for an ad account.
steps: Use the rough split the source gives for budget allocation: 70-90% top of funnel, ~20% middle of funnel, 5-10% bottom of funnel.
Recognize that campaign-structure budget separation is largely gone; budget allocation now comes from the volume of assets you produce at each stage.
Therefore allocate 70-90% of the volume of assets you make to high-awareness stages and about 20% to middle/bottom-of-funnel stages.
Protect the funnel: moving too much budget to bottom-of-funnel DPAs depletes the quantity of top-of-funnel users and can topple the whole funnel, declining overall ROAS.
Avoid overspending on DPAs just because their attributed ROAS looks strong.
caveats: These percentages are the source's stated rough split; the source notes there is a more precise bottom-of-funnel budget calculation it covers later.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Run Partnership (Whitelisting) Ads to Borrow Creator Audience Data
cards.summary: Partnership ads run through the creator's profile, using both handles' audience for targeting and feeling more authentic.
cards.use_when: When looking for a scalable, authentic-feeling acquisition ad type that leverages a creator's audience.
steps: Set up the ad to run through the creator's profile rather than the brand's, displaying one or both handles.
Use a setting that allows combinations (brand only, creator only, or both) so Meta split-tests the best mix.
Understand the mechanism: these use the audience data from both handles, so a contextually relevant creator's audience helps fuel cold targeting well beyond warm retargeting.
Pick a creator who is genuinely contextually relevant to your target demographic.
Expect a more authentic feel than standard brand ads, reducing the 'I'm being sold to' reaction.
The source reports some accounts running up to 40% of total ad spend through partnership/collaborator ads; not running them is described as a disadvantage.
caveats: The source warns the arbitrage window may be closing, so verify current effectiveness before over-committing.
The 40% figure is a source-stated example, not a benchmark.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Size Your Concept Test by Hit Rate
cards.summary: Launch at least 10 ads per new concept and scale volume to your account's actual hit rate to expect a winner.
cards.use_when: When testing a new concept and deciding how many ad variations to produce.
steps: Define the hypothesis explicitly: what exactly are you testing (generally the concept, especially one of the four variables: persona, angle, offer, format).
Build the full set of ads under that concept; a common mistake is building one, two or three ads and calling it a test.
The source states most accounts have a ~5% hit rate, so a new concept needs at least 20 ads to expect a winner mathematically.
Set a working floor of 10+ ads for a proper concept test rather than the arbitrary 3.
Launch into your structured testing campaign with concepts at adset level.
Analyze against the hypothesis: expected spend, expected conversions, expected ROI versus actuals.
If it worked, apply scaling strategies; then iterate, with iteration speed increasing as ad spend grows.
caveats: The 5% hit rate is the source's stated typical figure; measure your own account and adjust required volume accordingly.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Set Minimum Ads per Ad Set and Protect Working Learning Phases
cards.summary: Launch a minimum of three ads per ad set, and only inject new ads into underperforming ad sets, not winners.
cards.use_when: When deciding whether to add new ads to an existing ad set or spin up a new one.
steps: Set a floor of at least three ads per concept ad set; the upper limit is basically open and scale-dependent (the source cites 50-100 as a practical ceiling).
Recognize that adding new ads resets the learning phase to some degree because creative sequencing gets disrupted and Meta relearns spend distribution.
If an ad set is hitting KPI and scaling well, do not inject new ads; the source reports learning this the hard way after breaking sequencing on a winner.
If an ad set is underperforming its KPI, you can freely add ads, turn ads off, and restructure; breaking non-working sequencing is acceptable.
When adding genuinely new creative to a healthy concept, prefer launching a new ad set rather than modifying the existing winner.
caveats: The 50-100 upper ceiling is described loosely as 'kind of the sky based on spend'; adjust to account scale.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Don't reset the learning phase on a winning ad set
cards.summary: Protect performing ad sets from new-ad injections that reset sequencing and redistribute spend; only disrupt underperformers.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to add new ads into an ad set or campaign that is already hitting your KPI on Meta
steps: Check whether the ad set/campaign is hitting its KPI before touching it.

If it is hitting KPI, do not inject new ads into that ad set. Adding ads resets the learning phase and disrupts the sequencing Meta uses to distribute spend across existing creative, which risks breaking performance.
If it is missing KPI badly, treat it as open season: turn ads off, add as many new ads as you want. The source's reasoning is that a broken sequence is worth breaking because it isn't working anyway.

When you want more variations of a winning concept, do NOT pile them into the winning ad set. Build a separate ad set named for the same concept (e.g. 'concept one shoot two') so you can filter that they belong to one concept while keeping the original ad set untouched.
For the winning concept itself, scale by increasing budget rather than switching it off. The source calls turning off a winner to relaunch it in a scaling campaign a rookie mistake.
caveats: Source states this from personal experience of breaking a performing ad set years earlier.
The sequencing mechanic and learning-phase behaviour are Meta-specific and can change as the algorithm changes.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Amount spent as the top creative performance proxy
cards.summary: Rank creative by amount spent first, then roROAS/CPA, then CPC and CTR, then video hook and hold rates as diagnostics.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a creative report to decide which ads to keep, iterate, scale or kill
steps: Rank metrics in this reliability order: (1) amount spent, (2) roROAS or CPA, (3) CPC and CTR, (4) hook rate and hold rate for video.

Treat amount spent as the best proxy over extended periods because Meta sequences spend across ads and attribution goes only to the last ad. An ad with lower roROAS but double the spend of others is likely driving purchases elsewhere in the account and may be your top-funnel standout.
Check roROAS or CPA using 7-day click or incremental attribution to avoid last-click distortion.

Use CPC/CTR as a leading indicator, especially at the fringes. If your average CPC is around a threshold (the source uses a $3 CPC example) and no ad above it has ever been profitable, you can predict very-early-spend ads will never work because traffic is too expensive.

Use hook rate (people past 3 seconds) and hold rate (people past 15 seconds, though the source tracks several definitions) only as diagnostic tools for video. They don't correlate to conversion, but a bad hook rate tells you to swap the hook; a bad hold rate points at the bridge or body.
Combine metrics rather than relying on one before deciding to kill or iterate.
caveats: Hook and hold rate definitions vary; the source uses multiple definitions in their own reporting.
Thresholds like a $3 CPC are account averages, not universal benchmarks.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: CBO vs ABO is a risk-tolerance choice
cards.summary: CBO concentrates spend into few ads for higher ROI but more fatigue risk; ABO spreads spend to de-risk and manage product portfolios.
cards.use_when: Choosing campaign budget structure for a store, especially when running multiple products or when efficiency targets change
steps: Understand the mechanics: with CBO, the campaign distributes budget itself and Pareto's principle compounds — roughly 4% of ads can hold about 64% of total spend and revenue in the source's ad account breakdowns.
Accept the CBO trade-off: likely higher efficiency/ROI but higher risk. If those few ads fatigue, you have no backups.
Choose CBO if you need a quick efficiency spike and don't care about de-risking or testing right now.
Choose ABO-style manual control if you want a lower-risk steady state, more ads and products working, and protection against a single fatigue event.
For stores with a large product portfolio, avoid putting all products under one CBO, because spend concentrates into a few products (Pareto applies at product level too) and skews your assortment.
Note the source's own preference: they lean toward the lower-risk structure most of the time but switch to CBO in periods where efficiency has to come now, then return to a de-risked steady state.
caveats: The 80/20 and 4%/64% figures come from the source's own ad account data, not a universal guarantee.
Agencies are often KPI'd on efficiency and profit, which biases them toward CBO and toward squeezing winners short-term.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Shift creative mix from desire-led to pain-point-led
cards.summary: Retailers built on campaign shoots skew to desire-led creative; move the mix toward pain-point assets for performance.
cards.use_when: Auditing the creative mix for a fashion, retail or lifestyle store whose account was built from campaign photography
steps: Review your current ad account through a desire-vs-pain lens: count assets that build desire (models, aspirational shots that make people want the product) versus assets that address a customer pain point.
Recognise the source of the skew: campaign shoots only build desire and don't play to pain points at all, so accounts built on them become heavily desire-weighted.

Use the source's recommended target ratio as a starting heuristic: shift toward 60/40 pain-to-desire, with the strongest brands closer to 70/30, treating desire-led assets as the branding-driven portion and pain-led as performance-marketing assets.
Translate this ratio into your next shoot plan: brief additional concepts that open on a concrete customer frustration rather than a look.
The source's rule of thumb: the best performance marketing assets are the ones that sit on pain.
caveats: Ratios are the source's opinion/heuristic for the brands they audit, not an experimentally proven benchmark.
This is aimed particularly at nine-figure large retailers in the source's market; smaller brands may need different mixes.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Build bottom-of-funnel ads around buyer objections
cards.summary: Map why non-buyers didn't convert by objection type and produce retargeting creative that handles each one.
cards.use_when: Designing retargeting/BOF creative for a store with an established conversion rate
steps: Start from the maths: at a 5% site conversion rate, 95% didn't buy. List the likely reasons rather than assuming one cause.
Break the non-buyers into objection buckets. The source's example mix: ~20% price, ~20% brand trust, ~20% product quality, ~20% simply not ready yet.

Match creative to each objection: for price, show discounts, value anchoring, or cost-per-use angles (e.g. compare a supplement to the price of a coffee for the same caffeine). For brand trust, use social proof — customer counts, five-star review counts, UGC testimonials. For quality doubts, use UGC of the product in use, before/afters and demonstrations. For 'too soon', stay present with educational or lifestyle content.
Build your BOF asset mix proportionally to whichever objections actually dominate; the source treats objection handling as the primary purpose of a product ad in BOF retargeting.
Repeat the exercise for common high-volume product categories from your order data to make the objection mix accurate.
caveats: The percentages are illustrative examples from the source, not measured distributions in your account.
Price objection buyers may convert later on promotion, not at full price.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Volume beats everything only above a quality bar
cards.summary: Prioritise volume, then concept quality, hook strength, editing, UGC talent and storytelling — but only once each ad clears a minimum quality bar.
cards.use_when: Setting the output target and quality standard for your creative pipeline for a store's paid social programme
steps: Rank production priorities in this order: volume first, then concept quality, then hook strength, then editing quality, then UGC talent, then storytelling.
Define what a 7/10 ad looks like for your store: a documented bar covering concept elements, hook elements, and format matched to the stage of awareness.

Judge future ads against that bar. The source's claim is that among ads above the bar, even 10 top creative strategists cannot reliably pick the winner, so don't burn effort trying to predict the top 1%; just produce more ads that clear the bar.
Avoid 'junk volume': the source describes brands pushing thousands of ads a month that lack good concept, hook or awareness-matched format — the volume was real but under the bar.
Reinvest effort continuously into understanding and raising the minimum bar, then maximising volume above it.
caveats: The 7/10 bar is the source's analogy, not a formal rubric.
'Volume matters most' can be misread as licence to ship low-quality ads; the source explicitly warns against that.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Two ways to size monthly creative volume
cards.summary: Simple rule: one new ad per $1k monthly spend; better method: back-propagate from new-customer revenue target divided by average expected revenue per ad.
cards.use_when: Setting how many new ads your store needs to produce this month
steps: Quick estimate: produce one new ad per $1,000 of monthly ad spend (e.g. 30k/mo = 30 ads, 50k/mo = 50 ads). The source gives this in AUD and says it translates roughly fine to USD.
Better method: calculate average spend per ad. If you launched 500 ads and spent $500,000 over the last year, each ad averaged $1,000 spent.
Find average return per ad: either acquisition MER (new customer revenue / ad spend) or roROAS on a 7-day click basis. At roROAS 3 and $1,000 mean spend, expected revenue per ad is $3,000.
Back-propagate from target: divide your monthly new customer revenue target by expected revenue per ad. A $300k new-customer-revenue target ÷ $3,000 = 100 creatives per month.
Flex volume with the forecast through the year: as your expected new-customer revenue changes, creative volume should track the same shape.

Account for two gaps in the simple model: average time for an ad to earn its revenue (if it takes 4 months, required volume must be much higher), and the split between winners and losers (100 losing ads generate almost nothing; 100 winners can generate millions). Forecast winners and losers separately and layer the time component in.
caveats: The $1k-per-ad rule is a rough heuristic, not a precision forecast.
The detailed model requires your own historical spend, return and timing data to be meaningful.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Set creative production budget as a share of media spend by scale
cards.summary: 4–30k/mo spend: founder-led, time not money; 30–100k: ~25% of media budget to production; 100k+: asymptote to ~10%.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much of the paid social budget to allocate to creative production at your current spend level
steps: At 4–30k/month spend: run founder-led content and statics. Production budget is your time, not cash — the source says statics and founder-led video can get you to 30k/month spend without paid production. The founder should be creating it so they learn the ideation, scripting and editing process and can then KPI and train others.

At 30–100k/month: allocate about 25% of media budget to production (100k/month = 25k/month on creative). The source notes this is far more than most brands spend and is a stated reason many brands fail to scale.
Expect this range to feel uncomfortable — production cost is high relative to the business and feels off, but it democratises at scale.
Above 100k/month: let the percentage fall to around 10% of media budget. As a share of revenue, at 25% MER, 10% of media budget equals roughly 2.5% of total revenue.
Spend that allocation on diversity: UGC, partnership ads, an in-house or part-time static designer, and possibly a low-cost agency for another creative type such as VSSLs.
caveats: Percentages are the source's recommendations from agency practice, not measured industry standards.
Founder-led production at low spend requires genuine founder involvement; outsourcing without learning the craft undercuts the stated benefit.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Treat production spend as a revenue driver, not a cost centre
cards.summary: Case example: a 350k/mo brand stuck at 15 ads refused production spend; reworking old winners lifted results, but fatigue eventually reversed them.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to shift a slice of media budget into creative production on a high-spend, low-creative-volume store
steps: Diagnose the bottleneck before optimising media buying: the source describes a brand spending 350k/month with only ~15 live ads, where the media buyer over-segmented into ~25 campaigns and experimented with big caps and cost caps to squeeze those 15 ads, because there was nothing to work with creatively.
First response used here: relaunch and rework old performers still available in the account, taking 15 ads to about 60 without any new creative production.

That alone reportedly raised spend ~40k/month, cut CAC 20–30% and grew new-customer revenue ~28% — but the founder saw Meta spend as revenue-driving and production as a cost centre and refused further production.

Model the reallocation before deciding: the source proposed moving $10k/month from media to production to buy about 40 assets (some hook swaps, some statics) at an agency, roughly doubling active ads, and estimated this would unlock at least a 5% efficiency improvement. On 350k spend, 5% is about 17.5k, so either drop 17.5k of spend (having spent 10k, net ~7k gain) or keep spend flat and gain incremental revenue — at their then-3x return, an extra 40–50k/month.
Watch for the downside: when no new creative arrives, the 60 ads fatigue, ads get turned off, spend redistributes away and the account drifts back toward its previous level.
caveats: All figures come from one client case study and are examples, not promises.
The source's own agency proposed the reallocation, so the recommendation and the case study are not independent.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Test bulk creative and hook variants via Instagram trial reels
cards.summary: Post ads as trial reels with the CTA cut off to read viral reach and retention graphs before spending in Ads Manager.
cards.use_when: Validating a batch of new hooks or rough cuts cheaply before loading them into a paid account
steps: Take V1 of an asset and post it as a trial reel from the business or personal page, cutting the in-app CTA off the end.
Read two outputs: comparative reach (does the post travel at all relative to other trial reels) and the retention graph, which shows whether the drop-off is in the hook, bridge or body.

Use this before perfection: if captions or other details still need a round-2 fix, post V1 as a trial reel while round two is being edited, and gather feedback within about 24 hours before the final asset exists.

Use it especially for hook testing at volume: post ~20 hook variations as trial reels, see which retain best, and put only the top ~5 into the ad account instead of paying to test all 20. The source says they do this on all of their own ads.
caveats: The source frames this as tactical and time-sensitive ('as of April 2026') and says it may stop applying as algorithms change. Verify the current trial reel interface before relying on it.
Retention and reach metrics are diagnostics, not proof of conversion performance.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Understand total spend capacity and shape the fatigue curve
cards.summary: Every ad has a finite lifetime spend capacity; you can shape the curve to squeeze short-term cash or let high performers breathe longer.
cards.use_when: Deciding how hard to push a winning ad given inventory position, cash conversion cycle and growth rate
steps: Plot the ad's daily spend over time: spend rises as Meta distributes budget (or you raise it), plateaus around a maximum daily spend limit, then fatigues and gets pulled down or turned off. The area under that curve is the ad's total spend capacity.
Accept the two rules: every ad has a total spend capacity, and every ad will fatigue and eventually be turned off.

Choose the curve deliberately. Squeeze option: take the ad to a high daily budget to sell through inventory fast, accepting earlier fatigue and degraded MER. Breathe option: hold the ad at a low daily budget like $100 and aim for months of life rather than weeks.

Choose squeeze when you have inventory that must sell through this month for the P&L position; choose breathe when inventory is short, replenishment is pending, or growth is outrunning your cash conversion cycle.

Give whoever runs your account the wider business context (inventory, cash, growth) — the source warns an agency sees a winner and squeezes it to produce a strong 30–90 day case study and good roROAS reporting, which can ruin long-term account and inventory stability.
caveats: The source is describing agency incentives that may not apply to in-house teams or aligned agencies.
Full derivative modelling of the curve is approximate; use it as a directional decision tool.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Diagnose the two causes of creative fatigue
cards.summary: Fatigue comes from the ad itself going stale or from pushing too much spend through too small an audience.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why a previously strong ad is losing spend and deciding whether to iterate it or change targeting breadth
steps: Cause one — the ad is stale: it has reached maximum spend capacity, or it repeats the same visuals, concepts and value propositions targeting the same audience as other creatives in the account, which accelerates fatigue. Fix by rotating hooks, changing format, or introducing genuinely different concepts.

Cause two — the audience is too small: a highly specific persona has a maximum daily spend capacity you cannot exceed without driving frequency and wrecking profitability. Example used: creatine for men running sub-4-hour marathons, or in B2B, e-commerce CFOs in Australia running $100m+ businesses — only about 1,000–2,000 people, so $10k/day would hit each of them hundreds of times.

Estimate each persona's spend capacity and park spend there, rotating creative so you can keep hitting the audience as it churns (e.g. people enter a marathon-training audience, run their race, and leave; new people keep entering).

Scale further by widening the callout, not by over-spending on the narrow one: broadening from 'CFO of $100m+ e-commerce business' to 'e-commerce founders earning over 100k' dramatically increases daily spend capacity — but the source warns against going broad reflexively, because broader callouts force you to make better creative that resonates with more people.
Treat the sequencing as: highly specific persona callouts that raise creative quality first, then move broader once you hit scale.
caveats: The source states good top-of-funnel unaware ads are very hard and most brands shouldn't attempt them below roughly $50m+ scale.
Audience-size estimates in the examples are rough figures, not researched counts.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Four tactical responses once an ad fatigues
cards.summary: Iterate hooks, move to a cost cap campaign, duplicate ad sets (not recommended), port post IDs to a scaling campaign, or rotate formats.
cards.use_when: Choosing what to do with a fatigued ad instead of simply killing it
steps: Lead with iteration: take a hero ad that has started to fatigue and rotate new hooks onto it to extract more spend from the same asset.

Optionally move the ad into a cost cap campaign to pull more spend through it. The source says this works but fatigues the creative faster and is a short-term media buying tactic that won't materially change the business.
Duplicate ad sets: the source explicitly does not recommend this, calls it too tacky, and says it worked in the past but not now. Include only if you already believe it works.
Move the post ID of the creative into another campaign such as a scaling campaign so it keeps existing engagement. The source says this sometimes works but won't save the account.

Rotate formats as a variation of iteration: translate a strong video into a static, a strong VSSL into UGC, or a strong image into an unaware long-form copy static — the source notes these are quite different strategies.
Accept that these tactics only squeeze a little more from the back end of a creative. The real answer is the portfolio approach: have other performing ads to fall back on.
caveats: The source ranks duplicate ad sets as not recommended and scaling-campaign moves as unreliable.
None of these extend a creative's core capacity; they delay the turn-off.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Run media buying as portfolio and inventory management
cards.summary: Above ~50k/month, the media buyer's job is diversifying risk across ads and products and aligning the ad account with commercial objectives, not just maximising profit.
cards.use_when: Reviewing agency or media buyer performance against your actual commercial position (inventory, cash, sell-through)
steps: Above about 50k/month spend, treat the media buyer's core job as portfolio management across ads and products, aligning commercial objectives with what the ad account is doing.
Decide whether you want Pareto concentration in the account or whether to force against it structurally so you're not over-leveraged on a handful of ads. Run the same decision at product level.

Consider the P&L vs balance sheet trade-off: agencies optimise to maximum profit and efficiency because that's what they're KPI'd on, which can mean failing to sell through inventory. The source's example: a business with $2m profit on the P&L and $3m of unsold inventory on the balance sheet is negative $1m in cash.

If you're in that position, restructure the account to sell through stock even though returns and efficiency won't be optimal and you'll have to make creative around that stock — the source frames it as a hard pill that rebalances the business.
Make sure whoever runs your media is across your inventory position; the source states plainly that if the media buyer isn't across inventory, that isn't good.
caveats: The ~50k/month threshold is the source's heuristic.
Optimising for sell-through can visibly worsen reported efficiency, so expectations need to be set with whoever owns the P&L.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Split production effort across replication, iteration and net-new
cards.summary: Prioritise reproduction of winners most heavily, then iteration on near-misses, then net-new concepts — roughly 50–60/20–30/20–30.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to point your creative team's production hours each month
steps: Classify each planned asset into one of three types. Winning content replication: repeat or lightly rework assets that already worked (hook iterations, format translations, reposting strong organic). The source calls this by far the highest-impact content type for both paid and organic — reposting proven assets reaches new audiences repeatedly. Iterative content: fix underperformers via hook or format changes, or take a working concept to a new persona or a new offer. Net-new concepts: entirely new formats, angles and concepts.
Allocate roughly 50–60% of effort to replication, 20–30% to iteration and 20–30% to net-new, adjusting for performance and risk profile.
Do not allocate 0% to net-new: everything up the chain eventually fatigues and falls off, so new concepts must keep flowing up to feed replication.

Correct for your own bias: the source admits their organic content runs about 80–90% net-new and only 10–20% replication, and that replication consistently holds around 80% of views — evidence of overallocation to net-new.
caveats: The percentage split is the source's general recommendation and explicitly changes by business context.
The 80%-of-views figure is from the source's own organic content, not a universal result.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Brief creators properly and vet them via their prior briefs
cards.summary: Creator output quality is a product of your brief quality; vet creators by comparing past work to the brief behind it.
cards.use_when: Sourcing UGC creators or briefing in-house video for a store's ad scripts
steps: Before hiring, collect examples of the creator's past output — the source calls skipping this self-evidently bad.

Also request the brief behind each example. Comparing output against brief tells you how much scaffolding they need: if they produced something excellent from a terrible brief, you can send broad strokes; if the brief was extremely in-depth, you should match that level of detail.
Write the highest-quality, most in-depth brief you can for the highest output quality.
Don't force script adherence: ask for one take held to the script and one that feels more natural, then choose the better or run both.

Check regional fit separately: creators must be native to the market you're targeting. The source says an Australian accent translated into the US market underperforms, US creatives need native US accents, and UK-to-AU translates decently but native still wins. The script can be identical — only the local creator changes.
If you also post organic content that performs well, reuse it rather than only producing new material, since repeated posts reach people who haven't seen them.
caveats: The accent/market guidance is the source's observation from their own account experience, not a researched benchmark.
An in-depth brief is recommended but must be paired with a creator who can execute it.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Where AI helps and hurts in the creative pipeline
cards.summary: Automate briefing/scripting and production heavily with AI, keep human judgement in ideation and analysis.
cards.use_when: Deciding which creative workflow steps to hand to AI for a store's ad production
steps: Map the pipeline: ideation → briefing → production → publishing → analysis feeding back into ideation.

Do not automate ideation. The source's reasoning is that LLMs converge on the same outputs, so no amount of context, documentation, Reddit scraping or custom skills produces ideas differentiated from competitors. A creative strategist still has to validate concepting here.

Automate briefing and script writing heavily. Build a branded AI skill that walks through a questionnaire — who is the persona, what's the concept, what's the offer, long form or short, which stage of awareness — and outputs a brief or script said to be 99% of the way there, needing a ~1% tweak.
Automate production as far as the format allows. The source says VSSLs and static image ads can be about 90% AI-produced, and AI is native to the video editor role more broadly.

Be careful with AI in analysis: it won't respect your metric hierarchy and won't weight account structure or commercial context properly. The source says they use it in analysis but that it misses often and can actively point you in the wrong direction if used for core decisions.
The principle: skip automating the outer ends of the pipeline and maximise throughput in the middle (briefing and production).
caveats: The '99% there' and '90% AI' figures are the source's experience, not measured benchmarks.
The statement that LLM ideation always converges on the same output is the source's opinion at time of recording and may change as tools evolve.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Hire and incentivise a creative strategist
cards.summary: Creative strategy is primarily copywriting; source candidates from copywriters, other brands, or promote designers/editors, and consider a 3%-of-ad-spend variable.
cards.use_when: Building or restructuring the production team behind a store's paid social creative
steps: Fill three core roles: a video editor for video ads (AI-native strongly preferred, since it unlocks more assets and footage that doesn't yet exist), a designer for statics (both roles can be global, part-time outcome-based contractors or full-time), and a creative strategist.

Look for the strategist in this order: copywriters, because creative strategy is primarily copywriting — writing scripts, writing static briefs, ideating new personas — and LLMs have made the drafting part of copywriting less scarce, so the ideation is the valuable part. Alternatively, poach an existing creative strategist or backfill from your designer or video editor, which shortens the feedback loop because the same person can ideate, design and brief edits.
Understand the workflow you're hiring into: the strategist brings ideas and moves them into a branded AI skill that outputs the actual script for production.

Consider a variable component tied to results: the source describes paying creative strategists roughly 3% of ad spend based on the creatives they produce and brief, so they're directly incentivised to maximise hit rates.

Judge the model by scale: the source reports this works well on mid-size brands, but at very large spend a strategist could earn around $80,000 a month, at which point the model breaks and brands move away from it.
caveats: The 3% and $80,000/month figures are the source's observations of a practice, not standard rates.
The source notes creative strategist is a new role with few experienced candidates in market.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Start organic content before paid for small stores
cards.summary: Organic forces you to learn what content people actually watch, which compounds into paid creative quality.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a small or early-stage store should invest in organic before or alongside Meta spend
steps: Run the source's recommendation for smaller founders: post organically every single day and get good at identifying what good content looks like, rather than assuming paid comes first.
Watch what actually gains views and study retention graphs plus share and save rates — these teach you what holds attention.

The stated reason isn't that organic outperforms paid, but that organic forces you to become good at creative, and that skill compounds into paid ads when you know how to make content people want to watch.
Where you reuse organic output in paid, favour repetition of proven pieces: repeat the same content over and over, because every repetition reaches a new audience and tends to perform similarly.
Pair this with format discipline: identify the awareness stage of the piece and match the format to it, then move validated concepts from statics into video.
caveats: This is the source's forward-looking recommendation for 2026–2027, not a measured result.
Daily posting requires sustained founder or team time; it is a discipline commitment rather than a shortcut.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Meta Creative Team & Production Benchmarks by Monthly Ad Spend
cards.summary: Stage-gated playbook for how many creators, concepts and new assets to run at 4–30k, 30–100k and 100k+ monthly Meta spend.
cards.use_when: You're setting the creative org, output volume and budget split for your store's Meta ad program and need a scale-appropriate structure rather than copying a big brand's setup.
steps: At 4–30k/month: founders shoot the content themselves, an iPhone is fine, and you aim for a natural look. Limit yourself to three core concepts done well — the leverage is in script quality, not concept count. Allocate a high proportion to testing — roughly 60–80% of budget — because you lack the spend to scale winners yet. Use trial reels as a cheap way to validate ideas before committing production.

At 30–100k/month: bring on two to three UGC creators, direct about 25% of spend to production, expand to five to six concepts to start de-risking, and produce roughly 30–100 new creatives per month. Add a scaling campaign and begin introducing partnership (whitelisted/creator) ads.

At 100k+/month: stand up a full creative team — a scripter, an editor, four to six creators and a designer (part-time is acceptable). Commit a minimum of ~10% of ad budget to creative, run 8–10 active concepts, and produce at least 100 new assets per month (the source's rule of thumb of roughly $1k of spend per ad).
The source's framing: at 100k+ the thing you're actually buying is a system that outputs creative continuously — without it, creative becomes the permanent bottleneck.
caveats: These spend bands and ratios are the presenter's heuristics, not measured benchmarks — recalibrate against your own account.
The 100-assets figure is explicitly derived from a 'basic $1k per ad' formula, so it scales with spend rather than being a fixed target.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Splitting Production Budget Between Iteration and Net-New Concepts
cards.summary: Put most production money into iterating proven creative rather than designing brand-new concepts, because iteration drives the majority of performance.
cards.use_when: You're allocating a paid-social production budget or briefing a creator/editor team on what to make next month.
steps: In the production budget, deliberately weight the majority toward iteration on concepts that have already shown signal (new hooks, new opens, different angles on the same idea) rather than net-new concept design.
Treat net-new concepts as the smaller share — they seed the pipeline, but the source states iteration is what drives most performance.
Operationalise this by keeping a roster of proven concepts and versioning them (swapping the hook, the first three seconds, the visual treatment) before spending on fresh ideas.
Pair this with the stage-appropriate concept count so you don't spread iteration too thin across too many parent ideas.
caveats: This is the source's stated allocation principle; the exact split is not given as a hard number, so treat 'majority' as directional.
Requires a feedback loop — if you aren't tracking which ads are winning, you can't know what to iterate on.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Tracking Cost-per-Asset and Per-Ad ROI to Justify Creative Spend
cards.summary: Build a financial model that tracks cost per creative asset by source and profit contribution per ad, so you can tell whether each content type is worth producing.
cards.use_when: You're deciding whether to keep or cut a creator, agency or content format, or need to defend creative budget to a founder or CFO.
steps: Stand up a financial model that records cost per asset broken out by source (which creator, which agency, which internal team produced it).
Pair that with average profit contribution per ad from that source, so you can compare whether a more expensive creator's content actually earns its cost back.
Evaluate estimated contribution after product and variable order costs, media spend and allocated production costs. Media spend divided by production cost is not ROI.
Use the output to shift budget toward content sources whose cost per asset is justified by profit contribution, and away from ones that aren't.
This is presented as the 100k+/month standard, but the same logic can be applied at smaller scale with simpler tracking.
caveats: Attribution of profit to a single ad is inherently noisy; treat per-ad ROI as directional.
Requires discipline in tagging production costs to the assets they produced — without that tagging the model is meaningless.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Trial Reels and Partnership Ads as Cheap Creative Validation Levers
cards.summary: Use platform-native validation hacks — trial reels at small spend, partnership/whitelisted ads at scaling spend — to de-risk creative before heavy investment.
cards.use_when: You're at the top of a creative testing cycle and want to know which concepts or creator partnerships are worth scaling before committing full budget.
steps: At the 4–30k/month stage, use trial reels as a low-cost way to validate a concept before putting real production or media budget behind it.

At the 30–100k/month stage, begin introducing partnership (creator/whitelisted) ads as a way to branch out and de-risk — you're leveraging the creator's handle and audience rather than only your own account.
Route validated winners out of the trial/partnership layer and into your scaling campaign.
Keep the validation layer running continuously so you always have a pipeline of pre-vetted concepts feeding the scaling campaign.
caveats: Trial reels and partnership-ad features change over time — verify the current interface and eligibility rules in Meta Ads Manager before relying on them.
Validation performance on trial placements may not perfectly predict performance at scale.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Letting Creative Volume, Not Pre-Optimisation, Reveal What Good Looks Like
cards.summary: You cannot know what winning creative looks like in advance — build the volume loop (concepts, scripts, ads in account, feedback) and let the data define good.
cards.use_when: You're tempted to over-plan creative before launching, or you're deciding how much to invest up front in perfecting scripts and concepts.
steps: Accept the source's claim that for most advertisers creative is the binding constraint on Meta — media buying is no longer where the leverage is.
Instead of trying to predict winners, build the loop: generate concepts, script them, get ads into the account, read the feedback, and iterate.
Use your stage-appropriate concept and asset counts (three concepts at small spend, five to six mid, eight to ten at scale) as the input to that loop, not as a one-time launch exercise.
Protect the volume: the bottleneck at scale is almost always whether the creative machine keeps producing, not whether any single ad is perfect.
If you find yourself constantly scrambling for creative, treat that as the diagnosis that the production system — not the individual ad — is what needs fixing.
caveats: 'Volume solves it' is the presenter's opinion; quality and concept relevance still matter, and low-quality volume burns budget.
Small accounts have limited spend, so volume must be matched to the testing allocation (60–80% at 4–30k/month) rather than maximised blindly.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Two-Format Creative System: Top-of-Funnel Problem/Solution and Bottom-of-Funnel Objection Ads
cards.summary: Build only extreme top-of-funnel problem-solution ads and extreme bottom-of-funnel objection ads, letting middle-funnel coverage happen naturally.
cards.use_when: Deciding what creative concepts to brief for a paid social campaign, so you stop wasting production budget on vague middle-funnel ads.
steps: Split all creative into two formats: top-of-funnel problem/solution ads and bottom-of-funnel objection-handling ads.

For top-of-funnel, address the core problem the avatar has and position your product as the unique solution. Problems can be functional (back pain) or identity/emotional (clothing makes you feel cool, part of something).
For bottom-of-funnel, make one ad per objection (price vs. competitor, warranty/expiration, delivery speed, quality doubt). Show one specific proof point per ad rather than dumping all benefits.
Accept that longer, hook-heavy top-of-funnel ads will naturally bleed into the middle of the funnel; shorter or simpler versions of either format cover the middle-bottom gap.
Do not build dedicated middle-funnel creative unless you have a specific reason.
Run catalog/DPA retargeting to anyone who viewed similar products as the non-creative bottom-of-funnel layer.
caveats: The source presents this as the currently working approach in the 'Andromeda era'; funnel economics shift as platform algorithms change.
Skipping middle-funnel creative is a deliberate trade-off relying on natural spillover; some categories with long consideration cycles may need explicit middle creative.
cards.source_name: The ONLY 2 Ad Creative Formats You Need to Scale Facebook Ads.docx

cards.title: Creative Hit Rate: Measure Winning Ads Instead of Total Ads Launched
cards.summary: Define a creative hit rate as winning ads divided by total ads launched, and scale creative volume only when hit rate quality is maintained.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether to increase ad production volume, or auditing why a high-volume creative testing program is underperforming.
steps: Define a 'high-performing ad' upfront using two criteria: it spent more than 5% of total campaign budget AND hit your target CPA.
Calculate hit rate = (number of high-performing ads) / (total ads launched) × 100.

Interpret it: launching 100 ads with 5 winning ads is a 5% hit rate, described by the source as a solid, fairly normal benchmark. Volume negates luck, so 1,000 ads at the same hit rate implies ~50 winners.
Before producing more ads, ask whether each new ad has a genuine chance to be a winner. Only scale volume if the baseline quality holds.
When volume rises but hit rate falls, treat that as a signal you are diluting quality, not scaling.
caveats: The 5%-spend threshold and 5% hit rate are the source's own definitions and heuristics, not industry standards.
Increasing volume only compounds if hit rate is stable; otherwise you multiply low-quality spend.
cards.source_name: The ONLY 2 Ad Creative Formats You Need to Scale Facebook Ads.docx

cards.title: Avoid Flooding the Pixel With Low-Quality Creative That Creates Negative Events
cards.summary: Understand that Meta's pixel and delivery train on all traffic including non-converters, so unqualified clicks actively degrade targeting.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to bulk-upload thousands of AI/UGC ads, or diagnosing declining account performance despite rising spend.
steps: Recognize the mechanism: the pixel fires, sends signal events to Meta, and delivery optimizes based on the purchase event to find similar buyers at lower CPA.
Understand that the pixel also trains on negative events — bounces, carts not converted, unqualified traffic — not just purchases.
Realize that flooding an account with thousands of low-quality ads disperses budget and generates negative events that mis-train the pixel and degrade targeting accuracy.
Before scaling creative count, vet each ad for its likelihood of attracting the right avatar; reject ads likely to pull unqualified clicks even if they are cheap to produce.
Treat the pixel's recent event stream as a quality signal to protect, not just a volume number to grow.
caveats: This is the source's explanation of Meta pixel training, not a documented platform spec; algorithm behavior changes and should be re-verified in the current interface.
The source does not provide a quantified threshold for how many negative events cause harm.
cards.source_name: The ONLY 2 Ad Creative Formats You Need to Scale Facebook Ads.docx

cards.title: Avatar-and-Angle Framework for Top-of-Funnel Concepts
cards.summary: Turn one avatar's full list of problems into ad angles, then pair each angle with the avatar to form a top-of-funnel concept.
cards.use_when: Generating top-of-funnel ad concepts and creative briefs for a product, especially when stuck for angles.
steps: Define one avatar (your ICP) at a time — the specific person you are selling to.
List every problem that avatar has, including problems not obviously related to your product; each problem becomes a potential ad angle.
Combine one avatar with one angle to create a concept/packaged ad.
Write ads that explicitly call out the avatar and their problem, then position your product as the solution.

Note the source's claim that the algorithm tends to show ads mentioning a specific group to that group (e.g., an 'if you're ex-X' ad reaching ex-X people), reinforcing the need for explicit avatar callouts.
Repeat across multiple avatars who can buy the same product for different purposes — e.g., a greens product framed for GLP-1 weight-loss users vs. for hair growth.
caveats: The algorithm-matches-avatar behavior is the source's claim about the Andromeda era and may not hold universally or persist.
Listing unrelated problems can dilute relevance; the source frames it as a brainstorming step, then you select the strongest angles.
cards.source_name: The ONLY 2 Ad Creative Formats You Need to Scale Facebook Ads.docx

cards.title: Mine Bottom-of-Funnel Objections by Calling Checkout Abandoners
cards.summary: Discover real purchase objections by phoning customers who abandoned checkout and by writing down objections you already know, then build one objection ad each.
cards.use_when: Building bottom-of-funnel retargeting creative or diagnosing why add-to-cart does not convert to purchase.
steps: First, write down every objection to buying your product that you already know (price, shipping, trust, warranty).
Second, call customers who literally abandoned their checkout and ask why they did not purchase. The source calls this the best method for surfacing true bottom-of-funnel objections.
Convert each surfaced objection into its own ad: price objection → value/quality proof or competitor comparison; warranty objection → show the guarantee; delivery objection → show speed.
Keep each bottom-of-funnel ad focused on one objection and one proof point, not a full feature list.
Example from source: a hair product ad stating a single clinical claim, and a cookware ad leveraging a lifetime warranty to counter competitors' limited warranties.
caveats: Abandoned-checkout calls require customer contact data and may have low response rates; the source presents it as high-signal but does not quantify outcomes.
Results of example ads are illustrative, not guaranteed benchmarks.
cards.source_name: The ONLY 2 Ad Creative Formats You Need to Scale Facebook Ads.docx

cards.title: Structure the Ad Account as Avatar/Angle 'Packs' Inside One CBO Campaign
cards.summary: Use a single CBO prospecting campaign with many ad sets ('packs'), each grouping ads by a single avatar and angle or funnel position.
cards.use_when: Setting up or restructuring a Meta ad account so you can read results and control spend by avatar, angle and funnel stage.
steps: Create one core prospecting campaign (e.g., 'ML Prospecting') using auction buying and a Sales objective.
Set daily budget to where you are currently comfortable — the source warns not to use budget as a lever to increase spend, and suggests a rough floor of at least 1× your target CPA.
Choose bidding (highest volume or value) and keep budget scheduling at 'none'.
Set audience segment reporting: engaged segments = site visitors last 30 days and add-to-cart last 90 days; existing customers = 180-day purchasers (not all-time).
Name each ad set as a 'pack' with a sequence number plus avatar and angle, and label the funnel position (top or bottom).
Exclude existing customers from the prospecting campaign; leave placements wide open; select the correct dataset and the purchase conversion event.
Use a standard attribution setting (source uses 7-day click, 1-day engaged-view, 1-day view). Do not use dynamic creative or live video ads.

Launch each new batch of ads into a new pack. You can run dozens of packs in one campaign — the source reports accounts with 30–100 ad sets — which allows control via value rules, minimums and maximums instead of pausing ads.
Expect the pattern over time: top-of-funnel packs spend more and scale further at lower ROAS; bottom-of-funnel packs convert better but scale less.
