cards.title: Run a 12-interview pain-point research round
cards.summary: The source cites Stiehl and DeVries' claim that 12–15 one-on-one interviews surface about 80% of a segment's pain points, matching 7 focus groups.
cards.use_when: You need to identify the pains your product copy and ad hooks should address, and are weighing interviews against focus groups.
steps: Recruit 12 to 15 people from your target segment for one-on-one interviews. The source, citing Pain Killer Marketing (2008) by Chris Stiehl and Henry DeVries, says this generates about 80% of all possible pain points for the segment — the same as 7 focus groups of up to 12 participants each.
Run them as conversations rather than questionnaires, so you capture what people reveal about themselves beyond direct answers.

After at least 12 respondents, document and analyze everything. The source warns explicitly not to use this to validate your assumptions — look for new information, and highlight both the surprising and the repeated findings.

Cross-check the pains you hear through other channels: audit competitor sites to see which pains they hit on, use the Google Adwords keyword tool for phrases your audience searches, run PPC ads testing different pain points to see which get clicked most, monitor your segment on Twitter and their blogs, and find out what websites they commonly visit.
Translate each confirmed pain into how your product addresses or eradicates it, and use that in copy.
caveats: The 80% figure is the source's citation of a specific 2008 book, not a measured law; treat 12–15 as a starting heuristic.
Keyword tool names and interfaces may have changed; verify the current tool.
Sources disagree on methods — the source prefers interviews and casual conversations over formal focus groups.
cards.source_name: COPY HACKERS.docx

cards.title: Separate pain targeting from motivation reflection in copy
cards.summary: Great copy either neutralizes a critical pain or reflects a deep motivation — motivation is not a discount, a limited-time offer or your value proposition.
cards.use_when: You are drafting headline and hero copy for a PDP or landing page and need to decide whether to hit pain or aspiration.
steps: Recognize the two sides of crafting a message: targeting pain, and reflecting motivation including values. Your product must either address and neutralize or eradicate a critical pain, or pinpoint a key motivation.

Write motivation copy by reflecting, not describing, what drives the visitor. The source's example: Teresa, 39 and 65 pounds overweight, goes to a weight-loss site. Her real motivations are to prove herself against the skinny neighbor, attract an ideal partner, earn her mother's respect and love what she sees in the mirror — but she tells herself she wants information about weight loss. A million sites give information; the smart copy reflects the motivation, e.g. 'Embrace the Woman in the Mirror', supported with photos of two friends smiling coming out of a dressing room, testimonials from real women who love shopping now, and video and print case studies.
Do not write the raw motivation literally (the source rejects 'Become the Size Zero You See in Magazines' as too blunt) — write useful copy that reflects it.

Do not confuse motivation with discount or urgency: the source states that motivation is not a discount or a limited-time offer, and is not your value proposition, because a value proposition speaks to your unique solution while motivation speaks to the customer's pain.

If competitors or a broader category have already created the motivation, piggyback on it rather than recreating it. Example copy given: 'Americans who use software to manage their money sleep better at night', 'Find out where you're leaking cash so you can save more money & invest in your future', 'Categorize your expenses!'
Back any factual claim with a source, such as a link to the article where the research was published.
caveats: Motivation copy may not convert every visitor; the source's stated goals for it are to confirm the solution is what they thought it was, remind them they need a solution, keep them on the page, get them nodding, and move them to the next step.
Pain and motivation lists in the source are illustrative, not exhaustive.
cards.source_name: COPY HACKERS.docx

cards.title: Target 20–35% of visitors instead of 100%
cards.summary: Copy written for a narrow, highly qualified segment can convert far better than neutral copy written to offend no one.
cards.use_when: You are writing or revising a homepage headline, PDP headline or ad hook and feel pressure to keep it broad so it does not exclude anyone.
steps: Reject the neutral-house theory for stores. Real estate agents depersonalize a house because they need one buyer for one house; you need hundreds of buyers, which tempts you to neutralize your site into a 'beige blob'. The source's counter-argument: if you try to make every visitor happy you say nothing compelling enough to make anyone buy.
Write for your most qualified traffic — the source's band is 20–35% of visitors, and it states that even 22% is fine to write for.

Do the conversion math as the source frames it: if only 20% of visitors are in the segment and you convert half of them, your conversion rate becomes 10%; converting a quarter of that segment yields 5%, which the source describes as more than double the average for untargeted large-company sites.

Use direct-mail precedent: a piece promoted with 'How to Legally Rob Slot Machines in ANY Casino!' converted well enough to be mailed repeatedly in 2005 by taking the risk of being highly desirable to a select few rather than appealing to everyone.

Revise existing copy to speak directly to that segment. Make headlines more specific at minimum. The source's test: the more neutral and bland your copy is, the more likely you are not targeting a segment.

Take the segment-specific headline pattern from startups the source cites: CampaignMonitor 'Email marketing software for designers and their clients' (any industry could use it, but designers arrive most and are influencers), CollegeBudget 'Student-only deals, delivered daily', Reach.ly 'We connect hotels with guests in real time', Trulia 'Homes and local scoop for the real estate obsessed'.
Once the message is right for the segment, buy more traffic for that segment — the source expects better ROI than sending untargeted traffic to a targeted page.
caveats: The source's conversion arithmetic is illustrative, not a benchmark; the 20–35% band is the source's heuristic.
Do not let narrow targeting lock you out of expansion — the source notes that Reach.ly-style focused messages can be expanded as the business grows.
cards.source_name: COPY HACKERS.docx

cards.title: Build a product positioning document with five columns
cards.summary: List every feature, mark which are unique, map each to a customer pain and at least one benefit, then priority-rank the rows.
cards.use_when: You are preparing to write PDP copy, comparison content or in-product messaging and need one source of truth about what your product does and why it matters, or you sell multiple products and need one document per product.
steps: Create a table with five columns: Features, Unique to Us, Customer Pain Solved, Benefits, Priority.

In Features, list every single feature and leave nothing out. Even a feature you consider small — the source's example is a light switch on a lamp — may be the bullet that puts you above a competitor in someone's mind. Do not start writing copy or toying with words at this stage.

In Unique to Us, check the box when only your solution offers the feature; if a competitor offers it, list each competitor; if it is similar to a competitor's feature, briefly describe the similarity.
In Customer Pain Solved, use your earlier customer research to note which pain each feature solves or addresses, and tag which segment it solves for when you have several.

In Benefits, assign at least one express benefit to every feature; some features have several. If a feature has no express benefit and you have to stretch to make one fit, cut it from the list — the customer does not need to learn about it on your site.
Set Priority per row — the source uses high, medium, low or numbers or color-coding — to know what to emphasize versus subordinate when writing.
Create a separate document for each product variant, and reuse the document for every page, email and in-product message.
caveats: The source recommends spending real time making this document thorough and 'possibly ugly' — it is a listing exercise, not a wordsmithing exercise.
Benefits of how you do what you do (e.g. FSC-only paper, a playful bookkeeping look-and-feel, donating to 1% for the Planet, vegan-certified materials) sit outside features and need their own rows.
cards.source_name: COPY HACKERS.docx

cards.title: Distinguish features from benefits and write the customer's outcome
cards.summary: A description of what a feature does is not a benefit; the benefit is the value the specific buyer derives from it.
cards.use_when: You are writing PDP bullets or benefit blocks and keep restating specifications instead of outcomes.
steps: Use the source's working definitions: a feature is a part of your product that does a unique thing (a light switch on a lamp); a benefit is the outcome of what that feature does — the value the customer derives (you can easily fill a room with light or darken it).

Avoid the common mistake of treating the purpose of a feature as its benefit. Example: for an online cake service, gluten-free flour that prevents flare-ups for people with celiac and aligns with whole-food or vegan diets is still a description of the feature, not the benefit.

Ask who the buyer is, because the benefit changes per segment. For a grandmother who feels deep satisfaction when loved ones enjoy a meal, the benefit of a gluten-free cake is watching her granddaughter with celiac enjoy her birthday party like every other kid. For a teacher bringing a celebratory cake to school under gluten restrictions, the benefit is rewarding her students while keeping the principal and the PTA happy.
Judge a benefit by whether it tells the customer what is in it for them — how they will feel after using it and what improves in their lives — not merely what the feature will do.
Remember the source's ordering rule for copy: your copy is first about what the user wants, and second about how your product satisfies those wants.
caveats: Benefits that tap into motivations are described as powerful, but the source gives no measured lift figures for benefit-framed versus feature-framed copy.
cards.source_name: COPY HACKERS.docx

cards.title: Choose whether to lead with a benefit or a feature per audience
cards.summary: There is no universal rule that copy must lead with the benefit — some shoppers distrust soft benefit language and go straight to comparison charts.
cards.use_when: You are deciding what goes in the hero headline and first bullets of a PDP or landing page for a specific shopper type.
steps: Treat the top-priority message as your 'lead'. The source reports having seen a headline focused on a new product feature outperform a headline showing an expected benefit, so the decision is situational, driven by what your customer base needs at that moment.

Match the lead to shopper type. Some shoppers are suspicious of soft marketing messages — which many benefits unfortunately become. Others jump straight to comparison charts and catalogues to check the features. Others signed up because they heard about one cool feature. The source states none of these types would want you to lead with the benefit.

Whatever you lead with, support every feature with a benefit and every benefit with a feature or a related support point — the source's example of support is a snapshot of the interface design backing a benefit of enjoyable software.

Look at AnyNewBooks as a working pattern: the headline leads with the core benefit, the subhead supports it with the service feature of weekly notifications. The source derives at least three explicit benefits from that one feature: no cost so cash stays in your pocket; weekly cadence means no spam and no wasted seconds deleting emails; the emails come to you so you don't hunt for new books and risk missing something you would love.

Use a mix as Mint does on its How It Works page: the page headline speaks to features while addressing the overarching value proposition of power and simplicity, and the chunk headlines vary between benefits ('See all your accounts in one place', 'stay safe and secure') and features (autocategorization of transactions), each supported by a clear visual.
caveats: The source's cross-reference of feature-led versus benefit-led headline performance comes from the author's own observation, with no dataset, so it does not establish a general rule.

Do not summarize to fit a tight space: the source says a constrained copywriter should choose shorter, tighter words rather than dilute the message, because a summary is neither noticeable nor memorable and specifics stick.
cards.source_name: COPY HACKERS.docx

cards.title: Show don't tell: let design and visuals carry part of the message
cards.summary: Some of the strongest messages never appear as text — screenshots and visual design can prove a claim better than copy.
cards.use_when: You are building a PDP, How It Works page or feature section and deciding what to write versus what to show.
steps: Adopt the source's 'show don't tell' reading of Mint: rather than telling visitors the software is design-focused, the site's clean visual design demonstrates the benefit of easy, clean design.

Support each message chunk with a visual that either gives proof of the claim — the source's example is showing interface screenshots — or reinforces the message, as with a sign saying the service is free.
Where a screenshot, press logo, button, video demo or icon can replace copy, let it, but only without sacrificing clarity.

In the product positioning document, pair benefit rows with their support points (e.g. an interface snapshot supporting the benefit of enjoyable software) so writers know what asset to place next to the copy.
Note that good writing is good design in the source's framing — copy should guide design, not be squeezed into a template afterward.
caveats: The source's examples are drawn from Mint and AnyNewBooks as observed at the time of writing; page layouts have since changed.
cards.source_name: COPY HACKERS.docx

cards.title: Audit competitor and search language to skip wordsmithing
cards.summary: Messaging built from exact customer keywords, review phrases and competitor audits removes guesswork from value proposition writing.
cards.use_when: You need headline and value-proposition language for a PDP or ad set and are deciding between internal wording and market wording.
steps: Pull language from three external sources rather than from internal assumptions: exact search keywords your audience uses, phrases that appear in reviews, and competitor audits.
Use the Google Adwords keyword tool (verify the current tool name, since interfaces change) to find phrases your audience is searching, as the source recommends for uncovering pain points.
Audit competitors' sites to see which pain points they hit on and which features they claim, and record the overlaps in the Unique to Us column of your product positioning document.

Borrow motivation that competitors or the broader category have already created instead of building it yourself. The source's example: personal finance tools benefit from Intuit, major banks and TV shows like Til Debt Do Us Part having already convinced people they need to manage their money, so the store only has to remind people why they need the solution.
When you make a factual claim in the resulting copy, link or cite the research source — the source suggests this can be as simple as a link to the article where the research was published.
caveats: The source warns against 'wordsmithing' — rearranging internal messages — but does not claim external language alone produces conversion lift.
Competitor copy is itself unverified; treat competitor claims as language input, not as proven positioning.
cards.source_name: COPY HACKERS.docx

cards.title: Plan messaging for launch traffic waves
cards.summary: Startup traffic arrives in distinct waves with different motivations, and copy may need lines specifically written to reflect each wave's motivation.
cards.use_when: You are sequencing store launch content, early landing pages or ad campaigns and deciding which message to show as traffic sources shift.
steps: Map the waves the source describes: wave 1 is beta signups from friends, contacts and family who join the email list; wave 2 is media coverage sending specific segments such as developers from Hacker News and technophiles from TechCrunch who also join the list; wave 3 is launch day, when the email list floods the site and many visitors like the site on social networks while niche or foreign press sends a range of traffic; wave 4 brings invitations, blog posts and social recommendations — the 'Lookie Lous'.

Write to the dominant motivation of the current wave. In wave 1, visitors — including a mom who wants to support you and an ex-coworker who wants to pick apart the idea — are looking for the basics of what you are doing. Wave 2 visitors want more specifics. Waves 3 and 4 want to learn about the solution, learn about the company, and identify whether the solution solves X pain for them.
Expect that a value proposition alone may not cover the wave-specific motivation; the source says you will likely have to write lines of copy specifically focused on reflecting visitor motivation.

Write the copy to confirm the solution is what they thought it was, remind them they need a solution like yours, keep them on the page longer, get them nodding, and move them to the next part of the experience where conversion work continues.
caveats: Wave descriptions come from the source's 2011 startup context and media landscape; the sequencing pattern is transferable but the named channels are dated.
cards.source_name: COPY HACKERS.docx

cards.title: Test names and creative with cheap ad or shelf experiments
cards.summary: Tim Ferriss' low-budget testing approach — PPC-tested book titles and store-shelf cover tests — transfers to naming products and choosing creative.
cards.use_when: You are choosing a product name, collection name or ad creative set and want market evidence instead of internal preference.
steps: Use paid ad testing to decide naming. The source describes Ferriss buying PPC ads and testing various titles, then using the winning ad's title as the book's name.

Use physical placement to decide creative. Ferriss printed different covers and placed them on other books in a bookstore to see which ones customers gravitated to; the cover that attracted most people became the book's cover.

Translate to ecommerce: test candidate product names or collection names in ad copy and compare click-through; test hero creative variants by exposing them to traffic and watching what people engage with.
Treat these as cheap directional tests rather than definitive design decisions, and rely on the same PPC-through-click testing discipline the source recommends for segment testing.
caveats: The source presents these as examples of low-budget research, not as controlled experiments with reported lift figures.
Ferriss' result — the winning title became the book name — is a case example, not a guarantee that ad-tested names always outperform.
cards.source_name: COPY HACKERS.docx

cards.title: Fix headlines that target no one
cards.summary: Copy that could belong to any company in the category signals you are not targeting a segment — make headlines specific.
cards.use_when: You are auditing an existing homepage or PDP headline and it reads generic or interchangeable with competitors.
steps: Check for the failure pattern the source documents: LikeALittle's headline 'Hello! Welcome to LikeALittle! Connect with people near you' describes a campus-only anonymous flirting service but could be confused with any social network's headline. LearnVest's 'Take Control. Afford Your Dreams.' helps women organize their finances yet never mentions women on the homepage — the source calls this a miss.
Contrast with the targeted pattern: CampaignMonitor names designers, CollegeBudget names students, Reach.ly names hotels, Trulia names the real estate obsessed.
Apply the fix: make headlines more specific at minimum. The source's diagnostic is that the more neutral and bland the copy is, the more likely it is not targeting a segment.

Watch for the internal reason for vagueness — being too close to the project, deadline pressure, or believing investors won't fund something too narrow — and treat it as a risk rather than a reason to stay broad.
Recognize the value of being the company that 'gets' a segment: the source argues that if your product is built for one small market segment, own that and speak directly to it.
caveats: The cited sites and headlines reflect their state at the time of writing; some may have changed.
When testing ad copy rather than a durable headline, a broader hook may be appropriate for demand capture — this guidance is about segment-specific messaging, not a ban on any broad ad.
cards.source_name: COPY HACKERS.docx

cards.title: Decide whether to write copy in positive or negative framing
cards.summary: Marketing messages typically stem from solving pain, which is inherently negative, while marketing managers push for positive framing — the source flags this tension.
cards.use_when: You are writing PDP or ad copy about a problem the product solves and are choosing between pain-first and positive-outcome-first framing.
steps: Name the tension explicitly: most marketing messages are based on the idea of solving customer pain, which the source calls inherently negative, but marketing managers want messages written in positive ways.

Ask which side of the message you are writing. If you are targeting pain, your job is to neutralize or eradicate a critical pain for the segment. If you are reflecting motivation, the copy should express the desired outcome the visitor is already chasing — the source's example rewrites a blunt desire into 'Embrace the Woman in the Mirror' rather than naming the size-zero aspiration.

Do not substitute discounts or limited-time offers for genuine pain or motivation: the source states motivation is not a discount and not a limited-time offer, even where customers are price-sensitive.

Choose framing based on the segment's shopper type — the same audience that distrusts soft benefit language may respond better to a direct problem statement, while a motivation-led buyer responds better to outcome language.
Keep all claims factual and supported. The source notes that when making claims you must have support, such as a link to where the research was first published.
caveats: The source does not resolve the positive-versus-negative question with a rule; it presents the conflict without prescribing one side.
No measured comparison of positive versus negative copy is provided.
cards.source_name: COPY HACKERS.docx

cards.title: Run a research survey and select your target segments
cards.summary: Survey at least 12 people, look for surprising and repeated answers rather than validation, then shortlist segments by visit frequency and compensation.
cards.use_when: You are starting from limited customer knowledge and need to pick which segment your store copy and ads should speak to.
steps: Field a survey by email if you have the list, by phone, or in person at a real location.
Ask questions that get people to reveal themselves — demographics, favorite services and products, and motivations.

Collect at least 12 responses, then document and analyze everything. The source stresses you must not simply validate your assumptions; look for new information that helps you write copy to build the business rather than your ego.
Highlight both the surprising findings and the repeated findings.
Shortlist a segment by two conditions together: they visit your site frequently, and they compensate you with cash or referrals and likes.
Then buy PPC ads on Google targeted to each candidate segment and see which segments click through, accepting that the test costs money but is worthwhile if it pinpoints the single best fit.
caveats: 12 responses is the source's stated minimum for this exercise, not a statistical standard.
Asking respondents to do you a favor and adding 'please' is claimed to raise response rates; the source says to test it.
cards.source_name: COPY HACKERS.docx

cards.title: Show Don't Tell: Convey Benefits Through Design and UI
cards.summary: Your product's interface or page design can demonstrate a core benefit without a single word of copy.
cards.use_when: Designing a PDP, landing page or app onboarding where a core benefit (simplicity, speed, cleanliness) can be demonstrated visually instead of claimed in text.
steps: Identify one benefit you currently state in copy (e.g., 'clean, easy design', 'fast checkout', 'simple setup').

Ask whether the page itself can demonstrate that benefit rather than assert it: a stripped-back layout for a design-forward product, a 2-field checkout for a simplicity claim, an instant-loading demo for a speed claim.
Apply the Mint example as the pattern: Mint shows clean, easy visual design through their own web design instead of telling visitors they are design-focused.
Recognize that some of the strongest messages never appear as text on the page; audit your key pages for benefits you claim in words that could instead be embodied by the page experience.

Where the product or interface can't demonstrate the benefit directly, keep the copy claim but support it with a visual proof element (screenshot, before/after) rather than leaving it as a bare assertion.
caveats: Works best when the claimed benefit matches something the page itself can physically do; not every benefit is demonstrable this way.
Design-as-message still needs to be legible to a first-time visitor who doesn't know what to look for.
cards.source_name: COPY HACKERS.docx

cards.title: Build a Product Positioning Document Before Writing Copy
cards.summary: A structured table matching unique features to customer pains, benefits and priority ranking is the foundation for all page copy.
cards.use_when: Starting copy for a new product page, landing page or ad campaign and needing a documented, ranked source of messages before writing.
steps: Create a table with columns: Feature, Unique to Us?, Customer Pain Solved, Benefit, Priority.
List every feature of the product or offer, and mark which ones are genuinely unique versus table stakes in your category.
For each feature, write the specific customer pain it solves, then translate it into a customer-facing benefit (not a restated feature).
Assign a priority rank to each benefit; this ranking becomes the basis of your messaging hierarchy for every page you write.
Keep this document as a living reference and revisit it before each new page or campaign so copy stays consistent across sessions that may be weeks apart.
Source (Joanna Wiebe, Copy Hackers) insists this document is critical to writing compelling copy; treat completing it as a prerequisite, not an optional exercise.
caveats: Priority ranking is a working judgment, not a formula; revisit it as you learn from customer research and testing.
Unique features may still rank low on priority if they solve a pain few customers feel.
cards.source_name: COPY HACKERS.docx

cards.title: Choose Positive vs Negative Framing Based on What's Working
cards.summary: Neither positive nor negative framing wins universally; test both, but never attach your brand to a negative image you can't decisively remove.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to frame a headline, ad hook or landing page message around a customer pain versus a desired outcome.
steps: Recognize that many marketing managers demand only positive copy (avoiding 'don't', 'never', 'get rid of') while negative framings like 'DreamBox Gets Rid of SPAM' or 'Bankers Don't Want You to Use This Free Banking App' often capture attention more sharply.

Compare the paired examples directly when drafting: 'Now You Can Use Your Smart Phone to Reduce Your Bank Fees' vs. 'Bankers Don't Want You to Use This Free Banking App'; note that both classic positive campaigns (VW 'Think Small') and negative ones (Apple '1984') are remembered as historically great.
Test both framings on your page rather than picking on principle, per the source's advice that no one has made a definitive case for either.

The key warning: avoid creating a negative image and then tacking your brand on as the solution. If your solution can't decisively erase the negative feeling, hint at the negative rather than dragging it to the surface.

Do not rewrite existing negative copy that is already converting; the source's rule is 'if it ain't broke, don't fix it' — only revise negative copy if conversion rate is low or bounce/exit rate is high.
A hybrid can work, as in Miller Lite's 'Tastes great, less filling' — pair a positive and negative frame in one message.
caveats: The source explicitly refuses to declare a universal winner between positive and negative; treat any choice as testable, not settled.
Revise copy only on evidence of underperformance (low conversion, high bounce/exit), not on stylistic preference.
cards.source_name: COPY HACKERS.docx

cards.title: Use Keyword Research to Source Customer Language for Copy
cards.summary: AdWords search volume reveals the exact phrases customers use, which belong in your headlines, buttons and demos — not just your SEO tags.
cards.use_when: Writing headlines, subheads, meta titles, demo scripts or button copy for a product or category page and needing the customer's own vocabulary.
steps: Open Google AdWords keyword tool and enter at least one primary keyword or phrase you believe fits your product.

Review the global and local monthly search volumes to find higher-traffic related phrases; the source's example is Patrick McKenzie researching 'bingo card creator' and finding 'printable cards' has roughly 100x the traffic.
If a higher-traffic phrase is a genuine fit, write a landing page targeting that phrase (the source presents this as McKenzie's approach, not a universal mandate).
Record the keywords and use them to shape copy in H1 headlines, H2 subheads, URLs, meta titles, meta descriptions, demo scripts, screenshot captions, and the second line of multi-line buttons.
Treat AdWords keywords as often the exact phrases customers want to see on the page — the language they use and that resonates when they land.
The tool interface and availability change over time; verify the current keyword research interface before building a workflow around it.
caveats: The specific traffic multiplier (100x) is a single illustrative example, not a benchmark.
Keyword fit must be judged; not every high-volume phrase matches the product, and forcing it can distort messaging.
cards.source_name: COPY HACKERS.docx

cards.title: Run a Home-Page-Only Competitor Content Audit
cards.summary: Audit up to 10 competitors' home pages for value props, top messages, CTAs, guarantees and standout ideas to inform your own messaging strategy.
cards.use_when: Planning a new home page, category page or landing page and needing to know what messages prospects have already seen from competitors.
steps: Take your top keyword phrases, search them, and note the top 3 organic and PPC results for each; the companies ranking for your keywords are your competitors (source: what shows up at the top of SERPs for your keywords IS your competition).
Limit the audit to the home page of a maximum of 10 competitors.

For each, capture a screen of the home page and on a second page record five things: (1) the value proposition/headline, (2) top messages, (3) primary calls to action — language, visual design and page position, (4) special reasons to buy such as guarantees and assurances, (5) anything else seriously cool that wows you.
Work in a slide deck with two pages per site; the source uses PPT with a screen capture page and an audit page.

Synthesize: build a value proposition table (competitor, value prop, benefits highlighted such as 'security', 'ease', 'affordability'), a top messages table with tickmarks and a totals column, and a CTA table with tickmarks and totals.

Use the totals to identify messages that are either white noise from overuse or baseline expectations visitors hold — for example, the source's audit found 'Accept credit cards', 'Low/Competitive rates & fees' and 'Support' were widely used.
Remember the audit only describes what competitors say, not what works; assessment and testing of the messages comes later.
Optionally, recruit users through a usability testing service (source cites about $29 per user in 2010) to review competitor pages on a budget; verify current pricing.
caveats: The audit cannot tell you which competitor messages are effective; it only reveals what exists and is repeated.
A message common across competitors may be a necessary baseline expectation or may be exhausted white noise — the audit alone cannot distinguish these.
Pricing cited is from 2010 and should be verified.
cards.source_name: COPY HACKERS.docx

cards.title: Build a Messaging Hierarchy Tied to Where Users Look
cards.summary: Rank messages most-to-least important for your target visitor, then place each where users actually look rather than in priority order down the page.
cards.use_when: Laying out a landing page, home page or PDP and deciding which message goes above the fold, near buttons, or further down.
steps: Start from the priority ranking of features and benefits in your product positioning document.
Understand that hierarchy is not about ordering messages top-to-bottom on the page; it's about knowing where users look and putting the messages they need to see there.
Lead with the biggest point for your visitor (the reason they landed), then position supporting messages as they're needed — first they land for X, then you tell them Y, then you close the deal Z.

Make sure two things are true: messages are clearly organized so copy draws visitors through the page toward a primary CTA ('Learn More', 'Buy Now', 'Sign Up', 'Get Started'), and messages are logically positioned. Emotional decisions still require logically fed information to happen.
Audit a high-traffic page: are the messages you want people to see — strong social proof, a stellar benefit — near eye-catching elements like buttons, icons or images? If not, reorganize and test.

Write the hierarchy down if your team is less confident or copy sessions are spread out; the longer the gap between writing sessions, the more the hierarchy keeps you on track. Small startup teams may be able to hold it in their heads.

Consider the gaze-direction research: usability specialist James Breeze (UsableWorld) used eye tracking to find people follow the gaze of a person in a photo; if you have a stock photo of a person near a button, test having that person look toward the button.
caveats: The 'woman looking at button' effect is presented as testable, not proven for your page; the source frames it as worth an experiment.
Hierarchy exists to prevent drift across sessions, not to prescribe a rigid template for every page.
cards.source_name: COPY HACKERS.docx

cards.title: Simplify Ambiguous Offers Into One Concrete Statement
cards.summary: Simplify a fee or offer message to a single unambiguous condition; the source's Fidelity example quadrupled program customers in 4 months.
cards.use_when: Writing or revising an offer headline, promo banner, pricing page or loyalty/checkout message that currently contains vague terms.
steps: Identify whether your offer message contains ambiguity on any of these axes: what exactly is reduced/offered, what the qualifying amount or condition is, and which account or product the condition applies to.
The source's example: Fidelity's reduced-fee message was ambiguous on all three ('What sort of reduced fees? What is a certain amount? Is it checking, savings, or both?').
Rewrite as one concrete statement: 'No Fees If You Keep $400 In Your Savings Account.'
Per the source, customers in that program quadrupled within just 4 months after the simplification — treat this as a case example, not a promised result for your store.

Apply the same test to your ecommerce offers: shipping thresholds, bundle discounts and subscription terms should state the exact amount and exact condition in the headline itself rather than requiring a click or a FAQ visit.
caveats: The quadrupling result is a single reported case from a financial services program, not a benchmark for ecommerce or for every simplification.
Simplifying does not mean overpromising; keep the concrete terms accurate to what the offer actually delivers.
cards.source_name: COPY HACKERS.docx

cards.title: Write Unbelievable-but-True Copy and Back It With Credibility
cards.summary: A nearly-unbelievable line can outperform, but it must never be literally impossible and must be supported by clear examples on the page.
cards.use_when: Drafting a bold claim or hook for a PDP, landing page or ad where the benefit sounds too good to be ordinary.
steps: Recognize that longform sales copywriters routinely write lines that are almost impossible to believe, and this can work to your benefit.
Enforce the critical distinction: a nearly-unbelievable line is acceptable; an impossible-to-believe line is not.
Always support the almost-unbelievable message on the same page with clear examples that build credibility — proof, specifics or demonstrations.

Balance against the related insight that customers want to keep believing there are magic cures, that they deserve them, and that those solutions require little effort while saving time; people are willing to believe you have the miracle product.
The source's stance: do not exploit that willingness, but also don't hold back if you genuinely have a product that will rock their socks off — roll with the inertia of their desire to believe.
caveats: The credibility-support step is not optional; the source explicitly says an almost-unbelievable message should always be supported by examples.
This is the source's expressed opinion about customer psychology, not a measured result.
cards.source_name: COPY HACKERS.docx

cards.title: Leverage Related News for a Time-Sensitive Landing Page
cards.summary: When a competitor blunder or relevant news item breaks, build a long-form page around it to redirect demand while the motivation is fresh.
cards.use_when: An industry news event or competitor failure creates momentary interest your store can respond to with a landing page or campaign.
steps: Watch for news items related to your category that you can use in a non-nasty way; the source's criterion is explicitly that the use must not be nasty.

The example: a client's competitor made a major blunder, a national newspaper picked it up, and the team cited the article in a long-form 'open letter' page designed to lure people away from that competitor.
Combine a long-form page format with the news hook; the source states the long-form helped, but the motivation created by the news item was critical to the campaign's success.
Per the source, that campaign sold nearly double the forecast — treat as a case example, not a guarantee.
Move fast, since the motivation is tied to a news cycle; keep the page honest and cite the source rather than misrepresenting the event.
caveats: The nearly-double result is a single case study, not a benchmark.
The source insists on non-nasty use; using a competitor's misfortune in a way that reflects badly on you can backfire.
cards.source_name: COPY HACKERS.docx

cards.title: Overwrite, Then Cut Vigorously — Long Copy Works If Interesting
cards.summary: Write roughly 10x more than you need, then trim hard; fact-packed long copy outperforms dull short copy.
cards.use_when: Drafting a long-form landing page, sales page or product story and deciding how much to write and how hard to edit.
steps: Start with 10x more information than you need and write it out; per John Caples (quoted by the source), if you need a thousand words, write two thousand.
Then trim vigorously — the source states the second half is just as important as the first; write through the night, then spend the day editing.
Do not fear long copy: fact-packed messages carry a wallop, and if the ad is interesting, people will be hungry for all the copy you can give them; if it's dull, short copy won't save it.
Apply to ecommerce contexts such as PDP descriptions, long-form landing pages and email sequences: abundant specific facts plus aggressive cutting beats a thin page padded with filler.
caveats: Long copy only works when it remains interesting; length alone is not the goal.
The Caples quote is attributed secondhand and presented as a principle, not a tested standard.
cards.source_name: COPY HACKERS.docx

cards.title: Don't Over-Explain; Assume Less Analytical Readers
cards.summary: Readers aren't constantly scrutinizing every claim, so you don't need to justify each statement — but don't exploit their blind acceptance either.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much explanation and justification to include in page copy, descriptions or ad text without bloating it.
steps: Account for the fact that people make hundreds of thousands of decisions daily without thinking and blindly accept things because questioning everything is exhausting.
Because of this, you do not need to explain every statement you write; you can state a benefit without a supporting rationale for each line.
Yet the source pairs this with an explicit boundary: do not take advantage of this tendency — the following tip states clearly 'Don't take advantage of this.'
Practically, this means cutting unnecessary hedges and justifications, keeping copy tight, while still being truthful about what the product or offer does.
caveats: This sits in tension with the tip to support almost-unbelievable claims with credibility examples; the resolution is that bold claims need support, ordinary claims don't need exhaustive justification.
Assuming readers are less analytical is a heuristic, not a license for deceptive copy.
cards.source_name: COPY HACKERS.docx

cards.title: Treat Positioning as the Highest-Leverage Copy Decision
cards.summary: The source calls positioning the most important decision; decide it through research before writing a single word.
cards.use_when: Before writing any product page, category page or ad campaign — when deciding what your product fundamentally is in the customer's mind.
steps: Accept the source's claim that the most important decision you will make is how you position your product or service.

Study the cited repositioning examples: Ogilvy & Mather positioned Merrill Lynch not as a stockbroker but as a total financial services centre, and positioned American Express Travelers Cheques for domestic use as well as foreign travel.
Do research first — talk to customers, business contacts, anyone who will answer questions — to determine how to position.
Decide positioning before you write a word; the source argues that although you can change later, there's no reason to start on the wrong foot when you can start right.

Apply to ecommerce equivalents: deciding whether your store is 'cheapest', 'fastest to receive', 'the specialist for a specific use' or 'the bundle that removes decisions' is a positioning decision that should be made with customer input, not copywriting momentum.
caveats: The cited repositioning examples are historical agency cases, not ecommerce experiments; adapt the principle cautiously.
Positioning can be changed later, but the source recommends starting from a researched position.
cards.source_name: COPY HACKERS.docx

cards.title: Write Ads to Trigger the Life-Force 8 Biological Desires
cards.summary: Anchor product messaging to one of eight hardwired human desires that drive the majority of purchasing decisions.
cards.use_when: Choosing the core angle for a PDP headline, ad creative or launch campaign when deciding which emotional benefit to lead with.
steps: Reference the Life-Force 8: (1) survival/life enjoyment/life extension, (2) enjoyment of food and beverages, (3) freedom from fear, pain and danger, (4) sexual companionship, (5) comfortable living conditions, (6) to be superior/winning/keeping up with the Joneses, (7) care and protection of loved ones, (8) social approval.
Pick the single LF8 desire your product most credibly satisfies, then make that the dominant appeal across headline, hero image and first lines of body copy.

Treat the nine learned/secondary wants (be informed, curiosity, cleanliness, efficiency, convenience, dependability/quality, beauty and style, economy/profit, bargains) as supporting, not leading, arguments—the source argues they are far weaker because they are learned, not hardwired.

Test which LF8 angle your buyers respond to (see the Haldeman-Julius example: the same book retitled 'Quest for a Blonde Mistress' jumped from 5,000 to 50,000 copies, and 'How to Argue Logically' tripled sales) by running the same product under different LF8-framed headlines and comparing click-through and purchase conversion.
caveats: The book-title lift figures are a 1920s mail-order example, not a modern ecommerce benchmark.
Pick the desire your product genuinely satisfies—the source warns that appeals your product cannot deliver will fail.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Direct Mental Movies With Specific Visual Words
cards.summary: Replace vague benefit claims with specific visual language that makes prospects mentally simulate using the product.
cards.use_when: Writing product descriptions, ad body copy, landing page sections or video scripts where a generic benefit statement is falling flat.
steps: Start from a vague line ('Go somewhere and do something') and progressively add specificity: location, object, action, then sensory detail (the source's progression: go to the kitchen / open the oven / pull out the pizza / pull out the freshest, crispiest pizza you've ever eaten).
Use action verbs and concrete nouns so readers picture themselves performing steps with the product, not just reading a claim.
Add 'positive visual adjectives' (PVAs) sparingly at key moments to intensify the image.
Apply this to ecommerce PDPs: instead of 'high-quality nonstick pan', write copy that walks the buyer through the first meal they'll cook in it.

For video ads, script the sequence of images the viewer should see in their mind rather than listing features; the source's framing is that 'the first use of any product is inside the consumers' minds'.
caveats: Whitman's claim that imagery increases desire is a persuasion principle, not a measured conversion lift—test copy variants against your own baseline.
Overwriting dense imagery can hurt readability; the source also recommends clear readability formulas and simplicity.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Lead With 'What's In It For Me?' Benefits
cards.summary: Consumers care about what the product does for them, not company facts, equipment or process.
cards.use_when: Reviewing product pages, about sections, ad copy or brochures that currently describe the company, factory or product specs.
steps: Audit each asset for self-serving content: company history, staff counts, square footage, equipment photos, 'unusual camera angles'. The source cites Daniel Starch's research showing readers ignore factory-focused ads.
For each feature listed, write the corresponding consumer benefit and lead with the benefit.
Put the single biggest benefit in the headline.
Batch benefits throughout ('Bombard Your Readers With Benefits') rather than relying on one strong claim.
Use the Flesch readability ease concept and clear layout so benefit statements land fast.
caveats: This is the book's core 'advertising should move people to act' doctrine—it is a direct-response stance, not a brand-awareness stance; brand campaigns may weight emotion and imagery differently.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Build Fear Appeals With All Four Required Components
cards.summary: Fear only converts when it is strong, paired with a specific effective solution, and the prospect believes they can act.
cards.use_when: Writing ad copy or a landing page for a protective or problem-solving product (security, insurance, hygiene, safety gear, health supplements).
steps: Confirm your product genuinely resolves the fear; if it doesn't, the source says the appeal will fail.

Include all four elements (Pratkanis & Aronson, Age of Propaganda): (1) scare the prospect, (2) offer a specific recommendation to overcome the threat, (3) make the action seem effective, (4) make the prospect believe they can perform it.
Target existing, widely recognized fears rather than inventing new ones—e.g., sun damage sells sunscreen; UV damage to laundry does not sell detergent.
Support the solution with credibility boosters: testimonials, demos, free trials.
Use deadlines and scarcity ('limited offer', 'while supplies last') as a fear-of-loss variant, but still provide the clear path to buy.
caveats: Too much fear can paralyze rather than motivate (the source's 'deer in headlights' analogy).
The source explicitly ties ethical use to having a truly effective solution.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Use Ego Morphing to Sell Identity, Not Just Function
cards.summary: Present imagery and social proof that lets buyers see themselves as the kind of person who owns the product.
cards.use_when: Merchandising lifestyle, luxury, apparel, beauty or status-adjacent products where functional copy underperforms.
steps: Identify the desirable characteristic society associates with the product: physical attractiveness, intelligence, economic success, sexual prowess.
Show imagery of aspirational customers—per the source, perfume ads show attractive models who never even wear the product.
For stores without celebrity customers, create association: the book's example suggests giving free product to recognizable local figures, then referencing who uses your service.
Apply the social-proof version for B2B/service contexts: name the most rigorous clients ('why local bank presidents choose us') to transfer credibility to the average buyer.
Avoid heavy persuasion copy in these assets; let the image do the ego work.
caveats: This mostly applies to goods whose value is largely symbolic; commodity purchases usually need functional benefit copy.
False or misleading customer references would be deceptive—only state genuine relationships.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Pair the Scare With a Credible, Easy Solution
cards.summary: Fear appeals must translate into a believable, achievable action or they create inaction.
cards.use_when: Designing acquisition creative for problem-solution products like sanitizers, supplements, insurance or safety items.
steps: Diagnose your market's preexisting anxieties: for hand sanitizer, the source shows GOJO used surveys about unwashed hands and dirty money to make bacteria a foreground concern.
Lead with concrete facts about the risk, then present your product as the accessible fix (the source notes Purell's travel bottles made the solution easy).
For product pages, add a clear call to action with a low barrier (free shipping, sample, easy return).
Use deadline mechanics—'one-day sale', 'while supplies last'—to nudge action on the fear of missing out.
Validate the fear's credibility by targeting existing, widely-recognized fears rather than fringe concerns.
caveats: The book's sanitizer and mint ads are historical examples of positioning, not proof of your product's efficacy.
Exaggerated health or safety claims can breach advertising standards; keep claims substantiated.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Use Psychologically Potent Headlines to Stop the Scroll
cards.summary: The headline is the highest-leverage copy element; use proven starters and lead with the strongest benefit.
cards.use_when: Running paid social or display ads, writing email subject lines, or title-tagging a PDP or landing page.
steps: Write multiple candidate headlines around one dominant benefit, not a feature or product name.
Use the book's 22 headline-starter patterns (e.g., 'How to...', 'Who else...', question style) and question headlines, which the source lists as a separate power technique.
Include extreme specificity numbers where honest, per 'Crush Your Competition With Extreme Specificity'.
Add 'grabbers' above or before the headline (the source lists '12 ways to lure readers into your copy').
Test headlines as the primary variable; the source treats the headline as the biggest determining factor of whether copy gets read.
caveats: The '22 starters' are lists of formulas, not validated lifts; run A/B tests against your own audience.
Some patterns like rhetorical questions can fail for certain products or audiences.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Battle Human Inertia at the Point of Decision
cards.summary: Even a convinced buyer needs reasons to act now and an easy path to purchase.
cards.use_when: Optimizing checkout, cart recovery, subscription sign-up or any step where visitors have interest but don't convert.
steps: Add scarcity and deadlines to the offer: the source says fear of missing out (tied to the 'bargain' secondary want) pushes action.
Write a guarantee that reduces perceived risk ('Guarantees that Guarantee Higher Response').
Make buying frictionless: the source's hot lists include '13 Ways to Make Buying Easy'.
Use coupon offers and coupon-style CTAs ('The Coupon Persuader') where the audience is deal-motivated.
Avoid purely clever or entertaining copy that produces 'wow' reactions and zero action—measure purchase conversion, not likes or comments.
caveats: Fake scarcity or artificial deadlines are deceptive and can backfire; the source ties deadlines to a real bargain.
Guarantees must match what your operations can actually honor.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Borrow Credibility Through Social Proof and Authority
cards.summary: Prospects need to believe your claims before they buy; transfer credibility via testimonials, transfer and authority positioning.
cards.use_when: Adding trust elements to a PDP, landing page, sales letter or paid ad for a product with a skeptical or high-consideration audience.
steps: Use social proof: customer testimonials, user counts, reviews, and named companies that use the product (the book's 'Transfer—Credibility by Osmosis' and 'The Bandwagon Effect' principles).
Position yourself as an authority ('Authority Positioning' technique), for example by citing credentials or specialized experience.
Use 'examples vs. statistics': testimonials often beat bare statistics for emotional credibility, while stats support the rational case; the source lists both as principles #12 and #16.
Reinforce with 'The Inoculation Theory' in competitive markets: mention and defuse objections before the buyer reaches checkout.
For B2B or premium products, cite specific expert or peer groups ('why these types of buyers choose us').
caveats: Never fabricate reviews, testimonials or endorsements—this is deceptive and illegal in most jurisdictions.
Video and screenshot proof often work better than text claims, but require real customers.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Structure Copy for Clarity and Reinforce Key Points
cards.summary: Message clarity and repetition are separate, stackable persuasive techniques.
cards.use_when: Editing long-form sales pages, email sequences, or any asset that feels scattered or unclear after the first draft.
steps: Apply 'Message Organization'—structure with a clear single main claim, then supporting benefits in logical order (the book's AIDA framing: attention, interest, desire, action).
Use 'Repetition and Redundancy' to restate key claims and the offer at multiple points; the source includes the P.S. line as a restatement of the offer, often read first.
Use rhetorical questions sparingly to draw readers in and prompt agreement.

Apply the Elaboration Likelihood Model concept: decide whether the audience will process carefully (give strong arguments) or lightly (favor simple, familiar cues like count of reviews or brand familiarity).
Use 'message sidedness' knowingly—two-sided presentations can build credibility with skeptical audiences; one-sided may work for already-persuaded buyers.
caveats: Repetition beyond a point becomes noise; monitor engagement metrics for fatigue.
Two-sided messaging is a situational choice, not a universal rule.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Match Copy to the Buyer's Stage and End Goal
cards.summary: Persuasion step-by-step (Transtheoretical Model) and means-end chaining help you align message with where the buyer is and what they're really after.
cards.use_when: Planning email sequences, retargeting ads or content marketing where different segments need different messages.
steps: Map buyers to Transtheoretical stages — precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance — and change the CTA per stage: educational content to cold audiences, use-case demos and offers to warm, urgency and discounts to hot.

Apply the Means-End Chain: link product attributes → functional benefits → emotional end states; write copy that connects the product's most concrete attribute to a specific life outcome the buyer values.
For replenishment or subscription, use 'maintenance' framing: reminders, auto-refill, program benefits.
Test whether different segments respond to pain-avoidance or aspiration framing (fear vs. ego).
caveats: The book presents these as frameworks based on academic persuasion research; there are no ecommerce lift numbers cited.
Stage bands are conceptual, not numeric thresholds—avoid assuming specific conversion rates.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Apply Layout, Type and Color to Increase Readership
cards.summary: Formatting choices affect how many people actually read and act on your ad.
cards.use_when: Laying out a PDP, landing page, email or ad creative where copy is already strong but engagement is low.
steps: Prioritize 'The Psychology of Simplicity' and clean layout; avoid cluttered, clever, or self-referential design.
Place the strongest benefit visually prominent above the fold; apply 'The Psychology of Page and Section Positioning'.
Watch the 'Reverse-Type Pitfall' — low-contrast reversed text can cut readability.
Use the source's typeface and size psychology for scannability; avoid decorative fonts for body copy.
Wrap ads in white space ('Wrap Your Ads in White') and use color per the source's consumer color preferences chapter, testing your own palette where possible.
caveats: Color preference research predates current display contexts and can vary by audience; treat as guidance only.
The book's design rules are based on print-era observations; mobile rendering changes some assumptions.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Use Specificity and the Ogilvy Principle to Stand Out
cards.summary: Extreme specificity and following Ogilvy's evidence-based principles set your copy apart from vague competitor claims.
cards.use_when: Writing or editing any claim in a product description, ad or landing page that currently reads generically.
steps: Replace vague adjectives ('high quality', 'great value') with precise numbers, materials or outcomes—the source calls this 'Crush Your Competition With Extreme Specificity'.
Apply the 'Famous Ogilvy Principle' — study what the master copywriter concluded about headlines, body copy, and long vs. short content, rather than assuming shorter is always better.
Match 'Long Copy vs. Short' to the buying context: high-consideration and expensive products often justify long copy; impulse and low-cost products often do not.
Use the 'Unique Selling Proposition' tool — articulate a specific benefit no competitor can match and repeat it consistently.
Fill product pages with concrete detail (exact dimensions, materials, ingredient sources) to signal credibility.
caveats: Specificity must be true; unverifiable claims invite refunds and platform penalties.
Optimal copy length is audience- and offer-dependent; test on your own traffic.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Test Offers Like a Direct-Response Marketer
cards.summary: Treat the offer, not the copy alone, as the primary testable variable.
cards.use_when: Structuring an A/B testing roadmap for an ecommerce store's landing pages, PDPs or email campaigns.
steps: Follow 'Offer Testing' as a distinct step before obsessing over copy or creative—the source positions the offer as foundational to response.
Use 'Survey Power' and 'A Sales Letter in Survey's Clothing' to research what buyers actually want, and to disguise research as editorial content when appropriate.
Vary one element at a time and register actual response (purchase conversion), not just engagement.
Add 'Editorial Energizers' — sidebars, call-outs, and pull quotes — to increase readership of the offer.
Track coupon-style redemptions and multi-page vs. single-page formats where applicable.
caveats: The source's '100 secrets' include many pre-digital tactics; adapt them to current platforms and verify how each interface works before implementing.
Sample sizes on small stores make many tests statistically underpowered.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Prioritize Metrics That Reflect Action, Not Applause
cards.summary: Advertising's purpose is to make people act; measure purchases, not entertainment value.
cards.use_when: Setting up dashboards, reviewing a campaign's results, or justifying budget for a direct-response creative project.
steps: Define the target action for each asset: order, signup, quote request, or email opt-in.
Reject primary KPIs like 'Wow, great ad!' reactions, likes, or shares as proxies for sales.
Instrument the path from ad to purchase (link tracking, coupon codes, UTM parameters) so purchase conversion is attributable.
Treat copy and creative as tools to remove friction and provide a reason to act now, not to entertain.
When comparing variations, judge them on the target action, not aesthetic preference.
caveats: Some long-cycle or high-consideration products won't show immediate purchase conversion from paid traffic; measure assisted conversions and pipeline, not only last-click.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Use the 46-Point Killer Ad Checklist to Review Assets
cards.summary: A pre-launch checklist catches weak headlines, missing benefits, unclear offers and friction before spend.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a landing page, PDP, paid ad or email before it goes live.
steps: Pull the book's checklist categories: response superchargers, ways to convey value, ways to make buying easy, ways to boost coupon returns.
Check for headline strength (biggest benefit), clear single proposition, and specific support.
Check for urgency or deadline with a credible reason.
Check for an obvious, low-friction path to purchase (clear CTA, visible price, no unexpected steps).
Check for credibility signals (testimonials, guarantees, named proof).
Apply 'Give Yourself a Cleverectomy' — strip clever lines that don't drive action.
caveats: The checklist is drawn from print-era direct response; add modern essentials (mobile layout, page speed, trust badges, PCI compliance) it doesn't cover.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Close With a Restated Offer (The P.S. Principle)
cards.summary: The P.S. is often read first; use it to restate the offer and push action.
cards.use_when: Writing sales emails, sales pages or direct-mail-style landing page copy.
steps: Place an offer-restating P.S. at the end of every email and long-form sales page.
Repeat the offer and contact/CTA in the P.S.; the source emphasizes restating terms, price and action step.
For email, mirror this with a short postscript after the signature line containing the primary CTA link.
Use the same technique in ad captions and post-scripts for any long-form content.
caveats: In modern short-form social ads, there is rarely a place for a formal P.S.; prioritize the primary CTA instead.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Ego Appeal Through Envious Comparison
cards.summary: Show the buyer's peers envying them to trigger ego-driven purchase desire for premium products.
cards.use_when: Creating acquisition creative or PDP imagery for a premium, status-signalling product where the buyer's self-image drives the purchase.
steps: Identify whether your product is a 'trophy' purchase where visible ownership signals taste, success or status (luxury car, high-end gear, designer goods).

Build the scene around the buyer or owner being admired or envied by an equal-status peer, not just the product in isolation — the Rolls-Royce example shows a Mercedes driver squirming with envy at the stoplight.
Keep the peer plausibly the buyer's equal so the comparison stings; the Mercedes driver has status but less than the Rolls owner, which makes the desired upgrade feel attainable.
Note this is a peripheral-route cue: it works when purchase motivation is emotional and identity-based, per the source.
caveats: The source explicitly states not all products suit ego appeal; it fits status goods, not functional commodities.
The envy framing is the author's illustrative advertisement example, not a tested benchmark.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Transfer: Borrow Credibility From Respected Symbols
cards.summary: Use trusted institutional symbols, seals and expert cues so buyers question your sales argument less.
cards.use_when: Writing PDP copy, landing pages or ad creative for products where prospect skepticism — not awareness — is the main conversion blocker.
steps: Diagnose whether the real problem is disbelief: the source's frustrated advertiser had a good layout, photo, price and easy ordering but no sales because nobody believed him.
Identify people, groups or institutions your buyers already respect (medical bodies, professional guilds, national agencies, science, the Church, industry associations).
Get an official endorsement, testimonial or membership credential and then get permission to use their image, logo or a short video on your site or ads.

If a full endorsement is unavailable, spotlight recognized symbols that carry endorsement weight — the source cites the Good Housekeeping Seal of Approval and the official-looking logo of the National Guild of Hypnotists on a client's postcard.
Add authoritative-looking facts, figures and scientific-style graphs alongside the symbol to reinforce the transferred credibility.
Where relevant, surface an actual guarantee the trusted group stands behind; the Good Housekeeping seal promised refund or replacement within two years and functioned as a close-the-sale inducement.
caveats: The source notes many prospects use peripheral, non-critical thinking; if the purchase is high-cost and central-route, credibility cues alone are insufficient.
The hypnotist postcard example is an anecdote; the author states most recipients had never heard of the guild yet the credibility cue still functioned.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Bandwagon Effect: Link Products to Reference Groups
cards.summary: Persuade buyers by tying your product to aspirational, associative or dissociative reference groups they identify with.
cards.use_when: Choosing models, testimonials or lifestyle imagery for acquisition creative and brand positioning.
steps: Decide which of the three reference groups you are targeting: aspirational (groups the buyer wants to join), associative (groups sharing their ideals), or dissociative (groups they want to reject).

For aspirational influence, ensure prospects can easily identify with the people shown — match age and profile. For a racing bike-seat product with a median buyer age of 34, the source advises showing tour-winning pros like Lance Armstrong or Eddy Merckx, not elderly riders, casual 'Everyday Joe' riders, or your best-paying customer who isn't aspirational to the audience.

For associative influence, either appeal directly to the group's values in your creative, or disassociate from outside groups (the source cites the Gap's 'generation gap' name and youth-culture versus 'oldies' appeal), being aware you will alienate the groups you reject.
Choose your group axis: age, class, sex, geography, politics, education.
Write copy and imagery that tells buyers how buying makes them part of, keeps them in, or visibly distances them from a group — not just what features the product has.
caveats: The source cites Stec and Bernstein's Consensus-Implies-Correctness heuristic and Cialdini's comparison cues as support, but the store-specific lift is not quantified.
Dissociative framing offends the rejected group by design; judge whether alienating them damages your market.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Means-End Chain: Sell the Benefit of the Benefit
cards.summary: Write copy and imagery that points to the ultimate end result, so buyers evaluate the outcome instead of scrutinizing the product.
cards.use_when: Drafting PDP copy, hero headlines or ad hooks when the product's raw features are unremarkable or commodity-like.
steps: Run the source's 'why' chain on your product: 'The sign tells people who you are' → so they do business with you → so you sell products → so you make money. Keep asking 'what's the benefit of that?' until you reach the buyer's ultimate value.

Write copy and select images that always represent that positive end result, not the intermediate step: shovel buyers want attractive planted gardens, microwave buyers want time back, car buyers want to get from A to B with ego appeal as icing.
Shift the copy's focus so prospects are less likely to critically analyse product pros and cons and more likely to decide on the outcome it delivers.
Apply the Lexus example as a template: rather than selling the car's feel, sell that a realtor driving it looks more successful and therefore wins more listings.
caveats: The Lexus example comes from a fictional salesman's pitch, not a measured campaign; it is an illustration of the technique.
The source notes ego appeal is a layer on top of the core benefit, not a substitute for it.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Match Ad Content to Buyer Stage (Transtheoretical Model)
cards.summary: Identify whether prospects are unaware, considering, planning, buying or habitual, then write copy for that stage.
cards.use_when: Planning a campaign series, email flow or landing page for a product with varying buyer awareness.
steps: Classify your market using the source's five stages: Precontemplation (ignorant of your product or unaware they need it), Contemplation (aware and thinking about trying it), Preparation (planning, needs benefit/price detail), Action (ready to buy), Maintenance (regular repurchase).
Recognise your audience will be spread across stages at the same time.

Choose option one: write ads covering all five stages so each prospect finds their relevant chunk — include everything someone totally unfamiliar would need, including what it is, what's in it, why it's better and what it costs.
Choose option two: run a series of ads that progresses from stage one to stage five over time, each building on the last with increasing feature and benefit depth.
Match copy density to the stage: stage-one prospects need an introduction, stage-three prospects need benefit and advantage detail, stage-four prospects need a frictionless purchase path.
Reinforce existing attitudes where possible — the source states it is far easier to reinforce current behaviour than to change values.
caveats: Stage bands are a source-cited model (Prochaska 1994) applied to advertising; they are not a measurement system for your funnel.
The source does not give numeric thresholds for how many prospects sit in each stage.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Inoculation Theory: Pre-empt Competitors' Attacks
cards.summary: Warn prospects about competitors' claims and weak arguments in advance so they compare purchases through your filter.
cards.use_when: Writing comparison content, objection-handling copy or competitor-differentiation sections on PDPs and landing pages.
steps: Follow the source's three steps: (1) warn of an impending attack, (2) make a weak attack, (3) encourage a strong defence by prompting the prospect to articulate their own position.

Use the pizza example as a copy template: 'Our competitors tell you they use fresh mozzarella, but they don't tell you they buy it pre-shredded in bags; we hand-shred ours every morning.' Repeat the tell-you / don't-tell-you pattern for dough, delivery time and guarantees.
Take the consumer-advocate position and expose what to look out for, what's good, what's bad and what's suspect in your category, implying enough confidence to invite closer inspection.
Turn competitor criticisms of your brand into weak attacks your own copy answers, as the source notes advertisers do to reinforce loyalty.
Keep the attack weak; the source warns a strong attack risks weakening or reversing the prospect's attitude instead of hardening it.
caveats: The source insists the attack must be weak — overreaching can backfire.
This only works if your claims are legitimate; the source ties the technique's goodwill payoff to providing genuinely useful information.
An auto-body shop and pizza shop example are author illustrations, not measured results.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Belief Re-ranking: Change Beliefs Without Triggering Defensiveness
cards.summary: Change importance of beliefs or offer alternative evidence rather than telling buyers they're wrong.
cards.use_when: Writing copy to shift buyers off a habit or incumbent brand onto your product without triggering reactance.
steps: Choose between two routes: change the buyer's underlying beliefs by presenting emotional images (fear, humour, guilt) or factual evidence, or change the importance of beliefs they already hold.
Prefer reinforcing or undermining an existing belief over a wholesale change — the source states this is easier and more likely to succeed, and is the more popular persuasion strategy.

Reinforce a belief buyers already hold by adding supporting stats, reports, studies and testimonials, or everyday success stories they can identify with. Health-food advertisers add health-benefit claims to the healthy-diet belief the audience already holds.
Avoid head-on collision: instead of stating 'Milk is healthier than soda', present graphic factual evidence of soda's risks and milk's benefits side by side.
Aim for cognitive dissonance resolution — prospects amend beliefs to fit new perceptions — but accept that some will reject the ad outright; the source notes a 100% response rate is not realistic.
caveats: Prospects must remain unaware they're being influenced; the source states they should believe the decision is their own so it becomes cemented.
The baking soda toothpaste and kung fu examples show belief change over time, not a single-ad effect.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Elaboration Likelihood Model: Choose Central or Peripheral Copy
cards.summary: Match ad content to the buyer's thinking depth — heavy facts for high-consideration purchases, image and cues for low-stakes ones.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much evidence and data versus imagery and celebrity cues to put into a PDP, ad or landing page.
steps: Judge whether your product needs high personal relevance thinking (costly or important) or low-involvement processing (cheap, trivial, routine). A $928,000 house versus a can of pork and beans is the source's contrast.
For central-route products, pour on facts, stats, evidence, testimonials, studies, reports and case histories woven into the sales argument.
For peripheral-route products, load ads with colourful pleasant images, humour, popular subject matter or celebrity sponsorship — but still include fundamental data.

Even for low-involvement goods, state size, colour, weight, quantity and any measurable specification (the source cites TAPPI brightness rating for inkjet paper), and explicitly say how you're better than competitors.

Expect the payoff to differ: the source states central-route attitudes are more resistant to counter-persuasion and show greater attitude-behaviour consistency, while peripheral-route attitudes are easily changed.
caveats: The best route depends on the product; the source says don't use cues-heavy creative for luxury or high-cost items.
The distinction is the author's synthesis of the ELM, and the house/beans examples are illustrations rather than test data.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Cialdini's Six Cues (CLARCCS) for Peripheral-Route Ads
cards.summary: Deploy comparison, liking, authority, reciprocation, commitment/consistency and scarcity as mental shortcuts in low-consideration ad copy.
cards.use_when: Writing acquisition creative or PDP persuasion blocks for low-cost or impulse purchases where buyers won't deliberate deeply.
steps: Comparison: signal that a buyer's peers are already choosing your product ('everybody else is doing it'), leaning on the need to belong.

Liking: use likable spokespeople, ad characters or relatable users; the source notes the lynchpin is that the buyer must like the person, whether a catalog seller, a celebrity or a friend who bought before.

Authority: use official, intelligent or expert figures to endorse; the source notes actors who played doctors on TV still persuaded viewers even after being made to say 'I'm not really a doctor' — the cue survived disclosure.
Reciprocation: give something of value first (samples, gift certificates, free trials, even a dollar with a survey) so buyers feel obligated to return the favour.
Commitment/consistency and scarcity: use consistency pressure and limited availability to push compliance.

Use attractive faces in creative: the source cites research (Down & Lyons 1991) that attractive people are judged more trustworthy and likable, and notes men respond to pictures of men and women to pictures of women because of identification.
caveats: The source states these cues should not be your main tool when the purchase requires lots of thought, such as luxury or high-ticket items.
The author cautions against valuing the free gift cheaply — for reciprocation, give something of real value, not a junky logo key ring.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Reciprocation Offers That Kickstart Purchase
cards.summary: Give genuine value up front to create obligation and start the reciprocation loop toward a paid purchase.
cards.use_when: Designing first-order incentives, new-mover or new-customer offers, samples or lead magnets.
steps: Identify a free item of real value your buyer would want: a free entrée, free oil change or discount certificate rather than a disposable trinket.
Time it to a moment of need — the source cites Moving Targets sending gift certificates to people who just moved into a neighbourhood on behalf of restaurant and auto-shop clients.
