Deliver the free experience well; the source notes that if the customer was treated right and was satisfied, they are far more likely to return and become a loyal long-term customer.
Consider offering to a named local partner or audience segment so the gift also introduces your business.
Judge the giveaway against the source's warning: don't use junky, low-value items with just a logo and phone number — give something of value.
caveats: The source frames reciprocation as compelling but does not quantify return rates.
Moving Targets is a client example, not evidence your store will see the same conversion.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Prime Reciprocation with a Genuine Gift (Not a Trinket)
cards.summary: Give prospects a valuable, unrequested gift to trigger the pull of reciprocation and start new-customer relationships.
cards.use_when: Designing a new-customer acquisition offer, welcome insert, or sampling campaign for a store.
steps: Identify something of real perceived value you can give away: a free sample, a gift certificate, a free service, or a month of free access. Cialdini's reciprocation principle is triggered when you give first, unprompted.

Distinguish a gift from a favor or a thank-you: it must not be something they have to request, and must not be given in exchange for something they already did. That framing is what starts the reciprocation mindset.
Avoid low-value logo trinkets (keychains, cheap pens). The recipient should think 'wasn't that thoughtful?' - the value and thoughtfulness carry the effect.
Model new-mover style campaigns: gift certificates for free pizza, a free entree, or a free oil change on behalf of local clients, which introduce the business and set the reciprocation ball rolling.
Assume satisfied recipients return and often become long-term customers - but only if they were treated right during the gift experience. The gift opens the door; the experience has to hold it open.
caveats: The source's examples are from Moving Targets' new-mover mailings for restaurants and auto shops; the long-term-loyalty claim is the source's observation, not a measured benchmark.
A gift that the customer must request to receive is a favor, not a gift, and doesn't produce the same effect.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Commitment/Consistency and the Four-Walls Ad Structure
cards.summary: Build ads that pose a ladder of questions your prospect answers 'yes' to, boxing them into consistency with a stance they've already taken.
cards.use_when: Writing long-form sales copy, landing pages, or email sequences where you want to build momentum toward a purchase.
steps: Open with questions that elicit agreement on a reasonable stance: 'Are you afraid to walk the streets alone?' or 'Don't you wish there was an easy way to protect yourself?' Each 'yes' adds momentum to the next.
Stack the questions so each successive answer follows logically from the previous one, creating a snowball of interest and desire. This is Cialdini's commitment/consistency cue in ad form.
Close by presenting your product as the path that fulfills the position the prospect has already declared, then make the request (order, click, sign up).

Recognize this is strongest in person because social pressure is the engine. On paper there's no human interaction creating pressure to be consistent, so you must lean on copy and design techniques to push the reader through the full pitch to the call to action.
Use long-form direct-response structure to compensate: give the reader enough copy and encouragement to keep reading to the close.
caveats: The source explicitly notes the technique is more effective in person than in print; its print application is weaker.
The 'Tesla Sizzler' example is illustrative copy, not a product that exists.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Use Scarcity and Exclusivity to Increase Desire
cards.summary: Frame offers as limited in supply and access so the product appears both scarce and exclusive, raising consumer interest.
cards.use_when: Positioning a launch, sale, drop, or limited-quantity offer on a PDP, landing page, or campaign.
steps: Apply the scarcity cue with lines such as one-day sale, limited offer, only while supplies last, or first come first served. These make the product appear in short supply.

Combine scarcity with exclusivity for a stronger two-part effect: not just limited supply but restricted access. This differs from a plain deadline because it implies something others can't easily get.
If there is a genuine limited product drop or preorder capacity, state the actual quantity or ordering window; avoid service-enrollment scarcity examples.
The scarcity cue exploits the documented human pattern of wanting what we cannot have - the armrest you didn't want until someone took it.
caveats: The Cabbage Patch Kids example is offered by the source as historical illustration, not evidence that any scarcity claim will generate the same result.
Overused or artificial scarcity can backfire if prospects perceive the limits as fake; keep the constraint real.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Message Organization: Clarity Before Persuasion
cards.summary: If the prospect doesn't understand your message, no amount of testimonials or polish will persuade them - structure and simplify first.
cards.use_when: Reviewing PDP copy, ad copy, or any customer-facing message that feels crowded or confusing before sending it live.
steps: Accept the source's foundational claim: 'If you don't understand what I'm saying, I can't persuade you.' Poorly structured ads can also leave prospects with an inaccurate interpretation of your offer, which can hurt for a long time.

Treat message organization as a prerequisite to every other technique in the ad. Even strong benefits, slick materials, and glowing testimonials won't work if the message is disorganized or hard to follow.
Write simply and directly. Eugene Schwartz's framing, quoted in the source, is to 'write to the chimpanzee brain.'
Follow up with a dedicated simplicity pass (see readability card) - simple is not the same as easy; clear and plain communication takes deliberate practice.
caveats: The source treats this as the single foundational lesson; if you skip it, it warns ads will likely fail regardless of other technique quality.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Examples Beat Statistics: Trigger Self-Demonstration
cards.summary: Vivid examples make prospects imagine themselves using the product, which drives desire and purchase more than raw specifications.
cards.use_when: Writing product descriptions, PDP hero copy, and ad creatives for any product where emotion drives the purchase.
steps: Lead with a colorful example that puts the prospect in the driver's seat - the source calls this 'self-demonstration.' Get them imagining use before you list specs.

Recognize that well-written examples relate more closely to the prospect's personal experience and are easier to process (Petty & Cacioppo, 1986), which is why testimonials and endorsements dominate ads over fact lists.

Calibrate the examples-vs-statistics mix by product category: for beer, skip stats and show good times; for cars, lead with examples and include stats for performance, safety, or efficiency enthusiasts; for laser printers and other utilitarian products, stats (paper capacity, resolution, ink life, duty cycle) matter more; for landscape services, sell beauty, self-image, and convenience; for gyms, sell emotion with before/after photos and member testimonials.
Include both examples and statistics where relevant, but never at the expense of strong emotionally provocative examples. Set the ratio so you don't alienate either buyer type.
Let the product and buyer tell you the ratio rather than imposing one default.
caveats: The Rolls Royce example in the source is a stylistic demonstration, not a case study of measured sales lift.
Category recommendations in the source are the author's judgment; test against your own audience.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Two-Sided Messages: Compliment the Competition, Then Win
cards.summary: Present your competitor's strengths fairly, then show why you're better - this reads as credible and persuasive.
cards.use_when: Writing comparison pages, PDPs, or ads in a category with a well-known incumbent or a superior alternative that customers will discover anyway.
steps: Open by acknowledging what the competitor genuinely does well. The source's sample: 'Acme makes an excellent fly swatter, and they've been doing so for years.'
Pivot to the change in context or technology that makes your product the current better choice. The source's fly swatter ad moves from the 1940s-50s to 21st-century automation.

According to the research the source cites (Allen, 1991), two-sided messages are more persuasive than one-sided ones only when they stick to the format of defending your own position while also attacking the competition. The key is to advocate only one side - yours - while appearing fair and balanced.
Use comparison charts that show your advantages at a glance. The source argues most consumers are peripheral thinkers and read charts as 'all the research has been done for me.'
Point out concrete advantages rather than bashing: is yours faster, easier, cleaner, healthier, more fun, less expensive, more effective?
caveats: The source acknowledges central-route thinkers will question unchecked comparison facts and verify with the competitor - so only make claims you can back up.
Complimenting the competition is the source's recommended credibility play; it is not a universal rule that every ad must name competitors.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: The Takeaway Play: Tell Prospects Why Not to Buy
cards.summary: Telling people why they shouldn't buy can boost credibility and intensify desire among true prospects.
cards.use_when: Writing PDP copy, sales pages, or email for products where some buyers are a poor fit or where the offer risks seeming too good to be true.
steps: Identify the buyer who is genuinely not a good fit for the product - budget, use case, skill level, or needs.
State the disqualifier outright in your copy rather than hiding it. The source argues this builds credibility, and for true prospects it adds fire to their desire.
Treat this as the same takeaway mechanism the author uses in his own book: telling readers the book 'is not for you' to make them want it more.
Keep the disqualification honest and narrow so it filters misfit buyers without turning off the real target customer.
caveats: The source presents this as a persuasion principle, not a tested CRO result; test whether your audience responds well before rolling it out broadly.
Use sparingly - an onslaught of 'don't buy' can confuse or deter borderline buyers.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Repetition vs. Redundancy: Extend an Ad's Life Without Burning It Out
cards.summary: Repetition builds familiarity and trust, but overuse breeds contempt; re-present the same message in different formats to reset attention.
cards.use_when: Planning campaign flighting for a proven ad or a product's ongoing promotions.
steps: Accept the source's general claim that the 'seven times' figure is a heuristic, not a verified number. Repetition still matters: it breaks down disinterest, catches audiences who missed earlier exposures, and builds familiarity, acceptance, affinity, comfort, trust, and eventual sale.

Recognize the source's warning that there is an optimum level of repetition beyond which consumers become frustrated and 'turned off.' In a cited 1979 Petty & Cacioppo study, students who heard an argument three times supported it; agreement dropped considerably at five exposures, possibly due to tedium.

Do not use the study as a hard cap - the source explicitly says not to stop running ads after three times, since a college-spending study differs from product advertising. Use it as a caution to be sensitive to frequency.
Run different variations of the same ad rather than the same ad over and over. That is redundancy, not repetition - and it disguises the recycled message as new, extending its lifespan.
Apply multiple sources and multiple arguments: hearing the same message from different people with slightly different framings makes adoption of the belief much more likely.
caveats: The three-vs-five exposure study is a lab result the source itself frames as illustrative, not a campaign benchmark.
The source's own caveat applies: if the ad is making you money, keep it running despite repetition theory.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Rhetorical Questions: Use for Retention, Not Assumed Persuasion
cards.summary: Rhetorical questions may boost message retention and attention but the evidence on persuasion is mixed.
cards.use_when: Choosing headline or hook formats for ads, email subject lines, or PDP hero copy where you need attention or memory.
steps: Understand the mechanism: a rhetorical question is a statement disguised as a question. Our social training makes us try to answer questions, so the reader stops and thinks - which increases the likelihood they engage with the message (McCroskey, 1986).
Use it to grab attention when readers are skimming rather than thinking carefully, encouraging them to 'fire up some brain cells.'

According to the research the source reviews, the mixed evidence means the safest use is for message retention: questions designed to emphasize a point - rather than to persuade - are more likely to make your audience remember the message.

Classic examples to borrow the pattern from: 'Aren't you glad you use Dial? Don't you wish everyone did?' 'Who else wants a whiter wash - with no hard work?' 'How do you spell relief?' 'What would you do for a Klondike Bar?'
caveats: Some research cited in the source suggests rhetorical questions can make audiences feel pressured and cause them to scrutinize your message more critically and regard you as less of an authority.
A 1998 research analysis by Gayle, Preiss, and Allen found no appreciable influence on persuasion - treat it as a retention device, not a proven persuasion lever.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: WIIFM: Customers Buy Only When Believed Value Exceeds the Price
cards.summary: Prospects must first understand what's in it for them; without that, they won't even consider the trade.
cards.use_when: Reviewing your PDP or offer page to check whether the benefit to the buyer is front and center.
steps: Run the $20 envelope experiment on your own copy: ask yourself what a prospect would need to know before trading their money for your product. The source's workshop demonstrates prospects always ask 'what's in the envelope?' - the same as asking 'what's in it for me?'
Lead with benefits, not features. The source's plastic-bag-with-a-$20 example shows that once the benefit is visible, prospects are dramatically more willing to exchange money for it.
Frame the purchase as a value comparison: people buy when they believe your product is worth more than the dollars they exchange for it. That is the source's foundational principle of advertising.
Address loss aversion: buyers fear losing money, time, or both. Until they know the WIIFM, they hesitate even to engage with the offer.
caveats: The envelope and bag demonstrations are illustrative exercises, not measured ecommerce results.
WIIFM does not mean listing every feature - it means making the buyer's gain explicit and easy to grasp quickly.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Use Verifiable Evidence to Convert Belief into Purchase
cards.summary: Evidence - facts, figures, testimonials, endorsements, research, charts - persuades more effectively than claims you made yourself.
cards.use_when: Writing copy for higher-priced or considered-purchase products where prospects need justification before buying.
steps: Use the source's operational definition: evidence is 'any factual statement, object, or opinion not created by the source that is used by that source as support' (Reinhard, 1988). Facts, figures, testimonials, endorsements, research, and charts qualify. Your own claims do not.

Layer evidence on top of emotional appeal. You must provoke emotion to get the prospect excited enough to spend, but especially for costlier products you must supply enough reasoning so they can justify the purchase and satisfy their sense of responsibility.

Present evidence clearly and simply. Peripheral thinkers - most readers - won't work through dense data; they'll scan, decide, and move on. Colorful charts and graphs, plus quotes from trusted professionals, let them absorb the proof fast.
Anticipate the source's key point: buyers want to believe your claims (because believing lets them enjoy the benefits), and strong evidence is what lets them give themselves permission.
caveats: The source argues evidence is most effective with important or expensive products where buyers think carefully. Lower-cost impulse goods may rely more on emotion.
Central-route thinkers will scrutinize and check your evidence - make sure it holds up.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Length-Implies-Strength: Let Volume and Numbers Signal Credibility
cards.summary: Long, fact-packed copy and large numbers of testimonials or reasons make prospects infer the product must be legitimate.
cards.use_when: Writing sales pages, testimonials pages, or proof-heavy PDP sections for products where credibility is the main obstacle.
steps: Recognize the heuristic: prospects infer that a long ad with numerous credible facts is more likely true, similar to how a long polished speech makes you think the speaker knows the topic. The source calls this the Length-Implies-Strength heuristic (Stec & Bernstein, 1999).
Write long, engaging copy where the category supports it. Every additional block of copy is another opportunity to persuade and another cue that 'there must be something to it.'

Aggregate testimonials at volume. One satisfied-customer photo says one customer; dozens communicate powerful credibility by quantity alone. The source's client Jay Siff uses a four-page '101 Success Stories' brochure with 101 testimonials and photos.
Use simple lists of reasons. The source's Day-Timers ad gave 22 reasons to buy - hitting prospects from every angle and proving the product has merit through sheer number.
Package the volume into a named artifact - '101 Success Stories,' a numbered document, a Speak Out sheet - and repurpose it across formats so the quantity is visible at a glance.
caveats: The source explicitly acknowledges that length itself doesn't mean something is truthful - the heuristic is how people respond, not a guarantee of truth.
Overstuffing can hurt readability; balance the length with the simplicity prescriptions the source gives elsewhere.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Heuristics: Leverage Lazy-Brain Shortcuts in Ad Design
cards.summary: Because most buyers prefer fast, low-effort decisions, structure ads to deliver information in short, intuitive cues.
cards.use_when: Designing overall ad layouts, PDP structures, and proof blocks where customers are likely to skim.
steps: Accept that most consumers default to peripheral processing - quick, superficial judgments - because deep thought is effortful. Even the source's cited Edison quote summarizes the human preference for avoiding thinking.
Give the peripheral brain the information it needs in visible, glanceable form: numbered lists, testimonial counts, comparison charts, badges, and stacked social proof.

Use the three heuristics the source references: Length-Implies-Strength, Liking-Agreement (Balance Theory), and Consensus-Implies-Correctness. Liking maps to Cialdini's liking cue and consensus maps to social proof, so you can cover two of the three with those existing levers.

Remember that consumers will not verify claims. The source's example of a politician's 'Torpy's Tricky 200' document shows that numbered volume persuades even when few readers check. This is a warning as much as a tactic: because buyers don't verify, your credibility systems matter even more.
caveats: The source presents heuristics as effective persuasion tools but also warns they can be exploited dishonestly; the adversarial politician example is a cautionary story.
Central-route buyers will still check; don't rely on heuristics alone for high-stakes products.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: The Psychology of Simplicity: Readable Copy Is Non-Negotiable
cards.summary: Advertising exists to get people to act, so it must be written to be understood - simple, direct, and readable.
cards.use_when: Final QA on ad copy, PDP text, email, and any customer-facing copy before it ships.
steps: Apply the foundational rule: write so people can understand. The source calls this the #1 key to all effective written communication, and warns that an incomprehensible effective message is equivalent to no ad at all.
Treat clarity as a prerequisite: you may be advertising, but until someone reads and understands, you're just talking to yourself - and you don't need to pay to do that.
Audit readability yourself before publishing. The source notes there's no magic to it: you write, run the test, examine the score, and edit until it hits the range you want.
Tighten sentences and reduce sentence length where the copy reads slowly. Long sentences can require fewer words overall but demand more mental processing, which loses readers.
caveats: The source argues this is the foundation for everything else in the book - skip it and other techniques won't rescue the ad.
Clarity work is not just correct grammar; wordy but grammatically perfect copy can still fail the test.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Score Copy with the Flesch Reading Ease Formula
cards.summary: Use the Flesch Reading Ease Score in your writing tool to enforce readable copy across ads and pages.
cards.use_when: Editing product pages, ads, and email drafts for readability before publishing.
steps: Enable the readability statistics in your word processor. In Microsoft Word, the Flesch Reading Ease Score is available with a settings toggle. Verify the current location of that setting in your version, since interfaces change.

Score on a 1-to-100 scale - higher is easier. The source's grade mapping: 0-30 College grad, 30-50 College, 50-60 10th-12th grade, 60-70 8th-9th grade, 70-80 7th grade, 80-90 6th grade, 90-100 5th grade.
Use the source's comparative example to calibrate: 'John loves Mary' scores 92, 'John has a profound affection for Mary' scores 67, and a wordy 44-word version scores 32.
Consider the source's recommended targets: sentence length of approximately 11 words, refer to people by name or pronoun at least 14 times per 100 words, and about 70-80 percent one-syllable words.
Vary sentence lengths rather than writing uniformly short ones, so the copy sounds natural rather than robotic. The source warns against all three-letter words and uniformly tiny sentences.
caveats: The grade mapping and metrics are the source's presentation of the Flesch formula, not proven conversion benchmarks.
The source distinguishes readability from specificity - you still have to make the content definite, not just easy to decode.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Vary Your Tools but Keep a Readability Floor on Ad Copy
cards.summary: Ad copy that scores at postgraduate reading level loses mass audiences; keep the readability low enough for broad consumption.
cards.use_when: Deciding how technical or formal your product copy should be on a PDP or ad creative.
steps: Apply the source's core stat: only about 30 percent of U.S. 25- to 29-year-olds had completed a bachelor's degree or higher, and 3.4 million 16- to 24-year-olds were high school dropouts. Readable copy serves everyone; unreadable copy loses most of the market.
Compare the source's side-by-side test: a clear money-making offer scored 72.1 (6th-grade reading level), whereas a flowery version of the same offer scored 34.1 (college reading level).
Test your copy against your audience's norms by reading it aloud and checking grade level in your editor.
Avoid inflated sentence construction. The source specifically warns that putting effort into sounding academic can drop your message into a range most readers won't finish.
caveats: Even college-educated audiences can read longer copy well; the source's point is floor, not ceiling.
A lower reading score means easier, not less intelligent - the source is explicit about this distinction.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Rewrite Vague Claims with Short Words and Concrete Promises
cards.summary: Trade formal abstraction for specific, benefit-led phrasing that the reader can see and believe.
cards.use_when: Editing benefit claims, headlines, and PDP bullets to make them more concrete and persuasive.
steps: Replace abstract benefit language with specific, quantified, or vivid phrasing. The source's pair: 'Become financially successful' becomes 'You'll make up to $2,495 every week.'

Segment by audience and paint the specific outcome. The source's example: instead of 'Want your entire body to look more appealing?', write 'MEN! Do you want a rippling, rock-hard stomach? WOMEN! Do you want lean, luscious thighs?'

Watch for inflated vocabulary. The source warns that formal education pushes writers toward words like enervated, famished, elephantine, recalcitrant, and nefarious, and that using them in ads is effectively flushing money down the toilet.
Cut specific filler phrases the source calls out: 'and you'll enjoy same,' 'the aforementioned benefits,' 'you can liken this to,' and 'herein are 10 reasons.'
Use 'definite words' - nouns, proper names, pronouns, verbs, and specifics - so the reader does less interpretation. 'Joey ate chocolate' is more definite than 'Someone did something.'
caveats: The source's specific example headlines are stylistic demonstrations, not tested winners.
Don't swing to the other extreme of three-word sentences for every line; keep variety.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Run the Same Message Through Multiple Sources and Arguments
cards.summary: Present the same claim from several different people and lightly varied arguments to shift belief.
cards.use_when: Building testimonial blocks, review sections, creator partnerships, and multi-channel campaigns for one product.
steps: Collect the same core claim from multiple distinct sources - different customers, experts, or creators - rather than leaning on one testimonial.

Vary the exact argument each source makes, not the conclusion. The source's illustration: one person saying chocolate is healthy may or may not shift belief, but five people giving slightly different versions throughout the day is much more likely to change it.
Use this on long-form sales assets. The source notes that long, engaging copy with many testimonials and reasons builds belief through both quality and quantity.
Treat the multiple-sources approach as reinforcing the same message, distinct from repetition of one single ad; multiple-source variation resets attention while reinforcing the argument.
caveats: The source's 'chocolate' example is a hypothetical illustration of the multiple-source effect, not a measured study result.
Visible or obviously orchestrated testimonial campaigns can backfire on credibility; keep the sources genuine.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Plain-Language Rewrite of Product Copy
cards.summary: Strip school-taught 'big words' from product descriptions and ad copy so shoppers instantly understand what you sell.
cards.use_when: Rewriting a product page, category description, paid-ad copy or email when traffic bounces or copy reads like a corporate brochure.
steps: Scan the draft for inflated substitutes: 'enervated' for tired, 'famished' for hungry, 'elephantine' for big, 'recalcitrant' for stubborn, 'nefarious' for evil. Replace each with the everyday word.
Delete formal filler phrases the source calls out: 'and you'll enjoy same', 'the aforementioned benefits', 'you can liken this to', 'herein are 10 reasons'.
For each product-page bullet, read it aloud to a non-specialist; if they hesitate, cut or replace the word.
Ask whether the sentence tells the shopper what she gets, not how clever the writer is. The source argues copy has one job: to sell.
Apply the simplification to every asset you reuse (ad, PDP, landing page, email) because the trained habit follows you into every format.
Where a genuinely technical term is necessary for a niche audience (e.g., specs for pro buyers), keep it but define it in the same sentence.
caveats: The source's claim that unclear words 'flush money down the toilet' is opinionated; there is no measured conversion number attached.
Technical or expert audiences may expect precise terminology — simplify the surrounding sentence, not the term itself.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Short Sentences, Short Words, Short Paragraphs
cards.summary: Use one idea per sentence, ~11 words on average, and mostly one-syllable words to keep readers moving through sales copy.
cards.use_when: Formatting the body copy of a product landing page, sales email or catalog ad where you need prospects to read every selling point.
steps: Apply Flesch's targets as quoted by the source: about 70–80% of words should be one syllable, and sentences should average roughly 11 words.
Enforce the rule of one thought per sentence; put the next point in the next sentence rather than joining with 'and' or 'but'.
Keep regular paragraphs to about four or five short sentences so the page doesn't read as a wall of text.

Use the short-paragraph trick sparingly: pose a question or one-line statement, then answer or continue in the next paragraph in a few words (e.g., 'Would you like to know a secret way to make money watching TV? / I thought so. / Now let me explain...').
Check that opening sentences of the body are deliberately tiny — the source notes copywriter Drew Kaplan often opens paragraphs with two-to-four-word sentences like 'I confess.' or 'It's tough.'
Don't overdo the trick — the source warns mechanical-looking copy loses the effect.
caveats: Ogilvy's 'max 11 words in your opening paragraph' and the 70–80% one-syllable target are the source's cited heuristics, not tested conversion guarantees.
Repeating the two-to-four word pattern in every paragraph reads as gimmick; vary it.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Personal Pronoun Density for Warm Copy
cards.summary: Load headlines and body copy with 'you' and 'I' to turn mass advertising into personal communication.
cards.use_when: Drafting headlines, product descriptions or email subject lines that currently sound distant and corporate.
steps: Sprinkle 'you' and 'I' throughout every asset — the source says it is nearly impossible to overuse 'you' in well-written copy.
Start or end sentences with 'you': 'Do you…', 'Can you…', 'Would you…', 'Should you…'.
Write question prompts the source lists: 'May I ask you a question? May I ask your advice? Can I get your opinion? Did you know… Let me tell you… I think you'll like this idea…'.
Put 'you' in the headline itself, not just the body — the headline is where most skimmers stop.
Apply this to onboarding and retention emails too: framing the message as a one-to-one note raises its perceived relevance.
caveats: The source's claim that pronoun-heavy copy is 'the most effective kind' is an advertising convention, not a quantified result.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Feature-to-Benefit 'Big Deal' Translation
cards.summary: Convert every product spec into a WIIFM benefit by forcing each feature through the 'You benefit by…' test.
cards.use_when: Writing PDP bullets, bundle descriptions or ad copy from a spec sheet that currently lists only features.
steps: List each feature as a plain component (e.g., 'multiple ink tanks', '500-sheet tray', 'ultra-draft mode button').

For each, mentally shout 'BIG DEAL! What's in it for me?' then complete the sentence 'You benefit by…'. Example: multiple ink tanks → 'You benefit by saving money because you don't replace the whole cartridge when one color runs out.'
Keep the buyer's reaction as the copy — the source's printer example shows the prospect immediately self-identifies with the pain ('I spend a fortune for ink with my current printer').

Use the source's Rolls-Royce examples as the pattern: hand-selected leather → luxurious comfort in all climates; deep-pile wool carpeting → rich softness underfoot; 453-hp V-12 → power, control, supreme reliability; Spirit of Ecstasy hood ornament → feeling of power and 'arrived' status.
Run the same drill on every bundle or upsell item so cross-sell copy names the gain, not the components.
Strip anniversary notices, staff photos and company milestones unless they come with a price cut or buyer gain.
caveats: The feature/benefit split is the source's framing; a benefit that isn't credible becomes hype.
Do not convert a benefit into an unsupported numeric promise (e.g., 'save 50% on ink') unless your own product data supports it.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Biggest Benefit in the Headline
cards.summary: Put the single most important buyer benefit in the headline so 60% who only skim headlines still get the selling message.
cards.use_when: Writing or revising headlines for paid ads, emails, product pages or category banners.
steps: Write down the #1 reason a shopper would buy; that becomes the headline, not a brand name or vague claim.

Replace amorphous claims. The source's before/after: 'Louise Taylor Designs Homes of Distinction' → 'Award-Winning Interior Designer Louise Taylor Turns Your House Into a Gorgeous Model Home for Less than You Ever Dreamed Possible!'
Select the audience in the headline itself. The source contrasts 'We'll Help You Brighten Up Your Life and Save Big!' with the simple 'Need Lamps?' — the audience is instantly flagged.

Use the concrete-offer pattern when running a promotion: 'GIANT FILM SALE! All Rolls of 35mm Color Film are 25% Off—This Week Only!' or 'Attention Chocolate Lovers: Now Sink Your Teeth Into the 8½-Pound Fudge-Devil Volcano Pie—Absolutely Free!'.
Give the specific payoff over the 'tricks of the trade' framing: 'New Workshop Teaches You How to Boost Your Tips by 512%…or Your Money Back!' — though back claims you can substantiate.
caveats: The 60% headline-and-nothing-else and 3,000-exposure figures are the source's cited estimates; treat as directional.
Ogilvy's 'unless your headline sells, you wasted 90% of your money' is the source's quotation of an opinion, not a measured result.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Short vs. Long Headline Trade-off
cards.summary: Shorter headlines are read more, but readability does not guarantee effectiveness — benefit outweighs brevity.
cards.use_when: Choosing between a compact and a long, information-heavy headline for an ad, email subject line or PDP hero.
steps: Follow the source's two-rule priority: (1) always put the biggest benefit in the headline; (2) where two headlines are equally effective, the shorter one is read by more people.

Reference the source's cited readership bands by headline length: up to 3 words 87.3%; 4–6 words 86.3%; 7–9 words 84%; 10–12 words 82.5%; 13+ words 77.9%. Readership drops most sharply above 12 words.
Keep in mind the source's cognitive basis: people process roughly five to nine items in one act of attention, and grasp about five to six words in a single glance.
Accept occasional long headlines — the source notes well-written long headlines that flow into subheads can be remarkably effective in direct-response ads.
Do not chop a headline so short it loses audience selection or the benefit — the source states a short headline is not automatically an effective one.
caveats: Readership bands come from the source's cited 1939–40 Saturday Evening Post study and Starch research — dated figures, treat as directional.
Ogilvy and the source disagree on long vs. short: Ogilvy said longer headlines sell more. Choose per context.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: 22 Tested Headline Starters
cards.summary: Use a bank of proven opening words to set the tone of a headline while swapping in your specific product, offer and benefit.
cards.use_when: Stuck drafting headlines for a new product launch, promotion, category page or email campaign.
steps: Pick a starter word from the source's 22 and swap in your product: FREE, NEW, AT LAST, THIS, ANNOUNCING, WARNING!, JUST RELEASED, NOW, HERE'S, THESE, WHICH OF, FINALLY, LOOK, PRESENTING, INTRODUCING, HOW, AMAZING, DO YOU, WOULD YOU, CAN YOU, IF YOU, STARTING TODAY.
Match the starter to the buyer's awareness: 'Announcing' and 'Introducing' for launches; 'Warning!' for problem-solving offers; 'How' and 'Do you' for instructional angles.

Follow the patterned examples — 'How to Sing Like an American Idol in 90 Days or Less—Guaranteed'; 'If You Hate Cleaning Your Pool, This Ad Brings Good News!'; 'Would You Trade $2 for Our Famous Brick-Oven Pizza?'.
Anchor most headlines to John Caples' four qualities: self-interest, news, curiosity, and quick/easy way — self-interest and news usually carry the load.
Test multiple starters for the same product rather than committing to one, and check they still select a qualified audience.
caveats: The source warns against cute or clever headlines that don't target the right audience ('SEX!' for patio furniture) — the goal is the right eyeballs, not all eyeballs.
Free, guarantee and time-bound claims must match your actual offer and local advertising rules.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: 12 Openers That Bridge Headline to Body Copy
cards.summary: Pull the reader from the headline into the sales copy using one of 12 proven opening devices.
cards.use_when: The headline works but the body copy starts flat on a landing page, sales email or catalog ad.
steps: Choose a device and align it with the headline's promise: continue the thought; ask a question; quote a respected authority; give a free taste; challenge the reader to prove it works; start with a story of skepticism.

Add bandwagon, reporter, and personal-address options: tell what others are saying with a signed testimonial; write as a reporter ('Philadelphia, PA—A New York psychologist has just released the findings of a seven-year study…'); open directly with 'you' questions.

Use dramatic-story or super-detailed spec openers when the product story is emotional or technical — e.g., detailing an '8½ × 11-inch leatherbound, hardcover' book with 'over 327 pages, 10 information-filled chapters, and 45 of the most effective new communication tools'.
Try a very short first sentence to lure readers in: 'Don't you hate it?', 'It's so annoying!', 'I can't stand it!'.
Apply the 'free taste' opener on PDPs by giving one usable tip or sample step before the ask — the source shows it works in print.
caveats: Quoting an authority or publishing testimonials requires real, attributable sources — the source's examples are illustrative.
Super-detailed specs need accurate figures; guessing damages credibility on a PDP.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Break the Rectangle: Shape and Scroll-Stopping Design
cards.summary: Use shape difference — circular ads over the dominant square/rectangle — to stand out from competing placements.
cards.use_when: Placing display ads in a feed, marketplace or newsletter where your creative will sit cluttered among competitors.
steps: Acknowledge the source's observation that most print ads are square or rectangle simply because publishers optimize their sales space, not because square outperforms.
Ask the designer or printer to set the ad inside a circular border within the standard square space you buy; keep the copy layout normal rather than curving text around the interior.
Fill the area between the outer edge of the circle and inner edge of the square with a solid color (often black) so the circle is emphasized.
Give the horizontal-center area the most copy: a circle naturally offers more width at the middle than at top and bottom.
For ecommerce placements, translate the principle as stand-out creative in cluttered environments (distinctive shape or framing in a display slot) — not as a literal circle on a mobile feed.
caveats: The source's supporting evidence is Printer's Ink from decades ago in print — treat as directional, not a universal conversion result.
Ad platforms often control creative shape; test distinctiveness within the allowed format.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Never Reverse Long Body Type
cards.summary: White (or light) type on a dark background cuts legibility and slows reading — reserve it for short, large headlines.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a website, email or ad creative with dark backgrounds behind text.
steps: Check every text element: if body copy is lighter than its background, flip it to dark type on a light background.

Apply the source's cited evidence: G. Holmes (1931) found black-on-white text legible at ~66 inches versus ~55 inches for reversed; Daniel Starch measured a non-reversed reading speed just over six words per second versus just over four for reversed.
Note Paterson and Tinker's results: reversed passages read 4% less legibly when compared immediately after a normal passage, and 16% less legibly when participants read only reversed copy.
Keep the exception: reverse large headline type with few words out of a solid dark background (e.g., 'Free Chocolate Truffles!').
On a website, avoid dark hero sections with long light-grey paragraph copy; use a light card or overlay for body text.
caveats: Evidence is the source's citation of 1930s–1940s studies; more recent screen research may differ.
Dark mode interfaces are common and expected by many users — the principle applies to long-form sales copy, not necessarily UI text.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Extreme Specificity: Educate the Shopper With Detail
cards.summary: Describe your product's process, materials and numbers in exhaustive specifics so your listing feels more substantial than generic competitors.
cards.use_when: Writing a product page, brand story or category copy where competitors all use the same vague 'quality ingredients' language.
steps: List what you do that is invisible to the market — sourcing, process, preparation, craftsmanship, guarantees — and put it in the copy.

Contrast the source's two pizzerias: Luigi's ('wonderful home cooking' plus a coupon) versus Fratelli's, which specified fresh bread baked daily, from-scratch pasta, fresh herbs, pure cold-pressed virgin olive oil, spring water, Italian music, softly glowing candles.

Contrast the two hardware stores: the first listed categories at 'neighborhood-friendly prices'; Handyman Jack's cited 343 kinds of fasteners, 28 types of nails, 86 gauges of wire, 43 grit sizes of sandpaper, 16 hammer styles, 47 types of keys, 354,000 daily bolts and screws, top-name tools for less, and a no-nonsense money-back guarantee.
Use numerical specifics where they're honest: counts of SKUs, finishes, sizes, years of family craft (the source's four-generation, 80-year example).
Include sensory detail, not just data — 'golden and crusty bread', 'chewy interior crust' — to help shoppers pre-experience the product.
Understand the mechanism the source names: Length-Implies-Strength — because few competitors say these things, the one who does reads as bigger, more complete, more successful.
caveats: The source acknowledges some details are objectively trivial — the effect comes from the psychology of detail, not necessity.
Every count, source claim and guarantee must be true and verifiable or you risk consumer-protection exposure.
Unconfirmed adjectives like 'award-winning' should only accompany an actual award.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Ogilvy Two-Thirds Layout and Caption Rule
cards.summary: Structure ads and hero sections with a dominant visual, headline below it, and copy beneath — plus a selling caption under every image.
cards.use_when: Designing a display ad, print insert or a PDP/landing-page hero where the image-to-copy balance needs a proven arrangement.
steps: Use the Two-Thirds/One-Third (the 'Ogilvy') layout: top two thirds is one large photograph; headline directly beneath it; body copy below; company logo in the lower-right corner.
Or use the Reverse Ogilvy: photo on top third, headline beneath it, remaining two thirds sales copy, logo lower-right.
Start body copy with a drop cap — the source cites Ogilvy's claim of a 13% average readership increase.
Treat the headline and body copy as the photo's caption; the eye moves to the image first, then down.

Put a caption under every illustration — the source cites evidence that up to twice as many people read captions as body copy, and both Ogilvy and John Caples instructed copywriters to write selling captions.
caveats: Layout evidence is adapted from print research (Starch and Ogilvy); screen behavior and mobile layouts may differ.
The 13% drop-cap figure is attributed by the source to Ogilvy, not reinterpreted as a general benchmark.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Typeface Choice for Ease of Reading
cards.summary: Choose readable faces — serif for printed body text, initial caps for headlines — to prevent large chunks of readers abandoning copy.
cards.use_when: Specifying fonts for a catalog, print flyer, packaging, or the body text of a website or landing page.
steps: Use a serif face for body copy on paper: the source cites Wheildon's tests showing 66% comprehension for Garamond, versus less than 50% for Times Roman and 12.5% for Helvetica in one several-hundred-thousand-reader test.

Avoid excessively decorative fonts; the source singles out Flag Day-style, letter-obscuring faces as nearly unreadable, and notes research showing Cloister Black slowed reading by 16.5% and American Typewriter by 5.1%.

Choose from serif faces commonly recommended by practitioners the source names — Adobe Caslon, Adobe Garamond, ITC Stone Serif, Janson Text 55 Roman, Baskerville, Cheltenham Bold for headlines, Century, Caslon, Jenson, Courier for sales letters, Schoolbook for body.

Set headlines longer than a couple of words in initial caps rather than all caps: the source cites Paterson and Tinker's 11.8% readership drop for all caps, and a further test finding an 18.9% gap favoring initial caps.
Understand the mechanism for the caps rule — the eye recognizes words by outline, and all caps removes the ascender/descender variation that distinguishes words.
caveats: The serif/sans-serif comprehension figures are 1980s print studies from the source; screen rendering and resolution differ, and sans-serif is standard for digital UI.
The source itself notes no definitive study picking a single best serif; the practitioner preferences are opinions.
Comprehension percentages are source-cited findings, not conversion benchmarks.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Deadlines and Scarcity to Beat Buyer Inertia
cards.summary: Add a hard or soft deadline to every offer so prospects act while the salesperson is still in front of them.
cards.use_when: Finalizing a promotion, launch, restock or cart-abandon email where the CTA currently has no reason to act now.
steps: Decide between a hard deadline with a specific cut-off ('Sale Ends August 21st') or a soft deadline ('Quantities are Strictly Limited').

Use the source's standard phrases: 'Call Before April 5th', 'Supplies Are Strictly Limited', 'Offer Expires May 15', 'Price Guaranteed Only Until August 3', 'Offer Good Only Before 4 p.m.', 'Seating Is Limited to 50 Participants', 'NO Rain Checks Will Be Issued', 'Good Only for the First 50 Callers'.
Translate for ecommerce: countdown to end of sale, low-stock indicators, limited-run quantities, member-only windows, expiry on the discount code.

Apply the underlying psychology the source cites — Cialdini's scarcity weapon, where fear of loss gives deadlines their power — and note the source frames this as acting when the offer is presented, not just asking for the order.
Put the deadline in the headline, above the CTA and in the reminder email sequence.
caveats: A soft deadline like 'limited stock' must reflect real inventory constraints or it becomes a trust problem.
Fake countdown timers and always-on 'flash sales' can dilute the mechanism and trigger consumer-protection complaints in some jurisdictions.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Repeating 'You Learned' to Escalate Credibility
cards.summary: Use repeated paragraph leaders that echo the promise to speed reading, add tempo and imply volume of proof.
cards.use_when: Writing sales-page, webinar-recap or follow-up email copy where you need to consolidate the argument and drive the reader onward.
steps: Start consecutive paragraphs with the same leader phrase so the reader's eye is pulled down the page: 'YOU LEARNED…', 'We Guarantee…', 'We Promise…', 'You'll Receive…'.
In each follow-on paragraph, restate one point the reader has already been shown — the source's example repeats 'YOU LEARNED' across five paragraphs summarizing earlier lessons.
Alternate with benefit restatements so the repetition isn't pure self-congratulation — each leader should reintroduce a benefit or promise.
Use the technique at the summary page of a long PDP, in email sequences recapping earlier content, or on the post-purchase page to reanchor the value of the purchase.

Accept the source's rationale: the repetition increases perceived volume, and the source argues it can cause skeptical readers to doubt their own resistance because the copy sounds confident, specific and repeated.
caveats: The source acknowledges the reader may not actually have learned all the points being repeated — this is a persuasion technique, not an informational one.
Overusing paragraph leaders makes copy feel mechanical and can erode trust.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Choose headline and body type size for on-screen readability
cards.summary: Pick initial-cap headlines, Arial/Verdana sizing, and dark-on-light color to maximize online reading speed for ads and landing pages.
cards.use_when: Formatting headlines, body copy or a landing-page hero for on-screen reading (PDP, ad, email) where legibility affects completion.
steps: Set headlines in initial caps, not all caps. All-caps words form uniform rectangular outlines so the eye has fewer distinctive shapes to recognize, slowing reading; source cites an 18.9% gap favoring initial caps and Tinker's finding that all caps slowed reading.

For body text 12pt and larger, use Arial; below 12pt prefer Verdana but rarely go below 10pt. For a formal look use Georgia; for older audiences use 14pt. These come from multiple online legibility studies (Tullis/Boynton/Hersh; Bernard/Mills; Bernard et al.; Software Usability Research Laboratory), which the author synthesizes into one recommendation.
Set long headlines in black on white; white backgrounds read best, then yellow. Avoid reversing text out of dark backgrounds for long passages.
Remember paper and screen differ: print is ~300 dpi while Mac screens are ~72 dpi and Windows ~96 dpi, so a font that reads well in print may not read well online.
Verify current font availability and rendering on your actual storefront templates before standardizing, since interfaces change.
caveats: Recommendations are the author's synthesis of older readability studies, not a current controlled test of your audience or device mix.
Preference and speed results from these studies were sometimes mixed, so treat point sizes as heuristics, not hard rules.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Hire a real designer instead of self-designing sales materials
cards.summary: Use a vetted freelance designer or art-school student and always review samples before paying, because graphic software skills are not design skill.
cards.use_when: Producing product images, ad creative, packaging or sales collateral where amateur design risks a low-quality brand impression.
steps: Recognize the source's claim: owning design software does not make you a designer, and amateurish materials damage your image especially with prospects who don't know you.

To find a designer, call local ad agencies and ask to speak with the art or creative director, explaining you run a small business putting together an ad/brochure/flyer and asking for freelance recommendations; agencies usually work with several.

If hiring online, review the portfolio, ask the rate, and confirm whether billing is hourly or per project. Rates vary and some designers price by how large they think your company is, so the source advises not sounding big.
If budget is tight, call local graphic-arts schools for students who will work cheaply.
Before paying anyone, request samples; some will be excellent, others poor.
Note this card concerns creative production quality, not ad-media buying.
caveats: The source's remark that designers may charge based on perceived company size is an anecdotal opinion, not a pricing rule.
There is no implied benchmark for what a good designer costs.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Use questions to pull readers through copy
cards.summary: Open headlines, subheads and body copy with questions, especially 'Do you want...?' followed by a benefit, to keep prospects reading.
cards.use_when: Writing a product page, ad, email or sales letter where you need to hold attention from the headline into the body.
steps: Place questions in headlines, subheads and body copy. The source's stated mechanism is that a question creates an 'open loop' the reader wants to close, so they keep reading for the answer.
Use 'Do you want...?' openers followed immediately by a strong benefit, e.g., 'Do you want to DOUBLE, TRIPLE, even QUADRUPLE your self-confidence?'
Treat each sentence's job as earning the next: the purpose of the first sentence and paragraph is to get people to read the second.
Use questions as mini pop-quizzes in long-form content to keep readers alert and to make monologue feel like two-way conversation.
Note the source admits there is no scientific research supporting the NLP open-loop claim; the technique's justification is his observed readership effect.
caveats: Open-loop/NLP framing is attributed to NLP proponents only, without scientific support per the source itself.
Overusing questions can feel gimmicky; the source does not set a maximum.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Make sales letters personal, brochures detailed
cards.summary: Treat the sales letter as a one-on-one salesperson that meets prospects in their world, and the brochure as the sample-filled briefcase of complete details.
cards.use_when: Planning an email or sales letter versus a catalog/brochure, or deciding how personal versus detailed each piece of a campaign should be.
steps: Divide roles: the letter is the personal salesperson establishing rapport; the brochure is the impersonal briefcase of photos, samples and complete detail. Both work toward the same sale.

Write to 'meet the prospect in their world' by reflecting their language, age and situation. The source contrasts a stiff 'Dear Justin: The weekend is young...' opening against a casual 'Hey Justin... if you're sick and tired of staying home...' opening.
List every benefit first (not features), then rank them by importance to the customer, not to you. Put the #1 benefit in the opening of the letter.

Personalize salutations. 'Dear Bob' beats 'Dear Friend'; when you cannot personalize, use a transformation salutation like 'Dear Weekend Warrior' or 'Dear Soon-to-Be-Millionaire.' Never use 'Dear Occupant.'
Work the ideas of ease and quickness into the first sentence where relevant, since the source argues buyers respond to speed and ease.
caveats: These formatting prescriptions are the author's direct-marketing conventions; email and privacy norms may restrict personalization data today.
The source's example testimonial copy is illustrative, not a tested result.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Write teasers that survive the trash can
cards.summary: Design outer envelopes/carrier copy to look personal, not informational, so prospects open before trashing.
cards.use_when: Designing the subject line and sender presentation for a direct-mail or email campaign to a cold or loosely targeted list.
steps: Assume most mail is trashed within seconds and that many people open mail over a trash can, so you have only moments to grab attention.

Prefer nonspecific teasers such as 'PERSONAL ATTENTION OF:', 'PERSONAL LETTER FOR:' or 'IMPORTANT LETTER FOR:' over informational teasers. Informational teasers announce 'this is a sales pitch,' so the source advises using them only when the list is pin-point targeted to the offer.
Use physical cues that signal personal mail: brightly colored envelopes, a bloodred 'URGENT' stamp, and multiple small-denomination stamps instead of one stamp.

Write a personalized note next to the typed name, e.g., 'Eileen: Here's the Information We Talked About! —Drew,' or with an implied deadline such as 'Please Read This Letter Before 9:30 Tonight,' justifying the deadline in the letter.
Do not use mailing labels; they signal mass mailing. Feed envelopes through a printer, use a realistic handwriting font, or have a seniors group hand-address them.
caveats: Personal-looking tactics may conflict with spam regulations or brand standards in email; adapt carefully.
The source's preference for nonspecific teasers assumes the mailing list is not precisely targeted.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Build a Granny-style response device
cards.summary: Convert order forms into warm, easy-to-complete 'Personal Trial Certificates' with guarantee, scarcity and a business reply envelope.
cards.use_when: Designing a cart, order form or checkout page to reduce friction and lift completion rate.
steps: Rename the response device: instead of 'Order Form,' call it a 'Personal Trial Certificate' or 'Personal, No-Obligation Trial Certificate.'
Pre-fill the recipient's name and address. Print it on canary (yellow) paper so it stands out from other pieces.
Restate the offer on the form and place a bold 'YES!' check next to a box. The source cites John Caples' advice to show a small picture of what the buyer receives.
Play up the guarantee prominently, and put your mailing address, phone and web/email on the bottom in case the reader loses the rest. Put your name and address on all components.
Add scarcity and a deadline on the form itself, plus everywhere else in the mailing; without a deadline people tend to 'think about it.'
Include a business reply envelope (or a live stamp if you lack a reply permit), rubber-stamping 'RUSH! ORDER ENCLOSED!' or '24-HOUR PROCESSING' in red.
caveats: This is designed for direct mail; adapt the equivalent cart elements rather than literally mailing reply envelopes.
The source's claims about pre-filled forms and deadlines are his conventions, not measured benchmarks.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Collect testimonials systematically with permission
cards.summary: Request testimonials with a specific questionnaire and a signed usage release, compensating with copies of the finished piece or a small payment.
cards.use_when: Sourcing social proof for a product page, ad or brochure and needing documented permission to use customer quotes.
steps: Email or write customers: 'We want to make you famous!' and ask for their honest opinions for a new ad, brochure or website, offering, if they like, their photo.

Ask questions that produce quotable specifics, e.g., what they think of the service, what kind of response they get, how you compare to other providers, what they like best, whether prices are reasonable, and whether they'd recommend or hire you again.
Include a permission line granting you rights to use the quotes in complete or edited form, with checkboxes for with/without name and city/state, plus a signature and date line.

Provide consideration: the source says sending copies of the first printed piece in which the testimonial appears legally binds the agreement, or alternatively enclose $1.00 to cover their return expenses.
Pay the return postage with a self-addressed stamped envelope so the customer incurs no expense.
Always send the promised copies of the finished piece.
caveats: The source's description of 'consideration' is a lay legal explanation, not legal advice; confirm testimonial consent and compensation rules for your jurisdiction and platform.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Use the Guillotine Principle to grab attention with a face
cards.summary: Place a close-up human face looking directly at the reader in ads and pages to gain attention, warmth and trust.
cards.use_when: Choosing the main image for an ad, PDP, packaging or landing-page hero where stopping power and warmth matter.
steps: Add a photo of a person's head or face, looking directly at the reader. Faces are described as the best attention-getters.
Choose expression based on context: smiling is generally preferable, but a screaming, distorted face would be a shocker appropriate to a product like tear gas.
Show the founder's face for service and craft businesses (carpenter, dentist) to add warmth and convert a faceless business into a real person.
Even a tiny black-and-white photo will do; keep it simple.
Put the photo at the top of the ad and make the headline a quote from you, e.g., a headline reading 'Give Me 90 Minutes & I'll Show You How to Double...Triple...Quadruple Your Ad Response!'
Repeat your photo and name across ads; the source claims repeated exposure can build recognition over time.
caveats: Faces draw attention but the source gives no measured conversion lift; test against your audience and product.
A face that mismatches the offer's emotional tone can undercut the ad.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Sharpen copy with powerful visual adjectives (PVAs)
cards.summary: Replace generic product descriptions with concrete, sensory adjectives that let prospects picture and mentally demo the product.
cards.use_when: Rewriting commodity product or service descriptions where your offer looks like competitors' and needs to stand out.
steps: Swap bland descriptions for concrete imagery. The source's examples: 'Make lots of money' becomes 'Rake in $2,750 cash weekly'; 'Juicy red apples' becomes 'Mouth-watering, sugar-sweet, hand-picked apples'; 'Drink cleaner water' becomes 'Enjoy pure, crystal-clear, glacier-fresh water.'
For a specialty soap, describe the experience as splashing skin with 'liquid sunshine' or sliced Florida oranges, and rename a 'lather' as 'Sweet Orange-Cream Bubbles.'

Use the same technique for services: instead of 'Our expert cleaners will make your office sparkle like new,' specify walls and floors 'hospital-bright,' restrooms 'sparkling and sanitized,' carpets 'fluffy, fresh, and deodorized.'

The source's stated rationale: specific sensory words create clearer mental pictures and make you look more qualified and conscientious than competitors who tell only part of the story, so competitors appear to do less.
Apply to your weakest, most generic product copy first and compare response.
caveats: Source's claims of competitive advantage are persuasive argument, not tested data, and his own soap colleague pushed back that it was over the top.
Do not let PVAs override truth or compliance on claims like income or health.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Direct mental movies through the five senses (VAKOG)
cards.summary: Ramp up sensory detail across visual, auditory, kinesthetic, olfactory and gustatory channels so prospects mentally rehearse using the product before buying.
cards.use_when: Writing long-form sales copy, product pages or emails that must move a prospect from facts to purchase.
steps: Recognize that all experience blends five elements: Visual (sight), Auditory (sound), Kinesthetic (feeling/emotion), Olfactory (smell), Gustatory (taste). The source calls them internal representations (IRs).
Write to intensify these IRs so the reader experiences your product internally. Facts alone create few IRs and won't prime buying, per the source's pool-cleaner example.

Tour prospects through the product: name it, describe how it looks, sounds, feels and how using it changes their day. The source's pool-cleaner letter describes a hose like a 'blue manta ray,' a 'chuga-chuga-chuga' sound, sparkling water that 'smells better,' and piped-in 'piña coladas.'
Not every sense applies to every product; a printer won't sell taste, but can describe paper's smooth or cottony texture and how it feels to hold the stationery, creating quality associations.
Consider a 'step-out' authenticity move: a line that momentarily steps outside the ad to convey real-time, here-and-now genuineness.
Use this to justify longer copy; the source claims longer copy outsells short because it accumulates more IRs.
caveats: VAKOG and the long-copy claim are stated as the author's experience, not measured universal benchmarks; test against your audience.
Ethical and regulatory limits apply to exaggerated sensory promises and guarantees.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Battle inertia by making buying easy and asking for action
cards.summary: Lower effort on every step and make an explicit call to action, since people are lazy and avoid involvement.
cards.use_when: Optimizing checkout, signup, quote request or any conversion flow where prospects stall or abandon.
steps: Follow the source's two-step formula: make it easy to act, then ask for action. He warns these do not guarantee action but raise the odds.
Offer pre-filled forms where practical (name, address, credit card slot) and a postage-paid reply; remove roadblocks so the prospect says 'Gee, look how easy!'
Accept as many alternate payment forms as possible (major credit cards, checks, money orders, PayPal) and offer several shipping speeds, from ground to overnight.
Offer gift-wrapping, a strong guarantee to quell fear of loss, and payment plans like 'Just $14.99 a month for three months' to reduce the pain of spending.
Tell prospects exactly how to order, step by step; for retailers give address, phone, driving directions and hours.
Use phrase variants like 'It's Easy To Order!' or 'It's Easy to Get a FREE Estimate!' for your context.
caveats: This is the source's sales principle, not a guarantee; he explicitly disclaims that following these steps produces universal success.
Pre-filled and stored payment details carry privacy/security obligations today, unlike direct mail.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Differentiate with a unique selling proposition (USP)
cards.summary: Craft a real, truth-based gimmick or system that distinguishes your offer, since indistinguishable products give buyers no reason to prefer you.
cards.use_when: Positioning a product or store in a crowded category where your offer reads like generic sugar or salt.
steps: Accept the source's premise: when people can't distinguish you from competitors, they have no reason to prefer you. Commodity products get no preference.

Find or build a genuine differentiator and name it. Examples: not a hardware store but 'The Hardware Superstore!'; not an office cleaner but 'The Office Cleaning Technicians!'; not a real estate office but the 'Experts of the RapidSell System!'
If you don't have a named system, the source says create a real program you can name, so the USP reflects what's true.

Study his Nifty Fifty's diner example: they announce never using frozen beef, grinding burgers fresh daily, fresh-cut fries, no frozen onion rings, visible kitchen prep and the frying oil used. They are proactive about telling customers why they are great instead of hoping customers discover it.
Make sure the product or service is genuinely excellent, or you may educate buyers away from you.
caveats: The source stresses positioning should reflect what's true; an invented claim you can't back will backfire.
This is the author's opinion-driven framework; no conversion benchmarks are offered.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Positioning: turn a commodity into a category of one
cards.summary: Reframe your store from a generic product category into a distinctive, ownable identity so you stop blending in with competitors.
cards.use_when: You are writing your homepage headline, brand tagline, or About/positioning statement for a store that currently describes itself generically (e.g. 'quality home goods store').
steps: Replace generic category labels with a specific identity that implies a method, specialization, or system. Source examples: not 'office cleaner' but 'Office Cleaning Technicians'; not 'real estate office' but 'Experts of the RapidSell System'.

If the higher positioning doesn't exist yet, build a program or process and name it, then make it real (your stated identity must match actual operations). The source explicitly warns that saying you're an expert doesn't make you one.
Align the whole store experience to the claim: operations, supplier quality, packaging, support tone, and imagery must be congruent or word-of-mouth will expose the gap and the positioning will fail.
Audit every generic competitor phrase on your site and replace it with a specific, verifiable version of what you do differently.
caveats: The source insists the product/service must be genuinely excellent first, otherwise you 'educate your buyer away' from you.
Positioning is only as strong as the operational backing; promising 'technicians' while delivering untrained service backfires.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Make your ad hook 'specifically unique' instead of vague
cards.summary: Use concrete, specific, unexpected hooks instead of generic category claims to earn more readership and clicks.
cards.use_when: You are drafting ad creative or a product landing page headline in a crowded category where every competitor uses the same generic promise.
steps: Compare a generic headline ('Work from Home and Turn Your Email Into Big Profits') against a specific one ('19-Year Old College Kid Discovers Clever Way to Persuade People to Send You Money Via PayPal'). The source argues the specific one wins because it paints a clear mental picture.
Ask yourself: what's unique about my offer, my process, my product? Can I be the only one claiming this? Is there something unique about me I can leverage?

Use real, truthful specifics from your own operations (your size, your story, your method). The source gives examples like 'Big Bald Chris Teaches Wing Chun' and '6'5", 275-Pound Man Offers the BIGGEST Computer Discounts'—each is honest but vivid.
Back the distinctiveness with matching imagery (e.g. hire a photographer to emphasize the real attribute, like shooting from floor level to emphasize size).
caveats: Stay truthful—'find an intriguing way to say it' does not mean fabricate claims.
The source cites Starch Research that fresh/new headlines deliver higher 'Read Most' scores, but that is the source's cited finding, not your store's data.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Build an authority position and make content as the evidence
cards.summary: Become the recognized expert in your niche by publishing knowledge in many formats, which lowers buyer skepticism and builds trust before purchase.
cards.use_when: You want your store to be seen as the go-to expert in a niche, and you need to convert expertise into a concrete content and trust-building plan.
steps: Whoever writes your marketing must first regard their knowledge as valuable—the source defines this mindset shift as Step 1 of authority positioning.
Get a professional headshot in appropriate attire and put it on product pages, ads, emails, brochures, contracts—everywhere.

Publish short reports (the source suggests 3–10 pages, PDF and hardcopy) with your headshot and business name on the cover, e.g. 'How to Use 10 Little-Known Printing Secrets to Make Your Business Look More Professional'.

Run editorial-style Q&A 'columns' (3 short questions with short answers, headshot at top, business name/address/phone at bottom) in local papers—sometimes these are accepted free if they offer useful info.
Run free clinics/workshops with samples that teach the buyer how to judge quality, then let your offer do the selling.
Offer the reports as free lead magnets to anyone who comes in or registers.
caveats: The source's printer case study is one person's result; replicate the method, not a promised number.
Claims of authority must be backed by real demonstrated knowledge; the source explicitly states to assume 'excellent grasp on your subject' before adopting an authority stance.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Use a customer survey as a sales letter in disguise
cards.summary: Mail a short survey with an exclusive thank-you offer embedded to collect buyer insight and generate an easy incremental sale.
cards.use_when: You want to know what customers actually think and, at the same time, drive a repeat purchase or upgrade with minimal friction.
steps: Write a short personal letter (8.5x11 stationery) asking 5–6 questions about satisfaction, price perception, and likelihood to re-buy, using 1–10 scales for easy completion.
Add one open-ended question to surface free feedback, e.g. 'If you were the owner of my business, what would you do differently?'
At the end, embed an offer you would have offered anyway, framed as an exclusive thank-you only for survey respondents (e.g. a 50% off product, free consultation, or voucher).
Include a YES block and payment/confirmation mechanic so respondents can return payment with the survey, e.g. 'a $10 product for just $5—postage paid—only for survey respondents'.
Use mail-merge to make the letter look personal, not mass-produced.
Offer a free thank-you for taking the survey (e.g. a free slice) and limit response time to keep costs controlled.
caveats: The source claims this is effective for a wide range of businesses but warns the offer must feel like an exclusive thank-you, not a standard promo.
Feedback can be more valuable than the extra sales profit, but the survey response rate depends on list quality and ease of reply.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Format a survey for maximum response
cards.summary: Use a double postcard or one-page letter with a postage-paid reply envelope and mostly multiple-choice questions to maximize survey returns.
cards.use_when: You are physically mailing survey cards or letters to your customers and need the highest possible reply rate to make the feedback useful.
steps: Choose a format: a double postcard split by a perforation (one side addressed to recipient, the other is the survey card) OR a one-page 8.5x11 letter with a survey and stamp-free reply envelope.
Use a Business Reply Mail permit indicia on the reply card so respondents don't need a stamp; the source states ease is the secret of good survey response.
Keep everything short—ideally letter and survey fit on one page (front, both sides if needed)—to reduce handling and confusion.
Use semantic differential scales (1–10) for all questions where possible, e.g. 'On a scale 1 to 10, how likely are you to return to us within two weeks?'
Bribe respondents with a free item (e.g. free slice) but limit the response window to keep costs and logistics under control.
caveats: The source stresses the personal letter/envelope format gets more attention, but it means more manual processing than a digital survey.
The free reward and postage-paid reply are real costs that must be weighed against the value of the feedback.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Use 'grabbers' to force attention on your direct mail or package inserts
cards.summary: Attach a small physical object to your mailer or insert to create curiosity and a sense of obligation to read your offer.
cards.use_when: You send physical mail to prospects or include marketing inserts in shipments and need something that makes your piece stand out in the stack.
steps: Attach a small, relevant object to the top of the letter or insert (penny, dollar bill, sand baggy, chocolate wrapper, poorly printed sample) that relates to your offer.

Open with copy that names the grabber and immediately ties it to the promise, e.g. 'As you can see, I have attached a crisp one-dollar bill...I'll show you how to save 100 of these when you buy carpet'.
Match the grabber to your category: real estate—baggy of sand; collection agency—an NSF check; candy shop—a wrapper with a coupon for a free sample; printer—a poorly printed brochure.
Test with an A/B split: mail 500 letters with the grabber vs. 500 without, and compare response.
Ensure the grabber won't rip the envelope or create postal handling problems—consider bubble-wrap-lined envelopes for bulky items.
caveats: The source says the technique worked for Robert Collier in 1937 and should be tested; it is not a guarantee.
A grabber that is too bulky or sharp may damage the mail piece or get flagged by postal carriers.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Long copy outsells short copy—if you keep it interesting
cards.summary: Well-written long copy beats short copy because it satisfies both detail-hungry buyers and quick deciders, online and offline.
cards.use_when: You are deciding how much copy a sales page, product page, or email should carry, especially in a high-consideration purchase.
steps: Write enough to inform, build desire, convince, and motivate—restating benefits from several different angles and perspectives (e.g. how the customer will feel, how others will see them, how safe/practical it is).
Address both emotional and logical appeals so you speak to both peripheral and central-route thinkers (car ads are the source's model: status, safety, economy).
Pile on benefits, testimonials, and a warranty—the source calls this stacking social proof and fear-reduction.
Accept that some buyers decide after the headline, so long copy doesn't hurt them; it only gives more-information buyers what they need.
Don't pad—Gary Halbert's cited line is 'Copy can never be too long, only too boring.'
caveats: The source cites Ogilvy, Caples, Hopkins, and MarketingExperiments.com, and a single Online-Learning.com case where quadrupling homepage copy was associated with ~20% more enrollments—these are examples, not guarantees.
The source's claim is aggressive ('long copy invariably outsells short copy'), but the necessary condition is well-written, relevant copy—short copy is only right when there is little to say.
cards.source_name: Cashvertising.docx

cards.title: Make your ad look like editorial content to lift readership
cards.summary: Camouflage ads in the typeface, column width, and news voice of the publication so more readers stop and read.
cards.use_when: You place ads in newspapers, newsletters, or niche publications where ad blindness is high and you want higher readership.
steps: Write the ad as a news story: same typeface, column width, and leading as the surrounding articles, headline included.
Open with a news-style lead, e.g. 'Local Hypnotist Announces New Way to Quit Smoking in 48 Hours'.
