cards.summary: Increase total reach of each launch email by resending to non-openers with a fresh subject line and preview text.
cards.use_when: Planning launch or promotional email sends for a store and wanting more subscribers to see existing copy.
steps: Treat each new launch email as two assets: the original send and a resend to unopens.
Change both subject line and preview text on the resend. The source pre-writes two subject lines and two sets of preview text when preparing client launches, precisely for this.
If your list is small, she says just changing the subject line is fine; a new subject alone still splits the message.
Recognize why this matters: if only openers see each send, a large share of your list may never see that email; repeated resends recover those people and milk the copy you paid to write.
Schedule resends according to your chosen pacing (aggressive, moderate or relaxed).
Keep each send single-purpose; the resend is the same email, not a new offer.
caveats: Only subscribers who did not open the first send get the resend, so the total audience per send is split, not doubled.
Aggressive resends risk annoyance on small, engaged lists; the source acknowledges this depends on list size.
cards.source_name: Copywriting 101_ eCommerce copywriting course FOR BEGINNERS.docx

cards.title: Write the triple close: three sales emails on closing day
cards.summary: Send three strong sales emails on the final day of a launch instead of one, timed across morning, afternoon and evening.
cards.use_when: Final day of a store launch or promotion when you want to capture last-chance buyers across time zones.
steps: On the final launch day, send three separate strong sales emails rather than a single close. The source says she accidentally invented this after a client debated a morning/afternoon versus afternoon/evening close; doing all three handles time zones since you cannot know when people are home.
Keep each of the three a strong, direct sales email; these are the emails 8-10 of the 10-email launch structure.
Use urgency appropriate to the offer deadline: the source frames the triple close as a high-urgency finish to a launch.

Expect this to be high-volume; the source reports it as consistently successful, including in launches she says hit multi-six figures and a business that grew to around $2M annualized recurring revenue (her case examples, not guarantees).
Combine the triple close with the resend-to-unopens mechanic to maximize total reach on the closing day.
caveats: Three sales sends in one day is a strong cadence with unsubscribe risk; the source does not quantify churn.
She describes the triple close as her preferred, experimentally derived style, not a proven universal best practice.
cards.source_name: Copywriting 101_ eCommerce copywriting course FOR BEGINNERS.docx

cards.title: Write quick-win lesson emails for the middle of a launch
cards.summary: Use teach-then-soft-CTA emails in the launch middle, capping each with a reminder that the product is for sale.
cards.use_when: Filling the middle days of a store launch sequence with value that keeps the audience engaged without unsubscribing.
steps: Give one small win readers can apply immediately, drawn from something you would write as a blog post, video lesson or tutorial, and make sure it is related to what the product does.
Do not take anyone off the email in the lesson itself; teach the tip fully, then pivot at the end with a crutch CTA the source uses such as 'what's next', 'next step' or 'reminder'.

Write the CTA as a soft reminder that the product exists and has more and better strategies than the one just shared, e.g. 'if you love these strategies, just remember my product is available and has four other strategies way better than this one.'
Finish with a sign-off and a PS that capitalizes on the lesson: name the mistake the reader likely makes, point out the fuller fix the product provides, and link to full details.
Keep the single-purpose rule: this email teaches; the CTA is a reminder selling the product, not a second lesson.
caveats: Soft CTA wording ('what's next', 'reminder') is the presenter's personal crutch phrasing; test your own.
The lesson must be genuinely useful, or the reminder tactic reads as bait.
cards.source_name: Copywriting 101_ eCommerce copywriting course FOR BEGINNERS.docx

cards.title: Repurpose existing content into a launch email
cards.summary: Turn prior videos, live events, reading lists or tutorials into a middle-of-launch email that drives clicks to your offer.
cards.use_when: Running a launch sequence and needing email content without writing new assets from scratch.
steps: Inventory existing content: your brands' videos and blogs, external content, or a mix. The source uses this slot to teach while also taking readers off the email and to the content.

Option one, recommended reading list: show the book cover and name, link out (she links to Amazon), and write a short reason it matters, pulled from actual five-star review language. She listed around 10 books this way.

Option two, repurpose prior live content: after a client ran a five-day structured live stream lesson series in a 58,000-person Facebook group, she repackaged that into a launch email because not everyone had seen it.

Option three, topic-focused repurposing: turn existing videos or material into emails like 'five mistakes you're making with your resume' or 'how to network with agents', tying the theme to the product's promise.
Close the email with the same soft CTA framing used in lesson emails ('what's next', 'next step', 'reminder') plus a PS that reminds readers you are selling.
Keep the email single-purpose: one function per asset.
caveats: Repurposed content must relate to the offer, or the CTA feels disconnected.
Suggested reading lists that link to third-party sellers can send traffic off your funnel; weigh that against engagement value.
cards.source_name: Copywriting 101_ eCommerce copywriting course FOR BEGINNERS.docx

cards.title: Build testimonial and FAQ emails around objections
cards.summary: Use launch emails 2-7's success and FAQ slots to answer the specific objections blocking purchases.
cards.use_when: Filling launch sequence gaps with social proof and objection handling for a store offer.
steps: For the success email, choose format to fit industry and sales model: either one long, powerful testimonial or case study, or several testimonials.

Select testimonials by objection, not by general praise. The source stresses it is especially powerful when you understand the angles of objection people have and choose testimonials that speak directly to each one.

For the FAQ email, gather real questions from chat features on your site, emails to you, Facebook messages and page comments. The source says review this material for ideas if you do not already know what to include.

Open the FAQ email by acknowledging the questions, e.g. 'over the last few days I've been telling you about my product and you sent in so many great questions I wanted to address them all at once', then answer each question in turn.
End both emails with a reminder that you are selling and a CTA. The source keeps repeated crutch CTAs like 'reminder' and 'what's next'.
caveats: Objection mapping requires you to already know what blocks purchase; do the customer-research step if not.
The presenter's phrasing examples are templates to adapt, not scripts to clone.
cards.source_name: Copywriting 101_ eCommerce copywriting course FOR BEGINNERS.docx

cards.title: Use sentiment matching from reviews to mirror prospect language
cards.summary: Read five-star and one-star testimonials to capture the exact internal narrative prospects use to describe their problem.
cards.use_when: Writing store PDP, ad or email copy and needing the customer's actual words instead of brand wording.
steps: Read both 5-star and 1-star customer testimonials. The source's rule is to review both in order to mirror the exact internal narrative prospects use to describe their problems.
Pull phrasing and objections directly into copy: how happy buyers describe the outcome, and how unhappy buyers describe the failure, since both represent the prospect's inner monologue.
Use this research when writing review-highlight email content; she scanned Amazon five-star reviews and paraphrased their language as the reason to read listed books.
Apply the same language to ads, landing pages and product pages to close the gap between how the brand sees the transformation and how the prospect experiences the problem.

Recognize the underlying insight: as the business owner you have full context and passion for the transformation, but prospects come from a totally different background, and your job is to bridge the gap in their words.
caveats: Review language can be raw; adapt the emotion but keep the concrete and specific claims accurate.
One-star complaints may point to real product issues, not just copy problems; fix the product where relevant.
cards.source_name: Copywriting 101_ eCommerce copywriting course FOR BEGINNERS.docx

cards.title: Lead prospects from their reality to the primary conversion goal
cards.summary: Account for the gap between the owner's expert context and the prospect's everyday perspective when writing any asset.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why store copy about the transformation fails to land with prospects even though the product is good.
steps: Acknowledge the asymmetry: you are the expert with the full context and passion for the transformation your product delivers; prospects arrive with a totally different background and set of experiences.

Identify your primary conversion goal for the asset (a sale for most stores; for the source's consulting example it might be a free consultation), and write every step toward that goal in the prospect's terms, not yours.
Frame copy so it leads the prospect from where they are to the goal, not from where you are. The source calls understanding this gap 'absolutely key to everything else.'
Apply it across assets: ad, landing page and email should each assume the reader's starting point and move them one micro-decision closer to the goal.

Use your expertise only after connecting to the reader's reality; the source's acting-course example is that people care about her specific frameworks for getting into network TV from scratch, but not until the copy relates them to the reader.
caveats: This is a mindset framing from the source, not a measurement method.
Copy that skips the reader's starting point may still work short-term, but the source argues it underperforms.
cards.source_name: Copywriting 101_ eCommerce copywriting course FOR BEGINNERS.docx

cards.title: Triple Close: Three Cart-Close Emails in One Day
cards.summary: Send three short cart-closing emails across morning, afternoon and evening of the final day instead of one or two.
cards.use_when: Planning the final day of a launch or sale campaign (cart close, promotion deadline, drop ending) and deciding how many closing emails to schedule.
steps: Schedule three closing emails on the final day: one in the morning, one in the afternoon, one in the evening. The source's client debated morning+afternoon vs afternoon+evening; the resolution was to send all three.
Vary subject lines rather than repeating the same one — casual late-night lines like 'you up?' were used for the last send.
Keep each closing email short and text-only; the goal is a reminder to act before the deadline, not new persuasion.

Attribute the reported results to this source's experience: triple close reportedly doubled total launch revenue in one case, and adding the third email alone added roughly 15–25% of total launch revenue. Treat these as examples, not promised benchmarks.
Test it yourself against your previous single- or double-close baseline before assuming the same lift for your list.
caveats: The revenue claims come from the presenter's own launches and one client; do not treat 15–25% as a guaranteed lift.
Three sends in one day raises unsubscribes and spam complaints on less engaged lists — segment to recent openers/clickers where possible.
cards.source_name: Copywriting 101_ eCommerce copywriting course FOR BEGINNERS.docx

cards.title: Late-Night Subject Lines: Short, Lowercase, No Punctuation
cards.summary: Use very short, casual, lowercase subject lines for late-evening sends and avoid periods that signal 'stop reading'.
cards.use_when: Writing subject lines for evening or final-day emails in a launch, flash sale or abandoned-cart sequence.
steps: Write the subject line as a casual check-in: 'you up', 'you're still up', 'just checking in'. The presenter takes the cue from the widely cited 'Hello' subject line attributed to Obama's campaign email.
Use lowercase and skip punctuation; a period reads as a full stop and invites deletion. Exclamation points are described as tolerable.
Reserve your grammatically careful subject lines for other emails — deliberately break the rule for late-night sends.
The presenter reports roughly a 32% open rate on a 600k-contact list with these lines, noting that open rates normally fall as list size grows. Verify against your own list before adopting at scale.
Write the subject line last, after drafting the body from an email outline, so it matches the content.
caveats: The 32% figure is one list's result, not a benchmark; large-list open rates vary by sender reputation and segmentation.
Lowercase, informal lines may underperform for premium or B2B ecommerce audiences — test before rolling out.
cards.source_name: Copywriting 101_ eCommerce copywriting course FOR BEGINNERS.docx

cards.title: Text-Only Emails to Stay Out of Promotions and Spam
cards.summary: Send plain-text emails without HTML templates or heavy images so promotions copy doesn't get filtered or clipped.
cards.use_when: Setting up any ecommerce email sequence — welcome, launch, or replenishment — where deliverability to the primary inbox matters.
steps: Strip out fancy HTML templates from your ESP (Mailchimp, etc.). The presenter says 'throw them in the garbage' — templates push emails into the Promotions tab and spam.
Load all content as plain text; only include a picture when it carries the message (e.g. a book cover, or a video thumbnail with a superimposed play button hyperlinked to the video).
Keep total email size under roughly two megabytes; oversized emails get clipped by email clients, and images easily exceed that.
Give up ornate formatting so the effort you put into writing isn't wasted in spam folders.
Keep the copy tight — the source says you don't need 'sat words' or showy vocabulary.
caveats: The 2MB clipping threshold is described approximately ('like two megabytes or something') — verify your ESP and client behavior.
Pure text reduces visual merchandising; if you rely heavily on product imagery, use linked video thumbnails or send traffic to a landing page instead.
cards.source_name: Copywriting 101_ eCommerce copywriting course FOR BEGINNERS.docx

cards.title: Write Email Sequences From an Outline Before Drafting
cards.summary: Decide the number of emails and their function first, then fill in subject, preview, story and content for each.
cards.use_when: Starting any ecommerce email campaign — launch, welcome, replenishment or abandoned-cart — and deciding where to begin.
steps: Commit to a quantity up front before writing anything. The source uses ten emails for a launch and seven for a welcome sequence as defaults; deviate only deliberately.
Build an outline row-by-row for each email: number it 1 through N, then for each write out subject, preview text, story, today's content and PS content.
Fill in the outline like kindergarten class — literally write email one, email two, email three, and so on.
Make sure the outline expresses the through-line of the whole sequence and what each email contributes to the broader objective.
Start writing as soon as possible after the outline so you're not staring at a blank page unprepared.
caveats: The 10-for-launch and 7-for-welcome numbers are the presenter's defaults, described as classic standards, not universal requirements.
A too-short or too-long sequence may not fit your catalog or list — the point is deciding the count on purpose.
cards.source_name: Copywriting 101_ eCommerce copywriting course FOR BEGINNERS.docx

cards.title: Seven-Email Welcome Series for New Subscribers
cards.summary: Send a daily seven-day welcome automation that delivers a video lesson and a short pitch while engagement is highest.
cards.use_when: Setting up an ecommerce welcome automation for new email signups, especially for a product that benefits from tutorials.
steps: Send an email per day for seven days as an automation; you don't need to obsess over unopens — it's automated, not a campaign.
For each day, link a video from your YouTube channel: hyperlink a video thumbnail with a superimposed play button, and under it, describe what the viewer will learn.
Include a call to action like 'if you want to check it out, click here', plus a PS that names a benefit and links again.
Strike while the iron is hot — the moment people first join is the most engaged they'll ever be, so pack value into these first days.
Aim to build positive open behavior: frequent opens train the inbox to keep your emails in the primary tab rather than Promotions or spam.
caveats: The source speaks from the perspective of teaching and B2C ecommerce clients; a seven-day daily cadence may feel heavy for lower-velocity or replenishment-only stores.
The claim that opens train the inbox is a heuristic — inbox placement is a black box; verify with your own deliverability data.
cards.source_name: Copywriting 101_ eCommerce copywriting course FOR BEGINNERS.docx

cards.title: Ecommerce Welcome Email #1: Discount Plus a Three-Column Best-Seller Block
cards.summary: Open with a welcome discount and a simple three-column best-sellers grid, then follow with product-tutorial emails.
cards.use_when: Drafting the first email of an ecommerce welcome sequence for a product-led store.
steps: Subject/body: 'hey you're confirmed, welcome' — then give the discount. Name the audience something ('the squad', 'the crew', 'the family') and present a coupon like $10 off.
Below the coupon, add a simple three-column grid of best-selling products with title and image, and one link per column.
Use 'best-selling products' rather than 'our best-selling products' — the presenter keeps the phrasing modest and less self-referential.

Follow with six more welcome emails, each demonstrating a product through a tutorial — e.g. 'how to curl a pixie cut' or 'how to straighten very curly hair without frizz' — linking to a video that demonstrates the product.
Rinse and repeat the tutorial-plus-link format for all remaining emails.
caveats: The reported figures — $75k/month from the first email and $145k/month from the full sequence for a hair-tool brand — are one client's results, not a forecast.
Tutorial-based welcome emails work well for demonstrable products; pure commodity items may need a different first-email hook.
cards.source_name: Copywriting 101_ eCommerce copywriting course FOR BEGINNERS.docx

cards.title: Match Sales-Page Copy to Customer Awareness Stage
cards.summary: Set story length and proof density based on how aware the buyer is of their problem, the solution category, and your product.
cards.use_when: Writing a product sales page, long-form landing page or launch email and deciding how much story to tell before selling.
steps: Classify the audience on the awareness scale, drawn from the car-buying example: unaware (doesn't know the problem), problem-aware (knows a problem exists, not the solution), solution-aware (knows solutions exist — bikes, buses, cars), product-aware (has decided to buy a category and is choosing), and most aware (knows exactly which one they want).
For unaware and problem-aware audiences, build up the problem first with a longer story — describe common failed attempts (e.g. keto, zumba, rebound weight) and explain why nothing worked.
For solution- and product-aware audiences, shorten the story and add more testimonials and comparisons between options.
For most-aware buyers (the 'I want a Mercedes' stage), cut your story and sell the product — the source says 'shut up about your story' and show them their options.
Match the source's default: if your audience sits between problem- and solution-aware (roughly stages 3–4), use a medium to long story.
caveats: The stage framework is a heuristic, not a formula; some audiences straddle levels, and product-aware buyers still want price/availability clarity.
Awareness stages must be inferred from traffic source and customer research — don't assume your store's visitors are all the same stage.
cards.source_name: Copywriting 101_ eCommerce copywriting course FOR BEGINNERS.docx

cards.title: Sales-Page Template and Section Order
cards.summary: Copy a fixed section order — hero, story, proof, price positioning, objections, FAQs, repeated CTAs — to prevent incoherent pages.
cards.use_when: Building a sales page, product landing page or long-form collection page and deciding section-by-section structure.
steps: Write the hero section first: headline, sub-headline and a call to action. Don't name the product unless you're a household brand like mercedes.com or apple.com — a Mercedes-level brand can get away with it, a newer store cannot.
Write the story section at the length matching your audience's awareness stage.
Show why they need the product, then show what happens without it.
Insert testimonials and success stories, then position the price (offer stack or comparison).
Handle objections ('what if you took my money and I want it back?'), add FAQs, then more testimonials.
Slip in a call to action or pricing table every two or three content sections so the reader can buy at any point of readiness.
caveats: The source gives the template as a starting point and adapts it — don't treat section order as a rigid law.
The references to mercedes.com and apple.com are illustrative brand examples, not licensing to name-drop in your copy.
cards.source_name: Copywriting 101_ eCommerce copywriting course FOR BEGINNERS.docx

cards.title: Building a Cohesive Through-Line From Sub-Headers
cards.summary: Test sales-page cohesion by reading only the sub-headlines and checking whether they tell a complete story.
cards.use_when: Editing a sales page, landing page or launch sequence and deciding whether the sections connect.
steps: Isolate the sub-headlines and read them in sequence. Example from the source's purpose-course page: 'it's Monday morning, ugh'; 'it's Monday already, just five more minutes'; 'hey, at least it pays the bills'; 'we need a massive culture shift'.
If those lines don't tell a coherent story from problem to possibility, the page lacks a through-line and readers will drop off.
Rewrite sub-headlines to advance an argument in a logical order that matches how customers explain and feel about the problem.
Check the same coherence in your email sequence — each email's role in the arc should be visible from its outline position.
caveats: The 'number one problem' diagnosis is the presenter's opinion, not a measured finding.
This test works for long-form pages; short pages with one section rarely need a through-line.
cards.source_name: Copywriting 101_ eCommerce copywriting course FOR BEGINNERS.docx

cards.title: Sentiment Matching: Mine Reviews for Your Customer's Own Words
cards.summary: Read 5-star and 1-star reviews of competing or analogous products to learn the exact language customers use about the problem.
cards.use_when: Starting a product launch, PDP rewrite or ad campaign and needing customer language to write copy in.
steps: Read your own customer testimonials first if you have them.

If you don't, read reviews of competitors and analogous products: Amazon book, video or course reviews in the same category; if you're in relationships, look up another relationship coach with the same format.
Read both five-star reviews and one-star reviews — 5-star shows what people love, 1-star shows what they hate.
Use the findings to position the product: 'I'm not like the stuff you hate, but I am like the stuff you love'.
Note the exact words and phrases buyers use to describe their problem, and echo those words in the headline, story and object handling.
caveats: The source's example is a coaching business; the ecommerce translation is reading competitor product reviews to identify language — the demonstrated result was for non-ecommerce courses.
Amazon/course reviews may reflect different buyers than your store's audience; verify against your own customer support themes.
cards.source_name: Copywriting 101_ eCommerce copywriting course FOR BEGINNERS.docx

cards.title: Positioning the Price: Offer Stack or Apples-to-Oranges Comparison
cards.summary: Break your offer into individual features with value assigned, or compare your price against the cost of alternatives.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to present pricing on a sales page, bundle page or checkout for high-ticket or multi-part offers.
steps: Build an offer stack: list the individual features of the overall package and assign a value to each ('total X value, total investment starting at Y'). End with 'priceless' as the master-card-style kicker — the source uses this and reports it lands.
If itemizing features makes no sense for your offer, use an apples-to-oranges comparison instead.
Positive variant: show what it would cost for a trainer, a personal chef and a nutritionist making your menus — isn't it easier to pay $3.99 and get all of them?
Negative variant: show the cost of inaction — a heart attack is expensive, missing your daughter's wedding isn't worth skipping the payment.
Pick the variant that matches your audience's emotional driver; the source presents both as valid situational alternatives.
caveats: The 'total value' figures are marketing constructs — inflated itemized values can erode trust if the gap to price is absurd.
Negative fear-based framing can misfire with certain audiences and platforms; check ad policy and brand tone.
cards.source_name: Copywriting 101_ eCommerce copywriting course FOR BEGINNERS.docx

cards.title: Plan the Email Count Before You Write the Sequence
cards.summary: Decide the number of emails in a launch or welcome sequence up front, then fill in the outline.
cards.use_when: Starting a launch or welcome sequence and planning how many sends are needed.
steps: For a launch: default to ten emails unless you have a specific reason to deviate.
For a welcome sequence: default to seven emails.
State the target count out loud before writing so you know when the sequence is finished.
Work through the outline row-by-row (subject, preview, story, content, PS) — then start writing as soon as possible.
Map each email to a clear function in the broader objective so you know what each one is for.
caveats: These are the presenter's defaults, described as classic standards — not requirements for every catalog or audience.
Deviating is fine provided the deviation is deliberate, not accidental.
cards.source_name: Copywriting 101_ eCommerce copywriting course FOR BEGINNERS.docx

cards.title: Use Second-Person 'You' Copy and Drop Your Own Logic
cards.summary: Write in second person and reason with the customer's logic, not yours, since their background and framing differ from yours.
cards.use_when: Writing or editing email, PDP or ad copy where the copy favors the brand's reasoning over the buyer's.
steps: Audit drafts for first-person framing — 'we built', 'our process', 'our story' — and convert them to 'you' framing.
Avoid selling via your own logic chain; the customer arrives with a different set of experiences and their own narration of the problem.
Use sentiment matching (reviews, testimonials) to learn the customer's logic, then write to that logic.
Check each paragraph: does it help the reader see their situation more clearly, or explain your reasoning?
caveats: Second person is a default, not a prohibition on first-person in testimonials, brand story pages or about-us content.
Sentiment matching takes research time; skipping it and defaulting to your own logic defeats the purpose.
cards.source_name: Copywriting 101_ eCommerce copywriting course FOR BEGINNERS.docx

cards.title: Choosing Email Software: Mailchimp, ActiveCampaign, or Infusionsoft
cards.summary: Pick beginner, intermediate or enterprise email software based on list size and membership-site needs.
cards.use_when: Selecting an ESP for a growing ecommerce store and deciding when to migrate.
steps: If you're just starting and list size is small, Mailchimp is the source's recommendation — the presenter has worked with clients up to 165,000 contacts on it, though they moved those clients off once it got large.
At a few thousand subscribers, ActiveCampaign is described as a good intermediate step.
If you don't need Infusionsoft, the source says don't use it.

Infusionsoft is only justified in two cases per the source: (1) huge lists of roughly 600,000 to 1,000,000+ contacts, or (2) membership sites, where it integrates better with membership-site software than competing ESPs. The source says membership-site use justifies it at around 1,000+ members.
Otherwise, choose the lower-complexity tool and migrate up only when a trigger threshold is hit.
caveats: Tooling capability and pricing change frequently — verify current interfaces and plans before committing.
The list-size thresholds are the presenter's heuristics, not vendor limits; your own engagement and segmentation needs may force migration sooner.
cards.source_name: Copywriting 101_ eCommerce copywriting course FOR BEGINNERS.docx

cards.title: Use Short Headlines to Carry a Story Across a Page
cards.summary: Write sales-page headlines that function as a sequence of mini-lines telling the reader's story in order.
cards.use_when: Writing the hero section and section headers of a product or launch sales page.
steps: Write consecutive short lines that build a narrative arc — the source's example: 'you're starting an exciting journey'; 'Hollywood doesn't make it easy'; 'if you're serious about your craft'.
Tie each line to a customer-voiced belief rather than a brand claim: actors believe Hollywood is institutionally harder than it should be, and the copy validates that belief before selling.
Name the exact thing the audience already agrees on — actors constantly take classes, read trade magazines, attend casting workshops — so the copy speaks in-language.
Keep sections short enough that a reader skimming only headlines still gets the argument.
Make the last section a positioning and price section rather than another story beat.
caveats: The examples are drawn from coaching and acting courses, not ecommerce — transfer the structure of customer-voiced headline sequences, not the specific lines.
Story-heavy headlines can slow a product page for bottom-of-funnel traffic; consider testing short benefit headers there.
cards.source_name: Copywriting 101_ eCommerce copywriting course FOR BEGINNERS.docx

cards.title: Punctuation and Formatting Discipline in Subject Lines
cards.summary: Avoid punctuation that signals stopping and reserve periods for body copy, not the subject line.
cards.use_when: Reviewing subject lines in any ecommerce email campaign before launch.
steps: Do not use periods in subject lines — the source says a period means 'stop reading' and invites deletion.
Exclamation points are described as tolerable; keep everything else minimal.
Skip elaborate vocabulary and decorative phrasing; plain, spoken language outperforms ornate prose in the source's experience.
Apply these rules across the whole sequence, reserving grammatically careful lines for the body where tone matters more than open behavior.
caveats: These are the presenter's stated preferences from their own sending practice, not empirical standards; brand voice in some categories tolerates punctuation.
Test punctuation choices against your own open rates before treating them as rules.
cards.source_name: Copywriting 101_ eCommerce copywriting course FOR BEGINNERS.docx

cards.title: Start Writing Copy as Soon as Possible, Even by Hand
cards.summary: Get a first draft down quickly to avoid blank-page paralysis — outline first, then write fast.
cards.use_when: Failing to start a launch, welcome or PDP copy project because the scope feels overwhelming.
steps: Decide the email count or page sections in outline form before writing words (ten for launch, seven for welcome as defaults).
Write a full, rough line for each outline cell — subject, preview, story, content, PS — then start writing immediately.
Accept that the draft doesn't need to be clever; the outline does the thinking.
Don't freeze trying to pick perfect words; send the first draft into revision.
Use the same approach on a sales page: decide the story length first, then write the hero and build down.
caveats: Speed drafting works only after the outline phase — writing blind just produces incoherent copy faster.
The source's preference for committing quickly is a practice suggestion, not a quality guarantee.
cards.source_name: Copywriting 101_ eCommerce copywriting course FOR BEGINNERS.docx

cards.title: The four-step Google Ads pipeline: retrieval, elimination, ranking, auction
cards.summary: Understanding Google's internal ad-serving sequence explains why relevance, not budget, drives placement.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why Shopping or Search ads aren't showing, or deciding what to optimize first when a product campaign underperforms.
steps: Map your current campaigns against the four stages: retrieval (Google scans your landing page, titles, descriptions, images, price point, keywords, demographics to decide relevance), elimination (irrelevant or negative-scoring ads are discarded), ranking (surviving ads ordered by ad score), auction (CPC set by the buyer's intent and your relevance).
For retrieval optimization, treat your entire feed as your targeting data — fix weak images, vague titles, mismatched price points and missing attributes, since Google reads all of them.

For elimination, focus on what the source calls the ad score formula (DOJ-disclosed): bid x predicted click-through rate, minus a penalty variable (beta) reflecting user experience and landing page quality. Ads scoring negative are removed from the ranking entirely.
For ranking, once bid is automated and beta is low, the remaining lever is predicted CTR: make assets relevant to the searcher's history and current query.
Recognize the auction is pay-per-click, not pay-per-impression, so a weak click means real money spent without a purchase — relevant copy protects CPC.
Explain the audience-facing rationale to stakeholders: relevance gets you into the auction, keeps you from elimination, lifts your rank, and earns cheaper intent-rich clicks.
caveats: The ad score formula is attributed to DOJ disclosure in the source; treat the exact structure as the source's interpretation rather than verified Google documentation.
Position-click-share figures (40% for position one) come from the source's cited chart and should be validated against current SERP behavior before planning around them.
cards.source_name: ENTIRE google ads algorithm explained in 24 mins.docx

cards.title: Surface area scaling: duplicate products across pricing tiers to own the search page
cards.summary: Multiply one winning product into multiple listings differentiated by price tier so you occupy several ad slots at once.
cards.use_when: Product selection, merchandising and campaign structure decisions when a single hero SKU is already profitable and you want to grow without simply raising budget.
steps: Start with one product and one winning angle that is already converting.
Instead of only increasing budget on the original listing, duplicate the product several times (the source cites five to six duplicates).
For each duplicate, shift one axis: price tier (budget, standard, discount, premium, luxury), and adjust titles/images to match so each listing reads as a distinct offer rather than a clone.

Verify the newly created variants don't cannibalize the original: the source reports seeing little cannibalization between variants, but track blended CPC and conversion by variant before adding more.
Use the duplicated listings to compete for price-qualified queries (e.g. 'under $30' vs 'under $100') that a single mid-price listing would never enter.
Rebalance budget across variants based on which price tier is generating the better CPA/ROAS, not simply on the highest-volume variant.
caveats: The source's example of an operator appearing in six of seven slots is an anecdote from that operator's account, not a guaranteed outcome.
Maintaining many near-duplicate listings costs time in feed hygiene, price/stock sync and review — plan for the operational load.
cards.source_name: ENTIRE google ads algorithm explained in 24 mins.docx

cards.title: Differentiate duplicate listings with image angles matched to customer avatars
cards.summary: Instead of one product shot per SKU, create lifestyle/angle variants so each listing speaks to a different buyer persona.
cards.use_when: PDP/landing page and Shopping feed creative decisions when a single image set makes every product look like everyone else's.
steps: Take one product and separate images on a white background (the source claims this is what most competitors do) and ask which customer situations the product serves.
Create 2–4 variant images per product, each mapped to a distinct use case or avatar, e.g. leisure wear, active wear, corporate.
Match the visual context (setting, model, styling) to the persona's likely search intent so the shopper can see themselves using the product.

Note the source's claim that Google reads image content and demographics — if your images feature college students, Google may bias delivery toward them, so align avatar imagery with the audience you actually want.
Run duplicate listings with distinct image sets side by side to see whether the variant attracts a different click/order profile before expanding further.
Assign each variant a clear internal name matching the avatar so the merchandising team knows which listing serves whom.
caveats: Sources's avatar-image claim is the operator's interpretation of how Google infers audience from feed imagery, not documented Google behavior.
Producing genuine lifestyle variants per avatar is more expensive than editing one photo; only do this once the underlying product-converts.
cards.source_name: ENTIRE google ads algorithm explained in 24 mins.docx

cards.title: Write relevant, readable Shopping feed titles from product attributes
cards.summary: Use accurate product type, audience, attributes and use cases to clarify search relevance.
cards.use_when: Writing Shopping feed titles for actual product variants; adapt separately for PDP titles and Search ad headlines.
steps: Use the source attribute structure as a draft: product type, relevant qualifier, intended user, differentiator and variant details. Keep the result readable rather than stuffing every keyword.
For a heated jacket, include supported attributes such as USB rechargeable, intended use and color. More words do not guarantee eligibility for more searches.
Mine additional keywords in Google Ads Keyword Planner by entering the core product term, setting the target country, and exporting the returned search terms.
Feed the exported keyword list plus the title template into your preferred AI writing tool (the source uses Claude) to generate title variants in bulk.
Fill the description field too: use two paragraphs of natural copy that include use-case and person-specific keywords (winter, hunting, construction, poor circulation).
Keep real variants distinguishable with accurate attributes; do not create duplicate listings merely to repeat keywords.
caveats: The source algorithm explanation is a simplifying hypothesis, not a verified account of ranking. Verify current title limits and feed requirements before deployment.
cards.source_name: ENTIRE google ads algorithm explained in 24 mins.docx

cards.title: Set up a lean Performance Max campaign limited to Search and Shopping
cards.summary: Strip out Gmail, Display, Maps, Discover and YouTube placements in PMax to concentrate budget on high-intent surfaces.
cards.use_when: Campaign setup for an ecommerce account launching its main Google campaign, or auditing an existing PMax that is spending on low-intent placements.
steps: Create campaign without guidance, choose Performance Max, set the account goal to purchases, and select the Google Merchant Center feed.
Leave the bidding/target fields blank at first (do not set tROAS on a new account).
Set locations to presence, not presence-or-interest — the source says the default presence-or-interest wastes budget on people unlikely to buy.
Turn off TV screens under devices.
On the asset page, leave all headlines, YouTube creatives and email assets blank; keep only products selected.
Disable text, image and video enhancement so the system does not auto-expand into YouTube, Gmail or Display placements.
If the platform errors on publishing the empty asset group, create the asset group fully, publish, duplicate it, leave the duplicate blank, then pause the original — per the source's workaround.
Ignore the ad strength score; the source reports it is always 'poor' when running PMax this way and still performs.
caveats: Interface fields and names change; verify against the current Google Ads UI before instructing a media buyer to follow this exactly.
Single-campaign consolidation is the source's opinion — sometimes brand and standard shopping campaigns still need to be layered.
cards.source_name: ENTIRE google ads algorithm explained in 24 mins.docx

cards.title: Don't set a tROAS target before the account has conversion history
cards.summary: Premature tROAS targets throttle scaling; the source waits months before adding one.
cards.use_when: Deciding when to apply target ROAS to a Performance Max or Shopping campaign on a new or growing ecommerce account.
steps: Leave tROAS blank for the first roughly three months while you let PMax optimise against conversion data.
Wait until you see a plateau or efficiency drop before adding a target.
When adding a target, remember Google tROAS is the revenue target per ad dollar: 300% means you want $3 of revenue per $1 spent.
For campaigns that are already highly profitable, consider not adding a target at all — the source scaled a campaign to ~$500K spend without one to avoid limiting it.
If budget reaches roughly $20K–$30K/day and every incremental dollar returns less, layer in a standard shopping campaign rather than pushing budget higher on the same PMax campaign.
caveats: All dollar and timeframe figures are the source's operational heuristics from its own accounts, not benchmarks; profitability is store-specific.
Some accounts may be forced to set a target by the platform — check current requirements.
cards.source_name: ENTIRE google ads algorithm explained in 24 mins.docx

cards.title: Consolidate campaigns instead of segmenting by product line
cards.summary: Contrary to popular advice to run many separated campaigns, the source argues one consolidated campaign outperforms segmented structures in ecommerce.
cards.use_when: Campaign architecture decisions when deciding how many Google campaigns to run per product category.
steps: Audit the current account and count campaigns; the source's stated position is that consolidation beats segmentation.
Aim to run as few campaigns as possible — ideally one dominant performer — rather than splitting by niche, product line or avatar.
Allow exceptions where structure genuinely differs: brand search, standard shopping and PMax may all need to coexist.
When one campaign is hitting diminishing returns, layer a second campaign underneath rather than fragmenting the original.
Review conversion and cost data by campaign monthly to confirm the consolidated structure is still the most efficient arrangement.
caveats: This is a source-specific opinion that runs against common practitioner guidance — segment structure can be required in accounts with very different margin structures or regions.
Rigid consolidation can hide underperforming SKUs; keep SKU-level reporting regardless of campaign structure.
cards.source_name: ENTIRE google ads algorithm explained in 24 mins.docx

cards.title: Work the learning phase: 30 conversions in 30 days is the baseline, not a cap
cards.summary: Google's stated learning phase threshold is 30 conversions in 30 days, but aligned feeds can exit faster.
cards.use_when: Planning launch expectations and diagnosing persistent under-delivery after a new campaign or new ad account launch.
steps: Understand Google's definition per the source: 30 conversions within a 30-day window (roughly one conversion/day) exits the learning phase.
If the whole system is aligned — titles, descriptions, images, price, product selection — the source reports campaigns exiting learning in roughly the first week.
For new accounts, expect early instability: the source describes a typical trend of shaky first days, first order around day two or three, then multiple orders per day once Google has signal.
If a campaign stays in learning indefinitely, audit relevance alignment before increasing budget; poor alignment keeps Google from gathering usable customer data.
Reinforce wins by continuing to accumulate and double down on conversion data — the more conversions Google sees, the better its targeting.
Treat the 30-in-30 heuristic as a floor for accounts that are otherwise misaligned, not as a target to aim for.
caveats: The 30-in-30 figure is Google's stated definition per the source, and conversion counting rules vary by conversion action; verify current thresholds.
Faster exits reported by the source are from its own accounts and should not be promised.
cards.source_name: ENTIRE google ads algorithm explained in 24 mins.docx

cards.title: Weekly optimisation cadence: tROAS, budget, negative keywords, product pruning
cards.summary: A tight weekly Google Ads review cycle beats constant tinkering; the source changes only a few levers each week.
cards.use_when: Setting up an ecommerce account's recurring Google Ads management routine.
steps: Schedule a fixed weekly review (the source uses Sundays) and in most weeks only touch three things: tROAS, budget, or prune keywords/products.
Pull the campaign report and identify products getting the most clicks and keywords driving the most clicks — these are the winners to protect.
Identify products selling poorly and keywords wasting spend, then remove them.
Use early-data reviews: even at ~$100 spend you can see which products and keywords attract clicks.
When making the change, prefer one lever at a time so you can attribute the effect; the source typically changes only one of tROAS, budget or pruning per week.
Track the long-term trend line weekly rather than intraday — Google's returns are historically steadier across weeks than social platforms'.
caveats: No performance guarantees; the weekly cadence is the source's operating habit, not a proven optimal formula.
Over-frequent pruning can remove keywords still in an early learning stage — judge with enough impression/click data.
cards.source_name: ENTIRE google ads algorithm explained in 24 mins.docx

cards.title: Use Google's intent-by-relevance CPC model to gauge paid search economics
cards.summary: Google's modern CPC is described by the source as the customer's purchasing intent multiplied by the advertiser's relevance.
cards.use_when: Evaluating keyword/bid economics and deciding whether a mid-relevance advertiser should compete on a high-intent query.
steps: Think of each searcher in tiers of purchase intent (the source illustrates a 1x lightly-interested buyer up to a ~3x frequent ad buyer).
Think of each ad in tiers of relevance to the query (the most relevant seller gets the lowest multiplier, an irrelevant one a higher multiplier).
Multiply the two: the most relevant advertiser attracts the highest-intent buyer at a favourable CPC, while a less relevant advertiser pays far more for the same click.
Use this to justify why investing in relevance (titles, images, price tier) reduces effective CPCs and improves downstream conversion rate and average order value.
Before bidding aggressively on a broad term, confirm your listing genuinely matches the buyer's stated need — otherwise you are the advertiser paying the high multiplier.
Remember Google charges per click (not per impression like Facebook), so a poorly relevant click is pure loss — relevant copy and matching landing pages protect spend.
caveats: The specific multipliers (1x–3x, 1x–5x) are the source's illustrative numbers, not a published Google formula.
Relevance-driven CPC improvement compounds slowly and requires consistent feed quality.
cards.source_name: ENTIRE google ads algorithm explained in 24 mins.docx

cards.title: Add a branded search campaign to defend your brand term cheaply
cards.summary: A separate brand campaign ensures your store appears first when shoppers search your name.
cards.use_when: Defensive campaign setup for an established ecommerce brand seeing competitors or review sites outrank its own name in search.
steps: Confirm your brand name has meaningful search volume before building the campaign.
Set up a dedicated branded search campaign so that when a customer types your brand, your listing appears above competitors and review sites.
The source reports little cannibalisation between a brand campaign and general PMax spend and treats it as a low-cost defensive layer.
Monitor the brand campaign separately to confirm real incremental value rather than capturing clicks you would have won organically.
Keep expectations modest relative to PMax — the source characterises it as a small add-on that handles a fraction of revenue.
caveats: Attribution between brand search and organic remains difficult; ensure you are not paying for conversions you would get anyway.
Brand keywords have different CPC dynamics than generic terms.
cards.source_name: ENTIRE google ads algorithm explained in 24 mins.docx

cards.title: Treat beta (experience penalty) as the long-term ranking lever
cards.summary: The source's ad score formula subtracts a penalty for poor post-click experience, and that penalty decreases with persistent quality and conversion history.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to invest alongside acquisition — site speed, delivery reliability, customer experience — to lower paid search costs over time.
steps: Recognise that beta penalises slow landing pages, poor store experience and non-delivery; it lowers ad score and directly worsens eligibility and rank.
Treat reducing beta as a daily compounding effort: keep landing pages fast and accurate, ship orders on time, and avoid scam-adjacent practices.
Earn trust through accumulated conversions and good customer experiences, which the source says lowers beta and, in turn, reduces clicks costs and lifts ranking.

Look at long-term trends: the source argues Google is a long-horizon platform (returns sustained over 2–5 years) compared with the up/down volatility of social platforms, provided the fundamentals remain aligned.
Keep the same store/account running to build trust equity, rather than constantly starting fresh accounts.
Prioritise relevance-hitting work (titles, images, pricing) for quick PCTR gains while beta improves slowly through consistent operations.
caveats: The beta variable and its long-term effect are the source's framing, not Google-published mechanics; treat directionally.
The 2–5 year ROI claim is anecdotal to the source's accounts.
cards.source_name: ENTIRE google ads algorithm explained in 24 mins.docx

cards.title: Build a broad keyword pool with Keyword Planner before writing feed copy
cards.summary: Mine real search terms in Keyword Planner and feed them into title/description templates to widen your query coverage.
cards.use_when: Paid search or Shopping feed title and description creation, and expansion of a keyword strategy.
steps: Open Keyword Planner (free) from within Google Ads and enter the core product term.
Set the target country and run results to see the actual related search terms people use (e.g. for 'heated jacket': electric jacket, self-heating jacket, heated coat, heated hunting clothes).
Export the keyword list, then combine it with your structured title template (adjective, product, audience, USP, use cases, specifics).
Generate titles and two-paragraph descriptions in bulk with an AI writing tool, sitting every returned keyword into the relevant slot.
Load the generated titles/descriptions into the feed or campaign asset, checking that each title still reads as coherent customer-facing copy.
Repeat for each surface-area listing variant so its keyword pool reflects its specific price tier and avatar.
caveats: The Keyword Planner surface and export workflow change periodically; verify current UI steps.
Keyword-stuffed description copy can look spammy in customer-facing storefronts; keep the aggressive version for ad/feed fields.
cards.source_name: ENTIRE google ads algorithm explained in 24 mins.docx

cards.title: Prefer PVMs consolidations before adding new campaign types
cards.summary: Before introducing a new campaign type, confirm your current single campaign has genuinely plateaued.
cards.use_when: Scaling an ecommerce ad account when tempted to add campaign types to solve a performance plateau.
steps: Evaluate whether you have hit diminishing returns on the existing campaign — the source's trigger is often a budget around $20K–$30K/day where marginal return falls.
When that happens, layer a standard shopping campaign beneath the PMax rather than spreading budget across many new campaign types.
Keep brand search as a separate small layer for defensive coverage.
Only introduce additional campaign types when they address a specific structural need (brand, control over CPC via standard shopping) rather than a general wish for more reach.
If you do scale further, consider asset groups and tROAS adjustments before launching entirely new campaign categories.
Keep campaign count low: the source structured accounts so one campaign produced ~99% of revenue.
caveats: Thresholds cited are the source's own operating observations and vary by category and margin.
This consolidation bias can conflict with the needs of large accounts requiring geo or margin-based segmentation.
cards.source_name: ENTIRE google ads algorithm explained in 24 mins.docx

cards.title: Interview alignment: relevance across feed, landing page and price point
cards.summary: The algorithm scans the entire store surface as targeting data, so misaligned listings dilute delivery.
cards.use_when: Landing page and feed QA when diagnosing declining impressions, rising CPCs or low volume of conversions after a period of stability.
steps: Audit every attribute Google can read: titles, descriptions, images, price point, keywords, demographics implied by imagery.
For each duplication/surface-area variant, confirm the price, imagery and copy actually correspond to the buyer segment the listing is meant to attract.
For a variant pitched at a budget buyer, show budget-relevant imagery and price transparently on the landing page so post-click experience matches the ad.
Check landing page load speed — the source attributes beta penalties partly to slow pages.
Align ad copy language (use cases, audience) with the actual PDP copy so the searcher's expectation is met.
Fix the top few high-traffic listings first and measure whether CPC and CTR improve before touching the long tail.
caveats: The claim that Google scans landing-page speed into a beta penalty is the source's interpretation and should be considered directionally, not as verified mechanics.
Improvements compound over weeks; don't judge a listing change from a single day of data.
cards.source_name: ENTIRE google ads algorithm explained in 24 mins.docx

cards.title: Aim for high page position and read the clicks-per-position trade-off
cards.summary: Higher ranked positions capture disproportionately more click share, so ranking work is fundamentally a demand-capture play.
cards.use_when: Setting expectations for a Google campaign and prioritising rank/impression-share work over superficial creative prettiness.
steps: Use the source's cited click-share gradient (roughly 40% position one, ~20% position two, ~10% position three, ~7% position four) as a directional illustration of why rank matters.
Recognise that for a given query you are not up against thousands of advertisers, only the handful of listings competing for those slots.
Prioritise relevance work (feed titles, images, price tiers) which the source says raises PCTR, ad score and therefore rank.
Combine rank work with surface-area duplication so that even the lower slots you occupy are yours, multiplying the share you capture.
Track impression share and position over time to see whether the relevance changes actually shifted you upward.
caveats: The click-share percentages are the source's cited chart values and vary by query type, device and SERP layout today; validate with your own data.
Position one does not guarantee high conversion rate — poorly matched searchers may click and bounce.
cards.source_name: ENTIRE google ads algorithm explained in 24 mins.docx

cards.title: Google Ads is a demand-capture channel, not a fix for broken marketing
cards.summary: Treat Google Ads as a demand-capture engine that channels existing purchase intent, not as a rescue for weak product-market fit.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to launch or scale Google Ads for your store versus fixing offer, product and messaging first.
steps: Audit whether you already have a converting offer, an angle and messaging that works — the source recommends proving this on Meta first before scaling on Google.
Reframe Google's role: Meta/TikTok create demand, Google captures it, and email/SMS/backend flows retain customers and lift LTV.
Check your channel mix: the source sees Google as ideally about 20-30% of ecommerce revenue, with Google over-performing beyond that signalling other channels are underperforming.
Before spending, verify your landing pages convert; strong ads with poor pages only drive wasted spend.
Only scale Google once the offer, page and messaging are proven, because Google's comparative search results will expose any weakness.
caveats: The 20-30% revenue figure is the source's heuristic, not a universal benchmark; some stores legitimately exceed it.
This is the presenter's opinion; stores with no proven offer should prioritize offer and page testing before Google scaling.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Treat Google as four ad platforms in one
cards.summary: Plan Google as four distinct placements — search, shopping, YouTube and display — each covering a different intent level.
cards.use_when: Structuring a store's full Google Ads account and deciding which campaign types to build.
steps: Map Search to high-intent and problem-aware queries, from product-level searches down to vague problem searches.
Recognize Shopping as the highest-converting placement — the source reports it can be 60-80% of ecommerce Google ad revenue because image, title, price, offer and reviews appear together.
Use YouTube (including Shorts) for demand generation and top-of-funnel reach, not just direct response.
Reserve Display for remarketing first and cold reach only once you're spending tens of thousands per day.
For most brands, the source recommends focusing only on search, shopping and YouTube until the core is built out.
caveats: The 60-80% shopping share and tens-of-thousands-per-day display threshold are the source's stated heuristics, not universal figures.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Build a cold-customer magnet funnel across Google
cards.summary: Assemble top, middle and bottom-of-funnel Google campaigns so every awareness stage leads to a purchase path.
cards.use_when: Designing the full campaign architecture for an ecommerce store that wants to capture cold customers across Google.
steps: Top of funnel: run YouTube ads (Short), in-stream video and Google Display to generate attention and demand.
Route top-of-funnel traffic to advertorials, listicles, VSLs or quiz funnels before the product page.
Middle of funnel: use prospecting Search, Performance Max (search, shopping, discovery, display) and prospecting Shopping to capture existing demand.
Bottom of funnel: run Branded Search, Branded Shopping and dynamic remarketing targeting homepage and product page visitors.
Tie it together: visitors who drop off at add-to-cart get dynamically remarketed to the homepage or product page.
Name the result honestly: the source claims this combined setup yields a 3-5x return per dollar, but treat this as an example, not a guarantee.
caveats: The 3-5x return is the source's claim from their own client accounts, not a promise for your store.
Funnel pages such as quizzes and advertorials add build effort; the source does not specify minimum traffic to justify them.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Scale at break-even using LTV-to-CAC, not front-end ROAS
cards.summary: Focus on break-even new-customer ROAS/CPA and lifetime value rather than chasing isolated high front-end ROAS.
cards.use_when: Setting bid targets and budgets for a store deciding how aggressively to acquire customers.
steps: Calculate your break-even new-customer ROAS and break-even new-customer CPA so you know the ceiling you can spend per acquisition.
The source's core philosophy: scale ad spend until acquisition is break-even or slightly profitable on first purchase, then capture profit on repeat purchases.
Instead of only pushing CAC down, raise AOV on the first order and lift LTV via email/SMS, remarketing and new product releases.
If LTV is 3-5x, the source argues you can afford to spend 2-3x more to acquire the same customer while keeping the ratio intact.
Judge performance on blended marketing efficiency (total revenue vs total ad spend) rather than individual campaign ROAS alone.
The source states the advertiser who can spend the most to win a customer wins — enabled by a stronger backend, not just bigger budgets.
caveats: This is the presenter's stated scaling philosophy and their opinion on how to win auctions; not a rule for every store.
An LTV-based strategy assumes you have reliable cohort and backend data; otherwise it risks unprofitable spend.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Structure branded traffic separately before scaling
cards.summary: Isolate Branded Search and Branded Shopping from prospecting so Google doesn't waste budget converting people who already know you.
cards.use_when: Cleaning up campaign segmentation in a Google Ads account before increasing spend.
steps: Create a dedicated Branded Search campaign with absolute impression-share targeting to protect your brand terms and block competitor bids.
Create a separate Branded Shopping campaign distinct from your prospecting shopping.
Keep the rest of your budget (the source says 80-90%) on cold traffic, so branded terms don't soak up spend that was already going to convert.
Split prospecting from retargeting campaigns, and split branded from non-branded, so spend is directed at cold customers rather than easy conversions.
Watch for the distortion effect: if branded terms sit in prospecting campaigns, Google will spend on the easiest converters and starve the cold terms where new customers are.
caveats: The 80-90% cold-traffic split and absolute targeting are the source's recommendations; the right split varies by brand.
The source says competitor brand bidding is generally a waste because well-protected brands neutralize it.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: The cold customer magnet funnel structure
cards.summary: A three-layer Google setup — demand generation, demand capture, conversion — covering all awareness stages.
cards.use_when: Designing the full Google campaign architecture for an ecommerce store.
steps: Top of funnel (demand generation): YouTube ads (shorts and in-stream), non-brand search, display; use advertorials, listicles, VSLs or quiz funnels as landing pages.
Middle of funnel (demand capture): Performance Max, Standard Shopping, and Dynamic Search Ads to show products where demand already exists — this is where most ecommerce revenue comes from.
Bottom of funnel (conversion): Branded Search, Branded Shopping and Dynamic Remarketing in Merchant Center to convert high-intent visitors and maximize revenue.
Connect the layers: add-to-cart drop-offs are dynamically retargeted back to homepage or product page; brand-aware users get routed through branded search/shopping.
Verify the structure matches your current stage — brands relying only on a single campaign type will remain vulnerable to competitors.
caveats: The claimed 3-5x return applies to the source's example accounts, not a guaranteed outcome.
Fully building out this system takes roughly 1-4 months per the source; it is not an overnight setup.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Know the role of each ecommerce Google campaign type
cards.summary: Assign campaign types to specific jobs — PMax and Shopping for capture, search for intent, YouTube for demand generation.
cards.use_when: Choosing which campaign types to launch for a store at its current scale and deciding which to prioritize.
steps: Performance Max should be your biggest spender, combined with Standard Shopping to cover the shopping placement and win first-position auctions in your category.
Non-brand search targets high-intent queries plus problem statements and investment statements.
Branded search and branded shopping capture already-aware users cheaply and stop competitors bidding on your terms.
YouTube sits at the top of funnel to generate search volume and can run its own funnel simultaneously.
Dynamic remarketing ties it all together, re-targeting anyone who visited your homepage, product page or add-to-cart.
Only add YouTube and cold search campaigns once branded search, shopping and Performance Max are established.
caveats: The source warns Performance Max is black-box and must be controlled properly to avoid wasted spend.
Recommended ordering assumes a baseline of conversion data already exists.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: The three phases of ecommerce Google Ads growth
cards.summary: Sequence Google Ads growth — foundation/testing, then bidding and expansion, then scale — rather than launching everything at once.
cards.use_when: Deciding what to build first when launching or rebuilding a store's Google Ads account.
steps: Phase 1 (30-60 days): launch branded search, branded shopping and prospecting shopping; set up conversion tracking and analytics; use manual bidding to control spend while waiting for at least one conversion per day over 30 days.

Phase 2 (roughly months 2-6): shift to max conversions or tROAS based on margins and break-even ROAS; remove low-performing keywords; add retargeting and audience segmentation; launch YouTube and Performance Max.
Phase 3 (after ~6 months): increase budget on high-performing campaigns; expand to new search/shopping keywords using collected data; use Performance Max to scale with control.
Once the core is mature, add cold search and display if you have extra spend to build out the account fully.
Expect full build-out of a Google system covering ~90% of the inventory you'd bid on to take roughly 1-4 months.
caveats: The 30-60 day, 2-6 month and 6-month windows are the source's heuristics, not fixed rules.
Manual bidding in phase 1 assumes you can monitor and adjust spend regularly.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Trust Google's automation but set guardrails
cards.summary: Let Google optimize broadly while controlling the points that matter, rather than micromanaging or abandoning control.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much manual control to keep over keywords, bidding and targeting in a store's Google Ads account.
steps: Let the creative do the targeting: go broad on keywords and audiences, and avoid over-restricting to preset signals so Google can find new converting terms.
For standard shopping and branded search, keep tighter control — the source recommends absolute impression-share targeting on brand search.
Use automated bidding (tROAS/tCPA) only on campaigns where it makes sense, since Google bids in real time more efficiently than manual for those.
Set clear constraints: run negative keyword scripts to filter low-intent searches, and manually prune via search term reports daily.
Turn off Google's automated recommendations, and scale based on your own performance data, not Google's suggestions to spend more.
Where engagement metrics are weak (high bounce, low session duration), fix the landing page — Google can't fix bad conversion rates.
caveats: The default-to-automation advice is the source's opinion; some accounts may need more manual control.
Negative keyword automation still needs manual review of search terms.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Scale as a process, not an event
cards.summary: Scale spend in steps with daily, weekly and monthly routines that maintain efficiency before adding budget.
cards.use_when: Managing an existing store's Google Ads account and deciding when and how much to increase spend.
steps: Daily: review search terms and add negative keywords; monitor impression share and adjust bids toward the source's 50-60% impression-share target.

Weekly: scale winning campaigns against your break-even ROAS/CPA KPIs; optimize landing pages based on session duration and conversion performance; A/B test new ad copy and landing pages; do Weekly Merchant Center optimizations.
Monthly: increase budgets only if new-customer acquisition and blended ROAS are stable; run a full account review to catch disapprovals or gaps missed during daily/weekly work.
After each increase, confirm KPIs stay stable at the higher spend before scaling further.
If performance declines, fix the leak before increasing budget — the source stresses that scaling is about spending better, not just more.
caveats: The 50-60% impression-share target is the source's stated sweet spot, not a universal benchmark.
Session duration and conversion metrics should be read together, not as standalone signals.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Cut poor SKUs and cap brand spend for efficiency
cards.summary: Improve Google Ads efficiency by concentrating on hero products and limiting branded campaign spend to a small share of budget.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a store's product-level ad spend and branded campaign budgets to eliminate waste.
steps: Identify your hero product — the 80/20 product driving most Google revenue — and concentrate spend there.
Cut poor-performing SKUs rather than advertising every product; not all SKUs are scalable on Google per the source.
Cap branded campaign spend at a maximum of around 10% of monthly spend; the source prefers 3-8%.
Use tROAS/tCPA bidding to keep spend focused on efficient, converting traffic.
Target the goal of increasing acquisition without increasing waste, reviewing SKU-level and brand-level spend regularly.
caveats: The 10% maximum and 3-8% range are the source's heuristics; overspend thresholds vary by brand maturity and brand-name search volume.
Cutting SKUs should consider whether those products support cross-sell or LTV.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Expand beyond search and shopping with YouTube
cards.summary: Add YouTube and demand-gen campaigns to generate new search volume once native search demand is exhausted.
cards.use_when: Deciding when to move beyond search and shopping campaigns for a store hitting a growth ceiling.
steps: Monitor whether search volume on your product and target queries has gone stagnant.
Introduce YouTube ads (including Shorts) and demand-gen campaigns to expand audience reach beyond the limits of existing search volume.
Use YouTube-generated interest as new intent signals that feed Performance Max and shopping campaigns.
Capture the demand on Google's own channels before competitors bid on it.
The source argues YouTube is currently under-exploited with relatively low CPMs for ecommerce brands, so it's a growth opportunity.
caveats: The low-CPM claim is the source's assertion as of the recording and may not hold over time; verify current auction dynamics.
YouTube as primary demand generation is the source's opinion, not a universal rule for every brand.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Test and iterate ads and landing pages continuously
cards.summary: Run split tests on search ad copy, product feeds and landing pages so you always have a control to beat.
cards.use_when: Setting up ongoing optimization for a store's Google Ads and PDP/landing pages.
steps: A/B test search campaigns and product feeds weekly — new headlines, descriptions and CTAs.
Test landing-page variants too: different layouts and messaging flows, using conversion data to decide.
Keep multiple search ads per ad group as challengers rather than a single control; the goal is to beat the current best.
Automate reporting, bid adjustments and negative keyword scripts to free up time for testing.
The source's reasoning: even a small lift in conversion or CTR can meaningfully increase revenue and let you spend more to acquire customers.
caveats: The source views thinking you have the perfect ad without testing as a mistake; expect to run multiple variants.
Weekly testing cadence is the source's recommendation; test duration should respect statistical significance.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Make the offer the centerpiece of Google ads
cards.summary: Since Google shows your ad next to competitors, a stronger offer — shipping, BOGO, bundles — drives the click and conversion.
cards.use_when: Designing ad copy and promotions for a store competing in comparative Google search and shopping results.
steps: Because Google is a comparative shopping platform, decide what makes your offer visibly better than the alternatives shown alongside you.
Use shipping thresholds and frame free shipping as 'shipping on us' so customers feel they already have it.
Test offers like buy-one-get-one, buy-two-get-one, percentage off, or for high-AOV products (above roughly $100) a dollar amount off like $50 off.
Put the offer everywhere in the ad so it appears in the context shoppers compare.
Consider bundling to differentiate and simultaneously raise AOV, which gives more margin to advertise.
caveats: The above-$100 AOV suggestion and 'shipping on us' framing are the source's tips, not universal rules.
Offer strength must pair with a congruent landing page, or clicks won't convert.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Diagnose weak performance via landing page congruence
cards.summary: When ads get clicks but no conversions, check session duration and ad-page congruence before blaming the ads.
cards.use_when: Troubleshooting a store's Google Ads where impressions and clicks are strong but conversions are low.
steps: Separate the ad's job (get the click) from the landing page's job (make the sale).
Check average session duration as a proxy for whether the page matches what the ad promised.
If people bounce quickly, the page likely isn't relevant to what they clicked for — fix page relevance rather than the ad.
Confirm the offer shown in the ad also appears on the landing page so the shopper's expectation is met.
Only after ruling out page and congruence issues should you treat it as a targeting or ad-copy problem.
caveats: Average session duration is a rough proxy for congruence, not a definitive metric.
The source recommends prioritizing impression share, CPC, CTR, conversion rate and conversion count before session duration.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Prioritize AOV over COGS cuts for scalable unit economics
cards.summary: Improve ad scalability mainly by increasing average order value and leveraging LTV, not by squeezing down COGS.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether a store has the margin to run and scale Google Ads.
steps: Check that you have enough margin to reinvest into advertising; without margin you cannot scale.
Rather than focusing first on lowering COGS, the source argues to raise AOV because it offers more leverage without risking product quality or supplier relationships.
Increase AOV through stronger offers and bundles.
Factor LTV into how much you can afford to pay: a strong LTV may let you go break-even or slightly negative (the source gives a 0.8 example) and recover it over the next 12 months.
Set your break-even new-customer ROAS and CPA from these numbers, then align bids and budgets with them.
caveats: The 0.8 example is illustrative, not a standard; your acceptable first-order loss depends on your own cohort data.
The source's preference for AOV over COGS applies when product quality and supplier terms shouldn't be compromised.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Track the metrics that matter for ecommerce Google Ads
cards.summary: Monitor impression share, CPC, CTR, conversion rate and conversion count, plus average session duration, to steer campaigns.
cards.use_when: Building a reporting dashboard or weekly review for a store's Google Ads account.
steps: Track number of conversions and conversion rate to judge sales impact.
Track CTR and CPC to gauge ad relevance and auction competitiveness.
Prioritize impression share — the source ranks it highest because low share correlates with high CPC, low CTR and low conversion rate.
Add average session duration as a sixth metric to measure ad-to-page congruence.
Optimize for purchases, not add-to-carts or clicks, in ecommerce Google Ads.
Set these against your break-even new-customer ROAS and CPA to know how much you can bid.
caveats: The source's ordering of metric priority (impression share first) is their opinion, not an established standard.
Optimizing toward purchases assumes sufficient conversion volume; low-volume stores may need interim goals.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Diagnose Google Ads health in the right order
cards.summary: Use a fixed sequence of account-level metrics to find the real bottleneck before touching campaigns.
cards.use_when: Your Google Ads spend is rising but profit is flat, and you need to decide whether to fix creative, landing page, offer or campaign setup before scaling budget.
