steps: Pull six metrics: impression share, average CPC, CTR, conversion rate, number of conversions, and average session duration.
Read them in that priority order — the source treats impression share as the leading indicator: low impression share predicts high CPC, low CTR, low conversion rate and few conversions.
Treat average session duration as the congruence check between ad promise and landing page; short sessions suggest the ad and page are saying different things.
Only after those site/offer-level numbers look sound, move to Google Ads mechanics (conversion tracking, structure, creative, bids).
Interpret the benchmark contextually: lower impression share means competitors are outbidding or out-converting you, which is a spend/offer problem, not just a bidding problem.
caveats: The source asserts impression share is the single most important metric for ecommerce; this is a practitioner heuristic, not a Google-documented rule.
Session duration is the source's informal ad-to-page congruence proxy, not a formal diagnostic metric.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Set up Shopify-to-Google Ads purchase conversion tracking
cards.summary: Configure enhanced conversions with purchase as the primary goal, then correctly order the remaining funnel events.
cards.use_when: You are launching Google Ads or your reported conversions do not match Shopify orders and you need trustworthy purchase data before scaling.
steps: Install Google Analytics 4 via the Shopify Google & YouTube app first, then in Google Ads go to Goals > Settings and switch on enhanced conversions using the Google tag method.
In Goals > Conversions > Summary, create new conversion actions for purchase, add to cart, begin checkout and product view (page view).

For the purchase action: add to account-default goals, mark as primary, use different values per conversion, count every conversion, and set click-through window to 90 days and engage-view and view-through windows to 30 days.
Set attribution to data-driven and manage conversions through the Google tag.
Import the prebuilt Google Tag Manager container, then paste the conversion ID and each of the four conversion labels into the matching GTM constants and publish the workspace.
In Shopify admin > Settings > Customer Events, add a custom pixel, paste the GTM customer-event code, set your country code and insert your GTM container ID, then save and connect.
Finally, edit add to cart, begin checkout and product view to Secondary (observe only) so they do not drive bidding; keep purchase as the account default goal.
caveats: The exact menu paths and prebuilt container are from the source's 2025 workflow; verify current Google Ads and Shopify interfaces before following step by step.
Turning non-purchase events to secondary assumes purchase is your optimisation event — different goals may justify a different primary.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Structure campaigns by funnel stage and start at the bottom
cards.summary: Split cold, mid-funnel and branded campaigns so cold and branded conversion data stay visible and separately attributable.
cards.use_when: You are planning a Google Ads account architecture or reworking an account where branded and non-branded results are blended and unreadable.
steps: Top of funnel: YouTube Shorts and static assets run through Demand Gen, fed by your Meta winners at roughly $50/day, running fully broad with the creative doing the targeting.
Mid funnel: cold search, competitive search (only if it works well), Performance Max and cold Shopping.
Bottom funnel: branded search, branded shopping and dynamic remarketing.

If you are just starting, begin at the bottom of the funnel to accumulate conversions, then add one mid-funnel campaign — for ecommerce usually Shopping and PMax — and only move up-funnel once smart bidding is viable.
Exclude all customer lists from cold campaigns and exclude your brand from PMax so branded conversions do not inflate cold performance.
Keep branded search and branded shopping in separate campaigns so cheap branded conversions stay identifiable and marketing spend stays efficient.
caveats: The source's rule of thumb for smart bidding eligibility is about one conversion per day sustained over 30 days — treat as a heuristic, not a Google requirement.
Running your Meta winners as YouTube statics/shorts is a transfer assumption; test rather than assuming parity.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Write Google ads from audience research, not keyword lists
cards.summary: Ground search ads, shopping titles and YouTube angles in the language and motivations of the person searching.
cards.use_when: You are writing search ad copy, shopping titles or a YouTube short for a cold audience and need angle and language direction.
steps: Before writing anything, map the audience: the language they use, psychographics, problems, pains, goals, desires, why they buy and why they buy from you specifically.
Ask explicitly: what type of person searches this, what pain are they in, what problem are they solving, what desire or goal does the product fulfil.
Write search headlines, descriptions, images, callouts, site links and snippets that echo that language, since on Google the searcher is seeing every competitor's ad simultaneously.
In shopping ads, carry the same language into the title (for targeting) plus the promo extension, ratings and social proof that visually differentiate the listing.

For YouTube Shorts use heavy direct response: make the CTA explicit (click here, search this, tap the screen) and state the big offer and next step, because the platform is less purchase-oriented than Meta.
The source argues resonance, connection and offer are what make you stand out — not just being cheapest, since margin constrains price competition.
caveats: The claim that cheap price would win all else being equal is the source's framing; margin reality often prevents it.
Heavy-direct-response guidance is the source's opinion about YouTube's buying sophistication, not a measured universal rule.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Let Shopping and PMax discover your converting keywords
cards.summary: Use broad-match Shopping/PMax search term reports as first-party keyword research rather than guessing keywords upfront.
cards.use_when: You need real, purchase-confirmed search phrases for search campaigns, shopping titles or landing page copy.
steps: Launch Shopping and PMax broadly and let Google test a wide range of search terms automatically rather than pre-selecting keywords.
Read the search term report inside Google Ads and rank queries by impressions, CTR, conversions and CPC.
In Shopping, this also reveals what your product title is actually matching against, which tells you what your feed title is communicating.
Extract converting queries into exact and phrase match keywords in search campaigns — start with exact for proven winners, phrase for close variations.
Push the same winning phrases into product titles, PMax assets, YouTube angles, offers and landing page copy.
Exclude the low-performing and non-converting search terms to raise efficiency, then repeat: the loop is a flywheel, not a one-time task.
Example: a shopping feed surfaces 'best marathon shoes for flat feet' as converting, so you'd otherwise never have intuited that query and can now target it exactly and build copy around it.
caveats: This inverts traditional keyword-first research; the source recommends manual keyword research only for your very first search campaigns or when you need control.
The source claims broad will not work in search campaigns unless you are explicitly testing — validate data elsewhere first.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Use manual keyword tools only for the first rung
cards.summary: Seed initial search campaigns with third-party keyword data, then hand research over to Google's conversion data.
cards.use_when: You have no conversion history and must launch a first search campaign or decide initial product title targets.
steps: Use Google Keyword Planner on your main product category to find general product-level search phrases with high search volume and reasonable CPCs.
Use paid tools (Ahrefs, Semrush) to reverse-engineer competitor keywords, and SpyFu to see what competitors are bidding on.
Treat competitor bidding as weak evidence: the source says assume competitors may be bidding on terms that do not work for them.
Note the limitation: third-party data gives search volume and competitor behaviour but no purchase confirmation for your product.
Use these keywords only to seed, then let Shopping/PMax conversion data replace and refine them over time.
Best combined approach per the source: start broad with method one (let Google optimise for speed and scale), then layer traditional research for extra optimisation.
caveats: High search volume without buyer intent is a poor target; the source stresses buy intent over volume.
Keyword Planner and third-party tool interfaces change frequently — verify current functionality.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Set bids and budgets from unit economics, not habit
cards.summary: Choose bidding strategies per campaign type and let your margins and KPIs define how much you can afford to bid and spend.
cards.use_when: You are setting bid strategy and daily budget for branded, shopping, PMax or cold campaigns.
steps: Work backwards from unit economics: how much can you afford to spend per acquisition to beat competitors, and how much are you willing to spend to test versus scale.
Match strategy to campaign type: branded search runs on target impression share (the source calls it absolute target impression share); branded shopping runs on manual CPC where you control max CPC.
Mid-funnel and cold campaigns use smart bidding: maximise conversion value for ecommerce (more value per purchase), maximise conversions when you want volume, plus tROAS and tCPA variants.
Choose maximise conversions over value only when you know your break-even CPA and simply want as many actions as possible; otherwise value-based bidding is the ecommerce default per the source.
The source treats bids and budget as the last optimisation area — after creative, structure, tracking and offer — though it still matters.
Budget levels depend entirely on brand specifics: goals, KPIs, COGS and desired scale; there is no universal number.
caveats: The source explicitly gives a non-specific answer on budget size because it depends on individual brand economics — do not copy another brand's budget.
Smart bidding requires sufficient conversion volume to learn; bid strategy names and settings change, so verify in the current Google Ads interface.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Enrol the four GMC add-ons
cards.summary: Turn on dynamic remarketing, customer reviews, product ratings and promotions in Merchant Center to lift CTR and enable remarketing.
cards.use_when: You are setting up or auditing Google Merchant Center before running Shopping, PMax or remarketing.
steps: Go to Merchant Center Settings > Add-ons and check the Discover tab for programs you are not enrolled in.
Enable dynamic remarketing — the source says it is essential for the whole Google Ads system to function for ecommerce.
Enable Google customer reviews and product ratings to add trust signals that the source claims noticeably raise CTR and conversion rate on ads.
Enable promotions so your discount appears in the Shopping ad itself; the source argues a visible better offer wins the click and increases purchase likelihood.
Verify each add-on is actually active, not just available, before spending on feed campaigns.
caveats: CTR and conversion-rate lifts from reviews/ratings/promotions are stated by the source without specific measured figures — treat as directional.
Eligibility for some add-ons varies by country and account standing.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Complete GMC business info and branding to survive review
cards.summary: Fill business details, verified store, logo/colour assets and social profiles accurately to protect account standing.
cards.use_when: You are onboarding a store to Merchant Center or your account has warnings and you want to reduce suspension risk.
steps: In Business Info, enter details that exactly match your website: verify and claim your online store, provide your checkout link, accepted payment methods, and business logo and colours.
In the same screen use Edit logo and colours to upload square and rectangular logos plus a main and accent colour, so Shopping ads look on-brand and Google sees a complete, legitimate business.
Verify your website branding, payment methods and policies are genuinely consistent with what you enter — the source warns Google is ruthless about mismatches that lead to account suspension.
If in the US, enable business identity attributes: category options include woman-owned, veteran-owned, black-owned, Latino-owned and small business.
The source recommends selecting small business even for larger companies, citing the Bureau of Labor Statistics threshold of under $40 million annual revenue as qualifying as small.
Add social profiles (Instagram, Facebook and others) to make business information as complete as possible.
caveats: The small-business threshold is the source's interpretation of Bureau of Labor Statistics classification, not a Google eligibility rule — verify current Google criteria.
Identity attributes are flagged as a minor CTR/social-standing factor, not a major performance lever.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Lock shipping and returns as manual in GMC
cards.summary: Fix shipping and returns configuration inside Merchant Center so Shopify changes cannot desync policies and trigger suspension.
cards.use_when: You are configuring Merchant Center shipping/returns or your store changes shipping rates and you fear feed or policy mismatches.
steps: In the Shopify Google & YouTube sales channel, under product feed settings, set shipping settings to Manual setup in GMC so changes in Shopify do not auto-update Merchant Center.
The source's reasoning: a random sync change can create a mismatch with your stated shipping policy and a flag can escalate to account suspension.
In Merchant Center > Shipping and returns, add policies for every country you ship to, including differing speeds and methods (the example brand runs both US and Canada).
Enter an accurate ship-from location.
Add your returns policy inside GMC, link directly to the specific returns policy page, and ensure it mirrors what is on your site.
Treat a clear, strong return policy as effectively a requirement to run Merchant Center today, and as something Google checks when deciding to suspend.
caveats: Keeping settings manual means you must update GMC yourself when shipping genuinely changes — do it as part of the routine maintenance cycle.
Google's policy and feeds interfaces change; verify that manual-mode options still exist before relying on the workflow.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Audit feeds and fix 'needs attention' errors
cards.summary: Locate your primary feed and systematically clear product-level errors before scaling feed ads.
cards.use_when: You are diagnosing why feed ads underperform, or onboarding a store whose products are disapproved or warning-flagged.
steps: In Merchant Center settings, open Data sources to see every feed; with the Shopify Google & YouTube app the primary feed comes via the content API.
Identify your primary feed and any supplemental feeds, confirm the primary is updating, and note that promotions sources can also live here.
Go to Products > Needs attention to see Google's per-SKU issues; the example shows approved products missing an age group.
Work through the list systematically, fixing red errors and yellow warnings using Google's own stated fix instructions.
Make this a weekly routine: revisit Products and diagnostics each week and clear new red or yellow flags before they accumulate.
caveats: The source notes many brands never do this and blame Google Ads for what is a feed problem — expect meaningful time cost with large SKU counts.
Some errors only apply to specific categories (e.g. age group for certain verticals), so not every flag is relevant to every product.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Build product titles with the 130–150 character formula
cards.summary: Frontload high-volume keywords and differentiators in feed titles, placing brand first or last depending on brand strength.
cards.use_when: You are rewriting Shopping/PMax feed titles to raise relevance and win more qualifying impressions.
steps: Write titles of roughly 130–150 characters including: highest-volume keyword, product details (colour, size, quantity), second highest-volume keyword, differentiating angles/USPs, and brand name.
For a small brand pushing cold traffic, frontload the high-volume keywords and place the brand name at the end.
For a big brand that can leverage recognition in Shopping, place the brand name first and the high-volume keywords after.
Cover variant fields — colour, size, weight, format — so searchers know exactly what they are buying.
Apply the difference between high-volume keyword (the most product-aware term everyone uses), variants, USPs/angles and brand name in that structure.
Edit titles in Merchant Center > Products by opening the SKU and using Edit product, or manage them in a data feed tool like DataFeedWatch.
You can paste the formula and your product info into ChatGPT to generate a draft, then edit the keyword choices yourself.
caveats: The 130–150 character target is the source's recommendation; verify current Google title length limits before publishing.
The example 'Apple Watch band' title shows the pattern but is a case illustration, not a performance promise.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Write feed descriptions that survive policy review
cards.summary: Use the description for targeting and benefit copy, not promotions, and avoid website copy dumps.
cards.use_when: You are optimising feed descriptions for a store that simply imports Shopify product copy into Merchant Center.
steps: Check your current description: if it is auto-pulled from the Shopify product page, assume it is not optimised for feed targeting.
Write roughly 1,000 characters covering key features, USPs, a call to action and useful product information.
Frontload high-volume keywords at the start, in the style of an SEO article, because Google uses the description for targeting.
Exclude promotional text such as discount claims, because the source states that violates Google's policies.
Treat description as secondary in impact to the title, but still worth the effort because it expands the terms your product can match against.
caveats: The source calls the description less leveraged than the title — prioritise titles first.
Promotion language belongs in Merchant Center promotions, not the description; policy details can change, so verify current rules.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Choose feed images for context and standout
cards.summary: Test main images that show the product in use versus on plain backgrounds to improve Shopping ad click appeal.
cards.use_when: You are choosing or testing primary feed images for product pages and Shopping/PMax assets.
steps: Select the highest quality, most attention-grabbing image available for each SKU as the primary feed image.

Test the product alone on a clean background against the product in context: a sofa in a well-lit living room setup, golf clubs mid-swing on the green, an Apple Watch band shown on an actual Apple Watch.
Show a product in the context it was made for when the item alone is confusing — the Apple Watch band only makes sense attached to a watch.
Supplement with lifestyle images of people using the product for other placements.
For this source's example brand, the product-focused image performed best; treat that as their finding and run your own test rather than copying it.
caveats: The source is explicit that the best-performing image style is brand-specific — do not assume product-only wins for your category.
Main image choice can affect eligibility and performance simultaneously; check policy requirements alongside conversion appeal.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Fill product identifiers, categories and attributes accurately
cards.summary: Use GTINs, product type, category and filtering attributes to remove performance-limiting warnings and increase discoverability.
cards.use_when: Your feed shows warnings about identifiers or missing attributes, or you want products to appear under Shopping filters.
steps: Never change the product ID or SKU; let them import consistently from Shopify or a feed tool, because changing them disrupts history and targeting.
Provide GTIN, UPC, EAN, JAN or ISBN if your product has one — ask your supplier and register the barcode in the feed; custom-made products may legitimately lack one.
Set product type and Google product category for every SKU (the source suggests asking ChatGPT for a first draft), condition to new unless genuinely used, plus accurate price and availability.

Complete detailed attributes used in Shopping filters: colour, size, size type, sizing system by country, gender, material, pattern, age group for apparel; bundle status, adult and energy class where relevant.
Leave shipping and returns to pull from Shopify or the policies configured in GMC.
Add custom labels (e.g. label 1 for small bands, label 2 for large bands) so you can target and report on cohorts inside Google Ads.
Keep COGS, sell quantity and currency fields filled where applicable, though the source calls these minor for performance.
caveats: Missing correct identifiers create performance-limiting warnings rather than outright ban in most cases — still fix them early.
Attribute requirements and identifier rules vary by category and country; check current Merchant Center requirements.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Never edit price or availability inside GMC
cards.summary: Change price, availability and sale price only at source so Google does not flag a website mismatch.
cards.use_when: You are updating product pricing or stock and deciding where to make the change.
steps: Make all price, availability and sale price changes in Shopify (or your store platform), never directly in Merchant Center.
Let the change flow back into GMC through the feed so the value matches what a shopper sees on your site.
Understand the risk: Merchant Center checks for mismatches between the site price and the feed price, flags a warning, and repeated mismatches compound account risk.
Treat this as part of weekly and monthly maintenance: review feed values against the live site during routine checks.
If a value genuinely must change in GMC for a feed-only reason, confirm the source-of-truth logic first so the next sync does not overwrite or re-flag it.
caveats: The rule applies to price, availability and sale price specifically; other attributes such as titles and descriptions are edited in the feed.
This is the source's stated best practice for avoiding suspension — enforcement behaviour can change, so keep site and feed aligned regardless.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Earn the Shopping experience scorecard badge
cards.summary: Use Google's store quality scorecard to catch missing trust factors and differentiate listings with a trusted badge.
cards.use_when: You want Shopping listings to stand out against competitors and are looking for the highest-leverage remaining trust improvements.
steps: Open the Shopping experience scorecard in Merchant Center and read which components are missing or underperforming.
Work through the components it covers: shipping experience, return experience, purchase experience, browsing experience and promotion data.
Use the edit links to correct shipping details, returns information, purchase experience and browsing experience directly.
Aim to reach the exceptional tier, which the source says earns a trusted badge on Shopping listings and is measured comparatively against competitors.
Combine this with active product ratings and promotions (see the add-ons card) since they feed the same trust layer.
The source's own example sits at number one in its industry for this scorecard, which they attribute to a well-optimised Merchant Center — treat as their result, not a guarantee.
caveats: The badge is awarded comparatively against competitors in your industry, so you can improve and still not hold it.
Scorecard components and point thresholds change; check the current scorecard requirements.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Run a weekly and monthly GMC maintenance rhythm
cards.summary: Keep Merchant Center healthy with recurring checks for feed errors, policy drift and promotion dates.
cards.use_when: You run feed campaigns continuously and need an operating routine that prevents gradual account decay or suspension.
steps: Weekly: go through Products and diagnostics, fixing any new red errors and yellow warnings.
Monthly: briefly review your website shipping and returns policies against what is configured in Merchant Center and correct any drift.
When a new sale or promotion starts, add it to GMC promotions and set a proper end date; when the sale ends, make sure the promotion expires or is removed.
Keep the go-to-market discipline of never editing price, availability or sale price in GMC, so maintenance stays focused on feed hygiene rather than correcting mismatches.
Treat this as the ongoing layer on top of the one-time setup phases: account and business setup, shipping/returns/tax, feed health, and trust/visibility.
caveats: The source frames nine out of ten brands as not having Merchant Center set up correctly — expect setup debt, not just ongoing tweaks.
Promotion scheduling mistakes can leave stale offers live, so calendar the end dates.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Reduce Merchant Center suspension risk deliberately
cards.summary: Treat suspension as the highest-cost ecommerce event and run the checklist that keeps feed, Shopping and PMax running.
cards.use_when: You are auditing an account for suspension risk or your store has received warnings, mismatches or policy flags.
steps: Prioritise the most common triggers the source identifies: inaccurate business information, mismatched shipping and returns policies, and price/availability mismatches between site and feed.
Keep business info, checkout link, payment methods and branding accurate and consistent with the live site at all times.
Set shipping settings to manual in GMC and maintain policies per country with an accurate ship-from location.
Link directly to a real returns policy page and mirror the policy in Greenhouse Center configuration.
Clear feed errors and warnings weekly rather than letting them stack, and never edit price, availability or sale price inside GMC.
Recognise the stakes: a ban blocks feed ads, Shopping ads, and the strongest part of PMax for an ecommerce brand, so prevention work outranks other optimisation.
caveats: This is a prevention checklist, not an appeals process — a suspended account needs its own remediation path.
Google's policy enforcement and specific triggers are opaque and change; treat the list as risk reduction rather than a guarantee.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Product Feed Optimization Basics for Google Merchant Center
cards.summary: Keep feed titles, descriptions and images simple and accurate, sync availability automatically, and never edit sale price inside GMC.
cards.use_when: Optimizing your Google Merchant Center product feed so Shopping and PMax ads can serve correctly and convert.
steps: Do not overcomplicate feed titles, descriptions or images; the source argues keeping them simple and accurate works best and that most people overcomplicate this.
Never change your sale price inside Google Merchant Center itself — leave pricing to sync from your store so no mismatch can appear.
Make availability dynamic to real stock: anything out of stock must be marked sold out, or Google will flag you for showing 'in stock and ready to ship'.
Do the same pass across every SKU; note that scaling this is mostly manual work if you have many SKUs, but once correct it improves Shopping results.
caveats: The source claims results improve 'massively' but gives no measured benchmark — treat as directional.
GMC interface and feed rules change; verify current fields in the Merchant Center UI before editing.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Payment and Checkout Compliance Checks for GMC
cards.summary: Test payment methods, final price transparency, and discount codes on your checkout, because GMC bots audit all three.
cards.use_when: Preparing or auditing your store checkout to avoid Google Merchant Center suspension or promotion disapproval.
steps: Maintain SSL on checkout pages — confirm the checkout URL starts with HTTPS, which Google requires for secure transactions.
Test every payment method you list (PayPal, cards, crypto, Afterpay, etc.); listing a method that doesn't actually work at checkout is a GMC error and can suspend the account.

Verify final price transparency: taxes, state-level sales tax, and shipping fees by destination must all be reflected before payment and match the Shopify and GMC data. Run test orders to confirm calculations.
Test discount code functionality. A promotion won't go live in GMC unless the code applies at checkout; if an approved promotion stops working, that is a big flag.
caveats: GMC's checkout audit behaviour is described from the presenter's experience, not official documentation; verify current policy.
Promotion approval rules and deadlines change — check GMC help docs.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Listing Accuracy Checklist: Claims, Reviews, Links, Pricing
cards.summary: Make listing claims factual, reviews authentic, links correct and listed prices match checkout to prevent GMC misrepresentation flags.
cards.use_when: Auditing product listings and product pages before scaling Google Shopping or PMax spend.
steps: Review product claims for accuracy and remove exaggerated or unverifiable claims; stick to factual benefits. If making scientific claims, provide credible resources in listings, descriptions and on the landing page.
Verify review authenticity and recency. The presenter warns against fake reviews; he recommends a real review flow and pushing a review feed into GMC so star ratings show on Shopping listings.
Mark out-of-stock items as sold out and keep availability dynamic to real inventory — showing 'in stock and ready to ship' on an out-of-stock item is a violation.
Check every link, especially product page to shopping listing; broken or mismatched links can be flagged as a scam and lead to suspension.
Ensure listed price matches checkout price and discounts apply accurately; mismatches cause abandoned carts and GMC disapprovals.
caveats: The source calls unverifiable claims 'the biggest thing that hits brands' — his experience, not a published statistic.
Claim rules vary by category (e.g. health); confirm current Google misrepresentation policy.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Branding, Navigation and Legal Page Checks for GMC
cards.summary: Polish brand assets, keep footer links working and update legal pages to look like a reputable store in Google's eyes.
cards.use_when: Cleaning up store branding, navigation and policy pages so GMC bots see a trusted store.
steps: Optimize logo quality and placement and complete all brand information plus URL and business verification in GMC during setup.
Update homepage branding, messaging and visuals monthly — also a CRO move, but it keeps the store looking reputable rather than like a default theme.
Check navigation and hamburger menu for broken links and direct links to contact, home, products, about, return policy, shipping policy and subscription management. Google bots crawl these.
Review and update terms and conditions and ensure the privacy policy reflects current data practices; Shopify provides defaults to start from.
Test all footer links so return, about, terms of service, contact, shipping and subscription management policies are reachable from the footer, where Google verifies trust.
caveats: The source calls branding 'low leverage' for suspension risk but still worth doing.
Default theme usage is described as a trust signal risk — opinion, not a stated Google rule.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Shipping, Returns and Contact Info Sync for GMC
cards.summary: Keep shipping costs, courier details, returns policy and contact info synchronized between your site and GMC and review them monthly.
cards.use_when: Setting up or maintaining shipping, returns and contact sections to prevent GMC suspension.
steps: Match website shipping settings to GMC shipping and returns sections, including shipping cost and delivery times. The source shares a client case where shipping cost dropped after a courier change but GMC wasn't updated, causing a week-long suspension.
Name the courier services you actually use (UPS, FedEx, DHL) in both your shipping policy page and GMC shipping policy.
Confirm order tracking functionality works and that the courier provides tracking; customer service will feel it otherwise.

Write clear step-by-step return instructions in both your site returns policy and GMC, and link GMC to the site returns page. Missing returns, shipping or terms pages guarantees suspension per the source.
Update refund processing timings monthly, keep return periods current, test return links, and verify return address and timing monthly.

Verify physical business address monthly, test the customer service phone number, use a branded domain email (not Gmail), and cross-check contact details match across GMC, Google Ads and all Google accounts.
caveats: The week-long suspension is one client example, not a benchmark.
The claim that a phone number is required is softened by the source to 'or at least an easy way to contact you' — treat as preference.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Site Speed, Design and App Health as GMC Trust Signals
cards.summary: Fast, well-branded sites with working apps get better CPCs and store ratings; slow or broken stores risk GMC penalties.
cards.use_when: Improving site experience to protect Google Ads performance and Merchant Center standing.
steps: Test website loading speed and optimize user navigation paths. A slow site causes bounces, wastes paid clicks, and the source says Google marks you down versus competitors in CPCs and can cost you the trusted seller badge.
Update store design so it is properly branded and official: avoid default themes, use high-quality non-AI-generated images and clear fonts.
Make product images and descriptions congruent with what is shown in GMC — this helps conversion rate and keeps Google's view consistent.
Test all apps and plugins for functionality. Dead apps slow the store; broken actively-used apps create user-experience flags that escalate to GMC risk.
caveats: Slow-site CPC penalty and badge loss are the source's claims about Google behaviour; verify against current Google documentation.
No specific speed threshold is given.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: The 34-Item GMC Anti-Suspension Checklist by Frequency
cards.summary: Work a 34-point Google Merchant Center checklist split into daily, weekly, monthly and one-time tasks to avoid suspension.
cards.use_when: Building an ongoing ops routine for your Google Merchant Center account.
steps: Organize checks into the source's categories: payment and checkout, product listings, branding, shipping information, returns, legal compliance, contact info, and store design/performance.
Assign each item a frequency — daily, weekly, monthly or once — and actually do once-tasks during GMC setup (URL and business verification, branded email, terms defaults, SSL).
Do the full checklist deliberately rather than quickly: the presenter says pause, check each item in your GMC, and change it immediately if missing.
If you get suspended, assume it is one of these 34 items, since Google typically won't tell you the exact cause.
Keep the list as a living document and re-run it after any change to shipping, pricing or fulfilment suppliers.
caveats: The source calls the result 'bulletproof' and 'basically guaranteed' — that is confidence framing, not a guarantee.
Checklist content and GMC policy change; verify against current GMC help docs.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Build a Reusable Brand Context Profile with AI Before Writing Ad Copy
cards.summary: Train an LLM on your brand and product page to produce a reusable context profile for ads, landing pages and emails.
cards.use_when: Preparing to generate Google Ads assets, Meta copy, landing page copy or emails and needing consistent brand context.
steps: Give the AI a role, context, task, examples, constraints and desired output — the source calls this the best way to prompt anything.
Use a prompt casting the AI as a world-class direct response copywriter for ecommerce cold traffic, and feed it a PDF of a product page (e.g. save the page as PDF from the browser).

Have it audit the page for value proposition, emotional and logical persuasion, CTAs, voice of customer, proof mechanisms, offer positioning, copy structure, conversion blockers and missed psychological levers, plus optimization suggestions.

Run a second prompt casting it as an elite advertising strategist/deep researcher to map product intelligence, customer psychographics, competitors, keyword and intent mapping, and market positioning.
Save the resulting context profile offline or in Drive so you and your team can reuse it for any asset type.
caveats: The source has his own prompt pack; prompts shown are his workflow, not universal.
AI output quality depends on input quality — garbage in, garbage out.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Use AI Deep Research to Build Customer and Market Understanding
cards.summary: Run a deep research prompt in a research-capable model with your URL and product PDF to produce a long brand, audience and market brief.
cards.use_when: Replacing or supplementing weeks of manual customer and market research before writing ads or landing pages.
steps: Use AI to write the deep research prompt itself: instruct a prompt-engineer persona to produce a single detailed prompt for an elite advertising strategist covering brand, audience, positioning, product and voice.
Paste that prompt into a deep research tool with web access plus your store URL and the product page PDF.
Expect roughly 15–20 minutes of runtime; the source notes the tool shows its research trail (Reddit, YouTube, etc.), which can surface authentic voice-of-customer language.
Export the output (often 30+ pages) to Google Drive and archive it so you can update it later.
Mine the output for angles, offers, reframing, emotional and logical buy triggers and audience awareness levels before writing copy.
caveats: Presenter says Google's deep research is currently best and that this may go out of date; he also says this gets you about 80% of the way there, not 100%.
Tool choice and capabilities change quickly — verify current options.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Convert Research into JSON Context Profiles for Consistent Copy
cards.summary: Use an LLM to turn deep research into avatar, market and brand JSON profiles plus one combined context file.
cards.use_when: Structuring brand research so any AI session can instantly understand your store before generating copy.
steps: Prompt a strong writing model (the source uses Claude Sonnet 4) as a world-class AI prompt engineer and brand strategist, feeding it the full deep research document.

Have it produce four outputs: a customer avatar JSON, a market context JSON (pricing tiers, direct and indirect competitors, target keywords, competitive landscape), a brand context JSON, and a full combined context profile.
Use the combined profile as the paste-in context for any model when generating ad copy, landing pages or emails.
Keep the JSON files in Drive so your whole team can reuse them; note that long responses may pause and require 'continue'.
Expect detail like avatar psychographics, competitor mapping and offer positioning — the point is precision, not brevity.
caveats: JSON is used because it maps variables clearly for LLMs; it is a workflow choice, not a Google requirement.
Model names and best-model recommendations may change.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Generate All Google Ads Assets from a Context Profile
cards.summary: Paste your brand context plus a Google Ads JSON asset template into an LLM to produce RSA headlines, descriptions, sitelinks, callouts, snippets and PMax assets.
cards.use_when: Building Google Search or PMax campaign assets at scale without starting from a blank page.
steps: Load the full context profile into a fresh model session together with the Google Ads asset JSON template.
Prompt simply: create all the Google Ads assets needed for my brand.

Review outputs organized as Search and PMax assets — headlines (including long ones), descriptions, sitelinks, callouts, structured snippets, price extension suggestions, and asset variations by awareness level (problem, solution, product, most aware) plus competitor and responsive search ad examples.
Ask for a product feed Shopping title when needed; the model returns primary and alternative titles, keyword-optimized and competitive variations, promotional titles, and explains why they work.
Manually edit weak or off-brand lines — the source flags examples like 'aerospace grade materials' as bad and 'stop buying cheap wallets' as possibly off-brand.
caveats: The source says AI gets you roughly 80–90% of the way; human judgment supplies the rest.
The '$10M new customer revenue' figure is the agency's claim about its workflow, not a guaranteed result.
Verify character limits and current asset requirements in Google Ads.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Set Up a Branded Search Campaign to Protect and Capture Demand
cards.summary: Run a search campaign on exact-match brand terms with impression-share bidding to own the SERP, defend against competitors and feed cheap conversion data.
cards.use_when: Launching or optimizing paid search on your own brand name to capture searchers who saw you elsewhere.
steps: Create a Search campaign, optimize for the purchase conversion, name it clearly (agency + brand + 'search brand').

Use impression share bidding, not conversions, and set 'absolute top of search' to about 95%, with a max CPC around $3. In the source's experience brand clicks then cost about 1–2 cents, at most around 50 cents.
Turn off search and display network partners, target your own country using presence (not presence or interest), set English, and add observational audiences like customer list and GA traffic.
Add exact-match brand keywords such as [brand], [brand reviews], [brand discount code]; optionally add phrase match versions of best exact-match keywords for extra scope.
Write RSAs with brand + 'official site' + offer headlines and sales copy descriptions; add logo and business name; set a daily budget like $25.
Optimize by raising max CPC only if the budget won't spend, and never switch away from absolute top of search.
caveats: The source says you are often paying for some conversions that might have happened organically, but argues the space, defence and cheap conversion-data benefits justify it.
The $64 spend returning $1.5K and $858 returning 24 orders are specific examples, not benchmarks.
CPC and bidding options change — verify current Google Ads settings.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Why Every Ecommerce Brand Should Run a Branded Search Campaign
cards.summary: Branded search ads expand your SERP footprint, defend your brand from competitors and load cheap high-intent conversion data into your account.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to spend on your own brand terms in Google Ads.
steps: Take up more SERP space: paid ad at top plus organic results plus Shopping results leaves searchers surrounded by your brand.
Defend your branded term from competitors who may bid on it with 'us vs them' ads; the source says running early helps Google give you ad rank as the official advertiser.
Induce purchases from people who discovered you on Facebook or organic content and then search your name — an offer in the ad can move them from research to buying.
Feed your purchase conversion action with cheap, high-intent conversions that improve performance of Shopping, PMax and other campaigns.
Add buying-journey safety: a sponsored 'official site' result helps searchers trust they are on the real store rather than a knockoff or scammer.
caveats: SAS is where the source says competitor brand-bidding is most prevalent; ecommerce less so.
The source concedes most brand conversions would often happen organically anyway — the case is marginal gain and defence, not pure incremental revenue.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Set Up and Automate a Branded Shopping Campaign with Scripts
cards.summary: Create a Shopping campaign limited to branded terms and use scripts to automatically exclude non-branded search queries.
cards.use_when: Adding a high-leverage, fast-to-launch Shopping campaign to lift account efficiency and cheap sales.
steps: Duplicate or build a Shopping campaign structure, then exclude all non-branded terms so it only serves on branded queries.
Use a negative keyword script to automatically keep non-branded queries out of the campaign as search terms accumulate.
Match product feed titles and descriptions to brand naming so the campaign surfaces on brand searches.
Monitor and adjust exclusions regularly to prevent non-branded spend leaking into the branded campaign.
The source says this can be set up in a couple of clicks and lift ROAS and spend efficiency within about 24 hours.
caveats: The claim of uplift within 24 hours is the presenter's description, not a measured benchmark.
Script availability and Shopping campaign structure can change — verify current Google Ads interface and script sources.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Branded Search & Shopping Campaigns: Structure, Bidding & Exclusions
cards.summary: Build a manual-CPC branded shopping campaign plus branded search to protect your brand term, harvest cheap conversions and keep prospecting bids clean.
cards.use_when: Setting up or auditing paid search structure for a store that already gets branded searches and wants brand protection plus cheaper conversion data.
steps: Create a separate shopping campaign for branded traffic only (New campaign > Sales > conversion goal Purchases > Shopping > connect Merchant Center > choose Standard shopping, not Performance Max). Name it by brand + campaign type.

Set bidding to manual CPC with a low budget (the source uses ~$50/day) and high campaign priority. Turn off the search network; set locations to where you actually sell and set location options to 'Presence' only, never 'Presence or interest'.

Create a product group/ad group (e.g. all products in one group if the brand term applies to the whole catalog) with a ~$1 starting bid, then subdivide by product only when products differ enough that you want to see separate average CPCs.

Automatically exclude all non-branded terms via a Google Ads script (Tools > Bulk actions > Scripts) so only brand terms remain in the shopping listing. Verify the current script UI before copying anything.
Optionally run a parallel branded search campaign so a branded query shows both shopping and search ads, taking more of the above-the-fold SERP.

In the branded campaign, exclude your existing-customer list: export the customer list from your store backend, then Google Ads > Audiences > Exclusions > upload and exclude. Rationale: repeat buyers searching your name are buying, not browsing, so paying for that click is waste.
Optimize only via manual bids — do not switch to automated bidding; if search impression share is low, raise the max bid slightly instead.

Check whether you are paying for conversions that would have happened organically: the presenter states you usually are, and argues it is still worth it for brand protection, cheap conversion data feeding prospecting, and conversion data that Google uses to steer smart bidding.
Do not expect the campaign to stay clean on its own — continuously exclude non-branded terms and keep the Merchant Center feed optimized, since feed quality drives cost, visibility and click share.
caveats: Source is a Google Ads agency owner with a commercial interest; his 'you always need one' position is his opinion, not a measured benchmark.
Data showed competitors ranking on brand terms; the presenter notes this is mainly seen in software but applies to ecommerce too.
Branded campaigns mostly capture demand that already exists; treat them as protection and data harvesting, not incremental growth.
Automated keyword-removal scripts require account-specific edits and may change — verify the current script interface.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Cold Search Campaigns: Capture Problem-Aware Demand, Not Product-Aware Demand
cards.summary: Use broad-match cold search ads on problem-aware queries to reach people who don't know your brand, then tighten winners into exact match.
cards.use_when: Planning acquisition for a store whose product solves a specific problem and whose product-aware search demand is exhausted or too expensive.
steps: Set up a search campaign on the Google network only, objective Sales, single primary conversion action, campaigns optimized for purchase conversions.

Choose bidding: the source uses Maximize Conversions with the AI Max feature on for cold problem-aware terms. He reserves Maximize Clicks for testing product-market fit with broad investigative terms. Turn brand exclusions on so branded queries stay out of this cold campaign.
Set locations with 'Presence' (not presence or interest) limited to countries you actually ship to; set a daily budget you can hold for at least a few weeks of testing.
Build the ad group from many problem-phrased keywords, mixing exact and broad match; the source explicitly avoids phrase match. Start broad to see the full range of queries the market actually types.
Read the search terms report: mine converting broad queries, then promote proven ones to exact match so Google can optimize around them, and pause/remove terms with clicks but no conversions.

Judge terms on click-through rate, CPC and conversion rate together. In the case study, 'how to lower blood pressure' had a 7.5% CTR at 38p CPC and ~2.3% conversion; 'blood pressure supplements' had a higher conversion rate but also a higher CPC; 'how to reduce high blood pressure' had a ~9% CTR with few conversions.
Once a term proves itself, change the final URL for that keyword so the ad points to a page written for that exact query, rather than the generic default landing page.
Build out the ad with price extensions, structured snippets, callouts, sitelinks and a business logo to occupy more of the SERP.

Use dynamic keyword insertion in the headline so the searcher's own phrase appears in the ad (set a sensible default headline for when no keyword is inserted) and pin it; the source credits this congruence for an 8.32% cold CTR.
caveats: Case-study metrics (8.32% CTR, 3.82% cold conversion rate, ~£3.5k spend, £7.6k reported return) are from one UK supplement account over ~3 weeks and are examples, not benchmarks.
The presenter says Google-reported return figures are unreliable and recommends a third-party attribution tool as source of truth.
Broad match floods in irrelevant queries; it requires ongoing search-term review and negative work.

Send problem-aware cold traffic to an advertorial/educational sales letter, not a product page with a buy box — the source states you cannot present an offer to someone who is only problem-aware and brand-unaware.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Build Mini-Funnels Per Search Term for Cold Traffic
cards.summary: Match one landing page and one ad per high-volume problem-aware search phrase to convert cold searchers you already know are looking for.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many landing pages to build for paid search and where to spend page-creation effort on problem-aware traffic.
steps: List the problem-aware phrases in your niche with their monthly search volume (the source cites ~3.6k for 'how to lower blood pressure' as an example). Treat each phrase as a separate mini-funnel.
For each phrase, check the three constraints: can the ad get a strong CTR, what CPC can you tolerate at your COGS, and what conversion rate can the page achieve.

Apply constraint thinking: if CTR is already strong (the source reached ~8%) and CPC is acceptable, the biggest lever is conversion rate, so invest in the page for that phrase rather than rewriting the ad.

Create a landing page congruent with the phrase — e.g. for 'how to lower blood pressure' build an educational article/sales letter that lays out the problem and solutions, then presents your product as the solution. Avoid a generic advertorial when the phrase implies a different intent.
Point the keyword's final URL to that page (not just the default ad URL) so the same campaign can hold several mini-funnels.
Keep phrases you have not built a page for yet running to the default page; add pages only for phrases with real search volume and converting signal.

Expect different CPCs by intent: product-aware phrases ('blood pressure supplements') cost more per click than problem phrases, but the problem phrase can still have a lower cost per conversion because it is more congruent with the page.
Because volume is capped per phrase, treat each page as longevity infrastructure — a page converting at 10% CTR on ~4,000 views a quarter compounds over years of the brand's life.
caveats: Search volume limits reach per phrase; this is a demand-capture play, not a way to create new demand.
The conversion-rate estimates in the source are projections from a 3-week test, not a proof that page changes lift conversion.
Distinguish conversions at the page level (purchase conversion rate) from click-through rate on the ad; improving one does not automatically improve the other.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Performance Max: What It Is and Where It Fits in the Google Funnel
cards.summary: Treat Performance Max as a middle-of-funnel catch-all engine fed by signals, not a hands-off campaign that replaces search, shopping or YouTube.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to add Performance Max to a store's Google account and what budget share and role to assign it.
steps: Understand the incentive: the source argues Performance Max exists partly to force advertisers into YouTube, Display, Discovery and Gmail inventory that previously could not be monetized from search and shopping alone — so it is built to give Google revenue, but still useful to you.

Position Performance Max as the middle-of-funnel catch-all: it covers auctions and placements your search and shopping campaigns lose, and it retargets cold traffic from Meta, TikTok or organic that landed on the Google network via page-view/product-view signals.
Leave a separate top of funnel (YouTube shorts, in-stream, demand gen, display) and bottom of funnel (branded search, branded shopping, product-aware search and shopping).
Allocate roughly 20–30% of budget to Performance Max as a healthy share — the source's heuristic, not a calculated optimum. Use Performance Max as a core engine, not the entire vehicle.
Feed it strong signals before expecting performance: clean Merchant Center feed, optimized product titles, proper purchase conversion tracking, and high-quality creative assets.
Use it as a remarketing mechanism for cold visitors, but exclude brand terms so it does not claim your branded conversions.
Give it both demand capture and demand generation credit: it can catch existing searches/shopping intent and retarget cold visitors across placements within one campaign.
caveats: The source explicitly warns Performance Max is not set-and-forget; he has audited accounts with 90–100% of budget in 11 Performance Max campaigns.
Performance Max has limited reporting transparency, auto-bidding with no manual CPC control, and reduced placement control unless you add exclusions.
Applies to stores with clean feeds, proper conversion tracking and enough volume to satisfy smart bidding; otherwise the source recommends manual search and shopping first.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Qualify Your Store for Performance Max Before Launching
cards.summary: Screen for feed quality, tracking, budget and conversion volume before committing a store to Performance Max.
cards.use_when: Assessing whether a store is ready for Performance Max or should stay on manual search and manual shopping.
steps: Check the feed: is the Merchant Center product feed clean, complete and optimized? A poorly optimized feed disqualifies the store in the source's view.
Check tracking: is there one primary purchase conversion action firing accurately (Google & YouTube app for Shopify or Google tag), with no competing primary actions?
Check volume: can the store generate roughly 30–50 conversions per month, which the source gives as the minimum for smart bidding strategies to learn?
Check budget: does the store have at least $50–$100 per day available; the source treats tiny budgets as a bad fit and recommends manual search and manual shopping instead.
If any check fails, do not force Performance Max. Run manual shopping/search, fix the feed and tracking, then revisit.
When you do launch, accept that Performance Max may only be able to generalize from your conversion data — weak data means weak automation.
caveats: $50–$100/day and 30–50 conversions/month are source-specific readiness heuristics, not universal thresholds.
Being 'on shopping' matters because a store with no shopping presence has no feed signal for Performance Max to work with.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Set Up a Performance Max Campaign: Bidding, Locations, Devices, Exclusions
cards.summary: Configure a Performance Max campaign with the right bidding strategy, location targeting, device set and brand exclusions.
cards.use_when: Building a new Performance Max campaign inside a Google Ads account.
steps: New campaign > Sales > optimize for Purchases > Performance Max, connect Merchant Center, name with a clear convention.

Choose bidding: the source almost always uses Maximize Conversion Value with a target ROAS derived from the store's break-even ROAS, computed from COGS, gross margin and unit economics; the alternative is Maximize Conversions with a target CPA. Do not copy another brand's ROAS target — it is meaningless without their margin.

Leave the 'customer acquisition' bidding option off (source preference). Instead pursue new customers through offer, ad congruence and audience signals, and measure new-customer ROAS/CPA in a third-party attribution tool such as Triple Whale or Northbeam.
Set locations to the countries you sell in and the correct language; ignore EU political ads if outside the EU.
Add UTM parameters in campaign URL options (or set them post-publish in your attribution tool) so multi-channel reporting is clean.
Turn off tablets and TV screens (source: tablets never; TVs only for dedicated demand gen) and check device splits — mobile usually converts best; keep computers only if their metrics hold up.
Add brand exclusions; the source notes this is not foolproof.
Import customer lists, in-market audiences, custom-intent audiences based on high-intent keywords, competitor brand names and specific websites as audience signals.
Verify current Google Ads interface and feature names before following these steps, as this setup changes frequently.
caveats: Break-even ROAS/CPA is store-specific; there is no universal 'good' ROAS.
Performance Max only offers automated bidding (Maximize Conversions or Maximize Conversion Value), so you cannot control max CPC.
Brand exclusions in Performance Max are described by the source as incomplete protection; verify with brand queries in reporting.
The source's aversion to the customer-acquisition bidding toggle is an opinion, not a tested rule.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Structure Performance Max Around Signal Density, Not Campaign Count
cards.summary: Segment Performance Max by product category and country so signals concentrate in one campaign per audience type.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many Performance Max campaigns a store should run and how to split products and geographies.
steps: Split into separate Performance Max campaigns only where audiences and products are genuinely different (e.g. wallets vs luggage) — the source's rule of thumb is that if a shopper would search these separately, they belong in separate campaigns.
Also split by country or region when advertising in multiple locations; never run two locations in one Performance Max campaign.
Otherwise put everything into one campaign and use multiple asset groups inside it for collections or product types.
Match each asset group's targeting, messaging and audience signals to that specific product segment.
Avoid fragmenting signals across many campaigns and hoping Google optimizes at account level — the source states it does not.
Continually review product performance and remove SKUs that burn budget without converting.
Audit regularly for the failure pattern the source describes: 90–100% of budget concentrated in many Performance Max campaigns with misfired signals, and branded conversions costing $5–$10 per click.
caveats: The 'one campaign per category/country' guidance is a heuristic from the presenter's agency experience, not a controlled benchmark.
Asset-group-level reporting is limited compared to search and shopping, so mis-allocation can hide inside a campaign.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Select Products for Performance Max: Scalers, Zombie Asset Groups and 80/20
cards.summary: Choose the products Performance Max focuses on using the 80/20 principle, and quarantine underperformers instead of letting them dilute spend.
cards.use_when: Building or pruning the product list inside a Performance Max campaign.
steps: Apply the Pareto principle: first find the 20% of products generating 80% of revenue, and even the 4% generating 96%; start Performance Max there.
Pick the product that best leads on cold traffic as the primary scaler, i.e. the offer a brand-unaware buyer can be sold on.
Regularly review performance and remove SKUs that consume budget without converting.
For larger catalogs, create 'zombie asset groups' that group only underperforming products, so they can be tested without dragging down the main scaling campaign.
Do not neglect dedicated product pages for those zombie products, and still optimize them — some products simply do not work on Google, and the goal is to keep them from hurting your scalers.
Keep impressions and clicks concentrated on proven high-converting products because every impression and click in Performance Max is a budget decision.
caveats: This is the source's strategy, not a tested attribution model; the 80/20 and 4/96 splits are illustrative distributions.
Removing products from Performance Max does not mean they cannot sell elsewhere (email, organic, other channels).
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Handle Performance Max's Reporting, Placement and CPC Limitations
cards.summary: Mitigate Performance Max's attribution credit, placement leakage and uncontrolled CPC with third-party measurement, audits and exclusions.
cards.use_when: Auditing an existing Performance Max campaign for wasted spend or unreliable reporting.
steps: Use a third-party attribution tool (Triple Whale, Northbeam) as the source of truth because Performance Max can take credit for sales originating in other marketing channels.

Where campaign-level granularity is missing, apply a third-party reporting script (the source names Mike Rhodes'/Microscript as the gold standard) to get placement, cost and conversion detail inside the campaign. Note that Google is rolling out some equivalent transparency, but the source says it is not yet close.
Audit landing pages and placements Performance Max is serving to; if you see irrelevant placements, exclude them and turn off automations you never opted into.
Exclude branded terms inside the Performance Max account so brand conversions are not counted as Performance Max results.
When you cannot control CPC, decide whether the achieved CPC is sustainable at your cost-to-LTV ratio — the source argues that if the economics hold, CPC alone is not the metric to monitor.

Judge launch success weekly: if CPCs remain outside what your margins can sustain even with correct setup, the source's conclusion is that this channel/strategy may simply not be viable for that product and competition level.
Apply the same discipline to unit economics as for other platforms: the platform delivers conversions at a market CPA, and the question is whether your business can hold that CPA.
caveats: Reduced control is inherent to Performance Max bidding; you cannot set a manual max CPC.
Attribution overlap with other channels means platform-reported ROAS is usually optimistic.
Script tools and third-party features change; verify the current interface before implementing.
The 'if CPC is sustainable, don't worry about it' framing is the presenter's economics-based opinion; it still requires monitoring CPA against margin.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Audience Signals and Conversion Data Are the Real Performance Max Inputs
cards.summary: Supply customer lists, in-market and custom-intent audiences plus clean conversion tracking so Performance Max can start without a learning plateau.
cards.use_when: Launching a Performance Max campaign from a cold start or improving an underperforming one by changing its inputs.
steps: Verify account-level conversion tracking is accurate before launch: exactly one primary purchase conversion action, tied to your campaign goal, firing via the Google & YouTube app or Google tag.
Upload your customer list and, if allowed, in-market audiences that historically work.
Build custom-intent audiences from high-intent keywords, competitor brand names, specific sites and trigger behaviours relevant to your category.
Include the same audiences as signals even when running feed-only broad campaigns; Performance Max still needs an explicit definition of who your buyer is and is not.
Use exclusions to define who not to reach (existing customers, irrelevant audiences) alongside positive signals.
Expect Performance Max to find the right users eventually, but use strong signals to launch cold from scratch without a long ramp.
caveats: The source still relies on third-party reporting for new-customer measurement rather than the account-level 'customer acquisition' bidding option, which he never enables.
Signal quality depends on available data; a small store may not have enough customer list or conversion volume for full audience-building.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Use Search Terms and Landing Page Audits to Fix Google Ads Waste
cards.summary: Regularly review search terms and landing pages to remove non-converting queries and unreviewed placements that drain budget.
cards.use_when: Running weekly/monthly maintenance on Google search, shopping or Performance Max campaigns.
steps: Pull the search terms report and sort by conversions and conversion value.
Remove terms that receive clicks but no conversions, and promote converting broad terms to exact match so budget concentrates on proven queries.
Check whether your best-converting queries are being served by a generic landing page; if so, build a page congruent with that query and change the keyword's final URL.
In Performance Max, audit which landing pages placements are sending traffic to and exclude placements that would never convert.

Remember that the campaign build is only half the job: for shopping campaigns, most ongoing optimization happens in Google Merchant Center, so keep the feed updated or you will see higher cost, lower visibility and reduced click share.
Re-check audience exclusions (especially existing customers) so spend is reserved for net-new demand.
caveats: Search-term data requires statistical significance; a few clicks with no conversions is not conclusive proof that a term should be killed.
For search, keyword-level final URL changes interact with ad-level URLs; verify which URL the system is actually using in the current interface.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Performance Max campaign setup with category-specific asset groups
cards.summary: Build PMAX campaigns by splitting asset groups by product category, feeding Google matched headlines/imagery/landing pages, and using search and audience signals as a conversion flywheel.
cards.use_when: Launching or restructuring a Performance Max campaign for a store with multiple product categories (e.g. dresses, shoes, hats).
steps: Create an asset group per major product category rather than dumping all products into one asset group. Use listing group > 'selection of products' and filter by item ID to isolate that category's SKUs.
Fill brand guidelines (business name, logo, colors, fonts) so ad assets stay visually congruent.

Max out copy assets: 15 headlines, 5 long headlines, 5 descriptions — shortfall limits Google's combinations. (Agency uses an internal GPT to draft these; third-party tools may change, verify current availability.)
Supply up to 20 images: product, lifestyle, in-use, high-production; horizontal, square and vertical aspect ratios. Rotate weak images out over time.

Point the final URL to the matching collection page per asset group so searchers land on the exact category. If you use the brand homepage as final URL, Google can auto-route products — the source says test which approach works for your brand.

Load search themes (up to 50): your highest-volume, highest-converting terms pulled from Keyword Planner, existing search/shopping campaigns and demand-gen data. Add audience signals: customer lists, website visitors, competitive keywords/sites.
Set location to 'presence' only, select your language, and set brand exclusions as a first pass (source warns it is not foolproof; brand terms often need manual exclusion after launch).
Set budget at least $50/day, ideally $100/day, of what you can sustain.
caveats: Source says brand exclusions in settings are not a complete fix — expect to manually exclude branded search terms later.
Source disables tablets and TV screens for PMAX; TV screens only for dedicated demand-gen campaigns.
Source keeps only 'images' asset optimization on and disables text and final URL expansion to stop irrelevant landing-page text, sizing charts and support pages being pulled in.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Daily PMAX search-term and auction-insight hygiene
cards.summary: Review PMAX search-term insights every day to exclude irrelevant queries, catch branded leakage, and harvest new profitable keywords for search campaigns.
cards.use_when: Daily check on a running Performance Max campaign to protect budget and reallocate targeting.
steps: Open the PMAX campaign > Insights and reports. Review search terms that triggered the ad over the last 7 and 28 days.
Flag and exclude irrelevant search terms directly inside PMAX to stop wasted spend. The source frames this as building a 'firewall' around the campaign.
Watch for branded conversions appearing in PMAX search terms — brand is supposed to be excluded; if branded terms show up, exclude them immediately through the additional brand-exclusion process.
Read cost per conversion and CTR by search term; treat rising costs or falling CTR as a signal that ad assets need refreshing.
Harvest terms converting in PMAX but not covered by your search campaigns as candidates for dedicated search campaigns.
Check auction insights (impression share on Search and Shopping, last 28 days) to see who you are competing against.
Use audience insights to feed what is working back into demand-gen campaigns and to see which audiences respond to which assets.
caveats: This is described as the source's only required daily PMAX task; everything else is weekly or monthly.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Weekly PMAX product-level spend and SKU exclusion
cards.summary: Inspect which products actually receive PMAX budget weekly and exclude poor-performing or out-of-stock SKUs to protect efficiency.
cards.use_when: Weekly budget review for a Performance Max campaign with multiple products or categories.
steps: In the PMAX campaign, open the 'Products' view to see spend and performance at product level.
Confirm budget flows to best sellers and highest-margin products rather than defaulting to whatever Google picks.
Identify products that consume spend without converting, and products with weak CTR dragging the asset group down.
Exclude poor performers: Campaigns > Asset groups > View listing groups > exclude the specific products.
Keep excluded out-of-stock product pages out of PMAX until inventory returns — source lists removing out-of-stock URLs as part of exclusion hygiene.
Re-include a SKU only when you have inventory and want to test it again.
caveats: With a single-product brand the product-level view is trivial; the value appears when multiple products sit inside listing groups.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Weekly asset and landing-page exclusions in PMAX
cards.summary: Refresh low-performing ad assets weekly and exclude non-converting URLs from final URL expansion to keep spend on sales pages.
cards.use_when: Weekly creative and traffic-routing review inside a live Performance Max campaign.
steps: Campaigns > Asset groups > View asset details to see conversion data, clicks, CTR and conversion rate per headline, long headline, description and image.
Replace assets that get little or no spend or weak conversion performance each week; Google prioritizes high-performing assets, so removing weak ones lifts overall results.

If automatically created assets or final URL expansion is on, exclude irrelevant URLs: blog posts, about pages, sizing/fitness charts, shipping info, contact and customer-service pages, and other support pages that kill purchase momentum.
Find which pages are currently being served: Report editor > 'when and where your ad shows' > PMAX campaigns placement; then add those unwanted URLs to exclusions.
Also check the landing-page report: Report editor > Ads and assets > Landing pages, and list pages with high spend but low conversion rate as first candidates for exclusion or replacement.
Use analytics to find high-bounce pages and add them to the exclusion list.
caveats: Source treats asset optimization text and final URL expansion as risky because they pull irrelevant page text; keep only image/layout asset optimization on.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Monthly PMAX search-theme and customer-list refresh
cards.summary: Once a month, replace non-converting search themes with proven converters and re-upload your first-party customer list to sharpen signal quality.
cards.use_when: Monthly optimization cycle for PMAX audience and keyword signals.
steps: Pull top converting search terms from your search campaigns, shopping campaigns and PMAX itself.
Open Campaigns > Asset groups > edit signals and replace search themes that are not converting with the proven converting terms.
Confirm themes align with high-performing queries rather than legacy guesses.
Export new customer emails and phone numbers from your CRM (Shopify, Klaviyo etc.) for the previous period.
In Google Ads, go to Audience manager > your data segments > plus icon > Customer list > upload new list.
Set a monthly reminder to repeat, or automate the upload, so Google can find users similar to your best customers and improve retargeting effectiveness.
caveats: Customer-list targeting works from first-party data quality — stale or partial lists weaken the audience signal.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Break-even CPA and ROAS as your scaling baseline
cards.summary: Calculate the maximum you can spend to acquire a customer (break-even CPA) and the corresponding break-even ROAS from your own unit economics before scaling any campaign.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether you can profitably increase Google Ads budget, bids or a new channel's spend.
