Instead, check for clear separation between branded and non-branded campaigns; brand keywords appearing in non-brand campaigns (or vice versa) is an immediate red flag to fix.

Look at your non-branded campaigns' ROAS against acquisition MER. If they do not correlate, investigate three possibilities: (a) they are genuinely outperforming and you may be underspending on Google, (b) they are mislabeled — pulling brand or bottom-of-funnel traffic driven from other channels, or (c) there is a setup/attribution problem.
Only after ruling out (a) and (b) should you conclude it is a setup issue.
caveats: Google's attribution defaults and reports change; verify current settings in the interface.
Bottom-of-funnel and cross-channel halo effects make Google ROAS misreadings common in the source's experience.
cards.source_name: How We Audit 8 and 9 Figure Ad Accounts (Full Process).docx

cards.title: Isolate a test to resolve attribution ambiguity
cards.summary: When correlation between platform ROAS and business MER stays unresolved, run a controlled incrementality test instead of guessing.
cards.use_when: You cannot tell whether a platform (Meta, Google, TikTok) is genuinely driving incremental new-customer revenue.
steps: Once you have compared platform ROAS to acquisition MER and attribution-setting changes still do not reconcile them, do not keep spending on an assumption — design a test.
For eight- and nine-figure brands, the source uses causal geo-lift experiments, typically run over about 25 days, to validate a platform's incrementality.
For brand-spend incrementality, use a clustering algorithm to pull brand spend from selected states and measure the effect, if the business believes brand is incremental.
Write clear parameters before launching so the result is readable; the output should either confirm performance or confirm a setup problem.
caveats: ~25 days is the source's typical duration, not a fixed rule.
Geo tests require sufficient volume; the source frames this as an eight/nine-figure technique.
cards.source_name: How We Audit 8 and 9 Figure Ad Accounts (Full Process).docx

cards.title: Evaluate retention to set CAC targets
cards.summary: Benchmark gross-profit retention curves by day 90, 180, and 365 to decide how much first-purchase CAC you can tolerate.
cards.use_when: You are setting acquisition budget targets and need to know whether high first-order CAC is justified by repeat purchasing.
steps: Build a cohort analysis at gross profit level over time.
Examine the percentage growth in gross profit at day 90, day 180, and day 365.
Compare your curve against portfolio averages for comparable brands/categories — the source contrasts e.g. fashion brands against each other.

Use the result to adjust CAC tolerance: strong retention means a higher acceptable CAC and lower first-purchase GP-to-CAC requirement; poor retention means first purchase must be highly profitable because people do not buy again.
Feed the adjusted tolerance back into your new-customer KPI targets.
caveats: Pulling these numbers is described as complicated; the source does not give universal growth benchmarks in this video.
Comparisons are to the source's client-portfolio averages, which are category-dependent.
cards.source_name: How We Audit 8 and 9 Figure Ad Accounts (Full Process).docx

cards.title: One cold campaign until business complexity forces a split
cards.summary: Start account structure from a single cold campaign and require a defendable purpose for every additional campaign.
cards.use_when: You are restructuring a Meta or Google ad account or reviewing whether campaign count is inflated.
steps: Ask: how many campaigns exist, and what is the defendable purpose of each one? Write each purpose into a spreadsheet column next to the campaign.
Error-check each campaign against its stated purpose (exclusions, settings, creative) as you go.

Cut any campaign you cannot defend with a clear commercial argument and consolidate; the source says this is common even in accounts spending $1M–$5M/month, and consolidation usually improves performance.
Do not add complexity for spend's sake — the source says complexity is required by business complexity, not budget size.

Legitimate causes of fragmentation include multiple countries/sub-brands/regions where you want to shift budget selectively (e.g., Australia vs New Zealand), or a fast-turning product portfolio where you need to pull budget on one category (e.g., dresses) and read results quickly.
If your agency cannot articulate why each campaign exists, treat that as a reason to consolidate.
caveats: This is the source's operating thesis for their managed accounts, not an industry rule.
Meta 'campaign count' heuristics change with platform behavior; validate against current performance.
cards.source_name: How We Audit 8 and 9 Figure Ad Accounts (Full Process).docx

cards.title: Check frequency across new, engaged, and existing audiences
cards.summary: Use 30-day frequency on new/engaged/existing segments to find overspend and weak top-of-funnel content.
cards.use_when: You are diagnosing audience-segment budget distribution or diagnosing creative fatigue in your Meta account.
steps: Split budget analysis by three segments: new, engaged, and existing — the source says look at frequency, not percentage split, across these.
If 30-day frequency on existing is extreme (source example: 30), you are overspending on existing customers and should cut that spend.
If frequency on engaged is high (source example: 14), you have too much middle-of-funnel creative and should reduce it in favor of more top-of-funnel assets.
Treat high engaged frequency as a symptom of content that is not top-of-funnel enough, or of existing-customer spend bleeding into all campaigns instead of being controlled in a dedicated campaign.
Fix by launching more genuinely top-of-funnel assets and containing existing-customer spend to one dedicated campaign.
caveats: The 30 and 14 figures are illustrative source examples, not universal thresholds.
Ideal frequency varies by category and offer; do not treat a single frequency number as a target without context.
cards.source_name: How We Audit 8 and 9 Figure Ad Accounts (Full Process).docx

cards.title: Standardize on 7-day click plus 1-day engaged view
cards.summary: Adopt a single tight attribution setting across the account and keep it consistent.
cards.use_when: You are configuring Meta attribution settings or auditing whether settings are inconsistent across campaigns.
steps: Check whether attribution settings are consistent across all campaigns; inconsistency changes reported ROAS between campaigns and muddies comparisons.
Choose a tighter setting that correlates better with your P&L; the source's go-to is 7-day click plus 1-day engaged view.

Note the source's explanation for including engaged views: Meta changed the definition roughly three months before the video so that likes/comments/shares and 5-second views are no longer counted in 7-day click, so 7-day click plus 1-day engaged view is roughly equivalent to the previously preferred 7-day click.
Apply the same attribution setting everywhere, then use attribution-setting breakdowns when judging performance (see reconcile-platform-roas card).
caveats: The specific definition change and closure equivalence is time-sensitive; verify current Meta documentation.
A 'tighter' setting is a business-fit choice, not universally optimal — the source notes it correlates better with their P&L.
cards.source_name: How We Audit 8 and 9 Figure Ad Accounts (Full Process).docx

cards.title: Audit campaign naming against actual settings and creative
cards.summary: Confirm that campaign/adset naming matches the targeting, objective, and creative actually running underneath.
cards.use_when: You are doing a housekeeping pass or suspect high-ROAS 'cold' campaigns are mislabeled warm or existing-customer campaigns.
steps: For each campaign/adset, compare the name to the actual audience definition, placement, objective, and the ads beneath it.

Flag mismatches: source notes a campaign labeled 'cold top of funnel' frequently turns out to target existing customers and serve bottom-of-funnel assets, making its ROAS look great when it is not actually acquiring cold customers.

If names use awareness stages (e.g., 'problem aware'), verify the ads actually match that stage (a 'problem aware' adset running a bunch of solution-aware ads is a defect even if the name looks competent).
Treat naming mismatch as a diagnosis gap: the account is claiming something the traffic and creative are not delivering.
caveats: Naming conventions vary; the criterion is whether the label accurately describes the audience and creative, not a specific label format.
cards.source_name: How We Audit 8 and 9 Figure Ad Accounts (Full Process).docx

cards.title: Common Meta settings errors worth fixing
cards.summary: A short list of concrete Meta account errors: undefined segments, App Rewards placements, legacy lookalike/interest targeting on purchase objectives, missing existing-customer exclusions.
cards.use_when: You are doing a settings-and-targeting error sweep on a Meta account during a structure audit.
steps: Set definitions on new, engaged, and existing audiences rather than leaving them undefined.
Kill App Rewards placements — the source says they have never seen an App Rewards placement drive a single purchase, and local/store-driving engaged-view campaigns bleed into this placement.

Do not use legacy targeting methods (lookalikes, interest targeting) on purchase objectives for ecommerce; the source would not use them for 99% of accounts, reserving them for specific non-purchase cases.
Verify existing customers are actually excluded from cold campaigns.
Confirm naming matches settings and creative (see separate card).
caveats: '99% of accounts' and the no-purchases-from-App-Rewards claim are the source's stated opinions/experience, not measured benchmarks.
Placement options and defaults change over time; verify in the current ads manager.
cards.source_name: How We Audit 8 and 9 Figure Ad Accounts (Full Process).docx

cards.title: Google-specific audit checks: search terms, feed, currency
cards.summary: Audit Google by checking brand leakage in cold campaigns, Merchant Center feed completeness, and multi-currency feed setup.
cards.use_when: You are auditing Google Ads and Google Merchant Center ahead of a seasonal peak or a restructure.
steps: Open each cold campaign, go to search terms, and verify branded terms are not pulling through into cold campaigns.
Check the Google Merchant Center feed: optimize titles, fill in all relevant feed variables, and eliminate warnings and errors.

If selling across multiple countries, use a multi-currency feed — the source warns that running everything through a single currency triggers auto-conversion and adds tax as it presents in Shopping, hurting performance.
Then investigate the halo effect: Google often sits bottom-of-funnel, so check whether cold search-term demand is genuinely converting cold traffic.

If ROAS on non-brand campaigns does not correlate with acquisition MER after these checks, the source usually proposes an incrementality test for Google — but only when they suspect a halo effect or need rigorous validation.
caveats: The source notes Google can be a strong new-customer channel — one of their own brands was Google-only and reached a seven-figure run rate around 2019–2020 — so Google is not inherently bottom-of-funnel.
Feed and interface details change; verify current GMC and Google Ads UI.
cards.source_name: How We Audit 8 and 9 Figure Ad Accounts (Full Process).docx

cards.title: Creative volume rule: one new ad per $1,000 of monthly spend
cards.summary: Size your creative production requirement by anchoring new ads per month to monthly ad spend.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether creative volume is the bottleneck or setting a production target for your creative team or agency.
steps: Divide monthly ad spend by $1,000 to get a baseline monthly new-ad target (source example: $100k/month implies ~100 new ads per month).
Treat this as a rough rule of thumb, not a linear law — the source says at $1–3M/month you likely do not need 3,000 assets, and there are diminishing returns to raw creative volume at large scale.

If you need a more precise target, use one of two models: (a) a churn model — monthly churn rate of winners implies a replacement rate; combine with hit rate to back into volume; or (b) average winner spend and revenue generation — if an average winner generates $20k, use that and your win rate to back-propagate to volume.
If your actual output is far below the rule-of-thumb target, treat creative volume as a likely bottleneck.
caveats: $1,000/ad is explicitly a simplification; the source's real models are described as complicated.
Churn-model inputs (winner churn, hit rate, average winner revenue) are business-specific and must come from your own account.
cards.source_name: How We Audit 8 and 9 Figure Ad Accounts (Full Process).docx

cards.title: Separate volume, diversity, and quality as the creative bottleneck
cards.summary: Creative bottlenecks are one of exactly three: insufficient volume, insufficient concept diversity, or insufficient quality.
cards.use_when: You are diagnosing why creative performance has plateaued and need to pick the right fix.
steps: First check volume against your spend-based target (see the $1,000/new-ad card); if output is far off, that is the bottleneck.
If volume is fine, check diversity — specifically concept diversification, not format diversification (see concept-diversity card).

If both volume and diversity are adequate, assess quality by reading the actual scripts and content, judging angles, personas, scripting, talent, and offer. This is the hardest to systematize and requires direct-response marketing judgment; the source recommends looking at the ads directly and rescripting/reshooting what is weak.
Assign exactly one bottleneck at a time — the source emphasizes you only have one creative bottleneck at any moment; pick it and fix it before moving on.
caveats: Quality has no SOP in the source — it requires domain judgment and reviewing actual creative.
You may end up with a different bottleneck than the source would call it if your spend model differs.
cards.source_name: How We Audit 8 and 9 Figure Ad Accounts (Full Process).docx

cards.title: Diversify concepts, not just formats
cards.summary: Measure creative diversity by angle/offer/persona concept coverage rather than by mix of UGC, statics, and other formats.
cards.use_when: You are planning creative strategy for a scaling account or diagnosing why a single winning ad fatigues.
steps: Define concepts as a combination of angle, offer, and persona — not format (video vs static vs UGC). The source says people over-index on format diversity and under-index on concept diversity.

Illustration: a creatine brand spending $200k/month may be launching 200 ads/month but if all spend sits behind one concept (e.g., men 25–45, gym-performance angle, single bundle offer), it is not diverse — it is one concept being fatigued into the ground.

Set concept targets by spend band: sub-$100k/month, 1–3 concepts is fine; $100k–$500k/month, aim for around 2 winning concepts with 2–6 in testing; $500k+/month, aim for 3+ concepts and 4–5 core working funnels, unless you are targeting the US/worldwide where two scalable concepts can carry a lot of spend.
Sector-specific interpretation: in fashion, diverse concepts typically mean different products/categories; in CPG, typically different reframes of the same product.
If your concept coverage is far below the band for your spend, treat diversity as the creative bottleneck.
caveats: Concept-count targets are source heuristics, not verified benchmarks, and depend on market size and breadth.
Some format diversity is still needed (e.g., not running only statics); the point is to not over-index on format.
cards.source_name: How We Audit 8 and 9 Figure Ad Accounts (Full Process).docx

cards.title: Don't over-allocate to dynamic product ads
cards.summary: Keep DPAs as a small share of spend because they are bottom-of-funnel and rarely incremental.
cards.use_when: You are rebalancing spend inside a Meta account where DPAs are consuming the majority of budget.
steps: Check what percentage of account spend is in dynamic product ads.
If a large share (source flags accounts sitting near 70% of spend in DPAs), rebalance — DPAs are bottom of funnel and, in the source's view, not incremental.
Acknowledge DPAs can spend on cold and perform 'okay' there, but do not treat that as justification for the dominant share.
Move reallocated budget into diversified cold campaigns with concept-level creative.
caveats: '70%' and 'not incremental' are the source's observations/opinions, not measured facts across all accounts.
DPA performance varies by category and catalog size; validate with your own incrementality read.
cards.source_name: How We Audit 8 and 9 Figure Ad Accounts (Full Process).docx

cards.title: Analyze winners to replicate the source of success
cards.summary: When an ad wins, diagnose which variable caused the win and consciously replicate that variable.
cards.use_when: You have recently found a winning creative and are deciding whether to iterate on it or chase entirely new ideas.
steps: Do not abandon a winner to search for whatever comes next — the source says some accounts find a winner and never replicate on it.
Decompose the winner across variables: persona, angle, offer, format, script structure, influencer/talent, and any other material difference.
Identify which variable drove the result (the source asks explicitly: was it the persona, the angle, the format, the scripting, the influencer or the talent?).
Brief the creative team to produce variations that hold the winning variable constant and vary the rest, to validate and extend the win.
Feed this back into the creative roadmap so winners inform the next production cycle.
caveats: Attribution of a win to a single variable is inherently uncertain; treat it as a hypothesis to test in the next round.
Winners decay over time — this is about reinforcement, not indefinite reuse.
cards.source_name: How We Audit 8 and 9 Figure Ad Accounts (Full Process).docx

cards.title: Run creative production as a system with a feedback loop
cards.summary: Replace ad-hoc creative production with a continuous system that ingests performance feedback.
cards.use_when: You are setting up or reviewing your creative roadmap and production cadence against a scale target.
steps: Ask whether creative is shot reactively when ads are needed, or produced continuously against a roadmap.
If ad hoc, build a consistent production system that puts a high volume of assets into the account on an ongoing basis.
Include a feedback loop: performance data from live creative should feed back into the briefing and production process.
Set expected volume using the spend-based rule or a churn/average-winner model, and check whether production capacity genuinely matches it.
Align internal creative team skills or agency selection to the required volume and quality standard; the source notes this may require upskilling the team or changing creative agencies.
caveats: Source does not prescribe a specific production tool or headcount — the requirement is output against volume and quality targets.
Volume targets should be revisited as spend scales, per the diminishing-returns caveat.
cards.source_name: How We Audit 8 and 9 Figure Ad Accounts (Full Process).docx

cards.title: Drill down from business metrics to the ad that's the bottleneck
cards.summary: Trace a constraint top-down from business revenue to platform, campaign, adset, and ad to locate the actual driver.
cards.use_when: You have identified a top-level problem (e.g., rising CAC) and need to find where in the account it lives.
steps: Start at the top with business numbers: Shopify revenue, new customer revenue, and CAC.
Identify the level of the problem (e.g., CAC issue), then go into Meta and Google and determine which platform.
Within the failing platform, go into campaigns, then adsets, then ads, until you reach the element holding back performance.
Confirm the diagnosis with data-integrity checks (platform ROAS versus acquisition MER) before making structural decisions.
Sequence the fixes: generally data integrity first, then account structure, then creative — the source notes creative often has the highest impact but the longest fix time.
caveats: Order of fixes is a source heuristic, not a universal law; the appropriate sequence can vary with business context.
If your metrics are not trustworthy, do not attempt to diagnose deeper levels until the data-integrity layer is fixed.
cards.source_name: How We Audit 8 and 9 Figure Ad Accounts (Full Process).docx

cards.title: Fix data integrity before creative or account structure
cards.summary: If platform metrics do not correlate with business KPIs, treat that as the top-priority bottleneck before anything else.
cards.use_when: You are sequencing a paid-media turnaround and deciding what to fix first.
steps: Check whether a large gap exists between acquisition MER and platform-attributed ROAS.

If the gap is large and unresolved by attribution-setting changes, make data integrity the number-one bottleneck — the source's rationale is that you cannot do valid creative analysis or account structuring on metrics that are not causally tied to business outcomes.
Complete the data-integrity work first (attribution settings, breakdown-based reporting, fixed P&L and first-time P&L).
Then fix account structure, which the source describes as a relatively fast, high-leverage fix (consolidating campaigns, removing bleed into existing customers, fixing settings errors).
Then move into creative, which the source treats as high-impact but slow to fix because it requires structural changes to production capability.
caveats: This ordering is a source opinion based on their client portfolio, not an empirical sequence validated across all businesses.
Some businesses with accurate data may benefit from starting on creative instead.
cards.source_name: How We Audit 8 and 9 Figure Ad Accounts (Full Process).docx

cards.title: Ad account audit order: data → structure → creative
cards.summary: A prioritization sequence for auditing underperforming paid ad accounts: fix data integrity first, then account structure, then creative.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing a declining or flat paid acquisition program (Meta/Google) and deciding which fix to tackle first this quarter.
steps: Start with data integrity: verify tracking, pixel/events, attribution windows and reporting so decisions rest on trustworthy numbers. The source treats this as the highest commercial-impact item and the foundation for everything downstream.
Second, review account structure: campaign/ad set organization, budget allocation, consolidation vs fragmentation — the source places this as the number-two priority by commercial impact.
Third, move to creative: only once the data and structure are sound does creative testing become a reliable lever.

Note the source's distinction: by commercial impact the ranking is data, account structure, creative — but by time-to-implement the practical order is often data first, then account structure, then creative.
Apply the sequence as a recovery roadmap when a brand is going sideways or declining, rather than jumping straight to new creative.
caveats: This ordering is the presenter's framework/opinion, not a universal law; some accounts with obviously broken creative may warrant a different entry point.
The source describes its audit process at a high level in this section and does not detail the specific checks inside each phase.
cards.source_name: How We Audit 8 and 9 Figure Ad Accounts (Full Process).docx

cards.title: Write ads as salesmanship in print
cards.summary: Claude Hopkins' core test: every ad, headline, and creative decision should be judged by whether it would help a live salesperson close the sale to one prospect standing in front of him.
cards.use_when: Writing or reviewing any acquisition creative — Meta/TikTok ad, product page hero, landing page, or email subject line — and you need a single test to cut indecision.
steps: Before finalizing a creative, ask: 'Would this help a salesman sell the goods if I met the buyer in person?' If the line only exists to be clever or short, cut it.
Do not shorten copy just because people 'read very little.' Hopkins's point: you would never hand a real prospect to a salesman and cap him at 10 words. Length is not the constraint — relevance is.

Because advertising 'may appeal to thousands while the salesman will talk to one,' a mediocre ad damages every prospect at once, whereas a mediocre salesman only wastes one conversation. Apply the higher bar to the ad.

Rewrite any line that would embarrass a salesperson saying it face-to-face — especially boasts, brand commands, and 'avoid imitations' style warnings, which Hopkins says indicate a motive buyers cannot sympathize with.
Check the final creative against one question: does every sentence increase good impression and speak to the prospect's desire, not the advertiser's pride?
caveats: This is Hopkins's framework from early-1900s direct-response advertising; the 'salesman' test is a reasoning tool, not a measured conversion benchmark.
Longer copy is not automatically better — the test is relevance and sales-helpfulness, not word count.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

cards.title: Sell service, not your brand
cards.summary: Hopkins argues the two greatest faults in advertising are boasts and selfishness; replace 'buy my brand' appeals with a clearly unselfish offer of service to the customer.
cards.use_when: Drafting ad copy or landing page hero sections where the instinct is to lead with the brand name, product features, or company achievements.
steps: Identify every self-referential line in the creative — company history, plant size, awards, 'we're the best' claims — and tag each as a boast to be removed or reframed.
Rewrite each as the customer benefit that follows from it. The size of your plant, for example, becomes a reason the buyer gets faster shipping or lower risk.

Make the salesperson's plea match Hopkins's model: 'I was selling service... the advantage to myself was covered up in my efforts to please him.' The buyer should feel you are solving their problem, not asking a favor.

Apply the same to creative in competitive categories: Hopkins says you cannot enter a well-occupied field on a plain 'buy my brand' appeal, because it is repugnant. Offer exceptional service to induce switching from a favorite brand.

Re-audit existing top-of-funnel ads monthly. Hopkins's observation is that most advertisers merely 'cry a name' and their evident desire is selfish advantage — such advertising may pay somewhat but never as well as apparent unselfishness.
caveats: Hopkins presents this as a general principle ('argue for your own advantage and people will resist to the limit'), not a tested conversion lift.
Service framing still needs a real differentiator or specific promise; empty service language without substance is just another kind of vacancy.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

cards.title: Advertise to one person, not the masses
cards.summary: Treat every inquirer as an individual prospect who walked into a store, with a specific need — not as a mass to be sent the same generic catalog or ad.
cards.use_when: Setting up email capture, retargeting sequences, PDP recommendations, or paid traffic flows where all visitors currently get the same generic response.
steps: Segment the entry point by expressed intent. Hopkins's example: a woman writing about a sewing machine should receive the sewing-machine catalog with every style and price, not the full company catalog sent to all inquiries alike.

Add social proof local to the prospect. Hopkins sent names of every buyer in the inquirer's town and asked her to go see the machine and talk to owners. For ecommerce, substitute nearby reviews, UGC, or a demo they can inspect in person.
Treat 'people in the mass' as a mistake. Hopkins: 'We must get down to individuals. We must treat people in advertising as we treat them in person.'
Apply this to retargeting and email: an ad creative that speaks to the searched category won't work for a cold, broad audience — match the creative to the individual's demonstrated desire.
Build the flow so a person who showed one specific intent gets one specific, complete answer (product, price, proof) rather than being routed to everything you sell.
caveats: Hopkins describes this principle from letter-inquiry handling, not digital funnels; the metaphor is the transferable part, not the mechanics.
Personalizing by intent requires enough traffic or data per segment; below that, use one clear offer rather than leaking budget across thin segments.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

cards.title: Tell the pains you take (the Schlitz story)
cards.summary: Reveal the ordinary manufacturing and quality steps you take, even if competitors do the same, because nobody has told the story in print and it creates perceived distinction.
cards.use_when: Writing a product page, brand story section, or ad angle for a commodity-like product where you believe 'everyone does this, so it's not a differentiator.'
steps: Do first-hand research at the source of production — visit the facility, interview the operators, ask why every step exists. Hopkins saw plate-glass rooms, white wood-pulp filters, pipes cleaned twice daily, bottles cleaned four times by machinery, 4,000-ft artisan wells, six-month aging, and a mother yeast developed by 1,200 experiments.
Capture each step's purpose, not just its existence. For ecommerce, that could be inspection steps, material sourcing, QA thresholds, or fulfillment processes.

Resist the founder's reflex that it's just ordinary. Hopkins's clients said 'the processes we use are just the same as others' — his answer: 'Others have never told this story... It will startle everyone in print.'
Write the process into the PDP or ad as a purity/quality narrative with concrete numbers and specifics, giving your claim a visible meaning instead of merely repeating 'pure' or 'premium'.

Test this against your current PDP claims: 'the maker is too close to his product. He sees in his methods only the ordinary.' The steps you find boring are exactly what a buyer has never seen explained.
caveats: Schlitz allegedly went from fifth to neck-and-neck with first after the campaign — a case-study result attributed to the source, not a promised outcome.
The technique works only if the claimed process is true and verifiable; inventing hidden steps is not the method, and it can be easily exposed.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

cards.title: Sell painkillers, not prevention
cards.summary: Prevention and disaster-avoidance are weak appeals; Hopkins found people will do anything to cure a trouble but little to prevent it, so advertise rewards, beauty, happiness, and desirable outcomes.
cards.use_when: Choosing the angle for health, wellness, supplement, dental, financial, or maintenance-focused products where the default pitch is risk prevention.
steps: Write both angles for the same product: the prevention angle ('use this so your teeth don't decay') and the reward angle ('use this to become more attractive, happier, more cheerful').

Hopkins's Pepso dent decision: he resolved to advertise the toothpaste as a creator of beauty rather than a preventative. Apply the same shift to skincare, supplements, supplements-for-prevention, or device warranties.
Never picture the afflicted in creative. Hopkins says he never referred to disasters and every illustration he used showed attractive people. Shoot and select creators accordingly.
Frame recurring-purchase products around the positive identity the customer attains, not the loss they avoid, because that is what drives the buying psychology.

Use the appeal audit across the whole campaign: Hopkins says every campaign depends on its psychology and success is determined by right or wrong appeal — so pick one dominant psychological appeal and make all ad variants consistent with it before testing.
caveats: Hopkins made a reported million dollars on Pepso dent from this psychological choice — a dramatic historical case, not a benchmark for modern conversion rates.
Reward positioning must still be honest and compliant; beauty/outcome claims in regulated categories (supplements, health) may need legal review.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

cards.title: Sample the right way: require an effort
cards.summary: Free samples and demos work only when the user requests them or earns them; promiscuous sampling destroys perceived value, so gate samples behind an action.
cards.use_when: Designing lead magnets, free-trial offers, sample distribution, or PR-box mailers — deciding whether to send product free or require an opt-in.
steps: Do not propend samples on people who didn't ask. Hopkins: 'I have never found that it paid to give samples to people who do not request it... Products handed out without asking lose respect.'
Gate the sample behind a small action — filling out a request form, giving an email, completing a quiz. 'It is different when you force people to make an effort.'
Sequence it: 'We must arouse interest in our product before it has value to anybody.' Use the ad or PDP to create desire first, then offer the demo/sample as the response.

Use the demonstration principle the sample represents. Hopkins sold about 1 in 10 women when merely talking about his mother's silver polish, but nearly all when he could get inside the house and demonstrate it — 'a good product is its own best salesman.'
For ecommerce, replicate the demonstration with sampling programs, money-back guarantees, or in-home trials that require an explicit claim, then let the product do the selling.
caveats: Hopkins calls promiscuous sampling a 'very bad plan' from his direct-selling era; the transferable rule is that perceived value depends on an effort threshold, not on refusing all free sampling.
Gating raises friction — measure both claim rate and downstream conversion/repeat purchase rather than assuming fewer, better leads pay off.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

cards.title: Give your brand a human personality
cards.summary: People love people more than corporations; giving your product or brand a named, personal spokesperson makes the creation famous along with the person.
cards.use_when: Building brand identity, creator-led content, founder-led marketing, or repositioning a faceless ecommerce brand in categories where competitors are all 'soulless corporations.'
steps: Decide whether the founder, a named expert, or a recurring persona will front the brand. Hopkins used a persona called Professor Anderson with an actual person behind it and said he did this wherever possible.

Make the person the face and voice of the advertising — not a stock model or a logo — because 'personalities appeal while soulless corporations do not. Make a man famous, and you make his creation famous.'

Have the person talk about the product's accomplishments and its making, since 'all of us love to study men and their accomplishments.' For ecommerce, this can be founder storytelling on the PDP, creator-style ad creative, or an expert answering objections on video.
Keep the persona consistent across channels so the human becomes a recognizable asset, consistent with the 'stick to what works' rule for campaigns.
Apply it especially where the founder is uniquely qualified: the person who built the product knows every in and out and is the best advocate for why customers should buy.
caveats: The Professor Anderson example is historical; the transferable claim is that personality aids persuasion, not that every brand needs a fictional persona.
Invented authority personas can breach modern ad-platform policies and consumer trust if they misrepresent expertise — prefer a real named person.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

cards.title: Test, never assume your own taste predicts demand
cards.summary: Hopkins warns that judging products by personal preference has cost the advertising industry fortunes — the successes he doubted sold like crazy, so submit everything to the court of public opinion through testing.
cards.use_when: Deciding what products, creatives, or angles to launch or kill when you have a personal gut reaction for or against them.
steps: Separate your taste from the market's. Hopkins: 'We must never judge humanity by ourselves. The things we want, the things we like may appeal to a small minority.'
He explicitly says product selection goes wrong when operators reject products as 'stupid' that then sell hugely because the audience is billions of people, not the operator.

Write down your prediction before launching, then compare against actual performance — the practice mirrors Hopkins making mistakes in a small way and learning from each (he says he made no mistake twice).
Run small, cheap tests first rather than betting the campaign on a personal conviction, so the market rather than the operator adjudicates.
Record what worked and re-use it; Hopkins links this habit to developing enduring advertising principles, in contrast to repeatedly changing your mind based on your own impression of the creative.
caveats: Hopkins's argument is specifically against relying on personal preference and for empirical testing; it is not a formula for how many tests or what sample size to run.
Testing does not mean ignoring strategy or brand constraints — it means the audience, not the founder, is the judge of appeal.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

cards.title: Stay close to the buyer and the money
cards.summary: Hopkins advises studying actual sellers (including canvassers and door-to-door salesmen) to learn what appeals work, and positioning your work near revenue-generating activity so you can capture a share of the value created.
cards.use_when: Doing customer research for ad angles, or negotiating roles, contracts, or agency compensation tied to advertising and sales performance.
steps: Study real sellers up close. Hopkins spent hours under torchlight listening to pitchmen and canvassers and said: 'Study salesmen, canvassers, and fakers if you want to know how to sell goods.' For ecommerce, this means watching sales calls, reading support tickets and chat logs, and interviewing repeat buyers — not just reading dashboards.
Watch for reactions, not just stated preferences: when you're close to the buyer, 'you can hear, you can see what they reject, you can see what appeal lights up their eyes.'
Document the specific phrases and objections that recur and test them as ad angles, since direct-response salespeople are the closest real-world laboratory for appeals that work.

On compensation, apply Hopkins's 'stay close to the money' principle: he moved from the expense side of a business to the sales-generating side, then negotiated a share of the sales he brought in (e.g., asking for a portion of the million dollars in toothpaste sales he generated).
Evidence value created and ask for a share of measured incremental value rather than flat fees disconnected from results.
caveats: 'Stay close to the money' is a career/business principle from Hopkins's autobiography, not a prescribed commission structure; deal terms vary by role and market.
'Fakers' in Hopkins's era includes deceptive pitchmen — study the mechanics of persuasion, not tactics that mislead buyers.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

cards.title: Stick with the ad that works (moving parade)
cards.summary: You notice your own ads far more than customers do; Hopkins warns against changing successful campaigns out of boredom and says the best way to win new customers is usually the way that won millions.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to refresh or replace a profitable creative, offer, or PDP hero because it 'feels stale' internally.
steps: Before changing a working ad, distinguish internal boredom from market fatigue. 'The advertising becomes monotonous to the men who read every ad… they always come to want something new,' but customers have not read every ad.

Use the framing: you are not advertising to a standing army, you are advertising to a moving parade — most of your audience is seeing the message for the first time, which is why repetition across a changing audience keeps working.
Set a decision rule for refreshing: change when measured performance degrades, not on a fixed internal schedule or subjective creative boredom.
If you must change, keep the winning core (appeal, claim, offer) intact and swap the execution shell (imagery, format, channel), so you preserve what won millions and only vary the wrapper.
Record which principles have endured for you the way Hopkins kept his — this turns one-off wins into reusable rules rather than restarting from scratch each cycle.
caveats: This is Hopkins's stated preference for continuity, echoed later by David Ogilvy; some modern platforms show genuine creative fatigue, so treat 'never change' as the source's bias, not an absolute — reconcile with your own retention curves.
A moving parade still implies reach and frequency are being bought repeatedly; if you only ever reach the same small audience, repeated exposure can fatigue.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

cards.title: Judge advertising by salesmanship and the customer's mind
cards.summary: Hopkins treats advertising as multiplied salesmanship whose success or failure is determined by whether the psychological appeal matches human nature — not by cleverness or personal taste.
cards.use_when: Choosing an appeal/angle before writing a campaign, or diagnosing why a campaign isn't converting despite decent execution.
steps: State the appeal in one sentence before writing: prevention, status/beauty, convenience, effort saved, time saved, etc. Hopkins says 'every advertising campaign depends on its psychology. Success or failure is determined by the right or wrong appeal.'

Check the appeal against what humans actually do: people 'do little to prevent' trouble but pursue rewards, happiness, beauty, and cheer — so test one dominant positive-outcome appeal before loading multiple appeals into one ad.
Apply the salesmanship standard to every executional question (length, tone, claims): 'Ask yourself, would this help a salesman sell the goods?' rather than following generic copywriting rules.

Because advertising is 'multiplied salesmanship,' the same mediocre message reaches your whole audience, so errors cost more than in person — raise the bar on the main promise before polishing anything else.

Use customer perspective as the final filter: no manufacturer should conduct his own advertising because he is too close to the factory and tells what he takes pride in rather than what the customer wants to know.
caveats: The 'right or wrong appeal' is a directional principle, not a guarantee; categories and audiences differ, and regulated categories constrain appeal choices.
Hopkins's own framework favors positive-outcome appeals; some products genuinely sell on risk-avoidance (insurance, security), so treat it as a starting hypothesis to test, not law.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

cards.title: Prove the product, don't just talk about it
cards.summary: A dramatic demonstration converts far better than any argument; Hopkins sold roughly one in ten women by talk but nearly all by demonstration, and carried that principle into every campaign.
cards.use_when: Designing acquisition creative, PDP media, or landing page proof sections that currently rely on claims instead of showing the product working.
steps: Identify what a live demonstration would look like: the silver-polish example is the literal product applied to the buyer's own problem in front of them. For ecommerce, this means demo video, before/after, side-by-side, or a trial the customer physically experiences.
Prefer showing to arguing. Hopkins: 'No argument in the world can ever compare with one dramatic demonstration.' Replace persuasive copy with a visual proof asset where possible.
Get the product into the buyer's hands when feasible, since 'a good product is its own best salesman.' This is the rationale behind trials, guarantees, and in-home tests.
Choose demo formats that face the particular objection the buyer has — show cleaning power, fit, durability, or result timeline — rather than a generic brand film.
Keep demo creative central on the PDP and in paid ads, not buried; if the product genuinely wins on demonstration, make it the lead, not a supporting detail.
caveats: The one-in-ten versus 'nearly all' figures are Hopkins's door-to-door experience, not an ecommerce benchmark.
Demos must be accurate to real product performance; an exaggerated demo creates post-purchase returns and review damage.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

cards.title: Capitalizing on insights: put your money where your copy is
cards.summary: Hopkins bought shares in the brand whose sales his advertising would lift, capturing the value he helped create — a model for tying compensation or investment to measurable performance you drive.
cards.use_when: Structuring performance-based deals, agency compensation, affiliate arrangements, or deciding how to bet on a product angle you believe will outperform.
steps: Apply the principle that 'the big salaries are paid to the salesmen... and to the men in the factory who reduce costs,' i.e., value accrues near revenue and profit creation — position your work and compensation close to that lever.
If you believe your creative will materially lift a brand's sales, negotiate a share of measured incremental value or performance-based terms rather than purely time-based fees.

Hopkins's Pepso dent example: he bought shares for $13,000 at the start of the project; the position paid him $200,000 in dividends and later sold for $500,000. Use this as an illustration of aligning upside with the results of your own work, not a promised return.
Build measurement into the deal up front — agree on what constitutes incremental sales attributable to advertising before the campaign begins.
For an operator running their own store, the analogous move is to reinvest in the channels and product angles with proven incremental lift instead of spreading budget evenly.
caveats: The Pepso dent numbers are a historical case study, not a benchmark; many campaigns don't produce that outcome and share-of-upside deals require trusted attribution.
Tying compensation to performance only works when sales lift can be reliably attributed — otherwise you are negotiating over an unmeasurable number.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

cards.title: Do the work in volume with focus
cards.summary: Hopkins attributes his success to exceptional hours and volume of practice, not exceptional ability: working two or three times as much produces two or three times the mistakes and successes, and you learn from both.
cards.use_when: Building a sustainable creative testing cadence or deciding how much output an in-house or agency ecommerce marketing function should produce.
steps: Increase the volume of finished work — ads written, creatives shipped, tests run — rather than endlessly perfecting one asset, because volume is what generates both mistakes and successes to learn from.
Treat mistakes as the tuition: Hopkins says he learned from each and 'made no mistake twice,' turning errors into an operating record of enduring principles.
Pair volume with a learning log so insights from tests persist beyond the individual campaign and inform the next one.

Hopkins worked nights and Sundays (rarely an evening free for 16 years) and calls business a game he plays; the transferable mechanic is sustained focused repetitions in one domain, not the literal hours and not a recommendation to burn out.

Direct the volume at one thing you can go deep in — Hopkins says those with singular focus derive insights others simply won't have; for ecommerce, pick the domain (e.g., landing pages or paid creative) and do many deliberate reps.
caveats: Hopkins himself writes 'I am not advising others to follow my example' on the extreme hours; treat the durable lesson as focused volume, not the workaholism.
Volume without measurement or learning produces churn, not improvement — you still need to record what worked.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

cards.title: Reframe advertising questions around the buyer's desires
cards.summary: Almost every ad question can be answered by asking what a good salesman would say if the individual prospect stood before him — starting with the prospect's expressed desires, not your product facts.
cards.use_when: Resolving copy, offer, or page-layout debates inside a team where opinions conflict and no test data yet exists.
steps: Identify the prospect's expressed desire first: for the sewing machine inquirer it was a sewing machine; for your store it may be a specific use case, budget, or occasion. 'Consider the person who stands before you with certain expressed desires.'
Answer the ad question in that person's terms: 'However big your business, get down to the units, for those units are all that make size.'

Cut lines that serve the brand's interests instead of the prospect's. Hopkins says 'argue anything for your own advantage and people will resist to the limit... seem unselfishly to consider your customer's desires and they will naturally flock to you.'

Test the creative against the standard 'Say only what you think a good salesman should say if that prospect stood before him' — this resolves disputes without waiting for an A/B test when budget or traffic is limited.
Use this as a fast internal filter before running the more expensive statistical test on the remaining, genuinely ambiguous options.
caveats: This is a judgment framework, not a substitute for measurement; where traffic allows, still validate against conversion data.
What the prospect 'wants to know' is inferred, not given — validate assumptions with support tickets, reviews, and sales conversations.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

cards.title: Don't let success in one area convince you you can run any
cards.summary: Hopkins observes men make money in one business and lose it in others because success breeds the belief that they are super-businessmen — past success is not transferable competence.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to expand your store into an unrelated product category, new market, or a different business, especially when an existing product line is performing well.
steps: Inventory the specific competencies your current success depends on — sourcing, creative, fulfilment, audience — and ask which of these actually transfer to the proposed expansion.

Treat the planned move as a new business, not an extension of a proven one: Hopkins says 'it is curious how we all desire to excel in something outside of our own province. This leads many men astray.'
If expanding categories or markets, allocate a small test budget and staff it with people who do have domain experience, rather than assuming the core team's proven playbook carries over.
Watch for the moment confidence substitutes for evidence — the pattern Hopkins names is that one success makes people feel qualified to run anything.
Keep the proven core investment protected while the new venture is unproven, since losses in the new area can drain cash generated by the successful one.
caveats: This is a cautionary pattern, not a rule against diversification; adjacent expansions that share competencies may transfer well.
The claim is Hopkins's observation about businesses of his era; modern operators should still evaluate with their own data.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

cards.title: Earn the role by demonstrating the work, not just applying
cards.summary: When Hopkins wanted a senior advertising job at a company with one of the largest budgets, he had dozens of people write testimonials, ran a daily newspaper column sharing his learning, and applied alongside the evidence — and won the role.
cards.use_when: Pitching a major retailer partnership, applying for an in-house leadership role, or winning a large client when you have no direct relationship and the competition is strong.
steps: Prepare proof of skill from third parties: Hopkins had dozens of people send letters vouching for his copywriting ability — for ecommerce, gather retailer logos, GMV case studies, or client statements.

Create a public body of work that the decision-maker will encounter: Hopkins wrote a daily newspaper column on advertising sharing everything he learned, so the hiring decision-maker saw his expertise repeatedly.
Do all the standard moves too — apply, call, try to meet — but treat those as the baseline, not the winning move, since the testimonials and column are what differentiated him.

Aim the pitch at the decision-maker's actual need, echoing Lasker's recruiting speech: acknowledge the best available copy still isn't good enough, then ask for exactly what's needed (e.g., 'give me three ads that will start the campaign').

Make the ask concrete and tied to a result, as Lasker did when offering any car on the street charged to him in exchange for three campaign-starting ads — pair a clear deliverable with a clear reward.
caveats: The job win is an anecdote from Hopkins's career, not a hiring guaranteed by this method.
The newspaper-column tactic relied on local print reach; adapt the 'public proof of work' to channels your target buyer actually sees.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

cards.title: Write every ad as one-to-one salesmanship
cards.summary: Judge ad copy by asking whether it would help a salesman close a half-sold prospect standing in front of you.
cards.use_when: Drafting or reviewing any paid ad, product page or email where the prospect has already clicked or shown interest.
steps: Assume your reader already raised their hand — the headline or creative image earned the click, so treat the following copy as a live conversation with a warm prospect rather than a broadcast to a crowd.
For each line, ask: 'Would I say this to a buyer standing in front of me right now?' If it is something you'd only say to a mass audience, rewrite it.

Do not cap length artificially by a word count — as the source argues, confining a salesman to a set number of words would be an unthinkable handicap. Let the copy run as long as it stays interesting and useful to that one person.
Do what a good salesman does with a half-sold prospect: give enough specific information to prompt action, without boasting or showing off.
End with the equivalent of the natural close the salesman would reach — a service framed offer, not 'give me your money'.
caveats: The 'no length limit' view is Claude Hopkins' position; short-form ad formats and platform character limits may still force brevity, so adapt rather than abandon the principle.
Treat this as a copy-review heuristic, not a testable claim — you still need your own measured results.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

cards.title: Long copy works when it stays interesting
cards.summary: More telling produces more selling, provided the copy holds attention on something the prospect is already interested in.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a product page, landing page or advertorial should be short or long-form for an interested audience.
steps: Accept Hopkins' maxim 'the more you tell, the more you sell' — some of his most successful ads reportedly ran to around 15,000 words, framed as interesting information about a product the reader already showed interest in via the headline.
Make the copy interesting, not merely long: the source's logic is that people give time to what interests them if you make it interesting.
Only extend after the headline has confirmed interest; long copy shown to someone who never opted in is wasted.
Use this as a testable hypothesis on your own store: run a longer, information-rich variant against a short variant and measure purchase conversion, not just click-through.
caveats: The 15,000-word and other Hopkins figures describe a print-era direct response context; they are examples of what worked then, not benchmarks for modern feeds.
Do not confuse 'more you tell' with padding — Hopkins frames it as story and useful information, not repetition of features.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

cards.title: Frame ads around service, not buying requests
cards.summary: Ads that ask no one to buy and instead offer service convert better because buyers act to please themselves.
cards.use_when: Writing the offer framing and call to action for an ad, landing page or door-opener promotion.
steps: Assume the reader is selfish in the ordinary sense — they care nothing about your brand, interest or profit, and only seek service for themselves.
Avoid the appeal Hopkins calls unpopular: 'Buy my brand, give me the trade you give others, let me have the money.'
Build the ad around offered service: wanted information, cited advantages to users, a genuine benefit the reader gets whether or not they buy.

Model the door-to-door hairbrush case: 2,000 salespeople were sent to say 'I was sent here to give you a brush; take your choice from these samples.' The housewife, picking one brush, saw several she wanted and felt anxious to reciprocate the gift — producing the order without any direct ask.
Apply the same structure to your offer: let the prospect choose, experience or receive value first, so the purchase becomes the natural result.
caveats: Hopkins notes these seemingly altruistic ads are based on knowledge of human nature — they are designed, not accidental charity; do not mistake this for simply being nice.
The hairbrush example is historical anecdote, not a tested result for your category.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

cards.title: Spend most of your copy time on the headline
cards.summary: The headline selects and opens the door for the right readers; the entire return on an ad can hinge on it.
cards.use_when: Allocating copywriting time across a headline, subhead and body for an ad, landing page or PDP above-the-fold block.
steps: Follow Hopkins: the purpose of a headline is to pick out the people you could interest, like saying 'Hey there, Bill Jones' to one person in a crowd — headlines must not be misleading.
Recognize that most readers scan headlines and only some proceed to body copy (the source cites Ogilvy's estimate that roughly 80–90% read the headline versus the body).
Invest accordingly: Hopkins says he spent far more time on headlines than on the writing itself, often hours on a single headline and discarding scores before choosing.

Ask whether the promise — the actual benefit the customer gets from your product — is stated in the headline. The source's archetype: '1,000 songs in your pocket' puts the main appeal directly in the headline.
Because return depends on attracting the right sort of readers, cut any headline that pulls the wrong audience even if it pulls volume.
caveats: The 80–90% headline-versus-body figure is attributed here to Ogilvy, not established in the source text as a measurement; treat as a heuristic.
Hopkins reports headline changes sometimes multiplying returns five- to tenfold, and Ogilvy later reportedly saw 19-to-1 differences — these are historical observations, not guaranteed lift ranges.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

cards.title: Use specificity to make claims land
cards.summary: Definitive statements with real numbers carry weight; platitudes and generalities roll off and leave no impression.
cards.use_when: Rewriting generic benefit claims on ads, PDPs or landing pages into defensible, specific statements.
steps: Identify every claim of the type 'best in the world', 'lowest prices', 'high quality' — Hopkins says these are simply claiming the expected and have no impression whatsoever.
Replace each with a definitive statement carrying an actual figure or tested fact; Hopkins notes actual figures are not genuinely discounted, while specific facts carry full weight.

Study his examples: a clothing seller claimed 'my net profit is 3%' instead of 'lowest prices in America'; a razor maker advertised a '78-second shave', indicating actual test results, versus the generic 'quick shaves'.
Make sure any figure you deploy is true and verifiable for your own product — the technique derives its power from credibility, and a false specific damages it.
caveats: Hopkins' examples come from a pre-regulatory print era; modern advertising rules on comparative and substantiated claims apply, so verify every figure you publish.
Specificity multiplies the weight of an argument you already have — it cannot rescue an irrelevant or unwanted offer.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

cards.title: Exploit price perception and exclusivity psychology
cards.summary: Prices and group-restricted offers shape value perception independently of the underlying product.
cards.use_when: Framing price, tiered access, membership or VIP offers in ads and on site merchandising.
steps: Use the painting example: announced without a price, most passers-by ignored it; once told it cost $750,000, people returned and a crowd formed around it — price itself created attention and perceived value.
Consider deliberately signalling premium pricing rather than hiding it, if the product's positioning supports it, since people judge things largely by price.

Apply the tribal principle: offers limited to a defined class — veterans, lodge members, executives — outperform general offers, because those entitled to a group advantage will go a long way not to lose it.
Translate into ecommerce specifics: members-only drops, founders' pricing, a named customer segment ('for working chefs') on the landing page, or early access restricted to an email list.
Recognize Hopkins' broader point: an identical offer presented in different ways can bring multiplied returns, so the framing — not just the discount — is the lever.
caveats: The $750,000 figure is Hopkins' historical illustration, not a tested conversion result for your category.
Do not fabricate exclusivity or fake a group the customer cannot plausibly belong to; the principle rests on the buyer's belief in genuine entitlement.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

cards.title: Rewrite the same offer in different framings
cards.summary: An identical offer presented differently can multiply returns, so treat the framing itself as the test variable.
cards.use_when: Planning the next round of ad, landing page or email creative variants when the offer and price must stay fixed.
steps: Hold the offer constant — same product, same price, same discount — and change one framing element at a time: the headline, the group it is addressed to, the price presentation, or the degree of specificity.
Draw your variant ideas from the source's demonstrated framing levers: headline appeal, group-restricted versus general offer, price emphasis, and concise numbers instead of generalities.

Accept Hopkins' claim that, once you find a working ad, the best way to get new customers is the way you got the previous ones — repeat and iterate on what works rather than abandoning it for novelty.
Set up the comparison so you measure purchase conversion for the same audience, since different framings attract different readers and raw volume can mislead.
caveats: Keeping the same ad and re-running it versus rewriting it is a strategic call — Hopkins advocates repetition, but modern platform fatigue effects are outside his evidence.
Framing changes can pull a different audience, so compare conversion within comparable traffic, not across mismatched segments.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

cards.title: Research deeply to find the keystone fact
cards.summary: Long, tedious research often yields the single fact that becomes the backbone of a winning campaign.
cards.use_when: Preparing the creative brief or angle list for a new product launch or a stalled ad account.
steps: Before writing, gather full information on the subject, as Hopkins insists an ad writer must: read widely, including technical, dry or obscure material that was never written for marketers.

Accept that you may read volumes and find few usable facts — but one fact can be the keystone of the campaign. The source cites a toothpaste writer who read volumes of scientific matter and found in one volume the idea that 'helped make millions'.
He also cites the Rolls-Royce case, where a line found in an obscure engineering document became the basis for one of the most successful campaigns of all time.
For your store, hunt in the same terrain: supplier specs, factory documentation, warranties, ingredient sheets, support tickets, review language — places competitors have not mined for ad copy.
Treat research volume as the job: the source describes campaigns preceded by very large volumes of data and months of research, with the finished ad looking simple on purpose.
caveats: The 'millions' and campaign-success outcomes are historical case examples, not reproducible promises.
The source's maxim 'genius is the art of taking pains' is Hopkins' view of effort, not a guarantee that effort alone produces a winner.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

cards.title: Keep an enduring human-psychology checklist
cards.summary: Human nature is stable, so curiosity, price perception, belonging and self-interest remain reusable copy levers.
cards.use_when: Building a standing checklist or briefing template your team uses before shipping any ad or page.
steps: Adopt Hopkins' premise that human nature is perpetual — the same today as in Caesar's time — so the psychological principles you learn will never need to be unlearned.

Include curiosity on the checklist: he calls it one of the strongest human incentives and says it should be employed whenever possible, which in ecommerce terms means intriguing headlines and open loops rather than full disclosure upfront.
Include price perception: people judge things largely by price, so decide deliberately what your price signals.
Include belonging: group-limited offers beat general ones because people will work to keep an advantage tied to their group.
Include self-interest: readers act to please themselves, never to help your profit — test every draft against that filter.
Run the draft through the checklist and flag any claim that only serves the brand.
caveats: The claim that psychological principles are fixed and enduring is Hopkins' assertion; it should not be read as evidence that any specific tactic works on every platform today.
Individual execution still requires testing — the checklist generates candidates, not proven winners for your store.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

cards.title: Reconcile headline impact with measured conversion
cards.summary: Headline-driven return changes are large in the source's account, but must be verified on your own traffic and metrics.
cards.use_when: Setting expectations and measurement discipline before running a headline or creative test on your store.
steps: Note the source's claims: the identical ad run with various headlines differs tremendously in returns, and a headline change is said to multiply returns five to ten times; Ogilvy is cited as having seen differences up to 19 to 1.
Treat these as historical observations from print direct response, not as forecast ranges for your account — they justify investing in headlines and testing them.
Design your test so the headline is the isolated variable: same offer, same audience, same placement and creative where possible, differing only in headline.
Measure the metric that matches the goal — purchase conversion for a sales headline, qualified click-through if the headline's job is audience selection.
Remember Hopkins' framing that headline return depends on attracting the right sort of readers, so a lower-volume headline may be the winner if it brings better-qualified buyers.
caveats: Do not present the five-to-ten-times or 19-to-1 figures as expected lifts for a client or stakeholder; they are source-cited historical anecdotes.
Small-sample tests on niche stores may need longer runs or larger creative differences to show reliable effects.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

cards.title: Choose headlines that reveal interest, not conceal it
cards.summary: A headline should work like a news headline: help hurried readers pick out what interests them without misleading.
cards.use_when: Selecting among headline options for an ad, email subject line or landing page hero.
steps: Apply the source's stated purpose: to pick out the people you could interest, the way a newspaper headline lets readers choose what they wish to read.
Keep it truthful — Hopkins stresses that headlines must not be misleading, because attracting the wrong readers wastes the entire ad spend.
Account for hurry: people want to be amused or benefited, so the headline has to deliver one of those immediately.

Recognize that a profitable product may interest a reader more than anything else, but they will never know unless the headline tells them — so the headline must surface the specific interest rather than a vague tease.
Use the 'empty church' framing: you cannot educate or inspire a prospect who never clicked, so the hook must earn attention before any persuasion, teaching or product explanation begins.
caveats: The idea that you must entertain before you educate is the presenter's interpretation of Hopkins; treat it as editorial guidance, not Hopkins' own tested conclusion.
Do not let entertainment slide into misleading curiosity — Hopkins explicitly warns against headlines that conceal the interest they should reveal.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

cards.title: Match copy length and detail to the interested reader
cards.summary: Once a prospect has shown interest, give them enough information to act rather than cutting to an arbitrary word count.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much detail to include on a PDP, landing page or long-form ad for a considered purchase.
steps: Separate the two audiences: the uninterested scanner who never clicks and the interested prospect who arrived by clicking the headline or image.
For the interested prospect, follow the source's instruction to consider them as prospects standing before you seeking information, and give them enough to get action.
Do not apply mass-market brevity rules — the source argues that telling a salesman to use a certain number of words with a live prospect would be an unthinkable handicap.
Include the specific facts and service-oriented detail the prospect needs (Hopkins' razor example: a definitive '78-second shave' rather than 'quick shaves').
Review whether each added paragraph helps a half-sold buyer decide; cut content that only serves the brand or repeats the headline.
caveats: Length guidance is contingent on the prospect's existing interest — long copy shown to cold traffic or before the click is a different case the source does not address.
Platform formats (short video, display, character-limited ads) constrain this approach; apply it where the medium allows depth.
cards.source_name: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

cards.title: Run static-first creative volume instead of VSLs on Meta
cards.summary: Since Meta's Andromeda algorithm rewards sheer creative volume, prioritize a weekly static-ad production cadence over high-production video sales letters.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to allocate your creative budget and team time between video and static ad formats for a Meta campaign.
steps: Accept the source's premise: Andromeda behaves like a 'hungry panda' that needs an absurd volume of fresh creatives before ads fatigue, and producing that volume in video is expensive and slow.

Recognize Facebook can only serve so many video ads per user session, so the algorithm biases toward statics it can show more of per session; the presenter calls this the main reason his cheap native statics beat a VSL that took 2.5 months to produce.
Book one hour every week to produce fresh creatives from your winning offer/product; treat this as the core scaling activity, not a side task.
If you still want video, use proof-of-concept content that already works organically rather than polished productions built from scratch.
Test the format call yourself rather than assuming: the source's claim that statics 'all day of the week' beat video is the presenter's opinion based on his own account.
caveats: The claim that Meta structurally biases toward statics is the presenter's interpretation, not a confirmed platform mechanic.
His account reportedly runs 17 VSLs simultaneously, so his static preference comes from a context of very high existing video volume.
cards.source_name: Learn 97% of Meta Ads in Under 19 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Use identity triggers in ad copy instead of backend interest targeting
cards.summary: Insert a specific niche, demographic or category keyword directly into your winning ad's headline or body copy so the algorithm finds that buyer pocket for you.
cards.use_when: Preparing ad copy and targeting for a Meta campaign where you want to reach a specific customer segment without manual interest stacking.
steps: Find your best winning ad and identify the 20% of clients that represent 80% of revenue; note the niches they operate in.

Duplicate the winning ad and swap in one of those niches as a keyword: e.g. change '462 leads per week on autopilot' to '462 dental leads,' then repeat with 'lawyer leads,' 'property investment leads,' etc.
Launch the variants and review CTR; the source claims performance improves markedly and that new audience pockets open up that a generic ad would never reach.

Explain the mechanism as the presenter does: it is not a magic word but a category/identity word that feeds the algorithm a signal about who to look for, because the creative now functions as the targeting.
Apply the same idea to demographics: write copy variations for a 25-year-old woman versus a 30-year-old woman so the ad itself carries the targeting context.
caveats: This is one presenter's observed tactic, not a guarantee; validate CTR and cost per lead against your own control ad.
Do not paste niche keywords that misrepresent your offer just to chase a segment.
cards.source_name: Learn 97% of Meta Ads in Under 19 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Clone your winning ad into hundreds of AI-generated variations
cards.summary: Feed your winning ad to an LLM and generate hundreds of micro-variations targeted to specific demographics, then let CBO pick winners.
cards.use_when: Scaling a proven Meta ad that risks fatiguing, when you need more creative supply from one winning format.
steps: Do not turn off all non-winning ads and ride a single winner to death; the presenter calls that amateur hour because fatigue kills your only asset.

Give the winning ad to an LLM (he names Claude or his own tool Kong; verify current interfaces) with the premise: 'write to 100 people and none of them could tell this was written by a different person.'
Prompt it to rewrite for specific segments, e.g. 'now write this for 25-year-old women' and 'for a 30-year-old woman'; the copy should read almost the same but with details relevant to that person.
Sequence the work: body copy first, then headlines, then the creative itself.
Place all variations into a Campaign Budget Optimization (CBO) campaign and let Meta's AI shift spend toward the best performers.
caveats: The source says CBO cloning has not always been perfect; many ads in the campaign may receive no spend.
LLM output must still fit your offer and compliance requirements; a variant that reads differently to a real buyer defeats the premise.
cards.source_name: Learn 97% of Meta Ads in Under 19 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Rescue ignored ads with a zombie campaign
cards.summary: Revive high-conviction ads that got zero spend in the main CBO by launching them in an isolated ad set to force delivery.
cards.use_when: After running a CBO clone campaign, when several creatives you believe in recorded zero or near-zero spend.
steps: Collect all ads in the CBO campaign that received no spend but that you have high conviction are genuinely good ads.
Place those dead ads into a separate, isolated ad set — the 'zombie campaign' — and launch it.
The isolated structure forces delivery on ads the algorithm ignored in the primary campaign, letting you extract additional winners.
The source reports typically juicing out another 20% of ads that turn out to be winners; treat that as one operator's example, not a benchmark.
Feed any newly proven winners back into your main scaling structure.
caveats: This is the presenter's tactic and reported result; your extraction rate will vary with account, budget and creative quality.
Only run this for ads you genuinely believe in — it will not turn a weak creative into a winner.
cards.source_name: Learn 97% of Meta Ads in Under 19 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Make ads that do not look like ads
cards.summary: Produce paid creative that matches natively consumed content in your niche so it does not read as advertising and die on arrival.
cards.use_when: Developing acquisition creative for a Meta or TikTok campaign where polished ad-looking assets are underperforming.
steps: Reject the instinct to make ads 'pop off the feed' and hijack attention; the presenter notes people hate ads and install ad blockers by the hundreds of millions.
Find what content natively performs in your niche. His example: a 46-minute minimally edited YouTube video with millions of organic views is simply run as a paid ad, because it is already proven.

If you lack organic hits, create a burner account: set up fresh TikTok and Instagram accounts, follow all influencers and pages in your niche, and like their content so the platform surfaces the niche's most popular content on your feed.
Use whatever rises to the top of that burner feed as the template for the ads you produce and run.
The source claims this will outperform your current best-performing ad, which is his assertion, not a guaranteed result.
caveats: The performance claim is the presenter's opinion based on his accounts; validate with your own holdout or split test.
Native-looking creative still must comply with platform ad policies and your claims substantiation.
cards.source_name: Learn 97% of Meta Ads in Under 19 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Test broad targeting against interest stacking with identical creative
cards.summary: Run your best ad with no interest targeting alongside your stacked version and compare CPA after 7 days.
cards.use_when: Reviewing Meta targeting strategy when deciding whether to keep layered interest targeting or move to broad audiences.
steps: Duplicate your best winning creative that currently has interest stacking applied.
Create a version with no interest targeting — just pick a country such as Australia, the US or the UK — and let it run alongside the stacked version.
After 7 days, compare CPAs between the interest-stacked ad and the broad ad.
