Treat the underlying principle as the presenter states it: the creative is the targeting now, so more context in the creative lets Meta find the right people, and you should not try to beat Meta's engineers at targeting.
If broad wins, reinvest the time you spent on backend targeting into producing more creative.
caveats: The 7-day window is the source's suggested comparison period; small sample sizes can mislead, so check spend and conversion volume before concluding.
Broad targeting relies on strong creative context; running broad with a thin, generic ad may not replicate the result.
cards.source_name: Learn 97% of Meta Ads in Under 19 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Write long-form copy to widen Meta's context window
cards.summary: Give the algorithm a large amount of descriptive copy about exactly who you want so it can locate those buyers.
cards.use_when: Writing ad copy for a broad-targeting Meta campaign where the creative must carry the audience definition.
steps: Stop relying on short-form, very basic ad copy; the presenter argues this shrinks the context window Meta has about who you want.
Write long-form copy that explicitly describes the person you are targeting — their situation, role, and the niche keyword signals from your identity triggers.
Understand the causal chain the source asserts: limited context window for your creative means a limited pool of people Meta can target with it; more context expands the reachable audience.
Pair this with broad targeting settings so the algorithm does the placement work while the copy does the qualification.
Judge results on cost per acquisition, not on how polished the copy looks.
caveats: Long copy is not automatically better; it only helps if it contains genuine, accurate targeting context.
This is one operator's framing of how the algorithm uses creative context; validate against your own account data.
cards.source_name: Learn 97% of Meta Ads in Under 19 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Match your best ad headline to the landing page headline
cards.summary: Mirror the top-performing ad headline, subheadline and lead-in on your landing page to fix scent and lift conversion rate.
cards.use_when: Optimizing a landing page or PDP after ads are driving clicks but conversion rate and CPA are poor.
steps: Compare where effort goes: the source says most advertisers put 90% into ads and only 10% into landing pages, which causes high bounce when the page does not match what was clicked.

Find your best-performing headline by testing 20, 30 or 40 headline variants within an ad, since Meta exposes headlines to roughly a thousand times the people who click through, giving far more statistically significant data than the landing page.
Take the winner and mirror it on the landing page headline, subheadline and copy lead-in.
The presenter reports a minimum 15–20% conversion-rate increase from this alone; treat that as his observed result, not a benchmark.
Run a standing rule of at least three split tests at any time, mining insights from top ads and applying them to the page.
Immediate action: open your top 3 ads and put their headlines side by side with the page headline; fix any mismatch within 24 hours.
caveats: 15–20% is the presenter's personal reported lift, not a guaranteed outcome.
Message match helps conversion rate but only for traffic that was already qualified by the ad; it will not fix a weak offer.
cards.source_name: Learn 97% of Meta Ads in Under 19 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Retarget non-buyers with a different offer, not the same one louder
cards.summary: Serve people who did not buy a different product or service offer instead of repeating the same ad.
cards.use_when: Building retargeting campaigns for a store or service business with multiple products, to recapture non-converting traffic.
steps: Accept the premise that the number one reason people do not buy is that the offer or product was not right for them, so re-serving the same ad is futile.
Identify what each visitor clicked on — e.g. they came in for protein powder because that is the product they engaged with.

Retarget that audience with a different offer, e.g. creatine. The source describes protein powder at a 2–3x return and the non-buyer retargeting to creatine at around 6x, and says to trust the tactic rather than expect it to make intuitive sense.
Also use a free high-value content offer as the top-of-funnel; outbound calling every person who downloads it tells you their pains, fears, hopes, dreams and why they did not buy.

Build retargeting first as an objection-handling ad from those non-buyer reasons, then proof/testimonial carousels, then a CBO of best-performing ads for other products retargeted to the same audience.
caveats: The 2–3x vs 6x figures are the presenter's illustrated example, not a promised result.
Outbound calling every lead is appropriate for his service-style business; ecommerce stores without a call operation should adapt the objection-gathering step to surveys or post-purchase feedback.
cards.source_name: Learn 97% of Meta Ads in Under 19 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Scale against blended ROAS and net free cash flow, not platform ROAS
cards.summary: Evaluate changes in absolute store contribution and cash requirements when higher spend lowers reported ROAS.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to increase Meta ad budget when the presenter's peers hesitate because reported ROAS or cost per lead has worsened.
steps: Do not optimize to platform-level ROAS percentages; the presenter reframes the goal as blended ROAS across the whole business, and more importantly net free cash flow.
Distinguish break-even ROAS, a revenue-to-spend ratio, from allowable CPA, a currency amount per acquisition. Calculate both from the store cost model.

Test budget increases against allowable acquisition cost, available cash, inventory and a predefined loss limit; the source aggressive scaling stance is a hypothesis, not an instruction to spend without a ceiling.
Accept compression: the source gives the example that ROAS may fall from 15x to 5x or 10x to 5x, but the point is the absolute net cash generated by spending $100,000 versus $1,000 per month.
When someone reports ROAS dropping from 15 to 11 or cost per lead rising to $50, ask the reframing question: did you make more money in a 30-day period?
Block three hours a month to personally review the numbers rather than relying only on an analyst or media buyer.
caveats: Blended and net free cash flow require accurate, complete accounting; if COGS, fulfillment and refunds are excluded, a break-even ROAS is wrong.
Scaling to break-even assumes you can tolerate thin or zero profit per acquisition to buy market share; the presenter's opinion on this may not fit a cash-constrained store.
The 40x example is anecdotal.
cards.source_name: Learn 97% of Meta Ads in Under 19 Minutes.docx

cards.title: The Three-Question Copy Test (Visualize / Falsify / Distinct)
cards.summary: Run every product headline, ad line and PDP hook through three binary questions to find memorable, credible, ownable copy.
cards.use_when: You are writing or reviewing a product title, ad headline, PDP hero line, email subject or landing page hook and need a fast filter before shipping.
steps: Ask question one: 'Can I visualize it?' Close your eyes and try to picture the words. If nothing concrete appears, the line will not be remembered — cut or rewrite it.

Ask question two: 'Can I falsify it?' If the claim can only be judged as mush (e.g. 'great quality', 'better way'), it reads as filler. Aim for claims that are plainly true-or-false and can be proven.
Ask question three: 'Can nobody else say this?' If a rival store could paste your line onto their page unchanged, it is not positioning. Push until the line is bespoke to your product's facts.
Score: the source treats three 'no' answers as a signal you have written rubbish, and three 'yes' answers as a signal you are onto something. Review the copy line by line, not the whole ad.

Pair the test with the 'One Mississippi, Two Mississippi' speed check: show the creative to another person and if they don't 'get it' within about two seconds of reading, it is too slow for a feed or billboard context.
Keep scores as a personal screen, not a published benchmark — the source gives no data on conversion lift from passing the test.
caveats: A line can be visually concrete and falsifiable yet still irrelevant to purchase motivation; the test screens memorability and ownability, not demand.
Source's claim that 'if everyone gets it, you may be doing something wrong' is an opinion. Confusing the out-crowd can also simply lose sales — decide per audience.
The two-second read threshold is a presenter's heuristic, not a measured conversion rule.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Abstract-to-Concrete Zoom-In Exercise
cards.summary: Rewrite vague benefits by drilling down a two-column abstract/concrete sheet until you hit a picturable object or scenario.
cards.use_when: Your product benefits read as adjectives ('effective', 'convenient', 'premium') and you need concrete claims for ads, PDP bullets or category positioning.
steps: Take a sheet of paper and draw a vertical line down the middle. Write 'abstract' at the top of the left column and 'concrete' at the bottom of the right.
Write your current vague phrase in the left column (e.g. 'regain fitness', 'pretty people in big cities').
Ask repeatedly, 'What do I actually mean here?' and rewrite the phrase lower and lower in the right column, converting intangible words into objects, people, places or actions a reader can picture.
Worked example from the source: 'regain fitness' becomes 'getting people up off the couch to run 5K' — the source notes this is effectively the Couch to 5K naming logic.
Second worked example: 'worn by pretty people in big cities and old people elsewhere' becomes 'worn by supermodels in London and dads in Ohio' — two picturable people in a funny juxtaposition.
Use the resulting concrete phrasing directly as product name, headline or PDP bullet candidates, then run the three-question copy test on each.

Sharpen concrete words further where possible: source critique of a Tesla line suggested preferring 'tougher than an F-150' over 'better truck than an F-150' for shorter, more picturable, more ownable phrasing.
caveats: Drilling down takes real work and multiple rewrites; the source notes 'you can't just like' produce facts — research is required.
Concrete wording can be less searchable or less category-obvious; you may need one concrete emotional line plus one plain functional line on the same PDP.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: 'You Can't Talk, Only Point' — Replace Adjectives With Proof
cards.summary: Write copy by pointing at provable things (charts, objects, people, numbers) instead of using subjective adjectives.
cards.use_when: Your product page or ad is adjective-heavy ('high-quality', 'innovative') and you need provable claims, proof points or image directions.
steps: Set the constraint: describe the product using only statements that are objectively true or false — no 'good-looking', 'trustworthy', 'premium'.
Convert each adjective into a pointed fact. Source dating-app example: replace 'intelligent' with 'reads on the tube'; replace 'good-looking' with 'looks like Ryan Gosling, 6 foot 2'.
For a store context: replace 'durable' with a pointed artifact — a test result, a materials spec, a photo of the seam, a 50-year price chart, or the number of units returned.
Ask for each claim: which object, image or graph can I physically point at that makes this true? If none exists, the claim is wallpaper and should be cut or researched.

The source's gold example: instead of saying gold 'never goes out of fashion', point at the 50-year gold price chart, a castle, a family's gold stash, or Warren Buffett's portfolio allocation — then research which pointed fact actually motivates the buyer.
Translate pointed facts into visual and copy direction on the same PDP or ad unit so text and image reinforce each other.
caveats: Pointing at facts takes research effort; the source explicitly says it 'takes work — that's why it's better', so budget time before publishing.
Some pointed facts are true but unpersuasive ('350 million Americans'); choose facts that carry a story or tension.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Write Claims a Competitor Couldn't Sign
cards.summary: Distinctiveness test: reject any line a competitor could legitimately copy and force copy back to your product's unique facts.
cards.use_when: Your product is functionally similar to competitors (appliances, supplements, apparel) and you need positioning language that separates you in ads and merchandising.
steps: Draft the line, then ask: if a competitor pasted this onto their site, would it still be true for them? If yes, it fails. Credit the principle to Jim Durkey as cited by the source: never write an ad a competitor can sign.
When a line fails, return to product research rather than adjectives. Look for a fact only your product can state — a spec, history, founder story, user base or supply-chain detail.
Source example: Volvo's speedometer ad counts five dials on a rival's speedometer versus six on Volvo's — a fact only Volvo can point at, and a visual that aligns with the text.
Source example: Corvette's 'They don't write songs about Volvos' works because only Corvette can claim that songs (Post Malone, country music) reference Corvettes.
Source example: 'It takes 3.1 seconds to read this ad, the same time it takes a Model S to go 0-60' — a precise, falsifiable, product-specific fact that doubles as a reading-speed gag.
Apply the same exercise to category marketing: source cites Hinge's 'the dating app designed to be deleted', a line a rival dating app can't claim without contradicting its own retention model.
Use whatever survives as the hero line on the PDP, product ad or landing page; keep the plain functional description elsewhere for shoppers who need the category basics.
caveats: Distinctive lines can alienate the out-crowd; the source argues partial confusion is acceptable because it draws attention, but this is a judgement call for your audience size.
Do not invent brand facts to make a line distinctive — the distinctiveness has to come from something true about your product.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Facts First: Ground Every Ad In A Verifiable Fact
cards.summary: Start from a checkable fact (not a number by definition) and build the ad or PDP story from it.
cards.use_when: Your creative or product page feels like opinion, hype or wallpaper and you need a truthful anchor with an internal story.
steps: Locate the fact behind the claim — a spec, a consumption stat, a count, a sourcing detail, a history detail, or a documented behaviour. The source: 'when you say a fact, it guarantees you say something'.
Test the fact's interest level. Source says '350 million Americans' is true but not interesting; find the fact that has a story inside it.
Worked example: 'Asana spends around £345 million a year on sales and marketing' or 'Jack Kerouac wrote On the Road in three weeks' — facts that naturally raise a follow-up question.
Worked example: East-coast-to-London is a six-hour flight — too short to sleep, too long to be quick, which reframes the routine flight misery as a concrete argument.
Worked example: a fast-food worker pours factory ketchup into a Heinz bottle — a fact; the ad line 'even when it's not Heinz, it's Heinz' is built on top of the fact, not the reverse.
Apply to ads and PDPs by starting the copy draft with a facts list for the product, then finding the fact that carries the strongest story and leading with it.
For product claims on PDPs, pair the fact with a visual: chart, photo, spec table or diagram, so the fact is pointable rather than stated.
caveats: The source's dialogue presenters disagree on whether facts are inherently dry — this is a craft opinion. Facts need to carry tension, not just be accurate.
Verify any factual claim before publishing; the source gives sports, business and travel examples as illustrations, not as vetted evidence for your category.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: The Who-Who-Says-What-Well Framework For Copy Briefs
cards.summary: Structure any copy task as: who you're talking to, what you have to say, and saying it well — with visual context driving the format.
cards.use_when: You are briefing a designer, freelancer or yourself before writing an ad, email, PDP hero block or landing page and need to avoid vague inputs.
steps: Point A to Point B: define the buyer's current attitude and the desired attitude after reading, drawing on John Henley's line that the current attitude is the starting point and the desired attitude the finish line. Sketch the wire between them.

Piece 1 — Who you're talking to. Name the channel and moment: a person scrolling a feed, someone who has used your app for months without upgrading, a tourist on a street with a coffee in mind. Source example: Snapchat's Super Bowl ad targeted a moment an average 39-year-old viewer would never occupy.

Piece 2 — What you have to say. For product launches, this means having a belief or 'why' behind the product (the source cites the subscription-economy thesis behind Zuora as an example), so the copy carries a point of view rather than generic benefit lists.

Piece 3 — Say it well. The catchy phrase comes last; the brief must contain pieces 1 and 2 first. Source example: the Hinge brief would be 'an app for people who want long-term relationships and are fed up with dating apps' — the writer then turns that into 'the dating app designed to be deleted'.

Compress into a one-line format reminder: source offers 'coffee and pastry = £5' for a tourist walking past versus a 17-item detailed menu for someone already walking in — form follows the moment, not your internal product richness.

For static ads, layer visual hierarchy the way classic print ads do: eye first hits one element, then a second, then the story. The Hinge visual instead of the mascot is cited as an example of image doing the storytelling work.
Before final, put the draft in the context where it will be seen (see adjacent cards on pre-visualising).
caveats: Piece 2 requires an actual point of view; if your product has none, the framework will just produce polished filler.
The Snapchat and coffee-shop examples are the presenter's anecdotes, not measured outcomes.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Build The Ad In Figma, Not In Word — Design And Copy Are One
cards.summary: Write the ad, landing page or newsletter directly in its final visual layout so line breaks, hierarchy and copy are judged as the reader sees them.
cards.use_when: You are producing static ads, a landing page hero, email creative or a newsletter and copy and layout decisions are being made separately.
steps: Choose the live surface as the writing tool: source writes newsletters inside the email platform, ads inside Figma, and would pin a billboard mockup among competing billboards. Never draft in a plain doc for final layout.
Set placeholder images early so the copy is written around the visual shape, in the way source placed two placeholder illustrations before writing final lines.
Judge line breaks: source rewrote a line several times purely because it spilled onto two lines in the layout and looked messy — settle the copy until it fits the intended line count.
Use layout references from classic print ads (source cites a Volkswagen winter-preparation ad with structure to mirror) as models for hierarchy and density.
Iterate with design and wording together; source estimates the worked ad took roughly 2 days and about 25 rewrites.
For static ads, mock it into a feed or billboard context with other ads around it before signing off — the source warns that a clean isolated mockup lies about stopping power.
caveats: Writing in the tool is slower; if the surface is not fixed, at least prototype in the correct aspect ratio before sign-off.
Figma and other tool UIs change — verify current behaviour before enforcing a specific workflow with a team.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Pre-Visualise The Ad In Real Context (Feed, Billboard, Inbox)
cards.summary: Test stopping power by placing the creative where the buyer will actually see it, not against a blank canvas.
cards.use_when: You are approving static ad creatives, email headers or social hooks and want to know whether they grab attention in a busy feed.
steps: After designing the ad, pull it into a mockup with six or seven other ads around it and people walking past (source suggests this is how you'd test a billboard).
Ask: does it actually grab attention against that noise, not against the isolated Figma frame?
Apply the One Mississippi, Two Mississippi speed check to the in-context mockup: if the reader doesn't get it within about two seconds, the hook is too slow for the surface.

For email, write the newsletter directly inside the sending tool (the source uses ConvertKit) rather than in a Google doc, because line lengths shift when pasted and the reader will see the copy wrapped differently to the draft.

For store landing pages, view the hero on mobile in a browser with the surrounding UI and competitor tabs open — this is the ecommerce translation of the source's feed mockup method, not a claim from the source.
Do not skip the context mockup because the isolated design looks tidy — the source explicitly warns against judging a designed-but-isolated ad as if it were a real one.
caveats: A channel that is intentionally niche and only needs to resonate with an in-crowd may fail the two-second test by design; the source accepts this trade-off, though you should weigh it against lost reach.
No conversion benchmark is given; treat the two-second rule as a creative-floor check, not a performance prediction.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Conflict Pairing To Generate Ad Ideas (Sullivan's Line Down The Page)
cards.summary: Brainstorm ad concepts by listing two opposing ideas on either side of a page and writing the argument between them.
cards.use_when: You need a fresh static ad or landing page angle and your current drafts are flat feature lists.
steps: Draw a line down the middle of the page. On one side, write your product's benefit in plain terms — e.g. 'increase landing page conversions from 1% to 2%'.
On the other side, write the natural opposing choice or cost — e.g. 'spend twice as much on ads'.
Read the pair as an argument: which side is the ad opening with, and what does the reader need to hear to accept the second side?

Classify the conflict by enemy type if it helps: A = a different approach to the same problem, B = a belief disagreement, C = a direct competitor. Source uses Volkswagen's winter-preparation ad and Apple's Mac vs PC work as examples of C.
Write the header as a choice between the two sides: source ended up with 'Want to grow twice as fast? You have two choices.'
If the argument feels thin, keep pairing different opposing ideas and read them as arguments rather than as a slogan list.
Bring the resulting pair into design as a layout, leaning on the visual reference you have collected (source cites a Volkswagen ad layout as the template that made the final version work).
caveats: Source treats conflict as a loose brainstorming device — it explicitly says 'I don't take this too seriously, just draw a line and write opposites'. It is a generator, not a formula.
Conflicts that insult a customer segment or misstate the rival's product can backfire and create legal or community risk; keep the conflict factual.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Drafting By 'Bleeding The Ink Dry' — Spitball Then Curate
cards.summary: Generate a large volume of rough candidate lines without judging them, then select and refine down through many rewrites.
cards.use_when: You are stuck on a headline, hook or hero line and every draft you produce is either obvious or precious.
steps: Accept that the final line is almost never written directly. Source: 'I couldn't write that as it is on the screen right now.'
Spitball freely and badly. Source produced lines like 'Go fool Zuckerberg', 'Roll Monopoly dice', 'Hidden hope', 'Spaghetti at war' before arriving at usable material.
Compare it to running a dirty tap: the first output is muddy, and the goal is to keep flowing until it runs clean, without judging each early line.
After a burst of generation, pause and select. Source noted he couldn't tell good from bad after 2-3 hours of work and had to get trusted feedback — use a small group whose taste you respect.
Rewrite repeatedly around constraints (header length, line count, parallelism). Source's final had roughly 25 rewrites across about several days.
Stop when the structure, hierarchy and wording hold up against the visual mockup and pass the three-question copy test — source describes the moment as 'you literally can't' improve further.
Apply the same loop to PDP hero copy and email subject lines: run a batch of bad candidates through a screening pass rather than trying to write one perfect line.
caveats: High-volume iteration needs time budgeted; source spent days, which is impractical for daily ad rotations.
Ego check: source accepts he couldn't judge his own work after long sessions and relies on a small advisory group; without that, review bias can push you to ship weak work.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Build An Argument, Not A Claim — Small Believable Promises
cards.summary: Frame ads as arguments that move the buyer from a current to a desired belief, with modest believable claims rather than big hype.
cards.use_when: You are writing the hero section, email or paid ad for a conversion offer and want the claim to be credible rather than oversized.
steps: Treat copy as argument: the conclusion is the purchase, and the body of the ad is the reasoning.
Choose a claim the reader can plausibly accept. Source's completed ad argues 'learn copywriting' by claiming 'increase landing page conversions from 1% to 2%' rather than 'become a millionaire'.

Use in the argument the natural cost side of the choice: the source pairs learning copywriting against 'raise twice the cash, hire twice the staff, spend twice as much on ads, cross both your fingers'.

Change the frame of the offer so it saves the reader something instead of costing them. Source's other ad reframes '2 hours to learn copywriting' against '22,000 hours of writing over a career', turning a time cost into a time saving.

Amplify a small number by expanding its time frame. Source derives about 22,000 hours from roughly 4 hours a day writing x 300 days a year x a 30-year career — he notes the figures are his working assumptions, not sourced statistics.
Mirror the structure on the live page: place the choice or the argument visibly, not buried, and bold the key terms that carry the logic.
For ecommerce: replace generic 'premium' claims on a PDP with an argued comparison (e.g. cost per use, hours saved, replacements avoided) where the arithmetic is defensible.
caveats: The 22,000-hour figure is a personal estimate constructed with the words 'give or take'; do not present it as verified data for your own category.
Small believable claims are more credible but may be less click-magnetic than aggressive ones; the source prefers sincerity over hype, which is a positioning choice.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Positioning By Replacement And Smarter-Choice Framing
cards.summary: Define the product by what it replaces and by the smart, self-flattering decision it lets the buyer make.
cards.use_when: Your product is one of many similar options or has an obvious cheaper alternative, and you need a positioning line for PDP or ad creative.
steps: Ask 'what does it replace?' Source example: Athletic Greens' 'you're going to need a smaller cabinet' communication positions it as replacing a shelf of vitamins and supplements. In a store context this maps directly to bundle, refill and regimen language.
Point to the pain of the replaced behaviour: source names the morning-routine hassle of vitamin A, C, D, zinc as the pain point the positioning attacks.

Second framing tool: let the buyer feel smart, not just flattered. Source example: 'the sport sedan for people who inherited brains instead of wealth' — the buyer of a modest car is invited to see themselves as financially intelligent.

Source's paraphrase of the underlying principle: if you can make the customer feel like they're making a smart decision, you are doing something right. Attribute this to the source's paraphrase, not a measured result.

Check the framing is defensible: it should be a claim your actual product can support, and provable to the shopper. 'Smarter than buying a Ferrari' works only if you can point to running cost, resale or durability facts.
Use the positioning in the hero and the replacement language in the comparison or bundle block on a PDP — the source illustrates the replacement idea visually with the cabinet image.
Test against the three-question copy test: can the buyer visualize the replacement or the smart choice, is the claim falsifiable, and could a rival store say the same line?
caveats: The source's own caveat on the smarter-choice angle: some ads assume an in-crowd who will 'get it' instantly while others won't. In ecommerce that risks abandonment by a broader cold audience.
No conversion evidence is provided for these framings; treat them as copy hypotheses to test on your PDP or ad set.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: The One-Element Ad — Strip To The Essential Component
cards.summary: Reduce an ad to a single powerful element rather than the default header + subheader + picture + logo, if the single element can carry the message.
cards.use_when: You are designing static ads or PDP hero blocks with too much going on and want to increase stopping power.
steps: Start from the default spec — header, subheader, picture, logo — and then ask whether you can do the ad with just one of those.
Source cites Neil French via the episode: if you can do an ad with just one of those elements, you're onto a winner.

Worked example: the Economist 'I've never read The Economist — management trainee, aged 42' ad has no apparent subheader, no picture, and the logo absent in the standard position; the ad's identity comes from brand colour and the word 'Economist' embedded in the copy.
For ecommerce translation: test a static ad or PDP hero that is one compelling sentence and one visual, or even just one sentence, rather than the standard headline + subhead + CTA stack.
Keep the identification cues the brand owns (colour, distinctive typography, a recognisable phrase) so the stripped ad is still attributed to you, as the source notes for the Economist red.
Sequence is deliberate: the source points to the first line causing a question and the second line resolving it — 'It takes 3.1 seconds to read this ad / the same time it takes a Model S to go 0-60'.
Apply the One Mississippi, Two Mississippi check to the reduced ad before shipping.
caveats: The source's claim that one-element ads are 'a winner' is Neil French's craft opinion relayed by the presenter, not a measured rule.
Reduction can cost clarity for shoppers who scan for price, specification or shipping information; the stripped creative may need a denser supporting block on the same page.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Storytelling With Cultural Scaffolding, Not Mascots
cards.summary: Let imagery lean on shared cultural references the audience already holds instead of inventing mascots that fit an unrelated category tone.
cards.use_when: You are choosing the hero image or creative concept for a brand whose promise is serious and where a mascot or gimmick would clash.
steps: Ask what the audience already knows and feels about this category that the image can rest on. Source describes the Hinge hero image as resting on cultural scaffolding rather than inventing meaning.

Match the tone of the imagery to the emotional seriousness of the promise. The source argues Duolingo-style mascots suit a silly, funny category, while dating-for-marriage content should be real and not silly.

If the existing brand visual is doing the wrong emotional job, replace it. Source's example: he removed a mascot from a landing page he was working on, and considers the replacement image to have told the story better.

Build in the customer's next believed moment: the source reads the Hinge line as implying 'I'll meet someone, live happily ever after, and delete the app' — the image should reinforce that implied outcome, not just the feature.
Reject images that carry no shared reference and require explanation (the source's 'if everyone gets it, you might be doing something wrong' cuts the other way when the audience is cold).
For store landing pages, audit hero imagery for whether it references a customer-known situation (usage moment, occasion, aspiration) or just a fabricated brand prop.
caveats: The Hinge mascot removal and image choice is one practitioner's judgement — it is not an A/B test result.
Cultural scaffolding ages; an image referencing a current meme or celebrity decays quickly and may date the PDP.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Copy As Positioning: The Same Product, Sold Differently
cards.summary: Copy and branding can move identical commodities into completely different sales outcomes by positioning them differently.
cards.use_when: Your product is functionally similar to cheaper alternatives (commodity categories, private label comparisons) and you need a reason to exist beyond features.
steps: Accept the starting point: two physically similar products can differ only by positioning and reputation. Source compares a Snickers bar with a discontinued Fuse bar of similar appearance and taste, one of which reached the world's best-selling chocolate bar status.
Look for the existing positioning line that already owns a moment, before writing more copy. Snickers' 'You're not you when you're hungry' is cited as the example of a line that lands.

When the product itself is weak, shift the angle rather than improve the product. Source cites footballer Dave Kitson, who outsold Beckham, Lampard, Gerrard and Owen books by reframing marginal playing career material as behind-the-scenes Premier League exposé, released anonymously as The Secret Footballer.
The rule the source extracts from the Kitson story: ask 'what can I do that no one else is doing that people care about?'

Translate to ecommerce: for a functional commodity, find a credibly distinct angle — an access story, a supply-chain confession, an unusual usage occasion, a founder position — and write it into the PDP and ads, rather than adding adjective preambles.

Pair with brand-level positioning references the source uses, such as Ogilvy's 'we don't choose the whiskey, we choose the image' and 17 of 20 American teenagers choosing Apple — reminders that choice reasons sit outside the spec sheet.
Re-verify the copy against the three-question test once the angle is chosen.
caveats: Some of the source's material is presenter anecdote ('I think it's an example of a foundational principle'); the Snickers/Fuse comparison and the Kitson outcome are illustrations, not controlled evidence.
Positioning stories that lean on secrecy or consumer deception carry reputational risk; if adapting the Secret Footballer pattern, keep claims true and defensible.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Metonymy — Swap Literal Category Words For Visual Ones
cards.summary: Replace a literal category label in copy with a concrete, surprising stand-in that is more visual and memorable.
cards.use_when: Your PDP or ad copy uses category words ('device', 'subscription plan', 'storage') that read flat and you need a line that sticks.
steps: Identify the literal, correct word the copy is actually describing. Source example: what Apple really meant was '1,000 songs in your media player'.
Choose a stand-in that a reader can picture instead. Source substitutes 'pocket' — the ad becomes '1,000 songs in your pocket'.

Accept the deliberate imprecision: the source acknowledges the sentence doesn't literally make sense, and treats that as the point — 'pocket' is more visual, surprising and punchy than 'media player'.
Check what the swap does to the claim: it should sharpen imagery, not misstate what the product does, or create a claim you cannot substantiate on the PDP.
Use for hero lines, packaging-adjacent copy and ad headlines where brevity matters; keep the literal description available in specs or FAQs for shoppers who need it.

Test the substitute against the three-question copy test, and consider whether the substituted term itself is one a competitor could also use — the standing-in word should ideally feel owned by your brand.
caveats: The source treats metonymy as a technique, not a rule for every line — it's easy to push into nonsense if the stand-in word is not instantly picturable.
Product-page legal and factual copy may not tolerate substitution; keep the visual line and the literal spec separate.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Contrast and Juxtaposition As The Engine Of Memorability
cards.summary: Build memorable lines by putting two opposing ideas, numbers or images side by side and letting the tension do the work.
cards.use_when: You are writing a headline, subject line or hero copy and want it to stick without hype.
steps: Look for a pairing that creates a small tension. Source examples: 'supermodels in London and dads in Ohio'; 'tougher than an F-150, faster than a Porsche 911'.

In the De Beers example cited by the source, the line is 'how can you make two months' salary last forever?' — the source notes the line 'shouldn't work' because two months' salary and forever are in direct contradiction, which is why it sticks.
Where the numbers are involved, make the contrast do arithmetic or logic work: source's 'the difference between 1% and 2% is not just 1%, it's 100%' framed the whole ad's argument.
Structure an ad around the contrast as a two-option choice: source's finished ad sets 'throw money and pray' against 'learn copywriting', in parallel items.
Keep the two sides parallel in rhythm and word count where possible. Source highlights the repetition of 'twice' and 'both' across parallel lines as something worth pulling out with bolding.
For a store, apply this when a product is premium, cheaper-per-use, or has a surprising comparison: put the two numbers or outcomes side by side in hero and comparison blocks.
Verify both sides of the contrast are true on your PDP; the De Beers line works because the two sides are both real in the campaign, not because of wordplay alone.
caveats: Contrasts that drift into exaggeration break the falsifiable test and can invite complaints or platform flags.
The 'difference is 100%' framing is an argument about relative improvement, not a claim that every 1% lift yields doubled growth — source presents it as a copywriting argument, not a growth model.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: If Possible: Publish Sourced Feedback Loops In Ad Production
cards.summary: Route finished ad copy through a small circle of trusted-taste reviewers before shipping, especially after long drafting sessions.
cards.use_when: You have been writing the same ad, subject line or hero for hours and can't judge whether it's good; you have trusted colleagues or peers available.
steps: Recognise the moment: source says after 2-3 hours of writing he cannot tell what is good and what is not, and reaches out.
Send the candidate to a small group whose taste you respect, not an open pool — source sent the draft to a handful of people.

Give them the candidates side by side with the alternatives. In the source example, the options included 'Go fool Zuckerberg', 'the corporate way' and 'throw money and pray', and the feedback settled on 'throw money and pray' as the left header.
Treat feedback as signal on taste and clarity, not as a vote on raw ideas — the source kept elements from the rejected options elsewhere in the layout.
Feed the result into the next iteration, then run the same reviewers past the revised version if the structure changed materially.
For ecommerce, apply this to PDP hero and email subject lines where one-word or one-line differences swing click-through; keep the reviewing circle small and consistent.
caveats: Source's reviewers are chosen for taste, not statistical representativeness — their verdicts are not consumer research.
Do not outsource final judgement entirely; the source keeps working after feedback receives the verdict, and note that some channels may not have a reviewing circle at all.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Lead with facts instead of adjectives for ad and landing copy
cards.summary: Replace vague adjectives and opinions with specific, verifiable facts to make ad copy and product claims carry weight.
cards.use_when: Writing or auditing headline, PDP or ad copy where current claims feel vague ('high quality', 'unequal', 'sloppy') and you need credibility.
steps: Identify every adjective-based claim in the draft (e.g. 'better', 'unequal', 'sloppy', 'premium').
Convert each into a concrete fact, number, comparison or observable detail: instead of 'unequal' show the graph/difference; instead of 'Tiger was sloppy' say 'he averaged 7 fairways vs his usual 11'.

For ecommerce: replace 'our jeans are better made' with a spec (stitch count, denim weight, warranty length, number of returns per 1,000). Replace 'fast shipping' with the actual measured delivery time.
Once rooted in a fact, layer interpretation or momentum on top — the fact earns the right to the claim.
Keep a running 'arsenal' of facts about the product, brand and category so you're never writing from adjectives alone.
caveats: The source treats this as a principle, not a measured benchmark; the golf figures are an analogy, not ecommerce data.
Facts must be true and checkable — fabricated specificity destroys the credibility the technique is meant to create.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Structure a newsletter with five to six dense examples and built-in conflict
cards.summary: Harry Dry's newsletter formula: five to six concrete examples per issue, each containing conflict, written in short paragraphs.
cards.use_when: Planning an email newsletter, retention email or content send for an ecommerce audience where engagement matters more than list size.
steps: Treat the send as 'more letter than news' — open with a time-and-place personal intro (what you can see out the window, what's happening in your life) rather than a brand announcement.
Include five or six examples/items rather than one long piece; density is the value.
Build conflict into almost every example: use before/after, problem/solution, or 'how everyone else does it vs how this brand does it'.
Write the conflict by hinging on an implicit 'but' rather than repeatedly writing the word 'but' — narrate the turn naturally.
For ecommerce: frame a product story as 'every competitor positions X way; here's how we position it' or 'here was the problem, here's the fix' rather than a flat feature list.
Close with a conclusion so the letter has a shape.
caveats: Source notes engagement, not subscriber count, is the meaningful metric — 100k subscribers at ~50% open was cited as illustrative, not a target.
This is the writer's personal format, presented as his own method, not a universal rule.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Keep paragraphs to two lines and let each one earn its place
cards.summary: Short paragraphs help distracted readers move through copy, and force sharper self-editing.
cards.use_when: Formatting email, PDP or landing-page body copy that readers will skim on mobile or in a feed.
steps: Cap paragraphs at roughly two lines; the source reports never writing a paragraph longer than two lines in his newsletter since 2021.
Use the three-line test: if a paragraph runs to three lines, you're probably not explaining it clearly — cut words or sentences until it's two.
Treat short paragraphs as stepping stones the reader can 'swing between' when attention is low.
Give strong lines room to breathe by isolating them as their own short paragraph.

Apply a burrito test to each paragraph: pull one sentence out — if it still works without it, the sentence probably didn't belong there. (Kaplan's law of words: words not working for you are working against you.)
caveats: The source explicitly says he isn't claiming short paragraphs are inherently good or bad — it's his idiosyncratic style, chosen for readability and editing discipline.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Write simply by rewriting, not by trying to write simply the first time
cards.summary: Simplicity comes from repeated rewriting — write several versions of the same line and pick the best pieces.
cards.use_when: Drafting a headline, tagline or hero copy for a PDP or ad and the first pass feels clunky.
steps: Accept that you cannot write simply in the first draft; simplicity is an editing output.
Write a sentence or paragraph, then copy-paste and rewrite it several times, ending with four or five versions of the same line.
Deliberately allow some rewrites to be bad — the freedom to fail produces more original options.
Get better feedback by showing reviewers multiple versions rather than one; a reviewer can say 'use that sentence but put it in that one'.
Reference good writing guides (e.g. Zinsser's On Writing Well, Forsyth's Elements of Eloquence) if you want to go deeper.
For ecommerce: produce 4-5 hero headline variants for the same product page or ad and merge the strongest phrases across them.
caveats: The source says this process 'caused me a lot of turmoil over the years' and is unsure whether to recommend it — it is a personal method, not a guaranteed shortcut.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Use 'and' as a red flag when scoping a product or brand
cards.summary: The strength of an idea is inversely proportional to its scope — 'and' on a landing page usually signals a diluted offer.
cards.use_when: Writing landing pages, brand taglines or collection descriptions and deciding what the store or product actually stands for.
steps: Scan your landing page or tagline for 'and' joining multiple categories: 'we sell jeans and t-shirts and socks and have dressing rooms'.
Recognise this as a scope problem, not just a copy problem — it signals an unfocused offer.
Narrow to one thing done well, e.g. 'We make jeans. That's it.' The source cites this as Hiut Denim's tagline (worn by supermodels in London, dads in Ohio).
The same principle applies to images: the strongest covers/images are one clean concept (the Velvet Underground banana, Dark Side of the Moon prism) — one image beats seven unrelated ones.
For ecommerce: test whether a one-category message outperforms a multi-category message on the same traffic before broadening the scope.
caveats: Supported by brand examples, not by ecommerce conversion data; treat as a positioning heuristic to test, not a proven rule.
The source does not claim multi-category stores are wrong, only that the strongest ideas are narrow.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Structure copy by dividing it into named, parallel parts
cards.summary: Structure equals dividing lines plus parallelism — split a big idea into two or three labelled parts readers can hold onto.
cards.use_when: Writing a long-form sales page, PDP story, category page or ad narrative that currently feels like a wall of text.
steps: Take the large idea (e.g. 'copywriting') and divide it into buckets: who are you talking to, what are you saying, how are you saying it.
Use the 'two things that look like one' move: show that what readers think is one thing is actually two (e.g. 'get 100 readers' vs 'get the next 9,900 readers'), and use that as part one/part two.
Apply parallelism so the parts are grammatically and conceptually matched.
For ecommerce: split a product page into parallel, scannable parts (the problem / the product / the proof) rather than a single block of features.
Treat structure as chapters — 17 loose videos are like a book with no chapters; give the reader something cohesive to hold.
caveats: The source cites the 'That's interesting' paper (attributed to 1971) as the origin of the 'show two things are one / one thing is two' framing — treat the citation as his reference, not a verified fact.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Hold a high quality bar and never let it fall — ship only 9/10 work
cards.summary: Your work is your standards: define what 'good' looks like and refuse to publish anything below it.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a product page, ad, email or creative is ready to ship, especially under deadline pressure.
steps: Set an explicit bar: the source ships only 'nine out of ten plus' — if it doesn't meet it, it doesn't go out.
Accept that holding the bar will make some people angry, anxious or cause them to stop working with you — the mentor quoted says this is the price.
Define 'good' concretely: take a walk, come back, and ask 'can I take anything away from this?' If nothing can be removed and it reads line-to-line, it's done.
Use the 'worn by supermodels in London, dads in Ohio' test: a line you cannot add to or subtract from and improve is finished.
For ecommerce: apply the same check to hero copy and ad hooks before launch rather than shipping the first acceptable version.
caveats: The line 'you can't add a word to that ad' is the source's subjective standard of quality, not an objective benchmark.
Holding an absolute bar has real costs (slower shipping, friction with collaborators) that the source acknowledges.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Build conflict into ad creative using the implicit 'but'
cards.summary: Conflict (before/after, problem/solution, us-vs-them) makes messages memorable because humans remember relatively.
cards.use_when: Writing ad hooks, product stories or comparison sections where the copy reads flat and factual.
steps: Identify the implicit 'but' in the story: 'I woke up at 8:52 and started looking for clothes, but my mum ran up the stairs and told me not to do the interview in those shorts.'
Render it naturally — don't literally write 'but this happened, but this happened'.
Use the simplest conflict forms: before/after, here's the problem / here's the solution, here's how everyone else does it / here's how we do it.
Use contrast deliberately: pickle juice makes orange juice taste sweeter — the comparison makes each element memorable.
For ecommerce: frame a product story as 'here's how every other screen recorder positions itself; here's how Loom did it' (positioning conflict) or 'here's what went wrong, here's the fix'.
Human memory is relative, so pairing your product against a real alternative sharpens recall.
caveats: The Loom positioning story is the source's illustrative example of the technique, not a measurable result; the 'worth more than the whole screen recorder bucket combined' claim is his characterization.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Build a fact arsenal from first-hand experience, not invented detail
cards.summary: Writers like Ogilvy, Bukowski and Plath produced memorable work because they had direct experience of their subject — taste and conviction come from lived observation.
cards.use_when: Deciding what product details, founder stories or category observations to feature in your ad or PDP copy.
steps: Collect two kinds of experience: (1) direct observation — stand in the car, notice the loudest noise at 60 mph (Ogilvy's Rolls-Royce headline came from a motor magazine writer who actually did the drive); (2) long-term expertise — Bukowski worked as a postman for 20 years and wrote Post Office, Plath interned at a New York fashion magazine and wrote a disillusioned intern.
Translate this to ecommerce: actually use the product, talk to customers, note the specific detail a competitor couldn't claim ('loudest thing you can hear is the electric clock').
Look for the specific, concrete observation sitting right in front of you (the hail outside, the green tea, the mess) rather than reaching for generic phrases.
Avoid 'gumming together long strips of words already set in order by somebody else' — that is what the source says predictive AI does.
caveats: The Ogilvy 'increased Rolls-Royce sales by 50%' figure is given as the source's account of a historical ad, not a verified benchmark for you.
Whether these writers' backgrounds 'caused' their work is the source's interpretation, not a proven causal claim.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Use AI as a tool, but judge output by your taste and conviction
cards.summary: AI can assist research and drafting, but has no taste, no belief and no lived experience — your standards decide whether its output is good.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to use AI in writing PDP copy, ad copy or newsletters without producing generic output.
steps: Treat AI as a research and drafting tool, not an author — the source compares it to the pen-to-typewriter and film-to-digital switches, which didn't make work better on their own.
Before publishing AI-assisted copy, apply the quality bar test: can you subtract anything and improve it? Does it read line-to-line?
Check whether the copy contains genuine belief or conviction — AI 'does not believe something'; a good writer sees something, believes something and writes about it.
Check whether the copy contains specific observation or experience ('AI is predictive — it lays out what has been laid out before').
For ecommerce: use AI for volume variants, then merge and cut using your own judgement; don't ship the first generated version.
The source suggests if you believe AI will do a better job than you, it probably will — so maintain your own standard deliberately.
caveats: The source says the future of AI is unknown and calls it 'a great research tool'; he explicitly does not claim it cannot take your job, only that he doesn't think it can do what he does.
The generative-fill/Abbey Road example is an anecdote about taste, not evidence about AI's current capabilities.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Protect silence and focus before writing sessions
cards.summary: Starting the day with silence and a walk rather than a feed improves the quality of writing work.
cards.use_when: Scheduling time to write ad copy, product pages or a newsletter that actually needs to be good.
steps: Avoid opening TikTok/Instagram first thing — the source says it makes the day 'drudge' and slow.
Sit in silence, take a walk in the park with no earphones, and collect your thoughts before writing.
In shared writing retreats, the source and the Cultural Tutor agree not to talk until dinner (5 or 6 pm) to preserve intensity.
Apply this to ecommerce teams: block uninterrupted writing time for launch copy and creative rather than writing between meetings.
The source's operating principle is 'silence and action'.
caveats: This is a personal working habit from a solo writer, not a team or agency workflow, and has no controlled evidence behind it.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Treat Every Ad as a Salesman Held to Sales Standards
cards.summary: Judge advertising by whether it would help a real salesperson close a sale, not by whether it entertains or wins applause.
cards.use_when: Evaluating or briefing any ecommerce ad creative (Meta, TikTok, Google, email), or arbitrating disagreements about a headline, slogan or image in a campaign.
steps: Before approving any ad, ask the two diagnostic questions: 'Would this help a salesperson sell the goods?' and 'Would it help me sell them if I met the buyer in person?' If the answer is no for a functional reason, cut the element.

Reframe the ad's job: it is multiplied salesmanship addressing thousands, not a slogan or brand-awareness vehicle. Every dollar spent is a mistake multiplied across all your trade, so be more exacting than you would with a single sales rep.

Strip performative elements — clever conceits, literary style, attention-grabbing gimmicks — because any apparent attempt to sell creates resistance. People resent feeling over-influenced and suspect the pitch is not on merit.
Write to one typical individual buyer, not to 'people in the mass'; a blurred mass view produces generic copy that converts poorly.

Consider having a real sales conversation or watching customer support transcripts before writing — Hopkins notes some of the ablest ad men spent weeks selling door to door to learn which arguments landed.
If an element survives the salesperson test but is there for pride or aesthetics, keep it knowingly and record its cost, rather than assuming it is neutral.
caveats: Hopkins's rule is a directional filter, not a way to skip testing; the salesperson test alone does not substitute for keyed return data.
This is Hopkins's strong opinion, not an established law; brand-building and top-of-funnel creative can have value that direct-response metrics do not capture.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Write the Headline to Hail Only the Interested Segment
cards.summary: A headline's job is to pick out the specific subset of readers who can be interested in the product and address them directly.
cards.use_when: Writing or testing headlines for an ecommerce ad, PDP hero, email subject line or landing page, where you must attract the right buyer rather than maximize raw clicks.
steps: Identify the narrow segment your product actually serves and the reason they would care (e.g. corsets → women; cigars → smokers). Explicitly discard irrelevant audiences before writing.
Write the headline as a direct hail to that segment — Hopkins's 'Hey there, Bill Jones' in a crowd — so the right reader instantly knows the ad is for them.
Avoid blind or clever headlines even if they pull many more readers; the extra readers are mostly people with no use for your offer and the actual prospects may never realize the ad refers to them.

Test by keyed returns: Hopkins reports that running an identical ad with different headlines can multiply returns five to ten times, and he kept keyed returns on nearly 2,000 headlines for a single product.

Because one product has many uses (beauty, disease prevention, cleanliness), run a variety of ads so each appeal reaches its own audience; accept that a weaker appeal may still be profitable even at half the returns of the best one.
Compare each headline against actual cost per customer or per dollar of sale, not volume of clicks, before deciding which appeal is dominant and how to allocate ads.
caveats: The five-to-ten-times multiplier is Hopkins's historical mail-order observation, not a benchmark for your channel; verify with your own keyed tests.
Headline appeal differs per product line; do not copy another brand's winning headline style as a universal rule.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Replace Superlatives With Specific, Verifiable Claims
cards.summary: General claims and superlatives are discounted by readers; a precise number or process earns full weight.
cards.use_when: Writing PDP copy, ad copy, offer claims or comparison copy where you need a claim to be believed rather than dismissed as hype.
steps: Audit your copy for platitudes and superlatives — 'best in the world', 'lowest price in existence', 'pure', 'quality'. These claim only the expected and suggest careless truth, leading readers to discount everything you say.
Convert each into a specific, checkable fact: instead of 'more light' say 'three and one-third times the light'; instead of 'prices reduced' say 'prices reduced 25 percent'.

For pricing claims, a bold specific disclosure can outperform a superlative: a clothing advertiser replaced 'Lowest prices in America' with 'Our net profit is 3 percent' and business increased sensationally; likewise a car maker stated 'Our profit is 9 percent' and itemized $735 of hidden costs on a $1,500 car.

Turn ordinary brewing or manufacturing steps into specific story facts, as a brewer did — a plate-glass cooling room, 1,018 yeast experiments, water drawn from 4,000 feet — because these are mere essentials in the industry that no one has bothered to tell buyers.
Quantify tests and comparisons: '78-second shave', 'softens the beard in one minute', '130 formulas tested'. Such statements imply you actually tested and compared.
Use exact scope instead of elastic claims: 'Used by the peoples of 52 nations' rather than 'Used the world over'.
Check any number you put in copy is true and defensible; Hopkins treats a specific claim as either truth or a lie, and buyers treat it accordingly.
caveats: Do not invent figures, tests or percentages you cannot substantiate — a specific claim is a claim of fact.
Specificity only works once; rivals copied the '52 nations' phrasing, so periodically refresh the fact you lead with.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Lead With Service, Not a Buy Request
cards.summary: Offers that give the buyer something (trial, sample, useful information, risk-free approval) outsell ads that simply ask for the order.
cards.use_when: Designing an offer or acquisition creative for a hard-to-sell product, cold audience or high-consideration purchase where a direct 'buy now' ask is underperforming.
steps: Rewrite the ad around the buyer's side of the service — advantages to users, information they want — rather than the brand's interests. The self-interested appeal ('Buy my brand, give me the trade') is unpopular.
Consider offers that let the buyer prove the claim at no cost or risk: a sample, approval, trial period, or the first package paid for by the maker rather than given away.

Case evidence Hopkins cites: an electric sewing-machine motor maker stopped soliciting a purchase and offered a one-week in-home trial with a demonstrator; about nine in ten trials led to sales. Do not treat that rate as a forecast for your product, but the trial mechanism is the transferable idea.

Distinguish paid trials from freebies: both advertisers offered a full-size package to poorer-class buyers, but the one whose coupon let the buyer get a package the maker paid retail for succeeded, while the one who gave it free failed and lost trade — a free 15-cent package cheapened the product.

Make sampling opt-in rather than shoved at people: a housewife handed an unwanted sample pays it no respect; one who requests a sample after reading the story arrives knowing and expecting the claimed qualities.
For neighborhood or marketplace channels, mimic the brush-canvasser tactic: open by offering a choice of free samples so the prospect engages and reciprocates, rather than asking for an order first.
caveats: Approval and sample offers rely on people being honest; Hopkins reports losses are very small, but this is his mail-order-era experience, not a modern guarantee.
Repeated free sampling can train buyers to expect free product, making later purchase feel like a downgrade.
Physical sample programs have fulfillment and fraud costs that must be measured against incremental orders.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Tell the Full Story in One Ad — No Serials
cards.summary: Once you have a reader's attention, present every important claim in that single ad; do not split arguments across a series.
cards.use_when: Structuring ad copy, PDP or landing page content where you must decide how much of the argument to include and whether to serialise messaging across multiple touchpoints.
steps: Inventory your appealing claims by testing headline variants and comparing results; keep an accumulated list of claims that have proven to pull.
Put every claim on that list into each ad thereafter, because one fact appeals to one reader and another to another; omitting any one loses the percentage that fact would have convinced.
Refuse the serial-ad approach — 'continued in the next issue' ads rarely connect, and a person who has read and decided once is unlikely to reread, just as no one rereads a news item.

Apply the rule-of-thumb: a complete story may be one sentence for a low-consideration product like chewing gum, but it must still be reasonably complete; for high-consideration purchases it may run to columns — a car buyer read full columns and books before choosing.

Do not waste space addressing existing customers; they already read and decided and will not read your ads. Assume every reader is an unconverted prospect and write for them. You may advertise that their current product is poison and they would never see it.

Accept monotony for repeat readers: a complete story is always the same, and single mail-order ads have run year after year without diminishing returns because returns come from new readers, not repeat ones.
Note that brief ads are rarely keyed or traced; ignore untraced examples of 'short is better' and be guided by your own traced results.
caveats: The 'more you tell, the more you sell' maxim held in tested mail order; in modern short-form video and skippable ad units the format itself constrains copy length, so test the full-story principle within the format's limits.
Complete story does not mean padding; every line must carry an argument that has proven its pulling power.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Use Mail-Order Discipline as the Benchmark for All Ads
cards.summary: Ads that sell goods by direct response are the severest test of copy and a model for economy of space, pictures and words.
cards.use_when: Reviewing whether your ecommerce ad creative is wasting budget on decoration, big type or design quirks, or when you lack any keyed results to judge an ad by.
steps: Study long-running, clearly profitable direct-response ads and note the concrete patterns Hopkins identifies: small type (proved that larger type does not pay — doubling type doubles space while adding no added sales), no waste space or borders, no boasting, no palaver, no attempt to amuse.

Note their pictures: always to the point and earning their space, sized by their selling importance — a dress picture may take much space, minor items get small space. Pictures in untraced advertising may only produce whims.

Take the incubator case as a cautionary example, not a law: an advertiser added a silhouette row of chickens, increasing space 50 percent, and cost per reply rose exactly 50 percent with not one added sale, because incubator buyers were practical people looking for offers, not pictures.

Treat size as proportional only if utilized: a twice-larger ad brings about twice the returns and a four-times-larger ad about four times, but only when the larger space is used as well as the small — setting half-page copy in a page space doubles cost per return.

Key and trace your own ads wherever possible. In mail order, cost per reply and cost per dollar of sale are immediate and exact; in non-direct lines, compare towns, methods or cost of sales to get comparable data.
Base final conclusions on cost per customer or cost per dollar of sale, not raw reply volume — one ad may bring many worthless replies, another fewer valid ones.
caveats: Hopkins's examples (incubators, cycle ads) are era-specific; extract the principle of traced economy, not the specific formats.
Deliberately attractive design can have brand value; Hopkins allows this but insists you know and record what it costs in returns.
Some direct-response ads are ugly and crowded by design choice, not necessity; copy the tested pattern, not the ugliness.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Key and Trace Ads to Replace Guesswork With Fixed Principles
cards.summary: Repeated keyed tests, watched at cost-per-reply and cost-per-sale, convert advertising from gambling into a science with reusable laws.
cards.use_when: Setting up an experiment cadence for ecommerce ad creative, PDP tests, headline tests or offer tests, and deciding what metric to judge them on.
steps: Use a traceable mechanism — a coupon code, dedicated URL, unique reply mechanism — to measure the action each ad engenders, then compare one ad, headline, argument, size or picture against another.
Record every result with the headline and creative that produced it, so you accumulate a database of what pays rather than an anecdote.

Note the illustrative spread Hopkins gives: one five-dollar article's replies cost 85 cents, another submitted ad cost $14.20 per reply, and another brought replies at an average of 41 cents — on 250,000 replies a year the difference is enormous. Compare your figures to your own best, not to these.
Judge variations at the end of the chain — cost per customer or cost per dollar of sale — because cheap replies can be worthless ones.
When a method invariably proves best, promote it to a fixed principle and stop retesting it for that line; then reserve experimentation for the variable factors of people and products.
Where direct returns are impossible, run town-by-town, region-by-region or channel-by-channel comparisons measured by cost of sales to get an equivalent signal.
Expect your own judgment to be wrong often: Hopkins says one quickly loses conceit by learning how often judgment errs, 'often nine times in ten', which is why untraced preference is not evidence.
caveats: Small tests produce noisy results; Hopkins's agency compared thousands of ads and hundreds of lines to reach dependable conclusions.
Principles derived from one line may apply only to analogous undertakings; treat line-specific findings as hypotheses until tested in yours.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Apply Fixed Psychological Levers That Still Drive Buying
cards.summary: Human nature is stable, so curiosity, price-as-quality signals, personal ownership and class-restricted offers can be used deliberately to lift response.
cards.use_when: Designing ad angles, offer framing or PDP persuasion elements for an ecommerce product, notably when the product's real qualities are similar to competitors'.
steps: Use curiosity as a headline and angle device: Puffed Wheat and Puffed Rice succeeded largely on claims like 'grains puffed to 8 times the normal size' and '125 million steam explosions in every kernel' after failing without that framing.

Do not sell cheapness — sell the feeling the buyer can afford the best; treating buyers as unable to afford quality ('cheapness' appeals) causes resentment, whereas a department store's $1,000 Easter hat drew crowds of women who came to see it.

Use price and premium numbers as quality signals when relevant: a National Gallery painting was ignored until the catalog noted it cost $750,000, after which people returned to surround it. Stating a large sum paid for a formula (e.g. $100,000) won respect where a vague claim did not.

Prefer to send goods with no money down and collect later, rather than money-back guarantees: both refund and pay-later offers tested, and pay-in-a-week-if-you-like-them proved many times more impressive than refund promises.

Make ownership personal: offering to put the buyer's name in gilt on each book, with no other meaningful change, sold hundreds of thousands of books; a leather-covered book with the man's name on it, waiting to be requested, got nearly all recipients to respond and supply qualifying information.
Restrict offers to a named class (war veterans, lodge or sect members, executives), because those entitled to an advantage will go far not to lose it.

Handle substitution with an invitation rather than a warning: 'Look out for substitutes' failed as a selfish appeal, while 'Try our rivals too' — inviting comparison — corrected the situation and made buyers insist on the conspicuously superior brand.
caveats: These are Hopkins's tested mail-order examples; measure each lever in your own audience rather than assuming the same magnitude.
Fabricating a paid-price figure that is not true is a false claim; the $100,000 formula statement was presented as fact.
Name-personalisation and restricted offers can raise cost and complexity per order; check margin impact.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Use the Questionable Persona or Trusted Neighbour as the Seller
cards.summary: Attributing the offer to a credible human — a photographed, named dealer or a woman customers identify with — can beat an impersonal business offer.
cards.use_when: Building the 'from' identity for ecommerce ads, email, WhatsApp or DMs, especially for credit, instalment or higher-risk categories where trust is the barrier.
steps: Choose whether to speak as a company or as a named individual. Hopkins describes two side-by-side women's clothing instalment concerns: one made a bare business offer to poorer girls and the other put a motherly, dignified woman in charge, used her name on all ads and letters, and wrote like a friend — the impersonal rival had to quit.
Have the named persona sign all communications in their own voice and use their picture, so ads and correspondence reinforce the same trusted identity.

Position the persona's motivation as service to the buyer's situation — Hopkins's example: she knew what it meant for a girl not to dress her best and had long wanted to supply good clothes with all season to pay.

For credit or delayed-payment offers, use a warm recommendation to extend credit rather than a bare credit offer, which can seem like a reflection: tell the customer that a known, paying customer recommended her and that a credit account is open, no advance payment, order any time.

Adapt the neighbour-warrant tactic: a far-away guarantee is unremarkable, but a dealer who signs a written warrant to refund on request, in the buyer's own neighbourhood, made a fortune for one concern and has proved effective whenever tried.
Extend the same logic to marketplace or reseller trust signals: attribute the guarantee to a local, named party rather than an anonymous brand.
caveats: The persona must be real or clearly representational to the customer; inventing fake testimonials would be deceptive.
These are historical mail-order cases; the trust mechanism transfers but the specific credit-granting model may not fit every category.
Using a persona's photo and name across ads is a commitment; inconsistency between the persona and actual support weakens the effect.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Budget Ads Around Proven Claims, Not Around the Seller's Taste
cards.summary: The appeals you personally prefer rarely perform best, because you do not know enough people to average out their desires.
cards.use_when: Deciding which ad angles and headlines to scale in an ecommerce campaign, especially when your personal favourite is underperforming and a plain or surprising angle is winning.
steps: Assume your taste is not representative: Hopkins states outright that the appeals we like best will rarely prove best, so preference is not a reason to scale an ad.

Learn the dominant appeal on each line by comparison. For a soap, 'Keep Clean' and 'No animal fat' might attract few readers, 'It floats' might interest more, while a beauty or complexion headline might pull many times as many — you only know by testing.

Do not assume technical features persuade: an automobile headline about a good universal joint may fall flat because few buyers think about universal joints, while 'The Sportiest of Sport Bodies' may out-pull it fifty to one.
Let each tested appeal have its share of spend: an appeal that brings half the returns of the best can still be profitable, and you skip no paying field.

Run multiple distinct ads for overlapping audiences — Hopkins notes using twenty separate ads across twenty magazines because circulation overlaps and different percentages of people respond to different approaches.
Allocate spend across appeals in proportion to proven pulling power, learned through experiment, not through internal debate.
caveats: The 50-to-1 and five-to-ten-times figures are Hopkins's keyed mail-order examples; use them as illustrations of variance, not as expected effects.
Multiple ads raise production cost and testing complexity; protect enough budget per variant to reach a readable result.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Judge Pictures by Their Selling Cost, Not Their Charm
cards.summary: Pictures consume one-third to one-half of many campaign budgets, so each must earn its space through tested selling power.
cards.use_when: Approving or cutting images in ecommerce ad creative, PDP galleries or landing pages when deciding whether an image justifies its place and cost.
steps: Estimate the share of spend tied to visuals: Hopkins says from one-third to one-half of an advertising campaign is often staked on the power of the pictures, in space cost as well as production cost.
Do not use a picture merely because it is interesting, attention-getting or decorative; treat that as waste unless a test proves it pays.

Score each image on what it sells: in tested direct-response ads pictures are always to the point and act as salesmen in themselves, and their size is gauged by selling importance — a dress one is selling may occupy much space, minor items less.

Test image additions against cost per reply or cost per sale. The incubator advertiser added a row of silhouette chickens, increased space 50 percent, and his cost per reply rose exactly 50 percent with no added sales.

Infer from the incubator result that picture value is audience- and category-dependent: those buyers were practical people seeking attractive offers, not imagery. Do not generalise the result to image-driven categories such as apparel.
Compare the same ad with and without the picture before rolling a visual treatment out at scale.
caveats: The 50 percent cost increase is a single case study, not a rule; some ecommerce categories legitimately sell on imagery.
Pictures in untraced general advertising may teach little and result in whims, per Hopkins — so untested visual conventions are weak evidence.
This is Hopkins's opinion from mail-order testing; modern feed advertising may show different image dynamics that require your own tests.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Interview and Sell to Buyers Before Writing Copy
