cards.summary: Direct contact with prospective customers reveals the arguments and approaches that actually land, replacing expensive guesswork.
cards.use_when: Preparing copy for a product launch or a stalled ecommerce campaign where you have no reliable data on what buyers respond to.
steps: Talk to prospective buyers directly before planning the ad. Hopkins notes it was customary to interview hundreds of possible customers, and one of the ablest ad men spent weeks on a single article selling from house to house.
Use those conversations to learn what buyers want and which factors do not appeal, testing different forms of argument and approach as you go.
Alternatively send questionnaires to learn buyers' attitudes, or study support chats and reviews for the same signal-capture purpose.

Recognise the maker's blind spot: the maker knows manufacturing and the dealer side, but that very knowledge leads him astray about customers because his interests are not their interests — so treat internal assumptions as suspect.
Have the copywriter place themselves in the buyer's position to the exclusion of other perspectives; Hopkins calls this one of the most important determinants of success.
Use findings to build the claim list and headline variants for keyed testing rather than launching a fully untested campaign.
caveats: No method for determining purchasing preferences was found in the source text; the reliability of questionnaire responses is not established here.
Small interview samples may not represent your broader market; validate chat and interview insights with keyed tests before committing spend.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Use Test Campaigns to Set Spend Before Scaling
cards.summary: Small, keyed and traced tests establish which method pays before a full campaign commits ad budget.
cards.use_when: Planning the launch sequence and media budget for a new ecommerce product, market or creative concept before scaling spend.
steps: Run the ad in a limited, keyed test first and read the results at cost per reply and cost per dollar of sale before scaling to full campaign spend.
Where direct response is not measurable, run matched town or region tests measuring cost of sales, and compare scores of methods across those cells.
Record every variation compared — headline, setting, size, argument, picture — so the test yields reusable principles, not just a go/no-go.
Expect frequent wrong readings of your own judgment; Hopkins says one learns how often judgment errs, often nine times in ten, which is why untested scale-up is dangerous.

When you find an ad that pays, protect it: Hopkins cites Mr. Mead of the Mead Cycle Company saying he would not change a single word for $10,000, because the ads you see are the final results of many years of comparisons.
Refresh only when a tested replacement beats the incumbent; long-running winning creative should not be changed for novelty.
caveats: Small market tests may not generalise to national audiences or other channels; results are directional.
The mechanics of keyed coupons and traced mail-order ads are era-specific; translate the testing principle into trackable links, codes and post-purchase attribution appropriate to your stack.
Verify current platform testing and attribution interfaces before relying on any particular measurement setup.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Let Data Decide When Craft and Storytelling Pay
cards.summary: Every departure from tested direct-response economy has a measurable price; keep it only if you knowingly accept that cost.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest in brand-style or design-led ecommerce creative versus plain, response-driven creative, and when defending or cutting costly creative elements.
steps: Separate the two reasons a general ad departs from winning direct-response form: the advertiser does not know what the direct-response advertiser knows (advertising blindly), or he deliberately sacrifices a percentage of returns to gratify a desire.
For each costly choice — fine design, big type, entertainment value, untested image — name what it is for and estimate the return loss through a keyed comparison.

Test deviations one at a time so the cost of each extravagance can be attributed: Hopkins asserts every departure from the principles adds to selling cost and that the nearer you get to proved direct-response copy the more customers you get for the money.
Do it if you can afford it, but know the price: Hopkins compares deliberate aesthetic sacrifice to fine offices and buildings — justifiable for pride, but only if you know what you are paying.
When returns fall short, return to a proven model ad and eliminate the identified waste rather than adding more ornament.
Distinguish personal pride in the creative from the reader's response; Hopkins notes some advertisers fall into trying to be performers and seek applause instead of sales.
caveats: This is Hopkins's strongly stated position, tied to direct-response measurement; brand-equity effects are difficult to attribute and may justify intentional deviation where tests cannot capture their value.
The 'always closer to mail-order copy means more customers' claim is a generalisation from tested mail-order lines, not a universal law for every category.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Only trust ads you can trace
cards.summary: Judge every ad, creative choice and offer by keyed returns, never by opinion or imitation of untraced advertising.
cards.use_when: Choosing ad creative, headlines or offers for any campaign and deciding whose advice to follow.
steps: Key every ad so you can attribute replies, coupons, codes or store presentations to a specific ad, headline, plan or method.
Treat any ad that produces no traced result as unproven; refuse to copy a competitor's ad or follow an advertiser's style unless you know its measured returns.
Ignore opinions from anyone who cannot show their returns, including colleagues, printers and self-described experts; test their suggestions instead.
Note that brief, cryptic ads are almost never keyed — assume they were never measured, not that they work.
Accept that full, story-telling ads are the norm in traced mail-order advertising because long copy can be tracked and attributed.
Base changes to your creative on compared results, not on arguments around a table.
caveats: This is Hopkins' 1923 position; modern platforms give partial attribution and modelled conversions, so treat keyed data as directional for upper-funnel spend.
Some brand-building spend cannot be cleanly keyed; don't conclude it does nothing, only that you cannot yet price it.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Make your product its own best salesman with samples
cards.summary: Use samples not as giveaways but as interest filters that generate keyed prospects, cheaper follow-up and a fair product test.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether and how to run a sampling or trial offer for a physical product before scaling acquisition.
steps: Offer a sample so you can legitimately use the word 'Free', which the source says typically multiplies readers and can repay the sample cost several times over in extra attention.
Require effort before fulfilment — a cut-out coupon, phone call or store visit — so only interested prospects receive samples.
Never distribute samples promiscuously to homes or hand stocks to dealers to give away; the source says such samples cheapen the product and often never reach the buyer.
Samples and coupons both register interest, so use them to key and compare one ad, headline or plan against another.
Where international or out-of-area circulation would waste coupons, tell those readers to write for a sample and then route them to a local stockist.
Where offered, price at full-size package rather than half-price: before a prospect is converted, getting half price is about as hard as getting full price.
caveats: The source's numeric examples (costs of 15–70 cents per inquiry, fourfold response to store presentation) are dated mail-order figures, not current benchmarks.
Repeaters from sampling are a small percentage; Hopkins says the loss is usually smaller than the cost of policing it.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Deliver samples where people already shop
cards.summary: Local sample delivery at stores drastically reduces inquiry cost versus mail, and simultaneously builds distribution.
cards.use_when: Structuring a sample or coupon offer and choosing between mail fulfilment, phone response and local store redemption.
steps: Prefer coupons presented at a local store over mailed coupons; Hopkins reports the same ads bringing inquiries at 18–22 cents versus 70 cents by mail.
Offer multiple response routes where practical; in one case 70% of inquiries came by telephone rather than mail, because writing and stamps are a barrier.
If a newspaper's circulation reaches outside towns, tell those readers to write while routing local readers to stores — mailing a sample may convert someone who cannot then be supplied.
Have participating dealers return coupons promptly so you can follow up while interest is fresh.
Require a stock purchase to receive samples if only some stores can be supplied (e.g. a dozen samples with a dozen packages), then refer all inquiries to those stores.
Say 'only one sample to a home' and 'adults only' where children or hoarding would waste samples.
caveats: Some buyers or dealers may buy up papers for full-size-package coupons; the source advises not announcing the offer date and using Sunday papers.
Store demonstrations and promiscuous handouts are called out as poor use of samples unless interest is established first.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Use test campaigns to answer selling questions before you scale
cards.summary: Prove a new product, form, price or method in a few towns, measure cost and repeat purchase, then roll out with known economics.
cards.use_when: Launching a new product, new campaign or major creative change, or deciding whether to scale national spend.
steps: Pick four or five average towns (or other representative test cells) rather than relying on the opinions of you and your advisers.
Run the offer with a sample or free package to start users quickly, then measure: do they buy, do they repeat, how much do they buy, and how long until profit repays selling cost.
Compute cost per customer and revenue per customer from the test; Hopkins asserts averages from a small scale reliably predict the large scale.
Use the test to try alternative product forms; one advertiser found near-unanimous disapproval of a planned reformulation and 91% approval of a second form.
Use tests to try new methods on an already-successful campaign, without disturbing the running campaign; one food advertiser tried over 50 plans in five years and eventually cut selling cost 75%.
Let a challenger prove superior skill by running a few towns and comparing cost per result with the incumbent campaign.
caveats: Hopkins cites typical test costs of $1,000–$5,000; these are 1920s figures, and the general method — not the numbers — is the transferable part.
The dollar amounts and the 75% improvement are case examples, not promised results.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Judge a product by whether repeat sales repay acquisition cost
cards.summary: Before scaling, establish cost per customer, revenue per customer and payback time; short-lived, one-purchase items often can't be advertised profitably.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to advertise a new product, setting allowable acquisition cost, or comparing products for portfolio investment.
steps: Learn what a user spends per year, total consumption in the market and the percentage of readers the product appeals to — waste circulation drives cost.
Compute cost per customer from keyed tests rather than guesswork, and check whether purchases repeat and at what interval.

For single-purchase articles, assume acquisition cost roughly matches mail-order costs for comparable single items; Hopkins says mail-order sales on single articles rarely cost less than $2.50 each, and dealer-sold equivalents cost about as much.

Reject claims aimed at prevention rather than cure: Hopkins says people will pay a lot to cure trouble but little to prevent it, and a prevention claim may pull far less than an alternative benefit claim.
Ask whether the product lasts too long or appeals to too small a percentage, in which case most spend reaches non-buyers.
Project payback: if the ad cost returns before bills are due, the product can be advertised without investment; if it takes months, finance accordingly.
caveats: Numeric thresholds are 1923 US mail-order figures and should not be applied literally today.
Repeat-purchase rates and appeal percentages vary by line and must be measured for your own product.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Don't spend to educate a habit you can't own
cards.summary: Changing consumer habits is prohibitive for one advertiser; watch trends created by others and move in to satisfy demand at the right time.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a campaign that tries to create a new consumer habit, category or education objective rather than satisfy existing demand.
steps: Estimate the cost of converting non-users; Hopkins cites a dentifrice case where converts cost $20–$25 each, making the spend unrecoverable in a lifetime of sales.

If a habit change is needed to use your product, consider abandoning the education objective entirely rather than allocating a share of each ad to it — Hopkins calls partial funding 'the same folly on a smaller scale.'
Prefer satisfying already-created wants: monitor popular trends, fashions and newly created desires, then offer to satisfy them when demand appears (he cites yeast and antiseptics).
Consider shared category education only through cooperative funding across many producers, since no single advertiser can recoup the cost alone.
Check that your ad reaches newly converted buyers rather than re-educating people who already use the category.
caveats: Hopkins' cost figures are 1920s and line-specific; the principle — calculate convert cost before funding education — is what transfers.
Some modern brands do profitably create categories, but typically with capital, long horizons or shared spend.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Pick the claim that appeals to the most buyers
cards.summary: When a product has several true claims, feature the one with the widest appeal in headlines and relegate niche claims to body copy or occasional ads.
cards.use_when: Writing headlines and PDP copy for a product with multiple benefits, especially health, cosmetic or functional claims.
steps: List every true claim the product supports, then estimate what percentage of buyers each appeals to.

Feature the broadest, most attractive claim in headlines; Hopkins reports a toothpaste that prevents decay but also beautifies teeth succeeded by never featuring tooth trouble, while competitors centering on trouble pulled less.
Avoid letting a narrow claim contaminate a broad one: he says mentioning an eczema claim on a soap might destroy the beauty claim that appeals to nearly all buyers.
For claims appealing to roughly a quarter of customers, include them in a percentage of ads and probably in every ad's body copy, but don't make them the headline.
Test headlines against each other with keyed returns; Hopkins says one heading may pull ten times another, so guessing is unsafe.
Use exactness to strengthen a claim: instead of 'good food value,' state the laboratory figure (e.g. 425 calories per pint, equal to six eggs).
caveats: Appeal percentages must be measured for your product; the source's examples are illustrations, not benchmarks.
Some regulated categories restrict comparative or health claims; verify current rules before publishing.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Research the product exhaustively before writing
cards.summary: Weeks of reading, consumer canvassing and dealer research often surface the single fact that becomes the campaign's keystone.
cards.use_when: Preparing to write ad or PDP copy for a new product or entering a category you don't know well.
steps: Read widely in the product's technical or scientific literature; Hopkins describes weeks of medical reading on coffee that yielded one fact — caffeine's stimulation comes two hours after drinking — which reframed a caffeine-free coffee from a near-beer substitute into a full-pleasure product.

Interview consumers at scale: canvasses of all classes, thousands of home interviews and questionnaires to tens of thousands of prospects are the source's norm before a food or personal-care campaign.
Survey dealers and gather every rival's literature, claims and current advertising so you start with exact knowledge of what competitors are saying.

Count the addressable base before choosing the appeal: one pork-and-beans canvass found only 4% used canned beans, so the winning approach targeted home bakers rather than the 4% brand-choice minority.
Employ chemists or labs to verify or disprove claims; Hopkins warns that an untrue impressive assertion can bar you from good media and damage credibility.
Apply the same research approach to existing products when launching a new line or reformulation, not just new brands.
caveats: Research volume must fit the margin available on the product and the size of the opportunity.
Some canvass figures in the source are decades old; the practice of primary research, not the specific percentages, transfers.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Choose names and prices as strategy, not afterthoughts
cards.summary: Names that tell a story or create an exclusive category, and prices matched to volume versus margin needs, shape an entire campaign.
cards.use_when: Naming a product or line extension, and setting or repositioning price before advertising.
steps: For a name, weigh descriptive names that tell a story (Shredded Wheat, Cream of Wheat, Puffed Rice) against coined names that can become category names (Kodak, Karo, Jell-O, Vaseline) and prevent substitution.

Prefer a coined or owned name over a generic descriptor: Hopkins says Toasted Corn Flakes and Horlick's Malted Milk left the way open to perpetual substitution and lost much of the market they pioneered.
When setting price, decide between high volume at thin margin (Campbell's Soup, Palmolive, Ford) and high margin with small consumption per customer (a corn remedy used rarely).
Recognize that a high price can itself be an inducement where products are judged by price and buyers assume expensive means better.
Note that a price appealing to only about 10% of buyers multiplies the cost of selling by narrowing the field.
Check that the price leaves enough margin to fund the advertising required for the volume you need.
caveats: These are Hopkins' 1923 examples; subscription, SaaS and marketplace economics differ.
High-price-as-quality only works in categories where buyers use price as a quality signal.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Map the competitive field before choosing your angle
cards.summary: Study entrenched rivals' price, quality and claims, and find a real, tellable advantage that gives satisfied users a reason to switch.
cards.use_when: Entering an established category or launching against entrenched brands, and deciding whether to attack, differentiate or avoid the fight.
steps: Inventory the forces against you: rivals' prices, quality levels, claims and how strongly they are entrenched, including whether they created and typify the habit.
Accept that fields where one brand originated and typifies a habit are nearly impregnable; invasion requires a convincing advantage or superior sales copy, not a comparable product and a budget.

Work through substitution mechanics: for a new shaving soap, every prospect uses a rival and many are satisfied, so describe the individual — a man on a Pullman with his favourite soap — and determine what you could say to him personally to make him switch.
Win one specific customer type first: 'We cannot go after thousands of men until we learn how to win one.'
If the maker claims no distinction, hunt for an impressive fact about the product that competitors have not told; it doesn't need to be unique, only more convincing.
Plan defences against substitution from the start; a brand that only establishes a demand, without owning the name or claim, may lose the harvest it created.
caveats: Head-on attacks on habit-creating leaders usually fail regardless of copy quality.
The source's case is about physical goods sold through dealers; marketplaces and marketplaces-with-reviews face additional trust factors.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Get distribution before or alongside advertising
cards.summary: Advertising before availability wastes converts; use sample and coupon offers naming specific dealers to force stock and achieve distribution quickly.
cards.use_when: Running any campaign where consumers must be able to buy immediately after seeing the ad.
steps: Choose a distribution method — direct/mail order until volume forces retailers, referral of inquirers to stocked dealers, consignment to wholesalers, or named-dealer advertising — based on your line.
Start locally, naming specific dealers in the first ads; when other dealers see rivals named, they typically stock quickly if advertising pulls.

Use coupons good at any store for a full-size package: mail proofs of the ad to dealers in advance with a list of media and circulation, so each dealer sees coupon holders as cash sales they don't want to lose.
Where samples are used, supply participating stores with samples in proportion to a stock purchase, then refer inquiries to all stores to force general distribution.
Avoid sending free stock or starting with consignment as default methods; Hopkins calls free starter stock expensive relative to other options and consignment resented with difficult collections.
For outside circulation, route inquiries to a local store rather than mailing, so the supplying dealer gains a customer.
caveats: Coupons good for full-size packages risk being bought up in bulk; the source advises avoiding announced dates and using Sunday papers.
Methods vary by line and retailer power; test in representative markets before committing.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Don't buy dealer effort; buy customers
cards.summary: Dealer help, loading discounts and displays often shift sales between stores rather than growing total sales — spend that money on creating customers instead.
cards.use_when: Evaluating trade discounts, loading offers, display allowances and display placement as a route to sales growth.
steps: Test any dealer incentive by comparing total market sales, not sales at the promoted store: a window display may give one dealer a larger share without increasing your total.
Treat loading offers (e.g. one case free with ten) as requiring 10% more advertising-sold volume just to return the same revenue.
Recognize that most dealers push their own brands and that advertised lines carry thin margins and get price-cut, so anticipated extra effort is often not forthcoming.
Prefer sales made by conviction through advertising; Hopkins says customers won through casual recommendation rarely stick.
If you do fund display or trade promotions, compare cost per incremental customer against the equivalent spend on media that creates new buyers.
Accept that if customers cost you one dollar each, every wasted dollar is a lost customer; set this as your spend criterion.
caveats: Some categories — impulse, luxury, grocery — depend on display and shelf placement for discoverability; don't eliminate trade support without testing.
The source's argument assumes advertising is the primary demand creator, which may not hold for products without brand pull.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Positive ads beat negative appeals
cards.summary: Show the desired outcome and the envied life, not the problem or the afflicted customer; Hopkins claims positive ads pull four to one over negative ones.
cards.use_when: Choosing imagery, headlines and proof points for ads, PDP hero images or landing pages for beauty, health, apparel, education or self-improvement products.
steps: Replace 'before' imagery with 'after' imagery: show clear skin, not wrinkles; pretty teeth, not decayed ones; well-dressed people, not shabby ones.
Do not attack rivals, point out their faults or appear to knock competitors; apart from issues of media acceptance, the selfishness is obvious and costs trust.
Write invitations rather than accusations: 'Send now for this sample' rather than 'Why do you neglect this offer?', which implies the reader is already neglecting.
Assume readers will act and invite them to follow the crowd.
Where relevant, include a person who benefits from the transformation — the source notes beauty advertising gains from including an admiring man, since women use beauty to gain effect.
Keep every ad cheerful in tone; Hopkins says readers dodge a lugubrious advertiser.
caveats: The four-to-one figure is Hopkins' stated experience, not a general benchmark; test against your own audience.
Some categories respond to honest problem agitation; the source concedes negative appeals may work with 'the afflicted' and for remedies.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Keep a consistent advertising personality
cards.summary: Give your advertising a consistent, distinctive personality and don't change what has proved appealing; readers build confidence through repeated acquaintance.
cards.use_when: Setting tone of voice for an ongoing campaign and onboarding new writers or agencies who produce ad and PDP copy.
steps: Choose an individuality suited to the audience: rugged honesty where it counts, good-fellow tone where choice is a matter of favour, or authority where technical confidence is needed.
Attribute responsibility where possible — name the person who made an improvement or sign the ads — so a face rather than a soulless corporation speaks.
Give each writer your established tone before they draft: Hopkins says a new writer 'gets into the spirit adopted' and plays the part like an actor.

Never change an individuality that has proved appealing; readers recognize you by mannerisms as much as name, and appearing different every time undermines trust, forcing best friends to reacquaint themselves.
Allow a complete change only when a wrong approach forces it.
If you change, don't force traits that conflict with your audience's preferences; be distinctive without becoming eccentric or abnormal.
caveats: Consistency must not preserve a tone that a new test has disproven; the source permits a complete change when the tack is wrong.
Signed ads require the named person to be credible and available; otherwise the device backfires.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Make pictures argue only when letters wouldn't pay better
cards.summary: Pictures are often a third to a half of the campaign stake, so use them only when they out-sell the same space in type, and never merely to attract attention.
cards.use_when: Allocating space between imagery and copy in ads or on PDP and landing pages, and deciding art style.
steps: Before commissioning any image, ask whether the same space as persuasive type would sell more; if not, use type.

Use pictures to make a selling argument type can't make: products whose appearance drives desire (clothing, collars, food), or aspirational figures (successful men for business courses, admired women for beauty).
Test rather than assume — the source cites grains photographs beating figure drawings for one product and other pictures being a total loss.
Avoid eccentric, comic or frivolous imagery: it steals attention from the headline and appeal, and Hopkins argues no one patronizes a clown.

On art quality and colour, treat these as minor economies: good art pays at least as well as mediocre; colour generally pays only where it approximates the product (orange, desserts), not merely to attract attention.
Repeat a proven picture rather than replacing it: Hopkins argues new customers won't remember it, so repetition is an economy.
caveats: The 'third to a half of campaign stake' refers to space cost in print advertising; digital equivalents differ.
Art quality and colour questions have both viewpoints supported in the source and depend on the line and modern media.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Test copy letters like ads before sending at scale
cards.summary: Write and test multiple letters as you would ads; a letter reaching a half-sold prospect can either complete the sale or forfeit the impression.
cards.use_when: Designing follow-up emails, direct mail or outreach to prospects and previous buyers for an ecommerce list.
steps: Analyse which circular letters you personally act on or file; the ones that survive have a headline offering something you want or need to know, at a glance.
Recognise that half-sold prospects are the highest-value recipients: letters to inquirers and follow-ups complete a sale or forfeit the impression gained, so they matter as much as the original ad.
Before sending millions, send a few thousand split across many variants — one publisher tested 25 letters to a thousand prospects each — and learn which produces the best result.
Use the variant with the best measured returns; abandon a plan that tests unprofitable rather than rolling it out.
Where testing at scale isn't possible, base the letter on knowledge gained from prior tests, not assumptions.
Apply the same test-different-copy discipline to ad creative and landing pages, not just letters.
caveats: Assumes a list or inquiry base large enough to split into meaningful test cells.
The source is pre-digital; modern email and deliverability constraints change cadence but not the test-before-scale principle.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Eliminate costs that don't produce measurable sales
cards.summary: Weigh every project and method against a known cost per result, because small economies are irrelevant next to basic appeals that can halve or multiply results.
cards.use_when: Auditing any campaign spend — dealer allowances, displays, samples, art, media — and deciding where to cut or reallocate budget.
steps: Identify the few variables that can halve or multiply results — the appeal, the headline, the offer — and treat art quality, colour, specific ad details and dealer perks as minor economies.
For every spend line, run a comparison test: some towns with the treatment, some without, and compare total sales, not just sales at promoted outlets.
Note that questions can be settled cheaply by a test campaign rather than by argument; Hopkins calls it going to the court of last resort — buyers.

Estimate whether an effort is too costly in advance: if converting a habit or reaching a tiny minority means a per-customer cost that can't be repaid from the customer's lifetime spend, don't attempt it.
Consider that what can't be done profitably on a large scale usually can't be done on a small scale either; partial funding of a losing objective is the same folly, smaller.
Apply the same criteria you use for manufacturing costs to advertising, so every element is compared on cost and result.
caveats: Some brand and awareness spending is not immediately measurable; don't cut everything without a measurable return if you have strategic reasons and can measure over a longer horizon.
The source assumes a mail-order measurement framework; adapt the method to the measurement tools your channel supports.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Test letters and follow-ups with actual returns before full send
cards.summary: Keyed split tests across many letter variants pick the winner that gets the most responses, mirroring scientific ad testing.
cards.use_when: Running an email or direct-mail campaign (abandoned cart, replenishment reminder, win-back) and deciding which message to scale.
steps: Before sending millions of pieces, build a small test: the source publisher tries up to 25 letter variants, each mailed to about 1,000 prospects.
Key each variant so responses are traceable, then compare cost-per-result, not just open or reply counts.
Compute what results will cost; if the best variant appears unprofitable, abandon the plan rather than scaling a loser.
Roll out only the variant that pays best on actual returns.
For ecommerce: apply the same discipline to abandoned-cart, post-purchase, and replenishment flows — write several subject/body/offer variants, split a sample of the list, and scale the winner.
caveats: The source's 25-variant/1,000-prospect scale is a mail-order example, not a required benchmark; adapt sample size to your list and traffic.
Test where possible; where not possible, base the message on knowledge gained from prior tests.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Follow up inquirers along the original interest, not a new argument
cards.summary: A follow-up letter should complete the impression the prospect already formed, not restart with a different pitch.
cards.use_when: Writing follow-up emails to leads who requested a quote, sample, catalog, or signed up but did not buy.
steps: Identify what created the original interest (the ad, offer, or page that captured the lead).
Continue that same argument and promise in the follow-up — do not introduce a different selling angle or guess again.
Note which selling letters add urgency: a limit on the offer, an expiry date, or a stated cost of delay.
Add a specific inducement for immediate action rather than generic 'act now' language.
For ecommerce: if a lead downloaded a size guide, follow up on fit and selection rather than switching to a price/discount pitch unless price was the original hook.
caveats: Follow-up letters go to 'half-made converts,' so they are high-leverage; the wrong argument forfeits the impression already gained.
Offers must expire on a genuine date — the source's point is to force prompt decision, not to fake scarcity.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Give a compelling personal reason to order from you rather than a competitor's catalog
cards.summary: A gift or personal note enclosed with the catalog gives the buyer a reason to order from this vendor instead of the several competitors he also requested.
cards.use_when: Fulfilling catalog or sample requests in a category where buyers request multiple competing catalogs.
steps: Recognize the competition: an inquirer may send for three or four similar catalogs, so your catalog alone does not win the order.
Enclose a letter and a personal card with the catalog. Say you are a new customer and want to welcome them.
Ask them to enclose the card with their order so you can guarantee a gift — something they keep.
Differentiate the reason for old customers versus new customers (e.g., a different justification for the same gift).
Measure whether the gift pays for itself through larger sales per catalog; the source reports it paid several times over, so treat as an example to verify, not a promise.
caveats: The gift's payback is a reported case result, not a guaranteed outcome.
The curiosity the offer arouses must favor your catalog over alternatives; a weak reason will not beat a competing offer.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Price prompt action into your offer rather than losing to delay
cards.summary: You can afford to pay for immediate action; delay costs more than the inducement.
cards.use_when: Setting promotional mechanics (expiry windows, premiums, bundles) for a product launch or seasonal push.
steps: Strike while the iron is hot: ask for the decision at the moment of interest.
Offer an inducement for prompt action, or state what delay will cost the buyer.
Consider time-limited mechanics: the source cites an advertiser who got hundreds of thousands of women to buy six packages and send trademarks for a premium good for only one week.
Evaluate whether the premium or discount cost is less than the value of accelerated purchases and reduced delay.
For ecommerce: test expiring bundles or first-order premiums at checkout rather than always-on discounts.
caveats: The six-package/trademark/week-long premium is a case example, not a universal template.
The source warns no single tactic applies to two lines — ways of getting action are many, but principles are universal; test for your category.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Choose product names that either tell a selling story or accept a long earned-meaning path
cards.summary: A name displayed prominently should aid advertising; descriptive names do, meaningless coined names only pay off after long advertising.
cards.use_when: Naming a new product, bundle, or house brand where the name will be displayed in ads and on listings.
steps: Classify your candidate name: descriptive (May Breath, Cream of Wheat, Dutch Cleanser, Holeproof, Minute Tapioca) versus meaningless coinage (Kodak, Karo, Vaseline, Kotex, Lux, Postum).
If descriptive, note it can be both protected and self-explanatory, so display space earns its keep.
If coined, accept that the great majority of coined names never attain meaning; do not assume yours will.
Avoid names that consist of common descriptive ingredients (Syrup of Figs, Coconut Oil Shampoo, Tar Soap) — they invite substitution, force you into a comparison class, and cap pricing power.
Avoid unfortunate generic names (Toasted Corn Flakes, Malted Milk) where creating demand also creates demand for competitors using the same words.
Avoid frivolous coinages for a serious product; the source says frivolity almost prohibits respect.
caveats: Names have lost originators 'four-fifths of the trade they developed' in the source's examples — but these are historical cases, not predicted outcomes for your name.
On patented products, the right to a name expires with the patent (Castoria, Aspirin, Shredded Wheat Biscuit), so patent protection can itself be undesirable.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: When a common name is unavoidable, use the founder's name
cards.summary: A man's name as an auxiliary brand is better than a coined name because it signals personal pride in the product.
cards.use_when: Naming a product whose category term must be a common name (e.g., you must call it 'soap' or 'oil').
steps: Accept that the generic product word cannot be owned or protected.
Add a man's name as the auxiliary brand — the source says this is much better than a coined name because it shows someone is proud of his creation.
Recognize this naming decision as foundational: some names became the chief factors in success, others lost four-fifths of the trade their originators developed.
Display the name so it supplements, not replaces, the selling story; the service of the product, not the name, is the important thing.
caveats: The four-fifths figure is a historical example, not a benchmark.
The source's advice is directional and dated in its gender framing; the transferable principle is that an eponymous brand implies personal accountability.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Eliminate wasted ad display space telling no selling story
cards.summary: A vast amount of space is wasted displaying names and pictures that tell no selling story; modern advertising moves to cut that waste.
cards.use_when: Auditing ad creative or PDP hero modules where brand marks, logos, or decorative images occupy prime real estate.
steps: Tally how much of each ad or page is spent on name, logo, or decorative imagery versus selling content.
For each element, ask whether it advances the selling story; if not, cut or compress it.
Justify prominent name display only when the name itself aids advertising (descriptive names earn this; meaningless coinages do not).
For ecommerce: reduce oversized brand imagery on PDPs and ads unless it carries product information (ingredients, use case, proof).
caveats: The source is addressing print advertising; the ecommerce adaptation (PDP, thumbnails) is an analogy, not a documented result.
A strong, established brand can carry display value the source's era could not measure; test before stripping brand assets.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Key every ad so results can be known and proved
cards.summary: Ads that are unkeyed are spent blindly; the source argues you can prove an unprofitable ad's worthlessness with a simple keyed test.
cards.use_when: Setting up spend for any paid channel, landing page, or campaign where you cannot yet say whether it pays.
steps: Attach a key: a code, dedicated URL, offer, phone line, or unique ask that ties responses to a specific ad.
Stop running ads you know to be unprofitable, even if they have run for years — cost of a dollar doing a five-dollar job is waste.
Watch for the tell of unkeyed ads: frivolity, clever conceits, entertainment, and palaver a salesman could never say.
The source's blunt test: end an ad with an offer to pay five dollars to anyone who writes that they read it through; the scarcity of replies reveals how few actually read it.
Note that many unkeyed ads today were keyed at the beginning — they won on a small scale before ever running large scale.
caveats: The $5 read-through test is the source's illustrative device, not a recommended offer today; the principle is to build a measurable response key.
Keying measures response, not full attribution; combination effects in growing businesses can still leave advertising's share uncertain.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Judge ads by traced returns, not by whether you personally like them
cards.summary: Ads that look crowded or verbose to an admirer may be the top payers; the type with the best traced performance is the one to run.
cards.use_when: Deciding which creative or page style to scale when stakeholders have aesthetic preferences.
steps: Separate the roles: you may be seeking something to admire or entertain, but the buyer is seeking information to act on.
Check whether the ad is keyed; if keyed and among scores of traced ads, the style you dislike may be the best performer.
Let keyed returns, not taste, choose between a 'clean' ad and a dense/informational one.
Keep long-used unkeyed ads suspect; they may simply never have been tested.
For ecommerce: resist replacing a converting PDP because it looks cluttered until a keyed split test proves the new one wins.
caveats: This does not mean density always wins; the source's claim is that traced results should decide, not aesthetics.
Test infrastructure must be reliable or the comparison is meaningless.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Apply the storekeeper's discipline to national-scale spend
cards.summary: A storekeeper charges every line of an ad to a department and every inch must justify its cost next day; most national advertising is done without that justification.
cards.use_when: Allocating budget across product lines, departments, or channels where spend is currently credited only by overall business growth.
steps: Charge each line of your ad or campaign to the proper department/product — mirror the storekeeper who must justify every inch the next day.
Require each spend to justify its cost rather than presuming it pays because the business is growing.
Beware crediting advertising for growth from combined efforts: the source cites a $700,000/year advertiser who did not know if advertising was worth anything.
Move to 'safe and sure' small expenditures on known returns that can grow into big ones on a certainty rather than a guess.
For ecommerce: assign channel and campaign budgets to gross margin by product line and review cost per result, not blended revenue growth.
caveats: Combined effects make pure attribution hard; the source's answer is keying and small-scale proof, not perfect multi-touch attribution.
The $700,000 figure is a historical example of an unaware advertiser, not a threshold.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Treat advertising as a gamble to be removed, not a tonic to endorse
cards.summary: Spending because advertising worked for others is like taking a secret tonic on endorsement; if the business thrives, the tonic gets credit regardless.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether to launch or continue a paid channel because competitors or past results suggest it 'must' work.
steps: Identify whether current spend is justified by measured return or by presumption and others' endorsements.
If the business thrives, check that you are not simply crediting the tonic; if it fails, do not attribute it to fate.
Replace endorsement reasoning with a test: run a small, keyed campaign and measure cost per result before scaling.
Adopt the source's forecast that advertisers will be judged on known returns and only competent men survive — build the measurement habit before it is forced on you.
For ecommerce: apply this to new channel launches (a paid channel, an affiliate, a marketplace) with a defined test budget and kill criteria.
caveats: This is the source's argument and forecast, not an observed law; some brand advertising intentionally has delayed, hard-to-key effects.
Small tests may not capture long-horizon brand effects — note the limitation when deciding whether to abandon.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Win on a small scale before running on a large scale
cards.summary: Ads based on known statistics were keyed at the start and proved themselves at small scale before big rollout.
cards.use_when: Planning a product launch or campaign scale-up where you want evidence before committing large circulation or spend.
steps: Key the ad or campaign at the outset so results are attributable.
Prove the concept at small scale with actual returns.
Only then scale circulation or budget, using the winning variant.
Keep the keying discipline even after scaling to maintain known statistics.
For ecommerce: pilot a new product or creative on a small budget/audience, then expand based on measured cost per result; the source's 'millions of circulation' is the print-era analogy.
caveats: Scale itself can change results (auction dynamics, audience saturation); the source assumes the small-test winner holds up.
Not every product or channel permits small-scale testing — newsletters and follow-ups may have to rely on prior test knowledge instead.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Test follow-up sequences because they complete or forfeit the sale
cards.summary: Letters to inquirers and follow-up letters show the same differences as ads — some get action, some complete a sale, some forfeit the impression gained.
cards.use_when: Designing post-inquiry sequences (samples, quotes, cart abandonment) where the first contact only half-converted the buyer.
steps: Recognize follow-ups go to half-made converts, making them disproportionately important relative to their volume.
Where possible, test follow-up letters against each other with keyed responses; where not, base them on knowledge from past tests.
Check each letter for whether it completes the impression already gained or forfeits it.
Ensure the sequence drives toward immediate action via an inducement or a stated cost of delay.
For ecommerce: treat abandoned-cart and post-sample flows as testable creative, not boilerplate — split variants and measure completed-purchase rate.
caveats: The source treats follow-up importance as a general principle; it does not provide sequence-length or timing benchmarks.
Where testing is impossible (low volume), fall back on tested principles rather than inventing a new argument.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Match offer mechanics to the line, but keep the universal principles
cards.summary: Ways of getting action are many and rarely transfer directly between lines, but the underlying principles are universal.
cards.use_when: Adapting a proven promotion, premium, or urgency tactic from another category to your own product.
steps: Identify the principle behind a tactic (prompt decision, overcome delay, preference over substitutes) rather than copying the mechanic.
Do not assume one way of getting action applies to two lines; the source says rarely can one way be applied to two lines.
Design a category-appropriate mechanic that serves the same principle, then test it.
Consider that demand you create can be shared by competitors if your name or product term is generic — build a reason to buy from you specifically.
For ecommerce: a time-limited premium that worked in one vertical may need a different mechanic in another; validate before scaling.
caveats: The source is explicit that this is its view, not a tested universal mechanic; treat transfer as a hypothesis.
Descriptive names create category demand that other sellers can also capture, so pair naming with a distinct reason to choose you.
cards.source_name: Scientific Advertising.docx

cards.title: Choose the right TikTok ad format for each objective
cards.summary: Match in-feed, Spark Ads, search ads, and Shop ads to distinct ecommerce goals instead of defaulting to one format.
cards.use_when: Planning which TikTok ad type to build for a launch, a scaling push, a demand-capture play, or a native checkout offer.
steps: Pick in-feed ads as the default workhorse for most testing, scaling, and direct-conversion campaigns; they slot into the For You feed looking native, allow a custom CTA (Shop Now, Purchase, etc.), and are skippable.

Use Spark Ads when you already have a post (yours or a creator's) with organic traction: boosting it preserves the accumulated likes, comments, and shares, feels more native, and lets you validate creative organically first — the source credits this with higher CTR and lower CPA. Reach out to a creator whose post you want to boost and get their authorization code.

Use TikTok search ads to capture people actively searching your category (e.g., 'cell phone cases'); the sponsored result can be a video, not just text, letting you target keywords and diversify discoverability beyond the home feed. Use the keyword planner in the Ads Manager to source search keywords and negatives.

Use TikTok Shop ads / GMV Max when you want the order to check out natively inside the TikTok Shop app — the cart icon or CTA opens a native checkout with no shipping or card entry, and TikTok's affiliate platform can surface creators to make the shop videos you then promote.
Mix formats rather than relying on one, since each captures a different intent (browse, warm organic audience, active search, native purchase).
caveats: The source's CTR/CPA claims for Spark Ads are the presenter's assertions, not measured benchmarks.
Format names and setup flows are TikTok-specific and change over time; verify the current interface.
Ads in-feed appear roughly every four to five scrolls per the source's observation.
cards.source_name: The BEST TikTok Ads Course For Beginners in 2026.docx

cards.title: Set TikTok budgets to clear the learning phase
cards.summary: Configure daily ad-set budgets as a multiple of target CPA to gather ~25 conversions in 7 days before judging results.
cards.use_when: Setting launch budgets and ROAS targets for a new TikTok campaign or ad set for an ecommerce product.
steps: Set each ad set's daily budget to roughly two times your target CPA so the set can accumulate about 25 results within 7 days — the threshold the source uses to exit the learning phase.
Recognize that during the learning phase results are unstable; judge creative and targeting only after you've cleared it, not on day one or two.

For TikTok Shop GMV Max campaigns (which automate product-catalog promotion and creative delivery for native Shop checkouts), set your initial target ROAS slightly low on purpose to guarantee adequate delivery volume, then raise the target and scale spend upward once delivery is stable.
Treat the 2x-CPA / 25-conversion / 7-day figures as the source's heuristics for clearing the learning phase, not guaranteed mechanics; check your account's current reported learning-phase criteria.
caveats: The 2x CPA and 25-in-7-days numbers are the presenter's recommended heuristic, not a documented universal rule.
Setting target ROAS too high early can starve delivery; the defensive low-target approach trades some efficiency for volume.
cards.source_name: The BEST TikTok Ads Course For Beginners in 2026.docx

cards.title: Set up a TikTok Ads account for approval and safety
cards.summary: Complete the business, payment, audience, and brand-safety settings that keep a TikTok ad account deliverable and unbanned.
cards.use_when: Opening or hardening a TikTok ad account before spending on ecommerce campaigns.
steps: Fill in the account setup information (business name, website, industry, correct region, currency, time zone) — ads cannot run until this is complete.
Choose automatic payments rather than manual threshold payments so a winning ad keeps running instead of pausing when a spend threshold is hit.

Upload any documents TikTok requests; the source says completing document requests reduces the chance of the ad account being banned. Add a credit card as the payment method (recommended over PayPal) to minimize suspension risk.
In audience controls, set default targeting location and minimum age (e.g., 18+), and set excluded custom audiences if you have them — the source treats exclusions as advanced, skippable early on.

In the brand safety hub, choose standard inventory for most brands (avoiding expanded inventory placements) and exclude sensitive categories such as youth content, combat sports, gambling, and lotteries, plus any vertical-sensitive content you don't want associated with your brand.
Monitor the account health page (customer feedback and ad-group status) and fix any errors immediately to avoid flags or bans.
Verify current interface paths before making these changes.
caveats: Ads-credit offers (the source mentions up to $6,000 in TikTok ad credits) may change; check the current offer.
Document and verification requirements vary by region and account standing — the source says you may or may not need to upload documents.
cards.source_name: The BEST TikTok Ads Course For Beginners in 2026.docx

cards.title: Set up a TikTok Business Center and link all assets
cards.summary: Centralize users, ad accounts, organic accounts, pixels, catalogs, and shops in one Business Center for scalable access control.
cards.use_when: Managing an ecommerce brand's TikTok advertising with agencies, contractors, or multiple accounts and shops.
steps: Create a Business Center (via the left-hand menu in Ads Manager) if you'll give anyone else access or manage more than one account; an individual Ads Manager alone is enough only for a single solo advertiser.
Under users, add members by email and assign roles (admin, standard, finance, or financial analyst) so granular access is controlled.

Under accounts, link your advertising account. If it isn't auto-linked, request access using the ad account ID found in the Ads Manager. Note that requesting access to the account does not give every member access — you then assign individual users to that ad account.

Link your organic TikTok business account (via QR-code scan) with 'manage account' access (rather than 'deliver ads') for business use, and choose whether ads also show on your organic profile — the source recommends the 'show as ad only' option so A/B-tested hook variants don't clutter your feed.
Link your TikTok Shop to your assets so the ad account, organic account, and shop all talk to each other.
Under brand finances, set up payment management (finance/admin role required), and enable two-step authentication plus an allowed email domain in settings to restrict access.
caveats: Role and access flows are TikTok-specific and may change; verify the current interface.
Linking a Shop requires having a Shop already — set one up first if needed.
cards.source_name: The BEST TikTok Ads Course For Beginners in 2026.docx

cards.title: Install and verify the TikTok pixel before spending
cards.summary: Deploy the TikTok pixel with maximum data sharing and confirm events fire so campaigns can optimize toward purchase.
cards.use_when: Preparing a store to run TikTok ads optimized for add-to-cart or purchase events.
steps: In Ads Manager, go to Events Manager and connect a web conversion data source, entering your website; TikTok will detect your platform (e.g., Shopify) and suggest the best setup, including a manual option.
For Shopify, install the TikTok app (developer must be TikTok Inc.), then use the TikTok Ads setup tab to connect the correct TikTok for Business account, Business Center, and ad account.
Choose the maximum data-sharing model for the best optimization data, but confirm your privacy policy reflects that usage — the source flags they are not a lawyer and say to check your policy.
Confirm the pixel captures the full event set you care about: page view, view content, add to cart, search, initiate checkout, purchase, and payment-info-added.

Verify events fire correctly using either the Events Manager test-events tool (enter your URL) or the TikTok Pixel Helper Chrome extension, walking through view-content, add-to-cart, and checkout on your own store.
Treat a failing pixel as a blocker: without firing purchase/add-to-cart events you cannot optimize campaigns toward those outcomes and results will suffer.
caveats: The source says pixel setup is 'not recommended' to run ads without — but event availability depends on platform integration and privacy consent.
App names, tab labels, and setup flows may change; verify current TikTok/Shopify documentation.
cards.source_name: The BEST TikTok Ads Course For Beginners in 2026.docx

cards.title: Build a pain-solution ad with the 8-step structure
cards.summary: Sequence hook, problem, failed solution, product intro, feature-benefits, demo, desired result, and CTA in a TikTok ad.
cards.use_when: Writing a TikTok product ad for a problem-solving product (e.g., a foot-support or pain-relief item) that needs a clear narrative.
steps: Open with a hook that names the specific pain (e.g., forward head posture, plantar fasciitis) so the viewer self-identifies in the first seconds.
State the problem in the customer's situation — e.g., a podiatrist saying runs triggered their plantar fasciitis.
Optionally add a failed solution step: 'I tried these shoes and they didn't work' to make the eventual product feel earned.

Introduce your product as the recommended fix, then stack feature-benefits ('stabilized my foot to promote blood circulation,' 'targeted the root cause') — add as many as sound natural and non-repetitive.
Demo the product working, then state the desired result that directly resolves the opening pain, e.g., 'what I thought was a 3-month recovery is now 3 weeks.'

Close with a clear call to action (check them out / shop now). Lean on loss aversion: the source says humans are about twice as motivated to avoid pain as to gain something positive, so naming the pain is what drives the point home.
caveats: The 8-step formula and the 'twice as motivated by pain' ratio are the source's framing, not a guaranteed conversion formula.
The failed-solution step is optional per the source; including too many steps can bloat short ads.
cards.source_name: The BEST TikTok Ads Course For Beginners in 2026.docx

cards.title: Open ads with a curiosity gap
cards.summary: Use story, visual, or expectation-gap hooks so viewers must keep watching to resolve incomplete information.
cards.use_when: Writing the first three seconds of a TikTok ad when retention is the main problem.
steps: Use a story opener that promises a payoff the viewer needs closure on — e.g., 'you won't believe what happened...' before revealing it's about a soap brand.
Use a visual curiosity gap: show an unresolved scene, unusual setup, or a challenge ('can you remove this long bar?') that viewers want the answer to.
Use an expectation-setup hook with a specific timeline that promises an outcome — e.g., 'I used this for 4 weeks, here's what happened' — combining curiosity with specificity.
Use a 'don't do it' warning hook showing a person reacting to something off-screen, creating anticipation about what they're looking at.
Make the hook resolve into your product; the source says almost every TikTok hook should create some curiosity gap, and the extreme examples shown just make it more obvious.
caveats: Curiosity gaps that never connect to the product waste the hook; the resolution must be the ad's payoff.
The source's examples are from various advertisers; results are illustrative, not benchmarks.
cards.source_name: The BEST TikTok Ads Course For Beginners in 2026.docx

cards.title: Use pattern interrupts to beat the scroll reflex
cards.summary: Break the brain's prediction of 'normal content' with a visually unexpected opening before showing the product.
cards.use_when: Producing the opening shot of a TikTok ad when the video looks too much like everything else in the feed.
steps: Think of the feed as a prediction machine that filters out anything familiar; a pattern interrupt is anything the viewer didn't expect to see.
Try physical disruption shots — breaking or throwing an object — as a fast, single-shot opener, then cut to the product (used by luggage brands in the source's examples).
Try unexpected imagery or a surprising reveal (e.g., a product the audience didn't expect that brand to make) to force attention.
Try ASMR-style sensory openers (a satisfying pour, a texture close-up) as a subtler but still effective interrupt.

Try an exaggerated or surreal visual effect (the source shows an extreme AI-generated result) paired with a direct problem question, e.g., 'do you know what hard water does to your hair?' so the shock ties to the product problem.
Keep the interrupt as a brief opening beat before transitioning into the product, so it serves the ad rather than replacing it.
caveats: Stunts unrelated to the product can attract the wrong audience or hurt brand perception; tie the interrupt to the offer where possible.
Examples are the source's illustrative clips, not measured performance guarantees.
cards.source_name: The BEST TikTok Ads Course For Beginners in 2026.docx

cards.title: Apply authority bias in product ads
cards.summary: Borrow credibility visually or verbally — expert attire, first-person credentials, or a known face — so viewers trust the claim.
cards.use_when: Casting or scripting a TikTok ad for a product where trust is the conversion barrier (supplements, health, technical goods).
steps: Dress the spokesperson or shoot in settings that signal their authority: a chef's whites in a kitchen, a lab coat in a production facility, scrubs and a stethoscope for health claims.
Have the person state the credential in the first line — e.g., 'I own a restaurant myself, so I know good quality' or 'I am a chef' — so the bias triggers immediately, not midway through.
Show the process or 'eyes on every step' to reinforce expertise through transparency rather than just claiming it.
For larger budgets, use a celebrity (the source shows Mario Lopez) — the source notes this creates authority bias effectively but may exceed budget.

Note the source's caution that some examples imply expertise through costuming (scrubs, stethoscope) without confirming the person's credentials; the source presents this as common practice, so weigh the ethical and compliance risk for your brand.
caveats: Implying credentials via costume can violate ad-platform or legal standards for certain categories (e.g., health claims). The source presents this practice without endorsing its legality.
Celebrity placements require budget and usage rights.
cards.source_name: The BEST TikTok Ads Course For Beginners in 2026.docx

cards.title: Align ads with the buyer's identity
cards.summary: Write and cast ads that call out the identity the customer wants to occupy, not just the product's features.
cards.use_when: Positioning a TikTok ad for a lifestyle, wellness, hobby, or premium product where self-image drives purchase.
steps: Identify who the buyer wants to become or how they see themselves — a fit person, a 'serious professional,' an avid reader, 'kindle girlies,' 'physical book girlies.'
Call that identity out explicitly in the ad, verbally or visually, so the viewer feels the ad is for them (the source's reader-pillow ad names both kindle and physical-book identities repeatedly).
Match product language to that identity — e.g., 'more reps, more strength,' 'beast mode activated' for fitness buyers; 'the ring real men wear' for a masculine position.
Use customer-style identity phrases in the hook so viewers self-select in the first seconds.
Apply the same logic to any product: define the target identity, then make the ad a mirror of it.
caveats: Identity frames that patronize or exclude can backfire; keep the called-out identity genuine to your actual buyer.
Examples are the source's illustrative ads, not proven performance lifts.
cards.source_name: The BEST TikTok Ads Course For Beginners in 2026.docx

cards.title: Anchor price against a higher reference
cards.summary: Show a higher price or prior cost first, then your actual price, so the real price feels like a gain.
cards.use_when: Writing a TikTok ad or PDP creative for a value-focused or premium product where price is the objection.
steps: Open or structure the ad around a visible comparison: a near-identical item at a much higher price versus yours (the source shows a $35,000 vs $75,000 bracelet, and insurance quotes of $47 vs $98).
Anchor to a more expensive product, a more expensive service, or the pre-discount price of the same item.
Frame reductions as caused by a concrete reason (sale, comparison to competitors) rather than a vague 'cheaper.'
Keep the anchor credible — a comparison the viewer can plausibly believe; an absurd anchor undercuts trust.
Move from the anchor into the offer and CTA so the price relief converts into a click.
caveats: Comparison pricing must comply with advertising-truth rules in your market; the source treats it purely as a psychological tactic.
Anchors work only if the viewer accepts the reference price as real.
cards.source_name: The BEST TikTok Ads Course For Beginners in 2026.docx

cards.title: Build reciprocity with tutorial-style ads
cards.summary: Teach something genuinely useful before pitching so viewers feel compelled to give back by buying.
cards.use_when: Planning long-form or educational TikTok ad content for a considered-purchase product.
steps: Lead with real value: create a tutorial or explainer that solves a chunk of the customer's problem with no immediate pitch — the source cites a 22-minute dental-implant masterclass ad that the presenter says performs well.
Keep the teaching substantive so that by the end the viewer feels they've learned a lot and is primed to act.
Place the offer and CTA after the value delivery, e.g., a quote request or check-out at the end.
Consider long-form for high-consideration products where education reduces risk; short-form tutorial snippets can work for simpler products.
Treat reciprocity as one of the most underused tactics per the source — test it where your product benefits from explanation.
caveats: The 22-minute dental ad performance is the source's anecdote, not a benchmark for your category.
Long education-first ads can lose viewers; retention depends on the topic's pull.
cards.source_name: The BEST TikTok Ads Course For Beginners in 2026.docx

cards.title: Use scarcity and social proof in TikTok creatives
cards.summary: Trigger FOMO with restock/stock messaging and borrow trust with reviews, real customers, and follower counts.
cards.use_when: Writing ads for products with demand spikes, waitlists, or strong review bases where proof drives conversion.
steps: For scarcity, lean on restock framing: 'back in stock,' 'sold out three times this year,' or comments like 'when is the restock, please' shown on screen.
Show the FOMO as real social behavior (viewer comments asking for restock) rather than stating scarcity abstractly.
For social proof, overlay written reviews on the creative.
Interview real customers on camera about the product and use their reactions as proof.
Cite audience size or authority signals where relevant (the source shows an ad referencing 90K Instagram followers).
Combine proof types — text reviews, customer interviews, and comment screenshots — rather than relying on one.
caveats: Scarcity must be truthful; false stock claims are a legal and platform-compliance risk.
The source presents these as tactics with examples, not measured lift for every product.
cards.source_name: The BEST TikTok Ads Course For Beginners in 2026.docx

cards.title: Judge TikTok demand before committing budget
cards.summary: Weigh audience breadth, time spent, and social-commerce growth to decide how much to invest in TikTok for your store.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to open a TikTok acquisition channel at all, or how to justify the channel to a skeptical team.
steps: Check the audience match: the source cites TikTok's ~1 billion monthly active users, ~95 minutes daily time spent per user (top platform by time usage, growing yearly), and a demographic spread including 18-24 at 32%, 25-34 at 29%, and 45+ at 18%.
Note the source's point that older segments (45+) can have lower competition and lower CPMs, making them attractive when your product fits that audience.
Consider social-commerce momentum: the source cites TikTok Shop surpassing $20 billion and projected ~$30 billion by 2028 (eMarketer) and roughly 20% of the social-commerce market.
Recognize the algorithm's reach: even a zero-follower account can reach millions organically, and organic winners can then be amplified with ad spend (Spark Ads).
Use these figures as directional, not as guaranteed outcomes for your store.
caveats: Percentages and revenue projections are cited by the source and may be dated; re-verify current figures before using them in a business case.
Platform reach stats do not imply your product will convert at any particular rate.
cards.source_name: The BEST TikTok Ads Course For Beginners in 2026.docx

cards.title: Back-in-stock scarcity ads and comment mining
cards.summary: Use sold-out/restock messaging and customer comment sections to build authentic scarcity creative for ecommerce brands.
cards.use_when: Planning acquisition creative for a product that has sold out or restocked, or when you need low-cost ad concepts that signal real demand.
steps: Build a restock ad by leading with the fact that the product sold out (source example: 'This anti-aging serum sold out three times this year, and here's why people are raving about it').
Mine your own product comments and DMs for organic demand signals, e.g. customers commenting 'when is the restock, please' — screenshot or film these and use them directly in the ad.
Show the comment thread on screen as the hook so the scarcity proof is visible, not just claimed.
Pair the restock message with the reason people wanted it back (a specific benefit or review), so the ad is not only scarcity.
If the product is genuinely out of stock, run waitlist or back-in-stock notification creative to capture demand instead of pausing spend entirely.
caveats: Only use restock/sold-out claims you can substantiate; the source presents these as common patterns, not as verified performance guarantees.
Scarcity wears out — rotate restock angles so the claim stays credible.
cards.source_name: The BEST TikTok Ads Course For Beginners in 2026.docx

cards.title: Stack social proof in the first seconds of ad creative
cards.summary: Layer reviews, real-customer footage and follower counts into ads to lift credibility and performance.
cards.use_when: Producing ad creative for a PDP-driven campaign where you need higher trust and click-through on cold audiences.
steps: Add on-screen review cards (star ratings, quotes, before/after photos) over the product footage rather than relying on spoken claims alone.
Film or source real customer conversations — interview an actual buyer about the product and use their words as the ad script.
Include measurable authority signals where true, e.g. on-screen mention of follower counts like 90K Instagram followers, or the number of customers served.
Use founder/customer pregnancy, skin, fitness or lifestyle stories as testimonial narrative arcs, since the source shows these being used as identifiable real-person formats.
Match the social-proof format to the placement: short review overlays for cold traffic, long testimonial narrative for retargeting.
caveats: The source states more social proof tends to perform better but gives no benchmark; treat as a directional principle.
Never fabricate review counts or before/after results — social proof that can't be verified exposes the store to ad rejection and refunds.
cards.source_name: The BEST TikTok Ads Course For Beginners in 2026.docx

cards.title: Specificity principle for claim writing
cards.summary: Replace vague benefit claims with precise numbers, timeframes and percentages to make ad copy and PDP claims believable.
cards.use_when: Writing ad hooks, PDP headlines, bullets or email subject lines where claims currently sound generic and are being ignored.
steps: Audit each claim for specificity: vague claims get ignored; specific claims get believed (source rule).
Convert rounded/vague numbers into exact ones — source examples: 'lose weight fast' becomes 'lose 11 lb in 23 days'; 'boost your income' becomes 'made $4,387 in 12 days'.

For ecommerce, apply the same to product claims: '98% natural' instead of '100% natural' reads as more believable (source example), and day-by-day results ('watch how this changed my skin in 2 weeks') beat a single generic after shot.
Use numbered day or result progressions in creative (day 0 through day 20) to show the timeline behind the claim.
For stats-based hooks, use specific failure or success rates to create curiosity, e.g. the source's example referencing a percentage of coconut oil products failing.
Apply the same rewriting pass to PDP bullets and bundle descriptions so ad and landing page claims stay consistent.
caveats: Specific claims still need to be truthful and substantiated; the source is describing persuasive framing, not permission to invent numbers.
Odd, precise numbers feel more credible than round ones, but don't fabricate precision you can't back up.
cards.source_name: The BEST TikTok Ads Course For Beginners in 2026.docx

cards.title: Using TikTok Creative Center top ads for swipe files
cards.summary: Search and filter TikTok's free ads library to collect hook and format inspiration, while accounting for opt-in limitations.
cards.use_when: Sourcing ad inspiration or competitor research before shooting a new batch of TikTok creatives for your product category.
steps: Go to TikTok Creative Center and open the Ads Inspiration / Top Ads dashboard; verify the current navigation since TikTok's interface changes.
Filter minimally: the source recommends just country plus niche/industry, because each additional filter (including objective) narrows the pool of visible ads.
Set the date range to the last 180 days to maximize the number of ads returned.
Leave ad format open unless you specifically need one format; then sort by likes (e.g. top 1–20%) to surface the strongest performers.
Open the analytics panel on any ad to see likes, CTR, budget tier and the landing page URL — the landing page is useful for copying page structure, not just the creative.
Save ads into named collections inside Creative Center so swipe files stay organized by product or angle.
Use the keyword search for a specific term (e.g. 'protein'), but expect buggy or thin results for very niche keywords.
caveats: Ads only appear if the advertiser opted in; many large-spend brands deliberately opt out, so this library is not comprehensive.
High likes does not equal high purchase conversion — treat it as format/hook inspiration, not proof of sales performance.
cards.source_name: The BEST TikTok Ads Course For Beginners in 2026.docx

cards.title: TikTok One top ads insight for category creative angles
cards.summary: Use TikTok One's creative library and top-ads insight panel to extract category-level selling points and audience angles.
cards.use_when: Deciding which creative angles and selling points to test for a category (e.g. beauty, personal care) on TikTok Shop.
steps: Access TikTok One via the prompt inside Creative Center or via ad account > Tools > Creative Inspiration; use Explore Mode for the full library view.
Open Top Ads Insight and filter by category, region and a 30-day window.
Set the sort to top video views to see which creative approaches dominate that niche.

Use the breakdown table that lists target audience, physical product, applicable scenarios and specific selling points with example ads, and turn each selling point into a testable hook for your own product.
Cross-reference these angles with your own reviews and comments to pick which ones fit your product truthfully.
Re-check the tool periodically: the source notes some views (e.g. the creative-approach panel) were behaving unreliably at recording time.
caveats: The source found the overlap with Creative Center data high and some panels buggy or in rollout; verify what's currently functional before relying on it.
Selling-point examples are category-level inspiration, not validated results for your product.
cards.source_name: The BEST TikTok Ads Course For Beginners in 2026.docx

cards.title: Organized ad swipe files with a paid ad-spy tool
cards.summary: Build boards of competitor and category ads with a paid library that captures opted-out ads and offers strong search.
cards.use_when: Running frequent creative testing and needing a persistent, searchable swipe file across TikTok and other platforms, including competitor accounts.
steps: Choose the tool if you are producing ads regularly (the source calls it not worth it for one-off advertisers) and set up boards by angle, competitor or campaign, e.g. separate boards for each psychological principle, seasonal events like Black Friday, and each client.
Use filters to narrow by platform, format (video vs image) and niche, then apply to build a filtered feed of relevant ads.
Search by product keyword; the source reports noticeably better results than the free TikTok keyword search.
Spy on a specific brand to see all ads they are currently running across platforms, then save individual ads into the relevant board.
Review boards before each new creative sprint to pick angles and formats you haven't tested yet.
caveats: Paid tool; the source's preference is personal and based on frequent ad production, not a universal recommendation.
Tool names, pricing and interfaces change — verify current plans and features before subscribing.
cards.source_name: The BEST TikTok Ads Course For Beginners in 2026.docx

cards.title: TikTok Shop product research with Kalodata
