cards.title: Segment Retargeting Audiences by Funnel Stage
cards.summary: Build distinct retargeting audiences — product page viewers, ATC non-purchasers, checkout abandoners, category viewers, all visitors, past purchasers — so you can read ROAS, spend, and clicks per audience.
cards.use_when: Configuring Demand Gen (or other retargeting) campaign audiences for an ecommerce store and needing audience-level performance reporting.
steps: Create these segmented retargeting audiences, per the source's recommended list: product page viewers; add-to-cart users who did not purchase; abandoned cart users who started checkout but did not finish; category page viewers; all site visitors; and past purchasers (for repeat purchases and upsells).
Attach the audiences to your Demand Gen retargeting campaign with proper audience segmentation so performance is reported per audience rather than blended.
Read performance by audience — ROAS by audience, spend by audience, clicks by audience — to identify which segments actually work.
Shift budget and creative toward the audiences that perform and away from those that do not.
Keep past-purchaser audiences distinct because their role is repeat purchase and upsell, not first conversion.
Note that PMax does not provide this level of audience reporting, which is the core reason for running Demand Gen separately.
caveats: Audience sizes can be too small for reliable reporting in low-traffic stores; segmentation only pays off above a data threshold.
The audience list is the presenter's recommendation, not an exhaustive standard.
cards.source_name: The Best E-commerce Google Ads Strategy for 2026.docx

cards.title: Segment Demand Gen Reporting by Network and Optimize Creative Accordingly
cards.summary: Use Demand Gen's network/placement segmentation to see whether YouTube in-stream, Shorts, Discover, Gmail, or Display is driving results, then reallocate creative and budget to what works.
cards.use_when: Optimizing image/video retargeting creative and placement allocation for an ecommerce store running Demand Gen.
steps: In the Demand Gen campaign, click to segment by network so you can view performance at the individual ad or ad group level.
Evaluate each placement separately: YouTube in-stream, YouTube Shorts, Google Discover, Gmail, and the Display network.
Where a placement performs (for example, the source's illustration of Shorts outperforming Display), produce more creative suited to it — e.g., more portrait-format videos for Shorts.
Where a placement underperforms and cannot be fixed, consider turning it off entirely and focusing creative effort on the remaining placements.
Run creative variations and double down on what performs, cutting what does not.
Note that this level of creative testing and iteration is described as impossible within PMax, which hides placement data.
caveats: The Shorts-vs-Display example is illustrative, not a predicted outcome for your account.
Placement availability and labeling in Demand Gen change over time; verify in the current interface.
cards.source_name: The Best E-commerce Google Ads Strategy for 2026.docx

cards.title: The PMax ROAS-Floor Hack: Keep PMax as a De-Prioritized Safety Net
cards.summary: Set PMax's ROAS target far above your manual campaigns (e.g., manual at 300-400%, PMax at 600-700%) so higher manual bids win most auctions while PMax catches leftover queries and audiences.
cards.use_when: After building Standard Shopping, Search, and Demand Gen campaigns, deciding what to do with the existing Performance Max campaign.
steps: Do not pause or delete PMax — keep it active but de-prioritized.
Set PMax's ROAS target significantly higher than your new manual campaigns. The source's example: if manual campaigns run around 300-400% average ROAS target, set PMax to 600% or even 700%.

Understand the mechanism: lower ROAS targets in manual campaigns translate to higher CPC bids, so Google prioritizes those campaigns and they win more auctions, getting the lion's share of impressions and clicks.
Let PMax act as the catch-all: it picks up search queries your Search campaigns did not cover or audiences your Demand Gen campaigns missed.
Monitor that PMax is genuinely de-prioritized rather than still dominant, and adjust the target gap if it keeps taking meaningful volume.
Treat the 300-400 vs 600-700 numbers as an illustrative starting ratio, not a required setting.
caveats: This is the source's described hack, not a documented platform feature or guarantee.
ROAS targets must be meaningful in your own account's economics; the example numbers may be inappropriate for low-margin catalogs.
Behavior of platform bidding and target semantics can change; verify current mechanics before relying on the effect.
cards.source_name: The Best E-commerce Google Ads Strategy for 2026.docx

cards.title: Set Different ROAS Targets for Incremental vs Non-Incremental Traffic
cards.summary: Apply aggressive ROAS targets to high-intent branded traffic and lower targets to non-brand acquisition, so reported performance reflects true business growth instead of funnel re-engagement.
cards.use_when: Setting campaign-level ROAS targets or evaluating whether reported Google Ads ROAS represents genuine new-customer growth for an ecommerce store.
steps: Classify traffic by incrementality: branded and retargeting traffic is high-intent and easier to convert but often less incremental; non-brand acquisition is lower-intent but more likely to be a sale you would not otherwise have gotten.
Set aggressive (higher) ROAS targets on high-intent branded traffic.
Set lower ROAS targets on non-brand acquisition to allow more aggressive bidding for incremental growth.
Interpret blended or PMax-reported ROAS with caution: the source warns that strong ROAS can hide an over-reliance on retargeting and branded traffic that was already in the funnel.
Judge success by whether non-brand/incremental volume grows, not only by the headline ROAS figure.
Keep brand and non-brand reporting separated wherever possible so you can apply and monitor the distinct targets.
caveats: This is a strategic framing from the presenter, not a formula; appropriate target levels depend on margins and customer economics.
Incrementality is not directly measured by the platform's default ROAS reporting.
cards.source_name: The Best E-commerce Google Ads Strategy for 2026.docx

cards.title: Decide Between PMax-First and Manual Multi-Campaign Structures
cards.summary: Choose PMax alone for simplicity, or the three-component manual build (Standard Shopping + segregated Search + Demand Gen) when you have the time and expertise to scale beyond PMax's control limits.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much Google Ads campaign structure to operate for an ecommerce store, based on available time, skill, and scaling ambitions.
steps: Assess honestly whether you are a beginner or time-constrained operator: the source states PMax is a solid, efficient starting point for that situation.

If you want to scale beyond PMax's ceiling, build the three dedicated components instead: Standard Shopping campaigns, segregated Search campaigns (brand vs non-brand), and Demand Gen campaigns for image/video retargeting.
Expect the manual build to outperform PMax in each component when run properly, because each component gets custom structure and optimization PMax does not expose.
Plan for the management load: this structure requires keyword research, feed work, ad copy testing, audience segmentation, and ongoing bidding decisions.

If you lack the time or expertise, the source's alternative is to have an agency build and manage the structure for you, so the decision becomes build-in-house vs outsource rather than PMax vs manual.
Reassess periodically as data accumulates on which components beat the PMax baseline in your account.
caveats: The claim that the manual structure significantly outperforms PMax is the presenter's experience, supported by agency case examples rather than a controlled test.
Agency results cited (e.g., specific eyewear and bedding ROAS figures) are examples, not promises for other stores.
The source has a commercial interest in recommending the managed-service path.
cards.source_name: The Best E-commerce Google Ads Strategy for 2026.docx

cards.title: The Rule of One: Anchor Each Ad and Landing Page to a Single Big Idea
cards.summary: Michael Masterson's Rule of One says compelling sales messages center on one big idea rather than stacked selling points, with evidence from 91 of the top 100 offers.
cards.use_when: Deciding the core message for a paid social ad, landing page, advertorial, or PDP before briefing creative or writing copy.
steps: Before writing, select one big idea to be the 'tip of the spear' for the ad or page. Everything else is subordinate to it.
Apply Masterson's three tests to the candidate idea: it must be easy to understand, easy to believe, and interesting or unique. If it fails any test, keep hunting.
Strip out competing selling points. Masterson calls stacked, unrelated claims 'tossed salad copy' — throwing many selling points in hoping one sticks, which dilutes conversion power.

Make all sub-bullets, arguments, facts, and stories serve only to reinforce the single concept. A 'six morning strategies' list works only if all six are sub-points of one core benefit; if each is unrelated, it is a tossed salad.
Review your best-converting ads and check whether they share simplicity, directness, and clarity — use them as evidence for how narrow your message should be.
Recognize the hard part is choosing the one idea, not writing the copy. The writing gets simpler once the single idea is fixed.
caveats: The 91-of-100 claim comes from Masterson's review of top historical offers and is the source's evidence, not a guaranteed outcome at your scale.
The presenter's opinion that the best-converting ads are 'the ones that do best are the simplest' is a personal observation, not a universal rule.
cards.source_name: The Copy Rule I Learned From The Best Copywriter I Know.docx

cards.title: Audit Ad and Page Copy for 'Tossed Salad' Clutter
cards.summary: Diagnose cluttered messaging that stacks unrelated selling points, then consolidate it into one reinforcing argument.
cards.use_when: Reviewing an underperforming ad, landing page, or advertorial that has accumulated multiple selling points over iterations.
steps: Read the creative or page and list every distinct selling point, claim, and benefit that appears.
Flag any point that is not a sub-point of the same core idea — those are the tossed-salad elements.
Identify which single point is easiest to understand, easiest to believe, and most unique. That becomes the candidate big idea.
Rewrite remaining sub-bullets, stories, facts, and arguments so each one reinforces that one concept rather than introducing a new angle.
If a strong sub-point cannot be made to reinforce the core idea, cut it; do not keep it 'just in case'.
Re-read the final message and check that a stranger could state its one argument back in a sentence.
caveats: Cutting compelling-but-off-topic points is uncomfortable; the source frames that discomfort as the forcing function that improves selection.
This is a messaging framework, not a testing protocol — validate any rewrite with your own ad or page tests.
cards.source_name: The Copy Rule I Learned From The Best Copywriter I Know.docx

cards.title: Use the Rule of One to Force a Single USP
cards.summary: A USP should be one core proposition everyone immediately understands, not nineteen competing propositions.
cards.use_when: Defining or revising the unique selling proposition for a product launch, brand campaign, or product page.
steps: Gather every plausible selling proposition you have for the product or offer.
Apply Masterson's three criteria as a filter: easy to understand, easy to believe, counterintuitive or unique.
Select one proposition as the anchor. The source is explicit that you want one core selling proposition, not 19.
Position that proposition as the central claim of the ad, landing page, and any supporting advertorial.
Check that the proposition is believable — a counterintuitive claim that is not credible will not move buyers.
Use the selected USP to decide which supporting proof, testimonials, and facts belong on the page, and which to drop.
caveats: The source presents this as Masterson's framework rather than a tested rule; results depend on product and audience.
Uniqueness that isn't believable fails the framework's own test — don't chase novelty alone.
cards.source_name: The Copy Rule I Learned From The Best Copywriter I Know.docx

cards.title: Set Up a TikTok Business Center and Advertiser Account Cleanly
cards.summary: Create a dedicated TikTok Business Center with a business-domain email, verified advertiser account and backup payment method before spending on ads.
cards.use_when: You are launching a store's first TikTok ads and need foundational account infrastructure that supports smoother approvals and billing.
steps: Go to business.tiktok.com and click Get Started; sign up with a business email address rather than a personal one, because TikTok reportedly gives better ad approval rates with business domains.
Even if you already have a personal TikTok account, register with email and password so personal and business identities stay separate.
In the Business Center, add billing information, then click Add an Advertiser Account and create a new one; complete the business name and verification prompts.
Open Payment Management > Settings and add a credit card first for faster approval.
Add a backup payment method such as PayPal so a failed card debit does not trigger ad disapprovals.
Verify the current TikTok interface and any regional verification requirements, since the exact menu labels and steps change over time.
caveats: The approval-rate advantage for business domains is the presenter's recommendation, not an independently verified benchmark.
Exact URLs and menu names may change; confirm in the live ads manager.
cards.source_name: The Only TikTok Ads Tutorial You Will Ever Need (Beginner To Advanced).docx

cards.title: Install the TikTok Pixel Through Shopify Partner Integration
cards.summary: Install the TikTok Pixel via partner integration and confirm core conversion events such as complete payment are tracking before launch.
cards.use_when: You are preparing a Shopify store to run TikTok conversion campaigns and need reliable purchase event tracking.
steps: In Ads Manager, open Tools > Events > Get Started Web and select your website.
Choose Partner Integrations rather than manual setup when Shopify or Google Tag Manager is available, because partner syncing is simpler.
Authorize access and complete the onboarding flow; wait the short sync period.
Confirm the pixel shows as active on the right-hand side of the events screen, and verify core conversion events such as complete payment are being received.
If no partner integration is available, use manual setup and follow the on-screen instructions.
Verify the current interface, as event names and setup paths can change.
caveats: Pixel verification is a prerequisite; do not assume events are flowing just because installation appeared to succeed.
Partner integrations may not cover every store setup or region.
cards.source_name: The Only TikTok Ads Tutorial You Will Ever Need (Beginner To Advanced).docx

cards.title: Use the Three-Tier Campaign Pyramid for TikTok Ads
cards.summary: Structure TikTok campaigns as objective-level campaigns, experiment-level ad groups and creative-level ads to keep testing organized and scalable.
cards.use_when: You are building or restructuring a TikTok ad account for a product store and want clear separation between objectives, audiences and creatives.
steps: Create one campaign per main objective (for example, web conversions for a product store, lead generation for email capture, or traffic for early creative testing).
Under each campaign, create multiple ad groups that each control budget, targeting, schedule and bid, treating each ad group as a mini experiment testing something specific.
Inside each ad group, place multiple ad creatives (videos, copy, CTAs) so you can compare creative variations within the same audience and budget.
Avoid dumping your entire budget into a single ad group; spread spend across several experiment ad groups.
When reviewing results, judge each ad group independently, because the algorithm learns separately at the ad group level and a losing ad group does not drag down a winning one.
Use a naming convention covering product, objective and date (for example, 'shoes-conversion-Feb-04') to keep reporting readable.
Verify current UI naming, since TikTok periodically renames objectives and settings.
caveats: The source's claimed separation of ad group learning is based on the presenter's client experience, not published TikTok documentation.
This structure is a starting heuristic; high-spend accounts may consolidate ad groups differently.
cards.source_name: The Only TikTok Ads Tutorial You Will Ever Need (Beginner To Advanced).docx

cards.title: Configure a Conversion Ad Group with Broad Targeting and $50/Day
cards.summary: Set up a web-conversion ad group with pixel-based complete payment optimization, TikTok-only placement, broad demographic targeting and at least $50/day.
cards.use_when: You are creating the first TikTok conversion ad group for a store and need concrete settings and a defensible minimum budget.
steps: In the ad group, select your installed pixel under Data Connection and choose 'complete payment' (or another deep purchase event) as the optimization event.
Set Manual Placement and untick everything except TikTok if you want to focus on the main feed first.
Choose location (for example, United States) and a basic age range such as 18–35; keep gender generic and leave other targeting broad so the algorithm can find buyers.
Set the budget to at least $50 per day per ad group; the source argues lower spend will never generate enough data to identify what works.
Leave the schedule continuous rather than time-of-day optimization until you have evidence for scheduling changes.
Change the optimization goal from value to conversions.
Verify current optimization goal and placement labels in the live interface before launching.
caveats: The $50/day minimum is the presenter's stated heuristic after managing over $5M in TikTok spend for clients; it is not a platform guarantee.
Broad targeting assumes enough country-level audience volume; small markets may need broader settings.
cards.source_name: The Only TikTok Ads Tutorial You Will Ever Need (Beginner To Advanced).docx

cards.title: Build Three Custom Audiences, Then Lookalikes Instead of Direct Retargeting
cards.summary: Create 180-day web visitors, 30-day video completers and uploaded customer files as seeds, then use lookalike audiences in cold ad groups rather than targeting the seeds directly.
cards.use_when: You have a Shopify store with pixel traffic, video views or customer data and want to build TikTok audiences for prospecting campaigns.
steps: In Tools > Audience Manager, click Create Audience > Custom Audience.

Build three seed audiences: (1) web traffic page views in the last 180 days, (2) engagement audience of people who completed your videos in the last 30 days (100% watch), and (3) an uploaded customer CSV.
Name them clearly, such as '180 days web visitors', '30 days video views' and 'customer file'.
Do not target these seeds directly; instead click Create Lookalike Audience and select each custom audience as the source.

Set the lookalike location to the country you are targeting and generally use the 'balanced' setting for large markets like the U.S.; use broad for small markets such as Finland to keep the pool large enough to spend.
In the ad group, add the lookalike audience under Include Audience to tell TikTok to find more people similar to your seed.
Verify current audience manager options, as retention windows and lookalike settings are interface-dependent.
caveats: Retention windows and lookalike expansion options are platform-specific and can change; the 180-day and 30-day windows are the presenter's recommendations.
If seed audiences are very small, lookalikes may be ineffective.
cards.source_name: The Only TikTok Ads Tutorial You Will Ever Need (Beginner To Advanced).docx

cards.title: Keep Interest Targeting to Two or Three Broad Parent Categories
cards.summary: Limit TikTok interest targeting to a few broad parent categories because stacking 15+ interests raises spend and constrains the algorithm.
cards.use_when: You are setting interest targeting for a TikTok conversion ad group and are tempted to stack many detailed interests.
steps: Select no more than two to three broad, related interests, such as 'fashion and accessories' for an apparel store.
Choose parent categories rather than drilling into many sub-interests, so TikTok's algorithm can identify buyers.

Use the source's example as orientation: a fashion brand started with over 15 detailed interests and saw cost per result above $100 consistently; after stripping down to one broad fashion category, the source reports CPA dropped to 34–41 (currency unit not specified).
Treat this as a case study, not a promise; your category, price point and creative quality affect results.
Pair with behavioral targeting sparingly; the source generally uses only one behavior setting such as iOS 8 and above.
caveats: The reported CPA drop is a specific client case from the presenter's agency, not a general TikTok benchmark.
Broad interest targeting is a current recommendation; seasonal or niche products may need different treatment.
cards.source_name: The Only TikTok Ads Tutorial You Will Ever Need (Beginner To Advanced).docx

cards.title: Use a Four-Week Targeting Ladder to Refine Audiences Without Overspending
cards.summary: Start broad in week one and add one layer of targeting per week—basic interest, then lookalikes, then stacked winners—to gather data while controlling costs.
cards.use_when: You are launching or scaling a TikTok campaign and want a structured sequence for audience refinement instead of guessing all targeting at once.
steps: Week 1: run broad targeting with only location and basic age range.
Week 2: add one basic interest category that matches the product niche.
Week 3: introduce lookalike audiences built from your custom audience seeds (see the custom/lookalike card).
Week 4: stack winning audiences that performed in earlier weeks, combining lookalikes and proven interests.
Keep budget at the ad group level so each week's tests remain independently readable.
Use the weekly data to decide whether to keep, refine or kill audience configurations rather than making all changes at once.
caveats: The ladder is the presenter's current recommendation; the optimal pace depends on spend volume and how quickly your ad groups accumulate enough impressions.
Do not stack audiences before you have enough spend to learn from each testing layer.
cards.source_name: The Only TikTok Ads Tutorial You Will Ever Need (Beginner To Advanced).docx

cards.title: Apply the 3:3 Creative Testing Framework Across Hooks, Angles and CTAs
cards.summary: Test three hooks, three angles and three CTAs per product, with at least three distinct ad styles, to find converting creative combinations.
cards.use_when: You have a product to advertise on TikTok and need a structured creative testing plan rather than random video variations.
steps: For each product, create at least three distinct ad styles: a solution/problem video, a tutorial-style video and a lifestyle/UGC-testimonial video.
Within those, vary three hooks, three angles and three CTAs so each test has clear separation between variables.
Test the same creatives against different audiences, because the source reports some creatives bomb with cold traffic but perform well with warm traffic.
Use the winning hooks, angles and CTAs to build the next round of variations rather than changing everything at once.
Verify the current ad creation interface for how to duplicate or vary creatives across ad groups.
caveats: The '3:3 method' is the presenter's internal framework; the specific number of variations may need adjusting for lower budgets or smaller catalogs.
Results depend on product-market fit, offer and landing page, not creative variation alone.
cards.source_name: The Only TikTok Ads Tutorial You Will Ever Need (Beginner To Advanced).docx

cards.title: Structure a 3:2:1 Test: Three Creatives, Two Audiences, One Objective
cards.summary: Run a first test with three distinct ad creatives, two audience types and one clear objective over three to four days for roughly $300–400 total.
cards.use_when: You are launching a first paid test for a store and need a concrete test plan with budget, duration and audience options.
steps: Set the objective to a single clear conversion goal, such as web conversions or complete payment.
Allocate at least $50 per ad group per day for three to four days, giving a total test budget around $300–400.
Creative one: pain-solution video with the pain point as hook, a demo of the solution and a clear CTA.
Creative two: tutorial-style video with a how-to format, feature highlights and an educational angle.
Creative three: UGC testimonial with real results, before-and-after and an authentic feel.
Audience one: broad interest-based targeting using one or two relevant interests, no age restriction or demographic narrowing.
Audience two: lookalike audience based on purchases, narrowed to top markets such as the U.S. or U.K., with no extra restrictions.
Use distinct styles so the test has clear winners and losers rather than marginal differences.
caveats: The 3:2:1 structure and $300–400 budget are the presenter's recommended test; smaller stores may need to run shorter or lower-budget tests.
The source says this framework generated over eight figures in sales for their clients; treat as a case example, not a guarantee.
cards.source_name: The Only TikTok Ads Tutorial You Will Ever Need (Beginner To Advanced).docx

cards.title: Check Core TikTok Metrics in the First 24–72 Hours
cards.summary: Use early CTR, watch time and CPM thresholds to diagnose whether a TikTok ad is failing on creative, audience or hook before spending more.
cards.use_when: You have launched a TikTok ad group and need a fast, structured read on whether to fix, kill or scale it.
steps: Within the first 24 hours, check that CTR is above 1%, watch time is above 25% and CPM is under $15.
After three days, look for CPC under $2, add-to-cart cost below $10 and purchase cost under $30.
If CTR is below 1% within 24 hours, treat it as a creative problem and produce a stronger hook or transitions.
If CPM is above $20, treat it as an audience problem and adjust targeting.
If watch time is below 20%, treat the hook as insufficient and create variations of the first three seconds.
Kill the bottom 50% of ads after three days and double down on the winners with new variations.
Do not optimize any ad before spending at least $50 or reaching 1,000 impressions, because the data is not yet meaningful.
Verify current metric benchmarks, as the presenter's thresholds are TikTok-specific snapshots and may vary by market and product.
caveats: These thresholds (CTR >1%, watch time >25%, CPM <$15, CPC <$2, ATC <$10, purchase <$30) are the presenter's current heuristics, not universal benchmarks.
The $50 or 1,000-impression minimum is the source's stated floor for statistical significance; it does not guarantee a reliable read.
cards.source_name: The Only TikTok Ads Tutorial You Will Ever Need (Beginner To Advanced).docx

cards.title: Use the Diagnostic Checklist to Separate Creative Problems from Audience Problems
cards.summary: Map specific early performance failures to the right fix: weak hook, creative transitions or audience targeting.
cards.use_when: A TikTok ad group is underperforming and you need to decide whether to change the creative or the targeting before spending more.
steps: If CTR is low (below 1% in the first 24 hours), replace the creative with a stronger hook and better transitions rather than changing audiences first.
If CPM is high (above $20), adjust audience targeting and broaden or refine the audience setup; do not assume the creative is the sole cause.
If watch time is low (below 20%), remake the first three seconds specifically rather than overhauling the whole video.
Continue to check each metric independently within the first 24–72 hours, since multiple issues can coexist.
After three days, if the ad group is still weak, kill the bottom 50% and reinvest into winners instead of repeatedly patching failing creative.
Verify current platform reporting, as metric windows and definitions can change.
caveats: The thresholds are the presenter's stated TikTok benchmarks; different categories and markets may perform differently.
A low CTR can also result from poor product-market fit or a mismatched landing page, which the diagnostic does not cover.
cards.source_name: The Only TikTok Ads Tutorial You Will Ever Need (Beginner To Advanced).docx

cards.title: Use Native Video Formats and the Five Highest-Converting Hook Patterns
cards.summary: Make TikTok ads that look like organic content using UGC, POV or tutorial formats, and open with one of five hook patterns to stop the scroll.
cards.use_when: You are creating ad creative for a store on TikTok and need formats and hook patterns that match the platform rather than TV-style ads.
steps: Choose from the three formats the source says are performing: UGC, POV story and tutorial/how-to video.
Avoid making ads look like TV commercials; the moment content looks like an ad, viewers scroll past.
Open with one of five hook patterns: pattern interruption, controversial statement, curiosity gap, visual hook or time-based hook.
Aim to stop the scroll in the first three seconds and deliver on the hook's implied 'what's in it for me' quickly.
Use text overlays for silent viewers, fast pacing and multiple micro-CTAs throughout the video.
Verify current TikTok creative best practices, as formats and trending patterns change quickly.
caveats: The source's format and hook lists are current observations from the presenter's agency, not fixed platform rules.
Avoid claims or visuals that violate TikTok ad policies; native-looking creative still must comply with platform rules.
cards.source_name: The Only TikTok Ads Tutorial You Will Ever Need (Beginner To Advanced).docx

cards.title: Follow the 0–35 Second Ad Structure and Technical Specs
cards.summary: Build TikTok ads in four timed sections—hook, promise, proof, CTA—and meet minimum video specs such as 9:16 and 15–35 seconds.
cards.use_when: You are scripting and producing a TikTok ad for a store and want a concrete structure and export settings.
steps: Structure the first 0–3 seconds as the hook.
Use 3–15 seconds for the core promise or problem.
Use 15–30 seconds for proof and demonstration.
Use the final 30–35 seconds for the call to action.
Layer pattern interrupts every two seconds, text overlays for silent viewers and multiple micro-CTAs throughout the video.
Use emotional triggers such as before/after, transformations or validations.
Export at 9:16 aspect ratio (1080 x 1920), keep the file under 500 MB, and aim for a video length of 15–30 seconds; the source says their sweet spot is around 32 seconds.
Keep cuts every two to three seconds, use trending sounds from TikTok's library where appropriate, keep background music at most 80% volume and voiceover at -3 dB, and add captions for accessibility.
caveats: The 'sweet spot' length of 32 seconds is the presenter's finding, not a universal rule.
Technical specs such as 1080 x 1920, codec and file size may change; confirm current TikTok upload requirements.
Trending sounds for ads may have commercial-use restrictions; the source later notes using commercial music in CapCut for ads.
cards.source_name: The Only TikTok Ads Tutorial You Will Ever Need (Beginner To Advanced).docx

cards.title: Build a High-Retention Ad with an Undeniable Hook and Rhythmic Editing
cards.summary: Analyze a 30M-view TikTok ad to learn how a curiosity-driven hook, promised payoff and varied clip rhythm can sustain retention.
cards.use_when: You are editing a TikTok ad for a store and want to increase watch time and rewatch rate through pacing and payoff structure.
steps: Open with a hook that implies a clear 'what's in it for me', such as revealing an underrated resource or tool.
Keep the hook short—around two seconds—and deliver on its promise quickly so viewers feel rewarded.
Cut clips at varied lengths (some 3 seconds, some half a second) to create rhythm and avoid monotony.
Vary the audio and visual cadence: alternate speaking and silence, zoom in and out, and accelerate clips to create fast-to-slow pacing.
End by delivering the promised payoff, such as showing the actual tool or result.
If retention is the priority, test ads without a spoken call to action; the source says CTAs can damage retention and rewatch rate, and TikTok automatically adds a clickable button.
Verify current features, as automatic ad buttons and retention metrics are platform-dependent.
Note: the 30M views, 2.3M likes and 7% CTR are specific results from the source's client, not a guarantee.
caveats: The recommendation to omit a verbal CTA is the presenter's opinion based on retention metrics; it may not apply to every product or campaign objective.
Retention is one factor among many; conversion still depends on offer, landing page and product fit.
cards.source_name: The Only TikTok Ads Tutorial You Will Ever Need (Beginner To Advanced).docx

cards.title: Edit UGC-Style TikTok Ads in CapCut with the Agency Formula
cards.summary: Use CapCut to trim hooks, apply a 4K filter, add hook text, add commercially safe music and export at 1080p with a defined workflow.
cards.use_when: You are producing TikTok ad creative in-house and need a repeatable editing workflow with specific settings.
steps: Film clips with natural window light, a clean background, phone held vertically, in 3–5 second segments and from multiple angles.
In CapCut, create a project, drag in raw clips and click Adapt to convert everything to 9:16 vertical format.
Apply the 4K filter across the entire timeline as the base effect for UGC-style ads.
Trim the first clip to a maximum of three seconds and make it the strongest hook.

Add text over the hook clip using a readable font such as Gilroy Semi Bold or your brand font; adjust tracking tighter, position the text just above eye level and add a subtle stroke or outline if visibility is poor.
Apply a typewriter text animation to the hook text as a small pattern interrupt.
Add background music from CapCut's commercial music section—not TikTok sounds—to keep usage commercially safe; lower music to 70% if using a voiceover.
Export at 1080p, H.264, MP4, 60 fps and recommended bit rate. Always preview on a phone before uploading.
Structure the ad as hook, problem, solution, call to action and ensure text and pacing reflect that sequence.
caveats: CapCut's interface, filter names and export settings may change; verify the current app version.
The source recommends CapCut because it is free and TikTok-owned, but other editors can produce equivalent results.
Commercial music availability and licensing terms can change.
cards.source_name: The Only TikTok Ads Tutorial You Will Ever Need (Beginner To Advanced).docx

cards.title: Use a Naming Convention and Avoid Smart Campaigns for Cleaner Testing
cards.summary: Name campaigns by product, objective and date, and toggle off smart campaigns to preserve manual control over ad group testing.
cards.use_when: You are creating TikTok campaigns for a store and need reporting clarity plus full control over testing variables.
steps: Before launching, define a naming convention: product, objective and date (for example, 'shoes-conversion-Feb-04').
On the campaign creation screen, toggle off smart campaigns so you retain flexibility over ad group structure.
Apply the convention consistently across campaigns, ad groups and ads so labels stay readable in reporting.
Use the naming to quickly identify which product, objective and test date each row belongs to when reviewing performance.
Verify current TikTok naming and smart campaign options, as the interface and defaults change.
caveats: Smart campaigns may be useful in some accounts; the source recommends disabling them for the testing structure described.
Naming conventions are internal process, not a platform feature.
cards.source_name: The Only TikTok Ads Tutorial You Will Ever Need (Beginner To Advanced).docx

cards.title: Meta CPM inflation and the efficiency trade-off
cards.summary: Why Meta's ad costs rise every year and what that means for how you plan creative and offers on your store's account.
cards.use_when: Planning annual ad budget, forecasting CPM/CPA inflation, or explaining to a founder why yesterday's winning creative stopped being profitable.
steps: Understand Meta's core objective: maximizing revenue per user per minute. It grows this by adding ad inventory (more ads per feed, more surfaces) and by raising CPMs.
Accept that CPM inflation of roughly 20–30% year over year is the norm (the source measured this across 150M+ in spend; factor out natural dollar inflation).
Recognize Meta cannot simply make advertisers unprofitable, so alongside CPM increases it must improve conversion efficiency and ROI for advertisers.
Practical implication: a creative or offer that broke even 12 months ago may now be unprofitable. Bake CPM inflation into your target CPA and margin assumptions when setting bids and budgets.

Because Meta constantly rolls out updates (Andromeda, Gemini, smaller ones), treat every update as an attempt to raise ad-serving efficiency so it can charge more — expect to keep improving creative and landing pages, not just structure.
Verify current platform features and inflation figures in your own account before forecasting.
caveats: The 20–30% figure is the presenter's observation from their aggregated data and is cyclical with Black Friday; it is not a universal benchmark.
Some advertisers can still be profitable on Meta during CPM inflation, but the margin of safety narrows.
cards.source_name: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

cards.title: Last-click reality vs. Meta's multi-touch optimization
cards.summary: Why ad-level ROAS in the UI misleads budget decisions and why you should evaluate creative at the adset level.
cards.use_when: Deciding which ads to kill or scale, or reconciling an ad's reported ROAS with actually getting spend.
steps: Know that the platform shows last-click attribution, giving full credit to the final ad a user clicked before buying.
Meta itself optimizes across multi-touch sequences, spreading credit across the chain of impressions and clicks that led to the purchase.
Consequence: an ad that looks like a loser on last-click may still be genuinely contributing, and Meta may keep spending on it because it sees earlier or later value in the sequence.

Because bidding and optimization are inherited at the adset level (cost caps are set at adset, never ad level), evaluate creative performance and make budget decisions at the adset level, not the ad level.
When you see one ad soaking up credit while others look weak, ask whether they are part of a sequence before cutting them.
For incrementality you care about, use 7-day-click or incremental attribution views before reallocating budget — the source found an ad showing 7x ROAS that was actually 1.9x incremental.
caveats: The source's 7x vs 1.9x example is a single case, not a promised ratio.
Check current attribution and reporting options in the platform, since interfaces change.
cards.source_name: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

cards.title: Trust the algorithm's breakdown spend distribution
cards.summary: Why breakdowns (placement, age, gender, region) rarely justify restructuring, and how incremental returns explain apparent misallocation.
cards.use_when: Tempted to launch a dedicated campaign for a placement or demographic that shows higher ROAS in a breakdown report.
steps: When a breakdown shows one segment (e.g., Stories at 4x ROAS) beating another (Feed at 3x) yet getting less spend, don't assume Meta is misallocating.

Understand the breakdown effect: Meta is testing increments. It has already tried pushing more spend into the higher-base-return segment and hit zero incremental returns; the lower base-return segment still returns more on each additional dollar.
Metaphor: if an ad at $300/day gains nothing at $320 but another at $200/day earns more at $250, Meta routes spend to the second even though its base ROAS is lower.

Practical rule: unless you are a very experienced media buyer, do not implement changes based on complex breakdowns or ad-level ROAS. Beginners who over-segment breakdowns usually make commercially misaligned decisions and get worse performance.
Focus instead on the things with real leverage: creative, landing pages, and the structure of adsets.
caveats: There are genuine cases where spend distribution is wrong, but identifying them requires expertise the source says most advertisers lack.
Breakdown data is blended and does not capture incremental impact.
cards.source_name: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

cards.title: Creative-as-targeting and why broad targeting works
cards.summary: Meta's retrieval system now uses your creative to find buyers, so interest and lookalike targeting are largely obsolete.
cards.use_when: Setting up a new cold campaign or considering interest/lookalike tests instead of broad targeting.
steps: Shift from the old model (pick interests/lookalikes, then load creative) to the current model: load creative, leave targeting broad, and let Meta's retrieval system read the creative and serve it to relevant users.
Understand why interests are flawed: they record interaction (a like, comment, click) not intent. Someone posting 'I hate dogs' gets labeled interested in dogs.

Meta's modeling now behaves like a high-dimensional vector space (the source illustrates ~10,000 dimensions). Real-time interactions move each user through the space, and users cluster naturally; your ads are spread broadly and Meta finds the hotspots where people buy.
Fact: with broad targeting, Meta targets the whole space, finds buying hotspots, and as you scale the target area expands into colder people — which is why ads fatigue during scaling.
Replace interest-targeting tests with landing-page tests and CRO experiments, which the source says produce larger conversion-rate inflections.
Don't burn test budget on interest or lookalike audiences; the source asserts interests are flawed and lookalikes don't work.
caveats: Personal opinion attributed to the source: interest targeting 'shouldn't be in your account.' Some advertisers report niche cases where interests still help — validate in your own account.
Broad targeting requires strong creative; weak creative will simply fatigue faster as you scale.
cards.source_name: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

cards.title: Consolidation beats segmentation: the campaign-level data silo
cards.summary: Why fewer campaigns generally perform better and how conversion-data splitting at the campaign level drives that.
cards.use_when: Restructuring a Meta account that has many campaigns, or deciding whether to add a new campaign or adset for a new angle or product.
steps: Know the architecture: conversion data is siloed most strongly at the campaign level, shared more at the adset level, and inherited downward. Every added campaign chunks your conversion signal.
Example: 100 conversions/month split across four campaigns means each gets ~25 — less signal, worse optimization via small sample size bias.
Expect an efficiency boost when you push through roughly 100–200 conversions per month because Meta finally has enough signal to understand who to target.
Therefore consolidate up at the campaign level. At the adset level, segmentation swings efficiency only around 5–10% — you can segment or consolidate more freely there.
Do not stack multiple creatives into a single flexible ad: you lose insight into which creative is working, so you can't make more of the winner.
Exception: keep campaigns separate where unit economics differ, personas don't overlap, or regions need independent budget control.
caveats: The 5–10% adset swing and 100–200 conversion threshold are source heuristics, not universal constants.
Total consolidation into one campaign/one adset is a bad idea for ~90% of brands per the source; only a minority can get away with it.
cards.source_name: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

cards.title: Five diagnostic questions for account structure
cards.summary: The product, margin, persona, region and creative-volume questions to answer before designing any Meta structure.
cards.use_when: Designing or restructuring a store's Meta account to match the business's products, margins and goals.
steps: Ask how many product categories you have — more categories (with differing goals) generally require more segmentation.
Ask how wide the margin spread is — if margins vary substantially by category, you may need campaigns that prevent low-margin items from soaking up spend.
Ask whether you have multiple personas that genuinely don't overlap — non-overlapping personas belong in the structure; slightly tweaked versions of the same person don't.

Ask how many regions you sell in — multiple regions usually require campaign-level segmentation to control spend distribution and sell-through, especially if you hold inventory or have per-region revenue targets.
Ask what your creative throughput is — 10 ads/month allows little segmentation; 2,000 ads/month needs a methodical pipeline from testing into scaling structures.
Apply two non-negotiables: data integrity (the structure must produce readable, actionable data) and commercial alignment (the structure must reflect margins, goals, and categories that need spend).
caveats: There is no universal perfect structure; the answer depends on each business's specifics.
Structures that aren't readable are not actionable and force costly restructures.
cards.source_name: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

cards.title: Generic sub-$50k/month Meta structure
cards.summary: A simple, low-segmentation structure most small advertisers can run while testing concept-based creatives.
cards.use_when: Launching or cleaning up a Meta account spending under roughly $50k/month with limited creative volume.
steps: Run one dedicated testing campaign (CBO or ABO) with adsets built around concepts. A concept = Persona + Angle + Offer, and creatives are made under that combination.
Place 3–5 creatives per adset as a starting point; you can go higher if you genuinely have the creative volume, but most sub-$50k accounts don't.
When you make more creatives for a concept: if the adset is underperforming, add them to that same adset to try to revive it.
If the adset is hitting KPI, don't touch it — launch the new creatives in a new adset for the same concept. 'Never touch something that's working.'
Expect this to produce multiple adsets for one winning concept over time; that's fine and expected.
Exclude existing customers from the cold/testing campaign so retargeting purchases don't skew results.
Verify current campaign settings and audience-exclusion options in the platform before launching.
caveats: This generic structure is not tailored to any business; use the five diagnostic questions for a custom build.
The source states a hard rule — don't change a performing adset — which is an opinion based on media-buying experience, not a measured law.
cards.source_name: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

cards.title: Budgeting the retargeting support layer
cards.summary: Treat retargeting as a capped, small support campaign and calculate its budget from audience size, frequency and CPM.
cards.use_when: Setting or auditing retargeting/DPA spend for existing customers or engaged audiences.
steps: Define retargeting (DPAs, existing-customer ads) as a support layer, not a growth driver. Cap it rather than letting it scale with the account.
Calculate the retargeting budget with the formula: Total Audience Size × Desired Frequency × CPM.
Set a frequency ceiling: the source keeps existing-customer retargeting under a frequency of 7 on a 30-day rolling window.
For a small CPG-style account, the retargeting campaign may be as small as roughly $20/day — enough to capture incrementality without over-spending.
Exclude existing customers from cold campaigns so retargeting revenue doesn't overattribute into cold and push frequency up artificially.
In fashion, where existing-customer targeting is more incremental, split the retargeting campaign into two adsets (new arrivals and DPA) so DPA doesn't absorb all spend.
caveats: The formula's frequency and CPM inputs must come from your own account and audience estimates.
The $20/day and frequency-7 figures are source examples, not universal targets.
cards.source_name: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

cards.title: Calculating daily testing budgets by back-propagation
cards.summary: Derive the daily test budget from target conversions, expected CPA and test duration instead of guessing.
cards.use_when: Setting the daily spend for a specific creative or landing-page test and deciding how long to run it.
steps: Decide the target number of conversions you want the test to observe (enough for a meaningful read).
Multiply target conversions by expected CPA to get total test cost.
Divide by test duration in days (the source's example uses 7 days) to get the daily testing budget.
Example structure: 20 conversions × $30 CPA = $600 total; over 7 days that's ~$86/day.
Use this to back-propagate from business goals to the platform budget rather than picking a round number.
Keep the test budget separate from scaling spend so you can evaluate the outcome against a known conversion threshold.
caveats: All inputs are account-specific; the 7-day example is illustrative, not a required duration.
Conversion counts this small produce noisy reads, so treat the result as directional.
cards.source_name: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

cards.title: Choosing ABO vs CBO by conversion volume and signal
cards.summary: When to let the campaign distribute budget (CBO) versus controlling it per adset (ABO).
cards.use_when: Deciding campaign budget type for a store, especially with high AOV, low order volume, or risky product ranges.
steps: Default to CBO (Advantage campaign budget) when conversion volume is healthy: the algorithm distributes spend more efficiently than you will and can operate on an 80/20 pattern where 20% of ads get 80% of spend.

Switch toward ABO (adset-level budgets) when conversion volume is very low, e.g. a $10k AOV brand doing ~5 orders/day. With so little signal Meta optimizes upstream on CPC/CTR/hold rate, and those metrics have almost no correlation with revenue except at extremes.
Recognize the drawbacks of full CBO: no control over testing, no spend for new creatives, and dependence on one fatigue-prone winner.
Contrast with ABO: you control where spend is forced, which de-risks and enables testing, but a novice can burn money by forcing spend into weak adsets.
Rule of thumb from the source: an inexperienced in-house buyer should lean CBO; an experienced buyer can run mid-structure with controlled spend.
Audit case: a $20–30M furniture brand's consolidated CBO put 57% of spend into a DPA adset showing 7x ROAS but only 1.9x on incremental or 7-day-click — DPA overspend on cold audiences is common.
caveats: The furniture 7x vs 1.9x example is a single audit, not a universal pattern.
CPC/revenue correlation claim is the source's assertion; verify in your own data.
cards.source_name: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

cards.title: Segment accounts by unit economics and audience
cards.summary: When margin spread, non-overlapping personas, or high AOV/low volume make segmentation worth the added complexity.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to separate products, categories or audiences into their own campaigns despite the consolidation rule.
steps: Watch for margin spread: if category A carries 70% margin and category B 60%, or if distressed ('grade C') inventory must be discounted, consolidation can funnel spend into compressed-margin items and hurt contribution margin and branding.

Watch for non-overlapping personas: for a menswear/womenswear brand, put men's and women's ads in one adset and the adset gets confused — check via the gender breakdown whether women's ads are serving to men. Women buying for partners is directional and real, but the reverse is rarely efficient.
Watch for high AOV/low volume: a $10k AOV brand at ~5 orders/day lacks the signal for CBO to optimize on purchases, so its structure must differ from a typical account.
When you do segment, keep campaigns aligned to how the business thinks about products, margins and goals (commercial alignment).
Where possible, push category segmentation down to adsets rather than multiplying campaigns, to limit data chunking.
caveats: Segmentation carries a data-splitting cost; only segment for a concrete commercial reason.
The gender-mismatch audit pattern is a screening heuristic, not proof of poor performance in every category.
cards.source_name: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

cards.title: Worked example: CPG brand structure with one persona and two markets
cards.summary: How a one-product, one-persona, 70%-margin CPG brand at $5M/year should structure Meta for US and AU.
cards.use_when: Designing structure for a simple consumable product with high repeat rate and few personas.
steps: Use one consolidated cold campaign per country (one for US, one for AU) — do not manufacture extra personas at this revenue level.
Run creative testing at the adset level based on concepts, with most spend flowing to the one concept/persona currently performing.
Exclude existing customers from both cold campaigns — in CPG, returning-customer revenue will overattribute into cold and inflate frequency through self-retargeting.
Add a small existing-customer/retargeting campaign at very low spend (roughly $20/day at this size) to capture incremental revenue while holding frequency under 7 over 30 days.
Keep it simple: one advantage-plus-cold campaign per market plus a small retargeting layer.
Treat repeat-purchase behavior as the reason to exclude customers, not a reason to scale retargeting.
caveats: This is a source example for specific parameters (one product, one persona, 70% GM, $5M); changing any parameter may change the structure.
cards.source_name: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

cards.title: Worked example: fashion brand with SKUs, personas and regions
cards.summary: How a 50-SKU, four-persona fashion brand at $5M/year should structure Meta across AU/NZ and UK.
cards.use_when: Designing structure for a multi-category, multi-region store with discounting and seasonal differences.
steps: Create category campaigns (e.g., pants, tops, dresses) because purchase orders, revenue goals and sell-through differ per category and unsold stock goes to sale and erodes margin.
Consolidate AU and NZ into one campaign: NZ typically maxes out at 7–10% of total spend and orders fulfill from an Australian warehouse.

For the UK, decide based on inventory: if UK stock is held in Australia, you can consolidate regions and sell through stock anywhere; if you make UK seasonal purchase orders (northern vs southern hemisphere seasons), keep the UK separate.
If you keep separate regions, move category segmentation down to adsets inside one AU campaign and one UK campaign to avoid doubling to six campaigns — this also handles separate UK subdomains/URLs.
Add a DPA retargeting campaign to engaged audiences (e.g., 90-day site visitors).
Add an existing-customer retargeting campaign with two separate adsets — new arrivals and DPA — so DPA doesn't absorb all spend and you can keep showing new arrivals to repeat buyers.
Exclude existing customers from cold campaigns.
caveats: Region consolidation is contingent on where inventory physically sits and whether regions have independent targets.
Fashion existing-customer targeting is described as more incremental than other categories, which justifies the extra spend.
cards.source_name: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

cards.title: Page caps, whitelisting and regional pages
cards.summary: How to keep running high creative volume once you hit Meta's active-ad cap per page.
cards.use_when: Scaling weekly creative output and being blocked from launching more ads on a single page.
steps: Know the cap: Meta allows roughly 300–500 live ads per page, which high-volume accounts hit quickly.
Option 1 — duplicate pages: create multiple brand pages with minor differences (e.g., a different logo color) and run ads across them. Example cited: Gruns with ~15 Gunrs pages.
Option 2 — partnership ads: run ads through a real influencer/creator's page; often requires paying the creator if they have leverage.

Option 3 — whitelisting: create a third-party-style page (e.g., 'Fiber Health Magazine') and run the same or advertorial-adjusted ads through it; the third-party framing reduces the 'being sold to' feel.
Option 4 — regional pages: if you run separate country campaigns (UK, AU, US) and hit the cap, create per-country pages so each region gets its own cap.
The source would do all of these simultaneously and isn't concerned about consolidating onto a single page.
caveats: The exact cap changes over time — verify the current limit in Meta's interface.
Some advertisers have brand-team concerns about consolidating onto one page; the source notes some do.
cards.source_name: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

cards.title: What media buying still controls (and what's dead)
cards.summary: Prioritize structure, concept-level adsets and customer allocation over bids, budget tweaks and interest tests.
cards.use_when: Allocating media-buyer time across an account, or deciding which levers to pull for efficiency.
steps: Stop daily bid tweaks with cost/bid caps — the source calls this low-leverage; even if it yields ~5%, the same hours spent on better creative can double or triple the account.
Stop daily budget pacing for small accounts; it churns campaigns and decisions are made on tiny samples. Both were viable around 2019–2020 but not now.
Focus on account structure and architecture aligned with commercial objectives.
Focus on concept-level segmentation at the adset level (Persona + Angle + Offer).
Focus on controlling percent/dollar allocation to existing customers over time.
Replace interest-targeting tests with landing-page tests and CRO experiments on the site, which the source says move conversion rates more.
Recognize media buying still matters at high spend ($100k+/month), where the source estimates 10–20% efficiency lift from good buying; at ~$100/day it is not the main lever.
caveats: The 5% bid-tweak gain and 10–20% buying lift are the presenter's estimates, not measured benchmarks.
CRO-first emphasis is a strong opinion from the source, not a universal rule.
cards.source_name: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

cards.title: Concept definition and adset grouping rule
cards.summary: Group ads by Persona + Angle + Offer so each adset trains on one commercial idea.
cards.use_when: Building adsets or deciding which creatives belong together in a cold campaign.
steps: Define a concept as the intersection of Persona + Angle + Offer; build the creatives underneath that concept.
Place each concept in its own adset so Meta's targeting model learns one coherent audience rather than a mix.
Do not group unrelated creatives (e.g., men's and women's apparel) in one adset — adsets learn in isolation, so mixing confuses targeting and spreads the ad to everyone.

When adding creatives to an existing concept: if the adset is failing, add to it to try to revive performance; if it's hitting KPI, leave it untouched and add creatives as a new adset for the same concept.
Expect a single winning concept to proliferate into many adsets over time as you add fresh creative.
caveats: Ads-level reporting can still mislead due to sequencing, so judge at the adset level.
cards.source_name: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

cards.title: Why 2018-style interest segmentation stopped working
cards.summary: The historical shift from segmented interest structures to consolidating, creative-led buying.
cards.use_when: Understanding why a legacy agency's heavily segmented structure underperforms, or deciding whether to keep many interest adsets.
steps: Understand the old mechanic: each new adset served to ~1,000 random people and Meta zoned in based on that small sample, producing divergent results across identical adsets — which favored heavy segmentation.

Note the turning points: iOS 14 cut offsite signal used for interest grouping (the source cites about 30% of targeting signal lost), prompting a shift to creative-led retrieval; AI/inference investment further raised ad-serving efficiency; consolidation became preferred.
Recognize the current state: conversion data is siloed at the campaign level on every major platform (Meta campaigns/adsets/ads; Google campaigns/ad groups/ads), so segmentation chunks your learning.

Practical takeaway for an operator: legacy hyper-segmented structures, often run by cheaper agencies serving smaller businesses, are likely hurting performance — push toward consolidation and concept-based adsets.
If you are spending $10k–$20k/month with a cheap agency running legacy segmentation, this is directly relevant to your account.
caveats: The ~30% signal loss and small-sample history are the source's account; treat as historical context, not current measurement.
Consolidation is the general default but has exceptions for margin, personas and regions.
cards.source_name: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

cards.title: Three settings-style cleanups to audit before restructuring
cards.summary: A reminder to verify interface toggles and default settings before any restructure, plus the non-negotiable principles.
cards.use_when: Preparing a Meta account for restructuring or an audit.
steps: Before restructuring, check the account's settings and toggles for anything that only affects spend distribution and is not part of your intentional structure — the source lists turning off three settings as an immediate action.
Verify each toggle's current name and location directly in Meta Ads Manager, since Meta renames these frequently; the source intentionally did not rely on stable names.

Apply the two structural non-negotiables while cleaning up: data integrity (the structure must yield readable, actionable reporting) and commercial alignment (the structure must reflect product margins, categories, and goals).
Review whether your current campaigns hide categories that need spend or allow low-margin or end-of-life inventory to absorb budget.
Only after these checks, decide on consolidation vs. segmentation using the five diagnostic questions.
caveats: The specific 'three settings' are not named in the source text; do not guess them — confirm in the live interface.
Any settings advice is time-sensitive and should be validated against current Meta documentation.
cards.source_name: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

cards.title: Never Touch a Performing Ad Set — Fork It Instead
cards.summary: Preserve winning Meta ad sets untouched and route new creative and new spend into adjacent ad sets and campaigns to protect what already works.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to add new ad creative into an existing Meta ad set or spin it into a new one during creative testing or scaling.
steps: Judge the existing ad set first: if it is not hitting your CPA or ROAS KPI, drop new creatives directly into it and try to make it perform.
If it is hitting KPI, do not add anything to it. The source's stated number one rule of Meta media buying is never touch something that is working — do something next to it.
Launch the new concept as a separate ad set so the winning ad set keeps its learning and delivery undisturbed.
Accept the resulting sprawl: it is normal for six of ten ad sets to belong to a single winning concept made up of creative produced over time.
Layer in a scaling campaign only once an ad set genuinely outperforms target (the source's example is above a 5x return) and all soft metrics are strong.
When a winner plateaus at a spend ceiling, place the same post IDs into a scaling campaign while still scaling inside the testing campaign at ad set level.
caveats: Scaling-campaign duplication typically unlocks roughly an extra 20% daily spend on a good day — at $60/day base that is about $10, which the source says is not worth the complexity.
At roughly $400/day base the same move yields about $80/day, and doing it across ten top ads might unlock about $1,000/day, which the source considers worthwhile.
cards.source_name: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

cards.title: Exclude Existing Customers and Set 7-Day Click Attribution
cards.summary: Protect ad test integrity by excluding past purchasers from cold campaigns and reading results on 7-day click attribution.
cards.use_when: Configuring audience exclusions and attribution settings before launching cold acquisition campaigns or interpreting their results.
steps: Exclude existing customers from cold testing campaigns so repeat buyers do not flow through acquisition ads and make weak concepts look stronger than they are.
Set the account or campaign attribution to 7-day click so numbers reflect a consistent window rather than claiming conversions unrelated to the ad.
Enable audience segments in advertiser settings so you can later break down spend and ROAS by new, engaged and existing segments.
After setup, confirm existing-customer spend is near zero in the breakdown; any meaningful spend there signals your exclusion is broken.
When any number looks suspiciously strong, check the attribution window and audience segment breakdown before drawing a creative conclusion.
caveats: The source notes excluding existing customers matters less at very low spend scales but should still be done for clean testing.
Attribution windows and interface locations change; verify current placement in Ads Manager before relying on them.
cards.source_name: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

cards.title: Set Test Budgets by Back-Propagating from CPA
cards.summary: Size each ad set test budget as a multiple of target CPA (3x minimum, 5x preferred) so the test reaches a real yes/no decision.
cards.use_when: Setting ad set budgets and kill rules for a new creative concept test in a Meta account.
steps: Take your target CPA — for example $50 per customer — and multiply by three to get the spend threshold before deciding keep or kill (here $150).
At $150 spent: three or four conversions means keep running; two conversions is a yellow light — let it run another ~$50 before deciding; zero or one means cut it.
The source personally prefers waiting to 5x target CPA (here $250) where the client permits, because the first chunk of spend is learning who to target and efficiency usually improves after that.
At 5x there is no yellow light — the decision is strictly yes or no because enough spend volume exists to judge.
Apply the same logic to ad sets, not individual ads, since concepts are what you are validating.
If you cannot afford the multiplier threshold for a concept, you do not yet have the volume to evaluate it — fix other business levers first.
caveats: This is a stated rule of thumb, not a platform mechanic; the source is deliberately more generous than the standard because early spend is exploratory.
Low-conversion-volume businesses (high AOV, few purchases) need longer windows and may still struggle to reach clean thresholds.
cards.source_name: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

cards.title: Run Tests One Week to Capture Seasonality and Time-to-Purchase
cards.summary: Set test duration by balancing two forces — daily seasonality and time to purchase — typically landing near one week.
cards.use_when: Choosing how many days to let a creative or concept test run before reading results and making a kill or scale decision.
steps: Identify your daily seasonality: strong days and weak days will bias results if a test only runs on one slice of the week.

Identify your time to purchase: if buyers typically see two to four impressions over three to four days before purchasing, a one-day test kills the top-of-funnel ad that was warming those buyers, and other ads capture the conversion.
Balance the two variables to set a duration: one week is the source's general recommendation.
For larger, more stable businesses with short time to purchase, compress to three to four days.
For tiny budgets with long time to purchase and heavy daily seasonality, extend to 10–14 days.
Do not read results on windows shorter than the volume can support: the source would not read data on less than a 5-day period at the sub-$50k/month spend level.
caveats: Duration heuristics depend on conversion volume — the source notes a business doing a thousand conversions a day can read two-day windows while three conversions in three days cannot support short windows.
The goal is fast feedback loops for iteration, but not at the cost of biased reads.
cards.source_name: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

cards.title: KPI at Ad Set Level and Scale Budgets in 20% Daily Steps
cards.summary: Manage sub-$50k/month accounts by KPI-ing ad sets on target CPA or ROAS and raising winning budgets about 20% per day.
cards.use_when: Running routine optimization in a small Meta ad account where spend volume is too low for heavy campaign segmentation.
steps: Read performance at the ad set level against your target CPA or target ROAS over a reasonable rolling window.
If the ad set hits KPI, increase budget in roughly 20% increments per day rather than doubling.
If it misses KPI, diagnose why — what was wrong in that creative — then produce more ads and concepts, and either wind the ad set down or turn it off.
KPI the scaling campaign at the campaign level instead, since the source's structure has no ad set segmentation there.
KPI retargeting on incremental ROAS using an attribution breakdown, and watch frequency so it does not exceed about seven on a 30-day window.
Do not set ad set budgets using the legacy '50 conversions in a 7-day window' rule — for most businesses this back-propagates to far too much budget.
caveats: The source explicitly ties the 20% step and 5-day minimum window to this spend tier; larger accounts may behave differently.
The 50-conversion rule is criticized as producing oversized budgets relative to average order value and expected CPA.
cards.source_name: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

cards.title: Keep Account Structure Consolidated at Low Spend
cards.summary: At low spend, consolidate conversions into few campaigns, use structured creative testing, and avoid segmentation you cannot read.
cards.use_when: Designing a Meta account structure for a business spending under roughly $50k per month.
steps: Consolidate: with low conversion volume, keep segmentation minimal so all conversions pool into a small number of campaigns.
Use a structured creative testing campaign that forces spend through new ad sets so you can learn rather than waiting for the algorithm to allocate.
Do not build multiple campaigns, funnels or persona splits merely because spend feels high enough — you likely lack both volume and business complexity to justify it.
Only add campaigns when a specific commercial objective (a distinct funnel, persona, or product category with different economics) aligns with the business.
Verify any new campaign has enough conversion volume to produce readable data and a decision loop.
caveats: The source frames this as a framework, not an exact structure, because every business differs.
Adding segmentation solely for appearances breaks the data-integrity and commercial-alignment rules the structure is built on.
cards.source_name: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

cards.title: Layer Campaigns at $50k–$250k with a Commercial Reason
cards.summary: Add campaigns at mid-scale spend only when each one maps to a funnel, persona, or product with different economics and its own KPI.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to add campaigns or ad sets as a store's Meta spend scales from about $50k to $250k per month.
steps: For a single-SKU CPG brand, split campaigns by funnel/persona: the source's fish oil example runs one campaign targeting 65+ for arthritis with VSSLs, native statics, older-demographic testimonials and TV-style ads cut to UGC, and a second campaign repositioning the same product for 25–35 for brain health with different landing pages, different creators and heavier whitelisting.

For a multi-SKU fashion brand, split by commercial lever instead: a new-arrivals campaign to push sell-through, and a dedicated campaign for a category (for example pants) where LTV analysis shows higher first-purchase AOV and stronger repeat rates — accepting a higher CPA KPI because the customers are higher quality.
Keep the retargeting campaign existing-customer only unless a specific reason exists to add website visitors.
Give each new campaign a stated reason tied to margin, portfolio or persona rather than adding campaigns to look sophisticated.
Expect more ad sets as creative volume grows, and two or three cold campaigns rather than one.
caveats: The source warns against layering campaigns without a commercial objective — that breaks data-integrity and decision-loop fundamentals.
LTV-based category CPA targets require actual repeat-rate data, not assumption.
cards.source_name: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

cards.title: Build Creative Concepts as Persona × Angle × Offer × Ad Type
cards.summary: Run a concept matrix so ad sets map to structured concepts and creative output becomes directional rather than random.
cards.use_when: Planning monthly creative production and setting up ad set structure for a Meta account at mid to high spend.
steps: Define each concept as a combination of persona, angle, offer and ad type.

Worked teeth-whitening example: persona coffee drinkers, angle whitening without sensitivity, offer just the product, ad type UGC — then rotate many ad types under that ad set since ad type is flexible.
Second concept: persona brides, angle get ready for your wedding in 14 days, offer a 14-day bundle, ad type testimonial with before/after and process documentation.
Third concept: persona smokers, angle remove stains, offer a subscription (relevant because the problem persists), ad type founder-to-camera because the founder was a smoker.

Once a concept works, double down: build a dedicated landing page and funnel around it (the source's 'wedding in 14 day bundle' example) and scale it while continuing to develop other angles and personas.
Inspect results at concept level regularly and feed insights back into the next creative batch, directing more volume to winning concepts and attention to losing ones.
caveats: The source references a separate 30-minute video on creative concept building for depth.
The source says to launch roughly 100–300 new ads per month at $50k–$250k spend for growth — a stated volume target, not a platform requirement.
cards.source_name: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

cards.title: Use Concept Testing to Shape Retention and Product Strategy
cards.summary: Concept-level performance tells you who you are acquiring and in what proportions, which should feed retention flows and product expansion.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to route post-purchase retention, win-back and product portfolio decisions based on ad account persona data.
steps: Track which persona/angle concepts actually drive customers and in what share — for example the source's question of whether 40% of customers arrive as smokers and 40% as brides-to-be.
When a persona performs strongly (the bride example), increase creative volume, build a custom landing page, and adjust the offer to match.
Expand product categories to meet that audience, since you are now generating a steady stream of that customer type.

Build post-purchase retention and win-back flows specific to that customer's stage of life — the source's example sends a free gift after the wedding ('congrats on getting married') pulling the customer into a different product line.
Keep concept targeting niche enough to produce these persona insights; broad targeting yields no reliable persona data and bleeds inefficiency into the rest of the business.
caveats: This is applied reasoning from the source's framework, not a tested ecommerce result.
Requires enough conversion volume per concept to attribute customers reliably.
cards.source_name: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

cards.title: Run a Dedicated Promo Campaign to Protect Learning
cards.summary: Segment promotions into their own campaign so repeated promo launches do not disrupt testing and scaling learning.
cards.use_when: Running frequent promotions (the source's example runs every three to four weeks) in a Meta account with active testing and scaling campaigns.
steps: Pull all promo creative out of the testing and scaling campaigns and run it in a separate promo campaign.
Rationale: promos turn over fast, so launching them inside testing or scaling constantly turns ads off and launches new ones, disrupting campaign learning and unsettled results.
Accept that the promo campaign also targets a somewhat different customer — the source describes it as prioritizing price-sensitive consumers — so it warrants separate optimization.

Do the same extraction for any funnel that grows large enough to deserve its own KPI: in the source's example an advertorial funnel consuming about 30% of total spend was pulled into a dedicated campaign.
Keep testing and scaling campaigns stable, adding spend there rather than churning their composition.
caveats: Running promos every three to four weeks is the source's example, not a recommended promo cadence.
Dedicated campaigns add management overhead that is only justified at higher spend levels.
cards.source_name: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

cards.title: Consolidate Website-Visitor Retargeting into Cold Campaigns
cards.summary: For most accounts, skip a dedicated website-visitor retargeting campaign because existing campaigns already reach engaged audiences.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to build a website visitor retargeting campaign for a store's Meta account.
steps: Run the audience segment breakdown in Ads Manager to see spend, ROAS and share going to new, engaged and existing audiences — this requires audience segments to be enabled in advertiser settings.
Check whether the engaged (website visitor) segment already receives meaningful spend at meaningful frequency from your cold campaigns.
For most accounts — the source says about 90% — no dedicated website visitor campaign is needed because existing testing and scaling campaigns allocate enough spend there.
