cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads 2026 Free Course.docx

cards.title: Configure DSA Targets and Negatives by Category
cards.summary: Segment DSA ad groups by product theme and block non-commercial pages to avoid wasted spend on irrelevant queries.
cards.use_when: Setting up or cleaning up dynamic search ads for a multi-category store.
steps: Choose your ad targets: all landing pages from standard ad groups, URL-based rules (URL contains a category term), category equals, or specific URLs.
Segment at the ad group level by theme — one DSA ad group per category such as men's shoes, women's shoes, children's shoes — rather than mixing everything in one group.
Add negative ad targets for pages you don't want crawled or served against, such as privacy policy, blog pages and return policy, especially in the initial phase.
Once running, review your search term report frequently and continue adding irrelevant terms as negatives.
Apply the same bidding discipline as RSAs: manual bidding in a new account, then automated once conversions reach roughly 30+ per month per the source's heuristic.
caveats: DSA is best used to expand reach and mine new keywords alongside existing RSAs, not usually as the sole campaign type.
Google's autonomy means the landing page a visitor sees may differ from the one you'd pick.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads 2026 Free Course.docx

cards.title: Use DSA as a Test Proxy for Performance Max Search
cards.summary: Test search behavior with DSA before committing budget to Performance Max, since the search component behaves similarly.
cards.use_when: Planning a move into Performance Max or deciding whether to run DSA first for a store.
steps: If already running shopping or video campaigns, add DSA campaigns to generate readouts on how search within Performance Max is likely to perform.
Compare DSA search performance against your existing RSA performance to gauge whether adding Performance Max makes sense.
Use DSA for keyword mining at the same time: it can surface new converting search terms that RSA keyword research misses given the volume of new queries daily.
Feed any strong DSA search terms back as keywords in more tightly controlled campaigns.
caveats: This is the source's analogy, not a guaranteed equivalence — treat DSA results as directional evidence.
Performance Max behavior and interface change often; confirm current capabilities.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads 2026 Free Course.docx

cards.title: Decide Whether to Run Branded Search
cards.summary: Run branded search campaigns when competitors bid on your brand or you need early conversion data, and skip them when you already dominate organic with no competition.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to allocate budget to a branded search campaign for a store.
steps: Run branded search if competitors are bidding on your brand name, or if the account is new and needs easy conversion volume to feed machine learning.
Skip it (per the source, almost always) if there is no competitor bidding and your organic listing reliably shows first for brand queries, since you would just pay for traffic you already get.

If you run it, target exact match brand variations (brand, brand + shoes, brand reviews, brand men's) and map each to a relevant page — reviews page for review queries, collection page for category queries.
Add your brand as phrase match to capture untargeted long-tail brand terms, then promote converting search terms from the search term report into exact match keywords.
Exclude branded terms from all other search campaigns via negative keyword lists or brand exclusions, so non-brand campaigns are measured on genuinely incremental traffic.
caveats: The 'almost always skip' stance is the presenter's opinion and depends on your organic ranking and competitive reality.
Excluding brand from other campaigns matters for interpreting incrementality; not doing so inflates non-brand performance.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads 2026 Free Course.docx

cards.title: Branded Search Ad Copy, Bidding and 90% Impression Share
cards.summary: Use manual CPC, pin the brand in headline one and target 90%+ impression share on branded search so competitors cannot take bottom-funnel clicks.
cards.use_when: Setting up copy, bids and targets for a branded search campaign.
steps: Pin headline one to your brand name with an authority framing (for example 'brand official store'), since searchers are already looking for you.
Test multiple headline-two angles — offer, shipping, feature/benefit — but generally pair the brand headline with some form of offer.
Add multiple sitelinks to expand the ad and send users to collection pages, active promotions, bestsellers and a dedicated reviews page for trust.
Bid with manual CPC and aim for over 90% impression share, or use target impression share as an alternative; the source avoids automated bidding on branded campaigns.
Track the cost per conversion — the source expects branded conversions to cost only a couple of dollars — and investigate if it is materially higher.
caveats: The 'over 90% impression share' and 'couple of dollars' figures are the source's targets, not universal benchmarks; they will vary by market and competition.
The advice to never use automated bidding on branded campaigns is a strong presenter preference and should be treated as opinion.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads 2026 Free Course.docx

cards.title: Performance Max Basic Setup for Ecommerce
cards.summary: Configure Performance Max for purchase value, exclude your brand and hand it clean assets and first-party signals.
cards.use_when: Launching a Performance Max campaign for an ecommerce store.
steps: Create a new campaign, choose Sales, optimize for purchases, select Performance Max and link your Merchant Center account so products are available.
Choose conversion-value focus rather than conversion-count focus, since order values differ across the catalogue.
Leave the target ROAS field blank initially and let the campaign run on maximize conversions for the first 2–4 weeks so the algorithm can learn.

Set location and language, then add a brand exclusion (all brand spellings and misspellings) or a negative keyword list so the campaign does not serve on your own brand where dedicated branded campaigns exist.

Skip Google's AI asset generation and supply your own assets: roughly 6–7 headlines (30 characters each), long headlines (90 characters), and 3–4 descriptions (90 characters), plus images, videos, sitelinks and extensions.

Name each asset group by product theme and segment by theme rather than selecting all products, because centralizing copy, landing pages and creative around one theme is more coherent than letting Google bundle everything.
caveats: Interface layout for campaign creation changes; verify current steps in the account.
The source says more than 15 headlines is unnecessary but that filling slots is optional.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads 2026 Free Course.docx

cards.title: Performance Max Budget, Search Themes and Audience Signals
cards.summary: Set a PMax daily budget of at least 3x average CPA and use first-party customer lists as the main signal.
cards.use_when: Sizing budget and configuring signals at Performance Max launch for a store.
steps: Set the average daily budget at least at 3x your non-branded average CPA — for example, a $40 CPA implies a floor of about $120/day.
If the store cannot commit roughly $100/day to Performance Max, prefer running shopping and search campaigns instead of funneling a small budget into PMax.

Add search themes only if you deliberately want to push search hard inside PMax, using proven converting keywords or search terms from the account; otherwise omit them because they can cannibalize traffic from your search campaigns.

Add audience signals using first-party lists — all-time customers, top-value customers, or last-12-months customers — which the source has seen shorten the learning phase compared with leaving it blank or using custom/in-market segments.
caveats: The 3x average CPA budget rule and roughly $100/day minimum are the source's heuristics, not calculated requirements.
The source reports poorer performance when search themes are added throughout their accounts and mixed outside feedback on audience signals — treat both as directional.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads 2026 Free Course.docx

cards.title: Performance Max Learning Phase and Bid Progression
cards.summary: Give Performance Max 4–6 weeks and move from maximize conversion value to target ROAS once it reaches about 50 conversions per month.
cards.use_when: Managing an early-stage Performance Max campaign and deciding when to change bid strategy.
steps: Expect a long learning phase for Performance Max — sometimes 4–6 weeks — and avoid frequent structural changes that prolong it.
Start on maximize conversion value and review whether the campaign reaches roughly 50 conversions per month inside a single campaign.
At that point transition to target ROAS and set the target at or slightly below the campaign's actual ROAS so the algorithm keeps room to spend.
Then either scale by raising spend while holding the target, or gently raise the target ROAS as efficiency improves.
Review campaign structure changes only after the learning phase has settled.
caveats: The 50-conversions-per-month threshold is the source's heuristic and should be tested against your own campaign volume.
Setting target ROAS far above actual performance typically strangles spend rather than improving efficiency.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads 2026 Free Course.docx

cards.title: Ongoing Performance Max Optimization Checklist
cards.summary: Review search terms, negatives, channel mix, audiences and assets on a regular cadence because PMax is not set-and-forget.
cards.use_when: Running weekly or monthly optimization on a Performance Max campaign for a store.
steps: Review search term reports (and search categories) for irrelevant terms and add negatives; in new accounts or new campaigns check every 48–72 hours.
Check brand exclusions are in place for both your own brand and, if desired, competitor brands, keeping brand and non-brand traffic cleanly separated for honest performance measurement.

Review channel/new PMax reporting to see impressions, interactions, spend and purchase value by network — search vs shopping vs video — and use a script like the one credited to Mike Rose for asset-group level cost and top-product detail if in-platform reporting is incomplete.

Inspect audience segments for demographic and in-market skew (the source cites an example of 5x more clicks from one age band) and use those findings to build custom segments for this or other campaigns.
Review asset performance (headlines, descriptions), remove persistently poor performers and add fresh angles to test on a recurring basis.
caveats: Micro-script and channel reporting availability varies by account and UI state; verify current reporting before relying on it.
Asset performance labels are Google's representations, not ground-truth conversion measures.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads 2026 Free Course.docx

cards.title: Choose One or Two Performance Max Campaigns Over Sprawl
cards.summary: Consolidate PMax into one campaign with themed asset groups until budget allocation clearly justifies splitting out a scaling campaign.
cards.use_when: Structuring a store's Performance Max campaigns when deciding between consolidation and segmentation.
steps: When running significant shopping and manual search alongside PMax, consolidate into one PMax campaign with asset groups separated by theme (bestsellers, category two, category three).

If a theme — for example bestsellers — is not getting adequate budget, extract it into a second, scaling-focused PMax campaign with a more aggressive target aimed at known bestsellers and top converters.
Keep the remaining adjunctive categories in the efficiency-focused campaign.

Reach for consolidation first; the source notes most brands in the roughly $100k–500k/month Google Ads range still benefit most from consolidated structure, with segmentation becoming more worthwhile above that level and only in certain cases.
caveats: The $100k–500k per month range is the source's observation of its client base, not a formula.
Even above that level, the source says there are cases where segmentation is better — do not treat consolidation as an absolute rule.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads 2026 Free Course.docx

cards.title: Demand Gen for Remarketing to Cart Abandoners
cards.summary: Build remarketing with Demand Gen rather than Display, optimizing for purchases and targeting cart abandoners.
cards.use_when: Setting up a remarketing campaign to recover abandoned carts for an ecommerce store.
steps: Go to ads.google.com, open campaigns, create a new campaign, choose sales as the objective and purchases as the conversion focus.
Select Demand Gen as the campaign type, which serves image and video ads across YouTube, Discover, Gmail and the display network, so you can reach returning visitors without relying on display alone.
For the starter campaign in the source's example, target cart abandoners so the ads speak directly to people who reached the cart but did not complete a purchase.
Serve dynamic remarketing creative so the ads reference the products the visitor viewed.
Use Demand Gen for remarketing before display; the source reports Demand Gen far outperforming display for remarketing across its accounts.
caveats: The source's remarketing example is described as a setup demonstration — no specific conversion lift figures are given, so avoid assuming results.
Demand Gen placement and campaign creation options change frequently; verify the current interface.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads 2026 Free Course.docx

cards.title: Demand Gen remarketing setup for cart abandoners
cards.summary: Step-by-step Google Ads Demand Gen campaign configuration for retargeting imported cart-abandoner audiences with purchases as the conversion goal.
cards.use_when: Setting up a Google Ads retargeting campaign aimed at shoppers who added to cart but did not buy.
steps: Go to ads.google.com, click Campaigns, then the blue plus button and New campaign.
Choose Demand Gen as the campaign type; set objective to Sales and conversion focus to Purchases.
For a cart-abandoner campaign the source generally excludes the product feed and reports stronger performance without it.
Leave target cost per action unset initially; give the campaign a daily budget (the walkthrough used a £50/day example).
Set location and language at ad group level, and typically turn off TV screens under device targeting.
In the ad group, add your imported cart-abandoner audience as a custom audience and add no other audience signals.
Turn OFF optimized targeting — for remarketing you want only people who performed the desired action, not lookalike expansion.
Choose channels: the source excludes the Google Display Network and runs YouTube (in-stream, in-feed, Shorts, Discover) plus Gmail, which they report gives higher-quality traffic.
Pick an ad type based on the offer: single image for a strong simple offer, carousel image for high product variety, video when storytelling or offer nuance is needed.
caveats: The channel mix that works for one account may differ; the presenter explicitly says others will have different opinions on excluding Display.
Requires a large enough cart-abandoner list to be worth targeting.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads 2026 Free Course.docx

cards.title: Five objections that explain cart abandonment and how to answer them in ads
cards.summary: A five-bucket framework for diagnosing why shoppers abandon carts and matching each objection to specific remarketing ad creative.
cards.use_when: Writing retargeting ad creative or offer copy for cart abandoners, and choosing which objection to lead with.
steps: Bucket each abandonment reason into one of five objections; the source notes more than one can apply.
Complacency/distraction — the shopper was browsing casually and forgot. Answer with urgency so they feel the offer may expire; the source shows a high-urgency static creative as the example.

Price/value — 'too expensive.' Answer by justifying price, comparing to competitors, or using price-per-unit for CPG-style products; the source cites Harry's comparing a $16 refill against a market leader at $40, and positioning the product as an investment rather than a purchase.
Trust/credibility — 'is this company legit?' Answer with PR callouts, third-party review platforms (e.g. Trustpilot) and as much social proof as possible throughout the funnel.
Product efficacy — 'will this even work?' Answer with real customer photos and inset reviews so prospects see someone like themselves for whom it worked.

Logistic friction — shipping, delivery time, cost, returns. State your shipping/returns/warranty terms as attractively as your margins allow; the source's example shows free worldwide shipping and returns plus a 24-month warranty.
Once you see which objection audience responds to on remarketing, push that same signal (trust/social proof, etc.) up into higher-funnel creative to prevent abandonment earlier.
caveats: Not every brand can offer free worldwide shipping and returns; the source says to offer the most attractive options within your means.
Example competitor pricing and review screenshots are illustrative, not benchmarks.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads 2026 Free Course.docx

cards.title: Is YouTube a fit for your store? Four prerequisites
cards.summary: Qualifying criteria (AOV, demonstrability, patience, existing winning Meta creative) to check before committing to YouTube ads.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to add or launch a YouTube/Demand Gen channel for a DTC store.
steps: Check AOV: the source says a $25–$30 AOV makes success very unlikely; $75–$100 is ideal and anything above $50 is usually a workable starting point.
Check demonstrability: can you clearly show the product's value in video? If not, YouTube is likely the wrong channel.
Check patience and budget: expect choppy performance for an initial four-to-six-week period before deciding.
Check your Meta creative: you should already have winning ad creative on Meta before moving to YouTube — do not use YouTube as a creative testing ground.
Validate your offer on Meta first (faster feedback) and know your customer avatar in detail; the source says if you don't know your avatar inside out, do not touch YouTube ads.
If budget is already spread thin across acquisition channels, don't cannibalise a working channel to fund YouTube — consolidate on what works.
caveats: AOV thresholds are the presenter's working heuristics, not calculated benchmarks.
If AOV, demonstrability or patience are missing, the source recommends waiting rather than forcing the channel.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads 2026 Free Course.docx

cards.title: YouTube campaign configuration: Demand Gen, Shorts only, maximise conversions
cards.summary: How to configure a Demand Gen YouTube campaign (post Video Action deprecation) to run Shorts-only with mobile devices and learning-phase bidding.
cards.use_when: Launching a YouTube prospecting campaign and choosing channels, devices, bidding and budget.
steps: Use Demand Gen as the campaign type (Google deprecated Video Action campaigns in March 2025); objective Sales, goal Conversions.
In channels, select only YouTube Shorts — exclude in-stream, in-feed, Discover, Gmail and Display when running a Shorts-only play.
Exclude TVs, and generally exclude tablets; the source often (not always) excludes desktop to keep Shorts on mobile.
Turn OFF optimized targeting for a new campaign with a new audience; start narrow then expand. Test turning optimized targeting on later if you want the algorithm to expand.
Bid strategy: start on Maximize Conversions with a daily budget so Google can spend and learn; the source warns a Target CPA set with no data can suffocate spend and the campaign never takes off.
Expect choppy performance in the learning period (roughly pronounced for about two weeks) even if the setup is correct.

After about two weeks, wait for a consistent CPA pattern across a three-to-five-day window, then switch to Target CPA set at or slightly below current CPA (the source gives a $40 CPA → $35–$36 TCPA example when pushing efficiency early).
Budget rule of thumb: aim for about three times AOV as daily budget (e.g. $60 AOV → $180/day).
caveats: The source says allowing a higher TCPA lets more learning happen and optimises faster, but efficiency suffers short-term.
The Video Action deprecation and Demand Gen interface details are the source's account and may change — verify the current Google Ads interface.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads 2026 Free Course.docx

cards.title: Start narrow and expand horizontally on YouTube targeting
cards.summary: Why the source rejects Meta-style broad targeting on YouTube and instead builds three narrow audiences per product/avatar.
cards.use_when: Building audience targeting for a new YouTube or Demand Gen prospecting campaign.
steps: Treat YouTube differently from Meta: on Meta the creative is the targeting and the algorithm widens delivery itself; the source has not seen that behaviour on YouTube — on YouTube your targeting is actually the targeting.
Start with a narrow audience for your ICP, because most brands want efficiency early and niche products need their specific audience; you can always expand horizontally later.
Do not start broad and narrow later — the source says this constricts the algorithm and your success.
For each product vertical or customer avatar, apply the same top two-to-three proven Meta creatives across three separate ad groups.

Build three audiences: (1) a custom segment from search-intent keywords (e.g. 'no lace trainers for women', 'hands-free shoes'), (2) a custom segment from website/competitor sites your ICP visits pre-purchase, and (3) a lookalike audience seeded from first-party data.
Exclude your all-time customer list in every ad group so Google cannot harvest existing buyers and take credit for repeat purchases.
Add demographic refinement (e.g. females 25–44) to each audience when you know the avatar; the source sees this outperform broad demographics unless your product has truly broad appeal.
caveats: The presenter's own experience: in-market and affinity segments have never worked — 'they don't work in our experience' — but acknowledges this may change if YouTube follows Meta toward broad targeting.
Seed lookalikes from converters rather than all website visitors; most visitors won't convert.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads 2026 Free Course.docx

cards.title: YouTube Shorts creative specs and storytelling structure
cards.summary: Length, format, subtitle and hook-to-CTA structure for YouTube Shorts ads, tested first on Meta.
cards.use_when: Producing video creative for a YouTube Shorts or Demand Gen prospecting campaign.
steps: Use 20–60 second videos; longer is trending, with storytelling, social proof and expert endorsements outperforming sub-20-second content — but do not exceed 60 seconds.
Shoot 9:16 vertical for mobile-first; include subtitles because a large share watch without sound.
Confirm proof of concept on Meta (or TikTok) first — you should be moving winning creative across, not testing creative on YouTube.

Open with movement or curiosity: the source's Kizik example opens with someone rushing and falling while stepping into a shoe within the first one or two seconds — a scroll-stopping hook that also frames problem→solution.
Demonstrate the product visually — your USP must be showable; the source says if the product isn't visually demonstrable, YouTube isn't for you.
Around 60–70% in, consider stitching quick cuts of additional UGC creators' social proof alongside the main creator's narrative.
Close with a strong CTA backed by a real offer and urgency whenever possible.

In Google, you can add up to 20 images, a logo, up to five headlines and five descriptions; the source generally writes only a couple of offer-centric headlines and uses descriptions for objection handling and trust signals.
Test adaptive layouts with caution: results have been mixed and you may see unusual placements and asset deliveries when on.
caveats: The source has no strong opinion on adaptive layouts — mixed results only.
Headline/description counts and layout options are from the source's session; verify current Google Ads limits.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads 2026 Free Course.docx

cards.title: YouTube retargeting campaign with low-level spend
cards.summary: A separate no-guidance video-views campaign for retargeting warm audiences, with keyword/topic exclusions and CPV bidding.
cards.use_when: Adding a retargeting layer to a YouTube prospecting campaign for website visitors or cart abandoners.
steps: Create a campaign without guidance, select Video as the campaign type and Video views as the subtype — there is no fixed objective in this build.
Pick your retargeting audience: e.g. website visitors from the last 3 or 7 days, product viewers, or add-to-cart users.
Choose the format based on what works on Meta: skippable in-stream for longer horizontal storytelling full of social proof and offer urgency; Shorts for UGC retargeting.
Note that many Meta advertisers retarget with static creative because it's cheaper — this is an acceptable area for small YouTube tests.

For skippable in-stream, set keywords, topics and placements, but exclude the YouTube homepage, anything beyond YouTube (display network placements) and mobile apps/gaming apps to avoid low-quality placements.

Bid target cost per view, generally in the £/$0.10–$0.30 region — but expect a narrower audience (e.g. add-to-cart) to be more expensive per view than a broad website-visitor list, so let CPV breathe.
Err on the higher side initially and refine down once it has learned.
caveats: The $0.10–$0.30 CPV range varies widely by niche and by how much cold traffic costs you; it's a starting region, not a target.
Some advertisers do not run any YouTube retargeting and let Meta handle it — the source allows for this but recommends a small layer if cold YouTube spend is large.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads 2026 Free Course.docx

cards.title: Three things YouTube-winning brands do
cards.summary: The patterns the source says separate brands succeeding on YouTube from those wasting spend.
cards.use_when: Auditing whether your store is ready for YouTube ads and reviewing your playbook priorities.
steps: Prove creative on Meta first: everything is tested there and moved to YouTube only once it's known to work — never test creative on YouTube.
Layer YouTube on top of an already functional Shopping and Search bedrock; brand search, Shopping and prospecting campaigns should all be dialled in first.

Know your target audience deeply — what they search for, what sites they visit, what their pre-purchase behaviour is — because that determines how effective your custom segments are and how quickly the algorithm learns.

Track lead indicators during early launch when purchases may take a week or two to appear: view rate and placement watched, video played-to quartiles (25/50/75/100%), CTR, CPM, cost per view, impression frequency per user and average watch time per user.
Also fix lag indicators — landing page arrivals, add-to-carts and purchases — because the source warns many accounts have broken conversion tracking and are reporting fabricated success.
caveats: The $50m revenue and $2.4m-per-quarter figures are the agency's own reported results, not guarantees.
Referencing the presenter's stated four-year experience and agency work; treat as practitioner opinion.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads 2026 Free Course.docx

cards.title: Demand Gen image ad anatomy for remarketing
cards.summary: Front-end fields to complete in a Demand Gen image ad and how to use headlines/descriptions for offer and objection handling.
cards.use_when: Building or reviewing the asset group for a Demand Gen remarketing campaign.
steps: Name the ad and provide the final URL that clicks should land on.
Upload up to 20 images and add your logo; adaptive layouts from Google lets it fit more layout styles and aspect ratios by manipulating your assets.
Expect placements across YouTube, the Discover feed and Gmail when using Demand Gen.
Use up to five headlines and five descriptions, but the source usually writes only a couple of headlines when they are very offer-centric — you know what message you want served.
Write the headline around the offer (e.g. urgency) and use the description to close the deal with objection handling or trust signals.
Remember the audience already failed to buy once — the ad's job is to address the specific reason they did not convert.
Take care with adaptive layouts: the source reports mixed results and unusual placements/deliveries when enabled — be prepared if you turn it on.
caveats: Field limits (20 images, 5 headlines, 5 descriptions) and layout behaviour are as described in the source's session; verify against the current Google Ads interface.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads 2026 Free Course.docx

cards.title: Turn remarketing objection-learning into funnel-wide improvements
cards.summary: Use cart-abandoner retargeting as a testing ground, then push winning objection-handling into upper-funnel creative to reduce abandonment before it happens.
cards.use_when: Iterating on creative across a Google Ads account and trying to raise on-site conversion rate and ROAS.
steps: Build a large-enough cart-abandoner list so you can test multiple objection angles quickly against one performance measure.
Run single-image and other simple ad variants, each hammering one objection (urgency for complacency, price justification, trust/social proof, efficacy proof, logistics clarity).
Read the results: if trust/social proof wins with abandoners, you now know that group is holding back on credibility.
Push the winning signal up-funnel: add more social proof or trust signals to prospecting and higher-funnel ad creative so people don't reach the cart unconvinced.
Expect the payoff to show up as a higher site conversion rate and more positive feedback, which the source argues makes things more economically sensible and the account easier to scale.

Keep the remarketing creative specific to the abandonment stage rather than copying cold prospecting creative — the source criticises treating remarketing as a one-and-done with the same cold static assets.
caveats: This is the presenter's reasoning and observed pattern, not a measured causal result they document.
Requires a large enough remarketing list to test multiple objections effectively.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads 2026 Free Course.docx

cards.title: Reconcile Google remarketing with your Meta team
cards.summary: Cross-channel practice of sharing creative learnings between Google and Meta to make remarketing more effective on both.
cards.use_when: Coordinating paid social and paid search teams on retargeting creative and messaging.
steps: Share what creative is working on Meta with whoever runs Google remarketing, and vice versa, so the same winning angles are used on both platforms.
If your Meta team already has strong retargeting creative (often static for cost reasons), consider reusing those assets on YouTube Shorts or in-stream rather than building from scratch.
Run a full-funnel remarketing view across Google and Meta so prospects see consistent objection-handling wherever they re-encounter the brand.
Align on which objection each platform's retargeting is handling (e.g. Meta leans on cheap static social proof, Google leans on Shorts UGC) so the two layers complement rather than duplicate.
The source argues this coordination is the route to higher conversion rates across paid channels and more profitable scaling; the source explicitly frames it as their own observation.
caveats: No quantified benchmark is provided for the lift from coordination; treat as a qualitative recommendation.
Assumes you have both a Meta and Google presence with enough creative volume to share.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads 2026 Free Course.docx

cards.title: Launch order for an ecommerce Google Ads account
cards.summary: Sequence campaign types bottom-funnel first (Search/Shopping), then remarketing/PMax, then Demand Gen top-funnel last.
cards.use_when: Planning which campaign types to launch first for a new or restructured ecommerce Google Ads account.
steps: Start with Search and Shopping (bottom/mid funnel) so the account begins driving new customers and branded data immediately.

After the account has roughly 4–6 weeks of data (source's guideline, not strict — depends on budget, product, and sale volume; can be sooner at high spend), add step two: direct remarketing via video and display campaigns to users who visited, added to cart, or began checkout without purchasing.
Only introduce Demand Gen (step three) once bottom and mid-funnel are largely saturated, because top-of-funnel conversions cost more and bottom-funnel traffic converts cheaper and higher quality.
Exception the source allows: if you already run proven creatives on Meta and are a large account, you may port them into Demand Gen earlier for profitable cold acquisition.
For video cold traffic, use Demand Gen with video-only assets, since the older video campaign type is being sunset by Google (verify current interface).
caveats: The 4–6 week figure is a general guideline, explicitly variable by budget and sales volume.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Separate branded vs non-branded campaigns
cards.summary: Never mix branded and non-branded targeting in one campaign — split for new-customer acquisition, clean attribution, and correct algorithm signals.
cards.use_when: Structuring new Search or Shopping campaigns, or diagnosing muddled attribution and inflated metrics in an ecommerce account.
steps: Define branded search as any query containing your brand name with inherent brand intent (e.g., 'Peter's Pans'); non-branded as generic product terms (e.g., 'non-stick fry pan').
Split every campaign into a branded stream and a non-branded stream rather than combining them.
Add your brand terms as exact-match negative keywords in every non-branded campaign so branded searches cannot leak in and distort attribution.
Expect your scaling to come from non-branded campaigns; branded campaigns exist mainly to capture existing demand cheaply and feed the algorithm data.
In the account, keep budget allocated so branded campaigns do not accidentally absorb spend meant for non-branded growth.
caveats: Source holds the opinion that branded campaigns are 'absolutely necessary' and high-performing accounts always have one; he concedes some accounts benefit less. Treat this as his view; nothing in Google Ads is black-and-white.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Bid strategy progression: clicks first, then conversions
cards.summary: Start new accounts on Maximize Clicks to gather conversion data, then switch to Maximize Conversion Value or Target ROAS after enough conversions.
cards.use_when: Setting or reviewing bid strategy on a new ecommerce Google Ads account or one with too few conversions for smart bidding.
steps: Launch with Maximize Clicks so Google can win cheap clicks while the account has no conversion history.

Keep click-focused bidding until you have accumulated conversions; the source cites roughly 15–30 conversions per month as the threshold to consider moving to Maximize Conversion Value or Target ROAS, and mentions 10–15 conversions as an earlier consideration point.
Rationale: asking a conversion-based strategy to find conversions in an account that has never recorded one is like blindfolding an archer — Google does not know what to aim at.
Once conversions exist, switch the campaign to Maximize Conversion Value or Target ROAS to let smart bidding optimize toward revenue.
Aggregate conversion volume across the account when judging readiness, since the threshold is about signal volume, not any single campaign.
caveats: The 10–15 and 15–30 conversion figures are source-specific heuristics, not a documented calculation; treat as rough guides.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Use branded campaigns as cheap algorithm training data
cards.summary: Run low-budget branded Search/Shopping to supply Google cheap, high-quality conversion data that accelerates learning in non-branded campaigns.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to bid on your own brand terms in ecommerce Google Ads.
steps: Accept that branded bidders would have converted anyway, and value the campaign for data instead: branded conversions are the cheapest source of high-quality traffic and signal.
Let branded conversion data flow into the account so machine learning improves on more expensive new-customer non-branded efforts.
Cap spend realistically — for smaller brands the source suggests roughly $10–$20/day, larger brands up to about $50/day, rare to exceed $50/day in the US.
If you fully spend the daily budget, check search terms under insights and reports; if traffic matches your brand intent, raise the budget until captured.
Set customer acquisition (new-customer) targeting off in branded campaigns; returning existing customers are fine there.
caveats: Google will not spend your full branded budget if there is not enough branded search volume — a low delivery is normal for small brands.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Turn off Search Partners and Display Network for Search campaigns
cards.summary: Uncheck search partners and the Google Display Network in Search campaign settings to protect conversion quality.
cards.use_when: Configuring settings for a new ecommerce Search campaign, before launch.
steps: Leave the Google Search Partners Network unchecked: it adds reach but typically brings lower-quality traffic, fewer conversions, and higher cost per conversion.
Leave the Google Display Network unchecked too: if you want display placements, create a separate Display campaign.
Note both boxes are checked by default, so actively untick them each time you build a Search campaign.
Only reconsider search partners if you have absolutely exhausted everything available on Google proper — the source calls this a very rare scenario.
caveats: This is the source's default practice; he allows exceptions for saturated accounts but treats them as unusual.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Set location targeting to presence, not presence-or-interest
cards.summary: Use 'presence' location targeting so ads only serve people actually in the target country, not those merely interested in it.
cards.use_when: Configuring geographic targeting on any ecommerce Google Ads campaign, especially when selling only to specific countries.
steps: In campaign settings, enter the target location and narrow it as far as needed (country, state, city, postcode).
Open the location options dropdown and select 'presence' rather than 'presence or interest'.
Reason: presence-or-interest can serve ads to people outside your target country who are merely interested in it (e.g., someone abroad searching about it), wasting spend.
Optionally exclude regions you do not want to serve.
Combine with a language setting that matches your store, typically English unless you sell in other languages.
Leave audience segments off unless you have a specific demographic to target, and keep broad match keywords off for these campaigns.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Ignore Google's AI keyword and asset generation
cards.summary: Skip Google's automated keyword/asset generation during campaign setup — Google optimizes for its own revenue, not yours, and does not know your brand.
cards.use_when: Building new Search campaigns and facing Google's prompted tools or recommendations.
steps: On the keyword and asset generation screen, do not use the suggested AI keywords or headlines.
Apply the same skepticism throughout setup to any automated creation or automated change suggestions.
Rationale: Google will try to make as much money as they can, not necessarily as much for you, and knows your brand and customers less well than you do.
Add your own keywords manually with the intended match types instead.
Same logic applies to ad copy: the source says Google will tell you not to pin headlines; he disagrees and says pin when it improves relevance.
caveats: This is the source's strong opinion; other practitioners do use automated suggestions. Treat as a default stance, not a universal rule.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Step 2: add remarketing to re-engage non-converting visitors
cards.summary: Build direct remarketing campaigns (video and display) targeting site visitors who added to cart or began checkout but did not purchase.
cards.use_when: After initial Search/Shopping campaigns are running and you want to recover near-converting traffic in an ecommerce store.
steps: Build audience lists from site behavior: visited, added to cart, began checkout, and prior purchasers for repeat purchase.
Run video remarketing campaigns for these audiences; the source finds video most effective when creatives are high quality because they are more engaging.
Alternatively or additionally run display remarketing campaigns to re-approach non-purchasers and past buyers.
Add these campaigns only after roughly 4–6 weeks of account data (source's guideline, variable by budget and sales volume).
Expect these to lift both conversion rate and customer LTV by adding repeated touchpoints.
Keep the goal to push users over the edge toward purchase and to re-trigger past customers, not to retarget broadly.
caveats: The 4–6 week timing is a general guideline, not strict.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Use Performance Max correctly, or use feed-only PMax as a feed-led alternative
cards.summary: Test a feed-led retail PMax configuration against the store baseline without assuming strict audience or channel isolation.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a feed-led versus full-asset Performance Max campaign for an ecommerce product catalog.
steps: Confirm Merchant Center linkage, eligible products, accurate prices and stock, and tested purchase-value tracking.
Treat the source feed-only approach as a test of reduced manually supplied creative. Review the actual asset-generation and URL-expansion settings in the current interface.
Monitor channel delivery, product performance and new versus returning customer outcomes; compare contribution and acquisition cost with the existing Shopping or full-asset setup.
Do not classify the campaign as remarketing-only or promise Shopping-only delivery. Use a campaign with appropriate audience controls when strict remarketing is required.
caveats: Editorial correction: PMax audience signals do not impose strict targeting; omitting manual creative does not guarantee placement isolation. https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/14530785
Merchant Center data can generate assets automatically. Source examples of efficient feed-led campaigns are not delivery guarantees. https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/15865151
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Introduce Demand Gen last, for top-of-funnel cold traffic
cards.summary: Use Demand Gen (video-only or all-assets) for cold audiences only after bottom and mid-funnel campaigns are saturated.
cards.use_when: Deciding when and how to run cold top-of-funnel Google Ads for an ecommerce brand.
steps: Target people who may not know the product, the problem, or your brand — e.g., a kitchen-cookware ad asking 'Are you sick of food sticking to your pans?' then showing a high-quality creative.

Choose between video-only Demand Gen (YouTube ads via video assets, kept in the preferred/future-proof campaign type since old video campaigns are being sunset) and all-assets Demand Gen (serves across YouTube, display, search, and more).
Start with video-focused setups: the source notes all-assets campaigns typically yield lower efficiency on video.
Delay launch until bottom-of-funnel and mid-funnel campaigns are largely saturated, because top-of-funnel conversions cost more.
Run it as a standalone full-funnel layer independent of other channels once proven; if you already have proven Meta creatives and a large account, port them here earlier for profitable acquisition.
caveats: Efficiency/cost expectations are the source's guidance, not measured benchmarks; the video campaign sunset timing is forecast and should be verified.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Link Shopify and Merchant Center, then Merchant Center to Google Ads
cards.summary: Three-way linking (Shopify → Google Merchant Center → Google Ads) is the prerequisite for any Shopping or feed-based campaign.
cards.use_when: Preparing an ecommerce store to run Shopping or feed-based Google Ads for the first time.
steps: In Shopify, go to Sales channels → Google and YouTube and link your Google account and Merchant Center to Shopify, then link products.
If you have no Merchant Center, create one (merchants.google.com) and connect it to Shopify via that tab; allow a couple of hours for the link and product import.
In Google Ads, go to Tools → Data manager → connected products and connect Google Merchant Center if not already shown.
Verify your imported products appear on the Merchant Center products page before building campaigns.
If you are not on Shopify, use an equivalent linking solution for your platform (source notes most stores are Shopify but other tools exist).
caveats: Interface paths are as described at the time of recording; Google changes navigation, so verify current menus.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Feed product titles with informative keywords
cards.summary: Write Merchant Center product titles that include the full product name, key attributes, and brand so Google matches them to the right searches.
cards.use_when: Optimizing Merchant Center product data before running Shopping campaigns.
steps: Put the highly necessary product details first in the title, then attributes, then the brand name at the end.
Example structure: 'Black Non-Stick Frying Pan 38cm Diameter, Peter's Pans'.
Include keywords that reflect what shoppers actually search, so Google can target the product ad to the right queries.
Fill every available field (title, description, product type, category, price, sale price, GTIN, etc.) with high-quality information.
If you have a GTIN, include it; if not, do not worry and still complete the rest.
Do not agonize over perfection at this stage — get a correct, informative setup live first; deep optimization is a separate, longer effort.
caveats: Title keyword strategy must not include terms your product is not (see incorrect-attribute warning card).
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Product descriptions: use AI for keyword-rich copy, but never wrong attributes
cards.summary: Generate long Merchant Center descriptions with a tool like ChatGPT, but exclude any attribute the product does not actually have.
cards.use_when: Filling Merchant Center product description fields across a catalog without hand-writing every one.
steps: Use a detailed prompt, e.g., 'Write a 2,000-character product description for a black 38cm non-stick frying pan, including keywords a shopper might Google to trigger a Shopping ad.'
Treat the description as a keyword surface for Google's matching, not as marketing copy that must be hand-written.
Only include keywords for products and searches you actually want to appear for.
Exclude incorrect attributes: if a pan is not aluminum, do not write 'aluminum pan', or Google may serve it to aluminum or stainless steel pan searches and waste clicks.
Review generated descriptions before saving to catch any fabricated attributes.
Save your changes or the work is lost.
caveats: Wrong attribute terms cause Google to show the product to irrelevant searches, so cheap AI generation must still be checked.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Use feed management tools for large catalogs
cards.summary: For large product catalogs, use a feed management app rather than editing every Merchant Center field manually.
cards.use_when: Working with a large SKU count and standard Shopify–Merchant Center sync is too slow or limited.
steps: Recognize that manually filling every field does not scale for large catalogs.
Use a Shopify feed management plugin (the source names Srois, a Shopify plugin) to manage feeds more thoroughly than the automatic Google–Shopify integration.
Apply it to bulk-edit titles, descriptions, and attributes across many products.
If you have only a few products, skip this and hand-fill the fields — simpler and faster.
After any bulk changes, verify in Merchant Center that products imported and are eligible to serve.
caveats: The source explicitly does not go deep into optimization and promises a future guide; treat this as a starting point. Tool names and plugins change — verify availability.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Configure Shopping campaign objective and conversions
cards.summary: In Shopping campaign setup, select the sales objective and use only the purchase conversion goal — not add to cart or begin checkout.
cards.use_when: Creating a Shopping campaign for an ecommerce store and choosing conversion goals.
steps: In Campaigns, create a new campaign and choose the Sales objective (the source says this is the case ~99% of the time for ecommerce).
Set the account goal to purchases only; remove add to cart and begin checkout as conversion goals for this campaign.
Rationale: if Google can optimize to 'easy' micro-conversions, it may chase add-to-carts and never deliver purchases.
Ensure purchase conversion tracking is correctly installed before launch — bad tracking feeds poor data and undermines results.
Use a consistent campaign naming structure (campaign type → geography → focus, e.g., 'Shopping / USA / Non-Brand') so accounts are easy to review and audit.
caveats: Source treats purchases-only as the right default for ecommerce; it does not deny that add-to-cart and begin-checkout can be useful elsewhere in the account.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Use Search for category/collection intent, Shopping for specific products
cards.summary: Route broad category searches to Search campaigns pointed at collection pages, and specific-product searches to Shopping listings.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a keyword should be covered by a Search campaign or left to Shopping listings in an ecommerce account.
steps: For non-branded Search, target category/collection intent (e.g., 'non-stick pans') where the shopper wants to compare a range rather than one exact product.
Send those clicks to the matching collection page (e.g., /nonstickpans), not a single product page.
Use phrase match for these category keywords; phrase match can get broad, so monitor and add negatives.
Keep ad groups to one collection/category each — never mix two collections in one ad group, or Google may show a crockpot searcher a non-stick pan ad.
Use Shopping for the 'sniper' approach — when someone searches a specific product spec, the exact product listing shows with image, price, and shipping.
Only run category Search campaigns when a category is genuinely popular and data supports testing it; they are not essential in most ecommerce accounts.
caveats: Source states Search campaigns are not a big priority in ecommerce and he uses them infrequently; Shopping is the main driver.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Write branded vs non-branded Search ad copy
cards.summary: Include the brand name and pin it first in branded ads; emphasize range and guarantees in non-branded category ads.
cards.use_when: Writing RSA headlines and assets for branded or non-branded ecommerce Search campaigns.
steps: Branded ads: always include the brand name in a headline and pin it to position 1 so searchers instantly recognize your brand and click through.
Add a trust/social-proof headline (e.g., 'Ultimate Quality and Reliability') and an offer/CTA headline (e.g., a specific sale).
Non-branded category ads: the brand name is optional; instead lead with selection and reassurance, e.g., 'Huge Range of Non-Stick Pans' or a guarantee like '100% Guaranteed Not to Stick'.
For branded campaigns, set customer acquisition (new-customer) targeting off — returning customers are acceptable and desirable there.
Use only 3–5 headlines rather than filling all 15 so you can actually split test; too many headlines make testing impossible.
Pin headlines when it improves relevance, even though Google advises against pinning.
caveats: Source's anti-pinning position is a strong opinion that contradicts Google's recommendation; treat as a situational choice.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Fill out ad extensions to expand ad real estate
cards.summary: Use sitelinks, callouts, structured snippets, promotions, prices, business name and logo to enlarge ads, build trust and lift CTR.
cards.use_when: Building Search ad assets for an ecommerce campaign and trying to maximize click-through rate.
steps: Add sitelinks to relevant but not immediately-matching pages (bestselling product, a why-non-stick blog post, etc.) so interested users can self-route.
Add callouts and structured snippets for trust and to build out the ad's footprint on the search page.
Test promotions and price assets; the source says they are useful but not strictly necessary.
Skip calls and messages — not relevant for ecommerce brands.
Complete advertiser verification to enable business name and logo on ads; source calls this worth the hassle because it raises trust, especially against competitors in non-branded auctions.
Write these once with care — they can be reused across nearly every campaign, so quality copy pays off long-term.
caveats: Bigger ads correlate with higher click chance per the source; asset types and availability change, so verify what your account supports.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Set branded and category Search budgets
cards.summary: Keep branded budgets modest ($10–$50/day typical) and test category Search campaigns at roughly $20–$30/day based on AOV.
cards.use_when: Allocating daily budget to branded vs category Search campaigns for an ecommerce store.
steps: For branded campaigns, budget roughly $10–$20/day for smaller brands, up to about $50/day for larger brands; it is rare to exceed $50/day in the US.
Expect Google not to spend the full budget if branded search volume is low — a partial spend is normal.
For category Search campaigns, start around $20–$30/day to test, adjusting for AOV (higher AOV needs more budget to generate purchase volume) and total account budget.
If branded campaigns fully spend their budget, check search terms under insights and reports; if terms are aligned, increase budget until you capture the traffic.
Scale non-branded/category spend only when the data tells you it is warranted.
caveats: Figures are the source's rules of thumb, not benchmarks; actual spend depends on AOV, volume, and account size.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Use negative keywords to protect non-branded campaigns
cards.summary: Add your brand terms as negatives in every non-branded campaign to stop branded searches leaking in and inflating metrics.
cards.use_when: Building or auditing non-branded Search or Shopping campaigns in an ecommerce account.
steps: Go to the ad group or campaign keywords area and open the negative keywords section.
Add every branded term you target in your branded campaign — brand name, misspellings, no-space variants — as negatives in the non-branded campaign.
Example: if a shopper searches 'Peter's Pans non-stick frying pan', without the negative they could land in the non-branded ad group and distort attribution.
Use a shared negative keyword list so the same brand terms can be applied across all non-branded campaigns.
Beyond brand terms, monitor phrase-match traffic and add negatives for irrelevant queries as they appear.
Re-check search terms regularly since broad phrase match drifts over time.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Test category Search campaigns cautiously
cards.summary: Non-branded category Search campaigns are optional in ecommerce — only launch them when a popular category shows likely profitable demand.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether to add non-branded category Search campaigns alongside Shopping.
steps: Default to letting Shopping carry non-branded product demand; only test category Search when one category gets heavy traffic and users likely to buy.
Keep ad groups tightly themed to a single category or collection.
Use 3–5 phrase-match keywords per category ad group, maximum 10 — three well-chosen phrases often capture the traffic.
Point ads to the matching collection page for a seamless journey from query to page.
Start at roughly $20–$30/day for the test and scale only if data supports a profitable ROI.
Drop or pause the campaign if data does not show profitable demand.
caveats: Source is candid that he does not use category Search campaigns frequently and considers them non-essential in most ecommerce accounts.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Set up a first Standard Shopping campaign for bestsellers only
cards.summary: Launch Google Shopping by running only 5-10 bestseller products in a single ad group instead of dumping the whole catalog in one campaign.
cards.use_when: You are creating your first Google Shopping campaign and deciding which products to advertise.
steps: In Google Ads go to Campaigns > plus > Create, choose the Sales objective, and set conversion goals to purchases only (remove add-to-cart and begin-checkout as primary goals so Google doesn't chase the cheaper action). Verify the current interface before relying on exact menu paths.
Choose Shopping as the campaign type and select your linked Merchant Center account/feed; if multiple feeds exist, pick the correct one.
When Google pre-selects Performance Max, switch to Standard Shopping. The source advises avoiding PMAX when the account has no conversion data because it is likely to lose money without data.
Name the campaign consistently (e.g. 'Shopping | USA | Bestsellers | Max Clicks') so the products, geo and bid strategy are obvious.

Pick 5-10 known or predicted bestsellers (under 10 is the source's recommendation). Small catalogs in one campaign get attention spread thin if the budget is limited, and Google may latch onto weak products at mediocre ROAS.
caveats: Source-specific heuristic: 5-10 products, under 10. Not a benchmark.
Menu labels and defaults change; verify in the current UI.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Restrict a Shopping ad group to specific products by item ID
cards.summary: Use product group subdivisions and exclusion to make a bestsellers ad group run only the chosen products, not the whole feed.
cards.use_when: Your new Shopping ad group is showing all products and you want it to contain only bestsellers.
steps: Open Campaigns > Ad groups, select the campaign and ad group, then open the Product groups tab.
All products is enabled by default; click the plus to Add subdivision. Prefer subdividing by Item ID when the feed is not cleanly categorized.
Search each bestseller by name, select it, and repeat until all chosen products are listed, then Continue to edit bids and Save (do not change bid values on that screen).
The group now shows your selected products separately plus an 'everything else / all products' row.
Click the green status dot on the all-products row and change it to Exclude, leaving only the selected bestsellers enabled.
caveats: Excluding everything else means only the listed products can serve; re-check the list when you add or retire products.
Category subdivision only works if the Merchant Center feed is consistently categorized.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Choose a Shopping bid strategy based on account conversion data
cards.summary: Start a new Shopping campaign on Maximize Clicks, then graduate to Maximize Conversion Value and target ROAS as conversions accumulate.
cards.use_when: You are setting the bidding strategy for a Shopping campaign and need to decide between clicks and conversion-based bidding.
steps: With no conversion data in the account, select Maximize Clicks. The source states conversion-based bidding on a data-less account tends to perform poorly.
Once roughly 15+ conversions exist, consider switching to Maximize Conversion Value.
At roughly 30+ conversions per month with a consistent ROAS (source example: hovering around 2.5), consider adding a Target ROAS so Google holds performance near the level you were already achieving.
Optional: set a Maximum CPC bid limit only after you know your average CPC from performance columns, to clip outlier bids far above normal (source example: seeing $5 bids when average CPC is $1.20).
caveats: 15 and 30 conversions plus the 2.5 ROAS figure are source-specific heuristics, not established thresholds.
A Max CPC cap set too tight can suppress delivery.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Configure Shopping targeting: presence only, no search partners
cards.summary: Set geo targeting to presence-only, uncheck search network, and use all devices to keep Shopping spend on real in-market buyers.
cards.use_when: You are finalizing locations, networks and devices on a Shopping campaign.
steps: Uncheck the automatically-enabled Search Network option unless you have already fully saturated the Google network (source says leave it off by default).
Set devices to All Devices for most scenarios.

Select the target location (e.g. United States), then open Location options and choose Presence, not Presence or interest. Presence-or-interest can show ads to people outside the country who merely show interest in it.
Leave start and end dates as the creation date unless you have a specific flight.
caveats: Google may still optimize device delivery toward the best-performing devices.
Presence-vs-interest option is absent on some campaign types.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Exclude branded searches from a non-branded Shopping campaign
cards.summary: Add your brand name variations as exact-match negative keywords so your prospecting Shopping campaign stays non-branded.
cards.use_when: You run a Shopping campaign intended for new-customer, non-brand acquisition and want branded traffic excluded.
steps: Go to Campaigns > Audiences, keywords and content > Search keywords, and select the Shopping campaign.
Under Negative search keywords, click plus to add negatives.
Enter all brand-name variations (e.g. 'Peter's Pans', 'Peter's Pans frying pans') as exact match using square brackets so you exclude only those queries and not adjacent traffic.
Keep the campaign's targeting non-branded; branded traffic should be handled in a separate branded campaign.
caveats: Overly broad negatives can strip useful non-brand queries; exact match limits the blast radius.
Source attributes the branded/non-branded separation rationale to its overview module; the concept is that branded and prospecting traffic perform differently and should be measured separately.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Sequence a second all-products Shopping campaign after bestsellers prove out
cards.summary: Once bestsellers deliver consistent sales and ROAS, launch an all-products Shopping campaign with no exclusions to find the next winners.
cards.use_when: Your bestsellers Shopping campaign is producing consistent sales and you want to prospect for additional high-performing products.
steps: Confirm the bestsellers campaign has steady, consistent sales and a stable, profitable ROAS first.
Create a second Shopping campaign using the same setup but skip the product-group subdivision so all products remain enabled.
Run this all-products campaign as a discovery channel to identify more potential bestsellers.
Feed any discovered winners back into the bestsellers campaign structure and remove losers.
caveats: Source says to only do this after bestsellers are working, not at launch.
An all-products campaign can also be run as PMAX, but the source sticks to Shopping for this step.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Prune underperforming products from a bestsellers campaign
cards.summary: Exclude products from the bestsellers campaign that received meaningful spend and clicks but failed to perform.
cards.use_when: A bestsellers Shopping campaign is live and some products are dragging down overall ROAS.
steps: Review product-level performance to find items with substantial ad spend and clicks but weak or unprofitable returns.
Exclude those products from the bestsellers ad group using the product group exclusion flow.
Keep the bestsellers campaign reserved only for products that justify inclusion.
caveats: The source does not give a numeric spend or click threshold; use judgement and enough data before cutting.
Removing a product entirely stops it serving; it can be re-added or moved to the all-products campaign.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Add a low-budget branded Shopping campaign to capture branded product searches
cards.summary: If you have significant branded demand, run an all-products Shopping campaign with a brand-negative script at a small budget to show products for brand searches.
cards.use_when: You have meaningful branded search volume (from ads, organic or other channels) and are not fully capturing it with search campaigns.
steps: Set up a Shopping campaign with the same process as your standard campaign but leave all products enabled and exclude nothing.
Use a small budget sized to cover branded traffic only (source example: around $20/day).
Implement a branded Shopping script (source credits 'PBC masterminds' and provides a link) via Tools > Bulk actions > Scripts, copy the script and make the required modifications.
Verify the current script and its instructions before use, since third-party scripts and the interface change.
caveats: Only needed if you have substantial branded traffic; branded shopping campaigns are optional.
Source says you can also do this even if you simply want your products to appear on brand searches.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Check audience lists and tagging before any remarketing campaign
cards.summary: Ensure the Google Ads tag, GA4 and linked accounts are feeding audience lists, and wait until lists are large enough to target.
cards.use_when: You plan to run any display, video or PMAX remarketing campaign and need working audience data first.
steps: Open Tools > Shared library > Audience manager to see which audiences the account is tracking (some auto-created, some from other sources).
Prioritize the automatic setup: the Google Ads tag, GA4 linked through the data manager, and the Shopify link, which the source calls the easiest and most reliable for most stores.

Consider a customer match import plugin (source names 'Simprosys Custom Match list') to upload Shopify customers into Google Ads and feed purchase-converter data; the source describes it as cheap and optional, not required.
Wait until lists have accumulated enough users before launching remarketing; too-small lists make targeting ineffective.
caveats: Source does not specify a minimum list size, only that small lists won't allow effective targeting.
Plugin names and setup flows change; verify before implementing.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Set up a Display remarketing campaign for returning visitors
cards.summary: Build a low-budget Display campaign targeting all-site visitors with conversion-value bidding and strictly non-expanded targeting.
cards.use_when: You have re-engagement audiences populated and want to retarget past site visitors with Display image ads.
steps: Create a new campaign with Sales objective and purchases-only conversion goals, choose Display, and enter the landing page. Send users to a page designed for prior visitors (offer or deal page) if you have one; otherwise the base or relevant collection page.
Set geo with Presence only, leave most settings at defaults, and start budget low, around $10-15/day. The source warns that high Display budgets can push low-quality placements.

Use conversion-value bidding (Maximize Conversion Value), since remarketing is introduced when the account already has data. Target ROAS can be added later; if enabled early, set a very low target so it doesn't restrict delivery.
In targeting, choose audience segments from your data: Browse > How they've interacted with your business > website visitors, e.g. all users.
Uncheck Optimized Targeting, which is on by default. It expands delivery beyond your remarketing list, which defeats the purpose. The source says it has not performed well for this use.

Build the ad with at least the required landscape and square images; the source considers images more important than headlines/descriptions here. Creative should assume the viewer already knows the brand, e.g. a code offer like 'PETER30 for 30% off' rather than an introduction.
caveats: Source opinion: avoid optimized targeting on remarketing; stated as the presenter's experience, not a universal rule.
Budget figures are source examples, not benchmarks.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Run Video remarketing for site visitors with a product feed attached
cards.summary: Set up a YouTube video remarketing campaign using conversion bidding, tight site-visitor audiences, 3/day frequency cap, and product feed relevance.
cards.use_when: You want a more efficient remarketing channel than Display and are ready to retarget site visitors via YouTube.
steps: Create a campaign with Sales objective, purchases goal, and Video type. Note the source says Video campaigns were being upgraded to Demand Gen in early 2025; verify the current campaign types.
Use Maximize Conversions (source says Maximize Conversion Value is not available on video). Budget around $10-20/day; the source recommends roughly 10-15% of total account budget for remarketing.
Attach a Merchant Center product feed so relevant products show clickable below the ad (e.g. a non-stick pan ad paired with a non-stick pan feed), improving relevance and clickthrough.
Device: if running vertical YouTube Shorts only, target mobile phones; if running landscape and portrait, keep all devices and let Google optimize toward the best performers.
Set frequency capping to about 3 impressions per day. The source argues views beyond that rarely change opinion and waste spend.
Turn off video enhancements so Google doesn't auto-edit or crop your videos; you should know exactly what creative is running.

In the ad group, target all users (or specific segments like product viewers/abandoners), uncheck optimized targeting, and upload your video to YouTube (public or unlisted) and paste its URL. Add a CTA, headline and description, using the preview panels to see how each asset appears.
caveats: Source opinion: video remarketing is typically more efficient than image display remarketing; invest there first, but this is the presenter's observation.
Frequency cap of 3/day is a source recommendation, not a proven threshold.
Video campaign type may no longer exist; verify in the current interface.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Use 2-3 high-quality ad copy assets rather than filling every field
cards.summary: Write fewer, stronger headlines and descriptions in remarketing ads instead of padding out every asset suggestion.
cards.use_when: You are building a Display or Video remarketing ad and Google offers many headline/description slots.
steps: Provide at least one or two headlines and descriptions, which is enough to launch and run a little testing.
Stop there rather than filling every available slot; the source argues you end up populating the later ones with low-quality copy.
Tailor all copy and creative to the specific remarketing segment (all visitors, cart abandoners, product viewers) so it reads as re-engagement, not a first introduction.
If you test asset performance, use separate ads with different assets so you can compare cleanly.
caveats: Source opinion about asset quality versus quantity; not a tested rule.
Minimum required assets still must be supplied for the ad to run.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Position PMAX as a remarketing weapon alongside new-customer Shopping
cards.summary: Use PMAX to retarget Shopping customers with product listings, keeping Shopping as the new-customer acquisition funnel.
cards.use_when: You already have Shopping campaigns acquiring new customers and want a retargeting layer using PMAX.
steps: Keep the Shopping campaign as the new-customer funnel targeting non-branded searches (branded traffic excluded via negatives).
Set up a PMAX campaign whose strategic purpose is to retarget those shopping customers with shopping listings and high-intent ads.
Get the important PMAX settings right before launching; the source stresses that PMAX is very data- and algorithm-dependent and can waste money when not contained by the correct strategy.
Treat PMAX as reliant on existing account data, consistent with the source's advice to avoid using it at the outset when there is no data.
caveats: Source describes this PMAX-as-remarketing approach as a fairly new, specific strategy; the full PMAX settings walkthrough is in a later module, not this section.
Source states PMAX set up wrongly wastes money, and without data is likely to lose money.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Feed-Only Performance Max Alongside Standard Shopping
cards.summary: Test a feed-led retail PMax configuration against the store baseline without assuming strict audience or channel isolation.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a feed-led versus full-asset Performance Max campaign for an ecommerce product catalog.
steps: Confirm Merchant Center linkage, eligible products, accurate prices and stock, and tested purchase-value tracking.
Treat the source feed-only approach as a test of reduced manually supplied creative. Review the actual asset-generation and URL-expansion settings in the current interface.
Monitor channel delivery, product performance and new versus returning customer outcomes; compare contribution and acquisition cost with the existing Shopping or full-asset setup.
Do not classify the campaign as remarketing-only or promise Shopping-only delivery. Use a campaign with appropriate audience controls when strict remarketing is required.
caveats: Editorial correction: PMax audience signals do not impose strict targeting; omitting manual creative does not guarantee placement isolation. https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/14530785
Merchant Center data can generate assets automatically. Source examples of efficient feed-led campaigns are not delivery guarantees. https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/15865151
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Excluding Branded Traffic from PMAX to Protect Attribution
cards.summary: Build a negative keyword list of brand terms and apply it to PMAX so brand demand stays in branded Shopping and Search campaigns and PMAX only handles non-branded remarketing.
cards.use_when: Merchandising/measurement decision when PMAX is absorbing branded searches and inflating its apparent results while muddying which campaign actually drives new customers.
steps: Confirm you already run a separate branded Shopping campaign (and branded Search) that captures brand demand; this is the precondition for excluding brand from PMAX.
In the PMAX campaign, go to Audiences, keywords and content, then Search keywords, then Negative search keywords.
Add every brand variant customers might search, in exact match: brand name, brand plus product category, common misspellings and product-specific brand phrases.
Save them into a new shared negative keyword list named for brand exclusion so the same list can be reused across campaigns.

Because PMAX does not allow you to attach the list directly in the UI (as described in this course), use the Google support form to request the negative keyword list be applied to the PMAX campaign. Verify the current application method before relying on it.
Assign roles in reporting: branded Shopping and branded Search collect branded traffic only; non-branded Shopping drives new customers; PMAX catches past visitors and non-converting traffic.
Re-audit search terms periodically to identify new brand variants to add.
caveats: Requires an existing branded campaign structure; excluding brand without one loses brand traffic entirely.
The support-form route for applying negatives to PMAX is the presenter's workaround at time of recording and may be outdated.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Deciding Between Feed-Only PMAX and Asset-Filled PMAX
cards.summary: Test a feed-led retail PMax configuration against the store baseline without assuming strict audience or channel isolation.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a feed-led versus full-asset Performance Max campaign for an ecommerce product catalog.
steps: Confirm Merchant Center linkage, eligible products, accurate prices and stock, and tested purchase-value tracking.
Treat the source feed-only approach as a test of reduced manually supplied creative. Review the actual asset-generation and URL-expansion settings in the current interface.
Monitor channel delivery, product performance and new versus returning customer outcomes; compare contribution and acquisition cost with the existing Shopping or full-asset setup.
Do not classify the campaign as remarketing-only or promise Shopping-only delivery. Use a campaign with appropriate audience controls when strict remarketing is required.
caveats: Editorial correction: PMax audience signals do not impose strict targeting; omitting manual creative does not guarantee placement isolation. https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/14530785
Merchant Center data can generate assets automatically. Source examples of efficient feed-led campaigns are not delivery guarantees. https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/15865151
