cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Budgeting and Sequencing Demand Gen Campaigns
cards.summary: Sequence Demand Gen as the top-of-funnel step after PMAX, and allocate on the order of 30% of account budget when new-customer acquisition is the priority.
cards.use_when: Budget and rollout planning for a store deciding when to add Demand Gen and how much daily spend to commit relative to its existing Shopping/PMAX setup.
steps: Decide timing by budget: with a smaller budget and no proof on other platforms, implement Demand Gen after PMAX remarketing. With a high budget, existing proof on other platforms, and rapid scaling goals, implement it alongside PMAX (source treats this as step two versus step three).
Set the campaign as Sales objective, purchases conversion goal, Demand Gen campaign type.
Use best-seller products as the starting product set so the campaign accumulates data quickly and can be tested and iterated fast.
Enable the product feed with your Merchant Center account so catalog items appear alongside the video/image ads and shorten the path to purchase.

Start with conversion-based bidding and leave target CPA unchecked; the source argues you cannot know a realistic CPA before the campaign has data, and a misaligned target slows learning. Switch to conversion value bidding only if the account already has results to support it.

Set daily budget relative to AOV: the source's illustration is roughly $50/day at $10–20 AOV and $100+/day at around $50 AOV, and it recommends allocating about 30% of the full account budget to Demand Gen when focused on new customers (e.g. ~$150/day out of a $500/day account). Treat these as starting heuristics, not benchmarks.
Expect to invest meaningfully: the source states these campaigns need real budget to generate conversions.
caveats: Budget figures are the presenter's rough guidance tied to AOV and total budget, not tested benchmarks.
Converting new customers at '2+ ROAS' on cold traffic is presented as an observed example, not a promise.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Demand Gen Setup: Settings, Placements and Device Controls
cards.summary: Configure Demand Gen location, device and partner settings to keep spend on higher-quality placements and, where desired, bias video delivery toward Shorts.
cards.use_when: Technical setup of a Demand Gen campaign for a store that wants control over placement quality and format, especially when repurposing short-form social creatives.
steps: Set location and language at campaign level (or ad group level if you need variation). The source's example targets the US with English.
Disable Google video partners. The source compares them to low-quality display/search network placements and says results are worse than standard Google placements.
If you want to bias toward YouTube Shorts, narrow devices to mobile only. The source notes this increases the chance of Shorts placement but cannot guarantee it.

Understand the format selection caveat: if you assign a video only to Shorts, Google requires at least one video showing in each format for that choice to fully apply, and the source's observation is that it may still serve the video in other formats (in-stream, in-feed).
Turn off video enhancements so Google does not auto-edit your creatives into formats that may crop content or wording.
Note that device narrowing plus Shorts targeting together is the best available control for Shorts-specific delivery in the source's experience.
caveats: Format selection behavior is described as unclear in Google's documentation and the source's read is an assumption based on observed data.
Verify current placement and enhancement settings in the live interface, as these change frequently.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Structuring Demand Gen Ad Groups by Creative Theme
cards.summary: Split Demand Gen ad groups by creative theme (e.g. UGC product reviews) and keep image and product creatives in separate ad groups or campaigns for clean testing.
cards.use_when: Creative and ad-group planning when launching Demand Gen for a store that has multiple creative concepts or formats to test against a product set.
steps: Group creatives by theme, not by randomness: for example, one ad group containing three to five iterations of a UGC-style product review video for a specific product.

Pair each theme ad group with the matching product selection, e.g. select the specific item IDs for the stainless steel pans being reviewed, so creatives and catalog items stay relevant to each other.
Run video ads first. The source states video is the most effective and highest-return Demand Gen format it has seen, especially when you have proven Meta/TikTok/Snapchat creatives to port over.
Separate image ads (image + products format) into their own ad group, and consider a separate campaign; do not mix them into the video ad group.
Treat product ads as separate again, at minimum a distinct ad group. The source notes these are very new and it has limited data, so treat as experimental.
Point each ad to the most relevant URL: the specific product page when the ad promotes one product, or a relevant category/landing page when it covers a range.
Do not reuse another creator's YouTube video as your own ad creative; the source's example of pulling a random Short is illustrative only.
caveats: The claim that video is the highest-return format is the presenter's observation, not a benchmark.
Product ads are new with thin data in the source; results may differ.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Keeping Demand Gen Assets Few and Varied Enough to Test
cards.summary: Limit headlines/descriptions to one to three high-quality options per ad so split tests remain interpretable instead of exploding into untraceable combinations.
cards.use_when: Creative testing decision for a store setting up Demand Gen (or similar) ads that wants to know which messaging actually drives conversions.
steps: Fill only the fields that apply to the chosen format and keep optional asset counts low: the source recommends roughly one to three headlines, descriptions and long headlines for Demand Gen assets.
Recognize the combinatorial problem: five of each field multiplies into combinations you cannot attribute, making it impossible to know which headline performed.
Run identical ad content with only a single variable changed between ads so you can compare cleanly, rather than changing several fields at once.
Keep the copy extremely relevant to the specific product or theme of the ad group, and high quality over quantity.
Note that this low-count guidance is specific to Demand Gen-style assets; the source separately notes Search ads require at least three headlines, so do not apply the 'one to three' rule to Search.
caveats: Minimum asset counts differ by campaign type; check current platform requirements.
Single-variable testing assumes sufficient volume for significance; the source does not address low-volume cases.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Audience Signals in Demand Gen: Bias Toward Cold Reach
cards.summary: Leave Demand Gen targeting open or use a few in-market/search-theme signals, but never import your own customer or remarketing lists, which pushes it toward warm traffic.
cards.use_when: Targeting setup for a Demand Gen campaign when the goal is new-customer acquisition and you must avoid duplicating remarketing already handled by PMAX.
steps: Default to fully open targeting: the source reports this performs best for its Demand Gen campaigns.

If you do add signals, use external interest indicators only: roughly three to five search themes, one to two in-market segments, and a couple of demographic adjustments, kept conservative so testing stays interpretable.

Never include your own data: no customer lists, remarketing audiences, or converter audiences, since these direct Google toward people who already know the brand, which defeats the new-customer purpose.
Avoid affinity segments; the source considers them too broad and low-meaning.
Turn off optimized targeting. The source says it makes targeting go wide in ways that produce lower-quality traffic; testing it later is optional once you have results.
Test with and without signals to see which your account responds to, rather than assuming signals help.
caveats: The 'open targeting performs best' finding is the presenter's campaign experience, not a controlled benchmark.
Audience options and naming may change in Google's interface.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Assigning Funnel Roles Across the Google Ads Account
cards.summary: Map each campaign type to a funnel job — Shopping/Search for new and branded demand, Display/YouTube for remarketing, PMAX for product remarketing, Demand Gen for top-of-funnel cold reach.
cards.use_when: Whole-account architecture review for a store unsure whether campaigns are duplicating work, cannibalizing each other, or leaving a funnel stage uncovered.
steps: Assign non-branded Shopping as the new-customer acquisition driver; exclude past visitors and branded traffic there so it targets genuinely new buyers.
Assign branded Shopping and branded Search purely to collecting branded demand, nothing else.
Assign Display and YouTube remarketing to re-engage site visitors.
Assign Performance Max to product remarketing and follow-up: catching past visitors, branded-adjacent and non-converting traffic the Shopping campaign does not target.
Assign Demand Gen to the top of funnel: capturing new users and traffic on YouTube, Discover and Gmail, the closest Google surfaces to Meta/TikTok-style cold acquisition.
Sequence implementation: Shopping and branded campaigns first, then PMAX remarketing once conversions are consistent, then Demand Gen (or alongside PMAX if you have budget and scaling ambition).
Check each new campaign against this map before launch to confirm it does not duplicate another campaign's traffic.
caveats: The exact role boundaries depend on having separate branded and non-branded campaigns; without them, roles blur.
The source presents this as its recommended structure for ecommerce, not the only valid one.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Pre-Launch Checklist for Google Ads Campaign Settings
cards.summary: A short checklist of settings the source disables or verifies across PMAX and Demand Gen: auto-created assets, video enhancements, optimized targeting, video partners and video format coverage.
cards.use_when: Final QA before launching or editing a PMAX or Demand Gen campaign in a store's account, to avoid giving Google uncontrolled creative and placement decisions.
steps: Turn off automatically created assets in every campaign where the option appears; the source's rationale is that auto-created assets mean you don't know what is shown or what you are paying for, and it explicitly skips the asset-generation screens.
Turn off video enhancements in Demand Gen so Google does not reformat your creative.
Disable Google video partners in Demand Gen to avoid lower-quality placements.
Turn off optimized targeting in Demand Gen unless testing it deliberately after results exist.
Keep the source's underlying principle: maximize control over what is shown and where, and only delegate control when you can observe the results.
Resolve launch-blocking validation errors and inspect asset automation settings; do not assume every missing-asset warning can be ignored.
caveats: These are the presenter's control-first preferences, presented as opinion; some accounts may benefit from automation, which the source acknowledges only for targeting in specific cases.
Option locations and names in Google Ads change; verify in the current interface.
cards.source_name: Full Ecom Google Ads Course 2026 (100% FREE).docx

cards.title: Pre-diagnosis rules: change history, time horizon, conversion latency
cards.summary: Three checks to run before touching a Google Ads account that looks like it's underperforming.
cards.use_when: Before diagnosing or editing Google Ads when a store's revenue or ROAS appears to have dropped.
steps: Check change history first. If anyone (you, a teammate, the client, another agency) recently tweaked settings, bids, budgets, campaign structure or the website, assume that change is the cause before running any audit. Never make new changes on top of unexplained recent changes.
Extend the time horizon. Avoid diagnosing on a 1-day read; zoom out as far as the account's conversion volume allows so you are not making decisions off small-sample noise.

Check conversion latency. In Google Ads, conversions are attributed back to the click date, not the purchase date. So the last 3–4 days always look terrible on default conversion and ROAS columns, in every account.
Build a custom column using 'conversions by conversion time' (conversions credited to the day of purchase) to get a real-time read on the last few days.
Only after those three checks should you start level-one diagnosis; otherwise you risk changing a healthy account and pushing it into a worse position.
caveats: The speaker states last 3–4 days always look bad in every account — this is their framing of default attribution behavior, not a benchmark.
Redesigning the account (or multiple changes at once) risks a learning-phase reset that deepens the decline.
cards.source_name: How To Fix An Underperforming Google Ads Account.docx

cards.title: Level-one business check: cross-channel spend weighting and the revenue equation
cards.summary: Determine whether a revenue dip is even a Google problem by checking media mix share and which revenue-equation lever moved.
cards.use_when: When a store reports a revenue or efficiency drop and you must decide whether to investigate Google Ads, Meta/other channels, or the website first.
steps: Establish the media mix by spend share. If Google is only ~10% of spend (e.g., 90% Meta), a top-line revenue dip is very unlikely to be a Google issue — start elsewhere.
If spend is more evenly split (e.g., 65% Meta / 35% Google), still do due diligence on both, but start with the higher-spend platform.

Ask what else changed outside Google: did a promotion end, was there a creative refresh on Meta, did the offer change, did the business change something material? Get the client to confirm anything you're not across.
Decompose the revenue equation: Revenue = Conversion Rate × Average Order Value × Sessions. Identify which of the three fell.

Interpret the lever: AOV down points to product mix / upsell-cross-sell changes; conversion rate down points to landing page, offer or audience; sessions down points to a traffic source losing click volume.
Reconcile platform attribution against true business KPIs (revenue, profit contribution, MER/AMER) to distinguish a real business decline from a tracking or attribution error.
caveats: The speaker notes the majority of accounts they see skew to Meta — this is their client-base observation, not a universal rule.
If Google holds majority spend, run the Google drill first even though the general sequence favours the biggest spender.
cards.source_name: How To Fix An Underperforming Google Ads Account.docx

cards.title: Check seasonality against a forecast before diagnosing
cards.summary: Use forecasting to rule out expected seasonal dips so you don't run a multi-hour diagnostic on normal fluctuation.
cards.use_when: When a store's revenue dips and you need to decide whether the decline is a real anomaly or expected seasonality before investing time in root-cause work.
steps: Maintain a forecast for the business so each period has an expected revenue range rather than a single number.
When a dip appears, compare actual against the forecast for that period. If the dip is in line with expected seasonality, stop — do not run a diagnostic process to 'fix' something that was predicted.
If the dip is outside forecast, proceed to the cross-channel and revenue-equation checks.
Where forecasting is absent, treat any seasonal dip as a real problem and expect to burn hours diagnosing a fluctuation that will recur.
Keep the forecast updated so the comparison is meaningful over time.
caveats: The speaker's process treats an expected seasonal dip as requiring no action — this depends on the forecast being accurate; a bad forecast mislabels real declines as seasonality.
cards.source_name: How To Fix An Underperforming Google Ads Account.docx

cards.title: Prioritise diagnosis by spend: top-5 campaigns only
cards.summary: Ignore low-spend campaigns during diagnosis because even a doubled result there cannot move the business.
cards.use_when: When drilling into a Google Ads account to find the cause of a material business decline.
steps: In the campaign tab, sort by cost descending so the highest-spend campaigns sit at the top.

Do not spend diagnostic time below the top five campaigns by spend. Example: a campaign at 10% of budget doubling performance moves the business ~5%, and if Google is only 40% of your media mix, that is single-digit impact.
Theoretically a small campaign could be the cause, but the speaker argues it is unlikely; start where the impact is and work down only after the likely causes are cleared.
Ask the client's specific complaint against this lens: if it's a 10% ROAS decline on the fifth-biggest spender while business-level KPIs are up, it probably does not need investigating at all.
caveats: The 10%-budget and 40%-media-mix numbers are illustrative examples, not thresholds to apply as hard rules.
This is the speaker's prioritisation heuristic; a small campaign can occasionally be the root cause.
cards.source_name: How To Fix An Underperforming Google Ads Account.docx

cards.title: 90–180 day weekly overview scan before drilling into campaigns
cards.summary: A five-minute account-level scan of weekly metrics to find the inflection point and which metric changed.
cards.use_when: When starting the Google Ads portion of a diagnosis, before looking at individual campaigns.
steps: Set date range to the last 90–180 days and switch to a weekly view.
Stay in the Overview tab and rotate through each metric: cost, conversions, conversion value, cost per conversion, ROAS (conversion value ÷ cost), and CTR.
For each metric, note whether it went up, down or sideways and, critically, when the inflection point occurred (e.g., '3 March').
Move to the Campaign tab and work down from the top five spenders, asking which campaign contributed most to the metric change after that date.
Then drop to ad group level (or asset groups in PMax) and repeat the same exercise to see whether all groups moved or one specific group did.
Output two facts: which campaign type fell off, and which specific campaigns and ad groups within it.
caveats: The benefit of a weekly view is trend visibility; a shorter daily view reintroduces the small-sample and latency problems.
The five-minute figure is the speaker's expectation for an experienced operator, not a guarantee.
cards.source_name: How To Fix An Underperforming Google Ads Account.docx

cards.title: Match failure modes to campaign type: PMax and Shopping
cards.summary: Why identifying the campaign type first matters, and the specific failure modes to check for PMax and Shopping.
cards.use_when: When a Google Ads decline has been traced to a specific campaign and you need to know what to inspect.
steps: Understand that PMax, Shopping and Search decline for different reasons, so establish campaign type before troubleshooting.

PMax / Shopping check 1 — warm/cold drift: check the search term report for brand terms and the audience report for skew toward existing customers. If brand terms are appearing despite exclusions, or the audience skews warm, the exclusion is broken or target ROAS is pushed too high.

PMax / Shopping check 2 — feed health: feed quality drives most Shopping performance (the speaker says 80–90% of PMax performance comes from Shopping). Check products in the campaign for out-of-stock, turned-off or disapproved items, and verify the GMC feed for errors and warnings, including changed titles or descriptions.

PMax / Shopping check 3 — target ROAS: raising tROAS narrows targeting toward warmer, higher-conversion-probability buyers, likely pulling spend back and hurting new-customer acquisition. Cross-check new-customer ROAS in a third-party tool or natively in Google Ads; a higher tROAS typically shows worse NC ROAS.

PMax / Shopping check 4 — product bloat and stock churn: a rapidly growing SKU count flooding one campaign can hurt learning, and high-spend products going in and out of stock reset that product's learning and can affect the whole campaign.
Also check whether spend is being distributed into search partners with poor performance.
caveats: The 80–90% figure is the speaker's stated observation, not a measured benchmark.
Brand exclusion should already be in place — the check is a double-check, not a fix in itself.
cards.source_name: How To Fix An Underperforming Google Ads Account.docx

cards.title: Search campaign failure modes: search terms, auction insights, display leakage
cards.summary: Four specific checks for a declining Search campaign, including broad-match reallocation and display leakage.
cards.use_when: When diagnosis points to a Search campaign as the source of a performance decline.
steps: Search terms: split the report either side of the inflection point, sort by spend, and compare the top-spending terms and their efficiency. With broad match and smart bidding, a wild reallocation of spend across terms can be the cause even when overall volume looks similar.
Auction insights: compare before and after the inflection point. A new competitor entering the auction can raise CPCs or reduce your ability to enter auctions at all.
Target ROAS: the same failure mode as PMax — raising tROAS narrows targeting toward warmer buyers rather than magically improving efficiency.
Display leakage: confirm display is turned off for the campaign, or spend may be silently allocated to display, which correlates with the performance drop.
caveats: If search terms and efficiency look materially unchanged either side of the inflection point, move on rather than forcing a conclusion.
The display-leakage check is a specific Google Ads configuration risk; verify the current interface for where display settings live.
cards.source_name: How To Fix An Underperforming Google Ads Account.docx

cards.title: Metric decomposition: build the formulas before you touch anything
cards.summary: Every campaign KPI is the product of underlying metrics — learn the decomposition to reach the true root cause rather than the first visible symptom.
cards.use_when: When you've isolated a declining campaign metric and need to trace it down to the trigger that actually moved.
steps: Keep the two core formulas in mind: CPA = CPC ÷ conversion rate, and Clicks = Impressions × CTR. The speaker says these cover roughly 90% of troubleshooting.
At campaign level: attributed revenue is driven by CPC, conversion rate and AOV. Declining conversions come from fewer clicks, lower conversion rate, or broken tracking.

Understand AOV itself decomposes further: it's a blend of new-customer AOV and returning-customer AOV, each sitting on a distribution curve, and each order is mechanically driven by units per transaction and average unit retail.

Use this decomposition to get past superficial answers. Trying to fix AOV by asking 'what offer changed?' is not root cause; drilling into NC AOV, then the distribution curve, then whether UPT or AUR moved, is.
Write out which sub-metric moved and what triggered it before proposing any fix.
caveats: The 90% figure is the speaker's own estimate of coverage from those two formulas.
The speaker says infinite decomposition is possible; the value is choosing the next useful level, not expanding until the trail goes cold.
cards.source_name: How To Fix An Underperforming Google Ads Account.docx

cards.title: CPC troubleshooting: quality score, competition and premium auctions
cards.summary: Three explanations for rising CPC and how to tell whether higher CPC is actually a problem.
cards.use_when: When diagnosing a Google Ads efficiency decline where cost per click has risen.
steps: Add columns for Quality Score, Expected CTR, Ad Relevance and Landing Page Experience at keyword level. Compare before and after the inflection point.
Ad relevance is often the easiest to fix: make the ad copy more relevant to the search terms actually being served.
Expected CTR extrapolates current CTR into the future, so it improves only by making the ads materially better.

Landing page experience is the hardest to change: it requires dev work, and Google's re-crawl/rescoring cadence is unclear — the speaker reports it can take weeks to months even after the site is fixed.
Check auction insights before and after the dip to see if a new competitor entered the auction and is pushing up CPCs.
Consider whether you're now entering premium (more expensive) auctions as a result of a tROAS or bidding change — this is only a problem if those clicks aren't higher quality.
Treat CPC as a near-vanity metric: CPC up with conversion rate up keeps CPA flat and is fine; CPC up with conversion rate flat is the problem signal.
caveats: Landing page experience is presented as occasionally being the bottleneck despite the long, uncertain resync cycle.
Premium auction entry is not automatically bad — judge it on whether conversion rate compensates.
cards.source_name: How To Fix An Underperforming Google Ads Account.docx

cards.title: Conversion-rate troubleshooting: tracking, landing page, audience, learning, offer
cards.summary: Five ordered causes of a website conversion rate drop on Google traffic.
cards.use_when: When the conversion-rate leg of the revenue equation has fallen and you need to find which factor is responsible.
steps: Check tracking first: confirm conversion tracking still fires and that you aren't reading the last few days using default conversion columns instead of conversions by conversion time.

Check landing page changes: did the URL change, were prices changed, is a redirect pushing traffic elsewhere, were upsells/cross-sells added, did merchandising shift? The speaker treats this as the number one likely cause of a conversion rate decrease.

Check audience change: same page and site but lower-quality traffic from premium auctions converts worse, and vice versa. Inspect search terms for relevancy to the landing page and whether a bidding-strategy change is pushing toward a different audience.
Check learning phase: a large structural change to the account resets the learning phase, which reliably lowers conversion rates because the system enters the wrong auctions and sends poor traffic.
Check the offer: a promo ended, a discount was removed, or the free shipping threshold changed — all directly affect conversion rate.
caveats: A learning-phase reset from structural change can push you into a feedback loop of decline; avoid causing it unnecessarily.
The ordering reflects the speaker's experience, not a published causal test.
cards.source_name: How To Fix An Underperforming Google Ads Account.docx

cards.title: Volume troubleshooting: clicks = impressions × CTR, budget vs bid share loss
cards.summary: How to diagnose a loss of click volume, separating budget constraints from bid/quality constraints.
cards.use_when: When Google Ads efficiency is stable but volume (spend or revenue) has fallen and you need to find why clicks dropped.
steps: Split the click loss into impressions and CTR. Impressions falling means you're entering fewer auctions or your listings show less often.
Distinguish impression share lost to budget from impression share lost to bid. If you're hitting your daily budget cap, more impressions require more spend.
If click volume and impressions are both down while spend has been steady, the speaker says it's almost certainly a bid issue rather than a budget one.
Fix impression share lost to bid by working on its inputs: quality score, new competitors in the auction, and how aggressively you're entering auctions.
If CTR is the falling leg, look at ad fatigue (rare on Google, more plausible on search than Shopping) and audience mismatch — the ad may no longer fit the people and search terms it now serves.
Check ad copy for time mismatch (e.g., a summer sale still running after summer) and, on Shopping, check competitive pricing on the same products.
caveats: Ad fatigue is described as rare on Google, but the speaker allows for it in search ads.
The budget-vs-bid inference relies on spend being stable over the comparison period.
cards.source_name: How To Fix An Underperforming Google Ads Account.docx

cards.title: Competitive pricing scripts: pull products rather than match discounts
cards.summary: How a wholesaler used competitor price monitoring to avoid unprofitable Google Shopping auctions.
cards.use_when: When Google Shopping CTR and ROAS fall on specific products and you suspect a competitor has discounted the same items.
steps: Track competitor pricing on your key products in real time — the source describes a script monitoring a major competitor's website for price changes.
When a competitor cuts price materially (the example is 20–30% off), pull or de-prioritise the affected product in the campaign structure rather than continuing to force spend to it.
Rationale: continuing to run the product would mean ROAS falls off a cliff, and matching the discount would erode gross margin to almost nothing.
Use Impression Share lost to rank (search impression share lost {rank}) as the native Google Ads column for this signal.
Reintroduce the product when the competitive discount ends and the price gap closes.
caveats: This is one client example (a sunglasses wholesaler), not a guaranteed result.
Script availability and metric naming may change — verify the current Google Ads interface before building the workflow.
cards.source_name: How To Fix An Underperforming Google Ads Account.docx

cards.title: Default to fixes, not rebuilds — and protect the learning phase
cards.summary: Apply targeted fixes and allow time to read them, because a rebuild resets learning and can worsen the decline.
cards.use_when: When you've reached the root cause and are choosing between a targeted change and restructuring the account.
steps: Start with a fix, not a rebuild. Any rebuild triggers a learning reset, which the speaker says will likely put you in a worse position.
Evidence the danger: performance declines, so you make a big change, which causes further decline, which prompts another big change — a feedback loop until the account is in a bad state.
After applying a fix, allow enough time to determine whether it worked before layering another change.
Only if fixes don't work, or clearly won't bridge the gap to historical performance, consider a rebuild.

Before applying, ask honestly how much impact this specific change will make. Changing a headline is unlikely to fix an entire business decline unless a headline change was the original cause. Keep re-thinking the fix until you believe it's strong enough to move the problem area.
caveats: The speaker acknowledges situations dire enough that a 'kitchen sink' response is justified — in that case speed beats clean attribution of the fix.
The threshold for 'enough time' depends on the account's conversion volume, not a fixed window.
cards.source_name: How To Fix An Underperforming Google Ads Account.docx

cards.title: Isolate one fix at a time to preserve causal learning
cards.summary: Why applying multiple simultaneous fixes (the kitchen sink) prevents you from knowing what worked — and when to accept that trade-off.
cards.use_when: When deciding how many changes to apply to a landing page, offer or campaign after diagnosing a decline.
steps: Recognise the 'kitchen sink' problem: if you change the offer, redesign the landing page, and adjust traffic continuity all at once and performance recovers, you cannot identify which change mattered.
If the problem recurs later, you'll be unable to solve it without repeating the kitchen sink — you've learned nothing transferable.
Strip back to a smaller set of changes so the outcome is interpretable; this is where the speaker says the strategic judgement lies.
Assess severity first: a dire, urgent decline may justify a kitchen sink because fixing it matters more than knowing why; a mild dip rewards a clean, attributable test.
caveats: Isolating variables slows recovery — the trade-off must be weighed against severity.
This is a principle for interpretability, not a controlled-experiment protocol; the source doesn't specify sample-size or duration requirements.
cards.source_name: How To Fix An Underperforming Google Ads Account.docx

cards.title: Root-cause sentence test: don't touch the account until you can complete it
cards.summary: A gate before making any change — you must be able to state the metric, sub-metric, trigger and root cause in one sentence.
cards.use_when: Before applying any fix to a Google Ads account following a diagnostic process.
steps: Assemble the full chain from the top down: business KPIs → channel checks → campaign types → specific campaign → metric → sub-metric → trigger → root cause.

Check whether you can finish the sentence: 'this campaign is underperforming because this metric dropped, driven by this sub-metric, which was caused by this trigger, which itself was the root cause.'
If you cannot complete that sentence after the process, do not change the account.

Where the client points at a bottom-level metric (e.g., 'CPC is down on this ad'), zoom out first: check business-level KPIs and whether the issue matters to growth. Often it doesn't, and the hour is better spent elsewhere.
caveats: The speaker describes this order of investigation as the skill that separates strong performance marketers from habitual tweakers — it's their opinion, not a formal standard.
The gate can be overridden when a fix is clearly necessary for business continuity.
cards.source_name: How To Fix An Underperforming Google Ads Account.docx

cards.title: Diagnose Whether You Are Overspending or Underspending on Google Ads
cards.summary: Google sits bottom-of-funnel and captures demand other channels create, so most accounts either over-invest or wrongly starve Google of budget.
cards.use_when: Setting annual or quarterly budget allocation across Google, Meta, TikTok and affiliates, or deciding whether to increase Google spend when the platform reports high ROAS.
steps: Recognise the two failure modes: (1) overspend — Google looks efficient because it captures bottom-intent demand generated by Meta, TikTok and affiliates, so you push budget into spend that isn't incremental; (2) underspend — you believe Google is only bottom-funnel so you cap it at e.g. $10k/month while spending millions on Meta, even though your category has large cold search volume your product could serve.
To test which camp you're in, look at whether backend revenue moves when you increase Google spend, not just the in-platform ROAS figure.
If backend revenue does not track budget increases, you are likely overspending and should hold or redistribute, not scale further.
If backend revenue is constrained only because you never funded Google beyond a token amount, investigate cold search demand for your category terms before dismissing the platform.
Treat the source's >$10k/month anecdote as an illustration of the pattern, not a threshold for your store.
caveats: The two-camp framing is the source's heuristic; real accounts sit on a spectrum.
Attribution overlap between Google and upper-funnel channels makes either error easy to misdiagnose from platform numbers alone.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Consolidate Campaigns Before Segmenting Them
cards.summary: Campaigns learn in isolation, so splitting identical products across campaigns starves low-volume ones of conversion data and lowers ROAS.
cards.use_when: Auditing or restructuring campaign architecture (shopping, PMax, search) or when you see ROAS fall as you go down the campaign list.
steps: Map each campaign's 30-day conversion volume. If you run three shopping campaigns with 50, 20 and 10 conversions respectively, ignore the small amount of cross-campaign platform data sharing and model them as fully siloed.

The campaign with 10 conversions is modelling bids off 10 users' psychographic data — it cannot bid accurately and will underperform. This is why account structures typically show ROAS declining in line with conversion volume.
Merge products and budget into the highest-volume campaign to pool conversions (e.g. 90/month) so smart bidding has a larger dataset and produces more accurate auction bids.
Only re-segment once you can justify the split commercially — the default should be one campaign; each additional campaign must earn its place.
Validate any restructuring with backend revenue, since consolidated campaigns may look better in-platform for reasons unrelated to true incrementality.
caveats: Consolidation assumes products share margin profile, market and creative logic; merging different-margin or different-country products distorts bidding.
Platform-level data sharing exists to a degree; the silo model is a simplification for planning.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: The Four Justifications for Segmenting a Google Ads Account
cards.summary: Only brand vs non-brand, geography, margin/efficiency targets and product category justify splitting campaigns beyond the consolidated default.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to create an additional campaign for a product line, market or margin tier.
steps: Start from the default of one campaign; require heavy justification for every extra campaign.
1) Brand vs non-brand: never let a single PMax or shopping campaign cover both, because you want branded placements and cold acquisition managed separately.
2) Geography: selling in multiple countries always warrants campaign-level separation.

3) Margin or efficiency goals: a 70% gross-margin collection must not share a bidding strategy with a 35% margin collection. At a 300% target ROAS the 35% line is barely profitable while the 70% line is very profitable, and because Google usually can't see margin it will push all spend to whichever drives more revenue.
4) Product category: products that attract different personas (e.g. office chairs vs plants) should learn separately so each models its own audience.
When proposing a split, name which of the four variables it addresses — if none apply, consolidate.
caveats: The 70%/35% margin and 300% ROAS figures are illustrative.
Margin-based segmentation depends on having margin data available to feed the platform; otherwise you're relying on separate campaigns and bids.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Convert SKAGs into Single-Topic Ad Groups
cards.summary: Responsive Search Ads need large impression pools to exit learning, so one-keyword ad groups should be replaced by themed groups of 10–20 keywords.
cards.use_when: Restructuring search campaign ad groups, or inheriting an account still running Single Keyword Ad Groups.
steps: Understand why SKAGs died: an RSA contains up to 15 headlines, 4 descriptions and other assets, producing roughly 2,700 combinations. Google split-tests these against each other, and testing realistically needs about a quarter-million impressions to resolve.
A single exact-match keyword will never deliver that volume, so the ad stays stuck in learning and cannot optimise.
Restructure into single-topic ad groups: e.g. 'general plumbing', 'emergency plumbing', 'affordable plumbing'. Under each theme, place 10–20 themed keywords rather than one.
Write ads tuned to the theme so they are contextually relevant to every keyword in the group; the dynamic RSA then adjusts which headlines serve based on which keyword in the theme triggered.

When auditing an existing SKAG account, transition to single-topic groups and compare performance — the source reports better results consistently across audited accounts, while acknowledging rare accounts where SKAGs still work.
caveats: The quarter-million-impression figure is the source's testing heuristic, not a platform-published threshold.
The source's demonstrated example is a service business; the same logic is applied by the source to ecommerce search campaigns.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Fix the Seven Most Common Google Ads Setup Mistakes
cards.summary: A rapid audit list of configuration errors that quietly drain budget or corrupt measurement in ecommerce accounts.
cards.use_when: Running an account audit or onboarding a store's existing Google Ads account.
steps: 1) Don't use GA4 events as the primary conversion: the source reports a 10–15% (sometimes higher) attribution gap versus direct snippet code on the site.
2) Don't run a single asset group in a PMax campaign — build segmentation at asset-group level.
3) Don't pair broad match with Maximize Clicks: broad match needs a smart bidding strategy to work well.
4) Turn off display in search campaigns; the source rates display as one of the worst networks, especially for cold traffic.
5) Add negative keywords — both branded negatives on cold campaigns and general negatives in search campaigns.
6) Turn off auto-applied recommendations so Google stops making changes you didn't approve.
7) Set a naming convention: agency tag, region, campaign type (PMax/shopping/search), audience (cold/brand/theta), and optionally goal, so anyone can read the account.
caveats: The 10–15% GA4 gap is the source's observed figure and should be verified in your own setup.
Naming convention fields are the presenter's preference; adapt to your team.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Set Up PMax Asset Groups with Matching Listing Groups
cards.summary: PMax's single biggest error is one default asset group or multiple asset groups that all share the same products.
cards.use_when: Building or auditing a Performance Max campaign for an ecommerce store.
steps: Know the mechanics: an asset group holds images, headlines and descriptions used for search, display, YouTube, Discover and Gmail placements; its listing group holds the products from the Merchant Center feed that serve on Shopping.
If you accept the default single asset group, everything is bundled and creative can't be matched to intent.
If you build multiple asset groups but forget to customise each listing group, every asset group still contains all products — the segmentation does nothing.

Four reasons to segment: (1) creative relevance — a shopper who viewed jeans should be retargeted with jeans imagery and copy, not random catalogue items; (2) audience signals work better when granular, since you can signal 'in market for jeans' instead of vague 'fashion'; (3) search themes become specific; (4) you gain visibility into performance by asset group, e.g. seeing that tops are outperforming jeans due to seasonality and reallocating budget.

Apply the rules of thumb: one asset group per product type (chairs/tables/lighting/decor, or hand tools/power tools/fasteners/accessories), at least 15 products per asset group, never one product alone (it will get little spend).
caveats: The 15-product minimum is a flexible heuristic that depends on SKU count.
The source advises a minimum of three and maximum of about 20 asset groups; beyond 20 most businesses lack the complexity to justify it.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Use Brand Exclusions and Weigh What Actually Matters in PMax
cards.summary: Without brand exclusions a PMax campaign is effectively a retargeting campaign; the source ranks the variables that move PMax performance.
cards.use_when: Configuring or prioritising fixes inside an ecommerce PMax campaign.
steps: Exclude your brand from PMax. Two methods exist: (1) campaign settings → brand exclusions → add new brand, let Google index your branded terms and apply the brand list; (2) the newer capability to add negative keywords directly to PMax. The source recommends doing both as fail-safes so a missed variation is still caught by the list and vice versa.

After running PMax across ~250 accounts and consulting on ~400 more, the source ranks variables in this order: (1) the GMC feed — titles, descriptions, imagery (assuming PMax is prioritising Shopping); (2) brand exclusions; (3) asset and listing group structure plus the assets themselves; (4) bidding strategy; (5) audience signals and search themes.
Search themes and audience signals are signals, not targeting — they do not guarantee bids on those terms. Prioritise keywords that historically converted in your account rather than inventing them.

For mature accounts spending tens of thousands per month, the source reports audience signals and search themes are roughly a 1% lever at best; they matter mainly on new business, new product, new category or new asset group launches, where there is no conversion history.
Once a campaign has ~30 days of conversion data, Google bypasses the audience signal — the source states you could remove it with no performance impact.
Verify current interface locations for brand exclusion and negative keyword settings before acting, as Google changes these.
caveats: The ranking and agency-tested figures are the source's own observations, not published benchmarks.
The claim that audience signals stop mattering is explicitly flagged as potentially controversial.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Run a Feed-Only PMax and Check Actual Channel Delivery
cards.summary: Test a feed-led retail PMax configuration against the store baseline without assuming strict audience or channel isolation.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a feed-led versus full-asset Performance Max campaign for an ecommerce product catalog.
steps: Confirm Merchant Center linkage, eligible products, accurate prices and stock, and tested purchase-value tracking.
Treat the source feed-only approach as a test of reduced manually supplied creative. Review the actual asset-generation and URL-expansion settings in the current interface.
Monitor channel delivery, product performance and new versus returning customer outcomes; compare contribution and acquisition cost with the existing Shopping or full-asset setup.
Do not classify the campaign as remarketing-only or promise Shopping-only delivery. Use a campaign with appropriate audience controls when strict remarketing is required.
caveats: Editorial correction: PMax audience signals do not impose strict targeting; omitting manual creative does not guarantee placement isolation. https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/14530785
Merchant Center data can generate assets automatically. Source examples of efficient feed-led campaigns are not delivery guarantees. https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/15865151
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Use Max Conversion Value to Gather Data, Then Move to Target ROAS for Stability
cards.summary: Target ROAS does not raise average performance so much as flatten week-to-week volatility; Max Conversion Value makes bigger bets.
cards.use_when: Choosing or changing the bidding strategy on a PMax or shopping campaign.
steps: Launch on Maximize Conversion Value to accumulate conversion data, then roll into Target ROAS once data exists — this matches how the platform is designed to be used.

Expect the trade-off: Max Conversion Value produces large up-and-down swings as the algorithm makes bigger bets; Target ROAS smooths the distribution. The source notes total performance over the same period is roughly comparable — the difference is day-to-day reliability.
When setting the initial Target ROAS, look at trailing ROAS and set slightly below it (e.g. trailing 420–430% → set 400%).

Then watch for the trap: repeatedly nudging Target ROAS upward (400% → 425% → 450% → 500%) squeezes spend down until a new equilibrium. It looks like improved media buying, but the campaign is restricting who it bids on — the pool narrows toward warm audiences and existing customers rather than new ones.

If you need reliable daily revenue and don't need to chase incremental cold acquisition on that campaign, the higher target is a reasonable trade — but if you're already tight on volume, prefer a lower target and more spend.
caveats: Figures like 400–500% target ROAS are illustrative examples of the trap, not benchmarks.
The source frames the choice as reliability versus reach, not strictly better versus worse.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Build a Feeder Strategy: Cold Shopping Plus Warm PMax
cards.summary: A low-target-ROAS cold campaign reaches cheap auctions nobody else bids on, feeding a high-target-ROAS warm campaign that converts.
cards.use_when: Scaling cold new-customer acquisition on Google when PMax alone has plateaued and you suspect warm-traffic over-attribution.
steps: Set up two campaigns: (1) a broad, low-Target-ROAS campaign (source example as low as 50%, i.e. 0.5 ROAS) that will bid across the entire pool of users searching relevant terms; (2) a high-Target-ROAS campaign (source example 600%) that only targets warm, in-market, likely-to-buy users, often previous site visitors.

The logic: most advertisers only bid on the high-intent half of the user pool (people who have visited many sites and used purchase-relevant terms). Google sees the other half as low intent — first-time searchers with no site history — and almost nobody competes for those auctions, so clicks are cheap.
The cold campaign drives traffic cheaply; the warm campaign captures and converts it on second or third click. The source reports this works well across many accounts.
Practically, run standard shopping as the cold campaign (it is better at reaching cold audiences) and PMax as the high-target-ROAS retargeting leg.

Why this is needed: the source reports that in private discussions, major agency owners agree PMax substantially over-attributes — 50%+ of PMax conversions are repeat or warm customers it didn't acquire — while standard shopping under-attributes because PMax takes credit for the final click. Verified against ~250 accounts running PMax plus ~400 consulted ecommerce accounts.
caveats: The 0.5 and 6.0 ROAS levels are source examples; set your own bands against your margin and data.
The 50%+ over-attribution figure is an industry observation reported by the source, not a measured benchmark you can rely on for your account.
Feeder strategies require enough spend to fund a deliberately unprofitable cold campaign without hurting overall economics.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Recognise PMax's Ceiling and Reframe the Allocation Question
cards.summary: PMax is strong for smaller accounts but plateaus; the useful question is what percentage of spend goes to PMax versus standard shopping.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to keep scaling PMax or redistribute budget into standard shopping.
steps: If you are spending roughly $15–20k/month or less, PMax is useful to get the account moving and scaling.

As you scale PMax further, expect it to plateau. In the source's testing on large accounts scaled to $100k–$300k/month, doubling PMax budget while in-platform ROAS stayed at 5x did not move backend revenue.

Two common reactions both fail: raising budgets further, or raising the target ROAS. Both push more spend into warm and repeat traffic, so the in-platform ROAS may rise while the campaign becomes a 'glorified retargeting campaign'.
Accept that once PMax plateaus, further cold growth requires layering in standard shopping.

Measure the right thing: run a controlled ramp — scale one campaign type by 2x over 30 days and compare with another account ramping the other — and check backend revenue, not the in-platform ROAS. The source reports standard shopping consistently produced better incremental backend revenue despite its in-platform ROAS dropping (e.g. 5x → 4x → 3x) while PMax's stayed at 5x.

Reframe the planning question from 'should I run PMax?' to 'what percentage allocation should PMax versus standard shopping get?' — the source suggests roughly 20–40% to PMax for mid-to-upper-market ecommerce, with the majority in standard shopping.
caveats: The 20–40% allocation and $15–20k/month threshold are the source's heuristics, not universal rules.
The ramp test is illustrative and confounded by account differences; treat results as directional.
Lead-gen businesses should read 'shopping' as 'search'.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Choose Between the Three Standard Shopping Structures
cards.summary: Top-seller split, feeder strategy and labelizer automation suit different catalogue sizes and business models.
cards.use_when: Choosing a standard shopping campaign structure for an ecommerce catalogue.
steps: Structure 1 — top sellers split: put all top sellers in one standard shopping campaign and everything else in a second. This forces Pareto (aim for ~80% of spend on the top 20% of products) while keeping a testing budget on the long tail to promote new winners. Suitable for a large SKU count in a non-fashion category; not suitable for fashion or a 5–10 product business.
Structure 2 — feeder strategy: run standard shopping as the cold traffic engine feeding a high-target-ROAS campaign (see separate card).

Structure 3 — labelizer/flo boost tiers: split products into over-index, index, near-index, under-index and no-index based on 30-day rolling performance, with bidding strategy and budget tuned per tier. You can label manually for small catalogues or run an automated labelizer script that re-tiers products in real time.
The source only recommends the labelizer for catalogues with thousands of SKUs — for most businesses it adds segmentation complexity without enough upside.
Apply the same four segmentation justifications as everywhere else (brand, geography, margin, category) if you split further.
caveats: The source explicitly warns against the top-seller split for fashion and small catalogues.
80% of spend on the top 20% of products is a stated aim for that one structure, not a general rule.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Keep 80–90% of Ecommerce Google Spend in Shopping, Not Search
cards.summary: Shopping listings convey image, price, promos and comparison context pre-click, so they convert better than search ads in ecommerce.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to split budget between shopping and search campaigns for an ecommerce store.
steps: For ecommerce and retail, target roughly 80–90% of Google spend in shopping rather than search — the source's core recommendation for the category.

Reason: search ads give the user a headline, a description nobody reads and a couple of extensions. Shopping shows the product image, price, title, active promos or reviews, brand name and extensions, with about five competitors beside you so the shopper pre-selects the most relevant listing before clicking.

For visual categories like fashion this matters most: search ads for 'red dress' attract clicks from people who then bounce because the style isn't theirs; shopping ads filter that mismatch pre-click.

Exception to reverse the split: ecommerce businesses with a B2B component. The source reports search outperforms shopping there — e.g. selling bulk eyelashes to technicians and small businesses — because a business buyer often won't click a shopping listing whose price doesn't match the mental model of a business purchase.
Only push into search after you've saturated shopping and need additional volume.
caveats: The 80–90% allocation is the source's recommendation for ecommerce, not a measured optimum for every store.
The B2B exception is the source's observation and depends on your buyer type.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Choose Shopping vs Search by Buyer Type
cards.summary: Shopping captures most ecommerce leverage, but B2B-style bulk buyers on an ecommerce store often convert better through Search ads.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to split Google Ads budget between Shopping and Search when your store sells both to consumers and to businesses (bulk, wholesale, trade customers).
steps: Ask whether a meaningful share of your buyers purchase for a business reason: bulk quantities, trade/technician use, repeat supply, or known-supplier relationships.
Default to putting about 90% of ecommerce focus into Shopping, since that is where most consumer product discovery and greatest leverage sits.

Break that default when the store has a B2B component: B2B buyers tend to skip Shopping listings because shown unit prices feel wrong for the bulk deal they want, so they click Search ads instead. Example given: bulk eyelashes sold to technicians and small salons perform better on Search than Shopping.
If B2B applies, build Search campaigns around supplier-intent and bulk-intent language, and keep consumer Shopping running separately.
Segment B2B traffic and creative onto different landing pages so bulk pricing and trade terms aren't shown to consumer shoppers.
Judge by comparing cost per acquisition and revenue per click between the two channels in your own account rather than assuming the general rule applies.
caveats: The 90% Shopping figure is the source's rule of thumb for consumer ecommerce, not a benchmark for B2B-heavy stores.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Rebuild Google Shopping Product Titles for Keyword Reach
cards.summary: Structure Shopping feed titles around researched, converting search terms rather than internal product names, and generate variants from search term reports.
cards.use_when: Optimizing the Google Merchant Center feed so your product listings appear for more relevant search queries and earn more clicks.
steps: Pull the search term report and identify the query variants that already convert for that product type (for example 'formal dress', 'dissolvable creatine powder', 'clear', 'flavored', 'portable').
Move the brand name to the end of the title, or remove it entirely if nobody searches for your brand; the brand already appears lower in the Shopping listing.
Move the decorative or internal product name (for example 'Nathan dress') out of the prime position unless it is a recognised product name.
Lead with the highest-value relevant keyword plus product type so intent is clear to both the user and the algorithm.
Append as many relevant attributes as fit within the title character limit so you can be matched on more specific queries (for example colour or size attributes).
Continue adding researched keyword variants until the title is full.

If a product has variants (for example 50g, 100g, 500g packs) that each generate a separate Shopping listing, give each variant its own title, image and description aimed at a different keyword pool, even though they land on the same product page.
caveats: There is no golden title formula; base every change on your own historical search term data.
Roll title changes out gradually, not all at once; a bulk switch resets learning phases across campaigns.
This is a source-specific approach that should be validated against your own CTR and conversion results.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Diagnose and Break the Target ROAS Death Spiral
cards.summary: A target ROAS that keeps missing shrinks its own eligible audience until spend and conversions collapse, so reset the target aggressively when volume drops.
cards.use_when: Auditing a Google Ads account where spend has been gradually trailing off, or where target ROAS campaigns have stopped delivering volume.
steps: Look for the pattern over time: flat or rising spend, a dip in actual ROAS, then a steady decline in spend and conversions.

Understand the mechanism: the campaign stops hitting target ROAS, so it narrows the audience it bids on, which cuts conversions, which reduces the last 30-90 days of conversion data, which degrades the bidding model, causing a worse audience and further decline.
Recognise that seasonal dips, a strong product going out of stock, or any conversion drop can start the spiral through small sample sizes and worse targeting.
If you decide to lower the target ROAS, do it aggressively rather than in small steps; timid reductions commonly fail to arrest the decline.
Watch new accounts and recently onboarded campaigns for early signs so you can fix it before volume reaches zero.
Once volume recovers, avoid leaving target ROAS fixed permanently; rotate between restrictive and expansive strategies over longer periods to prevent over-siloing.
caveats: This is a mechanical failure pattern described by the source, not a universal rule; some campaigns with sufficient volume and stable history may hold a fixed target ROAS.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Pick Expansive vs Restrictive Bidding by Testing Appetite
cards.summary: Max conversion bidding spends ~30% of budget testing new audiences while target ROAS/CPA restrict auctions for efficiency, at the cost of siloing the account.
cards.use_when: Choosing or reviewing the bidding strategy for a Google Ads account and deciding whether you need scale discovery or tighter efficiency.
steps: Classify the strategy: maximize conversions and maximize conversion value are expansive because they can enter any auction; target CPA and target ROAS are restrictive because they only enter auctions that fit an efficiency target.

Use the rough concept that an expansive strategy allocates something like 30% of budget to testing new keywords, audiences, placements, regions and similar adjacent bets, which is what can unlock scale.

Assume a restrictive strategy has roughly 0% testing budget; how strict it really is depends on the gap between your achieved ROAS and the target. If you're hitting 4 and target is 4.5, testing is effectively zero; if you're hitting 5 and target is 2, it behaves more like max conversion value.

Weigh the trade-offs: expansive bidding wins auctions it otherwise wouldn't but also loses some it otherwise wouldn't, so it is higher risk; restrictive bidding is more efficient but silos you into one audience and demographic over time.
Rotate between the two over extended periods rather than staying on target ROAS permanently, to avoid a siloed negative feedback loop.
As a default for ecommerce, the source recommends going for value most of the time, because value bidding reflects product margin differences that pure conversion bidding ignores.
caveats: The 30% testing figure is an illustrative concept from the source, not a measured benchmark.
Bidding behaviour and available settings change; verify current strategy options in the Google Ads interface.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Maximize Conversion Value Instead of Conversions for Mixed-Margin Catalogs
cards.summary: Optimizing for conversions pushes spend to cheap products with low CPAs, so value-based bidding better reflects where the profitable orders actually are.
cards.use_when: Choosing between maximize conversions/target CPA and maximize conversion value/target ROAS when your catalog spans very different price points and margins.
steps: Model the failure case: a $40 t-shirt can acquire customers at, say, $20 CPA while a $200 jumper may cost $60 CPA, so a conversion-optimized campaign funnels nearly all budget into the t-shirt.
Check the ROAS of each: in the source example the t-shirt returns around 2x while the jumper returns around 3.5x, which is the outcome you'd prefer to fund.
Recognize that maximize conversions cannot distinguish these, because it optimizes for the lowest CPA and highest order count, not for value.
Switch ecommerce campaigns to value-based bidding (maximize conversion value or target ROAS) so the system weights higher-value orders.
Confirm your conversion tracking passes order value accurately before relying on value bidding, otherwise the model learns the wrong signal.
Review product-level spend after switching to verify budget is moving toward the higher-ROAS items you intended to fund.
caveats: The dollar figures are illustrative examples from the source, not ecommerce benchmarks.
Value bidding depends on accurate transaction value data; bad data will reinforce bad allocation.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Use Portfolio Bidding to Merge Learnings and Cap CPC
cards.summary: Account-level portfolio bid strategies let siloed campaigns share learning data and add max/min CPC limits on top of target ROAS or max value bidding.
cards.use_when: You have deliberately split campaigns into segments (brand, category, margin tiers) and want them to learn together, or you need to cap expensive clicks.
steps: Confirm you need the segmentation for a commercial reason, since the primary goal is still to have as few campaigns as possible.
Set up a portfolio bid strategy at the account level and apply it to the chosen campaigns so their conversion learnings are housed and modelled together rather than in isolation.

Use the portfolio to layer a maximum and minimum CPC on a target ROAS or maximize value strategy. Example: in high-end furniture where individual clicks can reach $10-$30, set a max CPC so the algorithm never buys a click above your profitable ceiling.
Treat this as the fix when too much segmentation has isolated campaigns from each other, since it recovers shared learning without rebuilding your structure.
Check whether the equivalent feature is available in your campaign types before designing a strategy around it; the source notes this capability differs by account tier and campaign type.
caveats: Portfolio bid strategies and CPC caps sit outside Pmax and Shopping in the source's account, so verify current availability in the Google Ads interface.
A max CPC cap restricts auctions, so set it from your own profitable spend ceiling rather than guessing low.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Exploit Search Campaign Smart Bidding Exploration
cards.summary: Search campaigns can use a smart bidding exploration setting that lets target ROAS bid outside its target in 10-30% bands to keep discovering new auctions.
cards.use_when: You run Search campaigns on target ROAS and want some of the scale benefits of expansive bidding without abandoning efficiency targets.
steps: Set the Search campaign to a restrictive strategy such as target ROAS as your efficiency baseline.
Enable the smart bidding exploration setting on the Search campaign so the algorithm can go outside the ROAS target in roughly 10-30% bands to test auctions it would otherwise skip.
Treat this as a middle ground between restrictive and expansive strategies, giving efficiency plus some discovery of new audiences.
Monitor whether the exploration produces incremental converting traffic or just erodes efficiency, and adjust the target accordingly.
Note that this option is not available on Pmax or Shopping in the source's experience, so it applies to Search only.
Verify the setting's current name and availability in the Google Ads interface, since platform settings change.
caveats: Source-specific recommendation; the setting may have moved, been renamed or changed scope.
Search campaigns are the source's secondary channel for most consumer ecommerce, so this tactic matters most where Search is already a focus.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Build Negative Keyword Discipline in the First 30 Days
cards.summary: Search campaigns need heavy negative keyword review early because broad targeting bleeds spend, then lighter ongoing management to avoid resetting learnings.
cards.use_when: Launching or taking over Search campaigns and controlling wasted spend on irrelevant queries.
steps: Expect the first 30 days to be the highest-leverage period for negative keywords, since campaigns go broad and pick up irrelevant terms.
Review negative keywords weekly in the first 30 days. If budgets are high, review daily to prevent keyword bleed and wasted spend.
From month one onward, drop the cadence to roughly weekly or nightly rather than constantly editing.
Avoid over-tweaking negatives, because every edit resets learnings and impacts performance.
Build a universal negative keyword list applied at account level so every new campaign inherits it automatically; search for an existing list, ask an LLM to draft one, or build your own.
Seed the list with clearly irrelevant themes such as jobs, careers, interns, hiring and salary, which should never receive your ads.
Use topic ad groups rather than keyword ad groups on the negative keyword side where you have thousands of SKUs; below that scale, this usually just overcomplicates the account.
caveats: The weekly/daily cadence depends on your budget level and search volume.
Exact negative keyword lists are not universal; audit yours against your catalog and business model.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Explain the Low Leverage of Average CPC
cards.summary: Average CPC is largely a vanity metric because traffic quality varies, so judge performance by conversion rate, AOV and ROAS instead.
cards.use_when: Reviewing Google Ads reporting or evaluating an agency's proposed CPC-focused optimization for your store.
steps: Write out the acquisition equation: cost per click drives traffic, and revenue equals conversion rate times average order value, so total return depends on all three.
Stop optimizing solely for the lowest CPC, since cheap clicks can be junk traffic that never converts and expensive clicks can be high-intent buyers.
Recognize that CPC and ROAS show very little relationship across large datasets, both at account and product level, in the source's analysis.
Keep only the peripheral extremes in mind: CPCs around $100 are almost certainly unprofitable, and CPCs around 10 cents are probably junk traffic.
Instead of chasing CPC, improve bidding quality by feeding the algorithm better conversion signals, quality score inputs and feed data so it bids on users likely to convert.
Measure success with ROAS and revenue per visitor rather than CPC movement.
caveats: The source presents this as a pattern observed across many accounts, not a formal benchmark; verify against your own account data.
This does not mean CPC is irrelevant in the extreme; extreme CPC levels still indicate a problem.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Win More Google Auctions by Raising Your Website's Conversion Rate
cards.summary: Because Google is an auction, a higher on-site conversion rate lets you afford higher bids than competitors and win more placements.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to invest to improve Google Ads performance when campaign settings have already been refined.
steps: Frame the auction logic: you and competitors bid on the same term, and whoever can pay the most wins the listing, the click and the conversion.
Accept that higher conversion rate is your lever to afford higher bids: if you convert twice as well as competitors, you can pay double per click and make the same money.
Apply the same logic to average order value: higher AOV extracts more revenue per click, so you can outbid competitors on the same traffic.
Use campaign structure, asset groups, audience signals and feed optimization to improve quality score so your bid effectively enters the auction lower than competitors'.
Recognize the counter-risk: a competitor with better conversion rate and AOV can outbid you even with worse ads and structure, so on-site performance ultimately caps what campaign work can achieve.
caveats: The doubled-conversion-rate example is an illustration of the auction mechanic, not a promise of results.
Without products and site improvements this advantage cannot be sustained.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Run Continuous Landing Page Split Tests on Search Ads
cards.summary: Duplicate ad groups with two ads pointing to two different landing pages, then rotate the winner against a new challenger every 30-60 days.
cards.use_when: Running Search campaigns and looking for the biggest lever beyond in-platform settings: improving the landing page conversion rate.
steps: Duplicate the ad in each ad group so ad one points to landing page one and ad two points to landing page two.
Keep the ads otherwise identical so the landing page is the variable under test.
Measure conversion rate over a 30-60 day period to give each page enough data.
Select the landing page with the higher conversion rate and make it the default.
Immediately start a new test: bring in landing page three as the challenger and compare it against the current winner.
Repeat the cycle so the campaign's average conversion rate rises over time, which raises the amount you can afford to bid.
Where possible, also test AOV improvements so revenue per visitor from the campaign rises alongside conversion rate.
caveats: The 30-60 day window is the source's guidance; lower-traffic ad groups may need longer or may not reach significance.
The source calls landing page testing one of the biggest levers in Search, but this is their opinion based on agency experience, not a measured benchmark.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Change Google Ads Budgets Slowly, Downward Faster
cards.summary: Google rewards slow methodical budget increases around 20%, and tolerates faster decreases, while other platforms allow quicker scaling.
cards.use_when: Scaling or pulling back spend on Google Ads campaigns after a winning period, or planning a promotion push.
steps: Increase Google Ads budgets in roughly 20% increments rather than doubling overnight; the source reports Google is a stable platform that responds badly to heavy budget changes.
Apply the same caution to bidding target changes: do not move target CPA or target ROAS overnight.
When reducing budgets from a high level, you can generally move faster with little instability or performance drop-off observed.
Treat other platforms differently: on Meta and TikTok you can increase budgets considerably faster than the Google 20% guideline.
Plan around the general principle that Google drives conversions consistently and wants slower, methodical changes, while other channels tolerate aggression.
caveats: The 20% increment is a widely repeated heuristic that the source confirms holds on Google specifically; it is not a calculated optimum.
Observed behaviour can change as the platform updates; validate on your own account.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Interpret 'Limited by Budget' as a Signal, Not a Rule
cards.summary: The limited-by-budget flag appears on almost every account regardless of spend level, so treat it as a hint to investigate incremental spend rather than proof it exists.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to raise campaign budgets when Google Ads reports campaigns are limited by budget.
steps: Read the flag as an indicator that the campaign could have entered more auctions if budget were available.

Do not treat it as proof that additional spend will be profitable; the source reports seeing it on nearly every account, even campaigns spending $5,000-$10,000 a day in a small total addressable market.
Investigate incremental spend by checking whether adding budget actually improves revenue and ROAS over a test period rather than accepting the flag at face value.
Combine the signal with other diagnostics: conversion volume trends, auction insights and marginal ROAS.
If incremental budget does not improve returns, leave the budget as is despite the flag.
caveats: Google's flag behaviour is the platform's own reporting and may change over time; verify current semantics.
Small total addressable markets can still show the flag even at very high spend, per the source's example.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Stagger Feed Title Rollouts to Protect Learning
cards.summary: Feed optimizations reset campaign learning, so roll title changes gradually and monitor CTR, CPC and returns in real time instead of switching everything at once.
cards.use_when: Applying Google Merchant Center title, image or attribute changes across a catalog with active Shopping and Pmax campaigns.
steps: Prioritize the highest-opportunity products or categories rather than the whole catalog at once.
Change a batch of titles, then watch campaign response before moving to the next batch.
Monitor click-through rate, CPC and return on spend for the changed listings in real time to see if the changes made a material difference.
Stop and redesign the keyword approach if results do not improve; test different researched keywords in titles instead.
Keep the baseline recorded so you can compare before and after the change.
Remember that a bulk switch resets learning phases on every campaign, which can put the account in a bad position.
caveats: There is no fixed batch size; pace depends on catalog size and campaign volume.
Feed changes can take time to propagate, so allow time before judging results.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx

cards.title: Optimize Shopping Images for Contrast, Not Just CTR
cards.summary: Shopping images occupy about 70% of the listing, so design them to attract the right buyer through contrast with competitor listings rather than maximizing clicks from everyone.
cards.use_when: Improving Google Shopping listing creative to lift click quality, not just click volume.
steps: Recognize the image dominates the listing, with price and title as secondary click drivers, so image work is high leverage.
Aim for the right clicks rather than maximum CTR: if you attract the wrong people, higher CTR does not help, mirroring the idea that a headline should hook the right reader, not everyone.
Study the listings you appear beside and build contrast, for example keeping a photo shoot but changing the background colour if competitors all use white backgrounds.
Supply images in the ratio Google expects, about 4x5, and override feed images via a supplementary feed if your defaults, such as fashion's 9x6, get autocropped badly.
Where brand recognition is limited, focus on visual differentiation rather than brand-led creative.
Review click-through and conversion quality together after image changes to confirm you attracted buyers rather than browsers.
caveats: The 70% real estate figure and 4x5 ratio are stated by the source and platform defaults may change; verify current Merchant Center image requirements.
Higher CTR alone is not the goal; validate with conversion and return data.
cards.source_name: The Only Google Ads Strategy You Need for 2026.docx
