Argue the three strategic benefits the source gives: (1) it lowers blended customer acquisition cost because paid traffic lands on site and converts to subscribers you can convert later for free; (2) it raises LTV through engineered repeat purchases instead of hoping customers return; (3) it builds an owned audience that compounds and reduces dependence on Meta/Google/TikTok CPMs and algorithm changes.

Map the counterfactual risk to your store: if the ad platform's CPMs double or your account is restricted tomorrow, how much of your revenue base can you still contact directly? That gap is your email opportunity size.

Translate the target into a monthly revenue number and compare against your current email-attributed revenue using a defined attribution window so the gap is measured consistently (see attribution card).
caveats: 30% is the presenter's stated benchmark from agency work, not a published industry statistic.
Changes to attribution windows will change the measured percentage; be consistent or compare like-for-like.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Complete the Klaviyo–Shopify integration and sync settings
cards.summary: Wire Shopify into Klaviyo correctly so subscriber capture, event tracking and anonymous activity all flow into one profile record.
cards.use_when: Initial account setup, a re-platform migration, or auditing why checkout/pop-up subscribers and browse events are missing from Klaviyo.
steps: During signup select 'sell products online', choose Shopify as the primary platform, and enter your Shopify URL. If migrating from another platform (e.g. Mailchimp), declare your existing list size so Klaviyo can guide sending-limit warmup; if new, select that you have no contacts.
Set your sender name (brand name, or 'Founder at Brand') and sender email address. This is what appears in the inbox, so it drives open behaviour as much as the subject line.
Turn on the Shopify app embed for on-site tracking inside your Shopify theme; without it Klaviyo cannot see on-site events.
Check 'sync your Shopify email subscribers to Klaviyo' and point them into your single main email list; mirror the same for SMS subscribers into one main SMS list.
Leave 'sync profiles and custom properties from Klaviyo to Shopify' unchecked — the source sees no strong reason for most brands to push Klaviyo data back into Shopify.

In Klaviyo data settings, enable anonymous visitor tracking. By default, views and add-to-carts before an email is captured are invisible, which suppresses browse-abandonment and cart-abandonment volume. Verify the current toggle location in your account, as the UI changes.
caveats: Anonymous visitor tracking means pre-opt-in behaviour becomes attached to the profile once they identify — disclose this in your privacy policy where required.
Menu names and toggles in Klaviyo change; confirm the current interface before instructing a team member.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Configure smart sending and attribution windows
cards.summary: Set the smart-sending window and choose attribution windows that match your consideration cycle, then exclude inflated data sources from reporting.
cards.use_when: Initial account configuration, or when email revenue reporting looks implausibly high/low and you need defensible numbers.
steps: In Settings > Email > Sender preferences, keep Smart Sending ON with the default 16-hour window so a subscriber does not receive a campaign within 16 hours of another email. This is the source's recommended default; it is customisable per brand.
Decide on 'ignore transactional messages': the source typically leaves this unchecked for most brands, meaning a just-purchased customer can still receive a marketing campaign.

Set open/click attribution windows to reflect your consideration cycle. Klaviyo's default is 5-day open / 5-day click. The source advises shorter for impulse-purchase products and longer for long-consideration products (e.g. $10k furniture with a ~30-day decision), but says do not stray far outside the 5/5 default as a conservative anchor.
In tracking/reporting exclusions, exclude transactional messages from attribution so order confirmations do not show up as revenue-driving email.

Exclude bot clicks (email and SMS) and exclude Apple Mail Privacy Protection opens from attribution data — since iOS 15, Apple pre-opens mail, generating fake opens that would otherwise claim credit for purchases.
Save, then re-check the reporting figures so you know whether your previous baseline was inflated.
caveats: Attribution windows determine how much credit email claims; changing them changes the 30% revenue KPI and all subsequent comparisons.
Apple privacy opens still appear in open-rate metrics generally unless filtered — for engagement segments, always filter with 'Apple privacy open is false'.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Set brand defaults, fonts and fallbacks for email design
cards.summary: Load logo, colours, socials and custom fonts with websafe fallbacks so every email and consent page renders on-brand across inboxes.
cards.use_when: Setting up Klaviyo for the first time, or when emails render in the wrong typeface or look unbranded on some devices.
steps: In the brand library, upload your logo — it appears in email headers and sometimes footers.
Set brand colours for accent, body text, buttons and links so templates inherit a consistent palette.
Set your primary font. Klaviyo does not support custom fonts natively for all inboxes; it supports websafe fonts, so pick the closest websafe match as the account default.
Add custom fonts separately. Google fonts and Adobe fonts can be selected directly. Fully custom fonts require the 'hosted web font' route with Klaviyo's hosting instructions.
Always define a fallback font — inbox providers such as Gmail may only render Google/web fonts, so an Adobe or bespoke typeface will silently substitute. Choose the closest visual match.
Add social icons in the brand settings so footers populate automatically without manual entry in every template.
Set brand voice if you use Klaviyo's AI copywriting, so generated copy matches tone.
caveats: Header links are rarely useful for most brands given the design approach shown in the course; they can be skipped.
Font rendering varies by inbox client; the fallback is what most recipients will actually see.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Authenticate your domain: dedicated sending domain, SPF, DKIM, DMARC
cards.summary: Stand up a branded sending subdomain with DNS records to protect sender reputation, and keep DMARC policy at p=none to avoid self-inflicted spam filtering.
cards.use_when: New Klaviyo account, domain migration, or diagnosing poor inbox placement despite good content.
steps: In Settings > Domains > Add domain, enter your root domain (e.g. brand.com) and then create a sending subdomain such as send.brand.com. This isolates marketing sending reputation from your root domain.
Choose the setup path: Klaviyo may offer an assisted integration partner (the source notes an 'Entry' integration option and that it may cost money); otherwise set up manually.

Select your domain provider, copy the generated DNS records (name and value) into your host's DNS settings (e.g. GoDaddy), then click verify. Verification can take up to 48 hours — only verify after records are actually published.
Add the SPF, DKIM and DMARC records the same way. SPF, DKIM and DMARC tell inbox providers you are who you claim to be and protect your brand from spoofers.

Critical: when creating the DMARC record, ensure the policy reads p=none, not reject or quarantine. With reject/quarantine, any email the provider thinks is spam goes straight to spam; with none, it continues to be delivered to inboxes. The source calls this a huge difference in delivered mail.
Confirm SPF/DKIM/DMARC are all passing before scaling volume.
caveats: The source presents p=none as the safer setting for deliverability; security teams may prefer stricter policies, which can suppress delivery.
DNS record formats and provider UIs differ; verify current instructions before editing live DNS.
DNS propagation delays mean urgent sends may go out unauthenticated if you leave setup to the last minute.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Maintain sender reputation with bounce, spam and engagement thresholds
cards.summary: Treat sender reputation like a credit score and monitor the three inputs — bounce rate, spam complaints and engagement — against the source's thresholds.
cards.use_when: Ongoing deliverability monitoring, or when opens collapse and you need to diagnose reputation damage.
steps: Understand the model: reputation is history-based and hard to rebuild once damaged; a good reputation gets primary inbox placement, a bad one gets spam or promotions tab.

Keep bounce rate under 1%. Bounces come from invalid addresses — e.g. a fake email submitted through a pop-up form still triggering the welcome or abandoned-cart flow. Suppress hard-bouncing addresses and consider preventing obviously fake form entries.

Keep spam complaint rate below 0.3%, and ideally below 0.1%, to stay inside Gmail and Yahoo's stricter 2024+ requirements. Locate these rates in your account reporting and review on a regular cadence.
Maximise positive engagement signals: opens, clicks and especially replies tell inbox providers people want to hear from you. Low opens and low clicks act as negative signals.
Send at a consistent cadence — the source cites an example of two campaigns a week plus flows sending daily — because erratic sending (long silence then a burst) is treated as a negative signal.
Fix the root cause before re-sending: low opens usually means wrong audience (see 180-day cleaning and engagement segments), not a subject-line problem.
caveats: Thresholds (0.3% complaint, 0.1% ideal, 1% bounce) are the source's targets and align with stated Gmail/Yahoo expectations; Google's published requirements should be checked for current limits.
Reputation damage is slow to reverse, so prevention, not remediation, is the practical strategy.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Clean unengaged subscribers and use engagement-tiered segments
cards.summary: Suppress subscribers inactive for 180+ days and work in 14/30/60/90-day engagement windows to protect primary inbox placement.
cards.use_when: Replenishment/list hygiene work, or when deliverability declines from sending to a stale list.
steps: Define the benchmark: suppress profiles inactive past 180 days. Someone who signed up two years ago and has not opened, clicked or visited since is near-certainly uninterested, and every send to them dilutes your reputation.

Build engagement filters using Klaviyo's activity windows rather than one blunt list. The source's framework uses 14-day, 30-day, 60-day and 90-day active windows to grade engagement tiers, letting you send the most aggressive cadence to the freshest tiers and reduce or suppress the tail.
Within the engaged segment, always filter out fake signals: require 'opened email where Apple privacy open is false' OR 'clicked email where bot click is false'.

Add recency carve-outs before suppressing: someone who subscribed in the last 14 days, or was active on site in the last 14 days, should stay in the engaged segment even with no opens — they may only have received one or two emails, or may be re-showing intent.
Put a time limit on the carve-out: if a site-active subscriber does not engage within roughly two weeks, they should drop back out rather than staying engaged status for six months on one visit.
Re-run the suppression periodically rather than once, so the tail is pruned continuously.
caveats: Suppression reduces list size and short-term sends; the source frames this as necessary for future inbox placement rather than a loss.
Engagement tiers only work if open/click tracking is filtered for Apple and bot events, otherwise inactive people will look engaged.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Configure preference pages and choose email opt-in deliberately
cards.summary: Match email signup confirmation and unsubscribe behavior to the store list-quality goals and applicable requirements.
cards.use_when: Account setup, when signup-to-list conversion is poor, or when unsubscribes look unbranded and abrupt.
steps: In Settings > Other, locate the four pages: preference page, subscribe page, email confirmation, and unsubscribe page.
Brand the preference page and offer meaningful topic or frequency choices without obstructing unsubscribe.
Edit the unsubscribe page to add brand-appropriate copy (e.g. a thank-you for being part of the brand) rather than a bare default page.

Evaluate single versus double opt-in for email using signup completion, list quality and applicable requirements. The source preference for single opt-in is not a universal instruction and does not automatically apply to SMS.
Check the footer of your email templates includes working preference and unsubscribe links.

If a person reports still receiving emails after unsubscribing, use the profile's three-dot menu > Suppress to remove them from all sends — a genuinely unsubscribed person receiving mail is a spam-complaint risk.
caveats: Single opt-in is the source's recommendation on volume grounds; double opt-in is stronger for consent quality and some regions' compliance expectations. GDPR-style consent rules may override the list-growth argument.
Suppression and unsubscribe are different states; both must be respected.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Map the customer journey before building flows and campaigns
cards.summary: Sequence every touchpoint — ad/organic, pop-up, welcome, campaigns, first purchase, repeat — so messages match what the subscriber already knows.
cards.use_when: Planning lifecycle architecture, or when you suspect campaigns and flows are contradicting each other.
steps: Trace the source's journey structure: first visit from Meta/organic/TikTok → pop-up form offer → first emails from automated flows (welcome/nurture, or abandoned cart if applicable) → recurring campaigns at least weekly → first order → post-purchase messaging designed to drive the next order.

At the pop-up checkpoint, check the ad or content creative the visitor arrived from, then write the pop-up offer to speak only to what that traffic already knows. Mismatched offers are the most common journey break.

Audit for cross-channel contradiction: the source's example failure is a first-time-customer discount sent to someone who has already placed five orders, which annoys and is unusable. Gate first-purchase offers to non-purchasers.
Assign each touchpoint a single job and audience stage so content, offer and copy align with where the person is.
Review flows and campaigns together on a schedule — this is the fix for the common pattern of channels being built 'in a silo'.
caveats: The journey is described as a typical sequence; not every store has a pop-up-first entry or a long nurture phase.
Journey logic is qualitative — treat it as an alignment discipline rather than a measurable model.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Use Klaviyo metrics as flow triggers and personalisation filters
cards.summary: Treat metrics (events) as the automation engine: they trigger flows and define who receives what.
cards.use_when: Building or debugging flows, especially abandoned checkout/cart, and building personalised dynamic content.
steps: Understand the three metric sources: Klaviyo-native (received email, opened, clicked, unsubscribed, marked spam, dropped), Shopify (ordered product, placed order, fulfilled, refunded, checkout started, order cancelled), and API/integration events from other apps.
Use metrics as flow triggers. The source's example: the 'Checkout Started' metric triggers the abandoned-checkout flow, with the first email sent about 2 hours later.
Use metrics as filters and conditions for who should receive an email and who should not — e.g. don't send a first-purchase offer to someone with a 'Placed Order' metric in their history.
Use metric properties for personalisation — an order metric carries what was purchased and for how much, enabling conditional and dynamic content.
Confirm each required event is actually firing end-to-end (place a test order, start a test checkout) before relying on it as a trigger, since missing metrics mean silent flow failures.
caveats: Because events drive triggers, a broken integration produces no errors — flows simply never fire. Test after every app or theme change.
Event names differ between Shopify and any custom API implementations; map them deliberately.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Read a Klaviyo profile to decide segmentation and personalisation
cards.summary: Use the profile page as the single richest record of a customer — subscription source, custom properties, predictive analytics, event timeline — to drive filters and dynamic content.
cards.use_when: Designing segments, splits and conditional content, or investigating why one customer received the wrong message.
steps: Check subscription status first: email/SMS opt-in state, how and when they subscribed, and which form they used. This determines whether they are mailable at all.

Review custom properties, which are brand-specific: source, prospect vs repeat purchaser flags, Shopify tags pulled through the integration, loyalty points balance. These are the fields you can filter on.
Review standard data: language, location (from IP or checkout address), most recent acquisition source, last site visit, profile created/updated timestamps, first/last active.
Read the event timeline on the right side to reconstruct the journey — active on site, submitted form, subscribed, each email open, product views, orders.
Open Metrics & Insights and edit which metrics appear at a glance (orders placed, revenue, fulfilled). Add loyalty or other integration metrics if useful.

Use predictive analytics fields: predicted CLV, predicted date of next order, and channel affinity (which channel the person prefers) to avoid double-sending email plus SMS to someone who prefers one channel.
Use recently viewed products for dynamic content — show that person the products they actually looked at rather than a static recommendation block.
caveats: Predictive analytics are model outputs and should inform, not dictate, targeting; the source frames them as attribution/hint data.
Custom properties only exist if you or an integration creates them; a missing property cannot be used as a filter.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Organise profiles into lists and segments, and never campaign to the whole list
cards.summary: Keep static lists for opt-in sources and welcome-flow triggers; use dynamic engagement-filtered segments for campaigns.
cards.use_when: Campaign sending setup, list growth tracking, or troubleshooting welcome flows sending the wrong message.
steps: Maintain one primary email list and one primary SMS list for organic opt-ins (pop-up forms and checkout). This concentrates welcome-flow triggering for your main traffic source.
Use lists for opt-ins and as welcome/nurture flow triggers only — lists are static and never change membership once a person is added.

Create separate lists for each non-organic import or campaign source (e.g. an Instagram giveaway). Reason 1: track how each source contributes to list growth. Reason 2: control welcome messaging — an Instagram giveaway subscriber should get a giveaway welcome, not the '10% off your first order' welcome.
Build dynamic segments for sending campaigns. Segments update continuously based on behaviour, purchase status, engagement and other profile data.
Apply the rule the source states emphatically: never send a campaign to your entire list, and it is rare to send to a list at all. Segments protect deliverability and personalisation.
Confirm each list has a distinct associated welcome flow before importing, so the flow-to-source mapping is not accidental.
caveats: Multiple lists mean multiple welcome flows to maintain; be deliberate about adding new ones.
List membership is permanent for people once added, so list-based sending will accumulate stale contacts — another reason to send via segments.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Build the engaged prospect and engaged customer segments
cards.summary: Create engagement-qualified segments that separate first-time prospects from returning customers, then use the campaign results to learn what converts each group.
cards.use_when: Setting up your campaign sending audience, or improving deliverability and personalisation for campaigns.
steps: Apply the core principle: only send campaigns to people who have shown they want to hear from you. Continuing to send to a subscriber who has not opened or clicked in two years is a certain negative signal with no upside.

Define engagement with OR conditions: opened email in the last 180 days (Apple privacy open = false) OR clicked email in the last 180 days (bot click = false) OR subscribed to a list in the last 14 days OR active on site at least once in the last 14 days.
Add the mailability condition AND can/cannot receive email marketing, so unsubscribed and suppressed profiles are excluded even if they meet other criteria.
Then split the segment into (a) prospects who have never purchased and (b) existing customers, and create both as reusable segments for every campaign send.

Rationale for splitting: after each campaign you can see purchase results by segment, distinguishing first-order conversion from repeat purchases. A single blended engaged segment hides whether a campaign acquired or retained.

Extend the split to brand-relevant axes where useful — the source's example is an apparel brand separating male-buyer and female-buyer history to see whether women's campaigns are being bought by men.
Keep engagement criteria attached to every derived segment, including interest-based ones. A customer who has purchased ten times but never opens email still hurts deliverability if mailed.
caveats: The 180-day and 14-day windows are the source's chosen thresholds, not proven optima; adjust to your purchase cycle.
The prospect/customer split is a reporting and learning device first; targeting value is a secondary benefit.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Style campaign creative by segment learning
cards.summary: Once prospect vs customer is separated, read which creative elements converted each group and repeat those elements in the channel aimed at that group.
cards.use_when: Writing campaign and welcome-series creative, or deciding what proof and offers to lead with for new vs returning buyers.
steps: Send campaigns to the split segments from the previous card so results are attributable to prospect or customer audiences.

After the send, compare conversion between segments and note which content elements appear to drive the result. The source's illustrative example: if a prospect-heavy campaign featuring lots of reviews converts prospects well, add more reviews to prospect-facing campaigns and to the welcome series.

Carry the learning forward by audience, not across the board: what works for first-time buyers does not automatically work for repeat buyers, because the two groups buy for fundamentally different reasons.

Apply the same logic to discounts: prospect segments are where first-purchase offers belong; customer segments should receive non-discount value (new arrivals, replenishment, loyalty, education) instead.
Iterate by changing one creative variable per send so the comparison remains interpretable.
caveats: This is a directional learning loop, not a controlled creative test; the source presents it as observed practice rather than a measured effect size.
Do not generalise a prospect creative win to customers without checking, and vice versa.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Employ retention and account-level setup: where email sits in the 2026 lifecycle
cards.summary: Commit to a measured email cadence and a five-flow automated core, then extend with gamification, zero-party-data quizzes and split desktop/mobile experiences.
cards.use_when: Roadmapping the lifecycle programme, deciding sending frequency, and prioritising which automations to build first.
steps: Set the base sending cadence at 3–4 campaigns per week, the source's recommended campaign frequency. Consistency matters as much as volume for reputation — erratic bursts are a negative signal.
Prioritise the five core Klaviyo automated flows: Welcome, Browse Abandonment, Abandoned Cart, Abandoned Checkout and Post-Purchase. These are the standard set to build before advanced work.
Give the welcome flow a fast clock: the first 72 hours after signup is the critical conversion window, with day zero driving the highest purchase volume. Put your best converting email first.

After the core is in place, add advanced tactics the source lists: active gamification such as spin-to-win or scratch-off capture, zero-party data collection quizzes, and separate split-tested desktop and mobile experiences rather than one responsive template.

Recognise that the inbox itself is now AI-curated (e.g. Gmail's AI inbox), so authentication, regular cleaning and engagement-tiered segmentation are the levers that put mail in the primary inbox rather than the promotions tab.
Track cadence, flow coverage and inbox placement as programme health metrics, and be prepared to iterate rather than set and forget.
caveats: 3–4 campaigns per week plus flow volume is aggressive for some audiences; the source also tells you to learn whether emails are wanted, so cadence should be validated against engagement and spam complaints.
The 72-hour welcome window and day-zero concentration are the source's observations across an agency portfolio, not a guarantee for every offer type.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Engagement windows as sliding retargeting filters
cards.summary: Add recent site activity to an engaged segment so returning non-openers get inbox access again, but only for a limited window.
cards.use_when: Building or auditing your campaign send segments, and deciding whether dormant subscribers should still receive campaigns.
steps: Define engagement with four OR conditions, each time-bounded: opened email at least once in the last 180 days (with Apple privacy open = false), clicked email at least once in the last 180 days (with bot click = false), subscribed to list at least once in the last 14 days, or been active on site at least once in the last 14 days.

Treat site activity as intent evidence the same way you would treat a site visitor from a paid ad you retarget for a week or two. Someone browsing your store again is showing intent, so let them back into the campaign audience.
Cap the grace period. A returning visitor who then stops opening should stay in the engaged segment for roughly two weeks, not six months; if they do not engage again in that window, remove them.
Combine the OR engagement block with AND conditions for mailability and purchase status, then save and check the profile count preview before sending.
Re-verify the current Klaviyo filter names and privacy/bot filter labels, since interface naming changes.
caveats: The 180/14-day windows are the source's chosen settings, not a universal benchmark; adjust for your send cadence and list size.
Using OR for the mailability condition would include nearly everyone, so mailability and order history must be AND-ed to the engagement block.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Build prospect and customer segments by cloning one definition
cards.summary: Create the six core segments by changing only the order-count condition and the engagement window, not by writing new definitions each time.
cards.use_when: Setting up your initial Klaviyo segment structure before launching campaigns or flows.
steps: Build the prospect segment first: any engagement condition met AND can receive email marketing AND placed order zero times overall time.
Clone it and change only the final condition to placed order at least once overall time to produce the one-time/existing customer version.
Create three engagement windows per group: 90-day, 180-day and 365-day engaged, for both prospects and existing customers — six segments in total.
Use the preview count in the segment builder to sanity-check each segment's size before creating it.
Verify the current Klaviyo segment builder condition wording before rebuilding, since filter labels change between interface versions.
caveats: Segment definitions only matter if the list feeding them is clean; prospects are defined as never-purchased, so order tracking must be wired to your store correctly.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Match offer intensity to engagement window
cards.summary: Send evergreen content to the most recently engaged segment and reserve big offers for the widest window.
cards.use_when: Deciding which campaign content and offers go to your 90-day versus 365-day engaged segments.
steps: Send evergreen content — no huge offers, no huge new product announcements — to the 90-day engaged segment, because these people have shown recent interest and will keep engaging without a discount incentive.
Send major sale moments such as Black Friday and large product launches to the 365-day engaged segment to attempt re-engagement with people who only want to hear from you a few times a year.
Think of the customer type who shops a brand once a year specifically for the big deal — they do not want constant updates but do want the announcement, so the big offer is your reason to reach them.
Keep evergreen, non-discount creative in the cadence for recent engagers so you are not training your best subscribers to wait for discounts.
caveats: This is the source's agency practice at Dispatch, not a tested universal rule; the split between evergreen and promotional content should follow what your audience responds to.
The 90/180/365 bands are source-specific heuristics, not calculated thresholds.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Never send campaigns to the full list — and never to segments that are too small
cards.summary: Require an engagement filter on every campaign, but avoid slicing your sends so narrowly that you cut your monthly shots at converting a subscriber.
cards.use_when: Planning campaign send frequency and audience selection across your prospect and purchaser segments.
steps: Always include some engagement criteria in the campaign audience; never send a campaign to your entire list.

Avoid splitting two weekly campaigns across two different small segments (for example one send to prospects only, one to one-time purchasers only), because it halves your recipients and each person gets half as many chances to buy.
Recognize that you cannot know whether a given person will buy on Tuesday or Friday, so cutting their exposure removes shots on goal rather than improving relevance.

Unless you have millions of subscribers and the resources to send high volumes to small segments, send broader evergreen content to all engaged subscribers and personalize within the email using dynamic content instead of segment exclusion.
The source puts the cutoff at brands doing under roughly $20M a year, where broad engaged sending is the better trade.
caveats: This is the presenter's strongly held opinion based on agency experience; it is a distribution argument, not a claim that personalization is worthless — pair it with dynamic content.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Build filters so each flow only fires for the right lifecycle state
cards.summary: Profile filters are checked before every flow send, letting a welcome series stop the moment someone purchases.
cards.use_when: Setting up or debugging any automated flow where purchase or customer-type status should change who receives it.
steps: Add a profile filter to the welcome series requiring that the person has placed order zero times overall time.
Rely on the fact that Klaviyo re-checks filters immediately before each email in the flow, so a subscriber who buys between email one and email two does not receive email two.
Extend the same pattern to other flow logic: for example, filter out known B2B customers from a DTC welcome series when your brand serves both segments.
Avoid using Klaviyo default flow templates for these flows; the source recommends building from scratch (build your own) so triggers, filters and timing match your actual customer journey.
Verify current filter names and trigger options in your Klaviyo account before configuring.
caveats: Profile filters only work as well as the data behind them; order and tag data must flow from your store into the profile.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Micro-commitment first step in the pop-up form
cards.summary: Split the pop-up into a 'claim the offer?' step before asking for the email, then collect SMS, then show a success page.
cards.use_when: Building or redesigning your sitewide pop-up form to convert more site traffic into subscribers.
steps: Step one, micro yes: present only the offer and two buttons, e.g. 'Claim 20% off' versus 'I'm not interested', with nothing asked in return. The micro commitment principle means someone who commits to wanting the offer is far more likely to give their email next.
Step two, email opt-in: make the email field required with a 'field is required' message and set the button action to submit form, routing to your master email list.
Step three, SMS opt-in: collect phone subscribers here even if you have not built out SMS marketing yet; you are otherwise leaving subscribers uncollected for no setup cost.
Step four, success page: either show the code or send it to the inbox/phone. The source prefers sending it, because the first open and click boosts your sender reputation.
Turn on the teaser so that if someone exits the form mid-way, a teaser stays on site and can reopen the form.
caveats: The micro-commitment structure is based on the source's agency A/B testing across hundreds of forms, but the results are their client data, not a guarantee for your brand.
Nine times out of ten the micro-commitment step tests better, per the source, but it is still worth an A/B test.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Form behavior settings that stop accidental opt-out loss
cards.summary: Small behavior toggles — no click-outside close, immediate load, no images — prevent losing subscribers who never see the offer.
cards.use_when: Configuring display and behavior settings on a pop-up form before going live.
steps: Uncheck 'click outside form to close' so the only exit is the X button. Otherwise a browsing visitor who clicks a product at the exact moment the pop-up appears closes the form never to reopen it.
Set the form to load immediately rather than on a time delay, which the source reports performs better.
Build without side images: with no image, attention goes straight to the offer, and the source says forms without images typically outperform those with images (still a good A/B test).
Show the form to all website visitors who are not already subscribed, and keep frequency rules in mind if you do not want repeat visitors to see it daily.
Check that the form renders correctly on both mobile and desktop rather than only on the device you are building on; most of your site traffic is mobile.
Verify current setting labels in your form builder, since interface wording changes.
caveats: Targeting all non-subscribers is the source's recommendation for maximum capture, but you may still exclude specific URLs such as the cart page where a discount could cut into margin on an imminent purchase.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Offer choice is the highest-leverage pop-up test
cards.summary: Run monthly A/B tests on the form offer first, then behavior, then copy, then design.
cards.use_when: Planning your recurring pop-up form experiment roadmap.
steps: Test the offer first: percent off versus dollar off, 10% versus 15%, free shipping, cash back, or free gift with purchase, since offer makes the biggest difference to opt-in rate.
If testing dollar off against percentage, take your AOV and pick a dollar amount that equals roughly 10% of that AOV, so the comparison is at least in the same value range.
Test behavior second: micro-commitment step versus none, zero-party data questions in the form, load timing (immediate versus delay), which pages trigger it, and exit intent.
Test copy third: short versus long copy, and whether to reveal the offer versus teasing a 'mystery offer'.
Test design last: image versus no image, product versus lifestyle imagery, and text sizes, especially if your customer base skews older.

Run a test every month; even a form already converting well is unlikely to be at its ceiling. Take the conversion-rate numbers the source cites for its own agency clients as an illustration of headroom, not as your target.
caveats: The source's claim that Klaviyo's 'excellent' badge threshold is not actually excellent is the presenter's opinion, not a verified platform fact; treat it as a reason to keep testing.
Offer data is audience-specific — your demographic may respond better to dollar off or free shipping than to percentage off.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Targeting and location rules for offer differentiation
cards.summary: Use URL, geography, UTM source and cart value rules to show the right offer in the right place.
cards.use_when: Setting up pop-up targeting rules for a sitewide form, a sale form, or a channel-specific offer test.
steps: Use URL rules to suppress the sitewide discount form where it hurts: for example exclude the cart page so an about-to-purchase visitor does not get handed extra margin away, and exclude a sale landing page if the sitewide discount cannot be stacked with the sale.
Use location rules, driven by IP-based location, to show different offers by country — for example a different offer for Canadian versus US visitors.
Use UTM parameters to target by traffic source: if traffic from one paid channel is much cheaper, you could test a richer offer for that source while showing the standard offer to everyone else.
Use cart content value to trigger a form only above a threshold, such as over $1,000 in cart, so a strong offer lands on a high-value basket.
Use targeting modes deliberately: show to all visitors for a sale link, show to email subscribers only when you want existing subscribers to opt into SMS if they skipped it.
Do not restrict the sitewide form to the homepage only; the source explicitly discourages that.
Verify the current targeting options and labels in your ESP, since these change.
caveats: Cart-value thresholds such as $1,000 are examples of what the tool supports, not recommended thresholds for your store.
Source-specific channel advice (for example TikTok versus Meta offers) depends on your own cost per acquisition and margin.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Master list plus engaged segments as the base setup
cards.summary: Create one master email list that all forms and checkout feed, and build engagement segments on top of it.
cards.use_when: Setting up or cleaning up your ESP account before building flows and campaigns.
steps: Create a single master email list fed by your pop-up form and checkout, so every acquisition source writes into the same list.
Use the segment builder for audiences built from behaviour, properties and events — lists for who opted in, segments for what they have done.

Know the condition types available: whether someone can receive email marketing (not unsubscribed or suppressed), what someone has or has not done across tracked metrics with either a date range or overall time, location proximity, and profile properties including store tags.
Use property and tag conditions to target, for example, people carrying a specific Shopify tag or people who viewed specific items, so campaigns and flows can be personalized on that data.
Connect SMS subscribers to a separate list, as recommended, rather than mixing phone and email subscribers on one list.
Verify current Klaviyo list/segment tabs and builder condition names before implementing.
caveats: A list implies opt-in consent; using segments to send to people who never opted in creates deliverability and compliance risk.
The segment builder's exact property and metric names depend on your integrations and may differ from the example.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Campaigns versus flows, and stopping message overlap
cards.summary: Flows capture behaviour-triggered lifecycle revenue; campaigns capture time-sensitive moments — and the two must be coordinated.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a recurring send should become an automation, and diagnosing high unsubscribe or spam complaint rates.
steps: Route repetitive sends into flows: if you find yourself sending the same campaign weekly, monthly, or daily, it is probably a behaviour-triggered automation instead.
Keep campaigns for genuinely one-off, time-sensitive moments such as a new sale, a product launch, seasonal content, or a new blog post.
Use flows to extract lifetime value from the customer journey and campaigns to capitalize on moments that will not repeat.

Before sending a campaign, check whether the same person is also due a welcome, abandoned cart, or post-purchase email in the same period; overlapping sends in a 24-hour window are a common cause of unsubscribes and spam complaints.
Audit the campaign and flow calendars together as one customer journey rather than as separate programs.
caveats: The source's observation about high unsubscribe and spam rates among audited brands is anecdotal from their agency work, not a measured benchmark.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Welcome series: trigger, filter and immediate code delivery
cards.summary: Trigger the welcome series on list addition, gate it to never-purchasers, and send the signup offer code immediately.
cards.use_when: Building your first automated welcome flow after someone subscribes via pop-up or checkout.
steps: Set the trigger to 'added to list' on the same master list your pop-up form writes to, so every new subscriber enters the flow.
Add a profile filter requiring zero orders overall time, so checkout subscribers and past purchasers are excluded.
Remove any initial time delay for the first email: send the redemption code as soon as someone signs up so the promise made in the pop-up is fulfilled while intent is highest.
Set email one's sender on your authenticated brand domain, and set reply-to to your customer support address so replies land in the service inbox.
Structure the series so that by the end, the subscriber fully understands why your brand is the one to buy from in your category, not just that a discount exists.
Use standardised flow and email naming (for example 'welcome series email number 1') so reporting views can trace performance back to its source.
Verify current trigger, filter and naming fields in your ESP before building.
caveats: Filter requirements differ by brand; the source adds B2B exclusions for brands serving both B2B and DTC, which may not apply to you.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Design emails outside the ESP with image slices
cards.summary: Build email creative in a design tool and slice it, so brand fonts render consistently instead of being replaced by fallbacks.
cards.use_when: Producing welcome, cart, post-purchase and campaign creative that must match your brand across devices and inboxes.
steps: Design in an external tool and export image slices, so the layout renders pixel for pixel the same on desktop and mobile; inside a template editor, headline wrapping and spacing differ across devices and inboxes, making QA harder.

Understand the font problem: custom fonts need a web-safe fallback, and whether the brand font actually displays depends on the recipient's device and inbox provider, so what you see in the preview is not what every recipient sees.

Keep the brand consistent from ad to site to pop-up to first email, because these touchpoints are where initial trust is built; a font that does not match the rest of the funnel breaks that consistency.
Place the product block inside your externally designed email if you want products in it, since the product block is the one thing that must be set up in the ESP.
Add a proper footer with social links and your organisation details and unsubscribe language; the ESP inserts a required unsubscribe link regardless, but a default one is ugly.
Verify current editor capabilities and footer compliance requirements in your ESP.
caveats: Fully image-sliced emails trade rendering control for reduced live-text accessibility and searchability; the source advocates the approach for branding fidelity, not as a universal standard.
If you lack design resources, the source says choosing a template is acceptable, while noting template images often cannot be edited in the ESP.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Dynamic product feeds for emails
cards.summary: Use the ESP product block to insert static or rule-based dynamic products from your store into emails.
cards.use_when: Adding product recommendations to welcome, browse, cart or campaign emails, especially when inventory and bestsellers change often.
steps: Place a product block in the email; choose static products when you want fixed SKUs, or dynamic products when the selection should be recalculated each send.
For dynamic feeds, set criteria such as bestselling products over a chosen window — the source shows options like the last 3 days or last 90 days — so the email reflects current demand.
Add filters to avoid unhelpful recommendations: exclude a category, set a minimum price, or exclude products with very low stock.

Choose deliberately between dynamic and static: a brand with constantly turning inventory and new styles may want current bestsellers, while a brand with ten always-in-stock SKUs may prefer to always show its two or three consistent bestsellers.
Save the feed and attach it to the email; the ESP recalculates the products at send time as the underlying data changes.
Verify current product-feed criteria and filter options in your ESP, since these change.
caveats: Dynamic feeds depend on accurate product, price and stock data flowing from your store; stale data will produce stale or out-of-stock recommendations.
The source's window examples (3 days, 90 days) are illustrations of available settings, not recommended values.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Design Welcome Emails Outside Klaviyo, Export as Image Slices
cards.summary: Build welcome emails in Figma, export sliced images, and assemble them in Klaviyo for branding consistency beyond what templates allow.
cards.use_when: Designing your first welcome email for a new subscriber, where you need a branded look that Klaviyo's template/HTML editor can't produce (e.g., custom graphic placement).
steps: Design the full welcome series in Figma (or similar design tool) with the logo, offer code, hero graphic, and body content laid out exactly as you want it.
Slice each visual block in the design into separate images and export each as PNG or JPEG.
In Klaviyo, drag in an image block, upload the exported slice, and compress it.
Repeat for each section, stacking image blocks until the email matches the Figma design.
Add subject line and preview text after the design is assembled.
Set one-day time delays between each welcome email, then set the emails live one by one.
caveats: This workflow assumes design work happens outside Klaviyo; Klaviyo's templates and HTML editor are described as too rigid for advanced layouts.
Image-heavy emails trade design control for text deliverability — the source does not address that tradeoff.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Welcome Series Content Blueprint for DTC Brands
cards.summary: Sequence five-plus welcome emails, each covering a different reason to buy, while keeping the pop-up offer visible in every email.
cards.use_when: Planning the content and sequence of your welcome flow after a subscriber joins via a pop-up offer.
steps: Email 1: deliver the pop-up offer code with the goal of getting the subscriber back to the site as fast as possible; include the logo plus one or two of: a short founder letter, brand values, USPs, or best-selling products/collections.
Add a one-day delay, then email 2: explain your unique selling points — why they should buy from you rather than competitors.
Email 3: guide subscribers to the best product for them by highlighting your top 3–5 best sellers or best-selling collections.
One-day delay, email 4: feature the brand story, framing why the subscriber should care (e.g., the market problem the brand was created to solve).
One-day delay, email 5: a direct us-vs-them comparison arguing why to buy from you over specific competitors.
Then spotlight customer reviews/testimonials, then answer FAQs (many prospects never visit your FAQ page).
Add brand-specific angle emails (e.g., heritage, trust) based on what your customers care about.
In every email, keep a banner or line reminding them their offer is still valid.
caveats: Presented as a baseline the source says fits ~99% of DTC brands based on their A/B tests, not a universal requirement.
Not every brand has a brand story that drives conversion; the source acknowledges this.
Withhold nothing that could help a subscriber convert — the goal is to give new subscribers everything they need to make a first purchase.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Trigger Abandoned Checkout on checkout started With Order Filtering
cards.summary: Set up the abandoned checkout flow on the checkout started metric (labeled 'abandoned cart' in Klaviyo) filtered to exclude completed orders.
cards.use_when: Building the abandoned checkout flow in Klaviyo and setting the trigger and flow filters.
steps: In Klaviyo flow templates, search 'checkout'; the abandoned cart reminder template is actually triggered by the checkout started metric — Klaviyo names it cart but it fires on checkout.

Confirm both an abandoned cart flow (added to cart trigger) and an abandoned checkout flow (checkout started trigger) exist, since a shopper who adds to cart without starting checkout will not enter the checkout flow.
Add filter: placed order zero times since starting this flow, so Klaviyo checks they haven't already purchased before sending.

Optionally add 'has not been in flow in the last X days' — the source keeps this at 2–3 days for clients so returning shoppers who restart checkout still get reminded, arguing interest justifies more sends.
caveats: Flow filter windows (2–3 days vs. longer suppression) are a source opinion, not a benchmark; longer windows avoid over-messaging but the source believes shorter windows make more money.
Verify current Klaviyo template naming and filter options in your account, as interface and labels can change.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Test email and SMS sequencing in abandonment flows
cards.summary: Compare coordinated channel sequences while preserving shopper permissions, purchase exclusions and contact limits.
cards.use_when: Configuring the channel logic in an abandoned checkout or abandoned cart flow when you have both email and SMS.
steps: Review Klaviyo's default template split, which sends SMS if reachable and only sends email 4 hours later if SMS is not possible.
Test the source simultaneous-send idea only for eligible recipients and within channel send-time and frequency rules; compare against a staggered sequence.
Reason: you cannot know whether a given shopper converts from SMS or email; email carries advantages like visuals that SMS lacks, and after an abandoned checkout every hour counts.
A/B test time delays (e.g., 4-hour vs. 2-hour first delay) for your own list rather than adopting a fixed default.
Recheck purchase exclusions before messages and keep SMS quiet-hour settings enabled. https://help.klaviyo.com/hc/en-us/articles/9352115400219
caveats: Source opinion that simultaneously sending beats SMS-first fallback; not backed by a cited benchmark.
Shorter time delays 'typically convert better' is the source's testing observation, and they say to A/B test per client.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Branch Abandonment Flows by Prospect vs. Existing Customer
cards.summary: Split abandoned checkout and cart flows into first-time prospects (welcome offer, product highlights, objections) and returning customers (loyalty/subscription incentives).
cards.use_when: Writing content and setting up conditional splits inside abandoned checkout and abandoned cart flows.
steps: Add a conditional split on 'has someone placed an order at least once over all time' — yes = existing customer, no = prospect.
For prospects: remind them of the welcome offer they're still eligible for, show their abandoned products via Klaviyo dynamic cart content, and restate why they should buy from you (USPs).

Use roughly a 20-hour delay between prospect emails as a starting point, then remind them of the offer and cart contents again and address 1–2 common objections (e.g., price, perceived value) using relevant customer reviews.
Include a minimum of three abandoned cart emails for prospects, with the third addressing another objection.
For existing customers: they are past the acquisition offer, so instead focus on other incentives — subscribe-and-save, loyalty programs, or other reasons to repurchase.
caveats: The ~20-hour delay is a starting point the source says varies by brand.
The three-email minimum is the source's stated floor, not a measured optimum.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Link Abandonment Emails Directly Back to Checkout
cards.summary: Use the checkout URL event variable on images and buttons so recovery emails return each shopper to their saved checkout, not the homepage.
cards.use_when: Setting up links in abandoned checkout/cart email images and buttons so shoppers don't have to re-add products.
steps: On all image slices in the abandoned checkout flow, set the link address to the curly-bracket event variable event.extra.checkout URL.
You can copy this link from the 'back to my cart' button that Klaviyo already includes in its abandoned cart template.
This directs each specific person back to the checkout they started, with their products ready so they only need to place the order.

For browse abandonment, do the equivalent: preview/test the email, open the event properties (product name, ID, price, URL), copy the product URL property, and paste it as the link on 'shop now' slices instead of Klaviyo's default organization URL.
caveats: Dynamic variable names are Klaviyo-specific and may change — verify in the current template and event preview.
Copying event properties requires previewing a real triggering event to see the field names.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Use Klaviyo Templates Only For Dynamic Cart Tables
cards.summary: Start abandonment flows from Klaviyo templates to inherit the working dynamic product table, then replace the design with your Figma-built email.
cards.use_when: Building abandoned cart, abandoned checkout, or browse abandonment emails where you need a dynamic product table but custom design.
steps: Create the flow from Klaviyo's template (e.g., 'abandoned cart reminder') so the trigger, filters, and dynamic content are pre-built.
The template includes a two-column table: column one pulls the product image via a dynamic variable, the other shows product title, quantity, and total.
Delete quantity or total cells if you don't want them shown, keeping just the product name.
Keep the graphic slices from your Figma design as separate image blocks above/below the dynamic table, mixing static design with the dynamic block.
Preview for different profiles to confirm the right product images and titles render per recipient.
Use the template primarily for the dynamic table because building that code from scratch is technical and time-consuming.
caveats: For post-purchase flows with no dynamic content, the source builds from scratch instead of using a template.
Verify current template structure and variable names in your Klaviyo account.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Fix Browse Abandonment Filters and Link to the Viewed Product
cards.summary: Add the missing added-to-cart filter to Klaviyo's browse abandonment template, then link each email to the specific viewed product, not the homepage.
cards.use_when: Setting up the browse abandonment flow for shoppers who viewed a product but took no further action.
steps: Use Klaviyo's browse abandonment template (trigger: viewed product), but note the default profile filters only exclude checkout started and placed order.
Add the missing filter: added to cart zero times since starting this flow, so only shoppers who haven't moved down the funnel receive it.
Keep 'has not been in flow in the last 30 days' as a reasonable default for most brands, since browse-stage interest doesn't justify frequent reminders.
Approve the source's warning about browse abandonment objectives: purchase intent is lower, so write copy that acknowledges this and consider suggesting other products.
Emphasize social proof heavily for this audience, as they haven't signaled purchase interest yet.

Branch prospects vs. existing customers and show the viewed products via the dynamic table; replace the template's organization-URL link with the product URL from the viewed-product event so 'shop now' goes to the product page, reducing friction.
caveats: The 30-day flow re-entry window is the source's default preference, not a calculated rule.
The source recommends more than the single email Klaviyo provides by default.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Design Post-Purchase Flows Around First-Time vs. Returning Customers
cards.summary: Split the placed-order flow so first-time buyers get onboarding, education, and a proactive service check-in while returning customers get loyalty and cross-sell messages.
cards.use_when: Planning the post-purchase flow that fires after an order, especially to improve first-purchase experience and repeat purchase.
steps: Trigger on placed order; add brand-specific filters (e.g., exclude subscription or B2B customers from the standard post-purchase content, or route them to a different flow).
Do not schedule sends at a fixed time of day (e.g., 9 a.m.) — instead keep relative timing like '1 day after' so emails land when that buyer is typically active.
For first-time buyers: thank them, then deliver education/resources and use cases so they get full value — a poor first experience makes a return purchase unlikely.
Include a proactive plain-text customer-service check-in email ('how's it going, let us know if you need help'), which most brands skip and which requires no staff time once automated.
Then move them toward a next purchase via subscription, loyalty, or other programs.
Set a conditional split on 'placed order equals 1 over all time' to separate first-timers from returning customers, who instead get loyalty appreciation and personalized cross-sells.
caveats: The source notes post-purchase flows are highly brand-specific, so filters and content must be set per brand rather than copied.
The anti-9 a.m. opinion assumes buyer activity patterns match purchase time; it is a stated rationale, not a tested benchmark.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Time Your Win-Back Flow Using Actual Repurchase Data
cards.summary: Calculate median and average days between purchases, take a point in between, and delay the win-back flow to that — not Klaviyo's default 90 days.
cards.use_when: Setting the initial time delay before your customer win-back flow sends its offer emails.
steps: Pull your order data (e.g., Shopify) and calculate the median and average number of days between a customer's purchases.
Choose a delay between the median and average rather than guessing.

Sanity-check the delay against your product's consumption cycle. Example from the source: a food/beverage product consumed within 30 days, with ~5 days shipping, means you can assume after ~45–50 days a customer has likely run out and may need a nudge.
Build the flow on the placed order trigger with filter 'placed order zero times since starting this flow' so anyone who repurchases drops out automatically.
Space the win-back emails with longer delays (e.g., 7 days and 5 days per the source) rather than one-day gaps, since you can't know exactly when the customer is ready.
Content should say 'we miss you,' present a special exclusive offer with urgency, and reiterate why your brand beats the competition before they lapse.
caveats: The 45–50 day example is a worked illustration, not a universal benchmark — derive your own from your data.
Klaviyo's default ~90-day delay should not be accepted uncritically per the source.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Build a Sunset Flow With a Segment Trigger and Profile Property
cards.summary: Identify unengaged subscribers with a segment, send three last-chance emails, then tag and suppress non-responders to protect deliverability and billing.
cards.use_when: Setting up the sunset flow to remove chronically unengaged subscribers from your active list.
steps: Build a segment: opened an email zero times in the last 180 days AND clicked an email zero times in the last 180 days AND can still receive email marketing (not already suppressed).
Create a flow triggered by 'added to segment' using that segment.
Add profile filters: opened email zero times since starting this flow OR clicked email zero times since starting this flow, so anyone who engages drops out.
Send three last-chance emails focused on a strong offer, with subject lines that highlight it; use a dynamic code so it can't leak.
In the final email, tell them they'll be removed from the list unless they engage.
After a further delay (e.g., 5 days), add a profile property update setting a boolean custom property (e.g., 'unengaged' = true) on anyone who never engaged.
Create a second segment for 'unengaged = true' AND still able to receive email marketing; once a month, export that segment as CSV and import it under suppressed profiles.
caveats: The 180-day engagement window is presented as 'usually good for most brands,' i.e., a heuristic.
Suppression reduces active profiles and can lower Klaviyo billing, but the source frames the primary benefit as deliverability protection.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Set Campaign Cadence From Data, Not Ambition
cards.summary: Increase send frequency only while CTR holds and unsubscribes/spam complaints stay flat, and only to a volume you can sustain.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many campaigns per week to send for a brand roughly doing $1M–$10M/year.
steps: Decide the target volume based on two questions: what volume maximizes the balance of engagement, deliverability, and ROI, and what volume can you realistically sustain week after week.
Track click-through rate, unsubscribe rate, and spam complaint rate as you increase frequency.
If you go from one to four emails per week and those metrics stay roughly flat, you can send more — the list is signaling it wants that volume.
If metrics deteriorate dramatically, reduce back toward the level that preserves them.
Choose a cadence you can actually commit to: the source warns against promising four per week and delivering four one week and one the next.
If needed, start at a sustainable two per week and invest in resources/team before increasing.
caveats: The $1M–$10M revenue range is the source's stated sweet spot for this guidance.
The 'metrics stay flat' test is described as a hypothetical illustration of the principle, not a fixed numeric threshold.
Falling out of cadence risks higher unsubscribes and spam complaints and reduced engagement for seasonal peaks like Black Friday.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Product and Collection Spotlight Campaigns
cards.summary: Build campaign emails around one product or a thematic collection, going deep on why that specific item is best rather than listing the catalog.
cards.use_when: Choosing what to send in a weekly/regular campaign, especially for products you assume customers don't want.
steps: Product spotlight: pick one product and go deep on the details that make it better than competitors — materials, ingredients, construction — surfacing details that exist on the product page but that customers overlook.
Frame the email around why someone should care about this product specifically, rather than letting it compete with the rest of the catalog.

Collection spotlight: group products by a theme or common thread rather than by store category. Example cited: a 'head-to-toe neutrals' collection that pulls from separate tops and bottoms categories.
Use this framing even for slower products — the source argues results often surprise brands that assume they aren't wanted.
caveats: The claim that spotlighting non-bestsellers 'shocks' brands is anecdotal from the source's agency work, not a measured benchmark.
The source reports these campaign types perform well for roughly 99% of brands based on agency data, not a controlled study.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Benefit-Focused Campaigns: One Benefit Per Email
cards.summary: Isolate a single product benefit and build an entire email around it instead of listing all benefits at once.
cards.use_when: Planning campaign content when you have multiple selling points and want higher conversion from a specific customer segment.
steps: List the reasons different customer segments might buy your product (e.g., water savings, durability, materials).
Pick one benefit that matters disproportionately to a segment on your list.
Devote a full email to that benefit and its 'what's in it for me' — treat a single product-page bullet as the whole email premise.
Example cited: a shower-head brand building an email around 'over a billion gallons saved' rather than listing it alongside other features.
This approach lets you send more campaigns without repeating yourself, speaking to different benefits in turn.
caveats: The source notes this works when one segment will overwhelmingly care about the angle — testing different angles is advised rather than assuming.
Not a universal rule for every product with only one benefit to offer.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Use Content and Education Campaigns to Seed Purchase Intent
cards.summary: Repurpose blog/social content or teach a problem in email, then tie it back to the product you sell.
cards.use_when: Filling the campaign calendar when you don't have a promotion running, or when your product needs category education.
steps: Content spotlight: reformat existing blog or Instagram/TikTok content into an email, or use email to drive subscribers to content they haven't seen on other channels.
Structure the email so the first section teases and links to the content, then a second section presents the product from that content as available to shop.

Example cited: a client blog post on spotting food-allergy signs was turned into an email that teased the post and linked out, then promoted the brand's allergen-introduction products — parents learn the signs, then get offered a solution.

Education spotlight: teach the category or ingredient deeply rather than listing benefits. Example cited: explaining everything about argan oil so readers connect the dots themselves, or a 'three reasons wet wipes are not your friend' email that makes the case against the alternative before presenting the brand's product.
Use weekly newsletters (creation or curation — memes, playlists, industry news) to stay top of mind affordably when time is tight.
caveats: The blog-email conversion success is an agency case example, not a guaranteed result.
Education angles work best when your product/ingredients genuinely benefit from explanation.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Six campaign types to rotate in your email calendar
cards.summary: Pick from evergreen content, weekly newsletter, cultural event, promo (teaser/launch/last-chance/reminder) and new-product-launch campaigns based on what the store needs that week.
cards.use_when: Planning next month's campaign calendar and deciding what kind of email to send each week.
steps: Evergreen content campaigns educate subscribers on a topic relevant to them and connect it back to why they'd buy from you (e.g., Tushy explaining a category issue and letting readers draw the conclusion to buy).

Weekly newsletters can be created or curated; if you are tight on time, curate — memes, an industry roundup, a monthly Spotify playlist — the goal is engagement and being a brand people want to hear from, not direct revenue.

Cultural event campaigns (Mother's Day, Father's Day, Black Friday, holidays) convert well because they tie your product to something already top-of-mind; explain why to buy for that reason (Absolut's 'serve one up for the moms who are selfless', Rebel Rabbit's 'survive the holiday hustle').

Promotional emails split into four: teaser (warn a sale is coming / SMS gets early access), launch (sale is live — concise, sell the click not the product), last chance (final day urgency), and reminders (for multi-week sales, remind throughout instead of only at start and end; Ready Set Food adds a reminder module at the bottom of evergreen sends).
New product launch announcements are typically among the highest revenue campaigns; send at least one the morning of launch with clear, benefit-led messaging about why the subscriber should care.
caveats: The revenue claims for new product launches are the presenter's guarantee/opinion, not a measured benchmark.
Newsletter-style sends often drive low revenue but high engagement — judge them on whether format can be changed to convert, not just revenue.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Message and offer matter 10x more than copy polish or design
cards.summary: Prioritize what you send (product, offer, audience fit) over how beautifully you say it; a mismatched offer cannot be designed into converting.
cards.use_when: Allocating limited time between writing/designing emails and deciding what to promote and which offer to run for a campaign.
steps: Before polishing a design, ask whether the product and offer actually fit the subscriber and the moment — e.g., promoting men's items for Mother's Day will not convert no matter how good the email looks.
Treat merchandising, offer choice and topic selection as the highest-ROI activity; get granular about what you talk about and what you feature.

For smaller brands especially, stop over-investing in pixel-perfect design and copywriting — the presenter reports auditing many brands that are overly focused on creative while the underlying offer or product choice is the real lever.
Decide the core message and offer first, then let the copy and design serve that message rather than distract from it.
Re-check any campaign where the featured product would not make sense to the recipient in that moment; swap the product or reframe the angle before sending.
caveats: This is the presenter's strong opinion based on client audits, not a measured experiment; design still affects clicks and conversions, so this is about relative priority, not ignoring design entirely.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Send campaigns to engaged segments only
cards.summary: Build a sending segment of engaged subscribers (e.g., 90-day engaged) and exclude recent buyers or other inappropriate groups, not the full list.
cards.use_when: Setting up the audience for any campaign in Klaviyo, especially new product launches or promos where some subscribers shouldn't receive it.
steps: Create engaged-time-window segments earlier (prospects engaged 90-day example) and select them in the 'send to' field of the campaign — do not send to raw lists.

Use the 'don't send to' option to exclude subscribers for whom the message is inappropriate; for a new product launch, exclude anyone who purchased in the same category in the last 3 days by building that segment and adding it to the exclusion.
Where a campaign resends to a narrower segment, choose that narrower segment separately (e.g., only those engaged in the last 30 days) to avoid over-mailing lower-engagement people.
Check estimated recipients in the final review — Klaviyo shows it as the sum of included segments minus excluded segments.
Verify your segments are updating as expected: if you want exclusions to reflect purchases at send time, use the 'determine recipients at send time' toggle when scheduling.
caveats: If 'determine recipients at send time' is not ticked, dynamic segments are evaluated at scheduling rather than at the send moment — this is the wrong choice when excluding recent buyers.
The specific engagement windows (90-day, 30-day, 3-day) are examples from the walkthrough, not universal thresholds.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Decide smart sending per campaign, not just at account level
cards.summary: Override account-level smart-sending per campaign to control whether a subscriber who just received another email gets this one.
cards.use_when: Scheduling a high-priority campaign such as a big product launch or flagship promo, and deciding whether to let smart sending hold it back.
steps: Understand what smart sending does: it suppresses subscribers who recently received other emails so you don't over-send in a short window.
Set the baseline smart-sending limitations at the account level in settings, then override per campaign when the content justifies it.
Ask the specific question the presenter suggests: if someone received an abandoned cart email or a welcome series email within the last 16 hours, do we still want them to see this campaign?
For a big new product launch, the presenter's guidance is to turn smart sending off for that campaign because the subscriber is likely to want to hear about it; for routine content, leave it on.
After scheduling, confirm the smart-sending state in the final review screen — Klaviyo flags if it was disabled so you can verify it was intentional.
caveats: Turning smart sending off for every campaign risks over-mailing and unsubscribes; this override is reserved for genuinely high-relevance sends in the presenter's view.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Set up a new-product-launch campaign in Klaviyo end to end
cards.summary: Walk-through for building, templating and scheduling a new-product-launch campaign in Klaviyo with the correct audience, template source, tracking and timing.
cards.use_when: Building and scheduling a new product launch (or similar announcement) campaign for a Shopify store.
steps: Go to the Campaigns tab, create a campaign, name it (e.g., 'new product launch'), set the send date, set type to email, and add campaign tags — tags help with later data analysis.
Choose the audience segment (engaged segment) and apply any exclusions in 'don't send to'.
Turn smart sending on or off for this campaign depending on launch priority.
Include UTM parameters in tracking before moving on.
Choose the creative path: reuse saved templates, use the Klaviyo email library and edit, or start new — if you built the email in Figma, use 'create new' and drag in each image slice to rebuild it.
Write the subject line (intriguing, e.g., 'It's finally here...') and preview text (adds a second reason to open, e.g., 'the product that everyone's been asking for').

Use the campaign sequence builder to optionally add a follow-up resend, then review settings — estimated recipients, subject, preview, content, from/reply addresses, unsubscribe link (required for compliance), and tracking.

Schedule or send, choosing an exact send time (e.g., 9:00 a.m. Eastern when the product goes live on Shopify) or recipient local time zone, and toggle 'determine recipients at send time' if segments need to update at send.
caveats: Klaviyo's interface changes over time; verify current menu labels and toggle locations before relying on these steps.
The 9:00 a.m. launch-alignment timing is an example, not a rule — align send time with when the product actually goes live on your store.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Add a follow-up resend to catch non-openers
cards.summary: Resend a campaign to people who didn't open the first send, with a different subject line and a narrower audience, using Klaviyo's one-click toggle or manual cloning.
cards.use_when: Maximizing reach of a high-priority campaign such as a new product launch or a time-sensitive promotion.
steps: In the campaign sequence builder, toggle the resend to anyone who didn't open the first email.
Write a different subject line for the resend — if the first subject line didn't engage them, try another angle (e.g., 'Brand T-shirts just in time for summer').
Narrow the resend audience — for example if the first send went to a 90-day engaged segment, resend only to those engaged in the last 30 days to avoid over-mailing less engaged subscribers.
Set the time delay: Klaviyo will not allow a delay under 48 hours on the built-in resend.
For situations where you need faster or multiple resends, clone the campaign and send it manually instead of using the resend toggle.
