caveats: The 48-hour minimum limit applies to the built-in resend feature — the presenter notes this is fine for non-time-sensitive sends but inadequate for fast events like Black Friday, where you clone and resend manually.
For Black Friday-type events the presenter suggests two or three resends of the same campaign to cut through inbox flooding — this is aggressive and should be weighed against unsubscribe risk.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Write copy that sells the click, not the product
cards.summary: For promos and launches, write email copy whose job is to get the subscriber to the website; education happens elsewhere.
cards.use_when: Writing a promo launch or new product launch email where the goal is to get subscribers clicking through to a product page.
steps: Recognize that the email's job is often to get the subscriber to the site — if they don't get there, they can't shop or buy.
Write copy that earns the click rather than fully selling the product in the email.

Use this especially when other campaigns or content have already done the educating — for example, a Black Friday promo email should just communicate the offer and get them out (Moment: 'up to 60% off sitewide, shop Black Friday deals').
Keep promo launch copy short and to the point — the presenter says the best promo launch campaigns are concise.
Ensure the destination (product page, collection page, landing page) carries the selling work, since the email is the doorway.
caveats: This is the presenter's recommended approach for promos and launches specifically, where awareness and interest already exist; for a cold or educational campaign, more explanation in the email may be needed.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Write to one core message per email and cut fluff
cards.summary: Confine each email to one (at most two) overarching themes and replace paragraphs with concise, scannable copy or icons.
cards.use_when: Drafting a welcome email, campaign or any email that is drifting toward a kitchen-sink of messages.
steps: Choose the single core message for the email — avoid the common mistake of packing a welcome email with bestsellers, FAQs, a founder note and reasons to love the products all at once.
Limit yourself to a maximum of one to two overarching themes across subject line, preview text and body.
Cut unnecessary words and avoid paragraphs — where an icon or visual element can carry the message, use it instead of a paragraph.
Remember that many subscribers won't read a paragraph — they'll see it, decide they don't have time, and move on.
Write consistently in your recognized brand voice once you've defined it — if you haven't defined it, get clear on who you are as a brand and who your customer is first.
Speak to your specific demographic rather than trying to be everything to everyone — messaging aimed at millennial women, for example, should use their language and their concerns.
caveats: The 'shorter attention spans' rationale is the presenter's assertion, not a cited study.
The one-to-two theme limit is a heuristic to improve clarity, not a hard technical rule.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Lead with benefits framed for your specific customer
cards.summary: Translate product features into the benefits that matter to your named audience segment, rather than repeating product details.
cards.use_when: Writing product copy for campaigns, subscription reminders or a new product launch where the subscriber needs a reason to care.
steps: Define the audience first (e.g., millennial women with kids vs Gen Z men) because the same product needs different benefit framing.
Convert product details into 'what's in it for them': instead of 'best beans grown in Ethiopia', say what the coffee does for the drinker.
Adapt the benefit to the audience: for a busy parent millennial woman, promote energy to get through the day; for a Gen Z male audience, promote productivity for late nights or energy for sports.
For a new product launch, ask 'why should they care?' and answer it explicitly in the email — do not leave the benefit only on the product page or packaging.
Example from the walkthrough (Moment, still orange drink): state the benefit plainly — fights stress, boosts mood, enhances focus — plus limited stock and a try-now CTA.
caveats: The examples are agency work shown in the course, not measured conversion results; the pattern is the transferable takeaway.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Subject lines and preview text: under 50 characters, frontload the value
cards.summary: Put the value in the first few words of the subject line, keep both under 50 characters, and use preview text to add detail or curiosity.
cards.use_when: Writing subject lines and preview text for any campaign where the subscriber sees only a truncated line in the inbox.
steps: Frontload the value: for a sitewide summer sale, do not write 'Summer's finally here, shop 50% off sitewide' — write '50% off sitewide' first, then use the preview text for the seasonal framing ('Summer's finally here, shop now').
Test that if someone only reads the first three words, they still understand the value.
Keep both subject line and preview text under 50 characters so truncation doesn't hide the offer.
Use preview text to complement the subject line with extra detail or a curiosity hook that gives another reason to open.
Don't over-invest in subject line perfection — the presenter says it is not the most important part of email marketing.
caveats: The 50-character guideline and the claim that subject lines aren't the most important part are the presenter's guidance, not measured benchmarks.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Use persuasion levers: urgency, scarcity, social proof, curiosity gaps
cards.summary: Layer proven persuasion devices into email copy to increase the drive to act.
cards.use_when: Writing a promo, launch or content email and looking for a reliable way to increase clicks and purchases.
steps: Urgency and scarcity: state when a deal ends ('ends tonight') or that quantity is limited — the presenter says these reliably increase interest and action; use them only when true.
Social proof: feature customer reviews, user-generated content, influencer testimonials or press mentions — anything from a voice other than the brand increases subscriber trust.
Curiosity gap: tease content instead of revealing all of it; for a blog post, show a snippet and invite the click to read more rather than pasting the full post.
Place the persuader where it supports the CTA (e.g., urgency near the redeem-by line, social proof near the product or checkout module).
Do not fabricate what these devices assert — the persuasive effect collapses if the deadline or scarcity isn't real.
caveats: The presenter frames these as effective/common but does not cite measured lift numbers; treat them as well-worn tactics, not guaranteed uplift.
Fake urgency or invented social proof risks trust and compliance problems.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Design in Figma, not in Klaviyo's drag-and-drop
cards.summary: Build emails in Figma and slice them into Klaviyo rather than designing in Klaviyo's template builder, to get clearer offer communication, stronger structure and better visuals.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to design email creative before uploading into Klaviyo for a campaign or flow.
steps: Plan creative in Figma first; the presenter says strong layout and visual results shown in real examples are simply not achievable in Klaviyo's builder.
When uploading, in the campaign template step choose 'create new' and drag in your image slices one by one until the email is built.
The presenter's two structural reasons a Figma email outperforms: (1) structure and layout clarity, (2) the visual elements inside.
Don't conclude your brand can't support beautiful email design — the presenter's agency file shows strong designs for bold, natural, luxe, playful and educational brands.
After upload, verify the email renders with your brand fonts and that the layout is scannable on mobile, since sliced-image builds can be inflexible.
caveats: The presenter's comparative walkthrough (three Klaviyo-designed emails vs client Figma emails) is illustrative, not a controlled test with click or revenue data.
Sliced-image emails can hurt accessibility, text rendering, and load speed; this tradeoff is not addressed in the source.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Structure each email section as header, subheader, body, image, CTA
cards.summary: Use a scannable section hierarchy — header, subheader, optional body copy, image and CTA — repeated per section to funnel the reader to a click.
cards.use_when: Designing a campaign or flow email layout, especially one with multiple product or content sections.
steps: Give each section clear headers and subheaders so the subscriber can scan without reading every word.
Use enough white space so distinct messages read as their own sections rather than merging into a clutter.
Follow the order the presenter calls a top performer: header, subheader, body copy if necessary, image, and CTA.
If the section has multiple sub-sections, repeat that order within each one (as in multi-section client examples).
Think of the layout as a visual funnel: the header creates awareness (top), body copy educates and builds interest (middle), the CTA is the ask (bottom).
Test for scannability by asking whether a subscriber can see the offer (e.g., 15% off sitewide), the CTA, the merchandised favorites and the shipping USP without reading paragraphs.
caveats: The specific order is the presenter's recommended hierarchy, not a proved universal rule; variations work when all elements are still clear.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Three visual must-do's: CTA near products, icons not bullets, clear promo code
cards.summary: Place CTAs directly under each promoted product, replace bullet points with icons, and make the promo code unmissable near the CTA.
cards.use_when: Finishing email visuals before sending a promo, collection or product-focused campaign.
steps: Put a CTA near each merchandised product so a subscriber whose eye is caught can go shop immediately — don't rely on the product image being clickable, as many brands don't even link it.
Replace bullet points with icons (e.g., check marks) wherever the message allows — icons reinforce the point visually and are more engaging than a text list.
For promotion emails, make the redemption code unmistakable: put it in bold immediately before the CTA (e.g., 'use code SUMMER15 at checkout').

Watch for code placement that subscribers can miss — if the subject line says 25% off but the code is buried and 'Shop now' is the dominant element, subscribers will click without knowing they need a code and will be surprised at checkout.
Use only high-resolution imagery, and only relevant imagery: don't place an unrelated product image next to a product, and don't use a woman in the hero of a men's clothing email.
caveats: The warnings (missed code, blurred imagery) come from the presenter's inbox audit experience, not a measured test.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Monthly Klaviyo analytics audit: list growth, campaigns, flows
cards.summary: Run a monthly review of subscriber growth, opt-in sources and campaign performance to catch breakage and double down on what converts.
cards.use_when: The recurring monthly review of email channel performance and technical health.
steps: Check list growth: in Profiles, view subscriber growth over 30 days; note total subscribers, net change, new vs lost subscribers and month-over-month trend.
Drill into opt-in sources to see where subscribers came from (Shopify checkout and pop-up forms typically dominate) and their trends.
Diagnose a drop: a checkout-subscriber drop that matches a proportional drop in purchases/checkouts on Shopify is not a concern; a big gap between the two suggests the integration may be broken.
For a pop-up drop, open the form and compare views and submit rate across periods — if views fell but submit rate held or rose, the drop is traffic-driven, not form-driven.
Review campaign performance sorted by revenue for the last 30 days; then look at click rate (interest in content/offer) and placed order rate (what drove purchases).
Find the lowest performers and decide whether to cut, or — as with high-engagement newsletters — change the format to convert the engagement that already exists.
Review AB tests in the experiments section, and if needed end tests manually, keeping the highest converter.
caveats: The 27% month-over-month figure and other numbers are walkthrough examples, not benchmarks.
Sorting by revenue is the presenter's top-KPI recommendation, not the only valid view — open rate and click rate explain why revenue changed.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Read open rate, click rate and placed orders as a diagnostic layer stack
cards.summary: Interpret the three campaign metrics separately: open rate reflects subject line/targeting/timing, click rate reflects content and offer interest, placed orders reflect what drove purchase.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why a specific campaign over- or under-performed and deciding what to change next time.
steps: Read open rate as a signal of subject line strength, targeting quality and send timing.
Read click rate as the metric for whether subscribers cared about the content and the offer — this is the metric to judge content/offer fit.
Read placed order rate (and revenue) as the indicator of what actually drove the purchase decision.

Expect divergence: a campaign can drive more clicks but fewer purchases (content is engaging but the reason to buy is weaker), and less-clicked campaigns can drive more revenue when the offer is a strong purchase moment (e.g., Father's Day gifting).

Use this reading to decide whether to fix subject line/targeting (low open), content/offer interest (low click), or offer strength (low orders), and check whether you're treating a high-engagement, low-revenue send (like a newsletter) as a failure when it's actually an audience-interest signal.
caveats: The presenter asserts benchmarks that you should at minimum see open rates above 30% and click rates above 0.5%, calling anything lower a likely deliverability problem; they also warn that universal benchmark numbers are not reliable without a deep account audit.
Machine opens can inflate open rates. Include click and purchase behavior in diagnosis; do not infer deliverability solely from opens. https://help.klaviyo.com/hc/en-us/articles/4416803987739
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Use revenue and order count together to catch high-AOV distortion
cards.summary: Sorting campaigns by revenue can hide that a lower-revenue campaign drove more purchases; check placed orders and AOV before drawing conclusions.
cards.use_when: Analyzing top and bottom campaigns to decide which products, collections or campaign types to repeat.
steps: Sort campaigns by revenue first, since revenue is the primary KPI when the goal is revenue growth.
Then check placed order counts alongside revenue, especially for brands with high-priced, high-value products.

Note that a higher-revenue campaign can drive fewer purchases (e.g., $300 more revenue but 15 purchases vs 22 on a lower-revenue campaign), and the fourth-best revenue campaign can have the most unique purchases of the month.
If you're promoting products or collections that pull average order value down, the presenter suggests that may be a reason not to focus on them as much.
Combine this with click rate to understand whether the issue is interest or unit economics.
caveats: The specific numbers cited are from one walkthrough example, not general benchmarks; AOV distortion patterns vary by store.
Revenue remains the presenter's recommended first KPI — this card is an adjustment to, not a replacement for, that.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Diagnose a subscriber drop by separating traffic from form performance
cards.summary: When list growth falls, check whether the drop traces to site traffic decline (not controllable in Klaviyo) or form conversion decline (controllable).
cards.use_when: Monthly growth review shows a drop in new email subscribers and you need to decide whether to act on the form.
steps: Open opt-in sources and compare Shopify checkout subscribers and pop-up subscribers against Shopify purchase and checkout-started trends — a proportional drop suggests the integration and channel are fine.
For pop-up forms, open the form's reporting and compare form views and submit rate across the last 30 days and the prior 30 days.
If views dropped roughly 20% but submit rate rose from 2.19% to 2.28%, the subscriber decline was traffic-driven, not a broken form; the presenter treats this as no cause for concern.
Check whether the submit rate dropped dramatically, since form conversion is what you can control in Klaviyo — optimize here if it did.
Where form conversion is the issue, run or review an AB test on the form (the walkthrough shows an example test improving submit rate from 3.11% to 4.29%).
caveats: Submit-rate figures and the 20% view drop come from the walkthrough example, not a general benchmark; traffic attribution to paid/organic varies by brand.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Interpret Klaviyo's AB test statistics before trusting a result
cards.summary: Klaviyo surfaces a win probability and statistical significance but flags that test-period winners can differ from overall-send winners due to random chance, so extend or enlarge tests.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to call an A/B test campaign, subject line or flow variation a winner and roll it out.
steps: Open each AB test in Klaviyo's experiments section and read the lift in click rate, open rate or placed order rate and the win probability.

Watch for the case where one variation had the highest result during the test window but a different variation had the highest result overall on the full send — Klaviyo notes this can occur due to random chance.
When that happens, follow the guidance the platform gives: increase the length of the AB test period and/or increase the test size and rerun, taking the result with a grain of salt.
Manually end tests once a month when needed and keep the highest-converting variation.
Set up the next test each month regardless of outcome — the presenter argues that not testing means guessing about what your subscribers care about.
caveats: Klaviyo's statistics UI and recommendations may change over time; verify the current interface.
The presenter frames A/B testing as essential but doesn't establish a specific minimum sample size or duration.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Read top-level business review to attribute email revenue and understand month-over-month shifts
cards.summary: Use Klaviyo's business review dashboard to see total Shopify revenue, attributed email revenue, email as a share of revenue, and the campaign vs flow split.
cards.use_when: Reporting monthly email performance to the store owner and deciding whether growth came from campaigns or flows.
steps: Open dashboards > business review, set your time period and choose the comparison: previous period, or previous year if the brand is very seasonal.
Note total store Shopify revenue and its month-over-month movement.
Note attributed revenue and the percentage of total revenue coming from email — in the walkthrough example, just under 40% and up 9% month over month.
Open the message type breakdown to separate campaign revenue from flow revenue and their respective trends (example: campaign revenue $43K, up 54% month over month; flow revenue down 16%).

When a number moves sharply, dig underneath it — see the campaign revenue overview with conversion value, revenue and total recipients to understand what drove the shift, rather than reporting the headline alone.
caveats: The revenue figures and percentages are from one client walkthrough and are not universal benchmarks.
Attributed revenue depends on the attribution model in use; verify the model before presenting numbers as email's true contribution.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Ensure every email adds value before it ships
cards.summary: Before scheduling any campaign or turning on a flow email, confirm it educates, entertains or solves a problem for the subscriber.
cards.use_when: Final pre-send check on any campaign or flow email to catch content that has no clear subscriber benefit.
steps: Ask the presenter's test question: why is my subscriber going to care about this, and will they be glad they opened it?
Answer against the three value types — does this email educate, entertain, or solve a problem?
If the answer is 'no' or 'I'm not sure', go back to the drawing board and rewrite rather than scheduling it.
Apply this equally to automated flow emails, not just campaigns.
Use the same question when assessing why a low-revenue but high-engagement newsletter performed the way it did — if subscribers enjoy it, change the format to drive revenue rather than cutting it.
caveats: The presenter's standard is subjective and their claim that new product launches are among the highest revenue campaigns is expressed as a personal guarantee, not a measured result.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Monthly email business review: campaign revenue decomposition
cards.summary: A repeatable month-over-month workflow for explaining why campaign revenue rose or fell by decomposing recipients, unique opens, unique clicks, conversions and AOV.
cards.use_when: Running a monthly email/retention performance review and you need to explain a revenue change rather than just report it.
steps: Pull total store revenue (e.g. Shopify), attributed email revenue, and email's share of total revenue; note month-over-month change in the email share.
Break attributed revenue into campaign revenue vs flow revenue and note each one's month-over-month change separately — they move for different reasons.
Under campaign revenue, look at conversion value, revenue and total recipients, then the metric rows beneath.
Test the 'we just sent more' hypothesis first: if total recipients only rose a few percent (e.g. ~3.5%) while revenue rose 54%, volume is not the explanation.
Then read the chain: unique opens, open rate, unique clicks, click rate. In the source's example unique opens +13.6%, open rate +9.8%, unique clicks +15.6%, click rate +11%.
Find the outlier — in that example unique conversions +40% and order conversion rate from email +37% — and ask what merchandising or offer caused it (a sale, a launch, or just education content).
Close the loop by checking top-performing campaigns this month vs last month to see which specific sends drove the outlier.
Ladder the metrics back up: revenue per recipient and AOV should explain the remaining gap between click growth and revenue growth (source example: RPR +49%, AOV +17%).
caveats: The source's numbers are one client's first month with an agency, not a benchmark; treat them as an example of the diagnostic logic.
The source recommends building a custom dashboard tool for this at scale; Klaviyo's native reporting gives similar insight with more manual work. Verify the current Klaviyo interface.
Numeric stage bands here are heuristics, not calculations.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Optimize for unique opens and unique clicks, not open rate and click rate
cards.summary: The source's stated agency philosophy: drive revenue by maximizing unique opens and unique clicks, accepting lower rates when sending more volume.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to add campaign sends or widen a segment, and deciding which metrics to report on and optimize.
steps: Translate every metric change into people counts: an open rate falling 10% while unique opens rise 40% means 40% more humans opened, all of whom are eligible to click.
Accept that sending three campaigns a week instead of one can mechanically lower open rate and click rate while raising unique clicks; do not treat the rate drop as failure.
Use unique opens as the leading indicator for how many people can act, and unique clicks as the leading indicator of real engagement and (per the source) inbox placement.

Watch for the source's stated pattern: unique conversions can rise far more than unique clicks (example: +15% clicks, +40% purchases) because of what happens on site — a sale or product launch, not the email alone.
Report unique metrics in your monthly review so volume decisions aren't punished by rate declines.
caveats: This is an attributed agency opinion ('at Dispatch we optimize for unique clicks'), not a universal law; it makes most sense for accounts deliberately scaling send volume.
Attributed revenue and unique conversions depend on your attribution window and platform tracking, so verify before treating a 40% swing as causal.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Diagnose falling email metrics by which metric moved
cards.summary: A decision map that attributes declining email performance to deliverability, content, or merchandising based on which metric is falling.
cards.use_when: A monthly review shows email revenue or engagement dropping and you need to decide where to investigate first.
steps: If open rates and unique opens are falling dramatically, investigate deliverability and list health first (sending to unengaged cohorts, list growth quality, sender reputation).
If unique clicks or click rate are falling, treat it as a content/engagement problem — the emails or subject matter aren't landing with that audience.

If unique conversions and order conversion rate are falling while clicks hold, treat it as a merchandising and offer problem: the products, offers, and CTAs in the campaigns aren't compelling enough to make people buy.
Ignore small month-to-month noise — the source treats sub-5% moves as normal fluctuation and looks for jumps over ~10%.
Check overlap and volume before blaming content: too many sends to the same people depresses rates without any content problem.
caveats: Apple Mail privacy protection inflates/unreliably measures opens, which is why the source distrusts open rate as a deliverability signal and prefers clicks.
These are diagnostic heuristics from the source, not statistically derived thresholds.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Flow revenue review: traffic first, then the flow chain
cards.summary: How to review flow analytics month over month, starting with site traffic as the dominant driver and then localising the drop to a specific flow.
cards.use_when: Monthly retention review of automated flows (welcome, abandoned cart, abandoned checkout, winback) when flow revenue moved.
steps: Gut-check site traffic first: flow revenue down ~30% is usually explained by ~30% fewer people seeing the popup, opting in, and entering the welcome flow. If traffic was up while flow revenue fell, that is the real red flag.
Split flow revenue into conversion value and recipients, then read recipients: up means more traffic or more emails added into the flows versus last month.
Read the engagement chain: unique opens, open rate, unique clicks, click rate. Ignore sub-5% moves; investigate >10% jumps.
If click rate fell meaningfully (example −15%), consider deliverability first, since opens are polluted by Apple Mail privacy; clicks are the primary placement signal.
Reconcile conversions vs revenue arithmetically: unique conversions −6% with revenue −15% implies AOV fell substantially — confirm in the AOV row (example: −15%).
Check AOV drivers: a sitewide sale (e.g. 15% off for the month) mechanically cuts flow AOV, as does dynamic content serving lower-priced products than the prior month.
Go to top-performing flows: expect welcome series then abandonment flows to lead; compare each flow's revenue to last month and open any flow with a large gap.
Inside a flow, use the per-email analytics to compare open and click rates against the prior month, and check skip counts for people being filtered out unintentionally.
caveats: The source notes Klaviyo does not natively surface per-flow delivery/click/RPR trends in one view; they use an external dashboard. Verify current Klaviyo reporting.
AOV movement in flows is often outside email's control (sitewide promotions), so don't attribute it to email execution without checking.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Audit flow skip logic when a flow's revenue drops
cards.summary: The number-one thing the source checks when a specific flow's revenue falls is whether people are being skipped out of it by filters and triggers.
cards.use_when: A specific flow (welcome, cart, post-purchase) lost revenue month over month and you've ruled out traffic.
steps: Open the flow and use the per-email analytics/skip view to compare this month against last month.

Read the skip count against deliveries as a ratio, not in isolation — the source gives an example of 620 skipped vs 190 delivered that they knew was intentional, versus cases where subscribers are skipped inadvertently.
Inspect trigger filters, conditional splits, and profile filters (e.g. 'has placed order 0 times since starting this flow') for conditions that are now excluding eligible people.
Check for overlap suppression: flows that don't send because the person is also receiving a campaign or another flow.
Fix unintended exclusions, then re-check opens, clicks, and purchases in the following period, since fewer deliveries mechanically ladders down to less of all three.
caveats: A high skip count is not automatically a bug; it can be by design. The source only flags it as the first thing to examine, not as proof of a problem.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Run one high-leverage campaign A/B test per month
cards.summary: Set up campaign split tests with placed order rate as the winning metric, 100% size distribution, and only one variable changed.
cards.use_when: Planning the monthly campaign experiment in Klaviyo or equivalent, and choosing what to test.
steps: Build version A (control), then use the platform's 'create A/B test' option and choose content or send-time test. Verify button names in the current interface.
For send-time tests, keep the copy and design identical and vary only the send hour; the source suggests click rate as the winning metric there, since opens are unreliable.
For content tests, do not spend the test on subject line or preview text — the source says after hundreds of tests, email body content is the highest-leverage test.

Test high-leverage content variables: the offer, which product types are featured, imagery type (lifestyle vs product, single image vs four-image layout, static vs GIF), and CTA copy (e.g. 'shop now' vs 'save now').
Change exactly one thing between A and B. Do not vary subject line and content together, or stack a second content change on top — you won't know which change caused the result.
Set the winning metric to placed order rate rather than open rate or even clicks, because the goal of every test is revenue.
Keep size distribution at 100% for most brands so the whole audience is split 50/50; a 40% holdout that decides the winner is not statistically meaningful for typical list sizes.
Name variations descriptively (e.g. 'one image hero' vs 'four image hero') so the result is readable later.
Log the test in the experiments section so the learning rolls into the next month's planning.
caveats: Source opinion: they always use placed order rate as the winning metric and say never to use open rate. This favours tests with enough volume to resolve on a downstream metric.
The source explicitly says most brands can't reach statistical significance on a partial-holdout test, so a 100% split is a volume-constrained compromise, not a significance guarantee.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Flow A/B tests with automatic distribution
cards.summary: Flow experiments differ from campaign tests because they run continuously, so the platform can shift traffic automatically toward the winner.
cards.use_when: Testing two versions of an email inside a flow (welcome, abandoned cart, post-purchase) while the flow stays live.
steps: Open the specific email inside the flow, keep the current version as A, and use the create A/B test action at the bottom of that email.
Set the same style of winning metric logic you use for campaigns — the source favours placed order rate as the revenue-linked goal.

Because flows collect data continuously, select the automatic distribution option: the platform initially sends ~50/50 and shifts allocation as its model identifies a winner, then sends only the winner once significance is reached. Verify this option still exists in the current interface.
Change only one element between the two versions, exactly as with campaign tests.
Monitor progress in the experiments section rather than judging on the first few days.
caveats: Automatic distribution depends on the platform's statistical model; results are only as trustworthy as the traffic volume in that flow email.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Reviewing completed and in-progress A/B tests
cards.summary: How the source decides to call a test and move on, including when to accept a high win probability without formal significance.
cards.use_when: Your monthly review of experiment results, or deciding whether to ship a variation and pick next month's test.
steps: Open the experiment/flow A/B test view and compare version A and B on click rate and placed order rate, not on open rate.
Read the reported win probability. In the source's example, version A showed a 98% win probability, which they describe as not statistically significant but supported by enough data to act.
Consider account size: the source notes smaller brands may never reach formal significance even after several months of running a test.
When one version is clearly driving more revenue and the difference is meaningful, declare the winner, keep it live, and move on to planning the next test rather than waiting indefinitely.
Carry the learning into the test roadmap — for example, if four images beat one, treat that as a hypothesis to build on, not a permanent rule.
caveats: Win probability is the platform's estimate, not proof; the source explicitly acknowledges the example was not statistically significant and still chose the winner.
This is a pragmatic agency judgment call, not a statistical standard — hold it to a higher bar for tests that would change pricing or core offer structure.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Monthly deliverability health check inside Klaviyo
cards.summary: Check account-level deliverability score, the recommended thresholds, and per-mailbox-provider reports every 30 days, with clicks as the primary placement signal.
cards.use_when: Monthly email operations review, or when open/click metrics have been sliding and you suspect inbox placement.
steps: Open the deliverability tab and read the deliverability score, which the source says is based on open rates, click rates, bounce rates, unsubscribe rates, and spam complaint rates; track it over time.

Compare your account rates to the platform's recommended healthy ranges. The source cites: open rate above 33% considered okay; click rate above 1.2% considered okay; bounce rate under 1%; unsubscribe rate under 0.3%; spam complaint rate under 0.01%. Re-check these numbers in the current interface as they change.

Prioritize keeping bounce and spam complaint rates well under the guidelines — the source treats those two as the hard limits; unsubscribe slightly above the recommendation is described as tolerable when send volume drives more revenue.
Read both sides of the account: recent campaigns and your flows, since flows contribute separately to sender reputation.

Every ~30 days open the reports section to see performance by mailbox provider; in the source's example Gmail and Verizon sat near 63-70% opens while Hotmail/Outlook were ~46% with a lower click rate, and G Suite showed both high bounce and high unsubscribe rates.
For weak providers, build tightly engaged segments specific to those providers to stop deteriorating reputation there.
Verify placement with click rate rather than open rate, since Apple Mail privacy inflation has made opens unreliable.
caveats: The thresholds above are Klaviyo's recommended values as presented in the source; verify current guidance before treating them as targets.
The source says deliverability problems generally stem from failing the basics (unengaged segments, excessive sending, flow/campaign overlap) rather than from technical setup.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Recover inbox placement by tightening the engagement segment
cards.summary: When opens and clicks are steadily falling, shrink from a 90-day engaged segment to 30- or 60-day engaged, then expand again as metrics recover.
cards.use_when: Deliverability remediation: your usual engaged segment is no longer producing healthy open and click rates.
steps: Confirm the trend is steady decline in both opens and clicks, not a one-month fluctuation (ignore sub-5% moves).
If you normally send to a 90-day engaged segment, switch campaign and flow sends to a 30-day or 60-day engaged segment so the audience is more recently active.
Hold that tighter segment until open and click rates climb back to healthy levels — the goal is to demonstrate to inbox providers that recipients want your mail.
Expand the window gradually (e.g. 30 → 60 → 90 days) rather than jumping straight back to the wide segment.
In parallel, check campaign/flow overlap so the same people aren't being hit twice, which drives unsubscribes and complaints.
caveats: Tightening segments reduces short-term reach and revenue; the source frames it as a deliberate trade to repair reputation.
No recovery timeline is given in the source; expect it to depend on your volume and reputation damage.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Dynamic content blocks to merge segmented campaigns into one send
cards.summary: Use show/hide logic on content blocks so a single campaign or flow email renders different offers, copy, or reminders based on saved profile properties.
cards.use_when: You would otherwise build two near-identical campaigns for different regions, tiers, or customer states (e.g. different free-shipping thresholds, unused acquisition offer, loyalty points balance).
steps: Inside the email block, open the block settings and find the display / show-hide logic area (verify current naming in the interface).
Choose the profile property and set a condition, e.g. country equals United States.
Match formatting exactly: the property value you type must use the same spelling and letters as stored on the profile — check a real US profile to copy the exact string (e.g. 'United States').
Duplicate the block and invert the logic for everyone else (does not equal United States), then edit the copy for that group (e.g. free shipping over $150 instead of $100).

Preview against test profiles that have the property set and unset — the source shows that a profile with no country set falls into the 'not United States' branch by default, so decide whether that default is acceptable.

Apply the same technique to other data you hold: show reviews based on zero-party data, remind prospects of an unused acquisition offer, or tell existing customers their current loyalty points balance.
Keep the blocks' content substantively different so personalisation is real, not cosmetic.
caveats: Incorrect or inconsistent property formatting silently routes people to the wrong variant — always test both branches.
Profiles missing the property fall to the negative branch; add an explicit fallback if the wrong message would be harmful.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Trigger a winback from expected next order date
cards.summary: Replace average-days-since-purchase winback timing with per-customer predictive date triggers so at-risk customers hear from you at their own predicted repurchase moment.
cards.use_when: Building or upgrading a winback / reactivation flow so timing is personalised rather than based on a list-wide average.
steps: Create a flow manually and look for the date-property trigger option rather than a time-delay trigger.
Select the expected-date-of-next-order property available on each profile.

Choose to trigger on the date property value (not before it), because that is the date the model expects the repurchase; the source's example fires at 12:00 p.m. local time. Verify trigger timing options in the current interface.
Set the flow to never repeat, since you don't want the same winback email firing monthly to someone who has already been contacted.
Add a profile filter requiring zero orders placed since entering the flow, so anyone who buys drops out.
Add a short delay (the source suggests ~5 days after the expected date) to give them a grace period before you introduce winback offers.
Optionally branch on predicted or historic customer lifetime value (e.g. CLV at least $1,000) to give high-value customers a more personalised, stronger offer.
Compare against a simple version of the same flow where you trigger on average days between orders, especially if you have limited data on an individual.
caveats: Predictive dates are model estimates from Klaviyo and are less reliable for customers with few orders; verify the property is populated before relying on the trigger.
Treating predicted high CLV customers as already-high-value is the source's suggestion for proactive retention, not a proven conversion lift.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Use predictive CLV and churn risk in flow splits
cards.summary: Apply Klaviyo's predicted analytics — next order date, churn risk, AOV, historic and predicted CLV — as branch conditions in flows rather than only reading them on profiles.
cards.use_when: Designing conditional splits in retention or winback flows to vary offer strength and personalisation by customer value.
steps: Locate the predictive properties on a customer profile (expected next order date, average time between orders, churn risk prediction, average order value, historic and predicted CLV) to confirm which are populated for your account.
Build a conditional split on customer lifetime value — either historic CLV at least $1,000, or predicted CLV above the threshold.
Send higher-value customers a more personalised, better discount in the winback path, on the reasoning that recovering them is worth more.
Use predicted CLV to treat promising customers as high value earlier, before they have reached the threshold historically.
As with any split, monitor performance per branch over time; the source treats this as personalisation upside and notes Klaviyo keeps improving these models.
caveats: This is presented as an opportunity, not a tested result; the source gives no lift figures.
Predictions require sufficient order history to be meaningful — thin accounts will have weak or empty values.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Build multichannel touchpoints into flows (email, SMS, push)
cards.summary: Layer SMS and push notifications into existing flows to add high-converting touchpoints at the right time, with time delays deciding channel order.
cards.use_when: Designing or upgrading an abandoned cart, abandonment, or similar conversion flow where you already have email and want more touchpoints.
steps: In Klaviyo settings, find the SMS and push notification sections and complete setup — you get a phone number and compliance tooling for SMS, and push requires a custom mobile app; verify current setup requirements in the interface.
Inside a flow, add an SMS or push step in addition to the email steps.
Sequence channels by intent: in an abandoned cart flow the source gives the example of sending SMS first to convert, then waiting ~2 hours and sending the email to anyone who hasn't purchased yet.
Rely on flow filters so someone who converts exits and doesn't receive the later, redundant touchpoint.
Keep the offer and message consistent across channels so the follow-up feels like one conversation.
caveats: Push notifications require your own mobile app; they are not available to a mobile-web-only store.
SMS has consent and compliance obligations that vary by region — the source only notes Klaviyo supplies the compliance pieces, not that setup alone makes you compliant.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Integrate ecommerce apps to drive flow triggers and segmentation
cards.summary: Connect the Shopify apps you already use so their events and properties flow into Klaviyo and can trigger automations or refine segments.
cards.use_when: Setting up or expanding a Klaviyo account and deciding which integrations to add first.
steps: Go to settings → integrations → add integrations and filter to all to see the available directory (source cites 187 live integrations); verify the current count in the interface.
Start by integrating the apps you already run on Shopify, not new apps you don't use yet. The source's path: check Shopify's app list, then search those app names in Klaviyo's integration settings.
Install directly from Klaviyo, and read the overview of what data the integration passes and which features it enables before connecting.
Note that many integrations are configured inside the third-party app, not in Klaviyo — the source's loyalty example has the API key, status, and event triggers managed in the app.

Map the resulting events to flows — the source's examples: a Recharge subscription pause triggers a flow to unpause; a reviews app passing 'left a review' prevents asking for a review on that product again.
Map synced properties (e.g. points balance, loyalty status, VIP tier name, birthday, referral URL) to segmentation and personalisation.
For ad platforms, pass email addresses from Klaviyo segments (e.g. a high-value purchaser segment) to Meta or Google for retargeting and lookalike audiences based on your own data.
caveats: Integration directory contents and setup screens change — verify in the current interface before following exact menu paths.
More integrations mean more data flowing, but the source advises starting with what you already use rather than integrating speculatively.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Trigger a birthday flow using loyalty app point properties
cards.summary: Use an integration event plus dynamic content to personalise a birthday email with the exact points earned and the customer's current balance.
cards.use_when: Running a loyalty-driven retention campaign where members earn birthday points and you want one email that renders per-customer numbers.
steps: Confirm the loyalty app passes a birthday event and the relevant profile properties (points earned on birthday, points balance, loyalty status, VIP tier) into Klaviyo.
Create a flow triggered by that metric, e.g. the loyalty app's customer-birthday event, then add the email step.
In the email, insert the event property for points earned in this specific event so each recipient sees their own number (e.g. 250 points earned).
Add personalisation and search the integration's properties to insert the customer's current points balance, which will differ per person (source example: 1,669 for one customer, 355 for another).
Use preview and test on the specific profile that triggered the metric to confirm the numbers render correctly, then check a second profile to confirm they differ.
If different tiers earn different birthday points, the event property handles the variation without separate emails.
Decide on placement — the source uses birthday as a trigger for both email and SMS — and whether to include a redeem link or code.
caveats: The flow only works if the integration reliably fires the birthday event and the event property is present; test the event before building the creative.
Copy used in the source's example is sample copy, not tested copy — build your own.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Use dynamic blocks to personalise shipping thresholds and offers in one send
cards.summary: Personalise a single email's messaging, offers, and reminders using property-driven conditionals instead of splitting one audience across multiple sends.
cards.use_when: Merchandising or offer communication that differs by country, tier, or subscriber state — free shipping thresholds, unused welcome offers, loyalty balances.
steps: Identify messages you currently split into multiple campaigns or segments — for example a US free-shipping-over-$100 message versus a rest-of-world free-shipping-over-$150 message.
Build one email and add a text block at the top for the first variant, then apply show/hide logic on the property that distinguishes the groups (e.g. country equals United States).
Duplicate the block, invert the logic, and rewrite the copy for the second group.

For offer reminders, show prospects the acquisition offer they haven't used yet, and show existing customers their current loyalty points balance — using properties the integrations push onto profiles.
For zero-party data, show different customer reviews or content based on what the subscriber told you.
Preview against multiple test profiles, including one missing the property, so you know which branch default behaviour sends them to.
The source also uses predictive data in the same spirit: a higher-value customer branch can receive a stronger offer.
caveats: Property formatting must match exactly what is stored on the profile, or the condition won't match.
Running one conditional email instead of multiple sends reduces work but means a single send's metrics mix groups — plan how you'll read results.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Non-discount email strategy: replace constant promos with objection-handling content
cards.summary: Build a broadcast email program that earns full-price sales by educating and handling objections instead of repeatedly discounting the whole list.
cards.use_when: Planning the overall email program for a store that currently relies on frequent sitewide discount blasts and is eroding margin.
steps: Audit current sends: count how often the whole list gets a % off promo versus value or education content; if discount-only is your main strategy, treat it as the problem to fix.
Reframe email's job as handling buyer objections one at a time and slowly educating the customer toward a full-price purchase, rather than converting every send.
Map the top objections a first-time buyer has (trust, 'who is this brand', 'why you over competitors', 'what do people say') and assign each to a content bucket.
Keep discounts as an optional fifth bucket: the source recommends roughly one sale/discount offer per month so list members feel rewarded for staying subscribed.
Send the non-discount program to the engaged segment at the target cadence rather than building heavy segmentation first; the source treats elaborate segmentation as unnecessary here.

Track unsubscribes and engagement alongside revenue when shifting to non-discount content, since the source's claim that this yields 30-50% of store revenue is a description of his own client results, not a guaranteed benchmark.
caveats: The revenue-share numbers come from the presenter's own client work and are examples, not promises.
A once-monthly discount is a recommendation, not a universal rule; margins and category norms vary.
cards.source_name: Complete Ecommerce Email Marketing Strategy For 2026.docx

cards.title: Send 3-4 broadcast emails per week to stay top-of-mind
cards.summary: A 3-4x weekly cadence to the engaged list is the source's tested sweet spot between irrelevance at low frequency and fatigue at high frequency.
cards.use_when: Setting or revising the sending frequency for your recurring (non-triggered) email campaigns.
steps: Assess your current cadence: 1-2 sends/week risks customers forgetting the brand, failing to form an opening habit, and weak sender reputation with inbox providers; 5-7/week risks high unsubscribes, diluted messaging, and revenue plateauing.
Target roughly 3-4 sends per week (about 16/month) to your engaged list as the source's default, based on his stated testing across 200+ brands.
Keep content quality as the gating factor: lower unsubscribes at this cadence depend on sending the right content mix, not just sending more.
Recognize the cadence is also a deliverability play -- consistent sending builds sender reputation so mail lands in the primary inbox.
Treat brand specifics as adjustable: the source explicitly says every brand is different, so use 3-4 as a starting heuristic and test against your own unsubscribe and revenue data.
caveats: 3-4x/week is a source-specific heuristic from his testing, not an industry benchmark; your list tolerance may differ.
High frequency without the right content mix will still drive unsubscribes and fatigue.
cards.source_name: Complete Ecommerce Email Marketing Strategy For 2026.docx

cards.title: Balance broadcasts across four non-discount content pillars plus an optional sales pillar
cards.summary: Rotate educational, social proof, community/brand, and product/collection content in roughly equal amounts, with sales as a smaller optional fifth bucket.
cards.use_when: Building a monthly email content calendar and deciding what each broadcast should be about.
steps: Define the four non-discount buckets: educational (FAQs, ingredient education, how-to, 'how you've been using it wrong', what's not in the product, what happens if you stop); social proof (testimonials, media features, real-people results, influencers); community/brand (mission, brand timeline/history, values, why we exist, founder notes); product/collection highlights (trending, spotlights, gift guides, seasonal must-haves, product breakdowns).
Add the optional fifth bucket: sales (teasers, launches, gift-with-purchase, mystery offers).
Aim for a roughly even split across pillars. The source's example: for a 10-email month, do about 2-3 of each pillar, e.g., ~3 educational, 3 social proof, 3 product, 3 community/brand, and 2 sales.
Keep the mix stable month to month so the list gets variety without becoming discount-dependent.
Use the pillar split as the input to a calendar (AI or manual) so each slot is assigned a type before writing copy.
caveats: The even-split ratio is an example from the presenter's own email revenue experience, not a calculated optimum.
Bucket labels and counts can flex with seasonality (e.g., gift guides near holidays).
cards.source_name: Complete Ecommerce Email Marketing Strategy For 2026.docx

cards.title: Turn macro topics into hyper-specific microtopics for each email
cards.summary: Each email should deliver one narrow, single-takeaway idea rather than a broad brand message or a list of benefits.
cards.use_when: Filling calendar slots with campaign topics and writing subject lines/headlines for value emails.
steps: Start from the brand's macro topic (e.g., 'holistic health' or 'mental performance') and break it into hyper-specific angles.

Write topics with a single takeaway, phrased concretely: 'three ways high performers use [product] to win the day', 'ingredient deep dive: what makes adaptogens powerful', 'how to use [product] for 30 days and what to expect', 'what happens if you stop using it', 'label decoder'.
Avoid generic topics like 'our product is amazing' or 'get better overall health' -- the source identifies specificity as what makes non-discount emails convert.
Tie social proof to a specific experience a reader may be having (e.g., collect testimonials from people who quit coffee for a 'finally ditched coffee' email) and pull matching quotes from the site.
If topic generation is hard, use the pattern library: educational angles, social proof angles, community/brand angles, product/collection angles, then sales angles.
caveats: Specificity of ingredient/health claims should satisfy any legal or regulatory constraints in your category.
cards.source_name: Complete Ecommerce Email Marketing Strategy For 2026.docx

cards.title: Use a two-step ChatGPT priming workflow to generate calendar ideas and copy
cards.summary: Prime the model with full brand/audience/USP context, then instruct it to output a punchy headline, sub-headline, and 2-3 sentences of body copy leading to a CTA.
cards.use_when: Generating a month of campaign ideas or drafting email copy fast, when you have brand and product context ready to feed in.
steps: Step 1 - Prime: feed the model all brand voice, product details, target audience, and unique selling propositions before asking for anything.
Step 2 - Instruct: ask for a punchy headline, a sub-headline, and exactly 2-3 sentences of body copy that lead to a CTA -- this mirrors the source's custom GPT ('email marketing brain') behavior.

Ask for a balanced calendar across the five content types; verify the output's pillar counts (e.g., the source's sample month returned 4 educational, 3 social proof, 2 community/brand, 2 product/collection, 3 sales across weeks of 3-4 sends).
For subject lines and preview text, treat them as the email's headline and sub-headline; the source argues sender name drives opens more than the subject line (a stated opinion, not a measured rule).
Always review and edit AI output -- the source notes it is 'not going to be perfect' (e.g., a missing CTA) and must be checked.
If the tool interface has changed since this source, re-verify menu options and prompts in the current interface before following the exact flow.
caveats: LLM output must be fact-checked against actual product/ingredient facts; the source pulls final facts from the brand's own site.
Custom GPT/tool specifics are vendor- and version-dependent and should be re-verified.
cards.source_name: Complete Ecommerce Email Marketing Strategy For 2026.docx

cards.title: Structure email layout as headline, sub-headline, short body, CTA, infographic, product block
cards.summary: A winning email uses a minimal, skimmable layout: headline, sub-headline, a little body copy, a CTA, an infographic/education section, then a product/CTA section at the bottom.
cards.use_when: Laying out any broadcast email before sending to design.
steps: Open the email with a clear headline and sub-headline that calls out a specific problem the reader has (e.g., 'brain fog has met its match').
Follow with a short block of body copy (a few sentences) that introduces the mechanism/benefit, then an immediate CTA.
Add a hero/graphic section, then an educational infographic section (e.g., ingredient breakdown) that visualizes the mechanism.
End with a product/CTA section -- choose the offer (starter kit, multi-pack, or subscription) and link the CTA to the product page.
Assemble this in a plain document (e.g., a table with a row per section) to visualize the email before handing to design.
Keep total copy minimal -- the source stresses how little text is used and credits the layout, not length, for conversion.
caveats: This is the source's demonstrated layout, not a proven maximum-conversion template; test variations.
cards.source_name: Complete Ecommerce Email Marketing Strategy For 2026.docx

cards.title: Mix graphic-based and text-based emails at roughly 3-4:1
cards.summary: Blend branded graphic emails with plain-text, native-looking founder emails at about 3-4 graphic emails for every one text email.
cards.use_when: Deciding the format (graphic vs plain-text) for each send in the calendar.
steps: Default to graphic-based emails for education and infographic content that readers skim.
Insert plain-text emails that look like a personal message from a real person (e.g., founder note) -- the source says his best-performing emails of all time are these text-based sends.
At the source's example cadence of 16 emails/month, send roughly 12 graphic and 4 text-based to hit the ~3-4:1 ratio.
Place text-based sends in the community/brand pillar where founder notes, mission, and behind-the-scenes content naturally fit.
Write the text email in a conversational first-person voice (e.g., 'Hey, James here... I built this because...'), keep it short, and make sure it still includes a CTA if the draft omits one.
caveats: The 3-4:1 ratio is the source's guideline, not a universal constant; test your own split.
Plain-text sends still need a CTA and a clear linking target to convert.
cards.source_name: Complete Ecommerce Email Marketing Strategy For 2026.docx

cards.title: Apply the skimable, clear/concise, engaging copywriting rules
cards.summary: Write every email so it can be skimmed in seconds: no blocks of copy, one takeaway, bolded main points, and an engaging (humorous, fun, or informative) tone.
cards.use_when: Drafting or editing the body copy and headlines of any broadcast email, given short reader attention.
steps: Skimmable: eliminate blocks of copy, break content into short sections, and use bolded points and headlines so a reader can scan and self-identify (e.g., bolding '12-14g protein', 'zero sugar', 'gluten-free' so a gluten-free reader stops).
Clear and concise: keep it short -- a headline, a few lines of body copy, a button, and a small supporting detail, rather than an essay.
Engaging: choose a tone that either entertains (humor, playful framing) or educates with genuinely useful information.
Use concrete stats and fun facts as engagement hooks where relevant (e.g., a stat about time spent somewhere, framed as a benefit) -- the source cites these as high-engagement devices.
Write copy and design together, planning how each line will look in the email rather than writing text first and designing later.
caveats: The 3-second attention claim is the source's framing, not a measured benchmark.
Humor and stat-driven copy should fit brand voice and avoid unsupported claims.
cards.source_name: Complete Ecommerce Email Marketing Strategy For 2026.docx

cards.title: Replace paragraph copy with infographics that communicate value in seconds
cards.summary: Use checklists, icon graphics, feature diagrams, timelines, numbered lists, comparison cards, tables, flowcharts, and graphs instead of dense text to convey the offer.
cards.use_when: Designing the education/benefit section of an email, or replacing a long benefits paragraph that isn't performing.
steps: Choose the infographic type by job: checklists for feature sets; icon graphics for calling out individual features; feature diagrams for what's inside the product; timelines for what a user feels over time (e.g., product effects); numbered lists for step sequences; comparison cards for 'us vs. them'; tables for structured specs; flowcharts to guide readers to the right product; graphs to visualize a stat instead of stating it.
Show the product ingredients/components visually alongside short labels rather than writing them out in prose (the source points to supplement brands that show everything you get visually).
Pair each infographic with minimal supporting copy (e.g., an ingredient name plus a one-line function such as 'reduces stress' / 'boosts focus').
Combine copy and design rather than treating them separately -- the source's core claim is that copy alone won't be read.
Treat the infographic as the education workhorse inside the standard email layout, placed after the hero/CTA and before the final product block.
caveats: The source's claim that infographics are a 'cheat code' is an opinion based on his experience, not a controlled benchmark.
Ingredient/benefit claims shown visually should still meet regulatory requirements for your category.
cards.source_name: Complete Ecommerce Email Marketing Strategy For 2026.docx

cards.title: Run plain-text vs long-form A/B tests on the same email
cards.summary: Test a short plain-text founder email against a longer ~250-word version of the same message to find what your list responds to.
cards.use_when: Optimizing a found er/community email where you're unsure whether short or longer copy converts better.
steps: Draft the short plain-text version first (e.g., a founder note with a PS and a CTA).
Have the same idea rewritten as a longer, ~250-word email to use as the variation, keeping the core message and offer constant.
Ensure both versions include a working CTA and link to the same destination so the test isolates length/format.
Run the test and let results decide -- the source frames long-form as sometimes worse and sometimes workable, so treat it as a question to answer with your own data rather than a universal rule.
Apply the winner to future sends in that pillar before testing additional variables.
caveats: The source presents this as an example test, not a reported result.
Long-form copy can still work in some cases; the source does not claim it always underperforms.
cards.source_name: Complete Ecommerce Email Marketing Strategy For 2026.docx

cards.title: Use sender name (not subject line) as the primary open-rate lever
cards.summary: The source argues opens are driven more by who the email is from than by the subject line, so write subject/preview text for intrigue, not for the open alone.
cards.use_when: Writing subject lines and preview text and deciding how much testing budget to spend on them.
steps: Treat the subject line and preview text as the email's headline and sub-headline rather than as a standalone open-rate hack.
Build sender recognition through the 3-4x/week cadence so the audience expects and recognizes your brand in the inbox.
Write subject lines that create intrigue without revealing the full story (e.g., naming the benefit but not the mechanism, so the reader opens to find out 'why').
Pair a curiosity-driven subject with preview text that builds on it and adds a concrete hook.
Test subject lines where you have spare testing capacity, but do not assume large open-rate swings -- the source describes their effect as smaller than commonly believed (a stated opinion).
caveats: This is a contested opinion; the source himself calls it 'controversial' and gives no measured data.
Sender name effects still depend on deliverability and list familiarity.
cards.source_name: Complete Ecommerce Email Marketing Strategy For 2026.docx

cards.title: Keep segmentation light for broadcast campaigns
cards.summary: For manual broadcast campaigns, the source says you can send to your engaged list without heavy segmentation.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much list segmentation effort to invest in your recurring broadcast program.
steps: Prioritize sending the right content mix and cadence to the engaged list over building complex segment logic.
Use the engaged segment as the default audience for the 3-4x/week broadcast program.

Note that this guidance is about manual/broadcast campaigns specifically; triggered lifecycle flows (cart abandonment, welcome series) are a separate, related discipline the source does not cover here.
Revisit segmentation only when list data or deliverability problems point to a need, rather than as a first step.
caveats: The source's stated scope is broadcast campaigns, not automated triggered flows.
Light segmentation is the source's recommendation for this context and may not suit every list or deliverability situation.
cards.source_name: Complete Ecommerce Email Marketing Strategy For 2026.docx

cards.title: Reframe the 2024 Ecommerce Market Before Planning Funnel Spend
cards.summary: Post-2020 stimulus-era buying behavior is gone; more brands and more skeptical buyers mean acquisition-first funnels underperform unless back-end conversion is engineered.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to allocate budget and effort between cold ad acquisition and post-click email capture/retention for your store.
steps: Recognize the market shift the source describes: in 2020–2023 stimulus money and few competitors made impulse purchases easy, while in 2024 buyers have less disposable income, far more brand options, and prior bad/scam experiences online.
Accept the practical implication: cold-traffic conversion rates hover around 1% or less, so paying repeatedly for cold retargeting rarely produces profit.
Rebalance toward profit rather than top-line revenue: capture emails at the point of first site visit so you can convert warmed traffic cheaply instead of re-buying the same click.
Keep paid ads for their real strength — acquiring attention and driving first/second visits — and use email for the conversion and follow-up work.
Plan operations accordingly: you need the back end (flows, campaigns, list growth) built before scaling ad spend, or you will churn spend at roughly break-even.
caveats: Market-evolution claims and 1% cold conversion figures are the presenter's observation, not measured benchmarks for your store; verify against your own analytics.
This is a strategic reallocation argument, not a directive to cut ads.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Build the 'Stand a Chance' Funnel: 10% Email Capture Instead of Paying to Retarget
cards.summary: Sending cold traffic only to a purchase means paying to retarget the 99% who leave; adding a 10% email opt-in step unlocks cheap repeated content.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing your site funnel to decide whether email capture is placed early enough to monetize cold ad traffic.
steps: Map your current funnel: ad click → site visit → purchase, and estimate how much of the traffic purchases versus leaves (the source describes ~1% purchasing and 99% leaving).
Add a capture layer on the same traffic so at least a portion opts in — the source targets 10% of website traffic becoming email subscribers.
Treat the opted-in segment as a cheap content channel: you can email them repeatedly at a fraction of a cent per send instead of paying for each retargeting impression.
Scale the math to your traffic: the source's illustration is 50,000 monthly site viewers × 10% = 5,000 new subscribers per month, giving you a compounding list that no longer costs per-touch.
Note the source's framing: a strong funnel does not guarantee winning, but a funnel without capture essentially guarantees churning ad spend.
caveats: 10% opt-in and 1% purchase figures are the presenter's targets/illustrations, not universal benchmarks.
Email revenue depends on the quality of content sent afterward, not just list size.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Use the Trust Threshold Model to Justify Content Over One-Shot Ads
cards.summary: Cold visitors can only be converted after enough content exposures cross a personal trust threshold, so repeated low-cost content beats expensive single ad impressions.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many touches and what mix of ads/email a product page visitor needs before you expect a purchase.
steps: Define your audience's trust threshold: the point where a shopper has seen enough information and repeated exposures to actually hand over money.
Accept the source's claim: you cannot convert truly cold audiences in ecommerce — only audiences that know, like and trust you.
Warm cold traffic by accumulating 'trust points' with content touches: ad impressions do this, but so do emails, and emails are cheap while impressions cost money each time.
Where paid ads are the only touch, note the cost: brands relying solely on paid content often break even on the first order and depend entirely on back-end repeat purchases.
So route a share of visitors into email (via pop-ups, opt-ins) so most of your content touches cost near zero and the same or higher conversion effect is achieved.
caveats: The 'trust threshold' is a conceptual model, not a measurable number; do not invent a required exposure count.
The source explicitly is not anti-ads — it positions ads as attention acquisition and email as conversion/content.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Win the Honeymoon Phase: Prioritize New Subscriber Capture
cards.summary: New subscribers are worth more than older ones because fresh interest and first-purchase intent peak right after opt-in.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to invest list-growth effort and how to sequence messaging for a newly opted-in shopper.
steps: Treat the window from opt-in through roughly the first or second purchase as the 'honeymoon phase', where the subscriber is most receptive to the brand.
Recognize this is especially strong when the opt-in followed an ad click or an on-site visit, because intent is still top of mind.
Prioritize capturing these fresh subscribers aggressively (pop-up, post-purchase checkbox) rather than relying on long-term list members who may have lost interest.
Send high-value content and offers to new subscribers promptly while the honeymoon phase is active, since new-subscriber value is highest then.
Keep serving long-term subscribers good content too, because interest decays and is only recovered through repeated useful sends.
Treat 'new subscriber' as a distinct segment from 'past buyer' in your flows and campaign logic rather than mailing everyone the same thing.
caveats: Honeymoon-phase value is the source's qualitative claim; measure your own new-subscriber revenue per contact.
The point is prioritization, not a claim that existing subscribers have no value.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Deploy the Four List-Growth Methods and Know Their Roles
cards.summary: Pop-up forms, post-purchase opt-ins, sign-up pages and embedded forms each capture a different traffic context, led by pop-ups converting ~10% of site traffic.
cards.use_when: Setting up or auditing all the places your store can convert traffic into email subscribers.
steps: Install pop-up forms as the primary capture mechanism — the source targets a well-built pop-up converting around 10% of website traffic.
Add a post-purchase opt-in checkbox (optionally pre-checked) so nearly every buyer lands on the list automatically.
Create dedicated sign-up pages you can link from social, blog content, giveaways or other external properties.
Add embedded sign-up forms on the homepage and footer with a clear incentive or reason to join.
Sequence implementation roughly in that order of effectiveness: pop-ups first, then post-purchase, then sign-up pages, then embeds.
Feed all four into the same flows and campaigns so no captured contact sits idle.
caveats: Effectiveness ranking is the source's rough ordering; audit your own opt-in rates per method.
Pop-up timing and design mistakes (see pop-up cards) can drag the 10% target well below 1–3%.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Balance Flows vs Campaigns at ~50/50 of Email Revenue
cards.summary: Automated flows should carry roughly half of email revenue, and drifting far outside that band signals under-built automations.
cards.use_when: Auditing whether your automated email revenue is carrying its fair share or whether you are over-relying on manual sends.
steps: Set up the core flows every ecommerce brand needs with action-based triggers, described by the source as: welcome (joins list), website abandonment (visits and leaves), browse abandonment (views product and leaves), cart abandonment (adds to cart and leaves), checkout abandonment (reaches checkout and leaves), post-purchase, and win-back (no purchase in 60 days).
Confirm each trigger is configured with the correct conditions/filters so it fires on the intended behavior rather than every visitor.
Measure the split between flow revenue and campaign revenue; aim for the source's healthy band of roughly 40/60 to 60/40.
If flows come in around 30% versus 70% campaigns, treat that as a signal there is substantial room to improve automations.
Use well-built flows to relieve pressure on campaigns — automated revenue means you don't have to compensate for a slow month with a burst of manual sends.
Use flows to capture high-intent abandonment and personalize post-purchase content around the specific item bought.
caveats: The 50/50 and 40–60% bands are the source's heuristics, not a calculated formula for your store.
Win-back timing of 60 days is the source's suggested default; adjust to your purchase cycle.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Run 3–4 Non-Discount Campaigns Weekly Using Microtopics
cards.summary: Send 3–4 emails per week, each built around one hyper-specific non-discount topic, to build a habit and avoid discount fatigue.
cards.use_when: Planning weekly campaign content when your list is over-exposed to sales and you need to maintain open attention without heavy discounting.
steps: Commit to a cadence of three to four campaigns per week — the source's tested rhythm for best conversion across audiences.
Make each email cover one microtopic (a single benefit, one ingredient, one feature, myth vs fact, a single customer review) rather than a comprehensive article that overwhelms readers.
Avoid 'needy' buyer-focused content that only says buy/discount/exclusive/gone-forever; instead use value content like tips and tricks, a founder message, favorite picks, or industry watch-outs.

Use the source's list of non-discount campaign angles as a library: single benefit, single feature, FAQ, what's inside, how it's made, how to use, back in stock, myth vs fact, brand progress update, customer transformation, treat yourself, tips and tricks, throwback content, staff picks, early access.
Cycle through topics so you don't repeat the same angle; sending 3–4 per week from the library yields months of content.

Frame non-discount sends as altruistic — present product and information and let buyers choose — which avoids burning out your discounts and positions you as a sought-after brand rather than a begging one.
Keep sales pitches as the minority so discounts retain their power.
caveats: The 3–4/week cadence is the source's tested recommendation for its client base; adjust to your audience's tolerance and measure unsubscribes.
The 'don't sell' framing is the presenter's opinion on brand positioning, not a universal rule — transactional lists may still need more offer-led content.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Build a Monthly Campaign Calendar from Key Dates Outward
