cards.summary: Plan each month by placing fixed sales, launches and holidays first, then adding supplementary emails and filling the gaps to hit 3–4 sends weekly.
cards.use_when: Creating next month's editorial/email calendar so campaigns are planned in advance rather than ad hoc.
steps: Open a blank calendar for the upcoming month and mark the important fixed dates: scheduled sales, product launches and holidays.
For each major event, add supplementary emails around it — the source's example is a sale launching on the 10th with a reminder on the 12th and a closer on the 14th.
For a product launch, add supporting emails such as a teaser ahead of the launch.
Once the anchor events and their supporting sends are placed, fill all remaining gaps with microtopic campaigns so you land at three to four sends per week.
Draw the filler topics from your non-discount campaign library (single benefit, FAQ, how-it's-made, customer transformation, etc.).
Repeat monthly so content planning is systematic rather than reactive.
caveats: The example dates and per-event supplement counts are illustrative; scale supplementary touches to event size.
Calendar density should be validated against your engagement metrics.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Diagnose the 9 Common Pop-Up Mistakes Killing Cost Per Acquisition
cards.summary: Most pop-ups under 1–3% because of weak offers, multi-field asks, wrong timing, slow load, small size, excess copy, unclear offers and a reflexively findable close button.
cards.use_when: Auditing an existing pop-up that is converting below target before redesigning it or testing offers.
steps: Check the offer first — it is the most important element; 'sign up for updates' is not an offer. If no discount, use a giveaway, guide or similar value.
Remove extra requests: ask only for email on screen one; request SMS or other fields only after the email submit.
Set the fire delay around 4–12 seconds — not instant (harms experience) and not ~30 seconds (too few people see it).
Fix load speed by compressing images (the source recommends tinypng.com for shrinking large files) and avoiding images on mobile and heavy files generally, so the form doesn't lag in.
Enlarge the form — the source's guidance is roughly 75% of the screen on desktop and as much of the mobile screen as possible, since bigger forms tested better.
Cut copy to the essential: remove implied lines like 'exclusive offers and promotions'; keep only the concrete offer (e.g., '10% off your first order').
Simplify visuals — reduce colors, fonts, images and competing headlines; plain, minimal styling can outperform busy designs.
Make the offer unmistakable and large; shoppers decide in roughly half a second whether to submit or exit.
Defeat the reflexive close: shoppers automatically hit the top-right X, so move the close control (e.g., lower in the form, a separate in-form button, or another corner) to force a look at the offer.
caveats: Close-button repositioning, size targets and delay ranges are the source's tested preferences; verify they don't increase bounce on your site.
Compression tooling and platform interfaces change — confirm current options in your provider.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Choose the Right Pop-Up Offer Based on Average Order Value
cards.summary: Offers must be worth exchanging an email for; use percentage discounts below ~$100 AOV, dollar amounts above ~$100, and creative non-discount offers otherwise.
cards.use_when: Selecting or testing the incentive on your pop-up when opt-in rate is low or you are setting up a new form.
steps: Test whether the offer passes the source's filter: would you personally trade your email for it?
If AOV is under $100, use percentage-off framing (at $50 AOV, '10% off' reads better than '$5 off').
If AOV is over $100, switch to dollar-off framing — the source's example: on a $500 AOV, '5% off' sounds weak while '$25 off' performs better; dollar-off tested better in their experience.

If discounting hurts margins, choose a creative alternative: monthly giveaway entry, free guide, free gift with order, free shipping (give away even if you already offer it), early access to deals, or a 'mystery discount' framing.
Whatever you pick, make it explicit and prominent — vague 'early access' or hidden offers cause exits.
Then run offer tests and evaluate trade-offs: compare opt-in rates for e.g. $10 off vs $15 off against the margin cost of the larger discount to judge whether the extra signups justify it.
caveats: The $100 AOV threshold for dollar-vs-percentage framing is the source's tested heuristic, not a universal rule.
Deeper discounts can improve opt-in rate while eroding margin — judge by total downstream value, not opt-in rate alone.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Run the 5-Step Pop-Up Build Process and a 7-Test Roadmap
cards.summary: Build pop-ups by establishing the offer, choosing form type, creating the form, running a checklist, then AB testing and iterating — expecting many tests before reaching ~10%.
cards.use_when: Standing up a new pop-up program or optimizing an existing form toward 8–12% opt-in.
steps: Step 1 — Establish the offer (single offer to start) guided by margin and opt-in performance.

Step 2 — Choose the form type. The source names five starting points; the recommended first tries are the 'classic' (straight to email, clear offer, no extra fields) and the 'micro-commit' (an extra step before the form, e.g. 'Do you want 10% off?'), then test the others against your audience.
Step 3 — Create the form in your email platform (the source demonstrates Klaviyo and Amped) following the offer and design rules.
Step 4 — Run the form through a pre-launch checklist covering the common mistakes before pushing live.
Step 5 — Set up AB tests, monitor results, and iterate: expect opt-in to move up and down across many variants before reaching the target.
Use the source's progress pattern as realistic: 2.5% → 3.3% → 4.1% → 3.7% etc., reaching around 10% only through continued testing (their example took roughly a fifth or sixth form iteration).
Treat plug-and-play templates as a starting point that is usually left under-optimized; sustained testing is what produces the gains.
caveats: 8–12% is the source's target range, and the client reaching ~10% is a case example, not a promise.
AB testing requires sufficient traffic to reach conclusions; avoid calling winners on tiny samples.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Design the offer before you design the popup
cards.summary: A popup form only converts when the incentive behind it is genuinely worth opting in for, so define a strong offer first and pick the form type second.
cards.use_when: You are planning a list-growth popup (email/SMS capture) and need to decide what incentive to put behind it before building anything.
steps: Write out the actual offer you will give in exchange for the email, and make it concrete and valuable ('here is 10% off your order') rather than vague or insider-ish ('sign up for early access').
Test whether you are genuinely willing to deliver that offer to every subscriber — if you are not, pick a different incentive such as free shipping, a dollar amount off, or a free guide.

Only after the offer is set, choose the form type to test: the source's recommended starters are the classic form (straight to email address) and the micro-commit form (a yes/no question before the email field).
Run classic and micro-commit head to head as your first test before adding complexity such as quizzes or gamified forms.
When comparing offers, don't judge only by opt-in rate — check what happens to conversion once those subscribers are on the list, since that is the outcome that matters.
caveats: Source opinion, not a universal law: strong offers beat weak ones, but the source also says copy matters less than the offer.
Platform pricing and template availability change; verify the current interface.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Micro-commit popups: ask a yes/no question before requesting the email
cards.summary: Adding a one-question commit step in front of the email field leverages consistency bias and can lift submit rates versus asking for the email immediately.
cards.use_when: You are building a capture popup and want a low-effort form variant to test against a straight-to-email classic form.
steps: Build a first step that asks a single yes/no question tied to the offer, e.g. 'Do you want 10% off your first order?' with buttons like 'Yes please' and 'No thanks'.
Configure the affirmative button action to advance to the next step in the form rather than submitting, so the email field appears only after the click.
Reuse the same visual styling across steps (clone the step in your form builder) so the design stays consistent and you don't rebuild formatting.
In the second step, restate the offer and take the email input; keep to one input per step.
Test this against the classic version. The source's rationale is consistency bias — once someone clicks, they are more likely to finish.
caveats: 'Works better in a lot of scenarios' is the source's claim from practice, not a documented benchmark; results depend on audience.
Adds a click before capture, so measure total subscribers, not just conversion rate.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Quiz and gamified popups as alternative capture formats
cards.summary: Quizzes trade a question for the discount and can convert better while collecting segmentation data; spin-to-win and reveal-the-discount forms convert strongly but read as tacky.
cards.use_when: You have already tested classic and micro-commit popups and want additional capture formats, or you need customer preference data for future segmentation.
steps: For a quiz form: ask a question that tells you something useful about the shopper (e.g. which problem they are trying to solve), then present the discount as the earned reward in exchange for that answer.
Tag respondents by their answer in your ESP so you can send segment-specific follow-up emails later.
For a spin-to-win or reveal-the-discount form: make the interaction reveal the reward, then gate claiming it with the email address; the source notes spin-to-win typically lands on the top prize.
Try these formats periodically or rotate them rather than making them your permanent default if your brand positioning depends on a premium look.
Compare formats by opt-in rate and downstream purchase conversion, and remember gamified formats may attract discount-motivated subscribers.
caveats: Source's view: spin-to-win 'converts like crazy' but makes the brand look cheap — a positioning trade-off, not a universal recommendation.
Quiz tools and gamified templates vary by platform; verify which templates your provider currently supports.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Hide the X and force a claim-or-decline decision
cards.summary: Making the close button invisible or replacing it with a visible 'no thanks' option forces shoppers to consciously decide on the offer instead of reflex-closing the popup.
cards.use_when: You are designing a popup whose current form is being reflex-closed in the top corner without the offer being read.
steps: Reduce the X icon's visibility (e.g. set its opacity to zero) so the offer is the first thing read.
Add your own secondary button beneath the primary claim button with copy such as 'No thanks, close form' so the shopper can still exit deliberately.
Style the decline button to be visually quiet — blank background, readable text — so it does not compete with the offer.
Keep the offer headline as the largest element on the form and reduce surrounding copy so it is unmistakably the focus.
Keep the required legal SMS consent language small (source suggests roughly size 8) rather than letting it dominate the layout.
caveats: Hiding the exit can frustrate shoppers; the source frames it as improving conversion but notes to keep an explicit decline path.
Accessibility and platform policies may restrict or dislike hidden close controls — check your provider and local requirements.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Mobile popup build: single-step capture with email then SMS as a separate step
cards.summary: A high-converting mobile popup keeps one input per step, telegraphs the offer, and sequences email capture before SMS rather than stacking both fields together.
cards.use_when: You are configuring a mobile capture popup in your ESP and want a concrete layout order and settings to start from.
steps: Start from a multi-step email and SMS template, then clone it into a mobile-only form so mobile and desktop data can be analyzed separately.
Set targeting to display on mobile only so the same design is not distorted across devices.
Step 1: email opt-in with the offer as the hero headline; Step 2: phone number for SMS; Step 3: a success message with the discount code and a 'start shopping' style button.
Do not place email and SMS inputs on the same step — the source states this hurts conversion.
In the success step, tell SMS subscribers to confirm on their device and mention that anyone who skips SMS still enters the email welcome flow, so email subscribers are not lost.
Check the success step has a working close/continue button since the X may be hidden.
caveats: Different ESPs name steps and templates differently; tutorial videos referenced in the source may be outdated.
The source's recommended form dimensions (roughly 750x500 on mobile) are a starting point for testing, not a proven optimum.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Desktop popup design: go bigger, use a side image, keep one offer
cards.summary: On desktop, a larger popup with a product image on the side and a single clear offer generally converts better than fly-outs or small embeds, at some cost to shopping experience.
cards.use_when: You are designing the desktop version of a capture popup and deciding on size, layout and imagery.
steps: Clone your mobile form into a desktop-only version, then set targeting to display on desktop only.
Use a popup (or a larger custom size) rather than a fly-out, since the source reports fly-outs as less effective.
Use a product or lifestyle image on one side of the form. The source says 'right image' was tested as working best, but recommends testing left, right and no image.
Compress any image before uploading to avoid a slow-loading form.
Verify the layout holds after swapping images, since uploads can reset sizing and formatting.
Ask whether you are willing to trade some browsing experience for a more prominent form; source says bigger forms generally convert better but are more intrusive.
caveats: 'Right image works best' is the source's testing experience, not a universal rule — test it.
Large popups can increase bounce for shoppers mid-browse; consider timing and frequency alongside size.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Form targeting: delay, frequency and avoiding exit-intent
cards.summary: Fire popups on a time delay roughly 4-12 seconds after arrival, set a multi-day suppression window after a close, and avoid showing immediately or relying on exit intent.
cards.use_when: You are setting the trigger and frequency rules for a popup and deciding when it appears and re-appears.
steps: Do not show the form immediately on load; the source recommends against it.
Set the trigger to a time-on-page delay rather than exit intent, which the source says misfires and isn't very good.
Start with a 4-second delay and test upward toward 12 seconds.
Set a frequency rule so that after someone closes the form, it does not reappear for several days — the source uses about 5 days as an example.
Restrict the form to the device type it was designed for (mobile-only or desktop-only) so each version's data stays clean.
Advance the delay gradually and compare total submits, not just conversion rate, when choosing a final value.
caveats: Time delay and frequency values are the source's starting heuristics; the right values depend on traffic volume, page speed and audience.
Some platforms offer scroll-depth and page-count triggers as alternatives the source did not recommend over a time delay.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Popup form QA checklist before launch
cards.summary: A short pre-launch checklist covering inputs per step, timing, load speed, size, copy length, offer prominence and close-button design catches the common conversion killers.
cards.use_when: You have built a popup and are about to publish it; use this to catch obvious issues before sending traffic.
steps: Confirm only one input is requested per step — never email and SMS together.
Confirm the time delay sits in the roughly 4-12 second range.
Confirm the form loads instantly with no lag when it fires.
Confirm the form covers at least about 75% of the screen so the offer is not easily ignored.
Trim body copy to under about 10 words on the form.
Confirm the offer itself is the largest visual element.
Confirm there is no visible dismissive X, or replace it with a close-form button / an unclear X placement so the shopper makes a decision.
Verify close functionality works on every step, including the success step, so users are not trapped.
caveats: The source presents these as a strong starting checklist for testing, not a guarantee of performance; a strong offer can compensate for one missed item.
'Covers 75% of screen' and 'under 10 words' are the source's heuristics, not measured benchmarks.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Seven A/B tests to run on popup forms, in rough priority order
cards.summary: Test offer first, then form type, close functionality, time delay, imagery, copy and color — but judge delay tests on total submits rather than conversion rate.
cards.use_when: You have a live popup form and need a testing backlog ordered by likely impact on subscriber volume and revenue.
steps: Offer first (highest leverage): test 10% off versus $10 off versus free shipping versus a free guide, and include a mystery-offer variant; evaluate both opt-in rate and post-opt-in purchase conversion.
Form type second: test popup versus full-page versus fly-out, and test variations within your chosen type.
Close functionality third: test a close-form button versus an X, and test where the close control sits.

Time delay fourth: compare 4 seconds versus 12 seconds. Judge by total submits, not conversion rate — a 30-second delay may show a higher conversion rate but far fewer total subscribers because few visitors stay that long.
Image content fifth: test different photos and placements; on mobile consider whether an image belongs as the form background.
Copy sixth: test longer versus shorter copy and different phrasing ('unlock my offer' versus 'you've got 10% off').
Colors last: simpler color palettes tend to produce better opt-ins than busy ones.
caveats: The source recommends running a test every couple of days; that cadence requires enough traffic to reach a read.
The illustrative comparison (3% to 4% opt-in on 10,000 visitors equals roughly 100 extra subscribers a month) is arithmetic, not a performance promise.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Popup platform choice: built-in ESP forms versus a specialist tool
cards.summary: Your ESP's native popup builder is usually good enough to start, but a dedicated popup platform typically performs better at an added monthly cost.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to build capture forms inside your email platform or subscribe to a dedicated popup tool.
steps: If your ESP is also your email sender, start with its native form builder and templates, then realistically customize them for ecommerce rather than using the default template as-is.

If popups are a meaningful growth channel and budget allows, evaluate a dedicated popup platform (the source cites one at roughly $100/month) and compare opt-in performance against your current forms.
When evaluating a specialist vendor, ask whether they will build your first forms for you as part of onboarding, and confirm what the editor can customize.
Inside a specialist editor, expect to edit copy, images and each step separately; formatting may need manual padding/spacing fixes per device view.
Set targeting (e.g. anonymous visitors) and a time-on-page trigger such as 4 seconds, then preview locally and on your live site before publishing.
Confirm any discount code referenced in the form is created in your store, or the form may fail to deliver the incentive.
caveats: Pricing, free tiers and editor features change frequently — verify current pricing and interface before committing.
The source states it has seen strong ROI from the specialist platform but does not provide a verified benchmark; treat this as testimonial, not proof.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Flows versus campaigns: what each is for and how to split revenue
cards.summary: Flows fire automatically when a shopper completes a trigger action and handle personalization across the journey; campaigns are manual sends to the list.
cards.use_when: You are planning your email program structure and deciding how much revenue to expect from automated sequences versus one-off sends.
steps: Define flows as sequences triggered by a specific shopper action (site visit, product view, add to cart, checkout start, purchase, long lapsed purchase); once activated they fire automatically for every qualifying shopper.
Define campaigns as manually created, manually sent emails to your list.
Set up flow triggers through your ecommerce platform integration so events (cart abandonment, purchase) fire the sequence automatically.
Aim for a rough balance — the source suggests targeting roughly 50% of revenue from flows and 50% from campaigns.
Prioritize personalization: different customers are at different journey stages and should receive different information, which is the core advantage of flows over blasts.
Treat this as ongoing work: flows need updating as brand, trends and customer base change.
caveats: The 50/50 split is the source's heuristic, not a calculation derived from data presented here.
Any revenue contribution figures quoted by the source are testimonials from its own client work, not forecasts for your store.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: The six baseline flows to build first, in order
cards.summary: Nail the basics — welcome, site abandon, browse abandon, cart abandon, checkout abandon, post-purchase and win-back — before investing in advanced cross-sell or upsell automations.
cards.use_when: You are deciding which automated email flows to build or fix next, and whether to invest in advanced segmentation or upsell logic.
steps: Welcome flow: 8 emails for new subscribers.
Site abandon flow: 1 email for someone who visited the site and left without deeper action.
Browse abandon flow: 5 emails for someone who viewed a product and left.
Cart abandon flow: 6-8 emails for someone who added to cart and left.
Checkout abandon flow: 6-8 emails for someone who started checkout and left.
Post-purchase flow: sequence after a purchase.
Win-back flow: for customers who purchased months ago and have gone quiet.

Audit your existing flows against these basics before adding advanced cross-sell, upsell or split tests — the source describes a case where a brand wanted advanced automations while the welcome flow was a single email and cart abandonment was not set up correctly.
caveats: Email counts per flow are the source's recommended structure; your optimal counts depend on catalog, price point and purchase frequency.
The described revenue improvement for one brand (roughly $45k to $133k in a month after fixing basics) is a case example, not a promised result.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Build flows in a mobile-first multi-step pattern you can clone across devices
cards.summary: Build the mobile popup first, clone it for desktop, and keep each step focused on one input so both versions can be measured separately.
cards.use_when: You are implementing capture forms across device types and want a repeatable build process rather than two independent designs.
steps: Build the mobile version first with the step sequence you want (micro-commit, email, SMS, success), then clone the form and convert the clone to desktop-only.
Set display rules per clone so mobile and desktop data are analyzed separately rather than as one blended report.
Ask your SMS platform how phone numbers collected in your ESP form flow into their system — the source notes SMS may live on a separate platform.
If you want a micro-commit variant, clone the form again and move the new question step to the front, deleting the email field from that step.
In a specialized popup platform, customize each step's copy and imagery individually, and check that padding and layout are re-applied after any image swap.
Preview both versions before publishing and confirm each step's button actions are correct (advance step versus submit form).
caveats: SMS and ESP integration specifics vary widely by platform and country regulations; verify consent language requirements.
Tutorials referenced in the source may not match current platform interfaces.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Prioritize core lifecycle flows over advanced segmentation
cards.summary: Build the seven basic email flows — welcome, site abandon, browse abandon, cart abandon, checkout abandon, post-purchase and win-back — before advanced segmentations.
cards.use_when: Planning your store's email lifecycle roadmap or deciding where to invest automation effort first.
steps: Adopt the seven core flows as your baseline stack: welcome (8 emails), site abandon (1 email), browse abandon (5 emails), cart abandon (6-8 emails), checkout abandon (6-8 emails), post-purchase (3+ emails) and win-back (3 emails).
Resist the urge to build complex hypersegmentation first — per the source, advanced segmentation 'takes a lot of effort for not as many results' as nailing the basics.
Treat the email counts and delays below as starting templates, not proven optima; the source explicitly says every brand must test.
Set each flow to fire on its own distinct trigger and use exit filters so a customer moves through the funnel rather than receiving overlapping flows.
After launch, move improvement effort into campaign testing (see the campaign-as-testing-ground card) rather than endless flow surgery.
caveats: The flow counts and delays are the presenter's base outlines for 7-8 figure brands, not universal benchmarks — you must test per account.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Welcome flow: 8-email structure with exit filter
cards.summary: A 4-10 email welcome series delivering your acquisition discount, brand story, hero products and social proof, with a purchase filter removing buyers mid-flow.
cards.use_when: Setting up the new-subscriber welcome automation after your popup/form captures an email.
steps: Trigger on someone joining your email list; add a filter that exits anyone who makes a purchase (0 purchases since starting the flow) so buyers don't keep receiving discount prompts and instead enter the post-purchase flow.
Email 1: strong introduction — deliver the welcome discount at the top of the email (not buried), plus USPs, light social proof and best sellers; keep it condensed.
Email 2: brand background — founding story, face to the name, team photo, and sprinkle social proof into the story.
Email 3: highlight best sellers and why they're good, reminding of the discount.
Email 4: urgency — discount is expiring soon, add risk reversals (guarantees, shipping promise) and testimonials.
Email 5: us-versus-them — clearly list why you differ from competitors the subscriber is likely also evaluating.
Email 6: heavy social proof — brand testimonials and any media features.
Email 7: last chance, kept super simple and aggressive.
Email 8: note from the founder — check in, offer support via reply, and offer an extended discount (source says this email usually does well).
Use 1-2 day delays between emails (source sometimes uses 2-3 days); remind recipients of the discount in every email.
caveats: Source acknowledges discomfort with discounting first purchase but argues list value repays it; that is an opinion, not measured proof.
Offer the founder a real reply channel only if you can handle responses.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Welcome flow's two acceptable outcomes
cards.summary: Design the welcome flow to either convert the curious subscriber or prime a future buyer whose objections are already answered.
cards.use_when: Setting success metrics and email content priorities for the welcome automation.
steps: Outcome A: convert subscribers who would otherwise have left, using a strong popup form plus a welcome flow that addresses objections as they arrive.
Outcome B: if they don't buy, treat the flow as objection-priming — deliver the information needed so that when the need arises, campaigns convert without fresh objection handling.
Keep every email discount-visible so both outcomes retain the incentive thread.
After the flow completes, move non-buyers into the regular campaign list rather than leaving them in the automation.
caveats: Outcome B is hard to measure directly; treat it as a content-hygiene principle rather than an attribution claim.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Site abandon flow: one-email nudge to keep browsing
cards.summary: A single email sent 2-4 hours after a site visit with no product view, aimed at re-engaging or routing visitors down the funnel.
cards.use_when: Adding a recovery flow for visitors who hit your homepage or category pages and leave without viewing a product.
steps: Trigger on 'active on site' (the source uses Klaviyo/Shopify); exit anyone who views a product, adds to cart, reaches checkout, or purchases, so they enter the deeper flows instead.
Add a suppression so a visitor can't receive this flow more than once in 30 days.
Wait 2-4 hours before sending; the source found this window best but says to test it.
Send one email: 'Do you need some help?' — remind them to keep shopping and surface best sellers, a few categories, and light social proof.
Keep the email deliberately simple — don't overload it; the goal is to push them deeper into the funnel, not to sell a specific item.
caveats: Site-visit frequency is low per visitor, so send consistency matters more than frequency here.
An exit-filter misconfiguration can cause visitors to receive this alongside deeper abandon flows.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Browse abandon flow: 5-email recap that escalates slowly
cards.summary: A 5-email sequence for product viewers who didn't add to cart or buy, starting with a fast reminder and saving discounts for later.
cards.use_when: Building the browse-abandonment automation for shoppers who viewed a PDP but didn't add to cart.
steps: Trigger on viewed product; exit anyone who adds to cart, starts checkout, or purchases; suppress repeat entrants for 30 days.
Wait 45 minutes before the first email (source says test the interval). Email 1 shows the exact product they viewed via dynamic content (e.g., Klaviyo's dynamic block) with a simple reminder.
Email 2 (1-2 days later): brand info and risk reversals, plus other products they can shop — the objection is buy-in on the brand.
Email 3: testimonials and social proof on the viewed item, with dynamic content showing what they abandoned.
Email 4: introduce a discount only after the free options — the source deliberately delays discounting to protect margins — framed as a 48-hour flash.
Email 5: short closer, 'expires in 24 hours', discount reminder.
Keep emails very simple and use dynamic blocks in each email so the visitor sees their actual product.
caveats: Do not wait a week — source says this is too long while attention is fresh.
Discount timing is a margin trade-off, not a proven revenue lift for your account; test.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Cart abandon and checkout abandon are two separate flows
cards.summary: Add-to-cart and checkout-start abandonment need distinct triggers and exit filters, even if they reuse the same email content.
cards.use_when: Auditing or building cart and checkout recovery automations.
steps: Recognize the difference: adding to cart is a different event from entering the payment/shipping checkout page, so each needs its own flow.
Cart abandon trigger: added to cart; exit filters should include 'placed order 0 times' and 'checkout started' so anyone further down the funnel enters checkout abandon instead.
Checkout abandon triggers on checkout start with its own exit filter on purchase.
Reuse the same email content across both flows — the source uses identical content with different triggers.

Source claims roughly 90% of brands audited lack a proper cart-abandon flow; verify your platform actually fires an abandoned-cart trigger (the source says Klaviyo added it via Shopify integration around September 2024) or build a custom trigger.
Run 6-8 emails; first email ~30 minutes after the trigger (source's recommendation, test it), then 1-2 day gaps.
caveats: Platform trigger availability changes — verify the current interface and event names in your platform before assuming it exists.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Cart/checkout abandon content sequence
cards.summary: Email-by-email content plan for cart and checkout abandonment that ends with tiered offers for first-time versus returning buyers.
cards.use_when: Writing the emails inside cart-abandon and checkout-abandon flows.
steps: Email 1: simple reminder of the abandoned product with a shop-now CTA and dynamic block showing the item.
Email 2: text-based nudge from the founder — informal, personal, 'you left something behind'.
Email 3: brand USPs and why to choose you over other stores the shopper is likely comparing.
Email 4: customer testimonials plus dynamic abandoned content.
Email 5: last-chance urgency — 'your order is expiring, we can't hold it much longer'.

Branch the final email: returning buyers get a founder check-in with support offer, no discount; first-time buyers get a discount opener (e.g., '15% off if you buy within 48 hours') followed by a founder 'everything okay?' discount closer.
Place the dynamic abandoned-product block at the top of every email and add cross-sell recommendations at the bottom.
caveats: The 15% / 48-hour figures are examples from the source, not calibrated thresholds for your store.
Discounting checkout abandoners can train customers to abandon deliberately — consider testing versus a no-discount branch.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Post-purchase flow: 3 emails that thank, bond, and enable
cards.summary: A short post-purchase sequence: immediate founder thank-you with add-on offer, social follow, then product-usage tips that drive repeat purchase.
cards.use_when: Building the automation that fires immediately after an order is placed.
steps: Trigger on order placed with no exit filter — everyone should receive it.

Email 1, sent immediately: text-based thank-you from the founder using the customer's first name, tying the order to your mission, offering support by reply, and including a PS add-to-order offer within 24 hours — the source calls this an immediate big purchase window.
Email 2, ~2 days later: invite them to your main social channel or community group to grow your owned audience.

Email 3, ~3 days later: 'how to get the most from your product' — usage tips, routines, pairing suggestions that naturally set up the upsell, plus a recommended-products block based on customer activity.
Keep it to about three emails; the source says four-plus is optional and three is fine.
caveats: The add-to-order offer window depends on your fulfillment speed; if orders ship same-day, combine the add-on offer into the order confirmation instead.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Win-back flow: fire at double the average repurchase interval
cards.summary: A simple 3-email re-engagement sequence timed at roughly twice the customer's average time between purchases.
cards.use_when: Setting up reactivation automation for customers who bought months ago.
steps: Set the trigger based on elapsed time since last order — if average time between purchases is ~45 days, fire at ~90 days (source's rule of thumb: double the interval), or use 60/90/120 days.
Exit anyone who makes a purchase after entering the flow.
Email 1: 'it's been a while' brand reminder with a comeback nudge and a dynamic recommendation based on the customer's last purchase.
Email 2 (about a week later): a unique, dynamically generated discount code per customer — the source says personalized codes convert better.
Email 3: text-based last-chance from the founder, warm and understanding, restating the expiring discount.
Keep the flow simple; the source argues most repeat purchases come from regular campaigns (3-4 sends per week), not the win-back flow, so treat it partly as customer experience.
caveats: The double-the-interval rule is a heuristic, not a measured formula, and only works if you have a reliable average repurchase interval.
Source's claim that ~99% of retention/repeat revenue comes from campaigns is the presenter's assertion, not a verified benchmark for your list.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Use campaigns as the testing ground for flow content
cards.summary: Rather than running many A/B tests inside flows, test angles in frequent campaigns and port winning emails into flows.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to optimize lifecycle emails when flow testing is slow and hard to track.
steps: Send 3-4 email campaigns per week (minimum 2) so you get fast, 24-hour data on angles and subject lines.

Track campaign performance; when an email wins, add its angle to the relevant flow: educational product-creation emails to the welcome flow (with discount added), usage-tip emails to the post-purchase flow, return-policy emails to the cart-abandon flow for risk reversal.
Avoid maintaining dozens of simultaneous active tests across triggers — the source says flows are hard to monitor at scale and need spreadsheets to track.
Only accept flow-specific test results when the sample is meaningful; wait for customer entry volume before judging a flow variant.
Document what went into which flow so you don't re-test identical angles repeatedly.
caveats: Campaign and flow audiences behave differently, so a campaign winner is a strong hypothesis, not a guaranteed flow winner.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Test flow time delays before content
cards.summary: Time delay from customer action to first email is described as the biggest, fastest lever in flow testing.
cards.use_when: Choosing and tuning send delays for site, browse, cart and checkout abandon flows.
steps: Pick one abandonment flow and test two delays for the first email — e.g., the source compared 30 minutes versus 4 hours for a website-abandon flow.

Evaluate on placed-order rate, not just opens: in the source's example, the 30-minute delay got better open and click rates, but the 4-hour delay produced a much higher placed-order rate on a large sample.
Do not assume faster is always better — the source explicitly says the placed-order result favored waiting longer in that case.
Apply findings per flow, since attention windows differ (browse: 45 minutes recommended; cart: ~30 minutes; site: 2-4 hours; win-back: weeks).
Re-test delays as your list and traffic composition change.
caveats: The 30-minute versus 4-hour comparison is one case study; the source calls it a large sample but it does not establish a universal best delay.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Long-form versus short-form flow emails
cards.summary: Test whether abandonment emails should walk through objections or just remind — short reminders often win on impulse purchases.
cards.use_when: Deciding email length and content depth in abandonment flows and campaigns.
steps: Test a long email that explicitly works through objections against a short one that just says 'you left this behind, shop now'.

In the source's comparison on ~2,000 recipients, the short email achieved a 0.2% placed-order rate and 2.4% click rate versus better performance for the quick reminder — use this as a hypothesis, not a rule.
Reason about intent: some abandoners need their objections talked through, while others have no objections and only need a reminder — segment or sequence accordingly.
Combine both in sequence where possible: short reminder first, longer objection-handling email later in the flow.
Judge by placed-order rate, not click rate alone, since long educational emails can earn clicks without purchases.
caveats: Single A/B example, not a universal result; the source stresses it must be tested per account.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Subject line and preview text tests to run
cards.summary: Specific subject-line variables worth A/B testing: discounts mentioned, emojis, ellipses, caps, and length.
cards.use_when: Running subject line experiments for campaigns or flow emails.
steps: Test including versus excluding discount mentions (e.g., 'sale').
Test including versus excluding emojis in subject lines and preview text.
Test ellipses ('...') versus plain endings.
Test ALL CAPS versus sentence case.
Test different urgency timeframes stated in the subject line.

Remember the source's caveat: subject-line test learnings are hard to transfer to future emails because so much varies — use them for immediate improvement rather than building a permanent subject-line rulebook.
caveats: High variability makes subject-line learnings less durable; expect to keep re-testing.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Graphic-heavy versus text-based email design
cards.summary: Text-based founder-style emails often outperform graphic-heavy ones, but the source says to balance and test.
cards.use_when: Choosing email format for flow emails such as founder nudges, thank-yous and last-chance messages.
steps: Build a plain-text-style email (little or no imagery) that reads as a personal message, e.g., a founder note sign-off.
Compare it against your standard template with heavy graphics on open rate, click rate and revenue.
In the source's example, the text-based founder email beat the graphic email on opens, clicks and revenue — treat this as a directional hypothesis for your list.
Use text-based design preferentially for personal messages — founder notes, thank-yous, cart nudges, win-back last chances — and keep graphic design for product showcases and social proof blocks.
Re-test when you see sales drops or list composition changes.
caveats: Performance varies by account; the source explicitly says to test rather than assume text always wins.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Promoting categories versus individual products in email
cards.summary: Test category-level promotion against specific-product promotion — higher-ticket stores in the source leaned toward categories.
cards.use_when: Deciding what to feature in campaign and flow email blocks, especially for higher-ticket catalogs.
steps: Create one variant featuring specific products ('shop this jacket') and one featuring categories ('shop jackets, shop pants').
Measure clicks and revenue, not just clicks.
In the source's higher-ticket store example, categories produced higher clicks and higher revenue, so they biased future emails toward category promotion.
Default to individual products when the flow is abandonment-driven and you can show the exact abandoned item dynamically.
Revisit the bias as catalog breadth and price points change.
caveats: Single-store example; the source presents it as a tested bias, not a universal rule.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Seed welcome-flow social proof with early testimonials
cards.summary: Use whatever review volume and testimonials you have, and place them where the sequence's doubts peak.
cards.use_when: Writing welcome-flow emails when you have a new or small brand with little social proof.
steps: Place light social proof in email 1, woven into the founder story rather than isolated.
Save the heavy-proof email (brand testimonials, media features) for email 6, after brand education and before the aggressive last-chance email.
Use existing proof even if modest — the source suggests sprinkling review counts or media mentions into the story rather than waiting for large numbers.
Add testimonials to the urgency email (email 4) for recipients still on the fence, and repeat proof inside browse/cart recovery emails for the exact item abandoned.
Do not fabricate proof; if the brand is new, use founder credibility and risk reversal instead of numerical claims.
caveats: The source does not prescribe a minimum review count — do not invent one.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Founder-message emails and when they convert
cards.summary: Persona-driven 'note from the founder' emails work across welcome, abandonment and win-back flows when kept simple and human.
cards.use_when: Writing personal-voice emails for welcome close, cart abandon, post-purchase thanks or win-back final send.
steps: Use the founder (or a named person) as sender with the customer's first name in the body.
Keep it short and text-based; the source says these perform well because recipients feel personally reached.
Offer a real support channel: invite recipients to reply to the email with questions.
In abandonment flows, use it as the second email or the last-chance email, offering support and occasionally extending the discount by a day.
In post-purchase, use it immediately after order placed to convey mission and offer add-ons within 24 hours.
Expect and prepare for support replies — the source notes these emails generate customer questions.
caveats: Requires a real inbox and response process; unmonitored replies can hurt trust.
Founder credibility must be genuine — do not invent a persona.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Customize flows with dynamic product blocks
cards.summary: Use platform dynamic content so recovery and recommendation emails show the exact product or a personalized suggestion per recipient.
cards.use_when: Building browse-abandon, cart-abandon, post-purchase and win-back emails in Klaviyo or a comparable platform.
steps: Add a dynamic block showing the abandoned product (image, name, price, link) at the top of browse and cart/checkout abandonment emails.
Use the platform's product-recommendation blocks based on the customer's activity in post-purchase and win-back emails.
Generate per-customer dynamic discount codes in win-back flows so each recipient feels their offer is unique — the source says these convert better.
In welcome-flow examples, keep discount code visible throughout; a generic graphic won't reproduce that per-recipient effect.
Verify the current name and setup of dynamic blocks in your platform, as interfaces change.
caveats: Dynamic blocks depend on your catalog and event data being clean; missing product data produces blank or wrong recommendations.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Run 3-4 email campaigns per week to carry retention
cards.summary: Regular campaigns, not just flows, drive most repeat purchases; keep send frequency at least two per week.
cards.use_when: Planning weekly retention calendar and deciding how much to rely on automation versus broadcasts.
steps: Send 3-4 campaigns per week (the source treats two as the floor).
Use these campaigns as your testing ground for angles that later get ported into flows.
Keep the win-back flow simple because recipients are still receiving your regular campaigns.
Expect most repeat purchases to come from campaigns — the source asserts around 99% of retention and repeat purchases, but treat this as the presenter's claim, not a measured figure for your list.
Watch engagement and unsubscribes when scaling frequency; adjust if list health degrades.
caveats: The 99% claim is an unverified assertion in the source; do not plan forecasts around it.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Risk reversal and urgency placement in sequence
cards.summary: Place urgency and risk reversals at the sequence point where they resolve the remaining objection, not in the first email.
cards.use_when: Ordering content in welcome, browse, cart and checkout abandonment sequences.
steps: In the welcome flow, deliver the incentive first, then USPs/product education, then social proof, then urgency ('discount expiring soon') with risk reversal (30-day guarantee, shipping promise), then heavy proof, then last chance.
In browse abandon, keep email 1 as a pure reminder, put risk reversal in email 2, and put the discount in email 4 with a 48-hour framing.
In cart/checkout abandon, keep the last chance email separate from the discount branch, giving returning buyers a no-discount founder note instead.
In win-back, reserve the unique discount for email 2 and the last-chance founder note for email 3.
Use short, specific urgency ('expires in 24 hours') rather than vague pressure.
caveats: Aggressive urgency in the last email may cost list goodwill; the source recommends testing timing and tone.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Why the welcome flow exists: email as the cheap way across the trust threshold
cards.summary: Use the welcome flow to send trust-building content at scale, because paid traffic alone makes a first-time buyer too expensive.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much budget and effort to put into the post-signup welcome flow versus buying more ad impressions.
steps: Start from the source's funnel math: only a small share of site traffic (he cites ~2%) is ready to buy on the first visit; the rest arrive with objections about brand legitimacy, product quality and price. Those objections cannot be answered by one ad, so buyers need repeated exposure — the source calls this crossing the 'trust threshold'.

Recognise that the only other channel that reaches people daily at low marginal cost is email — the source cites 4B+ global email users, 90%+ of the US population checking email daily, and average $44 returned per $1 spent on email versus roughly $2 per $1 on paid ads. Treat those ratios as the source's cited industry averages, not guaranteed results.

Apply to your store: for each objection on your PDP (does this work, is this brand real, is it worth the price), assign at least one email in the flow that answers it, so paid spend does not have to be repeated to convince the same person.
Keep the objective in mind for measurement: the welcome flow's job is partly immediate conversion and partly priming future purchases, so judging it only by its own revenue understates its value.
caveats: ROAS and percentage figures are the source's cited averages; your niche, price point and traffic source will differ.
Email only works if you are actually capturing addresses — without a popup or lead magnet, the flow has nobody to send to.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Set the welcome flow length and goal by price point and buying cycle
cards.summary: Run the welcome sequence over 7-14 days for typical AOV, stretching to months for high-ticket products with long consideration.
cards.use_when: Scoping how many emails and how many days your welcome/onboarding flow should cover before you write it.
steps: Default to a 7-14 day window for a normal AOV store — the source's typical recommendation.
If AOV is very high (he gives the example of a ~$5,000 product), extend the flow well beyond that, potentially over two months, because the buying decision itself takes longer.

Define two outcomes you are designing for: (a) converting the curious signups who would otherwise bounce, and (b) priming future customers by addressing objections up front. Priming shows up later, e.g. the source claims a campaign sent to a primed list can produce a far larger revenue day ($75k vs $5k in his illustrative example) — treat that as illustration, not a benchmark.
Plan the flow as separate, spread-out emails rather than a couple of dense ones, and pick an email count that matches the length of the consideration window.
caveats: The 7-14 day range and two-month high-ticket example are the source's heuristics, not tested universals.
The revenue comparison used to illustrate priming is an anecdote; do not promise it internally as a forecast.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Split dense welcome emails into short, skimmable, spread-out messages
cards.summary: Fix short-but-crammed welcome flows by cutting information per email and spreading it across more emails.
cards.use_when: Auditing an existing welcome flow that crams brand story, bestsellers, FAQ and offer into 2-3 long emails.
steps: Accept the skim reality: the source states customers spend at most roughly 5-7 seconds on an email, so the whole flow's information cannot live in two walls of text.
Keep body copy minimal — the source calls anything over about 100 words 'too much' for these emails. Use short headlines and one idea per email.
Structure every email so the reader can get the point in about three seconds: clear headline, one supporting proof or claim, discount reminder if one exists, and a button.
Place a button near the top of every email so nobody has to scroll to act, and repeat a button at the bottom for readers who reach the end.

Assign one job per email across the sequence (intro + incentive, brand story, bestseller, offer reminder, us-vs-them, social proof, last chance, founder note) rather than duplicating everything everywhere.
caveats: The 100-word and 5-7 second figures are the source's rules of thumb for ecommerce promo email, not formal research.
Short emails do not mean skipping the offer reminder — the source specifically criticises welcome emails that never restate the discount.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Email 1: deliver the incentive and prove legitimacy in the first screen
cards.summary: Open the welcome flow with a fast, purpose-built email that hands over the discount and gives enough proof to click now.
cards.use_when: Writing or rewriting the first email a new subscriber receives after opting in.
steps: Put the welcome and the discount at the very top with the incentive code visible and a shop-now button above the fold, so the discount-only crowd can convert without scrolling.
Add a short brand message headline (the source's example uses two words carrying the brand's positioning) so skimmers absorb what you stand for without reading a paragraph.
Include one short social proof element and one or two differentiators (USPs), then the discount and another button.
Show bestsellers below so people who do not know what to buy have a default choice, not a blank stare at your homepage.
Close with a bottom button — the source notes most people will not scroll back up to find a top button if they end up at the base of the email.
caveats: Design should be simple and clean; heavy layouts compete with the one action you want.
Only discount-led lead capture suits this email; if your opt-in is a lead magnet or content offer, deliver that instead.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Email 2: put a face to the brand to convert skeptical new signups
cards.summary: Use the brand-story email to humanise the store and address the 'who are these people, are they real' objection.
cards.use_when: Building the second email in the welcome flow for a store that customers find through ads and don't recognise.
steps: Assume the reason they have not purchased yet is partly that you are a faceless brand they stumbled on in an ad; the email's job is to make you feel like a real small company with a mission.
Include a founding story in about two sentences, the mission, and — critically — a real face (photo of founders or maker), plus the reason the brand was started.
State one or two differentiators (ingredients, process, sourcing) so the story is not only emotional but informative.
Remind them of the discount above the button; include the button and a brand-aesthetic image.
Do not expect this email to be a big revenue driver — the source says it will make some sales, but its real value is priming and trust building for later purchases.
caveats: A fabricated or stock 'founder' image undermines the trust the email is meant to build.
Emotional storytelling still needs factual product claims to satisfy skeptical buyers.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Email 3: use a bestseller email to collapse choice paralysis
cards.summary: Spotlight one or a few bestsellers with reasons, so undecided buyers don't have to choose between your whole catalogue.
cards.use_when: Designing the mid-flow email for a store with a large catalogue where new subscribers don't know what to buy.
steps: Apply the source's observation that customers want choices but hate making them — so make the decision for them by featuring one or a few bestsellers rather than the full range.

Give the bestseller a reason: not just the product name but specific, brief qualities (the example uses protein, fibre, prebiotics, plant ingredients), so the qualities you praise transfer to how the brand is perceived.
Use one or two words or short bullets per point rather than sentences; keep proof concrete, not essay-length.
Adapt the layout to a specific hero product, e.g. one shirt or one flavour, while keeping the same structure of headline, hero image, reasons, discount, buttons.
Close with a discount reminder and a button, ideally with a button near the top as well.
caveats: The 'wants choices but hates choosing' idea is the source's framing of consumer psychology, not a tested law.
Featuring a product that is actually out of stock or barely stocked will burn the trust this email builds.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Email 4: add urgency plus risk reversal to push the fence-sitters
cards.summary: Turn the coupon reminder into a decision email by combining time pressure, testimonials and guarantees.
cards.use_when: Writing the offer-reminder email mid-flow when subscribers are informed but still not purchasing.
steps: Write a headline that addresses the discount directly and states the code is expiring — the source's example pairs 'friendly reminder that your discount code is expiring' with 'we don't offer discounts often', which creates urgency and positions the brand as non-discount.

Add risk reversals that answer the remaining purchase objections: free shipping, satisfaction guarantee, easy/free returns. The source flags the absence of risk reversals as the main improvement available in this kind of email.
Use testimonials for trust, and consider pairing testimonials with individual products plus their discounts, so proof and offer sit together.
Make the button large and unmistakable so clicking is trivially easy on mobile; the source argues an oversized button drives a very high click rate.
Include a bottom link to browse the whole catalogue for readers who did not like the featured products.
caveats: Frequent fake urgency erodes credibility — only claim expirations you will actually enforce.
The 'we don't offer discounts often' line only works if it is true for your brand.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Email 5: answer 'why you instead of the competitor' head-on
cards.summary: Use a direct comparison email to let shoppers evaluate you against alternatives and conclude you win.
cards.use_when: Building the comparison email for a crowded niche where buyers are weighing several similar brands.
steps: Lead with the elephant in the room: in most niches there are thousands of alternatives, so state why someone should pick you.

Use a short comparison table or list with brief 1-3 word points (the source's example contrasts customisation vs non-customisable, simple ordering vs complicated ordering, thoughtful gifting vs standard delivery). Keep it fast to scan.
Follow the comparison with one expanded differentiator and an emotional benefit — the source's example describes what a delivered gourmet meal does for a corporate event or anniversary.
Add a short testimonial for proof, then the discount and a shop-now button — the source also recommends a discount banner at the top of the email.
Keep claims factual and comparable; you are giving shoppers the facts so they can choose, which is what the source argues makes the decision easy.
caveats: Naming competitors invites regulatory and legal risk in some markets — check the rules before comparing by brand name.
Overstated comparison points that customers can verify as false destroy the trust the rest of the flow built.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Email 6: dedicate a whole email to social proof
cards.summary: Use one email purely for testimonials, reviews and media mentions to certify that your brand and products are legitimate.
cards.use_when: Building the trust email in the welcome flow, especially for new or unfamiliar brands.
steps: Fill the email almost entirely with proof: customer testimonials, verified reviews, review counts and ratings, media features. The source argues that even someone who only sees the subject line learns you are confident enough to stand behind your product.

Visualise the rating distribution rather than just citing an average, and label reviews as verified — the source says his team tested that adding 'verified' next to a buyer's name improves conversions.
Put a strong testimonial high in the email so it is visible on open, then add further reviews or a rating graphic.
Include risk-reversal icons (secure payment, fast and free shipping, quality guarantee) and a button at the bottom for readers who are now in a buying mood.
Use this email to answer the 'will this product actually work for me' objection, which is a reason people delay, not a reason they buy immediately.
caveats: The claim that 'verified' next to a review lifts conversion is from the source's own testing, not a published benchmark.
Do not invent or aggregate reviews you cannot verify — unverifiable proof is more damaging than none.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Emails 7-8: close with hard urgency, then a founder's personal note
cards.summary: Finish the flow with a last-chance discount email followed by a plain-text founder message extending the offer and inviting replies.
cards.use_when: Writing the final two emails of a welcome flow, for subscribers who have received the whole sequence without buying.
steps: For email 7, keep it extremely simple: 'last chance' headline, product graphic, clear discount code, extreme urgency copy (the source's example ends the phrase with 'expires forever'), plus social proof icons and one big button.

For email 8, switch to a plain text-based message from the founder: brief intro, reminder that the welcome discount was not used, an extension for one more day, a single shop-now link, and an invitation to reply with questions.

Keep the text email to one action so there is nothing else to do but click; the source argues this simplicity, plus the personal tone, makes text-based founder emails among the highest-performing emails in the sequence.
Use the final email to surface an objection: invite replies and commit to a response time, so anyone stuck on a question can get it answered and then buy.
caveats: Treat the source's claim that text-based personal emails are top performers as his experience, not a universal result.
Only extend the discount if you intend to honour it; repeat extensions train subscribers to wait.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Configure the Clavio trigger and filter so buyers drop out of the flow
cards.summary: Install the welcome flow with a signup trigger and a zero-purchases filter so existing and new buyers don't keep receiving sales emails.
cards.use_when: Setting up or auditing the automation behind your welcome/onboarding email sequence.
steps: Set the trigger to the specific list subscribers join from your popup (the source's example uses subscription to the 'newsletter' list), matching whatever your opt-in form actually adds people to.
Add a flow filter set to 'placed order zero times since starting this flow' so a purchase removes the person from the sequence.
Optionally use 'zero times over all time' if you want to be certain past purchasers never enter the flow; the source notes this as a more conservative option.
Verify the settings in your own platform's current interface, since trigger and filter naming changes between versions and tools.
Recheck the filter whenever you add a new popup, form or list, because a mismatched trigger means the flow silently never fires.
caveats: The described Clavio trigger/filter wording is from the source's setup and may not match the current UI exactly.
If your store sells high-frequency consumables, excluding all past purchasers may be wrong — decide based on whether the flow is genuinely welcome-only.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Give the welcome flow a target conversion rate and a testing loop
cards.summary: Judge and improve the flow against a realistic conversion band, then compound gains with continuous A/B tests.
cards.use_when: Reviewing welcome flow performance or deciding whether to invest in optimisation work.
steps: Set expectations with the source's heuristic: a 10% conversion rate from the welcome flow is his stated gold standard, and 20% would be considered very strong. Do not treat these as guaranteed outcomes.
Accept that even at the gold standard, roughly 90% will not buy — so the flow's other job (priming) must continue through the rest of your email programme.

A/B test the specific elements the source prioritises: subject lines and preview text, the offer structure (e.g. $10 off vs 10% off vs free shipping vs a free item with first order), which products are featured, and text-based versus graphic-based versions of individual emails.
Also test linking to specific products versus linking to collections.
In Clavio, the source prefers running the split with a conditional split because the numbers are easier to read; confirm the current split test tooling in your platform.
Track small gains as compounding: his illustrative example is a store doing 100k/month with 10k from the flow, where a monthly 10% improvement adds ~1k in the first month and compounds thereafter.
caveats: 10% and 20% are the source's stated targets for welcome flows, not universal benchmarks.
The compounding arithmetic is an illustration, not a forecast; actual gains depend on traffic and repeatability.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Reuse winning campaigns as welcome-flow emails to save build time
cards.summary: Monitor your regular campaigns and insert proven ones into the welcome flow with a first-order code added.
cards.use_when: Optimising the welcome flow when you have limited time to write new emails.
steps: Send 3-4 campaigns per week to your list, mostly non-promotional, and watch which angles outperform.

When a campaign clearly crushes, adapt it for the flow: add a line such as 'use code XYZ for XYZ off your first order' and insert it into the sequence, or replace the weakest-performing welcome email.
Use this to avoid building net-new emails while still refreshing the flow's content.

Try campaign angles the source names as working well in welcome flows: myths vs facts in your industry, blog promotion, a specific product spotlight, a testimonial spotlight, a customer story, and product restock announcements.
Keep the flow's core structure (intro, story, bestseller, urgency, proof, last chance) even as individual emails are swapped.
caveats: Check the swapped email still fits the sequence logic and does not repeat what another email already says.
Campaigns written for existing subscribers may assume context a new subscriber lacks; adjust the copy accordingly.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Audit whether you actually have an abandoned cart flow (added-to-cart vs checkout started)
cards.summary: Most stores think they run an abandoned cart flow but the trigger is actually 'checkout started', leaving the much larger added-to-cart audience untracked and unrecovered.
cards.use_when: Auditing or rebuilding your cart/checkout recovery setup, or when your existing 'abandoned cart' flow underperforms despite being live.
steps: Open your ESP (Klaviyo, Mailchimp, etc.) and find the flow labeled 'abandoned cart' or 'abandoned checkout'. Read the actual trigger, not the name.

Distinguish the two events: 'added to cart' fires when someone puts an item in the cart on a product/landing page; 'checkout started' fires only after they click checkout and reach payment. These are one funnel step apart.

Klaviyo (via the Shopify integration) names the checkout-started flow 'abandoned cart' and adds it automatically; the added-to-cart metric is NOT installed by default. So a store can have 'an abandoned cart flow' that only catches far-down-funnel people.
Check Klaviyo > Metrics to see whether 'Added to Cart' exists. If it doesn't, you have no true cart flow and are missing everyone who carted but never reached checkout.

Install the added-to-cart snippet yourself (see the install card), then run a proper added-to-cart flow alongside the checkout-started flow. The source uses the same email content for both, cloned into two flows with different triggers.
caveats: Source is strongly worded that ~90% of brands he audits have this mislabeled flow; that is a presenter observation, not an audited benchmark.
Added-to-cart requires a manual snippet in most setups, so it is more technical than the auto-installed checkout trigger.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Why abandonment is so high and why recovery is high-leverage
cards.summary: 70-85% of carts are abandoned and 26% of abandoners later buy the same item from a competitor, so an unworked cart flow is cash and market share leaking daily.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much to invest in cart/checkout recovery, or building the internal case to prioritize it over other store work.
steps: Reframe the add-to-cart: it is only half the sale. The source argues that in a market with thousands of brands per niche, getting a cart add is not a strong buying signal, so you must keep working the lead.
Lead with the cost of inaction: every day a recovery flow is not live, abandoners are slipping away, and 26% of them reportedly buy the abandoned item from a competitor instead.
Segment abandoners by the reason they left so you can address each: hard objection (they weren't convinced), distraction (kid threw a plate), or 'buy later' intent (waiting for a paycheck).

Note that abandonment is now partly a browsing behavior: 59% of shoppers abandon just from browsing and use the cart as a 'save for later' / bookmark, like an Instagram like. That audience still needs a reminder.

Recognize that more than 30% of shoppers plan to buy later but don't, because they forget, change their mind, or spend the money elsewhere. Automated reminders exist to beat the forgetting and the competitor.
caveats: Statistics in the source (70-85% abandonment, 26% competitor purchase, 59% browsing, 30% plan-to-buy-later) are cited to external sources but presented without method detail; treat as directional.
The 'burning cash' framing is the presenter's opinion about the opportunity cost of an inactive flow.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Design the recovery flow around the customer's decision cycle, not 1-2 emails
cards.summary: A short recovery flow lets customers off the hook before they finish their real multi-day decision cycle, so extend it to a long, spread-out series with branching.
cards.use_when: Planning the length, spacing, and branching of an abandoned cart/checkout email sequence.
steps: Don't stop at one or two emails over a couple of days. The source's target is a flow of roughly 6-8 emails (plus discount/support branches) spread across about 10 days to 1-2 weeks, to match a two-week decision window.

Map why length matters: multiple reminders stop customers forgetting, keep you top of mind, give room to overcome objections, let good content out-position competitors, and give time for a considered decision.

Branch the flow instead of sending one generic series: split by product/collection left behind (for product-specific info and testimonials), and split by prior-purchase status (for whether to offer a discount).
Sequence by job: quick reminders first, then product-specific education and social proof, then a last-chance urgency email, then a buyer/non-buyer split into support vs discount emails.
Keep the added-to-cart and checkout-started flows separate triggers but duplicate the same content so you maintain one set of emails.
caveats: Length and spacing are the source's stated best practice, not a universal rule; every brand differs and the outline is a starting point, not a finished system.
Spacing/timing should be tested for your audience rather than assumed.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Write plain, item-first recovery copy that overcomes objections
cards.summary: Recovery emails should skip fluff and let the dynamic display of the actual abandoned item carry the sale, with copy aimed only at removing uncertainty.
cards.use_when: Writing copy for any abandoned cart or checkout email.
steps: Make the item the number-one feature. Showing the exact product they left behind via dynamic product sections is described as carrying ~80% of the selling, so don't bury it under graphics or long copy.
Keep copy short and to the point; the source states too many words or graphics distract the customer from completing the order.
Focus copy on overcoming objections only: quick points on shipping, product use, customer reviews, and answers to FAQs.
Use second-person, item-specific wording ('your order ships free') rather than generic broadcast copy ('all orders ship free') so it reads as addressed to them.
Answer the questions a hesitant buyer would ask (is it healthy, how long does it last, when will it arrive) with concise facts, not a blog article.
The source's stated purpose of every recovery email is narrow: remind, give the specific info needed to decide, and remove uncertainty about the buying process.
caveats: The '80% carried by the item' figure is the presenter's estimate, not a measured benchmark.
Tone can flex (one example uses playful copy), but the source still keeps product-specific substance central.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Conversion-optimized recovery email layout
cards.summary: Recovery email designs should be short and focused, with a clear headline, an immediately visible CTA, the abandoned item with details, and trust/reassurance elements.
cards.use_when: Designing or reviewing the template/layout for abandoned cart and checkout emails.
steps: Put a clear headline at the top that addresses the cart or states the value proposition (e.g., 'your order ships free').
Place a prominent CTA button very high in the email so the customer can click without scrolling after opening.
Display the abandoned item with all relevant info (name, price, image, link) via dynamic content.
Add supporting sections/icons only if they are useful: shipping info, use of product, reviews.
Stack risk-reversal and trust badges such as free returns, free return shipping, buy-now-pay-later, warranty, and 'talk with an expert'.
Keep the whole design short and sweet — the source repeatedly warns against fancy graphics and long layouts for recovery emails.
caveats: The layout principles are general recommendations; the specific example email (footwear brand) is illustrative, not a guaranteed result.
Fewer elements per email risks needing more emails to cover all objections, which the source accepts as part of the spread-out flow.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Email 1: the 30-minute quick reminder
cards.summary: The first recovery email is a near-pure reminder that shows the abandoned item and gets the warm, distracted customer over the edge.
cards.use_when: Setting up the first message and its send delay in a cart/checkout recovery flow.
steps: Time it short: the source typically sees best results sending email 1 about 30 minutes after abandonment; test 30/45 minutes against 1 hour and 4 hours, with 30-45 minutes usually winning.
Keep the email minimal: 'take another look / we saved your items' plus a 'complete my order' CTA — do not add fancy graphics or extra words that distract.
Show the specific items left behind via the dynamic product section.
Add a short social proof line and risk reversals (e.g., ships in 1-3 days, free swatches) to nudge hesitant buyers.
Purpose is narrow: simply remind the customer what they left behind and let them finish the order.
caveats: The 30-45 minute timing is the presenter's observed best result; validate on your own list.
A 'quick reminder' converts because the customer is still warm — it won't rescue cold or high-objection visitors.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Email 2: second reminder with expanded social proof
cards.summary: The follow-up reminder repeats the simple format but leans harder on social proof and risk reversal to catch people who needed another look or were waiting on a paycheck.
cards.use_when: Writing the second message in a recovery flow, roughly a day after the first.
steps: Reuse email 1's simple structure but add more social proof and risk-reversal than the first send.
Aim it at two groups: those who just needed another reminder, and those who were waiting (paycheck) or comparing competitors.

Include: a quick remark about the product, the dynamic product section, then expanded social proof and risk reversals (e.g., free shipping, free return shipping, buy-now-pay-later, warranty, chat with an expert).
Keep it simple and similar to email 1 rather than inventing a new format.
Let the extra reassurance carry skeptical buyers who weren't ready off a pure reminder.
caveats: Same structure as email 1 means the value depends on the strength of your actual proof and guarantees, not the reminder itself.
Timing is 'about a day later' per the source; adjust to your cycle.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Emails 3-4: split by product for specific info, then specific testimonials
