cards.summary: Branch the flow by the abandoned product to deliver product-specific information and then product-specific testimonials, which the source says convert skeptical customers better than generic proof.
cards.use_when: Building branching logic in the flow and creating product/collection-specific recovery content.
steps: Add a Klaviyo conditional split (or trigger split) based on which SKU/product/collection was left behind; you don't need one branch per product, a few main collections are enough.

Email 3 gives product-specific information and overcomes objections specific to that product — e.g., for a cereal, the nutrition facts (sugar, carbs, protein, fiber, gluten-free) and how it compares. Keep it to the necessary facts, not a long article.
Email 4 follows with testimonials specific to that same product (e.g., jacket abandonment gets jacket reviews, a 4.9/5 star rating with review count, customer quotes).
The source's stated reason: a product-specific testimonial converts higher than a generic website testimonial in abandonments, because it speaks directly to the item and the person.
Continue to include the dynamic product section in both.
Show proof of why this works via A/B tests — the source cites a product-display test that produced ~6x more conversions (1 vs 6 purchases) on a higher-ticket product despite lower opens.
caveats: ~6x conversion on a product-display test is a single cited test example, not a promised outcome.
Targeting like the disease/health claims in the cereal example may carry compliance considerations in some categories.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Email 5: last-chance urgency email
cards.summary: Once the customer has all the info, send a sparse urgency email with a hard deadline to push an impulse order, and reopen shopping to other options.
cards.use_when: Writing the mid-to-late recovery email that precedes the discount/support branch.
steps: Assume the customer now has the info from the product-specific and testimonial emails; the job of this email is to make them act.
Go hard on urgency: a harsh deadline and 'your order is expiring' framing to trigger an impulse finish.
Keep the format light: dynamic product section, urgency copy, social proof/risk-reversal icons, and finish-order CTA.
Add a 'keep shopping' option because some people simply don't want that specific item — by this point (roughly day five / fifth email) showing alternatives can re-capture them.
The source's rationale for delaying the 'keep shopping' suggestion: stay focused on the abandoned item in early emails, then broaden at the last-chance stage.
caveats: Harsh deadlines only work if they are credible; the source stresses being strict on last-chance deadlines, so don't make deadlines you don't honor.
Source preference for delaying 'keep shopping' is an opinion about focus, not a validated rule.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Email 6A: buyer branch — founder support email, no discount
cards.summary: For customers who have bought before, send a personal founder touch offering support and a final chance instead of a discount.
cards.use_when: Configuring the prior-purchase branch in a recovery flow and writing the no-discount variant.
steps: Split the flow on whether the customer has purchased before; send this no-discount variant to past buyers only.

Make it a plain text-style email from the founder (e.g., 'hey it's Mike, co-founder') to stand out from the rest of the sequence — the source notes this personal touch can make it one of the best-performing emails in the flow.

Order the content: personal touch about the abandoned item, then an offer of support ('reply to this email, we'll get back to you within 24 hours'), then a final chance to order with a short urgency window.
Keep it simple: founder voice, last chance, support offer.
Rationale given: past buyers are the segment you least want to discount, and an unaddressed objection could be the reason for abandonment, so offering help may recover the sale without margin loss.
caveats: The claim that this can be the best-performing email is the presenter's opinion based on client experience, not a guarantee.
A 24-hour reply promise requires you can actually meet it; slow support could backfire.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Email 6B: discount opener for first-time buyers, then a discount last-chance
cards.summary: For non-buyers, offer a simple flash discount with urgency, then follow with a discount last-chance email; keep both extremely simple and focused on the offer and the abandoned items.
cards.use_when: Setting up the non-buyer branch of a recovery flow that uses a discount to acquire first-time customers.
steps: Send this branch only to customers who have never purchased, so the discount isn't given away to buyers who would convert without it.

Email 6B: state the flash discount plainly (e.g., $10 off $200+) with urgency, plus the dynamic product section and a finish-my-order CTA. No elaborate graphics — the source says the dynamic section carries the load.
Email 7 (discount last-chance): heavy urgency on the discount ('last chance, 25% off your cart, code expires today'). Keep it minimal and strict on the deadline.

Email 8: for discount recipients who still didn't buy, mirror the founder support email but include the discount — personal founder touch, last chance to claim with the discount for a set window, and an offer of support with a reply-to-email.

Rationale given: first-order discounts are accepted because once someone tries the product they're much more likely to come back, so the discount is an acquisition cost, not a margin giveaway to loyal buyers.
caveats: Whether to discount at all, and the size/value threshold, is the presenter's choice ('depending on how averse you are to discounts'); he typically discounts only non-buyers or non-buyers in the last 60-90 days.
Discount depth and urgency must be honored; non-credible deadlines hurt trust.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Install the added-to-cart metric and trigger in Klaviyo
cards.summary: The added-to-cart event requires a two-step manual install (snippet on site, then verify in Klaviyo) because it is not added automatically like checkout-started.
cards.use_when: Setting up or troubleshooting a true abandoned cart flow that captures add-to-cart abandoners.
steps: Check Klaviyo > Metrics. If 'Added to Cart' is missing, you need to install it. Verify against Klaviyo's current help doc since the interface changes.
On the Shopify store, if your theme has custom liquid blocks and a section you can edit, go to the homepage/product section and paste the provided snippet in a custom liquid block, then Save.

If you don't have an editable custom liquid block, edit theme code instead: insert the snippet under the body tag, wrapped with an 'if product' condition above and 'endif' below, per the guide, then Save.
Test the snippet: append a UTM (email=whatever@youwant.com) to your store URL, visit the store, and add an item to the cart.
In Klaviyo, search the email from the UTM and open the profile's activity feed; confirm an 'Added to Cart' event appears and the metric now exists.

Set the flow trigger to 'Added to Cart' with filters: checkout started 0 times (so checkout abandoners route to the checkout flow instead), placed order 0 times, and not in this flow in the last 30 days. For the checkout-started flow, use the same filters minus the checkout exclusion.
caveats: Klaviyo's snippet and metric setup can change; verify against Klaviyo's current documentation rather than relying on a saved snippet.
Editing theme code incorrectly can break the store; the source says to contact Klaviyo support to get the correct dynamic sections if you get stuck.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Set up dynamic abandoned-item content (careful: cart and checkout variables differ)
cards.summary: Dynamic product sections are the core of recovery emails, but the added-to-cart and checkout-started variables are different, so content built for one won't work in the other.
cards.use_when: Building the item-display block in recovery emails and troubleshooting broken/altered images or links.
steps: For added-to-cart dynamic content, use a split block: image on the left using the event image URL variable, and text on the right with item name and price variables. Point the checkout/cart link to your cart page (e.g., yoursite.com/cart) if you have one, otherwise Klaviyo's link sends them to the item they viewed.
For checkout-started, the dynamic content is built as a table block that must be set to dynamic and customized, and it exposes more data because checkout passes more information from Shopify.
Always preview with Klaviyo's preview feature to confirm the dynamic content loads before the flow goes live.
Do not copy checkout dynamic content into the cart flow (or vice versa) — the triggers feed different information, so the variables won't map correctly.
If the dynamic sections won't work, ask Klaviyo support (chat) for the correct variables for your trigger.
caveats: Exact variable names and block options can change in Klaviyo; confirm current behavior in the app or with support.
Source says ideally you have a cart page; without one, the fallback link sends people to a single item, which is a weaker recovery experience.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Set up A/B tests inside the flow rather than on the email
cards.summary: The source prefers a conditional random-sample split within the Klaviyo flow over Klaviyo's built-in email test, because numbers are visible in the flow at a glance.
cards.use_when: Running experiments on recovery emails and wanting quick visibility into results.
steps: Add a conditional split to the flow and create a random sample so branches split the audience evenly.
Copy and paste the prior email into one branch as the variant.
Reconnect the flow so both branches rejoin the main path afterward.

Compare against Klaviyo's native 'create a test' option on the email itself; the source finds that harder to read because you must click into the email to see the data, whereas the flow method shows the numbers at a glance.
Use the flow-level view to decide winners and iterate.
caveats: The preference for flow-level splits is the presenter's workflow opinion, not an accuracy claim; both can be valid.
Random-sample sizing and statistical significance are not covered here — don't over-read small test results.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Small A/B tests can compound into large revenue gains
cards.summary: The source argues small, iterative A/B tests on recovery emails (subject lines, format, layout) can each add meaningful revenue that compounds, so the outline is only a starting point.
cards.use_when: Planning an ongoing optimization cadence for cart/checkout flows after initial launch.
steps: Treat the provided email outline as a starting point, not a finished system; every brand needs its own optimizations.
Test small iterations, because the source says small changes can make or break the success of abandonment flows.

Prioritize tests the source ran: subject line (one cited test tripled placed-order rate and roughly doubled click rate on the same volume), long-form vs short-form email (short-form reportedly better), content alignment (center vs left, cited at ~$5K extra in a month), product display (cited at ~6x conversions), text-based layout (cited at ~40% conversion boost), and email content (cited at ~2x conversions).
Do the math on compounding: the source frames repeated 25-50% revenue boosts as compounding over time, using a Warren Buffett analogy.
Run tests continuously rather than as one-offs, and pick one variable per test to keep results readable.
caveats: All the percentage examples are the source's reported client test results, not guaranteed outcomes; do not treat them as benchmarks.
The 25-50% revenue-boost range is the presenter's characterization of small-test upside; actual lift depends on your baseline and traffic.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Separate cart and checkout flows to avoid double-messaging
cards.summary: Because added-to-cart and checkout-started are different funnel events, you need two flows with exclusion filters so people aren't messaged twice or dropped from the wrong sequence.
cards.use_when: Configuring the triggers and filters of both recovery flows in Klaviyo.
steps: Build two flows: one triggered by 'Added to Cart', one triggered by 'Checkout Started'. Duplicate the same content into both so you maintain one set of emails.

On the added-to-cart flow, add filters: 'Checkout Started = 0 times since starting this flow' (so anyone who moves to checkout exits and enters the checkout flow instead), 'Placed Order = 0 times since starting this flow', and 'has not been in this flow in the last 30 days'.

On the checkout-started flow, use the same 'Placed Order = 0 times since starting this flow' and 'not in this flow in the last 30 days' filters, without the checkout exclusion (it's the trigger itself).
Confirm both flows fire correctly and that a person who adds to cart then proceeds to checkout doesn't receive both sequences simultaneously.
caveats: The 'last 30 days' re-entry window is the source's reset choice; adjust to your purchase frequency.
Exclusion logic depends on trigger direction; verify in Klaviyo that your filters behave as intended.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Adapt to the 2024 more-competitive buyer who does due diligence
cards.summary: With more stores and a warier, thinner-walleted buyer who shops around, recovery messaging must overcome distrust and comparison shopping, not just remind.
cards.use_when: Setting the tone and content strategy of recovery and lifecycle messaging in a crowded niche.
steps: Assume the buyer has been burned online before (late shipping, not just non-delivery), so proactively answer logistics and quality questions: when will it arrive, will it arrive intact, what do reviews say, how long does it last.
Assume the buyer is comparing you against many other brands in the same niche and may have added competitors' items to their cart too; your objection handling and content quality decide the win.
Lead with risk reversal and specifics (shipping time, returns, warranty, reviews) rather than broad claims.
Recognize shopping is entertainment for many buyers and carting is a bookmarking behavior, so reminders — not pressure — are often what's needed.
Account for tighter budgets versus the stimulus-era spend; a discount targeted only at non-buyers can help first-time acquisition.
caveats: This 2024 framing is the presenter's market read; timing-specific claims may age.
Not every niche has thousands of brands or scam-scarred buyers — calibrate the level of proof to your category.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Build a six-email post-purchase flow with timed emotional beats
cards.summary: Six-email post-purchase sequence timed to the buying window, mixing founder gratitude, upsell, and product education to lift repeat purchases without heavy discounting.
cards.use_when: Setting up or rebuilding the post-purchase email flow for your store (replenishment/retention), especially if you currently only send an order confirmation and shipping notice.
steps: Set the trigger to 'order placed' with no filter so every buyer enters.

Email 1 at 0 minutes: a plain, text-based thank-you from the founder. Split by purchase count (1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th+) and change the wording slightly each time (e.g., 'you're almost a VIP' for repeat buyers). Include four things: sincere thanks, mission reminder, support offer, and a P.S. inviting an add-on to the order.
Email 2 at ~24 hours: 'want to add more.' Send a general cross-sell of best sellers or split by product/category for curated recommendations tied to what they bought.
Email 3 at ~3 days: a 'get excited, your order is being handled' message. You don't need a delivery trigger — estimate timing and link products at the bottom.

Email 4 at ~6 days: 'how to get the most out of your product.' Split by what they ordered and give usage tips; add a recommended-product section to pair complementary items. This also reduces returns from misuse.
Email 5 at ~7 days: ask them to follow one social platform (pick a single one, not several).
Email 6 at ~1-2 weeks: a founder check-in asking how the order went, offering support, and optionally a review or repurchase prompt.
After launch, analyze numbers and add or remove emails over time — this is a starting point, not a fixed template.
caveats: Timing past the first day is estimated, not triggered by real delivery data.
The presenter's claimed $48,000 in 30 days is a single case example, not an expected result.
Higher-AOV products may see more buyer's remorse, so the reassurance emails matter more.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Exploit the 3-hour post-purchase buyer window
cards.summary: New buyers are far more likely to buy again within hours of ordering, so the first post-purchase email should arrive immediately with an add-on invitation.
cards.use_when: Designing the very first post-purchase email or deciding how aggressive to be with an immediate upsell after checkout.
steps: Send the first post-purchase email within minutes (the presenter's flow uses 0 minutes) rather than waiting a day.
Use the founder gratitude email as the vehicle for the add-on P.S. — it reads genuine rather than pushy, so an add-on invite feels low-pressure.
Reference the extra item the customer may have removed from their cart during checkout; a simple 'you can still add to your order' line is often enough to convert.
Split the message by purchase count so repeat buyers get wording that acknowledges their loyalty, which makes the same add-on ask feel more personal.
Track the placed-order rate of this single email; the presenter reports it converts unusually well for a plain text message.
caveats: The 27% figure for repurchase within the first three hours is cited as third-party research — treat it as directional, not a guaranteed lift for your store.
The presenter notes higher-AOV products carry more buyer's remorse, so push the gratitude/reassurance elements harder than the upsell.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Use founder-voice emails to build small-brand trust after purchase
cards.summary: Plain text founder emails outperform designed ones for post-purchase because they read as genuine and reinforce the 'buy from people' feeling.
cards.use_when: Writing the copy and format for post-purchase gratitude and check-in emails where you want authenticity over polish.
steps: Write from the founder personally, using a plain text format with no heavy graphics — even if the customer doesn't buy, the email reads as sincere.
Follow a fixed four-part order: (1) sincere thanks, (2) remind them of the brand mission, (3) offer support if they have questions, (4) encourage a repeat purchase or add-on.
Use subject lines that reflect purchase count: 'your order means the world' (first), 'thank you again' (second), 'third time's a charm' (third), VIP framing (fourth).

For the later check-in, write longer: reference the customer by name, the date of purchase, what results they should expect by now, cite a social-proof number (e.g., '150,000 others'), then offer the chance to shop and to reach out for support.
Expect this check-in to generate useful qualitative feedback because it reads as a personal follow-up.
caveats: The social-proof number must be real — do not invent customer counts or results.
Persona varies: some brands use the actual founder, others a VP or named team member. Keep the voice consistent with who is really writing.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Use product-education emails to cut returns and boost repeat orders
cards.summary: Teaching customers how to use what they bought improves their results, which reduces returns and makes them more likely to buy again.
cards.use_when: Writing post-purchase education emails (email 4 in the flow) or building usage guides for products with a learning curve.
steps: Split by what the customer ordered and give tips specific to that product, not generic advice.
Include simple steps to use the product plus tips and tricks — this improves their chance of getting good results, which they will otherwise blame the brand for missing.
Add a recommended-product section that shows how pairing with another product improves results — a subtle cross-sell framed as a benefit, not an ask.
Use subject lines like 'how to get the most,' 'tips and tricks,' or '[Product] 101' to set the expectation of value rather than a sale.
Reuse your strongest campaign content here: if a research or proof email performed well in campaigns, add it to the flow to reaffirm the purchase.
caveats: The presenter notes the recommended-product section is the sales element — keep the email's primary focus on value so it doesn't read as a hard sell.
Also cited as a way to 'stay fresh' by rotating successful campaign emails into flows over time.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Set post-purchase email frequency to 3-4 sends per week
cards.summary: The presenter's testing across many frequencies found 3-4 campaigns per week produced the highest revenue with the lowest unsubscribes.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many campaign emails (not flows) to send per week to your list.
steps: Choose a starting cadence of 3-4 campaigns per week — the presenter reports this outperformed both 1-2 per week and 5-7 per week on revenue and unsubscribes.
Avoid 1-2 per week: the presenter says people see ~70 ecommerce brands per day (490 per week), so a weekly send gets forgotten and breaks the habit of opening your emails.
Avoid 5-7 per week: while revenue rises, it plateaus, unsubscribes and complaints climb, and each message's impact is diluted.
Keep every email's weight equal by spreading 3-4 sends across the week rather than clustering.
Ramp gradually, as in the case where a client went from 2x to 4x per week and open rates went from under 50% to 61%.
caveats: These are the presenter's own A/B-tested findings, not a universal rule your list will match — test on your own audience.
The presenter warns that frequency is not the real lever: if you only send sales emails, even 1 per week will annoy your list.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Send non-discount content to stay top-of-mind and win repeat purchases
cards.summary: Content that educates and entertains keeps your brand in customers' minds without discounts, priming them to buy when a need arises.
cards.use_when: Planning campaign content for a list you don't want to burn with constant promos, or when trying to protect margins.
steps: Shift campaign content toward value: tips and tricks, founder messages, brand stories, ingredient or product explanations, and 'our favorites' picks.
Avoid relying on discount, buy-or-die, and 'gone forever' style emails — the presenter argues these read as needy and increase sales resistance.
Aim for a healthy balance of product education and product promotion in every campaign calendar.
Think of it as the 'top-of-mind effect': if you appear every other day, when a customer has a random need they think of you first.
Use content to create the 'right place, right time' effect — more sends means more chances a customer happens to be in a buying mood.
caveats: The point is to build a fan base and repeat purchases over time, not immediate sales on every send.
The presenter frames this as protection against rising ad costs and shrinking margins — situational, not a promise.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Structure every email around one micro-topic and one takeaway
cards.summary: Each email should cover one small digestible idea using a micro-topic, so the recipient remembers it in the few seconds they open.
cards.use_when: Choosing what each campaign email should say, or when you feel you have 'nothing to send.'
steps: Start from a large macro topic in your industry, product, or niche (e.g., for supplements: building muscle, burning fat, dieting, overall health).
Break each macro topic into many micro-topics — e.g., 'best foods for dieting,' 'how to lower your appetite naturally,' 'best supplements to support dieting,' 'ingredient highlight.'
Write one email per micro-topic and ask: 'What is the one thing I want the customer to know after reading this?'
Use the problem-process-solution framework to structure it: educate on a problem, then the process, then position your product as the solution.
Keep the takeaway to a single point — the presenter argues covering 6 topics means the customer remembers none, while one topic is remembered.
caveats: The 3-5 second open window is the presenter's framing for why short, single-topic emails work.
Micro-topics should still link back to a product benefit so education and positioning work in tandem.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Use the problem-process-solution framework to position your product
cards.summary: Educating on a problem and a process primes the reader so that positioning your product as the solution lands naturally as a purchase.
cards.use_when: Writing campaign emails where you want to sell without an explicit discount, or when introducing a product to skeptical buyers.
steps: Educate on the problem first: 'why most people fail at XYZ' or 'why most solutions in this industry are bad.'
Educate on the process: 'how to do XYZ,' 'how to overcome XYZ,' or 'the history / old way of XYZ.'
Present the solution by positioning your product as the answer, then reinforce with how and why it works and how to use it.
Answer the questions your customer is actually asking at each stage so their natural path leads toward the solution (your product).
Use this to earn trust points the buyer needs before making a decision, and to remove friction for the due-diligence they do before buying.
caveats: The presenter stresses subtly positioning the product — the education must be genuinely useful, not a disguised sales pitch.
The framework assumes you can articulate a real problem your product solves.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Generate unlimited micro-topics with a ChatGPT prompt
cards.summary: A single well-structured prompt can produce ~100 micro-topic ideas, enough for a year of non-discount campaign emails.
cards.use_when: Building or refreshing your campaign calendar when you need many content ideas quickly.
steps: Define your macro topics first (the big themes in your niche or product), then ask ChatGPT to generate micro-topics under each.
Use a prompt that requests ~100 micro-topic ideas tied to your product and industry, which the presenter says can cover a year of non-discount campaigns.
Review the output and select topics you can genuinely educate on — the presenter notes the best topics come naturally, and AI just gives starting points.
Recycle and refresh topics over time rather than discarding them, since the calendar is meant to keep evolving.
Test the resulting topics against your own knowledge of the niche before sending — AI output is a draft, not final copy.
caveats: The presenter emphasizes AI is 'not perfect' and the strongest ideas come from your own understanding of the market.
The presenter notes the specific prompt and results are available in the free doc — verify the current interface of ChatGPT, which changes.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Position email as warm-lead content between cold paid ads and repeat purchases
cards.summary: Email captures attention after paid ads acquire it, then uses cheap content to build trust and drive repeat purchases.
cards.use_when: Deciding which email touchpoints to fund and how email fits with your paid acquisition channels.
steps: Use paid ads (Meta, Google, etc.) for the initial acquisition — getting cold traffic to your site and gaining their attention.
Use email for the later stages: nurture the lead, hold their attention, and drive repeat purchases once they've bought.
Rely on email over paid ads for repeat content because email is cheaper, you own the list, and it's predictable to scale.
Use a pop-up to convert site visitors into subscribers, and plan for a known percentage of subscribers to purchase over time.
Treat email as 'paid ads to people who already know, like, and trust you' — same function of driving traffic, far lower cost.
caveats: The presenter stresses email needs paid ads to grow the list — this is not an argument against paid ads.
Ownership of your list is a key advantage: no third-party platform can shut down your email channel.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Understand the trust threshold before asking for a purchase
cards.summary: Customers need multiple exposures to your brand before they trust you enough to buy, so email content exists to accumulate those exposures.
cards.use_when: Setting expectations for email campaign performance with skeptical first-time buyers, or diagnosing low conversion from cold traffic.
steps: Assume most customers have been scammed online and do due diligence before buying — treat trust as the primary barrier, not price.
Recognize the 'trust threshold': the point where a customer trusts you enough to make a purchase (even if they don't need the product yet).
Deliver repeated exposures across multiple channels so that when a customer compares you with a competitor, you're the brand they've seen more often and gotten value from.
Use email as the cheap, repeatable channel to stack those exposures after the first paid touchpoint.
Expect that the customer who has seen you many times and gotten value will choose you over the brand they've only seen three times via paid ads.
caveats: The presenter's comparison (brand seen 8 times across channels vs. 3 times via ads) is a heuristic illustration, not a study result.
The trust threshold isn't measurable in a single number — the presenter describes it as an accumulation over time.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Run A/B tests on flows using the flow-level split, not the email-level test
cards.summary: The presenter recommends testing flow emails by adding a conditional split in the flow builder so results are visible without clicking into the email.
cards.use_when: Setting up an A/B test on an email inside a Klaviyo flow and choosing how to build the test.
steps: Add a conditional split to your flow and create a random sample to divide recipients between the two versions.
Copy and paste the original email, edit the copy or design for the variant, then reconnect the flow so both paths continue to the next step.
Use this method rather than the email-level 'create a test' button.
Check results by opening the flow itself — the presenter prefers this because you can see the numbers right when you open the flow without clicking into the individual email.
Review the split's overview numbers to decide which variant to keep.
caveats: This is a tool workflow in Klaviyo; the exact interface and button labels may have changed — verify in your current version.
The presenter prefers this method for visibility and flexibility, but notes it's an opinion, not the only correct approach.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Add winning campaign emails into your post-purchase flow
cards.summary: Reuse campaign emails that performed well by inserting them into flows, so proof and education content reinforces the purchase.
cards.use_when: Refreshing an existing post-purchase flow, or when you have a strong campaign email (e.g., a research/proof study) you want more mileage from.
steps: Identify campaign emails with strong performance — the presenter cites research-study or clinical-proof style emails as examples.
Add that email into the post-purchase flow at a point where it reaffirms the purchase (e.g., after the product arrives).
Frame it as reinforcing their decision — 'this is clinically proven' — rather than as a new pitch.
Keep testing by adding and subtracting emails over time rather than setting the flow and forgetting it.
Rotate content so customers in the flow don't see the same messages repeatedly.
caveats: Only reuse emails that actually performed well; a weak campaign email won't improve in the flow.
Any proof claims must be real and compliant — do not fabricate clinical or research claims.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Use email frequency to build habitual opens and the exposure effect
cards.summary: Frequent, consistent sends create a habit of opening and leverage familiarity to build loyalty and better open rates.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to send more or less often, or when open rates are declining from infrequent sends.
steps: Send frequently enough (the presenter's tested sweet spot: 3-4 per week) that customers expect and look out for your emails.
Make each email nice to look at and genuinely valuable, so each open delivers a small dopamine hit and they open the next one.
Reinforce the loop: content, engagement, familiarity, loyalty — each cycle strengthens the relationship.
Leverage the exposure effect — people learn to like what becomes familiar, so consistent good content turns subscribers into fans.
Expect open rates from infrequent sending to fall, not rise, because the habit of opening is broken.
caveats: The case mentioned — a client ramping from 2x to 4x per week saw open rates go from high 40s to 61% — is one example and partly reflects better content.
The exposure effect is the presenter's framing; it only works if the content genuinely delivers value.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: One-Benefit Email Framework
cards.summary: Build repeatable campaigns around a single product benefit so the takeaway sticks in three seconds.
cards.use_when: Planning your monthly email calendar and needing evergreen campaign angles for each product in the store.
steps: List 10+ distinct benefits per product, one benefit per email.
Spread them out at roughly two per month (five months of coverage).
State only one benefit per send; naming six benefits makes customers remember none.
Lead with the benefit in the headline and keep the email visually simple, as in the 'banish festive fogginess' and Seed '61% of people experience digestive discomfort' examples.
Reuse these campaigns repeatedly; repetition is how customers remember.
caveats: The 'three-second read' and two-per-month cadence are the source's heuristics, not tested benchmarks.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: One-Feature Email: Selling Ingredient and Spec Differentiation
cards.summary: Feature a single ingredient, material or spec to distinguish a product that otherwise sounds identical to competitors.
cards.use_when: Writing product emails when every competitor claims the same benefit (e.g. protein powder that all says 'gain muscle').
steps: Write out every material or ingredient in the product; each can anchor its own email.
Pick one feature per email rather than a benefits-only pitch — features like 'pre-digestive enzyme' or an AI capability are things people actively want to know.
Assume the customer does not know what you consider common sense (David Ogilvy's point); spell the feature out.
Show examples like 'tamanu oil' or 'what we mean by instantised creatine' — one specific item per email, not a list of five.
For non-consumables, substitute the material or construction detail (e.g. clothing fabric composition).
caveats: The source pushes back on 'benefits not features' as an oversimplification; both angles have a place.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Single-FAQ Email to Kill Objections
cards.summary: Answer one frequently asked customer question per email to overcome objections and quietly position the product.
cards.use_when: Mining support tickets and reviews for purchase objections to turn into campaign content.
steps: Gather real questions from your support team and product reviews.
Pick ONE question per email; a long FAQ dump gets ignored.

Answer directly, then bridge into why your product solves it — e.g. 'how long until creatine works' answered with a timeframe and a shop link, or 'does whitening hurt teeth' answered with the damage-free alternative.
Think like an alien who just discovered your product: what would they ask?
Note that what's obvious to you as the industry expert is not obvious to the buyer.
caveats: Timeframe numbers in examples are brand-specific; use your own verified claims.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: 'What's Inside' Email for Bundles and Consumables
cards.summary: Unpack everything included with an order in a skimmable list to remove pre-purchase uncertainty.
cards.use_when: Selling bundles, kits or consumable products where buyers don't know exactly what they'll receive.
steps: List every component of the bundle or product in a skimmable list format.
Include free extras customers don't know about (installation guides, video guides, replacement parts) — brands often give these away without ever telling buyers.
For consumables, list out everything in the food, beverage or supplement so buyers know what's entering their body.
Use examples like an AG1-style unboxing of the welcome kit, or a 'seven super ingredients' list that keeps each item brief.
Spread this across multiple emails rather than cramming everything into one.
caveats: Keep each item short; the goal is scannability, not depth.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: How-It's-Made and How-To-Use Emails
cards.summary: Turn your production process or usage instructions into a story-driven email that signals quality and removes complexity objections.
cards.use_when: Reducing hesitation on a product that seems complicated, or building brand story for a physical product.
steps: For 'how it's made': list every step from material gathering through factory, warehouse and shipment, or spotlight a single stage (e.g. 'we run every ingredient through three filters').
Present the process with clear graphics or a simple A-to-Z sequence — a beer-style 'malt, mash, boil, ferment, bottle, age' layout works well.
For 'how to use': write step-by-step instructions by actually using the product yourself and recording what you do.
If the product is simple to use, reframe as 'how to get the most out of X' or 'how to style X' instead.
Push the usage content into your post-purchase flow too; it fits both pre- and post-buy.
caveats: Don't assume the customer knows your process even if all your competitors do the same thing — saying it still signals quality.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Back-in-Stock Email Leveraging Popularity and Urgency
cards.summary: Use the back-in-stock angle to combine popularity proof with scarcity, even for products that never truly sold out.
cards.use_when: New inventory arrives, or you want a high-urgency campaign angle on restocked or returned items.
steps: Track when products or collections come back into stock.
Draft a full feature email around the return — e.g. 'the Spidey Suds is back', 'the full glass is back in a new style'.
Frame with limited-time language ('only here for a limited time') to add urgency.
If a product didn't actually go out of stock, you can still use the restock angle when you receive new inventory.
Buying signals to lean on: something went out of stock, so it's popular, and it may go out again.
caveats: This is an attention angle, not a factual emergency; don't fabricate sell-outs you didn't have.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Trending Product Email — Frame Future, Not Past
cards.summary: Promote best-performing products by framing them as upcoming trends rather than last season's favorites.
cards.use_when: Highlighting top sellers or building seasonal collection emails on your store.
steps: Pick the product or collection performing well and feature it.
Frame as future trending ('these have been heating up; hottest trend for summer 2024') rather than past trending ('what was popular last summer').
Create curated product selections linking to a collection page in Shopify-type platforms to lift conversions on the click-through.
Lean into seasons whenever possible — seasonal selling performs especially well.
Send these frequently; the source says you can't send too many.
caveats: 'Future beats past trending' is the source's observed pattern, not a proven conversion benchmark.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Reviews and Testimonials Email for Social Proof
cards.summary: Feature a small number of customer reviews or social comments to prove legitimacy and trigger herd behavior.
cards.use_when: Building trust for a newer brand or nudging hesitant subscribers with peer proof.
steps: Pull real reviews from your product pages and site.
Use a maximum of two long reviews, or a handful of short ones — as in the Greens example using dated social-media comments.
Include social media comments where possible; recent dated comments boost credibility.
Keep the email short and simple, essentially just quotes plus a CTA.
Testimonials do two jobs: prove you're a legit brand that delivers, and show others already bought and are happy.
caveats: Only use real testimonials; the source emphasizes authenticity.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Us vs Them Comparison Email
cards.summary: Compare your product against competitors in a clear table to help buyers choose you without begging for the sale.
cards.use_when: Competitive categories where buyers are weighing alternatives before purchase.
steps: Build a simple comparison table with digestible points — 'why we shine' or 'this product vs that product'.
Show facts; do not beg for the purchase or lose frame, which increases sales resistance.
Keep it skimmable so the customer can instantly see the differentiators.
End with a clear CTA like 'shop now' and product link.
Angle can also be used for product-vs-product within your own line.
caveats: Keep claims accurate and verifiable; a table format doesn't excuse unsubstantiated comparisons.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Myth vs Fact Email
cards.summary: Bust common industry misconceptions to overcome objections with an engaging, curiosity-driven premise.
cards.use_when: Your niche has persistent misinformation (sunscreen, supplements, etc.) that blocks purchases.
steps: Identify common misconceptions buyers hold about your product category.
Structure emails as 'myth: X / fact: Y', either one myth per email or rapid-fire several.
Use an intriguing headline, as in the sunscreen myth-busting example with multiple 'myth busted' sections.
Keep copy punchy — customers won't read long explanations.
Consider a series of myth emails; the source says series have worked well historically.
caveats: Long myth-vs-fact copy underperforms; condense and make it scannable.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Blog Promo Email That Sells the Click
cards.summary: Use a sneak peek to drive traffic to a blog post, warming subscribers and enabling soft-sell product placement.
cards.use_when: You have blog content and want engagement that moves people down the funnel without a hard pitch.
steps: Use an existing blog post with an intriguing headline.
Give only a sneak peek — withhold enough that clicking is worthwhile; do not dump the whole article into the email.
Sell the click aggressively via prominent buttons and a 'read more' / 'get the scoop' CTA.
Place product recommendations further down in the email after the article context.
Rationale: a subscriber clicking a blog is already committing to browsing, making later site shopping more likely; blog emails read as soft-sell and still drive sales.
caveats: The source criticizes its own examples for giving too much info; reduce to preserve click incentive.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Research Study Highlight Email
cards.summary: Cite a published study related to your niche to position the brand as an industry leader and lateral proof.
cards.use_when: Looking for high-credibility campaign content that your list rarely sees.
steps: Search Google Scholar for your industry niche; also possible via ChatGPT with a prompt.
Spend no more than a few minutes; read the abstract to judge applicability.
Pick a study that either busts a myth or supports an ingredient/material you use.
Connect it to your brand even if it's not a study of your own product — e.g. 'new study reveals the link between soft gums and inflammation', then show your product solves soft gums.
Lay out the study with a clear breakdown and a learn-more CTA.
caveats: The source says this shouldn't take more than a couple minutes to find a decent one.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Holiday Email Using Obscure Holidays
cards.summary: Anchor fun emails to unusual daily holidays connected to your niche rather than only major holidays.
cards.use_when: Filling campaign calendar gaps and adding engagement without overt promotion.
steps: Find random holidays; use sites like checkiday.com, blank calendar pages, or ChatGPT.
Pick one that connects to a product or niche (e.g. National Irish Coffee Day used by Jameson, National Hiking Day used by AllTrails).
Build a light, fun email around it with a natural product tie-in.
You can still send standard major-holiday emails; these add incremental volume and engagement.
caveats: Keep the tie-in plausible; a forced holiday-to-product link can feel gimmicky.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: 15 Rapid-Fire Campaign Angenres for Ecommerce Lists
cards.summary: A catalog of niche-agnostic email angles you can bolt onto a calendar when ideas run dry.
cards.use_when: When building monthly calendars and needing more micro-topic campaign angles across the store.
steps: Progress update: share company milestones and achievements — people like being part of a growing brand.
Customer transformation and before/after: real before-and-after narratives of product impact.
Puzzles and riddles: brain teasers related to your industry as a fun break.
Note from the founder: personal CEO message with news or insights.
Gift guide: curated recommendations (e.g. wedding season, summer).
Treat yourself: self-care excuse to buy.
Media publication: coverage in news or Shark Tank and similar.
Behind the scenes: warehouse/office footage or product stories.
Tips and tricks: valuable quick advice.
UGC: tagged customer photos, reviews and influencer content.
Sneak peeks: reward subscribers with early looks.
Flashback/Throwback: nostalgic content and past milestones.
Staff picks: bestsellers framed as individual staff favorites.
Brand values: showcase what the brand stands for.
caveats: Not one campaign type; use selectively against your list's appetite.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Building a Monthly Campaign Calendar
cards.summary: Sequence anchor dates, supplementary sends and micro-topic campaigns into a structured monthly calendar.
cards.use_when: Turning a library of campaign ideas into an actual send schedule for your store.
steps: Step 1: Determine important dates — holidays, product launches, sale dates — and insert them into the calendar first so everything else builds around them.
Step 2: Add supplementary emails around those anchors — reminders for sales, teasers for launches.
Step 3: Fill remaining gaps with micro-topic campaigns (one-benefit, one-feature, FAQ, etc.).
Aim for three to four campaigns per week, each on a micro-topic.
Example structure: a St Patrick's Day 20%-off sale, a new product drop, supplementary emails around each, and micro-topics filling the rest.
caveats: The three-to-four-per-week cadence is the source's heuristic from agency work; adjust to list health.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Segmentation: Dynamic Segments vs Static Lists
cards.summary: Understand segments as dynamic, self-updating subsets so you can send the right content to the right slice.
cards.use_when: Designing list architecture in Klaviyo or similar before building campaigns and flows.
steps: Distinguish lists (static, flat collections of people) from segments (dynamic, updating in real time based on criteria).
In Klaviyo, lists and segments live under the same area but segments are the dynamic ones.
Start with basics: email open behavior, click behavior, frequency.
Intermediate: recent store activity like abandoned cart, recent purchase.
Advanced: flow-specific engagement or product-category interest.
Before hypersegmenting (e.g. by favorite color), weigh the tradeoff — the source argues three to four broad campaigns to 50,000 will beat one to two narrow campaigns to 10,000 '99 times out of 100'.
caveats: That ratio is the source's claimed experience, not a measured guarantee; they do say there's a time and place for segmentation.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Email Engagement Segments for Deliverability
cards.summary: Build the core engaged/unengaged suppression sets that protect inbox placement and control sending costs.
cards.use_when: Setting up your base sending architecture so campaigns never blast the full list.
steps: Create an X-day engaged segment — 'opened an email at least once in last 60 days OR clicked in last 60 days' (the OR guards against missed open tracking).
Add 'has not bounced an email ever' to exclude dead/fake addresses.
Decide the X window: start at 30 days if new to segmentation, then expand to 60, 90, 120 as open rates climb.
Target at least 40% opens before expanding; when opens hit ~50%, open the window to the next tier and repeat.
Create an unengaged members segment (subscribed, opened at least once historically, but no open/click in ~90 days) and email them around once per month — or suppress entirely.
Never send general campaigns to the whole list except major moments like Black Friday, because non-openers damage deliverability with inbox providers.
caveats: The step-ladder and 40-50% thresholds are the source's recommendations, not universal benchmarks.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Store-Engagement Segments to Find Funnel Leaks
cards.summary: Segment by on-site behavior to spot where buyers drop off and target them directly.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing conversion loss and building targeted campaigns beyond flows.
steps: Viewed a product at least once in past 30 days but no purchase = interested customers.
Added to cart or started checkout in past 30 days but no purchase = high likelihood to purchase; engage these hard.
Placed an order = recent buyers.
Placed five-plus orders = VIP customers.
Viewed at least three products without purchasing = window shoppers.
Use these to track where people are lost — e.g. lots of product views but few add-to-carts signals a product-page problem.
Targeted campaigns (new colorway, special discount) can be sent only to product-category-interested segments without bothering the rest of the list.
caveats: Mostly used alongside flows; campaigns are added on top, not instead.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: High Potential Purchaser Segment
cards.summary: Create a segment of recent site-active non-buyers to send extra nudges on top of the engaged list.
cards.use_when: Running an extra sale or push to people who are actively shopping but haven't purchased.
steps: Definition: subscribed AND placed zero orders in past 30 days AND (active on site OR viewed product OR added to cart OR started checkout in past 30 days).
Use OR conditions between the activity triggers as a safety net for missed event tracking.
Send these people one to two extra emails per month on top of your engaged list sends — a targeted sale or extra push.
Reserve certain offers for this segment rather than the whole list so you don't discount for everyone.
caveats: Some conditions overlap intentionally; the source keeps them to guard against broken triggers.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: VIP Segment Built on Purchase Count
cards.summary: Define VIPs by order count rather than spend to make milestones predictable and promotable.
cards.use_when: Designing a loyalty/VIP segment and corresponding email cadence.
steps: Base definition: subscribed AND placed an order at least five times all-time.
Prefer purchase count over total spend because spend thresholds are harder to predict — someone at $900 toward $1,000 might buy a $20 item and miss the goal, causing frustration.
With a count-based threshold, after the fourth purchase you can notify them they're one order from VIP and a free gift.
Send VIPs at most one extra email per month on top of the engaged list.
Run a welcome flow for anyone entering the segment — thank them and give exclusive content or a generous offer.
Send a VIP-only offer at least once a quarter.
caveats: Five orders is the source's illustrative threshold; use one that fits your purchase frequency.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Winback and Unengaged: Distinguishing Two Recovery Segments
cards.summary: Keep email-unengaged and past-customer winback segments separate because they solve different problems.
cards.use_when: Building reactivation and repurchase campaigns for your list.
steps: Unengaged members = email-side: subscribed and once engaged but no open/click in ~90 days; email roughly monthly with a comeback offer.
Winback potential customers = purchase-side: past buyers who haven't purchased in a while; also email ~one extra per month on top of engaged sends.
Set the winback window to the store's typical inter-purchase interval — hot tubs might be years, supplements much shorter.
Regular campaigns to the engaged list can also be sent to the unengaged once a month as a low-effort recovery attempt.
Don't send every campaign to unengaged people; it drags down open rates and sender reputation.
caveats: The 90-day threshold isn't sacred; 120 days is similarly acceptable per the source.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Predictive Analytics for AOV, CLV and Replenishment Timing
cards.summary: Use Klaviyo predictive analytics to target high spenders, VIPs and near-repurchase groups.
cards.use_when: Upgrading segmentation beyond basic behavior to optimize offers and timing.
steps: Open Klaviyo predictive analytics and inspect average order value cohorts.
If store AOV is ~$50, build a segment with AOV $100+ and target them with bundle deals or large inventory-clearing offers.
Segment by predicted customer lifetime value to identify VIPs.
Segment by average time between purchases — e.g. if a cohort reorders every 45 days, fire a reminder flow around day 40.
Segment by predicted gender to tailor product recommendations and creative.
caveats: The source notes Klaviyo predictions aren't perfect — treat as directional data.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Location Segmentation for Pop-Ups and Regional Offers
cards.summary: Segment by geography to target local events, region-specific stores and compliance needs.
cards.use_when: Running pop-up shops, in-person events or country-specific storefronts.
steps: Build segments by city, state or country.
For an in-person event, target subscribers in that city (e.g. a San Diego pop-up).
Use location to handle compliance requirements and localized store experiences across countries.
Also useful for brand-headquarters-area promotions.
caveats: Requires reliable location data; some subscribers won't have it.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Cadence and Content Rule: Send Three to Four Emails a Week
cards.summary: High-frequency, high-quality campaigning to engaged segments outperforms low-frequency sending.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many campaigns per week to run and worried about unsubscribes.
steps: Send three to four campaigns per week to the engaged segment, per the source's experience across 50+ ecommerce brands.
Keep content strong; the source observed lower unsubscribe rates at this frequency than sending once a week.
Each campaign should be built on a distinct micro-topic so the list doesn't fatigue.
Frequency only works when paired with engagement segmentation; sending that much to unengaged people backfires on deliverability.
Use the calendar structure: metrics (3-4/wk) and topic diversity are both required.
caveats: The source's observation, not a universal rule; test against your own unsubscribe and spam rates.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Build core Klaviyo segments: VIP, winback, suppress, engaged
cards.summary: Four baseline segments (VIP, winback potential, suppress, unengaged) cover most lifecycle revenue without over-segmenting.
cards.use_when: Setting up or auditing your store's email segmentation and deciding which lists to actually send to and suppress.
steps: VIP: customer can receive marketing and has placed 5+ orders all-time. Source's base definition uses order count because it is simpler and more predictable than combining orders and spend (e.g. 5+ orders AND $500+); try VIPs with a special offer at least once a quarter.

Winback potential: customer can receive marketing, placed at least 1 order in the last 150 days, and 0 orders in the last 90 days — i.e. their last purchase fell in that 90-150 day window. Trigger a short flow when they enter; later in the flow, consider a discount for those who still haven't repurchased.

Suppress list (send nothing): opened 0 emails in the past 180 days, OR has ever bounced, OR has ever marked an email as spam. Review it monthly and mark those profiles suppressed in Klaviyo settings to protect deliverability and cut list-based billing costs.
Unengaged is strictly about email engagement; winback is strictly about past customers — keep them separate.
Tune the winback window to the average buying cycle: a supplement brand on 30-day servings might start winback around day 45; a hot-tub seller may need years between purchases.

Don't build dozens of tiny segments. The source's stated priority is to first have the basics done well — e.g. an 8-email abandoned-cart flow and a popup converting better than 3% — before chasing elaborate segmentation that may only add a few percent.
caveats: All thresholds above are the source's own base definitions, not validated benchmarks; adapt them to your store's order data and buying cycle.
Source is opinionated that beginners should fix basic flows and popup conversion before advanced segmentation; complex segments were framed as marginal gains.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Interest and cross-sell segments by product/category
cards.summary: Segment by viewed/added/checked-out/purchased product or category to send targeted launches or automated cross-sell flows.
cards.use_when: Planning a product drop, category promo, or automated cross-sell (e.g. buyer of one item toward a complementary item).
steps: Interest-in-X segment: customer can receive marketing AND has viewed an item at least once where the category/collection is X, OR added to cart where category is X, OR started checkout where collection is X, OR placed an order where collection is X (all over all time).
Use this for 1-2 extra sends per month on top of your engaged-list emails when you have a launch or sale tied to that product/category.

Cross-sell segment: customer can receive marketing AND has placed an order at least once all-time where collection equals the trigger product (e.g. bought white shoes). Then run a flow/email selling the match (white socks) and reference the exact item they bought.
Add a negative condition to protect the message: e.g. ordered protein at least once all-time AND ordered pre-workout 0 times all-time, so pre-workout buyers never get the pre-workout cross-sell.

In Klaviyo, viewed/added-to-cart metrics use Klaviyo's category values while Shopify-native triggers (started checkout, placed order) use collections — make sure your products are organized in Shopify so both line up.
caveats: Confirm current Klaviyo/Shopify metric names and filters in the live interface, as the terminology shifts between platforms and updates.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Resend unopened important emails with the campaign-ID segment trick
cards.summary: Build a 'received X email but didn't open' segment from the campaign message ID, then resend with new subject line and preview text 1-2 days later.
cards.use_when: Maximizing reach on high-value sends like Black Friday, a major product release, or a big announcement.
steps: Open the sent campaign in Klaviyo and copy the campaign message ID code from the URL.

Create a segment with two conditions: received email at least once all-time where message equals that code, AND opened email 0 times all-time where message equals that code. Klaviyo will resolve the campaign name for you.
Duplicate the original campaign and send it only to that segment, 1-2 days after the original.
Change the subject line and preview text so the resend doesn't read as a repeat to anyone who saw (but didn't open) the first.
Source frames this as an 'instant revenue booster' — if the original had e.g. a 60% open rate, 40% never saw it.
caveats: Treat any specific open-rate figure as an illustrative example, not a benchmark.
This is a case-by-case tactic, not a permanent dynamic segment — rebuild it per campaign.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Optimize email copy for the skim, not the read
cards.summary: Assume readers skim in seconds; break copy with line breaks, labels and bold main points so the email is understood in under three seconds.
cards.use_when: Writing or editing any campaign, welcome, or abandoned-cart email where copy currently appears as long paragraphs.
steps: Shift your mindset: design emails for skimming, not for reading, because inbox attention is short and readers open in bursts between tasks.
Avoid blocks of text entirely — long paragraphs make the eye skip past; split copy with line breaks, subheaders and distinct sections.
Bold your main points so the eye is forced to follow them; most people will read only the bolded lines, so those must carry the full message on their own.
Use body copy underneath each bold point as the supporting justification and proof for those who read further.
Turn enumerated benefits into short labeled lists or numbers instead of a paragraph — e.g. five points listed out with bolded labels rather than one dense block.
Use comparison layouts (us vs. them, empty vs. daily) with bold subheads so readers grasp the contrast without reading the details.
caveats: The specifics of how email clients render bold, formatting and line breaks vary — test appearance across devices before sending.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Clear and concise email copy: short and sweet, one takeaway
cards.summary: Keep emails to one to two scrolls and one clear takeaway; assume readers are overwhelmed and forget multiple points.
cards.use_when: Writing campaign or flow copy that risks cramming several benefits or messages into one send.
steps: Keep the email to roughly 1-2 phone scrolls maximum; source's guidance is shorter is better because only a few seconds of attention are available.
Choose ONE takeaway per email and build the headline around it — e.g. a matcha email solely about 'enhances the benefits of caffeine', or a hair-loss email solely about growth potential.
Ask yourself before sending: is there one clear thing the customer can take away? If the email tries to give 3+ takeaways, assume readers remember none.
Split a benefit-stuffed email into a series: instead of one email listing estimator, graphs, alerts, multi-cook view, etc., dedicate a whole email to each feature one at a time.

Cut implied information. On a welcome email, skip telling subscribers they get exclusive offers/insider access (they already know from the opt-in) and let the discount code sit in the clear space you save.
Every sentence should move the reader toward a purchase; delete fluff that only fills space.
caveats: Some emails (e.g. a flowchart or comparison email) are intentionally longer because the format itself is the engagement — length alone isn't the failure, unclear/multi-message copy is.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Write engaging copy: punchy, informational, entertaining
cards.summary: Trigger dopamine with dense punchy copy, real information, and humor/graphics — repetition kills engagement.
cards.use_when: Writing campaign copy that feels flat, corporate, or repetitive and is underperforming on opens and clicks.
steps: Make copy punchy: short but information-dense, evoking emotion. Example structure packs a stat plus a benefit into a tiny space (e.g. a toilet-time stat tied to a digestive product benefit rather than a bland feature list).

Make copy informational: give facts and education, because people want to make an educated purchase decision. Source's view is that anything that isn't information is fluff — 'highest quality ingredients' should be replaced with actual ingredient facts; aim for the reader to learn something every open.
Make copy entertaining: use jokes, puns, puzzles and graphics, since TikTok-era dopamine tolerance means new/novel content works and repetition does not.
Say 'we'll spill the milk' and lead with real facts instead of generic claims — the source's cereal example packs protein content and 'fewer cravings' into a playful, factual line.
Source's rule of thumb: if a reader can clearly name the one takeaway (e.g. 'golden root is good for you and it's in this product'), the copy is working.
caveats: Source is deliberately opinionated that copy needs humor and punch; brand-voice fit matters — a corporate/clinical brand may apply 'entertaining' more subtly and should test.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Use infographics as email 'secret sauce' to hit all copy principles
cards.summary: Infographics simultaneously make email skimmable, clear/concise and engaging — the source's highest-leverage copy ability.
cards.use_when: Designing email layouts when deciding how to present benefits, comparisons, or product education beyond plain text.
steps: Map your own copy into one of these infographic formats and hand it to a designer rather than writing blocks of text: checklists, icon graphics, feature diagrams, timelines, numbered lists, comparison charts (us vs. them), tables, flowcharts, and graphs.
Checklists: present benefits with checks so the reader's eye scoops them up without reading sentences; the designer can interpret the layout creatively.
Icon graphics: attach simple icons (vegan, gluten-free, soy-free, non-GMO) to the product so a knowledgeable viewer recognizes them without reading labels.
Feature diagrams: point call-outs at parts of the product image (e.g. 'large glossy violin-shaped leaves', 'upright trunk') to show exactly what the buyer receives.
Timelines: map when results appear (month 1/2/3) or brand history — useful in post-purchase flows and welcome campaigns.
Tables and comparison charts: lay out ingredient or plan differences side by side so undecided buyers can self-select; flowcharts demonstrate which product suits which use case.
Source's practice: include at least one infographic inside every email.
caveats: More creative formats (flowcharts, custom diagrams) take more production effort; the source notes it's a tradeoff against simply listing benefits.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Outline email copy in a doc against an existing template
cards.summary: Write copy by physically mapping layout, spacing and sections in a Google Doc modeled on a real email, then hand it to the designer.
cards.use_when: Briefing designers or building any email where you want control over layout placement, not just the words.
steps: Find an existing email you like (source searches sites like reallygoodemails.com or mill.com) and use it as the structural template.
In a Google Doc, recreate the email's structure visually: label the headline, sub-headline, hero section, body, bullets, tables, and every CTA position ('shop now').
Describe the visual treatment inline — e.g. 'simple hero section showing this on a GIF', 'try a new graphic style: table', 'fan favorites laid out here'.
Include notes on layout spacing and ordering rather than dumping all copy in a list, because list-only briefs give you no control over where copy lands (top vs. bottom) and how it affects conversion.
Keep every element mapped (headline → sub-headline → graphic → image of product → shop now) so the designer can execute without guessing.
caveats: This is a workflow recommendation from the source, not a tested result; adjust the doc format to your team's handoff process.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Prime ChatGPT with your brand, then request punchy hero copy
cards.summary: A two-step ChatGPT prompt — prime with brand/customer context, then request headline, sub-headline and CTA — to get a strong starting draft you edit.
cards.use_when: Facing a blank page on a campaign, drop, or launch email and needing a fast first draft to refine.
steps: Step 1 — Prime: tell ChatGPT your e-commerce brand, product types, mission/goal, USPs, what makes your products unique, customer demographics and ages, brand voice preference, and customer goals/aspirations. Then ask 'Are you ready to write copy based on the topics I give you?' It retains this context within the same chat window.

Newer models: paste your website URL and tell it to use the site as additional context (the source notes it can recognize the brand from the site, though this depends on the current interface — verify before relying on it).

Step 2 — Request: state the email type and topic ('graphic-based email campaign with minimal copy, topic X'), supply the topic details and USPs, then ask for a quick punchy headline, a slightly longer sub-headline, 2-3 sentences of body copy, and a 'shop now' CTA.
Treat the output as a starting point covering roughly the hero and bridge sections; add your own testimonials and further sections yourself.
Edit the draft to sound less like ChatGPT and more like your brand before sending.
caveats: Source's own view: it's always better to write it yourself and use ChatGPT only for a starting point; outputs need editing.
Prompt behavior and what the model retains can change with ChatGPT versions — re-verify what context it actually holds.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Prioritize basics before advanced segmentation and copy tricks
cards.summary: Audit whether core flows and popup form conversion are healthy before investing in elaborate segmentation.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to spend limited email/lifecycle effort when the store's fundamentals are still underperforming.
steps: Check the fundamentals first: does an abandoned-cart flow exist with around 8 emails, and is the popup form converting above 3%?
If those basics are missing or weak, fix them before building intricate interest/cross-sell segments, since low-hanging fruit usually outperforms fragmentation.
Source's stance: the fancier segmentation may only add a couple of percent in conversion or a little extra revenue, and shouldn't distract from the priority work.
Once basics are solid, layer in the more advanced segments (VIP, winback, interest, cross-sell) and copy tactics.
caveats: These specific figures (8 emails, 3% popup conversion) are the source's heuristics, not universal benchmarks — adapt to your store and test.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Write email copy with an AI prompt + real email outline
cards.summary: Copy a proven competitor email's structure, then use a ChatGPT prompt with brand/customer context to fill the copy.
cards.use_when: You need campaign email copy (best sellers, restock, promo) and want a repeatable fast workflow instead of a blank page.
steps: Find a real email you like from a swipe source (the source names reallygoodemails.com and mill.com; verify current URLs) for the niche you're mailing.
Map its blocks exactly as an outline: headline, body copy, sub-headline, product collection section with per-product blurbs, CTA, footer — this gives your designer a clear map.

Improve the skeleton before writing: the source presenter added a 'Shop Now' button at the top linking to the best-sellers page, because the original's buttons sat too low; keeping a CTA above the fold is a stated preference, not a measured rule.

Feed the AI a context block: brand name and what you sell, mission, what makes brand/products unique, ideal customer, brand voice (e.g. 'conversational, motivational, like a friendly coach who gives tough love'), customer goals, and your website URL.

Then give a second prompt: campaign format (e.g. graphic-based, minimal copy), topic, and explicit asks — punchy headline, longer sub-headline, then 2–3 sentences of copy leading into the Shop Now CTA.

Iterate in-thread: ask for multiple headline options, ask to make them more conversational or less corny, and switch direction if an angle stalls (the demo abandoned 'meet your MVPs' for 'PR day' because gym-goers recognize the term).
Write per-product blurbs yourself from real product descriptions — short, voice-matched lines like 'minimal and smooth, perfect for arm day' — rather than generic AI filler.
caveats: AI drafts need proofreading; the demo relied on Grammarly and manual editing.
Don't invent product claims; pull specifics from the actual product description page.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Treat subject lines as frames, and test them on revenue
cards.summary: Subject line and preview text change the psychological frame of the email and can triple sales with identical content, so pick winners by revenue not opens.
cards.use_when: Setting up or interpreting A/B tests on subject lines for any campaign email, especially abandoned cart.
steps: Accept the stated premise that a strong sender reputation plus consistently good content is what drives routine opens — the presenter argues subject lines 'should not matter' for opens and aims for opens driven by sender name, like a creator whose audience watches regardless of title.

Use subject/preview to set the buying frame instead of describing the email: the same email copy and design produced different sales depending on whether the frame was gentle ('did you mean to do this?') versus direct ('this is ready for you — check it out and buy').

In the source's abandoned-cart example, the two variants had near-identical opens (68% vs 69%) but very different place-order rates (11.6% vs 3.8%) and clicks (14% vs 6.8%) — treat these as one case, not a benchmark.
Configure your ESP test (e.g. Klaviyo A/B) to select the winner on revenue or place-order rate, not open rate, since opens can look equal while revenue diverges sharply.
Review results per email type: the frame that wins on a cart email may not be the frame that wins on a launch.
caveats: The presenter's claim that subject lines don't matter for opens is his opinion; he still writes them carefully because they move sales.
Single-case numbers are illustrative examples, not predictions.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Subject line framework: 2–5 words, title case, curiosity loop
cards.summary: Short title-case subject lines that open a curiosity loop and pair with one or two emojis are the source's default format.
cards.use_when: Drafting subject lines for any store campaign — launches, restocks, promos, educational sends.
steps: Keep it to 2–5 words so the notification is scannable while the recipient is scrolling another app; long sentence-like subject lines get swiped away, per the presenter.
Use title case because the presenter finds it reads as more official and reports a positive effect on opens.
End on an open loop: hint at the payoff but withhold it so the only way to close the loop is opening the email (his analogy: a song or movie title you can't recall nags at you).
Use 1–2 emojis, not on every send: 'A Taste Of Sunshine' (emotional pull), 'Myth. Busted.' (curiosity), 'They're Finally Here' (anticipation), 'It's Literally This Easy' (mild cocky challenge).

Puns and periods between words are allowed levers — the presenter likes periods for suspense and notes the reviewer's praise for 'Tallow Won't Fix This' / 'the grass-fed elephant in the room' as a strong curiosity pairing.
Test emoji placement (beginning vs end) rather than assuming; the presenter prefers putting two emojis adjacent when using two.
caveats: Everything here is the presenter's stated heuristic, not a measured rule; he reports 50–60% opens to engaged lists across his clients.
Avoid the overused word 'secret' and don't stack multiple ideas (e.g. restock + sale) unless you can phrase them together.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Preview text framework: support the headline, end with an ellipsis
cards.summary: Preview text should be a short supporting line that adds a second curiosity hook, often ending in '...' to prompt the open.
cards.use_when: Writing preview text for any email where the subject line has already been drafted.
steps: Treat subject line as headline and preview text as sub-headline; build a visible hierarchy (shorter title-case subject, slightly longer regular-case preview).
Add new information rather than repeating the subject — the preview should support and extend the hook.
Use dot-dot-dot endings occasionally; the presenter finds an ellipsis strongly opens loops, but advises not using it on every send.

Pair examples given: subject 'A Taste Of Sunshine' with preview 'This wasn't supposed to be made but now it's a bestseller...'; subject 'Myth. Busted.' with 'If you want the cold hard facts we got them...'; subject 'It's Literally This Easy' with 'No one is talking about this but it will make you more money...'.
For restocks, pair 'They're Back' with 'And they're on sale for now' — the 'for now' adds urgency while the preview reveals the sale the subject omitted.
Leave something withheld: the presenter criticizes previews like 'add this to your packing list' as lame and would move product/news detail into the preview while keeping the subject open-ended.
caveats: The presenter explicitly says not to overthink preview text; content quality and cadence are the primary drivers.
The 50–60% open figure is his agency's reported engaged-list average, not a universal expectation.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Build urgency and holidays into seasonal campaign angles
