cards.summary: Use real calendar holidays, seasonal timing and scarcity language to give a plain product email a reason to exist.
cards.use_when: Planning a promo or content email with no launch hook — e.g. a nut-bar brand needing a July send.
steps: Ask an AI assistant for obscure or relevant holidays for the upcoming month to generate campaign topics (the demo used National Coconut Day for a coconut bar).
Tie the product directly to the occasion so the email reads naturally rather than as a generic sale blast.
Add urgency in preview text when inventory is genuinely constrained: the reviewed example 'Some SKUs already closed. Get yours now.' was praised for urgency.
Note that sale-with-restock emails combine two messages; the presenter considered it acceptable only when phrased as one idea ('They're Back / And They're On Sale For Now').

For travel or summer positioning, use simple seasonal framing ('Vacation Time') but push the specificity into the preview; the presenter found 'Trusted For Travel' too thin and rewrote it toward a benefit claim the reader has to open to verify.
caveats: Holiday-driven emails work only if the product connects — forced occasion tie-ins read as filler.
Don't claim scarcity ('some SKUs already closed') unless it is true.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Diagnose and fix weak inbox subject lines
cards.summary: A short review checklist for improving live subject lines: cut length, front-load the hook, and give the preview a job.
cards.use_when: Reviewing your own scheduled campaigns before send, or auditing past sends to improve format.
steps: Cut long descriptive subject lines: 'All New Summer Hiking Essentials' was judged too long; suggested replacing with a punchy repeat like 'New New' and pushing the product list into preview text.

Lead with the strongest word or concept, not the category: the presenter would make 'The Sale?' the subject and 'Red White And All You...' the preview for a July 4th send, since 'Americana inspired favorites' was unnecessary.
Make short subject lines work with a longer preview: two-word subjects pair well with five-plus-word previews for visible hierarchy.
Don't capitalize seasons; 'built for summer' should read 'Built For Summer' under his title-case convention.
Avoid flat previews with no hook ('The perfect sun hoodie'); instead end with a metaphor or pun plus ellipsis.
Watch subject-line craft details: he dislikes two emojis split apart, all-caps used without reason, and overused words like 'secret'.
caveats: These are the presenter's stated preferences and style conventions, not tested rules; he recommends testing emoji placement and phrasing for your own list.
A/B results vary by audience and list engagement.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Prioritize content quality and cadence over subject-line tricks
cards.summary: The presenter argues opens should be earned by consistently valuable content and predictable send cadence, with subject lines used only to frame the sale.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much effort to invest in subject-line optimization versus email content and send frequency.
steps: Build the presumption of opening: send content good enough that recipients open on sender name, then associate that experience with the next send (the presenter compares it to a creator whose audience watches regardless of title).
Keep cadence consistent enough that subscribers expect you multiple times a week, similar to newspaper-reading habits — the source's stated goal is conditioning.
Accept that subject line and preview text still exist to drive sales, so continue testing them on revenue even under this philosophy.
When auditing a campaign that underperforms, first check whether the underlying offer/content is worth opening before blaming subject lines.
caveats: The 'subject lines don't matter' position is explicitly the presenter's opinion and may conflict with standard deliverability practice; he still writes and tests them.
Multiple weekly sends require enough content substance and list tolerance — not validated for every list size or niche in the source.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Rewrite subject lines as curiosity gap, then judge them by sales
cards.summary: Draft subject line and preview text as a curiosity hook, but validate them on sales/conversion rather than open rate.
cards.use_when: Writing or testing the subject line and preview text for a campaign email, especially a new product or back-in-stock send.
steps: Aim for curiosity so the reader has a reason to click. A worked example: a tallow product email subject framed as 'Tallow won't fix this' followed by the preview text 'the grass-fed elephant in the room' — the presenter called this a strong example because it appears to talk down the product, then hints at an unresolved 'elephant in the room'.

Write preview text as a continuation of the hook, not a repeat of the subject line. Example given: subject references vacation time, preview reads 'add this to your packing list...' to keep the reader wanting more.
Don't overthink the mechanics. The presenter's position is that if you send good content, people open regardless of the specific subject line and preview text.
Judge subject lines and preview text on sales rather than opens, and test what works for your own list. This is the presenter's stated rule, not a universal benchmark.
Note that sender name also drives opens, so keep it recognizable.
caveats: The 'send good content and people will open anyway' claim is the presenter's opinion, not a tested universal rule.
Testing on sales instead of opens is a slower validation loop and needs enough volume to read.
The tallow example is a demonstration the presenter invented live, not a measured result.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Design ecommerce emails in Figma instead of Canva
cards.summary: Use Figma for email design over Canva because layout control and organization hold up better at scale.
cards.use_when: Setting up the design tooling and file structure for a store's recurring email design workflow.
steps: Choose Figma over Canva. The presenter states Canva is too simplistic and hard to organize, and that Figma can be just as simple while producing better emails and offering extra capabilities.
Work at a fixed email width of 600px. Build sections as frames at that width so slices export cleanly later.
Ignore most of Figma's feature surface — the presenter estimates roughly 90% of what you see is unused. Rely on shapes, text, image fills, gradients, alignment tools and slicing.
Use the layers panel to select and edit nested elements. Selecting a layer highlights the corresponding element on canvas and exposes its properties (e.g. setting a logo width).
Hold the format-appropriate modifier key when cropping images inside a frame (the presenter uses command) so a hero image can be reduced, e.g. to 600x500, without breaking the layout.
caveats: Recommended tooling, not a measured conversion result.
The 600px width is the presenter's convention; verify against current email client rendering.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Write email copy as a layout brief before design starts
cards.summary: Hand designers a sectioned copy document that shows the intended layout so the design matches the copywriter's intent.
cards.use_when: Briefing an email design (in-house or freelance) for any campaign or flow, to avoid rework between copy and layout.
steps: Instead of listing 'headline / body / CTA' abstractly, write the copy in the order and shape of the intended email sections so the layout is implied.

For a back-in-stock email, the layout brief looked like: 'back in stock / they're back' headline, a small block of body copy, a button, a graphic, a core-values block, then fan favorites and bestsellers listed.

The presenter's reasoning: as a former copywriter, emails would turn out very differently from what was imagined, so laying it out gives more control and gives designers a starting point rather than a blank canvas.
Designers appreciate it because starting from nothing is hard; the brief becomes the scaffolding.
Pair this with a Figma template library so the shape in the brief maps to an existing section.
caveats: This is a process recommendation from the presenter's agency, not an A/B tested outcome.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Build a reusable email section template library
cards.summary: Keep pre-built hero, bridge and product section templates in Figma so each new email starts from a proven section.
cards.use_when: Producing email campaigns or flows regularly and wanting to cut design time while keeping section quality consistent.
steps: Create a template file containing multiple variants of hero sections, bridge sections and product sections. The presenter's file labels them e.g. 'hero section 7', '3', '2'.
Each hero template contains a headline, body copy, a button and a graphic slot — the standard hero anatomy used in the walkthrough.
When starting a new email, pick a matching template, paste it in, and use it as the reference while building the rest.
Keep the template library separate from the working email file so variants aren't accidentally edited in place.
The presenter offers these templates via newsletter signup; the mechanism matters less than maintaining your own consistent variants.
caveats: Only three section types are described (hero, bridge, product); extend the library to cover your own recurring sections.
Template reuse risks visual sameness — the source separately warns that identical layouts every send erode attention.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Gradient overlay to place text over a hero image without covering faces
cards.summary: Layer a black-to-transparent gradient rectangle over a hero photo to create readable space for headline, body and CTA.
cards.use_when: Building an email hero where the photo is the background and copy must sit on top of it.
steps: Set the hero image to 600px wide and align it to the frame.
Identify where text will sit and check it won't cover faces — in the walkthrough the subject's faces were in the upper area, so text was pushed lower.
Add a rectangle at 600px width over the image, fill it black, and drag it so it blends into the photo.
In the fill settings, switch to the gradient tab. Change direction from side-to-side to top-to-bottom.
Set the bottom gradient stop to fully transparent and keep the top stop black, so the overlay fades from solid at the top into the image at the bottom.
Adjust stop positions until the transition is smooth, then place headline and body copy on top.
Set the hero frame to roughly 600x500 so the next section isn't pushed far down the scroll.
caveats: Long hero sections force a long scroll before the next section — the presenter cropped the hero down for that reason.
Figma gradient controls may change; verify the current interface.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Build a CTA button with a rounded rectangle and correct layer order
cards.summary: Construct email CTA buttons as rounded rectangles with text layered on top, and fix z-order when text disappears.
cards.use_when: Creating the primary CTA in an email hero or section where no button template exists.
steps: Draw a rectangle, set corner radius (the presenter used ~65 initially) and increase corner rounding to get a pill shape.
Set the button fill to contrast with the section — white on the dark hero, black on white sections.
Add a text layer for the CTA label, e.g. 'shop best sellers' or 'shop now', and center it.
If the label is hidden, it's a layer-order problem: move the text above the rectangle in the layers panel so it renders in front.
Adjust button size and weight after placement rather than before; the presenter resized and bolded iteratively until it looked right.
caveats: No specific button size is established as a best practice — sizing was tuned by eye.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Put the first CTA button above the fold and keep buttons large
cards.summary: Place a large, visible CTA near the top of the email and remove competing nav buttons that dilute clicks.
cards.use_when: Restructuring an underperforming email template, or reviewing an existing template's CTA placement and button sizing.
steps: Check where the first button appears in the rendered email. In the Whoop teardown the first button sat very far down the email, so an opener would have to scroll substantially before being able to click — the presenter says this impairs click rates and ultimately sales.
Move a prominent button into the hero so every opener sees it without scrolling. In the redesigned Whoop email a large button sits at the very top.

Remove the top-of-email navigation row (Shop Women / Shop Men / category links). The presenter states that four or five buttons immediately on open overwhelm the reader, hurt conversions, and increase churn. Move navigation into the footer instead.

For Birkenstock, an audience with a significant older demographic, increase font sizes and button sizes. The presenter's framing: make the buttons big enough that 'even a blind person could click these'.

Use only one or two calls to action per email. The Birkenstock original had shop now, sign up for catalog, follow on Instagram, sign up for free membership, tag us on Instagram, and recommendations all in one email.
caveats: These are the presenter's conversion principles based on agency experience, not controlled test results. Treat 'four or five buttons overwhelm' as a heuristic to test on your own list and audience.
Accessibility framing about font and button size is a design heuristic, not a formal accessibility standard.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Give every product its own Shop Now button, or at minimum underline the product name
cards.summary: Make clickability obvious on each product tile so the reader can shop a specific item directly from the email.
cards.use_when: Laying out a product grid or multi-product section in a campaign email.
steps: Add an individual Shop Now button to each product shown. The presenter's rule: each item gets its own link so the customer knows they can click through to that specific product page.

If individual buttons aren't feasible in the layout, at minimum underline the product name so it reads as clickable. The Alo teardown found product tiles where it was unclear whether items were clickable at all.

Make the clickable element the anchor for the destination link when slicing (each image export carries only one link, so the button and the product photo must be separate slices if they point to different URLs).

Don't overload product tiles with copy. In the Gymshark walkthrough the presenter judged the email already had enough information and chose a lean tile: product image, product name, a short descriptor, a review count, and a Shop Now button.
caveats: The presenter frames the underlining fallback as clearly weaker than a real button.
No measured click-rate uplift is provided for either approach.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Add review counts and short product descriptors to fill out product tiles
cards.summary: Enrich each product tile with rating and a one-line product attribute so the section feels substantial without becoming cluttered.
cards.use_when: Designing or refreshing a multi-product email section that currently looks sparse.
steps: Insert a star icon and the review count for highly rated products. In the walkthrough the item was labeled with a rating such as 4.3 alongside a star graphic.
Lock star icon proportions before resizing. In Figma, changing width alone distorts a star; enable proportional scaling so width and height change together.

Add a short attribute line under the product name, e.g. 'light support' for a sports bra. Use lowercase or sentence case rather than all caps — Figma's text panel has an option to control case ('as typed' vs all caps).
Style the attribute in a smaller size and a gray color so it reads as secondary to the product name, then adjust spacing so tiles stay aligned.
The presenter's reasoning: the section looked bare, and review counts plus a small attribute add depth and information 'but not too much'.
caveats: Review counts are used as a credibility signal; only display real review figures from the storefront.
Exact tile content should be tested per brand — this is one worked example.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Build a visual theme and repeat it across sections for depth
cards.summary: Use gradients and repeated line motifs to make a flat email feel dimensional and cohesive.
cards.use_when: An email section or whole campaign design reads as flat, two-dimensional or off-brand.
steps: Diagnose flatness. On the Gymshark core-values section the presenter said it looked 'two-dimensional' — a plain white background with no depth.
Add soft gradients behind text blocks: draw a rectangle at 600px, place it behind the text, and set a gradient from a light gray into white or transparent, top-to-bottom to soften the block edge.
Apply the gradient block one subgroup at a time rather than across the whole section — the presenter tried behind everything, then chose to go block by block.

Carry a motif across sections. In the Gymshark build, thin black divider lines used in the core-values section were reused beside product images and in the product section to create depth and tie the email together.
Vary backgrounds between sections (the walkthrough alternated a dark hero with a white core-values section) so sections are visually distinguishable and the email isn't uniformly dark.
caveats: Gradient tuning was done by eye; the presenter adjusted stop position and lightness repeatedly before settling.
The presenter notes brand-fit was uncertain for a Birkenstock redesign, showing that a modern restyle can conflict with brand guidelines.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Use layering and grouping to keep long email files navigable
cards.summary: Group each email section into named frames with inner sub-groups so a long email file stays editable.
cards.use_when: Managing a large email design file that spans multiple sections and will need edits or reuse.
steps: Wrap the whole email in a single frame at the target width (600px) and name it after the brand, e.g. 'gymshark email'. Extend the frame height to make room as you add sections.
Group all layers belonging to a section into one group and name it by section: 'logo', 'hero section', 'bridge section'.
Within a section, group sub-elements further — the walkthrough grouped button elements into a 'button' group and renamed layers to 'headline' and 'subheadline'.
Order the groups top-to-bottom to match the email reading order so the layer tree mirrors the rendered email.
Do this as you build, not retroactively. The presenter admits skipping organization, then had to go back and clean it up.
caveats: Purely a file-management practice; no conversion implication.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Close with a general Shop Now CTA after the product section
cards.summary: End every product section with a broad shop CTA so readers who wanted none of the featured items still have a path.
cards.use_when: Finishing any email that displays a grid or list of specific products.
steps: After the individual product tiles, add one general CTA such as 'shop best sellers' or 'shop all tops'.
The presenter's rationale: the reader might not want any of the shown products but still wants to browse, so give them a general route — 'always always always' end product sections this way.
Center and align the button with the rest of the section, and adjust section background height as needed.
Where relevant, echo the CTA language used at the top of the email so the email bookends around a single shopping action.
In the Alo redesign, the product section closed with a general 'shop all tops' CTA plus a brand line ('experience the Alo difference').
caveats: The 'always' framing is the presenter's rule of thumb, not a tested law.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Build a footer with category shopping links plus trust icons
cards.summary: Treat the footer as the one section present in every email and use it for persistent shop-by-category links and social proof badges.
cards.use_when: Designing or revising the standard footer block used across all campaign and flow emails.
steps: Add shop-by-category links in the footer. The presenter argues this generates a large volume of clicks because readers who reach the bottom may not want the featured items, and the footer gives them somewhere to go instead of leaving.

Instead of separate emails segmented by gender, place two footer entries such as 'Women' and 'Men' so any email can serve both audiences. In the walkthrough these were rendered as labeled line sections rather than buttons.
Include social media icons in the footer so every email carries a follow path.

Include social proof / service icons. The Gymshark footer reused Afterpay, Klarna, free shipping or free returns, and world class support icons — screenshotting and reusing the brand's existing icons is the pragmatic route the presenter used.
Keep the footer visually cleaner than the body and align the category columns. The Birkenstock redesign laid categories in a column or two columns; the presenter states this performed better.
Add unsubscribe and legal blocks in the ESP (Klaviyo handles this) rather than designing them in Figma.
caveats: 'You get a ton of clicks' from footer buttons is the presenter's observation from agency work, not a published benchmark.
Trust badge icons must reflect services your store actually offers.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Vary layout, imagery and copy between sends to prevent subscriber fatigue
cards.summary: Redesign emails so each send looks different in layout, color, theme and copy tone rather than repeating one template.
cards.use_when: Planning an email calendar and choosing which template or layout each campaign will use.
steps: Audit recent sends for sameness. The presenter pulled four random Gymshark emails that used the same layout every time and called this out as the easiest way to lose attention and subscribers.
Vary layout, colors, themes and copy per send — the presenter's framing is that subscribers want novelty and varying 'dopamine'.

Match email imagery to the brand's social channels. The Gymshark emails used studio-only product photography while their Instagram was full of people and life, creating a disconnected experience; the redesigned emails used lifestyle imagery instead.

Build dedicated value and social-proof emails alongside promotional ones. Examples shown: a testimonial email ('by gym lovers for gym lovers') with verified review counts and a testimonial carousel, and a blog-style email breaking down dumbbell back exercises.
Include a shop path even in non-promotional emails (blog, educational) so a reader who wants to buy can do so without leaving the email journey.
caveats: The claim that repetition loses subscribers is the presenter's assertion, not a measured churn study.
The redesigned examples were made by the presenter's team from public assets; no revenue results are reported here.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Shift CTA copy from 'learn more' to a concrete value proposition
cards.summary: Replace generic learn-more language with the specific thing the customer gets, such as a free trial.
cards.use_when: Rewriting email hero copy and CTA labels for an offer-driven email.
steps: Identify the concrete thing the customer receives. For Whoop it was a free month trial — you can get a device sent to you and use it for a month, so that is what the presenter centered the CTAs on.
Rewrite 'learn more' CTAs. The presenter's argument: nobody wants to learn more, they want to be given something.

Show the value proposition directly in the hero rather than only listing features. The original copy ('discover how Whoop outperforms other wearables') listed features; the rewrite led with the offer.
Repeat the offer at the bottom of the email as a reminder, after the design has carried the reader down.

Keep tone matched to the audience — the presenter rewrote a line into a modern reference ('they not like us' / 'there's levels to this') to appeal to the audience of the moment, admitting brand-fit risk.
caveats: The tone-matching rewrite is unvalidated; the presenter notes uncertainty about whether such a restyle matches brand guidelines.
No conversion lift is reported for the copy changes.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Use vertical stacking over side-by-side layouts in email copy
cards.summary: Lay out comparative copy vertically rather than in back-and-forth columns for easier reading in email.
cards.use_when: Building a bridge or comparison section that contrasts the brand against competitors or alternatives.
steps: Take comparative copy out of side-by-side columns and stack it vertically. The presenter states that going back and forth is hard for the customer and that vertical layouts performed better in their work.
Use this in bridge sections. The Whoop redesign used a bridge contrasting the competitor and the brand: 'they give you numbers, we give you insights'.
Keep vertical blocks short and highly readable — the presenter described the goal as making it 'super easy to read'.
Pair the vertical block with a background transition (the Whoop redesign used a transition over the section) to make the section feel immersive like the brand's site.
Reserve the hero for the biggest share of design attention — the presenter's position is that about 75% of attention should go to the hero section.
caveats: The '75% of attention on the hero' figure is the presenter's heuristic, not a measured metric.
The vertical-layout preference is an observation from the presenter's work, not a controlled test.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Slice an email design into separate export images, one link each
cards.summary: Cut the finished Figma design into slices per link target and per manageable image size before export.
cards.use_when: Preparing a designed email for uploading into an ESP as a stack of image blocks.
steps: Use Figma's slice tool: highlight the region you want, position the slice precisely, then export it. Repeatedly copy and paste the slice, aligning each new slice to where the previous one ended.
Split any region that needs a different link into its own slice. Each uploaded image can carry only one link, so a row containing multiple buttons must be sliced apart for each destination.
Split product tiles individually so each product is separately clickable.
Keep slices from being too large. Oversized image files load slowly in the ESP and in the recipient's inbox.
Slice social icons into separate exports — in the walkthrough Facebook, Instagram and Pinterest each got its own slice.
Export at 2X and as JPEG in the walkthrough; verify export options in the current Figma interface since these settings can change.
caveats: A purely image-based email trades layout fidelity for editability — copy can't be edited in the ESP without a new export.
Slice boundaries must align exactly or sections will show seams.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Compress exported email images in a batch before uploading
cards.summary: Run all sliced email images through a batch compressor to cut file weight before uploading to the ESP.
cards.use_when: After slicing an email design and before building the campaign in the ESP.
steps: Batch-upload all slices to a compressor at once. The presenter used iloveimg.com's compress image tool.
Read the before/after figures. In the walkthrough a batch went from 1.72 MB to 327 KB — roughly an 80% reduction — and the tool had already downloaded the compressed set for re-upload.
Upload the compressed files, not the originals, into the ESP.
The presenter's stated reason for compressing is load speed inside the ESP and in the inbox, which connects to deliverability hygiene.
Combine this step with careful slicing so no single slice is large in the first place.
caveats: Compression settings and tool behavior change — verify the current interface and check quality after compressing.
The 1.72 MB to 327 KB result is a single example, not a guaranteed reduction ratio.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Assemble the sliced email in Klaviyo and attach links and alt text
cards.summary: Rebuild the sliced design in the ESP using stacked image blocks, then apply per-image links and fallback alt text.
cards.use_when: Building the actual sendable campaign from exported image slices in Klaviyo or a comparable ESP.
steps: Create a campaign, choose the sending list, and use a blank email template.
Delete all default blocks except the unsubscribe/legal footer, since Klaviyo supplies the compliance block.
Drag an image block in, upload the compressed slices, then duplicate the block repeatedly and replace each with the next slice in order.
Upload images directly rather than pulling from image URLs so each block can take its own link.

For the social icon row, insert a table block instead of stacked images. Change the cell content type to image, add a column so there are as many cells as icons, and set padding to zero so icons fill the cell.
Paste the destination URL into each image's link address — the logo to the homepage, each product button to its product page, category buttons to their collection pages.

Add alt text where it helps. The presenter's position is that alt text is barely used because image blocking is very rare, but they still add descriptive text mirroring the copy (e.g. 'they're back') so an image-less reader can follow.
Send yourself a preview and click through every link before sending. The presenter notes ESP interfaces change, so verify the current block and table settings in Klaviyo.
caveats: The 'image blocking is very rare' characterization is the presenter's own view — verify against your list's client mix before deprioritizing alt text.
Because the email is images, copy edits require re-slicing and a new export.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Keep site and email visual worlds consistent
cards.summary: Match email design language to the storefront and social channels so the email feels like the same brand.
cards.use_when: Reviewing email templates against the storefront and social presence before a redesign.
steps: Compare the immersion level of the site against the email. The presenter noted Whoop's site is futuristic and immersive with different colors and transitions, while the email was plain, black and white, and followed the same layout repeatedly.

Pull brand-appropriate visual elements from the site into the email — color, gradient transitions and graphic treatments — as the Whoop redesign did, and carry lifestyle imagery over from social as the Gymshark redesign did.

Where brand identity conflicts with a modern restyle, flag it rather than assuming the redesign is correct. The presenter explicitly doubted whether the modern Birkenstock take fitted the brand's guidelines even while demonstrating the conversion principles.
Use branded backdrops and set pieces rather than plain backgrounds — e.g. a testimonial email with the brand's logos in the background and testimonials over a phone frame.
Seasonalize imagery for fashion brands. For a November send the Alo redesign used a winter lifestyle photo, with the presenter noting images are changed by season to stay current.
caveats: No measurement supports the claim that consistency improves conversion; this is a design coherence argument.
Modernizing a legacy brand's look can violate brand guidelines — treat the Birkenstock example as a demonstration, not a recommendation to imitate blindly.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Redesign browse-abandonment automations to include a top CTA
cards.summary: Fix triggered browse follow-up emails that show products but give no path back to the store.
cards.use_when: Auditing or redesigning a browse-abandonment or recently-viewed automation that fires after a shopper browses a category.
steps: Check the trigger logic against what fired. In the Alo example the presenter browsed women's tops while shopping for a gift, and an email titled 'trending tops — definitely worth a second look' fired a few hours later, resurfacing tops.

Verify the email contains at least one CTA. The Alo example had no working buttons at all — no top button and no keep-shopping button at the bottom — which the presenter called out as a serious defect for a large brand.
Add a CTA button at the top so a distracted shopper returning hours later can continue immediately.
Make product tiles obviously clickable: individual Shop Now buttons per item, or at minimum underlined product names.
Fix font color and contrast problems — the presenter flagged a color/font issue in the Alo email that damaged readability.
Add shop-by-category links in the footer so a shopper who no longer wants the browsed category can pivot to bottoms or other collections rather than abandoning.
Match imagery to the season and rewrite copy playfully ('serve in your new top', 'grab your new piece') to reconnect with the shopper's context.
caveats: This is a teardown of the presenter's own triggered sample; the browse trigger logic is inferred, not confirmed from the brand's account.
No post-redesign performance data is provided.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Use an interactive mix-and-match block to demonstrate outfit combinations
cards.summary: Show a GIF or rotating block of bestsellers that customers can combine into outfits, then drive to a single shop CTA.
cards.use_when: Building a merchandising email that needs a fresh layout idea for promoting multiple bestsellers together.
steps: Frame the section around combining products rather than listing them: the Gymshark example used copy like 'mix and match our favorites' and 'back in stock for guaranteed shirt shredding pump'.
Build the section as a GIF that cycles through different items, so a single slot conveys multiple combinations.
Follow the interactive block with a final CTA and a shop-by-category footer so the reader has both the featured route and a broader browse route.
Pair this with an emotional hero (the same email used copy about the gym as a sanctuary and sweat drowning out doubt) to differentiate the send from standard catalog layouts.
The presenter's stated purpose is variability — giving subscribers a different experience versus a repeating template.
caveats: GIF support and animation behavior vary by email client; test rendering before sending.
No conversion performance is reported for this specific block.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Use testimonial and social-proof emails to build trust for later purchases
cards.summary: Send review-led emails that accumulate trust even when they don't convert immediately.
cards.use_when: Planning a non-discount campaign slot aimed at warming a list or an audience segment that hasn't purchased.
steps: Build the email around real reviews. The Gymshark example headlined 'by gym lovers for gym lovers' with 100+ verified reviews.
Lay testimonials over a device frame and bold the key phrases inside each testimonial so skim readers catch the point.
Place a large CTA button directly beneath the testimonials, before the photo gallery.
Use a gradient background that fades from a gray tone into white to transition into the closing section without a hard edge.
Include a photo gallery for branding value even if it isn't directly transactional.
The presenter's expectation for this format: even if the reader doesn't convert off the email, they accumulate trust so they may buy later. This is a stated intent, not a measured outcome.
caveats: Only quote real, verified reviews; the 100+ figure comes from the example.
The later-conversion claim is the presenter's rationale, not tracked attribution.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Use value and educational emails that still carry a shop path
cards.summary: Send content-led emails that teach something useful and still route readers toward products in the same send.
cards.use_when: Filling a campaign slot with value content instead of a promotion, especially for an audience that buys gear or apparel.
steps: Base the email on a topic the audience actually searches for. The Gymshark example was built from a blog on dumbbell back exercises you can do without a gym.
Headline it as a practical guide, e.g. 'top no-fuss dumbbell back exercises', with an aspirational image.
Break the topic into parts to give genuine value — the example walked through back anatomy ('back anatomy 101') before the exercises.
Keep shopping paths available: the footer shop-by-category buttons and any in-body product CTAs mean a reader who wants to buy doesn't have to leave the email journey.
The presenter's rationale for the format is that the footer shop buttons ensure 'even if you're doing a blog email or an educational email' there are still clickable shopping routes.
caveats: Educational content requires genuine subject-matter accuracy; the source does not address content sourcing or review.
No performance data is given for this format.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Design emails as image slices, then link buttons in Klaviyo
cards.summary: How to export a Figma email design as slice images, compress them, and rebuild it in Klaviyo with clickable links and alt-ready structure.
cards.use_when: You have approved email creative in Figma and need to ship it through your ESP (Klaviyo) for a campaign or flow.
steps: In Figma, use the Slice tool to cut the email into pieces aligned to where links differ (logo, each CTA, product blocks, footer). Export at 2x for quality, JPEG is fine.

Do not make one giant slice for a long section; oversized image files slow inbox loading. Keep slices roughly small enough that no single image is very large — the source treats ~600px wide sections as the practical outer limit.
Compress all slices before upload (the video used iloveimg.com; any compressor works). Example from the session: 2.84 MB of slices reduced to 469 KB.
In Klaviyo, create a campaign/flow email, delete the default blocks, and add image blocks one by one in order, uploading the compressed slices top to bottom.
Attach links to each image that represents a button so it routes to the correct page (blog, collection, product).
Keep the footer social/footer text area as editable Klaviyo blocks (not images) so you can change social network links and the unsubscribe link.
Add a block of real, visible-but-tiny text in the footer (source suggests size 5) drawn from your About Us copy to counteract an image-heavy email looking spammy to Gmail and help deliverability.
Verify current Klaviyo image-block and campaign interface before executing — UI changes over time.
caveats: Heavy image-only emails risk deliverability; the hidden/tiny text trick is a source recommendation, not a guaranteed deliverability fix.
Email clients may block images; ensure key text is not only inside images where possible.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Use a non-discount email strategy: brand, value, social proof
cards.summary: Build a three-email mix of branded, value, and social-proof emails that promote products subtly instead of discounting.
cards.use_when: Planning a campaign calendar or welcome/engagement flow and you want to protect margin rather than default to discount offers.
steps: Decide the angle per email up front: (1) a branded email carrying your brand voice and best sellers, (2) a value/education email, (3) a reviews/social-proof email.
For the branded email, lead with a strong tagline tied to the brand (the session used a 'do gym' angle) and tie it into best sellers.
For the value email, pick a blog post or educational concept that hits a customer pain point (e.g. training at home with dumbbells) and tease the click.
For the social-proof email, pull real testimonials from your site that overcome objections and span different customer types.
Promote products subtly throughout so the email does not feel salesy and add sales resistance, while still giving a clear path to buy.
Find inspiration by scrolling the brand's Instagram and site to mine community language and angles, then carry that into email instead of plain corporate layouts.
caveats: Non-discount emails aim to protect margin but may convert differently than a discount blast; the source presents this as his preferred approach, not a universal rule.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Source email angles from your own Instagram and website
cards.summary: Mine brand Instagram captions, community language, and site blogs to generate email ideas instead of designing from a blank page.
cards.use_when: You need campaign angles for a store and want ideas that feel on-brand and content-driven rather than purely promotional.
steps: Scroll the brand's Instagram to capture recurring community language and recurring phrases (the source noticed the brand treated 'gym' as a verb).
Turn a repeated phrase or community theme into a tagline you can build a whole email around.
Check whether the site has a blog and pick a post that addresses a real customer pain point (e.g. home workouts without machines).
For that post, plan a blog email that teases the click and drives traffic back to the site, where readers can also shop.
Pull testimonials from the site for a separate social-proof email.
Note where the brand's email looks corporate/bland versus its livelier Instagram, and set the goal of bringing that life into email.
caveats: This is a content-mining process, not a performance guarantee; the source's claim that it 'prints cash' is his framing.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Pick email layouts from an inspiration bank of proven brands
cards.summary: Reuse layouts and sections from successful brands' emails rather than inventing new structures each time.
cards.use_when: You are laying out a new campaign email and need proven section structures for hero, product, and footer blocks.
steps: Keep a swipe inbox/folder of emails from brands you follow so you have a bank of layouts and sections.
Mimic the winning structure for most emails: headline + body copy + button in the hero, especially a 'learn more' button for blog emails.
Prefer centering the hero button and putting it prominently rather than leaving it small and off to the side.
Lift section ideas such as a 'mix and match' product block or a 'chest/back anatomy' educational breakdown and adapt the content to your products.
Keep the CTA goal singular: the source notes you can have many buttons as long as they all push one decision, not several competing ones.
caveats: Copy the structure and layout, not another brand's copyrighted assets or copy.
Button size/placement preferences are the source's tested opinions; test on your own list.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Educate with a product 'bridge' section to justify the price
cards.summary: Add an educational section that names product features and ties them to customer benefits to give a reason to buy.
cards.use_when: Designing product or launch emails where the hero alone just says 'shop our shoes' without explaining why the product is good.
steps: After the hero, add a bridge/education section that names concrete product features (the source's example: engineered mesh, dura outsole, 4mm lugs).
Tie each feature to a benefit framed around the customer, not the product in isolation.
For a content/blog email, use the bridge to summarize and add value (e.g. break down the parts of a muscle and their function) so the email teaches something.
Keep teasing the click throughout so the reader goes to the site and can shop.
Use visuals that support the education (labeled images, arrows pointing to parts) to make it feel immersive rather than blocky.
caveats: Feature-to-benefit claims must be accurate for your product; do not invent specs.
The source's specific product specs are examples from one brand, not benchmarks.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Build product interest with a GIF 'mix and match' section
cards.summary: Create a flipping GIF that pairs tops and bottoms to help customers visualize a full outfit and click through.
cards.use_when: Designing a merch/bestseller email where you want to show multiple product combinations without a wall of static images.
steps: In Figma, create a 600px-wide frame and place the first product pairing image plus a circle/arrows overlay hinting at flipping.
Duplicate the frame and swap in the next top/bottom combination; repeat so it cycles tops while holding bottoms, then cycles bottoms.
Select all frames and run a GIF plugin (the source uses one called Gif Canvas) to generate the animated file.
Insert the GIF into the email design and verify playback in the preview; static Figma won't animate but the exported GIF will.
Add a 'shop now' button beneath the GIF.
Centering the GIF and giving it a clean button keeps the section usable across clients.
caveats: GIF file size matters for load time — keep the animation reasonably compact.
Verify plugin availability/behavior since Figma plugins can change.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Add texture, gradients, and depth so emails don't look flat
cards.summary: Use background texture, gradients, and layering tricks to make branded emails feel immersive rather than blocky.
cards.use_when: Your email sections look like flat white blocks and you want to add life and flow without changing the copy.
steps: Pull a subtle background texture from the brand site and place it behind the hero content, then send it to the back so it doesn't block content.
Use brand logos/logomarks as faint layered elements to add depth without distracting.
To blend a gray section into a white footer, create a full-width rectangle, apply a linear gradient, set the top stop to the section color and the bottom stop to white so it flows.
Use a background-removal plugin to cut a subject out of a photo, then place large outlined type behind the subject for a layered hero effect.
Apply drop shadows to make photographic elements stand out (the source nudges the shadow offset sideways for depth).
Use white/outlined text over dark image areas and add a black-to-transparent gradient behind text to keep it readable.
caveats: Layering and gradients add file size; compress assets before upload.
Verify current plugin names/behavior before relying on them.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Reduce thumb stretch: size and place CTAs for mobile taps
cards.summary: Put large, centered CTAs where a phone-holding thumb can easily reach, because small corner buttons hurt clicks.
cards.use_when: Placing buttons in an email hero or product section and deciding size and position for mobile readers.
steps: Avoid small buttons in the top-left corner: the source notes a right-handed thumb has to stretch to reach it, and says this measurably hurts conversions.
Make the primary CTA large enough to be unmissable (the source jokes even a blind person would see it).
Center the hero button and place it prominently rather than burying it.
Underline text links or use a clear 'shop now' button — the source says he has A/B tested this consistently and clicks rise when links are underlined or buttons are explicit.
Vary button placement occasionally so readers don't get the same layout every email, while keeping the key CTA prominent.
Give each product block its own shop-now button, then a general CTA for shoppers who don't want the featured items.
caveats: The thumb-reach and underline claims are the source's tested opinions; validate for your audience.
Button sizing should be checked against your template/rendering across major clients.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Give a fallback general CTA plus shop-by-collection at the bottom
cards.summary: Add a broad CTA and category links so shoppers who don't want the featured products still have a path to buy.
cards.use_when: An email features specific products or a niche angle (e.g. yoga) and you want it to convert non-targeted subscribers too.
steps: After listing featured products with their own CTAs, add a general 'shop now' so people who don't like those exact items can still browse.
At the bottom, add shop-by-collection/category links (the source's example used running, workout, casual, yoga) so subscribers not doing that activity still have options.
For activity-specific emails, add a line broadening the relevance (e.g. 'style doesn't stop at the mat') and show products plus testimonials.
End with a large category CTA.
Keep the email working for the whole list, not just the segment the angle targets.
caveats: More CTAs risk diluting the message; the source argues it's fine as long as they point to one overall decision (shopping).
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Use big aggregate review counts as a trust signal in emails
cards.summary: Surface verified review volume and select testimonials that answer objections to build trust and goodwill.
cards.use_when: Building a social-proof or reviews email, or adding a trust section to a product email.
steps: Use the aggregate verified-review figure (the source's example displayed '100,000+ verified reviews') as a big selling point instead of a precise small number.
Hand-pick testimonials that overcome specific objections and span customer types (the source made sure to include male and female reviewers).
Bold the main points inside each testimonial so the value reads at a glance.
Present testimonials visually (the source put them in framed text boxes on a phone graphic, with star icons made from shape tools).
Frame the email personally with a headline like 'by gym lovers for gym lovers' to counter a corporate feel.
Add a lifestyle photo gallery plus shop-now at the bottom to add life without overwhelming the reader.
Keep it simple: the source skipped featuring products in the social-proof email, focusing on trust, then a shop button.
caveats: The source states testimonials 'always help' based on testing for large brands; that's his opinion, not a universal result.
Display only review numbers you can substantiate.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Write blog emails that sell the click and teach on the way
cards.summary: Structure a content email so the reader clicks through to the full post while getting value in the email itself.
cards.use_when: Sending a blog/content email to drive site traffic and downstream purchases.
steps: Lead with headline + body copy + a 'learn more' button at the top so the click is easy.
Tease the content and sell the click in the body (the source framed it as a short list, e.g. 'top 5 dumbbell back exercises').
Add a bridge section that gives real value inline — summarize and break down the topic (the source used a 'back anatomy 101' breakdown of muscle parts and functions) so the email isn't just a teaser.
Connect each educational element back to the blog and site so readers who go deeper can shop.
Include multiple 'learn more' reminders down the email and end with product photos plus the CTA.
Use benefit/motivational copy to sell the click (the source emphasized the exercises work with minimal equipment and space, for busy-gym-to-small-living-room use).
caveats: Multiple CTAs are fine here because they all point to one action (reading the post); don't mix in competing goals.
Keep the inline education accurate and consistent with the linked post.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Lay out copy section-by-section before designing
cards.summary: Plan the email's sections and write the copy in a doc first so design and layout follow a clear structure.
cards.use_when: Starting a new campaign email and you want copy organized before touching the design tool.
steps: Lay out the email in a doc as distinct sections (headline, body, button, bridge, product block, footer) so you can see the structure.
Write each section's copy against that plan, matching the winning hero pattern (headline + body + button).

For brand-voice body copy, prompt an AI with the brand's voice and the desired tone (the source asked for two sentences in the brand's voice about the gym) and treat the output as a draft to work with, not final.
Reference successful brands' emails while writing to borrow proven section structures rather than reinventing layout.
Hand the sectioned doc to a designer with clear labels (e.g. 'insert photo gallery of lifestyle pictures', 'mix and match tops and bottoms') so they know what each block needs.
Keep a consistent footer across emails with shop-by buttons (e.g. men/women) and social links.
caveats: AI copy needs brand-voice checking; the source notes you sometimes have to work with the output.
This is a production workflow, not a performance claim.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Choose a design tool that supports advanced layout
cards.summary: Prefer a more capable design tool (Figma) over basic tools when building immersive, layered email designs.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to design campaign emails and needing layered type, gradients, background removal, and GIF plugins.
steps: Use Figma for composite/advanced email design: it organizes layers well and supports the plugins needed (background remover, GIF canvas).
Note that the source rates Canva as good but more basic and harder to organize — fine for simpler emails, limited for advanced effects.
Start each email with a 600px-wide frame as the canvas.
Build buttons from a rectangle (set corner radius, e.g. 30) plus a text layer, then color and size them.
Use shapes, images, text, strokes (outline type), gradients, and effects (drop shadow) to build immersive sections.
Verify current plugin availability and UI, since Figma plugins and menus change.
caveats: Tool preference is the source's opinion; use whatever your team can execute well.
Plugin-dependent steps may break if a plugin is removed or renamed.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Keep the CTA goal singular even with many buttons
cards.summary: A long email can have many buttons as long as they all drive one decision, not several competing ones.
cards.use_when: Designing a multi-section email and deciding how many CTAs to include.
steps: Pick the single action the email should drive (read the post, shop the collection, shop the product).
Repeat that same CTA down the email (the source used multiple 'learn more' buttons) rather than introducing new, different asks.
Place CTAs after key sections: hero, education bridge, product blocks, and bottom category links.
Avoid telling the customer too many different things in one email; competing goals dilute the click.
Use shop-by buttons in the footer (e.g. men/women) that still funnel toward shopping.
caveats: This is the source's working rule of thumb, not a tested universal law; monitor your own click-through by placement.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Compress email images to protect load time
cards.summary: Compress exported email slice images before upload so the email loads fast in the inbox.
cards.use_when: Preparing Figma slice exports for upload to your ESP.
steps: Export slices from Figma (the source exports at 2x for quality, JPEG format).
Run all slices through an image compressor before uploading (the source used iloveimg.com).
Check the size savings: the session went from 2.84 MB to 469 KB with little quality loss.
Keep each slice reasonably small; avoid one giant image for a long section.
Upload compressed slices into your ESP and rebuild the email there.
caveats: Aggressive compression can degrade quality; balance size against visual fidelity.
Verify current compressor interfaces as tools change.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Match email design and copy to the brand's voice
cards.summary: Carry the brand's visual identity, fonts, and tone into email so it doesn't read as generic or corporate.
cards.use_when: An email looks bland/corporate compared to the brand's social presence and you want it to feel on-brand.
steps: Use the actual brand font rather than a default font — the source notes it dramatically brings the design to life.
Pull real brand assets: logo, colors, background textures, lifestyle images from the brand's own channels.
Write copy in the brand's voice (the source prompted an AI to write in the brand's voice and then refined it).
Aim for an immersive, fun feel rather than blocky, plain-white sections.
Mirror the energy and community language of the brand's Instagram in the email.
Add life to flat sections with lifestyle imagery and color rather than plain studio product shots.
caveats: Brand-voice copy from AI must be checked against the brand's actual voice.
Visual taste judgments are subjective; the source's '10/10' ratings are his opinion.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Footer text block to offset image-heavy emails
cards.summary: Pad image-heavy campaigns with invisible footer text to reduce spammy image-to-text ratios in Gmail's eyes.
cards.use_when: Before scheduling a design-heavy campaign or hero-image email that contains little body copy, when you want to reduce the risk of promotions/spam placement.
steps: Recognize the pattern the source flags: if an email is mostly images with only a few lines of text, this can look 'fishy' to Gmail.
Found a campaign that uses almost no text? Compensate by adding a large block of real prose (the source copies a brand's About Us page) at the bottom of the email.
In the email builder, add a text block at the very bottom, paste the text, and center it.

Style it to be effectively invisible: set font size very small (the source uses size five), set font color to the same color as the background, and reduce line spacing (the source uses about 5%) so it consumes almost no vertical space.
Confirm the block is invisible in both desktop and mobile previews before sending.
Send a test preview to yourself and check layout, links and rendering before scheduling.
caveats: Presented by the source as a trick it likes to use, not a guaranteed deliverability fix; hidden text can itself be treated as a spam signal by some filters, so treat as an experiment and monitor placement.
Only use text you have the right to reuse (the source copies another brand's About page content, which is not advisable for your own commercial emails).
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Link and alt-text pass before a campaign goes out
cards.summary: Finish every email by wiring all image/button links and writing alt text, then test-send before scheduling.
cards.use_when: Final QA step on any campaign, after copy and design are done and before scheduling the send.
steps: Walk the email top to bottom and link every clickable element to the correct destination: the source links the main hero to the brand's home page, one section to the blog, and collection sections to the men's and women's category pages.
Match each link to the section's intent rather than defaulting everything to the homepage.
Add alt text to each image, briefly paraphrasing the message (the source's example: 'top no-fuss dumbbell back exercises').
Note that image blocking affects a very small share of recipients (source says under 1%), so alt text is secondary but quick to add.
Send yourself a test email and click every link, then check desktop and mobile rendering.
Only then schedule or send the campaign.
caveats: The source states alt text may sometimes help deliverability but is 'really not a big deal' — don't treat it as a major ranking lever.
Exact button locations and preview options in your ESP may change; verify in the current interface.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Treat deliverability as a sender reputation score
cards.summary: Inbox providers rank you like a credit score: good reputation lands in primary, bad lands in spam, mediocre lands in promotions.
cards.use_when: When diagnosing why campaigns aren't being seen, or when deciding whether low revenue is a content problem or a placement problem.
steps: Frame deliverability as your domain/IP 'credit score' — the question is whether you land in primary, promotions or spam.
Understand the provider's incentive: inbox providers only surface emails users want so users keep using the platform; they watch engagement as the signal.
Use open and click engagement as the practical proxy: if few people open or click, providers push you toward promotions or spam, which further reduces visibility — a self-reinforcing cycle.
Check the technical layer first: the source says if your ESP (e.g., Klaviyo) shows no warning at the top of the homepage about domain setup, assume technical requirements are already in place.
If technicals are fine, split the cause into two: either your emails are weak, or your sender reputation is poor and you are being filtered.
caveats: The credit-score framing is the source's analogy, not an official metric.
The source's claim that a clean ESP dashboard means you're fine is a simplification — authentication and domain setup still deserve a direct check.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Improve the emails before chasing technical fixes
cards.summary: The source's number-one deliverability lever is simply sending better, more varied, engaging email content.
cards.use_when: When open rates are low and you're tempted to look for technical hacks instead of fixing the content your list receives.
steps: Accept the source's framing: low engagement has two causes — emails people don't want to open, or poor sender reputation from placement.
Attack the content side first: the source calls sending better content the number-one lever it sees for deliverability gains.
Avoid the templated look: the source warns against 'send the same templated BS' where you drop a product into a template in five minutes with no clear value to the reader.
Instead vary the topic and format each send so opening gives a small reward — the source describes this as a dopamine loop where a good past email makes the next open more likely.
Use a clean design and genuinely good copy, and give people a reason to look forward to the send.
Keep the format varied (the source sends different topics and layouts rather than one repeated template).
caveats: This is the presenter's opinion grounded in agency experience, not a controlled benchmark.
Improved content still won't help if authentication and reputation basics are broken.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Build 14/30/60/90-day engaged segments
cards.summary: Create rolling engagement segments defined by opens or clicks in the last 14, 30, 60 and 90 days, excluding bounces.
cards.use_when: Setting up the segment structure before running a deliverability recovery, or before deciding who should be in your base sending list.
steps: In your ESP segment builder, create four segments keyed on recency: opened or clicked in the last 14, 30, 60 and 90 days.
Include an OR condition: opened email at least once in the window OR clicked email at least once in the window — the source adds this because click tracking can register without an open being logged.
Add a subscribed condition so only marketable contacts are included.
Add a condition requiring zero bounced emails.
Repeat the same structure for each window so the segments nest: 14-day inside 30-day inside 60-day inside 90-day.
Use these four segments as the gating logic for every campaign you send during recovery.
caveats: The source notes click tracking can be unreliable in some ESPs, so the OR condition is a fail-safe rather than a perfect measure.
Window lengths are the source's heuristics; adapt to your list size and send frequency.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Six-week deliverability recovery protocol
cards.summary: Warm reputation back by sending only to tight engaged segments, then expanding as open rates hold.
cards.use_when: When campaigns are landing in spam/promotions and you want a structured plan to regain primary inbox placement.
steps: Weeks 1–3: build the 14/30/60/90-day engaged segments, and turn off all automated flows except the high-engagement ones — welcome, browse abandon, cart abandon, checkout abandon and post-purchase. The source argues these are opened at a high clip (people want their discount, their cart reminder, their order info) and therefore boost credibility.
Weeks 1–3 onward: send three highly engaging campaigns per week to only the 14-day engaged list. The source argues sending one per week just stretches the same recovery over three times as long.
Expand only when earned: once the 14-day segment is consistently at 50%+ opens for three straight campaigns, add the 30-day segment at three sends per week.
Weeks 5–6: keep monitoring opens; if you dip below roughly 40–50%, tighten back to the smaller segment.
Continue expanding to the 60-day segment as opens hold near 50%, then to the 90-day segment.
Week 6+: treat the 90-day engaged list as your base sending list, and send one campaign per month to the full newsletter list to try to re-activate dormant contacts.
caveats: The 40–50% and 50%+ thresholds and the three-per-week cadence are the source's own heuristics from agency work, not industry standards.
Opening to the full list monthly works only if that campaign is genuinely engaging; the source says it can just be a normal email.
The source states its main client case went from the 20–30% open range to about 60% opens after roughly 60 days — a single example, not a promise.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Keep only high-engagement flows during recovery
cards.summary: Pause most automations and lean on welcome, abandon and post-purchase flows, which reliably earn high engagement.
cards.use_when: Deciding which automations to leave running while rebuilding sender reputation, or which flows to prioritize when you can't build everything at once.
steps: Turn off all flows except: welcome, browse abandonment, cart abandonment, checkout abandonment and post-purchase.
Keep the welcome flow because contacts just opted in for a discount and will open the first email delivering it.
Keep cart and checkout abandonment because the reminder about an item they were already considering earns strong engagement.
Keep post-purchase because customers want order information.
Understand why this matters during recovery: every send that gets opens and clicks is a vote of confidence with providers; flows generate those votes without needing new campaign content.
Re-enable the remaining flows once engagement and placement have recovered.
caveats: This is the source's recommended recovery posture, not a claim that other flows are worthless.
If a flow's own engagement is weak for your brand, including it dilutes the signal you're trying to send.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Three-to-four campaigns per week as your default cadence
cards.summary: Send 3–4 campaigns weekly to your engaged list to stay top of mind, provided the content is genuinely good.
cards.use_when: Setting your ongoing campaign frequency after recovery, or testing whether your current once-a-week rhythm is too thin.
steps: Adopt 3–4 campaigns per week to the engaged list as the default — the source reports this as the sweet spot in roughly 90% of the cases it has tested.
Accept the reasoning: if you send one email a week, people forget you and engagement decays.
Recognize the conditional: the source explicitly says if your emails are bad, 3–4 per week is too much; frequency only works when content is good.
Treat it as a compounding loop — good send, engagement, recognition, more engagement — rather than a one-off tactic.
Watch open and click rate on the engaged segments; if engagement collapses, the lever to pull is tighter segments and better content, not necessarily fewer sends.
caveats: The '90% of cases' figure is the presenter's own estimate from client work.
This cadence is asserted as opinion based on generated revenue; it is not a study and will not hold for brands with weak content or tiny lists.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Text-based emails vs graphic emails A/B test
cards.summary: Test pure-text campaigns against graphic campaigns; the source's example showed text winning on clicks and placed orders.
cards.use_when: Planning a weekly A/B test, especially for a best-sellers or product roundup campaign where you'd default to heavy graphics.
steps: Set up a split test where variant A is a fully graphic email (product imagery, banners) and variant B is a text-based email with no product imagery.
Run it on a campaign type where you assume graphics are required — the source's example was a best-sellers email, where the text version outperformed.
Reason about why text can win: almost everyone sends graphics, so plain text stands out in a crowded inbox.
Use the results to decide where text fits in your ongoing mix rather than replacing graphics entirely.
The source recommends keeping both formats in rotation and using each where it performs.
caveats: The source presents one brand's example results (text version showed roughly 50% better click rate and more placed orders) as an illustration, not a guaranteed outcome.
Results will vary by brand and audience — the source explicitly says to test rather than assume.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Judge subject-line tests on placed orders, not opens
cards.summary: Subject line can shift purchase behavior; measure its A/B test on placed order rate and revenue, not just open rate.
cards.use_when: Running subject-line tests on campaigns or abandonment emails, and deciding which subject line to roll out.
steps: Run the subject-line test as a proper split on the same email body.

Read the open rate as a check but make the decision on placed order rate and order value — the source's abandonment example had nearly identical opens (the higher-open variant was slightly ahead) yet 11.6% vs 3.8% placed order rate.

Test emotional framing: the source contrasts something lower-barrier like 'your order is ready to go / packed and ready, just click' against something like 'your order's waiting for you', and reports lower barrier-to-entry language driving the higher placed order rate.
Test an exclusivity angle too, since the source says subject lines can affect whether and how someone buys.
Repeat subject-line tests frequently (the source frames these as weekly tests), not once a month, and log placed order rate as the primary metric.
caveats: The specific 11.6% vs 3.8% figures come from one anonymized brand test and are not benchmarks.
Attribution on open rate can be noisy; the source itself notes open-rate differences may be variability.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Products vs categories in the email body
cards.summary: Test showing individual products against linking to category pages; higher-SKU brands may find individual products win.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to merchandise a campaign for a catalog with many SKUs — show specific products or send people to browse a category.
steps: If you sell many SKUs, run this test early with a client/brand, because the result shapes how you merchandise emails going forward (the source says it tests this very early).
Variant A: show or link categories — e.g., men's vs women's, or a category hub page.
Variant B: show individual products directly in the email (e.g., four men's products, four women's products).
The source's working hypothesis was that categories would win for a high-SKU store, but the test showed individual products had a higher click rate (1.14% vs 1.04%) and far more purchases.
Reason about why: when you give shoppers many category options they must keep searching; showing the product directly shortens the path.
Skip this test for single-product stores, and remember the outcome can flip by brand — the source says it sees both directions.
caveats: The source reports only one brand's numbers and notes another brand could see categories win.
The source declines to attribute the higher average order value to the email itself.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Long-form vs short-form email body copy
cards.summary: Test longer founder-story copy against a few lines of text with a clear CTA; short won in the source's welcome-flow test.
cards.use_when: Writing a welcome-flow email or any campaign where you're tempted to explain product science, origin story or background at length.
steps: Create variant A: long form, e.g., a note from the founder explaining why the product is good, with substantial background and product detail.
Create variant B: short form — the source's example was about six lines: a warm welcome, one interesting product fact, and a shop-now CTA.
Run both on a meaningful sample (the source's example used ~2,000 recipients per side) and read click rate and placed order rate.
In the source's test, the long version produced 2.4% clicks and a 0.2% placed order rate, while the short version produced 3.4% clicks and a 0.7% placed order rate.
Reason: people don't read every word; long copy buries the call to action, while short copy keeps the CTA visible.
Roll out the winner for that audience but keep testing, since the source notes the right length differs by audience.
caveats: One brand's test result; not a rule that short always wins.
The source's sample-size disclosure (~2,000 each side) is what it used to argue the result wasn't accidental — your own significance needs depend on your volumes.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Test send time of day for campaigns
cards.summary: Morning vs late-afternoon sends can swing engagement sharply; dial in your brand's best window.
cards.use_when: After you've settled cadence and content, when tuning when campaigns actually go out.
steps: Set up a same-day time split on a campaign — the source's example compared roughly 11 a.m. against 4 p.m.
Read open rate, click rate and placed order rate; the source's example showed 36% opens in the morning vs 26% in the late afternoon, with placed orders much higher earlier in the day.
Don't assume the intuitive answer: the source notes people often assume evenings or late afternoon work because shoppers are off work, but in its test the lunchtime-ish window performed better.
Account for the sample issue: the source cautions there were too few placed orders at the lower-performing time to lean on that metric alone.
Once you identify a better window, apply it persistently — the source frames the payoff as a fixed uplift per campaign that compounds over months.
Re-test occasionally, since the best window is brand-specific.
caveats: One brand's timing test with a thin placed-order sample; the source says results depend on the brand.
Send-time tools and inbox behavior change; verify how your ESP handles time-zone splits.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Test flow delay timing for site abandonment
cards.summary: A 30-minute reminder isn't always better than a 4-hour one — test delays in abandonment flows on placed order rate.
cards.use_when: Setting the delay on a browse/site abandonment flow or any reminder email where you've assumed 'strike while the iron is hot'.
steps: Set up a test on the flow's first delay: variant A sends around 30 minutes after abandonment, variant B waits about 4 hours.

Use the source's example as the hypothesis to challenge: the 30-minute version was assumed to be better because the visit was fresh, but it produced a much lower placed order rate (0.7%) than the 4-hour version, on a large sample.
Read engagement carefully: the fast version had fewer opens and clicks, which the source interprets as people not being ready yet; the later send reached them when they had time to buy.
Consider the context explanation: someone who abandons may be busy with kids or errands and still busy 30 minutes later, but settled in bed at night when the 4-hour reminder arrives.
Apply the same testing discipline to delays between later messages in the flow, not just the first email.
caveats: This is one brand's flow test; the source says delays will differ per flow and must be tested.
Placed order rate on a flow depends on attribution windows — verify how your ESP attributes flow revenue.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Branded text email vs plain native text email
cards.summary: Once you choose text-based sends, test a branded version (logo header/footer) against a fully plain native-format email.
cards.use_when: Executing text-based campaigns and deciding whether to include your logo and footer or send truly plain text.
steps: Define variant A — branded text: plain text body with your logo at the top (clickable, driving site visits) and your footer at the bottom, giving brand association.

Define variant B — plain text: nothing but text, rendered in the inbox provider's native format (white background, black text, like an email from a friend), usually a bit shorter and easier to digest.

Run the test and compare delivered volume, click rate and placed order rate; the source's example had 1,900 delivered on branded vs 1,400 on plain, similar revenue, but plain showed a higher placed order rate (1.7% vs 1.2%) and higher click rate (4% vs 3%).
Choose per message intent: the source suggests plain/perceived-personal for founder-voice emails ('hey, it's Max, the founder'), and branded text when the message comes from the brand itself.
Keep both in your rotation and lean toward the one performing better for your list.
caveats: One brand's test with modest delivered volumes; the source notes results depend on the brand and message.
The plain-text version sacrifices the clickable logo, which can cost some site traffic.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Weekly A/B test roster of high-leverage variables
cards.summary: Keep a standing list of high-leverage email variables and test one deliberately every week rather than tweaking two words monthly.
cards.use_when: Building a recurring experimentation plan for your email program so testing keeps producing revenue rather than becoming sporadic.
