steps: Treat these as your roster of high-leverage variables to work through: graphic vs text-based email; subject lines; products vs categories; long vs short form; campaign send time; flow delay timing; branded vs plain text.
Run them as real splits on meaningful samples — the source criticizes one-off 'change two words once a month' tests as not enough to maximize revenue.
Read the right metric per test: placed order rate and revenue for subject lines, products-vs-categories and flow timing; click rate plus placed order rate for format and length tests.
Rotate through the roster so each variable actually gets tested for your brand instead of assumed.
Log results and roll the winner into the standing program, then re-test periodically since audiences shift.
caveats: The source lists these variables from its own agency practice; they're a prioritization, not an exhaustive or statistically rigorous framework.
Small lists will struggle to reach significance on split tests — the source's own examples lean on ~2,000-per-side samples.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Prime an LLM with brand context before writing email copy
cards.summary: Feed the model exhaustive brand, product, customer and voice information first so later copy prompts have real context.
cards.use_when: Setting up an AI-assisted email copy workflow for a store before generating any campaign copy.
steps: Write a priming prompt that dumps in as much brand information as possible: what you sell, mission, brand story, what makes the brand unique, ideal customer, brand voice, goals and aspirations.
Use full paragraphs rather than quick sentences — the source stresses giving it as much space and information as you can.
Include the store's website link so the model can pull additional context from it.
Keep this priming block reusable so every subsequent copy prompt in the session inherits the same context.
Expect the model to need product-level facts (materials, positioning, specific product copy) closer to when you draft.
caveats: The source's example primer for a large apparel brand is described as 'pretty brief' — more is generally better.
Model behavior and supported features change; verify what your current tool does with links and long prompts.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Prompt for graphic-email copy structure, then iterate
cards.summary: Ask for graphic-campaign copy with a punchy headline, subheadline and short body leading to a shop-now CTA, then refine across several rounds.
cards.use_when: Drafting hero and body copy for a graphic campaign and you want structured output instead of a wall of generic AI prose.
steps: State the format explicitly: 'we're creating a graphic based email campaign with minimal copy to send to our customers' — the source says without 'graphic based' the model returns letter-style text.
State the topic in plain language, including the emotional angle (e.g., best sellers as your MVP in the gym, helping you break PRs).
Request a 'quick and punchy' headline — the source says without 'punchy' you get a 20-word headline.
Request a slightly longer subheadline plus 2–3 sentences of body copy leading into a shop-now CTA, mirroring the hero structure of headline → subheadline → body → button.
Treat the first output as a draft: iterate ('make it more unique', 'make the headline more conversational', 'give me more options for headlines') and combine your favorite fragments.
Do the final polish yourself — the source treats the model as a support player, not the finisher, and reports this is how its agency writes copy.
caveats: The source warns AI copy is recognizable via clichés ('you're in luck', 'crafting', 'enthusiasts', 'we're diving into the exciting world', 'unleash your potential') and should not be shipped as-is.
Prompt phrasing effectiveness is model- and version-dependent.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Generate a year of non-discount email topics from micro-topics
cards.summary: Use a macro-to-micro prompt to produce broad themes and specific subtopics that become a full year of educational, non-discount campaigns.
cards.use_when: Planning a campaign calendar and running out of non-discount angles, especially for niche or technical product categories.
steps: Write a prompt stating the niche, what you sell, your brand mission/benefits, your average customer and what they want.
Ask for 10 overarching, general topics that tie into product benefits and customer lives.

Ask for 10 very specific subtopics under each overarching topic, written to educate the customer and potentially position your product as a solution — the source's prompt produced roughly 100 usable ideas.

Treat the output as raw material: for a supplement brand the source got themes like holistic health and wellness, sustainable muscle building and the science of natural supplements, with subtopics like adaptogens and stress, sleep and muscle recovery, gut health, and mental health and fitness.
Turn each promising subtopic into one campaign, and let brand-specific angles you think of yourself take priority over the AI list.
Feed the best ideas into your 3–4-per-week cadence so non-discount content fills most of the calendar.
caveats: Output quality varies — the source notes some generated topics needed cleanup.
The source insists AI is only a starting point and should never be the sole source of your content.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Email Marketing 2025.docx

cards.title: Set SMS campaign frequency to 1–2 sends per week maximum
cards.summary: SMS hits the phone's primary app with a ding, so send far less often than email—one message per week as the default, occasionally two—to protect a hard-won list from unsubscribes.
cards.use_when: Deciding your monthly SMS campaign cadence and how many messages to schedule per week for your store's list.
steps: Treat 1 SMS per week as your standing default and 2 per week as the rare exception, reserving extra sends for big events.

Recognize SMS is more intrusive than email because it triggers a notification sound and vibration in a primary app; the source says it is not comparable to sending 4–5 emails per week without backlash.
Use segmentation and selective sending so only the relevant portion of the list gets each message, reducing annoyance while keeping total weekly volume low.
Watch unsubscribe rate as your primary guardrail: the source reports unsubscribe rates on SMS run much higher than email, and that they rise the more you send.
Plan a regular monthly cadence of roughly 1–2 sends per week rather than blasting everything at a launch and going silent.
caveats: The 1–2 per week figure is the presenter's tested recommendation, not an industry standard; test against your own unsubscribe and revenue data.
Back-to-back daily sends (e.g., flash sale launch day then last-chance day) are acceptable for major events per the source.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About SMS Marketing in 2025.docx

cards.title: Budget SMS copy using the rendered segment count
cards.summary: Estimate actual message segments after personalization, links and required text rather than relying on a universal 160-character cutoff.
cards.use_when: Writing and editing SMS campaign or flow copy before sending, to control per-message cost.
steps: Preview the fully rendered message, including personalization, links and opt-out text.
Standard GSM-7 SMS allows 160 characters in one segment; Unicode or emoji can reduce that to 70. Multipart limits differ.
Use the provider segment counter and current destination pricing to estimate total campaign cost.
Compare a concise version with the original on net contribution, preserving clarity and required information.
caveats: An emoji does not simply cost a fixed 35-50 characters; it can change encoding for the whole message. https://help.klaviyo.com/hc/en-us/articles/13502982552347
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About SMS Marketing in 2025.docx

cards.title: Check SMS encoding and segment cost before sending
cards.summary: Estimate actual message segments after personalization, links and required text rather than relying on a universal 160-character cutoff.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to include emojis in SMS campaign or flow copy to add visual interest without images.
steps: Preview the fully rendered message, including personalization, links and opt-out text.
Standard GSM-7 SMS allows 160 characters in one segment; Unicode or emoji can reduce that to 70. Multipart limits differ.
Use the provider segment counter and current destination pricing to estimate total campaign cost.
Compare a concise version with the original on net contribution, preserving clarity and required information.
caveats: An emoji does not simply cost a fixed 35-50 characters; it can change encoding for the whole message. https://help.klaviyo.com/hc/en-us/articles/13502982552347
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About SMS Marketing in 2025.docx

cards.title: Reserve MMS images for campaigns where they earn 2–3x the SMS revenue
cards.summary: MMS (image) messages cost 2–3 times more than plain SMS, so include a picture only when the message can plausibly generate two to three times the revenue of a text-only send.
cards.use_when: Choosing between a plain-text SMS and an image MMS for a product launch or campaign send.
steps: Default to plain-text SMS for your regular campaign and flow sends, since SMS itself is already far more expensive than email per message.
Before attaching an image, estimate whether the MMS send must produce 2–3x the revenue of the SMS version to break even on cost—the source says this is rarely achieved by one image.
Restrict MMS to situations where the visual is essential (e.g., a highly visual product drop) and you can defend the cost with expected revenue.
Compare MMS vs SMS versions of similar sends over time in your dashboard to see whether images genuinely lift response for your audience before scaling them up.
caveats: The 2–3x cost multiplier is the presenter's stated range; your provider's rate card may differ, so confirm actual per-message pricing.
The source's advice is to stick to SMS as much as possible, but treats MMS as a judgment call rather than a prohibition.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About SMS Marketing in 2025.docx

cards.title: Choose an SMS platform that consolidates with your existing email stack
cards.summary: Most SMS platforms do the same core things at similar prices, so pick one—ideally the same tool you already use for email—and ignore marginal AI feature comparisons.
cards.use_when: Selecting or switching an SMS provider for your store before building flows and campaigns.
steps: Check whether your current email platform also offers SMS; the source recommends Klaviyo users stay on Klaviyo to consolidate marketing in one place.
If considering alternatives, the source names Attentive and Postscript as solid options alongside Klaviyo.
Discount vendor comparisons built on novel AI features—the source argues these features are rarely used and the differences are marginal.
Note that the main platforms are similarly priced, so switching to save money is often not the deciding factor.
Expect the provider to support a dedicated phone number, data tracking, and automation setup; follow the provider's own setup guide, which the source says takes minutes.
Verify current pricing, feature sets and setup steps directly with the vendor, as these change.
caveats: The named tools reflect the source's opinion at time of recording; verify current capabilities and pricing.
There is no single 'correct' platform per the source—consolidation and simplicity are the main criteria.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About SMS Marketing in 2025.docx

cards.title: Grow the SMS list with a post-purchase opt-in checkbox
cards.summary: Add a marketing opt-in checkbox at checkout so every buyer passively contributes a phone number, giving you a growing list in the background.
cards.use_when: Setting up checkout and post-purchase list growth to continuously add SMS subscribers without extra traffic.
steps: Place a checkbox on the purchase/checkout page asking the buyer to agree to receive marketing messages.
Keep it on for all buyers so the list grows automatically with every order.
Position SMS opt-in alongside email opt-in so the same checkout flow captures both channels.
Treat this as the low-effort baseline channel; the source still calls pop-ups the most effective list-growth method, so run both.
Confirm your checkout and SMS platform support the consent capture and that opt-ins sync to the right list.
caveats: Post-purchase opt-ins yield fewer subscribers than a well-optimized pop-up per the source; they are a background contributor, not the main driver.
Consent and messaging regulations vary by region—confirm compliance for your markets.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About SMS Marketing in 2025.docx

cards.title: Delay the SMS/email pop-up trigger to 6–10 seconds after page load
cards.summary: Trigger signup pop-ups on a 6–10 second time delay—not scroll or exit intent—to maximize views without hurting site conversions.
cards.use_when: Configuring the trigger and display rules of a website pop-up form that captures email and SMS subscribers.
steps: Set the pop-up trigger to a time delay of about 6–10 seconds after the page loads, which the source says is not too soon and has been tested.
Avoid scroll-based or exit-intent triggers, which the source says can misfire; a simple time delay performs reliably.
Reject long delays: the source argues few visitors stay 30 seconds, so waiting that long means few people ever see the form.
Balance intrusiveness: the form should be seen by as many visitors as possible without harming website conversions, which is the stated fine line.
Monitor both form conversion rate and overall site conversion rate after launch to confirm the delay is not hurting purchases.
caveats: The 6–10 second window is the presenter's tested recommendation for their client set, not a universal optimum; test on your own traffic.
Pop-up timing interacts with page speed and device type—validate on mobile specifically.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About SMS Marketing in 2025.docx

cards.title: Build a two-step micro-commitment pop-up: email first, then phone
cards.summary: Ask for email in step one, then prompt for the phone number in step two with benefit-driven copy, which the source says converts roughly ten times better than asking for both at once.
cards.use_when: Designing the multi-step flow of a website signup pop-up to capture both email and SMS subscribers.
steps: Step one: state the offer plainly ('this is what you get') and ask only for the email address.
Step two: immediately prompt for the phone number with copy that ties it to completing the offer, e.g. 'finish signing up to get your discount'.
Use as few words as possible in both steps—simplicity is emphasized repeatedly.
Never ask for birthday, product preferences, or other fields in the same step; the source says extra fields kill completion.
Offer something of value—a discount, giveaway, or free guide—since the source notes people will not hand over a phone number for nothing.
Test the two-step version against a single combined field to confirm the lift in your own funnel.
caveats: The '10x better' comparison is the presenter's claim from their testing, not an independent benchmark.
Discount offers trade margin on the first purchase; the source assumes a strong email/SMS backend recovers that margin over time.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About SMS Marketing in 2025.docx

cards.title: Aim pop-up forms at 8–10% conversion vs the 2–3% baseline
cards.summary: Most audited brands convert only ~2–3% of visitors via pop-up; optimizing trigger, offer, and form simplicity can reach 8–10%, tripling list acquisition from same traffic.
cards.use_when: Benchmarking and improving the conversion rate of your site's email/SMS signup form against typical performance.
steps: Measure your current pop-up conversion rate (new subscribers divided by visitors who saw the form) to establish a baseline.
Compare against the source's observed baseline: most audited brands sit around 2–3%.
Apply the levers that drive the source's 8–10% results: a 6–10 second time delay, a strong offer, minimal copy, and the two-step email-then-phone flow.
Track the form's impact on total site conversion so you can confirm the extra visibility is not costing more sales than it creates.
Re-test offer strength separately from form design, since the source stresses you must give people a reason to sign up.
caveats: 8–10% is an outcome the presenter reports from their own optimization work, not a guaranteed result; it is a target, not a promise.
Results depend on traffic source, offer, and audience; poor-fit traffic may never reach those levels.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About SMS Marketing in 2025.docx

cards.title: Launch five core SMS automation flows before heavy campaign sending
cards.summary: Set up Welcome, Browse Abandonment, Cart Abandonment, Checkout Abandonment, and Win-back flows, keeping each short and high-ROI, since automations run in the background and earn clicks without extra effort.
cards.use_when: Building the automated SMS flow system for a store, or deciding which flows to prioritize first.
steps: Welcome flow: deliver the promised discount to new subscribers in about 2–3 SMS messages.
Browse abandonment: message users who viewed a product and left, prompting them to return and finish.
Cart abandonment and checkout abandonment: remind people who added to cart or reached checkout to complete the order with a direct link.
Win-back: re-engage customers who purchased months ago and have not returned, optionally with a discount.
Keep flow volume light—do not overload customers with messages, since flows are meant for quick, high-converting, high-ROI touches rather than retention nurturing.
Use your platform's templates and connect it to your store platform (e.g., Shopify) so triggers fire automatically; the source says setup is easy and templates exist for base flows.
caveats: The source says you 'really don't need too much' in flows—avoid adding many extra steps.
Template copy and trigger names may change in the platform interface; verify current setup steps in your tool.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About SMS Marketing in 2025.docx

cards.title: Keep SMS campaigns transactional, urgent, or announcement-based—not nurture
cards.summary: SMS campaigns should carry product drops, special offers, restocks, and announcements; pure nurture or social-proof content tends to get high unsubscribes and poor ROI on SMS.
cards.use_when: Choosing what content types belong in the SMS campaign calendar versus what should stay in email.
steps: Assign to SMS: product drops and launches, flash sales, special offers, back-in-stock/restock alerts, and important announcements.
Assign to email: nurture, educational, and social-proof content; the source says email is where you can nurture without annoying people.
Use angles that manufacture importance where relevant, e.g. a 'back in stock' message, since urgency fits the channel.
Send mostly transactional-style content on SMS and reserve the bulk of relationship-building content for email.
Cut any SMS campaign type that historically shows high unsubscribes and weak ROI in your own data, since the source found nurture/social-proof SMS underperformed.
caveats: This reflects the presenter's tested experience; your audience may tolerate more or less nurture content, so test.
Some announcement types (e.g., giveaways to grow social) are used as filler, not core revenue drivers.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About SMS Marketing in 2025.docx

cards.title: Model the SMS month around launches and flash sales, then fill the gaps
cards.summary: Anchor the SMS calendar on big events—product launches get 2–3 messages, flash sales get 2—then insert 2–3 filler campaigns (giveaway, restock) to keep a 1–2 per week cadence.
cards.use_when: Planning a store's monthly SMS campaign calendar around known launch and promotion dates.
steps: List the month's main events first; use the source's example of a brand with a Halloween product launch mid-month and a Halloween flash sale on the last two days.

For a product launch, plan about 2–3 messages: an announcement on launch day (likely the biggest sales driver), a reminder or low-stock/urgency message about a week later, and optionally a teaser 1–2 days before to build hype.
For a flash sale, send two messages: a launch message on day one and a last-chance message on the final day; the source says back-to-back daily sends are fine for big events.
Identify gaps of more than a week without an SMS and insert 2–3 filler campaigns, e.g. a social media giveaway driving to Instagram, or a 'restock' alert for a popular item.
Note the source's rationale for restock sends: an item that sold out proves popularity, and the restock itself creates urgency—you can even run one on an item that was not literally out of stock.
Count total sends against the 1–2 per week ceiling and trim if the calendar exceeds it.
caveats: The example calendar is an illustration for an eight-figure brand, not a template that fits every store size or category.
The suggested restock angle may not be appropriate if it misrepresents inventory availability.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About SMS Marketing in 2025.docx

cards.title: Test SMS send times; default to 11 a.m.–2 p.m. and 4–5 p.m.
cards.summary: There is no universal best send time, so test per audience; the source's safer windows are midday and early evening, avoiding pre-10 a.m. and post-7:30 p.m.
cards.use_when: Scheduling SMS campaigns and last-chance messages to maximize open and click response for your specific list.
steps: Run your own tests across times of day, since the source says every audience differs and there is no single right answer.
Use 11 a.m.–2 p.m. as the safest default window, when people are between morning and lunch.
Try early evening at 4–5 p.m. as a secondary window that the source says performs well.
Avoid sending before 10 a.m. (people sleep in) and after about 7:30 p.m. (people go to bed or turn off phones).
Schedule last-chance messages around 6–7 p.m. with a short deadline like '4 hours left', but not later than that window.
Track clicks and revenue by send hour over multiple sends before locking in a standard time.
caveats: These windows are the presenter's tested heuristics, not universal laws; confirm with your own A/B timing tests.
Timezone spread in your list can blur results—segment or schedule per timezone where your platform allows.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About SMS Marketing in 2025.docx

cards.title: Treat the SMS list as a channel asset for revenue you control
cards.summary: The source frames SMS as a near-guaranteed-seen channel with very high open rates and an owned list—unlike ad accounts that platforms can shut down—and reports major contribution to store revenue.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest budget and team time in building an SMS channel versus relying solely on paid acquisition.
steps: Evaluate SMS as an owned audience asset: contacts gave you their number, so they are not cold traffic and the list cannot be revoked by an ad platform.
Recognize the reach mechanic: the source cites an average 98% open rate because text messages are seen almost immediately by nearly everyone.
Expect automations to run continuously in the background after one-time setup, requiring only periodic checks and optimization.

Judge channel value against your store's revenue mix; the source cites an example brand generating $750k in 30 days from SMS (roughly 20% of total revenue) and $422k from automations alone in the same window.
Set expectations by tracking your own SMS-attributed revenue and automation click rates rather than adopting case-study numbers as targets.
caveats: The 98% open rate and the $750k/$422k figures are the presenter's cited examples, not benchmarks or promises; your results depend on list size, offer, and product.
Introductory framing of 'SMS is the future' is the presenter's opinion; treat it as a rationale for testing, not a guaranteed channel outcome.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About SMS Marketing in 2025.docx

cards.title: Choose an SMS platform: consolidate with email, then price-shop
cards.summary: Pick SMS in the same platform as your email for management simplicity, but get competing quotes since SMS pricing varies and features rarely matter.
cards.use_when: Selecting or renegotiating the SMS/text platform for your store's lifecycle messaging.
steps: Prioritize running SMS inside the same platform as your email (e.g., Klaviyo, Omnisend, Attentive) so lists, segments and reporting live in one place.
Because consolidation often costs more, request a quote from your current email provider for their SMS add-on.
Take that quote to the main SMS competitors (source names Attentive and Postscript as the 'big dogs'; others such as OneText exist) and ask them to beat it, letting them compete on price.

Decide mainly on price and ease of management. The source argues the platforms' differentiating AI features are unlikely to be used and 'the basics will drive 99% of your revenue,' so don't agonize over the choice.
caveats: This is the presenter's opinion (Max / Well Copy); platform pricing and feature sets change, so verify current quotes and contracts.
Platform names and capabilities are source-specific and may be outdated.
cards.source_name: How to Create a SMS Marketing Strategy For $10M Shopify Brands.docx

cards.title: Capture phone numbers in your popup from day one
cards.summary: Add an SMS phone field to your email popup now, even with no SMS program, so your text list compounds instead of starting from zero later.
cards.use_when: Designing or revising the email/SMS signup popup that captures subscribers at store entry.
steps: Include a phone-number field in your popup even if you have no SMS list yet. The source's argument: if you start collecting SMS today and only decide to use it a year later, you already have a large list to market to; if you wait, you have zero.

Use a popup tool optimized for SMS capture. The source recommends Alia (allpopups.com) over native platform popups, reporting native Klaviyo opt-ins around 3–4% vs. Alia submit rates around 9% and typically ~16% when the offer is strong.
Track phone opt-in rate as a headline metric; the source frames getting ~60% of ad traffic to hand over a phone number as a major cheap-conversion unlock.
Refresh offers/tests over time so capture rate is judged on its own, not against one weak offer.
caveats: Opt-in rates cited (3–4%, 9%, ~16%) are the presenter's observed figures for specific brands, not guaranteed benchmarks.
Tool names and interface details may change; verify current setup.
cards.source_name: How to Create a SMS Marketing Strategy For $10M Shopify Brands.docx

cards.title: Use a quiz popup and 'activate your discount' copy to lift phone capture
cards.summary: Lead with a micro-quiz before asking for contact info, and phrase the SMS ask as finishing the signup they already started.
cards.use_when: Building the SMS/phone opt-in step of your store popup to raise subscriber capture rate.
steps: Start the popup with a quiz or micro-commitment (source: 'this is what works') before requesting email or phone — engage the visitor first, then ask.
Choose a template that offers a discount (e.g., 10% off) and asks a qualifying question, then transitions to the contact step.
Change the button label from 'Continue' (which signals another required step) to 'Claim now' to reduce drop-off.

Replace generic SMS copy like 'Sign up for texts' or 'Get exclusive deals' with action-oriented continuity copy such as 'Finish signing up with text to activate your discount' — the visitor has already given email and wants the discount activated.
Do not stack an extra discount for SMS. The source reports no marginal impact from offering extra % off for the phone number.
caveats: Quiz-first flows and copy results are the presenter's experience, not a universal rule.
Source claims 15%+ opt-in is achievable but notes most forms they review sit at 5–6% submit rate.
cards.source_name: How to Create a SMS Marketing Strategy For $10M Shopify Brands.docx

cards.title: Treat SMS as high-urgency, low-frequency — not a nurture channel
cards.summary: SMS tolerates far fewer sends than email; reserve it for time-sensitive, worth-the-ding messages or you get punishing unsubscribe rates.
cards.use_when: Deciding what content belongs in SMS blasts vs. email, and setting the tone of your text program.
steps: Recognize the cost of intrusion: source reports SMS unsubscribe rates of 3–5% vs. roughly 0.3% for email, because a text is a phone ding the customer notices.
Send far less on SMS than on email. Cut nurture content (testimonials, brand storytelling, evergreen best-sellers) — the source says it 'doesn't work' on SMS and drives unsubscribes long-term.
Reserve SMS for high-urgency events: product launches, back-in-stock/restock alerts, flash sales, private events, insider details.
Make each text 'worth receiving' and get straight to the point; test whether a timely-urgency angle (e.g., 'selling fast this week') outperforms a generic nurture angle before scaling frequency.
caveats: Unsubscribe-rate comparison is the presenter's cited figure, not a site metric.
Source explicitly says this is a starting point; some brands they run send daily because it fits their context.
cards.source_name: How to Create a SMS Marketing Strategy For $10M Shopify Brands.docx

cards.title: Budget SMS copy using the rendered segment count
cards.summary: Estimate actual message segments after personalization, links and required text rather than relying on a universal 160-character cutoff.
cards.use_when: Writing and budgeting SMS campaign and flow messages, especially for large lists.
steps: Preview the fully rendered message, including personalization, links and opt-out text.
Standard GSM-7 SMS allows 160 characters in one segment; Unicode or emoji can reduce that to 70. Multipart limits differ.
Use the provider segment counter and current destination pricing to estimate total campaign cost.
Compare a concise version with the original on net contribution, preserving clarity and required information.
caveats: An emoji does not simply cost a fixed 35-50 characters; it can change encoding for the whole message. https://help.klaviyo.com/hc/en-us/articles/13502982552347
cards.source_name: How to Create a SMS Marketing Strategy For $10M Shopify Brands.docx

cards.title: Test SMS vs. MMS images on net profit, not revenue
cards.summary: Image (MMS) messages can lift revenue and buyer intent but cost ~3x, so decide by net profit after send cost, not top-line revenue.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to include product images in SMS campaigns or abandonment flows.
steps: Run A/B tests of identical messages with and without an image, and track revenue AND send cost for each version.
Source example: the image version generated ~1.3x more revenue but cost 3x to send — worse ROI on revenue, yet net-profit-positive once the extra revenue ($1,300 back on $200 extra spend) is counted.
Source example 2: no-image message did $620 revenue vs. $1,200 with image; the image cost only ~$15 more at low volume, so it was a clear win — showing results depend on list size and offer.
Note the behavioral pattern: image messages often get lower click-through (people see the product and click with higher intent), but can produce more revenue.

Use images deliberately for high-impact moments only (new flavor/product drop, key abandoned-cart/welcome messages). The source notes a 9-figure brand (Grain's) rarely uses images, reserving them for important sends.
caveats: Both examples are low-volume/single-brand results, explicitly not guarantees; the source warns it 'doesn't always play out this way.'
Retest on your own offers and list size, since cost scales with list size.
cards.source_name: How to Create a SMS Marketing Strategy For $10M Shopify Brands.docx

cards.title: Build the five core SMS flows (welcome + four abandonments + post-purchase)
cards.summary: Every brand should run a welcome flow, site/browse/cart/checkout abandonment, and a post-purchase replenishment or win-back flow.
cards.use_when: Setting up or auditing the automated (flow) side of an SMS program.
steps: Welcome flow: triggered when someone joins via the popup (often with a discount). Keep it simple — introduce the brand and drive the discount.

Four abandonment flows, kept dead simple: site abandoned (browsed site, no product page), browse abandoned (viewed a product page), cart abandoned (added to cart), checkout abandoned (reached checkout).
Post-purchase / replenishment / win-back flow: bring buyers back after their first order.
Keep abandonment messages single and simple (see the US compliance card) and split by new vs. returning buyers when you can.

Treat these basics as the moneymakers: the source reports one brand's core flows producing $517k, with $293k from welcome, $107k cart abandoned, $46k browse abandoned, $20k retention, and $13k site abandoned in a month.
caveats: Revenue figures are a single agency portfolio example, not a benchmark to expect.
Exact flow structure should be adjusted per brand context.
cards.source_name: How to Create a SMS Marketing Strategy For $10M Shopify Brands.docx

cards.title: Structure the SMS welcome flow: day 1, day 3, day 5
cards.summary: Send a tight three-message SMS welcome — intro with discount, educational reminder, then last-chance — inside a short window while subscribers are warm.
cards.use_when: Writing the SMS welcome series triggered by your popup signup.
steps: Send SMS 1 immediately: give the discount with no preamble (the person just signed up for it).
Send SMS 2 about 2 days later (day 3) with a bit of brand/differentiation info or a reminder of the discount.
Send SMS 3 on about day 5 as an 'absolute last chance' before the code expires.
Keep the window tight — do not delay sends by weeks; hit people while they're warm.

The more aggressive alternative (source cites Grain's) is a message every single day with the discount repeated, mixing in educational messages; the source frames both as valid but prefers the tighter three-message structure.
If doubling up, keep messages short: e.g., 'Welcome to [brand], here's 20% off, code WELCOME20, shop now,' then a last-chance text days later. A/B test images and delay timing.
caveats: Dense cadence (e.g., daily) should be tempered by your audience and follows compliance/consent rules.
Delay timings are recommendations, not tested universals.
cards.source_name: How to Create a SMS Marketing Strategy For $10M Shopify Brands.docx

cards.title: Send only one SMS per abandonment event (US compliance)
cards.summary: US rules limit abandonment flows to a single SMS per recipient within 48 hours, so keep cart/browse/checkout texts to one simple message.
cards.use_when: Setting up SMS cart, browse, site, or checkout abandonment flows, especially for US customers.
steps: Build each abandonment flow to send exactly one SMS per recipient — the source states sending more than one SMS in an abandonment flow is illegal in the US.
Schedule that single message to fire within 48 hours of the triggering event (source cites Klaviyo's built-in constraint of one SMS per recipient in cart abandonment within 48 hours).
Confirm the recipient has SMS consent before the flow sends.

Because you get one shot, make it simple: browse abandoned → 'Eyes on something? You have good taste. Keep shopping' (fire ~60 min after browse); cart/checkout → 'Looks like you forgot something — finish your order.'
Optionally test adding an MMS product image against plain text, and split buy-intent: give non-buyers a welcome discount code (e.g., 'use WILDWELCOME20') while keeping buyers' messages simpler.
Verify current carrier/platform compliance rules, which can change.
caveats: 48-hour/one-message rule is described for the US; other jurisdictions differ.
The source says this is a compliance ceiling, not a ceiling on how creative the single message can be.
cards.source_name: How to Create a SMS Marketing Strategy For $10M Shopify Brands.docx

cards.title: Time post-purchase and replenishment SMS to the buy cycle
cards.summary: Send a cross-sell/upsell SMS about 10–14 days after delivery and a replenishment reminder just before the product runs out.
cards.use_when: Building the post-purchase and replenishment SMS flow for your store.
steps: Send SMS 1 around day 10–14 after order delivery, while the buyer is in the honeymoon phase: ask if they're enjoying the product and suggest cross-sell/upsell or a repeat purchase.

For consumable/replenishment products, add SMS 2 timed to when the product runs out. Calculate it: e.g., Athletic Greens — 30-day supply plus 7-day delivery → send on ~day 35, 'are you running low? reorder.'
Hold offers initially; the source recommends not adding discounts to these early post-purchase messages until later.
Don't over-send: remember buyers also receive your campaign blasts, so two well-timed post-purchase messages are usually enough.
Consider keeping all win-back-style post-purchase messages in one flow triggered on order placement.
caveats: The source says this flow varies so much brand-to-brand that no single verified template applies; the athletic-greens math is an illustration.
Replenishment timing depends on your own product consumption and delivery cycle.
cards.source_name: How to Create a SMS Marketing Strategy For $10M Shopify Brands.docx

cards.title: Trigger SMS win-back at double the average time between purchases
cards.summary: Use 2x the customer's average reorder interval as the win-back trigger, then send a short 72-hour flash offer plus a last-chance reminder.
cards.use_when: Setting the trigger point and offer structure for an SMS win-back flow for lapsed buyers.
steps: Estimate average time between purchases for your store (e.g., 45 days) and multiply by two (→ ~90 days you'd likely consider a customer lapsed).
At that trigger, send SMS 1 with a flash offer, e.g., 'We miss you — here's 30% off, exclusive code, expires in 72 hours.'
Wait ~2 days and send SMS 2 as a last-chance/expiry reminder.
Keep it to roughly two messages; the source says these two plus your post-purchase sends are all you need before the cycle repeats.
Confirm your estimate with actual reorder-interval data rather than guessing.
caveats: '2x average time between purchases' is a source heuristic, not a universal law.
Offer depth (e.g., 30%) is an example; test margin impact before adopting.
cards.source_name: How to Create a SMS Marketing Strategy For $10M Shopify Brands.docx

cards.title: Cap SMS blasts at about two campaigns per week for most brands
cards.summary: Baseline around two SMS campaigns weekly, reserving higher frequency for launch-heavy or aggressive-acquisition brands with big lists.
cards.use_when: Setting the SMS campaign (blast) calendar and frequency for your store.
steps: Start with a baseline of about two SMS campaigns per week for a typical brand. Send at least one per week at minimum.
For aggressive-acquisition brands spending heavily (source cites Grain's), sending an SMS every single day to people who've never bought is acceptable if you have a large list and lots of news.
Ease off for existing buyers: for one-time-purchase or subscription brands, reduce frequency to buyers, and the source says don't text active subscribers at all.
During major sale pushes you can increase to daily or even two-a-day (source references a 9-figure brand's calendar), then return to baseline after the push.
Don't force sends: the source prefers saving SMS for big announcements to avoid unsubscribes — 'do not force out SMS if you don't have to.'
caveats: Frequency recommendations are the presenter's opinion and depend on list size, brand news and consent.
Buyer-vs-non-buyer cuts are specific to a sub/large-brand context.
cards.source_name: How to Create a SMS Marketing Strategy For $10M Shopify Brands.docx

cards.title: Plan an SMS campaign calendar around high-urgency events
cards.summary: Fill the SMS calendar with launches, restocks, time-boxed sales and timely trend/drop alerts — not evergreen nurture.
cards.use_when: Building the monthly SMS campaign calendar and choosing which messages to send.
steps: Anchor sends to genuinely urgent, timely events: product launches, back-in-stock/restock alerts, flash sales, private events, insider news, and time-boxed 'selling fast this week' trend alerts.
For a launch, send the announcement, then a reminder a couple days later (source example: sent on the 4th, reminder on the 6th).
Use SMS-exclusive flash sales — the source highlights exclusive-to-list offers as especially effective.

You can relabel messages with urgency even when literal urgency is absent (e.g., frame a past collection as a 'restock,' or a product as 'running low') because restocks perform well — but note the source's caution that non-urgent nurture performed worst and drove more unsubscribes.

Example: a brand sent just five SMS in a month (pre-order collection, list-exclusive free-item offer, framed restock, reminder, launch) and reports >$100k and 16% of total store revenue — showing a lean, intentional calendar can perform.
caveats: This revenue example is a single case, not a benchmark.
Framing messages as 'restock' or 'running low' when untrue is the source's tactic; consider trust and advertising-standards implications before using.
cards.source_name: How to Create a SMS Marketing Strategy For $10M Shopify Brands.docx

cards.title: Broadcast SMS to the full list with a tight exclusion list
cards.summary: Default to sending SMS to all subscribers and only suppress chronically unengaged numbers, cleaning monthly — deep engagement segmentation leaves money on the table.
cards.use_when: Segmenting your SMS list for campaign sends and deciding send exclusions.
steps: Send to all SMS subscribers rather than narrow engaged segments. The source notes people who never click a text still purchase (they see the message and go to the site directly).
Maintain a simple exclusion list: exclude a contact only after they've received ~15 texts with zero clicks ever.
Also exclude anyone you've bought from in ways that make them a poor target (e.g., don't text active subscribers on a subscription).
Clean the list about monthly to control cost, since SMS is expensive per send.
For big announcements (e.g., a New Year's Eve sale), send to the entire list with no exclusions.
Don't 'get too cute' building engaged segments — the source reports broadcasting usually makes the most money.
caveats: '15 texts with zero clicks' is a source heuristic, not a tested threshold.
Platform automation may handle exclusion lists differently; verify your setup.
cards.source_name: How to Create a SMS Marketing Strategy For $10M Shopify Brands.docx

cards.title: Test delays, offers and images before scaling SMS
cards.summary: Validate timing, offer and image choices with A/B tests and your own brand context rather than copying a template wholesale.
cards.use_when: Deciding what to change or expand once your core SMS flows and campaigns are running.
steps: Test message timing/delays (welcome day spacing, abandonment send windows, win-back trigger).
Test offers: whether a discount changes behavior, and how deep, before adding them to flows (source found no marginal lift from extra SMS discounts).
A/B test including images versus not in flows and campaigns, tracking net profit (revenue minus send cost) rather than revenue alone.
Keep the tests attached to the core flows the source says drive most revenue; add complexity only after the basics are measured.
Expect results to be brand-specific: the source explicitly says this isn't a copy-exactly recipe and cites running daily SMS or intricate flows for some brands.
caveats: Source advises treating its structure as a starting point, not scripture; verify with your own data.
Small-sample tests give directional, not definitive, reads.
cards.source_name: How to Create a SMS Marketing Strategy For $10M Shopify Brands.docx

cards.title: Three components of a converting email: copy, structure, design
cards.summary: Break every ecommerce email into copywriting, structure and graphic design, then evaluate each separately against the goal of driving a purchase click.
cards.use_when: Planning a campaign or flow email (promo, launch, replenishment reminder) and deciding where a weak performer is failing before redesigning it.
steps: Split the email into three layers: copy (headline, body, CTA wording, social proof), structure (the order and placement of sections and buttons), and graphic design (buttons, colors, imagery, flow between sections).

Judge each layer by whether it moves a skimming reader toward the product, not by whether it looks impressive; the presenter argues brands lose revenue by caring more about how the email looks than how it performs.

Diagnose a low-performing email by location: if readers don't reach the offer, fix structure/button placement first; if they reach it but don't click, test copy clarity and offer framing; if it feels cheap or off-brand, fix design.
Make copy and design reinforce each other — copy should be scannable in the same rhythm the design implies, with bolded points and short lines rather than dense paragraphs.
Keep the design engaging enough that subscribers don't unsubscribe even when a specific email doesn't convert, since the presenter treats return engagement as part of the same asset.
caveats: The $150M revenue figure is the presenter's agency claim, not a benchmark for any individual store.
The presenter runs a paid agency; design judgment is his opinion, not a tested rule.
cards.source_name: How to Design High Converting Ecommerce Emails In Figma.docx

cards.title: 'Button at the top' rule for non-scrollers
cards.summary: Place the logo, headline, short copy and a large primary CTA fully above the fold so non-scrolling readers still have a path to purchase.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing the hero section of any promotional or lifecycle email where you need clicks from subscribers who never scroll.
steps: Put everything a customer needs to decide at the very top: logo, benefit/pain headline, one or two short sentences of body copy, and the CTA button — nothing below the first screen is required to act.
Make the top button visually large; the presenter argues bigger buttons get more clicks and criticizes competitor emails where the hero button is small.
Treat the top block as an elevator pitch: it should summarize the single offer or benefit, not educate or list features.
Check where the fold actually lands on mobile in your ESP preview (the presenter reasons that most opens are mobile and non-scrollers never see below it).
Place the CTA button directly below the hero copy rather than after a graphic, so a reader who stops after two sentences can still click.
caveats: The exact fold position varies with device and ESP rendering; verify in preview rather than assuming a fixed pixel height.
Making every button huge is the presenter's stylistic preference, not a tested universal rule.
cards.source_name: How to Design High Converting Ecommerce Emails In Figma.docx

cards.title: Email structure: hero, bridge, repeated CTAs, footer navigation
cards.summary: Use a repeating structure — hero pitch with button, informational bridge with an infographic, benefit/product section with another button, then category-navigation footer.
cards.use_when: Building or templating a promotional email layout, or fixing an email where traffic stops partway down the page.
steps: Hero: headline calling out the pain or benefit, brief body copy, large CTA button, and a hero graphic.

Bridge: justify the hero claim with short informational blocks — the presenter shows benefit bullets, checklists, icons and ingredient highlights rather than paragraphs — and include a CTA button at the end of the section.
Add a final product or benefit section near the bottom with another CTA, so readers who scrolled the entire email still have a click target.
Repeat the button at the end of every major section, because a reader who finishes a section and finds no button simply leaves.
End with a footer containing 'shop by category' buttons (e.g., Men/Women) and additional links, to capture clicks from readers who reached the bottom but didn't want the featured product.
Use a strong us-versus-them or comparison block near the end when the product's advantage needs to be made explicit before the closing CTA.
caveats: The presenter's claim that category buttons in the footer recover lost clicks is his observation, not a measured result.
Too many buttons can dilute the primary action — choose based on the email's single goal.
cards.source_name: How to Design High Converting Ecommerce Emails In Figma.docx

cards.title: Make the email scroll feel seamless with gradients and flowing backgrounds
cards.summary: Use continuous background colors and gradients between sections so readers don't notice section breaks and keep scrolling into lower CTAs.
cards.use_when: Designing a long image-based email where readers drop off at section boundaries, or matching section backgrounds in Figma.
steps: Pick the main background color from the hero image or product photo so the palette is anchored to a real asset rather than chosen arbitrarily.
Keep a consistent background color throughout the email instead of alternating white and colored blocks, which the presenter calls 'blocky' and associates with drop-off at section ends.
Where two sections meet with slightly different shades, add a gradient rectangle that transitions from the top section's color to the bottom section's color so the seam disappears.
Sample exact colors from the image or existing brand assets using Figma's color picker (eyedropper) so text, buttons and background stay matched.
Repeat one accent color (e.g., the site's CTA red or an alert yellow) in small details — a discount bar, a 'last chance' label, button fills — to tie distant sections together.
Preview the full email scrolled top to bottom to confirm no visible banding between sections.
caveats: Gradients and background rectangles increase design complexity; the presenter uses a simpler first-pass layout before adding them.
The link between smooth flow and higher scroll depth is the presenter's reasoning, not measured data.
cards.source_name: How to Design High Converting Ecommerce Emails In Figma.docx

cards.title: Skimmable copy: pain headline, one-sentence body, three selling points
cards.summary: Write email copy for a three-second skim: call out the customer's pain in the headline, keep the largest block to one sentence, and sell on no more than three points.
cards.use_when: Writing or editing the copy for a promo, launch or replenishment email, especially when the current draft is paragraph-heavy.
steps: Open with a headline that names the reader's pain or situation — the Bite example asks 'What's in your toothpaste matters?' — then differentiate in the body copy (e.g., 'we'll never include harsh chemicals, plastic tubes, or toxic fillers').
Keep the largest body block in the email to roughly one sentence where every word is load-bearing; the presenter points out the biggest copy block in the Bite email is a single sentence.
Limit the selling argument to three specific points even if the product has more features, reasoning that readers can only hold about three things at once.
Move features into skimmable infographics — checklists, icons, timelines, short benefit labels highlighted larger than supporting text.
Use bold only on your own claims in comparison blocks; the presenter deliberately left competitor points unbolded in his ButcherBox-for-Pets build so the brand's advantages read first.
Structure the argument as: call out the problem, back it with punchy information, then tie in the product and stack the resulting benefits (e.g., healthier teeth, cleaner planet).
caveats: The 'three things' limit and 3-second attention span are the presenter's heuristics, not measured thresholds.
This style assumes a promo/consideration email; transactional emails may need more precise detail.
cards.source_name: How to Design High Converting Ecommerce Emails In Figma.docx

cards.title: Reverse-engineer competitor emails into a reusable copy template with ChatGPT
cards.summary: Feed a competitor email to ChatGPT, have it extract the structural template, then have it write new copy for your brand using that exact formula.
cards.use_when: You need fast email copy drafts and have identified competitor emails whose structure and angle perform well in your category.
steps: Collect a competitor email that you consider well-written and structurally proven for your market (the presenter uses Bite's email as the model).
Prompt ChatGPT to transcribe the email's copy into text.
Ask it to analyse that copy and produce a reusable template describing the structural formula (headline type, body sequence, CTA placement, proof points).
Supply your brand and product context, then ask it to write a new email following that exact template.

Let the model ask for the angle and positioning, then answer with a specific hook — the presenter used 'if your soap is white and perfect looking it's probably fake' with an 'ancient craft' positioning.
Review the output and edit before sending; the presenter says the draft took about two minutes and he would adjust details afterwards.
Keep the template on file so future emails re-use the same structure with different angles instead of prompting from scratch.
caveats: Treat output as a draft: verify claims, ingredient statements and any regulated language before sending.
Copying a competitor's structure is the presenter's recommended practice, not legal advice on copying their copy verbatim.
cards.source_name: How to Design High Converting Ecommerce Emails In Figma.docx

cards.title: Build emails as stacked image slices, not one giant image
cards.summary: Design the email in Figma, slice it into separate images for links and load speed, then stack them in the ESP.
cards.use_when: Producing an image-based email design and preparing assets for upload into Klaviyo, Omnisend or a similar ESP.
steps: Build the design inside a Figma frame, using roughly 600px width for the email as a starting dimension.
Draw Figma 'slice' frames over each logical block and export at 2x, so each export is a manageable file rather than one email-length image.
Slice by link destination, not just by visual section: because an image can only carry one link, split the footer logo, social icons and category buttons into separate slices with separate links.
Compress the exported JPEGs before upload; the presenter uses iLoveIMG's compress tool and reports one set dropping from 4.4 MB to 1.26 MB (about 72% smaller).
Upload the compressed images into the ESP and stack them in order, removing default image padding and side margins so the slices appear seamless.
Assign one destination link per image, and add brief alt text (e.g., the headline) for the case where images don't load.
Send a test email to your own inbox and check rendering and link behaviour before scheduling.
caveats: Figma's slice tool and ESP padding controls may change; verify the current interface before relying on exact menu steps.
Alt text is recommended but the presenter says he hasn't observed a clear deliverability impact from it.
cards.source_name: How to Design High Converting Ecommerce Emails In Figma.docx

cards.title: Hidden footer text to protect text-to-image deliverability ratio
cards.summary: Append a block of invisible body text at the bottom of image-heavy emails so spam filters see a healthy text-to-image ratio.
cards.use_when: Sending an email built mostly or entirely from images, where the HTML contains very little real text.
steps: Take a legitimate, on-brand text block such as your About Us copy and paste it at the very bottom of the email template.
Set the font size very small (the presenter cites size 5), tighten line spacing (he cites around 5%), and set the font colour to match the background so it is effectively invisible to readers.
Place it after the footer content so it doesn't interfere with the visible layout.
Keep using real, relevant brand copy rather than keyword spam, so the block still reads as genuine email text if inspected.
Verify the block doesn't break rendering or create extra scroll space by previewing the final email.
caveats: This is presented as a workaround that 'tricks' filters; it may violate ESP or mailbox-provider terms and could backfire if detected.
The presenter's claim that Gmail penalises image-heavy emails is his assertion, not documented platform policy; verify current deliverability guidance before adopting.
cards.source_name: How to Design High Converting Ecommerce Emails In Figma.docx

cards.title: Laying out an email design in Figma without advanced tools
cards.summary: Map the email as labelled placeholder blocks in a Figma frame first, then replace them with brand assets, so the layout is decided before detail work.
cards.use_when: Starting a new email design from scratch and you need to establish section order before choosing images and colours.
steps: Create a Figma design file and draw a frame of about 600px width and a height long enough for the expected copy.

Drop labelled text boxes for each section in order — logo, headline, body copy, CTA, graphic, sub-headline, body copy, infographic, CTA, footer — and size them roughly to the intended hierarchy (e.g., headline at ~30).
Use this map to decide section order and see the whole email at a glance; the presenter recommends this specifically for getting unstuck when you don't know where to start.
Import the brand logo and product images, dragging them into the frame; Figma shows centering guides automatically.
Paste prepared copy from a document, then adjust fonts (the presenter used Montserrat) and weights (semibold rather than bold) to bring the layout to life.
Build buttons by drawing a rectangle over the CTA text, grouping the two elements, and labelling the group (e.g., 'button one') so it can be copied and reused throughout the email.
Choose the palette after the hero image is placed, sampling from it, so gradients and accent colours match real assets.
caveats: Figma's menus and features change; verify current panel names if following step-by-step.
This walkthrough deliberately skips copywriting — bring finished copy into the layout rather than writing in Figma.
cards.source_name: How to Design High Converting Ecommerce Emails In Figma.docx

cards.title: Us-versus-them comparison block built with icon checkmarks
cards.summary: Create an explicit comparison graphic with checkmarks for your brand and X marks for competitors to make the product's advantages unmissable before the closing CTA.
cards.use_when: Writing the bridge or product-proof section of an email where the differentiator needs to be stated clearly (e.g., ingredient quality, sourcing, process).
steps: Place your brand on one side and a generic competitor label (e.g., 'most human-grade brands') on the other, using the logo and a simple 'us'/'them' header.
List your claims as short text points on your side and the corresponding competitor claims opposite; the presenter bolded only his brand's points to make them read first.
Add a checkmark icon to each of your points and an X icon to each competitor point; the presenter downloads free icons from the Noun Project.
Enclose each column in a rounded rectangle (Figma corner radius around 20) with a stroke outline, using a neutral background for the competitor column and white for yours so your side stands out.
Place the comparison in the bridge section, after the hero and before the final CTA, then repeat the CTA button immediately after it.
Keep the list short and skimmable — supporting copy above it should summarise the single strongest claim (e.g., 'not all human-grade dog food is created equal').
caveats: Comparative claims about competitors can carry legal and platform-advertising risk; substantiate any factual claim before publishing.
The presenter chose not to bold competitor points; this is a style choice, not a rule.
cards.source_name: How to Design High Converting Ecommerce Emails In Figma.docx

cards.title: Put footer navigation to work for non-buyers
cards.summary: Use the footer to offer category, quiz and social links so readers who scrolled past the featured product still have somewhere to click.
cards.use_when: Designing the bottom of a promotional email where the featured product may not match every reader.
steps: Repeat the primary CTA (e.g., a link to a plan-builder or quiz) as the lead footer element so scrollers land on the main action.
Add 'shop by category' buttons covering your main ranges so readers whose interest wasn't the featured product can still enter the store.
Include a small number of social links and a website link for readers not ready to buy.
In the Figma build, split these footer elements into separate slices so each button and icon can carry its own destination link.
Reinforce accent colours by giving the footer its own subtle background shape so it doesn't float without visual anchoring.
caveats: The presenter asserts this captures clicks from readers who reached the bottom, but provides no measured uplift data.
cards.source_name: How to Design High Converting Ecommerce Emails In Figma.docx

cards.title: Upload a finished image-design email into an ESP as stacked images
cards.summary: Set up a campaign, strip the template, upload compressed slices in order, remove padding, add links, then test and send.
cards.use_when: Publishing an image-based email built in Figma into Omnisend, Klaviyo or a similar platform.
steps: Create the campaign in the ESP, entering the subject line and preheader text (the presenter uses 'Last chance for 20% off' with preheader 'Open for your last gift opportunity').
Open any template to get a canvas, then delete the template blocks so you start from an empty email.
Add image elements one by one and upload your compressed slices, stacking them in the exact order they appear in the design.
Select each image block and remove image padding plus any frame side padding so the stacked slices align edge to edge and look like one continuous design.
Assign the destination link for each image — one link per image — and add short alt text describing the image.
Preview and send a test email to your own address, checking that the unsubscribe link is present (the ESP added one automatically in the walkthrough) and that links and rendering are correct.
Choose recipients — all subscribers or a specific segment with exclusions — review, then send.
caveats: Omnisend and other ESP interfaces change frequently; verify current campaign, padding and image-upload controls.
Sending entirely image-based emails means text-only recipients see alt text, so keep alt text meaningful.
cards.source_name: How to Design High Converting Ecommerce Emails In Figma.docx

cards.title: Image-only vs text-and-HTML emails: the presenter's position
cards.summary: The presenter argues image-only emails are standard practice among large brands and text/HTML is not required in 2026; treat this as a contested practice with real trade-offs.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to build an email as stacked images or as HTML text with styled blocks.
steps: Consider the presenter's evidence: he claims all of the 20-plus 7-9 figure brands he has worked with use image-only emails, and cites one roughly $200M/year brand doing so.
Weigh that against the costs: all content depends on images loading, so blocked images reduce the email to alt text, and text is not selectable, searchable or easy to edit.

If you go image-only, invest in the mitigating steps the presenter describes — compressed slices for load speed, alt text on every image, and hidden on-brand text at the bottom for deliverability ratio.
Still build a plain-text or HTML text version where your ESP supports it, so readers with images disabled get the offer and CTA.
Test rendering in your own inbox and in a preview tool before sending to the full list.
caveats: This is the presenter's opinion, partly informed by his agency's client base; it is not an established rule and contradicts common deliverability and accessibility guidance.
Image-only emails impair accessibility for screen readers and readers with images off — a real risk the source does not address.
cards.source_name: How to Design High Converting Ecommerce Emails In Figma.docx

cards.title: Compress and slice images to protect load time in the inbox
cards.summary: Keep individual email slices small and compress them before upload, because a single full-email image slows loading in the customer's inbox.
cards.use_when: Exporting a long designed email from Figma and preparing the files for ESP upload.
steps: Avoid exporting the entire email as one image; the presenter's stated reason is file size and slow loading in the inbox.
Slice the design into section-sized images and export at 2x for retina rendering.
Run all exports through an image compressor (the presenter uses iLoveIMG's compress image tool) before uploading.
Check the resulting file sizes; the presenter reports a sample set going from 4.4 MB to 1.26 MB after compression, roughly a 72% reduction, and treats smaller as better for load speed.
Upload the compressed files to the ESP and confirm they display at full width without visible quality loss or seams between slices.
caveats: The 4.4 MB to 1.26 MB figure is one example from the walkthrough, not a target threshold for every email.
Compression settings vary by tool; check quality after compressing rather than assuming it is lossless.
cards.source_name: How to Design High Converting Ecommerce Emails In Figma.docx

cards.title: Design principles that keep emails converting and subscribers subscribed
cards.summary: Use big buttons, matched accent colours, infographics and careful small details to make emails engaging without relying on flashy effects.
cards.use_when: Finishing or reviewing an email design before upload, especially when the layout works but feels flat or off-brand.
steps: Use large buttons throughout the email; the presenter points to Gymshark's oversized hero CTA as the model and says the bigger the button the more clicks.

Match accent colours across sections — the Gymshark example repeats green across image borders, callouts and buttons, and the presenter's own build carries the site's red through the discount bar, button and 'last chance' label.
Apply small depth details: a border and shadow on the button to give it a 3D feel, and a coloured border around the hero image so it pops against the background.
Use infographics instead of paragraphs — checklists, icons, comparison graphs (the presenter shows a graph making gummies look better than tablets) and highlighted key words.
Vary text weight (semibold vs regular, larger vs smaller) to create hierarchy rather than setting everything the same.
Add lifestyle or product imagery to finish the email and bring colour and realism into the layout.
Keep it restrained: the presenter's summary is to take the basics and elevate them rather than exploding the email with crazy colours.
caveats: Bigger buttons and repeated accent colours are the presenter's design opinions, supported by examples rather than controlled tests.
Engagement-focused design may not convert on a single send; the presenter frames it as protecting long-term subscriber engagement.
cards.source_name: How to Design High Converting Ecommerce Emails In Figma.docx

cards.title: Use conversational messaging to resolve product-purchase friction
cards.summary: When shoppers need help with product fit, compatibility or a cart decision.
cards.use_when: When shoppers need help with product fit, compatibility or a cart decision.
steps: Audit messages for a concrete question the shopper can answer easily.
Identify the store and use natural, clear language rather than pretending an automated message is a personal friend.
Route replies to someone able to answer product, delivery and returns questions.
Use the supported messaging channel for the recipient; do not assume blue bubbles improve every audience.
caveats: The source promotes an iMessage tool; its claimed channel advantage is not independently established.
cards.source_name: If I Started SMS Marketing in 2026, I'd Do This.docx

cards.title: Reduce signup fields while retaining clear messaging consent
cards.summary: When simplifying a store text-message signup form.
cards.use_when: When simplifying a store text-message signup form.
steps: Collect only information needed for this signup and a useful follow-up.
Keep the marketing permission and sender purpose clear; a phone number alone is not the marketing opt-in.
Do not remove information the checkout needs to fulfill the order.
Compare signup completion with downstream replies, purchases and opt-outs.
caveats: Merchant adaptation of the source form-friction principle.
cards.source_name: If I Started SMS Marketing in 2026, I'd Do This.docx

cards.title: Test concise conversational welcome messages
cards.summary: When welcoming a shopper who opted into the store messaging program.
cards.use_when: When welcoming a shopper who opted into the store messaging program.
steps: Deliver any promised signup benefit and identify the store.
Ask one useful question about product preferences or intended use if a response will change the help offered.
The source suggests a five-minute delay and short copy; test timing within applicable send-time and message-count controls.
Do not split one message into several merely to simulate a human or satisfy an arbitrary length limit.
caveats: The source five-minute and 80-character preferences are heuristics, not optimal limits or billing rules.
cards.source_name: If I Started SMS Marketing in 2026, I'd Do This.docx

cards.title: Hand product questions to a trained human
cards.summary: When a messaging flow receives replies requiring individualized help.
cards.use_when: When a messaging flow receives replies requiring individualized help.
steps: Route replies to the support or product-specialist queue.
Carry forward the relevant product and order context so the shopper does not repeat it.
Answer the question and offer the appropriate product, size guide or cart link.
Set a realistic response target and communicate availability.
caveats: Human support requires staffing; the source response-rate anecdotes do not establish purchase uplift.
cards.source_name: If I Started SMS Marketing in 2026, I'd Do This.docx

cards.title: Use short product demos to answer a shopper question
cards.summary: When a opted-in conversation needs a clearer product explanation than text.
cards.use_when: When a opted-in conversation needs a clearer product explanation than text.
steps: Choose a short product demonstration or voice explanation only when the channel and shopper support it.
Use the actual SKU and answer the specific question.
Provide a text alternative when media is inaccessible or unavailable.
Compare resolution and purchase outcomes with text-only support against production effort.
caveats: Merchant application of the source multimedia conversation idea; channel capabilities and costs differ.
cards.source_name: If I Started SMS Marketing in 2026, I'd Do This.docx

cards.title: Measure conversational messaging by purchases and support outcomes
cards.summary: When evaluating store messaging flows or comparing supported channels.
cards.use_when: When evaluating store messaging flows or comparing supported channels.
steps: Track delivery, replies, opt-outs, support resolution, purchases and net contribution after messaging cost.
Use consistent attribution windows and a comparable control when estimating incremental impact.
Separate product inquiries from service appointment show-up or sales-call close rates.
Treat the source reported twofold reply lift as an unverified vendor example, not expected purchase lift.
caveats: Replies alone do not establish revenue impact.
cards.source_name: If I Started SMS Marketing in 2026, I'd Do This.docx

cards.title: Email System Build Order: List Growth → Flows → Campaigns → Tests → Deliverability → AI
cards.summary: Build the email program in dependency order, starting with signup forms, because each layer's performance depends on the layer below it.
cards.use_when: Planning an email marketing roadmap or auditing why email revenue is flat before buying new tactics or tools.
steps: Sequence work as: (1) list growth via high-converting signup forms, (2) core automated flows, (3) campaigns, (4) A/B testing, (5) segmentation, (6) deliverability, (7) AI to accelerate production.
Justify the order: campaigns and flows monetize a list, so a weak capture layer caps everything downstream — no list growth means flow and campaign optimization has nothing to work on.
Diagnose your store against the three gaps the source names: missing key flows, campaigns sent without a strategy, and trying to fix performance without knowing which underlying layer is broken.
Deliverable: an audit of your own ESP account listing what to build, what to fix, and where the largest revenue opportunity sits — before adding new tools.
Use the audit output to decide whether the next project is signup form optimization, a missing flow, or a campaign calendar, rather than doing all three at once.
caveats: The order is the source's recommended build sequence for a new or underbuilt program; a mature program may need a different entry point based on measured gaps.
No numeric benchmark is attached to the roadmap itself — the individual layers carry their own source-specific figures.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Signup Form Offer Design and Margin Math
cards.summary: Pick the opt-in incentive by testing offer types against signup rate, welcome-flow conversion and attributed revenue, not signup rate alone.
cards.use_when: Choosing or refreshing the incentive on the popup, full-page or embedded opt-in form on the store.
steps: Treat the offer as the biggest lever on signup rate, ahead of design: the source states a strong offer with poor design still outperforms a poor offer beautifully designed.

Offer types to test: buy one get one free; buy one get one at 50% off; free gift with purchase of X; free digital product; free shipping; fixed dollar amount off; dollar amount off over a threshold; percentage off; percentage off over a threshold; percentage off a subscription; cashback; early access to a sale; mystery discount (source's personal favorite).
Evaluate each variant holistically: factor profit margin, signup rate, the welcome flow's conversion rate, and the revenue attributed to that welcome flow — not just the opt-in rate.
If AOV is around $200, the source notes $20 off and 10% off are equivalent in value but $20 off carries higher perceived value; still confirm with your own split test.
Note the source's general claim that anything under 10% off is less effective, and treat it as a starting hypothesis for testing rather than a rule.
When the offer changes, update the headline, CTA button and any teaser/quiz copy so the promise is consistent across every step of the form.
caveats: The sub-10% and $200 AOV figures are the source's heuristics, not established benchmarks — discount depth must be validated against your own margin structure.
Aggressive discounting can train customers to wait for discounts and compress margin; the source does not model this trade-off.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Standard Popup Structure: One Headline, One Field, One CTA, One Microcopy
cards.summary: Keep the opt-in form to four elements and remove every block that does not move the visitor toward the email field.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing the layout of a desktop popup opt-in or full-page signup form.
steps: Use this structure: offer stated in the headline; one input field per step; a benefit-driven CTA button; a microcopy line under the button.

Write the headline as the offer itself, e.g. 'Unlock 20% off your first order'. Do not hide the offer in body copy under a generic greeting — the source treats this as one of the most common mistakes.
Delete sub-headlines like 'Sign up for special offers and updates' — the source argues the value is self-evident and the block adds friction.
Simplify the email field placeholder to something like 'Enter your email here' so the expected input is unambiguous.
Style the input field background so it stands out from the popup background (e.g. light grey field on white popup) to make it easier to find.
Avoid the words 'sign up' and 'subscribe' in both the headline and CTA; instead state what the visitor gets, e.g. 'Get my discount now'.
Add a microcopy line under the CTA giving a second, less attractive option, e.g. 'No thanks'. The source cites research that two options make people likelier to choose than a single CTA.
Remove the US disclaimer text about agreeing to receive marketing email; if you sell into the EU, retention of privacy disclosures is a legal question the source flags rather than resolves.
Remove any 'no thanks' alternative that competes with the CTA, and remove supporting text boxes describing your promotions.
caveats: The 'remove US disclaimer' advice is the source's US-specific claim; EU privacy rules are explicitly said to be different — confirm with counsel for your markets.
The two-option microcopy relies on cited research the source does not name; test it on your own audience.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Micro-Commitment (Micro-Yes) Step Before the Email Field
cards.summary: Insert a one-question yes/no step before the email field to create commitment, then measure whether it lifts total signups for your audience.
cards.use_when: Optimizing the opt-in form flow on a popup to raise email capture rate.
steps: Clone the email opt-in step and place a stripped-down version before it: remove the input field, change the primary CTA to something like 'Yes please', and keep a secondary 'No thanks'.
Frame the question as the offer, e.g. 'Do you want 20% off your first order?', with emphasis on the number.
Clicking 'Yes please' advances to the email field step; clicking 'No thanks' closes the form.
Make the two-step flow visually coherent: logo, headline, one field or one question per screen.
Split test the micro-yes step on versus off; the source reports testing across more than 40 ecommerce brands where it usually increased signup conversion, but it is not universal.
Run the test separately on desktop and mobile, since the source says the micro step can win on one device and lose on the other.
Judge the result on total signups and downstream welcome-flow revenue, not on signup rate in isolation.
caveats: The 40-plus-brand experience is the source's own client work, not a controlled benchmark — treat as directional evidence, not a guarantee.
If the step is added without a clean 'No thanks' exit, the form becomes a dark pattern and may increase closes or complaints.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Timing, Frequency and Device Targeting Rules for Popups
