cards.summary: Test popup timing, repeat exposure and device-specific targeting to balance signups with the shopping experience.
cards.use_when: Configuring when and how often the opt-in popup fires on the storefront, generally or per device.
steps: Do not show the form immediately on load; switch targeting from 'immediately' to rule-based display so a visitor exiting right away is not interrupted.

Set a starting delay of about 6 seconds as the source's default, and test within a 4–12 second range. Too short disrupts the visit and reads as spam; too long means fewer visitors ever see the form, so a high signup rate on tiny volume still yields few subscribers.
Layer a scroll condition, with about 60% as the source's starting point, and optionally a minimum pages-viewed condition. The source leaves these conditions non-mandatory (AND logic off).
Handle repeat exposure: set the closed form to re-display after about 3 days instead of the default 5.
Build one desktop-only form and one mobile-only form rather than a single responsive form, so layout, timing and copy can differ by device and A/B results are not mixed.
On mobile, disable the exit-intent trigger — the source calls mobile exit intent unreliable and says it fires when people are not leaving, harming experience.

Exclude existing subscribers (e.g. 'don't show to existing profiles'), the cart page and the checkout page so visitors already about to purchase are not offered a discount, and exclude wholesale or other non-retail pages.
If you only ship to one country, restrict display by location so the offer is relevant.
caveats: The 6-second delay, 4–12 second range, 60% scroll and 3-day re-show are the source's recommended starting points, framed as things to split test rather than fixed rules.
Excluding the cart and checkout pages is a deliberate choice to protect full-price orders; if your checkout abandonment is high, test the alternative before assuming it is right for you.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Teaser / Floating Button Configuration
cards.summary: Keep a persistent teaser or floating button so visitors who close the popup still have a visible path back to the offer.
cards.use_when: Adding or reviewing the teaser (Klaviyo) or floating button (Aliyah/Shopify app) that accompanies the opt-in popup.
steps: Enable the teaser so it displays both before the form appears and after the form is closed.
On desktop, use a rectangular teaser carrying short offer text such as 'Save 20%' rather than a generic gift icon; style it for contrast (e.g. black background, white centered text).

On mobile, switch the teaser to a circle and shorten the text so it does not occupy the full bottom bar — the source notes that stacked elements such as loyalty promotions can collide with a full-width bar.
Verify the teaser does not overlap checkout, cart or other persistent UI.
Split test teaser present versus absent; the source reports the teaser lifts both signup rate and the absolute number of subscribers.
caveats: The claim that the teaser lifts both rate and absolute subscribers comes from the source's own testing and is not quantified.
If your storefront already has several floating elements, a persistent teaser may add clutter; the source itself acknowledges this case.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Post-Opt-In Success Page: Withhold the Code, Train Email Opens
cards.summary: Route new subscribers to their inbox for the discount instead of displaying it on the success page, to protect first-email engagement signals.
cards.use_when: Writing the success/confirmation screen copy that appears after a visitor submits their email on the opt-in form.
steps: Make the success page visually identical to the form: same logo, same fonts, same colours.
Write a future-pacing headline such as 'Your discount code is on its way' rather than revealing the code.
Add instructions: check your inbox for the confirmation message containing the discount code.
Add the fallback line: if no email arrives within 5 minutes, check your spam folder — the source says this pre-empts support tickets caused by deliverability issues.

The source deliberately does not display the discount code on this page, arguing it removes any reason to open the first welcome email; a low open rate on a brand-new subscriber's very first email is a negative signal to inbox providers.

Test the alternative if you have strong reason to believe instant code delivery converts better for your audience; the source acknowledges this is an active industry debate and states its own position rather than a universal rule.
caveats: Holding back the code risks losing subscribers who never check email; this is the deliberate trade-off the source chooses, not a proven best practice.
The deliverability reasoning is the presenter's explanation, not a documented provider policy.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Separate Desktop and Mobile Signup Forms
cards.summary: Clone the desktop form into a dedicated mobile form and fix the specific elements that break at small sizes.
cards.use_when: Adapting an existing opt-in popup for mobile traffic, or before starting device-level A/B tests.
steps: Clone the desktop form, name it as the mobile version, and set device targeting to mobile only; leave the original on desktop only.
Remove the exit-intent rule on mobile because the trigger is unreliable there.
Audit every element for size: check that fonts are legible and that nothing overflows the viewport.
Increase the call-to-action button height (the source uses about 70 px) and raise CTA label size (about 30 px) so the button is comfortably tappable.
Raise secondary action text (e.g. 'No thanks') to about 18 px.
Increase emphasis sizes where the offer number appears inside the form (source uses 60 px in the micro-commitment step).
Raise the input field height (about 70 px) and input text size (about 20 px) via the general styling settings.
Increase success-page body text to about 22 px.
Skip images on mobile entirely where possible, or compress the logo, because mobile load time depends on the visitor's connection — the source says images are a common conversion killer.
caveats: Pixel sizes are the source's working values on a specific ESP builder and reproduce that presenter's config, not a universal standard; verify against your own template and your current interface.
Because results can differ by device, keep desktop and mobile tested and reported separately rather than averaging them.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Redirect Your Signup Offer Away From Cart and Checkout Traffic
cards.summary: Suppress discount popups for visitors in the cart and checkout so you do not discount orders that would have completed at full price.
cards.use_when: Configuring URL inclusion and exclusion rules for the opt-in popup on an ecommerce store.
steps: Exclude the cart page from popup display so a visitor mid-cart is not interrupted or re-priced.
Exclude the checkout page so a visitor about to purchase at full price is not offered a discount.
Exclude wholesale, B2B or other non-retail pages where the consumer offer is irrelevant.
Keep display on product, collection, homepage and content pages where the visitor is still exploring and the capture is additive.
Review exclusions whenever the theme changes URLs or SPAs change the path structure, since URL rules can silently stop matching.
caveats: This reduces capture volume in exchange for protecting full-price conversion; if your cart or checkout abandonment is high, test whether the loss of capture outweighs the protection.
Excluding checkout does not solve abandonment — it must be paired with an abandoned-checkout flow.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Compress Signup Form Images to Protect Load Time
cards.summary: Run every image used in an opt-in form through compression before uploading, because load time is a major conversion killer.
cards.use_when: Preparing product or lifestyle imagery for a signup popup, full-page form or landing page opt-in.
steps: Compress images externally before uploading to the email platform; the source names TinyPNG and Squoosh.
Upload the compressed file to the form builder only after compression, because large originals slow the form down and long load times suppress conversion.
Write descriptive alt text for every image, including the logo — alt text is what visitors see when an image fails to load.
For mobile forms, avoid images altogether and compress the logo if you keep it, since mobile load speed depends on the visitor's connection.
Check that the logo or hero image does not push the email field below the fold on small screens.
caveats: Compression tools are third-party products whose interfaces and settings change — verify the current workflow before relying on instructions.
The source claims load time is a major conversion killer but gives no measured threshold for image weight.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Ten Common Signup Form Mistakes to Audit Against
cards.summary: Audit a live opt-in form against the source's recurring failure modes, led by a weak offer.
cards.use_when: Reviewing an underperforming opt-in form or onboarding a store's existing email capture setup.
steps: Offer too weak: if the incentive is not compelling, fix that first — the source ranks it above every design issue.

Asking too much in one step: collect email, phone, first name, birthday and similar data in separate steps; if you collect phone number or other fields, add them after the email step. The source warns that visitors willing to give an email but not a phone number may abandon the whole form, losing the email entirely.
Time delay too short or too long: balance visibility against positive experience (see delay guidance in the timing card).
Form too small: the source's guidance is that a bigger form captures attention better, and suggests testing popup versus full-screen.
Too much copy: no supporting text blocks explaining that subscribers will receive offers and promotions.
Offer missing from the headline: the offer should be the first thing read, not buried in body copy.
'Sign up' / 'subscribe' language in headline or CTA: replace with the benefit.
Single form for both devices: build and test desktop and mobile separately.
Slow-loading form: compress images; skip images on mobile.
Incentive revealed on the success page: direct people to the inbox instead (source's position; an industry debate).
caveats: These are the source's observed common mistakes, not a validated ranking of conversion impact beyond the stated ordering of offer first.
The phone-number advice assumes email is the primary identifier for your program; SMS-first brands may order capture differently.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Signup Form A/B Test Priority Order
cards.summary: Test signup form variables in descending order of leverage, starting with the offer.
cards.use_when: Planning the next round of opt-in experiments, or deciding which variable to change when form volume is too low to test everything at once.
steps: Test 1 — offer: the highest-leverage variable; a strong offer with weak design beats a weak offer with strong design per the source.
Test 2 — micro-commitment step on versus off: usually lifts conversion but not for every audience.
Test 3 — time delay: a shorter delay raises signup rate but lowers total signups, so judge on total signups.
Test 4 — popup versus full-page form: full-page has greater visibility and wins for some brands.
Test 5 — headline copy, e.g. 'Save 20% now', 'Get 20% now', 'Take 20% now', 'Unlock 20% off now', 'Your discount awaits', 'Do you want 20% off?'.
Test 6 — CTA button copy, e.g. 'Save 20% off now', 'Get 20% off now', 'Unlock my discount now', 'Reveal my discount now', 'I want my discount'.

Test 7 — microcopy under the CTA: test variants such as 'No thanks', 'No thanks, I'll pay full price', 'No spam guaranteed', or social proof like 'Rated 4.9/5 by 5,000 customers', and test having microcopy versus none.
Test 8 — colour and design: plain versus fully designed form, light versus dark form, input field colour, CTA colour. Lower leverage than the above.

Test 9 — image versus no image: an image can distract from the form, so test both; also test different images (the source gives a client example where an image with a dog far outperformed one without, and explicitly warns against generalising that).
Test 10 — SMS opt-in angle: same 20%-off question framed for phone capture, a higher discount for SMS than for email (e.g. 10% email vs 20% SMS), or positioning the SMS list as a VIP club.
caveats: Priority order is the presenter's ranking of leverage, not a measured effect-size table.
Most variables are low-leverage; do not spend signup-form test volume on colour before offer and flow structure are settled.
Each audience differs, so a variable that wins elsewhere may lose here.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Configure a Signup A/B Test: Manual 50/50 and Winner Selection
cards.summary: Set the traffic split manually rather than automatic so the platform does not call a winner on insufficient volume.
cards.use_when: Launching an A/B test on a popup or form inside your email platform.
steps: Create the test from the existing form, name it for the variable under test (e.g. 'offer test').

Set variant A as the current control and variant B as the challenger, then update every dependent element of variant B — for an offer test that means the headline, the email opt-in, the teaser and the form's design copy all reflect the new offer.

In test settings, set the traffic weight to manual 50/50 rather than automatic; the source's stated reason is that automatic allocation can favour a variant before there is enough volume to justify the conclusion.
Enable winner selection but do not automatically end the test, so a human reviews the result before rollout.
Measure on the same holistic basis used for offer decisions — signup rate plus welcome-flow conversion and attributed welcome-flow revenue — not signup rate alone.
Run device-specific tests separately rather than pooling desktop and mobile results.
caveats: The manual 50/50 preference is the presenter's stance, and it costs statistical efficiency compared with adaptive allocation; it trades speed for the operator's control.
No minimum sample size is given; you must set your own stopping rule before reading results.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Full-Screen Opt-In Forms and Zero-Party Data Quizzes
cards.summary: Use full-screen branded popups with a single question to capture intent data alongside the email address.
cards.use_when: Choosing a capture format, or adding a segmentation question at the point of opt-in for a Shopify store.
steps: Consider full-screen forms on both desktop and mobile rather than small popups, which the source argues hurt conversion; full-screen formats allow full brand treatment with background and imagery.
Lead with one question — the source recommends keeping it to a single question even though multi-question quizzes are possible — such as 'What are you shopping for today, myself or someone else?'.
Ask for motivation-relevant segmentation, e.g. for a health brand: lose weight, build muscle, or improve general health; for a gift-focused store, the recipient.
Use a 'No thanks' exit so the full-screen takeover is escapable.
Pass the zero-party answers through the platform integration into your email list so they become segmentation properties on the subscriber profile.
Review survey-answer performance reporting to see which answers correlate with higher purchase behaviour, then weight acquisition and campaign targeting toward those segments.
caveats: Full-screen popups are more intrusive; the source argues the format win justifies it, but this is not presented as a cross-store benchmark.
Collecting a question before the email adds a step; the source argues the micro-commitment outweighs the friction, but it must be tested.
Integration availability and the exact question/report UI vary by platform and change over time — verify the current interface.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Gamified Opt-In First Steps: Spin-to-Win and Scratch-Off
cards.summary: Test interactive first steps before the email field, using a guaranteed-win mechanic, and expect different winners per audience.
cards.use_when: Choosing the opening interaction on a full-screen capture form to raise engagement and signup rate.
steps: Spin-to-win: configure the wheel so every visitor receives a reward — the wheel always lands on the designated reward slice, and you may display other slices as decoy rewards. Choose the reward value (e.g. 5% or 10%).

Scratch-off: use the interactive scratch surface with framing copy such as 'Try your luck — scratch below to see what you win'; the reward is revealed on scratch, producing a first brand interaction before the email ask.
Place the mechanic as the first step, before the email field, so it functions as a micro-commitment.
Split test the gamified first step against a mini quiz and against a plain yes/no micro-commitment; the source reports the mini quiz or scratch-off usually win, but says every audience differs.
Judge on total subscribers and downstream revenue, not just the completion rate of the mechanic.
If you already run a strong baseline, test one mechanic at a time so you can attribute the change.
caveats: The source relates one brand moving from about 11% to about 14% conversion after adding a scratch-off, and separately a scratch-off revealing a discount; this is a single client anecdote, not a promised result.
The scratch-off is described as a newer feature; availability and behaviour should be verified in the current platform interface.
Decoy reward slices on a rigged wheel create a misleading expectation — weigh the engagement gain against trust and any local consumer-protection rules.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Deliverability Hygiene: Authentication, Engagement Tiers and List Cleaning
cards.summary: Implement SPF, DKIM and DMARC, segment by engagement recency, and suppress long-inactive subscribers to protect inbox placement.
cards.use_when: Setting up or auditing sending infrastructure and list health, especially before scaling campaign volume.
steps: Implement the technical authentication trio — SPF, DKIM and DMARC — on your sending domain so mailbox providers can verify you.
Segment by engagement recency using activity windows; the source names 14-day, 30-day, 60-day and 90-day active tiers as the segmentation structure.
Use those tiers to differentiate sending: mail the most recently engaged tiers most often and reduce frequency or exclude the least engaged tiers.
Clean the list by suppressing profiles that have been inactive past 180 days — the source's stated list-cleaning benchmark.
Monitor inbox placement and sender reputation, particularly as AI-driven inbox curation changes how mail is sorted and surfaced.
Re-check authentication records and suppression rules after any change of sending domain, ESP or marketing platform.
caveats: The 180-day suppression threshold and the 14/30/60/90-day windows are the source's heuristics, not calculations derived from your data — adjust for your purchase cycle and list size.
Suppressing inactive profiles reduces list size and can reduce short-term revenue; the source frames it as necessary for placement.
Authentication setup depends on your DNS provider and ESP interface, both of which change — verify current configuration steps.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Core Automated Flows to Build and the 72-Hour Purchase Window
cards.summary: Prioritise five automated flows, and treat the first 72 hours of a new subscriber's life as the highest-converting window.
cards.use_when: Deciding which lifecycle automations to build or fix next in an ecommerce email program.
steps: Build the five core flows: Welcome, Browse Abandonment, Abandoned Cart, Abandoned Checkout, and Post-Purchase.
Front-load the welcome flow: the source identifies the first 72 hours as the critical purchase window, with day zero driving the highest conversion volume.

Because day zero is the strongest, make the first welcome message carry the clearest offer and the clearest instruction (including where the discount code is), rather than saving the strongest message for later in the sequence.
Pair each core flow with the capture and campaign layers so browse, cart and checkout abandonment have a path back to purchase.
Review which flows exist and which are missing before adding new campaign volume — the source names missing key flows as one of the three common reasons email revenue is flat.
caveats: The 72-hour window and day-zero emphasis are the source's framing of welcome-flow behaviour, not a benchmark tied to a specific dataset shown.
Post-purchase flows serve retention, review and replenishment goals rather than immediate conversion; do not judge them purely on attributed revenue in the first days.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Email Campaign Cadence and Audience Strategy
cards.summary: Plan campaign volume around a 3–4 per week cadence, sent with a real strategy rather than ad hoc.
cards.use_when: Setting or reviewing the weekly campaign calendar and checking whether sends are strategic or random.
steps: Use 3 to 4 campaigns per week as the source's recommended cadence reference point for the campaign layer of the email system.
Ensure campaigns sit on top of a working list-growth and flow layer; the source names 'sending campaigns without a real strategy' as a common failure mode.
Align campaign sends to the engagement tiers established for deliverability so higher-frequency sends go to more recently active subscribers.
Treat the cadence as a starting hypothesis tied to list size and engagement — do not adopt it unchanged if your list is small or your engagement tiers are thin.
Review performance by segment rather than as a blended average, so a strong campaign to an engaged tier is not obscured by weak delivery to inactive profiles.
caveats: The 3–4 per week figure is the source's recommendation, not a derived benchmark, and should be adjusted to list size, purchase cycle and engagement.
Sending more frequently into unengaged segments increases complaint and spam risk, which works against the deliverability practices the same source recommends.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Use AI and Personalisation Tools Only After the Fundamentals Are In Place
cards.summary: Layer personalisation, zero-party data quizzes and split-tested desktop/mobile experiences onto a working capture-flow-campaign foundation rather than as a substitute for it.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest in AI personalisation, quiz tools or advanced targeting features before fixing list growth, flows or deliverability.
steps: Fix capture, flows, campaigns, segmentation and deliverability first; the source's stated reason is that most brands are missing key flows, sending without strategy, or treating symptoms, so advanced features amplify a broken base rather than fixing it.
Once the base works, add active gamification (spin-to-win, scratch-offs) and zero-party data collection quizzes to lift engagement and enrich profiles.
Split test distinct desktop and mobile experiences rather than assuming one experience transfers, because results diverge by device.
Route collected zero-party data into segmentation so it drives targeting and campaign decisions instead of sitting unused in the capture tool.
Re-evaluate the tool stack only when a measured gap remains after the fundamentals are in place.
caveats: The source is explicit that AI is a speed-and-efficiency layer applied last, not a solution to a missing flow or a deliverability problem.
Tool availability and integration behaviour change frequently; verify current capabilities in the interfaces you use.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Choose a popup first step: scratch-off, quiz, or micro-commitment
cards.summary: Evaluate three popup first-step formats (scratch-off, mini quiz, micro-commitment) to raise email signup rate before the email field appears.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to structure the first screen of your email capture popup so more store visitors begin the signup interaction.
steps: Recall the source's claimed example: for one ecom brand already converting at 11%, adding a scratch-off first step correlated with a move to 14%. Treat this as a single-case example, not a benchmark.

Pick scratch-off or mini quiz as your primary test if you want a more engaging, gamified first interaction with the brand; the source presenter rates these as likely to outperform older formats, based on what they see across client accounts.

Keep the older micro-commitment pattern as a backup test: a simple yes/no frame like 'claim 10% off or no thanks', or 'do you want a mystery discount?' followed by the email field. It still produces a decent signup rate.
Optionally test skipping the first step entirely and showing the email opt-in immediately. Both presenters advise against it, but it can suit audiences that don't respond to games.
Run the formats as real A/B tests on your own traffic and keep the winner, rather than adopting any one format permanently.
caveats: The 11% to 14% lift is a source-reported client result, not a guaranteed outcome.
The claim that quiz and scratch-off will 'probably' outperform micro-commitment is the presenter's observation, not a measured universal rule.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Decide whether the popup success page reveals the discount code or sends to email
cards.summary: Trade off immediate code delivery against first-email engagement and deliverability when configuring the signup success page.
cards.use_when: Configuring the success/reward step of your email signup popup and choosing between showing the discount immediately or routing the subscriber to their inbox.
steps: Option A (source presenter's preference): show no reward on the success page. Use a plain 'you're in' confirmation plus copy telling them to check their inbox for the code, and to check spam or the promotions tab if it hasn't arrived within 5 minutes.

Use this option when first-email engagement matters to you: the argument is that if the code is already in the popup, subscribers have no reason to open email one, and low opens on a brand-new subscriber's first email can signal spam to Gmail and push future sends to promotions or spam.
Option B: reveal the discount code on the success page with a 'shop now' button. This removes friction and lets people buy immediately, at the cost of weaker first-email engagement.

Test both, since the source describes the debate as roughly 50/50. The presenter reports their own client tests show only a minimal conversion downside for the no-reward option, offset by the welcome flow in the first 72 hours, plus deliverability upside.
If you switch to the no-reward option, make sure your first welcome email delivers the promised code clearly, or you create unnecessary friction.
caveats: The deliverability reasoning is the presenter's interpretation of how mailbox providers behave, not a documented provider rule.
Reported minimal conversion downside is from the presenter's own client tests and may not hold for your list.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Configure single vs double opt-in for popup signup forms
cards.summary: Choose email signup confirmation separately from how and when the promised reward is delivered.
cards.use_when: Setting the opt-in method on your signup form, which determines whether the discount is shown on-screen or delivered by email.
steps: Single opt-in adds an eligible email subscriber without a separate confirmation click; reward placement is a separate design choice.
Double opt-in requires confirmation before subscription. Explain the next step and verify delivery of the promised reward.
Configure email and SMS permission separately; verify current channel and provider requirements.
The presenter is not a fan of double opt-in because the confirm-click step reduces the number of new email subscribers you collect.
If you still want the first welcome email opened while using single opt-in, rely on the success-page copy rather than adding a confirmation click.
caveats: Provider recommendations (Postscript, Attentive) are stated as of the source and should be verified.
The list-size downside of double opt-in is the presenter's stated experience, not a measured range.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Set popup trigger timing, scroll depth, and exit intent
cards.summary: Configure time-delay, scroll-depth and exit-intent triggers for signup popups, with a 4s vs 12s test as the starting point.
cards.use_when: Choosing when the email capture popup appears on your store, to avoid interrupting visitors too early or missing them entirely.
steps: Set a time-delay trigger between 4 and 12 seconds. The presenter always uses this band and starts experimentation with 4 seconds versus 12 seconds, then dials in the exact timing.
Add a 60% scroll-depth trigger so the popup also fires for engaged readers who haven't hit the time threshold.
Add exit intent: on desktop this fires when the mouse leaves the site, on mobile when the user quickly scrolls up.
Where the tool allows, separate mobile-only and desktop-only rules so trigger behavior matches each device's exit behavior.

Test smart/predictive triggering as an addition to your manual triggers: the source describes it as an AI model that learns the best moment to show the popup and fires it in addition to basic triggers.

When testing smart triggering, expect the presenter's typical pattern: signup rate dips slightly while total signups rise, because the popup is shown more often. Both the presenter and the tool vendor favor leaving it on, with the caveat that some clients see the opposite.
caveats: The 4-12 second band and 60% scroll depth are the source's recommended starting points, not validated universal thresholds.
Smart triggering behavior is tool-specific (Aaliyah). Verify the current setting and its behavior in your own tool's interface.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Build signup-form targeting rules for new vs returning visitors
cards.summary: Use targeting rules to show a first-time capture popup to new visitors and separate popups to already-subscribed visitors.
cards.use_when: Setting up popup audiences so you capture new emails without annoying existing subscribers, or to collect extra data from people already on your list.
steps: For your main signup form, target new visitors who have not signed up for email and have not signed up for SMS. This is the standard configuration the source uses.
Set up a separate popup for returning visitors: has signed up for email or SMS, or is identified by a cookie.
Use the returning-visitor popup to collect zero-party data, or to move an email subscriber onto your SMS list with a dedicated SMS opt-in form.

Configure re-trigger suppression: choose how long before the same popup can be shown again (the source notes options from seconds to a year), and suppress if another popup was viewed in the last 15 seconds when running multiple popups.
Set an overall store theme/branding once and reuse it across every popup so new forms stay visually consistent.
caveats: Popup targeting terminology and available conditions vary between tools; verify field names in your current interface.
The 15-second popup suppression is an example setting, not a recommended optimal value.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Preview and QA signup popups across devices before publishing
cards.summary: Use preview and device-simulation tools to confirm the popup renders and animates correctly everywhere before pushing it live.
cards.use_when: Final QA before publishing a new email capture popup to your live storefront.
steps: Play the animation preview so you can see the popup as an end user experiences it, including multi-step transitions such as first step, email step, and reward step.
Review the form on simulated devices — the source demonstrates an iPhone 15 and a 4K desktop — to confirm layout holds on both small and very wide viewports.
Use the preview button in the top-right corner to open your actual website with the popup showing, verifying it appears correctly on the live storefront.
Confirm the teaser/floating button (step one) looks correct before the full popup opens.
Check styling levers left in the builder: colors, fonts, button styles, input styles.

After publishing, create the reward in the rewards section: select a static code from your Shopify discount codes, generate a unique code, or use a custom reward such as a giveaway. Aaliyah's more granular preview options are noted as an advantage compared with the Klaviyo signup form.
caveats: Device-simulation coverage and builder options are tool-specific; check what your popup tool currently offers.
Some preview functionality described here may not exist in Klaviyo's signup form.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Offer copy for signups: explicit discount vs mystery discount
cards.summary: Test mystery or exclusive offer copy against explicit percentage-off copy, especially at lower discount levels.
cards.use_when: Writing the headline and button copy of a signup popup to raise signup rate without changing your actual discount.
steps: Run a copy test between an explicit offer ('10% off', '50% off'), a mystery discount ('you've got a mystery discount'), an exclusive offer, and a special offer.
Choose variants based on discount depth: the source states that if your discount is 10% or less, testing copy like mystery discount or exclusive discount is recommended.
The presenter's own rule of thumb: everything under 20% off tends to work better with the mystery discount angle; they recommend the mystery discount angle even for discounts at 50% off or less.
Let the A/B test decide for your audience rather than applying the rule of thumb blindly — the presenter explicitly says the data should confirm it.

Use automated smart testing where available: the source describes an AI system that builds the variant (for example a fully generated mystery-discount version) and runs tests automatically, ending each test when results are significant and moving to the next.
caveats: The under-20%-off and 50%-off-less thresholds are the presenter's heuristics, not measured cutoffs.
The automated test sequencing is specific to Aaliyah's smart testing; other tools may require manual test setup.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Diagnose a monetization problem before blaming email or buying more traffic
cards.summary: Frame list and welcome-flow weakness as a monetization problem that leaks paid traffic and inflates CAC.
cards.use_when: Reviewing why paid acquisition costs keep rising and deciding whether to invest in welcome flows rather than more ad spend.
steps: Check whether you are overpaying for traffic and under-monetizing it: many brands buy Meta, Google, TikTok, influencer, affiliate and landing-page traffic and let visitors leave with only a pixel hit.
Treat the resulting dependence on buying ever more traffic to hold revenue flat as the signal of a leaking funnel, not a traffic shortage.

Audit the three consequences the source names: rising blended CAC from traffic leaking without converting; email getting blamed based on topline email revenue instead of whether the welcome series captures first-time buying intent; and over-reliance on retargeting to recover people you already paid for once.
Invest in the welcome series as the fastest lever: it monetizes people you already paid to attract, improves first-time buyer conversion and payback speed.
Use the welcome series to build trust at the exact moment a new subscriber is deciding whether you are worth buying from, since that trust gap is often the real blocker.
caveats: This is a diagnostic frame from the source, not a measured causal model; rising CAC can have other drivers.
The claim that most brands have a monetization problem rather than a traffic problem is the presenter's generalization.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Front-load the welcome flow around the first 72 hours
cards.summary: Structure the welcome flow to concentrate persuasion and sends in the first 72 hours after signup when momentum and intent peak.
cards.use_when: Designing or restructuring the welcome series cadence for new email subscribers.
steps: Recognize the pattern the source reports across accounts: the overwhelming majority of welcome-flow revenue is generated within the first three days after signup, with the highest number of conversions on day zero and a steep drop after that.
Avoid stretched-out 10-, 14-, or 21-day welcome flows built mainly to 'build a relationship'; the source argues this wastes the moment of highest intent.
Schedule two emails on day one: email 1A immediately after signup, then email 1B eight hours later as a plain-text reminder.
Add a 16-hour delay after 1B so you reach 24 hours, then send email two, and continue daily through email six.
Accept the tension: the first email usually generates the most revenue because people only want the promised offer, so the later emails are what separate mediocre welcome flows from strong ones.

Use the later emails to build conviction quickly via social proof, brand credibility, product education, objection handling, USPs, category guidance, bestsellers, founder credibility, or urgency — not all of them, but enough to reduce hesitation fast.
caveats: The 72-hour concentration and the day-zero peak come from the source's own account analytics; timing will vary by brand, price point and traffic source.
The specific 8-hour and 16-hour delays are the source's recommended cadence, not tested universal optima.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Set welcome flow trigger filters and disable smart sending
cards.summary: Configure the welcome flow entry trigger, zero-purchase filter, no re-entry, and per-email send settings so only new non-buyers get the welcome discount.
cards.use_when: Building or auditing the welcome flow automation settings in your ESP.
steps: Trigger the flow when someone is added to your main list (often the newsletter list).
Add a profile filter: has placed order zero times over all time. This prevents existing buyers who re-subscribe from receiving the welcome discount again.
Disable re-entry so a person can only go through the welcome series once.
If working from a default template, delete the split for existing customers and remove any conditional split you're not using, then rebuild the delays.
Add time delays of 8 hours after email 1A, then 16 hours after 1B, then one day before each subsequent email through email six.

Turn off smart sending on every flow email. The source's reasoning: smart sending skips anyone who received an email in the last (default) 16 hours, but flow emails are trigger-based and must be delivered. For campaigns, the source advises the opposite — turn smart sending on. Verify the current smart sending window settings in your ESP.
Enable UTM tracking on the flow emails.
caveats: Filter names and default behaviors differ between ESPs and change over time; verify in your current account.
The advice to turn smart sending off for flows assumes trigger-based flows; the presenter's rule is not a universal deliverability law.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Write welcome email 1A: deliver the code above the fold
cards.summary: Make the first welcome email a frictionless delivery of the promised code with product guidance and trust builders directly in the above-the-fold area.
cards.use_when: Drafting or rewriting the first email of the welcome series.
steps: Put the offer, the discount code, and a one-click call to action in the above-the-fold section — the part visible without scrolling on mobile or desktop. The source's rationale: an estimated 90-99% of people only see the above-fold area before leaving the email.
Do not bury the code or make subscribers work for it. The subscriber signed up for one thing; give it immediately rather than leading with brand news.
Below the fold, show one to three bestsellers or a 'start here' selection to route them to a specific product or category.
Add trust builders where applicable: reviews, press mentions, expert endorsements, social proof.
Add risk reversals where applicable: free shipping, free returns, warranty, free trial.

Keep the hero simple. The source's example ('Welcome to [brand], 10% off your first order, use code X') is deliberately plain but unambiguous, then repeats the code with a CTA at the bottom of the email.
caveats: The 90-99% above-fold-only figure is the presenter's estimate, not a measured statistic.
The described layout is a source example for one brand; the exact modules should match your product mix and AOV.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Send a same-day plain-text founder reminder as welcome email 1B
cards.summary: Add a short, human plain-text second email eight hours after the first to capture day-zero momentum.
cards.use_when: Adding a second welcome-flow email on the day of signup to recover subscribers who didn't buy immediately.
steps: Send it eight hours after email 1A. The source's reasoning: momentum is highest on day zero and waiting 24 hours wastes it.
Write it as a short, direct, human plain-text founder-style note, for example 'just making sure you saw your code'.
Include a reminder of the discount code, one or two simple product or category references (bestsellers, bundles, top categories, or the most logical first purchase), and a direct CTA to the site.
Do not add a designed template or design flourish; the format is the point because conversational, human-feeling emails tend to be rewarded by inbox providers through engagement, per the source.

Expect a meaningful incremental revenue contribution from this second same-day email. The source reports this repeatedly in their tests and addresses the common concern that two emails in one day feels like too much.
caveats: The claim that email 1B 'drives a surprising amount' of incremental revenue is the presenter's client experience, not a published benchmark.
Two emails in one day may be inappropriate for very low-frequency or high-consideration catalogs; test on your own list.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Use welcome email 2 to build brand trust with substance, not fluff
cards.summary: Answer 'who are you and why should I trust you' in a short trust-building email with a discount reminder and CTA.
cards.use_when: Writing the second-day welcome email that establishes credibility for new subscribers who haven't bought yet.
steps: Choose the trust angle that fits your niche: a founder story, mission statement, quality standards, ingredients, sourcing, craftsmanship, or product philosophy. It depends on the brand.
Include a reminder of the welcome discount, a clear trust-building narrative, brand backstory or mission only if it actually matters, founder presence only if credible and relevant, and a clear CTA.
Keep it short. The source explicitly warns against big paragraphs; the goal is to reduce uncertainty and increase belief in the brand, not to tell the founder's entire life story.
Use a founder photo where it humanizes the brand — the example pairs a founder introduction with her product/category context and repeats the discount code.
Avoid 'brand poetry' with no substance; every claim should help a hesitant shopper decide you're a legitimate choice versus the alternatives they're comparing.
caveats: The source gives no length target; 'not too long' is a judgment call.
Founder credibility framing is not appropriate for every brand or category.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Use welcome email 3 to guide overwhelmed subscribers to a first purchase
cards.summary: Reduce choice paralysis by naming one to three bestsellers with benefit-led positioning and a discount reminder.
cards.use_when: Writing the welcome-flow email that helps undecided subscribers pick a first product.
steps: Assume subscribers don't know what to do with the discount code; tell them explicitly rather than expecting them to figure out the catalog.
Feature one to three bestsellers or best collections as recommended starting points.

Use simple benefit-led positioning rather than specs. The source's example leads with outcomes (grams of plant-based carbs for fast energy, dual carbs for quick absorption, hydration and endurance in one) instead of product features.
Explain why these are the best starting points and set clear expectations.
Remind them of the welcome gift again, typically in a top bar and in the email body.
Keep the email focused on routing, not on additional persuasion angles — that job belongs to later emails.
caveats: Benefit-first framing is a general copywriting principle; the source's specific framing comes from a supplement/energy brand example.
One to three featured products is the source's guidance; catalogs with very narrow assortment may need a different treatment.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Welcome email 4: handle objections and differentiate at the product or category level
cards.summary: Answer unasked objections about price, quality and alternatives, then add real urgency tied to a credible discount code.
cards.use_when: Writing the welcome-flow email that targets subscribers still hesitating after the first three sends.
steps: Assume remaining hesitation is friction and answer the questions they haven't asked: why buy from you instead of a competitor, why the price is justified, why they should trust your quality, and why act now.
Include core brand or product/category-level differentiators plus objection handling.
Remind them of the discount and add real urgency — a clear deadline if applicable (the source example: 'hurry, this code expires in 48 hours').

Make urgency believable by using unique discount codes, or static codes that look unique. The source warns that generic codes like WELCOME10 make urgency look fake because everyone knows such a code won't expire.
Add a review to support the argument.
Keep the focus on trust and differentiation rather than another hard sell.
caveats: The 48-hour deadline is a source example; your deadline must match your actual discount expiry for the urgency to be honest.
Not every brand has product-level differentiators worth a dedicated email; adapt the angle.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Welcome email 5: escalate urgency with reviews that mirror buyer objections
cards.summary: Push for the first purchase using a tightened deadline and one to three specific, pain-point-matching reviews.
cards.use_when: Writing the welcome-flow email that uses a closing deadline plus social proof to convert hesitant subscribers.
steps: Communicate a clear urgency deadline and escalate from the prior email: if email 4 said 48 hours left, email 5 says 24 hours left. If you hadn't stated a deadline earlier, 48 hours is a usable starting point. The source notes the escalation depends on the chosen strategy.
Add one to three reviews.

Select reviews carefully: avoid generic reviews that just say 'great product'. Choose reviews that highlight a specific pain point or objection and make readers feel recognized, so the reviewer's outcome maps to the reader's situation.
Prefer one strong, specific review over three generic ones.
Keep the email straightforward — urgency plus social proof, no new persuasion angles.
caveats: Deadline escalation only works if the deadlines are real; repeated fake deadlines damage trust.
The source gives no data on optimal review count beyond preferring quality over quantity.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Welcome email 6: close with a final reason to act, and test the format
cards.summary: Deliver the final welcome-flow push with the offer, strong urgency, and either a designed or plain-text format chosen by testing.
cards.use_when: Writing the final email of the welcome series and choosing its format.
steps: Include a final reminder of the offer, strong urgency, and a clear indication of what to buy.
Choose the strongest support angle for your brand: reviews, authority signals, or risk reversals.
Test designed versus plain-text format for this email rather than assuming one wins.

One route the source uses often: after email 4 at 48 hours and email 5 at 24 hours, make email 6 an 'extended sale' sent as a plain-text founder email ('we've extended your welcome discount for another 24 hours, act fast').
A/B test the closing angle and treat this email's format as a variable, not a fixed rule.
Keep the momentum assumption realistic: later emails in the flow generate less than the day-zero content, so expect incremental rather than dramatic returns.
caveats: The 'extended sale' angle works well in the source's experience but implies the deadline was moved; only use it if it is truthful.
The source presents two routes (designed vs plain text) as alternatives to test, not as a settled best practice.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Add proven evergreen campaigns to the welcome flow for extra revenue
cards.summary: Extend the welcome series beyond the core emails by appending evergreen campaigns that performed well as broadcasts.
cards.use_when: Looking for incremental welcome-flow revenue after the core six-email structure is working.
steps: Review past campaigns and identify the ones that generated the best results for your brand.
Check whether those top performers are evergreen, meaning they remain relevant and usable all year.
Add the evergreen winners into the welcome flow after the closing emails.

Candidate campaign types the source names: how-tos, blog promotions, review or user-generated content, myth-busting emails, product highlights, subscription promos, bundles, gift guides, and educational emails.
Do not cap the welcome flow at seven emails. The source explicitly says not to cap it and treats this as an easy way to squeeze additional revenue.
Set expectations modestly: because momentum is concentrated in the first 72 hours, treat the appended emails as incremental additions rather than major revenue drivers.
caveats: Purely seasonal campaigns are not evergreen and shouldn't be appended as standing flow emails.
The source does not quantify the incremental revenue, only that it is additional.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Position browse abandonment as mid-funnel persuasion, not lost-sale recovery
cards.summary: Treat browse-abandonment emails as trust and objection-handling plays for comparing shoppers rather than as discount-driven cart recovery.
cards.use_when: Deciding the strategy and tone for a browse abandonment flow targeting product-page visitors who didn't add to cart.
steps: Separate intent levels: browse abandoners viewed a product page but did not add to cart, so they are usually comparing alternatives in evaluation mode, not recovering a near-sale.
Shift the priority order for this flow: trust matters more than urgency, objection handling matters more than giving away a discount, and positioning matters more than promotion.
Do not clone your cart abandonment flow. The source says most brands get this wrong by treating browse abandonment as a weaker cart abandonment flow.

Recognize the competitive reality the source describes: a visitor viewing your product page likely has competing product tabs open, so the flow's job is to stay in the decision process with controlled persuasion rather than desperation.
Use the flow for margin- and LTV-conscious brands: follow up without immediately discounting, and reserve discounts for the later escalation emails.
caveats: The 'three other tabs' description is the presenter's illustration of comparison behavior, not measured data.
For very short deliberation categories, browse abandonment may behave more like cart abandonment.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Set browse abandonment trigger filters and a 30-day cooldown
cards.summary: Configure the viewed-product trigger with zero-order, zero-checkout, zero-add-to-cart filters and a 30-day re-entry limit.
cards.use_when: Building or auditing the browse abandonment flow in your ESP so it fires only for genuinely unconverted browsers.
steps: Trigger the flow on viewed product.

Add profile filters so the email only sends if the person has placed order zero times since starting this flow, has checkout started zero times since starting this flow, and has added to cart zero times since starting this flow.
Allow re-entry after a 30-day time period to create a cooldown window.
If you run Shopify, use the Shopify added-to-cart trigger rather than the API added-to-cart trigger. The source flags this as important.

Do not split the browse abandonment flow between new and returning customers in most cases. Rationale: browse abandoners are low-intent window shoppers, and even previous buyers are re-evaluating and comparing you against alternatives.

Exception: if margins are extremely tight and you truly cannot afford an incentive for returning buyers, consider a conditional split. The source argues that for most brands doing serious volume, the incremental revenue outweighs the marginal discount cost precisely because these visitors were not high-intent to begin with.
Note the contrast with cart abandonment, where the source does recommend splitting returning customers from non-buyers because intent is higher.
caveats: Filter and trigger names differ by ESP and change over time; verify in your current account.
The no-split recommendation is the source's general preference with a stated margin-based exception, not an absolute rule.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Time the browse abandonment delays and use dynamic product blocks
cards.summary: Set the send delay by intent level and include a dynamic product block plus recommendations in every browse-abandonment email.
cards.use_when: Building the timing and core content of the browse abandonment sequence.
steps: Set the first delay to roughly 30-45 minutes up to 2 hours. The source tests this range, uses 1 hour for demonstration, and notes that closer to the purchase moment you should email sooner.
Calibrate by flow type: browse abandonment is around 2-4 hours at the loosest, cart abandonment shorter, and checkout abandonment shortest — as early as 15 minutes for the checkout flow.
Structure as a four-part sequence: email one is a simple reminder, email two builds trust, emails three and four introduce the discount.
Add a one-day delay between each email.
Include a dynamic product block in every email, showing the product the person viewed.

Build the block efficiently: copy a default template's dynamic product block, save it as universal/reusable content, and edit it to match your branding rather than building from scratch — the source says this saves a lot of time.
caveats: The delay ranges are source heuristics for relative urgency across flow types, not measured optima; test on your own traffic.
Dynamic product block features and universal content features are ESP-specific; verify availability.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Write browse abandonment email 1 as a light, timely reminder
cards.summary: Send a non-aggressive product reminder within hours of the page view, with a dynamic product block, recommendations and social proof.
cards.use_when: Drafting the first browse-abandonment email.
steps: Send it while the visit is still fresh — the source's range is 30 minutes to 2 hours after the product page view — so the person still remembers you.
Keep it non-aggressive and not sales-heavy. A simple 'you were looking at this, are you still interested?' angle is enough.
Include a dynamic product block showing the viewed product.
Include a recommendations feed, for example four other products related to the viewed product.
Add social proof such as reviews or user-generated content.
Use a clear headline and CTA above the fold with body copy containing the dynamic product block and a second CTA, plus a related-products section.
Expect this email alone to recover mainly high-intent browsers who simply got distracted — the source says that is what you're capturing at this stage.
caveats: The source's claim about what share of intent this recovers is qualitative, not measured.
Timing must be feasible with your ESP's trigger and delay configuration.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Write browse abandonment email 2 to remove friction, not add pressure
cards.summary: Lead with risk reversals, social proof and product guidance to address hesitation for comparison shoppers.
cards.use_when: Writing the second browse-abandonment email for viewers who ignored the first reminder.
steps: Assume the non-conversion reflects hesitation, which the source calls completely normal in browse abandonment.
Think like the buyer and address the questions they have: is this worth the price, is this legit, what if it doesn't fit or work or last, is there a better alternative.
Do not sell harder. Reduce uncertainty.
Lead with risk reversals if you have them: guarantees, trials, free shipping, free returns.
If you lack strong risk reversals, lean on social proof instead.
Include a dynamic product block to guide them back to the viewed product.
Add a brand-level reason to buy where you have one — the source's example uses a mission-based reason ('every tea they buy feeds five rescue dogs') with a supporting review.
Treat this email as especially important for higher AOV brands, which need more convincing before a first purchase.
caveats: The higher-AOV emphasis is the presenter's reasoning, not measured by AOV band.
Mission-based angles only fit brands that genuinely have them.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Browse abandonment email 3: diagnose hesitation type before escalating with a discount
cards.summary: Classify remaining hesitation as price sensitivity, comparison shopping, or procrastination and escalate the offer intelligently.
cards.use_when: Writing the third browse-abandonment email, where the audience has ignored both the reminder and the trust-building email.
steps: Accept the interpretation: after two ignored emails, non-conversion is hesitation rather than forgetfulness — they are not sure they should buy from your store.
Diagnose which of the three hesitation categories applies: price sensitivity, comparison shopping, or 'I'll buy later' procrastination.
Escalate with an offer only at this stage, not before. The source structures the flow so discounts appear in emails three and four, after the reminder and trust emails.
Match the escalation to the hesitation type rather than sending the same incentive to everyone.
For returning customers specifically, the source suggests the same escalation logic: a small incentive, a subscription option where applicable, a bundle angle, or a compelling reason to act now.
Aim to convert low intent into action rather than protecting loyalty perception — this is the source's stated goal for browse-abandonment sending.
caveats: The three hesitation categories are the source's framework, not a measured taxonomy.
Escalating discounts in browse abandonment can erode margin; the source accepts this trade-off for volume brands but notes the tight-margin exception.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Browse abandonment flow: 3-4 email escalation ladder
cards.summary: Structure a browse abandonment flow that escalates from reminder to trust-building to deadline-driven discount or subscription push over 4 emails.
cards.use_when: Building or auditing the browse abandonment flow for your store.
steps: Email 1: simple reminder with the viewed product in a dynamic product block plus CTA buttons, and risk reversals (guarantees, trials, free shipping/returns). Example shown: apparel brand 'every tea they buy feeds five rescue dogs' plus a review.
Email 2: trust/risk reversal angle — three deeper reasons why people buy from this brand, with a dynamic product block.
Email 3: treat remaining non-buyers as hesitant, not forgetful. Hesitation falls into one of three buckets: price sensitivity, comparison shopping, or 'I'll buy later' procrastination.

For email 3, choose one of two escalation options. Option A: small time-sensitive incentive with a clear 48-hour deadline, clean design, single clear CTA. Option B: if you sell replenishables, push subscribe-and-save (e.g., 10% off), a bundle, or a starter-kit discount to protect margin instead of discounting a one-time purchase.

Email 4: last chance before discount ends — plain-text email from the founder, short and direct, 24-hour deadline, reminding them of the code from the previous email. Source argues plain text at this stage feels personal while heavy design signals automation.

Optional in emails 3-4: show product recommendations via the Klaviyo product feed (e.g., 'you might like these') so non-buyers see other products. Furniture example also used a footer bar highlighting a physical store to build trust.
caveats: Source presents this ladder as its own recommended structure, not a universal rule.
The presenter explicitly says the browse flow is where they see brands 'overdo it' with banners and urgency graphics — simplifying is the point.

The source does not recommend splitting the browse flow between new and returning buyers because browse abandonment is low intent; even returning customers are comparison shopping. Only treat margins as the reason to split.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Abandoned cart vs abandoned checkout: build side by side
cards.summary: Use the same flow structure for abandoned cart and abandoned checkout, differing only in trigger and one flow filter.
cards.use_when: Setting up abandoned cart and abandoned checkout flows inside Klaviyo (verify current interface).
steps: In Klaviyo, go to Flows > Create flow, search 'cart' to find the cart flow (it may not appear in the Essentials list — verify current UI).
If your store is on Shopify, use the Shopify 'added to cart' trigger, not the generic one. Build the abandoned cart version first.
Set flow filters: checkout started zero times since starting this flow, placed order zero times since starting this flow, and (via 'has not been in the flow in the last 30 days') no recent re-entry.

Add the first time delay. Klaviyo defaults to 4 hours; the source says this is too long and recommends testing 15 minutes to 1 hour, e.g., 30 minutes. The principle: the closer to purchase intent, the sooner the email.
Send email 1 at ~30 minutes, email 2 one day later, email 3 one day later.
Add a conditional split: 'has placed order at least once (all time)' — yes = returning customer, no = non-buyer/first-time buyer.
Non-buyers get two further emails: email 4 with discount (48-hour deadline) and email 5 one day later with a final discount reminder (24-hour deadline).

Returning customers get the founder check-in email. Then clone the whole flow, rename to abandoned checkout, change the trigger to 'checkout started', and remove the 'checkout started zero times' filter since the trigger is now checkout started.
caveats: Exact Klaviyo menus, defaults and filter names may have changed — verify the current interface before implementing.
The 15-60 minute timing is a recommended starting point the presenter says to A/B test; it is not a proven benchmark.
Only apply the discount branch if your margins allow it.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Abandoned cart/checkout email content: 3-stage objection sequence
cards.summary: Content plan for what each abandoned cart/checkout email should contain: simple reminder, plastic-text founder check-in, then objection handling.
cards.use_when: Writing the copy for abandoned cart and abandoned checkout emails before any discount is offered.
steps: Email 1 (30 min-1 hour after abandonment): simple reminder only. No discount, no overselling. Most abandonment is distraction ('phone, a thousand things going on'), not a 'no'. Include a dynamic product block and your risk reversals (guarantees, trials, free shipping, free returns). Example: 'You left something tasty behind — complete my order — why spice fans love us — complete my order.'

Email 2 (1 day later): plain-text personalized check-in from the founder. Tone should feel like a one-to-one email. Angle: 'Noticed you were checking out this product — wanted to make sure you didn't run into issues. By the way, here's why people love us.' Keep it 2-3 short paragraphs max, end with a simple CTA and a link back to their cart. This also performs well with Gmail's AI inbox prioritizing conversational email (source's 2026 claim).

Email 3 (1 day later): objection handling, not 'our brand is awesome'. Address the real frictions: is it worth the price, shipping time, what if it doesn't fit, what if it doesn't work, what if it's not as good as the photos. Frame strongest USPs/products as answers to those objections (durability/warranty for price, certifications/press for trust, clear differentiation for comparison shopping). Include a dynamic product block.

Example of objection handling from a vape brand: 'British made quality' (addresses trust/offshore concerns), '8X cheaper than cigarettes' (price concern), '100% BPA free' (safety concern), 'highly rated service' (social proof).
caveats: This sequence deliberately holds discounts until escalation; the source argues giving discounts in email one destroys margins and trains customers to wait for discounts.
The claim that this structure is 'the highest converting' is the presenter's opinion, not a measured benchmark.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Discount vs no-discount fork: non-buyers vs returning customers
cards.summary: Split abandoned cart/checkout discounting: offer an escalating discount to first-time non-buyers, but only support or a smaller incentive to returning customers.
cards.use_when: Deciding who gets a discount code in your abandoned cart/checkout flow and how much.
steps: Add a conditional split after emails 1-3: 'has placed order at least once (all time)'. Yes = returning customer, No = non-buyer/first-time buyer.

Non-buyers (email 4): clean, simple, time-sensitive discount — code with a 48-hour deadline, dynamic product block, optional Klaviyo product feed recommendations, clear CTA. Examples shown: 'Take 10% off your cart, use code...', 'Enjoy 10% off today'.

Non-buyers (email 5): final push, plain-text from the founder with the code and a 24-hour deadline. Example: 'it's Melanie here, founder of... good news, you can still claim your offer with 10% off, use code...' This is the source's claim: plain text closes first-time buyers who are '90% convinced' but need a deadline.

Returning customers: no discount by default. Send one plain-text founder check-in offering concierge-level support — ask about sizing, specs, delivery, offer help. Source argues returning customers already trust the brand, are often just distracted, and may be comparison shopping for details, not loyalty.

If margins are solid and you want to discount returning customers, source recommends a smaller discount than non-buyers — their example: 5-10% instead of 50% for non-buyers. In that case, add the matching final reminder email one day later.
caveats: Discount amounts and deadlines (48h/24h) are source examples, not calibrated benchmarks.
Source specifically warns not to train loyal customers to expect full discounts — offering returning customers the same discount as non-buyers is the most common mistake the presenter calls out.
The 5-10% vs 50% example is illustrative, not a recommended ratio.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Post-purchase flow filters and timing
cards.summary: Set up a post-purchase flow with the right filters, filters that skip recent emailers, and a 10-minute first email delay.
cards.use_when: Setting up a post-purchase flow in Klaviyo that turns first-time buyers into repeat customers.
steps: Trigger: placed order. Set two flow filters: placed order zero times since starting this flow (so a second purchase re-triggers the flow and doesn't get the old one), and canceled order zero times since starting this flow.

Wait 10 minutes before the first email. Don't send immediately — the customer already receives your transactional order/shipping emails from Shopify or your commerce platform, so a separate thank-you would be redundant.

Turn OFF smart sending / 'skip recently emailed profiles' on every email in this flow. If a customer just bought from a campaign email, smart sending would suppress the post-purchase email, which is the opposite of what you want.

Add a conditional split: 'has placed order equals one (all time)' — Yes = first-time buyer; No = returning customer. Optionally split again at two purchases for a separate three-plus-purchase track, which the source says is worth it for some brands but not necessary for most.

Source's default structure: email 1 (thank you) at 10 minutes; email 2 (order on its way) 2 days later; email 3 (how-to, split by product/category); optional email 4 (social follow push); optional email 5 (loyalty program push); email 6 (post-delivery personal check-in from the founder).
caveats: Klaviyo menu names and smart-sending settings may have changed — verify current interface.
The 'order on its way' timing assumes standard shipping; adjust to your actual shipping times.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Post-purchase email content: 6-email sequence
cards.summary: Content plan for the post-purchase emails that reduce returns, build the relationship, and drive the first repeat purchase.
cards.use_when: Writing the emails in your post-purchase flow after a customer's first order.
steps: Email 1 (10 minutes): plain-text thank-you from the founder. Confirm order progress, offer support, tell them what to expect. For first-time buyers make it a memorable first impression; for returning customers express gratitude for loyalty. Include a link back to your site (source says even just a site link gets a strong post-purchase place-order rate) and optionally recommend a specific product to cross-sell — the biggest repeat-purchase window is the first 30 days.

Email 2 (2 days): 'your order is on its way'. Build excitement, reinforce the value of the purchase, and include recommendations — static blocks or the Klaviyo product feed. Examples: refills/cookbook/candle/kit for a spice brand; 'complete your stack' bundles pairing isolate with creatine or collagen for a nutrition brand; 'explore more' sabers plus a mystery saber (curiosity works).

Email 3: how-to email, split by product or product category so it's actually relevant to what they bought. Provide clear actionable tips, links to FAQs/manuals/videos, and reassurance they made a good choice. This reduces returns and improves experience.
Email 4 (optional): social media follow push — the more channels you hold a customer on, the better for repeat purchase.
Email 5 (optional): loyalty program push. Make the benefit immediately clear (points, discounts, rewards for shopping/reviewing/referring) — people only join for a clear benefit.

Email 6: post-delivery plain-text check-in from the founder — 'how did everything go?' The source says this is one of the highest-revenue emails because it shows genuine care and can invite the next purchase.
caveats: Source claims retained customers are 9x more likely to convert and repeat customers spend 67% more than new customers; it does not provide the study for either, so treat as attributed statistics, not your expected results.
Source claims 95% of customers receiving proactive post-purchase communication are less likely to return — also unaudited data, use as directional.
The 'most returning customers buy within 30 days' statement is from one client screenshot, not a universal benchmark.
Auto-applied source framing: how-to email 3 only makes sense if you have technical products; simple care instructions may be enough for apparel.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Post-purchase as the retention engine
cards.summary: Treat the first purchase as the start of the relationship, not the finish line, and use the post-purchase flow to drive repeat purchase and reduce returns.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much post-purchase and replenishment effort to invest after the first order.
steps: Reframe the first purchase as the beginning of the relationship — a weak post-purchase experience loses repeat purchases, referrals, trust, and lifetime value.
Prioritize the first 30 days: the source says most returning customers buy within 30 days of their initial order, so this is the window to improve first-to-second purchase rate.
Use the flow to reduce returns by reinforcing purchase value, giving usage/care tips, and building excitement — buyer's remorse is a major return driver and returns cut into margin.
Push replenishment appropriately within the post-purchase sequence: subscriptions or loyalty programs for replenishable products, and cross-sell/recommendations for everything else.
Multi-channel touchpoints (email + SMS + social) are described as ways to increase repurchase rate — the more places you hold the customer, the more often you can reach them.
caveats: The statistics cited (9x, 67%, 95%, 30-day window) are attributed to 'research' by the source without citations and are not benchmarks you should plan against.
Return-rate and repeat-purchase effects will vary by category and AOV; the source presents them as typical, not universal.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Email campaign frequency: aim for 3-4 per week
cards.summary: Send email campaigns 3-4 times per week so your brand stays top of mind without burning out the list.
cards.use_when: Deciding how often to send email campaigns to your ecommerce list.
steps: Sending once or twice a week feels respectful but backfires: subscribers can't place you, skip past you, and eventually forget you exist — 'less frequent doesn't mean less intrusive, it means less memorable'.

Sending 5-7 times a week (every day) can produce short-term revenue but drives fatigue, higher unsubscribes, lower engagement, and deliverability damage. The degradation is slow enough that brands often don't notice until it's done.

Target 3-4 campaigns per week. This keeps visibility without tipping into annoying, keeps engagement healthy, keeps churn manageable, and builds a consistent inbox presence rather than sporadic spikes.
Because the volume is high, campaigns must be short, valuable, and easy to act on — a couple of seconds to make an impression; nobody wants a wall of text from a brand they bought from once.
caveats: The 3-4x/week figure comes from the source's own testing across 120 ecommerce brands over 7 years; treat as a source-specific heuristic, not an industry benchmark.
Frequency should still be tuned to your list size, engagement and deliverability; the source itself notes the flood of what you send matters as much as how often.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Campaign mix: don't let promos dominate the calendar
cards.summary: Balance your campaign calendar across seven categories instead of leaning on discounts, or you train subscribers to wait for sales.
cards.use_when: Building or auditing your monthly/quarterly email campaign calendar.
steps: All campaign emails fall into one of seven buckets: promos/special offers; holiday/special events; product launches; product highlights; social proof; value-based/educational; company updates.

Audit your calendar against those buckets. Most ecom brands over-index on promos because discounts drive immediate sales — but if every email is a promotion, subscribers learn to wait for the next deal and only buy at a discount, which kills margin.
Add a subtler cost: constant 'buy now' emails make a brand feel desperate, and the source says desperate doesn't sell.

Replace some promo volume with trust-building content. Source argues that in 2026 customers are skeptical, research and compare, and trust is what sits between being on your list and buying. Trust takes repetition across multiple touchpoints, not one clever subject line.
The practical payoff the source claims: when customers trust you, they buy without needing a discount, improving both conversion rate and margins.
caveats: The 'seven categories' is a planning framework used by the source, not a data-driven taxonomy.
The source does not say promos are bad — it says they should sit alongside trust-building content, with discounts having a time and place.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Non-discounted campaign idea bank (social proof + education)
cards.summary: A list of social proof and educational campaign angles you can send without discounting.
cards.use_when: Filling your campaign calendar with non-discounted emails that build trust with your list.
steps: Social proof angles: testimonials, user-generated content, press mentions, media features, influencer reviews, before-and-after results from real customers, review roundups around one product or benefit, trust badges/certifications, star-rating highlights across platforms like Trustpilot or Google, peer video testimonials, customer milestones (long-time buyer or achievement), and community numbers (customers served, orders shipped, countries reached).

Education angles: blog/article highlights, research highlights, myths debunked, FAQs, industry trends, common mistakes and fixes, glossary emails breaking down jargon, beginner's guides, advanced tips, debunking a competitor claim, expert interviews, book/resource recommendations, a single surprising 'stat of the week', your most-asked question pulled from support or social comments, and an ingredient/material spotlight explaining why one component matters.
Use these to build trust through teaching — source argues that genuinely useful content makes you a credible source, not just another brand in the inbox.
Keep each email short and easy to act on, since you're sending 3-4 per week.
caveats: These are the source's idea prompts, not tested angles with known performance.
Claims like 'educational content is one of the most effective trust builders' are the presenter's argument, not measured results.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Non-discounted campaign idea bank (product, brand, occasion, engagement)
cards.summary: Product-focused, brand/culture, occasion and interactive campaign angles that sell without discounts.
cards.use_when: Planning campaign emails that highlight products or brand story rather than cutting price.
