steps: Product-focused angles: bestsellers, new arrivals, trending products, staff picks, back-in-stock, bundles, essentials, gift guides, 'gift yourself', feature highlights, benefit highlights, us-vs-them competitor framing, problem-to-solution, before-and-after, how-to-use, how-it's-made, tips and tricks, coming-soon sneak peeks, limited-edition/seasonal (creates urgency without discounting), product comparisons to help choose between two of your own products, subscription/loyalty highlights, most underrated product, fan favorite, founder's pick, packaging highlight, product origin story, sensory description (food, beauty, lifestyle), complimentary products (soft cross-sell), build-a-routine, most gifted, and customer-favorite combinations/bundles.

Brand and culture angles: brand story, founder story, meet the team, behind the scenes, recent developments, brand USPs, day in the life, community spotlight, brand values in action, 'our story so far' timeline, why we started, what we refuse to do (powerful trust/differentiation angle), mistakes you've made (rare, memorable, transparent), manufacturing process, suppliers/partners, team tradition, and growth announcements.

Calendar/occasion angles: holidays, awareness days tied naturally to your niche, seasonal transitions, brand milestones (anniversaries, subscriber counts, units sold), new year/new routine, back to school, new season preview, end-of-year reflection.

Engagement angles: quiz/survey teaser to find the right product, poll results tied back to products, 'ask us anything' (also good for deliverability), pick your favorites votes, challenge emails, waitlist/early access invites, referral program spotlights, and loyalty program updates.
caveats: This is a long prompt list from the source, not a prioritization or performance ranking.
It is not evidence that any single angle converts; test within your own list.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Campaign calendar tool setup and the minimum fields to track
cards.summary: Maintain a campaign calendar in any tool, tracking status, ownership, content and results at minimum.
cards.use_when: Setting up or cleaning up the production calendar your team uses to plan campaign emails.
steps: Choose a tool based on how you work; the source says the tool matters less than consistent use. Options discussed: Notion (flexible visual workspace), Airtable (stronger filtering/sorting across high volumes, used by the source's agency), ClickUp or Monday (if your team already lives in a project management tool), or Google Sheets (underrated and sufficient for a simple setup everyone can access).

Whatever the tool, track at least: campaign status, owner, send/planned date, campaign category, subject line and/or angle, main content or offer, and links to creative or the live campaign so the full campaign list doesn't become a graveyard.
Use the tracked category column to enforce the non-promo mix — if every row says 'promo', your calendar is out of balance.
Review the calendar on a regular cadence so you always know what is drafted, which email is next, and which tested angle hasn't been reused.
caveats: The exact field list belongs to the source's own system; add fields that reflect how your team actually works.
Tool features and interfaces change — verify current functionality before standardizing on one.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Run a campaign calendar in a tool your team will actually open
cards.summary: Choose the lightest project tool your team already uses, then track six fields per campaign.
cards.use_when: Setting up or replacing the email campaign planning system before a month of sends.
steps: Pick the tool by team behavior, not features: Notion suits visual, flexible team workspaces; Airtable is stronger for filtering/sorting large campaign volumes across many clients; ClickUp or Monday make sense if the team already lives in a PM tool and wants email alongside other marketing work; Google Sheets is enough for a basic, universally accessible start.

Track these fields for every campaign: send date, campaign type, segment, status, and owner. Status values used by the source: idea, copywriting, design, implementation, ready to review, scheduled, sent.
Use the owner field to name the person responsible for that specific step, not a general team.

Note this is agency-practitioner experience, not a benchmark: the presenter reports switching tools over ~4 years and currently using Airtable; Google Sheets is described as underrated and sufficient.
Verify the current UI and plan limits in whichever tool you choose, since interfaces change.
caveats: Tool recommendations reflect one agency's workflow; a small store may never outgrow Sheets.
A calendar only helps if it is updated consistently.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Send campaigns only to engaged subscribers
cards.summary: Suppress unengaged profiles from campaigns to protect deliverability and inbox placement.
cards.use_when: Deciding the send list for any ecommerce campaign, especially after engagement or revenue has declined.
steps: Stop blasting the full email list; the source calls this one of the most common and costly email mistakes because unengaged sends hurt deliverability and push even strong campaigns into spam.
Define an engaged segment in Klaviyo as people who opened or clicked within the last 30, 60, or 90 days.
Choose the window based on your list size and sending volume — the source treats 30/60/90 as options, not a fixed rule.
Send campaigns to that engaged segment only, and use deliverability/segmentation tutorials from the source's channel for setup detail.
Verify current Klaviyo segment and suppression mechanics before building, since interfaces change.
caveats: Aggressive suppression shrinks the addressable list; the method deliberately trades raw reach for inbox placement.
The text does not state a numeric deliverability benchmark for this change — treat any lift as audience-dependent.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Anchor the calendar with fixed dates before filling content
cards.summary: Lock non-negotiable sends first, then build all remaining campaigns around them.
cards.use_when: Starting a new month of email campaign planning for a store with launches, restocks, or planned promotions.
steps: Open the calendar and mark every already-decided event for the month: product launches, back-in-stock products, planned sales or promotions, brand milestones and announcements.
Treat these as anchors — do not place any other content until they are in.
Layer optional holidays and awareness days on top afterward; find lesser-known dates via nationaltoday.com by searching the target month.

Cap date-based emails at one or two per month, and remember you don't have to discount for them — relevant content alone is enough. Example from the source: a coffee brand owns National Coffee Day, but could also fit World Sleep Day or National Productivity Day if the positioning supports it.
Avoid firing a 'national day' email every week; the source says it becomes annoying.
caveats: Fixed-date clarity matters most when launches and promotions are already budgeted; for stores with no fixed events, holidays become the anchor instead.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Keep sales events to one per month or fewer
cards.summary: Rare promotions preserve full-price conversion and avoid training customers to wait for discounts.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many discount or sale emails to schedule in a month and how to protect margin.
steps: Limit sales events to a maximum of one per month; the source says every other month is even better.

Recognize the two costs of frequent discounting: subscribers learn to wait for the next sale instead of buying at full price, and the brand becomes perceived as a discount brand — a perception the source calls very hard to reverse.
Treat scarcity as the mechanism: when the audience knows you rarely discount, a promotion creates urgency; when a sale is always around the corner, it creates patience.
When planning the month, place the single sale event as a fixed anchor and build non-promotional campaigns around it.
Sequence the calendar so full-price product and value campaigns sit in the weeks before and after the event rather than piling on more offers.
caveats: This is the presenter's stated opinion ('I cannot stress this enough'), not a measured benchmark; inventory clearing or seasonal retail realities may justify more.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Reuse existing blog, video and social content for campaigns
cards.summary: Mine your own content library before writing anything new, and match each piece to the right season.
cards.use_when: Filling empty calendar slots for a store that lacks new creative bandwidth.
steps: Inventory existing blogs, YouTube videos, social posts, podcasts or any content generally useful to your audience.
Match each piece to the right time of year: a summer skincare routine blog fits May or June, not November.
Choose one of two routes per piece: tease the most interesting part and link to the full blog/video, or summarize the key takeaway and link directly to a relevant product.
Mix or test the two routes against each other over time to learn what the audience prefers.

If the content library is thin, search Google for topics the audience cares about and write a short educational email based on what you find — the source notes you don't need to be the original source of information, only the clear presenter who connects it to your brand.
Verify current platform features if you plan to automate this reuse inside an ESP.
caveats: Out-of-season content recycling can feel disconnected; timing the piece matters as much as the piece itself.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Plan a month of campaigns with an AI context block
cards.summary: Feed AI brand, audience, cadence, fixed dates and a campaign-idea list, then refine its draft.
cards.use_when: Drafting a full month of email campaign ideas quickly instead of brainstorming from a blank calendar.
steps: Build a context block containing: brand name and what you sell; target customer and their problems; sending frequency (the source recommends three to four campaigns per week); the month being planned; fixed dates already locked in; content already placed; and the full list of campaign types from the source's library (downloadable via the free email marketing course linked in the video description).

Prompt the AI (the source uses Claude; ChatGPT or Gemini also work) with a structured request: brand, customer, cadence, month, locked dates, the campaign-type list, then 'fill in the remaining slots with specific campaign ideas from the list that make sense for our brand and audience, including send date, campaign type, and a two-line angle description.'

Review every suggestion against three questions: does it make sense for our brand right now; do we have the content, images and reviews to execute it; and is the overall mix balanced across the seven campaign categories.
Swap out anything that doesn't fit and fill gaps from the idea list.
Expect the source's claimed time of roughly 10–20 minutes for a full month; treat that as the presenter's experience, not a guaranteed benchmark.
caveats: The output is a draft — the source explicitly says you won't use every suggestion as-is and will refine from there.
AI planning quality depends entirely on context quality; thin inputs produce generic calendars.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Pressure-test the finished calendar with AI before finalizing
cards.summary: Paste the completed calendar into AI to flag imbalance, repetition and over-promotion before it goes live.
cards.use_when: Doing a final quality check on a completed monthly email calendar.
steps: Once the calendar is filled in, paste it back into AI with a review prompt: 'Here's my email campaign calendar for [month]. Review the mix across campaign types and the weekly cadence. Flag anything that looks unbalanced, repetitive, or too promotional, and suggest alternatives where needed.'
Use the output as a cheap pre-check that catches problems before they reach the list and before the human mix check.
Treat AI comments as input, not verdict — the source says they are often genuinely useful but still require your judgment.
Follow with the manual monthly and weekly mix checks described in the calendar-balance process.
Verify current AI tool availability/features if you rely on a specific model.
caveats: This is a supplementary check, not a replacement for reviewing the calendar yourself.
AI cannot know your inventory, creative readiness or margin situation.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Check monthly mix across the seven campaign categories
cards.summary: Audit campaign balance by category before finalizing, pulling anything above roughly one-third promotional.
cards.use_when: Finalizing a monthly email campaign calendar and checking whether it is too sales-heavy.
steps: Spread the month's campaigns across the seven campaign categories used in the source's framework.

Check the rough monthly ranges the source says work well for most ecommerce brands: one to two promotional or discount emails, four to six product-focused emails, four to six value or education emails, two to four social proof emails, and two to four brand emails.
If more than a third of the content is promotional, remove some promotional sends and replace them with content or social proof emails.
Treat the ranges as starting heuristics, not targets to force — the source presents them as a rough balance that works for most brands.
Verify the category definitions in your own system if you use an ESP-native calendar.
caveats: The bands are source-specific heuristics, not a calculated benchmark; list size, seasonality and launch cadence can shift them.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Alternate campaign types within each week, not just across the month
cards.summary: Avoid clustering similar campaign types in one week — no two consecutive emails should share a type.
cards.use_when: Sequencing a week of sends and checking why engagement dips despite a balanced monthly mix.
steps: Apply the rule: no two consecutive emails should be the same campaign type. If Monday is a testimonial, Wednesday cannot be another social proof send.
Fix the common failure mode where a brand batches all social proof into one week, leaves only product highlights in the next, and produces a pattern subscribers start to ignore.
Use the source's example well-paced week for four sends per week: Monday educational, Wednesday product-focused, Friday social proof, Sunday brand.
Check that the week delivers a complete experience — the subscriber is educated, shown a product, given proof it works, and connected to the brand.
Apply this week by week when finalizing the calendar rather than only auditing the month as a whole.
caveats: Cadence depends on your sending frequency; three sends a week needs a different sequence than four.
This is a source heuristic for variety, not an experimentally validated optimum.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Build a two-week execution buffer before sends go out
cards.summary: Always have emails two weeks ahead — written, designed and sitting ready for review.
cards.use_when: Fixing late, rushed campaign production that degrades email quality and coverage.
steps: Make two weeks of runway a non-negotiable workflow standard: emails going out in two weeks are already written, designed and queued for review.

Recognize what writing the day before produces: quality drops, you default to promotions because they are easier under pressure, coordination with fixed dates is missed, and errors slip through with no time to catch them.
Work backward from the calendar: two weeks before send date, the campaign should already be drafted; one week before, designed and reviewed.
Use the buffer to coordinate launches, restocks and sale anchors with the surrounding campaign content.
The source acknowledges this is difficult for many ecommerce brands but says to put in the effort to establish it.
caveats: Requires enough creative and merchandising capacity to stay ahead; a hard backlog can make the two-week rule feel unattainable at first.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Run a 20–30 minute monthly performance review
cards.summary: Review opens, clicks and revenue by campaign each month to find patterns the calendar can encode.
cards.use_when: End-of-month review before planning the next month's email calendar.
steps: Spend 20–30 minutes at month end reviewing what went out and how it performed.
Identify campaigns with the highest open rates; identify campaigns that drove the most clicks and revenue; identify underperformers and reason about why they underperformed.
Keep the analysis shallow enough to be sustainable — the goal is spotting patterns, not a deep statistical study.
Feed the patterns back into next month's calendar: repeat the formats, angles and timings that worked and drop the ones that consistently underperformed.
Repeat monthly so the calendar sharpens over time.
caveats: The presenter calls this super important, but the 20–30 minute figure is his own cadence, not a measured optimum.
Small lists may not produce statistically meaningful monthly patterns.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Put the product in every email, leading with value
cards.summary: Even non-promotional emails should present the product as the natural solution to a taught problem.
cards.use_when: Writing education, brand or social proof campaigns that risk becoming product-free content.
steps: Ensure every email — including those with nothing to do with a promotion — has your product somewhere in the picture.
Lead with value: teach the audience about a problem, then position the product as the natural solution. The source frames this as useful rather than pushy.
Rotate angles across the calendar so the relationship builds from different directions: build trust with social proof one week, educate the next, show behind-the-scenes the week after.
Track that all these angles ultimately move the same needle — a compounding relationship that makes selling easier over time.
Treat the campaign calendar as a system, not a hunt for a single killer email.
caveats: This is the presenter's positioning philosophy; heavily editorial or community-led brands may deliberately separate content from product.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Restrict SMS campaigns to launches, restocks and sales
cards.summary: Use SMS sparingly for highest-impact moments and keep routine sends in email.
cards.use_when: Deciding which campaign calendar items get SMS versus email, especially outside the US.
steps: Use SMS only for three use cases: product launches, restocks and sales events.
Route everything else on the campaign calendar to email — the source says email does the job at a fraction of the cost.
Stop treating SMS like email: sending SMS campaigns every week burns through the SMS list and racks up costs, particularly outside the US and in Europe where rates are significantly higher.
Monitor your SMS cost per send; the source states ROI outside these three use cases rarely makes sense given the cost.

If based in Europe, test WhatsApp as an alternative — it is far more common there, cost per message is much lower than traditional SMS in most European markets, and the source says brands testing it now have an advantage as the channel matures.
caveats: WhatsApp-for-ecommerce is described as still early; expect a learning curve and verify current platform support.
This is the presenter's stated philosophy ('use it sparingly'), not an experimental result.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Build a systematic AB testing mindset before running tests
cards.summary: Test on a schedule, from written hypotheses, with enough data, judged on revenue.
cards.use_when: Setting up an ecommerce email testing program or auditing why past tests produced no usable learning.
steps: Test consistently: run new tests every two to four weeks depending on volume. The source notes a brand doing over $100k/month has far more traffic and can test much faster than one doing around $10k/month.

Write a clear hypothesis stating what you're testing, why, and the expected outcome. Instead of 'test two subject lines,' write 'adding an emoji to the subject line will increase the open rate because it will make the email stand out in the inbox.'

Collect sufficient data before concluding. Source guidelines: at least 3–5,000 impressions per variant OR at least 15 days runtime for signup forms (7 days may be enough in some situations, but 15 is the general advice); at least 1,000 recipients per variant for flows; 500 recipients per variant can occasionally be enough if the gap is very large.
Judge on revenue as the ultimate metric — the source says revenue decides roughly 95% of tests. Sometimes a lower click rate produces more revenue, and that trade is worth taking.
Avoid the trap of endlessly testing only subject lines because they are easy; a winner with no hypothesis behind it teaches nothing transferable.
caveats: The 3–5k / 15-day / 1,000-recipient figures are the source's general guidelines, explicitly qualified as situation-dependent, not universal law.
Random tests without hypotheses produce winners you cannot reuse.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Rank signup form tests by impact and work top-down
cards.summary: Start with the offer, then micro-step, delay, form type, copy, design, and finally SMS angle.
cards.use_when: Prioritizing which signup form (popup) experiments to run first to grow the email list.
steps: Run the top-10 signup form tests in order of impact, starting at number one, to get the biggest gains fastest. The primary KPI for all of them is submit rate.

1. Offer/incentive — biggest impact by far; if the offer is bad, other hacks move submit rate only marginally (the source cites roughly 2% to 2.2% style gains). Options: BOGO, buy one get one 50% off, free gift with purchase, free digital product, free shipping, dollar-amount threshold, subscription incentive, cash back, early sale access (strong at Black Friday), mystery discount (the source's personal favorite).

2. Micro-step vs no micro-step — asking for a small commitment ('claim my deal' vs 'no thanks, I'll pay full price') before requesting the email. Spikes submit rate for most brands but not all; test separately for mobile and desktop because results often differ by device.
3. Time delay — default 6 seconds; test the 4–12 second range. Shorter delays can lower sign rate while raising total signups because more people see the form.
4. Scroll amount — default 60%, test 30–90%; also test exit intent on/off.
5. Popup vs full-page form (flyout forms, in the source's experience, never beat popups).
6. Headline copy — 'claim your mystery discount' style direct headlines; avoid 'welcome to Nike' or 'sign up for product updates.'
7. CTA button copy — first person tends to win ('claim my deal,' 'unlock my discount'); 'claim my deal' cited as consistently strong.
8. Microcopy — e.g. 'no thanks, I'll rather pay full price'; also test microcopy vs none.
9. Design/colors — plain simple forms tend to beat fully branded designs (black CTA on white, gray input fields for contrast).
10. Image vs no image and SMS signup angle.

Take a holistic view on the offer test: a higher submit rate that produces much weaker welcome flow conversion may not be worth it, though you can keep nurturing those subscribers through other flows.
caveats: The ranking is the agency's own analysis of their signup form tests, not a published benchmark.
Being on-brand may conflict with the better-converting plain design; the source chooses conversion but says test it yourself.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Choose signup form images by device, not aesthetics
cards.summary: Use human faces or pets on desktop forms, skip images on mobile to protect load speed.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether and which image to place in a popup or signup form.
steps: Test image vs no image per brand and niche — some perform better with a hero image, others plain.
When using an image, follow the source's observed hierarchy: images with pets work best when applicable to the brand; images with human faces next; static product images perform weakest.
Use the image as a visual cue toward the headline (the source's example shows people looking at the logo/headline text) — this pattern is described as working well.
Skip images on mobile forms: mobile users are often on slower 4G/5G connections and loading speed matters.
If you do use images on desktop forms, compress them to protect load speed.
caveats: Pet imagery only makes sense if it fits the brand; forcing it is not recommended.
These image preferences are agency observations, not measured benchmarks.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Test SMS signup angles against the email offer
cards.summary: Compare same-offer, better-offer and VIP-club angles for adding SMS subscribers.
cards.use_when: Building or optimizing the SMS opt-in step, especially when email signup already exists.
steps: Decide which of three angles to test for SMS signup: the same incentive as the email list; a stronger incentive for SMS after someone joins the email list (for example 10% off email vs 50% off SMS); or the VIP club angle covering special discounts, pre-sales and early access.
Run these as split tests rather than assuming the VIP angle wins.
Remember SMS opt-ins carry ongoing send costs and compliance obligations, so a cheap opt-in that converts poorly downstream is not automatically good.
Verify current SMS consent and compliance requirements for your region before launching the test.
caveats: The source gives the three angles as test options without ranking them.
SMS economics differ sharply outside the US, which changes how much an aggressive SMS offer is worth.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Test the first email of every flow first
cards.summary: The first flow email carries by far the highest impact — spend limited testing time there.
cards.use_when: Allocating limited experimentation capacity across abandoned cart, browse, checkout, welcome and winback flows.
steps: Prioritize tests on the first email of each flow; the source states it has the highest impact by far across hundreds of ecommerce stores analyzed.
Do not spend testing time on email six of a browse abandonment flow while email one is untested.

Rank flow tests for the first email by expected impact: time delays, product block structure (hero image vs dynamic block above the fold), plain text vs designed, copy length and angle, then subject line and sender name.
Test the whole flow's time-delay structure only after you have optimized the first email's delay.
Recognize that flows generate the source's stated 40–70% of email revenue, which is why this reallocation matters.
caveats: The 40–70% flow-revenue figure is the source's claim from client work, not a universal constant.
A flow's later emails still matter for total revenue, just less per unit of testing effort.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Test flow time delays with flow-type reference ranges
cards.summary: Tune when the first flow email fires, using source ranges by abandonment type.
cards.use_when: Setting or testing send delays in site, browse, cart and checkout abandonment flows.
steps: Decide which of two delay tests to run: the whole delay structure, or just the delay on email one. Do the email-one test first because email one has the most impact.

Compare an aggressive cart sequence (email one, then email two 12 hours later, then three and four at 12-hour intervals) against a regular day-by-day sequence; the source says aggressive works well for some brands.

Use these starting windows for the first email by flow type: site abandonment 1–4 hours; browse abandonment 30 minutes to 2 hours; cart abandonment 50 minutes to 1 hour; checkout abandonment 50 minutes to 1 hour.
Note the general pattern: the further down the customer journey, the shorter the appropriate delay.
Set it up as a conditional split — a 50% random sample waits one duration and 50% waits another — then collect enough data before judging.
Verify current flow-split configuration in Klaviyo, since the interface changes.
caveats: The ranges are source-observed starting points ('massive differences' between brands), not fixed best practice.
Running the delay test without sufficient recipients per branch produces noise.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Test product blocks, dynamic feeds and hero images in flows
cards.summary: Compare recommendation formats and email structure to raise flow revenue.
cards.use_when: Optimizing abandoned browse, cart and checkout emails, and cross-sell or winback flows.
steps: Test product blocks vs product category blocks: some audiences want specific product recommendations, others prefer browsing general collections. Test this in welcome email one, abandonment series, post-purchase cross-sell, winback and campaigns — and re-test per situation, because a winner in welcome email one does not carry over to winback.

Test static product blocks vs the Klaviyo product feed (which uses purchase, viewing and all-time history for recommendations). This is only relevant for stores with a large catalog, where specific recommendations are hypothesized to beat static random products.

For abandonment series, test a hero image vs no hero image. Current structure is often a header image with a dynamic product block below; the alternative is a short headline with the dynamic product block above the fold so the exact viewed or carted product is the first thing the reader sees.
Judge all of these on revenue, not just clicks.
caveats: Hero-image results vary substantially by niche, per the source.
The dynamic-feed vs static test requires enough catalog and data volume to be meaningful.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Test plain-text vs designed emails and copy variables in flows
cards.summary: Plain-text founder messages, copy length, tone and angle are high-impact flow tests worth running.
cards.use_when: Deciding email format and copy style for flow emails, particularly discount-bearing final emails.
steps: Split test plain text vs fully designed emails; some brands see plain text perform very well.

Run this test on the first flow email (highest impact) and on the last email of the flow, especially when it contains a discount — a personal plain-text message from the founder is cited as performing well in certain niches.
Test short copy (max three to five sentences) vs long, multi-paragraph copy.
Test branded tone of voice vs direct-response style (harder sell).

Test angle vs angle: pick the pain point used to persuade in one email and split test it against a different pain point; the source notes this is trickier to set up but can reveal which pain point triggers the most revenue.
Judge on revenue rather than open or click rate.
caveats: The source calls copy a broad subject with many possible variables; results are brand-specific.
Angle testing is harder to isolate because the two emails necessarily differ in more than one way.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Test landing page destinations from flow emails
cards.summary: Compare collection page, product page, homepage and dedicated landing pages on end revenue.
cards.use_when: Choosing where flow or campaign email links should send shoppers.
steps: Set up the test in Klaviyo even though it is not strictly an email AB test, then measure the end result — revenue, not clicks.
Compare destinations such as collection page vs product page, homepage vs collection page, and a regular product page vs a purpose-built product landing page.
Apply the general principle of making the desired action as easy as possible, which normally argues for the product page as the closest step to purchase.
Still test the alternatives: the source notes collection or homepage can sometimes produce a better user experience and more revenue.
Run this for campaigns too, where the same destination question recurs with each new send.
caveats: Landing page tests mix many variables at once, so results are harder to generalize across campaigns.
The source gives no numeric expectation for the size of the effect.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Use manual 50/50 splits instead of automatic winner selection
cards.summary: Avoid staggered sends that deliver the winning variant at a suboptimal time on early, noisy data.
cards.use_when: Configuring any Klaviyo AB test for campaigns or flows.
steps: Always choose a manual 50/50 split: send version A to half and version B to half, 100% test size, 0% automatic winner rollout.

Reject the automatic option (send 20% to A, 20% to B, then the winner to the remaining 60% after a few hours) for two stated reasons: the largest segment receives the email at a time that is not your optimal send time, and two to three hours is too short a window to determine a winner.
Select place order rate as the winning metric for campaigns.
Analyze results after a couple of days, then apply the learning to future sends.
For flows, either let the test run while the sample accumulates or review after reaching the recipient threshold.
Verify current Klaviyo test configuration options before building.
caveats: Manual splits delay the winner reaching the full list, which is acceptable because you learn for future sends rather than optimize one send.
The source attributes low statistical significance partly to auto-selection's short window.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Run systematic campaign-side tests, starting with send time
cards.summary: Send time is a top campaign variable; also test angles, landing pages, feeds, subject lines and sender names.
cards.use_when: Deciding what to test on recurring newsletter-style campaigns rather than flows.
steps: Prioritize send time and date — the source calls it capable of dramatically affecting opens and revenue. Run exploratory tests at least five times to find audience-specific patterns.
Look at revenue alongside open rate: a 7 a.m. send may win opens while a 2 p.m. send wins revenue, and the source says to favor revenue.
Test email angles: which pain points or brand USPs trigger the best response.
Test landing pages (collection vs product vs homepage vs dedicated page), and dynamic Klaviyo feed vs static product blocks.

Also test subject lines, sender names and CTA buttons, but recognize campaigns are trickier than flows because each send has new content — a CTA winner on campaign A may not transfer to campaign B sent at a different time or with a different type.
Verify current Klaviyo reporting fields when comparing revenue across send-time tests.
caveats: Campaign tests rarely produce clean generalizable rules because content changes every send.
The five-run minimum for send-time exploration is the source's recommendation, not a statistical guarantee.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Deprioritize subject line, sender name and CTA button tests
cards.summary: These are easy but low-impact — run them after the high-impact tests are exhausted.
cards.use_when: Choosing which email tests to run when testing capacity is limited.
steps: Recognize that subject line tests are easy and fast but generally do not have the biggest revenue impact; the source warns against falling into the trap of only testing subject lines.
When testing subject lines, still make them strategic: emoji vs no emoji, first name vs no first name, urgency vs no urgency, offer in subject line vs preview text, specific numbers vs none.
Test sender name (e.g. 'Apple' vs 'Tim from Apple'), which is interesting especially for plain-text founder emails and can boost open rate, but again has modest revenue impact.
Recognize CTA button tests (text, size, color — 'buy now' vs 'shop now', regular vs high-contrast color) as the lowest-impact test on the flow list; don't start here even though it is popular.
Sequence these after time delays, product blocks, plain text, copy and landing page tests are done.
caveats: The source explicitly calls CTA button testing low impact and warns against starting there.
Subject line and sender name tests still consume send volume and recipients, so they are not free.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Set the upper bound on test duration and sample per variant
cards.summary: Aim for around two weeks per test and at least 1,000 recipients per variant before concluding.
cards.use_when: Deciding when to call an email AB test and move to the next one.
steps: Wait for at least 1,000 recipients per variant as the rule of thumb for flows.
Accept 500 recipients per variant only when the difference between variations is already massive.

Plan roughly two weeks per test so multiple tests can run per month, and note the source's qualified exception: 7 days can be enough in some situations, but 15 days is the general advice for flows and signup forms.

For signup forms, require at least 3–5,000 impressions per variant or 15 days of runtime, whichever takes longer — even if 3–5,000 impressions arrive in a single day, stretch the test over multiple days.
Scale test throughput to list volume: higher-traffic brands reach thresholds faster and can test more per month; smaller brands need more calendar time per test.
caveats: These thresholds are the source's general guidelines, explicitly described as situation-dependent rather than a statistical formula.
Concluding early on a small sample produces false winners that then get applied to future sends.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Build segments that start with marketing eligibility
cards.summary: Every Klaviyo segment should first filter on who can legally receive marketing, with extra GDPR handling in Europe.
cards.use_when: Creating or auditing send segments for campaigns and flows, especially in Europe.
steps: Create the segment under Lists & Segments → Create → Segment.
Add the mandatory starting condition 'person can receive email marketing' so the segment only targets active profiles who can be marketed to.
If based in the US, this condition is sufficient.

If based in Europe, add a further filter for subscription/consent status under GDPR-aware rules, because the ability to receive marketing does not equal consent. Example from the source: someone who entered their email at checkout can receive email marketing but is not officially subscribed; similarly, a purchaser who never consented to email marketing.
Build segmentation to make campaigns relevant to recipients rather than as an advanced extra.
Verify current Klaviyo segment condition names and European consent handling, since both the interface and privacy requirements change.
caveats: The source cautions that European rules add complexity beyond the single eligibility condition; confirm your own compliance obligations.
Segments built without the eligibility filter risk sending to profiles that should be suppressed.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Build an engaged-90-day segment as your campaign workhorse
cards.summary: Construct an engaged segment combining email and site activity with OR logic, then clone it across 14/30/60/90/120-day windows.
cards.use_when: Setting up campaign send audiences or starting deliverability recovery in Klaviyo.
steps: Create a segment starting with the condition 'person can receive email marketing' as a base for every segment you build.

Add condition: 'has opened email at least once in the last 90 days', then clone that condition and set it to 'has clicked email at least once in the last 90 days' — keep logic on OR, because an open may fail to track while a click registers.

Keep everything on OR and add further conditions: placed order at least once in last 90 days, checkout started at least once, active on site at least once. Do not add 'viewed product' or 'added to cart' because these are already captured by active-on-site.
Clone the segment and swap the timeframe to 14, 30, 60 and 120 days so you have a ladder of engagement windows.
If you have severe spam issues, temporarily drop the website conditions and use only opened/clicked email until open rates recover.
Use the engaged-90 segment as the default audience for most campaigns; use tighter windows (14/30) when repairing deliverability.
caveats: The source reports typically achieving 50%+ open rates with engaged-90 segments for its clients; this is a source-specific experience, not a guaranteed benchmark.

For EU lists you must filter further on 'because person subscribed' due to GDPR consent rules; US-based lists can rely on 'can receive email marketing' alone, though subscribed contacts usually engage better.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Mandatory exclusion segments for every campaign
cards.summary: Create suppression segments for spam markers and bounced addresses and apply them to all sends.
cards.use_when: Before sending any campaign, or during a list-cleaning pass.
steps: Build a 'marked as spam' exclusion segment: person can receive email marketing AND has marked email as spam at least once over all time.

Build a bounce exclusion segment with two branches: has bounced email at least 4 times over all time where bounce type = soft, OR has bounced email at least once over all time where bounce type = hard.
Treat hard bounces as permanent (suppress after one) and soft bounces as temporary (allow up to four attempts before suppressing).
Add these as exclusions on every single campaign you send.
To remove them permanently, open the segment, click the three-dot menu, choose 'suppress current members', then bulk suppress.
Allow roughly one to two hours for Klaviyo to update suppression counts depending on segment size.

Maintain an 'all but unsubscribed and suppressed' master segment: can receive email marketing, email does not contain the text 'q.com' (bot addresses), and has marked email as spam zero times over all time.
Send to this master segment roughly one to two times per month to give unengaged people a chance to re-engage without burning your reputation.
caveats: Always send campaigns to segments, not lists, per the source's stated preference.
Bot filters and suppression counts may need refreshing as data changes; re-check segment membership over time.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Build unengaged segments that exclude past customers
cards.summary: Create 120-day and 180-day unengaged segments using AND logic that quarantine never-purchasers but retain past buyers.
cards.use_when: Building sunset flows and long-term suppression rules to protect deliverability and reduce Klaviyo costs.
steps: Create unengaged-120: opened email zero times in last 120 days AND clicked email zero times in last 120 days AND placed order zero times over all time AND checkout started zero times in last 120 days AND active on site zero times in last 120 days.
Use AND here, not OR — you want fully inactive contacts, the opposite of the engaged-segment logic.
Set placed order to 'zero times over all time' (not 120 days) so that anyone who ever bought stays on the list and can still be re-activated.
Clone to unengaged-180 (six months) and use it as an exclusion segment and periodic suppression source.
Use unengaged-120 as the trigger audience for a sunset/unengaged reactivation flow.
Suppress the 180-day group over time if they never purchased, because removing them improves deliverability and lowers Klaviyo cost.
caveats: The source deliberately keeps past buyers on the list indefinitely, reasoning that a customer from over a year ago can still be reactivated; this is a judgment call you can adjust to your margin structure.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Specialty segments for buyer-stage targeting
cards.summary: Create first-time buyer, returning customer, non-buyer and VIP segments to target differentiated offers.
cards.use_when: Planning sales events, loyalty messaging or new-customer reactivation offers.
steps: First-time buyers: placed order = 1 over all time AND can receive email marketing — use for a specific second-purchase offer.
Returning customers: placed order at least 2 times over all time — differentiate loyalty messaging from first-timer messaging.

Non-buyers: placed order zero times over all time — during sales events the source gives non-buyers an extra discount on top of the event discount, since existing customers don't need the extra nudge.
VIPs: define per brand, e.g. placed order at least 4 times over all time, or total spend at 3–4× AOV.

High potentials: checkout started, added to cart, viewed product, or active on site at least once in the last 30 days, AND did not place an order in the last 30 days — use as a base for a targeted flow or one-off offer.
Win-back: placed order at least once in the last 6 months but zero times in the last 90 days — use as the base for a win-back flow or a one-off campaign.
caveats: VIP thresholds differ by brand and niche; the source explicitly says there is no universal definition — set thresholds from your own AOV and repeat-purchase data.
The extra-discount-for-non-buyers tactic is the source's agency practice; validate margin impact before adopting.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Diagnose deliverability with placement testing and Klaviyo metrics
cards.summary: Use inbox placement tools and Klaviyo's deliverability tab to find whether the problem is placement, provider or geography.
cards.use_when: Open rates are consistently low and you need to locate the cause before changing strategy.
steps: Treat open rates consistently below 30–35% as a likely inbox placement problem (the source cites 50%+ as achievable for engaged segments, so far below that signals an issue).

Option 1: send a test campaign to a seed list via a placement tool (the source names GlockApps) to see primary-inbox, promotions and spam split, blocklist status and IP reputation; the source suggests running this monthly.
Option 2: in Klaviyo, open the last five sent campaigns and go to the deliverability tab to review open rate, click rate, bounce rate, unsubscribe rate and spam complaint rate.
Check 'performance by inbox provider' — a problem may exist only with Hotmail/Outlook while Gmail is healthy.
Check 'performance by country' — if one country underperforms, send only to a tighter engaged segment there for a while to rebuild engagement.
caveats: Tool names and menu locations change; verify current interfaces before relying on paths.
The 30–35% and 50%+ figures are the source's heuristics for its own clients, not universal benchmarks.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Four-step technical setup for email sending
cards.summary: Configure branded sending domain, default sender, DMARC and optionally BIMI as the baseline deliverability setup.
cards.use_when: Initial Klaviyo setup or auditing an account with unexplained placement problems.
steps: Add a branded sending domain in Klaviyo under Settings > Account > Domains; enter the root domain and add the required DNS records until status shows live.
Set your default sender email address to an address ending in the branded domain (e.g. hello@yourbrand.com) — never a free-mail or unrelated domain.
Add a DMARC record as a TXT record with name '_dmarc' in your DNS; the source identifies this as the most commonly missing piece when auditing ecommerce brands.
Verify DMARC with a free checker tool (the source names GlockApps' DMARC checker) to confirm the record resolves correctly.

Optionally implement BIMI to authenticate your logo in the inbox and, on some clients, display a blue verification check; the source cites roughly $1,500/year and says it's worth considering for eight- and nine-figure brands, sometimes seven-figure.
Treat technical setup as necessary but rarely the main cause — the source states it rarely fixes a deliverability problem on its own.
caveats: BIMI requires DNS configuration and provider support (Gmail, Yahoo and some Apple versions per the source); costs and requirements should be verified at implementation time.
DMARC/SPF/DKIM values must match your specific provider's current instructions.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Five-step list-cleaning protocol
cards.summary: Suppress five categories of dead weight to cut costs and improve sender reputation.
cards.use_when: Any account with a large list and low engagement, or as a periodic hygiene pass.
steps: Segment 1 — long-term unengaged: opened email zero times in last 90 days, clicked zero, active on site zero in last 180 days, placed order zero times in last 365 days, received email at least 10 times in last 180 days, and can receive email marketing.
Segment 2 — no recent sends: active or created at least a year ago, received email zero times in the last year, active on site zero times in the last year, and can still receive email marketing.
Segment 3 — never opened: active or created at least a year ago and received email zero times over all time (i.e. essentially never contacted).
Segment 4 — spam markers: marked email as spam at least once over all time.
Segment 5 — bounces: soft bounced 4+ times over all time OR hard bounced at least once.
Suppress each segment via the three-dot menu > suppress current members > bulk suppress; wait one to two hours for Klaviyo to process.
Result: remaining list is engaged or semi-engaged, and you stop signaling to Gmail/Outlook that you mail people who report or reject you.
caveats: Suppression is not reversible in bulk without re-adding contacts, so apply segments carefully and confirm counts before bulk suppressing.
The '10 emails in 180 days' and '365 days' thresholds are the source's cleaning heuristics; seasonality or low-frequency programs may justify adapting them.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Ramp deliverability back with a staged engagement ladder
cards.summary: Recover inbox placement by sending only to progressively wider engaged segments while watching open rate gates.
cards.use_when: A store has a known deliverability problem (consistently low opens, spam complaints) and needs a recovery sequence.
steps: Week 1–2: turn off all flows except welcome, post-purchase and browse/checkout abandonment.
Week 1–2: send 3 campaigns per week only to the engaged-14-day segment (6 emails total).
After 2 weeks, check those campaigns' open rates. If at or above 50%, move up. If below 50%, repeat another 2 weeks at 14 days.
If still below 50%, strip website activity from the engaged segments and use only opened/clicked email conditions.
Then send 3 campaigns/week for 2 weeks to engaged-30; re-check. Expect a small dip but require it to stay near 50% to advance; otherwise repeat 2 more weeks.
Continue the same two-week-per-stage process for engaged-60 and engaged-90.
Once engaged-90 is stable, make it your main campaign audience and turn all flows back on.
If opens trend toward 60%, you can keep widening to 120/150/180 days while staying above 50%, though the source still recommends keeping the majority of sends at engaged-90.
caveats: The 50% open-rate gate is the source's operational target for its own clients, not a universal benchmark.
Ramp speed depends on list size and existing reputation; smaller engaged windows may send very few emails in week one.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Make emails readable to Gmail's AI filter
cards.summary: Replace image-only email elements with live text so AI inbox systems can parse and prioritize your emails.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing campaign templates for inbox placement.
steps: Write descriptive alt text for every image — say what is shown and include any discount and code (e.g. 'person eating pizza — 15% off with code X').
Switch from design product blocks to Klaviyo's native product blocks so product information is live text rather than baked into an image.
Use live-text top bars for offers instead of image banners.
Put live text in the footer: product category links, loyalty status, store locator, support information.
Keep sending plain-text emails regularly (the source suggests 1–3 per month) for AI readability and strong engagement.
Do not abandon design entirely — the requirement is that the email is understandable without reading the images.
Keep the above-the-fold section highly optimized since most readers never scroll: a single clear primary call to action with a contrasting button.
caveats: This is the source's forward-looking adaptation to Gmail's AI features; results will vary as inbox providers change behavior.
Plain-text emails should still carry your brand voice and offer, not be blank utility messages.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Structure emails for clicks and replies, not just opens
cards.summary: Adopt conventions that maximize the metrics inbox providers weigh most: clicks, replies and engagement diversity.
cards.use_when: Writing or redesigning campaign templates after a low click-through or low reply rate.
steps: Use conversational subject lines; the source's test is whether a friend would send that subject line to a friend — if not, Gmail is likely to classify it as promotional.
Keep emails short and use shorter body copy.
Include a single primary call to action above the fold with a contrasting button.
Share only 3–5 products per email, for example in a 2×2 grid, each with its own 'shop now' button, and end with a 'shop all' button for people who don't like the featured items.
Periodically send plain-text emails to invite replies; the source stresses that replies are a powerful human-interaction signal for Gmail.
Use live-text footer links to product categories, which the source reports reliably lifts click rates.
Avoid sending a heavily promotional email every single week; mix in non-promotional sends.
caveats: The source's click-rate targets (5%+ minimum, explicitly rejecting Klaviyo's reported 1–1.2% benchmark) are its own opinion and depend on list quality and offer strength.
Reply invitations only work if someone monitors and responds to the inbox.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Use AI to analyze exported campaign analytics
cards.summary: Export Klaviyo campaign data and prompt an AI to surface bottlenecks and prioritized tests.
cards.use_when: You lack analyst bandwidth and need a quick diagnostic of recent campaign performance.
steps: In Klaviyo, go to Campaigns, open the three-dot menu and choose 'export analytics'.
Select the time range (year-to-date or at least the last 90 days), choose email only (or include SMS), and include all A/B test message variations.
Export the CSV and upload it to an AI assistant (the source uses ChatGPT).
Prompt it as an email marketing data specialist and ask for a specific number of data-backed observations with recommendations.
Example framing the source used: 'analyze this data set and give me 10 observations with recommendations on how to improve it'.

Use the output to identify bottleneck metrics (e.g. high uncorrected opens but low unique clicks) and get concrete next actions like redesigning templates around one above-fold CTA, adding contrasting buttons and shortening copy.
Look for the AI's diagnosis of day-of-week and send-time patterns, subject-line features (e.g. emoji presence) and bounce spikes, then design controlled tests from those hypotheses.
caveats: Treat AI recommendations as hypotheses to test, not instructions; the AI may propose test windows or KPIs that don't match your business.
The source notes it optimizes for placed-order rate rather than open rate when testing send times, since opens can be high in the morning while purchases concentrate in the evening.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Use AI to diagnose flow performance and prioritize tests
cards.summary: Export Klaviyo flow analytics, analyze with AI, then focus testing on the flows and emails carrying the most revenue.
cards.use_when: Deciding which email flow to optimize next, or auditing a mature automation program.
steps: In Klaviyo, go to Flows, open the options menu and choose 'export analytics'.
Select at least the last 90 days (year-to-date is fine), aggregate by day, include all A/B test message variations, and export the CSV.
Prompt the AI as an email marketing data specialist to analyze the flow data set and return a set number of data-backed observations with concrete recommendations.
Use the output to rank flows by revenue contribution and to identify where a small lift compounds most.
Prioritize A/B tests on the highest-volume, highest-revenue flow rather than low-traffic emails, because a lift on a flow with few recipients barely moves the business.
Follow up with a focused prompt on one flow (e.g. the welcome series) to get email-by-email findings and prioritized actions.
caveats: This is the source's workflow with ChatGPT on its agency client data; the specific observation counts and findings are examples, not promises.
AI output quality depends on data completeness and the clarity of your prompt; always verify claims against the raw CSV before acting.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Where welcome-flow revenue actually concentrates
cards.summary: Expect the first email of a welcome series to carry most revenue and rethink the purpose of later emails.
cards.use_when: Auditing or rebuilding a welcome/onboarding flow.
steps: Export welcome-flow analytics and check revenue by email. In the source's case, email one contributed roughly 88% of welcome-series revenue and the flow generated a large share of total flow revenue.
Accept that email one converting hardest is natural — subscribers sign up to use the discount they just saw.
Treat emails two through five-plus as nurture for the majority not ready to buy, with the goal of guiding them toward a future first purchase rather than matching email one's revenue.
If trailing emails generate zero revenue, consider shortening the series or repurposing them as behavior-based follow-ups rather than sending low-impact messages.
A/B test subject lines on email one first, since that is where volume is highest and any lift compounds fastest.
caveats: The 88% figure comes from one client's data set in the source and should be treated as an illustrative example, not a benchmark you should expect.
The source still notes that email marketing ROI is high, so cutting later emails should be justified by their poor incremental performance, not just low revenue.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Spot under-monetized flows and channel gaps
cards.summary: Use flow analytics to find flows with high opens but weak clicks or orders, and consider SMS as a follow-up for non-clickers.
cards.use_when: Reviewing browse abandonment, cart abandonment and cross-channel follow-up performance.
steps: For each flow, compare open rate, click rate and order rate; the source's example flagged a browse flow with 42% opens but only ~2.3% clicks and a 6% order rate.
Where clicks are weak relative to opens, add dynamic product blocks and a single hero call to action to rebuild intent.

For non-clickers, consider an SMS follow-up if your SMS flow shows strong revenue per recipient — in the source's case the SMS browse flow showed €1.70 per recipient while the email version underperformed.

Check for channel-specific gaps: the source's analysis flagged checkout abandonment traffic as small, SMS checkout as a hidden gem, post-purchase leaving money on the table and win-back flows barely converting.
Prioritize the fixes with the highest combination of traffic volume and revenue impact.
caveats: The specific rates and €1.70 per-recipient figure are one client's data used as an illustration, not a benchmark.
SMS follow-up requires separate consent collection and compliance, which the source does not detail here.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: 2026 deliverability KPI targets for ecommerce email
cards.summary: Set measurement thresholds for open, click, spam-complaint and unsubscribe rates before diagnosing strategy.
cards.use_when: Reviewing Klaviyo campaign health or setting reporting thresholds for an email program.
steps: Open rate: target at least 45% minimum, ideally 50% or higher, on engaged segments.
Click rate: target 5% or higher; the source explicitly argues against Klaviyo's suggested 1–1.2% benchmark because it forces overly tight segments.
Spam complaint rate: keep at 0.01% or lower and actively monitor it.

Unsubscribe rate: aim for 0.3% or lower, but treat it as less critical than in the past because one-click unsubscribe in Gmail has raised unsubscribe rates and unsubscribes don't directly hurt deliverability.
Still minimize unsubscribes because a shrinking list costs long-term revenue.
Track provider- and country-level breakdowns in addition to overall numbers, since averages can mask local problems.
caveats: These thresholds are the source's recommendations for its own client work, not industry standards; they depend heavily on list source and offer strength.
The source's disagreement with Klaviyo's click-rate guidance is an opinion — test against your own conversion economics rather than adopting either figure blindly.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Sequence the email system as a connected chain, not isolated tactics
cards.summary: Build ecommerce email in a dependency order where signup feeds flows, flows capture intent, campaigns create momentum, tests sharpen winners and deliverability keeps it all reaching the inbox.
cards.use_when: When planning the next quarter of email work or deciding which email project to start next in an ecommerce store.
steps: Start with list growth: the source argues that without a steady stream of new subscribers every other email effort operates on a shrinking audience, so fix signup capture before adding complexity elsewhere.
Layer the five core flows next: welcome, browse abandonment, abandoned cart, abandoned checkout and post-purchase. These capture existing intent rather than trying to manufacture it.
Add campaigns after flows: campaigns create momentum with your list, but they work better when triggered flows are already catching high-intent behaviour.
Add A/B testing only on top of already-working elements; the source frames testing as sharpening what works, not as a rescue tool for broken flows.
Layer segmentation to keep sends relevant, then treat deliverability as the foundation that decides whether any of it reaches the inbox.
Use AI last, as an execution accelerator across the whole system rather than a replacement for the structure.
Work through the sections one at a time as a buildout roadmap instead of implementing everything at once.
caveats: The source is a course summary from an agency that also sells buildout services; the sequencing is the presenter's framework, not a measured benchmark.
Stores with a large existing list but weak capture may reasonably prioritise flows over list growth.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Audit your email program against the six-layer dependency model
cards.summary: Use a six-layer checklist (signup, flows, campaigns, testing, segmentation, deliverability) to find the weakest link limiting email revenue.
cards.use_when: When email revenue has plateaued and you need to diagnose which stage of the ecommerce email program to invest in next.
steps: List the six layers: list growth/signup forms, core triggered flows, campaigns, A/B testing, segmentation and deliverability.
For each layer, record whether it exists, how it is performing and whether the layer above it depends on it.

Look for breaks in the chain: signup forms feeding flows, flows capturing intent, campaigns creating momentum, tests sharpening winners, segmentation keeping messages relevant and deliverability getting mail to the inbox.
Prioritise the earliest broken link, because later layers inherit problems from earlier ones; a great campaign calendar wastes effort if subscribers are not being captured or mail is not landing.
Implement fixes sequentially rather than simultaneously so you can tell what changed outcomes.
Expect the payoff to be a cleaner system with better timing and more relevant messaging, not simply a higher volume of sends.
caveats: This is the presenter's diagnostic framing from an email course, not a validated scoring model; treat layer priority as a judgement call for your store.
If you sell agency services or build systems for clients, this audit works the same way for a client account, but the source's own pitch to book a buildout call is not a required step.
cards.source_name: Klaviyo email.docx

cards.title: Write 12 months of emails in one sitting
cards.summary: Block out a full year of emails in a single session so the perceived cost of starting an email program collapses.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to start or restart a store email program and dreading the ongoing workload.
steps: Commit to a small, finite batch first: 12 or 24 emails, not an open-ended commitment.
Sit down once and write them all in one block (Hormozi says 24 emails took him roughly half a day).
Realize from that session that a year of list communication costs about half a day, which reframes email as cheap rather than as another plate to spin.
Start with once a month if you have never mailed; treat anything beyond the pre-written batch as bonus.
Prefer a quality threshold over a rigid cadence if committing to a schedule makes your writing worse — send when you have good material, not to satisfy a calendar.
caveats: Source-specific: this is Hormozi's own framing of his hesitation; the half-day figure is his, not a benchmark.
Batching works for evergreen tactical content; it is poorly suited to inventory drops, launches or time-sensitive promotions.
cards.source_name: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Plain-text email format to stay out of the Promotions tab
cards.summary: Format marketing emails to look like a personal note — text-heavy, no images, one or two links — so filters treat them as real correspondence.
cards.use_when: Planning the HTML/template for any store campaign email, especially retention and re-engagement sends.
steps: Write the email as mostly text with a handful of sentences, approximating an everyday email between two people.
Send zero images where possible; if you must, keep them minimal, since image-heavy 'Vegas Strip' promotional layouts read as pure promotion to filters.
Limit to one or two links maximum per email.
Remove money-related language from the body and subject where you can — Hormozi observed more money words correlate with a higher share landing in the Promotions tab.
Ask recipients to reply as part of the flow (see the Reply Yes card) because replies signal engagement to providers.
Mentally model the provider's objective: they want to deliver the highest-quality inbox experience, so align with that instead of hunting hacks.
caveats: The source notes 16.9% of B2B marketing emails never reach the inbox at all, driven by domain reputation — plain text is one input, not a silver bullet.
No images means you cannot show product photography, so this format suits tactical/editorial sends more than visual product launches.
cards.source_name: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes.docx

cards.title: The Money Minute structure: reward on every step
cards.summary: Use a fixed four-part email skeleton that rewards the reader for opening, for reading, and for clicking.
cards.use_when: Designing the standard template for a recurring store newsletter or retention email.
steps: Open with an immediate one-glance reward — a quote, a striking line or a tweet — so the reader is paid back the instant they open.
Follow with one single tactical idea, kept to roughly 200 words (about a minute of reading); resist adding a second concept.
Frame the tactic as problem → solution → how: name a condition that makes the solution necessary, give the solution, then the concrete tactic.
Insert a contextual CTA that bridges from that specific content rather than a generic copy-pasted button.
Close with a P.S., because after the subject line it is the most-read part of an email.
Keep the format identical every send so readers know exactly what they are getting — the McDonalds principle: same shape, different quality burger each time.
caveats: Hormozi explicitly says the 200-word limit is his format choice, not a rule of law — his colleague Lila sends longer story-based emails to higher-revenue segments and they perform well.
Placement of CTA vs P.S. is flexible; the source says there is no science to it.
cards.source_name: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Reward every step with a feedback-loop email design
cards.summary: Behavior repeats when it was rewarded last time, so design each email so opening, reading and clicking each deliver a payoff.
cards.use_when: Restructuring an underperforming store newsletter or welcome sequence where readers open but never act.
steps: Analyze behavior as after-the-fact reward, not as a preceding trigger: people repeat actions that previously paid off.
Reward the open with a one-glance payoff at the very top of the body (quote, punchline, striking stat).
Reward the read with a complete, usable tactic — the reader should be able to apply it to their business immediately.
Reward the click by placing high-value hidden content behind the link (a video, a deeper document) rather than duplicating the email content.
Protect the loop: one bad email can break the habit, so prefer extending a silence over sending something weak.
Accept that failing to earn opens and clicks eventually pushes the sender toward the Promotions tab — the source calls this 'email death'.
caveats: A single poor send can undo accumulated trust, so the model punishes volume without quality.
Rewards must be real; promising value behind a link and not delivering it is treated by the source as the worst outcome.
cards.source_name: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Reply Yes onboarding to train provider reputation
cards.summary: Require new subscribers to reply 'Yes' to receive the lead magnet, so engagement signals raise sender reputation.
cards.use_when: Setting up or revising the welcome and lead-magnet delivery flow for a store's opt-in.
steps: Structure the welcome email so the lead magnet is delivered only after the subscriber replies 'Yes'.
Give a reason to reply by making the reward clearly worth the action (e.g. an exclusive chapter or asset).
Use the pre-reward moment to sell regular communication, not just the freebie — subscribers who only want the magnet will ignore everything after.
Place the lead magnet mention near the end, after you have sold the ongoing value, so you surprise and delight before giving the promised item.
Inside the gated asset, continue the loop by pointing to specific pages and asking for further engagement.
Treat this as building domain reputation with inbox providers — many small positive signals rather than one hack.
caveats: Reputation is cumulative; the source describes it as '100 golden BBs', not a single silver bullet.
Reply-gating adds friction, so it will reduce raw opt-in-to-magnet completion compared with instant delivery.
cards.source_name: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Make unsubscribing easy to protect deliverability
cards.summary: Reduce friction on unsubscribes because dormant subscribers hurt domain reputation more than people who leave cleanly.
cards.use_when: Configuring the unsubscribe link, preference center and list hygiene for a store's email program.
steps: Make the unsubscribe action visible and simple rather than buried or requiring a support request.
Reason from deliverability: uninterested subscribers who stay on the list drag down domain-level sending reputation over time.
Treat a subscriber who unsubscribes as still aware of your brand — they may still buy later through another channel or inbox, so do not treat it as a loss.
Accept a higher unsubscribe rate on your first send in a long while — the source calls this 'shaking the tree', effectively pulling forward churn.
Benchmark against it: Hormozi reports over 1% on his first-ever send, settling to roughly 0.42% per email, and treats the program as healthy as long as list growth between sends exceeds unsubscribes.
caveats: The 1% / 0.42% figures are one sender's list, not a target for all stores.
If unsubscribes exceed growth, the reasoning inverts and the cadence or content is the problem.
cards.source_name: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Segment the list by qualifier answers at opt-in
cards.summary: Collect qualifiers like revenue band or business stage at signup and send content matched to the segment.
cards.use_when: Designing the opt-in form and deciding who receives which store campaign or educational email.
steps: Add qualifying questions to the opt-in — for example revenue band, whether they run a business, or product-usage level for a store.
Route sends by segment (e.g. a specific tactic only to the 500k+ group, another to 0–100k).
Recognize that mismatch, not email quality, is usually why a send underperforms — advanced content to beginners or the reverse reads as 'not for me'.
Encourage honest answers: subscribers who lie to get the 'better' tier receive content that does not apply to them.
Cite the cited study result as context only: HubSpot research referenced in the source found segmented lists produced a 791% increase in email ROI.
caveats: The 791% ROI lift is a third-party study result cited by the source, not a promise for your list.
Every extra opt-in field costs signups, so weigh the segmentation gain against form friction.
cards.source_name: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Make CTR the primary email metric, not open rate
cards.summary: Track clicked actions over opens because Apple privacy changes make open data unreliable and CTR is what predicts revenue.
cards.use_when: Choosing the KPI for a store email program and reviewing send-to-send performance.
steps: Decide on the definition first: CTR can mean clicks as a share of all recipients, or of those who opened — the two produce very different numbers.
Use clicks-as-share-of-sent as the metric tied to action, since it is independent of open-tracking accuracy.
Report both so you can tell an open-rate problem from a click-rate problem.
Evaluate over a rolling period rather than per email, balancing 'deposit' sends against harder 'withdraw' asks.
Use the source's own figures only as orientation: roughly 35.7% open rate and 8.5% CTR across three months on his list, which he treats as a strong CTR.
Accept that open-rate accuracy is degraded by privacy changes and treat it as directional.
caveats: The 35.7% / 8.5% figures are one sender's list — not a benchmark to hold yourself to.
The source states he is confident in CTR but not in the open-rate reporting.
cards.source_name: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Split-test subject lines on a slice, then send the winner
cards.summary: Test subject lines (and preview text) on a small portion of the list, then blast the winning variant to the rest.
cards.use_when: Optimizing subject-line performance for recurring brand emails or product campaigns.
steps: Create two variants of the subject line and let the platform send each to a small percentage of the list.
Wait for the winner to emerge, then send that variant to the remainder.
Model the same pattern used for video thumbnails: automated variant testing picks the better performer.
Weigh brand consistency: if you are building a named recurring format, keeping the same prefix every time can cost some short-term open rate in exchange for a habit-driven long-term open.
Optimize the preview text as a separate asset — it is the first roughly 150 characters shown and the source reports up to a 24% open-rate lift from crafting it (source-reported figure).
Do not let the preview default to the first 150 characters of the body, which is often a greeting and carries no curiosity value.
caveats: The 24% preview-text lift is attributed to the source's reported experience, not a guaranteed result.
Fixing a branded subject prefix sacrifices subject-line testing upside; the source frames this as a deliberate trade-off.
cards.source_name: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Send at the right day and hour for B2C vs B2B
cards.summary: Match send day and time window to audience type, since consumer and business inboxes peak differently.
cards.use_when: Scheduling a store's campaign or newsletter sends across a week.
steps: For B2C, prefer Monday and Tuesday based on Nielsen/Neil Patel data cited in the source, with about an 18% average open-rate increase.
For B2B, prefer Wednesday (source notes Wednesday delivered a comparable lift to the B2C Monday/Tuesday effect).
Justify it as attention availability: consumers are more distracted early week; business buyers catch their breath midweek.
Send in the pre-lunch and post-lunch windows — roughly 10:00–noon and 1:00–3:00 — since the first thing in the morning is dominated by genuine business mail.
If you operate in a single time zone, use these windows deliberately; if your list is spread internationally, do not over-invest in timing precision.
Pick a reference time zone and stay consistent with it.
caveats: These day/time effects are described as small lifts, not transformative — the source calls them 'golden BBs'.
Relevance drops sharply for multi-time-zone audiences.
cards.source_name: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Keep cadence high but content value-only
cards.summary: Send roughly three times a week if every send is genuinely valuable, and fold the CTA into the value rather than running separate promo emails.
cards.use_when: Setting the sending frequency and give/ask balance for a store's list.
steps: Start at once a month if you are not mailing, then increase as quality holds.
Target about three sends a week only when content stays strictly value-driven; the source reports this as the sweet spot after talking to experienced email marketers.
Skip the classic promo/educational rotation: make every email valuable and simply make the path to your offer easily available, the way a link-in-bio works.
Remove the need to balance a give/ask ratio by never treating a send as pure ask.
Note the alternative: the source personally dislikes committing to a cadence and prefers sending when he has good material.
If frequency is harming quality, lower frequency rather than lower quality.
caveats: 'Three times a week' is passed on as advice from other email marketers, explicitly labelled as not a rule.
Emailing more often than a store can produce honest value is expected to burn the list.
cards.source_name: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Optimize for mobile rendering before sending
cards.summary: Check how every email renders on mobile, since most recipients will read it there and poor rendering kills clicks.
cards.use_when: Final QA before sending any store email, especially image- or layout-heavy templates.
steps: Preview the email in both desktop and mobile formats before sending.
