Fix layout breakage now, because images and multi-column blocks are the most likely to mangle on small screens.
Weigh the mobile share: the source cites roughly 58–60% of global internet traffic on mobile devices.
Treat broken rendering as a direct CTR problem — the source says unprofessional-looking mobile layouts plummet click-through rates, with e-commerce most at risk because of heavy imagery.
Consider that plain-text, image-free email sidesteps most mobile rendering risk entirely (see the plain-text card).
caveats: The 58–60% mobile traffic figure is global internet traffic, not email opens specifically.
Mobile preview tools vary by client and interface — verify in your current email platform.
cards.source_name: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Confine links and CTAs to one per objective
cards.summary: Use one or two links per email, each tied to a distinct audience or objective, instead of sprinkling many links.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many links and buttons a store email should contain.
steps: Raise the link count deliberately: the source disagrees with the common 'one link only' rule and says one or two is safe.
Require a clear reason for a reader to pick one link over another — each link should serve a different objective or audience.
Avoid five or more links, which the source calls aggressive.
Put a genuinely interesting nugget in the email and send readers to the full asset rather than pasting the whole blog post into the email.
Treat clicks as training: each rewarded click makes the next click more likely, so build the habit deliberately over time.
Keep the CTA contextual — the bridge into the link should follow from the email's specific content, not from a stock button pasted into every send.
caveats: Click training only works if the destination is good; a weak linked asset degrades future click behavior.
The one-link rule is a real practice elsewhere — this is presented as a situational alternative, not an absolute.
cards.source_name: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Use annual renewal fees to lift revenue without touching the headline price
cards.summary: Add a one-time annual fee on top of a monthly subscription, charged after the first year, to increase revenue without hurting front-end conversion.
cards.use_when: Pricing a subscription, membership or replenishment program in a store.
steps: Set the annual fee at about one to three months of the monthly price.
Charge it only after the subscriber has stayed a year, so it never appears in the advertised entry price that drives signups.
Reason about timing: someone who has already stayed twelve months is unlikely to leave over it.
Estimate the impact: the source states the fee adds roughly 8–24% to revenue at no added cost, and on a 20% margin business that can roughly double profit.
Example from the source: a $39/month plan with a $99 annual renewal moves annual revenue per customer from $468 to $567, a 21% increase and an effective $47/month.
Keep advertised pricing unchanged because advertised price drives conversion.
caveats: All figures are the source's illustrative math, not tested results across businesses.
This works for recurring/recurring-charge models; it does not transfer to one-off product sales.
Disclose the fee clearly in terms of service to avoid chargeback and trust damage.
cards.source_name: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Turn testimonials into hooks by asking for the worst moment
cards.summary: Collect testimonial answers as a specific worst-moment story rather than a before/after narrative, so the quote works as an ad hook.
cards.use_when: Sourcing customer testimonials for a store's PDP, ads or email content.
steps: Stop asking customers how life was before your product — that produces long stories with no usable hook.
Instead ask one question: what was the worst moment?
Expect a moment, not a summary; the specificity is what makes the hook powerful.

Compare the source's own examples: 'two months away from shutting our doors', 'barely making enough to survive', and two separate testimonials that ended the month with $0 of profit — the detail, not the general struggle, is the value.
Analyze which hooks win by reviewing many testimonials together (the source reviewed 2,500 and found the best shared a pain-based hook).
Deploy the resulting line as the opening of an ad, the first line of an email, or the top of a review block.
caveats: The 2,500-review finding is from Gym Launch testimonials in a coaching context; the transfer to a store's reviews is an adaptation.
Pain-based hooks suit acquisition creative; testimonials used as reassurance on a PDP may need a different, outcome-focused framing.
cards.source_name: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Give away a peeled-off bonus to make list membership worth something
cards.summary: Create exclusive assets that only list subscribers receive, so opt-in is sold on ongoing membership rather than the lead magnet alone.
cards.use_when: Designing the incentive stack for a store's email opt-in.
steps: Identify work you already produced that is valuable but does not fit its main container — the source describes writing book chapters that did not flow with the book.
Finish that material to full quality and reserve it as a subscriber-only gift.
Make it platform-specific so there is a reason to be on the email list specifically, not just somewhere.
Separate the recruitment message: sell regular communication first, then mention the free asset by the way.
Back it with anticipation — tell subscribers a larger announcement is coming and they will hear it first.
Verify the asset is genuinely good before gating it, because unsubscribing after a disappointing reward is the outcome the source says he worries about most.
caveats: A weak lead magnet followed by nothing of ongoing value causes immediate unsubscribes or permanent dormancy.
Exclusive-asset creation requires genuinely spare finished work; manufacturing filler defeats the purpose.
cards.source_name: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Prioritize fast follow-up over almost everything else
cards.summary: Respond to an opt-in within seconds — the source says it could quadruple sales and argues it should be the first operational priority.
cards.use_when: Deciding what to fix first in a store's lead handling and conversion process.
steps: Set up a system that calls or reaches a lead within about 60 seconds of opting in.
Cite the source's basis: an HBR study he refers to showed an average 391% increase in sales, which he translates as roughly quadrupling.
Run the prioritization test: if nothing else on the roadmap can quadruple sales, this should be the first priority.
Reframe staffing as self-funding: the source argues you can afford the coverage out of the sales lift it produces.
Treat it as simple to understand and hard to operate — the constraint is coverage and process, not the idea.
caveats: The 391% is a study figure cited by the source, not a guaranteed outcome for your store.
This applies to businesses with a sales follow-up step — direct-to-consumer self-serve checkouts may have no equivalent action.
cards.source_name: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Focus effort on CTR over open rate over time
cards.summary: Optimize the rolling click-through rate rather than individual sends, treating high-value hard asks as withdrawals against softer sends.
cards.use_when: Planning a store's monthly email mix and reviewing whether the program is trending up or down.
steps: Decide deliberately which sends are deposits (pure value, low ask) and which are withdrawals (a real conversion push).
Avoid asking for the click with equal pressure in every send, since that erodes response over time.
Deliver hidden high-value content behind links — the source cites Google Drive links to video sales letters and other gated assets as an effective pattern — to keep clicks rewarding.
Watch the rolling metric rather than the single send; the source evaluates CTR across a period, not per email.
Note the source's own orientation numbers as context only: about 8.5% CTR, which he interprets as roughly 8,500 clicks per 100,000 sends.
Expect that training the audience to click is what governs future deliverability, since providers read engagement as quality.
caveats: Google Drive link tactics are described by the source as a 2011-era advanced tactic — test whether it still behaves that way in current inbox environments.
The 8.5% CTR is one sender's list, not a benchmark.
cards.source_name: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Use native-style links for deliverability
cards.summary: Route clicks to links that inbox providers already recognize as legitimate rather than to raw hosted sales pages.
cards.use_when: Choosing where a store's email link should point — sales page, video or gated document.
steps: Prefer links to mainstream properties the provider understands, such as a video platform link.
For a sales letter or video sales letter, host the asset where the provider can identify the file type rather than on an unfamiliar domain.
Test rough, duct-taped-looking assets too — the source says they sometimes convert better than polished destinations.
Label this as a 2011-era tactic and verify current behavior before relying on it.
Pair it with the broader principle: align with the provider's objective of delivering high-quality mail rather than looking for hacks.
caveats: The source explicitly flags this as an old tactic, and provider routing behavior changes — verify before depending on it.
Hosting sensitive assets on third-party storage may not suit branded or gated commercial offers.
cards.source_name: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Pre-flight: run audience + objection research before drafting any email copy
cards.summary: Run a few hours of structured research on competitor ads, Amazon reviews, podcasts and social profiles to build a research doc you write emails from.
cards.use_when: You are about to write a campaign, welcome flow or promo email and don't yet have written pain points, angles and objections for the product.
steps: Decide the product you're writing for and the country/demo you're targeting (the source uses the US as the biggest DTC market as an example) before touching any copy tool.

In Facebook Ad Library, search the product category, filter by country, set ad category to 'All ads' and media type to 'Video' — the source argues video is more telling because only slightly bigger brands can run UGC video.

Sort to find competitors running many ad variations (the source points to one running 85 versions vs. another with 5) — many variations suggests a working angle. Open the competitor's page > About > Page transparency > Ads to see the whole history.
Open the product page and record the USPs, ingredients, bundle offers and claims the competitor is making.
Start a plain Notion page as an idea dump (the source says no template is needed) and list product benefits, keywords, and the angle the competitor is leading with.
Do this over multiple products and save findings. The source claims a few hours up front makes each email 10–20 minutes to write.
The output is a single research doc you will pull banner angle, review selection, benefit copy and guarantee messaging from.
caveats: The source's time estimates (few hours research, 10–20 minutes per email) are his own experience, not a benchmark.
Filtering by only video ads skips image-based competitors that may also be performing.
cards.source_name: Master Email Copywriting for E-commerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Mine Amazon reviews for pre-purchase objections, not praise
cards.summary: Read most-recent Amazon reviews of competing and adjacent products to collect the specific objections (taste, difficulty of use, lead content, purification) you'll neutralise in copy.
cards.use_when: You are building objection-handling copy, review blocks or a guarantee for a consumable or problem-solution product.
steps: Go to the Amazon of the country you're targeting and search the product category plus adjacent categories (source example: sea moss and shilajit for a supplement brand).
Pick products with a good volume of reviews, then filter to Most Recent — the source says top reviews are not always that useful.
Scroll the negative and mixed reviews and list every practical complaint: difficult to scoop, air-dries, tastes bitter, hard to swallow, no energy increase, no noticeable change.
Log category-level objections, not just one brand's: in the source example, lead content and lack of lab testing appear across shilajit products because they're sourced from different regions.
Note positive reviews too — for sea moss the source found repeated 'easy to swallow / no bad taste' praise, showing taste is the category's buying barrier.
Spend roughly 30–60 minutes per product category doing this, then decide how your product's process (e.g. purification method) answers each objection.
Extend the same mining to Trustpilot, the Better Business Bureau, comment sections on the brand's and competitors' social posts, and podcast comment sections.
caveats: The source doesn't trust reviews posted on the product page itself because they can be faked — prefer Amazon and third-party review sites.
30–60 minutes is the source's suggested minimum, not a validated threshold.
Watch for regulated or medical claims when turning objections into copy.
cards.source_name: Master Email Copywriting for E-commerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Pressure-test the market by searching Facebook Ad Library for problem keywords
cards.summary: Search Ad Library for the underlying problem (e.g. hair loss) rather than your product name to see what solutions already exist and what people complain about.
cards.use_when: You are deciding which angle or mechanism to lead with in acquisition emails or cold traffic and want evidence your framing is unsolved elsewhere.
steps: Type the problem phrase, not the product, into Facebook Ad Library (source example: 'hair loss').
Look at the incumbent solutions that flood the results — in the source example, minoxidil ads.
Note the objections people raise about those solutions: the source says minoxidil is effective but carries hormone influences and side effects.
Position your product as the alternative the incumbent's customers are already looking for — in the source example, holistic or natural alternatives like sea moss or collagen.
Turn that gap into the angle you lead acquisition emails with, then feed it into the banner block and the benefit highlight copy.
Cross-check whether the complaint pattern also shows up in Amazon reviews of those incumbent products before committing to the angle.
caveats: The minoxidil side-effect claim is the presenter's assertion about what people say in the market, not a verified medical statement — verify before using in copy.
Ad Library interfaces and filters change; verify the current UI before instructing a team member.
cards.source_name: Master Email Copywriting for E-commerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Extrapolate benefits into underlying insecurities to write empathetic copy
cards.summary: Map each surface product benefit down to the specific insecurity it compensates for, then write to the insecurity rather than the feature.
cards.use_when: You are writing longer-form benefit highlight copy or story blocks and the current draft reads generic or feature-led.
steps: List each product benefit plainly (source example: boosted energy, fat loss and muscle gain, thicker fuller hair, intense detoxification, improved skin).
For each, write the immediate consequence (muscle gain leads to feeling and looking more confident).

Then push one level deeper to the social or identity insecurity: not being able to approach people, nervousness in social settings, feeling inferior, seeing acne first every time you look in a mirror.

Decide which benefits are 'perks' and which are true insecurity anchors — the source argues fat loss, muscle gain, hair loss and low testosterone carry much more emotional weight for men than energy or detox.
Write benefit copy aimed at the insecurity, then resolve it with your product's mechanism (e.g. mineral deficiency, not personal failing).
Keep the deep version to one benefit per email block; use icon-plus-short-label benefit rows when you need to show several at once.
Keep the tone that of a friend trying to help, matching the short 100–300 word length of ecommerce emails rather than long-form advertorial.
caveats: The source presents this as his own psychological extrapolation technique, not a researched model of buyer behaviour.
Deeper insecurity angles can drift into regulated claims — the source notes he must imply rather than state them.
cards.source_name: Master Email Copywriting for E-commerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Shift the blame outward to remove shame from the buying decision
cards.summary: Redirect responsibility for the customer's problem onto external factors so the reader is the victim rather than the cause, lowering the emotional cost of buying.
cards.use_when: You are writing problem-solution copy for a category where the customer may feel personally responsible for their problem (damaged hair, low energy, poor skin, low testosterone).
steps: Identify the behaviour the customer is privately blaming themselves for.
Name the external cause instead: the source's example is telling women with damaged hair that chemical-laden hair dyes from large corporations ruined it, not their years of dyeing it.
For a supplement brand the equivalent is framing symptoms as a biological deficiency rather than a personality flaw — e.g. nerves before approaching someone are a testosterone issue, not shyness.
Present your product as the remedy that reverses damage which was not the customer's fault in the first place.
Use this framing in the banner angle, benefit highlight copy and the objection-handling review you select, so the whole email is consistent.
Keep it honest: the source frames this as ethical only when the external explanation is true, not as a manipulation tactic.
caveats: The source explicitly calls this an ethical copy tactic — if the external blame is fabricated, the claim becomes deceptive.
Avoid naming competitor brands or making unsubstantiated accusations about specific companies.
cards.source_name: Master Email Copywriting for E-commerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Build emails from modular blocks instead of writing long-form direct response
cards.summary: Treat every ecommerce email as an assembly of standard blocks (banner, CTA, review, product display, benefit highlight, content/story, countdown, featured-on, guarantee) and write copy per block.
cards.use_when: You are briefing a designer, creating Klaviyo templates, or training a junior writer on how to produce campaign and flow emails quickly.
steps: Write out the block list you'll use: banner, CTA, review, product display, benefit highlights, content or story, countdown timer, featured on, guarantee.
Note which blocks carry real copy (story and benefit blocks) versus which are largely design (logo, footer, product display).
For each email, pick only the blocks the email's goal needs — a launch email may be banner + countdown + product display + guarantee; a story email may be banner + long content block + review.
Draft each block independently rather than writing a continuous letter, since ecommerce copy is short-form and design-led (the source puts typical emails at 100–300 words).
Hand the block-level copy to the designer so they know what goes on each visual element.
Build a reusable library of your own block designs so future emails are assembled rather than designed from scratch.
Expect the copywriting itself to become fast — the source claims 10–20 minutes per email — once your research doc and block library exist.
caveats: This is the presenter's own framework for ecommerce brands; it is not appropriate for long-form advertorial funnels.
Design-tool specifics (the source demos Canva and mentions Figma as more professional) change over time — verify current capabilities.
cards.source_name: Master Email Copywriting for E-commerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Write the banner block to state the email's purpose above the fold
cards.summary: The banner is everything visible on a phone without scrolling, so its job is to state the email's offer or intent in one eye-catching hit.
cards.use_when: You are drafting the top of a promotional, launch or flow email and want to maximise scroll-through to the rest of the message.
steps: Design and write for the mobile above-the-fold area only — the source compares the banner to opening a letter with 'I am writing to [purpose]'.
Make it eye-catching and state the goal or offer of the email plainly.
Optimise the aspect ratio for mobile phones so the key text isn't cropped halfway.
Check the offer and CTA text are fully visible without scrolling.
Expect roughly 9 out of 10 emails to have some form of banner — either a short strip or a longer one containing a CTA — so treat it as standard, not optional.
Measure success by whether the reader reaches the next block of the email, since a cut-off or vague banner suppresses everything below it.
caveats: The source's '9 out of 10 emails have a banner' is his own observation, not a study result.
Banner rendering varies by inbox client; test in the clients your list actually uses.
cards.source_name: Master Email Copywriting for E-commerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Keep CTA button copy to a single clear instruction
cards.summary: Button text only needs to tell the reader where to click and what happens next — the source says this is not hard to write and shouldn't be overthought.
cards.use_when: You are filling in button labels across a campaign, flow or template in your ESP.
steps: Write the action the reader is taking: Shop Now, Order Today, Learn More are the source's standard examples.
Match the label to the intent of the email block above it — a countdown-driven offer email uses an order-oriented button, an education email uses a learn-more button.
Keep it short enough to render on a mobile button without wrapping or truncating.
Avoid loading the button with persuasion; the persuasion lives in the banner, benefit and review blocks.
caveats: The source gives this minimal attention by design — treat this as the low-effort block, not a place to test elaborate copy unless you have reason to.
cards.source_name: Master Email Copywriting for E-commerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Select review blocks that answer a specific known objection
cards.summary: Replace generic 'I love it' testimonials with reviews that directly neutralise a pre-purchase anxiety you identified in research.
cards.use_when: You are populating the social-proof block of an email or flow and want it to move undecided readers rather than decorate the email.
steps: Pull your research doc and list the top objections the audience has before buying.

Match each review slot to one objection — for a sea moss/shilajit brand the source would pick one review about better hair and nails and one from a busy person whose energy improved without changing their lifestyle.
Avoid reviews that only express general satisfaction, because the source argues they don't help the reader decide whether the product is for them.
Pair reviews with UGC photos selectively: it can strengthen credibility, but the source warns against attaching a face to sensitive objections (his example is erectile dysfunction).
Choose which objections are safe to pair with a face and which should stay anonymous, respecting the reviewer's privacy.
Keep the review text short enough to sit in a mobile block.
caveats: The privacy caution about matching faces to sensitive objections is the source's guidance, and he advises using UGC 'with caution' rather than as a rule.
Do not assume a review that answers one objection answers the rest — one objection per review slot.
cards.source_name: Master Email Copywriting for E-commerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Choose the product display layout before writing the copy
cards.summary: Decide between row-by-row and grid formats based on how much copy each product needs and how it will render on a phone.
cards.use_when: You are laying out a merchandising email that features one hero product or several SKUs.
steps: If the product needs descriptive copy alongside its image and CTA, use a row-by-row layout — the source uses this when copy accompanies the product.
If you're showing several products with only an image and title, use a 2x2 grid, which fits a product image plus title without shrinking the text.
Avoid wide grids like 3x2: the source warns products render too small on mobile for people to distinguish text.
Envision the mobile rendering before writing the copy, because the column count determines how many words each product can carry.
Write copy to the space the layout allows rather than the reverse.
caveats: Grid thresholds are the source's design judgement, not a tested rule — verify against your own template's mobile rendering.
The source demos in Canva for smaller brands and says Figma gives more professional output for larger teams.
cards.source_name: Master Email Copywriting for E-commerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Choose icon rows or longer copy for benefit highlights
cards.summary: Icon rows let you show several benefits at once; longer copy lets you tackle one benefit and its underlying insecurity in depth.
cards.use_when: You are writing the benefits section of an email and deciding how much persuasive copy to attach to each claim.
steps: For the icon route, write short benefit labels — the source's examples are boosted energy, fat loss and muscle gain, thicker fuller hair, intense detoxification — and attach custom icons that visually match each claim rather than a generic tick.

For the long-copy route, focus on one benefit per block, open with the insecurity the benefit resolves, then resolve it with the product's mechanism (source example: acne is a mineral deficiency, and adding those minerals can help acne scars heal over time).
Don't try to write deep emotional copy for perk-level benefits such as energy or detox; the source says you can't dive into insecurities with those angles.
Match block choice to email length — icon rows for short promo emails, one long benefit block for story or education emails.
Refine the first-draft sentence structure before shipping, since the source's own first-draft example is deliberately rough.
caveats: The acne/mineral mechanism is the presenter's illustrative copy example, not a clinically established claim — do not reuse mechanisms you haven't verified for your own product.
Keep regulated health claims out of benefit copy.
cards.source_name: Master Email Copywriting for E-commerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Use fact-only content and story blocks when you don't know copywriting tactics
cards.summary: For founders writing their own emails, content blocks can simply present a study or a factual founding story — no framework required — and still sell.
cards.use_when: You are a small brand owner writing an education, brand-story or ingredient email without a copywriter or an established voice-of-customer library.
steps: For a content block, state the fact plainly — the source's example is a study showing a 200mg dose of shilajit over two weeks raised average testosterone in the control group by 42% — and stop there.
Support it with a simple chart if you can; the source says that alone constitutes the content block.

For a story block, narrate facts in first person: the source's example is a founder seeing genetically receding hairlines in the family, learning prevention is the best cure, discovering micronutrient deficiencies, sourcing sea moss through relatives and shipping it through customs, then selling it after friends had results.
Resist inserting copywriting frameworks — the source's point is that both examples sell on facts alone.
Keep the block short enough to sit between a banner and a product display.
caveats: Any study statistic you cite must be real and must actually support the claim for your product; the source's 42% figure is his own illustrative example, not a citable result.
Verify the study before publishing, and check how the claim sits with advertising regulations in your market.
cards.source_name: Master Email Copywriting for E-commerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Use countdown timers to back an urgency claim
cards.summary: A countdown timer only works as urgency if it is tied to a real, expiring claim such as a 24-hour discount code.
cards.use_when: You are running a launch or sale email where an offer genuinely expires and you want urgency without writing more persuasive copy.
steps: Only deploy the timer when there is a real deadline — the source's example is a discount code expiring in 24 hours; the timer just substantiates the claim.
Place it as its own block, typically near the offer or CTA.
Use the tool the source recommends, countdownmail.com, which he describes as roughly $10/month with unlimited uses.
Build a reusable countdown block in your ESP so future launches take minutes.
Verify current pricing, ESP integrations and rendering behaviour of whichever countdown tool you choose before building it into a core template.
caveats: A countdown attached to a deadline that resets or never actually expires damages trust; the source ties urgency to a genuine offer.
Tool pricing and interfaces change — confirm before committing.
cards.source_name: Master Email Copywriting for E-commerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Feature logos as an authority block using 'as seen on' wording
cards.summary: The featured-on block is a simple trust signal: two wordings and a row of publication or show logos.
cards.use_when: You are adding a credibility layer to a welcome, launch or promotion email and have genuine press or media appearances to show.
steps: Use one of the two standard wordings: 'As seen on' or 'Featured on' — the source says that is all the copy needed.
Lay out the logos of the outlets you've genuinely appeared in, for example Shark Tank or a relevant industry publication.
Place it where it reinforces trust, typically after the banner or alongside the product display.
Confirm you actually appeared in every logo you show — the source presents this purely as displaying real PR.
caveats: The source treats this as a copy-light block, so don't expect it to carry the email; its job is trust reinforcement only.
cards.source_name: Master Email Copywriting for E-commerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Reverse risk with a long unconditional guarantee — and expect fewer returns
cards.summary: Offer a long guarantee window on consumables to remove the fear of loss; the source argues a 180-day window will return less than a 30-day window in practice.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to add a guarantee block to acquisition or first-purchase emails and how long the window should be.
steps: Identify the two fears the guarantee addresses — being scammed, and the product not working for them, both described by the source as a fear of loss rather than a product objection.
Offer an unconditional guarantee window and state it plainly in its own block on first-purchase and acquisition emails.

Consider a long window such as 180 days over a short one such as 30 days: the source explains that with 30 days buyers hold themselves to the deadline and return, while with 180 days they procrastinate past the point of bothering and often forget entirely.

If you're a bootstrapped brand worried about refund exposure, note the source's claim that guarantees barely move return or refund rates and that a longer window lowers them further on lower-ticket consumables.
Repeat the guarantee in the flows most likely to be a customer's first purchase.
caveats: This is the presenter's stated '180-day guarantee paradox' based on his own brand experience, not a published benchmark — test the window on your own refund data before adopting it.
Check consumer-law requirements for guarantee and refund statements in your selling markets.
A guarantee block doesn't replace answering objections — pair it with objection-handling reviews.
cards.source_name: Master Email Copywriting for E-commerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Profile followers and ad comments to pin down who actually buys
cards.summary: Scan a competitor's Instagram followers and comment sections to infer the real demographics, age ranges and interests of the buying audience.
cards.use_when: You need a sharper customer profile for email segmentation, creative angles or list targeting and analytics only gives you aggregate age and gender.
steps: Open a competitor's Instagram and read comments on their latest posts for language and objections.
Look at the top followers of a brand with a niche audience and open individual profiles — the source suggests checking roughly 50 to 75 to get a sense of the pattern.
Record what recurs across those profiles: the source's example is seeing posts about motorbikes, fishing or holistic wellness and inferring that is the buyer's real interest set.
Use Google Analytics and Facebook audience analytics for the baseline age range, gender and interest data if you have it, but treat the profile scan as the psychographic layer on top.
Feed the findings back into the research doc alongside benefit and objection data.
Use the profile to write the banner angle and select reviews for the email.
caveats: This is observational inference, not statistically valid sampling — don't treat a 50–75 profile scan as audience research that stands alone.
Review platform data-use terms before systematically scraping or viewing profiles.
cards.source_name: Master Email Copywriting for E-commerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Test SMS/email send frequency with a holdout to prove incrementality
cards.summary: Design a cohort split (normal / zero / double) to measure whether extra messages actually lift revenue before scaling budget.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to increase lifecycle message cadence or justify a growing SMS bill to leadership.
steps: Split your subscriber base into three cohorts: hold steady at current cadence (for example 50%), send nothing at all (for example 25%), and send double the cadence (for example 25%).
Run for a full cycle long enough to capture conversion behavior—Postscript's test moved brands from roughly one text per week to two.
Compare revenue per subscriber across cohorts against the true holdout, not just platform-attributed revenue, to see incremental lift.
If 2x shows a statistically significant revenue lift over holdout, raise cadence; if not, keep the baseline.
Note that in the test described, more sending produced higher ROI with ~98% confidence the 2x group yielded significantly more revenue—treat this as one brand's result, not a universal benchmark.
caveats: Every SMS has a real per-message cost, unlike email, so incremental revenue must clear the toll.
Attribution tools report what happened; only a holdout shows what would have happened otherwise.
cards.source_name: Rethinking SMS Marketing for Ecommerce_ AI, RCS & LTV.docx

cards.title: Set an SMS frequency baseline using subscriber LTV and unsub rate
cards.summary: Use subscriber LTV (acquisition rate, messages per subscriber, revenue per message, unsub rate) to find the send cadence that maximizes revenue without spiking unsubscribes.
cards.use_when: Setting or revising monthly SMS cadence and worried about annoying the list.
steps: Track four metrics: % of list subscribing (acquisition rate), messages sent per subscriber per month, revenue per message, and unsubscribe rate.
Watch unsubscribes inside the first 30 days as the key signal of over-messaging.
Start near Postscript's observed sweet spot of roughly 8–10 texts per subscriber per month, which they report generates high returns with essentially zero impact on baseline unsub rate.
Do not assume this is fixed—the correct baseline must be tested per brand by mapping the relationship between messages per subscriber, revenue, and unsub rate.
Use the data, not gut fear of 'annoying people'—if frequency were a problem, it would surface in the unsub metric.
Recognize real spread across brands: some large brands send ~2 texts/subscriber (e.g., a subscription-first model), while others (e.g., Grüns) send ~20+ in the first 30–45 days.
caveats: 8–10/month is Postscript's observed range, not a guaranteed optimum for every store.
High-frequency brands often accept higher spend for a specific goal such as converting to subscription; low-frequency brands may be filtering out long-term non-buyers to avoid fees.
cards.source_name: Rethinking SMS Marketing for Ecommerce_ AI, RCS & LTV.docx

cards.title: Treat SMS as an acquisition channel, not just retention
cards.summary: Most people who give you a phone number haven't bought yet, so SMS flows are the welcome mat for paid traffic—manage and optimize them like performance marketing.
cards.use_when: Allocating team ownership, budget, or optimization effort across paid acquisition and lifecycle channels.
steps: Recognize that the first action a Meta/Google click often triggers is the signup popup—so SMS/email pop-ups and welcome flows are part of the acquisition funnel.

Track that roughly 25% of compliant double-opt-in subscribers buy within 30 days (Postscript's cross-brand figure); the remaining ~75% are unconverted subscribers whose first-purchase objections still need handling.
Treat the pop-up → welcome series as your acquisition engine, distinct from campaigns that serve retention at day 15/30/45.
Align org structure so one leader sees paid, creative, ecom, and retention—Postscript and operators report that siloed teams miss second-order effects (e.g., an ad change tanking SMS list growth).
Test pop-up changes against full-site conversion rate, not just opt-in rate, because a pop-up can lift signups while hurting checkout.
An operator predicts retention will become the next frontier as paid channels saturate—an opinion, not a guarantee.
caveats: The 25% figure is an aggregate across Postscript's ~25,000 brands, not a target for your store.
Centralizing teams is a recommendation from practitioners, not a proven universal structure.
cards.source_name: Rethinking SMS Marketing for Ecommerce_ AI, RCS & LTV.docx

cards.title: Add a question to lifecycle flows to start conversations
cards.summary: The lowest-effort entry to conversational commerce is appending a simple question to an existing flow message and reading the replies.
cards.use_when: Starting conversational commerce or sourcing zero-party data without new tooling.
steps: Pick any existing flow (welcome series, abandoned cart, delivery follow-up).
After the standard link or message, append a plain question such as 'Is there anything else I can help you with today?' or 'Do you have any questions I can answer?'

Test it: one operator split a 6-message welcome flow, with the variant ending in a question, and it performed well; keep the standard flow to convert the easy 25% then use the question to catch marginal prospects where conversation is required.
Expect volume—operators report brands getting thousands of replies in the first week when they ask.
Mine the replies for objection themes and use them to guide future flows and ad copy.
Extend this to more touchpoints: post-delivery usage questions, winback, long-consideration prospects.
caveats: For short-consideration, low-ticket impulse buys (e.g., a wallet before Father's Day), conversation at the end of the flow is sufficient—going conversation-first is overkill.
For long-consideration or high-ticket categories (e.g., a $1,000 sofa with a ~90-day window), consider putting conversation earlier to compress the decision.
cards.source_name: Rethinking SMS Marketing for Ecommerce_ AI, RCS & LTV.docx

cards.title: Match conversation strategy to consideration period and ticket size
cards.summary: When and how aggressively to open conversations depends on how long buyers deliberate and how high the stakes are.
cards.use_when: Designing whether flows should lead with conversation or stay broadcast-first for a given product category.
steps: Identify your category's consideration period (time from click/opt-in to purchase).
For short, impulse-driven buys, run a normal broadcast flow and reserve conversation for the end to handle stragglers.
For long-consideration or high-ticket items, place conversation earlier—the source compares it to putting your best salesperson in front of a shopper while they compare you to competitors.
For one-time-to-subscription conversion, which carries an outsized value bump, lean conversation-heavy to handle objections and upsell.
Use winback and unconverted-senior-subscriber segments as conversation targets, since they've engaged with texts but never bought.
Post-delivery, ask a follow-up question about product usage to open a dialogue at the best moment for repeat purchase.
caveats: Consideration-period length is a judgment call per category; the source gives 90 days as an example for furniture, not a rule.
cards.source_name: Rethinking SMS Marketing for Ecommerce_ AI, RCS & LTV.docx

cards.title: Use conversation data to build real zero-party customer attributes
cards.summary: Conversations surface static facts and ephemeral attributes you can operationalize across text and your CDP.
cards.use_when: Enriching subscriber profiles with personalization data and building one-to-one messaging.
steps: Instrument conversational replies so the content is queryable, not just answered in the moment.
Separate static data (a purchase made a year ago, a SKU, a subscription tier) from ephemeral data that changes over time (a child ages from 1 to 2, seasonal location, a fitness or health change).
Push attributes into your CRM/CDP so they can inform messaging beyond SMS—the source is building toward API/MCP access so personas like Claude can consume them (verify current availability).
Build triggers around ephemeral attributes: a daughter's next birthday, a season change, a size change after a weight-loss journey.
Treat this as the path to 'audience of one' personalization marketers have chased but lacked data to execute.

Example of the kind of data conversations yield: a belt brand learned a wife buys for her husband, that he was on a health journey down 40 lbs, and that his size would keep changing—actionable but not obtainable from browsing data alone.
Operators report subscribers who have a conversation with the brand show ~1.5x higher lifetime value—an internal metric, not a guarantee.
caveats: Postscript's API/MCP access was in development at the recording—check current product docs.
The 1.5x LTV lift is the vendor's observed metric; validate on your own list.
cards.source_name: Rethinking SMS Marketing for Ecommerce_ AI, RCS & LTV.docx

cards.title: Use SMS/MMS/RCS as distinct channels and enable RCS for richer actions
cards.summary: RCS is a separate messaging channel with SMS fallback that raises the creative ceiling with carousels, video, and native action buttons.
cards.use_when: Planning SMS creative formats and considering RCS rollouts for launches or drops.
steps: Understand RCS is not SMS/MMS—it's its own protocol; if a recipient can't receive RCS, messages fall back to SMS in tools like Postscript.
Use RCS for rich formats: carousel scrolling, video, and native action buttons.
For product drops, use the iOS calendar action button so recipients can add a launch date directly instead of a vague 'watch this space' text.
Exploit native CTAs that integrate with the phone to expand use cases on the messaging channel.
Operators report outsized performance on RCS over SMS/MMS—treat as early directional signal, not a benchmark.
Confirm current carrier/device support and platform interface before committing budget, as RCS availability and features change.
caveats: RCS performance claims are early-stage and vendor-reported.
Feature availability (e.g., iOS calendar) varies by platform and time—verify in your messaging tool.
cards.source_name: Rethinking SMS Marketing for Ecommerce_ AI, RCS & LTV.docx

cards.title: Adapt to customer data through conversations
cards.summary: Persistent conversations uncover the objections preventing purchase that no PDP can pre-empt, so build a process to capture and act on those objections.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing mid-funnel purchase blockers and reducing friction at PDP and checkout.
steps: Run ongoing conversations on your list to capture live objections people don't broadcast anywhere else.

Look for objections that are too specific to design for: e.g., a shopper who would only buy 'Miracle Balm' if assured it holds up to a 5-hour-a-day gardening/sweating regimen, or a buyer whose cart total ($75) exceeded her budget ($68) and who needed a small offer to close.
Use conversational tools to handle these at the moment of decision (the source's Shopper AI handles shade-matching and small price-gap offers automatically).
Query conversation archives to surface trends and recurring blockers (the source's 'Ask Shopper' feature).
Feed the discovered objections back into PDP copy, FAQ, and ad creative so future traffic self-serves.
Treat conversation logs as arguably your richest consumer-insight stream, since many brands never text customers at all.
caveats: The specific brand examples (Jones Road, belts) are illustrative, not benchmarks.
Automated handling of price-gap offers requires merchant-defined guardrails—set them deliberately.
cards.source_name: Rethinking SMS Marketing for Ecommerce_ AI, RCS & LTV.docx

cards.title: Chase incremental value in retention channels as paid channels saturate
cards.summary: As the curve of paid acquisition flattens, finer optimization of lifecycle messaging on owned channels becomes the marginal growth lever.
cards.use_when: Setting next-quarter growth priorities and allocating between paid acquisition and lifecycle optimization.
steps: Recognize that as paid opportunities are exhausted, marginal value moves into retention channels—the source quotes a CMO predicting retention would become the topic of focus after everybody exhausts paid incrementality.
Shift toward precise optimization: for example, deciding whether 50K, 75K, or 100K of monthly SMS spend is most efficient at the margin, not just whether the current spend works.
Scrutinize the SMS bill as a meaningful cost that lives between SaaS costs and performance marketing on the P&L—as it scales, so should the demand for incrementality evidence.
Partner with a vendor or team willing to 'grade their own homework' with holdouts on large spend.
Separate lead conversion (subscribing) from purchase conversion (buying) and from close rate—holdouts and cohort measurement track whether the channel produced net-new purchases.
caveats: The CMO's retention prediction is a forecast, not a law.
Retention-only isn't universal—brands with long consideration periods should still invest in top-of-funnel acquisition.
cards.source_name: Rethinking SMS Marketing for Ecommerce_ AI, RCS & LTV.docx

cards.title: Align pop-ups, flows, and campaigns to the true purchase decision
cards.summary: Pop-ups and welcome flows are acquisition touch points; campaigns are retention—design and own them accordingly.
cards.use_when: Deciding ownership and testing scope for pop-ups, welcome series, and campaigns.
steps: Treat the pop-up and welcome flow as part of the acquisition engine (ad → lander → pop-up → flow), because that chain is the first interaction with many paid visitors.
Treat campaigns as a retention touchpoint where you speak to subscribers at day 15/30/45 with launches and first-party-data-driven messages.
Ensure at least one leader sees both the flow and site behavior so signals aren't missed—e.g., an ad change lowering SMS list growth below forecast.
Test pop-up experience against full-site conversion rate, not just opt-in rate, to catch changes that hurt checkout.
Recognize the 'customer journey as a line' is misleading—people interact with all touchpoints in non-linear ways, so siloed assembly-line thinking invalidates decisions.
Follow the source's 'just ask' rule: solicit conversations at the acquisition stage to intercept people who look like a converted customer but have a first-purchase objection.
caveats: Full-site A/B testing of pop-ups requires sufficient traffic to detect conversion-rate impact.
Org restructuring is contextual—not every store can centralize teams.
cards.source_name: Rethinking SMS Marketing for Ecommerce_ AI, RCS & LTV.docx

cards.title: RCS vs SMS/MMS: what changes in the message
cards.summary: RCS is a distinct messaging protocol with SMS fallback that upgrades text-only or single-image messages into rich carousels, video, web views and native action buttons.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to pilot RCS for campaign sends or transactional/drop messaging, and scoping which message formats to build for it.
steps: Understand RCS as a separate protocol from SMS/MMS, not a formatting tweak: SMS is text-only, MMS adds an image, RCS supports carousels, scrolling, video and embedded web views inside the messaging thread. Where a recipient can't receive RCS, the message falls back to SMS, so keep an SMS-safe version of every send.

Exploit native phone integrations for commerce use cases: action buttons can be programmed as any CTA, and calendar functionality lets a pre-launch drop message offer 'add to calendar' instead of 'watch this space' — replacing a reminder prompt with an actual saved event.
Know that consumers are already trained on this interaction pattern (iMessage-style rich bubbles have existed for years), so richer messages don't require teaching the customer new behavior.
Treat RCS as an early-adopter inbox-distinction play: the present lift partly comes from standing out versus SMS-only brands, and the source expects that advantage to diminish as adoption grows.
Weigh the cost: RCS is somewhat more expensive than SMS because carriers take a cut, so a pilot should be judged on incremental performance, not just message-level cost.
caveats: The source's claim of outsized RCS performance over SMS/MMS is a current observation from one provider and its brand base, not a benchmark; the source itself names carrier cost/performance as the main threat to the channel.
RCS availability details vary and change quickly — verify current device and carrier coverage before planning a send.
Live brand example mentioned: one brand switched to RCS with a holdout group running to measure incremental impact.
cards.source_name: Rethinking SMS Marketing for Ecommerce_ AI, RCS & LTV.docx

cards.title: Test RCS by holding out or running a clean flow
cards.summary: Operationalize an RCS switch with either a holdout group for incremental read or a deliberately simple one-to-one flow for a cleaner test signal.
cards.use_when: Launching or planning a first RCS campaign and needing to decide how to structure the test so results are trustworthy.
steps: Choose your measurement design up front. One option discussed: run a holdout so you can read the incremental impact of the new RCS experience versus the baseline SMS path. The other option: keep the RCS flow deliberately one-to-one and simple first, then test richer elements (carousels, cards) so the effect of each addition is cleaner.
If you change flow and format at the same time, you can't attribute lift to RCS versus your new creative — separate the protocol change from the creative change where possible.
Only after a clean baseline read should you layer richer formats: carousels for recommendations, web views for expanded browsing, action buttons for CTAs.
Build the SMS fallback version of each RCS send so the holdout/control experience is a true comparison, not a broken message.
caveats: The source only states this as an intended approach ('we'll probably go a little bit more one to one and then we'll test to get a cleaner read') — it is a plan, not a proven result.
Early-adopter novelty effects can inflate RCS lift; expect the advantage to shrink as more brands adopt the channel.
cards.source_name: Rethinking SMS Marketing for Ecommerce_ AI, RCS & LTV.docx

cards.title: Conversational carousels for product recommendation
cards.summary: Use RCS carousels inside a conversational thread to answer 'what do you recommend' with a small set of tailored best-sellers plus a native web view.
cards.use_when: Merchandising and PDP/landing-page substitution inside SMS/RCS: when a customer asks for a recommendation and you need to move them to a purchase path in-thread.
steps: Treat the conversational recommendation as a replacement for sending bare links. Where the old flow produced a few links in reply to 'I'm buying for a guy who likes the outdoors — what do you recommend?', the richer flow returns a carousel of three items curated for that buyer type.
Constrain the carousel to a small, opinionated set (the source uses three) so the customer makes a choice rather than browsing a catalog in a text thread.
Lean on attached web view so the customer can expand into a native browser experience inside the messaging app — the whole browse-to-buy path stays in the thread.
Use the carousel to serve best-seller logic for a persona/use-case rather than one generic product, and feed objection data from these conversations back into your other flows.
Because the format relies on consumer familiarity with in-thread rich content, no new customer education is needed; the constraint is building the recommendation logic behind it.
caveats: The recommendation-carousel capability is described as a future/planned application by the source, not a documented live result.
Named brand (Ridge) is used illustratively — do not treat it as evidence of conversion lift.
cards.source_name: Rethinking SMS Marketing for Ecommerce_ AI, RCS & LTV.docx

cards.title: List growth first: fix pop-up opt-in rate
cards.summary: For a $5–10M brand trying to grow SMS, the highest-leverage first move is on-site opt-in rate, because list size is the top of the funnel for every downstream send.
cards.use_when: Auditing SMS as an acquisition/growth channel and deciding where to spend first effort on list growth.
steps: Start with on-site opt-in. The source names it the fastest way to grow an SMS list, ahead of other capture methods, because it sits at the very top of your own-channel funnel and pays off in every future campaign.
If you do nothing else, fix the pop-up acquisition rate first — treat it as the single most important list-growth lever before adding new flows or formats.
Add fun/compelling content to the pop-up to lift opt-in rate; one brand explicitly says they had been under-optimizing pop-ups and are now doing it aggressively.
Make this an owned-site-team responsibility: the source recommends having your site team drive the opt-in effort aggressively and watch that the metric trends up.

Recognize the strategic logic: more numbers means more people you can text, and the source long considered list-growth capability the main differentiator between SMS providers (now shifting toward features like conversational commerce and RCS).
caveats: The $5–10M annual revenue band is the source's own framing for who should prioritize this, not a universal threshold.
The claim that on-site opt-in is 'the best' capture method is the source's opinion, stated alongside acknowledgement that other methods exist.
cards.source_name: Rethinking SMS Marketing for Ecommerce_ AI, RCS & LTV.docx

cards.title: Raise send cadence until unsubscribe rate ticks up
cards.summary: Increase message frequency one send at a time and let unsubscribe rate find your new ceiling, then treat that as the baseline.
cards.use_when: Setting campaign cadence for an established SMS program and deciding how many sends per week the list can absorb.
steps: Starting from your current cadence, add one more message per week (or one every two weeks if you send infrequently) as an increment, not a one-time jump.
Measure the unsubscribe rate after each increment and keep pushing until you see the unsubscribe rate begin to tick up — that inflection is where you stop and reset the baseline.
Do not treat the send-frequency question as separate from revenue: the point is to see how the added sends affect overall revenue from the channel, so track channel revenue alongside unsubscribes.
Once you find the ceiling, hold that cadence as your new baseline rather than reverting to the old, more conservative one.
Repeat the exercise periodically, since list composition and tolerance shift over time.
caveats: This is the source's recommended operating heuristic, not a measured benchmark; the correct ceiling differs by list and offer.
Pushing cadence without watching unsubscribe (and other list-health signals) can degrade the channel — the source explicitly uses unsub rate as the stop signal.
cards.source_name: Rethinking SMS Marketing for Ecommerce_ AI, RCS & LTV.docx

cards.title: Ask customers why they didn't buy to feed all flows
cards.summary: Run conversational questions to surface purchase objections, then push that learning into your team and every flow — not just to generate incremental revenue.
cards.use_when: Running conversational SMS and using customer-research output to improve abandoned-cart, win-back, PDP and objection-handling flows.
steps: Start a conversational thread that asks questions rather than only pushing offers; the goal is to learn why people aren't purchasing, not solely to drive a sale in the thread.

Capture the objection reasons as customer insight and route them into the team's decision-making as fast as possible — the source treats asking customers directly as the fastest way to get this data into the team's head.
Apply the objections to your existing flows: if the recurring objection is shipping, sizing, price or trust, adjust the flow copy/offer that handles that stage.
Use the same mechanism to feed conversational recommendation logic (e.g., carousels of best-sellers for a stated use case) once you know the buyer intents coming in.
Run this before/alongside cadence expansion so you know what to say when you add sends.
caveats: The source frames conversational questions as valuable mainly for objection insight and revenue; it does not supply benchmarks or expected response rates.
If you use an AI 'shopper' assistant for conversational replies (the source's provider offers one), verify current capability and QA the answers before scaling.
cards.source_name: Rethinking SMS Marketing for Ecommerce_ AI, RCS & LTV.docx

cards.title: Capture experiment learnings causally so the model earns trust
cards.summary: Operationalizing incrementality means running geo-lift and causal experiments and feeding them into your measurement model, so channel decisions are informed by tested lift rather than a black box.
cards.use_when: Attributing and budgeting across SMS/email/paid channels where you need to know which sends add incremental revenue versus cannibalize.
steps: Run structured experiments — the source uses a platform for all experiments and geo-lift testing — rather than inferring incrementality from last-click channel revenue.

Feed causal experiment results into your measurement mix model so the model is calibrated on tested lift; the source specifically values having experiments inform the MM ('causal MM') so it isn't a black box.
Use the resulting incrementality read to set the channel roadmap and budget, not just to report on past performance.
Apply the same framework to media mix and SMS sends so cadence and format decisions rest on observed lift rather than raw attributed revenue.
Build the muscle to distinguish lead conversion, purchase conversion and lift in this context before acting on the numbers.
caveats: This appears inside a sponsorship segment for a causal-MM vendor; treat the tool endorsement as promotional and evaluate measurement tools independently.
Causal-MM methodology and availability change — verify current product behavior before relying on it.
cards.source_name: Rethinking SMS Marketing for Ecommerce_ AI, RCS & LTV.docx

cards.title: Tactical SMS starting order for a mid-size brand
cards.summary: The source's recommended sequence for a $5–10M brand under-using SMS: fix pop-up opt-in, then expand cadence until unsubs rise, then add conversational questions.
cards.use_when: Prioritizing the first 30–90 days of an SMS improvement program when the team is lean and everything feels urgent.
steps: Step 1 — List growth: maximize subscribers through the on-site opt-in/pop-up and fix its acquisition rate first; this is the top of your owned-channel funnel and pays off later.
Step 2 — Cadence: add one send per interval and monitor unsubscribe rate, resetting your baseline at the point unsubs start rising; watch total channel revenue with it.
Step 3 — Conversation: begin asking customers questions to learn objections and purchase intent, and route those insights into all your flows.

Step 4 — Tooling/partner: if the team is lean and cannot execute the above, the source's own advice is to pick a hands-on platform that will push you toward the latest capabilities, accepting that this is the presenter's commercial pitch.
Sequence matters: list size and opt-in rate bound what cadence and conversation can deliver, so don't start by adding formats if your capture is weak.
caveats: The $5–10M band is the presenter's segmentation; smaller and larger brands may need a different order.
Step 4 is a vendor recommendation from the vendor's own employee and should not be read as an independent assessment.
cards.source_name: Rethinking SMS Marketing for Ecommerce_ AI, RCS & LTV.docx

cards.title: Checklist cadence: SMS/retention program for a growing brand
cards.summary: Small ecommerce teams run everything interconnected and hourly, so list health, cadence and message content should be managed as one operating rhythm.
cards.use_when: Running the day-to-day SMS/email lifecycle for a small ecom team and setting the review rhythm for list, cadence and messaging.
steps: Treat SMS/retention as small-team, high-frequency work: the source frames ecom as small teams doing big numbers where every hour matters and list, cadence and content are interconnected, so avoid optimizing one in isolation.
Keep a standing check on three top-of-funnel metrics together: pop-up opt-in rate (list growth), unsubscribe rate (list health), and channel revenue (output).
Change one lever at a time — a cadence increment or a format change — so you can tell what moved the unsubscribe rate.
Feed conversational objections back into the flows on a regular loop so the talking points stay current with what customers actually say.
Assign ownership: the source recommends the site team drive pop-up capture aggressively and watch the trend.
caveats: This is a synthesis of the source's advice rather than a single prescribed process.
Cadence and ceiling differ by list; no universal numeric target is established in the source.
cards.source_name: Rethinking SMS Marketing for Ecommerce_ AI, RCS & LTV.docx

cards.title: Sizing the SMS channel for your store
cards.summary: SMS is an owned retention channel; source argues it should account for at least 5–15% of brand total sales and cites client SMS bills under $1,000/month producing tens of thousands monthly.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to launch or resource an SMS channel, or benchmarking whether your current SMS program is underperforming relative to the channel's potential.
steps: Treat SMS as an owned retention channel like email: the list is not subject to ad auctions or algorithm changes, so revenue compounds month over month once built.

Judge the channel on its sales-share contribution. The source's benchmark: done correctly, SMS should account for at least 5–15% of total brand sales. Treat this as the presenter's agency heuristic, not a computed industry figure.
Compare channel cost to revenue: the source cites several client accounts spending less than $1,000/month on SMS to generate tens of thousands per month. Case-study result, not a promise.

Check a simple list-size math argument before investing: going from 5,000 to 10,000 subscribers on identical campaigns does not double orders (diminishing returns) — the source's illustrative example is roughly 100 orders becoming 160–180, not 200. Growth still compounds, so not growing caps your ceiling.
Audit which capabilities you already have in email before layering SMS, since most SMS revenue comes from omni-channel flows shared with email.
caveats: 5–15% of sales and the sub-$1,000-bill examples come from the presenter's agency clients; your category, list quality and offer mix will differ.
Diminishing returns are real: more subscribers from unqualified traffic dilutes performance.
cards.source_name: The Only Ecommerce SMS Marketing Video You'll Ever Need.docx

cards.title: Choose and configure an SMS platform for Shopify-style ecommerce
cards.summary: Pick Klaviyo, Attentive or Postscript — they all do the same core job — and configure number verification, subscriber import, signup forms, opt-out language, smart sending, quiet hours and keyword responses.
cards.use_when: Setting up an SMS sending account for the first time, or migrating existing SMS subscribers into a platform that also holds your email.
steps: Choose a platform: the source names Klaviyo, Attentive and Postscript and says all three send essentially the same simple texts, so you cannot go badly wrong. It prefers Klaviyo so email and SMS flows live under one flow view rather than splitting email in Klaviyo and SMS in Attentive/Postscript.
In platform settings, start SMS setup, pick your sending country, and verify a toll-free number. Note the source's caution: Canadian numbers can cost two SMS credits instead of one.
Upload your existing SMS subscriber list from CSV or other file so previously collected consent carries over.
Create the signup form — the platform states you need a form to keep collecting SMS subscribers; also keep an email pop-up active.
Set opt-out language to whatever you prefer (e.g. 'unsub') under message add-ons.
In sender preferences, decide on smart sending: when on, a subscriber will not receive more than one SMS campaign within a 24-hour window. Toggle per your cadence.
Leave SMS quiet hours on default — it blocks delivery during the restricted hours rather than sending.
Set keyword responses (e.g. texting JOIN to your number adds the person to the list and can trigger a discount), plus short links and terms. Verify the current interface, since menus change.
caveats: Platform UIs and pricing change; verify current setup screens, credit costs and quiet-hour defaults before relying on this walkthrough.
Country-specific costs and rules differ — the source only demonstrates a US setup.
cards.source_name: The Only Ecommerce SMS Marketing Video You'll Ever Need.docx

cards.title: Two-step pop-up to convert email visitors into SMS subscribers
cards.summary: Split email and SMS into separate pop-up steps, lead with your best offer in the email step, and use 'finish signing up with text to activate 20% off' style copy on the SMS step.
cards.use_when: Building or redesigning an onsite pop-up whose goal is to grow an SMS list from traffic you are already paying for.
steps: Do not put many fields on one pop-up. Avoid asking for first name, last name, occupation, location and phone all at once; each extra field is a hurdle that suppresses opt-in.
Make the pop-up two steps: an email step first, then an SMS step. Smaller sequential hurdles convert better than one large ask.

Decide the offer architecture. Many brands offer less for email and a bonus for SMS (e.g. 15% email, extra 5% SMS). The source disagrees: it prefers giving the best offer up front to email, because you get far more email opt-ins, then re-words the SMS step to capture SMS subscribers anyway. Test both if you are unsure.

Use the source's tested SMS step copy: 'finish signing up with text to activate 20% off' — i.e. tell the visitor the SMS step is what activates the discount they already saw, rather than dangling a new incentive.
Time the pop-up. The source's recommended delay is 6 to 10 seconds after page load — enough for the visitor to engage with the page before being interrupted.
Track opt-in rate separately for the email step and the SMS step so you can tell which step is losing people.
caveats: 'Finish signing up with text to activate 20% off' is the source's tested wording across its accounts, not a universal guarantee; validate on your own traffic.
Whether the best offer goes up front or is split between email and SMS is contested — the source presents its preference against the common alternative, not a proven rule.
cards.source_name: The Only Ecommerce SMS Marketing Video You'll Ever Need.docx

cards.title: Other SMS list-growth levers beyond the pop-up
cards.summary: The pop-up is the single biggest SMS list driver; the source frames seven growth methods and treats list growth as non-negotiable because an ungrown list caps campaign and flow reach.
cards.use_when: Planning next quarter's SMS subscriber acquisition when pop-up opt-ins alone are not adding enough subscribers.
steps: Make the onsite pop-up your primary method — the source calls it by far the number one way it grows client SMS lists.
Add keyword opt-ins: configure a JOIN-style keyword so people who text it join the list and can claim a discount. Promote the keyword offsite where phone-first audiences are.

Use the flow-generated opt-in surface: your existing SMS flows and signup forms are additional points where consent is captured, so make sure forms are live on the site rather than only in the platform.

Only count qualified buyers as valuable subscribers. The source is explicit that the larger the list of actual buyers, the larger the impact; bought or unqualified numbers add cost and unsubscribes without proportional orders.

Accept diminishing returns in your forecasting: doubling the list does not double orders on identical campaigns, but still increases order volume. Model the channel on incremental lift, not a linear multiple.
Review weekly whether opt-ins are trending with traffic — a flat list with growing traffic means the capture surfaces are failing.
caveats: The source says growth specifics are 'a whole other video' — treat this as a list of levers to prioritize, not complete build instructions.
Keyword-based opt-in rules and required confirmation language vary by jurisdiction; verify compliance with your SMS platform and counsel.
cards.source_name: The Only Ecommerce SMS Marketing Video You'll Ever Need.docx

cards.title: Write SMS campaigns that only say things worth interrupting for
cards.summary: SMS cannot afford to be vague: use clear, direct intents — sales, early access, restocks, back-in-stock, launches — because a 160-character message has no room for bland nurture content.
cards.use_when: Drafting the SMS slot in your campaign calendar, or reviewing a flat-performing SMS calendar that is heavy on general brand messaging.
steps: Cut broad, general and vague campaigns. In a short text there is not enough room to build curiosity, so a non-specific message fails to capture attention.
Anchor each campaign to a clear intention with an obvious click reason: sale, early access, restock/back-in-stock alert, new product launch.
Keep the message within the 160-character limit; going over splits the message into multiple parts and you are billed for more than one SMS.

Avoid MMS (image) messages unless the image is essential: the source notes images cost substantially more than a standard text. Compare marginal revenue against marginal send cost before defaulting to MMS.
Test SMS concepts against your email calendar — many campaigns are stronger as an email plus a spaced SMS reminder about the same event than as two independent messages.
caveats: 160-character single-message billing and MMS costing are platform/carrier-specific; confirm current pricing in your SMS provider.
The source's direct-intent list reflects its own accounts and does not rule out well-executed brand campaigns — it warns that vague content is the main failure mode.
cards.source_name: The Only Ecommerce SMS Marketing Video You'll Ever Need.docx

cards.title: Set SMS sending frequency: one to two campaigns per week, never more
cards.summary: Keep SMS at about one campaign per week (two only for brands pushing over 8 figures annually), because frequency above that drives unsubscribes and annoyance faster than it adds revenue.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many SMS campaign sends per week to schedule, or diagnosing an unsubscribe rate climbing above 1%.
steps: Start at roughly one SMS campaign per week. The source says this is the sweet spot it has personally found with clients.

If the brand is pushing over 8 figures annually, you may experiment with two campaigns per week. Anything more than two is likely overkill and produces higher unsubscribe rates with diminishing returns.
Set an unsubscribe-rate tripwire: above 1% means slow down your sending. Below 1% is normal; below 0.5% is excellent.

Adjust frequency by purchase cadence. Apparel can be bought roughly once a quarter, so more contact is tolerable; a furniture brand bought once every 18 months will not convert from a casual SMS, so pushing the same cadence will burn the list. Split test within your category.
Treat SMS as an intimate, personal channel: every send to a phone number is an intrusion, so only send when there is something concrete worth the interruption.
caveats: One to two per week is a source-specific heuristic from an agency's client base, not a calculated optimal derived from data; the source explicitly says to split test and that the number is industry-specific.
The 'over 8 figures annually' threshold is the presenter's rule of thumb.
cards.source_name: The Only Ecommerce SMS Marketing Video You'll Ever Need.docx

cards.title: Build a calendar from retail events, not nurture filler
cards.summary: Plan SMS around fixed retail moments — back-in-stock, seasonal launches, gifting holidays, big sale weekends, VIP early access, product spotlights and flash sales — with big events getting multiple sends.
cards.use_when: Laying out next month's SMS campaign calendar for a fashion or seasonal ecommerce brand.
steps: Start with the fixed calendar: slot the big sale events first (the source's example uses Memorial Day, which got multiple sends rather than one).

Give major sales more than one send: e.g. a sale-start SMS on the Friday, an SMS on the actual holiday, and a VIP/subscriber early-access SMS on the Thursday before. Multiple sends on one event are a deliberate lever, not waste.
Add seasonal relevance: back-in-stock for returning items, introducing the season's collection, and a mid-season clearance send highlighting the sale section (source example: up to 50% off).
Layer gifting holidays that match the audience (e.g. Mother's Day for a women's fashion list).
Add a product-focus send spotlighting the hero product from the new collection, and an occasional one-day or weekend flash sale on a specific collection or few products.
Leave room for one brand/community-focused send with a call to action that is not purely transactional.
Keep the monthly count at one to two per week even when the calendar looks full, then split test whether raising frequency on a big event beats adding a new event.
caveats: The source populated about two SMS messages per week in its May example and immediately said your brand does not need to do that — it is an illustration, not a target.
Campaign-type effectiveness varies by category and purchase cycle; the source says to split test rather than copy the calendar.
cards.source_name: The Only Ecommerce SMS Marketing Video You'll Ever Need.docx

cards.title: Schedule SMS outside quiet hours and coordinate email timing
cards.summary: Choose recipient-appropriate send times and test email/SMS spacing without treating a source time window as universal.
cards.use_when: Choosing send times for SMS campaigns and pairing them with the day's email send.
steps: Apply current regional and recipient-local quiet-hour settings before scheduling; do not rely on one universal time band.
Target the late morning to early afternoon window. The source's found sweet spot is roughly 11:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m., when people are on lunch or on a break.
Test a deliberate interval between related email and SMS messages; the source suggests about five to six hours as a starting hypothesis.
Use the pairing deliberately for launches and offers: the customer sees the email in the morning and the SMS in the afternoon, giving the same message a second chance on a second device.
Check how the current platform skips or defers each message type at quiet hours and whether a delayed offer will still be valid.
caveats: The source late-morning preference is anecdotal; timing depends on recipients and current platform controls. https://help.klaviyo.com/hc/en-us/articles/4408737146651
cards.source_name: The Only Ecommerce SMS Marketing Video You'll Ever Need.docx

cards.title: Run SMS as a single-message omni-channel flow
cards.summary: Automated SMS flows are triggered by list signup, cart abandonment or product browse; most may legally contain only one SMS message (welcome is the exception with two), and they should run blended with email in one flow.
cards.use_when: Building the abandoned-cart, browse-abandonment and welcome automations for a store, or auditing whether existing SMS flows are compliant.
steps: Set up the three flows the source says drive the majority of revenue: welcome, abandoned cart, and browse abandonment.
Respect the one-message rule: for most flows you may only send a single SMS message, because additional messages are non-compliant. The abandoned-cart flow, for example, should have exactly one SMS.

Use the welcome-flow exception: you may have two SMS messages in the welcome flow. The source suggests the second goes out 2–3 days after the first, e.g. 'your 10% off is waiting' pointing to bestsellers.
Write the welcome message plainly: thank them for signing up, deliver the first-purchase discount code (source example: 10% off), and tell them to go shop.

Build the flows as omni-channel — SMS and email blended in the same automation — so email carries the longer content and SMS carries the short reminder. Klaviyo is preferred precisely because both appear under one flow.

Rely on the timing advantage: an abandoned cart SMS firing a couple of hours after the abandonment reaches the customer while intent is still high, and may reach someone who is on their phone but not checking email that day.
Plan for maintenance: the source says you get about 90% of the work done up front, then you split test, optimize and refresh periodically — do not literally set and forget.
Add a conversion incentive inside abandonment flows if margins allow; the source says customers receiving an extra incentive in the flow are more likely to convert.
caveats: The one-message-per-flow compliance rule and the two-message welcome exception are the source's stated understanding of SMS regulation; confirm current carrier and legal requirements before scaling.
The source cites a client generating over $100,000 per month from one SMS flow — a case study, not an expected result.
Extra abandonment incentives train customers to abandon; the source presents the tactic without addressing that risk.
cards.source_name: The Only Ecommerce SMS Marketing Video You'll Ever Need.docx

cards.title: Measure SMS on clicks, unsubscribes and delivery — not open rates
