cards.summary: Open rate is a vanity metric for SMS; target a 5–15% click rate, keep unsubscribe below 1% (excellent below 0.5%) and delivery above 90–95%.
cards.use_when: Reporting on SMS campaign performance, or setting up the dashboard and review cadence for the SMS channel.
steps: Ignore SMS open rates. The source calls them a vanity metric; click rate is the true read on engagement.
Target click rate of at least 5%, up to about 15%.
Keep unsubscribe rate below 1%; the source calls below 0.5% excellent. Above 1% means you are sending too much.
Keep delivery rate above 90% (good) and above 95% (excellent).

Diagnose and fix: for low click rates, tighten the engaged segment you send to and make the campaigns more direct. For high unsubscribe rates, send fewer messages, send to a more tightly engaged segment, and drop any informational/non-sales campaign. For low revenue per SMS, switch up the types of campaigns you send.

Review Cadence: check the platform about once a day for how the day's campaign is doing; weekly, review trends, line up the week's campaigns and inspect flows; monthly, compare performance to prior months and choose one or two structural changes (e.g. send two campaigns for the next big sale instead of one) to test.
caveats: During list growth, expect the unsubscribe rate to run higher simply because new subscribers are less engaged — the source notes this and does not treat early unsubscribes as a failure.
The 5–15% click and sub-1% unsubscribe bands are the source's recommended targets, not guaranteed results for every category.
cards.source_name: The Only Ecommerce SMS Marketing Video You'll Ever Need.docx

cards.title: Avoid wasting budget through non-compliance and message-length errors
cards.summary: SMS law is stricter than email: never send to anyone who has not explicitly opted in, keep most flows to one message, avoid MMS costs, stay inside quiet hours and watch the 160-character limit.
cards.use_when: Auditing SMS list segments and send rules before a campaign, or onboarding a new SMS platform to reduce avoidable spend and legal risk.
steps: Segment only explicit SMS opt-ins. Unlike email, you cannot send SMS marketing to anyone who has not explicitly opted in — build the audience filter carefully and exclude ambiguous consent.
Keep most automated flows to one SMS message; the welcome flow is the only exception allowing two.
Enable quiet hours so no message is delivered before 8:00 a.m. or after 9:00 p.m.
Keep messages within 160 characters to avoid being billed for multiple message parts.
Default to standard SMS rather than MMS — images cost substantially more — and only choose MMS when the creative is essential to the offer.
Be aware of country-level credit costs (the source notes Canadian numbers may cost two credits versus one) when budgeting sends.
caveats: These rules are the source's stated compliance guidance and vary by jurisdiction and platform; verify with your SMS provider and legal counsel.
Explicit opt-in requirements mean purchased or scraped phone lists cannot be used for marketing.
cards.source_name: The Only Ecommerce SMS Marketing Video You'll Ever Need.docx

cards.title: Klaviyo (or similar ESP) account setup essentials for a new store
cards.summary: Order of operations for launching an email platform: connect store, choose opt-in mode, set up a branded sending domain and DMARC before sending anything.
cards.use_when: Launching or migrating the store's email lifecycle platform (Klaviyo or similar) and deciding which technical settings must exist before the first campaign or flow sends.
steps: Create the account and connect the store so purchase and browse events flow in automatically (the source connects a Shopify store URL during onboarding).

Choose the sending software against these criteria: easy setup and support, strong signup-form builder, strong flow builder, strong campaign builder, good email editor, data/segmentation capability, and built-in A/B testing. The source names Klaviyo (industry leader on technical setup, forms, flows, campaigns, segmentation, testing) and SendLane (newer, praised support) as the two it would pick; verify current pricing and feature sets before deciding.

Decide single vs double opt-in. Double opt-in requires a confirmation click before subscribing: higher list quality, fewer subscribers because many never open the confirmation email. The source's preference is single opt-in, relying on engagement segmentation to suppress non-openers later.
Set up a branded/dedicated sending domain by adding the provided NS records and TXT record at your DNS provider (e.g. GoDaddy, Google Domains/Squarespace) so mail appears to come from your brand.

Add a DMARC TXT record at the root host; start with policy p=none (reporting only) with an aggregate-report address you control, then move to quarantine/reject once reports look clean. Use a DMARC record generator if needed, and use a separate inbox for reports.
Turn on smart sending (the source uses a ~16-hour window) so a contact does not receive another email within that window; adjust to your cadence.
Set attribution: last-interacted email within 5 days, and tick the option excluding Apple privacy opens so inflated opens don't earn revenue credit. SMS attribution defaults to 1 day.
Enable anonymous visitor tracking so pre-identification browsing is backfilled onto the profile once identified.
Set up brand assets (logo, colors, fonts from Google/Adobe with a web-safe fallback), design the preference/subscribe/unsubscribe pages in brand style, and turn on automatic UTM parameters for links.
Verify the domain shows as active before sending; propagation takes time.
caveats: Sending without a branded sending domain and DMARC risks filtering under Gmail/Yahoo 2024 inbox standards.
UI paths and setting names change; verify inside the current interface.
Attribution windows and smart-sending windows are conventions, not universal rules.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Rate signup forms against a 2–4% baseline and target 8–12%
cards.summary: Typical ecommerce brands convert 2–4% of visitors into subscribers while optimized popups reach around 8–12%, so judge forms against the high-converting band.
cards.use_when: Benchmarking the store's email capture rate and deciding whether the popup needs a rebuild to hit list-growth targets.
steps: Pull your current subscriber conversion rate (new subscribers divided by site sessions) for the same period.
If you are near 2–4% of visitors, treat the form as underperforming; the source's high-converting target is roughly 8–12% of traffic entering the list.
Do not rely on a footer signup form alone — the source's testing repeatedly shows popups outperform other form types despite bounce-rate objections.
Rebuild toward the high-converting pattern: strong offer in the headline, single email field, prominent CTA button, secondary 'no thanks' option, and separate mobile and desktop forms.
Track list growth and form submit rate weekly so improvements are visible and not assumed.
caveats: 2–4% and 8–12% are the source's observed ranges, not guarantees; your traffic mix, price point and brand strength shift the achievable rate.
Very broad or very narrow display rules can hit a high submit rate while total signups stay low — always pair submit rate with total subscribers.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Build a high-converting popup: offer, headline, single field, big CTA
cards.summary: Popup anatomy that converts: an attractive offer stated in the headline, one email field, a large contrasting CTA, and a de-emphasized alternate option.
cards.use_when: Designing or redesigning the email capture popup for the storefront.
steps: Pick the incentive first — form success hinges on the offer more than on design. Research from the source's client work: for AOV around $200, $20 off often beats 10% off because '$20' reads larger than '10%'; anything below roughly 10% off is usually too weak unless your AOV is very high. Alternatives: BOGO, BOGO at 50%, free gift with purchase, free digital product, free shipping, cash back, early access (strong at Black Friday), mystery discount.
Write the headline around the offer, e.g. 'Unlock 10% off your first order' — avoid 'sign up'/'subscribe' language and never bury the offer in body copy.
Use one field: email. Ask for phone, name or preferences only in a second step after the email is captured.
Set placeholder to something explicit like 'Enter your email here' and give the input field a contrasting fill (e.g. light grey) so it is obviously an input.
Make the CTA large (the source uses ~70px height vs the ~54px default) and contrasting; note bigger buttons correlate with higher conversion, but not absurdly large.
Give a de-emphasized second choice, e.g. 'No thanks, I'd rather pay full price' — two options (one attractive, one unattractive) lift signups versus one button.
Keep the legal microcopy only where required (GDPR/EU); the source removes it for US stores.
Compress all images (e.g. tinyPNG) since faster loading correlates with more conversions; add alt text to every image.

Consider hiding the X: the source resizes it to minimum and matches its color to the background, since a visible second exit reduces signups — this is ethically debatable, and a 'no thanks' button already exists.
caveats: The source's claims about hiding the X and about button size are practitioner observations, not universal benchmarks.
Offer preference (e.g. % vs $ at the same AOV) should still be tested in your store.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Timing and display rules for capture popups
cards.summary: Display the popup after 4–10 seconds or 40–80% scroll (the source uses ~6s / ~60%) and treat the OR-vs-AND rule toggle as the main audience-size lever.
cards.use_when: Configuring when the store's popup appears so it captures engaged visitors without annoying first-timers.
steps: Never display immediately on page load; the source calls it a conversion killer because the visitor doesn't know the brand yet.
Choose rule-based display: time delay, scroll depth, exit intent, or a combination.
For desktop, use exit intent plus a time delay plus a scroll threshold; the source uses ~6 seconds and ~60% scroll, saying 4–10 seconds and 40–80% scroll are viable and should be split tested.

Leave the OR toggle on (only all conditions met = AND). With OR, the form shows on exit OR after the delay OR after the scroll — a wider audience; the source never uses AND because it targets far too few people.
Set reappearance frequency: default 5 days, the source often uses 3, and tick 'don't show again if submitted or if the go-to-URL button was clicked'.
Target only non-subscribers ('don't show to existing profiles') so current subscribers aren't re-prompted.
Exclude URLs such as cart/checkout, /wholesale and landing pages you're running paid traffic to, so you don't discount a visitor who is already about to buy.
Optionally include/exclude visitor locations based on shipping coverage.
Use a separate display setup for a list you already own: e.g. show an SMS-only signup form to existing email subscribers.
caveats: Earlier display = more total signups but lower submit rate; later display = higher submit rate but a smaller exposed audience. Both metrics must be read together.
Frequency, delay and scroll settings are brand-dependent; the source insists they be tested.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Always build separate mobile and desktop popups
cards.summary: One form for both devices fails: clone the desktop form into a mobile-only version and resize fields, buttons and teasers for touch.
cards.use_when: Finishing the capture popup build and preparing it for mobile traffic, which is most of an ecommerce store's visitors.
steps: Clone the desktop form and rename it explicitly (e.g. 'mobile' / 'desktop').
Set device targeting to mobile only on the clone, then adjust timing rules — drop exit intent on mobile because it is unreliable and annoying there.
Increase input field and CTA size for thumbs: the source sets input text ~20px, input height ~70px, CTA height ~80px and CTA/microcopy text ~20–24px, versus smaller desktop values.
Add extra padding above the CTA and between elements so users don't mistap.
Skip the side image on mobile (no room); keep the layout vertical.
Rework the teaser shape for small screens (e.g. rectangle to circle or corner tab) and shrink the text to fit.
Enlarge success-page text (the source uses ~22–24px) so the confirmation is readable on a phone.
Check the teaser placement against other on-site widgets (chatbot, loyalty promo, load-time banners) so nothing overlaps.
caveats: Sizes in the source are examples from one build, not fixed specs; adjust to your brand and test.
The two-form approach doubles maintenance — apply the same edits to both when you change an offer.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Withhold the discount code from the success page
cards.summary: Show 'check your inbox' on the post-signup success page so the first welcome email earns the open and the code, protecting deliverability and inbox training.
cards.use_when: Designing the popup success page and the first welcome email after email capture.
steps: Do not print the discount code on the success page — the source argues it removes any reason to open the first welcome email, which tanks the open rate, which in turn harms sending reputation and the whole email system.
Replace it with a headline like 'Your discount is on its way — check your inbox for your confirmation and code'.
Add a fallback line: didn't receive it within 5 minutes, check spam — new subscribers on Gmail are especially likely to land in spam, and this line reduces support tickets.
Style that spam note in bold so it stands out.
Match the success page visually to the opt-in (same logo, image, colors).
Deliver the actual code inside the first welcome-series email, training recipients to open your mail over time.
caveats: This delays the shopper's purchase by one email-open step; some brands may decide the immediate-purchase tradeoff is worth testing.
The source states this as a strong preference for the email system's health, not a tested universal result.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Teaser tab: keep the capture offer permanently reachable
cards.summary: A small persistent tab ('Save 10% now') lets visitors reopen the popup after closing it and adds a second capture surface.
cards.use_when: Adding a persistent capture element to the storefront after a visitor dismisses the popup.
steps: Pick a shape (rectangle, circle, corner tab) and position it so it does not collide with your chatbot, loyalty widget or promo bar — check the live site on both devices.
Write short benefit text such as 'Save 10% now' and make it bold.
Choose when it shows: before the form, after the form is closed, or before and after (the source uses before and after).
Give it a high-contrast background relative to the site (e.g. black tab with white text) and raise transparency to zero.
On mobile, switch to a smaller circle or corner shape so it doesn't cover content.
Test the placement against your actual pages, since overlapping on-site elements are a common failure.
caveats: A permanently visible tab can feel pushy on content-heavy pages; still A/B test whether it lifts total signups.
Positioning must be rechecked whenever you change your theme or add third-party widgets.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Ten signup-form mistakes to audit before scaling list growth
cards.summary: Diagnostic checklist of the ten most common popup failures, from weak offers and too many fields to slow images and codes given away too early.
cards.use_when: Auditing an existing store popup that gets traffic but converts poorly.
steps: 1. Weak offer: the offer, not the design, drives signup; anything under ~10% off is generally ineffective unless AOV is very high.
2. Asking too much in step one: email only in the first step; move phone/name to a later step.
3. Wrong time delay: too short disrupts the visit and converts poorly; too long means few visitors ever see it — the source's range is roughly 4–10 seconds (up to 12).
4. Form too small: bigger forms get noticed; the source even suggests trying a full-page form as a test.
5. Too much copy: one headline, one field, one CTA button, microcopy — no paragraphs about exclusive offers.
6. Offer hidden in body copy: put the offer in the headline, largest and clearest.
7. Using 'sign up'/'subscribe' wording — people avoid those words.
8. One form for mobile and desktop.
9. Slow-loading images — compress with tinyPNG or similar.
10. Discount code given on the success page instead of in the welcome email.
caveats: These are the source's practitioner observations from client work, not controlled benchmarks.
Fixes 1, 3, 5 and 6 interact — changing only one may not move the submit rate.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: A/B test the offer holistically, not by signup rate alone
cards.summary: When split testing signup incentives, judge by welcome-flow placed-order rate, AOV and attributed revenue together, not the form's submit rate.
cards.use_when: Deciding which popup incentive (percentage off, dollar off, BOGO, gift, free shipping, mystery discount) the store should run.
steps: List candidate offers to test: percentage off, dollar amount off, dollar amount off above a threshold, free shipping, BOGO, BOGO at 50%, free gift with purchase, free digital product, subscription incentive, cash back, early access (strong at Black Friday), mystery discount (the discount is revealed only in the first welcome email; the source reports strong submit rates with this).
Run each offer against a control form and let enough traffic accumulate to compare.

Do not judge on form submit rate alone: the source reports a client case where a new offer had a lower welcome-flow placed-order rate but a much higher AOV and higher attributed welcome-flow revenue, so total revenue was higher.
Track per-variant: form submit rate, welcome-flow placed-order rate, welcome-flow AOV, and attributed welcome-flow revenue.
Choose the offer that wins on revenue, and if an offer is a good fit for a specific segment (e.g. early access for VIPs), route it accordingly.
caveats: Offer outcomes are store- and price-point-specific; the client result is an example, not a promise.
Testing many offers simultaneously fragments traffic and delays significance.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Add a micro-yes step before the email field
cards.summary: A prior 'Do you want 10% off?' commitment step can lift submit rates by getting an initial yes, but the source reports it works better for some brands without it.
cards.use_when: Optimizing the capture popup's form structure with an extra qualifying step.
steps: Clone your email opt-in step and place the clone in front of it in the form flow.
Rewrite it as a question rather than a command, e.g. 'Do you want 10% off your first order?' instead of a statement.
Keep the flow: micro-yes question, then a teed-up yes action, then the email field.
The rationale the source gives: a first micro-commitment makes people more likely to say yes to the next step.
A/B test micro-yes versus no micro-yes — the source says most brands see a submit-rate spike with it, but for some brands the version without it wins.
caveats: Adds a click of friction; only keep it if your test shows a net gain in subscribers or revenue, not just submit rate.
Effect varies by audience and offer strength.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Reap the main email lifecycle payoff: LTV and AOV, not only last-click revenue
cards.summary: Email's core value is raising customer lifetime value and average order value and reducing reliance on paid ads, not just collecting one-off email revenue.
cards.use_when: Planning the email channel's role in the store's overall acquisition and retention mix, and justifying budget and effort.
steps: Define objectives clearly: grow the list rapidly, and convert first-time buyers into returning customers.
Position email next to, not instead of, paid ads: the source argues a store should not rely solely on paid traffic and treats email as an essential complementary channel.
Use email to build a relationship that makes a customer more valuable than a one-time ad-driven buyer.
Measure email's effect on LTV and AOV in addition to attributed revenue, since those are the outcomes the source attributes to the channel.
Run standalone campaigns roughly a couple of times per week to nurture traffic into first purchase and first buyers into repeats.
Use the offered campaign-calendar template as a planning artifact for the quarter.
caveats: The dollar results cited in the source (e.g. 34–52% of revenue, revenue uplifts versus prior periods) come from that agency's clients — treat as illustrative examples, not benchmarks.
Attribution of total revenue growth to email is questionable when paid spend, seasonality or product launches also changed.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Micro-yes signup step: ask for consent before email capture
cards.summary: Inserting a 'Do you want 10% off?' micro-commitment step before the email field can lift signup conversion, but must be split-tested per brand.
cards.use_when: Designing or A/B testing the newsletter/SMS signup form (popup or full page) for an ecommerce store.
steps: Add a step before the email opt-in that asks only a yes/no question, e.g. 'Do you want 10% off your first order?' with a single CTA button ('Yes please') and no input field.
Remove the email input field from this step; clicking the button submits the micro-form and advances to the real email opt-in, which triggers the welcome flow.
Keep microcopy under the button (e.g. 'No thanks, I'll pay full price', 'No spam guaranteed') to give an exit route.
Split-test the form with and without the micro-yes step and compare the signup conversion rate for your own brand.
Because the source reports that the micro-yes gives a spike in signups for most brands but some brands perform better without it, always validate rather than assume.
caveats: Benefit is brand-dependent; source explicitly says to split-test it.
The micro-yes is a lead-conversion (signup) tactic, not a purchase-conversion result.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Signup form tests: delay, format, and audience size
cards.summary: Test popup delay, popup vs full page, and other form variables on total signups, not just signup rate.
cards.use_when: Optimizing the newsletter signup popup for an ecommerce store, deciding timing and format.
steps: Run a time-delay A/B test, e.g. 4 seconds vs 12 seconds, and track total number of signups, not only the signup rate.
Expect a shorter delay to lower the signup rate but possibly raise total signups because the form is shown to a larger audience.
Test a popup form against a full-page form and compare signup rate and total signups.
Test headline copy: 'Save 10% now', 'Get 10% now', 'Take 10% off now', 'Unlock 10% off now', 'Your discount awaits', 'Do you want 10% off'.
Test CTA button text: 'Save 10% off now', 'Get 10% off now', 'Unlock my discount now', 'Reveal my discount now', 'I want my discount'.
Test microcopy variants such as 'No thanks, I'll pay full price', 'No sales spam guaranteed', 'Rated 4.9/5 by 5,000 customers'.
caveats: Signup rate and total signups can move in opposite directions; the source stresses watching total volume.
Exact lift numbers are not promised; treat headline/CTA effects as testable, not guaranteed.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Visual signup form tests: color, images, and imagery content
cards.summary: Test plain vs designed, light vs dark, contrasting fields, and image presence/content on the signup form.
cards.use_when: Designing the visual layout of an ecommerce newsletter popup or signup page.
steps: Split-test a plain simple form against a fully designed form.
Split-test a white form against a black form, and test input-field colors (contrasting color vs plain white).
Test the CTA button color.
Split-test a centered form with no side image against a form with a side image.
When using images, test image content: the source cites a blanket brand where a blanket with a dog on it outperformed a plain blanket image.
caveats: The blanket-with-dog result is a single brand example, not a universal benchmark.
Image relevance to the product/category may matter more than image presence alone.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: SMS opt-in angles after email signup
cards.summary: Test offer-equivalence vs upgraded offer vs VIP-club angle for the SMS opt-in step.
cards.use_when: Adding or optimizing an SMS list opt-in step within the email signup flow.
steps: Build the SMS signup as an extra step after the email opt-in.
Angle 1: use the same offer for SMS as email (e.g. 10% off both), and test it.
Angle 2: offer a better SMS-only offer, e.g. email signup says 10% off, next step says 'Do you want 15% off? Sign up for SMS', and test it.
Angle 3: use a VIP Club angle — email opt-in offers 10% off, SMS step offers 'Join our VIP Club for exclusive sales, pre-sales, early access', and test it.
Split-test the angles against each other and measure SMS opt-in rate.
caveats: The source presents these as testable angles, not guaranteed winners.
Higher SMS discounts can erode margin; choose based on your own unit economics.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Flow structure and profile filters in Klaviyo
cards.summary: Understand flow triggers, profile filters (order/cart/checkout exclusions), and profile properties to prevent overlapping emails.
cards.use_when: Building or auditing Klaviyo flows for an ecommerce store so customers don't receive conflicting sequences.
steps: Pick a trigger based on customer journey stage: active on site, viewed product, added to cart, checkout started, placed order, or added to list/segment.
After confirming a trigger, note it cannot be changed without duplicating the flow.

Add profile filters under the trigger, e.g. 'has placed order 0 times since starting this flow', 'has checkout started 0 times since starting this flow', 'has added to cart 0 times since starting this flow'.
For welcome series, add 'placed order 0 times', 'checkout started 0 times', and 'added to cart 0 times since starting this flow' so buyers and cart/checkout abandoners exit the welcome sequence.
Consider excluding 'viewed product' and 'active on site' as well, but source prefers not to exclude those from welcome since browse/site abandonment flows are short and early in the journey.
Use profile property updates (e.g. set 'in_welcome_series = true' at flow start, false at end) to segment flow participants in or out of regular campaigns.
Use conditional splits with 'placed order since starting flow' to route buyers to a post-purchase email vs continuing the welcome series, or use a random 50/50 split to A/B test flow strategies.
caveats: Trigger choice is locked after confirmation; you must duplicate the flow to change it.
Excluding checkout-started and added-to-cart from a welcome series is the source's preferred approach but is presented as a judgment call.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Use past profiles to backfill newly launched flows
cards.summary: Backfill a new flow so eligible customers enter at the correct stage instead of waiting for the delay to elapse.
cards.use_when: Launching a winback, re-engagement, or time-delayed flow and wanting it to act on past behavior immediately.
steps: Open the flow's Manage Flow settings and choose 'Add past profiles'.
Choose 'throughout the flow' so profiles are added based on where they would be if the flow had been live earlier, rather than only at the beginning.

Example: a winback flow triggered 90 days after last order — adding past profiles throughout the flow lets someone whose last order was 80 days ago receive the first email in 10 days instead of waiting 90 days.
Select 'eligible profiles' as the whole list or a specific segment.
Note that flows containing dynamic coupons cannot use past profiles; if you need past profiles and a discount, use a static code instead.
caveats: Past-profile backfill is unavailable for dynamic coupon flows — a real trade-off if you rely on dynamic codes.
Adding profiles to the beginning vs throughout the flow produces very different behavior; choose deliberately.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Turn off smart sending for flows, keep it on for campaigns
cards.summary: Disable smart sending in flows so abandoned-cart/checkout emails aren't skipped; keep it enabled for campaigns.
cards.use_when: Configuring send settings inside any Klaviyo flow email for an ecommerce store.
steps: In each flow email's settings, uncheck 'Skip recently emailed profile' (smart sending) and save.
Rationale: if a customer already received a campaign or other email within the last 16 hours, smart sending would skip them from a cart abandonment flow — losing high-intent, high-revenue sends.
For campaigns, keep smart sending on in ~99.9% of cases unless there's a specific reason to disable it.
The default smart-sending window is 16 hours and can be edited in general email settings (e.g. 8 hours), but the flow-level decision stays the same: off for flows.
Enable UTM tracking in the same settings block (and optionally custom tracking) so revenue and behavior attribution works with Google Analytics.
caveats: Source treats 'off for flows, on for campaigns' as its own strong rule; validate against your own send-frequency and deliverability data.
Disabling smart sending can increase total email volume, which matters for spam-complaint rates.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Welcome series structure: 7 emails with distinct angles
cards.summary: Build a welcome series that delivers the incentive fast, then rotates through brand story, bestsellers, reviews, USP comparison, and expiring-discount urgency.
cards.use_when: Building or rewriting the welcome flow for an ecommerce store after newsletter signup.
steps: Email 1: deliver the discount code immediately (the promised incentive).
Email 2 (~1 day later): brand story — founder message, origin, mission, what sets you apart — to build trust before pushing product.
Email 3 (~1 day later): bestsellers; dive into unique features/benefits and the end result for the customer; cap at ~3–5 bestsellers depending on brand.
Email 4 (~2 days later): reviews/UGC/press mentions — prioritize reviews about the specific pain points your subscriber has, not generic 'highly recommended' quotes.
Email 5 (~2 days later): 'us vs them' USP comparison, since subscribers are comparing you to competitors.
Email 6 (~2 days later): either a 48-hour discount reminder or a new/higher discount with a 48-hour deadline (source's split of two routes).
Email 7 (~1 day later): 24-hour discount expiry as a plain-text email from the founder — plain text tends to improve deliverability and adds a personal touch.
Remind subscribers of the discount code in every email, but give each email its own distinct angle.
Add profile filters (placed order, checkout started, added to cart = 0 since starting flow) so buyers and cart/checkout abandoners exit the welcome series.
caveats: The 3-day and 4-day defaults from Klaviyo are presented as slower than the source's preference; both are options, not proven superior.
Fake urgency is explicitly cautioned against — make sure stated deadlines are real.
Timing and email count are the source's opinion, not tested benchmarks.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Site abandonment flow: trigger, delay, and one guiding email
cards.summary: Build a site-abandonment flow for visitors who never viewed a product, using the active-on-site trigger and a 1–4 hour delay.
cards.use_when: Recovering early-stage site visitors (homepage/blog visitors who did not view a product) for an ecommerce store.
steps: Create a flow with the 'active on site' API trigger.
Add profile filters: 'has placed order 0 times', 'checkout started 0 times', 'added to cart 0 times', and 'viewed product 0 times since starting this flow' so anyone advancing in the journey exits.
Add a time delay before email 1 of 1–4 hours; source suggests earlier journey stages can wait longer.
Send one email that acts as a shop assistant: 'Is this what you're looking for?' with links to relevant collections or specific products depending on your catalog size.
A/B test 1 hour vs 4 hours, and test 'guide to collections' vs 'guide to bestsellers' to see which drives product views.
Turn off smart sending and enable UTM tracking in the email settings.
caveats: The flow normally has a single email because these visitors are early in the journey and not yet high-intent.
No default Klaviyo template exists for site abandonment; you must build it yourself.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Browse abandonment flow: trigger, filters, and review-led emails
cards.summary: Set up a browse-abandonment flow triggered by viewed product, with product-specific reviews and a discount only after several emails.
cards.use_when: Re-engaging shoppers who viewed a product but never added to cart on an ecommerce store.
steps: Use the 'viewed product' trigger.
Add profile filters: 'checkout started 0 times', 'placed order 0 times', 'added to cart 0 times since starting this flow', and 'has not been in flow for the last 30 days'.
Set the first-email delay — Klaviyo defaults to 2 hours; test 1 hour vs 3 hours and narrow down.
Email 1: simple 'Did you see something you like?' reminder of the viewed product.
Email 2 (~1 day later): reviews, UGC, press mentions to build confidence in the specific product.
Use trigger filters to build product- or collection-specific browse flows, and make USP/review content specific to the viewed product — the source says specificity converts better.
Delay any discount until around email 4–5; source argues giving discounts immediately trains shoppers to wait for codes.
Aim for a 4–6 email sequence; turn off smart sending and enable UTM tracking.
caveats: 'Wait to discount' is the source's opinion, not a tested benchmark across all stores.
The 30-day flow suppression window is a default recommendation; your repurchase cycle and catalog should guide the choice.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Abandoned cart flow: trigger distinction and 6–8 email structure
cards.summary: Build a true added-to-cart abandonment flow (not the mislabeled checkout default) with a 30-minute-to-2-hour delay and staged email angles.
cards.use_when: Setting up or fixing the abandoned cart sequence for an ecommerce store in Klaviyo.
steps: Select a Klaviyo template whose trigger is 'added to cart' — the popular 'abandoned cart' template actually uses 'checkout started', so verify the trigger before building.

Add profile filters: 'checkout started 0 times', 'placed order 0 times', and 'has not been in flow for the last X days' (Klaviyo defaults to 7 days; source prefers ~14 days, adjusting for repurchase frequency).
Set the first-email delay to 30 minutes–2 hours (Klaviyo default 4 hours is described as long), and A/B test 30 minutes vs 2 hours.
Email 1: short reminder that the item is still in cart.
Email 2 (~1 day later): reviews/UGC/press — the more specific to the exact product, the better.
Email 3: objection handling — address reasons someone might hesitate to finish the purchase.
Email 4: specific USPs of the product/brand.
Email 5 (~1 day later): first discount (e.g. X% off) with 48-hour urgency, because a discount without urgency gives no reason to buy now.
Email 6 (~1 day later): 24-hour deadline reminder.
Emails 7–8 options: raise the discount, or send a plain-text founder email offering an extended 24-hour sale.
Monitor spam-complaint, unsubscribe, and open rates as you lengthen the sequence; source warns long sequences (14–20+ emails) become annoying.
caveats: Sources disagree on sequence length and suppression windows; treat 6–8 emails and 14 days as source preferences, not industry standards.
Discounts should reflect margin realities; the source explicitly ties higher discounts to margins.
Adding a post-purchase branch inside the cart flow is described as a common but not recommended pattern — the source prefers separate flows.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Checkout abandonment flow: same structure, different objections
cards.summary: Clone the abandoned cart flow and retarget checkout starters with content tailored to late-stage objections like shipping costs.
cards.use_when: Recovering shoppers who started checkout but did not complete the purchase on an ecommerce store.
steps: Clone the abandoned cart flow and change its trigger to 'checkout started'.
Remove the 'checkout started 0 times' profile filter (no longer relevant); keep 'placed order 0 times since starting this flow' and the flow-suppression window.
Reuse the cart sequence structure but tailor copy to checkout-stage objections — the source cites surprise shipping costs as a common blocker.
Consider offering free shipping instead of a percentage discount when shipping is the likely objection; source argues free shipping can cost less (for a $200 AOV) while converting the customer.
Adjust reviews, USP content, and discount amounts to the later stage; these customers are one step closer to purchase.
Keep discount timing late in the sequence (around email 5) and use urgency with any discount.
caveats: The free-shipping-vs-discount trade-off depends on your margins and AOV; source gives a $200 AOV example, not a universal rule.
Separate cart and checkout flows are both needed; do not rely on a single 'abandoned cart' template for both.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Time-delay heuristics by journey stage
cards.summary: First-email delays should shorten as the customer moves from browsing to checkout, and each delay should be split-tested.
cards.use_when: Setting or tuning the first-email delay inside ecommerce abandonment flows.
steps: Site abandonment (no product viewed): 1–4 hours.
Browse abandonment (product viewed): ~1–3 hours; Klaviyo default ~2 hours.
Cart abandonment (added to cart): 30 minutes–2 hours; Klaviyo default 4 hours described as too long.
Checkout abandonment: shortest delay, since intent is highest (structure follows cart flow with faster timing).
Run A/B tests at each stage (e.g. 1 hour vs 4 hours for site abandonment) and narrow toward the best-performing delay.

Inside time delays, you can also delay until a specific time of day or weekday, and choose store timezone, recipient local timezone, or specific days — use these to align sends with typical browsing/buying times.
caveats: These are source heuristics, not tested universal timings — the source repeatedly says to split-test.
Correct timing depends on niche, audience, and purchase frequency.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Subject line, preview text, and sender name optimization
cards.summary: Treat preview text as a second subject line, test sender names, and keep sender email consistent across all sends.
cards.use_when: Configuring email metadata for ecommerce flows and campaigns in Klaviyo.
steps: In each email's edit settings, fill in subject line, preview text, sender name, and sender email address.
Write a distinct, compelling preview text — the source calls it your second subject line; do not skip it.
Note that plain-text emails have no preview text field, so only the subject line applies.
Test sender name variants, e.g. a founder's name vs the company name, especially in welcome series.
Use the same sender email address across all flows and campaigns to protect deliverability and consistency.
Preview the email in desktop and mobile views before publishing.
caveats: Plain-text emails can't use preview text, so you must rely on subject line alone — plan accordingly.
No specific subject-line lift figures are given; treat this as a testable area.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Bulk flow action status and flow analytics
cards.summary: Use flow-level settings to publish/draft all emails at once and analyze flow performance over custom time frames.
cards.use_when: Managing, launching, or reviewing ecommerce email flows in Klaviyo.
steps: In the flow's Manage Flow settings, update action statuses to set all emails to live, manual, or draft at once rather than editing each email individually.
Add flow name and tags to keep flows organized.
Use the Show Analytics view and select a time frame (including custom) to review flow performance.
Use flow history to see changes over time.
Note that trigger selection is permanent at the flow level; to change a trigger, duplicate the flow.
caveats: Bulk status changes apply to all emails in the flow — verify no email is intentionally paused before switching to live.
Klaviyo's interface changes frequently (the source notes the company was running UX tests in 2024), so verify current menu locations.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Decide whether to use Klaviyo's default flow templates
cards.summary: Klaviyo's prebuilt templates are a starting point for beginners, but custom-built flows typically convert better.
cards.use_when: Choosing whether to start an ecommerce flow from a Klaviyo template or build from scratch.
steps: When creating a flow, browse Klaviyo's prebuilt flows by goal (e.g. prevent lost sales, nurture subscribers) if you lack email marketing experience.
Recognize that default templates are not optimized for your specific brand and audience.
If you have the capability, build custom flows from scratch; the source recommends this approach for better conversion.
If you do use a template, review and adjust triggers, delays, and content before launching — never ship a template unedited.
Note the source's view: something is better than nothing, but custom flow work is worth the effort.
caveats: 'Custom flows convert better than templates' is the source's opinion, not a measured benchmark.
Template availability and naming in Klaviyo change; verify current options in the interface.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Exclude engaged customers from overlapping flows
cards.summary: Use profile filters so customers advance to the next journey stage without receiving overlapping flows.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing ecommerce email flow logic to prevent a customer receiving conflicting or repetitive sequences.
steps: For each pre-purchase flow, add exclusion filters for later journey events: e.g. welcome series excludes placed order, checkout started, and added to cart.
Site abandonment excludes placed order, checkout started, added to cart, and viewed product since starting the flow.
Browse abandonment excludes checkout started, placed order, and added to cart since starting the flow.
Cart abandonment excludes checkout started and placed order since starting the flow.
Checkout abandonment excludes only placed order since starting the flow.
Set a 'has not been in flow for the last X days' filter (30 days for browse, 7–14 days for cart/checkout) to prevent re-triggering the same flow too often.
Rationale: overlapping flows send too many emails, which can trigger spam complaints and erode trust.
caveats: Whether to exclude active-on-site and viewed-product from the welcome series is a judgment call; source prefers not to exclude those because their flows are short.
Flow-suppression windows should match your repurchase cycle — a 7-day window is fine for weekly replenishment but too short for long repurchase cycles.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Use trigger filters for product- and collection-specific flows
cards.summary: Trigger filters let you limit browse/cart abandonment flows to specific products or collections for more relevant messaging.
cards.use_when: Building product-specific or collection-specific abandonment sequences in Klaviyo for an ecommerce catalog.
steps: Open the flow's trigger settings and add a trigger filter under Add trigger filter.
Select dimensions to include or exclude specific products or collections — e.g. only send a browse-abandonment flow for a high-margin collection.
Use trigger filters when you want different sequences for different product categories, each with its own reviews, USPs, and objections.
For site abandonment flows, trigger filters are generally not used because no product has been viewed yet.
Combine trigger filters with specific review/UGC content about the exact product or collection to increase relevance.
caveats: The more product-specific flows you build, the more maintenance overhead; prioritize products/collections with enough traffic to justify it.
Klaviyo's trigger-filter UI may move between versions; verify current setup in the interface.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Use plain-text founder emails and real urgency for final conversion
cards.summary: End long flows with a plain-text founder email that carries real, verifiable urgency rather than a designed template.
cards.use_when: Writing the final emails of ecommerce welcome, cart, checkout, or browse sequences to convert holdouts.
steps: Send the final email as plain text rather than a designed template — the source says plain text generally delivers better and feels more personal.
Send it from the founder's name (a real or fictional person at the company), using the founder's voice.
Use explicit urgency such as 'your discount expires in 24 hours', and make it true — the source stresses not using fake urgency.
For discount expiry, use a dynamic coupon code so the deadline is genuine; avoid static codes like 'WELCOME10' as the urgency mechanism.
Options for the final push: extended sale for 24 hours only, a higher discount, or a founder plain-text last-chance email.
In welcome series, place this plain-text founder email around email 7; in cart/checkout flows, use it around emails 6–8.
caveats: Fake urgency damages trust; use dynamic codes or genuinely expiring offers.
Plain-text emails cannot include preview text, so the subject line carries the full burden.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Clone the Core Pre-Purchase Flows Instead of Building from Scratch
cards.summary: Build the five essential pre-purchase flows (welcome, site abandon, browse abandon, cart abandon, checkout abandon) by cloning one proven template and swapping the trigger and one filter.
cards.use_when: Standing up pre-purchase automation for a store from zero, or when you need to ship cart/checkout abandonment emails quickly without redesigning content for each.
steps: Establish one pre-purchase flow as your structural template (commonly the abandoned cart flow). It holds the general email structure, delays, and offer logic you'll reuse.
Clone it and rename for the next flow. Change the trigger to the matching event — for a checkout abandonment flow, the trigger is 'Checkout Started'.

Add or remove profile filters so the flow only targets people who haven't already bought. For abandoned cart/checkout, a common filter is 'Placed Order zero times since starting this flow' so buyers don't get further abandon emails.
Keep an additional filter such as 'has not been in this flow in the last 7 days' to avoid re-enrolling people too soon.

Keep the general content structure but rewrite the copy toward the specific objection — for checkout abandonment the reason is different (usually payment/logistics friction) than for cart abandonment.
Note the source positions the welcome, site abandon, browse abandon, cart abandon, and checkout abandon flows as the essential pre-purchase set.
caveats: The filter logic and trigger names are platform-specific (Klaviyo/Shopify) — verify the current interface before building.
Cloning is a starting point; you must tailor the content, not just the trigger.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Add a Cancelled-Order Filter to Post-Purchase Flows
cards.summary: Protect post-purchase flows from sending to people who cancelled their order by adding a 'cancelled order zero times' profile filter at the trigger.
cards.use_when: Setting up a post-purchase or customer thank-you flow, where someone could place an order and then cancel before the flow finishes sending.
steps: Set the trigger to 'Placed Order'.
Add a profile filter that reads roughly 'Placed Order / Cancelled Order equals zero times since starting this flow' — the source's default is 'cancelled order zero times since starting the flow'.
Rationale from the source: a customer can place an order and then cancel it, and you don't want them receiving the rest of the thank-you/upsell content after a cancellation.
Optionally make trigger filters based on specific collections or products if you want product-specific post-purchase flows.
Ensure this filter sits before the first send so it gates the whole flow, not just one email.
caveats: Filter naming and availability depend on the ESP and its cancel-order support — verify in the current interface.
Product/collection-specific post-purchase flows require your ESP to expose product data on the order event.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Time Your First Post-Purchase Email Around Transactional Emails
cards.summary: Delay the first post-purchase email ~30 minutes instead of sending instantly, because the transactional order-confirmation email already fires immediately.
cards.use_when: Designing the first email in a post-purchase/customer thank-you flow, deciding the initial send delay.
steps: Recognize that a purchase immediately triggers transactional emails (order confirmation, shipping updates) from your store platform. The source notes these go out right away if your system is configured correctly.
Avoid sending your marketing post-purchase email instantly so you don't 'support-bomb' the customer with multiple emails at once.
The source's default is to wait roughly 30 minutes after purchase before the first post-purchase email.
Use the delay to let the transactional confirmation land first, then follow with the branded thank-you.
Keep the first marketing email light on logistics (the transactional email already covers shipping) — just reinforce trust and set expectations.
caveats: The 30-minute delay is the presenter's preferred default, not a benchmark — adjust based on your transactional setup and product.
If your platform's transactional emails are delayed or missing, fix that first rather than compensating in the flow.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Split Post-Purchase Email 1 by First-Time vs Returning Buyer, Then Merge Paths
cards.summary: Branch the first post-purchase email on order count to give first-time and returning buyers different thank-you copy, then recombine into one path for the rest of the flow.
cards.use_when: Building the branching logic of a post-purchase flow and deciding which portions should be segmented.
steps: After the initial delay, add a conditional split on 'Placed Order equals 1 overall time' — Yes routes to first-time buyer content, No routes to returning/repeat customer content.
Write different Email 1 copy for each branch: acknowledge whether they're new or returning, and set the tone accordingly.
Turn OFF smart sending on these transactional-style thank-you emails so they send as intended rather than being delayed/skipped.
The source notes you can extend the split further — e.g., buyers with ~4 purchases could be treated as VIPs with different content — but first-time vs returning is the useful baseline.
After Email 1, merge both branches back into a single path and send the same content (Email 2 onward) to everyone; the source treats this as the default unless you have reason to keep separating.
Decide per your brand whether returning customers even need emails 2+; the source keeps both and merges.
caveats: This is a conditional-split pattern specific to the platform; verify the operator options available.
Whether to keep returning customers in the full flow is a judgment call — test for your audience.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Use the First Post-Purchase Email to Reduce Buyer's Remorse and Cross-Sell Softly
cards.summary: Send a plain-text founder/team thank-you email that builds trust after payment and adds a low-pressure 'add to your order' cross-sell line.
cards.use_when: Writing the first post-purchase email content, especially for the 24–48 hours after purchase when doubt peaks.
steps: Send it as a plain-text email written from the founder or team to feel personal.
Acknowledge the purchase and explicitly recognize whether the buyer is first-time or returning — the source calls this 'really important' for feeling appreciated.

Address buyer's remorse: the source explains that in the 24–48 hours after paying but before receiving the product, buyers second-guess whether the purchase was worth it and whether the brand is trustworthy.
Include a short reassurance line like 'we're preparing your order and will keep you updated on shipping' — you don't need to repeat full logistics since transactional emails cover that.

Add a soft cross-sell line: 'if you want to add something to your order, click here' linking to the store, so the extra item ships with the original order — the source says this increases average order value and reports good results.
Keep the primary goal trust-building; treat the AOV lift as a side effect, not the main aim.
caveats: The AOV benefit is the source's reported experience, not a guaranteed result.
The cross-sell only works operationally if you can actually combine shipments — confirm your fulfillment supports it.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Sequence the Post-Purchase Flow Around Shipping, Usage, Loyalty, Reviews and Cross-Sell
cards.summary: Structure the post-purchase flow as: thank-you (30 min) → excitement/usage guide (~2 days) → loyalty intro (~10 days) → review request (+3 days) → cross-sell with deadline emails.
cards.use_when: Mapping the full email sequence and delays of a post-purchase flow for a physical product.
steps: Email 1 (~30 min): thank-you and buyer's remorse reduction (see related card).

Email 2 (~2 days): build excitement for delivery by giving product usage instructions. This future-paces the customer using the product, reduces buyer's remorse, and pre-empts support questions. If you sell multiple product types, use product-based splits to tailor this email to the item bought.

Email 3 (~10 days): introduce your loyalty program. The source argues this is the moment the customer is happy having received and tried the product, making it a natural point to enroll them and move a first-time buyer toward repeating. Note: the delay depends on your shipping times — the source sets it after expected delivery.

Email 4 (~+3 days): ask for a review, since by now the customer has enough usage to have formed an opinion. Offer a discount code as a thank-you for reviewing — the source notes it's optional but useful because even non-reviewers get a code and may rebuy.

Email 5 & 6 (~7 days later, then +1 day): cross-sell with a discount and a 48-hour deadline, followed by a plain-text 24-hour deadline email from the founder. The source says founder plain-text emails 'work so well.'

The delay to delivery and the review ask depend on your product type and shipping times; adjust accordingly. If you sell consumables, the source notes you can add a 'replacement reminder' (e.g., a 30-day product prompting at day ~25).
caveats: Delays are the presenter's defaults and depend on shipping and product type — validate against your own data.

The source flags review flows may be better as a separate flow when using a dedicated review platform (e.g., Judge.me) with its own triggers; otherwise you can host the ask inside the post-purchase flow.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Target the First-to-Second Purchase Gap as the Hardest Retention Step
cards.summary: Prioritize converting a first-time buyer into a second-time buyer, since the source says this is the most difficult transition, versus repeat-buyer reorders which come more easily.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to invest retention/win-back effort — loyalty, post-purchase, and win-back flows — and setting expectations for which cohort to focus on.
steps: Recognize the source's framing: going from a first-time buyer to a second-time buyer is the hardest step; once a customer has bought 2–3 times, getting them to buy again is comparatively easy.
Design the post-purchase flow (loyalty intro, review request, cross-sell) specifically to shorten that first-to-second gap.
Use the win-back flow to catch first-time buyers who never returned within your typical buying cycle (see win-back card).
In the loyalty introduction email, emphasize earning points and discounts on the next purchase to lower the barrier for a second order.
Treat first-time buyer retention as the metric to watch, not just total repeat rate.
caveats: This is the presenter's framing of relative difficulty, not a measured benchmark — your category may differ.
Durability and consumable products may have structurally shorter repurchase cycles than the source's general claim.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Set Win-Back Timing from Your Own Buying Cycle Data
cards.summary: Trigger a customer win-back flow off a purchase plus a wait equal to your brand's typical repurchase cycle, then verify the delay against your Shopify data and A/B test it.
cards.use_when: Configuring the trigger and delay for a customer win-back flow for lapsed customers.
steps: Set the trigger to 'Placed Order' and add a profile filter like 'Placed Order zero times since starting this flow' so buyers exit.

Choose the wait based on your brand's buying cycle — research how long customers typically take to repurchase (the source suggests checking your Shopify data). The source notes the platform default is ~75 days but that 40 or 90 days may fit better for your brand.
A/B test the delay for your store to find what works best.
Use the platform's 'add past profiles' feature (bulk enrollment) so people who would already have been at the right point in the flow are enrolled without waiting the full delay.
Build the content: Email 1 ('it's been a while') highlights new arrivals or specific collections; the source suggests the default two-email win-back is thin and you can expand it.
caveats: 75 days is a platform default, not a benchmark — derive your own delay from data.
Bulk/past-profile enrollment behavior depends on your ESP — verify the feature before relying on it.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Escalate Win-Back Offers Slowly with Long Delays to Avoid Annoying Lapsed Customers
cards.summary: In a win-back flow, start non-discounted, introduce a discount only after two emails, then escalate, using longer delays between emails since lapsed subscribers are less engaged.
cards.use_when: Writing the email sequence and offer cadence for a customer win-back flow.
steps: Email 1: no discount — 'it's been a while', guide toward new arrivals or collections.
Email 2 (short gap, the source suggests ~3 days rather than the default 15): reinforcement/reminder, still non-discounted.
Email 3 (~7 days later): first discount with a 48-hour deadline if they haven't converted.
Email 4 (~1 day later): another deadline email, optionally plain text, with a 24-hour deadline.
Emails 5 & 6 (~2 weeks later): a higher/second discount with 48-hour and 24-hour deadlines, possibly plain text again.

Use longer time delays throughout because recipients are disengaged; the source warns that sending many emails in a short window to lapsed customers risks annoyance, spam complaints, and deliverability damage.
A/B test this flow heavily — the source singles out win-back as one that deserves a lot of testing, especially for reactivating first-time buyers.
caveats: Recommended delays are the presenter's defaults — adjust to your brand and test.
Discount escalation erodes margin if overused; the source ties offer discipline to list health (see campaign-mix card).
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Run a Sunset Flow to Re-Engage or Suppress Unengaged Subscribers
cards.summary: Send a plain-text sunset flow to unengaged subscribers whose only goal is an open (re-engagement), and update a profile property to suppress those who never open.
cards.use_when: Cleaning your list and protecting deliverability by identifying and suppressing subscribers who haven't engaged in a long window (e.g., 90–120+ days).
steps: Trigger the flow off your unengaged segment (defined later in the course via segmentation) — subscribers who haven't opened in roughly 90, 120 days, or longer, depending on the segment you choose.
Write Email 1 as a plain-text 'you haven't opened in a while — are you still interested? If not, click here to unsubscribe.' Actively inviting the unsubscribe is intentional.
Send Emails 2 and 3 using your highest-permissible discount and clickbait-style subject lines — the only goal is to get an open, which re-engages the subscriber so campaigns can resume.
Use plain text throughout because the source reports it delivers better than designed emails and reads more personally, improving the chance of landing in the primary inbox.
If a subscriber doesn't open any email in the flow, update a profile property (e.g., 'unengaged = true') and build a segment on that property so you can suppress them.
The source's framing: you'd rather have people unsubscribe than stay on the list costing you money and risking spam complaints.
caveats: The source states this flow won't generate much revenue — its purpose is list hygiene/deliverability, not sales.
The 90/120-day window is a segment choice, not a fixed threshold — set it from your own data.
Verify property/segment tooling in your current ESP interface.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Have the Five Core Flows Plus Win-Back and Sunset in Place
cards.summary: Prioritize the essential lifecycle flows the source calls the biggest money-makers: welcome series, site abandon, browse abandon, cart abandon, checkout abandon, post-purchase, win-back, and sunset.
cards.use_when: Auditing which automation flows a store still needs, or sequencing which flows to build first.
steps: Confirm the pre-purchase set exists: welcome series, site abandon, browse abandon, cart abandon, checkout abandon.
Confirm post-purchase and customer win-back exist as post-purchase flows.
Confirm the sunset flow exists for list hygiene.
The source singles out the welcome series, cart abandon, and browse abandon as the most important flows to keep optimizing over time — treat them as ongoing optimization targets, not set-and-forget.

Beyond the core, the source lists optional/extended flows as the possibilities are 'endless': bounceback offer right after purchase, back-in-stock, replacement reminder (e.g., a 30-day consumable prompted at ~day 25), product/data-based cross-sell flows, and a tailored 'highly engaged but never purchased' window-shopper flow.
caveats: Which flows are 'biggest money-makers' is the presenter's assessment, not a measured benchmark across stores.
Build order should consider your data volume — some flows (e.g., back-in-stock) need inventory/restock events to exist.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Turn Smart Sending Off for Flows, On for Campaigns
cards.summary: Disable smart sending in flows so intended emails always send, but keep it enabled in campaigns ~99.9% of the time; enable UTM tracking on campaigns.
cards.use_when: Configuring flow and campaign send settings to control when emails are skipped versus always delivered.
steps: In flows, turn smart sending OFF — the source says you always want flow emails to send as designed rather than being suppressed by recent-email logic.
For example, turn off smart sending on the post-purchase thank-you emails so they aren't skipped.
In campaigns, turn smart sending ON (the source says ~99.9% of the time) — this is the 'skip recently emailed profiles' toggle, avoiding duplicate sends to people who were just emailed.
Enable UTM tracking on campaigns.

When preparing a campaign, set the recipient list (start with the main/newsletter list but send to engaged people — see segmentation), confirm smart sending, then proceed to content, subject line, preview text, sender name, and sender address.
caveats: Smart sending behavior and toggle location are platform-specific — verify in the current interface.
Sending only to engaged people interacts with list hygiene; don't rely on smart sending as a substitute for a clean list.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Choose Among Drag-and-Drop, Plain Text, or HTML Email Editors
cards.summary: Prefer the drag-and-drop editor for most marketing emails, use plain text for personal/deliverability-sensitive sends, and avoid raw HTML due to rendering issues.
cards.use_when: Deciding which email editor to use when building a campaign or flow email.
steps: Default to the drag-and-drop editor for most campaigns — it's the source's go-to for designed emails.

Use plain text (text-only) emails occasionally to feel more personal and improve deliverability; use them specifically in deliverability-sensitive flows like post-purchase thank-yous and the sunset flow, and for founder deadline emails.
Avoid raw HTML: the source says you'll 'almost guaranteed' hit mobile/desktop rendering issues and it's hard to get pixel-perfect across browsers and apps.
In the builder, create a blank email (or use the template library / saved templates) and assemble using the editor.
After building, exit the editor, review the email, and double-check recipients, smart-sending setting, and subject line before scheduling or sending.
caveats: These are the presenter's preferences, not absolute rules — some stores may have the design resources to make HTML work.
Template availability and exact editor names vary by ESP version — verify the current interface.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Use Seven Campaign Buckets to Source Email Ideas
cards.summary: Classify every campaign idea into one of seven buckets — promos, holidays/events, product launches, product highlights, social proof, value-based, and company updates — to keep your calendar varied.
cards.use_when: Generating campaign ideas and building a varied campaign calendar that doesn't fatigue your list.
steps: Bucket 1 — Promos and special offers: discounts.
Bucket 2 — Holidays, special events, Black Friday, Christmas.
Bucket 3 — Product launches: launch a new product with one or a sequence of emails.

Bucket 4 — Product highlights: problem→product-solution angles, us-vs-them/competitor comparisons, bundles, essentials round-ups (e.g., top three skincare essentials), bestsellers, new arrivals, gift guides (strong in Q4 and before Valentine's), subscription content, back-in-stock/restock, ingredients and benefits.
Bucket 5 — Social proof: reviews, user-generated content, influencer messages, press mentions.
Bucket 6 — Value-based: blogs, articles, myths, how-tos that give value (strong if you have blog content).
Bucket 7 — Company updates: brand updates, founder story, behind-the-scenes, product development.
When planning a month, make sure you have a good mix spanning different buckets rather than leaning on one.
caveats: The seven buckets are the source's organizing framework; not every brand will use all seven evenly.
Some buckets (value-based, social proof) depend on assets — blog content, reviews, UGC — that you may need to build first.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Cap Discount Frequency with a 5:1 to 10:1 Non-Discount Ratio
cards.summary: Keep at least a 5:1 ratio of non-discounted to discounted emails (the source prefers 10:1 and a max of one discount email per month) to protect brand perception and long-term results.
cards.use_when: Planning campaign cadence and deciding how often to deploy discounts across your email calendar.
steps: Use at least a 5:1 ratio — five non-discounted emails for every one discounted email, as the minimum.
For the source's own clients, target 10:1 (ten non-discounted per discounted) and cap discounts at roughly one per month.
Be aware of Q4/Black Friday as the exception where discounting increases.
In other months the source sometimes runs two months with zero discounts for some clients.

Rationale from the source: constantly giving discounts trains your audience to ignore them ('you already did it last week'), so a rare discount creates real excitement; it also protects brand reputation and margin.
This applies both to standalone campaigns and to the offer logic inside win-back and sunset flows — escalate offers rather than front-loading them.
caveats: The 5:1 and 10:1 ratios and the one-per-month cap are the presenter's recommendations, not universal rules — set for your margin and category.
Q4 is explicitly called out as an exception.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Set Campaign Frequency from Revenue Tier, Then Adjust by Metrics
cards.summary: Use rough revenue tiers (under 50k → 2–3/week; over 50k → 3–4/week; over 200k → 4–5/week) as a starting point, then adjust based on open and unsubscribe rates, never going above ~5/week.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many campaigns per week to send, and whether to scale frequency up or pull back.
steps: Starting guideline: stores under ~50k/month send roughly 2–3 campaigns/week.
Stores over ~50k/month target roughly 3–4 campaigns/week.
Stores over ~200k/month total revenue can send roughly 4–5 campaigns/week.
The source's sweet spot for most clients is ~3–4 campaigns/week; it would 'almost never' go above 5/week, since that reads as spammy — unless you segment so each person only receives ~3/week.
Adjust by data: if you currently send 1/week and open rate is above ~30% with low unsubscribes, you can increase to 2/week. If already at 2/week with open rate above ~30%, increase to 3/week.
Pull back: if you send 4/week with open rate below ~30% and high unsubscribes, don't increase even if revenue is high — instead clean your list and possibly drop back to 3/week.
Never decide frequency on gut feel — always look at the brand's data.
caveats: The revenue tiers, 3–4/week sweet spot, ~5/week ceiling, and 30% open-rate threshold are the source's rough heuristics, not measured industry benchmarks.
Higher frequency is only safe with solid segmentation so individual subscribers receive fewer messages.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Plan the Campaign Calendar by Layering Events, Value Content, and Company News
cards.summary: Build a monthly campaign calendar in four steps: list relevant holidays/events, pick value-based content, add company events, then fill gaps with the remaining buckets — keeping a varied mix.
cards.use_when: Building out a month's campaign schedule and filling empty send slots with a non-repetitive mix.
steps: Step 1 — List key holidays and events, not just generalized ones. Consider days crucial to your brand and audience. Use a resource like nationaltoday.com, pick the target month, and list events that fit your brand (e.g., 'Sunscreen/Sun Safety Month' for a sunscreen seller). Don't leverage everything — pick what's relevant.

Step 2 — Choose value-based content for the time of year — for instance, a 'top five skincare tips for fall' blog works in October but not May. YouTube content and existing blogs can be reused. Two routes: (a) summarize the blog and link to the full blog as the main CTA, or (b) summarize the blog and link to the products mentioned as the main CTA. The source says test both; if you have no blog, use Google to research valuable content and write an email around it.
Step 3 — Add company events: back-in-stock, product launches (or a full sequence), upcoming holidays → gift guide, etc.

Step 4 — Fill remaining blank slots with the other buckets: share user-generated content, reviews, address a common audience problem and tie it to your product, bust a myth in your niche and link a product.

Layer the mix — e.g., in an August example the source set a product highlight every Sunday, value-based email Tuesdays, a VIP flash sale, a review email, and a company update, with sends on Tuesday/Thursday/Sunday.
caveats: nationaltoday.com and calendar image tools are external tools — verify current availability; the specific holidays shown are examples, not endorsements of any holiday as universally relevant.
The route that yields better results (link to blog vs link to products) differs by audience — the source insists you split-test rather than assume.
Don't over-complicate or over-use holidays, and don't attach a discount to every event.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Run Campaign Calendar Planning in a Shared Planning Tool
cards.summary: Track your email calendar consistently in a shared tool (Airtable, Notion, ClickUp, Monday, or a Google Sheet) so everyone involved sees the same plan.
cards.use_when: Setting up the operational workflow and documentation for planning and shipping campaigns.
steps: Choose a planning tool — the source has used Notion and now uses Airtable, but notes ClickUp, Monday, and even a Google Sheet work fine.
The tool choice doesn't matter; the source stresses the only requirements are consistency, logging everything, and clarity for everyone involved in the process.
Optionally sketch the month visually first — e.g., a blank calendar page image imported into a whiteboard tool — then transfer the plan into your tracker.
Once the rough calendar exists, build it out in whichever tool you selected.
Keep it maintained as you produce and send, so the calendar reflects reality (not just the plan).
caveats: Tool names are examples; the operative point is consistent, shared logging, not the specific software.
This is a process/workflow recommendation, not a performance claim.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Design Emails for Conversion, Not Just Aesthetics — Favor Simplicity
cards.summary: Treat email design as a conversion mechanism: use simple, digestible layouts with a clear value proposition, no blobs of text, and no excessive colors or callouts.
cards.use_when: Designing campaign and flow emails, especially deciding how much copy and visual decoration to include.
steps: Adopt the 'clean, tidy room vs messy room' framing: long paragraphs of text and too many colors are uninviting; a clear, uncluttered layout invites reading.
Keep the email simple and to the point: one clear value proposition and a unique mechanism toward the end state — no blobs of text, no excessive callouts, nothing over the top.
The source notes email design has shifted away from long-form copy toward simplicity because subscribers either lack the time or already expect persuasive fluff and tune it out.
Remember the core principle: more friction → less conversion; less friction → more conversion. Aim to reduce friction in layout and copy.
The source's example: a clearance email needs only two lines of copy plus a designed CTA button — not a wall of text to say '40% off clearance.'
Ensure the email visually matches your website branding, since the source treats brand consistency as a primary reason design matters.
caveats: This reflects a shift the source observed over recent years in e-commerce email — it's directional advice, not a hard rule for every brand or audience.
Simpler design still needs a strong offer/copy — design alone won't convert.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Use Visual Hierarchies (Z, Inverted Triangle, F Patterns) to Guide the Eye to the CTA
cards.summary: Arrange email elements along familiar eye-movement patterns — zigzag/Z, inverted triangle, or F — so the reader flows naturally toward the main CTA button.
cards.use_when: Laying out an email's sections and deciding where to place headlines, body copy, images, and the CTA button.
steps: Z/zigzag pattern: alternate elements left-right following natural eye movement, with lines or imagery guiding the eye toward the different elements. The source cites Magic Spoon as a strong example, using generous whitespace and little copy.

Inverted triangle: place an attention-grabbing headline at the wide top, then narrow the focus down through body copy to the primary CTA button at the point. The source cites Dr. Squatch as an example.

F pattern: headline, then body copy, then CTA — simple and familiar. The source cites a lollipop brand example and says you 'can't go wrong' with it, but also warns to vary patterns so it doesn't get monotonous.
Keep the goal clear: focus the reader toward the CTA button, which takes them to your site where a purchase can happen.
Use visual hierarchies to reduce the bouncing between ideas; the more the reader has to jump around, the higher the friction and the more likely they close the email.
caveats: These patterns are the source's framework, not tested performance guarantees — apply them in your brand's style and test.
The source notes the F pattern is simple and safe but can get boring, so alternate patterns over time.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Replace Long Paragraphs with Visual Formats (Checklists, Tables, Comparisons)
cards.summary: Swap text-heavy explanations for visuals like checklists, comparison tables, and graphs, which are easier to digest and reduce friction.
cards.use_when: Writing email body copy that would otherwise become a long paragraph, especially product comparisons or multi-point explanations.
steps: Replace long paragraphs with visuals — the source names checklists, comparison tables, and graphs as examples that are 'way easier to digest.'

Example from Magic Spoon: use a visual sequence ('Rise. Spoon. Shuffle to your kitchen. Pour Magic Spoon into the bowl.') leading to another CTA, communicating the promise visually rather than in prose.
