Example from Magic Mind: instead of explaining each hormone in a paragraph, present the information as a checklist of a few checkpoints — the source says readers are far more likely to read the checklist than the paragraph.
Example from a bar brand: instead of a paragraph comparing bars, use a comparison table so benefits and differences are immediately clear.
Keep emails short and snappy rather than one big wall of text.
Note the source's framing that copy and design 'integrate with each other' — you're not writing copy and then decorating it, you're designing as you write.
caveats: Visual formats still need accurate content — the presentation changes, not the substance.
Very simple products or single-idea emails may not need a comparison/checklist; don't force a visual where two lines suffice.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Treat the Above-the-Fold Section as Decisive — Include Headline, Support, and CTA
cards.summary: Optimize the visible-without-scrolling section with an attention-grabbing headline, supporting image/text, and a call to action button, since most readers decide whether to continue from it.
cards.use_when: Designing the top of any email — campaign or flow — where you choose what appears before the reader scrolls.
steps: Define the above-the-fold section as the viewable area of the email before scrolling on desktop or mobile (the term comes from newspapers optimizing their most visible part).

The source readopts the 'people just bounce' assumption and argues, based on its own client data, that above-the-fold optimization still matters — including on mobile — because most viewing and clicking happens there.
Include an attention-grabbing headline: readers decide in a few seconds whether to continue.
Include supporting brand image and/or text that clarifies what the email is about.
Include an interesting call to action button within this section so readers can act immediately.

Example from Ritual: 'Enjoy 30% off for Memorial Day — shop now' with an aesthetic image and a CTA button makes the email's purpose instantly clear on mobile. Another example (Dr. Squatch) uses an arrow to guide the eye toward the CTA.
caveats: The source explicitly notes there's ongoing debate about whether above-the-fold optimization still matters; its position is that it does, backed by its own data — but this is the presenter's view, not a universal law.
The specific brand examples are illustrations, not endorsements or guarantees.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Build a Modular Figma Email Template Library for Fast, Varied Design
cards.summary: Maintain a Figma library of interchangeable section templates (headers, product sections, body sections, review blocks) so email design starts from building blocks rather than a blank canvas.
cards.use_when: Setting up an email design system, especially when producing many emails or serving multiple brands and needing variation.
steps: Use a cloud design tool like Figma so designers and clients can collaborate on email designs.
Build basic template blocks: multiple header sections, product sections, body sections, and review blocks — the source's agency made roughly 25 header section variations alone.

For each block type, create many variations (e.g., header with logo + title + text + CTA + image; header with logo + title + CTA; centered vs with/without supporting text; 2×2 product grids; zigzag product layouts; multiple review display styles).
Assemble a full email by picking and matching sections, then layer your brand's fonts, colors, and styling on top — every brand's final design differs by its own branding.
Include body-section visuals like checklists and other data visualizations, not just body copy.
The source says this is especially helpful when producing many emails across clients where appearing original and varied is otherwise difficult.
caveats: The specific template counts and section types are the source agency's setup — build what fits your brand and volume.
Figma is the source's tool of choice for agency/client collaboration; other design tools can serve the same modular purpose.
Templates are a starting point — you must apply branding to avoid generic-looking emails.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Slice a Figma email into image sections before importing to Klaviyo
cards.summary: Cut a designed email into separate exported images so each block loads fast and can carry its own product link.
cards.use_when: Importing a Figma-designed campaign into Klaviyo or another ESP, or diagnosing slow/clipped campaign emails.
steps: Do not export the whole email as one image: the file is large, loads slowly in the inbox, can cause deliverability problems, and allows only one link for the entire email.
In Figma, switch the tool from Frame to Slice and select logical sections: hero/header, section titles, each product block, call-to-action button, footer.
Leave short text elements (headings, section labels, legal lines) out of the slices if you plan to rebuild them as real text in the ESP, because real text helps deliverability.
Export each slice as PNG or JPG, then compress all of them (e.g. TinyPNG, Squoosh, iLoveIMG) — one example reduced the hero from ~2 MB to ~522 KB and other slices by 50–74%.
Upload the compressed images into the ESP and reconstruct the email block by block, then add text blocks, padding, links and alt text.
Keep the mandatory unsubscribe block; delete other default ESP blocks before rebuilding.
Verify the current Figma export and ESP upload interfaces, since both change.
caveats: Compression ratios vary by image; check quality after compression.
Slicing is only needed for image-heavy designed emails; text-heavy templates may not need it.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Set alt text, deep links and auto-applied discount codes on email images
cards.summary: Every email image needs descriptive alt text and a deep link, ideally with the discount code embedded so it applies automatically at checkout.
cards.use_when: Building or QAing a campaign in an ESP, specifically linking product images and setting alt attributes.
steps: Fill in alt text for every image: it shows if the image fails to load and is read by inbox providers such as Gmail to understand the email.
Write the alt text as a short description including the offer, e.g. '20% off shower products with code DIRTYDISCOUNT'.
Link each image to the most specific relevant page — a category/collection page or a single product page — never just the homepage.

Embed the discount code in the URL if the platform supports it (the source demonstrates a redirect parameter after the domain containing the code and destination collection), so the code is applied automatically at checkout.
Test each modified URL in a browser before sending to confirm it resolves and the discount applies.
Run through every link in the ESP preview on desktop and mobile to catch broken or wrong destinations.
caveats: The exact URL/discount parameter format depends on the store platform; the source's example is one implementation — verify what your platform supports.
Auto-applying the code reduces friction, but is not a replacement for showing the code in the email copy.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Size, pad and fix email images so they render correctly on mobile
cards.summary: Import images with generous padding and toggle full-width text on mobile to avoid awkward desktop padding on small screens.
cards.use_when: Finalizing email layout in an ESP drag-and-drop builder and checking the mobile preview.
steps: Set base text styles before assembling: roughly 18px desktop and at least 16px mobile, line spacing around 1.5, and a chosen alignment — adjust to brand.

After importing each image, set block padding — the source adds about 20px top and bottom between sections to recreate the whitespace from the design file, since whitespace makes content easier to digest.
Where sections sit directly above each other, add padding only on the bottom to avoid doubling spacing.
When a text block keeps desktop side padding in the mobile preview (visible as an over-indented paragraph), enable the full-width-on-mobile toggle on that block.
Use the preview to compare desktop and mobile against the original design before scheduling.
Verify padding controls, since ESP builders change their padding UI over time.
caveats: Exact pixel values are the source's preference, not a rule; match the original design and brand.
Sending a real test to your own inbox and checking mobile and desktop is the final step before scheduling.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Cap products per campaign email at three to four and keep the offer above the fold
cards.summary: Limit product blocks in a campaign and make offer, code and CTA visible without scrolling to protect both deliverability and choice.
cards.use_when: Designing or reviewing a promotional campaign's layout and product selection.
steps: Put the headline offer, the discount code and a large CTA in the above-the-fold hero so nothing important requires scrolling.
In the source's Dollar Shave Club example, the original email only showed the discount code far below a small button; the revamp moved code and a big CTA to the top.
Limit the email to a maximum of three to four product blocks — the source argues too many links hurt deliverability and too many options stop people choosing.
Use a zigzag or other visual hierarchy to present the chosen product blocks rather than a flat list.
Repeat the offer and code with another CTA in the closing body copy.
Include multiple category links in the footer so recipients who don't want the promoted category can still find something relevant.
caveats: The three-to-four maximum is the source's recommendation, not a measured benchmark.
The example is a redesign illustration, not a reported conversion result.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Build reusable universal blocks for footer and repeated email sections
cards.summary: Save recurring email sections as ESP universal blocks so one edit updates every campaign that includes them.
cards.use_when: Setting up an ESP template system or updating a footer/category block across past and future campaigns.
steps: Build the section once (commonly the footer with category links and social icons) inside the ESP.
Save it as a universal/reusable block rather than rebuilding it per campaign.
Insert the universal block into every campaign and flow email that needs it.
When a change is needed — e.g. adding a product category — edit the universal block once and it updates across all emails using it, instead of editing each campaign.
Also export the footer slice from design files so the block has consistent imagery.
caveats: Only sections that should be identical everywhere belong in a universal block; campaign-specific content should stay local.
Feature naming and behavior vary by ESP — confirm in your platform's current docs.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Use the four segmentation types to decide what to build first
cards.summary: Choose segment logic from behavioral, demographic, engagement-level and purchase-history dimensions before building in the ESP.
cards.use_when: Planning a store's segmentation structure or assigning messages to different customer groups.
steps: Behavioral: group by actions — recent purchasers, frequent site visitors, or product viewers who didn't buy — useful for triggering personalized emails.
Demographic: group by age, gender or location — useful for regional promotions or demographic-specific collections (e.g. fashion lines).
Engagement-level: group by how people interact with your emails — frequent openers, rare openers, and those who haven't opened in a while.
Purchase history: group by past purchases, total spend or purchase frequency — useful for recommending similar products or loyalty offers.
Map each planned campaign, flow or offer to the segment type that carries the right intent, then build only those segments.
caveats: Types overlap in practice; the point is choosing the right logic per message, not using all four everywhere.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Build engaged segments across 30/60/90/120-day windows including website activity
cards.summary: Create cloneable engaged segments that blend order, checkout, cart, product-view and site-activity signals, then clone for each time window.
cards.use_when: Deciding who receives regular campaigns, or building the audience logic for retention and reactivation.
steps: Start with the condition that the person can receive email marketing so suppressed profiles are excluded.

Add conditions (using OR between engagement events): placed order at least once, started checkout at least once, added to cart at least once, viewed product at least once, active on site at least once — all within the window (the source uses 120 days as the base).
The source includes website activity alongside email opens/clicks because someone may ignore emails but still browse the brand.
Optionally create a second version using email metrics only (opened email or clicked email in the window) if you want email-specific engagement.
Clone the 120-day segment and change the window to 90, 60 and 30 days rather than rebuilding from scratch; add 14/7 or 180/365-day versions as needed.
Expect segment computation to run in the background; you can leave the page while the ESP processes it.
caveats: The 30/60/90/120 ladder is a source recommendation, not a settled standard.
Segments may be auto-moved to inactive after a period (the source mentions ~45 days in Klaviyo) and require reactivation.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Build buyer, non-buyer and repeat-buyer segments for tailored messaging
cards.summary: Segment buyers by purchase count and separate non-buyers, since a first-time buyer and a five-time buyer need different treatment.
cards.use_when: Planning campaigns and flows that treat new, repeat and never-purchased customers differently.
steps: All buyers: person can receive email marketing AND placed order at least once over all time.
First-time buyers: clone the buyers segment and set placed order equals 1 over all time.
2x buyers: placed order equals 2 over all time; 3x+ (VIP candidates): placed order at least 3 over all time.
Non-buyers: placed order 0 times over all time — this list-only, never-purchased group should get different campaigns and flows than repeat buyers because their mindset differs.
Use these groups to size your customer base (how many buyers, first-timers, repeat buyers, never-bought) and to target appropriate offers.
caveats: Cloning and editing one base segment is faster than building each from scratch.
Thresholds (e.g. 3+ = VIP candidate) are starting points, not fixed definitions.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Build abandonment and window-shopper segments for targeted recovery campaigns
cards.summary: Segment people who started checkout or added to cart but didn't buy, and high-intent browsers who never purchased.
cards.use_when: Designing cart/checkout abandonment campaigns and browser-targeting flows.
steps: Abandoners: person can receive email marketing AND (started checkout at least once in last 90 days OR added to cart at least once in last 90 days) AND placed order 0 times in last 90 days.
Send this group a specific recovery campaign, e.g. a final-chance offer.

Window shoppers: (viewed product at least twice in last 30 days OR active on site at least twice in last 30 days OR clicked an email twice in last 30 days) AND placed order 0 times overall AND person can receive email marketing.
Adjust the 'twice' threshold up or down based on your traffic volume and check the resulting segment size before building the flow.
Give each segment its own tailored flow rather than one generic abandoned-browse email.
caveats: The 90-day and 30-day windows and the 'twice' threshold are source defaults to test against your own data, not benchmarks.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Define VIP segments by purchase count or spend relative to AOV
cards.summary: Combine a repeat-purchase threshold with a spend threshold around four times AOV to identify VIPs, tuned to your brand.
cards.use_when: Setting up loyalty or VIP targeting, or deciding which customers get premium treatment.
steps: Start with person can receive email marketing.

Add a purchase-count condition (the source's example: placed order at least 4 times over all time) OR a revenue condition (e.g. revenue at least $200 over all time where the revenue metric is available from the store integration).
Set the revenue threshold as a multiple of AOV — the source suggests roughly 4x AOV as a base (AOV $50 → $200 minimum).
Adjust the multiple (some brands treat 2x AOV or two purchases as VIP) and decide whether to use all-time or a trailing period such as one year.
Use the VIP segment for loyalty rewards or premium offers.
caveats: The 4x AOV figure is the source's suggested starting point, explicitly described as not set in stone and brand-dependent.
The revenue condition requires a connected store integration; without it, only purchase-count logic is available.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Build unengaged segments, then suppress or exclude them
cards.summary: Identify recipients with no opens, clicks, orders or site activity plus enough received emails, then suppress them or send a sunset flow.
cards.use_when: List hygiene, deliverability protection and building a sunset/re-engagement flow.
steps: Person can receive email marketing AND placed order 0, started checkout 0, added to cart 0 and viewed product 0 times in the window. Include all website metrics — the source notes that 'active on site' sometimes fails to fire, so redundant events prevent false positives.
Add email metrics: opened email 0 times AND clicked email 0 times in the window.

Add a 'received at least N emails' condition so people had a chance to engage. The source suggests at least 6 emails in the window if you send roughly three campaigns a week; treat this as trial-and-error and check segment size.

Clone the 120-day version and change windows to 90, 60, 30, 180 and 365 days. For the 365-day version the source uses email-only metrics — e.g. 0 opens and 0 clicks in 365 days with at least ~12 emails received — as a strict clean-up list.
To act on it, use the ESP's 'suppress current members' option on the segment rather than exporting/importing CSVs, and use the unengaged segment as the trigger for a sunset flow.
caveats: The six-email and window values are tuning parameters, not universal thresholds.
Suppressing is irreversible for future sends; review the segment contents before suppressing.
Do not exclude soft bouncers immediately — see the bounce segment approach.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Create bounced-email and spam-complaint segments and exclude them by default
cards.summary: Segment hard and soft bounces and spam complaints separately, suppress hard bounces immediately and exclude all three from every campaign.
cards.use_when: Protecting sender reputation and cleaning your sending list in the ESP.
steps: Spam complaints: person can receive email marketing AND person has marked email as spam at least once over all time. Exclude this segment from all campaigns by default and suppress them.
Hard bounces: bounced email at least once over all time where bounce type equals hard — suppress immediately.
Soft bounces: bounced email at least 4 times over all time where bounce type equals soft — tolerate a few because inboxes can be temporarily full, but exclude after repeated soft bounces.
Instead of suppressing daily by hand, add these segments to your campaigns' default exclusion list; suppress only when you want them gone for good.
Note the bounce-type and spam-marked conditions require the relevant integration/event data to be available in the account.
caveats: The 4x soft-bounce threshold is the source's example; tune to your list.
Suppression removes the profile from future sends; exclusions are reversible — choose per intent.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Split subject line and preview text to stay readable on mobile
cards.summary: Short subject lines plus a complementary preview text raise the chance the whole first impression is read on a small screen.
cards.use_when: Writing campaign subject lines and preheaders for a store's promotions or content sends.
steps: Treat the subject line's only job as getting the open; it must create curiosity or intrigue and stand out in a crowded inbox.
Treat the preview text as a second subject line — many brands skip or waste it by focusing only on the subject line.
Follow up on the subject line's promise in the preview text and tease the content without lying; a high open rate from a broken promise leads to spam complaints or unsubscribes.

Avoid full sentences: use a few words in the subject line and a few in the preview text. Because most opens happen on mobile, a long subject line is cut off — split one long idea between the two fields.
Do not promise in subject/preview what the email doesn't deliver.
caveats: The segment cuts off after listing the email's headline; exact character limits are not specified in the source.
Open rates are not the only goal — delivering the promise protects sender reputation.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Write email headlines as outcomes, not features
cards.summary: Headlines in the header section should sell the reader's benefit or outcome rather than product specifications.
cards.use_when: Writing the hero/header copy for a product or promotional campaign email.
steps: Make the headline the first thing readers see in the header section, so it carries the hook.

Translate features into outcomes. The source's Apple examples: '1,000 songs in your pocket' (iPod) resonates more than the storage spec, 'it's all screen' (iPhone X) and 'full screen ahead' (Apple Watch).
Ask what the reader gets, not what the product has, and phrase the headline that way.
In the Dollar Shave Club example the headline was the offer itself — 20% off shower products — because it is immediately clear what to expect and grabs attention.
Keep it short enough to survive mobile rendering in the header block.
caveats: The Apple and Dollar Shave Club examples are illustrations of the principle, not performance benchmarks.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Apply reading-level, brevity and one-message rules to email body copy
cards.summary: Body copy should read at roughly a fifth-grade level, cut 20–30% of words, focus on one thing, and flow sentence to sentence.
cards.use_when: Drafting or editing campaign body copy and product-block descriptions.
steps: Write at approximately a fifth-grade reading level — the source cites marketing research that this is easiest to understand — and check drafts with a readability tool such as Hemingway.
Use the tool as a guide, not an absolute: keep the brand's tone and voice.
Read the copy aloud and delete fluff; the source finds most drafts can lose about 20–30% of words once spoken.
Focus each email on one thing. Ten emails about one benefit is more digestible than one email covering many things; short attention spans mean multiple messages are forgotten.
Make every sentence pull the reader to the next one, so the copy flows naturally toward the CTA.
Keep sentences short and snappy, and use tools like Grammarly to catch spelling/grammar errors that look unprofessional.
caveats: The fifth-grade and 20–30% figures come from the source's cited research and experience; treat as heuristics.
Readability scores can conflict with brand voice — balance them.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Do audience research before writing, and use copy frameworks as invisible scaffolding
cards.summary: Spend most of the copywriting effort on understanding the audience; let frameworks like AIDA or PAS shape copy without forcing the structure.
cards.use_when: Preparing to write a campaign or flow sequence for a specific customer group.
steps: Before writing, research the target audience: pain points, what makes them happy, what they want to hear from you, what makes them tick. The source estimates roughly 80% research and 20% writing, especially early on.
Write copy that answers 'would I read my own newsletter?' — make it interesting to the recipient, not just about the product.
Use frameworks as reference points: AIDA (attention, interest, desire, action) or PAS (pain, agitate, solve). The source notes these are rarely applied literally in modern email.
Check completed copy against the frameworks — good copy almost always fits one of them naturally.
Show personality and sound human; the source observes top brands all inject personality rather than generic lines.

Use humor where it fits the brand and audience — the source suggests it works especially well for younger (roughly under-30) audiences — and use contractions ('you're', 'you'd', 'they've') to sound like talking to a friend.
Provide value above all: frameworks, active voice and readability only finish copy that is genuinely useful.
caveats: The 80/20 research-to-writing split is the source's heuristic, not a measured benchmark.
Humor and voice must match the brand and audience; it is not universal.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Cut copy: easy words, active voice, no fluff
cards.summary: Final-pass editing removes adverbs, passive voice, alliteration and complexity so copy reads fast and sounds human.
cards.use_when: Final editing pass on campaign copy, PDP copy or ad copy before scheduling.
steps: Read the draft aloud, then remove words and sentences that add nothing — target cutting roughly 20–30%.
Delete adverbs.
Convert passive voice to active voice.
Avoid alliteration and complicated/rare words; keep language simple.
Use contractions (they've, you'd, you're) to make copy conversational.
Confirm the remaining copy still conveys one clear message and leads to the CTA.
caveats: This is the source's editing checklist, not a guaranteed conversion improvement.
Brand tone may justify keeping some stylistic language — judge against the audience.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Prioritize A/B tests by recipient volume, not by ease
cards.summary: Focus split tests on the emails and flows in your account that reach the most recipients so any win compounds across revenue.
cards.use_when: Deciding which email or flow to test next when you can only run a limited number of experiments per month on your store's lifecycle program.
steps: Map each flow and campaign to its monthly recipient volume and revenue contribution before choosing a test target.
Rank the biggest levers first: welcome series, abandoned checkout, abandoned cart, and post-purchase/winback flows, plus the first 2-3 emails of each.
Within those, test high-recipient emails before testing minor flows that only reach tens of recipients per month.
Treat improvements on a 20-recipient flow as marginal: it may lift that flow's conversion, but it will not move overall store revenue materially.
Allocate test slots so at least the majority of experiments land on the top flows and top campaign sends.
caveats: The source frames this as advice for general ecommerce stores, especially under roughly $100K/month; large multi-million-dollar stores can afford to chase smaller levers.
Recipient volume ranking depends on your own account data, not a fixed universal list.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Test send time against place order rate, not open rate
cards.summary: Run send-time split tests with place order rate as the winning metric because the hour with the best open rate is often not the hour with the most orders.
cards.use_when: Scheduling campaign sends and deciding whether to trust Klaviyo's Smart Send Time or run your own send-time test.
steps: Create an A/B test on the campaign and choose 'test send time' rather than relying only on Smart Send Time.
Pick two clearly different times (for example 7 a.m. versus 7 p.m.) to start with a meaningful contrast.
In the test settings, set the winning metric to place order rate, not click rate and definitely not open rate, since revenue and placed orders are the KPIs that matter.
Keep size distribution at 100 and track links separately per variation so you can attribute results correctly.
Run the comparison across roughly 5-10 campaigns before concluding; one campaign is effectively zero data.
Once a winner emerges, narrow the test (for example 7 a.m. versus 11 a.m., then 11 a.m. versus 2 p.m.) to pinpoint the best window.
caveats: The source states it has repeatedly seen the best open-rate time differ from the best place-order time, but notes this is not universal across all brands.
The 5-10 campaign range is a heuristic that depends on audience size and revenue level, not a fixed rule.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Test content structure in campaigns, not just subject lines
cards.summary: Run campaign content tests (product blocks vs none, bestsellers vs categories) because the learning transfers to flows and future sends, unlike one-off subject line tests.
cards.use_when: Planning campaign experiments and choosing which content variables to vary in your store's promotional and evergreen sends.
steps: Set up an A/B test on content rather than only on subject lines, since subject-line results on a one-time campaign cannot be reused elsewhere.
Version A: original email with product blocks. Version B: same email without product blocks. Compare results.
Run a second variant type on sitewide sales: one version highlighting three bestsellers versus one version highlighting product categories or new arrivals.
Set the winning metric to place order rate where possible; the source notes Klaviyo does not allow place order rate for subject-line tests, so click rate is the next-best option there.
Run each content test across multiple campaigns before drawing conclusions and before applying the pattern to flows.
caveats: Subject-line tests on one-off campaigns yield data you cannot act on elsewhere; the source recommends deprioritizing them for that reason.
Place order rate is not selectable as a winner metric for all test types in Klaviyo; verify the current interface.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Use 50/50 manual distribution for email A/B tests
cards.summary: Turn off Klaviyo's automatic distribution and split traffic 50/50 so you keep control of the test and have enough data for a sound winner decision.
cards.use_when: Configuring test settings for subject line or content A/B tests in campaigns and flows.
steps: In the test settings, turn off 'automatically chosen distribution' and set the split manually to 50/50.
Expect automatic distribution to shift more sends toward whichever variant Klaviyo currently favors, which can bias the comparison.
Accept the tradeoff: manual 50/50 requires you to check and analyze the test yourself, which the source's agency prefers because it wants full control.
If you lack time to monitor tests, the source says enabling automatic distribution is acceptable.
For winner selection, the default is click rate; configure to open rate if needed, but note place order rate is not available for subject-line tests, and click rate is the better fallback.
Leave the winner-selection method on 'test by statistical significance' or choose the time limit; alternatively switch it off and pick the winner manually.
Write a note on the test explaining your hypothesis so you can interpret it later.
caveats: These are the source's stated preferences from agency practice, not universal requirements.
Automatic distribution behavior and test-setting labels in Klaviyo may change; verify the current interface.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: A/B test abandonment flow timing with conditional splits
cards.summary: Test the delay before your abandoned cart and abandoned browse emails by building two flow paths with different wait times, then narrow toward the best delay.
cards.use_when: Optimizing abandoned cart, abandoned checkout, or browse abandonment flow timing to lift placed orders while watching spam complaint rate.
steps: Add a conditional split at the top of the flow and set the condition to a random sample of 50%.
Set the 'yes' path to one delay (for example 2 hours) and the 'no' path to another (for example 1 hour) so the difference at the start is meaningful.

Duplicate every email so each path carries the full sequence rather than rejoining after the first email; the source prefers this because email 1 may perform worse at the longer delay while emails 2-3 perform better, and you want the full picture.
After results come in, narrow the comparison (for example test 2 hours versus 3 hours) to pinpoint the ideal delay.
Monitor spam complaint rate alongside placed order rate, since timing changes affect both.
Repeat the same conditional-split approach for browse abandonment, starting with a wider gap such as 1 hour versus 3 hours.
caveats: Splitting every email into two paths multiplies maintenance work; the source prefers it for full-sequence visibility, but it is a tradeoff.
Ideal delays are store-specific; the 1/2/3/4-hour values are illustrative test values, not benchmarks.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Flow subject lines are worth testing, campaign subject lines usually are not
cards.summary: Test subject lines in flows because they run indefinitely, but deprioritize campaign subject-line tests whose results you cannot reuse.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to spend subject-line testing effort across your welcome, abandonment, and post-purchase flows versus one-time campaigns.
steps: For flow emails, go to the email you want to test, hit 'create a test', and enter an alternative subject line (for example 'did you see something you liked' versus 'oops you forgot something').
Run the subject-line test on flows because they send continuously, so a winning line keeps producing results over time.
For campaigns, treat subject-line testing as low-value: the send is one-time, so a winner gives you little actionable information afterward.
Instead of campaign subject lines, direct campaign test effort toward send times and content variations that inform your flows and future campaigns.
Still set the winning metric responsibly: use click rate when place order rate is not selectable.
caveats: This is the source's stated preference and a judgment about actionability, not a claim that subject lines never matter.
Klaviyo's test-creation flow and available metrics may change; verify the current interface.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Skip CTA-color split tests at small store scale
cards.summary: Button-color A/B tests (yellow vs red) are generally not worth running for stores under roughly $100K/month because the expected lift is too small.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to allocate limited testing capacity for a small or mid-size store's email program, signup forms, or above-the-fold email content.
steps: Recognize that CTA color tests usually show meaningful differences only for very large senders, in the source's experience brands doing multiple millions per month with very large audiences.
For stores under about $100K/month, redirect that test slot to bigger levers: flow timing, content structure, and first-email variants in top flows.
If you do test above-the-fold email content, test headlines and calls to action rather than only button color.
Note that color tests are technically possible and can produce a difference; the source's position is that the gain is minor relative to effort at small scale.
caveats: The ~$100K/month threshold and the 'millions per month' scale are the source's heuristics based on agency observation, not measured benchmarks.
A large-audience brand may legitimately find color tests worthwhile.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Write email copy that earns attention through value, not cleverness alone
cards.summary: Voice and personality make copy less robotic, but value to the reader is what drives response; build the email around a clear, useful offer first.
cards.use_when: Drafting campaign or flow email copy for product launches, promos, or category sales that need to fit your brand voice.
steps: Lead with value: the source frames value as more than half the battle, with tone and formatting tips finishing the job.
Make the headline immediately clear about what the reader gets, for example a percent-off product sale, so attention is grabbed by clarity as well as offers.

Write body copy in the brand's voice rather than generic promo language; a line that is a little edgy or funny fits a brand like Dollar Shave Club, whereas a generic 'hurry, selling out fast' line can convert but fits worse.
Call out the discount code explicitly and pair it with a clear call-to-action button such as 'save now'.
Insert recommended product blocks, then close with body copy that continues the same on-brand tone rather than reverting to generic urgency.
Keep sentences short and snappy as a finishing pass after the value and voice are right.
caveats: The Dollar Shave Club example is the source's constructed demo, not a measured performance case study.
Brand-voice edginess is not a universal rule; a generic line may still convert.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Structure promo emails around headline, code, CTA, products, and closing copy
cards.summary: A tested promotional email layout moves from a clear attention-grabbing headline through an explicit discount code and CTA to recommended products and on-brand closing copy.
cards.use_when: Building the layout and copy order for a discount or category-sale email in your store's campaign calendar.
steps: Open with an attention-grabbing headline that makes the offer immediately clear, such as '20% off shower products'.
Follow with body copy written in your brand's tone so the email reads as a fit for your audience rather than a template.
State the discount code prominently and place a clear call-to-action button, for example 'save now'.
Add 'recommended for you' product blocks so recipients can act on the offer without leaving the email's context.
Close with additional body copy that reinforces the sale and repeats the code, keeping the same voice throughout.
Compare your draft against the generic alternative (plain percent-off plus urgency) to check whether your version is genuinely more on-brand.
caveats: This layout comes from the source's demo campaign, not from a documented A/B test result.
A generic urgency line may perform acceptably; brand fit is the differentiator the source argues for.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Track place order rate as the primary email KPI hierarchy
cards.summary: Optimize emails for revenue and place order rate first, then click rate, and treat open rate as the least important metric in the chain.
cards.use_when: Choosing the winning metric for any email A/B test or deciding which send-time or content variant to adopt in your store.
steps: Set revenue and place order rate as the top-level KPIs for email decisions.
Rank click rate second and open rate last, since higher opens do not reliably translate to more orders.
When comparing send times or content variants, prefer the option producing more placed orders even if its open rate is lower.
Where a platform does not allow place order rate as the winner metric (the source notes this limitation for subject-line tests in Klaviyo), fall back to click rate rather than open rate.
Check the platform's current metric options before configuring, since available selections can change.
caveats: The source reports that the best open-rate time often differs from the best place-order time, but this is agency observation rather than a universal law.
Metric availability in Klaviyo varies by test type.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Sequence send-time tests from wide contrast to narrow pinpointing
cards.summary: Find your best send time by first testing two very different hours, then progressively narrowing around the winner across multiple campaigns.
cards.use_when: Establishing a default campaign send time for your store instead of relying on a single Smart Send Time suggestion.
steps: Start with a wide contrast between the two test times so any real difference is detectable.
Let the test run across several campaigns (the source suggests roughly 5-10) rather than judging from one send.
Take the winning hour and pair it against a neighboring hour in the next round, for example 7 a.m. versus 11 a.m.
Repeat with a progressively tighter bracket, for example 11 a.m. versus 2 p.m., converging on the best window.
Apply the resulting send time as your default, but keep monitoring place order rate rather than assuming the optimum is fixed.
caveats: The number of campaigns needed scales with audience size and revenue in the source's framing; 5-10 is a heuristic.
Results are brand-specific and may shift with seasonality or list changes.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Expect to customize templates to your brand instead of copying them
cards.summary: Templates and flows give you a starting blueprint, but each store must test which retargeting flows, designs, and campaigns its own customers respond to.
cards.use_when: Rolling out a new email program or onboarding templates into your store and setting realistic expectations for iteration.
steps: Treat any provided template as a starting point, not a finished system; the source states not every template will fit a brand's needs.
Determine through testing which flows retarget your customers best, which email design engages them most, and which campaigns they want to see.
Accept trial and error as part of finding the right system, strategy, design, and flows for your specific store.
Prioritize iteration on high-recipient flows and sends so your trial and error produces compounding learning.
caveats: The source promotes a paid service with a stated 20% revenue guarantee in 60 days; such claims are the presenter's marketing and are not independent evidence.
No specific template or design is guaranteed to fit a given store.
cards.source_name: _Klaviyo Email Marketing FULL COURSE 2025.docx

cards.title: Prioritize money pages over blog content in ecommerce SEO
cards.summary: Prioritize transactional collection and product intent, then assess supporting content by store-specific revenue contribution.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to allocate SEO budget and content effort across collection/product pages versus a blog for a Shopify store.
steps: List your transactional 'money pages': product and collection/category pages that correspond to keywords a shopper would use when ready to buy.
Rank each candidate by whether a searcher using that keyword is likely to purchase now (e.g. 'natural face wash' vs 'why should I use natural face wash').
Prioritize building out and ranking collection pages for the highest-intent keywords first; treat informational blog posts as secondary or skip them.
Measure direct and assisted conversions from blog content in this store; the source's 0%-2% range is not a universal benchmark.

For a brand struggling with this, the source's example was building roughly 40 new collection pages in the first 3-4 months, which coincided with organic search revenue rising from ~$2K/month to over $10K/month (case example, not a benchmark).
Measure success by organic search revenue, not traffic growth, since traffic without conversions is a sunk cost.
caveats: The source's stance is strongly anti-blog; some stores with high-consideration products may still benefit from informational content, so treat this as a prioritization rule, not an absolute ban.
Case-study revenue jumps are single examples, not guaranteed outcomes.
cards.source_name: $40,000,000 Worth of Ecommerce SEO Advice in 11 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Simplify technical SEO to four essentials
cards.summary: Focus technical SEO only on crawlability/indexing, no broken links, good mobile/desktop UX, and clear page hierarchy.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a technical SEO audit or agency pitch and deciding which fixes are actually worth doing on a store.
steps: Confirm your key pages are crawlable and indexed properly — the source says if Google cannot find key pages, nothing else matters.
Fix broken links (404s), since they hurt user experience and rankings.
Ensure good mobile and desktop UX: fast enough, easy to navigate, not confusing.
Establish clear hierarchy so Google and users understand which pages (e.g. collections) are most important.
Ignore most other technical items pushed by agencies: meta descriptions have not been a ranking factor since 2014 (per source), and minor speed fixes are helpful but not necessary.
If an agency/freelancer pitches endless technical fixes, the source advises caution — treat that as a warning sign rather than a requirement.
caveats: The source's opinion that meta descriptions and minor speed fixes don't matter is presented as its own view; actual importance can vary and Google's documented rankings do involve page experience signals.
Hierarchy still matters and should be verified with internal linking structure.
cards.source_name: $40,000,000 Worth of Ecommerce SEO Advice in 11 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Evaluate relevant existing-page placements for store referrals
cards.summary: The source prefers existing-page placements; evaluate the relevant audience and cost while qualifying paid links.
cards.use_when: Planning a backlink acquisition campaign or budget and choosing between link insertion and guest posting for a store.
steps: Compile a list of sites in your niche that accept guest posts or link insertions.
Find contact information using a scraping/contact tool like hunter.io (verify current tool).
Ask about editorial relevance and sponsorship terms; qualify any paid placement with sponsored or nofollow.
Evaluate candidate pages on domain rating, domain traffic, page traffic, and relevance before buying.
Prefer link insertions over guest posts: the source reports insertions cost roughly 20-30% less on average because the owner just tweaks existing content rather than publishing a new piece.
Prefer pages that already have established traffic, since a guest post has no guarantee of traffic while an inserted link on a live page already benefits from that page's traffic.
Alternatively, use link marketplaces, but expect them to be roughly 20-60% more expensive than direct outreach because they handle the outreach for you — reach out directly if cash-constrained.
caveats: Prices ($100-$400 average per insertion, per source) are the presenter's current spend, not a fixed market rate.
The '20-30% cheaper' and '20-60% marketplace markup' figures are source-specific observations; verify current pricing before budgeting.

Editorial qualification: paid placements must use rel="sponsored" or rel="nofollow"; do not buy unqualified links to manipulate rankings. Assess sponsored placements by relevant referral traffic and commercial value, not promised ranking credit.
cards.source_name: $40,000,000 Worth of Ecommerce SEO Advice in 11 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Aim for a modest number of quality backlinks, not thousands
cards.summary: For most ecommerce keywords you likely need only 10-20 relevant high-quality backlinks rather than thousands of low-quality ones.
cards.use_when: Setting link-building targets or evaluating a cheap SEO offer that promises large volumes of links.
steps: Recognize that sites with thousands of backlinks still often fail to rank number one, so volume alone is not the goal.
Target roughly 10-20 relevant, authoritative links for many keywords (source's heuristic, not a fixed rule).
Avoid cheap SEO services, agencies and freelancers that flood your site with garbage links, since these can hurt rather than help rankings.
Spend link budget on relevance, authority and traffic rather than sheer count.
Blend link insertions with other methods (digital PR, relationship-based outreach) rather than relying on one source alone.
caveats: The '10-20 backlinks' figure is a heuristic the presenter gives for 'a lot of keywords,' not an established threshold; different niches and competitiveness levels vary.
Quality and relevance matter more than any exact number.

Editorial qualification: paid placements must use rel="sponsored" or rel="nofollow"; do not buy unqualified links to manipulate rankings. Assess sponsored placements by relevant referral traffic and commercial value, not promised ranking credit.
cards.source_name: $40,000,000 Worth of Ecommerce SEO Advice in 11 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Apply the 80/20 rule to SEO effort and revenue
cards.summary: Roughly 80% of SEO revenue growth comes from 20% of effort: optimizing money pages and acquiring quality backlinks.
cards.use_when: Allocating limited SEO time or budget across reporting, technical fixes, content and link building for a store.
steps: Identify the two highest-leverage activities: building/optimizing transactional money pages and acquiring quality backlinks.
Concentrate most of your impact (the source estimates ~20% of time) on these two activities.
Accept that reporting, technical SEO, blog content and internal linking may consume ~80% of time yet drive the minority of revenue growth.
Stop trying to do everything: explicitly deprioritize low-revenue SEO tasks during limited-capacity periods.
Track organic search revenue as the primary success metric and reallocate toward whichever of the two levers is underfunded.
caveats: 80/20 is a heuristic framing from the source, not a measured calculation; actual effort/revenue split varies by store.
The source is a marketer promoting its own approach; treat the ratio as an orientation, not a guarantee.
cards.source_name: $40,000,000 Worth of Ecommerce SEO Advice in 11 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Track organic search revenue as the primary SEO KPI
cards.summary: Judge SEO by organic search revenue, not traffic, rankings or vanity blog metrics.
cards.use_when: Reviewing an SEO agency's monthly reporting or deciding whether SEO spend is working for your store.
steps: Set organic search revenue as the number one KPI for all SEO work.
Ignore or discount reporting focused on traffic growth, blog impressions and keyword rankings that don't correspond to revenue.
Benchmark against paid spend: the source cites a brand paying two agencies ~$5K/month each (~$120K/year) that never exceeded ~$2K/month in organic revenue — a net-negative spend.
If organic revenue isn't increasing after a reasonable period, treat the SEO program as not working and change approach.
Use paid-search/CPC signals (e.g. Google Ads Keyword Planner data) to validate whether a keyword is commercial before investing.
caveats: The revenue-vs-spend example is one case study, not a universal benchmark; timelines for SEO results vary.
Some early-stage SEO work legitimately takes time before revenue appears, so a short evaluation window can be misleading.
cards.source_name: $40,000,000 Worth of Ecommerce SEO Advice in 11 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Use a lean SEO tool stack: Semrush, Google Keyword Planner, Screaming Frog
cards.summary: Run ecommerce SEO with three tools: an all-in-one suite, a free keyword planner, and a crawler.
cards.use_when: Choosing or trimming SEO tool subscriptions and setting up keyword and technical research for a store.
steps: Use Semrush (or an equivalent all-in-one) for competitor analysis, keyword research, backlink gap analysis and copycat strategies.
Use Google Ads Keyword Planner as a free keyword research tool you likely already have access to if you run Google Ads.
Note that Keyword Planner gives search-volume ranges, not exact numbers: fine for small keywords, but the gap between 10K and 100K is substantial, so treat large-range keywords cautiously.
Use average CPC (bottom-of-page bid) as a proxy for commercial intent where paid tools give keyword difficulty, since Keyword Planner does not provide difficulty.
Use Screaming Frog for technical crawls (404s, missing H1s/H2s, titles, meta descriptions, URLs, canonicals); it is free for up to 500 URLs, so small sites can use it free.
Verify current pricing and free-tier limits before committing, as tools change over time.
caveats: Semrush pricing/features and Screaming Frog's free URL limit change over time; verify the current interface.
Keyword Planner volume ranges are approximations, and CPC is a proxy for intent, not a difficulty score.
cards.source_name: $40,000,000 Worth of Ecommerce SEO Advice in 11 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Build standout content and relationships for free organic links
cards.summary: Earn links via journalist/blogger relationships and standout content, but expect it to be slow and costly relative to paid links.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest in digital PR and link-worthy content versus paid link acquisition for a store.
steps: If pursuing free/organic links, expand a roster of journalists and bloggers who cover your niche and build relationships over time.
Create genuinely standout content or assets (source calls this the hardest and least scalable link method) that others choose to link to.
Expect to burn through many pieces of content before earning the first organic link.

Budget realistically: the source estimates earning links via digital PR costs around $5K/month; if you're earning links purely organically, it's typically because you're already a high-domain-authority brand (DR 70-80).
Weigh organic link building against cheaper link insertions, which the source prefers for most brands.
caveats: The $5K/month digital PR figure and DR 70-80 claim are the presenter's observations, not established benchmarks.
Organic link building is slow and less scalable; do not expect near-term results.

Editorial qualification: paid placements must use rel="sponsored" or rel="nofollow"; do not buy unqualified links to manipulate rankings. Assess sponsored placements by relevant referral traffic and commercial value, not promised ranking credit.
cards.source_name: $40,000,000 Worth of Ecommerce SEO Advice in 11 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Build a keyword strategy combining money pages and backlinks
cards.summary: Combine transactional keyword targeting on collection pages with a small set of quality backlinks to drive organic revenue.
cards.use_when: Planning a quarter of SEO work for a store: which pages to create/optimize and which links to acquire.
steps: Do keyword research to identify transactional keywords (category/product intent) rather than informational ones.
Map top keywords to new or existing collection pages, creating pages where gaps exist (source case: ~40 new collection pages).
Build 10-20 quality backlinks to those money pages via link insertions and relevant outreach.
Deprioritize informational blog keywords unless they support a transactional page.
Review organic search revenue after 3-6 months and reallocate toward pages/keywords showing traction.
Keep the plan lean: the source argues success comes from focusing on money pages plus backlinks, not from doing everything.
caveats: The ~40-page example is a single case; the number of pages needed depends on catalog and niche.
Timelines in the source's examples (3-11 months) are illustrative, not promises.

Editorial qualification: paid placements must use rel="sponsored" or rel="nofollow"; do not buy unqualified links to manipulate rankings. Assess sponsored placements by relevant referral traffic and commercial value, not promised ranking credit.
cards.source_name: $40,000,000 Worth of Ecommerce SEO Advice in 11 Minutes.docx

cards.title: Technical SEO on Shopify: Audit Order and Purpose
cards.summary: Run a three-step Shopify technical SEO audit (manual, crawl, Search Console) as the foundation before content or link work.
cards.use_when: Before investing in content marketing or link building for your store; when organic rankings are stagnant and you don't know if the technical foundation is broken.
steps: Understand the mechanism: Google spends a limited crawl budget per site, so cleaning up duplicates and low-value pages lowers the 'cost of retrieval' and improves your odds of ranking.

Step 1 - Manually review the store for the known Shopify issue classes: product URL duplication from collection paths, auto-generated tag/vendor/type pages, unredirected deleted products, variant duplication, missing structured data.

Step 2 - Crawl the whole site with a crawler such as Sitebulb, using the Chrome (JS-rendering) crawler and a mobile user agent since Google uses mobile-first indexing. Enable structured data checks in crawl settings.
Step 3 - Open Google Search Console and review Page Indexing for 404s, 'crawled - currently not indexed,' robots.txt blocks, and the Shopping/Enhancements structured data reports.
Prioritize critical and high-severity crawl issues first, then work down the list. Fix redirects on unintended 404s (301 to the relevant live page) to recover traffic and preserve link equity.
caveats: Presenter's opinion: technical SEO is the mandatory first step; skipping it undermines even excellent content and backlinks.
Sitebulb and GSC interfaces change - verify current menu names.
Large stores with thousands of pages are most affected, but small stores still benefit.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Fix Shopify Product URL Duplication (Within-Collection Paths)
cards.summary: Remove the within-collection URL parameter in Shopify theme code so product links always resolve to the canonical /products/ URL.
cards.use_when: When auditing technical SEO on a Shopify store and product URLs appear as /collections/x/products/y when navigated from a collection.
steps: Navigate to a product via two different collections and confirm the URL changes (e.g., .../collections/healthy-beef-jerky/products/... vs .../collections/jerky/products/...).
View source and locate the canonical tag: Shopify usually still points canonical to the clean /products/handle URL, so Google needs to reconcile multiple URLs and duplicates waste crawl budget.
Go to Shopify admin > Online Store > Edit code, open Snippets and find the product grid snippet (commonly main-collection-product-grid.liquid or another file with 'grid' in the name).
Search the snippet for 'within_collection' and delete that parameter, then save. Repeat for all instances of within_collection across theme files.
Note that some newer themes already omit this parameter - if you can't find it, no action is needed.
caveats: Editing this can break URL-derived breadcrumbs - see the breadcrumb meta field card.
Always back up your theme before editing; if unsure, ask a developer or AI assistant where to place code.
Remove from every occurrence, not just the first.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Rebuild Shopify Breadcrumbs With a Meta Field After URL Fix
cards.summary: Shopify builds breadcrumbs from the URL path, so fixing product URLs breaks them - store collection links in a breadcrumb meta field and render from that.
cards.use_when: After removing the within_collection parameter (or any time breadcrumbs on product/collection pages disappear or show wrong hierarchy).
steps: In Shopify admin, go to Content > Metaobjects > Manage definitions, select Products, and create a new definition such as 'breadcrumb'.
Set it to global and choose type URL (avoid the collection type, which can create issues).
For each product, store the URL of the collection it belongs to in that meta field.
Modify the theme's breadcrumb section/snippet to render the link from that meta field instead of Shopify's default URL-derived breadcrumb.
This also gives manual control over what each breadcrumb says rather than relying on URL parsing.
caveats: Best done with at least some theme code comfort; the source suggests asking ChatGPT to help place the code if non-developer.
Best practice: same manual meta-field approach for collection pages.
Full how-to code isn't fully given here - verify instructions in current Shopify theme docs.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: No-Index Auto-Generated Tag, Vendor, Type, and Utility Pages
cards.summary: Shopify generates thin tag/vendor/type/utility pages that can't be customized, so set them to noindex, follow.
cards.use_when: When the store has many product tags (sizes, colors, skin types) or blog tags, or when GSC shows many thin/duplicate pages indexed.
steps: Understand the issue: tags with spaces become ugly URLs, auto-generated tag pages can't have unique titles/H1s/meta descriptions, and sites with thousands of products/posts produce thousands of thin duplicate pages.
For product tags and blog tags, add the provided noindex, follow code snippet to your theme.liquid file.
For vendor and product-type pages, add the corresponding noindex, follow snippets to theme.liquid as well.
Also noindex site utility pages: all collections, all products, new products - they target no keywords and serve no SEO purpose.
Do NOT index tags you actually want: create a real dedicated collection page for that tag instead (e.g., 'moisturizers for dry skin'), so you control H1, URL, title, and content.
caveats: Find the correct spot in theme.liquid via a developer or AI assistant - Shopify's theme structure varies by theme.
Noindex, follow preserves link equity while preventing indexation.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Custom robots.txt on Shopify: Block Low-Value Pages
cards.summary: Create a custom robots.txt in a Shopify template to block crawling of auto-generated, duplicate, and low-value pages.
cards.use_when: After you have set low-value pages to noindex, as defense-in-depth to save crawl budget from duplicate/tag/vendor churn.
steps: Go to Shopify admin > Online Store > Edit code > Templates and click Add a new template, selecting the robots.txt template type.
Add rules blocking crawling of: all product collections, vendor pages, product type pages, product tag pages, and blog tag pages.
Replace any placeholder domain with your real domain in the snippets.
Check your current robots.txt by visiting yourdomain.com/robots.txt.
PREREQUISITE: Only block these if you already fixed the product URL duplication, since mismatched rules can create crawl problems for products.
caveats: Proceed with caution - the presenter explicitly warns that these rules can cause crawl issues if you don't fully understand them.
If already noindexed via other means, robots.txt changes add redundancy rather than new treatment.
Verify current Shopify template behavior against live docs before deploying.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Manage Variant Duplication: Merge or Canonicalize
cards.summary: Merge low-search-volume variants into one product, or keep them but point canonical tags at the primary product URL.
cards.use_when: When color/size variants each create near-duplicate product listings (e.g., cotton sock green vs cotton sock black) with no distinct descriptions or search volume.
steps: Assess whether the variant difference has meaningful search demand and whether the variant page would have genuinely unique content (description, H1, title).
Option 1 - Merge: create one Shopify product with the variants as options, keeping one URL and one content set. This keeps the site clean and avoids duplicate pages.
Option 2 - Canonicalize: create separate variant products but use a custom metafield holding the canonical URL, editable in bulk via Shopify admin (paste the primary product URL for each variant).
Or update the theme to read that canonical metafield and emit the canonical tag - ask a developer or AI assistant for placement.
Goal either way: search engines index only the primary product page while users can still browse variants.
caveats: Do not create separate variant pages when there is no significant search volume - that creates thin duplicates.
Presenter's judgment, not a hard benchmark; the threshold of 'significant search volume' is contextual.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Redirect Deleted Products to Preserve Redirect Path and Link Equity
cards.summary: Never let deleted product URLs 404 - 301 redirect them to a related product or collection to keep visitors and link equity.
cards.use_when: Whenever a product is removed or discontinued and was previously live, especially if it received traffic or backlinks.
steps: Before or immediately after deleting, go to Shopify admin > Online Store > Navigation > View URL redirects.
Add a redirect from the deleted product URL to a relevant replacement product or collection page - not the homepage unless nothing relevant exists.
Save the redirect.
Confirm in Google Search Console that old URLs return 301s rather than 404s.
This preserves link equity from any external links to the deleted product and prevents bad user experiences.
caveats: A 404 does not automatically harm rankings, but redirecting relevant pages preserves equity and UX per the source's practice.
Redirect to genuinely relevant pages; redirecting everything to the homepage is noted as suboptimal.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Remove Pages from Shopify Sitemaps Correctly (Avoid the Hidden SEO Trap)
cards.summary: Shopify requires manual sitemap exclusion, and the hidden SEO checkbox also forces noindex, nofollow - use the theme meta tag instead.
cards.use_when: When you canonicalize or want to exclude pages from the sitemap without preventing them from ranking (e.g., variant or parameter pages).
steps: Unlike WordPress, Shopify does NOT automatically remove canonicalized/noindexed pages from the sitemap.
Shopify exposes a hidden SEO field for products/pages (accessible via a special admin URL path; verify current mechanics). Setting its toggle to true removes the URL from the sitemap.
CAUTION: setting the hidden SEO toggle also sets the page to noindex, nofollow - bad if you only wanted sitemap exclusion.
To bypass that side effect, edit theme.liquid, find the relevant section, and replace it with the provided code snippet so the page is excluded from the sitemap without noindex, nofollow.
Test by requesting the sitemap after the change.
caveats: Editing theme code without developer experience risks breaking structured output; the presenter advises caution.
Shopify admin internals change - validate the current hidden SEO field behavior before relying on it.
Sitemaps support discovery; submission does not guarantee crawling, indexing or rankings.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Implement Product, Article, and Breadcrumb Structured Data
cards.summary: Verify and enrich schema so products show price, ratings, shipping, and returns in search results, and breadcrumbs show hierarchy.
cards.use_when: When you want rich snippets for product and blog listings, or when auditing technical SEO to ensure schema is valid.
steps: Product schema: most Shopify themes include basic product schema, but verify it is actually output and includes the key properties your theme supports (price, availability, ratings, shipping/return info where relevant).
Article schema for blog posts: check the theme's default output and verify key properties are present; blog articles pulling in rich results supports content-led SEO.
BreadcrumbList schema: check the theme's breadcrumbs.liquid snippet under Snippets to ensure it emits BreadcrumbList markup that reflects your site hierarchy.
Use GSC's Shopping/Enhancements structured data report and a crawler's structured data check to catch errors (often trivial, like a missing comma).
If implementation is beyond you, get a developer - the payoff is richer SERP presentation and clearer context for Google.
caveats: Exact key property lists weren't enumerated in the source; verify against schema.org and current Google rich results requirements.
Schema issues can silently lose rich snippet eligibility.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Posture Site Speed: Avoid Bloat Rather Than Optimize
cards.summary: Shopify is fast out of the box; site speed work mostly means avoiding heavy themes, oversized images, and unused/unconditional apps.
cards.use_when: When store pages feel slow, mobile conversion lags, or before adding new apps, sliders, or hero assets.
steps: Acknowledge the baseline: Shopify's hosting, browser caching, and CDN make a bare store fast. Speed degrades from added factors.
Diagnose with Google PageSpeed Insights to see actual bottlenecks and third-party impact.
Apply the fixes in priority order: lightweight theme, image format/size optimization, lazy loading, removing dead app code, conditional app scripts, minification.
Treat speed as both a conversion lever (bounce/abandonment) and a (modest) ranking signal, per the source's cited data.
caveats: The source cites Semrush/Search Engine Watch graphics for speed-to-conversion and speed-to-ranking relationships but reports the ranking effect as slight.
Precise speed benchmarks vary by store and connection; no universal target is established here.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Choose Lightweight Themes and Cut Hero/Grid Bloat
cards.summary: Prefer lean themes (Dawn free; Palo Alto paid) and replace sliders, carousels, and oversized grids with simpler components.
cards.use_when: At store build time or when auditing an existing Shopify theme that feels sluggish on mobile.
steps: If starting fresh, choose a lightweight, efficiently coded theme: Dawn is suggested for free, Palo Alto when budget allows.
Audit an existing theme for bloat: count sliders/carousels, hero styles, and oversized product grids.
Replace a slider with a single static hero image.
Cut product carousels from large counts (the source's example: 64 items) to a manageable number (~8) if the design allows.
These structural simplifications improve speed without needing code-level optimization.
caveats: Theme recommendations reflect the presenter's opinion and may date; verify current theme marketplace options.
Reducing components can affect merchandising/design - balance speed with conversion needs.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Optimize Image Format and Compression for Speed
cards.summary: Use WebP/JPEG for product images, WebP/PNG for hero text graphics, SVG for logos, and auto-compress with an app.
cards.use_when: When preparing product photography, hero images, logos, or auditing an image-heavy collection page.
steps: Choose format by role: WebP or JPEG for product photos; WebP for hero images and text graphics (good quality/size balance); PNG for lossless/absolute clarity; SVG for logos and icons (vector, crisp, tiny).
Compress existing images app-side: the source uses Crush Pixels (Shopify app) which auto-compresses on upload, commonly cutting file sizes ~50%.
For manual compression, the source cites Crush Pics app results (nearly identical visual quality, ~50% smaller).
Resize images before upload so you never upload desktop-resolution images for mobile consumption.
Adopt srcset for responsive images: let browsers load an appropriately sized source per device - mobile loads small, high-DPI loads large.
caveats: Percentages cited are the presenter's example, not a guaranteed benchmark.
srcset requires theme code edits - may need a developer.
App names/features change; verify current Shopify app listings.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Lazy Load Offscreen Images on Collection Pages
cards.summary: Delay loading images until they approach the viewport so long product grids don't load every image up front.
cards.use_when: On collection/category pages with many product images (e.g., 36-grid) where only the first rows are visible at load.
steps: Understand the mechanism: by default the browser loads every image at once, but only the first visible rows matter for initial load time.
Add the lazysizes.js library to the theme's assets folder.
Modify theme.liquid to include the lazysizes.js script.
Update image tags: replace the src attribute with data-src and add the lazyload class to the image.
Save and test on mobile - offscreen images should only load as the user scrolls.
caveats: Over-lazy-loading above-the-fold images can hurt LCP - do not lazy-load the hero.
Source gives one library (lazysizes); modern browsers support native loading='lazy' as an alternative to verify.
Requires theme code deployment; back up first.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Audit and Remove Unused App Code from Themes
cards.summary: Uninstalling a Shopify app often leaves its scripts behind in the theme, so sweep with PageSpeed Insights and remove orphan code.
cards.use_when: After uninstalling apps, or when third-party script overhead is flagged on the store.
steps: Recognize that uninstalling an app does not always remove its code injections from the theme.
Run Google PageSpeed Insights and read the 'Reduce the impact of third-party code' findings.
Look for scripts serving from domains of apps you no longer use, and any code not serving the current setup.
Remove obsolete app code from theme files, or have a developer do it to avoid breaking live functionality.
Only install essential apps; where possible, bake functionality into theme code instead of adding another app.
caveats: Removing the wrong snippet can break live features - the source recommends a developer for pinpoint-safe removal.
There's no built-in Shopify 'app cleanup' guarantee; residue varies by app.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Conditionally Load App Scripts by Page Type
cards.summary: Load each app's scripts only on pages where they're needed instead of sitewide via theme.liquid.
cards.use_when: When review widgets, zoom scripts, custom-option code, or social share buttons load on every page and slow unrelated pages.
steps: Identify where each app's scripts currently load (typically theme.liquid sitewide).
Map scripts to pages: product previews/reviews, image zoom, custom options -> product pages only; social share buttons -> blog posts only.
In theme.liquid or relevant templates, wrap each script in a Liquid condition so it only renders on the matching template (e.g., only when template contains 'product').
Save and verify the feature still works on its intended page and no longer loads elsewhere.
If uncomfortable with code, have a developer implement the conditionals.
caveats: Conditional includes can break if apps assume their scripts load globally - test each feature.
Requires theme edit and periodic re-audit when apps update.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Minify JavaScript and CSS to Reduce File Size
cards.summary: Strip comments, spacing, and line breaks from JS/CSS to shrink files and speed up loading.
cards.use_when: When PageSpeed or an audit shows unminified JS/CSS asset opportunities on the store.
steps: Understand minification: remove developer-only characters (spaces, line breaks, comments) without changing functionality.
For a no-code route, use a Shopify app like File Optimizer to auto-minify assets.
For manual JS minification, use a tool such as JSCompress.
For CSS, Shopify offers a built-in route - the source notes you can convert CSS to the .doc.css form (verify current Shopify asset/SCSS handling).
Apply, then re-run PageSpeed to confirm reduced transfer sizes.
caveats: Keep an unminified copy for future editing.
App names and Shopify's built-in CSS handling evolve - verify current dashboard options.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Speed up a Shopify store by minifying CSS/JS
cards.summary: Remove whitespace, line breaks and comments from CSS/JS to cut file size and speed up page load.
cards.use_when: When auditing storefront page speed and deciding whether technical asset optimisation is worth the effort before other work.
steps: Understand the principle: browsers don't need the spacing, line breaks and comments developers add for readability, so removing them shrinks files without changing functionality.
For a manual route, run JavaScript through a JS compressor and CSS through a CSS minifier.

Shopify gives a built-in option: name CSS files with the .css.liquid extension and Shopify minifies them automatically — verify the current accepted file extension in Shopify's docs before relying on this.
For non-developers, an app such as File Optimizer can automate minification of JS and CSS files.
Recommend getting a developer involved if you are not confident, because broken scripts can break cart or product functionality.
caveats: The source presents minification as one part of a broader speed playbook; it is not claimed to be sufficient alone.
Test on a duplicate theme before pushing live.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Async and defer non-essential scripts
cards.summary: Load chat widgets, analytics and tracking scripts asynchronously or deferred so the page renders and becomes interactive sooner.
cards.use_when: When third-party scripts (live chat, analytics, tracking pixels) are blocking rendering and hurting storefront speed.
steps: Classify each script: non-essential scripts are those that don't affect core site functionality — live chat widgets, analytics and tracking tags are the source's examples.
For asynchronous loading, add the async attribute to the script tag; the script downloads in parallel and executes as soon as possible.
For deferred loading, add the defer attribute; the script downloads in parallel but executes after the main content has parsed.
Both approaches let the page render and become interactive faster by moving non-critical script work out of the critical path.
