Have a developer implement this carefully and test checkout, cart and product-page interactions afterwards to confirm nothing breaks.
caveats: The source says this should be done carefully, preferably by a developer, to avoid negative impact on site functionality.
Do not defer scripts that the cart, variant picker or checkout depends on.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Use resource hints and preload to cut load times
cards.summary: Add preload, prefetch, DNS-prefetch and preconnect link elements in the head to control how and when key resources load.
cards.use_when: When optimising storefront load speed for above-the-fold assets, next-page navigation, or third-party domains like analytics and social buttons.
steps: Add a link element with the appropriate rel attribute and the resource URL, placed in the head of the HTML so it is acted upon early in page load.
Use preload for resources needed immediately on the current page (for example a hero image or critical font).
Use prefetch for resources needed for future pages, which makes subsequent navigation snappier.
Use DNS-prefetch and preconnect for third-party resources you know will be used, such as analytics or social media buttons.
Verify the exact syntax in current Shopify theme documentation before editing, since theme structure and supported tags can change.
caveats: The source describes implementation as fairly simple but the actual edits sit in theme code and need testing.
Resource hints are one part of site speed, not a fix for heavy images or bloated apps.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Frame keyword research around customer thought process, not just volume
cards.summary: Keyword research is uncovering the search terms people use when looking for your products, services or information — it maps the customer's thought process.
cards.use_when: When planning which collections, product pages and blog posts to build or optimise for organic search on a Shopify store.
steps: Start from a seed product term (the source's example is blackout curtains) and ask what a real customer would type, not what you would call the product.
Generate variations across dimensions: material (linen blackout curtains), room (blackout curtains for bedroom), question form (do blackout curtains keep heat out), and buyer vs explorer phrasing.
Recognise that each variation can attract a different audience or indicate a different stage of the buying journey.
Use the research to decide which pages to prioritise, which questions to answer with content, and what competitors are already targeting.
Expect the output to serve four things: more long-tail visibility, more relevant traffic, better conversion from high-buyer-intent terms, and a sharper content strategy.
caveats: The source stresses that rankings and search volume alone are not the point; search intent understanding is.
No specific volume thresholds are given.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Build a topical map instead of a flat keyword list
cards.summary: A topical map is keyword research extended into a roadmap of every topic and page needed to be seen as the authority in your niche.
cards.use_when: When a store has scattered SEO pages and you need a single plan for which collections, subcollections and blog posts should exist.
steps: Understand the goal: outline every topic you need to cover to be recognised as the leading expert in your industry, not just a list of keywords.
Pull the matching keywords for your seed topic from a tool such as Semrush — the source's example found roughly 21,000 keywords containing 'blackout curtain' — and note their volumes and difficulty.

Cluster keywords by search intent so you know which group of terms can be served by one page rather than many; the source recommends Keyword Cupid for automatic clustering based on SERP similarity, or you can cluster manually.
Prioritise by volume, then move the highest-volume clusters into a keyword map that lists keyword, volume, and cluster.
In a second tab (the topical map), assign each cluster a page type — collection, product or blog post — plus a primary keyword, secondary keywords, URL, volume, current rankings and status.
Track publication status and, for published pages, whether each needs a content refresh, a quick-win optimisation, or no change.
Use additional sources such as Wikipedia, Google Trends, competitor sites and Exploding Topics to find topics you missed.
caveats: The presenter uses this as their own preferred method and says it is 'keyword research on steroids'; it is not the only valid approach.
Keyword Cupid and Semrush are the tools the source names; interfaces and pricing change, so verify current features.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Decide page type by what ranks in positions 1–3
cards.summary: Match your target page type (collection, product, or blog post) to the content type Google already rewards for that keyword.
cards.use_when: When a keyword cluster could plausibly be served by a collection page, a product page or a blog post and you need to choose.
steps: Search the keyword and inspect what type of pages occupy the top three results.
If the top three are collection pages (as with 'blackout curtains'), target the keyword with a collection page.
If the results are informational articles (as with 'blackout curtain alternatives'), target the keyword with a blog post.
If results are mixed, lean toward whatever occupies positions 1–3, because that is where you want to be and Google is signalling the content type it wants.

Then apply the buyer's perspective: someone searching a broad category term probably wants options (collection page), while a very specific query like a product name, size, or unusual feature combination suggests a specific product (product page).
Note that very specific product-page keywords may have little to no search volume, which raises the separate question of whether those pages are worth indexing at all.
caveats: The source calls deciding page type 'a little tricky'; intent is the deciding factor, not a fixed rule.
Google's SERPs shift over time, so re-check before committing a build.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Prioritise bottom-of-funnel pages first on Shopify
cards.summary: Start SEO with collection and product pages, because they lead directly to revenue and pay back fastest.
cards.use_when: When deciding what to optimise first across hundreds of existing collection and product pages.
steps: Rank page priorities in this order: bottom-of-funnel pages (collections and products) first, blog posts later, because bottom-of-funnel pages lead to revenue growth and let you see return on the SEO effort sooner.
Within those pages, open Google Search Console and sort by number of impressions to find low-hanging fruit — pages already close to the top three where a visibility improvement could convert quickly.

Look for the small subtopics where search engines already treat you as an authority; these pages tend to receive the most impressions, and optimising them plus closely related pages moves the needle faster than switching to an unrelated collection.
Pair that with a Keyword Gap analysis: enter your domain plus a few competitors, and review the keywords competitors rank for that you don't.

If your backlink profile is stronger than the competitor's, the source argues you should be able to outrank them on those gap terms — this is most powerful for well-established brands with strong link profiles.
caveats: The prioritisation rationale is the presenter's experience, not a measured benchmark.
Keyword Gap relies on backlink-profile strength; a weaker-profile store should not assume it can outrank the competitor.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: One topic per page, many secondary keywords per page
cards.summary: Cluster a primary keyword with its close variants on one page, and split genuinely different topics onto separate pages.
cards.use_when: When mapping keywords to URLs so one page can rank for many terms without competing against your own pages.
steps: Set one primary keyword per page — it goes in the H1, the URL and the title tag.

Add secondary keywords that are variations of, or closely related to, the primary keyword: singular/plural variants, common misspellings (the source's example is 'block out curtains'), and attribute variants that would still be served by the same page and product set.
Split topics that would clearly show different products: white blackout curtains and pink blackout curtains should not share a page because they require different product results.

Cluster manually, or use a tool such as Keyword Cupid, which the source says clusters based on the Google algorithm — if the SERPs for two keywords are similar, it clusters them together, removing the guesswork.
Remember the rule is one topic per page, not one keyword per page; a single page legitimately ranks for many keywords.
caveats: Cluster tools are only as good as their SERP data and change over time.
The source states this as its own operating rule for Shopify stores, not as a Google-documented requirement.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Assign URL types: collections for options, products for specifics, homepage for breadth
cards.summary: Collection pages capture broad transactional terms, product pages capture highly specific ones, and the homepage targets broad high-level keywords.
cards.use_when: When deciding whether a keyword should live on a collection, a product page, or the homepage.
steps: Assign to collection pages the transactional and option-seeking terms: brand names, features, colours, materials, styles — anything where the searcher wants a variety of choices.
Assign to product pages only truly specific queries, e.g. a combination like 'aqua blue room darkening curtains' that signals a specific product; size and niche feature searches also fit here.
Accept that collection pages will usually outconvert product pages for broad terms, because a collection offering many options better matches what the searcher wants.
Use the homepage for broad, high-level keywords (the source's curtain-shop example is 'buy curtains online'), while individual collections cover narrower categories.

Check for cannibalisation: make sure the homepage keyword isn't also the target of a collection page (a bicycle store using 'buy bicycles online' on the homepage should not also target it with a collection).
caveats: The source notes it is debatable whether highly specific product pages with no search volume are worth indexing at all, and that some stores may be better off pushing crawl toward collections.
The source argues there is no SEO problem with reusing the same products across multiple collections when it makes sense to users.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Derive site structure and internal links from the topical map
cards.summary: A clean topical map becomes a site structure of homepage, collections and subcollections that mirrors how search engines expect topics to relate.
cards.use_when: When building or restructuring catalogue hierarchy and internal links for a Shopify store.
steps: Take the topical map and turn it into a hierarchy: homepage at the top, then primary collections (e.g. blackout curtains, sheer curtains, lace curtains, kitchen curtains), then subcollections under a parent.
Create subcollections by attribute — by room (blackout curtains for bedroom), by material (linen blackout curtains), by colour (white blackout curtains).
Treat each collection page as dedicated to one specific product category and one specific topic, so pages stay unique from one another.
Use the mental model that a search query is a question and your page is an answer; the easier you make the question-to-answer match, the higher you are likely to rank.

Feature subcollections inside their parent collection pages — the source's example is MyProtein's whey protein page linking to dairy-free protein, clear protein drinks and protein blends — which improves navigation and makes the hierarchy easy for search engines to crawl.
Note that Shopify has no native subcollection feature; you create a new collection and treat it as a subcollection.
caveats: Crawl-depth guidance ('lower depth is better') comes from studies the source cites generally, not from a specific controlled test.
Restructuring URLs on a live store needs redirect planning, which this section does not cover.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Spot and fix keyword cannibalisation
cards.summary: Cannibalisation is multiple pages on your site competing for the same keyword, which confuses search engines about which page to rank.
cards.use_when: When a collection, product or blog page isn't ranking as expected and you suspect competing pages on the same store.
steps: Check for overlapping targets: a collection page and a product page both targeting the same keyword (e.g. both targeting 'blackout curtains') is a cannibalisation problem.
Check content redundancy: blog posts targeting keywords already covered by collection pages.
Check keyword overuse — spreading the same keyword across many pages on the assumption it improves rankings, which the source says actually confuses search engines.
Fix by applying one page per topic: give each page one primary keyword and split overlapping pages into distinct, genuinely different topics rather than near-duplicates.
Keep secondary keywords on each page so you still capture variants without creating new competing pages.

Also look for near-duplicate collection ideas: pages like 'top rated gardening tools', 'most popular gardening tools' and 'gardening tools on sale' will compete for the same keywords and offer no unique value.
caveats: The failure mode described (internal competition confusing search engines) is the source's explanation; it is not framed as a documented ranking factor.
Merging or deleting pages affects existing traffic — check Search Console data before removing URLs.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Expand broad topics into subcollections without creating redundancy
cards.summary: Splitting a broad category into focused subcollections captures more search entry points, but only where each page has a genuinely distinct offer.
cards.use_when: When deciding whether to break a large collection into subcollections or keep it as one page.
steps: Create as many genuinely distinct collections and subcollections as the catalogue supports, because each one is an additional search entry point and increases total addressable market.
Split by meaningful dimensions: for a vacuum collection, the source suggests stick, upright, handheld and robotic vacuums.
Use a 'shop by' menu structure (by size, type, colour, feature) as a brainstorming device for which collections and subcollections your brand could have.
Use keyword tools such as Semrush to confirm the splits have search demand: enter the main keyword (e.g. vacuum cleaner) and review the containing keywords with difficulty and monthly volume.

Reuse products across multiple collections where it makes sense to users — the source says a cordless vacuum and a stick vacuum collection can both legitimately contain the same product without SEO problems.
Do not create near-duplicate pages (e.g. three 'best/top/sale gardening tools' pages); those compete with each other and add no unique value.
caveats: The source does not give a numeric threshold for when a category is broad enough to split; it describes the expand-vs-consolidate line as thin and requiring judgement.
The 'over 80% of organic revenue from collection pages for stores with 50+ products' figure is the presenter's stated generalisation, not a measured benchmark for your store.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Stick to your core topic and avoid diluting relevance
cards.summary: Publishing content far outside your topical map dilutes the site's perceived expertise and can cost rankings on core topics.
cards.use_when: When considering a new category, blog theme, or shoulder niche that sits outside your store's existing topic focus.
steps: Map how close a new topic sits to your core in Google's knowledge graph: blackout curtains, sheer curtains and linen curtains are close together; tablecloths are noticeably further; an unrelated category is furthest.
Keep publishing inside the topical map where every piece of content reinforces authority on the subjects you have chosen to cover.

Treat the source's warning as a live risk, not theoretical: the presenter describes a site that dominated a niche, expanded into shoulder niches, ranked briefly for a few months, and then lost rankings — search engines recrawled the site, judged it no longer sticking to its core competencies, and rankings dropped for the main topic too, not just the new one.
Before expanding, ask whether the new content would confuse both users and search engines about the site's actual purpose.
If expanding, do it only after the core topical map is maximally covered.
caveats: This is a practitioner's account of one overexpansion experience, not a controlled study or a promise about any specific site.
The 'few months' timeline and the loss of core rankings are specific to that case.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Optimise the main menu for fewer clicks to product
cards.summary: Match main-menu structure to catalogue size: minimal for small stores, direct subcategory access for large, shop-by-x for varied ranges.
cards.use_when: When designing or revising the storefront main navigation to improve usability and crawl efficiency.
steps: For small catalogues with few product categories, a simple 'Shop' menu may be sufficient — the source's example is an outdoor brand using a single 'shop gear' entry that routes to core collections.

For large catalogues with many categories (protein, bestsellers, creatine, amino acids, pre-workout), give direct menu access to subcategories like whey, clear, vegan and blended protein so users don't have to click through a parent first.

For stores with varied collections — by brand, style or goal — use a 'shop by x' navigation directly in the main menu; the source's example offers blinds by type, colour, window type, room and feature.
Set the goal as minimising the number of clicks needed to reach a desired product for both users and search engines.
Keep in mind the two stated benefits: better user experience (lower bounce, higher conversion) and SEO benefits (crawl efficiency, link equity distribution, reduced crawl depth).
caveats: The claim that lower crawl depth typically means better rankings is attributed to studies in general, not to a controlled test by the source.
Menu complexity can hurt mobile usability — the source does not address mobile specifics.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Make the homepage a hub for high-volume collections
cards.summary: Feature your highest-search-volume collection pages prominently at the top of the homepage to serve users and push backlink equity into money pages.
cards.use_when: When designing homepage layout and choosing which collections to surface first.
steps: Identify which collection pages have the highest search volume — those likely reflect what your audience is most interested in.
Feature them prominently at the top of the homepage using banners or featured sections so they are instantly accessible.
Aim for as few clicks as possible from homepage to those collections.
Add engaging content or promotions around those featured collections to draw attention.

Understand the SEO logic: the homepage usually has the most backlinks and is the most visited page, so linking out to high-volume collections passes backlink equity to pages whose ranking potential you want to improve.
Study the source's example: a blinds retailer whose homepage essentially mirrors its main menu, with shop-by-type, shop-by-colour, most-popular and shop-by-room sections.
caveats: The link-equity distribution rationale is standard SEO reasoning presented by the source, not a measured result from a test.
Don't overload the homepage to the point of slowing load time.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Handle faceted navigation correctly on Shopify
cards.summary: Default Shopify filter URLs are parameter-based and are not indexed, so keyword-targeted filters need their own dedicated collection pages.
cards.use_when: When deciding whether to add filters to a collection page and whether those filters should rank for anything.
steps: Decide whether faceted navigation is needed at all: a store with a few products likely doesn't need it, while a store with hundreds or thousands of SKUs likely does.

Understand the default: most Shopify themes use URL parameters for filters, and those parameter URLs are not indexed by search engines, which simplifies the site structure but means filtered pages won't rank for specific keywords.
If you want to target a specific keyword inside a filter dimension, manually create a dedicated collection page for it.
Treat that manual creation as a benefit, not a workaround: a dedicated collection lets you add unique content and customise the page, which a parameter-filtered view cannot.
Choose which filter dimensions to offer based on what helps customers narrow down (size, colour, price; the source's example uses food texture, flavour, special diet and life stage).
caveats: This describes default Shopify theme behaviour; confirm how your specific theme and apps handle filter URLs before assuming filters won't index.
The source frames faceted navigation mainly as a large-catalogue tool.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Build product grids for both users and crawlers
cards.summary: Avoid JavaScript-loaded product grids, show 36–48 products per page, and put useful product details directly in the grid.
cards.use_when: When setting up or redesigning collection page product grids on a Shopify store.
steps: Do not load product grids with JavaScript — the source says search engines typically struggle to crawl JavaScript content efficiently; use the default Shopify Search & Discovery app to generate grids instead.
Show roughly 36 to 48 products per page, aiming for as many as possible without compromising site speed, to avoid excessive pagination (the source's example is 21 pages for one collection).

Use numbered pagination rather than previous/next controls, because users and crawlers cannot skip to a specific page otherwise — the source notes some stores only offer next/previous, which forces multiple clicks to reach page five.
Add product details into the grid — colour options, a short description, size, pickup or delivery — so customers can decide without clicking through to the product page.
Treat the added detail as both a UX improvement and extra page content, which the source says adds relevance and usually leads to higher rankings.
Add faceted navigation for brands with heavy SKU counts (the source's benchmark: roughly 200 SKUs means customers will struggle to find items without filters).
caveats: The 36–48 figure is the presenter's recommendation, explicitly conditioned on not slowing the site.
The SKU/collection relationship ('over 50 products → collections drive 80%+ of organic revenue') is the source's generalisation, not a measured statistic for your store.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Add breadcrumbs, tag-style links and related products to product pages
cards.summary: Use three internal-link patterns on product pages to strengthen navigation, distribute link equity and aid discovery.
cards.use_when: When auditing product page template and internal linking on a Shopify store.
steps: Add breadcrumbs that give a clear path back to broader categories; the source notes most Shopify themes include this by default, so check whether yours does.

Add tag-style category links that let shoppers explore related collections and products — the source's example is a fishing tackle product page linking to vertical jigs, ice fishing jigs, blade baits, shown near the product description.
Add a related products section to boost sales and reduce navigation clicks; the source's example is Amazon's related-products row.
Recognise the combined SEO effect: these patterns distribute link equity more effectively and improve discoverability across the product range.
Treat this as often underused on Shopify stores hosting thousands of products, where effective linking on product pages meaningfully improves site structure.
caveats: Shopify theme support varies, so verify whether breadcrumbs and tag-style links are native or need code/apps.
The source presents the sales lift from related products as a benefit rather than citing a measured uplift.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Optimise the three key on-page elements on collection pages
cards.summary: Title tag, URL and H1 are the first elements search engines crawl and the strongest signal of what the page is about.
cards.use_when: When writing or rewriting collection page metadata for a Shopify store.
steps: Place the target keyword as close to the start of the title tag as possible — if the target is 'vegan protein powder', lead with that phrase.
Use up to roughly 60 characters in the title tag; if you aren't near 60, add secondary keywords or modifiers like 'buy online' or 'shop', or longer-tail variants of the target keyword.
Set the H1 to the target keyword itself — 'vegan protein powder' as the H1 if that is the target.
Keep the URL as short as possible and mirror the target keyword — the source's direction is simply 'vegan protein powder' as the slug.
Remember the broader principle: one page per topic, one primary keyword per page plus secondary keywords.
caveats: The ~60 character guidance is presented as a working rule of thumb, not a hard limit enforced by Google.
Shopify auto-generates some of these fields, so check for template overrides.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Decide what to do with a page: publish, refresh, or quick-win
cards.summary: Track each mapped topic's publication and performance status so the topical map becomes an actionable worklist rather than a document.
cards.use_when: When turning a completed keyword/topical map into a prioritised production and optimisation queue.
steps: Build a keyword map first that lists keywords with their search volumes, then cluster them.
Carry each cluster into the topical map tab and assign: primary keyword, secondary keywords, page type (collection, product or blog post), URL, main keyword volume, and current ranking.
Mark whether the page is published or not.
For published pages, record the decision: needs a content refresh, leave as is, or apply SEO quick wins.
For unpublished pages, the goal is simply to publish that piece of content.
Keep the two tabs separate — keyword map for research, topical map for the live plan — so volume prioritisation stays visible while you work.
caveats: The source describes its own template workflow; the specific columns are the presenter's structure, not a standard.
The template link is referenced in the original training material.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Shopify Collection Page Content Stack
cards.summary: Layered content template for collection pages: short description, detailed description, FAQ accordion, featured reviews.
cards.use_when: Building or rewriting a Shopify collection/category page template to rank and convert.
steps: Place a short collection description (2 lines max) below the H1 and above the product grid. It should state what the collection is or why to buy it — mobile users skip large text blocks, so keep it terse.

Add a detailed collection description below the product grid, 500–1,000 words. Cover what differentiates the collection from other brands, features and benefits, certifications, and usage instructions.
Insert an FAQ accordion below the detailed description; closed accordions cost no visible space so they don't hurt UX.
Feature 3 manually selected product reviews at the bottom of the page, choosing reviews that contain the target keyword so they help SEO and conversion.
Use simple HTML or custom metafields for the featured reviews rather than a heavy review widget, to avoid slowing the page.
caveats: The source frames collecting at least 80% of SEO revenue through collection pages as its own prior claim — treat it as the presenter's heuristic, not a measured benchmark.
Content must improve user experience; AI-stuffed keyword content that doesn't help users won't help rankings.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Splitting One Shopify Description into Short and Detailed Sections
cards.summary: Technical method to serve a short collection description above and a long one below the product grid using Shopify template code.
cards.use_when: A theme only exposes one collection description field but you need both a short top summary and a long bottom description.
steps: Find the collection template liquid file and locate where `collection.description` is output.
Replace that output with a split-code snippet so the part of the description typed above the split marker renders in the original position (below the H1, above the grid).
Add a second snippet below the product grid so anything typed after the split marker renders there as the detailed description.
Alternative: use a 'read more' link — show two lines below the H1 and reveal the long description on click by pasting the provided theme code and a small JavaScript snippet.
If implementation is unclear, paste the code into a general AI assistant and ask it to walk through adapting it to your theme.
caveats: Requires editing theme liquid and HTML directly; back up the theme before editing.
Code is for the theme as demonstrated; verify it works with your specific Shopify theme version.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Why Add Unique Content to Hundreds of Collection Pages
cards.summary: Strategic rationale for adding human-written content to every collection page: big retailers can't or won't, so it's your ranking opening.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest in content for each collection page when you have many collections.
steps: Recognize that large retailers (Amazon, Target) typically serve auto-generated pages built from the search term, usually just a product grid, with no dedicated optimized collection page.
Accept that adding content to 200–500 pages is laborious, and treat that difficulty as the competitive moat — competitors won't do it.
Apply the short-description / detailed-description / FAQ / featured-reviews template consistently across collections.
Verify the content is tasteful and user-focused; keyword stuffing or AI content that doesn't improve UX won't deliver.
caveats: The claim that this outranks competitors is the presenter's opinion, not a measured guarantee.
Content quality bar applies — volume alone without UX value won't help.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Product Detail Info and Faceted Navigation on Collection Pages
cards.summary: Add specification-style product details and filtering directly on collection pages to improve UX and relevance.
cards.use_when: Optimizing a collection page for user experience and adding unique content, especially with many SKUs.
steps: Show product details (size, color, pickup/delivery or similar attributes) directly in the collection grid so customers don't need to click into a product to decide.
For brands with large catalogs (the source uses ~200 SKUs as the threshold), add faceted navigation so customers can filter the product grid and find items.
Treat the added on-page detail as extra unique content that signals relevance to search engines.
Combine product details with the standard content sections (short description, detailed description, FAQ, reviews).
caveats: Faceted navigation typically requires an app or theme configuration; verify the current setup and avoid creating crawlable duplicate URLs.
No specific traffic or ranking numbers are promised.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: FAQ Accordions on Collection and Product Pages
cards.summary: Add FAQ accordions sourced from People Also Ask, with lightweight code and structured data.
cards.use_when: Adding an FAQ section to collection or product pages to answer pre-purchase questions and earn rich results.
steps: Source questions by searching your target term in Google and reviewing the People Also Ask section.
Implement as a closed accordion so the section doesn't dominate the page visually.
Add a lightweight, accessible FAQ answering genuine pre-purchase questions; do not justify it with promised FAQ rich results.
Place the accordion after the detailed description (collection pages) or in the FAQ section of the product template.
caveats: The source notes FAQ-rich-snippet display has been declining on the SERP — implement anyway for UX and potential value.
Structured data does not guarantee rich snippet display.
Use store FAQs to answer shopper questions. Do not promise Google FAQ rich results or treat FAQ markup as a ranking requirement; verify current search feature support.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Featured Reviews on Collection Pages
cards.summary: Manually place 3 keyword-rich customer reviews at the bottom of collection pages for both conversion and SEO.
cards.use_when: Improving collection page conversion and adding unique content without a heavy review app.
steps: Manually select three strong product reviews to feature at the bottom of the collection page.
Choose reviews that contain your target keywords so the section carries SEO value alongside conversion value.
Implement with simple HTML in the description or custom metafields rather than a review app or widget that could slow the page.
Refresh featured reviews periodically to keep them relevant to the collection.
caveats: The source asserts there are no downsides — verify reviews are genuine and compliant with platform disclosure rules.
Review apps vary; using metafields may require theme tweaks.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Deciding Whether to Rank a Product Page vs a Collection Page
cards.summary: Use SERP inspection of the target term to decide whether to build a product page or a collection page.
cards.use_when: Allocating SEO effort to either a product page or a collection page for a specific keyword.
steps: Google the exact search term and observe what type of pages rank — product pages or category/collection pages.
If results are mostly collection pages (e.g., 'flower seeds'), rank a collection page; you're unlikely to outrank the format Google prefers with a product page.
If results are mostly product pages (e.g., 'lavender essential oil'), build the product page.
When results are mixed — which the source calls common — ask what a customer would want: a single specific product or a choice of options; match the format to that intent.
Cross-check with keyword volume: if the specific product has no search volume, target the broader term with a collection page instead, or noindex the product page.
caveats: SERP composition changes over time; re-check before committing.
The presenter's framing of 'follow what Google prefers' is an operational heuristic, not a rule.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Evaluating Search Volume Before Investing in Product Page SEO
cards.summary: Decide whether to optimize, or noindex, product pages based on whether their (often invented) names actually get searched.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to spend SEO effort across a large product catalog with many custom-named SKUs.
steps: Check whether each product's name or specific attributes have search volume.

If products are made-up names (e.g., fishing lures like 'Hack Attack Flipping Jig') or hyper-specific fabric items ('silk/spandex stretch crepe sheen blue' vs navy), optimize the broader collection pages instead (e.g., 'bass fishing lures', 'eco-friendly fabrics').
If individual product pages do have volume (e.g., 'rosemary essential oil'), rank them — even lower volume, they attract highly targeted traffic.
For product pages with no search volume, consider removing them from the index rather than investing resources in ranking them.
caveats: This is a prioritizing heuristic, not a strict rule — a store's business model and product mix can change the call.
Conversion rate figures for product-page SEO traffic (presented as 5–15%) are the source's observed range, not a benchmark guarantee.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Handling Discontinued and Out-of-Stock Product Pages
cards.summary: Never delete ranking discontinued/out-of-stock product pages — keep them live with replacement CTAs or restock notifications.
cards.use_when: Managing product pages for items that are discontinued or temporarily out of stock.
steps: Keep the page active rather than deleting it — deletion sends the URL to a 404 and loses any traffic and rankings it held.
For discontinued products, replace the purchase option with a button linking to related or alternative products (the source references REI's 'shop similar products' pattern).
For out-of-stock products, keep the page and replace add-to-cart with a 'notify me when available' subscription (the source references Brewmate's pattern).
Acknowledge that rankings may decline temporarily if competitors have the item in stock — zero purchase conversion signals the page isn't satisfying searchers.
Restock quickly and implement the above to make recovery of rankings more likely.
Use 'shop similar products' and notification CTAs to keep users engaged so search engines still see the page as valuable.
caveats: Ranking loss during stockouts is the source's interpretation, not a documented algorithm rule.
Notify-me requires email capture and back-in-stock tooling.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Product Page Content Template for Shopify SEO
cards.summary: Structured product page layout: short description, features/benefits, spec table, detailed description, FAQ, reviews, images.
cards.use_when: Rebuilding a product page template for SEO and conversion on Shopify.
steps: H1 = product name plus target keyword.
Short description on top: 50–150 words explaining what it is and why to buy; include the product name.
Features and benefits: bullet points highlighting unique features (most users skim).
Specifications in a table format — includes technical specs, weight, dimensions, size, material — because tables can earn rich snippets and improve clarity.
Detailed description below: 500–1,000 words covering differentiators, expanded benefits, ingredients, suggested use; keep it tight since the goal is still conversion.
FAQ accordion answering pre-purchase questions with lightweight code that auto-adds FAQ structured data.
Product reviews at the bottom; collect reviews via post-purchase email asking for a review in exchange for a discount.
caveats: Spec-table rich snippets have been appearing less on the SERP, per the source — keep the table for UX and possible rich results anyway.
Word-count ranges (50–150, 500–1,000) are the source's recommended ranges, not a measured rule.
Use store FAQs to answer shopper questions. Do not promise Google FAQ rich results or treat FAQ markup as a ranking requirement; verify current search feature support.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Product Page Images, Alt Text, and XML Sitemap
cards.summary: Image SEO for product pages: descriptive filenames, alt text, WebP/JPEG, compression, lazy loading, sitemap inclusion.
cards.use_when: Optimizing images on product pages to improve conversion and SEO, and ensuring images are indexable.
steps: Show the product clearly, highlight key features, and demonstrate usage (including lifestyle photos so customers can imagine using the product).
Avoid generic filenames; name images with the product name plus what's happening in the image.
Write descriptive alt text describing what's happening in the image.
Use WebP or JPEG to lower file size without losing quality.
Optimize image dimensions and compress files; a one-click image optimization app/plugin is suggested for doing this at scale.
Implement lazy loading so images load as needed rather than all at once.
Create an XML sitemap that lists all images, not just the primary product image.
caveats: Compression tools and apps change; verify the current app or plugin interface and compatibility with your theme.
Sitemaps support discovery; submission does not guarantee crawling, indexing or rankings.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Product Page Structured Data: Product, Review, FAQ, Breadcrumb
cards.summary: The four schema types product pages should use, and why rich snippets increase CTR.
cards.use_when: Adding or verifying structured data on product pages to earn rich snippets.
steps: Implement Product schema (price range, availability, return policy can show on the SERP).
Implement Review schema to get star ratings; make sure the review app you use supports review markup out of the box, and double-check that it's active.
Implement FAQPage schema via a lightweight FAQ accordion.
Implement Breadcrumb schema alongside on-page breadcrumbs for the SERP breadcrumb display.
Treat schema as a CTR lever: the source contrasts a listing lacking rich results (Wayfair, one line, less SERP real estate) with one showing star rating, price range, and return policy (Walmart).
caveats: Most review apps implement review markup, but the source notes you must always verify it's working.
Rich snippet display isn't guaranteed even with correct schema.
Use store FAQs to answer shopper questions. Do not promise Google FAQ rich results or treat FAQ markup as a ranking requirement; verify current search feature support.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Breadcrumbs, Tag-Style Category Links, and Related Product Modules
cards.summary: On-page navigation elements that support internal linking and user navigation on product pages.
cards.use_when: Improving product page navigation, internal linking, and discoverability on Shopify.
steps: Add breadcrumb links at the top of the product page (e.g., Best Buy pattern) and apply Breadcrumb schema for the SERP breadcrumb display.
Add tag-style category links where applicable so customers can explore related collections, categories, or products based on how they found the item.
Add 'frequently bought together' or 'products related to this item' sections recommending similar or complementary products.
Treat these as both conversion and SEO tools: they increase average order value and improve navigation, and easier navigation helps search engines crawl the site.
caveats: Keep related-product links genuinely relevant; irrelevant links dilute the signals the modules are meant to create.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: When a Shopify Store Needs a Blog
cards.summary: Blog content ranks informational terms and, more importantly, supports collection page rankings via internal linking and topical authority.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest in a blog and how much to prioritize it for an ecommerce store.
steps: Identify search terms with informational intent that shopping pages can't rank for — e.g., 'best cold press juicer' returns informational results, so a listicle/blog review is required.
Publish the blog post (and related posts on juicer types and usage) alongside the shopping pages so you capture that traffic.

Recognize the main benefit per the source: blog posts support the rankings of shopping/collection pages through internal linking and topical authority — the source claims ~80% of SEO revenue typically flows through collection pages.
Convert blog traffic into revenue by embedding direct product CTAs, capturing emails via a discount popup, and running retargeting ads to blog visitors who didn't purchase.
caveats: The 80% revenue-through-collection-pages figure is the presenter's heuristic, not a universal calculation.
Informational content takes time to rank; treat it as support for commercial pages.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Optimizing Blog Post Titles, H1, URL, and Meta Description
cards.summary: The three on-page SEO elements for blogs plus the meta description, and where to set them in Shopify.
cards.use_when: Creating or auditing a Shopify blog post for on-page SEO.
steps: Title tag: put the target keyword at the start, stay within ~60 characters (the source's guidance), and add long-tail keywords or modifiers where possible.
H1: keep it simple — essentially the target keyword, e.g., 'types of women's underwear'.
URL: keep it short and use the target keyword, mirroring the H1.
In Shopify, scroll to the bottom of the blog post editor and click 'Edit website SEO' to set the page title, meta description, and URL handle.
Include the target keyword in the meta description — it doesn't materially help rankings per the source, but the keyword appears bolded on the SERP, improving click-through rate.
caveats: Character limits are the presenter's stated guidance; SERP truncation varies.
Meta descriptions affect CTR, not rankings per the source.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Writing Blog Content That Beats What Ranks
cards.summary: Match or exceed the structure and comprehensiveness of the pages currently ranking for your target term.
cards.use_when: Drafting a blog post meant to rank for a specific informational keyword.
steps: Source post ideas from your topical map (built during keyword research) rather than random keyword lists.
Inspect the pages currently ranking for the term; note their structure and headings.
Make your post cover at least the same topics and subtopics, ideally more, so it provides comprehensive coverage of related questions your audience asks.
Judge depth, not just breadth — topical authority considers how thorough each post is, so avoid thin content.
Break up text with a mix of images, videos, infographics, tables, and charts; the source cites Quirky Quinn's infographic-heavy 'types of women's underwear' post as an example.
Use these visuals to influence engagement metrics (bounce rate, time on page) that indirectly help SEO.
caveats: No specific content-length or visitor-duration benchmarks are established.
Visual engagement effects on SEO are described as indirect, not guaranteed.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Embedding Product CTAs and Internal Links in Blog Posts
cards.summary: Place relevant product CTAs and contextual internal links to convert blog readers and pass authority to shopping pages.
cards.use_when: Monetizing blog traffic and using blog posts to strengthen product/collection pages.
steps: Embed relevant direct product CTAs within posts or at the end, chosen to match the post topic (e.g., a hip-and-joint-supplements post ends with a CTA to that product).
Build internal links from blog posts to shopping pages and to other relevant blog posts, creating a thematic network that helps search engines understand the site and distributes page authority.

Instead of building all backlinks to shopping pages (which looks unnatural), build backlinks to good blog posts and internally link those posts to shopping pages to distribute link equity more naturally.
Implement the internal links deliberately — the source notes many agencies publish blog content without appropriate internal links, wasting the SEO value.
caveats: Internal linking to shopping pages distributes authority but doesn't replace direct backlinks entirely.
Keep links relevant; link-stuffing dilutes relevance signals.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Building Topical Authority One Cluster at a Time
cards.summary: Fully cover a single topic cluster before expanding to adjacent topics so search engines recognize your expertise.
cards.use_when: Planning blog/content production across topics for an ecommerce store.
steps: Pick one topic cluster (e.g., cold press juicers) and publish all content around that topic: how to make cold press juice, whether it's healthy, why it's better, etc.
Understand that one collection page alone won't build authority — comprehensive coverage of the topic is what establishes topical relevance.

Once authority is established in a cluster, expand gradually to related topics (e.g., masticating juicers) by creating a connection post such as 'cold press vs masticating juicers' first, then building out that next cluster.
Use the approach to differentiate from large retailers (Amazon, Target, eBay) that can't produce these supporting blog posts and therefore can't claim industry-level topical authority.
caveats: The 'one cluster at a time' sequencing is the source's recommended method, not a proven universal rule.
Timelines vary; no specific ranking timeline is guaranteed.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: What Ecommerce Link Building Is and Why It Matters
cards.summary: Backlinks act as votes of confidence; competitive keywords are won by sites with hundreds or thousands of backlinks.
cards.use_when: Planning off-page SEO for a Shopify or ecommerce brand.
steps: Treat backlinks as votes from other sites signaling that yours is valuable and trustworthy to search engines.
Check the backlink profiles of the top-ranking sites for your competitive keywords — the source says you'll typically see hundreds or thousands of backlinks.
Build a deliberate backlink strategy rather than relying on on-page SEO alone.
Understand the five link types covered as relevant to ecommerce brands: foundational, guest posting/niche edits, and others to be detailed in the full link-building training.
caveats: The presenter is Chris Graham, co-founder of 607 Media, in charge of off-page SEO — treat his claims as his professional view.
Backlink counts cited are the source's general observation, not a fixed benchmark for any niche.

Editorial qualification: paid placements must use rel="sponsored" or rel="nofollow"; do not buy unqualified links to manipulate rankings. Assess sponsored placements by relevant referral traffic and commercial value, not promised ranking credit.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Foundational Links for a New Ecommerce Site
cards.summary: Basic directory and social links establish that your store exists and signal what it's about.
cards.use_when: Onboarding a new ecommerce site with no backlink profile.
steps: Claim basic links such as business directories and social media profiles.
Treat these as easy-to-acquire foundation signals rather than ranking drivers — they tell search engines your site exists and is not fake.
Use them to send early relevance signals about what your site is about.
Layer guest posting and niche edits on top of foundational links once they're in place.
caveats: Foundational links alone won't rank competitive terms; they're a starting base, not a strategy.

Editorial qualification: paid placements must use rel="sponsored" or rel="nofollow"; do not buy unqualified links to manipulate rankings. Assess sponsored placements by relevant referral traffic and commercial value, not promised ranking credit.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Map the five link-building types to an ecommerce backlink mix
cards.summary: Foundational, guest post, niche edit, expert-quote, linkable-asset and digital-PR links each play a different role in a Shopify store's off-page profile.
cards.use_when: Planning a quarterly off-page SEO plan for a store and deciding where to spend outreach time and budget.
steps: Treat foundational links (social profiles, business/citation directories, Web 2.0 sites) as the base layer that signals your site exists and what it is about; the source says these are mostly free and Google-endorsed, so build them first before anything else.

Make guest posts and niche edits the 'bread and butter' for ecommerce: guest posts let you control content, anchor text and the target URL, so you can point a link from an interior-design blog to a specific curtain collection page. Niche edits add your link to an already-published, already-trafficked article, which the source argues is faster and often more powerful because existing pages pass link equity immediately.

Use expert-quote platforms (the source calls it HARO, now rebranded Connectively — verify the current name/interface) to answer journalist queries in your category, e.g. advice on choosing curtains for bright rooms, and earn editorial links when quoted.
Build linkable assets (comprehensive guides, infographics, calculators) on your own site, then do light outreach to relevant sites telling them the asset exists and asking for a link.
Use digital PR — a data-driven insight or press release pitched to journalists and bloggers — when you want the highest-quality editorial links.

Decide per link whether to target the domain or a collection/product page: the source recommends 50–75% of links to the main domain in the first ~3 months, with the rest on low-hanging-fruit collection pages.
caveats: The 50–75% domain-share rule is the source's rule of thumb for the first three months, to be adjusted afterward based on competition and results.
Tool names (Semrush, Ahrefs, HARO/Connectively, Snov.io, Hunter) change interfaces and pricing — verify current functionality.

Editorial qualification: paid placements must use rel="sponsored" or rel="nofollow"; do not buy unqualified links to manipulate rankings. Assess sponsored placements by relevant referral traffic and commercial value, not promised ranking credit.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Judge a backlink's quality before pursuing it
cards.summary: Six factors — follow status, anchor text, topical relevance, authority metrics, link target page and site quality — determine whether a backlink helps or hurts your store.
cards.use_when: Vetting a prospect site or an inbound link offer before you write a guest post, accept a placement or pay a fee.
steps: Check dofollow vs nofollow: dofollow links pass value; nofollow passes little. The source says a natural mix is fine, but focus effort on dofollow links.

Review anchor text: the visible clickable text should be descriptive and relevant, e.g. 'office chairs' for an office-chair page, so search engines receive the right topical signal. Keep it natural — over-optimized anchor patterns stand out against competitors.

Assess page-level relevance and site-level relevance: the article should relate to the page it links to, and the host site should sit in or near your industry (an interior-design site is a good fit for a curtain brand).
Check authority metrics (Moz Domain Authority, Ahrefs Domain Rating): aim higher, but treat them as manipulable — read them alongside the other factors rather than as the sole test.

Consider the linked page: send links to the page you actually want to rank, such as a collection page, but don't wildly exceed competitor link counts — if competitors have ~10 links to a page, building 30 'sticks out like a sore thumb' and risks penalties.
Prefer a few high-quality links over many low-quality ones.
caveats: Authority metrics can be gamed; the source explicitly says to interpret them in context, not in isolation.
The source presents over-building relative to competitors as a penalty risk; this is the presenter's framing, not a stated Google threshold.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Run a link-gap analysis and set a monthly link target
cards.summary: Compare your filtered dofollow referring-domain count against SEO competitors to derive a concrete monthly backlink goal.
cards.use_when: Setting link-building targets for a store and deciding how many placements per month to buy or earn.
steps: In Semrush or Ahrefs, filter your backlinks to dofollow only and to referring domains with DR/DA of at least 30 (the source's chosen floor). Count the result — e.g. 105 referring domains.
Apply the identical filters to your SEO competitors' profiles; the source analyzed three or more and averaged around 203 referring domains in its example.
Subtract your count from the competitor average (203 − 105 = ~98 referring domains needed) to size the gap.
Convert the gap into a cadence: spreading 98 links over 24 months is about 4 new links per month, but the source recommends aiming for roughly 6–8 per month to keep pace as competitors also build.
Re-run the link-gap analysis periodically to confirm you are still competitive.
caveats: The 105/203/98 figures are an illustrative example, not a benchmark for any particular niche.
The DR/DA 30 filter is a source-specific heuristic; adjust the floor upward if your own profile is stronger.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Screen spam links with a five-point checklist
cards.summary: Before accepting or paying for a placement, verify the site is real, topically relevant, has organic traffic and has quality backlinks of its own.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a paid link offer, an inbound guest-post pitch or an email offering backlinks for a store.
steps: Check it is a real site people care about: open it, judge design and content quality, and see whether it writes about one industry or about everything — general 'we cover anything' blogs are often link-selling sites to avoid.
Check history with the Wayback Machine: if the domain previously covered a different topic (the source's example: a former casino site now presenting as interior design), treat that as a red flag.
Check niche relevance: the site should discuss what your brand is about. Avoid general blogs built solely to sell links.
Check organic traffic: look for real traffic that is trending upward or at least stable. The source's bare minimum is 1,000 visitors per month, and sudden traffic dips can signal a penalty.
Check the site's own backlink quality: if the host site's inbound links are poor, it passes poor link equity to you.
Avoid bought links from cheap marketplaces (the source cites Fiverr and unsolicited backlink emails) — low quality at best, ranking damage at worst.
caveats: The 1,000-visitors-per-month minimum is the source's stated bare minimum, not an industry standard.
The source notes you can double-check cheap links because some may be fine, but says they usually are not.

Editorial qualification: paid placements must use rel="sponsored" or rel="nofollow"; do not buy unqualified links to manipulate rankings. Assess sponsored placements by relevant referral traffic and commercial value, not promised ranking credit.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Build foundational links and citations as the base layer
cards.summary: Set up social profiles, directory listings and Web 2.0 pages so search engines can identify your store as a real entity before you pursue editorial links.
cards.use_when: Launching a new store or a new brand with no backlink profile, before starting guest posting or outreach.
steps: Build foundational links — social profiles, business directory and local citations, plus Web 2.0 pages such as Medium or Behance. The source frames this as 'entity stacking': helping Google understand who you are so it can rank you.
Do not just create the profile and drop your URL in the about page: fill in the full business information and post some content and images so the listing sends strong identity signals.

For citations, prepare a standard data set: business name, owner name, address, city, telephone, website URL, business description, target keywords (e.g. shopping-page keywords) and logo. The source says you likely already have this and AI can help draft descriptions.
Target at least 30 foundational links — the source's own internal target, described as safe and free, though fewer may suffice.
Consider outsourcing citation building, as the source does, because doing it manually takes a lot of time.
caveats: The 30-link target is the source's internal goal, not a calculated requirement.
Vanity or incomplete profiles add little; the value is in filled-out, active listings.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Prioritize low-hanging-fruit collection pages for links
cards.summary: Use Semrush's organic research to find pages ranking in positions 4–10, then send links there because they are closest to converting rankings into revenue.
cards.use_when: Choosing which collection or category pages to build links to this month on a store.
steps: Open Semrush's Organic Research tool for your domain and filter positions to 4–10.
The output is the set of your pages sitting on page one but not yet in the top three — the source's 'low-hanging fruit' that can be pushed into the top three fastest.
Pick roughly three to five of these pages per month depending on your link-building budget, and save them as your monthly link targets alongside the main domain.
Balance this against the source's 50–75% domain-share rule for the first three months: juice the root domain while also pushing the easiest collection pages.
Rebalance toward collection pages after a few months based on competition and observed results.
caveats: The instruction is written for Semrush but the source says it is translatable to Ahrefs.
The 3–5 pages and 50–75% domain split are rules of thumb, explicitly dependent on brand age and existing link profile.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Prospect link targets by scraping competitors' guest-post backlinks
cards.summary: Identify true SEO competitors, scrape their placement-type backlinks in Semrush, then filter the export to reachable, healthy, relevant sites.
cards.use_when: Building an outreach prospect list for a store's guest posting and niche edit campaign.
steps: Determine SEO competition — the brands winning the SERPs for your target keywords, which may differ from your brand competitors. Use Semrush's Keyword Overview to read the SERP for a key term such as 'sheer curtains'.

Pick mid-sized niche competitors rather than giants: the source excluded Target, Walmart and Ikea because scraping their backlinks yields mostly unreachable or irrelevant prospects. Collect at least five SEO competitor domains.

In Semrush Backlink Analytics, open the Backlinks tab for a competitor and filter to: dofollow links, one link per referring domain, 'content' placement (so the link sits inside article content, implying a guest post), and platform = blog. Export the results.

Run the exported domains through Semrush's Bulk Analysis tool set to root domain, then filter to sites with monthly visits greater than 1,000 and an authority score of 15 or above (raise the threshold if your own profile is stronger).
Repeat for the other SEO competitors to build a refined prospect list.
If the list is thin, expand prospecting beyond SEO competitors to any site in your niche, or in adjacent niches (for curtain brands: interior design, home improvement, family/mom blogs).
caveats: The 1,000 visits and authority-score 15 thresholds are the source's heuristics.
Stay natural: the source warns against clearly irrelevant placements, e.g. an outdoor blog linking to a curtain brand.

Editorial qualification: paid placements must use rel="sponsored" or rel="nofollow"; do not buy unqualified links to manipulate rankings. Assess sponsored placements by relevant referral traffic and commercial value, not promised ranking credit.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Find contact details for link prospects
cards.summary: Use email-finding tools for speed, or fall back to manual site inspection, personal emails and contact forms.
cards.use_when: Turning a filtered prospect list into a sendable outreach list for guest posts or niche edits.
steps: Use a paid email-finding tool as the primary route — the source recommends Snov.io based on its results and clean lists, and notes Hunter.io as another option used by some SEOs; verify current pricing and data coverage.

If not paying for tools, go site by site into the contact page and look for a named person's email (chris@domain.com) rather than a generic inbox (info@domain.com), because a real person is less likely to bin the message.
Check the about page for owner names, then find their social profiles and reach out there.
Use site contact forms: the source says these almost always reach the site owner, and a well-crafted message can get a reply.
Send direct messages on social platforms referencing their site and asking whether they accept guest posts.
caveats: Manual research takes far more time and may not yield a usable contact, which is why the source prefers paid tools.
Tool names and capabilities change; confirm the current product before subscribing.

Editorial qualification: paid placements must use rel="sponsored" or rel="nofollow"; do not buy unqualified links to manipulate rankings. Assess sponsored placements by relevant referral traffic and commercial value, not promised ranking credit.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Write outreach subject lines and bodies that get opened and answered
cards.summary: Personalize subject lines with curiosity, humor or a question, and keep the body short, specific and clear about wanting a dofollow guest post.
cards.use_when: Drafting the first outreach email to a blog or site owner to request a guest post placement.
steps: Make the subject line both highly relevant and attention-grabbing — the source says if it only grabs attention without relevance, it reads as spam. Include the recipient's name and their domain, e.g. 'Quick question, Chris, about curtains.com'.
Use curiosity: a question about their own site works because it piques the owner's interest.
Use humor where it fits your niche — the source says jokes in the subject plus a matching answer in the body have worked well for them, and suggests testing combinations of tactics in your own niche.
In the body, state your intention to write content for their site and the type of content you specialize in, and make clear a dofollow link is desired.
Say explicitly that you are willing to pay any publishing fee if required — the source says you will most likely pay for these links.
Keep it short and to the point, and customize the free template rather than sending it verbatim: the source argues generic templates underperform because everyone has the same one.
caveats: The source states Google does not officially support buying links and may treat manipulative links as link spam, while asserting that paid links are widely used and work when done properly — treat this as the source's position, not a safe harbor.
The claim that a well-crafted message beats ~70% of template users is the source's assertion, not a measured benchmark.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Warm Up Cold Outreach Sending Accounts Before Guest Post Pitching
cards.summary: Set up cold email sending accounts for guest post outreach by warming them up and ramping volume slowly to stay out of spam filters.
cards.use_when: Preparing the email sending infrastructure for a link-building or blogger-outreach campaign on behalf of an ecommerce store.
steps: Choose an outreach sending tool. The source recommends Instantly as its top pick; Hunter (for finding prospect emails) also has an outreach feature, plus Lemlist and GMass are named options. Verify current pricing and features, as tools change.

Warm up each sending account first: send a small volume of emails that are designed to be opened, read, and replied to (not cold pitches), gradually increasing that volume until the account builds a healthy sending reputation.
After warm-up, begin with roughly 20 cold emails per day from each account and increase little by little over a few weeks.

Limit how many email accounts you create under one domain — the source says too many 'at-yourdomain.com' accounts starts to look suspicious. If you need high volume, buy additional related domains and set up accounts under those.
Complete the technical setup (SPF/DKIM-type configuration) the platform guides you through before sending.
caveats: Tool names, free trials, and interfaces change — verify on the provider site.
The 20-emails-per-day starting figure is the source's heuristic, not a universal rule.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Make Guest Post Pitches Unique Instead of Reusing a Template
cards.summary: Generic outreach templates get ignored, so tailor each pitch to the specific site's niche and audience to beat the template-using majority.
cards.use_when: Writing the outreach email to a blog or site you want to earn a guest post or link from.
steps: Start from a short, direct template: introduce yourself by name and domain, and state your request plainly.
Before sending, research the specific site and its audience, then clearly explain what the value of your proposed post would be for that audience.
Personalize the message so it reads as crafted for that site rather than mass-sent.
Keep it to a quick question format that is easy for the recipient to reply to.

Expect to outperform the roughly 70% of senders who rely on a generic template — the source's claim, based on the reasoning that a widely-shared free template loses effectiveness as more people use it.
caveats: The 70% figure is the presenter's assertion, not a measured benchmark.
Template personalization improves reply odds but does not guarantee acceptance.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Close and Negotiate the Guest Post Link, Then Run Final Vetting
cards.summary: Structure the back half of an outreach conversation — vet the site, negotiate terms, and always drive toward securing the link.
cards.use_when: Replying to a positive outreach response and deciding whether and at what price to place a guest post or link on that site.
steps: Treat any reply asking for clarification as a positive signal, not just an outright yes.

Run final vetting on the site: check language/locale, security, organic traffic, and other quality metrics using SEMrush or your tool of choice. Much of this may already have been filtered earlier, but double-check before committing.

Once the site passes vetting, negotiate terms — if you are buying the link, discuss price. Use SEMrush Authority Score-based pricing benchmarks as rough guidance, but treat them as flexible: a highly relevant site with strong traffic may reasonably cost more.
Remember the goal throughout: secure the link, whether free or paid. Each step should move you closer to that.
caveats: Pricing benchmarks are the source's rough guidance and can shift with inflation and time.
A positive reply is a question or interest, not yet a placed link — keep negotiating.

Editorial qualification: paid placements must use rel="sponsored" or rel="nofollow"; do not buy unqualified links to manipulate rankings. Assess sponsored placements by relevant referral traffic and commercial value, not promised ranking credit.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Write a Guest Post That Fits the Host Site's Audience
cards.summary: Craft guest post content around the host blog's readers — not your store's customers — so the post reads as genuinely valuable and earns the link.
cards.use_when: Writing a guest post for a partner blog (e.g., an interior design site) that will link back to one of your store's pages, such as a product collection.
steps: Identify the host site's actual audience and write for them. Example: for an interior design blog, write for interior designers and design enthusiasts, not for your curtain shoppers.
Pick a topic that is directly relevant to the page you want to link to. For a sheer curtains collection page on a curtain store, the guest post should be about sheer curtains.

Define your target page first, then generate title ideas — you can use AI (e.g., ChatGPT) to brainstorm titles and descriptions that combine the target keyword with the host blog's theme, then refine the output through iteration.
Choose a title that contains the target keyword and also fits the host blog's topic (the source's example: a title including 'sheer curtains' for an interior design blog).
Write 600–1,200 words unless the host specifies otherwise; note that some hosts who want longer, high-quality content are willing to publish without a fee, so a free link may be worth extra length.
Keep grammar, structure, and coherence human-readable; the source's reasoning is that content readable by humans is readable by search engines.
Offer fresh insight and a friendly, approachable tone — a good guest post can also position your brand as a thought leader in its niche.
caveats: Content-length guidance varies (the source gives both 500–1,000 and 600–1,200); treat it as directional, and defer to the host's requirements.
AI output needs refinement — the source notes you often have to 'wrestle' with it.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Place Guest Post Anchors Naturally and Near the Top
cards.summary: Embed the backlink anchor inside a relevant sentence near the top of the post rather than isolating it on an awkward 'check us out' line.
cards.use_when: Adding the link back to your store's collection or product page while writing a guest post.
steps: Write the anchor into a relevant sentence within the body content, close to the top of the post.
Aim for seamless integration where the link enhances rather than interrupts the reading experience.
Avoid isolating the link in a standalone spot (e.g., 'check out sheer curtains here'). The source notes some sites require this format for link inserts, but it is not ideal.
Incorporate the target keyword near the beginning of the title where practical, and use keywords in subheadings only where they fit naturally — forcing them in is risky.
Prioritize natural placement over hitting every keyword-stuffing opportunity.
caveats: Some hosts mandate a fixed anchor placement (often for link inserts); when they do, accept the constrained format.
Over-optimizing headings with keywords can read as unnatural and is risky.

Editorial qualification: paid placements must use rel="sponsored" or rel="nofollow"; do not buy unqualified links to manipulate rankings. Assess sponsored placements by relevant referral traffic and commercial value, not promised ranking credit.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Diversify Anchor Text and Mirror Competitor Backlink Profiles
cards.summary: Use mostly partial-match, URL, brand, and miscellaneous anchors rather than exact matches, and calibrate the mix by studying your top competitors' backlink profiles.
cards.use_when: Deciding what anchor text to use when placing guest posts or link inserts to a specific store page.
steps: Understand the anchor types: exact (identical to the target keyword, e.g., 'sheer curtains'), partial (includes keyword words or adds to them, e.g., 'sheer curtains like these'), URL (the literal page URL), brand (your store name), topical (related terms like 'home decor curtains'), and miscellaneous ('click here' or the linked page's title).
Use mostly partials, URLs, and miscellaneous anchors in the early months of link building — this is the safest default.
Reserve exact-match anchors for very good, high-value sites, and even then use only one or a few. Using the same exact anchor across every backlink can look unnatural to search engines.
Use synonyms and near-variations of your keyword to add partial-match diversity.
To determine the ideal mix, analyze the backlink profiles of your top three competitors — match the anchor-type ratio that dominates your space so you don't stand out as an outlier.
caveats: The source says an unnatural ratio is a risk to avoid, not a guaranteed penalty — 'better safe than sorry.'
Rigid ratios can be relaxed once your profile is more established (the source suggests around months six to seven you can start optimizing further).
Exact-match ratios are the source's opinion, not a search-engine-stated rule.

Editorial qualification: paid placements must use rel="sponsored" or rel="nofollow"; do not buy unqualified links to manipulate rankings. Assess sponsored placements by relevant referral traffic and commercial value, not promised ranking credit.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide to Shopify SEO - Full Course (4+ Hour Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Run Final Checks After a Guest Post Goes Live
cards.summary: Verify the live link meets your requirements before counting it as a success.
cards.use_when: After a host publishes your guest post, to confirm the link is correct and valuable.
steps: Check that the link resolves to the intended store page; paid or sponsored links must be qualified with sponsored or nofollow rather than requiring do-follow.
Confirm the link is contextual — it sits in a good, relevant sentence rather than sticking out awkwardly.
