The source's generalization: for roughly 60% of brands they work with, discount-acquired customers have substantially worse LTV — but this does not apply to all brands (the source cites some 9-figure retailers where it doesn't), so pull your own numbers.
Investigate cause: discounts open you to a wider, price-motivated demographic that doesn't repeat buy once prices return to normal.
Adjust acquisition strategy based on findings — if discounted cohorts are worse, weigh the front-end lift against long-term quality before scaling the offer.
caveats: The ~60% figure is the source's generalization across its client base, not a universal rule.
Some large retailers see no LTV penalty from discount acquisition.
Cohort quality takes time to measure; don't overreact to early signals.
cards.source_name: The Complete E-Commerce Retention Masterclass.docx

cards.title: Use zero-party data to improve acquisition targeting
cards.summary: Collect zero-party data (customer preferences, problems, motivations) to define personas and angles, then feed top- and bottom-customer insights back into paid ads.
cards.use_when: You are designing acquisition creative, personas, or angles, or setting up post-purchase surveys to inform paid media.
steps: Distinguish first-party data (email, phone, name) from zero-party data (personal info shared by the customer): what they do on weekends, what problem the product solves, what they like about the brand.
Collect zero-party data via surveys (post-purchase surveys mentioned as a method) and store it tied to customer records.
Analyze the top 20% of customers (which the source says typically drive 80% of revenue): identify their persona, the angles they responded to, and the offer they purchased on.
Force those top-20% patterns into paid ads and overallocate spend toward them to acquire more lookalike customers.

Analyze the bottom 20% of customers: identify their personas, angles, and offers — often these came in on an angle misaligned with the product (e.g., a skin-health supplement acquired on an 'energy' angle), causing returns, refunds, and no repurchase.
Exclude or reduce front-end spend on misaligned angles even if they show strong front-end ROAS, because the mismatch produces low-quality customers.
caveats: The 20/80 revenue split is the source's stated typical pattern, not a fixed rule.
Misaligned-angle detection often only surfaces through customer support feedback or surveys, so set up a capture mechanism.
Persona and angle insights require connecting post-purchase survey data to ad performance data.
cards.source_name: The Complete E-Commerce Retention Masterclass.docx

cards.title: Measure engaged-segment growth as your core retention KPI
cards.summary: Track the size of your engaged audience over time as the primary email retention metric, rather than optimizing each broadcast in isolation.
cards.use_when: You are setting retention KPIs, reviewing email/SMS performance, or deciding whether a reactivation strategy is working.
steps: Make the primary retention KPI the size of your engaged segment and whether it grows over time, not just per-campaign open or click rates.
Recompute the engaged segment on a consistent lookback window (source examples: ~180/220/280 days) so growth is comparable period to period.
When adding dormant subscribers back into sends, measure how many convert from unengaged to engaged and roll them into the engaged segment to capture net growth.
Use marketing calendar peaks to accelerate engaged growth: push strong offers to re-engaged subscribers when conversion is most likely.
Review engaged-segment growth over months (source cites 6–9 month windows) rather than week to week, and adjust sampling batch sizes accordingly.
Pair segment-growth tracking with broader retention metrics (repeat rate, VIP revenue share) to ensure growth is producing revenue, not just opens.
caveats: Engagement definitions and lookback windows are source-specific; adapt to your lifecycle.
Open rates are increasingly unreliable as an engagement signal; on-site actions like add-to-cart and checkout starts strengthen the definition.
The source's +40% YoY BFCM result is an anecdote, not a benchmark.
cards.source_name: The Complete E-Commerce Retention Masterclass.docx

cards.title: Reward VIPs with exclusivity rather than broad discounts
cards.summary: Give VIPs exclusive products, early access, perks, and experiences instead of treating them like the general list.
cards.use_when: You are designing VIP campaigns, a loyalty program, or flow pathways and want to increase VIP revenue without cheapening the relationship.
steps: Identify your VIP segment (revenue/profit leaders) and separate it from the general list in both campaign and flow builds.
Offer exclusivity rather than discounts: the source cites exclusive products, private sales, early access, offline experiences, and community/event perks as effective VIP rewards.
Use VIP campaigns for reminders about loyalty-program perks and benefits already attached to their account, since VIPs may not track these.
Build VIP branches into automated flows (VIP pathways) so the perks and treatment are consistent beyond campaigns.
Follow the 80% reach / 20% specific-goal campaign split, using VIP-focused campaigns as the more targeted 20% when driving VIP revenue is a goal.
Only invest in VIP programs when VIP revenue is your actual constraint; otherwise prioritize other constraints such as first-to-second order conversion first.
caveats: VIP rewards should not simply mirror general-list tactics; the source advises against treating VIPs like everyone else.
The source cautions against chasing VIP incrementality when your real constraint lies elsewhere.
cards.source_name: The Complete E-Commerce Retention Masterclass.docx

cards.title: Define desired customer emotions before designing the experience
cards.summary: Work backwards from the feelings and behaviors you want customers to have rather than pitching a product first.
cards.use_when: Designing your store's overall experience strategy, or briefing any change to the PDP, cart, post-purchase email or packaging.
steps: Instead of starting with your product and hoping customers adopt it, define the behavioral outputs you want from your customer (reorder, review, refer, subscribe) and work backwards to the proposition and experience that will produce them.
Recall a recent purchase experience of your own, then ask three questions: what happened, how did it make me feel, what did I do about it. Use this to see how feeling drives action.
Map your store's real touchpoints (ad click, PDP, cart, confirmation email, delivery, unboxing, support) and write the intended emotion for each.
Check for imbalance: if every design choice serves business metrics like AOV or urgency, customer trust can be compromised. Consider both rational and emotional needs.
Treat this as a living exercise rather than a one-off project; experiences keep evolving.
caveats: The presenter frames this as a general CX principle, not a tested ecommerce tactic.
Urgency devices like 'only two seats left at this price' were shown as stress-inducing examples, though no ecommerce sales outcome is given.
cards.source_name: _Introduction to Customer Experience (CX).docx

cards.title: Put a 'customer chair' in your merchandising decisions
cards.summary: Use an explicit customer-perspective check so customer needs appear on the agenda before business metrics do.
cards.use_when: Running a weekly trading, merchandising or roadmap meeting for your store where decisions about products, promotions or site changes get made.
steps: Model the practice the presenter attributes to Amazon: an empty 'customer chair' in every meeting room representing the customer, so every decision is tested against 'would our customer like this'.
Adapt for a store team: add a standing first agenda item that states the customer impact of each decision before revenue impact.
Audit whether the customer is present at all in your leadership discussions. When the presenter asks executives for their latest board protocol, the customer is very often not even on the agenda.
When someone argues for a tactic purely on business grounds, ask what the customer feels at that moment of the journey and whether trust is affected.
Consider the side benefit the presenter notes: acting as if the customer is present also tends to make meetings more efficient.
caveats: This is a described Amazon practice, not a measured ecommerce result.
It is a cultural device rather than a metric - pair it with actual customer data.
cards.source_name: _Introduction to Customer Experience (CX).docx

cards.title: Assess where your store sits on the random-to-differentiated CX spectrum
cards.summary: Diagnose whether your customer experience is accidental, designed or differentiated, and budget years not quarters for the transition.
cards.use_when: Reviewing your post-purchase experience and deciding how much to invest in standardising it versus differentiating it.
steps: Classify your current state honestly. Random: interactions vary by who handles them, so ordering, delivery and support outcomes are unpredictable and the presenter says this carries unnecessary cost. Intentional: a shared vision, strategy and cross-functional commitment mean everyone can think customer first, and this is where you start getting profitable. Differentiated: everyone everywhere acts in the customer's interest and you stand apart.
Look for signs of 'random' in your own operation: inconsistent reply times, variable packaging, support answers that depend on which agent picks up the ticket.

Recognise that the presenter estimates roughly 80% of companies are random, about 15% intentional and roughly 5% differentiated, and that a journey from random to differentiated takes about eight years from scratch.
Use the diagnosis to set realistic milestones for your store rather than expecting overnight transformation.
caveats: The 80/15/5 split and the eight-year journey are the presenter's figures, not a calculation you can verify for your own store.
The fish-licensing example she calls least customer-centric is an illustrative anecdote.
cards.source_name: _Introduction to Customer Experience (CX).docx

cards.title: Rank what customers actually value before your product
cards.summary: Corporate attitude, ease of business and helpful support outrank product quality in customers' ranking of favourite brands.
cards.use_when: Prioritising the retention and post-purchase roadmap: which improvement to fund first in support, ease, personalisation or product.
steps: Note the presenter's reported ranking from polling customers on what favourite brands do: number one is corporate attitude and doing good, then being easy to do business with, then being helpful when there is a problem, then the attitude of the people, then personalisation.
Observe that product or service only appears around sixth place, followed by consistency - most of the top of the list is emotional and relational.

Translate this into store budget allocation: audit how much you spend developing things that are not the product, versus how much goes into making the store easier to buy from and support better when something goes wrong.
Run the same reflection on your own customers: which of those attributes would they name as your number one?
Consider that the answer may depend on your product category, so don't take the order as universal.
caveats: This ranking comes from an informal live poll, not stated ecommerce research; treat it as a heuristic.
The presenter explicitly notes importance varies by product and service.
cards.source_name: _Introduction to Customer Experience (CX).docx

cards.title: Use purpose and word of mouth instead of pure differentiation on product
cards.summary: Products, price and quality are hard to differentiate, so treat experience and advocacy as the competitive edge.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to invest for competitive advantage in a crowded product category or a store selling easily-copied goods.
steps: Accept the presenter's premise that product, service, quality and price are difficult to differentiate because copying is fast and cheap; customer experience is the part less easily replicated.
Recognise that all three - product, process and people - together create something to be experienced; experience is not a substitute for the rest.
Act on the mechanism: if a customer can get the same product elsewhere, the reason to return is the experience. Otherwise they buy where it feels better.
Invest in word of mouth, which the presenter cites as trusted more than any other form of marketing (she quotes 92% of customers trusting family and friend recommendations).

Note the market shift she describes: customers buy from companies that do good, employees want to work for them, and investors look for social impact alongside return - the presenter links doing good to 78% of advocacy. Use this as direction, not a guaranteed conversion lever.
caveats: The 78% and 92% figures are quoted by the presenter without sourcing in this session.
Doing good is argued as a commercial advantage, not proven to lift store conversion.
cards.source_name: _Introduction to Customer Experience (CX).docx

cards.title: Ask employees what customers think before surveying customers
cards.summary: Skip intrusive surveys and start with front-line employee judgement plus data you already hold.
cards.use_when: Setting up or rethinking your store's voice-of-customer measurement, satisfaction tracking or post-purchase feedback programme.
steps: Take the presenter's position as an opinion, not a rule: she says do not measure anything that bothers your customers, because people hate surveys, and that millions of better ways exist.
Start with your own homework: find what facts and measures you already possess that reveal the answers you want. She names Lean Six Sigma quality tools as useful here.

If you have a few employees, ask them what they think the customer thinks. They are closest to reality and will feel valued; a store's front-line support and fulfilment staff often hear the real complaints.
Before asking employees, prepare a plan for acting on their feedback, because asking and then doing nothing can break employee performance and trust.
Walk in your customers' shoes: talk to customers and ask them directly rather than sending surveys.
Do not outsource judgements that are yours - the presenter's hotel example argues that asking a guest whether the room was in good shape is something the director should have checked personally.
caveats: This directly contradicts common practice of running satisfaction surveys; the presenter positions it as opposed to many of her global colleagues.
She also warns against surveys that exist to flatter the company or to whip employees, claiming the results are rarely budgeted for or acted on.
cards.source_name: _Introduction to Customer Experience (CX).docx

cards.title: Map the customer journey, not your internal processes
cards.summary: Journey mapping is the core tool for seeing the experience as the customer lives it and deciding where to focus improvements.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing where your post-purchase experience breaks down and deciding which fulfilment, email or support step to fix first.
steps: Adopt the presenter's distinction: customers do not experience processes, they experience a journey. If they cannot feel, hear, see or touch it, it is a process, not a journey.
Map the journey end to end from the customer's side, which gives an outside-in view of the experience they actually have, plus a realistic picture of where risk sits.
Use the map to see where to put focus where it matters most to both customers and business results, rather than fixing whatever is easiest.
Before mapping, ask how capable your current processes are of delivering the journey you want, and whether you have actually decided what service or product experience you intend to deliver is.

While mapping, run 'what if' risks and decide in advance how staff should react in difficult situations, for example giving employees checklists for a customer requesting something unusual. The presenter says the map surfaces scenarios even if they never occur.
Treat journey mapping as an ongoing management tool, not a one-time workshop output.
caveats: The presenter runs a full workshop on this; one session cannot substitute for that depth.
She frames it as a tool to answer the capability question, not a guarantee of results.
cards.source_name: _Introduction to Customer Experience (CX).docx

cards.title: Run the three-part CX framework: strategy, measurement, people
cards.summary: Apply a simple framework covering intended experience, journey-based measurement and the culture that enables delivery.
cards.use_when: Structuring a customer experience programme across your store's merchandising, fulfilment, support and team.
steps: Part one, strategy: answer whether you know who your customers are emotionally, what experience you want them to have, and whether everyone in the organisation knows their part in delivering that journey. Most organisations, the presenter says, have not defined the intended experience at all.

Part two, measurement: use customer journey mapping plus other measures, asking whether you measure from the customer's perspective rather than internal metrics only, and what your improvement priorities are.

Part three, people: create the culture and environment that lets people act in the customer's interest. Ask whether your people know the strategy, whether they are ambassadors of the intended experience, and how processes and people enable delivery.
Note the presenter's point that this framework still applies if you work alone in your own company.
Treat the three parts as puzzle pieces: having some without connecting them means you cannot see the picture or where the benefit is greatest.
Given how the presenter describes silo thinking as the single biggest breaker of CX strategy, ensure the three parts are linked rather than owned by separate functions.
caveats: The framework is presented as a global best-practice simplification from a partner, not validated against ecommerce performance data.
She spends roughly half a day on the strategy portion alone in her three-day trainings, so a quick pass is shallow.
cards.source_name: _Introduction to Customer Experience (CX).docx

cards.title: Define who your customer is, emotionally as well as demographically
cards.summary: Before deciding the experience, know customers' motivators, attitudes, values and purposes beyond your product.
cards.use_when: Building customer personas or researching buyers to inform PDP copy, post-purchase messaging and retention offers.
steps: Work through the presenter's questions for each core segment: what are their key motivators, not just around your product or service but generally; what are their attitudes towards your products; what do they value in a business relationship; and what personal purposes do they have.
Ask whether your organisation is set up to understand how you are making customers feel, not just what they buy.
Follow the sequencing logic: decide who your customer is and what you do for them before deciding what the experience should be.
Recognise the limit the presenter sets: being customer-centric does not mean always doing what the customer asks, but the experience should be good enough that word of mouth spreads.
Use the resulting understanding to shape both the intended emotion at each touchpoint and the practical choices behind them.
caveats: This is a questioning framework; the source does not prescribe specific research methods beyond walking in customers' shoes and talking to them.
The presenter notes that claiming to know your customer is common but knowing them in depth is where most organisations fall short.
cards.source_name: _Introduction to Customer Experience (CX).docx

cards.title: Write a customer experience strategy as an umbrella over the whole store
cards.summary: Define what you want customers to feel across the journey and translate it into principles and practical actions.
cards.use_when: Creating a documented CX strategy that governs store design, fulfilment choices, support tone and team behaviour.
steps: Separate this strategy from commercial segmentation. The presenter distinguishes a customer strategy that says which segments to target from the experience strategy that states what you want customers to feel across their whole journey with you.
Anchor it under business purpose, corporate objectives and business strategy, so the experience strategy acts as an umbrella over everything you do.
Include three elements: what the experience is - what you want customers to feel; the customer principles you live by; and what each principle translates to in practice.
Then define the actions that make the intended experience actually happen, rather than leaving it as a statement.

Use the presenter's three strategy questions as a completeness check: do you know who your customers are (emotionally), what you want their experience to be, and whether everyone knows their part in delivering it.
caveats: The presenter notes most organisations have not even defined the experience they want, and lack of clarity here makes measurement very hard.
She stresses this is not a one-off annual exercise: it keeps evolving.
cards.source_name: _Introduction to Customer Experience (CX).docx

cards.title: Give the CX function cross-functional ownership, led from the top
cards.summary: Customer experience is a leadership and culture question, not a marketing department job.
cards.use_when: Deciding who owns customer experience in a growing store team and how it connects across marketing, fulfilment and support.
steps: Expect the common question the presenter gets about who should be in charge, and treat 'everyone' as incomplete: there should be one owner who holds it together.
Adopt her view that mature organisations have a customer experience function working cross-functionally, like a quality function, rather than treating CX as merely an external marketing activity.

Extend the principle into operations: in a production or fulfilment setting, the people assembling and packing should act in the customer's interest through the right quality and by treating each other well, because how employees are treated tends to reflect how customers end up being treated.

Place ultimate accountability with the CEO and leadership team, since the presenter calls customer experience a leadership question, like quality, where responsibility sits with everyone in the process.
Watch for silo thinking, which she identifies as the one thing that makes or breaks a CX strategy coming to life and the source of random experiences.
caveats: This is her opinion based on consulting experience, not an ecommerce-specific study.
She answers a listener who assumed marketing owns CX: marketing only covers part of it.
cards.source_name: _Introduction to Customer Experience (CX).docx

cards.title: Create a shared experience vision to motivate front-line staff
cards.summary: Define what customers and employees should experience together so support staff can translate product pride into helping customers.
cards.use_when: Improving support quality, agent motivation and consistency in how your store's team handles customer problems.
steps: Start from the presenter's experience managing customer support in robotics: engineers love their products like a baby, and the shift required is translating that mindset into helping customers with the product, not just helping the product.
Create a shared, common and consistent strategy together with the team: what do we want our customers to experience, and what do we want each other to experience.

Apply the same logic to employees as to customers - what do employees need, what enables them to deliver a great experience, what motivates them - and explicitly connect employee experience to delivery of the business.
Avoid the common mistake of running employee experience separately from customer experience; the presenter says most companies disconnect the two.
Accept that this kind of mindset shift takes years, not weeks.

When customers ask for one thing but need another, rely on the culture and open processes you have built, and prepare scenario guidance from journey mapping so staff can handle such conversations without being over-scripted.
caveats: The presenter says the product-minded attitude shift takes years.
She notes she is not a sales expert, so the guidance on converting a customer to a different need is directional.
cards.source_name: _Introduction to Customer Experience (CX).docx

cards.title: Apply the same CX principles to B2B and less emotional categories
cards.summary: B2B buyers are still people, so journey, strategy and measurement principles carry over unchanged.
cards.use_when: Selling to businesses, public sector or any buyer where you assume customer experience is a consumer-only concern.
steps: Adopt the presenter's answer to the B2B question: there is no real difference, because whatever the organisation, you meet a human, and every customer is a person.
Reject the internal objection she reports hearing - 'we're in B2B, we don't have to think about customer experience' - since every customer still has a journey with you regardless.
Keep the same principles, methodologies and strategies, while noting her remark that B2C is somewhat more advanced in CX practice, so there may be more external examples to borrow from.
For your store, map the buying journey of the person placing the order, not just the company's procurement process, including approval steps as part of the journey.
Use the same measurement questions - intended experience, journey, customer-perspective measures, improvement priorities - even where the emotional signals differ in intensity.
caveats: The presenter's own background is B2B, so this is her assessment rather than a comparative study.
She acknowledges B2C practice leads B2B, so some adaptation may be needed for your category.
cards.source_name: _Introduction to Customer Experience (CX).docx

cards.title: Make experience a deliberate design, not a chance outcome
cards.summary: Experiences happen whether or not you design them, so choose the experience and process deliberately.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much to standardise post-purchase touchpoints such as order confirmation, shipping updates, packaging and returns handling.
steps: Accept the presenter's premise that every customer already has an experience with you whether or not you have decided what it should be, and experiences do not happen by chance - they happen by designing them.

Choose a starting point deliberately. She cites Steve Jobs taking over Apple in 1997 when sales were in steady decline, telling employees Apple had too many products and was just hoping people would buy them, then starting with the customer experience and working backwards to the technology.
Apply the same inversion to a store: define the intended purchasing experience first, then decide the tech, tools and processes that deliver it.
Watch what others deliver in your category, because customer expectations are rising through experiences like Amazon, Airbnb and Uber, and tolerance levels erode when things just work.
Use your intended experience as the standard against which new tactics and tools are judged before adoption.
caveats: The Apple account is a historical anecdote the presenter retells, not a store case study.
She presents competition on product, price and quality as difficult, meaning experience design is where deliberate choice pays off.
cards.source_name: _Introduction to Customer Experience (CX).docx

cards.title: Build a Bill of Materials Before Anything Else
cards.summary: A bill of materials breaks unit cost into every component and sub-vendor so COGS becomes a controllable, negotiable line instead of a mystery number.
cards.use_when: Setting up or renegotiating product sourcing for any physical-goods store, and before you start sourcing a new SKU or assume your landed cost is fixed.
steps: List every component of the finished unit (e.g. a gold solitaire ring = diamond, gold, labor, factory overhead, factory margin).
For each component, capture: component cost, sub-supplier/source, lead time, country of origin, and payment terms.
Get the sub-vendor layer too — your factory may not make its own inputs (lab-grown diamonds, gold, zippers, chipsets).

Split out labor and factory overhead as separate lines; these are the hardest to ask about but the ones that reveal where the money is. Verify sourcing claims (e.g. test that 'organic cotton' is actually organic).
Track component prices that move intraday or monthly (gold, diamonds, chipsets) so a supplier's markup stays visible and you can reprice when markets move.
Review the BOM with your supplier at least yearly and request price-break thresholds per line item.
Use the BOM as the first audit when acquiring or taking over a store: ~99 of 100 founders in the source's M&A experience did not have one.
caveats: The source says a BOM is worth building once you spend roughly $1M/year on COGS (~$100k/month to supplier), and some businesses benefit as low as ~$2.5M annual revenue; it is a judgment call below that.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Use BOM to Rethink Product Specs, Not Just Costs
cards.summary: Once you see every component's cost, you can engineer margin by changing materials, karat purity, or SKU tiers rather than only squeezing the supplier.
cards.use_when: Merchandising and product-development decisions — deciding what materials, specs, and SKU variants to sell and at what price.
steps: After building the BOM, ask structural questions per SKU: can this be made in a cheaper input (e.g. 10K vs 14K gold)? Can a premium tier be offered that lets you raise price more than cost?
Test whether a higher-end variant can be priced $200 above the base version while adding only ~$100 of real cost, creating more absolute dollars of margin.
Check whether you actually need every spec — if a component is a small share of COGS, price is your lever; if it's a large share, material substitution is your lever.
Feed these findings back into product selection so you choose SKUs whose component structure you can actually control.
Keep monitoring the component markets: a price move can swing a SKU's economics and force a repricing decision.
caveats: The source's example: Linear raised prices ~six times in 18 months as gold rose and still grew, because luxury-brand competitors left a gap — do not assume your category has that pricing power.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Enter Supplier Negotiations From a Position of Redundancy
cards.summary: Before asking a supplier to cut cost, do your homework so you already know the benchmark cost and have alternate suppliers mapped — leverage comes from preparation.
cards.use_when: Preparing for a cost-down negotiation with a factory or new supplier, or onboarding a supplier for a new product line.
steps: Before negotiating, buy and reverse-engineer competitor samples and map alternative suppliers for every key component.
Talk to heads of procurement at larger incumbent brands in your category to learn the industry-standard factory margin band (e.g. the source cites jewelry factories at ~5–9% EBITDA).
Come in with the BOM already drafted from other suppliers so the conversation starts from knowledge, not hope.
Ask each supplier to build their own BOM to your template rather than sending your current supplier's BOM — you want their independently sourced component costs.
Always maintain at least one viable alternate factory so you can act if the incumbent won't move.
caveats: The source's rule: if the factory won't budge, find another factory — but this only works if you actually built the redundancy first. If you entered the relationship giving the factory too much power, leverage is hard to recover.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Frame Cost-Downs as a Growth Partnership, Not a Squeeze
cards.summary: Present cost reduction to suppliers as fueling volume growth for both sides — share your P&L vision and translate it into units and dollars they care about.
cards.use_when: Making the first cost-down request to an existing factory, or resetting terms after acquiring a store or scaling a product line.
steps: Signal new ownership or new ambition explicitly ('I bought this because I plan to 5x it'), then explain you want both parties to win.
Share an abstracted P&L (e.g. 20% COGS, 40% marketing, 10% profit) and show where the savings go — funnel them into marketing to drive more volume, not into your pocket.
Translate the growth vision into units, since factories care about units, not your ad spend: 'we buy 1M units now, we want 10M by 2030.'
Walk them through the price-break thresholds you need per component and ask when each line item drops.
Offer to split financing or cost burden to show partnership (the source paid 80% of financing cost, factory 20% in one case).
Test whether their margin is abnormal for your industry before pushing hard — opening your books makes the conversation collaborative rather than confrontational.
caveats: This works only if you have a credible growth story and (ideally) benchmarks for normal margins in the category; a supplier with thin margins has nothing to give.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Ask for Volume Price Breaks on Every BOM Line
cards.summary: Negotiate component-level price breaks tied to unit volumes, understanding that factory economics rest on machine and labor utilization.
cards.use_when: Setting up volume tiers with a factory, planning a purchase order schedule, or forecasting COGS at higher volumes.
steps: For each BOM line (cotton, labor, zippers, polishing/QC, etc.), ask: at what volume does this price drop?
Frame it around the supplier's utilization — how much of their dedicated line is used, where is idle machine or fixed-labor capacity you can fill?
Reconcile invoices with the supplier line-by-line (the source has production leads sit with suppliers to do this), so credits for hitting thresholds are actually applied.
Track price breaks on sub-components too, since suppliers pass through their own sub-vendor economies of scale (e.g. a big zipper maker gives the factory a discount that should flow to you).

Consider internalizing procurement of key components (buying gold/diamonds/chips directly and supplying your assembler) to capture the sub-vendor margin, but only once you can manage the inventory price risk.
caveats: The source frames these as credits applied after you hit overage volumes, not blanket discounts — build the mechanism into the agreement. Internalizing components also exposes you to commodity price swings.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Use Payment Terms to Widen Your Float, Not to Chase Sales
cards.summary: Your real float is payment terms minus production lead time, so extending net terms buys you error tolerance and free cash flow.
cards.use_when: Deciding what payment terms to request from suppliers and how much working capital to hold before scaling ad spend or order volume.
steps: Map the actual deposit, invoice, shipping, receipt, sale and processor-payout dates. If net 90 begins when production starts and stock arrives in 30 days, 60 days remain before payment; a different contractual start changes this calculation.
Push for longer net terms as you mature — the source went from net 7 to net 90, citing net 180 as an extreme others use.
Recognize the most valuable outcome is margin of error: marketing is a daily variable cost you can switch off, a purchase order is not.
Factor in inventory mistakes (e.g. wrong size mix on rings) that eat your float in the real world.
Target consignment if you can get it: the factory owns goods until you sell, converting a made-to-order business to near-dropship cash dynamics.
caveats: Consignment is easiest with categories where the supplier can reclaim/resell inventory (the source notes gold's melt value and Hong Kong fulfillment made it feasible for one business); it isn't universally available.
Time from warehouse arrival to sale and payout consumes the remaining headroom; payment terms alone do not establish cash conversion.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Understand Supplier Financing to Unlock Better Terms
cards.summary: Factories use credit insurance and invoice factoring, so your P&L, not just the PO, determines the terms you can get — clean books matter.
cards.use_when: Negotiating extended terms or consignment, and when a supplier says they can't afford to float you.
steps: Ask whether the supplier can use export credit insurance or receivables finance. The source describes insurance-supported factoring; approval, advance rates and cost depend on the insurer, bank and buyer.
Request a written quote for alternative payment terms with financing charges and conditions separated from product price.
Support the credit audit: credit insurers grade you A/B/C using management accounts and payment history, and a past dispute can land you a low grade that blocks terms.
Keep books clean and pay on time to maintain a good grade — an unresolved supplier dispute from years prior cost the source a C rating.
Add financing cost as an explicit BOM line so the burden-sharing conversation is concrete (e.g. '$6/unit now, $5 if we double volume').
caveats: Rating is done by the insurer, not the factory, and low grades block financing; it can take time and effort to repair. Works best where the supplier is in a credit-insured export ecosystem (e.g. China).
The source's roughly 6% annual rate and grading examples are historical observations, not current available terms or approval guarantees.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Compare supplier credit with other working-capital options
cards.summary: The goal across BOM, price breaks and terms is a supplier relationship where they finance your inventory and dividends.
cards.use_when: Designing your overall sourcing/finance strategy and deciding what to prioritize as you scale purchasing.
steps: Stack the levers in order: BOM for cost visibility, then component price breaks, then long payment terms, then consignment.
Compare actual dated payments, fees, required security and downside obligations across supplier credit and alternatives; the source's lender cost examples are not current quotes.
Express financing charges in currency and over the financed period; an annual rate on a balance is not automatically the same percentage of COGS or revenue.
Keep the supplier relationship collaborative and share your vision so they become an eager partner rather than a lender of last resort.
Choose terms that preserve cash under slower sell-through, defects and delays rather than assuming every saving should fund more advertising.
caveats: This is Roman Khan's stated approach; results are his own and reflect a specific business mix and scale, not a guarantee. Long terms and consignment still require a supplier willing to extend them.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Build Component-Redundancy and Market-Monitoring Discipline
cards.summary: Actively re-source commodity components on an ongoing basis rather than one-time — keep multiple vendors and spot-check market prices.
cards.use_when: Managing replenishment and ongoing COGS after initial sourcing is set up.
steps: For commodities with public pricing (e.g. gold, lab-grown diamonds), pull current market prices monthly; diamonds in particular need quotes from 6–7 sub-vendors per month.
Attend the main industry trade fairs (the source notes chipset fairs that happen twice a year) to meet alternative and better suppliers, not just keep your current one.
Expect the supplier to carry an inventory-risk markup on top of component cost; that markup is your negotiation target.
Track component price moves that can force a repricing or spec change, and decide proactively: raise price (and test whether volume holds) or substitute materials.
Consider a hedging/diversification posture: the source notes buying components directly can also let you profit on a commodity rally, though this adds risk.
caveats: Component concentration risk is real — the source notes one supplier made up ~70% of COGS. Fully internalizing procurement exposes you directly to commodity volatility and inventory risk.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Pause Growth When Input and Tariff Shocks Hit
cards.summary: When duties, tariffs or commodity moves make the unit economics unsafe, it is acceptable to deliberately slow growth and hold flat while you rework sourcing.
cards.use_when: Fulfillment and sourcing planning when tariffs, duties, or input costs spike and your margins are compressed.
steps: Map your product's exposure: where is it produced (country of origin) and what duties/tariffs apply, from your BOM's country-of-origin column.

If exposure is unmanageable, decide explicitly to hold revenue flat rather than push volume at broken economics (the source paused growth for about a year on an India-produced business during high tariffs).
Use the pause to renegotiate with the supplier — if their margins were inflated, ask for a concession while conditions are bad.
As duties recede, be ready to resume growth and expect to give some margin back to the supplier ('pay a little more for COGS').
caveats: This is a scale- and category-specific move from the source; not every business can afford a flat year. The trade relationship with the supplier is central — transparent BOM data made the concession conversation possible.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Close Books Monthly and Dividend From Free Cash, Not EBITDA
cards.summary: Track actual cash generation monthly and fund only needed working capital before taking distributions — EBITDA is not cash.
cards.use_when: Setting a monthly schedule for taking money out of the store and deciding how much cash to retain to fund growth.
steps: Close the books by the 15th of each month for the prior month: revenue, COGS (cash and accrual), opex, profit.
Separate EBITDA from free cash flow — the source stresses the gap between profit and cash actually in the bank.
Estimate the working capital the coming months require for planned growth before withdrawing anything (e.g. if growing 80%, size the reserve accordingly).
Only dividend what is genuinely free after that reserve; the source projects taking ~65–75% of free cash flow out as distributions.
Automate/pre-derive the process so monthly distributions become routine, turning profit into actual cash in your account.
caveats: The source's distribution range is his own projection, not a universal benchmark. Without management accounts (the source says ~70% of the M&A founders he meets lack them), this is not possible — the cadence has to be built first.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Audit Margin Reality: COGS Is Your Biggest Lever
cards.summary: Opex and marketing are relatively predictable; COGS is the biggest controllable swing factor, which is why sourcing discipline beats growth-at-all-costs.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to spend optimization effort — sourcing vs marketing vs overhead — and reviewing whether your business is genuinely profitable in cash terms.
steps: Break the P&L into revenue, COGS, marketing, overhead; note that overhead and mature marketing are fairly predictable, while COGS is the largest moving variable.
Compare component-price moves (e.g. COGS jumping from ~15% to ~30% of revenue if gold doubles) against your ability to reprice or substitute.
Focus cost-down effort on COGS sourcing rather than assuming it's fixed; you can always find new vendors, whereas ad costs follow platform rules.
Measure true margin bands and recognize that sub-10% EBITDA becomes fragile under a single rental, platform, or freight shock.
Decide whether your category is genuinely profitable enough to keep scaling or whether you need to change the product/sourcing structure first.
caveats: The source's benchmark observations (many stores sub-10% EBITDA, some 20–25%) come from his own M&A pipeline and may not represent your category. He is openly 'dividend first,' which prioritizes cash extraction over growth velocity — a value judgment, not a universal rule.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Bill of Materials as the Foundation of Supply Chain Profit
cards.summary: A bill of material (BOM) is the foundational layer for any physical-goods business and the starting point for supply chain optimization and cash extraction.
cards.use_when: Setting up or auditing sourcing and COGS for a physical product store, or planning a cost-reduction or margin-improvement initiative across SKUs.
steps: Build a complete bill of materials for every sellable SKU: all components, packaging, inserts, and variable costs (shipping, duties, fees) that make up true landed cost.
Treat the BOM as the base of the profit pyramid — everything downstream (management accounts, free cash flow, distributions) depends on it being accurate.
For stores already doing millions in revenue, reconcile the BOM against actual supplier invoices and freight costs to find gaps and margin leaks.
Use the BOM to standardize margin accounting across all SKUs, and revisit it whenever a cost input (freight, packaging, supplier pricing) moves.
caveats: Speech-to-text garbled 'BOM' as 'bum' — the actual concept is bill of material.
The claim that BOM is 'by far' the most foundational input is the source's opinion, framed as advice to operators of physical goods.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Free Cash Flow vs. Enterprise Value: Which Game Is Your Store Playing
cards.summary: Businesses should be mapped on a quadrant of free cash flow versus enterprise value, because cash extraction tactics and exit options differ entirely between the two.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to optimize a store for ongoing cash distributions versus building a sellable, valued enterprise.
steps: Map your business on two axes: free cash flow (money taken out monthly) and enterprise value (multiple a buyer would pay).
Recognize the classic dropship pattern — high free cash flow, near-zero enterprise value — and decide whether that is intentional or a trap.
If you want enterprise value, invest in brand, durable systems, management accounts, and audited financials rather than just ad arbitrage.
Note that with strong enterprise value you gain access to additional levers (like dividend recaps) that pure cash-flow businesses cannot pull.
caveats: The source asserts most online sellers 'are probably not a brand' — a strong opinion, not a measured fact.
No numeric thresholds define each quadrant; the framework is qualitative.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Offer Optimization as the #1 Meta Scaling Lever
cards.summary: For most stuck Meta accounts, the biggest lever is a stale or weak offer rather than new creatives or bidding changes.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing a paid-social account that has plateaued despite healthy spend, or planning a growth push on a store in the $5–50M range.
steps: Audit your current offers and ask whether they are aggressive and compelling enough for the category — the source says 90% of stuck accounts fail here.
Test offer constructs like buy-two-get-three, BOGO, free gifts at cart or checkout, and email-capture discounts.
Change offers before changing everything else — the source reports >50% lifts from offer changes alone with the same creatives.
Model the variable cost of each offer (extra units, packaging, dimensional weight shipping) and compute profit per visitor, not just revenue per visitor.
Test small discount deltas: the source says 10% vs 15% had zero impact, but 10% vs 20% showed a real delta.
caveats: The source's specific lift numbers come from their portfolio and are examples, not benchmarks.
Do not blankly increase offer aggressiveness — extra units can inflate shipping and fulfillment costs and shrink profit.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Rotating Hooks and Angles Before Adding Media Budget
cards.summary: When the offer is solid but the account is stuck, the bottleneck is breadth of hooks and angles for the product.
cards.use_when: Scaling creative testing on Meta or planning a new creative sprint for a single hero SKU.
steps: Count how many distinct hooks and angles you currently run — the source says founders often stall at 3–4.
Recruit new angles from categories the product touches: use-case, occupation, gifting occasion, social proof, and objection handling.
Study outlier ads from adjacent categories for the opening frame, not just the product story (the source cites a personal-assistant gifting angle for jewelry).
Volume-test angles with consistent production sprints and kill losers quickly; expect only a fraction to print.
Feed the winning frameworks back into your production brief so new variants stay aligned with the proven promise.
caveats: Creative testing is not a substitute for a weak offer — the source treats offer as lever #1 and hooks as lever #2.
No fixed 'correct' hook count is given; the direction is 'more than 3–4.'
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Influencer-Specific Landing Pages That Mirror the Ad
cards.summary: Matching the ad to a personalized collection page in the same order the products appeared produced a large conversion lift.
cards.use_when: Building or rebuilding landing pages for influencer or whitelisted ads, or diagnosing a creative-to-page mismatch killing conversion.
steps: When an influencer ad promotes multiple products, build a dedicated collection page featuring their name, face, and code.
Order products on the landing page to match the chronological order they appeared in the ad.
Ensure the lead product or first-shown product sits above the fold on the collection page.
Add creator quote and lifestyle imagery where the page permits (e.g., supplements, single-product pages).
Test against your current generic collection pages and measure conversion rate.
caveats: The 30% conversion lift is a source-reported number from their own portfolio, not a universal benchmark.
The technique works best when the ad shows a finite product set; catalog mashup b-roll was said to underperform single- or aligned-product ads.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Using Partnership Ads to Bridge the Trust Gap
cards.summary: Whitelisting creator content as partnership ads adds trust signals and diversity to a Meta account that standard brand ads cannot.
cards.use_when: Scaling paid social for high-AOV or considered-purchase products, or diversifying a Meta ad account dominated by brand-owned creatives.
steps: Give creators the ability to hand over ad code and page rights for their content (Meta's partnership ads, modeled on TikTok Spark ads).
Aim for a meaningful whitelisted share of your ad library — the source runs roughly 40–50% partnership content.
Lean on real, aged creator profiles so the ad reads as a person rather than a brand, which the source says matters especially for high-AOV products.
Compensate creators in ways that match your cash-flow discipline; the source uses fixed fees, often broken into a daily rate with a short cancellation or trial window (they cite ~10–14 days).
Alternatively test variable or percentage-of-spend compensation for select creators, recognizing it can create operational mess if terms are inconsistent.
caveats: The source says most operators were not running partnership ads at the time of recording — early-adopter framing, not proven universal performance.
Comparing fixed-fee vs. variable-fee compensation is unresolved in the source; each is presented as a situational alternative.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Paying Creators a Trial Daily Rate Before Committing
cards.summary: Compensate whitelisted creators with a fixed daily rate and a short trial window so media spend is predictable and risk is bounded.
cards.use_when: Negotiating influencer or partnership-ad deals when you cannot forecast whether the asset will convert.
steps: Convert a monthly creator fee into a daily rate (e.g., source cites ~$10k/month broken into a daily figure).
Set a trial period (source references ~10–14 days) with a breakout or cancellation clause so you can stop paying if the creative does not perform.
Frame the deal transparently: you will pay the day rate, you want to see performance, and you want to manage risk.
Consider paying a modest kicker or higher rate during the trial period to reflect the creator's upfront production work.
Keep deal terms across creators consistent — the source says spread of terms across too many creators creates operational chaos.
caveats: The source notes they are still second-guessing this model versus variable compensation after seeing other operators pay much larger variable fees.
Daily rate, trial length, and kicker are source-specific to the source's portfolio; not universally applicable benchmarks.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: One-Day-Click ROAS with Post-Purchase Survey Multiplier
cards.summary: Use platform-independent 1-day click ROAS tempered by post-purchase survey data to extrapolate lifetime performance and judge whether an ad account can be scaled profitably.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to scale spend on Meta and other channels when multi-touch attribution is judged unreliable, especially for considered-purchase products.
steps: Track 1-day click ROAS in a cross-channel tool like Northbeam as your source of truth, since the platform-agnostic number is comparable across time.
Run a post-purchase survey asking 'when did you first hear of us' with bins like today, past week, past two weeks, month, six months, a year.
Assume the pessimistic case that only 1-day click conversions drove revenue — zero credit to view-through.
Multiply the immediate share (e.g., 20–25% for a jewelry brand) into 1-day click ROAS to estimate lifetime ROAS: a 0.5 one-day click implies roughly 2.0 lifetime under that assumption.
Compare the extrapolated lifetime ROAS against your breakeven ROAS to decide whether to keep scaling.
caveats: The percentages cited are sourced from their portfolio and seasons and are not benchmarks.
Northbeam's internal LTV calculations were not trusted by the source — they run the math themselves on top of the 1-day-click number.
The extrapolation is deliberately conservative (no view-through credit), which can understate performance in some windows.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Post-Purchase Survey Questions Worth Copying
cards.summary: Post-purchase surveys can reveal acquisition source, timing, competitive set, and even who to book next as an influencer.
cards.use_when: Building or refreshing a post-purchase survey on Shopify to inform creative, media mix, and influencer booking decisions.
steps: Ask where the customer heard of you (channel, platform) and when (today, week, month, six months, year) to feed the 1-day-click multiplier.
Ask basic demographics relevant to your category (age, gender) for targeting and persona scoring.
Ask which other brands they considered before buying — useful for competitive creative and positioning work.
Ask which influencer should represent the brand — the source uses this field to find and book influencers.
Deploy via a lightweight Shopify survey app, run it continuously, and refresh the question set when new hypotheses emerge.
caveats: Customers do not always remember accurately — treat responses as directional evidence, not instrumentation.
The exact survey wording and app were referenced but not fully specified in the source; pick a compatible Shopify tool and verify current options.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: YouTube Influencer Strategy: Patience and Portfolio Math
cards.summary: YouTube influencer ad reads are a venture-style portfolio play that requires deep payback tolerance and CPM-by-cohort pricing across personas.
cards.use_when: Planning or scaling a YouTube influencer program for a physical product brand, especially ones with broad audiences.
steps: Accept long payback windows — the source notes YouTube payback can exceed 30 days, so the account must stomach slow returns.
Budget for portfolio outcomes: the source describes ~100 booked influencers where ~20 print and pay for the 80 that do not.
Build a CPM scorecard by persona (gamer, hobbyist, mom, etc.) so each creator is priced to expected value, not gut feel.
Back into profit: the source's true north star is whether a $10k placement can generate a defined dividend amount after all costs, not just ROAS.
Focus on persona-fit and production quality of the read — a great ad read on a compatible audience is what unlocks outlier CPM efficiency.
caveats: The source's own spend dropped from early years (~$20M) to steady-state (~$4–7M/year), so this is not a 'spend more' recommendation.
YouTube CPMs are described as opaque and non-transparent — do not take a single CPM as a market rate.
Results like a $2 CAC at six-figure scale come from a specific creator and were described as an outlier, not a norm.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Is Amazon or Google Shopping Under-Weighted in Your Mix?
cards.summary: Channel mix should reflect category demand capture, not a default 'Meta-first' assumption — Google Shopping and YouTube are still major drivers for certain categories.
cards.use_when: Reviewing channel allocation for a store whose category has clear search demand (jewelry, electronics, tools) but is over-indexed on Meta.
steps: Map category demand: if buyers search for the product type (e.g., earbuds, jewelry), Google Shopping and YouTube likely deserve share.
Split paid media across Meta, Google (Shopping and YouTube), Amazon ads, and influencer so no single channel carries the whole account.
Consider that the source positions Meta at ~40–45%, Google ~20%, AppLovin 5–10%, and influencer for a portfolio spending near $100M — treat this as one operator's skew, not a target.
Re-evaluate TikTok spend explicitly: the source says they were 'sleeping on' TikTok despite evidence other operators scale on it, especially in younger-audience categories.
Reallocate based on incrementality, not legacy habit — verify with 1-day-click ROAS to compare channel-level performance over time.
caveats: The exact mix percentages are from one operator's portfolio and year.
TikTok and AppLovin channel economics change quickly — re-check current platform interfaces and reporting before making decisions.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Vivid Vision: Writing a Letter to Your Future Self as an Operator
cards.summary: Writing a dated letter from your future self clarifies what business and life outcomes you are actually building toward, which then guides strategy and risk-taking.
cards.use_when: Annual or multi-year planning for an ecommerce brand — choosing which markets, channels, or business models to build toward.
steps: Pick a specific future date (e.g., a birthday 5–10 years out) and write a letter to yourself as the person you will be then.
Describe outcomes across roles: operator, owner, family member, community member — not just revenue or exit numbers.
Use the letter to define the end state you are playing toward (e.g., being recognized as a meaningful stakeholder in a category) so day-to-day decisions align with it.
Revisit the letter on a schedule and compare current strategy against it — especially when considering concentrated bets or category pivots.
Reduce friction by being specific: dates, roles, and named outcomes work better than generalized aspirations.
caveats: The source frames this as 'manifestation,' not a rigorous operating plan; treat it as a direction-setter, not a forecast.
No specific number of categories or length of letter is prescribed.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Second-Mover Advantage in AI Adoption
cards.summary: The source argues for being a fast follower on AI tools — waiting to see what demonstrably moves profit before retooling teams around hype.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much resource to commit to AI tools and headcount for ecommerce operations, creative, and fulfillment.
steps: Define a payback test up front (source example: 'if I spend $10k on tokens I want at least $10k more in dividends').
Identify which team members already deliver real AI-driven value on operational problems, and work outward from them rather than mandating blanket rollouts.
Prioritize AI use cases tied to margin, dividend, or operating cost — not novelty adoption for its own sake.
Reassess periodically as the platform landscape shifts, since the source notes this is a fast-moving area.
caveats: The source says they had 'very little to show' from vibe-coding personally, even while eight team members were delivering — this is an honest mixed result, not a case for or against AI.
Any specific tooling or vendor mentioned may have changed — verify current interfaces before standardizing.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Automate influencer sourcing and outreach to scale partnership ads
cards.summary: Use AI to automate the find, screen, outreach and media-kit negotiation steps of influencer marketing so you can multiply conversations per week without adding headcount.
cards.use_when: Planning influencer/partnership ad acquisition and trying to increase creator volume for TikTok/Meta partnership ads.
steps: Map the current manual workflow end to end: source/screen creators against a written brand-fit brief, outreach, request media kit, negotiate a rebuttal to the quoted rate, and offer a performance kicker if it performs.

Automate the repetitive stages with AI while keeping the brand-fit judgment human: the presenter argues the person screening must effectively be the customer to understand the audience, and says a head of influence for one brand would not do a good job for a different brand.
Set volume targets: the presenter scaled from ~500 real creator conversations per week (creators with 100k+ audience) to 200–300 per day after automating, with a goal of 500 per day.
Treat it as a one-time build plus ongoing optimization rather than a variable opex problem.
Keep the negotiation logic explicit: counter the media kit rate with a stated CPM baseline and offer a kicker if performance is strong.
caveats: Results are the presenter's own example, not a benchmark; exact conversation volume depends on niche and team.
The presenter concedes AI UGC creators are not there yet for his scale (quality and legality), so he automates the process, not the creator itself.
Verify current AI tooling and platform rules before building.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Back a human-first creative thesis while hedging on AI ads
cards.summary: The presenter bets platforms will reward real-human partnership ads over AI slop, but flags regulation and unclear platform incentives as real risks.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to allocate creative budget between human influencer/partnership ads and AI-generated statics/video.
steps: Use AI-generated static ads freely: the presenter says all his statics are now AI, while continuing to invest in human creators for video.

Lean budget into partnership ads and TikTok influencers because, in a market commoditized by Amazon and AI, the presenter argues people want to buy from real humans and platforms will reward real people in-feed.
Hedge: acknowledge the opposing possibility that platforms will simply push whatever AI ads perform better for them regardless of 'human' sentiment.
Track regulatory developments: the presenter notes New York banned AI UGC ads with fines, as an opposing force to AI creative growth.
Treat AI-video parity with human UGC as a matter of when, not if, and re-test periodically rather than committing permanently.
caveats: This is the presenter's stated opinion/bet, not a proven rule.
Predictions about platform behavior and timelines are explicitly uncertain (the other speaker predicted 30–50% AI video by end of next year; presenter declined to commit).
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Localize pricing, language and merchandising to unlock non-US revenue
cards.summary: Model localization on a best-in-class case: per-market languages, localized pricing, and market-specific merchandising, not just one translated site.
cards.use_when: Expanding a DTC store into international markets or improving conversion in existing non-US traffic.
steps: Study a strong localizer as a reference: the presenter cites Caseify (phone cases) as localizing languages, pricing and even merchandising per market (UK vs China vs Korea, e.g. region-relevant collab/character cases).
Go beyond translated copy: the presenter says for a brand big in Asia the site should use Asian models and local languages (Chinese, Thai, Vietnamese) matching the countries shipped to.
Localize pricing per market rather than converting one currency blindly.
Note the presenter's own varied international mix (roughly 60% US/Canada, 40% non-North America; one brand ~35% US, 65% non-US) as context for why localization scales.
Treat localization as a distinct operating capability, not a one-off translation project.
caveats: The presenter says his own team is currently bad at localization, so treat this as a target state, not a described proven process.
Named companies are referenced as examples, not guaranteed benchmarks.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Level 1 international shipping: one 3PL, one global campaign, best creatives
cards.summary: A simple first step for cross-border: house light inventory in a Hong Kong 3PL and run one Meta campaign with all best-performing North America creatives against every shippable country.
cards.use_when: Starting international expansion for a light-product store (e.g. phone cases, small electronics) with limited operational resources.
steps: If the product is small/light, store inventory with a Hong Kong 3PL and ship out of there; the presenter calls this simple and fast for light goods.
Run one new global Meta campaign with one ad set, loading it with all your best-performing North America creatives.
Include all countries you can physically ship to at a reasonable price in that single ad set.
Run ads in English to start; localize language/imagery later as a second optimization level.
Then optimize variable costs (shipping and fulfillment) as the 'level one' cost unlock for international markets.
caveats: Applies most cleanly to light products; heavier or bulky goods need different logistics.
The presenter notes even US-fulfilled orders can sometimes ship cheaper from Hong Kong via a cross-border logistics provider, delivering in ~4.5 days on average in his example.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Cross-border logistics can beat domestic fulfillment on cost and speed
cards.summary: A cross-border provider that dropships from Asia to US customers in under 5 days can be cheaper than domestic end-to-end fulfillment.
cards.use_when: Evaluating fulfillment options or trying to reduce shipping cost and delivery time for a US-facing store.
steps: Compare total landed cost of domestic 3PL/fulfillment versus shipping direct from an Asia-based cross-border provider for your specific SKUs and volumes.

Use the presenter's data point as a hypothesis to test: he says it is cheaper for him to ship US orders from Hong Kong via Quinc Logistics than to fulfill end-to-end inside the US, averaging ~4.5 days to a US customer.
Look for providers that built internal infrastructure to consolidate dropship from China, India and Asia into fast, cheap US delivery.
If a provider externalizes this capability to other brands, treat it as a sourcing lever to negotiate.
caveats: Specific costs and delivery times are the presenter's example, not a benchmark; terms vary and should be verified with current providers.
Brand facts about named companies should be checked before relying on them.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Build a daily red/green/blue P&L report with mandatory explanations
cards.summary: Automate a daily Slack report of revenue, spend and key metrics with color status, and require the responsible owner to explain every miss in-thread.
cards.use_when: Setting up operating cadence and accountability for an ecommerce P&L.
steps: Produce a daily Slack update (AI-generated in the presenter's case, previously via virtual assistants) showing budgeted vs actual for revenue, ad spend, ROAS, repeat rate and other P&L lines by day.
Use color codes: e.g. one color for miss vs budget, another for beat, another for off-forecast; the presenter uses red/green/blue.
Publish to a town-hall-style channel everyone can see.
Require the accountable owner to reply in-thread whenever a metric is red, explaining why and the corrective plan (an SOP exists for each color).
If the same metric is off-forecast repeatedly (the presenter says many blue lights three days in a row), require an explanation of why the budget/forecast was so wrong to begin with.
caveats: Compounding small daily improvements is the presenter's motivating rationale, not a measured guarantee.
He notes he has not yet applied AI to the per-person reporting layer out of respect for individuals.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Run a daily task channel with every direct report
cards.summary: Each team member posts a morning plan and end-of-day completion plus time allocation, letting a leader spot overload and misplaced effort.
cards.use_when: Managing an ecommerce team's productivity and diagnosing why a channel (e.g. PPC) is missing targets.
steps: Create a personal daily-task channel per team member; the presenter has ~70 such channels for his front-office staff.
Each morning the person posts the 3 things they want to accomplish today plus the rest of their to-do list.
Each evening they post what got done (with check marks) and a breakdown of how time was spent (e.g. 30 min email, 1 hour Meta ad manager, 30 min Google ad manager).
Use the time-allocation logs to decide whether someone needs support, is overloaded, or is spending time on non-impactful work.
Cross-reference the individual channel with the macro P&L channel: if PPC metrics are red, check whether the owner is under-investing hours in creative production.
Use the accumulated logs as a factual basis for six-month reviews instead of relying on memory.
caveats: High-intensity, hands-on management style; the presenter frames it as a deliberate choice, not a fit for every manager or team.
Requires consistent participation to be useful.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Reframe micromanagement as structured recurring feedback
cards.summary: The presenter says micromanagement fails only when it is unprompted, random and unstructured; make it predictable, daily and consistent to train juniors.
cards.use_when: Onboarding or developing junior ecommerce operators and deciding whether/how closely to manage them.
steps: Give feedback at a predictable, consistent daily frequency rather than randomly.
Make the feedback structured and expected, so the recipient knows when and how it will come.
Pair frequent feedback with a system (daily P&L colors, daily task channels) so the leader is 'in the weeds' without being bogged down.
Lead by example: the presenter says leaders should also solicit and accept feedback, and participate in the same systems.
Hire for attitude toward feedback: filter for people who treat feedback as a gift and who are self-deprecating rather than defensive.
caveats: This is the presenter's explicitly contrarian opinion ('micromanaging is a great word'); it is a strong style choice, not a universal best practice.
The pattern is presented as training-focused, most relevant to junior employees.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Adopt the A Method's five-step hiring sequence
cards.summary: Scorecard, screening, topgrading, competency/culture, then reference-checked offer — a standardized sequence that made hiring comparable and durable.
cards.use_when: Building out an ecommerce team (e.g. head of finance or other key hires) and wanting a repeatable process to reduce early attrition.
steps: Step 1 — Scorecard: define outcomes and the specific attributes/competencies the role truly needs (and what it does NOT need, e.g. a head of finance does not need to be charismatic or extroverted).
Step 2 — Screening: a standardized, role-agnostic 15–20 minute set of macro questions any recruiter can run, with maniacal notes passed to the hiring manager.
Step 3 — Topgrading: a 30–60 minute deep, chronological walk through each résumé role, filling gaps (e.g. what happened between two jobs) and chasing flagged concerns.
Step 4 — Competency and culture: a domain case study (often with dummy data and deliberate traps) plus a cultural-fit questionnaire (e.g. comfort with constant feedback).
Step 5 — Reference-checked offer: make the offer conditional on 2–3 reference calls for senior hires, asking standardized questions tied to what screening/topgrading surfaced to get past fluff.
Keep a straight line through the doc: everything should reconcile, with no zigs or zags.
caveats: The presenter credits this method (plus learning from a near-bankruptcy) as central to scaling from ~$50M to $200M; that is his own case, not a proven benchmark.
He says reference calls are worthless for most people unless run through this standardized process.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Write a role scorecard that separates outcomes from attributes
cards.summary: Define what the role must deliver and the specific competences/attributes needed, and explicitly list what does not matter to remove interviewer bias.
cards.use_when: Writing a job description or evaluating candidates for an ecommerce role (e.g. head of finance).
steps: List concrete outcomes (e.g. build financial models, produce management accounts, run audits, budgeting, monitoring and risk).
List the real competencies (e.g. extreme attention to detail/OCD, strong analytical skills, decent problem solving, a get-it-done hands-on attitude).

Explicitly name irrelevant traits to avoid bias: the presenter says for head of finance he does not need charisma, extroversion or someone who excites him in the interview — he wants the boxes ticked.
Use the scorecard to align everyone involved in hiring (hiring manager, CEO, future manager) before interviewing.
In the screening, test career goals against the role's growth path (e.g. an aspiring CFO fits a head-of-finance stepping-stone hire; someone who wants to coast is a bad fit).
caveats: Some competency specifics (extreme OCD) may vary by company, though the presenter says head-of-finance competencies are largely consistent across companies.
Bias-removal is the goal; results depend on disciplined use.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Use screening booby-trap questions to test fit and flag deep-dive topics
cards.summary: A short standardized screen with deliberately probing questions surfaces fit and generates hypotheses to drill into during topgrading.
cards.use_when: Running first-round screens for any ecommerce role and deciding who advances.
steps: Ask one question from each core area: what are your career goals; what are you really good at professionally; what are you not good at professionally; who were your last five managers and how would they rate you 1–10; and why do you want to work here.
For the rating question, use the framing 'if I called [manager] and asked him to rate you 1–10, how would he rate you?' and probe 'why an 8 and not a 9' to get past polite answers.
Note red flags but don't resolve them in screening — carry them forward. Example: a candidate citing lateness on deliverables gets a note to probe prioritization in topgrading.
Use role-specific deal-breakers: for head of finance, disliking repetitive process work is a disqualifier because closing the books must be owned by this person.
Leave ~10 minutes at the end for the candidate's questions and always sell the company, even if you plan to reject, so the candidate leaves excited.
caveats: Screening alone does not resolve the flags it surfaces; that is topgrading's job.
The 'always be selling' closing is a nuance the presenter adds beyond the book, based on his own experience.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Topgrade candidates chronologically to find gaps and inflated titles
cards.summary: Walk every résumé role in order to verify what someone was actually hired to do versus their title, and to fill timeline gaps.
cards.use_when: Second-stage interviews where you need to verify a candidate's real track record before an ecommerce hire.
steps: Go role by role through the CV rather than accepting the summary.
Distinguish hired-title from final-title: the presenter's own example — hired as entrepreneur-in-residence, left as managing director — and ask what it actually took to progress.
Ask what the person was actually hired to do, what they did, and what results they drove in each role.
Probe chronological gaps: the presenter looks for holes (e.g. what were you doing between these two jobs, what went wrong).
Allocate 30–60 minutes for this stage, deeper than the 15–20 minute screen.
caveats: Takes real time per candidate; best reserved for those who passed screening.
Effectiveness depends on the interviewer's domain knowledge to judge the answers.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Use case studies with traps plus a culture questionnaire
