Anonymous campaigns can confuse or annoy audiences if the payoff is weak or the brand connection is unclear.
Works best when you have a distribution point or retailer ready at reveal time.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Native in-game placements that hand out real value
cards.summary: Put real products or discount codes inside games and communities your customers already inhabit, rather than interrupting them with ads.
cards.use_when: Acquisition creative and campaign planning when your audience spends leisure time in games, forums, or niche communities.
steps: Identify the digital spaces where your customers already spend leisure time - the source's case, Mercado Livre, used Call of Duty's 'Prop Hunt' mode where players disguise as furniture.
Hide real, usable value in the experience: Mercado Livre placed more than 420 real products in custom in-game maps, which players could find and redeem.
Add a cultural figure or character only if it fits the audience - the campaign featured footballer Neymar Jr. as a playable character.
Design the integration to feel native to the experience, so it doesn't read as an ad insertion.

Prepare for the volume: the source reports the campaign generated over R$7 million in sales, 5.2 million total views, and 600,000 real-time interactions, and won a 2025 Cannes Grand Prix in Gaming Entertainment.
caveats: The reported results come from a large platform's flagship campaign with agency support; they are not achievable on a small brand budget.
Game integrations typically require partnership agreements, platform permissions, and significant production cost.
Custom map or in-game item work is technically complex; verify current platform tools before planning.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Festival activation: solve a real attendee problem
cards.summary: Bring a service or truck to an event and relieve an actual pain point rather than pitching your catalog.
cards.use_when: Experiential marketing planning when you want brand affection from a defined physical audience.
steps: Identify the concrete hardships your customers face at the event - the source's case, Privalia at Lollapalooza in Brazil, targeted mud, heat, and long lines.

Deliver something that solves that problem on the spot, even if it isn't directly your product; the source frames this as the essence of guerrilla marketing - unconventional means used to promote the brand by solving real problems.
Position the brand as helpful and human rather than transactional so the goodwill translates into loyalty.
Capture the moment for social sharing, since the value comes from word of mouth after the event.
Keep the activation low-cost relative to reach; the format's whole appeal is high impact per dollar.
caveats: This is a non-ecommerce example from a marketplace brand; applying it to a product store requires adapting the activation to your category.
No conversion or revenue figures are given in the source, so treat the outcome as brand goodwill rather than attributable sales.
Event permissions and local regulations apply.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Own an underserved or taboo topic in your category
cards.summary: Address a topic competitors avoid, on the platform where that audience talks, and measure CPA against your other channels.
cards.use_when: Acquisition channel selection and content strategy when your category has an underserved audience and competitors avoid the subject.
steps: Identify topics in your category that competitors avoid or handle poorly - the source's case, Maxfem, tackled feminine intimate health in Brazil.
Pick a social platform where that audience is already discussing the topic, and build a community around authentic, sensitive treatment rather than a hard sell. Maxfem used TikTok Shop.
Measure CPA against your existing media mix: the source reports Maxfem achieved a CPA 40% lower than other media, qualified leads up 42%, and TikTok Shop revenue 170% above target.
Keep the treatment respectful and accurate - the source emphasizes authenticity and sensitivity as the reason the approach resonated.
Use the platform's commerce features to convert from the same content that built the community.
caveats: The specific figures (40% lower CPA, 42% more qualified leads, 170% of target) are one brand's reported case study results, not benchmarks.
Taboo-adjacent marketing carries reputational risk; mistakes are hard to reverse.
Platform moderation and advertising policies may restrict health-adjacent claims.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Crowdfunding or pre-order to validate demand before inventory
cards.summary: Use an audience plus a crowdfunding launch to prove demand and generate marketing before committing to stock.
cards.use_when: Product selection and inventory planning for a new SKU when you have an audience but don't want to carry unsold inventory risk.
steps: Launch the product as a crowdfunding campaign or pre-order rather than buying inventory first - the source's case, GIZMART in Japan, launched the Keychron Nape Pro trackball device this way.
Use the campaign as both validation and marketing; the source reports it reached 100 million yen in GMV within the first 12 hours and surpassed 300 million yen total.
Leverage your existing media audience or community for the initial push, since the model depends on people already paying attention to you.
Treat the crowdfunding result as a demand signal before scaling production.
Keep communication clear about delivery timelines so backers aren't surprised.
caveats: The yen figures are one platform's debut project, not a forecast.
Crowdfunding creates delivery obligations and reputational risk if you miss timelines.
Works best with an existing audience; cold launches rarely hit meaningful numbers.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Build the digital experience that replaces in-store trust
cards.summary: Over-invest in education, photography, and transparency to sell a high-consideration product sight-unseen.
cards.use_when: PDP and landing page design for categories where customers must touch or see the product before buying.
steps: Identify the trust barrier in your category first - the source's case, Miss Amara, sells premium rugs customers never touch.

Over-invest in the specific assets that replace the showroom: detailed education content, high-quality photography, styling inspiration, and transparent product information. Miss Amara reportedly built a $26 million business on this approach.
Provide enough information that customers can visualize the product in their own space, rather than a single hero image with minimal specs.
Extend the same standard across new markets as you expand - the source notes Miss Amara added sites in Hong Kong, New Zealand, and the US.
Treat confidence-building content as conversion infrastructure, not as a marketing extra.
caveats: The $26 million figure is one brand's reported scale, not a benchmark for the approach.
High-quality photography and education content carry real production cost.
If the underlying product quality doesn't match the presentation, trust breaks on the first order.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Community as co-creators: high-touch insider programs
cards.summary: Make your best customers insiders with events, early access, and input into products before automating anything.
cards.use_when: Retention and community strategy when you want customers who actively promote the brand, not just repeat buyers.
steps: Start small and personal: the source's case, Heaven Mayhem, launched with 20 one-of-a-kind necklaces and the founder DMing everyone who liked a post.
Host recurring high-touch events - monthly Zoom calls, girls' nights for around 150 community members, and office visits for matcha and product try-ons.
Ask the community for feedback on products and give them early access to new releases so they feel like insiders.
Let the relationship run both ways: when customers feel like co-creators, the source says they become evangelists with a stake in the brand's success.
Only automate after the manual pattern has proven the community actually engages - the source firmly frames high-touch work as the defensible advantage.
caveats: 150-person events and regular office visits are expensive in founder time and only pay off over a long horizon.
Community building doesn't scale linearly; growth requires deliberate rituals as membership expands.
This is a case study, not a guarantee that co-creation produces promotion.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Build community before product, and let feedback shape the catalog
cards.summary: Gather an audience first, ask what they want, and let the product emerge from those conversations.
cards.use_when: New product line or category entry where you can afford to test direction with an audience before committing to design and inventory.
steps: Spend months building an audience before the product exists - the source's case, Gully Labs in India, spent six months publishing about why India needed a desi sneaker brand before making a shoe.
Ask the community direct questions about what they actually want to wear, and feed answers into product decisions.
Shape the product from that feedback, so the launch audience is already invested in the outcome.
Continue using the community as a feedback loop after launch rather than switching to standard top-down development.
Use the audience itself as your launch distribution so you are not paying to acquire your first customers.
caveats: Six months of pre-build work is a significant runway commitment with no revenue.
Community feedback can skew toward a vocal minority; validate before over-committing.
This is a reported case, not evidence that community-first guarantees product fit.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Run a no-ads week experiment to test organic dependence
cards.summary: Pause paid acquisition for a short window and measure what organic traffic, content, and personal outreach can carry.
cards.use_when: Acquisition strategy review when you suspect the business depends entirely on paid channels.
steps: Pick a defined window (the source suggests a 'no-ads week') and pause paid acquisition during it.
Use the freed time to create content, engage your community directly, and reach out to customers personally rather than simply switching spend off and waiting.
Measure what happens to organic traffic and conversions during and after the pause, so you learn your true organic baseline.

Use the result as evidence for how much brand-building infrastructure you actually need versus how much you're renting via ads. The source's example, Province of Canada, reportedly generated over $100,000 in revenue in months without spending a dollar on ads in its first five years.
Repeat periodically to track whether your organic share is improving over time.
caveats: A week is too short to judge a long-run organic strategy; treat it as a snapshot, not a verdict.
The $100,000 figure and five-year timeline come from one brand's reported story.
Stopping ads temporarily can depress algorithmic or retargeting performance beyond the pause window.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Turn customers into co-creators through structured feedback
cards.summary: Create a visible feedback loop so customers see their input shaping the product.
cards.use_when: Product roadmap and retention planning for a marketplace or catalog where customer experience drives repeat purchase.
steps: Build a structured channel for feedback - surveys, community calls, or a dedicated inbox - rather than relying on ad-hoc comments.

Pay attention to how people actually experience the product or platform, not just what they say they want. The source's case, Bon Magasinage in Canada, had the founder track what worked, what didn't, and what could improve in the resale platform.
Act on the feedback visibly, and show customers that their input changed something.
Use the loop to focus your roadmap so you don't build features or products nobody wants.
Track loyalty and repeat behavior as the outcome of the loop, not just satisfaction scores.
caveats: This is a non-ecommerce-specific example from a second-hand fashion platform; adapt the mechanism to your own category.
No numeric results are reported, so treat the outcome as qualitative.
Feedback channels can be gamed by vocal outliers if you don't segment responses.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Question category assumptions to find structural advantage
cards.summary: Look for beliefs everyone in your category accepts as true, then test whether they're actually wrong.
cards.use_when: Strategy and product selection when your category commoditizes and you need a structural cost or positioning edge.
steps: List the assumptions everyone in your category treats as fixed - for Kogan.com, the assumption was that Australians wouldn't buy big-ticket electronics online.
Pick the assumption with the biggest upside if it turns out to be false, and test it with an actual product offer rather than a survey.
Support the bet structurally: Kogan reportedly built its own tech stack and went direct to manufacturers so digital efficiency could strip waste and pass savings to customers.
Lean into the resulting cost position when conditions shift - the source notes the company turned cost-of-living pressures into a growth engine, with gross margins rising as fixed costs fell.
Revisit the assumption list periodically as technology and consumer behavior change.
caveats: The $10 billion business scale is a single Australian company's outcome and not a template for margin structure.
Structural advantages like direct-to-manufacturer require capital and operational capability.
Assumptions sometimes hold for a reason; testing them can burn real inventory and cash.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Creator-first commerce: let affiliates drive discovery
cards.summary: Build creator and affiliate relationships and make their content the primary discovery and conversion engine.
cards.use_when: Acquisition channel planning when you want third-party content to carry discovery rather than your own ads.
steps: Recruit creators who genuinely fit your niche and give them tools and freedom to make content that feels authentic to them, following the source's description of Natura's creator and affiliate-first approach on TikTok.
Use a commerce platform that supports the model end-to-end for discovery, connection, and conversion - Natura used TikTok Shop as the central platform.
Let creator content serve as the reference point for the wider ecosystem, so you're not producing every asset yourself.

Seed product to creators for independent, unscripted reactions rather than heavily sponsored scripts. The source's other case, Swiss Arabian, had creators order independently and share unboxing content on Instagram and TikTok.
Track creator-attributed revenue separately so you can prune and invest appropriately.
caveats: Creator content is less controllable than your own; you can't force a narrative.
The source reports no specific performance numbers for these campaigns, so treat the model as directional.
Affiliate/creator disclosure rules apply in most markets.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: TikTok-first international expansion without local infrastructure
cards.summary: Test new markets through a platform that handles logistics and payments, before committing to offices or distributors.
cards.use_when: International expansion planning when you want to validate demand abroad without fixed local costs.
steps: Verify seller and product eligibility, fulfillment, payment support, fees and local obligations in the target market before assuming a platform removes the need for local infrastructure.
Verify demand in one market with a small product selection before expanding the range.
Use tailored campaigns and creator partnerships per market rather than one global creative approach.

Build awareness on the platform first, then expand into marketplaces like Amazon once demand is proven - the source describes MBX using a 'TikTok-first model' and TikTok's cross-border selling features.
Keep market entry reversible until you see repeatable unit economics.
caveats: The source reports no revenue figures for these expansions; treat the method as a low-commitment test, not a proven growth engine.
Platform logistics, fees, and cross-border features change frequently - verify current capabilities in your target markets.
Localization quality determines whether a test reflects real demand or a bad translation.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Make your benefit entertaining and culturally specific
cards.summary: Convert a functional product benefit into a jingle-led, shareable, culturally resonant format.
cards.use_when: Paid and organic creative strategy when your product benefit is utilitarian and forgettable.
steps: Identify your flattest functional benefit - the source's case, the Carrefour app in the Middle East, had to communicate that online shopping is easy.
Translate it into an entertaining format: Carrefour used a jingle-led, social-first approach with a culturally specific line rather than a feature list.
Localize the creative to the culture and language of the audience rather than running a translated global asset.
Design for sharing first - a memorable hook, character, or sound that spreads on social platforms.
Test the entertaining version against your standard functional creative to see whether recall and conversion improve.
caveats: Humour and jingles are easy to get wrong; cultural missteps can backfire.
No performance figures are reported in the source for this campaign.
Entertainment-led creative still needs a clear next step to convert.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Publish lifestyle content and monetize with matching products
cards.summary: Define a worldview your brand represents, publish content expressing it, and curate products that embody it.
cards.use_when: Content strategy and category positioning when you want customers to come for the content and stay for the products.
steps: Write down the worldview your brand stands for - what you believe about your category, your customers, and how they should live. The source's model, Hokuoh Kurashi no Doguten, built content around design, craft, food, and everyday life and let commerce follow from it.
Ask the test question the source poses: what content would my customers consume even if I never sold them anything?
Create that content consistently, and treat the store as an extension of the editorial voice rather than a separate entity.
Curate products that naturally fit the world you've built, so the offer feels like an extension of the content rather than an interruption.
Measure the audience you build as well as the revenue, since the model is explicitly a slower, zero-advertising-cost growth path.
caveats: The source describes this as a studied model rather than a campaign with published conversion metrics.
Editorial capability is a real operating cost; content-led commerce fails on thin or inconsistent content.
Long payback period; not suitable if you need near-term acquisition efficiency.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Position stores as community hubs and spotlight real people
cards.summary: Treat physical retail as a creative and community space, and reduce paid influencer activity in favour of authentic figures.
cards.use_when: Retail expansion and brand-building decisions when you want intrinsic community pull rather than rented attention.
steps: Position stores as creative hubs and community spaces rather than pure distribution channels - the source's case, Kotn in Canada, invested in brick-and-mortar with that framing.
Dramatically reduce sponsored influencer campaigns and instead spotlight third-culture figures and real customers who embody your values.
Ensure the values the brand stands for are specific and lived, not generic purpose language, so the community can genuinely self-select.
Create physical or digital spaces where that community can gather, and let the retail footprint carry the brand story.
Accept a slower, more intrinsic growth curve in exchange for a customer base drawn to the brand's point of view.
caveats: Physical retail adds fixed cost and risk; the approach depends on foot traffic economics in your market.
No performance figures are reported in the source for the reduction in sponsored influencer spend.
Authenticity claims are fragile - a mismatch between values and operations undermines the whole position.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Align your offer with a cultural or political moment
cards.summary: Identify a moment your customers care about and build a curated offer that lets them act on that sentiment.
cards.use_when: Product selection and bundle design when a cultural shift drives customers toward local or values-aligned buying.
steps: Watch for cultural or political moments that create purchasing intent in your market - the source's case, Common Goods in Canada, launched a Buy Canadian marketplace in response to US trade tensions.
Design the offer so acting on the sentiment is easy: the example used curated gift boxes filled with Canadian products rather than a sprawling catalog.
Only align where the fit is authentic; the source frames riding a moment of goodwill as valid only if the brand genuinely serves it.
Be ready for demand spikes: the source reports traffic surged after launch.
Plan for what happens after the moment fades, since trend-aligned traffic can be temporary.
caveats: Politically framed positioning can alienate customers on the other side of the issue.
The 'traffic surged' result is a single founder's account with no figures.
Trend-driven demand may not convert to durable repeat customers.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Run livestream selling with timed drops and real-time bidding
cards.summary: Collapse the distance between content and checkout by selling live with limited-time listings and auctions.
cards.use_when: Merchandising and channel testing for products that benefit from demonstration, storytelling, or collector appeal.
steps: Choose products that reward demonstration or storytelling - the source's case, eBay Live in Australia, blends livestream entertainment with real-time bidding and timed drops.
Compress the buy window: timed listings, one-off drops, and auctions create the urgency that makes live selling work.
Keep the checkout inside the live format so viewers who are already engaged can buy immediately without leaving.
Use the format for collector or inventory-heavy categories where real-time chat and bidding add value.

Run it on any live platform you already have - the source notes Instagram Live, TikTok Live, or YouTube Live can substitute for a dedicated platform - and verify current commerce features since platform capabilities change.
caveats: Requires host skill and preparation; low-energy streams convert poorly.
No performance figures are reported in the source for these formats.
Auction mechanics carry consumer-protection and platform-rule considerations.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Use a mystery hook to break through campaign noise
cards.summary: Launch a teasing format with an unexplained premise, then reveal it as an ad for your sale or product.
cards.use_when: Campaign creative planning around a major promotion when standard announcement assets are being ignored.
steps: Create a piece of content whose premise is intriguing on its own - the source's case, Lazada, released 'haunted CCTV footage' ahead of a 9.9 sale.
Delay the reveal so curiosity drives people to investigate before they know it's an ad.
Make the reveal worth the curiosity: Lazada's footage turned out to be an ad for 'Scarily Good Deals', so the payoff connected directly to the sale.
Keep the tone consistent with your brand personality - the source frames this as suitable for playful or daring brands.
Use it specifically to break through during high-noise sale periods when everyone is shouting promotions.
caveats: Clickbait-style hooks that don't pay off damage trust and can draw platform penalties.
No sales or engagement figures are reported in the source for this campaign.
Mystery formats are risky for brands with conservative audiences.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Shift from discount positioning to cultural relevance
cards.summary: Invest in visual identity and influencer-led storytelling so customers see you as a style source, not a discount channel.
cards.use_when: Brand positioning review when price competition is destroying margin and you want to compete on taste instead.
steps: Audit how much of your communication is discount-led; if price is the main reason customers shop with you, the source's argument is that you have no durable position.

Build three things deliberately: a bold visual identity, influencer-led storytelling, and omnichannel integration - the source's case, ZALORA in Southeast Asia, structured its campaign around those pillars.
Partner with a diverse ecosystem of creators across your markets rather than a single face, so the story feels broad and credible.
Shift the message from 'buy cheap clothes' to 'here is style inspiration', which is the repositioning the source credits with the brand's award recognition.
Measure brand metrics alongside conversion to confirm the shift is landing.
caveats: No performance figures are reported; the outcome cited is an industry award, not a sales result.
Brand repositioning is slow and expensive and won't fix a broken unit economics model on its own.
Discount-led competitors may take your price-sensitive customers during the transition.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Turn a small store into a community with events and social
cards.summary: Use social media and recurring events to transform a small online retailer into a community destination.
cards.use_when: Community and local marketing for a small store that can't outspend larger competitors.
steps: Use social media to tell your story and attract people who care about what you carry, following the source's case of Bailey Books in Canada.
Host events - virtual or in-person - that bring your community together; the source notes events don't need to be elaborate, just create space for connection.
Build an event calendar as an ongoing asset rather than a one-off launch activity.
Let the community, not the catalog, be the reason people return, which the source frames as something a purely online store cannot replicate.
Accept that the payoff is slower and harder to attribute than paid acquisition.
caveats: This is a bookstore case, not a product ecommerce playbook; adapt carefully to your category.
No revenue or traffic figures are reported in the source.
Events consume staff time and only work if you can sustain them.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Establish community-driven product development for resale or marketplace models
cards.summary: Let customer experience feedback directly shape platform and product evolution, and make the changes visible.
cards.use_when: Retention and product roadmap decisions for second-hand, marketplace, or community-driven commerce.
steps: Create a direct line from users to the founder or product owner so friction is heard early - the source's case, Bon Magasinage, had the founder tracking what worked, what didn't, and what could improve.
Focus on the experience of using the platform, not just the products listed on it.
Make improvements visible to the community so they see their feedback produced a change.
Strengthen loyalty through demonstrated responsiveness rather than loyalty discounts.
Use the feedback loop as a substitute for expensive market research if you have an engaged user base.
caveats: The source reports no numeric outcomes for this case.
This is a resale marketplace example; the mechanism transfers but the specifics may not.
Reactive feedback loops can produce feature sprawl if you act on every request.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Design a Wild Bet by Breaking a Category Convention
cards.summary: A step-by-step playbook for turning a constraining category 'rule' into a differentiated, hedged ecommerce experiment.
cards.use_when: You want to design one deliberate, differentiating store initiative (drop, loyalty mechanic, community play, campaign) instead of another incremental tactic.
steps: Step 1 — List the unwritten rules of your category (e.g. 'you must spend on paid ads to grow', 'loyalty points should never expire', 'discounts are the only urgency lever', 'you can't sell big-ticket online', 'you need a physical store to build community'). Pick the single rule that feels most constraining as your target.

Step 2 — Study adjacent industries for transplantable models: luxury fashion, gaming, hospitality, live events, collectibles, financial markets. Source examples: Last Crumb borrowed streetwear drop mechanics, Haus & Kinder borrowed gaming FOMO mechanics, Mercari borrowed experiential retail.
Define the target segment, hypothesis, total cash and labor cap, duration, baseline or holdout, and stop condition. Limit downside rather than assuming it can always be hedged.
Step 4 — Execute with obsessive detail; wild bets live or die on execution (packaging, paper stock, photography, delivery scripts).
Track referrals, repeat purchase and incremental contribution after all program costs; treat attention and earned-media estimates as separate signals.
At the planned review, scale, revise or stop based on the evidence; do not treat a single viral outcome as repeatable proof.
Step 7 — Document what you did, why it worked, and the results, then systemize it for repetition.
caveats: Run most wild bets cheaply; the source explicitly states most will fail.
Case results cited (e.g. Huckberry 3.5x LTV, Lulu and Georgia 78.5% incremental revenue) are examples, not benchmarks or promises.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: The 'Doesn't Scale' Philosophy for Defensible Ecommerce Advantage
cards.summary: Tactics that resist easy scaling (manual effort, personalization, human touch) create differentiation because competitors can't commoditize them.
cards.use_when: You're deciding where to invest founder time versus automation in acquisition, onboarding, or early-customer experience.
steps: Apply the core principles from Paul Graham's essay and Y Combinator case studies: recruit users one by one (Airbnb founders photographed New York listings door-to-door; Stripe installed the product for early customers personally; DoorDash founders delivered food themselves).
Go where your users are rather than waiting for them. If your buyers are on TikTok, be on TikTok; if at Coachella, be at Coachella.
Over-deliver beyond expectation: handwritten note, surprise gift, personal follow-up. These create stories customers retell.
Ask for referrals personally and make referring easy and rewarding rather than routing it entirely through automation.
Do manually what you'll automate later — manual work yields insights no dashboard gives.
Belief behind the method: if a tactic scales easily, everyone does it and it becomes commoditized.
caveats: Source framing, not a rule for every channel; paid media and automation still appear throughout the source's other examples.
Ecommerce application: the source's demonstrated cases are mostly DTC brands; treat analogies for your own store as hypotheses to test.
Source examples (Province of Canada, Heaven Mayhem, Benjie, Gully Labs) are illustrations without guaranteed replication.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Five Low-Cost 'Doesn't Scale' Ecommerce Experiments
cards.summary: Concrete, cheap founder-led tests — from the 20-customers exercise to a no-ads week — designed to surface customer insight and referrals.
cards.use_when: You want to test unscalable, human-touch tactics in acquisition, retention, or product development without a big budget.
steps: The '20 customers' exercise: imagine you could only have 20 customers. Write down every touchpoint from discovery to post-purchase, then identify where you can add a manual, human touch.
The 'founder's inbox' test: for one month forward every customer-service email to the founder and reply personally. The source claims you'll learn more in 30 days than in a year of surveys.
The 'unscalable gift' experiment: pick your top 10 customers from the last quarter, send a handwritten note and a small unexpected gift, and track whether they reorder and refer.
Adapt the source's no-ads-week idea as a bounded acquisition experiment; set a maximum acceptable revenue loss and account for campaign disruption before changing an established paid channel.

The 'community first' approach: before launching your next product, spend six months building an audience and gathering feedback (as Gully Labs did), letting the product emerge from community conversation.
caveats: Timelines and counts (20 customers, 30 days, 10 gifts, 6 months) are the source's suggestions, not validated thresholds.
Founder-inbox replies only work while volume is low; it is an early-stage diagnostic, not a permanent support model.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Programmatic Direct Mail for Abandoned-Cart and Browse Retargeting
cards.summary: Bring the abandoned-cart reminder into the physical mail stream with personalized product imagery and frequency caps.
cards.use_when: You have high cart or browse abandonment on high-consideration products and want a retargeting channel beyond email and ads.
steps: Send programmatic direct mail showing the specific product the customer abandoned or personalized recommendations based on browsing. Source examples: Furn mailed 514 A4 letters in C5 envelopes showcasing abandoned products and reported a 40% return rate; Lulu and Georgia, via PebblePost, reported 80% identity match, 22x iROAS, and a 78.5% increase in overall incremental revenue using mail sent within days of a browsing session.
Prioritize high-value carts and long consideration cycles; the source says it works best where customers need multiple touchpoints before buying.
Keep creative simple and clear, featuring the abandoned item or recommendation.

Set a frequency cap to avoid over-saturation. Magazine.co.uk limited customers to one mailing every 30 days and reported 38.81% higher conversions, personalized to the exact magazines left in the basket.
Measure incremental lift against a control group rather than comparing mail recipients only to non-mail cohorts.
caveats: All figures are vendor/partner-reported campaign results and should not be treated as expected benchmarks.
Programmatic DM requires identity-matching coverage; results depend on match rate.
Verify current vendor capabilities and pricing with the provider before budgeting.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Triggered Direct Mail Mapped to Ecommerce Journeys
cards.summary: Treat physical mail as a behavioral trigger inside existing automations — welcome, abandoned cart, post-purchase, win-back — with content tailored by cohort.
cards.use_when: You are mapping lifecycle automations (welcome, abandoned cart, post-purchase, win-back) and want to decide where a physical mailer adds value.
steps: Map your key ecommerce journeys first: welcome, abandoned cart, post-purchase, win-back.
Identify which journey steps would gain from a physical touch — typically high-value moments where attention is scarce.

Dynamically personalize content and offers by customer cohort and purchase history. DukesHill, a UK food retailer, ran a data-led triggered mail program with cohort-tailored content and offers and reported 22% more conversions.
Integrate direct-mail triggers into your existing automation platform so behavior fires the mailer the same way it fires an email.

Use QR codes or unique URLs to track engagement, then feed that engagement data back to trigger digital follow-ups, as Harlow Timber did with a Black Friday email that earned an 88% open rate across 12,000 contacts after direct-mail engagement.
caveats: Reported lifts (22% conversions, 88% open rate) are single-campaign examples, not guaranteed baselines.
Triggered mail adds cost and production lead time versus email; reserve it for segments where the math works.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Direct Mail for Second Purchase and Membership Onboarding
cards.summary: Use personalized physical letters at two high-leverage moments: first-to-second purchase and new loyalty-club membership.
cards.use_when: You are deciding how to move first-time buyers to a repeat purchase or how to onboard new loyalty/club members.
steps: Identify the moment in the customer lifecycle when a second purchase is most likely — the source suggests around 30–60 days after first purchase — and send a personalized letter with a specific offer or recommendation based on the first purchase.
Fressnapf's second-purchase campaign to 15,000 customers used personalized letters via optilyz and reported ROI of 6 and doubled conversion rate; a separate reactivation campaign also performed well.

For membership programs, send a physical welcome kit to new members with a personalized note, a small gift, and clear benefits information. GOLDNER's personalized welcome letters across seven European countries reported conversion rates ranging from 3.4% to 13.6%.
Treat tangibility of the first contact and depth of personalization as the stated success factors.
Track reorder and referral behavior for recipients so you can judge whether the letter earned its cost.
caveats: The 30–60 day window is a source suggestion, not a validated universal rule; find your own repurchase interval from order data.
The 3.4%–13.6% range reflects GOLDNER's multi-country campaign, not a target for your store.
ROI calculations depend on margin assumptions; define yours before claiming results.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Evaluate third-party audience data for an ecommerce direct-mail test
cards.summary: Assess audience relevance, data provenance and permitted use before a third-party acquisition mailing.
cards.use_when: You're planning acquisition or win-back against named competitors (e.g. meal-kit or subscription categories) and need targeting data.
steps: Engage a data partner to build distinct behavioral segments for acquisition and win-back campaigns.
Ask the provider to explain how audience segments and mailing addresses are obtained and used; a claim of anonymized insights does not make address-based targeting anonymous.
Craft specific messaging that incentivizes switching from the identified competitor.
Segregate acquisition and win-back creative: win-back speaks to a prior relationship, conquesting speaks to a competitor's value proposition.
Confirm GDPR and local privacy compliance for data sourcing and mailing before launching.
caveats: Requires third-party data partnership and compliance review; not a DIY tactic.
The source shows the structure HelloFresh used; it does not publish performance numbers.
The source's campaign label does not establish compliance for a new store, dataset or market.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Reflect Brand Values in Direct Mail Materials
cards.summary: Make paper stock, printing and messaging consistent with sustainability or premium positioning so the physical mailer reinforces rather than contradicts the brand.
cards.use_when: Your brand positioning rests on sustainability or premium quality and you are planning a direct mail or direct-mail retargeting program.
steps: Check that the mail format matches the brand promise: recycled paper and sustainable printing for sustainability-led brands; heavier stock and craft for premium ones.
Write messaging that reinforces the same positioning the site and packaging carry.

For relevance and sustainability, show the customer their own abandoned or recommended products rather than generic catalog pages, as Woolroom did via Paperplanes when testing personalized direct mail for abandoned or recommended products.
Pair personalization with an extra incentive to visit the site.
As a rule of execution from the design playbook, treat paper stock as a detail that matters once you have committed to mail.
caveats: The source does not provide verified sales figures for Woolroom; it describes the test design and brand alignment.
Verify current sustainable-printing and paper certifications with your print partner.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Personalized Direct Mail for High-Value B2B Proposals (Wholesale, Corporate Gifts, Trade)
cards.summary: Tightly defined target personas plus personalized direct mail inside a multi-touch ABM campaign for large accounts.
cards.use_when: You sell wholesale, corporate gifting, bulk or trade accounts where a single account is worth substantial revenue.
steps: Define a small number of target personas — the M&S Corporate Gifts program defined three — and tighten the focus of outreach rather than mailing broadly.
Build a list of high-value prospects; the source example contacted 100 prospects.
Send personalized direct mail to those prospects as one touch within a larger multi-touch campaign, not as a standalone stunt.
Use the physical mailer as the touch that breaks through digital noise, then follow with the rest of the account-based sequence.

Apply the same personalized mailing approach to inactive customer re-engagement where account value justifies the cost; the source cites Harlow Timber coupling direct mail with QR codes and a digital follow-up.
caveats: Very small prospect counts are appropriate only when account value justifies per-piece cost.
The source reports that sales rose but gives no numeric benchmark for the M&S campaign.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Build a Sticky Buying Moment Around Culture, Not a Generic Sale
cards.summary: Ride a cultural or political moment your customers care about, and make acting on it easy with pre-curated bundles.
cards.use_when: You are planning seasonal merchandising, bundles, or a campaign and deciding whether a cultural moment is an authentic fit for your store.
steps: Identify the cultural or political moments that genuinely matter to your customer base; the source example is Canadian buying sentiment amid US trade tensions.
Only align if your brand can do it authentically; the source frames authenticity as the condition for the goodwill.
Convert sentiment into an easy purchase: Common Goods launched curated gift boxes filled with Canadian products so customers did not have to assemble the decision themselves, and traffic surged.
Apply this to ecommerce merchandising by bundling your own or partner products into a ready-made 'act on this value' box rather than just changing banner copy.
Spotlight real customers or community members who embody the value rather than paid influencers.
caveats: Political alignment carries backlash risk with customers who disagree; the source does not discuss downside cases.
Traffic surges from a moment are not automatically conversion or retention gains; measure beyond visits.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Automate Rule-Based Operations Before Chasing Wild Bets
cards.summary: Use AI to absorb repetitive customer service, outreach and content tasks so solo operators can spend judgment on the bets that matter.
cards.use_when: You are a small or solo ecommerce team deciding what to automate versus what to keep manual.
steps: Audit the business for tasks that are repetitive and rule-based — the source names personalized emails, customer-service responses, and content creation.
Automate those with AI tools to reach a volume a solo founder could not match manually, per the 'AI Gothpreneur' model.
Reserve founder time for strategy and creative work, and for the wild bets that require human judgment.
Do not automate the high-touch 'doesn't scale' moments the source treats as differentiation (personal follow-ups, referral asks, over-delivery).
As with any AI tooling, verify the current capabilities, pricing and data-handling terms of each provider before committing.
caveats: This is a LinkedIn-post model, not a measured case study; no performance data is presented.
The source pairs this with human-touch differentiation elsewhere, so automation is not a blanket prescription.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Scarcity, Clout and Exclusive Drops: Borrowing Streetwear Mechanics
cards.summary: Design product or campaign drops using scarcity and status so the release itself becomes the story.
cards.use_when: You are planning a product drop, limited release, or landing page for a new item and want it to spread without paid ads.
steps: Borrow the drop model from a different industry: the source points to Last Crumb, which spent a year on brand work (including photography) before launch, with the product already developed and tested; the piece was framed around scarcity, clout and Michelin-star ambition, with $120 cookie drops.
Use scarcity deliberately — limited quantities or timed windows — and make exclusivity part of the packaging and drop experience.
Invest disproportionately in the visual and material details that signal status: photography, packaging, unboxing.
Time the drop so audience attention is already built (Gully Labs built an audience for six months before the product).
Measure the drop by word-of-mouth and LTV of engaged buyers, not by paid-media ROAS.
caveats: Scarcity can damage trust if it is faked or repeated too often; the source presents it as an ambitious brand-building choice, not a default.
The $120 price point is a brand-specific example.
cards.source_name: Wild bets.docx

cards.title: Calculate true gross margin with the "all in until it's in" COGS rule
cards.summary: Define COGS as every cost incurred to get a product onto the warehouse shelf ready to sell, so gross margin reflects reality rather than guesswork.
cards.use_when: When setting product prices, deciding which sales channels to sell on, or reviewing whether a SKU is actually profitable.
steps: Identify purchase and attributable inbound/conversion costs that bring inventory to its present location and condition; not every incremental cost qualifies.
Include supplier purchase price less applicable discounts, inbound freight and non-recoverable duties under the accounting policy.
Allocate shared inbound costs across SKUs using a documented driver such as weight, volume or value.
Carry qualifying costs in inventory until the goods are sold, then recognize the related COGS.
Recalculate landed unit cost when supplier prices, exchange rates or freight change.
caveats: The source is an accounting practitioner's guidance for statutory reporting; different KPIs such as contribution margin may be more useful internally than statutory COGS for some decisions.
Manufacturers have an additional layer of cost above simple bought-in goods; the walkthrough assumes a buy-and-resell model.
cards.source_name: Calculating COGS_ What Ecommerce Businesses Get Wrong.docx

cards.title: Sort each expense into COGS or operating expense before reporting margin
cards.summary: Use a consistent above-the-line/below-the-line split so gross profit comparisons across periods and channels mean something.
cards.use_when: When preparing monthly management accounts, evaluating channel profitability (Amazon vs Shopify), or diagnosing why profit does not match sales growth.
steps: Document the applicable accounting policy for inventory, cost of sales, fulfillment and selling expenses; timing before or after sale alone is not the classification test.
Track purchase cost, attributable inbound freight and duties as eligible inventory cost, expensed when sold.
Track outbound shipping, transaction fees, ads and storage separately so internal contribution can be reconciled to accounting gross profit.
Treat sale-price discounts in net revenue as applicable; do not automatically classify coupons as operating expenses.
Apply consistent definitions across Shopify, Amazon and reporting periods.
caveats: Rules described are for statutory/compliance accounts in the presenter's jurisdictions; internal KPI reporting may deliberately deviate.
cards.source_name: Calculating COGS_ What Ecommerce Businesses Get Wrong.docx

cards.title: Split packaging into product packaging (COGS) and shipping packaging (expense)
cards.summary: Distinguish the retail box that is part of the product from the transit box it ships in, since the two often arrive on one supplier invoice.
cards.use_when: When coding packaging supplier invoices, or when packaging spend is large enough to distort margin on fragile or gift-oriented products.
steps: Ask of each packaging item: does it sit on the shelf as part of what the customer buys? The branded retail box, inner tray and any presentation element is COGS.
Anything whose only job is to survive transit — the plain outer carton, void fill, tape, labels — is a shipping/operating expense.
When one invoice contains both types, split the line items before posting rather than coding the whole invoice to one account.
For multipacks or gift sets where the outer box is part of the offer, treat that box as product packaging and keep it in COGS.
Review the split whenever you change packaging suppliers, since mixed invoices are the common source of misclassification.
caveats: The retail-box rule comes from physical retail logic the source explicitly extends to ecommerce; there can be genuine grey areas for premium unboxing experiences — pick a defensible treatment and apply it consistently.
cards.source_name: Calculating COGS_ What Ecommerce Businesses Get Wrong.docx

cards.title: Separate dropship product and shipping costs in margin analysis
cards.summary: Compare dropship and stocked orders on complete order contribution, with a documented accounting policy.
cards.use_when: When calculating margin for a drop-shipped product line, or when deciding whether to offer free shipping on a SKU.
steps: Separate supplier product charges, inbound costs where relevant and customer-delivery charges.
Document how bundled supplier invoices are allocated and reported under the applicable policy.
Do not let free versus separately charged shipping alone determine accounting classification.
Include all merchant-paid delivery costs when comparing order contribution for stocked and dropship products.
Reconcile internal contribution reporting with the accountant's inventory and expense classifications.
caveats: Presented as a general rule with explicit exceptions, not a universal standard; confirm treatment with your accountant for statutory accounts.
Deciding whether to negotiate freight or find suppliers sits outside this method — that is a sourcing decision.
cards.source_name: Calculating COGS_ What Ecommerce Businesses Get Wrong.docx

cards.title: Code customer returns correctly and turn returns into a second sale
cards.summary: Classify the return cost accurately, then consider voucher or exchange offers that recover the sale — noting the extra accounting complexity they create.
cards.use_when: When managing return rates in apparel or other high-return categories, and when designing return-flow offers at the returns step.
steps: Track return shipping separately using the documented accounting policy.
Assess returned inventory condition, recoverable value and refurbishment costs; do not automatically capitalize all return labor or post it immediately to COGS.

At the point of return, consider offering a voucher, discount, alternative item or upsell. The source reports success from encouraging a replacement purchase at the return step, based on the observation that the original item simply wasn't quite right.
Consider prepaid return labels at a negotiated discounted rate as a way to control return-shipping cost.
Expect the accounting to get harder when returns generate vouchers or discounts: you must track what was actually sold, at what margin, net of the incentive.
If returns are material, track return-specific metrics alongside standard gross margin rather than forcing everything into one COGS figure.
caveats: The returns-to-resale offer is reported as an observed pattern, not a benchmarked result; test it against your own margin after vouchers and discounts.
Given rising shipping costs, the source notes free shipping and free returns are increasingly hard to sustain profitably.
cards.source_name: Calculating COGS_ What Ecommerce Businesses Get Wrong.docx

cards.title: Capture freight and duty against the right purchase order at the time it happens
cards.summary: Stop accumulating unattributed freight and duty invoices; attach each cost to the purchase it belongs to so landed cost can actually be calculated.
cards.use_when: When inbound logistics costs are piling up unallocated, or when setting up the purchasing workflow for a growing ecommerce operation.
steps: When raising a purchase order, record the agreed unit price and verify it against the supplier invoice that later hits the financials.
At the moment a freight or duty invoice arrives, identify which purchase order(s) it relates to and record the cost against them — do not file it to be sorted out later.
Avoid the common failure mode the source describes: a growing pile of freight and duty invoices never matched back to the products they belong to.
When one shipment carries multiple products, allocate the total freight or duty across them, weighting where the cost differs by unit (bulk, weight or value).
Treat this as a people-and-process discipline first; software helps execute it but does not replace defining who captures what and when.
caveats: Spreadsheets can work at small scale, but the source advises inventory management software as the business scales and allocations become weighted.
Specific inventory-management or accounting apps are mentioned in the source as vendor material; verify current features and integrations before selecting one.
cards.source_name: Calculating COGS_ What Ecommerce Businesses Get Wrong.docx

cards.title: Move from spreadsheets to weighted landed-cost allocation as SKU count grows
cards.summary: Attribute lump-sum freight and duty down to unit level so every SKU shows a true cost, using software once manual weighting becomes unreliable.
cards.use_when: When you sell many SKUs per shipment and cannot tell whether individual products are profitable, or when preparing to scale purchasing.
steps: Recognise the problem shape: costs arrive as lump sums (one container, one duty invoice) but decisions are made per SKU.
Choose an allocation basis — the source notes you may have ordered three or four different items and the freight or duty needs to be weighted differently across them.
Do the weighting consistently for every shipment; inconsistent bases across months make margin trends meaningless.
Move to inventory management software when volume or SKU count makes spreadsheet weighting error-prone, so landed cost is computed automatically per item.
Verify that the software's output ties back to the actual freight and duty invoices you received before relying on the margins it reports.
caveats: The source flags a vendor relationship behind this recommendation; treat it as a capability requirement, not a specific product endorsement.
No specific trigger volume for switching from spreadsheets is given — judge it by error rate and time cost, not a fixed number.
cards.source_name: Calculating COGS_ What Ecommerce Businesses Get Wrong.docx

cards.title: Classify supplier discounts and credits against product cost
cards.summary: Reduce COGS when a supplier discounts goods you are buying; handle credits carefully where stock has moved back.
cards.use_when: When posting supplier credit notes, rebates or discounts and deciding whether they lower unit cost or sit as income.
steps: Match supplier discounts and rebates to the affected goods and original purchase orders.
Reduce eligible inventory purchase cost for unsold affected goods and related cost of sales for sold goods as required by the accounting policy.
Record supplier returns with the corresponding stock movement and credit note.
Do not automatically post product-cost rebates as unrelated income.
Reconcile accruals and subsequent credits consistently; recognition is not a discretionary choice between past and future periods.
caveats: The source hedges this point ('it depends', 'generally speaking'), particularly for credits tied to stock movement — confirm with your accountant.
cards.source_name: Calculating COGS_ What Ecommerce Businesses Get Wrong.docx

cards.title: Troubleshoot a slipping P&L by reading upward, not sideways
cards.summary: Use the P&L hierarchy to locate which line above a missed target is causing the miss instead of guessing at an ads problem.
cards.use_when: Monthly or weekly review when net profit, contribution margin or gross margin misses target and you need to decide whether to cut spend, fix returns, reprice or renegotiate freight.
steps: Build the P&L as a stacked ladder: Revenue, Cost of Delivery, Gross Margin, Marketing (MEA), Contribution Margin, OPEX, EBITDA, Interest, Net Profit.
Express every line as a percentage of revenue as well as dollars, and track month-over-month movement rather than a single snapshot.

Apply the fault rule: if a target line is missed, the cause is everything above it. Missed EBITDA = OPEX, MEA or cost of delivery. Missed contribution margin = MEA or cost of delivery. Missed gross margin = cost of delivery or revenue (both gross and net).
Chase the specific lever inside the guilty line: refunds, discounts, shipping collected at checkout, landed cost, pick/pack, transaction fees, or media spend.

Set your contribution margin target by working up from the bottom: net profit target + forecast OPEX = required contribution margin, in both percent and dollars. A $1M net target with $1M OPEX requires $2M contribution margin.
Check whether revenue growth came from gross revenue or from a shrinking refund/discount allowance, since accounting software usually only surfaces net.
caveats: Contribution margin is used loosely — the source defines CM1 as product margin, CM2 as gross margin, CM3 as the revenue-minus-cost-of-delivery-minus-marketing figure; confirm which a report means.
Source is an agency operator's framing at 7–9 figure brands; percentage bands are illustrative, not benchmarks.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Separate gross and net revenue to find hidden profit
cards.summary: Gross-to-net breakdown exposes refunds, discounts and shipping collected as the real revenue levers most accounting software hides.
cards.use_when: When revenue moved between two periods and you cannot explain it from marketing or OPEX, or when you are deciding where to hunt for margin before cutting ad spend.
steps: Pull gross revenue, refunds/chargebacks, discount allowance and shipping collected separately, per period. Shopify shows this gross-to-net view; many platforms and accounting tools (Xero, QuickBooks) show only net or a cash read.
Compare the same gross number across months and check whether the net movement came from refunds or discounts rather than new demand.

Treat each line as a lever: fewer refunds, fewer discount codes redeemed, and more shipping collected at checkout all increase net revenue without extra traffic. The source claims most stores under-collect shipping at checkout.
If a gross-to-net view is not flowing into your accounting software, have your bookkeeper reconcile it into a custom report so decisions are not made off a net-only figure.
Investigate refund-rate spikes by product and cohort before assuming a media problem, especially in fashion where the source says refund rates have been seen from 10% up to 80%.
caveats: Gross-to-net detail may require custom reporting work; the source notes this gap exists in most accounting stacks.
Raising shipping collected is a pricing/offer change — test conversion impact before rolling out.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Recalculate contribution and break-even acquisition cost before discounting
cards.summary: Model discounted net revenue against all variable order costs before setting acquisition targets.
cards.use_when: Pricing and offer decisions — planning a promo, a bundle, a gift-with-purchase, or a clearance push, and setting the media efficiency target that promo must hit.
steps: Calculate pre-ad contribution per order as net revenue less landed product cost, fulfillment, payment fees and expected return costs, without double-counting discounts or refunds.
With $100 net revenue and $60 variable costs, contribution is $40; break-even CAC is $40 and revenue ROAS is 100/40 = 2.5.
At $70 discounted net revenue and unchanged $60 costs, contribution is $10: break-even CAC is $10 and ROAS is 70/10 = 7.
Compare a bundle or gift-with-purchase using actual basket costs and measured incremental conversion; a $4 gift does not guarantee another $100 sale.
Check clearance cash recovery separately from profitable ongoing acquisition.
caveats: Break-even here excludes fixed overhead and target profit; set a lower operating CAC ceiling.
Shipping, fees and returns can change with the offer; use store-specific assumptions.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Calculate pre-marketing contribution using explicit delivery costs
cards.summary: Separate accounting gross profit from the management contribution metric used to fund ecommerce acquisition.
cards.use_when: Before setting marketing KPIs on a product, deciding whether to keep or cut a SKU, or comparing your margin to competitor pricing.
steps: Start from revenue excluding pass-through taxes and recorded discounts/refunds.
Subtract landed product cost, fulfillment, outbound shipping, payment fees and incremental expected return costs exactly once.
Illustration: $100 collected less $9 tax gives $91 revenue. Product $30 + inbound $4 + outbound $11 + pick/pack $4 + fees $3 + assumed return loss $15 leaves $24 contribution, or 24/91 = 26.4%.
If the $15 includes revenue refunds, remove those from the revenue denominator too; document the definition rather than mixing net and gross bases.
Use pre-ad contribution dollars to fund acquisition, overhead and target profit; calculate separately for each SKU and channel.
caveats: This is an internal contribution model, not a universal statutory COGS classification.
The source calls its full-delivery metric gross margin; preserve explicit included costs when comparing reports.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Split variable and fixed marketing costs inside the P&L
cards.summary: Media spend, influencer fees and agency retainers are variable (MEA); in-house creative teams are fixed (OPEX) — miscategorising either distorts contribution margin.
cards.use_when: Structuring your P&L for monthly review, or deciding whether to bring creative production in-house versus using agencies and freelancers.
steps: Put media spend, influencer payments, events and out-of-home into MEA — anything variable with revenue.
Classify content production by whether it is fixed or flexes with demand. A permanent in-house team is OPEX.
Recognise that creative demand flexes seasonally (flat Q1, June spike, heavy November–December), so a fixed team is underworked, overloaded and then briefly right-sized through the year.
Cover the flex with agencies or short-term hires and route those costs to MEA as variable spend; the source notes some brands put all creative in MEA, which is a legitimate brand-level choice.

Keep OPEX genuinely fixed as you scale so margin percentage expands; the source argues seven-figure founders routinely let OPEX grow faster than MEA and cost of delivery, leaving profit flat in dollars.
caveats: Treating all creative as MEA flatters gross margin but reduces comparability to prior periods; pick one convention and keep it consistent.
The margin-expansion logic assumes OPEX stays flat — it does not hold if you add headcount ahead of revenue.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Waterfall pricing from bottom to top
cards.summary: Price by working from a contribution margin target through CAC, returns, fulfillment and COGS up to a price — then test it against competitors and cut the SKU if it fails.
cards.use_when: Launching a new product, repricing an existing one, or evaluating whether a hero SKU can carry paid acquisition.
steps: Set a target post-ad contribution rate on net revenue, allowing room for overhead and profit.
Estimate dollar costs per order: product, shipping, fulfillment, CAC and expected return losses.
For fixed dollar costs C and percentage charges f, solve net price P = C / (1 - target contribution rate - f). The denominator must be positive.
Use one currency and revenue basis; do not add a percentage directly to dollar costs or double-count returns.
Compare the required price with competing offers and test willingness to pay before committing to the SKU.
Stress-test CAC, return rates and fulfillment costs after launch.
caveats: The source estimates roughly 40% of startups price using keystone, a rough impression rather than a study.
CAC estimates for new products are uncertain; revisit the model once real acquisition data exists.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Read product-level economics to beat maximize-conversions bidding
cards.summary: Per-product CAC versus contribution margin reveals which SKUs deserve paid spend, because default bidding optimises the cheapest CPA rather than the most profitable sale.
cards.use_when: Campaign structure and budget allocation decisions when a low-CPA product is absorbing spend while a higher-margin product under-sells.
steps: Build a product-level table: retail price, cost of goods, gross margin dollars, CAC, contribution margin per sale.

Source example: a $90 hoodie with $21 COGS gives $69 gross margin; at $45 CAC it yields $24 contribution. A cheaper t-shirt with $27 gross margin at $15 CAC yields $12 — half the contribution despite a lower CPA.

Recognise that maximize-conversions bidding on Meta, Google or TikTok will send spend to the lowest-CPA item, which here is the less profitable product. Switching to maximize conversion value also fails here, because the hoodie has the worse ROAS.
Fix it structurally: segment campaigns by product category using product-level economics, or split budgets so high-contribution products get deliberate spend.

Apply a cannibalisation test: if a SKU acquires at an implausibly low cost, it may sell organically without media. Cutting spend there can lift its contribution per order and free budget for products that genuinely need paid support to clear.
Revisit allocation for omni-channel and large brands where in-store or organic demand inflates apparent efficiency.
caveats: The dollar figures are a single illustrative example, not category benchmarks.
Organic-versus-paid attribution is a judgement call; avoid cutting spend on a SKU without a holdout test.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Geo-lift testing to measure true incremental spend
cards.summary: Select control and treatment regions, hold out spend, and compare actual revenue against predicted counterfactual revenue.
cards.use_when: When platform ROAS is untrustworthy and you need to decide how much more (or less) to spend in paid media, or validate a channel's real contribution before scaling budget.
steps: Choose a control region and a treatment region with reasonably comparable demand and seasonality, and define the test window up front.
Hold out spend in the control region for the test period rather than relying on platform-reported lift.
Build a predicted counterfactual revenue for the control region from its pre-test history (and, where possible, comparable regions).
Measure the difference between actual revenue and predicted counterfactual revenue as the incremental effect of the spend.
Feed the incremental result back into CAC and break-even modelling rather than into platform-reported CPA.
Treat this as the answer to the source's core argument that attribution is unreliable and the gap between the ad account and the bank account is where brands get into trouble.
caveats: Region comparability and seasonality are the main failure modes; the source gives the design but no minimum viable region count or duration.
Results are estimates, not proof of channel-level causation, especially in small samples.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Forecast new and returning revenue as separate models
cards.summary: New customer revenue is driven by marketing inputs; returning revenue is driven by cohort decay rates and product launches — mixing them produces a forecast nobody can act on.
cards.use_when: Annual or quarterly planning, budget setting, or when deciding how hard to push acquisition versus retention investment.
steps: Build two separate forecast models. New customer revenue: forecast marketing spend and expected new-customer CAC, then derive new customers and multiply by new-customer AOV.
Returning customer revenue: apply historical cohort decay rates to existing customer cohorts and layer on expected product launches or restock events.
Keep new-customer AOV and gross profit separate from blended AOV, since returning customers carry higher AOV and inflate blended figures.

Source illustration: $200k monthly revenue split $140k new and $60k returning; at $50k ad spend and 50% gross margin, new-customer contribution is about $20k while returning contributes roughly $27.5k after ~$2.5k of retention tooling and agency cost — i.e. most profit came from repeat buyers.
Use the split to decide whether acquisition can be subsidised by repeat profit, and how much.
caveats: The revenue split is described by the source as typical for a business of that size; it is an example, not a benchmark.
Cohort decay rates degrade if assortment, pricing or market conditions change; refresh them regularly.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Fix CAC measurement before setting CAC targets
cards.summary: Use total ad spend divided by new customers, and pair CAC against first-purchase gross profit on new customers only.
cards.use_when: Setting acquisition targets, reviewing agency performance, or diagnosing why a 'healthy' blended CAC is not producing profit.
steps: Calculate CAC as total advertising spend over the period divided by total new customers acquired in that period — not platform CPA, which runs on attributed numbers and typically flatters the result.
Refuse channel-level CAC breakdowns; the source argues attribution makes per-channel deltas unreliable.
Pair CAC against gross profit on first purchase, not blended AOV times a possibly-wrong gross margin percentage. New customers typically have lower AOV and heavier discount-driven front-end offers.

Worked check: a $100 blended AOV at an assumed 70% gross margin looks like $70 GP and a comfortable $35 CAC — but if the new-customer AOV is really $90 and front-end discounting compresses margin, true first-purchase GP might be $50, making the CAC target wrong.
Answer 'what is a good CAC?' as a non-question: a $100 CAC against $10,000 first-order GP is excellent; a $100 CAC against $20 GP is a loss. Judge CAC only relative to first-purchase gross profit.
caveats: Attribution-free CAC is a deliberate simplification; channel decisions then rely on experiments such as geo-lift.
Requires clean new-versus-returning customer tagging in your platform and analytics.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Separate new-customer and returning-customer profit contribution
cards.summary: Compute contribution margin on new and returning revenue separately to see where the business actually makes money.
cards.use_when: Deciding budget split between acquisition and retention, or when a founder wants to increase ad spend but the profit source is unclear.
steps: Split monthly revenue into new-customer revenue and returning-customer revenue.
For new customers: new revenue minus ad spend, minus cost of delivery/gross margin, equals new-customer profit contribution.
For returning customers: returning revenue minus gross margin cost, minus retention tooling (email/SMS platform) and any retention agency, equals returning-customer profit contribution.

Source illustration: $140k new revenue minus $50k ad spend at 50% gross margin gives ~$20k; $60k returning revenue minus ~$2.5k tooling and agency gives ~$27.5k — the smaller revenue stream produced the larger profit.
Use the returning-customer profit pool to judge how aggressively you can subsidise new-customer acquisition, and whether increasing new-customer spend is self-funding.
Route the result into retention planning: repeat purchase is driven by product, experience and brand, not by media spend.
caveats: Requires reliable customer-cohort tagging and defensible gross-margin figures.
Retention tooling and agency costs vary widely; use your actual invoices.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Measure 90/180-day LTGP, not open-ended LTV
cards.summary: Restrict customer value to a fixed window and use gross profit rather than revenue so acquisition bids are grounded.
cards.use_when: Setting maximum allowable CAC for CPG, fashion or subscription models where first-order profitability is negative or thin.
steps: Cap the measurement window — the source recommends 90-day or 180-day windows because LTV keeps rising as you extend the horizon, even where it asymptotes.

Compute lifetime gross profit (LTGP), not revenue-based LTV. Many tools report LTV as revenue; in e-commerce the distinction matters because software-style LTV is often close to gross profit while e-commerce LTV is not.
Compare LTGP against CAC to establish payback. The source notes most agencies run a 3–6 month CAC payback period, and CPG brands frequently lose money on first purchase.
Expect competitors with larger repeat value to outbid you at auction; if your LTGP is thin, paying their CAC level is not viable.
Use the window-consistent LTGP to set the ceiling bid, then check it against the 90/180-day actuals before scaling.
caveats: Window choice changes the answer; compare cohorts measured over the same window only.
Cohort LTGP is backward-looking and can overstate value for brands with changing retention.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Ring-fence OPEX to protect margin while scaling
cards.summary: In e-commerce the growth lever is marketing, not headcount or software, so overinflating OPEX flattens profit as revenue grows.
cards.use_when: Budget review when revenue is growing but net profit is flat in dollars, or when deciding whether to hire, add software or upsize an office.
steps: Define OPEX as anything not in cost of delivery or marketing. The three big buckets are people, software and office/fulfillment space.

Keep true fulfillment costs — 3PL, warehouse, and warehouse staff doing pick/pack/ship — inside cost of delivery. Allocate warehouse staff per order (source example: $400/day ÷ 100 packages = $4/order) and have your bookkeeper tag and reclassify them into a custom P&L so gross margin stays accurate.
Keep everyone not directly fulfilling orders (head of marketing, head of operations) in OPEX.

Model the intended scaling shape: OPEX flat, marketing and cost of delivery rising with revenue, so profit expands as a percentage. Watch for OPEX rising faster than revenue, which leaves profit flat.

Be sceptical of 'reinvest in the business' leading to hiring and software that do not drive revenue. Marketing is the revenue lever; people set the skill ceiling but poor hires inflate cost without output.
Put interest expense below EBITDA, never in OPEX — it is financing leverage, and buyers evaluating EBITDA zero out loans.
caveats: The source argues OPEX should stay near-fixed, which assumes no step changes in headcount or systems; treat it as a discipline target, not an absolute.
The source concedes seven-figure brands often lack the skill to hire top talent, so the advice is to delay heavy people investment rather than never hire.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Use EBITDA and net profit as distinct decision numbers
cards.summary: Track EBITDA, net income and cash flow separately when financing inventory or planning owner distributions.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether to take on inventory financing, setting owner distributions, or preparing numbers for a buyer or investor.
steps: Build the management P&L with explicit product, fulfillment, advertising and operating costs.
Bridge EBITDA minus depreciation and amortisation to EBIT, then subtract interest and tax and include applicable non-operating items to reach net income.
Record loan principal repayments in the cash forecast, not as a P&L expense.
Bridge net income to cash using non-cash expenses, working capital, capital spending and financing.
Use the cash forecast and obligations when deciding distributions; positive EBITDA or net income alone is insufficient.
caveats: The percentages in the example are illustrative, not target benchmarks for any category.
EBITDA ignores working capital swings that dominate e-commerce cash.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Use product-level contribution margin to decide where paid spend goes
cards.summary: Break P&L economics down to the individual product so you can move ad budget from products that would sell anyway to products that need paid help.
cards.use_when: Deciding ad budget allocation across products, or whether a hero product should receive paid spend at all
steps: Build a per-product (or per-SKU) unit economics sheet: price, variable costs, contribution margin per order — the source suggests tools like Google Sheets if you don't have this.
Separate products into those selling efficiently on paid vs those that appear to sell regardless of spend (high organic/retail sell-through, suspiciously high efficiency).
Ask the counterfactual: would these people have bought this product anyway without the ad spend? For omni-channel or large brands, this is often yes for established heroes.

If yes, pull paid spend off that product — the source's example lifts contribution margin on that order by $15–$27 by not spending — and reallocate the budget to a product that genuinely needs paid media to drive sell-through (e.g., the hoodie that isn't moving organically).
Build this product-level view into the decision-making routine, not a one-off spreadsheet.
caveats: The $15–$27 margin lift is a single worked example, not a benchmark.
Cutting spend on a product that actually was incrementally driven by ads would lose sales — validate with incrementality testing where budget justifies it.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Measurement pyramid: platform metrics, finance-grade KPIs, incrementality
