cards.summary: Rank your marketing metrics in a reliability pyramid — platform ROAS/CPA at the bottom, finance-grade KPIs in the middle, incrementality testing at the top.
cards.use_when: Setting up or auditing which marketing metrics you report on and make budget decisions from
steps: Bottom tier: in-platform ROAS, CPA, CTR, multi-touch attribution tools (e.g., Triple Whale). Fast feedback but lowest reliability — use only for directional campaign/ad feedback inside a single platform.

Middle tier: finance-grade KPIs such as acquisition MER, blended MER, profit contribution and CAC — calculated from actual new-customer counts, actual new-customer revenue, and actual ad spend, not platform-attributed numbers.
Top tier: incrementality testing (geo holdouts) — most reliable but slow, can only be run infrequently, and needs data-science capability.
Accept the trade-off as you move up: reliability improves but speed decreases. Finance-grade metrics need longer windows before you act on their movements.
The source says incrementality testing is likely not applicable to ~80% of operators; it matters mainly for businesses spending over roughly $10M/month, omni-channel or multi-market.
Never compare ROAS across platforms (e.g., Google campaign vs Meta campaign) — different attribution models and funnel positions make the numbers non-comparable.
caveats: The 80%/20% and $10M/month figures are the source's heuristics for who needs incrementality testing, not a hard rule.
The source explicitly warns against building DIY geo holdouts without proper data-science test design.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Why platform ROAS misleads: all attribution is correlation
cards.summary: Platform attribution connects correlated events, not causation, and systematically over-credits bottom-of-funnel — so ROAS misleads budget decisions.
cards.use_when: Interpreting channel-level ROAS reports or defending/attacking a channel's budget based on platform numbers
steps: Recognise that an ad click followed by a purchase is correlation, not proven causation — the source's analogy is ice cream sales and swimming deaths both rising in summer.
Account for the funnel sequence: billboard/TV/influencer creates awareness, a Meta ad 'closes' the sale, and only the Meta click gets attributed. Top-of-funnel gets no credit.

Look for the TikTok→Meta→Google pattern: TikTok drives new-market impressions without much click-off, Meta retargets and captures the demand in-platform, Google captures branded search. Increasing TikTok spend raises Meta and Google ROAS, not TikTok's.
Do not let a C-suite reader use raw cross-platform ROAS to cut TikTok and pile into Google — that removes top-of-funnel generation, and bottom-of-funnel stops working without it.
Use platform ROAS only within a platform (e.g., two Meta campaigns side by side) for directional reads.
caveats: The TikTok→Meta→Google dynamic is explicitly framed as a current, possibly time-dependent observation for some large retail brands, not a universal law.
The source notes other attribution limitations exist beyond those covered.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Use finance-grade KPIs instead of platform-attributed numbers
cards.summary: Acquisition MER, blended MER, profit contribution and CAC calculate from actual new-customer revenue and actual ad spend, making them more reliable than platform metrics.
cards.use_when: Choosing which marketing efficiency numbers to report and act on for budget decisions
steps: Acquisition MER = new-customer revenue ÷ ad spend. New-customer revenue ÷ ad spend — the source's example yields 1.4 from $100 revenue and $50 spend (reported as the multiple, not the percentage form).
Calculate from actual financial records: real new-customer counts, real new-customer revenue, real ad spend — not from platform attribution.
Do not rely on the blended MER (total revenue ÷ ad spend) for indexing paid media performance — it includes returning-customer revenue that would have returned anyway.
Always delineate finance-grade metrics into new-customer-based versions. If blended MER is 2 but new-customer MER is 1.4, the acquisition strategy may not be profitable at all.
Expect these KPIs to move slower than platform metrics — read them over longer periods before acting.
caveats: The source flags being hesitant about including MER precisely because of the returning-customer contamination problem.
The example numbers ($100 revenue, $50 spend, 1.4 new-customer MER) are illustrative calculations.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Benchmark LTGP:CAC at fixed time horizons
cards.summary: LTGP to CAC contextualises acquisition cost with customer gross profit — but must be time-boxed (30, 90, sometimes 365 days) to avoid overspending on distant lifetime value.
cards.use_when: Setting acquisition efficiency targets or auditing whether your CAC is defensible
steps: LTGP:CAC = gross profit per customer ÷ cost to acquire that customer. Example: $100 GP ÷ $33 CAC = 3.33.
Never use an unrestricted lifetime value window — the source warns that value measured across years can cause overspending on cash you won't realise for 4+ years.
Measure across two horizons: 30-day LTGP:CAC and 90-day LTGP:CAC; add 365-day only where the acquisition strategy is aggressive.

Interpret the bands as the source's heuristics: below 1.0 means losing money on acquisition — the source says most audited brands here lack the retention to support it and it's usually poor acquisition efficiency, not a strategy. 1.0–2.0 is also generally not a good position, tolerable mainly for CPG with genuinely excellent retention or when investor-funded growth throttling is required.
2.0–3.0 is the optimal zone to scale budgets. Above 3.0 is also a mistake per the source — leaving money on the table by under-leveraging paid media.
To hit the bottom of the optimal range: take first-purchase gross profit and divide by 2 — $100 GP implies $50 target CAC.
caveats: The 1/2/3 bands are the source's stated benchmarks, not a derived formula.
Below-1 performance can stem from thin gross profit (source suggests under ~$70 GP on first order is likely a problem) rather than CAC alone.
The source notes most operators overestimate their retention quality and that 0.01% of brands can genuinely operate below 1.0.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Exclude view-through conversions and existing customers from platform reporting
cards.summary: View-through conversions and existing-customer spend inflate platform ROAS — use 7-day click and check audience breakdowns and frequency.
cards.use_when: Configuring Meta attribution settings or auditing where ad budget is being spent
steps: Use 7-day click (not view-through) as the optimisation and reporting window on Meta. The source says 7-day click ROAS is highly correlated with acquisition MER in most businesses.
Understand view-through: a user sees the ad, doesn't click, buys within 24 hours, and Meta claims the conversion — many of these buyers would have bought anyway (often existing customers).
Break down by audience segments to see how much spend goes to existing customers.

Pull the frequency column and ensure 7-day frequency is under 8 — above 8 the source says you are definitely overspending because you are serving existing customers more than eight times a month, which isn't incremental.
Remember the platform incentive: platforms favour existing-customer spend and expanding attribution windows because over-attribution drives more spend.
caveats: The frequency ceiling of 8 is the source's stated heuristic.
Correlation between 7-day click ROAS and acquisition MER is stated as typical ('in most businesses'), not guaranteed.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Budget existing-customer retargeting from customer count × frequency, not a % of spend
cards.summary: Calculate existing-customer ad spend from number of existing customers × desired frequency × CPM rather than targeting a percentage of total budget.
cards.use_when: Setting retargeting/existing-customer budgets or responding to the question 'what % should go to existing customers?'
steps: Reject the percentage-allocation framing — the source calls it a bad way to look at the problem, because brands with 80% of revenue from existing customers would derive an unmanageable percentage.
Formula: existing customers × desired monthly frequency × CPM = required monthly spend.
Example: 300,000 existing customers × 3 exposures × $2.50 CPM = $2,250/month.
Get the CPM from the platform's audience segment breakdown for existing customers — the source notes $2.50 is unrealistically low and real CPMs will be higher.
Change the variables (customer count, frequency 3–6, actual CPM) to get your spend figure.

Expect the result to be far lower than intuition suggests — the source reports large brands assuming hundreds of thousands per month when $10k–$40k at a 3–6 frequency is typically sufficient, and has seen tiny businesses spending $40k/month on existing customers.
caveats: The $2.50 CPM example is fabricated for illustration.
The source states the amount needed is typically much less than operators assume, but exact figures depend on your CPM and list size.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: The profit frontier: solve for the next best dollar
cards.summary: Allocate spend by finding the marginal return of the next $10,000 on each channel, and stop each channel where incremental acquisition MER hits break-even.
cards.use_when: Deciding incremental budget allocation across channels or whether to pull budget from one channel into another
steps: Frame the question as: if we spend an extra $10,000 next month, where does it get the best incremental impact?

For each primary channel (Meta, Google, TikTok), estimate the revenue return of an additional $10,000 on top of current spend — ideally via controlled incrementality tests, or intuitively over time for seven-figure brands.
Run the inverse too: could $10,000 pulled from Google and reallocated to Meta return better (e.g., 2x on the marginal Google dollar vs 4x on new-customer revenue on Meta)?
Push each channel up to the point where it makes no more profit past that marginal dollar — the profit frontier is where incremental acquisition MER reaches break-even, and that's where you stop.
Only after reaching the profit frontier on your three primary channels should you add tertiary channels.
Avoid spreading spend across many tertiary channels before the primaries are maxed out.
caveats: The source says the only way to truly understand marginal returns is incrementality testing; intuition or marketing-mix models are substitutes at lower revenue thresholds.
The 2x/4x figures are illustrative of the reallocation logic, not benchmarks.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Grade inventory to drive paid-media decisions on slow-moving stock
cards.summary: Grade inventory A–D by sell-through and use paid media to liquidate grade B/C/D stock back into cash — a job profit-KPI'd agencies often ignore.
cards.use_when: Planning product launches, SKU rationalisation, or deciding whether to push clearance inventory through ads at break-even or a slight loss
steps: Grade inventory by movement: A = fast-moving (focus on not going out of stock), B = medium/low sell-through, C/D = barely or not moving.
Check Shopify's auto-ranked inventory grades (source points to the Products tab; verify current interface location).
When a launch lands in C/D (the source's example: $1M ordered, only $100k sold, 400 days of cover), calculate days of inventory on hand and prioritise turning it back into cash.

Use paid media deliberately on C/D stock: dedicate it its own isolated ad funnel (it doesn't have to sit on the main site), use whitelisting pages, or push it into a new country where heavy discounting won't erode brand equity in the primary market.
Accept break-even or slight-loss selling on dead stock as a cash-conversion decision, not a profit decision.
Rationalise SKU count as new products are introduced so inventory on the balance sheet doesn't keep growing.
Give the paid media team visibility of inventory grades — the source warns agencies KPI'd purely on profit will starve grade B/C/D inventory of spend.
caveats: Source notes most brands cannot reposition a single product into a large TAM the way supplement brands (Grenade, AG1, IM8) can, so product launches are needed — and many fail.
The $1M/400-days figures are illustrative.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Cash conversion cycle explains why ecommerce can't scale arbitrarily fast
cards.summary: CCC (DIIO + DSO − DPO) plus supplier lead time and payment terms caps real growth speed regardless of ad efficiency.
cards.use_when: Setting growth targets, planning purchase orders, or evaluating whether rapid ad-spend scaling is fundable
steps: Formula: cash conversion cycle = days inventory outstanding + days sales outstanding − days payable outstanding.
Work through the compounding: if $50 gross profit lets you buy 11 units next cycle and yields $55, which buys 12, inventory purchasing grows only incrementally off prior gross profit.
Add supplier lead time — e.g., a 90-day lead time with full upfront payment means you must fund inventory 90 days before selling it, potentially forcing a 90-day stockout while waiting for cash.

Levers to fix it: negotiate better supplier terms (e.g., only 20% upfront, paying the balance on shipment — the source's example reduces stockout from 90 days to ~20), reduce lead time via a different manufacturer, or use inventory financing.
Compare financing cost, repayment timing, guarantees and collateral in actual quotes; stress-test slower sales before borrowing.
caveats: The source describes spend rising from $20k to $200k per month, a tenfold increase, with substantial inventory financing; this is an anecdote, not a benchmark.
Growth capacity depends on working capital, supplier terms, lead times and margins; no universal annual growth ceiling follows from this example.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Resolve the CFO vs CMO spend-cut reflex with inventory reality
cards.summary: When unsold inventory is stuck, cutting media can deepen a revenue decline — sometimes the correct move is to raise MAR temporarily to liquidate stock.
cards.use_when: Responding to a cash squeeze or a CFO request to cut marketing budget when inventory isn't selling
steps: Recognise the typical scenario: inventory from November still unsold in February (some in grade C/D), so finance proposes cutting media spend ~40% to preserve cash.

Understand why the P&L reflex fires: revenue dips, marketing as a percentage spikes (e.g., from 25% to 30%), profitability falls (e.g., from 30% to 25%), and finance concludes marketing has got out of control.
Check first whether marketing is actually driving the revenue. If media spend is cut, revenue dips further, and the cuts become cyclical — less spend, less revenue, lower profit, more cuts.

Consider the counterintuitive fix: increase marketing spend in the short term (source's example: deliberately lift MAR from 30% to 35%) purely to liquidate grade C/D inventory and turn it back into cash, restoring the prior revenue position faster.
Frame the decision as converting aged inventory to cash, not as an efficiency improvement.
Ensure marketing and finance have shared visibility of inventory grades so this conversation happens before the squeeze.
caveats: The 40%/25–30%/35% figures are the source's illustrative example.
The source frames the CFO's initial reaction as logical from the P&L alone — the issue is context the P&L doesn't show.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Forecast new-customer and returning-customer revenue separately
cards.summary: Forecast new and returning revenue as separate models because they have different underlying inputs — spend-driven vs cohort/event-driven.
cards.use_when: Building an ecommerce revenue forecast, budget or KPI target
steps: Rule one of DTC forecasting per the source: always forecast new-customer revenue separately from returning-customer revenue.
New-customer revenue is driven primarily by marketing inputs: ad spend, plus events and influencers where applicable, plus any tertiary channels.

Returning-customer revenue is driven by product launches, marketing events (e.g., discount periods), direct channels (email/SMS) and other reasons for customers to come back — ad spend contributes only a little.
Practise input-based forecasting: forecast the inputs (spend, launch calendar, events) and derive the output, rather than extrapolating the revenue line directly.
Look backwards at inputs to justify the number, not just at last period's revenue.
caveats: The delineation is the source's stated cardinal rule for DTC forecasting.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Build returning-customer forecasts from cohort repeat rates
cards.summary: Project next month's returning revenue by ageing every historical new-customer cohort through its average repeat rate and returning AOV, then adjusting for seasonality and events.
cards.use_when: Forecasting returning-customer revenue for next month's budget or board plan
steps: Build a cohort table of new customers acquired each month going back to your earliest data (e.g., Jan 2021 onward).
Derive the repeat rate by customer age: e.g., 7% in month 1, 6%, 4%, 2%, 1%, tapering to a small asymptote.

For each cohort, take its original new-customer count, apply the average repeat rate for the month it is about to enter (e.g., month 32 ≈ 0.1%), then multiply by returning-customer AOV (e.g., $100 → 100 × 0.1% × $100 = $1).
Sum across every cohort to get the returning-customer revenue expectation for next month.
Expect this method to land within roughly 10% accuracy on its own.

To tighten to 1–2% accuracy: (1) apply a seasonality factor from the last 3 years of returning-customer revenue seasonality, and (2) superimpose planned marketing events/product launches with their expected revenue realisation.
caveats: The 10% and 1–2% accuracy figures are the source's reported outcomes, not guarantees.
Requires sufficient cohort history to extrapolate old cohorts.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Model new-customer revenue by regression of spend vs acquisition MER
cards.summary: Plot daily spend against acquisition MER, strip outlier periods, fit a regression, and back-propagate from the new-customer revenue goal to see whether it's achievable.
cards.use_when: Forecasting new-customer revenue at a given spend level, or sanity-checking a growth target
steps: Plot daily data for the last year or so: acquisition MER on the y-axis, spend on the x-axis.
Fit a logarithmic or linear regression (whichever fits best) to get expected efficiency at a given spend level.

Remove outliers before fitting: sales periods, Black Friday/November periods (they overstate BAU efficiency), and any low-spend days below the minimum you'd realistically run (source's example: exclude days under $1,000).
Read the fitted line to answer: at $8,000/day, roughly what efficiency should we expect?

Back-propagate from the goal: for a target of, say, $100,000 new-customer revenue at 4x acquisition MER, go to 4 on the graph and read across to find the required spend — then check whether that spend is feasible.
If the answer is no, identify the actual input or lever that will beat last year's average: a marketing event, a new product launch, a new channel, or a step change in creative production.
Treat the gap between realistic expectation and target as the central forecasting exercise — there will always be a delta.
caveats: Other channels (influencers, etc.) require bespoke modelling rather than this paid-ads regression.
The source frames this level of modelling as critical at 8–9 figure scale; smaller brands may use simpler approaches.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Don't overallocate to bottom-of-funnel because it shows the best ROAS
cards.summary: Bottom-of-funnel campaigns always show the best platform ROAS and top-of-funnel the worst, so shifting budget toward the 6x and away from the 2x usually reduces incremental growth.
cards.use_when: Reallocating budget between campaigns or channels based on platform ROAS reads
steps: Expect the pattern: bottom-of-funnel (retargeting, branded search) will always attribute highest; top-of-funnel will attribute lowest.
When you see Meta at 2x and Google at 6x, do not simply move budget to Google — the source says the 6x is likely over-attributing because of its funnel position, branded terms, or retargeting.
Assume better incremental impact likely sits further up funnel, even with weaker in-platform numbers.
Validate only within a controlled test if you are making a significant reallocation, and check whether the pattern holds for your specific business.
If you increase budgets into bottom-of-funnel on the strength of its ROAS, expect non-growth — the source describes this as a common mistake.
caveats: The source says 'likely' and 'probably' — the bottom-of-funnel over-attribution is a tendency, not a certainty, and should be verified with testing per business.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Allocate part of marketing expense to brand, not just performance
cards.summary: Beyond roughly $1M–20M, performance marketing alone hits diminishing returns; brand associations built outside the ad account are what keep ad-account metrics strong at scale.
cards.use_when: Setting overall marketing budget allocation or planning acquisition strategy past a performance plateau
steps: Recognise the plateau: as daily ad spend pushes past roughly $30k–$40k/day, performance marketing alone stops getting further, per the source's stated experience.

Understand why large brands (e.g., $300M/year) can show better CPMs, CTRs, CPCs, CVRs and ROAS than $8M/year brands at 20x the volume: market saturation and associations built outside the ad account make the in-platform metrics look good.
Budget explicitly for branding efforts as a line on the P&L — associations in market delivered where your customers already are: events, areas, creators and content they consume.
Do not expect individual brand activations to show directly profitable ROI; the effect is the overarching association driving purchases that won't be attributed to performance campaigns.

The source's examples: buying running gear because every running influencer followed wears the brand; buying premium activewear because of a perception of quality built through creative and campaign shoots, not product experience at purchase.
caveats: The $1M–$20M brute-force range and the $30k–$40k/day plateau are the source's stated observations, not hard thresholds.
Individual brand activations likely won't show direct profitable ROI — the source says this is expected and accepted.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Know your gross margin and variable costs as the base of all finance decisions
cards.summary: The source's first key takeaway: understand gross margin, how to calculate it correctly, and the difference between product margin and gross margin.
cards.use_when: Reviewing unit economics, setting pricing or acquisition targets, or preparing a P&L for a marketing decision
steps: Identify all variable costs that belong in the margin calculation, not just product cost.
Distinguish product margin from gross margin — the source calls this a required distinction and lists it as takeaway number one.
Use the corrected gross margin as the basis for downstream metrics: contribution margin by product, CAC targets, LTGP:CAC, and profit contribution.
Check whether thin first-order gross profit is the real constraint on acquisition (the source flags under roughly $70 GP on first order as likely a problem), rather than immediately blaming CAC.
caveats: The source lists this as one of five closing takeaways and does not detail the full variable-cost build-up in this section.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Five core finance practices to run an ecommerce brand
cards.summary: A closing checklist of five financial operating habits—margin literacy, live dashboards, new/returning separation, cash vs P&L plays, and constraint diagnosis.
cards.use_when: Setting your store's monthly financial operating rhythm or auditing which finance disciplines your team is missing before scaling spend.
steps: 1) Know your gross margin and calculate it correctly: identify variable costs, and distinguish product margin from gross margin and how each flows into contribution margin. Use these definitions consistently across the team.

2) Define your metrics and build live dashboards—not daily ROAS reports. Track acquisition MER, profit contribution, and ideally LTGP to CAC. The source argues weekly ROAS reporting is unproductive for core decision-making.

3) Separate new vs returning customer metrics: track new-customer economics, acquisition MER, new-customer profit contribution, new-customer revenue and new-customer cohort size separately, because the underlying levers differ (and feed forecasting).

Coordinate inventory and advertising: additional borrowing raises interest expense and reduces cash/net profit. Interest alone does not change MER (revenue/ad spend); model sales and spend separately.

5) Use the P&L to identify the constraint in the business: structure it out, set KPIs at each level, and when you fall below target look above that level in the P&L to find what changed and which lever to pull.
Attribute the daily-vs-weekly ROAS stance to the source as an opinion, not a universal rule.
caveats: The daily-vs-weekly ROAS preference is the presenter's opinion, not an established benchmark.
The five-point list is a summary framework; it does not define numeric thresholds for any metric.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Structure your P&L as a constraint-diagnosis tool
cards.summary: Read the P&L line by line, set KPIs at each level, and when a KPI drops look one level up to find the changed lever and correct course.
cards.use_when: When a store's profit or efficiency metric falls below target and you need to locate the actual constraint rather than reflexively cutting ad spend.
steps: 1) Structure your P&L so each level has a clear definition (revenue, product margin, gross margin, contribution margin, profitability).
2) Set a target KPI for each level.
3) When you start falling below KPI at a given level, look above that level in the P&L to understand what changed—which variable cost, margin, or efficiency levers moved.
4) Pull the specific lever that rectifies the deviation and course-correct back to target rather than adjusting budgets arbitrarily.
5) Per the source, this is the single overarching purpose of the P&L: to identify the constraint in the business. Treat the P&L as a diagnostic map, not a reporting artifact.

Coordinate inventory and advertising: additional borrowing raises interest expense and reduces cash/net profit. Interest alone does not change MER (revenue/ad spend); model sales and spend separately.
caveats: The source does not specify exact KPI targets or tolerances; you must set them for your own business.
The practice assumes a correctly structured P&L where each level's variable costs are properly assigned.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Budget brand as a P&L expense line, not just performance marketing
cards.summary: High-quality brand associations, messaging and creative can drive purchases that performance ads would not, so brand deserves deliberate budget allocation.
cards.use_when: Deciding store budget allocation between performance marketing and brand-building (creative campaigns, positioning work) as you scale.
steps: 1) Recognize that some purchases are driven by perception of quality created through overarching associations, messaging, and campaign creative—the source describes two personal purchases that happened through brand, not through a performance ad or Google ad.
2) Do not understate brand's role: the source says it becomes unbelievably important as you continue to scale.
3) Treat brand as a budget allocation—an expense on the P&L—rather than an optional residual of leftover ad budget.
4) Apply to ecommerce: invest in the campaign shoots and creative that shape quality perception on PDPs and in ads, and account for that spend when calculating contribution margin.
Note this is the presenter's judgment from anecdote, not measured attribution.
caveats: The two purchases cited are personal anecdotes; they are examples, not proof of a generalizable result.
Brand's effect may be hard to attribute in standard performance reporting—avoid forcing brand spend into a last-click metric.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Align marketing strategy with SKU inventory to prioritize cash turnover
cards.summary: When cash is the constraint, deliberately accept lower profitability or MER to move inventory into cash, coordinating marketing and inventory teams.
cards.use_when: Replenishment, pricing or promotion planning when a store is cash-constrained and holding slow-moving SKUs.
steps: 1) Maintain constant communication between the marketing team (or agency) and whoever owns inventory, covering inventory position across the different SKUs.

Coordinate inventory and advertising: additional borrowing raises interest expense and reduces cash/net profit. Interest alone does not change MER (revenue/ad spend); model sales and spend separately.
3) Where inventory is overstocked, apply strategies that intentionally decrease profitability, decrease acquisition MER or decrease efficiency in order to prioritize turnover of inventory into cash.
4) Evaluate whether that trade makes the business overall healthier before executing.
This is an inventory-merchandising decision, not a universal rule to discount.
caveats: The source frames this as situational—only when cash conversion cycle is the actual constraint.
It gives no specific discount depth, turnover target or interest threshold; decide those from your own numbers.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Build a 48-month subscription financial model from ad spend down
cards.summary: Excel layout for forecasting a DTC subscription business: assumptions tab in blue, customer acquisition tab driving orders, then a monthly P&L out to 48 months.
cards.use_when: You need to plan store operations, model a raise, or test whether your ad budget and churn can produce a profitable subscription business before committing spend.
steps: Set a 48-month timeline (M1–M48) across the top; freeze panes so the active cell keeps time labels visible as you scroll right.
Colour-code inputs: hard-coded assumptions in dark blue, all formulas in black, so anyone editing the file knows which numbers they may change and which are calculated.
On an acquisition tab, start with monthly advertising spend (e.g. $5,000 ramping to $15,000 by month 7, then growing ~7.5%/month) and a paid CAC assumption.
Compute new customers = ad spend / paid CAC for each month. Model CAC improving over year 1 (e.g. $35 down to $20) as organic and email list growth lower blended acquisition cost.
Apply a monthly churn rate (the example uses a flat 15%) to recurring customers: retained = prior total customers x (1 - churn), so total orders = new + recurring.
Build the P&L from these order volumes: gross revenue = AOV x orders; subtract discounts and refunds (both applied only to new-order revenue) to get net revenue.
Feed COGS (product, packaging, fulfillment, customer service, merchant fees) and opex (personnel, advertising, other marketing, tech, an unallocated 'unknown' bucket) to land on operating income.
Add a roll-up summary tab that sums each quarter across years, plus starting cash and cash balance, to calculate runway in months.
caveats: All figures (CAC, churn, AOV, cost percentages) are illustrative assumptions, not benchmarks; replace them with your own data.
A flat churn rate is a simplification — real cohorts often churn differently in early vs later months.
The model is a planning sandbox; it does not predict actual performance.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Discounts vs CAC: when a discount is mathematically neutral
cards.summary: If a discount lifts conversion enough that CAC falls by the same dollar amount, post-marketing per-order contribution margin is unchanged — so discounting is a CAC substitute, not automatically a margin loss.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to run a discount or promo on a PDP, landing page or email flow, and whether the discount is actually cheaper than buying the same customers through paid ads.
steps: Work out your current paid CAC per new customer (total paid marketing / new customer orders).
Estimate how much the discount lifts first-order conversion, and translate that lift into the implied reduction in cost per acquired customer — a discount effectively subsidises acquisition.
Compare the discount's dollar cost per incremental new order against the CAC you would otherwise pay for that order.

If the discount reduces effective acquisition cost by roughly the same dollar amount it gives away, the post-marketing contribution per order is identical — choose on the basis of which produces the volume and quality of customers you want.

When discounting deeply, attach the discount explicitly to an on-ramp into a loyalty or subscription program so the acquired customer has a path to recurring contribution rather than being a one-off transaction.
Model several discount scenarios in your financial model and pick the one that maximises total company profit at your fixed ad budget, not the one with the highest conversion.
caveats: The neutrality claim only holds when the discount changes acquisition cost by the same dollar amount; larger discounts still reduce margin.
The source explicitly warns against using deep discounts for standard one-off flash sales — they should be tied to a loyalty/subscription on-ramp.
Conversion lift estimates are assumptions until tested.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Split COGS into product and fulfillment to read ecommerce margins
cards.summary: Separate product cost from fulfillment cost instead of lumping them into one COGS line, so you can see product gross profit and fulfillment drag independently.
cards.use_when: Reviewing monthly store P&L, diagnosing why margins moved, or deciding whether a shipping, pick-and-pack or packaging decision is eroding profitability.
steps: On your income statement, split COGS into (a) product cost (materials, manufacturing) and (b) fulfillment (shipping, pick and pack, packaging, other delivery charges).
Calculate product gross profit = revenue - product COGS, and express it as a percentage of revenue (the example shows roughly 73% converting to product gross profit).
Calculate contribution margin = revenue - product COGS - fulfillment. This is what remains to fund marketing, payroll and other opex.

Divide each individual fulfillment line by revenue month by month to pinpoint which charge is moving — the example shows pick-and-pack and packaging holding roughly stable while shipping and other charges crept up.
Track these percentages over several months; stable product and fulfillment percentages indicate predictable margins, while a swing in one line tells you where to intervene.
Use contribution margin per order (total contribution margin / total orders) as the number to compare against cost per new order.
caveats: Splitting COGS this way is the presenter's preference for ecommerce analysis; accountants will usually report a single COGS line.
Percentage shifts can reflect product mix change rather than true cost inflation.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Read a monthly P&L as percent of revenue to spot trajectory and margin drift
cards.summary: Lay revenue down through product cost, fulfillment, marketing and opex as percentages of revenue to see growth, margin predictability and where profitability broke.
cards.use_when: Monthly or quarterly store review: assessing whether the business is growing, whether margins are stable, and which line caused a profitable month to turn into a loss.
steps: Present the period side by side with a percent-of-revenue column next to every dollar line.
Order the lines: revenue, product COGS, product gross profit, fulfillment, contribution margin, marketing, post-marketing contribution, opex, operating income.
Check trajectory first: is revenue increasing month over month and are margins predictable or drifting?
Compare contribution margin % across months — stable percentages (e.g. ~42–43%) mean cost structure is under control.
Watch marketing as a percentage of revenue: it will bounce around when scaling, and a jump (e.g. 29% to 39%) can be the single cause of a loss month even when contribution margin held.
Trace the loss to a line before reacting — in the example, an August marketing spike pushed operating income from +7.5% to -2.2% and back to +6.4%.
Aim for break-even or better on the first order, since ecommerce repeat behaviour is generally limited; only exceptional stores are strongly profitable on the first order after marketing.
caveats: Saying ecommerce has 'generally' limited repeat behaviour is the presenter's generalisation; repeat-heavy categories exist.
Percentages can mask absolute-scale changes; read both.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Compute per-order unit economics: AOV, product cost, fulfillment, contribution
cards.summary: Divide each P&L line by total orders to get AOV, product cost per order, fulfillment per order and contribution margin per order.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing whether each order is actually profitable before marketing, and comparing month-to-month stability of your order-level economics.
steps: AOV = total revenue / total orders (example: $232).
Product COGS per order = total product COGS / total orders (example: $62).
Fulfillment per order = total fulfillment / total orders (example: $71).
Contribution margin per order = AOV - product cost per order - fulfillment per order (example: $99).
Drag the formulas across months to see whether per-order economics are consistent; in the example contribution margin per order stayed stable even as revenue grew.

For noisy months, compute a trailing average: total revenue / total orders, total product COGS / total orders, total fulfillment / total orders across the whole period (example: $238 AOV, $64 product, $74 fulfillment, ~$100 contribution).
Keep customer counts, order counts and unit counts distinct — orders exceed customers, and units exceed orders when baskets average more than one item.
caveats: Blended per-order figures hide product-mix differences and seasonality.
AOV varies by promotion and channel; a trailing average may hide a recent shift.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Add per-unit product economics to find your most profitable SKU
cards.summary: Calculate revenue, product gross profit and contribution margin per unit for each top SKU, because blended per-order numbers hide product-mix differences.
cards.use_when: Product selection, pricing and merchandising decisions — deciding which SKUs to push, bundle or drop based on margin per unit rather than revenue share alone.
steps: Pull a report that isolates sales by product; the summary financials report will not give you this.
For each top SKU, calculate average revenue per unit, product gross profit per unit and contribution margin per unit.

Compare both absolute dollars and percentages of revenue. Example: Product A (60% of sales) earns $230 revenue, $163 product profit (71% of revenue) and $92 contribution (40% of revenue); Product B (25% of sales) earns $122 revenue, $104 product profit (86% of revenue) and $74 contribution (61% of revenue).

Note the tension: Product A is more profitable per unit in dollars, Product B is more profitable as a percentage of revenue — the right choice depends on whether you optimise for cash per order or margin rate.
Compare per-unit contribution to the blended contribution margin per order: in the example the average order has higher contribution than either product alone, because customers buy multiple units.
Use the result to decide which SKUs to feature on the PDP, which to bundle together, and where a small markup is defensible.
caveats: Per-unit data requires a separate report; a channel- or order-level report will not produce it.
Higher margin-rate products can still be worse if their lower absolute contribution does not cover acquisition cost.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Calculate blended CAC from total marketing and new customer orders
cards.summary: CAC/CPA is total marketing spend divided by new customer orders only — returning orders are excluded because they carry little paid marketing cost.
cards.use_when: Setting or auditing acquisition budgets, and comparing what you pay per new customer against the contribution margin that customer produces.
steps: Pull total new customer orders for the period and total marketing spend for the same period; do not include returning customer orders in the denominator.
Blended CAC = total marketing / total new customer orders (the example shows $74, $113, $100 across three months, $97 blended).
Compare blended CAC against contribution margin per new order: in the example, only the month where marketing cost per new order exceeded contribution margin per order was also the loss month.

To go beyond a blended figure, build the funnel by channel and stage — top-of-funnel exposure and nurturing activities (content), then conversion activities (deals, discounts) — to calculate channel-level CAC for Facebook, Google and other sources.
Use channel-level CAC to shift budget toward the sources whose CAC sits comfortably below contribution margin, and investigate the ones that do not.
caveats: Blended CAC mixes channels and is only directionally correct; channel CAC requires funnel-level tracking.
A single month's CAC can be distorted by campaign timing and seasonality; the source suggests trailing averages for noisy data.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Build customer retention cohorts to measure true repeat purchase behaviour
cards.summary: Group customers by first purchase month and track their orders over subsequent months to see real lifetime purchase frequency, not just first-month averages.
cards.use_when: Forecasting LTV, judging whether a subscription or replenishment offer is working, or deciding whether retention spend is justified by actual repeat behaviour.
steps: Define cohorts by the month of a customer's first purchase; anyone repurchasing later stays in their original cohort (e.g. March = 167 first-time customers, April = 436, May = 659).
For each cohort, record orders in each subsequent month of lifetime (M2, M3, M4...), reading the grid diagonally to reconstruct total orders in a given calendar month.

Compute orders per customer over the observed window: the March cohort's 167 customers placed 330 orders in six months, about 1.98 orders each — nearly double the ~1.2 orders a customer appears to place in their first month.

To reconstruct a month's total orders, add that month's new customer orders to the diagonal of prior cohorts' later-lifetime orders (e.g. June new + May's M2 + April's M3 + March's M4 = recurring orders).
Use cohort order counts, not raw averages of all customers, to estimate LTV and to check whether CAC is recovered over the customer's real lifetime.
caveats: Cohorts require large data sets and a long enough history to read later months.
Early months of a cohort are incomplete; do not read M6 counts as that cohort's final behaviour.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Define LTV as lifetime contribution margin and test it against CAC
cards.summary: Customer lifetime value is the total contribution margin a customer generates across their whole relationship — compare it to the marketing investment that acquired them to see if the model is profitable.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to scale ad spend, raise prices, launch a subscription, or accept a slower payback in exchange for profitable scale.
steps: Define LTV as cumulative contribution margin (revenue minus product cost minus fulfillment) across all a customer's purchases, not as revenue.
Derive it from retention cohorts rather than blended averages — the source is explicit that cohorts tell a more exact story.
Compare LTV against CAC per new customer, and also check whether individual orders cover their own marketing cost, since ecommerce generally shows limited repeat behaviour.
If first-order contribution margin is below CAC, the business depends on repeat purchases to become profitable — validate that assumption with cohort data before scaling spend.
Use the split between first-order economics and lifetime economics to decide whether to push for break-even on the first order or accept a payback period across later orders.
caveats: LTV built on incomplete cohorts will overstate or understate the truth depending on maturity.
The recommendation to be break-even or better on every order is the presenter's stated preference, not a universal rule.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Simplify a startup payroll model with salary x headcount ÷ 12
cards.summary: Forecast personnel cost from role salaries and headcount assumptions, plus a benefits load, instead of building a named-employee payroll.
cards.use_when: Building or updating the opex section of a startup or store financial model where you need a defensible payroll line without individual offer letters.
steps: List roles (marketing/sales, merchandising, product, technology, executive/admin) with an average annual salary per role.
Add benefits as a percentage of payroll — the example uses 25% in the US for healthcare, payroll taxes and 401k matching.
For each month and role, calculate salary / 12 x number of people in that role; lock the salary cell with F4 (absolute reference) so the formula copies across all 48 columns.
Lay out headcount as a separate grid of numbers per role per month, so hiring plans (e.g. add one person when revenue hits a milestone, then hold) are explicit and editable.
Sum all role salaries, multiply by the benefits percentage, and show total personnel as its own bold line.
Make the hiring plan narratively logical — the point of the model is that an investor can read it and see a plan for spending a round sensibly, not too fast.
caveats: Average salary per role is a simplification; real payroll varies by seniority and location.
The 25% benefits load is a US-specific example assumption.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Include an unallocated 'unknown' opex bucket
cards.summary: Reserve a percentage of revenue in the model for expenses you cannot yet name, so the forecast does not understate cash burn.
cards.use_when: Building the opex section of a store financial model or budget, especially pre-launch or when scaling into new channels with uncertain costs.
steps: Create an 'other opex' category calculated as a fixed percentage of revenue (the example uses 10% of revenue in perpetuity).
Treat it as a deliberate catch-all for known-unknowns — tooling, agency retainers, contractors, one-off costs you have not scoped.
Keep it separate from the identified lines (advertising, other marketing such as PR or Facebook consultants, technology/hardware/software) so you can still see and edit those individually.
When actuals arrive, move spend out of the unknown bucket into named categories rather than letting it grow silently.
caveats: The 10% figure is an illustrative assumption in the source model, not a benchmark.
A catch-all can mask poor cost discipline if it is never reviewed against actuals.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Set up a quarterly roll-up with starting cash to calculate runway
cards.summary: A summary tab that sums quarters and years across a starting cash balance shows how long the business can operate before it needs more funding.
cards.use_when: Founder or investor reporting: answering how far a raised amount stretches, when cash turns negative, and which year the business becomes profitable.
steps: Create a roll-up tab that only sums cells from the monthly model — do not recalculate anything there.
Lay quarters across the top (Q1–Q4 with a full-year total) and years down the side.
Include the key lines only: gross revenue, net revenue, COGS, gross profit, gross margin %, advertising, merchandising, personnel, other opex, total opex, operating income.
Add starting cash (the amount raised) and calculate each period's cash balance as opening balance plus the period's loss or profit.
Calculate runway as the number of periods until the cash balance turns negative — in the example, $3M with those assumptions lasted about two years, going negative early in year 3.
Sanity-check the roll-up against the monthly model: summing the last 12 months of operating profit in both should match (the example checks $508,419).
caveats: Runway is only as good as the underlying assumptions; the source stresses that actuals will differ.
Fundraising takes time, so the source advises knowing the runway well in advance and starting the raise early.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Format a financial model for fast reading: colours, brackets, freeze panes
cards.summary: Use consistent colour conventions, accounting format with zero-suppression, and freeze panes so a large model stays readable and auditable.
cards.use_when: Building or reviewing any store P&L or financial model that others will read or edit.
steps: Apply the convention: dark blue = hard-coded input, black = formula, so editors instantly see what is safe to change.
Put a top and double-bottom border around the most important lines — revenue, gross profit, operating profit — so the eye lands on them in a dense sheet.
Use accounting format on key totals and suppress zeros so the model stays clean without noise.
Freeze panes so time headers and category labels remain visible while scrolling in both directions.
Build models without the mouse where possible (absolute cell references, border shortcuts via the keyboard) — the source says this pays back as models grow large.
Format with restraint: the source notes some people waste time over-formatting, but a little is worth doing.
caveats: Formatting conventions only help if everyone editing the file follows them.
The colour convention is a modelling norm, not a technical requirement.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Build a standard VC-style 4-year model — and know its limits
cards.summary: Venture investors typically want about four years of monthly projections; the source demonstrates a 48-month model from a $3M raise for a coffee subscription.
cards.use_when: Preparing a data room or investor conversation, or stress-testing whether your store's plan supports the growth story a raise implies.
steps: Extend the monthly model to 48 months (four years) and keep the assumptions on a separate, colour-coded tab.
Drive the whole model from a handful of core inputs: advertising spend, paid CAC, churn, AOV, discount and refund rates, and cost percentages.
Show the trajectory explicitly in the roll-up: rising gross margin, revenue growth, and the year of maximum loss versus the year the business reaches operating profit.
Use the model to test improvements — the source suggests checking whether better packaging or product-cost percentages move your break-even month earlier.
In the worked example, the business first turns profitable around month 45; that is a property of those assumptions, not a general rule.
Present both the premise and the fragility: this model is only as credible as the assumptions inside it, so be ready to defend each one.
caveats: A four-year horizon is the VC convention shown here, not a universal forecasting rule.
The example's break-even month and $1.9M monthly revenue at month 48 are outputs of the sample assumptions, not targets.
The source's own caveat: the model exists to test whether the idea can make money at all.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Cohort Table Mechanics: Reading Repeat Orders Diagonally
cards.summary: How to build and read a customer cohort table so repeat revenue and lifetime order counts are calculated correctly.
cards.use_when: Building or auditing a monthly cohort report to decide whether repeat-purchase revenue justifies acquisition spend.
steps: Lay out a grid: one row per acquisition month, one column per subsequent month of customer lifetime (month 0, month 1, month 2...).

Row totals give new customer orders in that month; the diagonal is what produces recurring orders in a given month. For June: take May's second month, April's third month, March's fourth month and sum them.
Verify the diagonal sum ties to the returning-customer orders figure reported for that month (in the source example, three diagonal cells summed to 122 recurring orders).

Read the average orders-per-customer by lifetime length: the source cohort showed roughly 1.2 orders in the first month rising to nearly double within six months, and cumulative orders of 1.67 by five months, 1.63 by four.

Use the cohort with the longest history to set your lifetime-orders assumption; the presenter used 1.98 orders for a cohort with the most historical data, explicitly choosing conservatism over extrapolating month 7-9 growth.
Recompute the table every month; if early cohorts' later months keep rising, your lifetime-orders estimate is stale.
caveats: Cohort-derived lifetime orders are only reliable for cohorts old enough to have lived through the period you're measuring; newer cohorts will understate repeat behavior.
The 1.98 figure is a source-specific example, not a benchmark for your store.
Do not read across rows instead of diagonally; that misstates which cohort produced a given month's repeat orders.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: From First-Order Economics to Lifetime Value
cards.summary: Step-by-step build of first-order contribution margin, LTV, and the CM:CAC ratio so you can see whether acquisition pays back.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether current ad spend is profitable on a first-order and lifetime basis before scaling acquisition.
steps: Compute first-order revenue as AOV times one order; in the source example AOV $138 produced $138 revenue, and subtracting product and fulfillment cost left $100 contribution margin.
Divide contribution margin by CAC for the first-order ratio; at $100 CM versus $97 CAC the ratio was 1.02, i.e. about $2 of profit on the first order.
For lifetime, multiply AOV and each cost line by the cohort-derived lifetime order count (here 1.98): revenue went from $238 to $469 and lifetime contribution margin to $197.

If no additional marketing was spent to drive repeat orders (customers returned via email list/organic), hold CAC flat and divide lifetime CM by the same CAC: $197 / $97 = 2.02, or about $99 profit per customer.
Interpret the result: a business that is roughly break-even on order one but 2x on lifetime can be profitable on every order once repeat purchases arrive; the presenter called this strong health.
caveats: Holding CAC flat for repeat orders assumes no incremental remarketing cost; if you pay to re-acquire or retarget, load that cost in.
First-order contribution margin below your CAC is only acceptable when the cohort data shows meaningful repeat orders.
The numbers here are one illustrative case, not target benchmarks for every store.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Why 50% Off Sitewide Destroys Black Friday Unit Economics
cards.summary: The mechanical reason a sitewide percentage discount loses money even when traffic and conversion spike.
cards.use_when: Planning Black Friday or any sitewide promo and choosing between percentage discount and a multi-unit offer.
steps: Model baseline first: in the source example, 1.75% conversion, $75 CAC, $135 AOV, $124 after refunds/returns, $21 product COGS, $19 fulfillment COGS, leaving $84 contribution margin and only $9 after CAC.

Then model 50% off: conversion typically jumps to 4-5% and CAC can fall to about $33, but most buyers take one unit, cutting gross order value to about $68 and net order value to roughly 55% of normal AOV when returns/refunds are not offered.
Critical point: product and fulfillment COGS stay essentially fixed. In the example CM fell to $29 against $33 CAC, so every customer lost money - the presenter said he has seen this many times.
Watch the volume illusion: orders may jump from 5,000 to 20,000 and revenue skyrockets while contribution margin after CAC goes negative.
Warning sign for your store: a business already at only $9 CM-after-CAC per order ($50,000 on 5,000 orders) cannot absorb a 50% price cut.
caveats: Discounting also gives back revenue you would have collected from customers who would have bought anyway.

The presenter's stated policy: make money on the first order at Black Friday, because Black Friday customers have notoriously poor retention and many buy only once. Subscription brands may rationally choose otherwise.
The specific conversion, CAC and COGS figures are one brand's example, not universal.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: BOGO / Two-for-One as a Black Friday Cash Machine
cards.summary: Replace sitewide percentage discounts with a two-for-one or gift-with-purchase to deliver perceived value without giving back revenue.
cards.use_when: Designing a seasonal promotion where you want the conversion lift of a deep discount but positive per-order profit.
steps: Recognize the psychological equivalence: two-for-one reads to the customer as twice the product for half the price, so you generally get a similar conversion-rate and CAC lift to 50% off.

Model the mechanics: at $135 AOV with no returns, product COGS doubles from $21 to $42, shipping rises only marginally since both units ship in one box, and merchant fees stay around $4 because revenue is similar to a normal order.
Result in the source example: contribution margin of $69 versus $29 on the 50%-off promo, and CM after a lowered CAC of about $33 came to $36 - more than the brand made on a normal non-promo order.
Compare at equal volume: at the same 20,000 orders, the two-for-one generated roughly twice the revenue of 50% off and on the order of three-quarters of a million dollars in the example.
Generalize to your product mix: if unit COGS is low, test buy-two-get-one-free or another gift-with-purchase structure rather than a straight percentage cut.
Run the numbers for your own COGS before committing; the presenter's recommendation is to model it, not to assume it.
caveats: Only works when marginal product cost is low relative to price; heavy or expensive-to-ship goods erode the advantage.
Shipping cost per unit is assumed to rise only marginally because units ship together - verify with your 3PL rate card.
The dollar figures are a single illustrative case, not promised results.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: The Core Unit Economics Stack: CAC, AOV, CM, LTV and Their Ratios
cards.summary: Definitions and relationships for the five metrics that determine whether an ecommerce business model can work.
cards.use_when: Setting up your ecommerce financial model or explaining unit economics to your team before scaling spend.
steps: Define CAC as the marketing investment to acquire a customer for the first time, AOV as average basket size per order, and contribution margin as what's left from an order after direct per-order costs (product plus fulfillment).
Distinguish contribution margin (one order) from customer lifetime value (profit across the series of orders a customer makes) - LTV is CM extended over the customer's lifetime order count.
Compute CM:CAC as the first-order test and LTV:CAC as the lifetime test; a $100 CAC against $100 CM per order across five orders yields $500 profit and an LTV:CAC of 5.
Set the goal stated by the presenter: every incremental customer should be more profitable than the last, which means margins rise as the business scales.
Treat deteriorating unit economics as a hard stop: at 10x size, worsening economics can drive profit to zero or negative.
caveats: Ratios here are defined from the source's modeling approach; adapt the cost buckets to what your P&L actually captures.
LTV:CAC of 1.0 is not acceptable by the presenter's standard because it leaves nothing to cover overhead.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Two Valid Models: Break Even on Order One, or Lose Early and Earn Later
cards.summary: When it is safe to lose money on the first order and when you must be profitable on it.
cards.use_when: Deciding how aggressively to bid on acquisition for one-time-purchase versus repeat-purchase product lines.
steps: Route one: hold margins and break even or better on the first order - required for product categories where most customers buy once, such as many apparel items.

Route two: run a very high lifetime order count (the source cites customers buying 5, 10, 15 times) so a first-order loss is recovered on the tail; the presenter cautions this only works for highly consumable or repeat-purchase products.
For repeat-consumable categories, consider subscribe-and-save / subscription box pricing as an antidote to low lifetime order counts.
Set the guardrail stated in the source: aim to at minimum break even on the first order for most businesses; only deliberately exceed that when the cohort data proves repeat behavior.
For one-time-buy categories, be careful about running CM:CAC below 1 on the first order - the presenter explicitly warns against it there.
caveats: A CM:CAC below 1 is only defensible with demonstrated high repeat rates; the source calls running it otherwise a way to lose money on every customer.
The 5-15 lifetime order range is the source's characterization of certain consumable businesses, not a benchmark for yours.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Ecom Gross Margin vs Contribution Margin: Two Different Buckets
cards.summary: Separating product-level costs from per-order fulfillment costs so you know which costs scale with each order and which vary by shipment.
cards.use_when: Building your P&L model or diagnosing why margin differs between orders and shipping destinations.
steps: Bucket one - product costs: manufacturing, import freight, duties and taxes, i.e. everything to get product to the fulfillment center and ready to ship. In the source example this was 27% of a $175 order, or $47.
Bucket one result is the ecom gross margin: revenue minus product costs ($175 - $47 = $128 in the example).
Bucket two - fulfillment costs: pick and pack, materials, 3PL charges and shipping. These vary order by order, with shipping usually the largest line.
Contribution margin = revenue minus both buckets; in the example $175 - $47 - $40 of fulfillment = $83, and CAC should be at or below that $83.
Use the split diagnostically: product costs should be stable and improve with scale/supply-chain fixes, while fulfillment costs need per-destination or per-weight scrutiny.
caveats: This naming convention (ecom gross margin) is the source's, and differs from standard GAAP gross margin presentation.
Fulfillment cost variability means blended averages can hide unprofitable shipping lanes.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Healthy Unit Economics Benchmarks Across the Business Lifecycle
cards.summary: How CAC, AOV, contribution margin and lifetime orders typically move from idea stage to late stage in a strong business.
cards.use_when: Benchmarking your own unit economics against a stage-appropriate expectation before raising or deploying growth capital.
steps: Idea phase (vision only): the source's plan was $65 CAC, $165 AOV, 60% contribution margin, 3 lifetime orders, giving $99 CM per order, 1.5 CM:CAC and roughly 5x LTV:CAC.
Launch phase: low CAC from friends/family but AOV only about $89 due to discounts and 39% contribution margin, with 1 lifetime order - CM:CAC around 1.0 is acceptable here.

Early stage (early channel fit, e.g. Facebook ads plus organic Instagram): 2,500 orders, $68 CAC, $134 AOV, $49 CM, older cohorts showing 1.7 lifetime orders and $112 LTV; CM:CAC about 1.0 and LTV:CAC about 1.6.
Growth phase: CAC drops slightly with organic mix, AOV normalizes to $148, CM 51%, LTV $196; CM:CAC 1.4 and LTV:CAC approaching 4.

Late stage: 250,000 orders, blended CAC down to $48, AOV up to $162 through more products and bundling, CM up to 65% from larger production runs and a fixed supply chain, 3.1 lifetime orders; CM:CAC 2.1 and LTV:CAC 6.7.
Target stated by the presenter: CM:CAC better than 1 at every stage, and roughly 5x or better LTV:CAC for a late-stage business driven by repeat customers.
caveats: These are the presenter's illustrative benchmark trajectories, not measured industry medians.
Excellent businesses can show 3-5x CM:CAC on the first order alone; matching 1.0 is not the ceiling.
Discounted periods legitimately lower AOV and margin - read them against the same period, not peak months.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Sub-Optimal Pattern: Rising CAC With Flat Contribution Margin
cards.summary: The failure mode where a business scales spend faster than it fixes economics, losing money on every customer.
cards.use_when: Reviewing whether an influx of funding should be spent on more acquisition or on fixing supply chain and retention first.
steps: Watch for CAC rising while AOV and contribution margin stay flat or drift down (the source example: 68 to 79 CAC, then 123, then 149, as ad spend increased).
Check lifetime orders in the same review: in the example they only rose to 1.2, then 1.5, then 1.8, so repeat behavior never covered the rising acquisition cost.
Compute the ratios: CM:CAC fell below 1 on the first order and LTV:CAC landed at 0.87 and then 1.0 - which the presenter says leaves no money to cover opex.
Diagnose the actual constraint before adding budget: the example attributed weak contribution margin to unoptimized supply chain, a mislocated distribution center and air freight.
Verdict stated in the source: this business should not be scaling until unit economics are fixed, even if it raised a large Series A/B.
caveats: An LTV:CAC of exactly 1.0 is not a passing grade by the presenter's standard.
Some businesses with strong repeat buyers can run CM:CAC below 1 on the first order; one-time-buy businesses cannot.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Splitting COGS Into Product and Fulfillment Buckets for Promo Modeling
cards.summary: The two-bucket COGS structure used to compare promotions and normal trading side by side.
cards.use_when: Building a promo P&L for Black Friday, bundles or free shipping tests, or recalculating contribution margin per order.
steps: Product COGS bucket: manufacturing cost plus duties and taxes, packaging, and inbound freight to the fulfillment center - in the example $15 manufacturing plus $6 other = $21.
Fulfillment COGS bucket: shipping and packing ($12), warehouse storage and pick costs ($3), and merchant/payment processing fees ($4) = $19 in the example.

Net AOV should be reduced for returns and refunds before computing anything else; the source notes losing roughly 5-10% of gross revenue to returns/refunds in many verticals ($135 to $124 in the example).
Contribution margin = net AOV minus both buckets ($124 - $21 - $19 = $84), then subtract CAC to get CM-after-CAC ($84 - $75 = $9).
When modeling a promo, hold product COGS fixed and adjust only the lines that actually move (merchant fees on lower revenue, marginally higher shipping for extra units in the same box).
caveats: The 5-10% returns figure is described as typical for many verticals, not universal - use your own returns data.
Promo best practice of not offering refunds or returns is a modeling assumption you must decide on deliberately.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Three-Statement Model as the Diagnostic for a Profitable-but-Cash-Poor Store
cards.summary: Why ecommerce stores show positive net income and falling cash, and which statement lines to inspect in order.
cards.use_when: Investigating why your store's bank balance declines in months when the P&L shows profit.
steps: Orient with three lines side by side first: revenue (~$415K/month in the example), net income (positive every month), and free cash flow (negative $22K, then varying wildly - only two of six months had both net income and FCF positive).
Then walk the income statement for structural mismatches: product cost is not matched to when you buy inventory, only when you sell it.
Check depreciation versus real asset spend - depreciation is a smoothed, non-cash charge that hides lumpy purchase timing.
Check debt: interest shows on the P&L but loan principal repayments only appear on the balance sheet, so debt activity is invisible in net income.
Check taxes: the P&L may accrue monthly while actual quarterly estimated payments leave in lumps.
Then read the balance sheet for inventory changes (increase = cash out), accounts receivable, and capitalized software, before reconciling to the cash flow statement.
caveats: Positive net income is described as often misleading for startups; free cash flow clarifies what is really happening.
Some months with negative net income can increase cash - the source shows this pattern, so never infer cash direction from the P&L alone.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Balance Sheet Cash Traps: Inventory, Capitalized Software, Quarterly Taxes
cards.summary: The three balance-sheet movements that most often explain cash going out while the P&L looks healthy.
cards.use_when: Planning a buying season, an engineering spend, or a tax payment quarter and forecasting whether cash can support it.
steps: Inventory: buying product is a lumpy cash outflow parked on the balance sheet. In the example, inventory rose $113K in one month (335 to 448) and this was the main driver of a $95K negative FCF on $77K net income; when inventory draws down, cash converts back in.

Capitalized software: payroll on engineers is moved off the P&L onto the balance sheet and amortized (typically 36 months for software). The example spent $240K over six months on the platform while only $40K hit the P&L.
Quarterly taxes: the P&L accrues monthly (e.g. $25K), but the balance sheet shows taxes building up and then leaving in lump payments (about $80K, then about $100K to the government).
Line of credit: reading the balance sheet showed roughly $25K/month of principal being paid down - cash leaving that never appears in net income.
Practical forecasting rule: before committing to an inventory buy, an engineering hire or a big marketing push, forecast the cash out date, not just the expense recognition date.
caveats: Capitalization rules and useful-life assumptions vary; confirm with your accountant rather than defaulting to 36 months.
This case is a constructed teaching model, so the dollar amounts are illustrative.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Reading the Cash Flow Statement: Operating, Investing, Financing
cards.summary: How each section of the cash flow statement maps to ecommerce activity so you can trace where cash actually moves.
cards.use_when: Reviewing monthly cash movements and classifying spend the way a lender or investor will read it.
steps: Operating section starts with net income from the P&L, then adjusts: accounts receivable up = cash negative (customers owe you); accounts payable up = cash positive (you still owe suppliers); depreciation is stripped back out as non-cash; inventory change is booked from the balance sheet movement.
Investing section holds long-term asset purchases - buying assets, investing in the software platform, buying shares in another company. Salary paid one month is an expense, not an investment.
Financing section holds anything about capital structure: owner distributions, loans taken or repaid, outside capital in. Not day-to-day operations.
Free cash flow = operating cash flow minus investing cash flow; it is the money left after internal operations are fully funded, with no further obligations other than financing.
Use FCF as the decision number for what you can do next: pay down debt, take a distribution, or fund the next inventory buy.
caveats: The definition given is operating cash flow minus investing cash flow - some practitioners compute it other ways; be explicit about which you use.
In the example, one month showed net income of only $140 while cash flow was $272, so never substitute one for the other.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Diagnosing Gross Margin Drops During Promo Months
cards.summary: Tracking gross margin percentage month over month to catch discount-driven margin erosion separate from volume effects.
cards.use_when: Reviewing monthly performance after a sale event to see whether volume gains were bought with margin.
steps: Track gross margin as a percentage of revenue, not just dollars, alongside order counts.
In the example, orders scaled from 3,000 to about 5,000, and in the month where orders more than doubled the gross margin percentage fell - the source attributes this directly to running a discount.

Cross-check the discount story against the COGS breakdown lines (product cost, import duty and inbound freight, pick and pack, shipping, merchant fees) to confirm the drop is price-driven rather than cost-driven.
Confirm recovery: the example then shows gross margin recovering in following months as discounting stops.
Use this pattern to set expectations before a promo: decide in advance what margin dilution you accept for the volume, and measure the actual against it the following month.
caveats: The source does not give a specific acceptable margin-dilution threshold; set your own based on contribution margin after CAC.
A margin drop coinciding with a supply-chain cost increase (air freight, for instance) will look similar - check COGS lines individually.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Free cash flow vs net income: inventory and tax timing as cash drivers
cards.summary: Read the cash flow statement to see why free cash flow diverges from net income, driven mainly by inventory build/sell-through and tax payment timing.
cards.use_when: Monthly or quarterly cash review for your store, especially when net income looks positive but your bank balance is falling, or you are deciding how much inventory to buy for the next selling season.
steps: Pull the cash flow statement alongside the income statement, not instead of it. Attribution: ecommerce finance commentary treats the cash flow statement as the operational view of the business.

Compare the change in inventory line to net income. If inventory rose (e.g., 335 to 448 in the source example), that is a cash outflow even though it may sit as an asset; if inventory fell because you sold through it, that is a cash inflow.

Check tax payments as a separate line. In the source example, months with tax payments showed cash out, and months with no payment effectively conserved cash — the payment timing, not the underlying tax liability, moved the number.

List the other large lumpy items (e.g., paying a software engineering team 100k in one month) and note them so you understand which month you 'lost' cash because of investment rather than trading losses.

Reconcile: explain the gap between net income and free cash flow by naming the specific drivers (large inventory purchase plus engineering payments; or sell-through of inventory plus no tax payment plus little engineering spend).

Use free cash flow as the operational view and net cash flow (after financing) as the holistic view: it answers whether the business can pay its debts and run itself at the same time. In the source example net cash flow was slightly lower than free cash flow because of leverage.

Warning sign from the source: ecommerce businesses often go broke not because they lose money per customer, but because they run out of liquidity from bad working capital dynamics — so treat the cash statement as the survival document, not the income statement.
caveats: The specific figures (335 to 448 inventory, 77k net income vs -95k free cash flow, 140 vs 272) are one case-study example, not benchmarks.
Net cash flow after financing is less operational because whether you have a loan is somewhat unrelated to how the business itself operates.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Calculate contribution margin per order and post-marketing contribution
cards.summary: Structure an ecommerce P&L into net revenue, product COGS, gross margin, fulfillment, contribution margin, CAC and post-marketing contribution so each expense can be optimized separately.
cards.use_when: Setting or reviewing product-level and order-level profitability, or diagnosing why a store that looks profitable at gross margin is not producing operating income.
steps: Start at gross revenue (product sales plus tax collected where applicable) and subtract discounts and returns, then add shipping income you charge customers. Result: net revenue, which is effectively your AOV after discounts and returns for the period.

Split COGS into product cost (manufacturing plus import freight plus duties/taxes to get product to the warehouse) and keep it separate from fulfillment cost (pick and pack, packing materials, 3PL charges, shipping to customer). A generic P&L lumps these together; splitting them is what lets you see which line is moving.
Compute gross margin = net revenue minus product COGS. In the source case study it ran about 70–75%.
Compute contribution margin = net revenue minus product COGS minus fulfillment. In the source example, $134 net revenue with $64 contribution margin, just under 50%.

Compute CAC as total marketing spend divided by first-time purchases, then post-marketing contribution = contribution margin minus CAC. Source example: $22 and $12 post-marketing contribution per order, i.e. profitable on the first order at roughly a 1.5 contribution-margin-to-CAC ratio.
Check merchant/credit card processing fees and include them — the source uses about 2.75% of revenue as a working assumption.
