Finally subtract operating expense per order to reach operating income. In the source example opex was about $8 and $6 per order and operating income was 11% and 5%, i.e. about $15 and $6 profit per unit.

Remember the leverage: small per-order changes (knocking a couple of dollars out of one line) multiplied across thousands of orders is the difference between tens of thousands of losses and tens of thousands of profit.
caveats: Gross margin is the highest figure, contribution margin lower, post-marketing contribution lowest — mixing the terms (calling gross margin contribution margin) causes wrong decisions.
All percentages in the source are one case-study supplement brand in a specific period; do not treat them as targets.

After the first order, returning customers generally carry little or no marketing cost, so first-order profitability is the ideal state — the source calls businesses with strong first-order profit exceptional.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Treat discount and CAC as one acquisition cost pool
cards.summary: Discounts and marketing spend are mathematically equivalent per-customer costs, so combine them into a single budget and optimize the split for total profit, not per-customer margin.
cards.use_when: Planning next quarter's promotional calendar and ad budget, or deciding whether a deeper discount or more ad spend will grow profit for the whole store.
steps: Build the scenario grid with the same ad spend in every column, then vary the discount. Source case: $100,000 spend, $1.50 per click blended, ~66,667 sessions in all scenarios, undiscounted price $200, COGS $75 ($50 product + $25 fulfillment).

Convert discount into a conversion-rate assumption. Source assumptions: 0% discount → 1.5% website conversion → 1,000 purchases → $100 CAC; $30 discount → 2.2% → 1,433 purchases → $70 CAC; $60 discount → 3.8% → 2,500 purchases → $40 CAC.

Compute contribution margin post-CAC per customer for each scenario. In the source, all three land at $25 per customer, because discount plus CAC totals $100 in every scenario: 0% + $100, $30 + $70, $60 + $40.

Now total it up across the whole business. Source results: scenario A $200,000 sales, $125,000 pre-marketing contribution, $25,000 post-marketing; scenario B $243,000, $136,000, $36,000; scenario C $350,000, $162,000, $63,000. The deepest-discount scenario produced the most total profit in this particular case.
Do not assume the deepest discount always wins. The source states it can go both ways: some brands make more money by shrinking revenue with spectacular unit economics on a smaller base of customers.

Reframe your planning as one pool: 'we will spend $X this year on demand creation — how do we split it between discounts and ad platforms to maximize sales and profit?' Treat the discount line and the marketing line as two forms of the same cost of acquisition.

Prefer attaching your best discounts to a loyalty or subscription on-ramp rather than a flash sale. The source argues flash-sale converters often will not buy without a big discount, while customers who join a loyalty or subscription program have self-selected into higher lifetime value.
Run this as a future-strategy split test with identical spend before committing to the deeper discount calendar.
caveats: The 1.5%/2.2%/3.8% conversion lifts and the $1.50 CPC are assumptions illustrating the method, not measured benchmarks.
Deep discounting can damage brand — the source explicitly says it is not advocating discounting 'like crazy'.
The result is highly sensitive to whether the assumed conversion lift from discounting actually materializes; if it does not, the deeper-discount scenario loses money.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Price prepaid bundles by comparing margin loss against retention gain
cards.summary: Prepaid multi-order bundles cut per-order margin but lock in multiple orders, so evaluate them on total lifetime profit rather than the discounted order's gross profit alone.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to launch or expand 3/6/12-order prepaid bundles, subscribe-and-save tiers, or any offer that trades discount depth for committed repeat orders.
steps: Model three segments side by side: one-time buyers, a three-order prepaid, and a six-order prepaid. Source assumptions: $80 undiscounted AOV, $19 product COGS, $15 fulfillment, $34 total COGS, $46 gross profit and 58% gross margin for one-time buyers.

Apply the discount and record the margin hit: 25% off for three orders gives ~$60 collected vs $80, gross profit falls to $26; 30% off for six orders gives ~$56 collected, gross profit falls to $22 and margin to about 39%. The source notes gross profit is roughly cut in half at the six-order tier.
Expect most operators to conclude at this point that the discount is not viable. That is the moment to add the retention data rather than stopping.
Model retention on a cohort of 1,000 new customers over 12 months. One-time buyers: about 10% reach order 2, 5% reach order 3, 3% reach order 4 → 1.2 average orders per customer in year one.

Three-order prepaid: 100% retention for three consecutive months, then roughly 50% roll off and 50% re-enroll, repeating → about 5.6 average orders in 12 months. Six-order prepaid: 100% retention for six months, then ~50% churn/re-enroll → about 9 average orders.

Multiply lifetime orders by gross profit per order. One-time: 1.2 × $46 = ~$54 LTV. Three-order prepaid: 5.6 × $26 = ~$146 LTV (about +169%, +$92). Six-order prepaid: 9 × $22 = ~$198 LTV (about 4x, +$144 per enrolling customer).

Then model the mix effect, because only a fraction of customers will take prepaid. Source sandbox: shifting from 100% one-time to 85% one-time / 10% three-order / 5% six-order raises weighted-average LTV from $54 to $71, about +30% on the same customer base, flowing to gross profit and operating income.

Consider prepaid as a working-capital tool as well as an LTV tool: collecting cash upfront can let you finance the inventory you will ship to that customer with their own money (negative net working capital), which the source notes is common in B2B SaaS and education but rare in ecommerce.
caveats: The retention curves (10% to order 2, 50% prepaid roll-off and re-enroll) are described as realistic for the presenter's merchants, not guaranteed results.
LTV figures ignore the marketing cost to acquire those customers, so a prepaid tier with lower cash collected can produce lower LTV-to-CAC than a one-time buyer if acquisition cost is unchanged.
Prepaid cash is partly a liability: you owe fulfillment over future months, so spent prepaid cash is not free profit.

The source also notes increasing discounts over the customer lifetime (e.g. 10% first, 15% second, 20% third, 25% fourth+) as an alternative to flat subscribe-and-save, because flat incentives get customers who subscribe for the one-time offer and cancel.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Build separate unit economics for transactional vs subscription customers
cards.summary: Transactional and subscription customers have different AOVs, discounts and cost structures, so model their unit economics on separate rows before forecasting any revenue.
cards.use_when: Building or rebuilding a subscription-box or subscribe-and-save financial model, or deciding whether subscription revenue is actually more profitable than your ad hoc channel.
steps: Build two unit-economics tabs or row sets: transactional (ad hoc, no loyalty program) and subscription. The source treats this as necessary because their retention behavior is very different and mixing them hides the truth.
For transactional: start from undiscounted AOV ($90 in the source), back out refunds (4% assumed) and discounts (5% assumed, e.g. email-capture offer), giving net AOV of about $81.99.

For subscription: undiscounted AOV is usually lower ($75 assumed) because subscribers buy smaller, more frequent orders, with 4% refunds and an average 20% subscribe-and-save discount, giving about $57 collected.

Break COGS into product cost and fulfillment separately and scale each to the AOV. Source transactional: about $7 product and $16.20 fulfillment; source subscription: about $6.50 product and $5.50 fulfillment on the smaller basket.
Add credit card processing at about 2.75% of collected revenue in both cases.
Resulting source figures: transactional contribution margin about $56, roughly 68%; subscription contribution margin about $33.40, roughly 59%. The subscription order is less profitable per order.

Do not stop at the per-order comparison. The source states subscription customers usually generate three to five times as much revenue per customer on a lifetime basis, which more than repays the lower per-order margin — hence the need to forecast retention separately before judging the channel.
caveats: 50–70% gross margin is described as typical for supplements specifically; do not carry that expectation to other categories.

The source simplifies to a single flat 20% subscribe-and-save for modeling purposes while noting that real high-retention programs use increasing discounts over the customer lifetime or prepaid bundles, which the source says can drive roughly 2.5x more lifetime spend than flat subscribe-and-save 20%.
All percentages are assumptions in a demonstration model, not measured results for a real brand.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Forecast ad spend divided by CAC to drive new customer counts
cards.summary: In a subscription-box model, marketing spend is the master lever: ad spend divided by CAC yields new customers, and everything downstream flows from it.
cards.use_when: Building a 36-month growth forecast, sizing cash needs or runway, or testing how sensitive your plan is to CAC improvements.
steps: Lay out monthly ad spend as a ramp rather than a flat number. Source example: $5,000 in month 1, $10,000 month 2, then +$5,000 per month for six months, then +$10,000 per month for the next six, then +$15,000 per month through month 24, then +$25,000 per month, ending around $570,000 per month at month 36.
Divide ad spend by CAC to produce new customers acquired that month. This is the mechanism that converts a budget decision into customer counts and, via unit economics, into revenue and margin.

Set CAC assumptions by price point and channel mix rather than by ambition. Source starting point for a product around this price: $100 CAC initially, dropping to $75 through month 12 and $60 after that as brand awareness and organic grow.

Explicitly acknowledge that CAC is unknowable before launch — it depends on copy, product, brand awareness and audience — so treat these as placeholders to be replaced with your observed CAC after you go to market.
Note the wide legitimate spread: some brands at scale have CAC far below $100 due to heavy organic, while brands relying on paid to a very niche audience can be far above.

Use CAC break-even as the sanity check: if you lose money after CAC on every customer, scaling ad spend multiplies the loss rather than the business. Determine your per-order post-marketing contribution before increasing the ramp.

Revisit and re-tune ad spend, conversion and CAC at the end of the model build — the source describes this as the normal iteration loop, and it is also how you answer 'how much cash do we burn to reach a given revenue level'.
Separate the new-customer counts into transactional and subscription streams, since only a portion of acquired customers will be sold directly into subscription.
caveats: CAC of $100/$75/$60 are illustrative assumptions for one supplement business, not benchmarks.
The ad-spend ramp and 36-month horizon are a demonstration model; substitute your own capacity, funding and observed CAC path.
Acquisition cost is only one side — the model is invalid if the retention assumptions it feeds are not grounded in your own cohort data.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Turn a contribution-margin model into a pricing and negotiation checklist
cards.summary: Because net margin per order is thin, identify each controllable line — freight, duties, pick and pack, packaging, 3PL, payment fees — and quantify what a dollar saved on each is worth at your order volume.
cards.use_when: Negotiating with a 3PL, carrier or supplier, evaluating a packaging change, or deciding where to spend optimization effort in an ecommerce P&L.
steps: Lay out the full net revenue to operating income waterfall per unit so every cost is visible on its own line: gross revenue, discounts, returns, shipping income, net revenue, product cost, import freight, duties and taxes, gross margin, pick and pack, packing materials, 3PL charges, shipping to customer, merchant fees, contribution margin, marketing, post-marketing contribution, opex, operating income.

Track each line period over period as both a dollar per order and a percent of net revenue. In the source case, product COGS moved from 29% to 27% of net revenue, pick and pack declined month over month (possibly from a better warehouse system), and fulfillment totaled $31 then $35 per order.

Watch the lines the source flags as volatile and worth close attention: import freight, duties and taxes, and shipping to customer — the presenter specifically notes freight costs varying wildly and shipping being a key management area for ecommerce.

Quantify the payoff of a fix: if you can negotiate or eliminate a couple of dollars from any individual expense, that becomes an extra few dollars per order, which across thousands of orders changes profit by tens of thousands.

Include payment processing explicitly. The source assumes about 2.75% of revenue for credit card processing in a subscription model and $3.65 to $3.79 per order in the case study — a line that scales with revenue and can be negotiated.

Compare margins across periods and treat per-unit visibility as the point: a standard P&L that lumps all product and fulfillment costs into one COGS bucket hides whether the unit economics are improving or deteriorating.
caveats: The case study's 29%/27% COGS, $31/$35 fulfillment and $3.65/$3.79 merchant fees are one brand's figures for two months, not benchmarks.

Fulfillment scope differs by product and location, so which charges fall into it will vary; the source recommends defining your own margin definitions and measuring them consistently rather than assuming an industry standard.
Saving a dollar only matters at volume — at low order counts the same per-order improvement is negligible.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Define gross margin, contribution margin and post-marketing contribution consistently
cards.summary: Treat gross margin, contribution margin and post-marketing contribution as three distinct measures with different purposes, and use contribution margin as the base you optimize back from.
cards.use_when: Setting up your store's reporting definitions, briefing an analyst or account manager, or comparing your margins against others' quoted figures.
steps: Define gross margin as revenue minus product cost only — the profit made at the product level, and the highest of the three percentages. Example given: sell for $100, cost $20 to make and get to the warehouse, gross margin about $80.

Define contribution margin as revenue minus product cost minus fulfillment — everything needed to sell and deliver the product to the customer's door. The source treats this as the profit you have available to spend on marketing and other operating expenses, and the margin you work back from when optimizing the business.

Define post-marketing contribution as contribution margin minus marketing spend — the test of whether you actually made a profit after producing, delivering and acquiring the customer. The source calls this the lowest and a very important view of whether the business generates profit.

Keep the terms separate in your reports even though people use gross margin and contribution margin interchangeably; the source recommends defining them according to how you run your business and then measuring them as unique ideas.

Use contribution margin as the ceiling on what you can spend to acquire a customer. In the source case, $64 contribution margin means you have roughly $64 to spend before breaking even on the product.

Interpret the CAC ratio accordingly: contribution margin to CAC of about 1.5 on the first order in the source example meant profitable on the first order, so all subsequent orders were effectively pure profit because they carry little or no marketing.
caveats: The source notes these terms are commonly used interchangeably in the industry, so when comparing to external figures, verify which definition the other party is using.
Contribution margin excluding marketing can look healthy while post-marketing contribution is negative, which is why the source insists both be tracked.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Build a Linked Acquisition-to-Retention Model for Transactional + Subscription Mix
cards.summary: Forecast ad-hoc and subscription customer streams separately so you can see how each drives revenue, profit and LTV in a blended subscription business.
cards.use_when: Financial planning for a store selling both one-time purchases and subscriptions (subscription box, supplements, consumables) where you need to model growth, breakeven and cash needs.
steps: Split new customers into transactional vs subscription each month, and transition the split over time: source's scenario starts at 60% transactional / 40% subscription in months 1-3, moves to 50/50 in months 4-6, and settles at 30/70 after a default-to-subscription cart change.

Model transactional repeat purchasing with a rolling return rate: divide returning customers last month by total customers acquired in the trailing 6 months. Source's example uses ~3.3% of the 6-month customer base returning in any given month.
Apply that return rate to the trailing 6-month customer count month by month, growing the trailing window as the store accumulates history.

Model subscriptions with a monthly churn rate, applied to the prior month's active subscriber base (not to this month's new signups). Source uses 25% monthly churn as a conservative subscription-box assumption.

Compute subscription lifetime orders as 1 / churn rate (25% churn = 4 orders), and transactional lifetime orders via the geometric series 1 / (1 - annual retention rate). Source's 40% annual retention gives ~1.7 lifetime orders.

Feed each stream's orders through separate AOV, refund/discount and per-unit COGS assumptions to produce revenue, COGS, contribution margin and LTV, then consolidate into an income statement and compute the blended, conversion-weighted LTV.
Expose CAC, LTV, LTV/CAC and LTV-CAC per segment and blended; plan to revise CAC each month as real market data replaces assumptions.
caveats: The 3.3% return rate, 25% churn and stated split percentages are source-scenario illustrations, not benchmarks — backtest them against your own trailing data before relying on them.
Weighting blended LTV by conversion split rather than revenue share changes the result; state which basis you use.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Forecast Marketing Spend into New Customers via CAC Assumptions
cards.summary: Convert a monthly ad budget into expected new customers by dividing spend by an assumed and iteratively updated CAC.
cards.use_when: Setting or pressure-testing monthly ad spend and growth targets for a store, and checking whether the acquired customers can ever be profitable.
steps: Set a CAC assumption per period — the source starts at $100 for the first few months, steps to $75 through month 12 and $60 thereafter in one scenario — and note that brands with strong organic can run far lower while niche paid-only brands run higher.
Divide monthly spend by CAC, rounded to a whole number, to get expected new customers (source example: $5,000 / $100 = 50 new customers).
Multiply forward across months to build the new-customer forecast, then push those customers into retention and subscription models to produce revenue.

As you scale, replace the assumption with observed CAC from your own market data and re-forecast, since CAC depends on copy, product, brand awareness and audience targeting and cannot be known before you go to market.
Check the resultant LTV against CAC — the source argues that if LTV is below CAC you lose money on every customer relationship and there is no viable business at that point.
caveats: The $100/$75/$60 ladder is a source-specific modeling example, not a benchmark; your CAC is only knowable after real market testing.
Blended CAC can mask segment differences — a profitable subscription cohort may subsidize an unprofitable transactional cohort.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Use Trigger Events to Shift New Customers from One-Time to Subscription
cards.summary: Sequence offer, discount and cart-default changes over months to lift the subscription share of new customers toward a 30/70 steady state.
cards.use_when: Designing subscription upsell offers, discount structures and cart/checkout defaults for a store trying to move from mostly one-time sales to recurring revenue.
steps: Start with a strong subscribe-and-save offer at checkout to capture the easy subscribers — source scenario reaches ~40% subscription signups in months 1-3.
Strengthen the subscription offer further (months 4-6, target ~50%) and then shift discount strategy: remove or reduce discounts on one-time purchases and tilt discounts toward subscribers.

From roughly month 10 onward, default the cart to subscription so buyers must actively switch back to one-time purchase. The source reports about a 60-70% increase in new subscription signups when defaulting the cart to subscription (data from the source's own platform, OrderGroove).
Lock the resulting 30% transactional / 70% subscription new-customer split as the steady state and carry it through the rest of the model.
Verify the default-to-subscription and checkout options available in your current platform before planning this change, since interfaces differ and change.
caveats: The 60-70% uplift figure is the source's own platform data from defaulting carts to subscription — treat as an example, not a guaranteed result.
Aggressive defaults and asymmetric discounts can annoy customers or invite cancellations; the source does not quantify downside.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Forecast Transactional Repeat Customers with a 6-Month Rolling Return Rate
cards.summary: Estimate how many one-time buyers return each month by applying a measured return rate to the trailing six months of acquired customers.
cards.use_when: Modeling repeat revenue and LTV for non-subscription customers where you cannot simply use 1/churn.
steps: Measure the historical return rate: total returning customers in a month divided by the total customers acquired over the trailing six months. The source typically sees figures like 3-5%.

Forecast forward by multiplying each month's trailing 6-month customer count by that rate, starting with only the data you actually have in early months and expanding the window to a full six months as history accrues.
Watch how the returning cohort accumulates: in the source's example, repeat transactional customers reach 576/month (vs 2,850 new) by month 36.
Convert the model into lifetime orders using the geometric series 1 / (1 - annual retention rate); the source's 3.3% monthly rate implies ~40% annual retention and ~1.7 lifetime orders.
Multiply lifetime orders by contribution margin per order (not revenue) to get transactional LTV — the source treats lifetime contribution margin as the meaningful LTV definition.
caveats: The rate must be measured from your own 6 months of data; 3.3% is the source's illustration.
The method assumes returning behaviour is reasonably stable; launches, seasonality or product changes can distort it.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Compute Subscription Lifetime Orders from Monthly Churn
cards.summary: Estimate lifetime subscription orders from billed periods, order frequency and contribution per shipment.
cards.use_when: Comparing subscriber versus one-time-buyer value to decide how hard to push subscription conversion and how much you can afford to spend acquiring subscribers.
steps: Estimate churn for the store's actual billing period; the source's 25% monthly churn is an illustration.
Expected active periods are 1/churn in a constant-churn model. Orders equal active periods times orders per period; four periods mean four orders only with one shipment each period.
Multiply expected orders by contribution per shipment after discounts, fulfillment and returns.
Compare observed subscription and one-time-purchase cohorts, including acquisition cost and cash payback.
Blend cohort values only with matching acquisition cohorts and realistic subscription conversion rates.
caveats: 1/churn assumes a constant churn rate over the customer's life, which rarely holds exactly.
Subscribers often carry a lower contribution margin per order (bigger discount) even though lifetime value is higher — model both margin and lifetime, not just one.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Report Post-Marketing Contribution Margin as the Core Profitability Gauge
cards.summary: Track contribution margin minus marketing each month to know whether the store can fund payroll and overhead at all.
cards.use_when: Monthly P&L review or investor reporting for any ecommerce store, especially when early customers are heavily first-time buyers.
steps: Compute contribution margin (revenue minus COGS) for the month, then subtract total marketing spend to get post-marketing contribution margin.
Interpret a negative figure as structurally unprofitable: the source's position is that if gross profit minus marketing is not positive, no amount of operating efficiency produces company profit.

Watch the trend rather than one month: in the source's scenario post-marketing contribution margin is negative early because there are few returning customers, and turns positive once the repeat/subscription base builds, because returning customers carry no CAC.
Use the metric to set the pace of hiring and overhead — payroll and other opex must fit under the post-marketing contribution margin for operating profit to exist.
Cross-check against LTV minus CAC as the unit-economics view of the same idea.
caveats: The source's timeline for reaching positive post-marketing contribution margin is scenario-specific and depends on retention build-up.
This is the source's strongly held operating view; it is a useful discipline, not a universal accounting rule.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Build a Simple Bucketed Payroll and Opex Forecast
cards.summary: Forecast people costs by functional bucket and headcount, then layer non-payroll opex to reach operating income.
cards.use_when: Building or updating a store's operating expense forecast and finding the month where operating income turns positive.
steps: Define a few functional buckets that match how you actually staff — e.g. marketing, creative, operations, exec/admin — and put an average salary per bucket, since early-stage stores often keep marketing/creative in-house while outsourcing engineering and other functions.
Forecast headcount per bucket by month and multiply salary/12 by headcount, locking the salary column so the formula copies across months correctly.
Add ~25% on top of salary for benefits, taxes and similar costs to get true employee cost.
Forecast non-payroll opex accounts (other marketing/influencer work, consultants/1099s, software, miscellaneous) as manual line items and copy them across months.

Compute operating income (also called EBIT) as contribution margin minus all operating expenses; in the source's scenario operating income turns positive in month 17 and reaches a 19% EBIT margin by month 36.
Avoid bloated multi-tab, hundreds-of-rows payroll models unless genuinely necessary — the source recommends this quick bucketed approach instead.
caveats: The 25% loading and the month-17/19% margin outcomes are source-scenario assumptions, not benchmarks.
Outsourced vs in-house staffing mixes change the shape of this forecast; adjust buckets to your reality.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Model tax losses separately from book losses and cash tax payments
cards.summary: Keep tax-loss assumptions explicit when forecasting cash for a store approaching profitability.
cards.use_when: Cash planning and investor communications for an unprofitable-early store that is turning profitable, to avoid over-forecasting tax outflows.
steps: Separate accounting losses from tax losses in the forecast.
Have the accountant confirm eligible carryforwards, restrictions, applicable rates and payment dates for the entity.
Apply only confirmed usable losses to forecast taxable income; do not assume every operating loss shields later profit.
Do not recognize a deferred tax asset automatically from accumulated losses; confirm the applicable recognition requirements.
Maintain a cash-tax calendar and downside case without uncertain relief.
caveats: The source's tax rate and eleven-month shelter are historical scenario assumptions, not current rules.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Forecast Inventory with Lead Time and Cycle Time Before You Model Cash
cards.summary: Work out when to place purchase orders by pairing supplier lead time with expected sell-through cycle, then cost each PO.
cards.use_when: Replenishment planning for any physical-product store to avoid stockouts and to see the true cash hit of inventory buys.
steps: Pull forecast order volumes from the demand model to know how many units each month must be fulfilled.
Set a lead time (source scenario: 3 months from order to receipt at the fulfillment center) and a cycle time (source scenario: 4 months of sell-through).
Order enough today so that inventory arriving after the lead time lasts through the cycle: order in month 1, receive in month 4, cover 4 months, then place the next PO.
Roll starting inventory minus orders each month, adding received POs when they land, to project inventory balances.
Cost each PO using a weighted-average product COGS across your order mix — the source weights transactional COGS ($7.70) and subscription COGS ($6.50) by order share to get ~$7.20 average.
Scale the PO cadence to reality (the source models quarterly-ish POs, but monthly POs may be needed) and stress-test demand because you are committing cash months before revenue.
caveats: Lead and cycle times are supply-chain specific; the source's 3-month lead and 4-month cycle are illustrative.
A single-SKU simplification is used — more SKUs multiply complexity substantially.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Build a Mini Cash Flow Statement to Find Working Capital Needs and Runway
cards.summary: Reconcile net income with inventory purchases to project real cash burn and how much capital the store must raise.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much funding or cash buffer the store needs and when, especially for inventory-heavy CPG or subscription-box businesses.
steps: In a simplified bridge, start with net income, add back inventory COGS expensed, then subtract all actual inventory supplier cash payments, whether goods have sold or not.
Add other non-cash and working-capital adjustments separately. Do not also subtract inventory/payables movements already captured by the supplier-payment bridge.
Add any starting capital (source scenario begins with $500k raised) and roll the cash balance month by month.
Expect cash to be choppier than net income: the source's example shows cash going negative around month 8 and again needing a large inventory outlay shortly after.

Use the trough of the cash curve to size the raise: in the source's example, the business needed roughly $1-1.5M cumulative to reach profitability even though operating income turned positive earlier.
Separately note the store's revenue run rate (last month's revenue x 12) as a real-time pacing metric alongside trailing 12-month actuals, and be explicit which one you quote.
caveats: This mini cash flow ignores other assets and liabilities by design — it is not a full three-statement model.
Capital need figures are the source's scenario and depend heavily on lead times, payment terms and growth rate.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Gross Revenue to Net Revenue Bridge: Report Refunds and Discounts Separately
cards.summary: Show gross revenue, then refunds/returns, then discounts, then net revenue — and split net revenue between first-time and repeat customers.
cards.use_when: Designing the monthly reporting pack or income statement presentation so you can see how much revenue discounts and refunds consume.
steps: Start with gross revenue from transactions times undiscounted AOV (source example: $2,700 AOV).
Subtract the refund/return rate (source assumes 4%) to quantify give-back.
Subtract discounts to arrive at net revenue, applying the appropriate net AOV per segment — the source notes subscription AOV is lower than one-time AOV.

Split net revenue into first-time vs returning/subscription-repeat revenue so you can see recurring revenue growing over time and shifting to the majority of the business (source scenario crosses to over 80% subscription revenue by month 36).
Use the split to verify your strategic direction: in a subscription business, repeat subscription revenue should eventually dwarf both first-time subscriptions and transactional revenue.
caveats: The 4% refund rate and AOV figures are the source's scenario assumptions.
Net revenue per segment requires segment-specific AOVs; using a blended AOV will misstate segment economics.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Reconcile Your Model: Gross Profit Percentage Must Match Unit Economics
cards.summary: Use the gross profit rate as an arithmetic check that every revenue and COGS line is forecast correctly.
cards.use_when: After building or editing a financial model, before presenting numbers to investors or using them for decisions.
steps: Compute the blended gross profit percentage from the rolled-up income statement (revenue minus COGS, divided by revenue).
Compare it to the gross profit percentage implied by the bottom-up unit economics (AOV minus per-unit COGS and fees).
If they don't match by segment (the source checks transactional and subscription separately), you have a formula or referencing error somewhere in the model — find and fix it.
Repeat this check each time you change AOV, discount, refund or COGS assumptions.

Track blended gross margin alongside segment margins, since a mix shift toward subscriptions (lower gross margin percentage but higher lifetime value) can lower blended margin while improving the business.
caveats: A match confirms internal consistency, not that your assumptions are correct — wrong-but-consistent inputs still produce a wrong model.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Consolidate Segments and Report the Ecommerce KPI Set
cards.summary: Roll transactional and subscription segments into one business view and report a fixed monthly KPI set to spot direction, not just level.
cards.use_when: Monthly management or investor reporting for a mixed one-time/subscription store; setting which numbers get tracked every month.
steps: Sum orders, gross revenue, net revenue, COGS and contribution margin across both segments to get the company total (source example reaches ~$1.6M net revenue per month by month 36).
Report annualized run rate (monthly revenue x 12) at the top, alongside trailing-12-month actuals, and be explicit which is which — the source prefers quoting run rate as the real-time pacing metric.
Report the subscription vs transactional revenue split and track it flipping toward subscription (source target: 80%+ subscription revenue).
Report CAC, blended LTV, LTV/CAC and LTV minus CAC per segment and weighted average.
Report post-marketing contribution margin and operating income/EBIT margin as the profitability lines.
Watch the LTV/CAC ratio trend: the source's scenario starts at 1.09 (barely above breakeven given the assumed CAC) and reaches 2 by month 36 through falling CAC and a richer subscription mix.
caveats: The source does not label 1.09 vs 2 as industry benchmarks; they are that scenario's trajectory.
Blended LTV requires a stated weighting basis (conversion mix vs revenue mix), or the ratio is ambiguous.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Churn rate only applies to subscriptions — use retention for one-off stores
cards.summary: Churn rate measures the share of subscription customers who cancel in a period; non-subscription ecommerce must use cohort retention instead.
cards.use_when: Choosing which metric to track for a subscription box, replenishment program or membership versus a one-off direct-to-consumer catalog.
steps: Confirm the customer is continuously rebilled (monthly box, annual membership, replenishment program). Only then does churn apply.
If customers buy one order at a time with no rebill, do not report churn — build a cohortized retention table instead, organized by the month of first purchase.

Specify the time window whenever you quote churn: monthly churn and annual churn are not comparable numbers. Source example: a monthly churn rate of 11% means 11% of subscribers cancel each month, while an annual churn rate of 11% means 11% cancel each year.
For B2B or long-cycle subscriptions (billing every 90 days or every two to four years), match the churn window to the billing cycle or the metric will mislead.
For a subscription store, track churn as a leading indicator of customer lifetime and therefore of ad-spend tolerance.
caveats: Source is explicit that churn simply does not apply to non-subscription businesses; using it there produces meaningless numbers.
Do not quote a churn figure without its time unit.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Calculate churn against the prior period's base, not the current month
cards.summary: Churn = cancellations in a period divided by subscriptions at the start of that period, because cancellations happen at renewal from the prior cohort.
cards.use_when: Reporting or setting targets for monthly churn on a subscription store, and auditing any churn number a team or agency has provided.
steps: Gather three figures per period: starting subscribers, new subscribers added in the period, and cancellations in the period.

Divide cancellations by the subscriber base from the prior period — not by the ending or current total. Source example: 100 customers in month one, 50 new in month two, 9 cancellations in month two → churn is 9/100 = 9%, not 9/141 = 6%.
Roll the formula forward across periods to see the trend: the source example moves 9%, 13%, 17%, 11%, 16% across months.
Apply the identical logic annually: source example with 53 customers in year one, 31 new, and 18 cancellations gives 18/53 = 34% annual churn.
Note that a growing subscriber count can coexist with high churn — the total hides the leak, which is why you need the split inputs.
caveats: Without new-customer and cancellation counts you cannot calculate churn; a simple beginning-versus-ending subscriber count is insufficient.
The source's own example shows monthly churn in the ~9–17% range and annual churn ~20–40%, which look wildly different but are two different periods, not a contradiction.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Convert churn into average customer lifetime with 1/churn
cards.summary: Average customer lifetime equals 1 divided by the churn rate over the same period, which lets you compare monthly and annual subscriptions on one scale.
cards.use_when: Comparing payback and LTV scenarios across subscription plans, renewal frequencies or box programs when you need a common lifetime figure in months.
steps: Under constant churn per billing period, expected active billed periods are approximately 1/churn, including the first active period.
At 25% monthly churn this is four monthly periods; multiply by orders per active period to estimate orders.
An annual renewal model with 40% annual churn gives 2.5 annual billed periods; it is not identical to a monthly cancellation model.
Compare plans using their actual billing and cancellation schedules and observed cohort revenue.
Treat lower churn as a scenario to validate, not guaranteed permission to increase CAC.
caveats: This is a simplified constant-churn model; it assumes a steady churn rate and does not capture cohort-to-cohort quality differences.
The source's churn bands (25% down to 5% monthly) are illustrative scenarios, not benchmarks for a given store or category.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Build a cohort retention table as the only valid retention view
cards.summary: Organize customers by first-purchase month and track the same group forward; do not try to read retention from aggregate monthly totals.
cards.use_when: Setting up retention reporting for a subscription or repeat-purchase store, or evaluating a data/analytics tool purchase for the store.
steps: Define cohorts by the month of a customer's first purchase. Each cohort row begins at month zero with that group's original count.
In each later column, show how many of that original group purchased or remained subscribed — always referencing the original group, not the prior month's survivors.
Compute retention by dividing a month's count by the locked original cohort count (lock the cohort column in the spreadsheet so it doesn't shift).

Read a single month of business diagonally across the table, because a given calendar month contains different relationship ages from different cohorts. Source example: 85 total purchasers in April come from four different cohorts.

Watch for cohort quality drift — source example shows a July cohort retaining 91% at the same point where the January cohort retained 74%, possibly due to a different acquisition event or customer profile.
Anticipate the diagonal shape: recent cohorts have empty future cells and older cohorts have no future cells.
caveats: Source recommends pulling this from your database with SQL or an analyst, but notes spreadsheet, analytics plugins and GA cohort features can also produce it; verify what your current analytics tool actually supports.
Aggregate retention across all customers hides the drift that makes cohort tables valuable.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Track net revenue retention separately from customer retention
cards.summary: Build a revenue-by-cohort table so you can see whether surviving customers spend more or less over time, not just how many remain.
cards.use_when: Assessing a subscription store where add-ons, upsells, box upgrades or price changes are meant to lift revenue per customer over time.
steps: Build the same cohort grid but populate cells with revenue from each cohort in each period, then apply the same locked denominator formula you use for the customer table.
Interpret above 100%: in the source example 22 customers in months one and two produced the same headcount but more revenue — expansion revenue from an additional purchase or offer.
Use this to evaluate whether merchandising actions (bundles, add-ons, tier upgrades, promotional deals) are actually expanding the relationship after acquisition.

Note the source's observation that some of the best software businesses see net dollar retention exceeding 150%; it is a directional statement about expansion-led models, not a target for a physical-goods box.
Where revenue per customer falls while headcount holds, discounting or product mix is eroding value even if churn looks fine.
caveats: Above-100% net dollar retention is a positive outcome, not a data error — do not treat it as a bug when reviewing reports.
The 150% figure comes from SaaS observation in the source and is not an established benchmark for subscription box or physical-goods stores.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Derive customer lifetime value per cohort in three columns
cards.summary: Cumulative lifetime revenue divided by the original cohort size, multiplied by gross margin, gives the LTV you should actually set CAC against.
cards.use_when: Setting the maximum allowable customer acquisition cost for a subscription or replenishment offer, or stress-testing a media plan's breakeven.
steps: Build cumulative lifetime revenue per cohort by adding each month's revenue to the running total. Source example: a cohort buying $1,750 in month zero reached $14,000 cumulative by month 11.
Divide cumulative revenue by the locked original cohort headcount to get average cumulative revenue per acquired customer — source example: $406 per customer across 35 customers.
Multiply by gross margin to get LTV. Source assumption used 65% gross margin, turning $406 of revenue into roughly $264 of lifetime gross profit.
Sanity-check the first-purchase view: in the source example a customer initially spent $50 with only $33 of gross profit against a $115 CAC, so month-one economics alone look impossible.
Trace the crossover month by month — source example reached $65 cumulative gross profit by purchase two, $95 by purchase three and $123 by purchase four, surpassing the $115 CAC there.
Use the resulting LTV to set the CAC ceiling and to justify spend that looks unprofitable on the first order.
caveats: The source's $50/month, 65% margin, $115 CAC figures are illustrative modeling assumptions, not benchmarks.
Gross margin here excludes marketing and overhead — do not substitute net margin or the payback math breaks.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Calculate CAC payback from cohorts, not from flat monthly gross profit
cards.summary: Dividing CAC by a single month's gross profit ignores churn; real payback must sum declining cohort gross profit until cumulative profit covers CAC.
cards.use_when: Deciding how fast a subscription or replenishment offer repays acquisition spend before scaling the media budget.
steps: Estimate payback the naive way first to see the size of the error: source example takes $28 monthly gross profit against $90 CAC and reports 3.2 months.
Layer in retention by order: source high-churn cohort of 3,500 buyers retained 100% at order one, 75% at order two and 50% at order three, with most customers gone by order 18.
Multiply CAC by the full original cohort count to get total marketing outlay — 3,500 × $90 = $315,000 in the source example.
Sum gross profit across periods using each period's surviving customer count, then find when cumulative gross profit crosses total CAC. Source high-churn example breaks even around month 8, not 3.2.

Repeat for a lower-churn cohort: source software-style example retained 45% at 12 months and 15% at 24 months, breaking even around month 9 against a 7.1-month naive estimate — roughly a 27% error versus roughly 150% in the high-churn case.
Scenario-test CAC itself: the source notes a move from $125 to $225 CAC shifted breakeven from about month 5 to about month 11.
caveats: The source warns payback is 'almost always' calculated incorrectly and that errors typically make real payback 20–100% (sometimes 200%) longer than reported.
Source numbers are worked examples, not universal benchmarks; rates vary by category and retention curve.
If your subscription allows skipping or irregular order frequency, count payback in number of orders rather than months.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Inspect what survives after payback, not just whether you break even
cards.summary: Two cohorts can both repay CAC while only one generates meaningful profit afterward, so read the tail of the cohort, not the breakeven date alone.
cards.use_when: Comparing subscription offers, pricing tiers or market segments before committing incremental media budget, or deciding whether to reprice a program.
steps: After computing cumulative gross profit against CAC, look at how much profit accrues beyond breakeven. In the source's high-churn example the cohort repays CAC but barely generates profit afterward.
In the source's lower-churn example, a still-large active base keeps producing profit after payback, lifting the lifetime-to-CAC ratio toward roughly 2x and continuing higher.
Treat a business that only reaches breakeven as having unresolved unit economics — the source states it would need to rethink pricing and other fundamentals.

Check whether your low-churn users might simply be people who forget to cancel, which you could exploit by splitting the range into a low-churn and a high-churn part; if that is what is happening, your targeting already selects for the low-churn segment and you should keep doing so.
Use the breakeven-plus-tail picture to choose between offer designs rather than ranking them on acquisition cost alone.
caveats: The 2x LTV-to-CAC figure appears in the source as an outcome of one illustrative scenario, not a required threshold.
Judging a store purely on payback speed can favour offers that never become profitable.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Choose subscription-compatible products and structure the offer
cards.summary: Subscriptions work for consumables and continuous needs; the recurring cadence, skippability and bundling of the offer drive the metrics.
cards.use_when: Selecting which SKUs to put on subscription or replenishment, and configuring cadence, bundles or memberships before launch.
steps: Filter the catalog for items customers buy repeatedly: food, beverages, supplements, skincare, coffee, pet supplies, office consumables. Source is explicit that durable one-time purchases like mattresses or computers do not fit.
Decide cadence deliberately. Source notes billing can be monthly, every 90 days, or multi-year in B2B — the cadence determines which churn window and payback unit (months or orders) is meaningful.
Consider bundling or curating the shipment (mixed discovery boxes, surprise formats) as a way to keep the recurring order interesting rather than a straight reorder.
Add mechanics that lift revenue per surviving customer — prepaid terms, memberships, bundles — and then verify the effect in the net-revenue-retention table rather than assuming it worked.
Expect that consumers evaluate the recurring commitment, not just the product, so the value of each delivery must justify the next charge.
caveats: The source presents these as the standard shapes of the subscription box model, not as proof any given SKU will retain.
Skippable or low-frequency subscriptions make month-based payback unreliable — measure in orders.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Recognize the churn-driven hurdles subscription boxes face with investors
cards.summary: High churn plus heavy acquisition spend makes subscription physical-goods stores hard to fund; sharp unit economics and retention data are what overcome it.
cards.use_when: Preparing a subscription store for fundraising, a board update or an internal go/no-go decision on scaling spend.
steps: Expect the comparison to software: the source notes VCs favour low-churn software economics over physical subscription boxes, so lead with cohort retention and LTV data, not revenue growth.
Present cohort retention, net revenue retention and cohort-based CAC payback together — the source says this cohort view is among the first things a venture investor asks for.

Use the Dollar Shave Club precedent carefully: the source cites its roughly $1B acquisition by Unilever in 2016 as what put the model on the map, driven by an extremely low price point (~$1 blades plus ~$3.99 shipping, ~$5 total) and mostly organic/guerrilla marketing because paid acquisition at ~$50 per conversion was unaffordable.
Derive the strategic lesson for your own store: when order value is very low, paid acquisition math may not close and you need organic or content-led demand instead.

Do not treat the acquisition outcome as evidence that any low-price subscription will be valued that way — the source cites it as a story, and the retention figures referenced came from third-party scraped transaction estimates.
caveats: The $1B acquisition and $1/$3.99 pricing are historical facts about one company, not transferable targets.
The retention figures for that case came from a site scraping third-party transaction data and are estimates.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Convert monthly and annual churn on a consistent survival basis
cards.summary: Normalize subscription churn through retained-customer survival before comparing rates.
cards.use_when: Comparing retention between plans or channels with different billing frequencies, or reviewing a subscription store's dashboard with mixed units.
steps: For constant monthly churn m, annual churn = 1 - (1-m)^12.
For annual churn a, equivalent constant monthly churn = 1 - (1-a)^(1/12).
A 40% annual churn rate corresponds to about 4.17% monthly churn under this assumption.
Use actual billing periods for lifetime revenue and payback: annual upfront subscriptions differ from monthly cancel-anytime plans.
Compare equivalent cohorts, observation windows and cancellation definitions.
caveats: These conversions assume constant churn and no reactivation; real cohort survival may differ.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Read one calendar month diagonally across the cohort table
cards.summary: A single month's total revenue comes from many cohorts at different relationship ages, so totals hide which cohort is deteriorating.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing a revenue or order decline on a subscription store when top-line reporting looks stable, or reviewing a monthly performance deck.
steps: Recognize that a month's transaction total is the sum of different cohort ages — source example: April's 85 purchasers include the April cohort in month zero, the March cohort in month one, the February cohort in month two and the January cohort in month three.
When a metric moves, trace it back to which rows are changing: early-month weakness points to acquisition, later-month weakness points to retention or product experience.
Note that recent cohort rows are incomplete by construction — cells beyond the latest month available are empty, which is why the table looks diagonal.
Compare cohorts at matched relationship ages (month 3 versus month 3), never at matched calendar dates.
caveats: Requires data organized by customer first-purchase month; if your platform cannot produce this, the analysis cannot be done from totals alone.
Small cohorts produce noisy retention percentages; do not overreact to single-month swings.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Build the cohort model in a spreadsheet with locked denominators
cards.summary: The cohort, cumulative revenue and LTV tables come from a small set of formulas with an absolute column reference to the original cohort size.
cards.use_when: Standing up repeatable retention and LTV reporting for a subscription store without waiting on engineering resources.
steps: Create one row per monthly cohort with the cohort's first-purchase count in the month-zero column, then populate purchases or subscribers per period.
Write the retention formula as current-period value divided by the original cohort value with the cohort column locked (F4 in Excel adds the $), then copy across the row.
Reuse the same divisor for the revenue table to produce net revenue retention, and for cumulative revenue divided by cohort size to produce revenue per customer.
Multiply revenue per customer by gross margin to get LTV, locking the gross-margin assumption cell so you can flex it in scenario analysis.
Delete future cells that have no data rather than leaving zeros, so the table stays readable.
Source notes startups typically have an analyst or data scientist write SQL against the database to produce the underlying table, and that the format is industry standard.
caveats: The source provides its model as a downloadable Excel file; free-template links and current analytics features may change — verify before relying on them.
Spreadsheet models must be refreshed when cohorts age; stale tables give false comfort.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Unit economics first: profit per order before anything else
cards.summary: Break down a single order's price, costs and gross margin before evaluating growth or marketing spend.
cards.use_when: You are launching or auditing a subscription box or physical product and need to know whether the business can make money per order before scaling ads.
steps: Write down the average order value (AOV). In the source case study, the subscription box was priced at $39/month with shipping baked in because customers expect free shipping — you mark up the price to absorb shipping rather than charging for it separately.
List every cost for one order: product cost (source example: $8.64), fulfillment/pick-and-pack at a third-party warehouse ($4.50), and shipping ($0.30) — total COGS $20.39.
Subtract COGS from AOV to get gross profit per order ($18.61 in the example).
Divide gross profit by AOV to get gross profit margin — 48% in the example.
The source is emphatic: if you don't know how much you make on one order, stop everything and figure it out first.
Keep this margin figure with you — you will multiply every lifetime revenue number by it to convert revenue into profit-based LTV.
caveats: Costs are illustrative, not benchmarks; substitute your own quotes for fulfillment and shipping.
Fulfillment and shipping are separate vendors in the source's example — do not conflate them.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Use churn-rate lifetime as a fast fallback, not the real answer
cards.summary: A quick LTV approximation from churn rate and gross profit per order, useful only when you have no cohort data.
cards.use_when: You have a new subscription store with almost no retention history and need a rough LTV for early ad spend decisions.
steps: Estimate monthly churn rate: the percent of subscribers who cancel each month. Source case: 27%.
Compute average customer lifetime as 1 / churn rate. At 27% churn that is 3.7 months.
Multiply gross profit per order by the average lifetime to get LTV. $18.61 × 3.7 = $69 of gross profit per customer.
Use this number as a ceiling on marketing spend to acquire one new customer.

Treat it as a placeholder: the source says churn rate doesn't capture customer lifetime well because cancellation is front-loaded (see Dollar Shave Club: roughly 25% took off in the first month, but only about 10% churned across the entire second year).
Switch to cohort retention as soon as you have enough data — the source says once a company has more than a couple of people, retention cohorts are the way to think about it.
caveats: Assumes a roughly constant churn rate; real retention varies by how long the customer has been subscribed.
Source calls this a 'lazy' calculation to use only when you have nothing better.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Read a retention cohort table to calculate lifetime revenue
cards.summary: Organize repeat purchases by signup month to see true retention, cumulative revenue and profit-based LTV over time.
cards.use_when: You have several months of subscription or repeat-purchase data and need a defensible customer lifetime value for ad budget decisions.
steps: Sort customers into cohorts by their first purchase month; label that month zero and each subsequent month 1, 2, 3…

Populate each cohort row with the number (or percentage) of that original group who purchase in each later month. Example: 100 bought in January, 81 came back in month one, 75 in month two, 45 in month three.
Divide each month's count by the starting month's count to express retention as a percentage.
Add a cumulative revenue row: sum each month's revenue from that cohort. The January cohort generated $3,750 in month zero and nearly $12,000 cumulatively by month three.
Divide cumulative revenue by the original cohort size to get lifetime revenue per customer ($116 in the example).

Multiply lifetime revenue by the gross profit margin (48%) to convert it into profit-based LTV — source example showed LTV building from about $18 in month one to $33, $47 and $55 over the next months.
Repeat each month as new data arrives; the curve tells you when LTV stops meaningfully increasing.
caveats: Works for non-subscription stores too — just read repeat purchases of the same cohort over time, as the source notes for gift-buying businesses.
Churn rate and cohort churn will disagree; the cohort view is more accurate because cancellation varies across the customer lifecycle.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Blended vs paid CAC: calculate both and know why
cards.summary: Split acquisition cost into blended (all spend / all new customers) and paid-only (ad spend / paid-attributed new customers) to judge whether growth is scalable.
cards.use_when: You run paid ads plus organic channels and need to decide whether you can profitably increase ad budget.
steps: Collect monthly ad spend, total new customers, and the split of new customers attributed to paid vs non-paid channels using Google Analytics, Google Ads and Facebook Ads Manager.
Compute blended CAC: total ad spend ÷ total new customers. Source example: $6,500 ÷ 134 = $48.51 per new customer.
Compute paid CAC: ad spend ÷ paid-attributed new customers. Source example: $6,500 ÷ 101 = $64.
Always exclude returning customers from the denominator — including them produces a meaningless CAC, since CAC is about acquiring the first purchase.
Compare paid CAC to LTV ($69 in the example — yes, profitable, but 'barely').
Ask whether organic traffic is scalable; the source notes paid channels can scale from $500/day to $20,000/day quickly, while organic often cannot — so paid CAC is the number that constrains growth.
caveats: Channel splits require tracking setup; not every store will have it.
Blended CAC flatters performance when a large share of new customers come from non-scalable organic sources such as friends and family.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Interpret the LTV:CAC ratio with the source's heuristics
cards.summary: Ratio of lifetime gross profit to acquisition cost signals whether the store can self-fund growth or needs outside capital.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to raise ad spend aggressively, seek investment, or fix retention/COGS first.
steps: Divide LTV by CAC. Source example: $69 LTV ÷ $48.50 blended CAC = 1.4.

Read the ratio against the source's stated bands: 1.0 is the bare minimum (you make no money before operating expenses); 2–3 is the target for growing profitably; mature SaaS businesses can see up to 6 because their lifetimes span many years.
If the ratio is low, the source's framing is that you will lose money on the early orders of each customer and need investment to bridge until customers become profitable.
If LTV is much higher than CAC, the source says the business can raise venture capital comparatively easily — investors are judging product stickiness and whether marketing scales without CAC rising.
Remember the ratio is based on gross profit only; payroll, fixed costs and other opex come out afterward.
caveats: The 2–3 and 'SaaS up to 6' figures are the presenter's heuristics, not universal benchmarks.
Ratio depends on which CAC you use (blended was 1.4 vs paid 1.4/1.4 — recalculate with paid CAC for a stricter view).
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Lever 1: Raise LTV by cutting churn and adding pause options
cards.summary: Small reductions in monthly churn have the largest single effect on lifetime value for subscription stores.
cards.use_when: Your LTV:CAC ratio is thin and you are looking for the highest-leverage place to improve subscription economics.
steps: Quantify the effect first using the churn shortcut: reducing churn from 27% to 20% raised LTV from $69 to $93 — a 35% increase in the source model.

Before cancellation, offer to pause or switch cadence: customers often cancel because they haven't finished the current box; letting them skip a month or take the box every other month keeps them subscribed.
Build email marketing that reminds, delights and drives repeat purchases, and invest in unusually responsive customer service to catch cancellations in the moment.
Requires automation — the source stresses you must respond fast enough to intercept the cancel intent.
Track retention at cohort level so you can see whether a pause option improves months 2–3 rather than just delaying churn.
caveats: The 27%→20% figures are from the source's illustrative model, not a predicted result for your store.
Pause options can mask churn rather than prevent it; watch whether customers resume or drift away.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Lever 2: Raise AOV without competing on price
cards.summary: Upsells, tiers and value-based branding raise revenue per order and improve LTV.
cards.use_when: You want to raise LTV per subscriber without finding entirely new customers.
steps: Introduce tiers or upsells — e.g., a basic box at $39 and a premium box at $49 with more items. Higher revenue per order flows straight into lifetime value.
Build brand loyalty deliberately: the source argues customers who love the brand become less price-sensitive, which gives you pricing power.
Avoid competing on price — customers who buy because you are cheap focus on price, and the source notes they may keep buying a product they dislike for the price alone.
Combine with retention work: the same loyalty that supports price increases also reduces churn, compounding LTV from both directions.
Recalculate LTV after any tier change, since the mix shift alters both AOV and retention.
caveats: The source's tier prices are examples, not targets for your catalogue.
Price increases can damage retention if the perceived value does not justify them.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Lever 3: Renegotiate COGS as volume grows
cards.summary: Product, fulfillment and shipping costs all fall with scale, increasing LTV without changing price or retention.
cards.use_when: You have grown order volume and want to convert scale into higher lifetime value and contribution margin.
steps: Decompose COGS into product cost, fulfillment and shipping, as in the source's $8.64 / $4.50 / $0.30 breakdown.
At low volume (source example: ~50 orders/month) you get the worst pricing — small production batches and small-volume fulfillment contracts.
At thousands of orders per month, buy product in larger wholesale quantities (the source models product cost dropping to about $7) and renegotiate the fulfillment contract (to about $4 per order).
Negotiate shipping rates as well — the source models shipping falling to about $6.50 in that line item, and notes every COGS line can be negotiated down.
Rerun your LTV model after renegotiation: in the source's illustration the combined reductions lifted LTV from $69 to about $80.
Attack LTV from every front simultaneously — retention, AOV and COGS — and keep re-checking it.
caveats: The renegotiated figures are illustrative model inputs, not quotes you should expect.
Some volume thresholds may be needed before suppliers or 3PLs will reprice.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Decide how long a window to use for LTV
cards.summary: Choose an observation window by finding the point where cumulative cohort revenue stops meaningfully increasing.
cards.use_when: You need to fix a defensible LTV horizon for budgeting or investor conversations, especially for non-subscription or seasonal stores.
steps: Build a simple model: start with a cohort (e.g., 1,000 customers), apply a monthly churn rate (e.g., 25%), and track remaining customers month by month.
Multiply monthly remaining customers by AOV and accumulate into a running cumulative revenue total.
Extend the model month by month and watch where additional months add negligible revenue — the source's example stopped around month 12.
Use the cumulative total at that plateau as your customer lifetime revenue, then multiply by gross profit margin for LTV.

For non-subscription stores, build the same view as a cohort: how many people bought in a given month, and how their repeat purchases accumulate over time; the source still recommends a longer window than a first-purchase-only view.

For seasonal gift-buying stores (Mother's Day, Christmas), the source warns LTV is not limited to the first 60–90 days — a customer acquired once may return across holidays for years, so model a multi-year window.
caveats: A 60–90 day LTV view understates businesses with long repurchase cycles; the source explicitly calls this out for gift products.
The plateau month depends entirely on your retention curve — there is no universal window.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Model paid Amazon launch orders and uncertain organic follow-on sales
cards.summary: Assess launch advertising against contribution and a conservative organic-sales scenario.
cards.use_when: You are launching a physical product on Amazon and deciding how much to lose on early ad-driven sales.
steps: Forecast paid orders using realistic ad cost and order contribution after marketplace fees and fulfillment.
Model organic sales separately rather than assuming paid orders guarantee ranking or reviews.
Request authentic feedback only through permitted marketplace processes; do not buy or incentivize reviews.
Compare a no-organic-uplift downside with the source's growth scenario before funding the launch.
caveats: Source review counts and launch economics are illustrative, not universal thresholds or current marketplace rules.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Model lifetime orders per customer before committing ad budget
cards.summary: Estimate how many times a customer repurchases to convert first-order profit into true lifetime value.
cards.use_when: You sell a consumable product and need to justify acquisition spend above first-order margin.
steps: Estimate average repurchase count from your own data — the source suggests looking across emails or an existing sales platform; the example used 2.2 lifetime purchases for a consumable like protein powder.
Multiply gross profit per order by lifetime orders: $43 × 2.2 ≈ $95 of lifetime profit in the example.
Deduct acquisition cost incurred only on the first order (about $40 in the example) to see the net profit per acquired customer.
Compare lifetime profit to CAC to sanity-check: source ratio came to 2.3, indicating paid acquisition still makes money over the customer's life.
Be conservative where you have no data — the source treats this as an assumption to revisit, not a fixed truth.
caveats: The 2.2× multiple is an example assumption, not a category benchmark.
Applies best to consumables; one-time-purchase products need a different LTV basis.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Sequence the forecast from marketing spend forward
cards.summary: Forecast ecommerce financials by starting with marketing budget, converting it to orders via CAC, then deriving inventory and cash needs.
cards.use_when: You are building a financial model for a new ecommerce or Amazon FBA business and need to know how much inventory and cash to line up.
steps: Start with the marketing budget line by month — the source's example began at $1,000, rose to $1,500, then increased $1,000/month out to month 16.
Apply CAC to convert spend into expected new orders (source example CAC: $41 per order).
Translate orders into units of inventory needed, remembering you must purchase inventory well in advance — the source notes checks of $10,000–$50,000 for stock before any revenue.
Model cash timing explicitly: inventory is paid for before Amazon or customers pay you, so the model must show when cash goes out versus comes in.
Add a cohort/LTV layer to show when paid orders turn profitable through organic sales and repeat purchases.
Use Excel hygiene as the source does: freeze panes on months and cost categories so assumptions stay visible as you build across months.
caveats: The marketing budget trajectory and $41 CAC are source examples, not projections.
Cash timing is the main risk in FBA businesses — the source highlights large upfront inventory payments as the core challenge.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Subscription retention benchmarking lesson from Dollar Shave Club
cards.summary: High long-tail retention, not high first-month retention, made a low-AOV subscription valuable.
cards.use_when: You are evaluating or building a low-price subscription and need to understand what makes the model worth investing in.
steps: Look beyond first-month churn: in the Dollar Shave Club cohort cited, roughly 25% of a monthly cohort cancelled within the first month, but retention recovered — about 76% remained one month after signup and around 82% the following month, possibly reflecting pause-and-reactivate features.
Track the long tail: about 51% remained after 10 months, and the second year lost only about 10 percentage points (roughly 51% to 41%), with about 37% still subscribed at 24 months.
Translate retention into revenue: at $5/month, 10 months is $50 and 24 months is $120 per retained customer — the source argues this long tail, not the monthly price, is what produced the valuation.
Apply the lesson to your own subscriber model: small AOV subscriptions can work if the retention curve flattens, which justifies higher acquisition spend.

Also note the source's counterweight: the company grew through low-cost organic/guerrilla marketing because it could not afford ~$50 per paid conversion — a retention story alone did not carry the acquisition.
caveats: The source explicitly warns that very few subscription box businesses see this kind of retention — it is a success story, not a typical outcome.
Cohort data came from a third-party site that scrapes transaction data; treat the exact percentages as estimates.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Build an Amazon FBA order forecast from marketing spend
cards.summary: Model paid orders from a monthly marketing budget divided by CAC, then layer a paid-to-organic ratio that grows as reviews accumulate.
cards.use_when: You are planning a new Amazon FBA product launch or replenishment cycle and need a 12-18 month order forecast before deciding how much inventory to buy and how much cash to raise.
steps: Set a monthly marketing budget row (example: $1,000 in month 1, $1,500 in month 2, +$1,000 each month thereafter as the business scales).
Compute paid orders per month with =ROUND(marketing budget / CAC, 0). At $1,500 spend and $41 CAC that yields 36 orders.
Add a paid-to-organic ratio that starts very low (the source uses 10%, meaning a few friends/family purchases) and rises over time. Compute organic orders as =ROUND(paid orders * ratio, 0).

Increase the ratio by a fixed step per month (source example: +10 percentage points per month) on the assumption that after roughly four to five months and ~300 orders you have accumulated enough reviews to start ranking organically.
Total orders = paid + organic, and this drives the revenue, COGS, fulfillment and inventory rows.
Freeze panes so the month header row and column labels stay visible as you scroll the model.
caveats: The 10%-per-month organic ramp and the 4-5 month review threshold are the presenter's illustrative assumptions, not measured benchmarks; tune them to your category and review velocity.
The model assumes a stable CAC; if CAC rises with spend, split the marketing row into channels.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Model inventory timing with a lead-time lag row
cards.summary: Offset inventory purchases by the supplier lead time so the model shows when stock actually arrives and when you go negative.
cards.use_when: You are building or auditing a cash model for a physical product where stock is bought months before it can be sold.
steps: Add an inventory-purchase row for the units you pay for each month (example: 250 units at $25 = $6,300).
Add an 'inventory arrival' row that simply equals the purchase row shifted forward by the lead time — the source uses a four-month lag, so a month-2 purchase arrives in month 5.
Add a total inventory row: previous month's total inventory − units sold that month + units arriving that month.
Copy the formula across all months and hunt for negative values. A negative number means you are out of stock and cannot sell; the goal is to time purchases so total inventory never goes negative.
Use the negative months as the trigger to size the next purchase (source example: 500 units, then 1,500, then 4,000 as order volume compounds).
Multiply each purchase quantity by unit cost to get the cash outlay, and note that a 4,000-unit buy at $25 is $100,000 — this is the number that drives the financing question.
caveats: Ignore the common shortcut of expensing unit cost proportional to orders; as a founder your cash leaves in lumps, and the inventory-investment row is what reflects reality.
Lead time should include production plus freight plus inbound receiving to Amazon.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Forecast inventory funding gaps with a monthly cash bridge
cards.summary: Separate units-sold profit from supplier-payment timing to find when an ecommerce store needs cash.
cards.use_when: You have an order and inventory forecast and need to quantify the funding gap before committing to a launch or a scaling plan.
steps: Forecast net sales and COGS for units sold; inventory purchases do not automatically become that month's COGS.
Build a cash schedule from opening cash plus customer receipts, less supplier deposits and balances, fulfillment, ads, overhead, taxes, capital spending and financing payments.
Add financing proceeds separately; reconcile closing cash to the next month's opening balance.
If starting from net income instead, adjust for non-cash items and working capital; do not subtract inventory cash twice.
Identify the lowest closing cash and add a reserve for slower sell-through, delayed payouts and higher returns.
caveats: The source's example shows months where total profit is slightly positive while cash is deeply negative — profit and cash diverge whenever you prepay inventory.
This model excludes taxes, returns and payment processing unless you add rows for them.
cards.source_name: Finance for eCommerce (1).docx

cards.title: Evaluate non-dilutive inventory and marketing financing
cards.summary: Revenue-share financing lets you fund inventory without selling equity, repaid as a percentage of revenue plus a flat fee.
cards.use_when: Your cash model shows a funding gap for inventory or paid acquisition and you are weighing equity dilution against revenue-based financing.
