cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Run three AI creative workflows as a test
cards.summary: Test human-only, human-briefed-AI, and AI-independent creative workflows to see which produces the best-performing ad variants for your store.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much human input to put into ad creative generation for paid acquisition.
steps: Set up three parallel workflows for the same product: (1) humans write the ad concepts unaided, (2) humans brief the AI then AI produces the creative, (3) AI generates concepts and creative independently against a defined optimization target.
Give each workflow the same outcome goal (e.g., purchases or ROAS on Meta) so results are comparable.
Run the variants as actual ads and let platform data decide the winner rather than internal taste.
Note that the source cites a study (via a podcast guest) where the AI-independent workflow outperformed both human-in-the-loop models.
Apply the winning model to scale, but keep a human check on brand and legal-sensitive claims.
caveats: The study is cited second-hand and not detailed; treat the result as a prompt to test, not a proven universal rule.
The presenter's opinion that humans are the limiting factor in creative is his view, not an established benchmark.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Measure AI revenue contribution including LLM commerce
cards.summary: Track whether LLMs become a real revenue driver, defined by the source as up to 10% of revenue sourced from or occurring within LLMs for some businesses.
cards.use_when: Forecasting marketing mix, budgeting for AI-commerce readiness, or deciding whether to invest in LLM product-feed setup for your store.
steps: Add LLM/AI-assistant traffic and assisted conversions to analytics as a distinct channel.
Define 'real' contribution using the source's heuristic of up to 10% of revenue sourced from or occurring within LLMs for some businesses.
Feed clean product feed data to LLMs using the protocols referenced in the source: ACM, UCM, and data from Shopify/Google; verify current specs before implementing.
Pair this with your website's role: the presenter argues the website is diminishing in value and commerce is becoming omnipresent (LLMs, glasses, TikTok Shop, retail, Amazon).
Invest with a longer time horizon since this is a counter-cyclical bet, per the source.
caveats: The 10% figure is the presenter's forecast for 'some businesses,' not a benchmark.
Protocol names and LLM commerce interfaces change; verify current documentation.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Follow transaction toward discovery
cards.summary: Put your transactions where people already discover products, because transaction always moves to the point of discovery.
cards.use_when: Deciding which sales channels to open or prioritize (TikTok Shop, Amazon, LLM, retail).
steps: Map where your customers currently discover your product category.
List every channel where discovery happens and whether purchase is possible there today.
Reduce friction between discovery and purchase (fewer clicks, in-platform checkout, shoppable content).
Prioritize the channel with the most attention and least purchase friction.
Reassess as discovery shifts; the source frames this as omnipresent commerce, not just omnichannel.
caveats: The priority of each channel depends on your category and customer; no universal channel ranking is implied.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Fit creative format to product complexity and funnel stage
cards.summary: Match ad format to how much information a buyer needs, then place the explanation either in the ad or the landing page.
cards.use_when: Choosing between static image and video ads and deciding what the landing page must do for a specific product.
steps: For each product, write out everything a buyer needs to know to purchase (source's 3D printer example lists plastic type, size, heat, kid-safety, software).
If the product is simple and understood, a static image ad can be highly effective and the landing page carries the rest.
If the product is complex, use longer-form video to answer questions in the ad, then drop the buyer into checkout.
If you run a static image ad for a complex product, the landing page must be excellent and cover all the questions.
Design the whole funnel (ad plus landing page) to collectively answer every question the buyer has.
caveats: The presenter rejects the image-vs-video framing as a false binary; format matters only relative to the product and funnel.
No specific format is claimed as a universal winner.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Test distinctive ecommerce creative while controlling unprofitable ad spend
cards.summary: Use the source's preference for fresh creative as a testing hypothesis within contribution and inventory limits.
cards.use_when: Managing a live ad account and planning creative rotation for the next quarter.
steps: Keep a proven ecommerce creative control while testing product demonstrations, objections and customer evidence in new formats.
Set evaluation windows and acceptable acquisition cost using the store's contribution and cash constraints.
Pause or reduce spend when losses, stock shortages or misleading claims warrant it.
Compare incremental profitable sales rather than assuming novelty or continuous spend always wins.
caveats: The source's never-stop-advertising advice is an opinion, not a rule for every store.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Treat creative as a sales obligation, not art
cards.summary: Judge creative by whether it drives a business outcome, using David Ogilvy's principle that it is only creative if it sells.
cards.use_when: Evaluating creative concepts or briefing a creative team or agency for your store.
steps: When reviewing creative, ask whether it drives a measurable business outcome rather than whether you like it.
Subordinate personal artistic preference to results in creative reviews.
Set the expectation with your creative team that ad work is evaluated on sales outcomes, not aesthetics.
Use this as the tiebreaker when a concept is liked internally but not performing.
caveats: Attributed to David Ogilvy via the source; it is a principle, not a numeric benchmark.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Write good-role / bad-role documents
cards.summary: Define what a role looks like when done badly as well as well, using the good/bad software engineer format.
cards.use_when: Writing job descriptions or onboarding docs for ecommerce roles like media buyer, retention manager, or merchandiser.
steps: Write paired statements: a good media buyer does X, a bad media buyer does Y.
Cover both the aspirational behaviors and the detrimental behaviors that can come alongside them.
Print and post the document so team members can check their behavior daily.
Use the same format for any role in your store (email marketer, buyer, ops manager).
caveats: Source notes this comes from an a16z-type document (possibly Ben Horowitz); attribution is uncertain.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Map influencer types to what you actually need
cards.summary: Influencers deliver trust, distribution, or content assets, and your job is to know which you need.
cards.use_when: Planning influencer or creator spend for your store and choosing who to work with.
steps: Identify which resource you need: (1) access to a trusting audience (e.g., a doctor for a skincare brand), (2) access to distribution at scale, or (3) content assets you can run in your ad account.
Match the person to the resource; someone with a huge audience but little trust is not the same asset as someone with a small, trusted audience.
Use their name as social proof where relevant: on your deck, your PDP, or your ad creative.
Recognize the highest-value scenario is when a partner provides trust, distribution, and assets together.
Reflect on the source's point that the two greatest influences on purchase ever are a recommendation from someone you trust and price; work those into your influencer plan.
caveats: Best case (all three) is rare; budget accordingly.
No CPM or conversion benchmarks are given.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Build a media arm to drive negative CAC
cards.summary: Use owned media to offset marketing cost so acquisition can become profit-generating rather than a pure expense.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest in content, podcast, or media as a customer acquisition channel for your brand.
steps: Decide first which business model the media serves: if you sell products, media drives awareness and offsets the marketing line; if you sell media itself, you need far more generalized reach.
If your model is product sales, build content aimed at a narrow, high-trust audience and let sponsorship or media revenue offset your marketing costs.
Track marketing as an offsetting revenue line so acquisition cost can trend negative.
Scale media spend only relative to the revenue it can drive back to the core business.
Recognize that a niche audience can command high CPMs from sponsors whose customer value is massive (the source cites banking/fintech sponsors).
caveats: The negative-CAC and 30%+ operating margin figures come from the presenter's service agency, not an ecommerce brand; adapt, don't assume identical results.
The presenter notes that a pure media business would require generalizing and dumbing down content, so don't blindly copy a niche strategy if media is the product.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Align dashboards to financial incentives
cards.summary: If financial incentives don't match the dashboard you show people, their behavior won't match it either.
cards.use_when: Setting team metrics or performance incentives for ecommerce roles like media buying, merchandising, or retention.
steps: Identify the primary financial metric you care about (the source's example: shareholder value).
Design dashboards so the reported metrics track the same outcome you're incentivized by.
Check that employee financial incentives point the same direction as the dashboard, or behavior will diverge.
Use equity or ownership to tie long-term behavior to that outcome.
caveats: Stated as a strong belief ('incentives drive action') by the source, not as an experimental finding.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Expect harder output-expectation setting from AI
cards.summary: AI raises the ceiling on possible output so fast that rightsizing team expectations becomes the hardest management problem.
cards.use_when: Setting creative volume targets or performance expectations for a marketing or ecommerce team now that AI tools are in use.
steps: Recognize the source's question: should a marketing team produce 5, 5,000, or 50,000 pieces of creative? There is no established answer.
Set expectations relative to outcomes rather than volume, since volume ceilings have shifted dramatically.
Use AI to produce a larger exploration set and let measured results, not headcount, define what's achievable.
Revisit team targets regularly, since what took 90 days can now take minutes per the source's outbound example.
caveats: The source explicitly calls misaligned expectations his hardest current problem; this is an open question, not a solved method.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Start with free cash flow, not net income, to judge business health
cards.summary: Use operating cash flow and capital spending alongside net income to assess an ecommerce store's available cash.
cards.use_when: Monthly or quarterly financial review of an ecommerce store, when net income looks healthy but the cash balance is shrinking or we are unsure whether to hire, buy inventory or take on debt.
steps: Reconcile net income to operating cash flow using non-cash expenses and working-capital movements.
A common free cash flow definition is operating cash flow minus positive cash capital expenditure; state the definition used.
Do not subtract a negative investing cash flow number or assume every investing transaction is capital expenditure.
Depreciation and amortisation affect profit but are non-cash expenses in that period.
Add financing flows separately to explain the change in bank cash; borrowing can raise cash without improving free cash flow.
caveats: The three-statement logic applies to all business models, but the specific swing factors differ — for ecommerce, inventory and capitalised development dominated.
Depreciation, debt principal repayments and capitalised software are invisible on the income statement, so a P&L-only review will systematically miss cash drains.
cards.source_name: Understanding Free Cash Flow for eCommerce Startups _ Finance Case Study.docx

cards.title: Map the three cash flow statement sections to store activities
cards.summary: Operating, investing and financing sections each capture different cash movements, and knowing which section an ecommerce transaction belongs to prevents misreading cash health.
cards.use_when: When setting up or reviewing an ecommerce cash flow statement and deciding where to record inventory buys, software build costs, loan drawdowns or owner distributions.
steps: Operating cash flow (also called cash flow from operations): everything related to running day-to-day operations — paying salaries, marketing, fulfilment and supplier bills. Start this section with net income linked from the income statement, then adjust.

Investing cash flow: purchases of long-term assets such as warehouse equipment, a software platform, or shares in another company. A one-month employee salary is an expense (operating), not an investment.
Financing cash flow: non-operational capital movements — owner distributions, money lent into the business, loan proceeds or repayments. This reflects capital structure, not trading performance.

Adjust operating cash flow for balance sheet movements: a rise in accounts receivable is negative to cash (customers owe you), a rise in accounts payable is positive (you owe suppliers and hold cash longer), and depreciation is stripped back out because it never left the bank.
Apply the same treatment to inventory: an increase in the inventory balance (e.g. 335k to 448k) is a cash outflow, and a decrease means you converted stock into sales and released cash.
Only after completing all three sections do you arrive at free cash flow, which the source describes as cash with no further obligations other than financing.
caveats: The exact interface and line-item naming varies by accounting software and template; verify current layouts when building or importing statements.
The source teaches the general structure via one ecommerce example, so line items specific to your store may need judgement.
cards.source_name: Understanding Free Cash Flow for eCommerce Startups _ Finance Case Study.docx

cards.title: Why inventory purchases make a profitable store run out of cash
cards.summary: Buying stock in large lumps hits cash in the purchase month while the cost only reaches the P&L when goods sell, so profitable periods can coincide with cash shortages.
cards.use_when: Planning inventory replenishment or a seasonal stock buy for an ecommerce store, or explaining why a high-revenue month did not improve the bank balance.
steps: Compare units-sold COGS with inventory purchased and supplier payment dates.
Track deposits, balances due, inventory receipts and payables to explain cash timing.
An inventory balance increase is not automatically an equal cash payment; supplier credit and prepayments change the bridge.
Forecast cash at planned reorder dates and stress-test slower sell-through.
caveats: The case study numbers are illustrative of one store's model, not benchmarks for expected inventory turns or margin levels.
Inventory dynamics will differ by model — made-to-order, dropship or pre-order stores carry very different cash timing.
cards.source_name: Understanding Free Cash Flow for eCommerce Startups _ Finance Case Study.docx

cards.title: Discount-driven revenue spikes lower gross margin percentage
cards.summary: In the case study, the month where orders more than doubled during a sale also saw gross margin percentage drop, so monitor margin percentage alongside revenue volume.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to run a sitewide sale, promotion or discount event, and evaluating the margin consequence after the event.
steps: Track gross margin as a percentage of revenue every period, not just gross profit in absolute terms. In the case study the percentage is relatively stable until the promotional month.

Expect a promotional month to increase order volume while lowering margin percentage, because products are sold at a discount — in the case study orders roughly doubled in the sale month and margin percentage declined.
After the sale, watch whether margin percentage recovers to the pre-sale baseline, as it does in the following months of the case study.

Combine this with the cash view: a sale that lifts volume but is paired with a large inventory build can still consume cash, so evaluate the promotion on margin percentage, free cash flow and inventory movement together.

Use the sale-month pattern to plan cash: if you discount to move stock, you may release inventory cash even as margin percentage falls, which the case study shows as a free cash flow higher than net income in the sell-through month.
caveats: The case study does not establish a target margin band or a discount depth that is safe; treat its figures as an illustration of the relationship rather than a rule.
A margin drop may be acceptable for strategic reasons (clearing stock, acquiring customers) that a P&L percentage alone will not capture.
cards.source_name: Understanding Free Cash Flow for eCommerce Startups _ Finance Case Study.docx

cards.title: Capitalised software development hides cash outflow from the P&L
cards.summary: Capitalising developer payroll pushes cost to the balance sheet and spreads it over its useful life, so the P&L shows a fraction of the actual cash being spent.
cards.use_when: Budgeting for building or extending a custom storefront, app or platform with an in-house or contracted engineering team, and reviewing why cash is leaving faster than reported expenses suggest.
steps: Separate software costs expensed immediately from costs qualifying for capitalization under the applicable policy.
Record actual cash paid even where the P&L recognizes amortisation over later periods.
Reconcile asset additions, amortisation, payables and non-cash changes; the asset balance change alone is not cash spending.
Subtract relevant capitalized development cash expenditure in the stated free cash flow definition.
Treat the source's amortisation period as an example, not a rule for every ecommerce platform.
caveats: Amortisation periods vary (the source says usually three, sometimes five years depending on what is purchased), so use your own accounting policy rather than the illustrative 36 months.
Capitalisation rules and thresholds differ by jurisdiction and accountant guidance — confirm treatment with your accountant.
cards.source_name: Understanding Free Cash Flow for eCommerce Startups _ Finance Case Study.docx

cards.title: Schedule cash tax payments using the store's actual tax calendar
cards.summary: Profit-based monthly tax estimates can differ from actual payment dates; reserve cash for the confirmed schedule.
cards.use_when: Forecasting store cash needs around quarter-end and reconciling monthly reported profit with actual cash movement in the bank.
steps: Obtain the entity's actual tax payment calendar and amounts from the accountant.
Forecast payments in the periods cash is due, whether monthly, quarterly or another schedule.
Reconcile tax expense, tax payable and payments.
Keep cash reserved for upcoming obligations out of discretionary spending decisions.
caveats: Payment frequency and estimation rules vary by country and entity type; verify your own tax calendar rather than assuming quarterly.
The case study amounts are illustrative and should not be used as expected tax rates.
cards.source_name: Understanding Free Cash Flow for eCommerce Startups _ Finance Case Study.docx

cards.title: Debt principal repayments never appear on the income statement
cards.summary: Only interest on debt hits the P&L; principal repayments show up on the balance sheet and financing section, so loan drawdowns and repayments distort cash without changing reported profit.
cards.use_when: Managing a store line of credit, merchant cash advance or term loan, and judging whether reported profitability reflects the real cash burden of debt.
steps: On the income statement, look for the interest line: it confirms there is debt but shows nothing about principal movements, since debt repayments do not appear in the P&L.
On the balance sheet, track the movement in the debt or line of credit balance. In the case study the line of credit is being paid down by about 25,000 per month.
Record principal reductions in the financing section of the cash flow statement, where money coming into or out of the business for non-operational purposes belongs.

When assessing store health, use net cash flow (after financing) rather than free cash flow to answer whether the business can pay its debts and run itself at the same time — the source notes net cash flow is lower than free cash flow whenever the business has leverage.
When deciding whether to draw more on a credit line for inventory or marketing, model the impact of the additional principal repayments on future months, not just the interest expense.
caveats: The source states net cash flow relates to debt service and is therefore a less operational measure than free cash flow; do not use it alone to evaluate trading performance.
Financing structures differ (revolvers, term loans, merchant advances); map the actual repayment schedule of your facility before modelling.
cards.source_name: Understanding Free Cash Flow for eCommerce Startups _ Finance Case Study.docx

cards.title: Reconcile a profitable month against a negative free cash flow month
cards.summary: Working through the case study month by month shows how to attribute a cash shortfall to specific balance sheet movements rather than to profitability.
cards.use_when: After a month where the store reported a profit but the bank balance dropped, to identify the exact causes before deciding on corrective action.
steps: Start the operating section with that month's net income and then adjust for each balance sheet change: receivables up is negative to cash, payables up is positive, depreciation is added back, and inventory increases are subtracted.
In the case study month with net income of 77k and free cash flow of -95k, the main driver was a very large inventory purchase, compounded by payments to software engineers building the platform.

In the contrasting month with net income of 140 and free cash flow of 272, the opposite dynamic applied: the store sold through a lot of inventory without buying more, paid little to the engineering team, and made no tax payment, so cash accumulated on the balance sheet.
Rank the causes by size for the month in question — inventory movement, capitalised development spend, tax timing and debt repayments are the recurring candidates in an ecommerce model.

Convert the finding into an operational decision: if the shortfall was an intentional inventory build, confirm the sell-through timeline and cash runway; if it was unplanned, address the specific driver before repeating the spend.
caveats: The case study's figures illustrate method, not your expected outcomes; apply the adjustment logic to your own numbers.
A single-month reconciliation can be distorted by seasonal or one-off items, so examine several consecutive periods before concluding.
cards.source_name: Understanding Free Cash Flow for eCommerce Startups _ Finance Case Study.docx

cards.title: Separate near-cash expenses from non-cash items when reading the P&L
cards.summary: Most operating expense lines equal their cash outlay, but depreciation and product cost do not, so identify which expenses reflect money actually leaving the bank.
cards.use_when: Reviewing the store's operating expense structure to decide where cash can realistically be cut versus where cuts only change reported profit.
steps: Walk each operating expense line and classify it: personnel, ad spend, marketing consultants, insurance, office rent, software and miscellaneous generally have a cash outlay equal to the reported amount, as the source notes for a 96k monthly personnel cost.

Flag depreciation as non-cash: you purchase assets and then spread the cost, usually over three or sometimes five years depending on what is purchased, so the P&L figure does not show how much cash went out.
Flag cost of goods sold as non-cash in timing terms: you are not buying products as you sell them, you are buying in large chunks and warehousing them.
When you need to cut cash quickly, target the lines where cash outlay equals expense (payroll, marketing, rent), since cutting depreciation does not release cash.

Rebuild the true monthly outflow from the cash flow statement rather than the P&L before making spending decisions, and check whether depreciation is increasing over time, which signals the business is buying assets.
caveats: Some expenses may be prepaid or accrued, so the reported amount may not equal cash in the period even for nominally cash expenses.
The source presents this as a general structure; the classification of any specific line depends on your accounting treatment.
cards.source_name: Understanding Free Cash Flow for eCommerce Startups _ Finance Case Study.docx

cards.title: Track the three statements together to see what the P&L omits
cards.summary: The income statement captures unit economics, the balance sheet reveals asset, debt and inventory movements, and the cash flow statement ties them into actual cash change.
cards.use_when: Building or reviewing the store's monthly reporting pack, or when a single statement gives a misleading picture of ecommerce health.
steps: Use the income statement to judge roughly whether the unit economics say the business should make money — the source describes net income as answering that question, not the cash question.

Move to the balance sheet to see what the P&L hides: inventory balances, capitalised software, tax liability build-up and loan balances. Assets should always equal liabilities plus equity as a basic check.

Read the cash flow statement to convert those balance sheet movements into cash impacts, since it is where inventory swings, capitalised development spend, tax payments and loan repayments become visible.

Use the case study's opening contradiction as a diagnostic template: a store profitable on the P&L but losing cash is usually moving inventory, capitalising development, paying down debt or timing tax — not mis-stating revenue.

Because the concept applies to all business models, apply the same three-statement read to subscriptions, marketplaces or retail, adjusting for which balance sheet items dominate (e.g. deferred revenue for subscriptions, inventory for retail).
caveats: The source assumes familiarity with the three-statement model and links a template; if you cannot build one, the reconciliation logic is harder to apply directly.
The case study deliberately uses an ecommerce business because it exhibits nearly every dimension of cash complexity — other models omit some of these drivers.
cards.source_name: Understanding Free Cash Flow for eCommerce Startups _ Finance Case Study.docx

cards.title: COGS Drives Unit Economics and Valuation
cards.summary: Why COGS accuracy matters for ecommerce operators: it sets the cash left per unit for marketing and R&D and drives gross margin used in valuations.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a product can fund its own acquisition and reinvestment, or preparing gross margin figures for investors or lenders.
steps: Take the sale price of a unit. Subtract only the true cost of delivering that unit (materials, direct labor, factory overhead, freight-in, packaging, or for digital: servers, delivery APIs, support and implementation wages depending on model).

The remaining gross profit per unit is the pool available for marketing, R&D and overhead. If gross profit per unit cannot cover customer acquisition cost plus contribution to overhead, the unit is not economically viable at that price.
Recognise that external valuers look at revenue growth and gross margin together; a misclassified cost that understates COGS inflates gross margin and distorts the valuation multiple.
Use the corrected gross margin to decide whether to make more of the same product, reprice, or discontinue and build a new product.
Keep a simple per-SKU gross profit calculation so repricing and promotion decisions are grounded in the same numbers shown to investors.
caveats: Gross margin is not the only valuation input; growth, retention and market matter too.
The source frames this for finance leaders and founders; the application to SKU-level decisions is an adaptation of that principle.
cards.source_name: Why CFOs Obsess Over COGs.docx

cards.title: Separate inbound inventory freight from customer delivery costs
cards.summary: Document the cost's economic purpose and accounting policy, then include variable selling and delivery costs in ecommerce contribution analysis.
cards.use_when: Setting up the chart of accounts or reviewing shipping cost treatment for an ecommerce store that ships physical products to customers.
steps: Identify what the charge purchases: inventory, customer delivery, support, referral or another service.
Use the applicable accounting policy for statutory classification rather than a universal label from another business model.
Track the charge separately per order or channel where possible.
Reconcile gross profit to contribution after variable fulfillment, commissions and support costs before setting CAC limits.
caveats: Service and software examples in the source do not establish universal COGS rules for a physical-product store.
cards.source_name: Why CFOs Obsess Over COGs.docx

cards.title: CPG vs SaaS Cost Structures and Margin Benchmarks
cards.summary: CPG/manufacturing carries high tangible COGS and 20-40% gross margins; SaaS carries lower labor/server COGS and 70-90% gross margins.
cards.use_when: Choosing which product model to build or expand, or sanity-checking whether your store's gross margin is in a normal range for its category.
steps: For a tangible/CPG product, build COGS from raw materials, direct manufacturing labor, factory overhead (rent, equipment depreciation, maintenance, utilities), freight-in and packaging.
For a software/digital product, build COGS from server or hosting cost, third-party delivery APIs and tools, customer support wages and implementation/onboarding wages.
Compare your gross margin against the source's rule of thumb: roughly 20-40% for CPG/manufacturing and 70-90% for SaaS. The source cites a baby-food manufacturer at about 30% as typical.

When deciding where to build, weigh margin against distribution opportunity: the source notes a CPG product may take a small slice of a very large pie, while SaaS offers higher margin but depends on your skills and idea.
Do not treat the benchmarks as targets; use them to flag whether a cost has been misclassified or a price is structurally too low.
caveats: The 20-40% and 70-90% bands are the source's rule-of-thumb heuristics, not calculated thresholds for any specific store.
A CPG product with strong distribution can win on absolute profit despite low margin.
cards.source_name: Why CFOs Obsess Over COGs.docx

cards.title: Balance Sheet to P&L Timing for Inventory Versus Services
cards.summary: CPG costs sit on the balance sheet as inventory until sale, while many SaaS costs like wages hit the P&L immediately.
cards.use_when: Forecasting cash and monthly profitability, or explaining to a founder-investor why a stock build-up hurts cash before it hits COGS.
steps: For physical products, capitalise inventory (including freight-in) as an asset on the balance sheet when produced or purchased, then move it to COGS on the P&L only when the item sells.
Understand that building stock consumes cash now and reduces reported profit later — useful when planning seasonal buys or bulk purchasing for cost savings.

For a SaaS/digital product, most COGS (support wages, implementation wages) hits the P&L immediately; only capitalised fixed assets such as owned servers or computers flow from the balance sheet into COGS via depreciation over time.
If you rent server capacity (AWS/Azure), the monthly fee goes straight to COGS rather than being depreciated.
Use this distinction when forecasting: a stock-heavy quarter depresses cash before it depresses profit, while a services-heavy quarter depresses profit immediately.
caveats: The source notes most modern small companies rent rather than own servers; ownership changes the accounting treatment.
Inventory costing methods (e.g. FIFO/weighted average) are not covered here.
cards.source_name: Why CFOs Obsess Over COGs.docx

cards.title: Classify ecommerce customer support costs consistently
cards.summary: Document the cost's economic purpose and accounting policy, then include variable selling and delivery costs in ecommerce contribution analysis.
cards.use_when: Allocating team costs for a subscription or membership store so that gross margin and retention investment are reported correctly.
steps: Identify what the charge purchases: inventory, customer delivery, support, referral or another service.
Use the applicable accounting policy for statutory classification rather than a universal label from another business model.
Track the charge separately per order or channel where possible.
Reconcile gross profit to contribution after variable fulfillment, commissions and support costs before setting CAC limits.
caveats: Service and software examples in the source do not establish universal COGS rules for a physical-product store.
cards.source_name: Why CFOs Obsess Over COGs.docx

cards.title: Separate partner commissions from product acquisition cost
cards.summary: Document the cost's economic purpose and accounting policy, then include variable selling and delivery costs in ecommerce contribution analysis.
cards.use_when: Recording affiliate, marketplace or channel-partner commissions for an ecommerce store to keep gross margin meaningful.
steps: Identify what the charge purchases: inventory, customer delivery, support, referral or another service.
Use the applicable accounting policy for statutory classification rather than a universal label from another business model.
Track the charge separately per order or channel where possible.
Reconcile gross profit to contribution after variable fulfillment, commissions and support costs before setting CAC limits.
caveats: Service and software examples in the source do not establish universal COGS rules for a physical-product store.
cards.source_name: Why CFOs Obsess Over COGs.docx

cards.title: Tie Server and Hosting Costs to Business Usage
cards.summary: Cloud costs (AWS/Azure) left unchecked rise quickly; reconcile them to customer or usage growth with engineering.
cards.use_when: Running a hosted or usage-based digital store, app or subscription platform where cloud spend is a major COGS line.
steps: Treat monthly AWS/Azure fees as COGS for a rented-server model (owned hardware instead flows in as depreciation).
Track cloud cost against usage or number of accounts so that adding a customer does not double your cost unnecessarily.
Build a per-customer or per-usage view of infrastructure cost so you can see whether economics improve or degrade as you scale.
Hold periodic meetings between finance and engineering to review how cost should move as the business grows — the source flags this as the practical control.
When onboarding a new enterprise account, tie the incremental infrastructure cost to that account so pricing reflects real delivery cost.
caveats: The source describes the meeting cadence as a practice to adopt, not a proven benchmark.
Cloud pricing and dashboards change; verify the current AWS/Azure cost tools before building reports.
cards.source_name: Why CFOs Obsess Over COGs.docx

cards.title: Waste Control: Expiry Rotation, Fire Sales and Inventory Controls
cards.summary: Reduce COGS leakage by moving near-expiry stock first, using fire sales to clear aged goods, logging stock in/out, and counting periodically.
cards.use_when: Managing perishable or seasonal inventory and shrink in an ecommerce warehouse or 3PL.
steps: Track expiration and obsolescence dates per SKU and ship stock with the nearest expiration first, before touching stock with a longer window.
When stock is very close to expiry, run a fire sale to move it quickly at much lower margin rather than losing it entirely.
Log inventory when it enters and when it leaves the warehouse, and run periodic physical counts — the source identifies missing outbound logging as the control gap that enables theft.
Investigate recurring count variances as a signal of shrink or process error, and feed the cost back into your COGS assumptions.
Use the same rotation logic for seasonal goods: move the oldest season first and discount aggressively before the next season lands.
caveats: Fire sales protect cash but depress margin; the source presents them as a last-resort recovery, not routine strategy.
Physical counting frequency depends on volume and risk.
cards.source_name: Why CFOs Obsess Over COGs.docx

cards.title: Correct COGS Gives a Trustworthy Gross Margin Signal
cards.summary: Accurate elements and timing of COGS produce the gross margin that informs unit economics and business decisions.
cards.use_when: Reviewing monthly accounts before making product-line, pricing or discontinue decisions.
steps: Audit each COGS line for correct inclusion: goods-related costs in, selling and promotion costs out.
Audit timing: match cost to the period the sale occurs, not when the invoice arrived, for physical goods.
After corrections, recalculate gross margin and check whether it still supports the price, the acquisition cost and the overhead contribution.
Use the corrected margin to answer the operational question the source highlights: can you make more of this product, or should you discontinue and build something new?
Repeat the audit when the model changes — for example when you move from self-fulfilment to a 3PL, or from owned to rented infrastructure.
caveats: The source does not prescribe an audit cadence; monthly or quarterly review is a reasonable adaptation.
Correct accounting alone will not fix a product whose unit economics do not work.
cards.source_name: Why CFOs Obsess Over COGs.docx

cards.title: Run the 3x3 loop: Commit, Check-in, Close for ecommerce teams
cards.summary: High-performing teams agree on goals, roles and norms upfront, then repeatedly check in and close the gap between what they say and what they do.
cards.use_when: Standing up or fixing the team structure behind a store's merchandising, content, ads or fulfillment operations.
steps: Step 1 — Commit: hold an explicit conversation about three foundations: goals (what we want to achieve), roles (who does what), and norms (how we share information and make decisions). The source stresses these must be explicit and openly discussed, not assumed.

Step 2 — Check-in: on a recurring basis, revisit those commitments: are we still behind these goals, and does our working style still hold? Mario Musa calls the natural tendency 'drift' — teams get pulled by multiple projects and responsibilities, so goals/roles/norms decay without revisits.
Step 3 — Close: identify the 'saying-doing gap' between stated intentions and actual behavior, then close it in small, specific steps rather than grand overhauls.

Pay attention to the environment around each change and adjust it so the small steps are supported, and be a 'realistic optimist' — think ahead about what will get in the way instead of assuming plans will just work.

Repeat the loop continuously; the source frames it as iterative, not a one-time onboarding event. Ecommerce example: after a catalogue-wide launch has drifted, re-convene, restate the goal (say, conversion on the top 20 SKUs), re-confirm who owns PDP content vs. ad creative vs. inventory, and agree one small test per week.
caveats: No fixed ratio of check-in time to working time emerged — Mario explicitly says 'it depends' on the team's appetite for process; the important point is that check-ins happen at all.
Framework is from observation of executive simulation teams, not from measured ecommerce experiments.
cards.source_name: Building High Performance Teams – How-To Tips from Wharton Fellow_Author.docx

cards.title: Write goals you can actually check against
cards.summary: Explicit, conversational agreement on goals, roles and norms beats silent assumptions and lets teams detect drift later.
cards.use_when: Setting quarterly goals for a store team or agreeing who owns which channel before a busy trading period.
steps: Treat goal-setting as a conversation, not a document drop: the source says teams need to be explicit and have a 'really good conversation' about goals, roles and norms together.
Ensure norms are covered alongside goals — how the team shares information and makes decisions is a first-class part of the foundation, not an afterthought.

Because drift is 'natural' and 'almost inevitable' as people juggle multiple teams and projects, keep the agreed goals few and small enough to re-read and check against later; Mario advises focusing on a few things rather than a lot, since teams get overwhelmed by goals that are too big.

Reuse the same written goals at check-ins: the check-in step asks 'what do we want to do, how do we work together, are we still committed?' — this only works if the original aims were specific enough to compare against.

Ecommerce application: for a peak-season push, agree the goal (e.g. which product lines or margin targets matter), the roles (who owns pricing, who owns creative, who owns stock cover), and the norms (how decisions on discounts get made), then revisit weekly.
caveats: The source gives no numeric target-setting method or KPI formula; it is a conversation framework, not a measurement system.
Overly detailed goal documents risk contradicting the 'keep it simple and manageable' advice.
cards.source_name: Building High Performance Teams – How-To Tips from Wharton Fellow_Author.docx

cards.title: Close the saying-doing gap with small, environment-aware steps
cards.summary: The core of team improvement is shrinking the gap between stated intentions and daily behavior using small targeted changes and realistic optimism.
cards.use_when: When a store team keeps agreeing on plans in meetings but day-to-day execution on pricing, listings or fulfilment keeps slipping.
steps: Diagnose the gap honestly: compare what the team said it would do (goals, roles, norms) with what is actually happening each week.
Choose small steps targeted at specific changes rather than one big reform — the source says the most effective way to close the gap is 'in small steps... targeted at really specific changes.'
Engineer the environment to support each step: pay attention to the conditions around the team and try to create an environment that makes the new behaviour easy.
Adopt 'realistic optimism' over pure optimism: think ahead about what could block the intended action and plan for it, rather than assuming it will happen.

Loop the change back into the check-in: after taking the small step, revisit whether the gap has narrowed, then pick the next small step. Ecommerce application: instead of a store-wide 'improve conversion' push, change one thing — e.g. whose job it is to fix out-of-stock PDPs each morning — and remove the blocker that stopped them.
caveats: Small steps are a deliberate trade-off; the source does not promise that incremental change fixes structural problems.
Realistic optimism requires time to think ahead about obstacles, which can conflict with firefighting during a live sale.
cards.source_name: Building High Performance Teams – How-To Tips from Wharton Fellow_Author.docx

cards.title: Three guidelines for better check-in conversations
cards.summary: Pay attention to styles, hold one-on-ones, and focus on a few topics to make team check-ins productive rather than performative.
cards.use_when: Running team rituals such as weekly ops standups, launch retros or trading reviews where conversations get stuck or unproductive.
steps: Address style differences explicitly: people vary on extroversion/introversion and on comfort with conflict; have a conversation about those styles so the team knows how to talk to each other.
Use one-on-ones as a primary trust-building channel: group dialogue alone becomes complex because of group dynamics, so pair dialogue with group time to build relationships.

Keep the agenda narrow: focus on a few things rather than a lot, because teams 'typically get overwhelmed' when trying to do too much or when goals are too big. Simplicity makes the conversation manageable.
Combine all three: the source argues that if you attend to how you talk to each other and simplify what you talk about, you tend to get a better conversation than if you do neither.

Ecommerce application: in a weekly trading meeting, restrict the agenda to two or three metrics/decisions rather than every channel, and hold separate 1:1s with merchandising, paid media and ops leads before the group review.
caveats: No formula is given for how much time to spend in 1:1s versus group check-ins; use judgement based on the team.
The source presents these as guidelines, not mandatory rules.
cards.source_name: Building High Performance Teams – How-To Tips from Wharton Fellow_Author.docx

cards.title: Match the work to teams vs. individuals
cards.summary: Not every task belongs to a team: expert, highly creative and time-critical work is often faster and better done by one person, while multi-perspective problems suit teams.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to assign a store task — e.g. writing a product page, setting pricing, or solving a merchandising problem — to an individual or a group.
steps: Identify tasks that should probably stay individual: the source lists work requiring specialised expertise, highly creative work, and situations where time is really short, because individuals tend to be more efficient than groups when speed matters.

Note the source's example: writing a report is likened to creative individual work; in an ecommerce context, drafting a product description or a campaign concept can be treated the same way, then reviewed by the team.
Reserve the team for problems requiring multiple perspectives and multiple sources of expertise — that is the condition the source identifies as appropriate for team work.

When you do convene a team, apply the 3x3 steps (commit to goals, roles and norms, check in, close gaps) rather than assuming the group will organise itself, since groups often fail to maximise potential because they don't organise well.
Ecommerce application: let one specialist own the copy or the bid strategy, but convene merchandising, marketing and supply chain when deciding which categories to back next season.
caveats: The source gives directional guidance rather than a decision matrix; boundaries between 'expert' and 'multi-perspective' work require judgement.
It notes there is lots of evidence groups generally don't maximise potential — this is a general claim, not an ecommerce-specific benchmark.
cards.source_name: Building High Performance Teams – How-To Tips from Wharton Fellow_Author.docx

cards.title: Common team failure modes: hero reliance, plan-worship, role neglect
cards.summary: Three recurring mistakes undermine teams: over-relying on one person, focusing on the plan instead of execution, and never defining who does what.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why a store launch or seasonal plan stalls after a good planning meeting.
steps: Avoid the 'great person' trap: the source calls relying too much on one strong-vision, dominant person the 'great person theory' and says it is 'almost always a big mistake' to focus too much on one individual. Spread critical knowledge so the store isn't dependent on one merchandiser or one ads buyer.
Don't stop at the plan: teams commonly focus too much on simply making a plan and not on how to execute it and organise people around it. Add an execution/organisation step after planning.

Do not leave roles implicit: a common mistake is having a good goals discussion, then saying 'let's go do it' without agreeing who does what, which means efforts aren't maximised. Explicitly assign ownership.
Build the fix into the routine: the source ties execution and roles back to the commit and check-in steps, so revisit role assignments when circumstances change.
Ecommerce application: after a promotional calendar is set, list each campaign and name the single owner for creative, pricing and stock, then review ownership at the next check-in.
caveats: These are observed common errors from a simulation setting, not quantified failure rates.
Spreading ownership must be balanced against accountability; the source does not prescribe how many owners per task.
cards.source_name: Building High Performance Teams – How-To Tips from Wharton Fellow_Author.docx

cards.title: Build psychological safety so people actually speak up
cards.summary: Psychological safety — people feeling able to share thoughts — improves decisions and collaboration, but most people withhold what they think.
cards.use_when: When store meetings produce silence or polite agreement but the real problems (stockouts, bad creative, weak margins) surface only later.
steps: Assume the default is withholding: the source says most of the time people do not speak their minds, and cites research that well over half the time people are not sharing what they are thinking and feeling.
Treat more information as better: if people share more, decisions and collaboration improve, so create an environment where they feel safe to speak.
Build safety through concrete behaviours identified in the source: building trust, having good one-on-one conversations, listening, and showing empathy and that you care.

Prioritise it: if focusing on one thing, the source says it would be creating an environment of psychological safety; it calls psychological safety an apparently soft factor that plays a big role in delivering results ('the soft stuff is the hard stuff').
Ecommerce application: in post-mortems on failed launches or promotions, explicitly ask what people were worried about but didn't raise, and protect the person who names the uncomfortable problem.
caveats: Psychological safety is presented as a strong opinion by the author, with general research cited but no specific study figures beyond 'well over half'.
It takes sustained one-on-one effort; it is not achieved by declaring a meeting 'safe'.
cards.source_name: Building High Performance Teams – How-To Tips from Wharton Fellow_Author.docx

cards.title: Know when to go fast and when to go slow
cards.summary: Match speed to task type: skip heavy team process when speed is essential, and slow down for formation and multi-perspective decisions.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much process to apply to a same-day flash sale versus a long-term category or assortment decision.
steps: Borrow the fast/slow distinction: Mario references Kahneman's Thinking Fast and Slow and applies it to teams — 'when you need to go fast maybe don't pay so much attention to team process.'
Go slow when team process is genuinely important: for example when you need to pull in multiple perspectives, that is when to be deliberate about how the team forms and how it has its conversations.

Set the right expectation for check-ins: there is no fixed ratio of check-in to working time; some teams have a large appetite and need for process and will check in more, while 'get it done' teams will check in less. What matters is that check-ins happen, with judgement on how much time to spend.
Distinguish task type when choosing: pair this with the source's split between individual-suitable work (expert, creative, time-short) and team-suitable work (multi-perspective problems).
Ecommerce application: let one person push a time-critical price change; convene the cross-functional team to deliberate on which categories to invest in or how to restructure the subscription offer.
caveats: 'It depends' is the source's own answer on check-in frequency — avoid turning this into a fixed cadence rule.
The fast/slow framing is an analogy to Kahneman's work, not a validated ecommerce decision rule.
cards.source_name: Building High Performance Teams – How-To Tips from Wharton Fellow_Author.docx

cards.title: Build landed unit cost and contribution per ecommerce order
cards.summary: Calculate product and delivery costs separately from advertising and overhead so pricing decisions use a consistent contribution measure.
cards.use_when: Pricing a product, deciding whether a SKU is viable, or setting up daily profit reporting in Shopify/Triple Whale.
steps: Start with net sales excluding pass-through taxes and recorded discounts/refunds.
Allocate inbound freight to units using a documented driver. A $11,000 container carrying 1,000 identical units adds $11 per unit, not $1.
Include manufacturing, applicable non-recoverable duties, inbound freight, pick/pack, outbound delivery, storage allocation and payment fees without double-counting.
Subtract advertising acquisition cost to calculate post-ad contribution; it is not net profit until remaining overhead and other expenses are considered.
Record landed product costs in the store/reporting system and reconcile fulfillment and advertising separately; verify the current integration.
Test the resulting contribution at plausible prices and acquisition costs before ordering; no single landed-cost-to-retail ratio guarantees viability.
caveats: Use current lane- and product-specific duty inputs from the responsible specialist, not blanket country assumptions.
This is a management contribution model; keep accounting classifications documented.
cards.source_name: Complete E-commerce Operations Guide.docx

cards.title: Write a tech pack to control supplier quality and prove non-conformance
cards.summary: A tech pack documents drawings, fabric GSM, measurements, hardware, graphics and labels so manufacturing errors can be proven and disputed.
cards.use_when: Developing or re-sourcing any physical product, especially apparel, before placing a large purchase order.
steps: Include: (1) complete drawing with print placement, shape and colours; (2) fabric details — GSM/thickness, softness, colour references (strike-offs), and treatment specs like acid wash; (3) precise measurements for grading across S/M/L/XL; (4) graphics; (5) hardware (zips, pockets, closures); (6) labels and swing tags with company name and correct positioning — wrong or missing labels can trigger regional fines; and (7) packaging specs.

Keep physical reference samples of fabrics and strike-offs. When quality complaints arrive, cut a standard-size square of fabric and weigh it against the spec GSM to prove the supplier used thinner, wrong fabric — this is how Oodie resolved 'too thin' complaints and got replacements.
Use the tech pack to brief a second supplier for competitive quotes and to switch factories without redeveloping the product.
If needed, commission a tech-pack creator using a defined deliverable and current quote; the source's under-$200 price is anecdotal.
Retain the agreed tech pack, purchase order and supplier messages for quality disputes; platform protection is subject to current terms and does not guarantee a refund.
Any product has a tech pack; it just becomes more complex for injection-moulded or hardware-heavy goods.
caveats: The source's quality-improvement estimate is not a guarantee.
Document ownership, usage and exclusivity terms separately; neither the supplier nor the buyer automatically owns all IP merely because of this workflow.
cards.source_name: Complete E-commerce Operations Guide.docx

cards.title: Negotiate MOQ, price and lead time as one trade-off set
cards.summary: Treat supplier MOQ, unit price and manufacturing lead time as the three levers to balance against cash flow and retail price.
cards.use_when: Selecting a supplier or placing a first or repeat purchase order.
steps: Obtain the supplier's actual minimum order quantity, unit price and manufacturing lead time; small custom runs may be possible at different economics.

Choose deliberately between higher price/lower MOQ (fits a small budget) and higher price/lower lead time (fits brands that want faster cash-flow turns). The source notes Oodie sometimes paid more for lower lead time.
Run the landed cost against your intended retail before committing. If landed cost forces a retail price that kills demand, do not launch that variant.

Write refund/tolerance terms into the supplier relationship before transferring large sums: what happens if product arrives different, tolerance for wrong quantities, and how you verify claimed quantities.
Resolve important specifications, ownership and remedies in agreed terms before committing funds; relationship-building does not establish these rights.
Compare multiple factories and consider de-speccing the product to hit a viable cost — the source estimates ~20% price improvement is achievable through comparison and negotiation.
caveats: MOQs, contract terms and savings depend on supplier and product; the source's 20% saving is an example, not a benchmark.
cards.source_name: Complete E-commerce Operations Guide.docx

cards.title: Order against the outputs: operations as an input→process→output system
cards.summary: Model operations as inputs → processes → outputs, and judge every change by whether it improves the customer-facing output while cutting inputs and process load.
cards.use_when: Deciding which operational initiative to fund or fix (warehouse change, automation, forecasting hire) and how to justify it against marketing spend.
steps: Define the output as the customer experience, not an internal metric. A process improvement that doesn't change what the customer receives is not the goal.
Reduce inputs (cost) and process load (labour/steps) through automation and negotiation to get more output for less — this is the lens for every freight, 3PL and supplier decision.

Use the two-brand cost comparison to justify the work: if brand A lands product at $21 and brand B at $28 due to worse freight, courier, product and warehousing terms, brand A has ~$7 more per unit to spend on marketing — improving CAC headroom and profit.
Test this by comparing parallel supplier/3PL/freight quotes on freight (e.g. $5 vs $6), product ($10 vs $12), courier ($5 vs $8), storage ($1 vs $2).
Treat operations as weeding a garden: without consistent cadence, the sales/marketing 'plants' stop producing as much.
Assign ownership to a COO-type role once you can afford it; below roughly $1M revenue, the founder often holds all these roles.
caveats: The $21/$28 and 20% figures are illustrative example numbers from the source, not a standard.
Needs dedicated ops attention to realise — the source attributes missed growth to lacking an ops role during a demand spike.
cards.source_name: Complete E-commerce Operations Guide.docx

cards.title: Build a critical path to hit launch and seasonal deadlines
cards.summary: A critical path sequences every product-development step with durations and dates so slips are visible and you avoid missing peak trading windows.
cards.use_when: Planning any product launch or seasonal buying cycle where missing a ship date means stranded inventory (e.g. Christmas).
steps: List every step: strike-offs/prints, first sample, revised sample, production sample, QC, bulk production, freight, and inbound to warehouse.
Sequence them in order and assign a duration to each (e.g. DHL sample from China ~5 days).

Set dates against each step from the target launch/ship date and use a project tool (Monday.com, Asana, Notion, Excel) with reminders for overdue tasks; on slip, push downstream dates or identify slack.
Assign an owner to each step and monitor daily. Don't let suppliers edit the critical path themselves — they can manipulate dates and you lose visibility.

Book a QC agent for the first, and ideally second/third, production run: they visit the factory, weigh and measure product against the tech pack and check Pantone colour. Alibaba has an inbuilt QC function; SGS also does compliance.
Work backwards from the Christmas shipping cut-off — failing to receive samples on time cascades to missing peak trade and leaves you holding stock through January/February.
caveats: Tooling changes; the specific apps named may differ in current interface.
QC via Alibaba or SGS incurs cost and lead time of its own.
cards.source_name: Complete E-commerce Operations Guide.docx

cards.title: Forecast demand on an in-stock window, not a raw calendar period
cards.summary: Base forecasts on periods you were actually in stock and on comparable prior-year/month velocity, then apply a growth rate.
cards.use_when: Replenishment planning for any SKU before placing a purchase order.
steps: Never forecast from a period containing stockouts. If you were out of stock 15 days of a 30-day month, use the 15 in-stock days and extrapolate — the source notes forecast misses of 50% common when this is ignored.
If under ~1 year of history or growing fast, use month-on-month: e.g. 100→120→145→175 suggests ~20% growth and a linear-to-slightly-exponential projection for the next month.

Where seasonality dominates (most ecommerce due to Black Friday and holiday gifting), build a month-by-month curve: e.g. Jul 200, Aug 210, Sep 205, Oct 2,000, Nov 4,000, then a sharp drop after the Christmas shipping cut-off.
Find product-driven seasonality via Google Trends (e.g. 'beach tent' spikes in summer) and account for northern vs southern hemisphere opposites.
Apply a growth-rate assumption (e.g. 20–40% monthly) in your tool or Excel, then output two answers: sell-out date and replenishment quantity.
Review on a weekly, fortnightly or monthly cadence; picking the wrong comparison window is the top forecasting error.
caveats: Growth-rate figures are source examples, not targets.
Too much inventory ties up all profit and cash (existential risk); too little yields zero revenue against fixed costs.
cards.source_name: Complete E-commerce Operations Guide.docx

cards.title: Set lead time, days-of-stock and safety stock inputs in the forecast tool
cards.summary: Feed supplier lead time, target days of stock and a small safety-stock buffer into the planner so sell-out and reorder-point outputs are realistic.
cards.use_when: Configuring replenishment thresholds and deciding how much working capital to commit to inventory.
steps: Enter supplier manufacturing lead time (e.g. 100 days) — longer lead times push the tool to trigger orders earlier.
Set target days of stock based on volatility and available capital: typical ranges are 4, 8 or 12 weeks.

Add 5–10 days safety stock as a buffer only after padding lead time with your average (rather than best-case) figure — the source says safety stock shouldn't really be needed if lead time is properly padded.
Use the tool output to get sell-out date and replenishment amount, then raise the purchase order.

Simple calculators (e.g. Inventory Planner, which the source recommends and uses; verify current features) or a custom Excel sheet both work — the goal is visibility on prior results to make future assumptions.
Consider hiring an ops manager (not necessarily a dedicated demand planner) to run this weekly once you're profitable and paying yourself.
caveats: Days-of-stock values are source heuristics that depend on industry, business age, volatility and cash.
Demand-planning tools exist (NetSuite, Walmart-grade systems); the source still ends up back at Excel for flexibility.
cards.source_name: Complete E-commerce Operations Guide.docx

cards.title: Use purchase orders as the single cross-functional source of truth
cards.summary: A PO is more than an invoice — it must be visible to finance, ops, marketing and customer service so stock arrival and discontinuations are coordinated.
cards.use_when: Raising, landing or discontinuing any stock order, and coordinating teams around inbound inventory.
steps: Create a formal PO (product, price, quantities, ship-to, terms) rather than just an ad-hoc Alibaba order.
Route it to finance (for invoice payment), ops (for inbound stock timing), and marketing (so they time promotions to arrivals).
Flag discontinuations and near-landing POs to customer service so agents don't refund or promise products you can't supply.
Adopt an ERP once you're past roughly $30–50M revenue — the source says an ERP handles ~90% of these ops functions; below that a spreadsheet/PM tool can suffice.
Keep the PO as the reference in Alibaba Trade Assurance disputes alongside the tech pack.
caveats: The $30–50M ERP threshold is the source's heuristic.
Fragmented POs across Alibaba and internal tools are the common failure mode to avoid.
cards.source_name: Complete E-commerce Operations Guide.docx

cards.title: Protect against 3PL failure with SLAs and multi-warehouse RFPs
cards.summary: Specify picked-on-time, delivered-on-time and cycle-count SLAs, and run a request-for-pricing across multiple warehouses to create competitive bids.
cards.use_when: Selecting or reviewing a 3PL, or negotiating fulfilment rates and service guarantees.
steps: Write a 3PL RFP ('Request for Pricing') that submits your volume forecasts and product dimensions to several warehouses so they bid competitively against each other.
Require in the SLA: picked-on-time guarantees, delivered-on-time tracking, and mandated bi-annual cycle counts.
Compare rates across providers for courier, pick-pack and storage, and factor these into unit economics.

Treat the 3PL as an existential dependency: the source describes a provider failing to ship during a forecast $45–50M October/November peak, causing promotions to be switched off, wrong products shipped and an estimated $20M+ in lost revenue.
Build trust and references — the source maintains a vetted list of ~10 3PLs and recommends introduction, noting the relationship is hard to get right.
Keep a contingency path (alternate 3PL, ability to switch) because a contracted underperformer is hard to fix mid-peak.
caveats: The $20M loss and $45–50M peak are the source's own case figures, not a benchmark.
The source discloses affiliate/relationship interests in its 3PL list.
cards.source_name: Complete E-commerce Operations Guide.docx

cards.title: Keep import duties and collected sales taxes separate in the cost model
cards.summary: Use verified import-cost inputs and net-revenue reporting rather than treating all tax amounts as the same expense.
cards.use_when: Building landed cost for cross-border sourcing or setting up tax handling in the store backend.
steps: Obtain the applicable product classification, origin, destination and current duty/tax treatment from the responsible customs or tax specialist.
Add confirmed non-recoverable import costs to the model; do not infer zero duty from a country pair or trade agreement alone.
Separate taxes collected for remittance from net revenue, and identify recoverable versus non-recoverable amounts.
Configure store collection and reporting against the confirmed requirements; a generic tax checkbox is not a complete setup.
Reconcile the modeled amounts with actual invoices and settlements.
caveats: The source's country-level examples are not verified current rates or permissions.
cards.source_name: Complete E-commerce Operations Guide.docx

cards.title: Choose supplier co-development vs independent product design
cards.summary: Compare supplier co-development with independently commissioned design on cost, control and documented rights.
cards.use_when: Committing to a product development route for a new or differentiated product.
steps: For supplier co-development, clarify existing designs, customization, reuse rights and what is included in the quote.
For independent design, commission clear deliverables and ownership/usage terms, then seek comparable manufacturing quotes using the tech pack.
Document tooling, design rights, confidentiality and exclusivity separately rather than assuming one development route guarantees ownership or defensibility.
Compare total development cost, lead time, manufacturability and customer demand before choosing.
caveats: Rights depend on agreements and applicable law; exclusivity and enforceability are not guaranteed by a tech pack.
cards.source_name: Complete E-commerce Operations Guide.docx

cards.title: Run forecasting continuously to avoid the two existential inventory failures
cards.summary: Selling out or over-ordering are both business-ending risks; forecast so cash isn't trapped in inventory while peak is covered.
cards.use_when: Deciding SKU expansion and seasonal buy quantities under cash constraints.
steps: Recognise both failure modes: under-ordering yields $0 revenue against fixed costs; over-ordering ties up all profits in inventory so you can't acquire customers or pay taxes.
Expand SKUs cautiously — adding colour/size variants multiplies the forecast risk and capital requirement.

Note the retail baseline (big-box retailers work to ~5% forecast variance); fast-growing ecommerce misses by far more — the source cites 50% misses. Build for that uncertainty with days of stock and buffer rather than pretending to precision.
For very new products, forecast from comparable existing products and recent marketing performance as your best guest.

The source attributes much of Oodie's miss during the COVID-driven ecommerce surge — a forecast $45–50M peak period — to having no ops/planning role, estimating the business could have been 30–40% larger with one.
Set a review cadence (weekly/fortnightly/monthly) and assign an owner.
caveats: The 30–40% opportunity and 50% miss are the source's own estimates.
Retailer 5% variance is the industry baseline cited, not achievable for most ecommerce.
cards.source_name: Complete E-commerce Operations Guide.docx

cards.title: Purchase order visibility across departments
cards.summary: A PO is a cross-functional document; keep it in a shared internal system so finance, ops, marketing and customer service act on the same truth.
cards.use_when: Setting up or auditing how purchase orders are recorded and shared before a replenishment order is placed or while stock is in transit.
steps: Recognise that a PO affects finance (paying supplier invoices and deposits), operations (stock arrival timing), marketing (when to push a product) and customer service (refund/discontinuation decisions on inbound stock).
Keep the authoritative PO in your accounting software (e.g. Xero, MYOB) so it matches supplier deposits and final payments.
Create a second shared sheet (Google Drive/Sheets or Airtable) that the whole team can view, containing SKU-level product list, quantities and PO number.
Add freight details as they arrive: estimated departure date, ETA, vessel number, bill of lading; for air freight a tracking number plus estimated dates.
Update ETAs whenever the vessel is pushed back and notify the affected teams via Slack or comments so no one acts on stale assumptions.
Do not let suppliers edit the internal sheet; route supplier changes through one channel (e.g. Alibaba) which the team can access.
Before discontinuing a product or mass-refunding, check the sheet for a PO about to land to avoid paying for stock you cannot sell.
caveats: This manual approach is a stopgap; a source-cited view is that brands above roughly $30–50M revenue usually need an ERP (~$200k to $500k+ to implement, e.g. NetSuite cited as expensive, Fulfil cited via Ridge).
cards.source_name: Complete E-commerce Operations Guide.docx

cards.title: Auditing 3PL invoices against actual order volume
cards.summary: Reconstruct per-order 3PL costs from your own sales data monthly rather than accepting the invoice at face value.
cards.use_when: Monthly reconciliation of a 3PL bill, or comparing 3PL quotes when switching providers.
steps: Break 3PL pricing into three components: pick-and-pack (per-item fulfilment cost), inbound (unloading container/air freight into the warehouse), and outbound (carrier shipping cost).
Decide per business whether inbound is material enough to include in unit economics; source notes it is sometimes small enough to ignore.

Record outbound separately because each 3PL holds its own carrier account (e.g. UPS, Australia Post, Royal Mail) and rates vary hugely — a high-volume 3PL may pass on excellent rates, a brand-new one may not.
Build a spreadsheet estimating each cost category from your Shopify sales for the period and compare against the invoice.
Watch for blended pricing that hides where costs sit; source reports roughly 30–40% of clients were overcharged in some cost areas by accepting courier or 3PL figures without checking.
Track storage separately — usually immaterial unless products are large, but audit it anyway.
caveats: The 30–40% overcharge figure is one operator's client sample, not a benchmark.
Cheapest 3PL is not automatically best; source argues for a mutually profitable relationship, not squeezing the provider on every order.
cards.source_name: Complete E-commerce Operations Guide.docx

cards.title: Running an RFP to select a 3PL
cards.summary: Use a structured request-for-pricing with forecasts and product dimensions to make 3PLs compete, then inspect facilities before signing.
cards.use_when: Choosing or replacing a third-party logistics provider.
steps: Assemble a master document with product dimensions, previous results, and — most importantly — forecasts; a growing business should present growth to get providers competing for the account.
Send the same document to multiple 3PLs so you can compare quotes on identical assumptions.
Visit the facility or at least see interior footage; refusal to show facilities is a red flag (source cites a prospective 3PL using stolen supermarket trolleys to move product).
Look for a barcode-scanning operation on both inbound and outbound — without scanning, missing stock becomes unresolvable finger-pointing.
Assess whether you are a valuable customer: being the smallest or largest account on their book affects the service you get, and sales-team behaviour is an indicator.
Confirm barcodes, cycle-count frequency and pick-time guarantees are written into the service level agreement.
Give forecasts you realistically intend to hit — wild forecasts cause over-staffing and erode the relationship.
caveats: Source view is that the cheapest option is not always best and a zero-sum relationship with the 3PL tends to backfire.
cards.source_name: Complete E-commerce Operations Guide.docx

cards.title: Writing an SLA with pick-time penalties for peak periods
cards.summary: Make pick and ship commitments explicit and attach consequences so peak-season failures do not become your brand's negative reviews.
cards.use_when: Negotiating or renewing a 3PL contract, especially before Black Friday or Christmas.
steps: Require an SLA stating promised pick time (e.g. within 24–48h) and ship time, with explicit consequences if missed — source suggests a pick discount or a free pick.
Recognise peak risk: if a 3PL under-forecasts its own staff, your pick time can blow out to 7 days and carrier backlogs compound the delay.
Include cycle counts in the SLA — source recommends counting fast-selling SKUs regularly and doing at least two full cycle counts per year.
Send an advance shipping notice and comply with agreed booking requirements before inbound deliveries to reduce avoidable receiving delays and charges; an ASN alone does not rule out fees.
Track delivered-on-time from your own customer-service data; if it drops below about 95%, investigate whether the cause is pick time or carrier lag before asking for discounts or refunds.
Expect delivered-on-time to be your internal metric rather than something 3PLs will guarantee in the SLA.
caveats: The 95% delivered-on-time threshold is a source-stated internal trigger for investigation, not a contractual standard.
SLA terms and pick-time windows vary by provider and market; verify the current contract language.
cards.source_name: Complete E-commerce Operations Guide.docx

cards.title: Designing the customer service tier split
cards.summary: Route simple tickets to international agents and nuanced tickets to local agents close to internal teams — and be sceptical of the assumption that offshore is always cheaper.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to staff and structure the customer support function, particularly when scaling past a few agents.
steps: Reject the default assumption that international (e.g. Philippines, Fiji) agents are automatically cheaper — source argues efficiency can be roughly double locally, so the real cost depends on training and ticket routing.
Split tickets by complexity: send easier, repeatable tickets to the international team and nuanced tickets to local agents who sit closer to internal sources of truth.
For larger businesses, use a blended model; for smaller businesses either route can work.
Account for public holidays: international teams may stay available during your selling market's holidays, though they have their own holidays and time-zone gaps.
Build training programmes and clear macros so agents resolve tickets without needing to escalate repeatedly.
Use international capacity for peak-season ramping — it is easier to add and train offshore agents than to scale a local team quickly, but be transparent about the peak expectation.
caveats: Source describes this as its preferred structure from experience, not a universal rule; test routing against your own ticket mix and quality data.
cards.source_name: Complete E-commerce Operations Guide.docx

cards.title: Cost per ticket and resolution-time diagnostics
cards.summary: Track cost per service, resolution time and touch points to find whether support problems come from systems, information access, or staffing.
cards.use_when: Reviewing customer service performance and support cost during monthly operations or before peak planning.
steps: Compute cost per service as total support expense (software plus agent cost) divided by number of tickets, and aim to keep it roughly stable across the year even as sales and ticket volume swing.
Fix the higher resolution time against causes: not enough visible internal information, slow agents or poor systems, or weak macros that force manual answers.
