Before approving big growth, confirm the company's existing operational problems wouldn't be exacerbated — in the source, politics would be made worse by absorbing a new team.

If the person is underutilized, change their assignment instead: assign ownership of the function where their existing skill is strongest and which the business actually needs (in the source, an ex-sales leader takes over sales).
Let peers make the case for the reassignment rather than the leader selling it; the person is more likely to convert when the argument comes from colleagues.
Require the reassigned person to fix the specific dysfunction they complained about — in the source, silence about priorities in their own team.
caveats: The acquisition figures in the source are fictional case detail, not a template for evaluating real deals.
A big acquisition can still be right; the source's point is the sequence — resolve internal capability and politics first, then grow.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Run a Five Dysfunctions Team Diagnostic
cards.summary: Score your leadership team against the five dysfunctions with a 15-statement questionnaire to find which layer is broken before you fix anything else.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why your ecommerce leadership team (merchandising, growth, ops, supply chain) makes slow or reversed decisions before choosing an intervention like restructuring or new hires.
steps: Have every member of the leadership team rate 15 statements on a 3/2/1 scale (3 = usually, 2 = sometimes, 1 = rarely), answering honestly and without over-thinking.

Group the scores: Trust = statements 4, 6, 12; Fear of Conflict = 1, 7, 10; Lack of Commitment = 3, 8, 13; Avoidance of Accountability = 2, 11, 14; Inattention to Results = 5, 9, 15. Total each group.

Interpret per the source's heuristics: 8–9 suggests the dysfunction is not a problem, 6–7 suggests it could be a problem, 3–5 suggests it needs to be addressed. Treat these as rough indicators, not precise measurements.
Compare members' scores rather than only averaging them — large discrepancies are themselves diagnostic of a trust problem.
Discuss the results as a team and agree on one behavioral change to test over the next quarter.
Re-run the diagnostic periodically, because the source stresses that even strong teams drift back toward dysfunction without constant work.
caveats: The scoring bands are the author's practical heuristics, not validated psychometrics; do not treat a 6 as a verdict.
Self-report scores can be gamed or unconsciously flattering; the conversation about discrepancies matters more than the number.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Model the Five Dysfunctions as a Chain, Not Five Projects
cards.summary: Trust, conflict, commitment, accountability and results are a sequential stack — breaking one link undermines the whole team, so diagnose in order rather than fixing symptoms independently.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to invest management effort when your ecommerce team shows several problems at once (missed launch dates, silent meetings, finger-pointing between merchandising and fulfillment).
steps: Map the chain: absence of trust → fear of conflict → lack of commitment → avoidance of accountability → inattention to results.

Check the bottom link first. If leaders hide mistakes and weaknesses, unfiltered debate about assortment, pricing or promo plans will not happen, and any 'commitment' is feigned agreement in the meeting.
Trace a current failure backward through the chain — e.g. a launch that slipped because nobody challenged an unrealistic date, because nobody trusted the person who owned it.
Address the lowest broken link first instead of launching an accountability program on top of a trust problem.
State the positive behaviors you want instead: trust one another, debate ideas unfiltered, commit to decisions, hold peers accountable, focus on collective results.
caveats: The model is the source's framework, not an empirically proven causal chain; treat ordering as a practical heuristic.
The source notes the behaviors are simple in theory but demand discipline and persistence that few teams sustain, so expect months, not weeks.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Behavioral Signs That Distinguish Trusting From Distrusting Teams
cards.summary: Compare your team's observable behaviors against the source's lists of trust symptoms to decide whether the problem is a trust deficit or something else.
cards.use_when: Assessing your ecommerce leadership or cross-functional team (e.g. growth, merchandising and supply chain) after a pattern of stalled decisions or unusual turnover.
steps: Look for the distrust markers the source lists: concealing weaknesses and mistakes, hesitating to ask for or offer help, jumping to conclusions about others' intentions, failing to tap colleagues' expertise, spending time managing how one appears, holding grudges, dreading meetings.

Look for the trust markers: admitting mistakes, asking for help, accepting questions about one's own area, giving the benefit of the doubt before reaching a negative conclusion, offering feedback and assistance, offering and accepting apologies without hesitation, looking forward to working together.
Score which side the majority of observed behavior falls on for your team, and note specific incidents rather than impressions.
If distrust dominates, avoid jumping straight to accountability or results initiatives; build trust first.
caveats: The source's lists are practitioner observations, not a validated instrument.
Distrust is expensive in ways that are hard to measure directly (the source argues it consumes time and energy better spent on the work), so resist demands for a hard ROI before acting.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Define Trust as Vulnerability, Not Reliability
cards.summary: Team trust means peers are confident each other's intentions are good enough to be open about weaknesses and mistakes — predictability alone is not enough.
cards.use_when: Evaluating why your ecommerce team avoids surfacing bad news about a failing SKU, a vendor delay, or a campaign that underperformed, even when individuals reliably deliver their assigned work.
steps: Separate the two meanings of trust: (a) predictability based on past delivery, and (b) vulnerability-based trust — the confidence that you can expose weaknesses, skill gaps, mistakes and requests for help without it being used against you.
Recognize that high performers often learned to be competitive and protective of their reputations, so turning that instinct off for the team is a real cost they must choose to pay.
Ask directly in a team setting whether people can admit an error without damage; the answer is the diagnostic.
Model it: leaders and senior operators should be the first to name their own mistake or gap.
Note that distrust shows up as time spent being strategically political and managing how one appears, not just as interpersonal friction.
caveats: The source stresses this is difficult and slow — vulnerability-based trust requires shared experience over time, repeated follow-through and understanding of individuals' unique attributes.
Distinguish carefully: reliability is still needed; the point is that it is insufficient for a cohesive team.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Personal Histories Exercise for Faster Team Trust
cards.summary: A sub-hour, low-risk exercise where team members share non-sensitive biographical facts to build empathy and prevent unfair behavioral attributions.
cards.use_when: Kicking off a newly formed ecommerce leadership team, integrating a new head of merchandising or supply chain, or restarting a burned-out cross-functional group after a bad quarter.
steps: In a meeting, go around the table and have each person answer a short list of low-sensitivity questions: number of siblings, hometown, unique childhood challenges, favorite hobbies, first job, worst job.
Keep it moderately personal but not overly sensitive; the goal is relatability, not disclosure of private struggles.
Run it as a discussion, not a form; the value comes from hearing each other, not from the answers themselves.
Expect this to take at least 30 minutes.
Follow up by scheduling regular working sessions where the resulting familiarity can be reinforced, because the source warns trust erodes without continued interaction.
Apply it specifically to dependencies your team has — e.g. the person who forecasts demand learning how the marketing lead came to their role can soften routine interdepartmental friction.
caveats: This is a first step, not a trust program; the source says vulnerability-based trust cannot be achieved overnight and requires shared experiences over time.
The author states these exercises must be paired with regular follow-up in daily work, or momentum is lost.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Team Effectiveness Exercise: One Contribution, One Needed Improvement
cards.summary: Each member names the single most important contribution a peer makes and the one thing that peer must improve or stop, reported one person at a time starting with the leader.
cards.use_when: When a team is functional enough to handle direct feedback but still has unspoken performance or behavior problems — for example, a merchandising lead whose dismissiveness is quietly degrading planning meetings.
steps: Frame it: every member will identify, for each peer, the single most important contribution they make to the team and the one area they must improve or eliminate for the team's good.
Start with the team leader so the leader is subject to the same scrutiny first, setting the norm.
Take one person at a time, with all responses reported while that person listens and does not defend.
Keep each pass tight — the source reports that roughly an hour is enough for a team, yielding both constructive and positive information.
Follow up on each identified development area in subsequent one-on-ones so it does not become a one-off exercise.
Book at least 60 minutes minimum.
caveats: The source acknowledges this is more rigorous and riskier than the personal histories exercise; it may feel intrusive and dangerous at first.
It assumes some baseline trust; the source notes even relatively dysfunctional teams can often make it work with surprisingly little tension, but results vary.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Use Personality Profiles to Reduce Team Friction
cards.summary: Behavioral preference profiles such as the MBTI give nonjudgmental descriptions of how people think, speak and act, making peer friction easier to interpret and manage.
cards.use_when: When recurring clashes between, say, a data-driven growth lead and an intuitive brand/creative lead are being read as personal conflict instead of stylistic difference.
steps: Choose a profiling tool that is nonjudgmental (no type is better than another), research-based rather than astrology-like, and in which participants actively identify their own type rather than receiving a verdict from a printout or score.
The author's stated preference is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator; a number of alternatives are also used by different audiences.
Have the whole team complete it and share results openly, then discuss how each type tends to communicate, decide and handle disagreement.
Use the shared vocabulary in live disagreements to reframe stylistic clashes before they become personal.
Revisit profiles when new members join, as the source shows for a new marketing VP who was walked through the model and then had his Myers-Briggs results reviewed with him.
Budget at least four hours of minimum time for these tools.
caveats: The source notes many such tools require a licensed consultant, which it says matters to avoid misuse of their implications.
Profiles explain style, not competence; the author positions them as trust-building and conflict-handling aids, not performance verdicts.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Keep 360-Degree Feedback Out of Compensation
cards.summary: A 360-degree program works only if it is a pure development tool, divorced entirely from pay and formal performance evaluation.
cards.use_when: Rolling out peer feedback across ecommerce functions (merchandising, marketing, ops) and deciding whether it will feed into reviews or salary decisions.
steps: Separate the program from any compensation or formal evaluation link; the source says even a slight connection invites dangerous political undertones.
Position it explicitly as developmental: it lets people identify strengths and weaknesses with no repercussions.
Brief participants before collecting input so they understand the firewall from pay and ratings.
Use outputs to design individual development plans and follow-up conversations, not scores in a review file.
Repeat annually or on a cycle rather than continuously, so it remains a deliberate exercise rather than a constant channel for criticism.
caveats: The author flags this as riskier than other trust tools because peers make specific judgments and deliver constructive criticism directly.
Without the firewall from compensation, the source expects the program to become political and lose its developmental value.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Vulnerability Must Start With the Leader — And Cannot Be Staged
cards.summary: The leader must go first in exposing weakness, create an environment that does not punish it, and never fake it for effect.
cards.use_when: When you, as founder or ecommerce lead, want the team to surface bad news about a channel, a vendor, or an assortment bet earlier — but the team still filters what they tell you.
steps: Open with a genuine disclosure of a mistake or limitation of your own, before asking anyone else to be open.

Watch for subtle punishment of vulnerability — interrupting, sarcasm, or sidelining someone after they admit a failure — and stop it immediately, because the source argues even well-intentioned teams discourage trust this way.
Do not perform vulnerability as a technique; the source states one of the best ways to lose a team's trust is to feign vulnerability to manipulate others' emotions.
Choose disclosures that are real and relevant to work rather than manufactured personal drama.
Reinforce vulnerability by continuing to ask for input on your own decisions and by visibly acting on what you learn.
caveats: The source is a business fable-style treatment; the leader-first rule is a stated principle, not an experimentally verified threshold.
Exposure carries real risk in the short term — the author frames it as risking face so subordinates will take the same risk.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Distinguish Productive Ideological Conflict From Personal Attack
cards.summary: Healthy conflict is confined to concepts and ideas and may look passionate or emotional from outside, while personality-focused attacks are destructive and should be ruled out.
cards.use_when: Setting norms for how your ecommerce team debates pricing changes, discount depth, channel budget or a new bundle — before the next planning meeting.
steps: Agree the rule: debate is about concepts and ideas; personality-focused and mean-spirited attacks are out.

Expect passion, emotion and frustration in legitimate debate, and do not intervene merely because it looks heated; the source says an outside observer could mistake productive conflict for unproductive discord.
Judge by outcome: good conflict ends quickly with the best available answer and no residual resentment, and leaves people ready for the next issue.
Treat avoidance as the real risk — the source argues suppressed disagreement pushes people into back-channel personal attacks, which are nastier than open argument over issues.
Stop the common practice of taking contested topics 'off-line' as a euphemism for deferring them indefinitely.
caveats: The line between passionate debate and personal attack is often only clear in retrospect; the purpose test (best solution in the shortest time) is the source's proposed standard.
The source notes conflict is taboo at work and gets harder to permit the higher up the management chain you go, so norms must be actively maintained.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Assign a Miner of Conflict to Surface Buried Disagreements
cards.summary: Designate someone in each meeting to extract buried disagreements and force the team to work through them, staying in the discussion until resolution.
cards.use_when: Running an ecommerce planning or S&OP-style meeting where unresolved issues (inventory commitments, promo calendar, channel budget) keep resurfacing instead of being settled.
steps: Recognize the symptom: issues that reappear meeting after meeting without resolution usually mean the real disagreement was never surfaced.
Assign the miner role for a given meeting or discussion — a person whose job is to call out sensitive issues and push the team to work through them.
Require the miner to stay objective and to commit to staying with the conflict until it resolves, rather than letting the group move on.
Rotate or specify who holds the role so it does not become one person's permanent burden.
Close the loop by recording the resolution and the specific calls to action.
caveats: This takes courage and confidence from the person holding the role; in low-trust teams it can be read as aggression.
The source presents it as a technique for teams that tend to avoid conflict, not a universal meeting requirement.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Use 'Real-Time Permission' to Keep Difficult Debates Going
cards.summary: When people start retreating from heated debate, interrupt to tell them the discomfort is appropriate and to keep going — then confirm afterward that the conflict was healthy.
cards.use_when: Facilitating a contentious ecommerce decision — cutting a channel, changing a returns policy, repricing a hero SKU — and watching participants soften their position to reduce tension.
steps: Watch for body language and speech that signal discomfort: hedging, apologizing for a point, or dropping a position mid-argument.
Interrupt briefly to explicitly grant permission: state that this level of disagreement is necessary and expected, and that they should continue.
Let the debate continue rather than resolving it yourself; the source notes this drains tension and gives participants confidence to keep going.
After the meeting, remind the group that the conflict they just had was good for the team and not something to avoid.
Note the source's observation that nobody fully gets used to conflict; if it is not a little uncomfortable, it is probably not real.
Keep the leader's protective instinct in check — the source warns leaders often interrupt disagreements prematurely and rob people of the chance to build conflict-management skills.
caveats: The source acknowledges it can sound paternal; it describes it as remarkably effective but not a fixed protocol.
Overprotective intervention is the specific failure mode the author warns against for leaders promoting healthy conflict.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Use the Thomas-Kilmann Instrument for Conflict Style Awareness
cards.summary: The TKI helps team members see their default approach to conflict so they can choose tactics deliberately rather than reflexively.
cards.use_when: When the same ecommerce peers repeatedly collide in the same way (e.g. one always yields on assortment calls, another always competes and forces a winner) and you want to change the pattern.
steps: Have team members complete the Thomas-Kilmann Conflict Mode Instrument.
Review each person's dominant modes and discuss when each mode is appropriate — competing, avoiding, compromising, accommodating, collaborating.
In live debate, name the mode being used and ask whether it is the right choice for this issue.
Use the shared vocabulary instead of attributing recurring friction to personality.
Pair this with other behavioral-preference tools, since the source notes most personality instruments describe how different types handle conflict.
caveats: This addresses conflict style only; on its own it will not fix a trust deficit underneath.
The source treats it as a supporting tool, mentioning it in one paragraph rather than prescribing a full procedure.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Separate Conflict About Issues From Your Team's Job
cards.summary: Leaders arguing about issues in a meeting is the work, not a symptom — resolving it there prevents pushing unsolvable problems down to their teams.
cards.use_when: A leadership meeting over the sales budget, headcount or channel investment turns tense and someone argues the team has regressed.
steps: Reframe the moment: when leaders debate an issue rather than attack each other, that is the healthy conflict you have been trying to build.
Recognize that letting leaders hash out these disagreements gives their teams clear direction instead of forcing subordinates to solve problems they have no authority to solve.
Confirm the disagreement is about the issue — e.g. whether to add sales headcount versus controlling quota inflation — rather than about which person is right.
Land the decision and communicate it down as clear direction, so the debate translates into action rather than lingering ambiguity.
Expect residual discomfort; the source shows participants reporting it still feels like fighting even when it is productive.
caveats: The source's example includes a direct clash between two executives that initially alarmed the rest of the team, illustrating that intensity alone is not a failure signal.
Do not use this framing to excuse personal attacks; the distinction between issue conflict and interpersonal conflict still applies.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Prepare the Team for the Dip After Early Progress
cards.summary: Warn the team explicitly that progress will be invisible in results for a while, and that groups often slide backward, so early behavioral wins are not mistaken for a finished job.
cards.use_when: Right after an offsite or process reset, before the next quarter's numbers land — so the ecommerce team does not revert when channel performance and morale still look flat.
steps: Tell the team directly that there will be days they will wonder if anything changed, and that behavioral change takes longer than a few weeks to show up in the bottom line.
State plainly that teams further along have slid backward, so discipline and persistence are the actual risk factors.

Keep the pace up after the initial burst: the source shows the leader continued to push on behavior — calling out smugness in meetings, forcing a peer to confront the team about unresponsiveness, and working through budget fights late into the night.
Track leading behavioral signals rather than only financial results in the interim — for example, whether people stay together during breaks and whether meetings are louder and more animated.
Treat laughter and eagerness to schedule follow-up as informal progress markers, as the source does for a recovering team.
caveats: The source is a fable; the observation that the team laughed more and stayed together is anecdotal, not a measured benchmark.
Optimism should be tempered deliberately — the author has the leader 'let the air out of the balloon' precisely to avoid over-confidence.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Address Individual Behavior Problems Directly, With Specific Evidence
cards.summary: When a leader's behavior is damaging the team, name it plainly and concretely, tolerate the emotional response, and hold the behavioral requirement firm.
cards.use_when: Handling a genuinely damaging team member — a merchandising or marketing lead whose dismissiveness is undermining peers — and deciding whether to attempt a turnaround or an exit.
steps: Go directly to the core issue at the start: state that the person is not a fit for the team and does not appear to want to be there, rather than opening with tangential feedback.

When they ask for the basis, give specific, observed behavior rather than general impressions — the source's example lists eye-rolling, disrespectful remarks toward a peer, and refusal to attend a company priority training.
Expect shock and denial. The source shows the person may genuinely not see it, or may be being coy; either way, repeat the specifics calmly.
Handle the counter-moves: blame-shifting (peers don't respect me), escalation threats (referencing the board or legal action), and claims that the behavior would change elsewhere.
Make the actual requirement clear — either complete and fast behavioral change or departure — and acknowledge honestly that you are not sure they want to do it.
Do not volunteer concessions in the room; the source shows the leader deliberately said she would see what she could do rather than immediately agreeing to a severance and equity request.
If it ends in departure, get a real agreement: severance, vesting and the official record, worked out with HR.
caveats: This is a fable; the dialogue is illustrative and the specific severance and equity terms are not a template.
The source frames the leader's job as building a functioning team, not avoiding board confrontation, which is a strong stance stated by the character.
Candid feedback of the harshest kind (such as telling the person they seem bitter) is the character's choice, not a recommended universal script.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Address destructive behavior even when a store specialist delivers strong results
cards.summary: Tolerating a high producer's destructive behavior makes the manager — not the individual — responsible for the team's performance collapse.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to protect a top-performing ecommerce buyer, media buyer or engineer whose poor collaboration is driving colleagues out.
steps: Watch the pattern the source describes: a top performer produces better work than anyone, peers complain repeatedly, the manager half-heartedly addresses it and then shields the performer because output looks good.
Recognize the second-order effects: other people's load increases, morale deteriorates, and the department's overall output declines even though the star is still producing.
Refuse to resolve the tension by rewarding the behavior — in the source's cautionary story, the manager promoted the difficult performer, and three of seven analysts quit within two weeks.
Attribute the performance problem to your tolerance of the behavior, not to the individual alone.
Set specific collaboration expectations and follow the organization's performance process; assess documented behavior and team impact before any role or employment decision.
caveats: The story is a fable with a dramatic outcome; do not read the reported 50 percent productivity impact or the one-month recovery as measured benchmarks.
The source's lesson is specifically that manager tolerance is the causal factor, which may overstate the individual leader's role in complex team outcomes.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Let Departures Be Mourned, Then Reframe the Decision
cards.summary: Even the removal of a difficult team member triggers mourning and self-doubt among peers; address it openly rather than letting it dampen the work.
cards.use_when: After terminating or losing a senior ecommerce leader, and noticing the leadership team's energy and meeting quality drop in the following days.
steps: Name the elephant explicitly in the next team meeting and ask how people feel about the departure.
Expect the standard concerns: fear of losing another executive, worry about the function, and the question of who is next.

Resist defending the departed person's performance record in order to avoid a fight — the source's leader wanted to argue that the person was never really part of the team but stayed quiet and listened first.

Answer with a personal story of a comparable mistake if you have one; the source's leader told a story about tolerating a destructive top performer and being fired herself, concluding 'they fired the right person.'
Land the message that the departure was done to protect the team: 'I don't plan on losing any of you.'
Expect a symbolic reaction beyond the individual — the source notes employee concern after a departure often reflects what the change signals rather than the loss of that specific person.
caveats: The story's device is a leader sharing a career failure; the specific narrative is illustrative, not a required script.
Mourning a difficult colleague's departure is described as nearly universal by the source, even when the person was the source of the problem.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Sequence the Communication After a Senior Departure
cards.summary: Announce a departure plainly to the team, hold legal detail back, and handle employee and press messaging with a single consistent line.
cards.use_when: Managing the internal and external messaging after a senior ecommerce leader leaves — before employees hear it from someone else or a trade publication calls.
steps: Tell the leadership team first, and state the confidentiality basis in advance because of legal issues related to departed employees.
Give a direct reason without unnecessary detail: the person was unwilling to adjust behavior and it was hurting the team, so you asked them to leave.
Answer the practical questions the team will actually ask: how the person took it, what happens to the function, what employees and press will be told.
For the function, name the interim plan — look for a successor while extending responsibility to strong internal people — and express confidence in that plan.
For employees and press, use one simple line: the person is moving on. The source stresses there is little flexibility about disclosing sensitive information.
Do not let initial reactions drive the message; the source argues that if the team makes visible progress, employees and analysts will settle, and many employees will not be surprised at all.
caveats: The source's example is a story; legal and disclosure obligations vary by jurisdiction and should involve counsel and HR.
The claim that employees 'won't be that surprised' is a character's expectation, not a measured outcome.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Run an Internal vs External Succession Debate, Then Decide
cards.summary: Have the team debate the replacement decision openly, then make the call yourself and state the criteria the hire must demonstrate.
cards.use_when: Filling a senior ecommerce vacancy — head of marketing, merchandising or supply chain — when there is pressure to promote internally from the existing team.
steps: Let the team debate whether to promote one of the departed leader's direct reports or hire externally, and let the disagreement run rather than shutting it down.
Before deciding, explicitly invite final input: ask whether anyone has anything else to add.

Make the call and explain the criterion you used — the source's leader said she wanted someone who could grow the department and help with branding, and saw no internal candidate close to that right now.
State the hiring bar in team terms: candidates must demonstrate trust, engage in conflict, commit to group decisions, hold peers accountable, and focus on team results rather than personal ego.
Involve the team in the search rather than keeping it with the leader — the source has every member interview candidates.
Assign a single owner to organize the search.
caveats: The source's leader overrode a divided team; this is one situational choice, and the text does not establish that external hiring is generally better.
A public statement that no internal candidate is ready can damage morale; the source does not address that risk.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Onboard a New Executive Through the Team, Not a Manual
cards.summary: Have existing team members each teach one dysfunction to the newcomer, then review working style and launch into real debates immediately.
cards.use_when: Integrating a new senior hire — a marketing, supply chain or growth leader — into an established leadership team.
steps: Assign different existing members to explain one dysfunction each, so the whole team participates in the onboarding rather than the leader delivering a presentation.
Cover the team's operating mechanics: each peer's role and responsibilities and the collective goals.
Review the newcomer's personality or behavioral-preference profile alongside the team's, and explain how peers tend to work and disagree.
Move straight into live work: the source has the team launch into passionate debates on the same day, ending them with crystal-clear agreements and no lingering bitterness.
Let the newcomer observe peers holding each other accountable directly, and keep bringing discussions back to results if tension rises.
caveats: The source is a fable; the very quick integration described is illustrative and depends on the team already functioning well.
A new hire may find direct peer confrontation uncomfortable at first; the source shows that discomfort coexisting with enthusiasm to join.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Review leadership span when store coordination becomes unwieldy
cards.summary: Reconsider decision ownership and reporting relationships when an expanding store leadership group slows execution.
cards.use_when: Your ecommerce company has grown past roughly a couple of hundred employees and the leadership meeting has become too large for fluid, substantive discussion.
steps: Identify which ecommerce leadership decisions stall because too many people attend or ownership is unclear.
Consider grouping related functions, such as supply chain and fulfillment under operations, while retaining specialist input on relevant decisions.
Test a smaller decision group without copying the fictional source's exact headcount or reporting structure.
Explain affected responsibilities and escalation paths individually, then publish the revised ownership map.
Review whether decisions and cross-functional handoffs improve before treating additional hierarchy as the answer.
caveats: The 'larger company, smaller top team' rule is the source's stated belief, not a measured threshold; the specific headcount and reporting structure come from the story's example.
Reducing direct reports can feel like a demotion; the source shows that peers will raise this concern, so address it explicitly.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Use TKI to Understand Conflict Styles on the Team
cards.summary: The Thomas-Kilmann Conflict Mode Instrument helps team members see their natural conflict inclinations so they can make more strategic choices about which approach fits each situation.
cards.use_when: Team friction is slowing a merchandising, pricing, or vendor-negotiation decision, and the operator wants to help the team choose an appropriate conflict approach rather than defaulting to their habits.
steps: Have team members identify their default conflict mode (competition, collaboration, compromise, avoidance, accommodation) using the TKI or a similar self-assessment.
Use the shared vocabulary to discuss which mode fits the current issue — e.g., a fast pricing response may need competition or compromise, while a vendor agreement may need collaboration.
Pair the assessment with direct conversation so team members see their own resistance patterns and can deliberately choose a more useful approach for the specific decision at hand.
caveats: The source presents the TKI as one helpful tool among several; it is not a prescriptive rule for every conflict.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Leader Restraint During Team Conflict
cards.summary: Leaders who jump in to protect members from disagreement deprive the team of the chance to develop conflict-management skills; restraint is the harder and more effective choice.
cards.use_when: An operator is tempted to step into a merchandising or marketing disagreement between team members because they fear the conflict is becoming unproductive.
steps: Recognize the urge to protect team members from harm is often a premature interruption of a disagreement that could resolve itself.

Allow resolution to occur naturally even when it looks messy; the source compares overprotection to parents who shield children from sibling quarrels, which strains relationships and leaves people hungry for resolution.
Model appropriate conflict behavior personally — avoiding necessary conflict is the surest way to let the dysfunction thrive.
Accept that losing control of the team during conflict does not mean failing as a leader; it often means the team is building its own capacity.
caveats: The source acknowledges this is difficult; the leader must still intervene if the team truly fails, but that should be a rare occurrence.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Commitment Comes from Clarity and Buy-In, Not Consensus
cards.summary: Great teams make clear, timely decisions and achieve full buy-in even when members disagree, understanding that consensus is not required for support.
cards.use_when: An operator is trying to get the whole team behind a product launch, pricing change, or campaign decision and is tempted to delay until everyone agrees.
steps: Separate the need for buy-in from the desire for consensus: reasonable people do not need to get their way, only to know their opinions were heard and considered.
Ensure everyone's ideas are genuinely aired, then rally around whatever decision the group or leader makes.
When there's an impasse, let the leader make the call rather than forcing false agreement.
Push for closure on clear decisions even without full certainty; the source argues a decision is better than no decision.
Recognize that unresolved commitment gaps at the top multiply into larger alignment problems downstream, especially for teams executing across departments.
caveats: This is the source's philosophy, not a universal rule; some decisions genuinely need more information, and the source still values research and analysis.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Use Cascading Messaging to Align the Team and the Organization
cards.summary: A short end-of-meeting exercise where the team reviews key decisions and agrees what to communicate prevents small executive misalignments from becoming major discrepancies downstream.
cards.use_when: A weekly or quarterly ecommerce team meeting is ending and decisions need to be communicated to store staff, vendors, or cross-functional partners.
steps: At the end of the meeting, spend at least 10 minutes explicitly reviewing the key decisions made.
Agree on what needs to be communicated to employees or other constituencies about each decision.
Identify which decisions should remain confidential and which must be communicated quickly and comprehensively.
Use the exercise to surface misalignment — often team members learn they are not on the same page and clarify outcomes before putting anything into action.
Send a consistent message so employees are not receiving contradictory statements from managers who attended the same meeting.
caveats: The source says the exercise takes a minimum of 10 minutes; skipping it undermines the alignment it is meant to create.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Set and Honor Decision Deadlines
cards.summary: Clear deadlines for decisions — including intermediate milestones — are a primary tool for overcoming commitment dysfunction and preventing costly ambiguity.
cards.use_when: An ecommerce team is stalling on a pricing decision, assortment change, or campaign launch and keeps revisiting the same debate.
steps: Set a clear deadline for when each decision will be made, and honor the date with discipline and rigidity.
Commit to deadlines for intermediate decisions and milestones as well as final ones, so misalignment is identified before costs become too great.
Treat timing as a critical part of clarity: ambiguity about when a decision will be made is the biggest enemy of a commitment-prone team.
Review whether the team is honoring deadlines at the start of each meeting, and address missed dates directly.
caveats: Deadlines work only if they are actually honored; a deadline that slips without consequence reinforces the dysfunction.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Worst-Case Scenario and Contingency Planning to Reduce Fear of Deciding
cards.summary: Briefly clarifying the worst-case outcome of a decision lets a hesitant team see that the costs of being wrong are survivable and smaller than imagined.
cards.use_when: A team is frozen on a high-stakes decision such as entering a new channel, launching a major product, or committing to a large marketing spend.
steps: Before or during the decision, briefly discuss contingency plans for what happens if the decision is wrong.
Even better, clarify the worst-case scenario explicitly so the team can see the cost is survivable and less damaging than assumed.
Use this to reduce the fear that is driving delay and paralysis.
Once the worst case is understood, move to closure and commit to the chosen path.
caveats: This is a fear-reduction tool, not a substitute for analysis; it is for teams that overvalue certainty, not for teams that routinely underanalyze decisions.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Low-Risk Exposure Therapy for Commitment-Phobic Teams
cards.summary: Deliberately making decisions in low-risk situations with substantial discussion but little analysis builds the team's confidence and reveals it overvalues lengthy study.
cards.use_when: An ecommerce team habitually delays decisions until exhaustive analysis is done, and the operator wants to build the muscle of deciding without perfect information.
steps: Choose a genuinely low-risk decision — a small site change, a minor campaign tweak, a low-stakes vendor choice.
Force a decision after substantial discussion but little additional analysis or research.
Afterward, review the quality of the decision and compare it to what the team expected.
Use the result to show that the decision was not much different from what lengthy study would have produced.
Gradually apply the same confidence to higher-stakes decisions.
caveats: The source explicitly says this is not a claim that research and analysis are unnecessary; teams with this dysfunction tend to overvalue them, which is the problem being corrected.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Leader's Role in Building Commitment
cards.summary: The leader must be comfortable being wrong, constantly push for closure, and avoid placing too high a premium on certainty or consensus.
cards.use_when: An operator leads a team that keeps deferring decisions and needs to set the tone that bold decisions with course-correction are acceptable.
steps: Accept the prospect of making a decision that ultimately turns out to be wrong, and communicate that acceptance to the team.
Constantly push the group for closure around issues rather than letting discussions continue indefinitely.
Hold the team to the schedules it has set, including intermediate milestones.
Avoid signaling that certainty or consensus is required before a decision can be made.
caveats: The source frames this as the leader's responsibility more than any other member's, but it does not mean the leader decides everything; the point is to create conditions for commitment.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Peer Accountability Over Bureaucratic Performance Management
cards.summary: The most effective way to maintain high standards is peer pressure — team members calling each other on behavior — which reduces the need for excessive bureaucracy.
cards.use_when: An ecommerce team has performance or behavior problems and the operator is considering adding new policies or formal corrective processes.
steps: Define accountability as the willingness of team members to call peers on performance or behaviors that might hurt the team.
Encourage team members to 'enter the danger' and have difficult conversations rather than avoid them.
Recognize that close teammates sometimes avoid accountability because they fear damaging the relationship — but the source argues this erodes trust and breeds resentment.
Hold one another accountable to demonstrate respect and high expectations, which the source says strengthens relationships.
Rely on peer pressure as the most efficient way to maintain standards, reducing the need for bureaucratic corrective action.
caveats: This is the source's stated opinion that peer pressure is the most effective and efficient means; it is not a universal rule that formal performance management is never needed.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Publication of Goals and Standards Enables Accountability
cards.summary: Publicly clarifying what the team must achieve, who delivers what, and how everyone must behave makes accountability concrete and removes ambiguity.
cards.use_when: An operator wants to make it easier for team members to hold each other accountable on a new initiative or across a cross-functional project.
steps: Clarify publicly what the team needs to achieve, who needs to deliver what, and how everyone must behave in order to succeed.
Keep the agreements in the open so no one can easily ignore them.
Even after the team has initially committed to a plan or behavioral standards, revisit and re-publish them rather than assuming everyone remembers or agrees.
Use the published goals as the reference point for peer-to-peer feedback and progress reviews.
caveats: The enemy of accountability is ambiguity; if goals and standards stay vague or private, peer accountability is much harder.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Simple and Regular Progress Reviews for Accountability
cards.summary: A little structure goes a long way: regular verbal or written communication about how teammates are doing against stated objectives prevents avoidance of accountability.
cards.use_when: An ecommerce team is not giving each other feedback on performance, and the operator wants a lightweight review rhythm that surfaces problems early.
steps: Set an expectation that team members regularly communicate with one another about how they feel teammates are doing against stated objectives and standards.
Choose a format — verbal or written — and keep it simple and consistent.
Do not rely on team members to do this on their own with no clear expectations or structure; the source says that invites avoidance.
Use the reviews to identify potential problems quickly by questioning one another's approaches without hesitation.
caveats: The source emphasizes structure, not heavy process; the goal is regular, simple reviews rather than a new bureaucratic system.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Team Rewards to Build a Culture of Accountability
cards.summary: Shifting rewards from individual performance to team achievement creates a culture where peers are unlikely to stand by quietly while someone fails to pull their weight.
cards.use_when: An operator is designing incentives for a store team — merchandising, marketing, fulfillment — and wants execution to depend on collective results rather than individual metrics alone.
steps: Shift rewards away from individual performance toward team achievement where the work is genuinely interdependent.
Recognize that when the team shares in the outcome, members are unlikely to stand by quietly and let the team fail because a peer is not pulling their weight.
Combine team rewards with published goals and simple progress reviews so the team knows what the shared standard is.
The leader remains the ultimate arbiter of discipline if the team itself fails, but this should be a rare occurrence.
caveats: The source notes that relying on rewards alone is problematic if it assumes financial motivation is the sole driver of behavior; team rewards are one tool among several.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Leader's Role: Avoid the Accountability Vacuum
cards.summary: Strong leaders can accidentally become the only source of discipline; the goal is to let the team be the primary accountability mechanism, with the leader as rare final arbiter.
cards.use_when: An operator finds that team members only raise problems to them, not to each other, and wants to shift accountability to the team.
steps: Notice if your own strength as a leader is creating an accountability vacuum — team members may assume the leader will handle discipline, so they hold back.
Actively encourage and allow the team to serve as the first and primary accountability mechanism.
Communicate clearly that accountability is a shared team responsibility, not a consensus approach where anyone can opt out.
Reserve your own intervention as the ultimate arbiter of discipline when the team itself fails — rare, but clear to everyone.
caveats: The source warns that stepping in too often recreates the vacuum; stepping in too little risks the team never developing its own accountability.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Focus on Results, Not Team or Individual Status
cards.summary: The ultimate dysfunction is caring about something other than collective goals; teams get distracted by team status (just belonging) or individual status (personal advancement).
cards.use_when: An ecommerce team seems comfortable but is not hitting growth or profitability goals, or members are optimizing for their own function rather than the store's collective outcome.
steps: Diagnose whether the team is focused on team status — being satisfied by merely belonging to the group — or individual status — enhancing personal position at the expense of the team.
Define specific objectives and clearly defined outcomes, recognizing that results include outcome-based performance, not only financial metrics.
Make the collective results of the group more important to each individual than their own goals.
Watch for symptoms: stagnation, failing to grow, rarely defeating competitors, losing achievement-oriented employees, and being easily distracted.
Address the root cause directly — the source says no amount of trust, conflict, commitment, or accountability can compensate for a lack of desire to win.
caveats: The source's examples include nonprofits, political groups, and prestigious companies that fall into the status trap; the dysfunction is not limited to commercial teams.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Public Declaration of Results
cards.summary: Teams that publicly commit to specific results are more likely to work with a passionate, even desperate desire to achieve them; 'we'll do our best' is a subtle preparation for failure.
cards.use_when: An operator wants a team or the whole store organization to raise its ambition and accountability around a growth or turnaround target.
steps: Define the specific results the team intends to achieve.
Make public proclamations about intended success to the team, the company, or relevant constituencies.
Use the public commitment to focus attention and effort, as the source says teams that commit publicly work harder to achieve the result.
Avoid the soft framing of 'we'll do our best,' which the source says subtly prepares the team for failure.
caveats: The source notes that for athletic teams, public guarantees can unnecessarily provoke opponents; for most teams, public commitment is helpful. It is a motivational tool, not a guarantee of the outcome.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Results-Based Rewards
cards.summary: Tying rewards, especially compensation, to the achievement of specific outcomes keeps attention on results, though relying on this alone assumes financial motivation is the sole driver.
cards.use_when: An operator is setting bonuses or recognition for a team and wants to avoid rewarding effort in the absence of results.
steps: Tie rewards, especially compensation, to the achievement of specific outcomes.
Avoid letting someone take home a bonus merely for 'trying hard' when the result was not achieved, because the source says this signals that achieving the outcome may not be important.
Use rewards as one of several tools, not the only one, since relying on them alone assumes financial motivation is the sole driver of behavior.
Combine with public declaration of results and clear goals so the team understands what outcomes are being rewarded.
caveats: The source explicitly warns that relying on rewards alone is problematic; pair it with other practices.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Leader Sets the Tone for Results Focus
cards.summary: If team members sense the leader values anything other than results, they take that as permission to do the same; leaders must be selfless and objective in rewards and recognition.
cards.use_when: An operator wants to build or repair a results-focused culture and is examining whether their own behavior is reinforcing or undermining it.
steps: Audit what you personally reward and recognize — if it is not results, the team will follow suit.
Be selfless and objective in reserving rewards and recognition for those who make real contributions to the achievement of group goals.
Avoid signaling that status, tenure, or personal relationships matter more than achieving outcomes.
Model the focus on results consistently, since the source says the leader sets the tone more for this dysfunction than for any of the others.
caveats: The source's claim is that the leader sets the tone more for this dysfunction than others; it does not mean the leader alone is responsible for results.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Kathryn's Meeting Cadence: How Much Time a Strong Team Spends Together
cards.summary: Kathryn's model shows a management team spending roughly eight days per quarter together — fewer than three days per month — which saves time by eliminating confusion and minimizing redundant effort.
cards.use_when: An operator is deciding how much meeting time the management team needs and is weighing 'real work' against structured team time.
steps: Adopt an annual planning meeting and leadership development retreat (three days, off-site) covering budget, strategy, leadership training, succession planning, and cascading messaging.

Hold quarterly staff meetings (two days, off-site) for major goal reviews, financial review, strategic discussions, employee performance, key issue resolution, team development, and cascading messages.
Run weekly staff meetings (two hours, on-site) for key activity review, goal progress, sales review, customer review, tactical issue resolution, and cascading messages.
Schedule ad hoc topical meetings (two hours, on-site) for strategic issues that cannot be adequately discussed in the weekly meeting.
Recognize that spending this time together actually saves time by reducing confusion and redundant communication, even though most management teams resist it.
caveats: The source presents Kathryn's methods as one way to run a management team, not the only way; the numbers are a model, not a universal prescription.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Choose FBA or FBM before setting up a seller account
cards.summary: FBA hands pick/pack/ship to Amazon for per-order fees; FBM means you ship yourself, and the source's preference is FBA for a semi-passive operation.
cards.use_when: Deciding your fulfilment model before registering an Amazon seller account or sourcing inventory.
steps: Understand the two models: FBA (Fulfilment by Amazon) means you send stock to Amazon's warehouse and they pick, pack and ship each order, charging fulfilment fees that reduce your margin. FBM (Fulfilment by Merchant) means you ship every order yourself.

Source view: the presenter chooses FBA because he wants a lifestyle, semi-passive business rather than packing orders at home. Treat this as his personal preference, not a universal rule — FBM can suit heavy, fragile, low-volume or made-to-order items.
Note that your choice changes the fee lines in every profitability calculation, so fix the model before you analyse products.
If in doubt, run one small FBA test batch and compare actual per-unit fulfilment fees against your own shipping cost before committing your full range.
Verify current fee schedules and programme terms in Seller Central, as Amazon changes them.
caveats: Source is a single practitioner's preference, not a benchmark; FBM is not inherently worse.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide To Amazon FBA In 2025 (1).docx

cards.title: Pick an Amazon business model: arbitrage, wholesale or private label
cards.summary: The three Amazon selling routes differ in capital, competition and learning curve; the source suggests starting with arbitrage/wholesale before private label.
cards.use_when: Choosing which Amazon selling model to launch next quarter and how much capital to allocate.
steps: Map the three routes as the source describes them: (1) Retail/online arbitrage — buy discounted stock from supermarkets or retail websites and resell on Amazon; lowest capital, quick-cash but not scalable and often capped (e.g. quantity limits per order). (2) Wholesale — buy branded products in bulk from a wholesaler or the brand and resell at retail price; more scalable, no need to create demand or run ads, source cites roughly £1,000 starting capital. (3) Private label — create your own brand, source from China, build your own listing and run ads; source cites roughly £5,000–£10,000 needed for stock, ads, images, listing, barcodes and trademark.
Note the trade-off the source highlights: wholesale means other sellers can buy the same branded product and compete on your listing; private label removes that but raises cost and learning curve.
His recommendation for beginners is to start with wholesale or arbitrage to learn how Amazon works, then move to private label — cite this as his opinion, not a rule.
Choose your route now because it determines which product-analysis checks (BSR, seller count, ROI) are even relevant.
caveats: Arbitrage and wholesale-specific sourcing metrics (BSR, seller counts, 30% ROI) do not transfer to private label or your own DTC store.
Capital figures are the presenter's stated examples, not guarantees.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide To Amazon FBA In 2025 (1).docx

cards.title: Register a UK Amazon Professional seller account and pass verification
cards.summary: Practical setup sequence for a UK seller account, including the live video verification call and proof documents you must have ready.
cards.use_when: Opening a new Amazon seller account in the UK and preparing for identity verification.
steps: Go to the Amazon seller sign-up page for your marketplace (e.g. sell on Amazon UK) and register either with an existing shopping account or a new one.

Compare current UK Individual and Professional charges and needed features. Do not mistake a volume-based cost recommendation for a hard unit limit; use current local prices rather than assuming US fees apply.
Register the account under the name of someone who holds both a valid proof of ID and a proof of address, because verification checks both.
Expect a live verification video call with an Amazon employee where you hold your ID next to your face, and be ready to upload your proof-of-address document.
After submitting, verification commonly completes within 72 hours (the source has seen it take as little as 1–2 hours), then add your bank/charge and payment details in Seller Central.
If the account is rejected, suspended or deactivated, you can appeal directly or engage a specialist to prepare a detailed appeal.
Reasons cited for rejection include details not matching your ID documents, a previously suspended account, or missing information Amazon requested.
caveats: Specific fees and timelines are UK- and date-specific; verify the current sign-up interface and fees in Seller Central.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide To Amazon FBA In 2025 (1).docx

cards.title: Set up a seller account you can actually trade from
cards.summary: The account needs verified identity, a linked bank account and the correct plan before any listing work begins.
cards.use_when: Preparing a newly approved seller account before adding your first ASIN.
steps: Before you can sell, complete the tasks the dashboard flags, including adding the bank account Amazon will use to pay you and to charge fees.
Do not begin sourcing or shipping until verification has passed and payment details are registered, otherwise you cannot receive funds.
Keep your proof of ID and proof of address consistent with the name on the account so future reviews or reinstatements are simpler.
Set your account to the correct marketplace and only enable the marketplaces you actually intend to sell in when creating listings, so you do not accidentally expose stock abroad.
Treat the account as the asset: the source notes suspensions are a real risk, and appeals are harder once a prior suspension exists.
caveats: The exact dashboard tasks and screens change; follow the current on-screen guidance.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide To Amazon FBA In 2025 (1).docx

cards.title: Analyse a resale ASIN with four pass/fail checks
cards.summary: Screen any wholesale or arbitrage product against BSR, seller count, Amazon-as-competitor and ROI before buying.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to buy a specific branded ASIN for Amazon wholesale or arbitrage.
steps: Check Best Seller Rank, found under the listing's 'see all information' or product-details area. The source's rule of thumb is BSR under 100,000, because the lower the rank the faster the product sells — treat 100,000 as his guideline, not a fixed law.
Check actual selling eligibility, authentic supply documentation and whether the product exactly matches the ASIN. Competitor seller count is not proof of permission to sell.

Check Amazon is not on the listing. Open the buy box and check 'sold by' — if it says Amazon, avoid it, because Amazon typically undercuts and wins the buy box (cited case: Amazon priced more than £10 below the next cheapest seller). 'Amazon Warehouse' is acceptable because it is used stock.

Check ROI of at least 30%. Use Amazon's revenue calculator with the ASIN, set your sell price (source suggests matching the lowest FBA seller), enter cost of goods, and compute ROI = profit ÷ cost of goods × 100.
Only sell if all four checks pass. The source allows one adjustment: for a fast-selling item he would accept around 20% ROI.
caveats: BSR and 30% ROI are this presenter's arbitrage/wholesale heuristics, not universal standards, and are not appropriate for private label or DTC.
Check gating/eligibility and current fee structures before buying.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide To Amazon FBA In 2025 (1).docx

cards.title: Calculate Amazon contribution, inventory ROI and applicable fee taxes
cards.summary: Include the complete per-unit cost stack and the seller's actual tax treatment when screening inventory.
cards.use_when: Judging whether a UK ASIN clears your profit threshold before committing to buy stock.
steps: Use the marketplace revenue calculator with the actual ASIN or dimensions, price, weight and fulfillment method.
Include landed product cost, selling and fulfillment fees, prep, labels, inbound charges, storage, expected returns and advertising where relevant.
Check fee invoices and the business's tax treatment; include non-recoverable tax costs and do not automatically add a blanket VAT percentage to every estimate.
Inventory ROI = contribution per unit / inventory cost per unit x 100; define the cost base consistently. £5.40 / £25 = 21.6%.
Compare contribution, inventory turnover and cash exposure together; the source's 20-30% thresholds are heuristics, not universal profit requirements.
caveats: Contribution is not final net profit after all overhead.
Use the relevant marketplace and verified tax inputs; calculator estimates may omit some costs.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide To Amazon FBA In 2025 (1).docx

cards.title: Run a 10–50 unit test order before committing to wholesale stock
cards.summary: The first order for any new wholesale product should be small so you can validate sell-through, competition and eligibility before scaling.
cards.use_when: Placing your first purchase order for a newly validated wholesale ASIN.
steps: Buy a test shipment of roughly 10 to 50 units rather than a full pallet on your first order, as the source recommends.

Use the test to check three things: whether the product actually sells at your price, whether other sellers jump on and undercut you, and whether the product has any restrictions or problems (e.g. gating) that leave you holding stock.
Compare the test result against your original product checks (BSR, seller count, ROI) before reordering in volume.
Only scale the order once the test shows the margin holding at real selling prices after Amazon fees and VAT.
Model the downside explicitly: the source's warning is that if you order 400 units and the product is restricted or undercut, your cash is trapped in unsellable inventory.
caveats: Test size is described as a range for beginners; some gated categories may require 10–100 units plus a supplier invoice to become eligible.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide To Amazon FBA In 2025 (1).docx

cards.title: Add an existing ASIN to your inventory instead of creating a listing
cards.summary: Match existing listings by ASIN, sell at the lowest FBA price and select Amazon's barcode to avoid commingled stock.
cards.use_when: Listing a validated wholesale or arbitrage product you are ready to sell on Amazon.
steps: In Seller Central go to Catalog > Add Product, paste the product's ASIN (found under 'see all information') and search rather than building a brand-new listing.

If the result says condition new 'apply to sell' you are gated. To get ungated the source's method is to buy 10 units — sometimes 100 — of the exact product from a wholesale supplier and upload an invoice matching your Amazon account or company name.
Once eligible, set condition as New and click 'Sell this product'; you are joining the existing listing, not creating one.
Price to match or sit close to the lowest FBA seller on the listing. Filter the other-sellers view by Prime to isolate FBA sellers.
Set fulfilment channel to Amazon (FBA) and disable any other marketplaces you do not want to sell in, then save and finish.

At the barcode field choose 'Amazon's barcode only' even if the product already has a manufacturer barcode, so Amazon can attribute commingled shipments to you rather than confusing your stock with another seller's on the same ASIN.
Allow around 15 minutes for the offer to appear in your inventory.
caveats: Gating thresholds and invoice requirements vary by category and brand; verify with Seller Central.
Sticking your own Amazon barcode over the manufacturer barcode is the source's commingling safeguard — this alters the physical unit, so confirm it does not conflict with the brand's requirements.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide To Amazon FBA In 2025 (1).docx

cards.title: Create an FBA shipping plan and respect box size and weight limits
cards.summary: Create an inbound plan from actual units, packaging and current marketplace requirements.
cards.use_when: Building a shipment plan to send stock from your premises into an Amazon fulfilment centre.
steps: Start the current Send to Amazon or replenishment workflow with the correct origin and inventory.
Check category-specific prep, expiration, barcode and labeling requirements; fragility alone does not determine prep needs.
Confirm who will prepare and label each unit before dispatch; do not assume Amazon offers the services shown in an older tutorial.
Enter accurate unit counts, box contents, dimensions and weights; check current limits and exceptions for the receiving marketplace.
Choose an eligible parcel or pallet route and compare actual carrier charges.
Check charges and cancellation terms before confirming; do not assume a universal 24-hour free cancellation window.
caveats: Source UK dimensions, label fees and carrier recommendations are historical examples, not current global requirements.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide To Amazon FBA In 2025 (1).docx

cards.title: Print SKU and box labels and schedule a UPS collection
cards.summary: After confirming the shipment you still must print labels, get the tracking ID and book a UPS pickup — receiving tracking alone is not the end of the process.
cards.use_when: Finalising an FBA shipment after confirming charges in Seller Central.
steps: Print SKU/unit labels, choosing standard or thermal format for your printer. On a normal A4 printer the source uses A4 label sheets so the labels print and peel off.
Print box labels and carrier labels on A4 label sheets (he cites 1 x 139mm or equivalent templates) — you will get a UPS label and an Amazon box label.
Do not stop when tracking details appear. Copy the tracking ID from 'view tracking details'.
Go to UPS's schedule-a-pickup page, confirm you have a prepaid UPS shipping label, and paste the tracking ID; separate multiple tracking IDs with commas.
Enter your address, the number of packages/boxes, and the total weight, then flag whether the shipment exceeds 32kg.
Choose the collection date and a 4-hour window (the source notes UPS offers something like 11:00–15:00 or 12:00–17:00 and you cannot shrink the window); alternatively drop off at a collection point.
Review and confirm the booking; from collection onwards Amazon handles picking, packing and shipping to customers.
caveats: Carrier interfaces, offered time windows and templates change — verify the current UPS booking flow.
The drop-off vs collection choice affects cost and control; the source simply prefers collection for convenience.
cards.source_name: Beginners Guide To Amazon FBA In 2025 (1).docx

cards.title: Anti-portfolio: products to avoid when selecting an FBA item
cards.summary: Reject cheap, seasonal, trendy, gated, and patented products before spending on inventory to avoid dead stock and price wars.
cards.use_when: Screening candidate products for a new Amazon FBA listing before committing capital to inventory.
steps: Rule out cheap products (roughly under $10 retail): the source argues a $7–8 flimsy item generates bad reviews, invites low-barrier competitors, and lets PPC clicks of about $1 consume all profit within two or three clicks.
Reject seasonal and trend-driven items, which leave you holding unsellable inventory and paying long-term storage fees once demand passes.
Reject restricted/gated categories and patented products — the source reports having ordered inventory he then could not sell because Amazon blocked the category or the item was patented.
Treat these as elimination criteria first, before evaluating upside: the speaker claims applying them saves tens of thousands of dollars, and that getting product selection wrong means failure.
Note this is one seller's opinion and heuristic, not a platform rule; verify current category gating and IP status per item before ordering.
caveats: The $10 price floor and '$1/click' figure are illustrative from the source, not measured benchmarks.
Some sellers profitably run cheap or seasonal products; the source's guidance assumes a paid-PPC-led launch model.
cards.source_name: COMPLETE Amazon FBA Product Research Masterclass.docx

cards.title: Four viability criteria for a target FBA product
cards.summary: Target premium-priced products with 30%+ net margin, problem-solving function, and low brand dominance.
cards.use_when: Building the shortlist of products worth deeper keyword and competitor analysis for an Amazon launch.
steps: Require a net profit margin of 30% or more after landed cost (product, shipping, duties, taxes) and FBA fees; treat below 30% as a discard signal per the source.
Set a minimum retail price around $25+; the speaker says his most profitable items are over $30 because higher ticket absorbs PPC and margin pressure.
Confirm the product solves a specific problem — the source frames this as 'dollars follow value' — since a better-resolved problem drives reviews, credibility, and repeat demand.
Check brand dominance: avoid categories where one legacy brand owns most of the sales (the source's example is Adidas/Nike/Puma soccer balls) and prefer niches where sales are spread across sellers.
Write the margin math out per unit before sourcing; the source criticizes sellers who don't know their FBA fees or landed cost.
caveats: 30% net margin and $25 minimum price are the source's heuristics, not industry standards; they vary by category and business model.
Low brand dominance is judged qualitatively — the source gives no numeric threshold for 'spread out' sales.
cards.source_name: COMPLETE Amazon FBA Product Research Masterclass.docx

cards.title: Keyword variability test: count the ways a product is searched
cards.summary: Prefer products describable by many distinct long-tail keywords so you can rank on multiple first-page terms instead of one contested head term.
cards.use_when: Deciding between two candidate products, or judging whether a niche offers cheap organic entry for a new Amazon listing.
steps: Take your candidate product and list the distinct ways a customer might search for it — the source's phone-case example: slim, green, wallet, waterproof, for men, for women.
Prefer products with dozens or hundreds of descriptive variants; these give many low-hanging long-tail terms to target in listing copy and launch PPC.
Discard or downgrade products with only one or two monolithic keywords — ranking becomes a single contested battle with no cheap entry points.
For ecommerce merchandising, apply the same test when writing PDP titles and bullet copy: cover the distinct descriptive variants rather than repeating one head term.
Validate the actual search demand for each variant in a keyword tool before building the listing around it.
caveats: The source gives no numeric minimum for 'enough' keywords — 'dozens' and '10/20/30/100' are illustrative.
Keyword counts and search volumes change over time; re-verify before committing.
cards.source_name: COMPLETE Amazon FBA Product Research Masterclass.docx

cards.title: Price-disparity check on Page 1 search results
cards.summary: Discard products whose Page 1 prices are tightly clustered; prefer wide spreads so you do not compete solely on price.
cards.use_when: Validating a candidate product's pricing power before sourcing inventory for an Amazon listing.
steps: Search the product's main keyword on Amazon and record the price of the first-page organic listings.
Example of a bad result from the source: 'tongue scraper' showed Page 1 prices from $6.99 to $12.99 — a roughly $6 spread — meaning near-identical products compete only on price and reviews.
Example of a good result: the same kind of product appearing at $20 and $100 on Page 1, showing buyers pay for something other than lowest price.
Discard products where all Page 1 results sit in a narrow band (the source cites $7–$13 as a discard band).
Use the spread to inform your own pricing and differentiation strategy: wide spread means positioning, bundling, or quality upgrades can justify a higher price.
caveats: Prices on Page 1 shift with promotions, coupons, and seasonality; sample more than once.
Wide price spread does not guarantee you can occupy the high end — it signals room to try, not capacity to win.
cards.source_name: COMPLETE Amazon FBA Product Research Masterclass.docx

cards.title: Helium 10 Black Box filter stack for finding weak competitors
cards.summary: A strict numeric filter set to isolate high-revenue, low-sophistication, ungated FBA competitors.
cards.use_when: Running a first-pass product scan in Helium 10 Black Box (Products tab) to generate raw candidates for an Amazon FBA launch.
steps: Open Helium 10 → Tools → Black Box → Products tab (verify the current interface, as tooling changes).

Set Category to an ungated one: the source names Home & Kitchen, Patio Lawn & Garden, Pet Supplies, Office Products, Industrial & Scientific, Kitchen & Dining, Sports & Outdoors, Tools & Home Improvement, and warns Baby, CDs/Vinyl, and some Electronics (batteries) cause gating problems.
Set Review Count Max = 300 to exclude dominant listings with tens of thousands of reviews.
Set Price = $25 to $60 (adjust upward with your budget) to avoid the cheap-product trap.
Set Monthly Revenue = $5,000 to $20,000 to cap the inventory and marketing capital required; the source warns a $30k/month product demands a large budget for stock and ads.
Set Listing Age Minimum = 8 months to filter out fads and validate evergreen demand.
Set Image Count Max = 4 to surface sellers with weak listings — the source calls sub-4-image sellers 'clueless' and therefore beatable.
The source's example run returned 500+ matching products; do not copy his exact filters wholesale — vary categories so you are not chasing the same products as everyone else.
caveats: These are the presenter's personal heuristics, not proven thresholds; the source explicitly says not to follow the exact filters.
Revenue and review estimates from any tool are modeled, not actual seller data.
Verify current filter names and availability in your Helium 10 subscription.
cards.source_name: COMPLETE Amazon FBA Product Research Masterclass.docx

cards.title: Review mining: turn 4.1–4.3 star sellers into a product spec
cards.summary: Sort results by lowest rating, find mediocre-but-selling products, and read 1-star reviews to extract the exact improvements to brief a supplier.
cards.use_when: Turning a shortlisted FBA candidate into a manufacturing brief before contacting suppliers.
steps: In Helium 10 Black Box results, sort by review rating from lowest to highest to surface products with real demand but unresolved quality problems.
Target products rated roughly 4.1–4.3 stars still generating over $5,000/month — they sell despite flaws, meaning fixes should lift conversion.

Open the 1-star reviews and read them for concrete physical complaints: fit, size, color options, durability, missing features. The source's example found a sun shade with 12% one-star reviews and photoshopped listing images.
Translate each recurring complaint into a specific requirement in your supplier brief (materials, dimensions, added options), then advertise the fix in your listing.
Repeat for your own post-launch PDP: mine 1–3 star reviews of competitors and of your own product to prioritize the next iteration.
