steps: Frame SOP creation as the price of advancement, not a chore: 'You cannot become a manager and make more money unless you document your job so we can hire someone under you.' The source reports securing full compliance this way.
Have employees write their own replacement docs — the person doing the job documents the job.
Tie documentation structurally to the promotion path so each role's output is a documented system the next hire can be trained against.
For ecommerce: use this to document repeatable functions (media buying, email flows, PDP builds, fulfillment steps) so you can add staff without re-explaining from scratch.
Pair with a central task system and weekly check-ins so documented processes are actually followed and kept current.
caveats: This is a management technique the source advocates and reports as effective; results depend on a credible promotion path. Do not present the tactic as a guaranteed outcome.
cards.source_name: $1B Marketer Explains_ How to Scale an Ecommerce Brand in 2026.docx

cards.title: Shift the CAC Question From 'Lower It' to 'Make It Work'
cards.summary: Rather than grinding to cut CAC from ~$70 to ~$60, improve retention and lifetime gross profit so your current CAC becomes profitable.
cards.use_when: Acquisition and pricing decisions — when paid traffic is near break-even and cutting CAC further feels hard or not worth the effort.
steps: Recognize the difficulty: the source (citing Jordan Manard) notes cutting CAC from ~$70 to ~$60 on well-run ad accounts takes enormous effort once you're doing a decent job.
Instead of asking 'how do I drive CAC down?', ask 'how do I make this CAC make sense for my brand?' — i.e. raise the value behind each customer.
Focus on retention: improving repeat purchase and back-end revenue raises lifetime gross profit, which raises the CAC you can afford.
Use email/SMS to drive the no-acquisition-cost repeat purchases — the source's point that getting the same customer 15 times beats getting a customer once.
Treat first-purchase profit as important but not the whole game: the source would rather have a massive back end than a great one-time front end.
caveats: The $70→$60 figures are the source's example, not a benchmark.
You must still handle first-purchase profitability — the source says don't neglect it; the shift is about the overall equation.
cards.source_name: $1B Marketer Explains_ How to Scale an Ecommerce Brand in 2026.docx

cards.title: Prefer Influencer/Affiliate Virality on TikTok Over Paid-Only Traffic
cards.summary: The source names TikTok creator-economy virality (commission-only influencer posts) as the largest current traffic arbitrage opportunity.
cards.use_when: Acquisition channel decisions — when evaluating where to allocate attention and paid budget across channels.
steps: Pursue TikTok Shop / creator-economy virality where you pay only commission, making the cost structure downside-light versus paid clicks.
Focus on getting creators to achieve organic virality — the source says this is the biggest arbitrage because you're not paying per click upfront.
Pair virality with a strong back end: the source's core point is that arbitrage on traffic alone matters less than lifetime gross profit, so pair cheap reach with retention.

For AI-driven creative (image ads, thumbnails, most videos), the source says he uses AI heavily — but for TikTok he still uses real people because he wants the organic reach of whoever posts on their own page.

Note the source's view that AI creative rivals real production in most cases; he estimates ~90% quality at far less effort — but uses real talent when depending on a celebrity or the organic reach of a real account.
caveats: Channel arbitrage shifts month to month — the source stresses it changes frequently, so verify current conditions.
The ~90% quality estimate is the source's opinion, not a measured benchmark.
cards.source_name: $1B Marketer Explains_ How to Scale an Ecommerce Brand in 2026.docx

cards.title: Centralize AI/automation requests in one intake form and prioritize them on a shared board
cards.summary: Collect internal automation and AI requests through one form, filter them in a recurring leadership review, and only push the approved ones onto a single prioritized project board with time estimates.
cards.use_when: You want to systematize internal automation and tooling work for an ecommerce operation (product data sync, inventory alerts, ad reporting, customer-service macros) instead of letting requests ping-pong across the team.
steps: Open a single submission form (e.g., a Google Form) where managers submit requests in a structured format: 'we need a robot/automation that does XYZ', plus the context and access it requires.
Have each manager gather ideas from their own team first, then submit on the team's behalf, so the form is not flooded with duplicates and low-priority requests.
Review submissions on a fixed cadence (the source used every other week) in a leadership meeting and rank them by how many people the solution would help.
Only move approved items onto a shared project board (the source used ClickUp); submissions existing on the form is not the same as being accepted for work.
Require the person building it to attach an estimate (e.g., two days, three days) and any missing context or access (e.g., Facebook Ads access) directly on the board item.
Keep work strictly top-to-bottom by priority, hold a short weekly review of tasks in flight, and let people message an always-available chat channel to unblock context and access requests.

Track value beyond cost: the source frames one dedicated builder at roughly $40k/year replacing what previously cost $40k/month in app development — treat that as the source's own historical comparison, not a benchmark.
caveats: The $40k/year vs $40k/month figures are the source's personal historical comparison, not a market benchmark.
The form is a filter, not an approval — most submissions should never reach the board.
Access granting (ad accounts, platforms) needs whoever owns credentials to be reachable quickly, or items stall.
cards.source_name: $1B Marketer Explains_ How to Scale an Ecommerce Brand in 2026.docx

cards.title: Get manager buy-in before rolling out any cross-store initiative
cards.summary: Before pushing a new company-wide process, validate it with the managers who will run it and reframe the 'why' in terms of what's in it for the person doing the work.
cards.use_when: You are about to standardize a recurring ecommerce task across many stores or clients — a new weekly reporting ritual, a PDP refresh checklist, a review-request process — and need it to actually get done without you checking every instance.
steps: Talk to the managers who would enforce the change before announcing it. Ask whether it helps them or is a waste of time.
Listen for existing overlap: they may already do something similar that you didn't know about, which may be enough.
State the explicit why behind the task. If you can't justify it clearly, expect it to be treated as busy work and deprioritized.

Frame the why around the person's benefit, not just the company's. The source's example: SOP write-ups were sold as 'this is how you become a manager instead of becoming a support bot for your own hires.'
Match the explanation to the audience — the source's observation is that smarter people are more likely to refuse a task they can't justify, so vagueness costs you most with your best people.
Deliver the rollout with a deadline. The SOP example was completed in two weeks once the reason was clear.
If a manager says it's unnecessary, either adjust the initiative or drop it — a mandated task with no accepted why will be half-done.
caveats: This is the source's stated management approach, not a tested universal rule; some mandatory changes genuinely can't be justified individually and may require a different enforcement mechanism.
The two-week SOP completion is a source anecdote, not a benchmark for your team.
cards.source_name: $1B Marketer Explains_ How to Scale an Ecommerce Brand in 2026.docx

cards.title: Handle entrepreneurial hires with a clear verbal commitment and a clean exit norm
cards.summary: The source deliberately hires entrepreneurial people for roles like media buying and dev/automation, asks for a spoken minimum commitment, and keeps exits clean and relationship-preserving.
cards.use_when: You're hiring for a growth-critical ecommerce role (paid media, retention/CRM, CRO/dev, creative production) and are weighing a strong candidate who openly plans to build their own business.
steps: Recognize the trade: the source views entrepreneurial candidates as typically the strongest performers and accepts that they will eventually leave — the duration of output matters more than longevity.
Before hiring, ask for a clear spoken commitment. The source's figure is at least two years in exchange for investment in them, done as a verbal pact rather than a contract.
State what you'll give in return: the source commits to supporting their eventual entrepreneurial move rather than blocking it.
Set an exit norm in advance, e.g., roughly three months' notice, and honor it by planning a transition rather than a sudden handoff.
When people leave under those terms, keep referring business to each other — the source says former employees have referred clients back and attended paid events.

Treat broken exits as a permanent signal: the source says he warns others against hiring someone who burned the relationship, so your behavior on exit is durable reputation data in this small ecosystem.
caveats: The two-year commitment is verbal and unenforceable by design; it works on relationship capital, not paperwork.
This trades team stability for peak talent — if a role needs multi-year continuity, this approach may not fit.
The source's positive recall of former employees is his own account.
cards.source_name: $1B Marketer Explains_ How to Scale an Ecommerce Brand in 2026.docx

cards.title: Ask 'can I hand this off?' before 'should I handle this?'
cards.summary: Make delegation the default first question so your own time is reserved for the few high-leverage plays only you can execute, with a personal idea-capture list so big swings don't get buried.
cards.use_when: You're the operator of an ecommerce brand and your day is full of requests, fires and small tasks while ad campaigns, partnerships and bigger merchandising plays keep getting postponed.
steps: Replace the default question 'should I handle this?' with 'can I give this to someone else?' and route it there first.
Triaging inbound is part of the job: the source sorts messages into hand-off, ignore, or delete-and-forget, and explicitly labels some requests as a waste of his time.
Account for what meetings cost: the source's comparison is that an hour on calls reaches about one person, while the same hour distributing instructions by text/Slack/WhatsApp can reach many.
This is not anti-meeting — the source says one-on-one depth-building calls are important; the point is that delegating execution buys back time for those and for bigger thinking.
Maintain a single running capture list (the source pins a WhatsApp chat with himself as his first pinned chat) and dump every ad concept, revenue idea, and contact to follow up with into it.
Review that list daily and execute on entries as fast as possible, so ideas don't drown under client fires and launches.
Reserve the freed time for the plays only you own — e.g., a large international campaign or partnership — because those won't be delegated to anyone on the team.
caveats: The source's hourly reach estimates are illustrative, not measured.
Delegation still requires someone competent to receive the work; handing off without a capable owner just moves the failure.
Expect a margin hit early: you fund the freed time before the bigger play pays off, which the source acknowledges is a real cost.
cards.source_name: $1B Marketer Explains_ How to Scale an Ecommerce Brand in 2026.docx

cards.title: Break the 'bigger box' trap before scaling past a plateau
cards.summary: The source warns that growing revenue by piling tasks onto the same founder-built machine just enlarges the box you're trapped in, so periodically rebuild the foundation instead.
cards.use_when: Your ecommerce brand has reached a revenue plateau (the source names around $100k/month as a reflection point) and your own hours are scaling up with revenue instead of staying flat.
steps: At a plateau, stop optimizing the current machine and audit the foundation instead: which functions still depend on you personally?
Ask the rework question directly — 'what has to change so I'm not working like a horse for the next tier of revenue?' — rather than assuming more revenue requires more of your labor.
Shift execution to people who own it, even at the cost of lower personal margin in the short term; the source explicitly trades margin for time.
Redirect the freed capacity into high-leverage moves you can't delegate: bigger campaigns, bigger deals, personal brand building.
Use delegation (see the hand-off-first card) as the mechanism, and keep a small number of large initiatives on your own plate.
Revisit the question at each plateau instead of once — the source presents it as a recurring checkpoint, not a one-time fix.
caveats: The ~$100k/month figure is the source's own heuristic reflection point, not a calculated threshold.
Deliberately accepting lower margin is a strategic choice with cash-flow consequences; it assumes you have the runway.
The source's framing is aimed at agency owners but the foundation-rebuild logic applies to any operator-built business.
cards.source_name: $1B Marketer Explains_ How to Scale an Ecommerce Brand in 2026.docx

cards.title: Build the founder's personal brand as a distribution asset, not a vanity project
cards.summary: The source's top takeaway from a founder event: the operators with the most inbound opportunities all had large personal brands, so start publishing earlier rather than later.
cards.use_when: You run an ecommerce brand and want a durable channel for partnerships, creator collabs, retail/distribution deals or inbound talent that doesn't depend on paid acquisition.
steps: Treat personal brand as infrastructure you start now, not after you've 'made it' — the source's point is that waiting is the mistake, and he notes regret about not starting a podcast years earlier.

Notice the pattern the source cites from the event: the founders receiving a stream of opportunities were the ones with big personal brands — treat that as an observed pattern, not proof of causation.
Pair publishing with the relationship behaviors that compound: doing goodwill, providing value, and staying in touch with people across roles and companies.
Use the time freed by delegation to do this consistently, since it competes with day-to-day operations for the same hours.
Seek proximity to people ahead of you, including by investing in their businesses where that's an option, which the source describes as a trust-deepening mechanism beyond ordinary networking.
Keep the door open with former colleagues and employers — the source treats these relationships as a source of future favors, introductions and referrals.
caveats: The source's claim that big personal brands caused the opportunities is an association he observed at one event, not a measured result.
Investing in others' businesses to build relationships carries financial risk and is unrelated to marketing performance.
Publishing takes months to compound; don't expect near-term acquisition impact.
cards.source_name: $1B Marketer Explains_ How to Scale an Ecommerce Brand in 2026.docx

cards.title: Separate New vs Existing Customer Ad Spend
cards.summary: Segment paid media reporting by new and returning customers so you can see whether spend is buying growth or just harvesting people who would buy anyway.
cards.use_when: Auditing or restructuring paid acquisition for your store when topline revenue has plateaued despite a reported 'healthy' ROAS.
steps: Split your ad account reporting so new-customer and existing-customer spend and revenue are tracked separately, not blended into one campaign total. In the source's audits, many brands never delineate between the two at all.

Index your key metrics against new-customer revenue rather than total revenue, because returning-customer revenue is largely a function of your product, model and industry, not incremental ad performance.

Pull frequency on existing customers — how many times existing customers see your ads every 30 days. The presenter says he pulls this in every audit and commonly sees 20 to 100; something around 10 is offered as an informal, not universal, target.

If existing-customer frequency is very high, treat pulling that budget as a candidate test rather than an automatic win — the source notes 10 to 20 frequency may occasionally still be incremental, but usually is not.
Confirm the change with a platform conversion-lift (geo-holdout) experiment on the existing-customer campaign rather than trusting reported ROAS.
caveats: Frequency bands (10, 20-100) are the presenter's rule-of-thumb from audits, not an established benchmark.
Conversion-lift experiments are platform features; verify current availability and setup in your ad platform's interface.
A nine-figure CPG brand reportedly showed negligible incrementality on existing-customer spend, but this is one example, not a guarantee for your store.
cards.source_name: 5 eCommerce Myths Keeping You Stuck.docx

cards.title: Why ROAS Is a Flawed Primary KPI
cards.summary: ROAS fails as a north-star metric because it is last-click, easily skewed by existing customers, and drives budget misallocation toward bottom-of-funnel.
cards.use_when: Choosing which marketing KPI to report to leadership or to optimize daily spend against for your store.
steps: Recognize three structural limits of ROAS: it can be skewed by existing customers, it reflects the last click rather than what created awareness, and it is distorted by whatever attribution settings are in use.

Note that branded search and retargeting campaigns naturally show high ROAS because they capture high-intent traffic that would likely have converted anyway, while genuinely awareness-building activity (the source's example is TV) has a return that is unmeasurable at that layer.

Test any metric against the source's rule: if a metric does not hold up across every context, it is probably flawed. The presenters argue incrementality, net profit, new-customer acquisition cost and CLTV survive context changes, while ROAS does not.

Where you still use ROAS, treat it as directional context, and note that some large-brand performance operators aim for the lowest ROAS at which they can acquire customers profitably rather than maximizing ROAS.
For large or multi-channel operations, be aware that ROAS has been reported up to executives for a long time, so repositioning the KPI may be slow and political.
caveats: The claim that ROAS should never be a primary KPI is the presenters' strong opinion, not a universal rule.
The claim that top US operators 'optimize for lowest ROAS possible' is the speaker's observation of an unnamed cohort, not a documented benchmark.
Attribution and platform metric behavior changes; verify current platform reporting before acting.
cards.source_name: 5 eCommerce Myths Keeping You Stuck.docx

cards.title: Split Klaviyo Attributed Revenue by New vs Returning
cards.summary: Klaviyo-attributed revenue is a useful north-star but is inflated by default view-through-style settings and should be split by customer type.
cards.use_when: Setting or reviewing your email/SMS retention KPIs and deciding whether to optimize campaigns for attributed revenue.
steps: Understand what Klaviyo's default attribution captures: the source describes it as 5-day open, 5-day click and says the open component functions essentially as a view-through metric that credits emails for purchases high-intent customers were going to make anyway.
Use attributed revenue as a directional north star: if it is rising, you are probably reaching converting people — but do not treat it as the definitive measure of retention success.
Split attributed revenue between new and returning customers. The source argues Klaviyo's impact on a new customer is far less incremental than on a returning customer.

Do not chase revenue-per-campaign as a primary KPI. Optimizing for it drives aggressive cadence — touching as many people as possible before they buy — which the presenters say can damage brand and customer attention.

Benchmark against the Klaviyo default settings if useful, since most users run them, but treat reported increments as needing conversion-lift or incrementality validation before you make budget calls.
caveats: Default attribution windows are platform behavior that can change; verify current Klaviyo attribution settings and options in the interface.

The source is critiquing an ad claim that '50% of revenue from Klaviyo' is a benchmark; the presenters call this meaningless as a guarantee and say the figure depends on business model (furniture vs supplements).
Incrementality of email to new vs returning customers is described as nuanced and ultimately needs testing, not assumption.
cards.source_name: 5 eCommerce Myths Keeping You Stuck.docx

cards.title: Frequency Audit as a First Step to Cutting Existing-Customer Waste
cards.summary: A simple frequency check in the ad account reveals how heavily you are re-targeting buyers and gives an intuitive basis for pulling budget.
cards.use_when: Preparing an audit or budget-review of your store's paid media, especially existing-customer targeting.
steps: Pull the frequency metric for existing-customer audiences over the last 30 days in your ad platform.
Compare against a rough sense of what is reasonable: the presenter offers around 10 exposures per 30 days as a plausible point of reference, while noting most audits he sees run 20 to 100.

If frequency is far above that, treat the excess budget as a candidate for reallocation, but frame it as a hypothesis — the source explicitly says moving from 10 to 20 may occasionally be incremental.
Where you can, follow up with a platform conversion-lift or geo-holdout experiment on that campaign to measure actual incremental contribution rather than relying on frequency alone.

Segment repeat buyers who have gone quiet on owned channels (e.g. purchased and unsubscribed) as the limited case where paid re-acquisition of existing customers may be reasonable — the source notes it is 'something smart to do' versus blindly targeting all existing customers.
caveats: Frequency thresholds are the speaker's heuristics from audits, not documented benchmarks.
Even a careful re-acquisition test on existing customers reportedly did nothing in the source's example; treat any spend there as experimental.
Conversion-lift experiment features, setup and reporting windows vary by platform; verify current interface.
cards.source_name: 5 eCommerce Myths Keeping You Stuck.docx

cards.title: Match Ad Spend Allocation to Your Repurchase Cycle
cards.summary: How much to spend re-targeting existing customers depends on how often your product can realistically be repurchased.
cards.use_when: Deciding budget split between acquisition and existing/retention-oriented paid media for your specific product category.
steps: Estimate your category's natural repurchase cycle. The source contrasts high-ticket furniture (repurchased roughly once every five years, per the presenter) with fast-moving consumables that generate frequent returns.
For long repurchase cycles, expect poor cohort lift and avoid spending heavily on paid ads to people who have already bought.

For fast-moving consumables with high likelihood of returns, a small amount of spend on specific segments may be justified — the source's example is people who purchased and unsubscribed, whom direct channels can no longer reach.
Rather than blanket-targeting existing customers, define narrow segments (unsubscribed buyers, lapsed repeat cohorts) where owned channels cannot reach them.
Validate any such spend with an incrementality or conversion-lift test before scaling, since even smart-looking segments may test as non-incremental.
caveats: The furniture and consumable examples are illustrative; confirm your own cohort data rather than assuming a category norm.
The source does not give a numeric budget split; treat any allocation as a business-specific judgment.
cards.source_name: 5 eCommerce Myths Keeping You Stuck.docx

cards.title: Treat Awareness-Funnel Spend Cautiously but Recognize It Drives Sales
cards.summary: Top-of-funnel activity can be genuinely valuable yet unmeasurable in last-click systems, so it gets under-funded relative to retargeting.
cards.use_when: Allocating budget across the funnel and interpreting reports that show strong branded/retargeting ROAS versus weak upper-funnel numbers.
steps: Recognize that last-click attribution will credit branded search and retargeting for conversions influenced by earlier awareness activity, making upper-funnel spend look bad.
Expect that if you only fund what reports well, you will systematically overallocate to bottom-of-funnel and to existing customers.
Use an alternative like incrementality testing or geo-holdouts where possible to estimate the upper-funnel contribution that platform reporting hides.

Accept that some awareness channels (the source cites TV) may not have a directly measurable return at that layer, only a downstream effect — reflect this in how you judge them rather than writing them off.
When you can't measure directly, treat the decision as a judgment call and keep the spend bounded and reviewable rather than either ignoring it or scaling it blindly.
caveats: This is a structural limitation of attribution systems, not a license to spend without any measurement.
Incrementality testing methods vary in rigor and availability; use the strongest option your platform and budget allow.
cards.source_name: 5 eCommerce Myths Keeping You Stuck.docx

cards.title: Measure Retention by Fundamentals, Not Email KPIs
cards.summary: Retention is primarily driven by product, portfolio, customer experience and pricing; email and owned media amplify, they rarely fix, weak retention.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing poor repeat purchase rates before investing in more email flows, upsells or cross-sells.
steps: First establish your baseline: check whether a meaningful portion of customers return on their own without marketing intervention. The source says you should; if you don't, extra marketing will not create it.

Walk the retention drivers the source lists — product quality, product portfolio, repeatability, customer experience, competitive landscape, pricing and the broader economy — and treat them as the upstream causes.
Use email and owned media to amplify those fundamentals: the source notes good brands use email to foster community, build loyalty and VIP programs, and run abandonment sequences.

In flows, prioritize communicating things that affect the customer experience — the source's example is that complex or instruction-dependent products should be explained rather than immediately pushed toward an upsell or cross-sell.
Treat Klaviyo (or any ESP) as a channel that can improve or worsen experience, but not as the fix for deep retention problems.
caveats: This is the presenters' strong opinion ('retention is not a flows problem, most of the time') and is framed against common agency pitches — it is a prioritization argument, not a claim that flows are unimportant.
The five-driver list is a conversational enumeration, not a formal framework.
cards.source_name: 5 eCommerce Myths Keeping You Stuck.docx

cards.title: Tie Spend Scaling to Net Profit, Not Absolute Budget
cards.summary: Scaling is not the same as increasing spend; the source reframes the goal as profitable growth rather than revenue at any cost.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to raise ad budgets, or evaluating advice that tells you to simply spend more on Meta.
steps: Question the assumption that a higher budget equals a bigger business. The source's counter is that anyone can increase spend without making more money.

Assess scaling against profit-focused metrics (net profit, CLTV, cash flow) rather than revenue or ROAS alone. The presenters note the industry narrative moved toward profit and cash-flow focus after the 2020-era growth-at-all-costs period.

If you do raise budget, watch revenue returns tightly and be ready to pull back. The source acknowledges that in the earlier era, a simple meaningful budget bump plus a few weeks sometimes produced more revenue — but that this is not reliable now.

Be aware that reported metrics from different channels (e.g. a much higher attributed number from email than from Meta) can mislead executive or owner decisions about where to add resources; treat channel-reported returns skeptically.
Where you are a young or small business, prioritize not going broke over matching competitors' spend levels.
caveats: The source gives no numeric profit benchmark of its own; a reference to a 20% net profit figure is attributed to another commentator, not presented as a universal rule.
The earlier-era advice to 'just increase budget' is described as having worked in a specific time window; it is not a current recommendation.
cards.source_name: 5 eCommerce Myths Keeping You Stuck.docx

cards.title: Score Metrics by Whether They Hold Up in Any Context
cards.summary: A practical filter for choosing KPIs: prefer metrics that remain meaningful no matter the business model, time frame or channel.
cards.use_when: Selecting which metrics to hold as your north star and which to demote to context-only when managing your store's performance.
steps: List your current KPIs and, for each, ask whether it would still make sense across different business models, time windows and channels.
Keep as top-level metrics the ones that survive that test. The source names incrementality, net profit, customer lifetime value and new-customer acquisition cost as examples.
Demote context-dependent metrics — the source names ROAS and Klaviyo attributed revenue — to supporting indicators, since they can break or fail to influence net profit in some contexts.
When a context-dependent metric moves sharply, investigate before reacting, especially if the movement coincides with channel-reported returns that may not be incremental.
Revisit the list periodically, since platform reporting and attribution behavior change and can reintroduce context-dependence.
caveats: This is the speaker's personal framework, presented as a heuristic, not an established measurement standard.
Even the surviving metrics require correct calculation and clean data; the source does not specify formulas.
cards.source_name: 5 eCommerce Myths Keeping You Stuck.docx

cards.title: Debug a Reported ROAS That Doesn't Match Topline
cards.summary: When reported ROAS stays healthy but revenue is flat, the likely cause is that spend is harvesting existing or high-intent buyers rather than acquiring new ones.
cards.use_when: Investigating a store where the ad account reports a 'healthy' ROAS (e.g. 4-5x) but total revenue has plateaued for months.
steps: Compare reported ROAS against topline revenue trend over the same period. If ROAS is 'fine' but revenue has not moved or is flat year on year, the metric and the business are telling different stories.
Check whether new and existing customer spend are separated at all — the presenters say many brands don't segment this, which hides the problem.
Look for spend concentrated on existing customers, high-intent organic audiences, and retargeting, which produces short-term high ROAS that eventually dries up as the pool is exhausted.

Note that a growing audience of followers or subscribers who have not purchased can look like incremental opportunity but is really high-intent traffic you already own being pushed through the funnel, which dries up too.
Set new-customer revenue (not total revenue) as the framing metric to reveal the underlying acquisition trend.
caveats: The 4-5x ROAS figure is a client example cited in the source, not a benchmark for good or bad performance.
The pattern described is a diagnostic hypothesis; confirm with segmentation and, ideally, incrementality testing.
cards.source_name: 5 eCommerce Myths Keeping You Stuck.docx

cards.title: Contrast as the Core Marketing Principle
cards.summary: Make every ad, email and store asset stand out from the noise by doing the opposite of what the market already sees.
cards.use_when: Planning acquisition creative or email subject lines and unsure whether the idea will get noticed in a crowded feed or inbox.
steps: Audit what the top competitors and top content creators in your niche are already doing — thumbnail style, hook formats, email subject patterns, PDP copy tone.
Ask 'how can I do the exact opposite?' for each element and pick the reversal that still serves your offer.
Apply contrast at the asset level: subject lines, hooks, creative format, even the page layout the customer lands on.
Treat the source's 'mad scientist' framing as a mindset: the goal is not to look like everyone else, it's to break the scrolling or inbox-clearing habit.
caveats: Contrast is the source's opinionated framework, not a measured benchmark; a contrarian format that confuses the buyer can hurt conversion.
Requires knowing the category norm first — contrast without a baseline is just noise.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Purple Ocean: Carve a Segment Inside a Proven Market
cards.summary: Enter a market with proven demand, then narrow to a hyperspecific segment you can own 100% instead of fighting for a slice of a red ocean.
cards.use_when: Choosing which product or angle to launch, or repositioning an existing store into a defensible niche.
steps: Confirm the parent market has proven demand (search trends, existing competing offers) rather than betting on creating new desire.
Identify a narrow slice — demographic, life stage, use case or single angle — where few or no offers specialize.
Build the product and PDP positioning around that slice so the buyer feels it was made specifically for them.

The source's examples: beef organ supplements positioned for women's life stages, nootropics positioned for entrepreneurs, pillowcases positioned around overnight acne. The demonstrated mechanism is the targeting and positioning, not the products themselves.
Accept that you are not inventing a new category — you are transferring existing desire from the proven market into your narrower offer.
caveats: The source calls blue ocean (no competition, no proven demand) and red ocean (proven demand, profits competed away) both bad options; purple ocean is the middle, and the source says it must be created, not found.
Segment size must still be big enough to sustain the offer — the source gives no numeric threshold.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Mass Desire Cannot Be Created, Only Transferred
cards.summary: Stop trying to educate the market into wanting your product; channel an existing desire into your offer instead.
cards.use_when: Writing PDP copy, ads or a landing page and wondering whether you need to explain why the customer should care.
steps: Identify the desire your market already holds (from search terms, customer calls, forum language) before writing a single line.
Write copy that connects that existing desire to your product rather than teaching a new problem from scratch.
If your only angle is 'we need to educate people', treat that as a signal to find a proven-demand angle instead.
Use the source's formulation — attributed to Eugene Schwartz — as the decision rule: mass desire can only be transferred, not created.
caveats: This is a direct-response principle the source endorses, not an empirical benchmark; some genuinely new categories have been built, though the source treats that as the rare exception.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Disguise Marketing So It Doesn't Read as an Ad
cards.summary: The highest-performing ad formats work because they don't look like promotions — the same principle behind advertorials, native statics and quiz funnels.
cards.use_when: Designing acquisition creative or landing pages and deciding between obvious ad formats and editorial-style formats.
steps: Balance two moves: contrast to get noticed, and disguise so the customer doesn't feel sold to.
Use formats that read like content — advertorial pages, quiz funnels, native-style ads — while still leading to your offer.
Recognize the principle is decades old (the source cites Gary Halbert's direct-mail observation that people sort mail over the recycling bin) — the format changes, the principle doesn't.
When a format becomes publicly hyped, expect performance to decline as the market floods it; rotate formats while keeping the underlying principle.
caveats: Native/advertorial formats must still comply with platform disclosure rules and local advertising law — the source does not address compliance.
This is the presenter's framework; it is not a guarantee that disguised formats outperform every explicit ad.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Stage-of-Sophistication Check Before Entering a Market
cards.summary: Most markets are at stage four sophistication or later, so an average claim won't work — you need a new mechanism or a new angle.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether a product angle or ad claim is strong enough to compete in a saturated category.
steps: Assess the market using the source's stages (attributed to Eugene Schwartz): stage 1 just make a claim, stage 2 compete on bigger claims, stage 3 build a mechanism, later stages require a new angle or identification.
If competitors are already making inflated claims (stage 2–3), do not enter with a slightly better claim — build a distinct mechanism or niche.
Use the cigarette industry as the source's illustrative example of a market passing through every stage; treat that as illustration, not a template.
Combine with purple ocean positioning: the new mechanism is what lets a small operator avoid head-on competition with funded incumbents.
caveats: Stage bands are a source-specific heuristic, not a measured calculation; the source gives no metric for assigning a stage.
The source says 'most markets are stage four or greater' as an opinion, not a measured fact.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: No Clean Hands: Founders Build Their Own Creatives
cards.summary: Founders should manually write copy and build ads in the early stage to develop market intuition, even though it doesn't scale.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to outsource all ad creative and copy at store launch, or to build the first batch yourself.
steps: Write the first ads, hooks, PDP copy and emails yourself rather than delegating everything from day one.
Accept the messy iteration cycle — the source's illustration is a founder testing 50 dropshipping products with zero winners before the skill compounds.
Treat the manual work as market research: every creative you build teaches you how your customer actually reacts.
Only layer in specialists once you personally understand which hooks and angles convert.
caveats: The source's 50-failures story is a personal anecdote, not a required path; the point is reps and intuition, not the specific number.
This conflicts with a pure leverage/outsourcing approach — the source presents it as a deliberate early-stage trade-off, not a permanent rule.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Money Loves Speed: Shrink the Test-to-Iteration Loop
cards.summary: Compress the time between getting early data and shipping the next variation — sometimes to the same day.
cards.use_when: Running paid creative tests or PDP/offer experiments and deciding how fast to iterate after early signal.
steps: Apply the scientific method quickly: question → hypothesis → test → data → next hypothesis.
When a new ad shows early positive indicators with meaningful data, iterate on that ad partway through the same day rather than waiting for a full cycle.
Keep a tight feedback loop on creative, PDP and offer tests so decisions happen on recent data.
The source frames speed as a structural advantage for small operators vs. slow corporate competitors.
caveats: The source conditions iteration on 'positive early signals with significant data' — acting on thin data is the failure mode, not the method.
No specific spend, CTR or CPA threshold is given for 'positive signal'; set your own with enough data to trust it.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Assume Nothing Until the Data Speaks
cards.summary: Every belief about what will convert is an assumption until a test produces data — and ugly creative often wins.
cards.use_when: Choosing between ad concepts, PDP variants or offers, especially when the team has a strong aesthetic preference.
steps: List the assumptions behind each creative or page decision (this will convert, this looks better, this angle is stronger).
Test them rather than debating them; treat only measured outcomes as real.
Expect ugly, low-production creative to sometimes outspend polished work — the source calls this 'ugly ads = pretty profits' and attributes it to clarity beating aesthetics.
Optimize for clarity of message over production value when resources are limited.
caveats: The source's own framing is that ugly ads *often* win, not that polish never matters — a poor-quality ad can also just fail.
Low-production formats must still meet platform policy and brand-safety requirements for your category.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Write Copy to One Stage of Awareness at a Time
cards.summary: Every prospect sits at a different awareness stage; mixing stages in one asset means you're talking to no one.
cards.use_when: Writing PDP copy, ad hooks or email flows and deciding how much problem-explanation the piece needs.
steps: Classify the audience stage for the asset: unaware, problem aware, solution aware, product aware, or most aware.
Write as if speaking to one hyperspecific person at that stage — do not blend an unaware buyer's framing with a solution-aware buyer's framing in the same piece.
Sequence assets across stages: cold ads speak to problem/unaware, retargeting and email flows speak to product/most aware.
Extract the exact language for each stage from customer research so the copy sounds like the buyer's own words.
caveats: Stages are a copywriting framework the source treats as foundational, not a measured segmentation model.
The source claims you can lead someone from problem aware to product aware, but not speak to unaware and product-aware buyers identically.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Research First: 80% Research, Then Write and Chief
cards.summary: Spend most of the copy process on research from real customer conversations, then write and review with the customer's language.
cards.use_when: Preparing to write a PDP, ad script or email sequence and allocating time across research, drafting and editing.
steps: Allocate roughly 80% of time to research, 5% to writing, 15% to 'chiefing' (reviewing the copy through both the customer's lens and a copywriter's lens) — the source's heuristic.
Prioritize transcripts and calls with your own customers over public forums; the source cites a real customer phrase lifted word-for-word into a top-performing ad hook.
Extract Voice of Customer (VOC) language — the exact phrases buyers use about the problem and desired outcome — and reuse it in hooks and PDP copy.
Use AI deep-research tools to consolidate psychographic and emotional research faster, but still ground it in first-party customer language.
caveats: The 80/5/15 split is the source's rule of thumb, not a measured benchmark.
Public forum research is described as inferior to first-party calls, which requires a system to actually reach customers.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Talk to Your Own Customers for Hook Material
cards.summary: Direct customer conversations produce the most valuable research — specific phrases that become profitable hooks.
cards.use_when: Building a research pipeline for ad hooks, PDP copy or email subject lines and deciding whether forums are enough.
steps: Set up a repeatable process to call or interview customers (the source's team ran calls and reviewed transcripts).
Listen for exact, oddly specific phrases describing the problem — these are candidate hooks.
Test lifted phrases as ad hooks or subject lines; the source reports one customer's exact phrase became one of the most profitable ads in the account.
Use the same transcripts to improve product decisions, not just marketing.
caveats: The source's 'most profitable ad' result is one anecdote, not a guaranteed outcome.
Requires access to customers — early stores with zero buyers must source language another way first.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Hook Anatomy: 80% Copy, 15% Visual, 5% Audio
cards.summary: A video hook is three ingredients — treat the copy as the dominant lever, the scroll stopper as secondary and audio as the smallest needle-mover.
cards.use_when: Producing video ad creative or short-form content and deciding where to spend effort.
steps: Write the first one or two sentences first and hardest — the source weights copy at roughly 80% of hook performance.
Add a scroll stopper (the opening visual) worth about 15%; the test is whether it makes someone say 'what did I just watch?'
Treat audio (voiceover, music) as the smallest mover at roughly 5% — a simple voiceover typically suffices.
Source your scroll stopper from clips that make you and others react viscerally, then test them in ads manager.
caveats: The 80/15/5 weighting is the presenter's stated heuristic, not a measured benchmark.
The 'what did I just watch' test is a source opinion about attention-grabbing visuals; shock value that misrepresents the product can hurt trust and may breach ad policy.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Punch-in-the-Gut Hook Writing
cards.summary: Open with a first line so vivid it feels like a punch, and prioritize clarity over cleverness.
cards.use_when: Writing ad hooks, email subject lines or landing-page headlines where the first line decides whether the rest is read.
steps: Use the PIG framework (punch in the gut, attributed to Chris Haddad): make the first sentence visceral and emotional, good or bad.
During review, repeat the source's editing prompt — 'make this punch harder' — on hooks, subject lines and headlines specifically.
Strip cleverness: if the line is trying to impress, rewrite it to be crystal clear.
Target roughly a fifth-grade reading level (up to eighth grade at most) for hooks and core copy.
Spend disproportionate time here — the source says up to 90% of the effort belongs on the first line/seconds.
caveats: The source's 90% attention figure and reading-level targets are stated rules of thumb, not measured results.
Over-punching without clarity or accuracy can mislead buyers and create refund or policy problems.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Swipe the Philosophy, Not the Words
cards.summary: When borrowing from winning ads, extract the underlying principle and rebuild it for your market instead of rewriting the copy one-to-one.
cards.use_when: Researching competitor or classic ads for inspiration before producing your own creative.
steps: Identify high-performing ads and ask what principle makes them work (contrast, disguise, emotional delta, mechanism).
Do not copy-paste and swap a few words — the source says you learn nothing that way and it only works marginally.
Rewrite from the principle for your specific niche, product and customer language.
Keep a swipe file organized by principle rather than by ad format so you can apply it across ads, emails and PDPs.
caveats: Directly copying competitor copy also carries legal and platform risk — the source advocates principle-level swiping, which avoids this.
This is the presenter's opinion on skill-building; some operators do get short-term lift from close swipes.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Legal Litmus Test for Market Saturation
cards.summary: Once a tactic is being publicly hyped on social media, the source assumes early operators have used it for months or years and it is already getting crowded.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to build a store strategy around a tactic or format you just saw trending online.
steps: When a format (native statics, adveditorials, a new creative style) becomes widely discussed, assume adoption is already advanced.
Prefer building on the underlying principle — content that doesn't look like an ad — rather than the specific hyped format.
Watch for declining performance in a format as public discussion rises; rotate to a less-crowded execution.
Use trend tools to separate rising demand (worth entering) from rising tactic chatter (already crowded).
caveats: This is a heuristic from the presenter's experience, not a measured rule; some publicly discussed tactics still work.
The source's claim about performance decline after broad discussion is anecdotal across accounts he observed.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Emotional Delta: Meet Buyers Where They Are, Lift, Then Return
cards.summary: Copy works hardest when it meets the buyer's current emotional state, raises it, then brings them back so the gap drives action.
cards.use_when: Structuring the emotional arc of a sales page, VSL or long-form ad.
steps: Identify the dominant emotional state of the audience (the source uses survival-niche fear as an example).
Open by meeting them there in their own language, rather than starting from an elevated aspirational tone.
Lift the copy toward courage, willingness or relief to show what solving the problem feels like.
Return them to their current reality so the contrast between where they are and where they could be creates the pull to act.
The source's illustration is entrepreneurs who lose wealth a second time feeling it more sharply than the first — that recalled peak makes the return-to-baseline gap acute.
caveats: The 'map of consciousness' framing is the source's own blend of David Hawkins' material with copywriting; it is a creative framework, not an empirical model.
Avoid manufacturing fear or distress in ways that misrepresent the product or exploit vulnerable buyers.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Copy Is Not Content — Separate the Two Functions
cards.summary: Content chases views and engagement; copy chases sales — treat them as opposite ends of a spectrum and don't expect one to do the other's job.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to repurpose social content into ads or sales pages, or how to allocate budget between content and direct-response assets.
steps: Classify each asset: content sits on the brand/engagement end, copy sits on the direct-response/sales end.
Do not assume a popular content piece will convert — the source cites Peter Kell testing VSLs built from content and reporting every one failed.
Build dedicated direct-response copy for anything whose job is sales (PDP, VSL, ad, email offer).
Use content for top-of-funnel attention and audience building, but route sales through purpose-built copy.
caveats: The source says copy is king and claims small audiences with strong copy can outearn larger audiences — an opinionated position, not a measured finding.
Content-driven brands with integrated commerce sometimes do convert content directly; the source treats that as the exception.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Compare Against Your Own Data, Not Other Operators
cards.summary: Comparing early results to other people's highlight reels creates demoralization without improving decisions.
cards.use_when: During a stretch of failed product tests or soft launch performance, when deciding whether to quit or keep iterating.
steps: When a batch of tests fails, review your own results for learning rather than comparing to publicly reported wins.
Expect long dry spells: the source's illustration is 50 failed dropshipping product tests before profitability.

The source also reports a near-overnight reversal — roughly nine months of losses followed by recovery and multiples of it within two to three months — as an example that timing can shift quickly, not as a promise.
Keep decisions anchored on your data and runway rather than on others' timelines.
caveats: 'Trust the process' is motivational framing; it is not a reason to ignore unit economics or to keep funding a failing offer indefinitely.
The $9,000 loss and $20,000 balance are personal anecdotes, not benchmarks.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Break the Rule Once You Know It (Contrarian Testing)
cards.summary: Learn the standard marketing rules first, then deliberately test against them — treating dogma as an untested assumption.
cards.use_when: When the team rejects a creative or offer idea because it 'violates best practice'.
steps: Before breaking a rule, verify you know the conventional play and why it exists.
Convert the rule into a testable hypothesis and run it as an experiment rather than accepting it.
Actively test variables others dismiss as silly — the source frames this as the mad-scientist posture.
Use counter-intuitive wins as ego checks that improve calibration.
caveats: The source notes most marketing rules were invented by ordinary practitioners decades ago and then repeated — good reason to test, but not proof the rules never worked.
Rules that are platform policies, legal requirements or safety constraints are not optional to break.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Swipe philosophies, not copy, to build ad frameworks
cards.summary: Extract the reusable psychological framework behind a winning ad instead of rewriting its copy for your niche.
cards.use_when: You are researching acquisition creative for a new product launch and deciding what to model your ad angles and hooks on.
steps: Collect ads or brand assets that are already performing in adjacent or same-category markets as reference data.
For each, don't transcribe the copy. Instead ask: what belief is being installed, what mechanism is claimed, what objection is being pre-empted, and in what order?
Write the extracted pattern as a reusable framework (e.g. 'problem-agitate-unconventional-cause-proof-offer') that drops into any niche.
File these frameworks in a persistent library so each new campaign starts from accumulated patterns, not a blank page.
When you do adapt a single ad closely, treat it as a shortcut that expires; the underlying framework is what keeps working when the creative is fatigued.
Feed your framework library into whatever AI writing tool you use so generated variants inherit the principle, not one competitor's wording.
caveats: The source argues one-to-one swiping works a little but does not build durable skill; that is the presenter's opinion, not a measured rule.
Do not copy a competitor's claims or proof points into your own ads — only the structural pattern.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Remove variables: launch on proven demand
cards.summary: Before adding a new product, ad or offer, eliminate the unknowns you can control — especially unproven product demand.
cards.use_when: You are selecting a product to launch or deciding whether to test an entirely new, never-before-sold SKU.
steps: List the variables that determine whether a launch succeeds: media buying, creative, copy, hook, product, market, platform algorithm, etc. The source claims this list can run to 30-40 items.
Cross off anything you can control or verify before testing — most importantly, whether people already buy this category of product.

Prefer markets where demand is already validated: people searching, competitors selling, reviews and category spend already exist. The source says the strongest marketers he knows hunt for proven markets, not unicorns.
Run experiments that change one variable at a time so a result can be attributed; a totally unproven product stacks an extra unknown on top of every other unknown.
Treat 'success is subtraction' as the presenter's framing: the goal is to reduce the number of things that could explain a failed launch.
caveats: The presenter notes that an unproven unicorn product can occasionally win big — he explicitly allows for the exception but argues it's unnecessary risk for most.
The 30-40 variable estimate is a rhetorical figure, not a measured count.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Optimize ads for clarity, not production polish
cards.summary: The source argues ugly, clear ads often outspend cinematic ones; stop optimizing for aesthetics and optimize for message clarity.
cards.use_when: You are briefing a creative team, editing a video ad, or deciding whether to spend budget on higher production value for your store's paid creative.
steps: Read the ad without visuals: does a stranger understand what you sell, who it's for, why it's different and what to do next within the first seconds?
Identify which elements exist only for aesthetics (cinematic b-roll, trend-sound montage, brand film) and cut or demote them if they delay the promise.
Put the strongest claim, the clearest demonstration and the reason to believe in the earliest frames you can.
When comparing a polished and a plain version, test the plain version against the same audience and offer; judge on conversion and spend, not on how the ad looks to you.
Recognize that the presenter's claim is that the clarity of the copy, not ugliness itself, drives the result — there is no proportional 'uglier = more money' rule.
caveats: This is the source's stated opinion based on his own ads; it is not a universal law and some polished creative does perform.
Clarity-first creative still has to comply with platform creative quality rules and brand standards.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Optimize the three economics: ads, funnel, backend
cards.summary: Break business economics into ad economics, funnel economics and backend economics, each with its own two-sided objective.
cards.use_when: You are setting targets for your store's ad account and funnel, or diagnosing which layer is underperforming.
steps: Ads layer: track ad spend, CPM, CPC and CTR. Objective is the lowest cost of traffic at the highest quality — the source warns that the cheapest traffic (e.g. sub-$1 CPM in some geos) is worthless if those users don't buy.
Funnel layer: track conversion rate and average order value (AOV). Objective is the most conversions at the highest possible AOV per order.
Backend layer: track repeat purchase rate, subscriptions, MRR/ARR. Objective is maximizing customer lifetime value (LTV) — the average total cash a customer produces over their relationship with you.
Example of the distinction: a $100 purchase means AOV $100 and LTV $100; if that customer buys again in a few months, LTV becomes $200 while AOV stays $100.
Work the three together: cheap qualified traffic, high conversions at high AOV, then lift LTV via subscription, replenishment or ascension offers.
Note the presenter's disagreement with the camp that says pick either high AOV or an LTV/repeat play — he asserts you can run both.
caveats: The high-AOV-plus-strong-LTV position is the presenter's opinion and he acknowledges it is debatable.
Platform metric names and definitions change; verify current reporting definitions before building dashboards on them.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Use AOV and LTV as levers on your ad bids
cards.summary: A higher-value customer lets you outbid competitors for the same auction because acquiring a customer is the hard part.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest in AOV-raising bundles, upsells or post-purchase offers rather than only optimizing ad creative.
steps: Compute your customer acquisition cost (CAC) and your average revenue per customer from one purchase (AOV).
Compute total revenue per acquired customer over time (LTV) for your store — repeat orders, subscriptions, ascension offers.

If two sellers pay the same $50 CAC but one's customer is worth $80 and yours is worth $100, the source argues you can now spend up to roughly $70 to acquire a customer while the competitor can only sustain $50.
Treat 'the business that can afford to spend the most to acquire a customer wins' as a quoted Dan Kennedy line cited by the presenter, not a proof about your auction.
Raise AOV through bundles, cross-sells, minimum-order offers or plan tiers, and raise LTV through subscription/replenishment or a clear next step after purchase.
Reinvest the extra margin into your bidding headroom to pursue growth rather than only margin.
caveats: The $50/$80/$100 example is illustrative; margins, refunds and fees mean the real extra spendable amount is smaller than the gross difference.
Platform auction mechanics are not purely bid-driven, so extra headroom does not guarantee you win a given impression.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Target a 3:1 LTV-to-CAC ratio as a baseline
cards.summary: LTV:CAC is the source's baseline business health metric, with different targets depending on business model.
cards.use_when: Sanity-checking whether your store's acquisition cost is sustainable before scaling ad spend or raising budgets.
steps: Compute LTV as the average total cash collected from a customer over their lifetime with your brand.
Compute CAC as the blended cost to acquire a customer, including ad spend and media costs.
Divide LTV by CAC to get the ratio; the source suggests 3:1 as a bare minimum for most models.
If the ratio is comfortable, put additional cash back into acquisition to scale; the source notes that scaling often makes CAC worse and requires more creative, so headroom matters.
Recompute the ratio for your model — the source says high-ticket models run very different KPIs from ecom.
caveats: The 3:1 baseline and the 7-10:1 high-ticket range are the source's heuristics, not an industry calculation you should treat as a hard threshold.
LTV assumptions based on projected repeat rates can flatter the ratio; use actual cohort data where possible.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Build retention into the backend from day one
cards.summary: The source argues mastery of LTV is the most common driver in sustainably scaled businesses, achieved through subscription, replenishment or ascension.
cards.use_when: Designing whether your store should push subscriptions or replenishment offers versus one-off purchases.
steps: Map your current repeat purchase rate and the intervals at which customers naturally reorder.

For consumable categories, offer a subscription or auto-replenish option that matches a realistic reorder cadence (the source cites 30-, 60- or 90-day cycles) and make it available at checkout or post-purchase.
For non-consumable or service-like offers, design a next step to move customers up rather than relying on repeated identical purchases.
Track repeat purchase rate and customer LTV as their own KPIs, not as a byproduct of ad reporting.
Recognize that when repeat purchase is zero, LTV equals AOV — the source treats that as a backend constraint to fix.
Accept that CAC is unlikely to fall as you scale; the source argues you'll need to keep adding new creative, so retention is the more durable lever.
caveats: Subscription and replenishment mechanics vary by payment platform and region — verify the current implementation.
Forcing all buyers into subscription can raise friction or cancellations; the source presents it as the norm in consumable categories, not a universal rule.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Treat platform-attributed data as approximate
cards.summary: Post-tracking-policy ad-platform reporting can over- or under-attribute by double digits, so verify with an independent source.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to kill or scale an ad based solely on metrics shown inside the ad platform.
steps: Assume in-platform conversion counts can be off in either direction — the source estimates anywhere from 5-10% on the low end up to 30-50% on the high end.
Use a third-party attribution or analytics tool alongside platform data to establish your own reconciled conversion count.
Reconcile the differences before you make budget decisions; the source warns you can otherwise optimize toward ads that are actually losing money.
Set a policy for which number you trust for reporting, and apply it consistently so scaling decisions aren't based on noise.
Re-check attribution periodically — the source notes platform and OS updates have changed definitions of counts like landing page views and content views.
caveats: The 5-10%/30-50% error ranges are the presenter's estimates, not a measured benchmark, and specific values will drift with platform and privacy-policy changes.
Third-party attribution tools also have limitations; no single source should be treated as exact.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Find the constraint, not the symptom
cards.summary: A bad conversion rate or high checkout drop-off is an indicator of a constraint, not the constraint itself — the source's 'hose' model.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why a funnel step underperforms before spending on redesign or new creative.
steps: Picture the business as a hose; kinks are constraints, and water is traffic and orders.
Track drop-off and KPIs for every funnel step: ad metrics (CPC, CPM, CTR), then landing page view-to-add-to-cart, add-to-cart-to-checkout, and checkout-to-purchase.
Example the source gives: healthy CPM, CPC and CTR with a weak conversion rate is not a constraint — it's a signal that the funnel is the bottleneck, so look deeper.
Example of a real root cause: a very high checkout-page drop-off traced to the store's payment processor not being set up at all.
Focus all effort on the identified constraint until flow improves, then re-measure, since constraint moves as you scale.
caveats: The source warns you will not see every constraint in your own business; partners or outside reviewers can surface what you miss.
A single funnel-step metric can have multiple causes; the point is to instrument each step so you can trace where the loss occurs.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Try to break your funnel before you launch
cards.summary: The source recommends aggressively trying to break your own funnel rather than only quality-checking it — customers will find the gaps if you don't.
cards.use_when: Running pre-launch QA on a new product page, checkout flow, offer or landing page.
steps: Walk the complete purchase path yourself as a first-time visitor: ad or entry point, landing page, product selection, cart, checkout, payment, confirmation.
Test payments deliberately — the source's example was a funnel with high checkout abandonment because the payment processor was never actually set up.
Test failure paths and edge cases: sold-out variants, expired coupons, discount stacking, mobile keyboards, address fields, and post-purchase emails.
Attempt to break the experience on purpose (back button, refresh mid-checkout, interrupted payment) rather than only confirming the happy path works.
Fix what you find before spending on traffic; the source describes launching untested funnels as common and avoidable.
caveats: This is a pre-launch QA discipline, not permission to test real customer funds or commit fraud.
Test environments may behave differently from live payment systems — verify with a real low-value transaction when acceptable.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Use entropy thinking to plan scaling headroom
cards.summary: The source argues systems drift toward disorder as you scale, and only deliberate added energy — time, people or systems — keeps things working.
cards.use_when: Planning how to keep operations — fulfillment, creative pipeline and ad management — intact while increasing order volume.
steps: Assume things you built will degrade, including a winning creative, offer or copy that has been performing; the source treats decay as a fundamental law rather than a failure.
Identify where the bottleneck will appear first as volume grows — creative production, order processing, support or inventory.
Inject one of three forms of 'energy' the source names: your own hours (limited), hires/human capital, or systems and AI tools.

For an ecommerce operation, examples of injecting energy could mean another creative editor, a product data/feed system or an AI-assisted merchandising workflow — but choose based on your actual bottleneck.
Keep external review in place so problems are caught before they compound, since the source argues you cannot see all issues in your own business alone.
Reassess as you scale, because the source claims everything gets harder, including rising CAC, not easier.
caveats: Entropy is used as a metaphor from physics; it is not a predictive model for business outcomes.
Adding people or tools without fixing the actual constraint adds cost without improving throughput.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Treat 'intuition' as accumulated test data, not a launch signal
cards.summary: The source argues gut feel about a product or ad represents pattern experience, and that beginners without test history are mostly rationalizing a cognitive bias.
cards.use_when: You feel certain a product or creative will work and are about to launch it without validated demand.
steps: Ask how many tests in this category you have personally observed — the source frames the claimed 10,000 to 20,000 hours of accumulated data as the basis for useful pattern sense.
If you don't have that history, treat your feeling as a hypothesis to test rather than a reason to commit budget.
Even with experience, the source states he is still wrong frequently — build in the expectation that any given test may fail.
Convert the hypothesis into a structured test with defined variables and success criteria instead of scaling on conviction.
For product selection specifically, replace 'I can feel it' with evidence that people already buy the category.
caveats: This is the presenter's strongly held opinion, delivered bluntly — treat it as a caution against unsupported confidence rather than a rule that experience means nothing.
Experience genuinely does improve judgment in some settings; the source's point is about the unverifiable confidence of beginners.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Simulate customer conversations with AI avatars
cards.summary: When you lack customer research access, the source suggests building AI personas from your research docs to rehearse and mine customer language.
cards.use_when: You need customer insight for copy or positioning but have no customers, can't run interviews, or need more angles.
steps: Write down your research: audience beliefs, objections, prior purchases and buying triggers, ideally from real data if you have it.
Build a small bot or prompt that instructs an AI to act as a specific customer who holds those beliefs — the source suggests one persona per buying angle.
Add your research material as the knowledge source so the persona draws on your findings rather than generic assumptions.
Conduct the conversation hands-free (the source describes walking while talking with earbuds) and ask what made them buy, what they feared and what they compared.
Capture verbatim language and objections to reuse in ads, PDP copy and offer framing.
Repeat across personas to compare angles before committing spend.
caveats: AI personas reflect the inputs you give them; they are not evidence of real customer behavior and should not replace actual customer data when it is available.
Do not confuse simulated insight with validated market research.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Keep pushing AI capability past the 'chatbot' stage
cards.summary: The source frames AI as a multiplier across every metric and urges operators to stay current as capability evolves.
cards.use_when: Deciding how deeply to adopt AI across your store's marketing, operations or support rather than only using one chat tool.
steps: Treat LLM chat as the entry level: useful for copy, research synthesis and analysis.
Move to workflows where tools are chained to complete repeatable tasks with less manual input.
Then to individual agents that can autonomously complete a task, and — as capability permits — coordinated multi-agent systems for a single goal.
Apply AI against specific metrics in your economics, rather than only as a creative generator: research, copy variants, image/creative production, customer support, analytics reconciliation.
Build your own urgency about staying current, since the source argues the adoption window narrows as capability becomes mainstream.
Evaluate any new tool against a specific task in your store rather than adopting it for novelty.
caveats: The five-stage ladder (LLMs → workflows → agents → agentic → AGI) is the presenter's framing, not an established taxonomy, and stage labels shift as tools change.
Verify current capabilities and interfaces of any AI tool before designing processes around specific features.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Elevate a commoditized category with display-worthy packaging
cards.summary: Choose premium packaging and fragrance design that makes a boring product something customers leave on the counter, justifying a higher price.
cards.use_when: Setting branding and price positioning for a commodity product (deodorant, soap, basics, staples) where competing on price destroys margin.
steps: Identify the category's default assumption — for body care, that the product is hidden in a drawer. Design the physical product so it looks intentional and displayable (countertop, shelf, desk).
Treat packaging as the primary price-justification mechanism: a premium look lets you hold a higher price point than competitors in the same functional category.
Raise the sensory experience to a premium standard: make a deodorant smell like a sophisticated perfume rather than only single-note peppermint or lavender, so the product feels like fine fragrance.
When briefing designers and fragrance houses, specify the display context (counter, bathroom, gym bag) so the visual and scent both support being shown off, not concealed.
caveats: Source example (Salt and Stone, body care) is a case example, not a guaranteed margin outcome.
Premium design raises packaging cost; verify unit economics before committing price positioning.
cards.source_name: 9-Figure Founder_ How To Build a Brand That's Impossible To Copy.docx

cards.title: Follow the hero product, even if it wasn't the original bet
cards.summary: Launch with an anchor product but let actual sales data redirect the brand toward whichever SKU becomes the hero.
cards.use_when: Deciding which product to lead with in merchandising, ads and PDP hierarchy when early sales don't match the launch plan.
steps: Launch with a clear, focused entry product (in the Salt and Stone example, sunscreen) to define the brand and shelf presence.
Track SKU performance closely in the first selling cycles; identify which product pulls the most volume and repeat purchase.
When a different SKU (e.g., deodorant) becomes the bestseller, reallocate merchandising hierarchy, ad creative and inventory depth to it rather than defending the original plan.
Keep the original product in the line if it supports positioning and cross-sell, but center the brand's story and acquisition spend on the proven hero.
Measure hero status through repeat purchases and multi-channel sell-through, not just launch-week sell-in.
caveats: The source's sunscreen-to-deodorant pivot is one brand's outcome; the timing and volume support for a pivot will differ by store.
Reallocating to the hero can starve a viable secondary line — set an explicit review window before cutting.
cards.source_name: 9-Figure Founder_ How To Build a Brand That's Impossible To Copy.docx

cards.title: Use a taste-maker inner circle for product approval
cards.summary: Route final scent or design approval through a small trusted circle of discerning customers rather than relying only on trained technical experts.
cards.use_when: Approving a final sensory product decision (fragrance, flavor, texture, color) before committing to production and launch.
steps: Use trained perfumers or specialists ('noses') to develop candidate versions of the product.
Do not let technical experts make the final call alone; assemble a tight inner circle of taste-makers — trusted people with taste representative of your target buyer.
Have the circle evaluate candidate versions blind against the intended positioning and price point.
Only approve a version that satisfies both the technical standard and the taste-makers' gut response.
Iterate rather than settle: the Salt and Stone deodorant went through about 8 formula generations before release.
caveats: The source's '8 generations' and inner-circle method are one brand's process, not a required benchmark.
A circle too close to the founder can create bias — include people who will say no.
cards.source_name: 9-Figure Founder_ How To Build a Brand That's Impossible To Copy.docx

cards.title: Source contract manufacturers by reverse-engineering big-brand supply chains
cards.summary: Find capable factories by identifying who manufactures for large established brands, then map those chains to your own product.
cards.use_when: Sourcing a first contract manufacturer or adding capacity and you don't know which factories can actually meet quality and scale.
steps: Identify large, quality-driven brands in adjacent categories (e.g., Oakley) that demonstrate the manufacturing quality you want.
Research who makes their products — through supplier registries, packaging markings, trade relationships, industry contacts — to build a target factory list.
Approach those factories directly with your product spec, volumes and quality requirements.
Vet each factory on capacity and certifications, not just willingness to take the job.
Confirm they can scale with you before committing: small brands that rush vetting can get locked into a manufacturer unable to grow with demand.
caveats: Source warns that small brands often skip the vetting big brands perform.
Big-brand factory relationships and disclosure practices change; verify current sourcing options rather than assuming a list stays valid.
