The source notes that if the same brand were relaunched tomorrow with the same assets, those ads would perform poorly in isolation.

Before copying a competitor's creative or lander, ask what ecosystem support you actually have: brand recognition, returning purchasers, email/SMS list, organic traffic, and existing first-party data.
If you lack that ecosystem, expect weaker cold-traffic response and compensate with tighter targeting, stronger offer specificity, or problem-first creative rather than brand-vibe creative.
Treat dramatic competitor results as contextual to their situation, not transferable benchmarks.
caveats: This is a presenter's opinion drawn from one brand teardown, not a universal law.
The 0.4% ROAS figure cited for a hypothetical relaunch is illustrative, not a measured benchmark.
cards.source_name: Alo Yoga Teardown_ Creative, Offers, Landers & Acquisition.docx

cards.title: Sending Paid Traffic to a Category Grid: When It Works
cards.summary: Driving paid traffic to a category grid is defensible for fashion brands with heavy on-site merchandising effort, but risky elsewhere—custom landers are the safer default.
cards.use_when: Choosing between a category grid and a custom landing page as the destination for paid ad traffic
steps: Assess whether you are in fashion or another fast-merchandised category where browsing a filtered grid matches buyer intent; the source considers this defensible only in that context and questionable otherwise.
If you are not in fashion, default to custom landing pages tailored to the ad's promise instead of a raw category grid.
If you do send traffic to a category grid, assign a specific team member to own its conversion rate and watch it closely.
Have that owner continuously adjust the filtering, sort order, and product ordering top-to-bottom as products go out of stock, size curves shift, and new products arrive.
Re-evaluate the grid regularly, because a stale grid with out-of-stock or poorly ordered items will erode click-to-cart conversion.
caveats: Fashion-specific advice; the source explicitly warns non-fashion brands to be careful.
Category grids require ongoing labor, so don't choose one unless you can staff the maintenance.
cards.source_name: Alo Yoga Teardown_ Creative, Offers, Landers & Acquisition.docx

cards.title: Stop Rebuilding the Ad Account Every Few Weeks
cards.summary: The source advises against churning creative every ~24 days and rebuilding the account every ~3 weeks, arguing you should squeeze winning ads instead.
cards.use_when: Setting your paid-social creative refresh cadence and deciding whether to retire or retain winners
steps: Recognize that constant account rebuilds keep the account 'fresh' and align with a front-end brand-distribution strategy, but sacrifice the compounding performance of proven winners.
When you have a winning ad, keep running it rather than retiring it on a fixed schedule; the source says it has never seen double-downing on winners fail for a fashion brand.
If a winner is selling out, place quick replenishment orders to keep stock available—the source cites getting more inventory within about 3 to 4 weeks as the enabling condition.

When you find a winning product, keep ordering and running it for as long as the market wants it, since you have likely found a trend to lean into; use it to convert new customers who then become repeat buyers.
Reserve creative churn for fatiguing or losing ads, not for winners.
caveats: The 24-day creative cycle and 3-week account rebuild are descriptions of the teardown brand's practice, not recommended benchmarks.
Doubling down assumes reliable replenishment; without it you'll just run out of stock.
cards.source_name: Alo Yoga Teardown_ Creative, Offers, Landers & Acquisition.docx

cards.title: Plan preseason acquisition as part of the full Black Friday budget
cards.summary: Evaluate early-season demand building alongside sale-period margin, cash and delayed conversion.
cards.use_when: Planning Q4 / Black Friday budget allocation for your store and deciding how much to spend before sale week versus during it.
steps: Define the full planning window explicitly: September is outside calendar Q4, which runs October through December.
Assess how earlier traffic converts during the sale using mature cohorts and, where feasible, an incrementality test.
Model sale discounts, product margin and repeat purchase assumptions before setting CAC tolerance.
Treat the source's 31-43% September-October allocation as a portfolio heuristic for an extended seasonal plan, not a universal Q4 requirement.
Reconcile spend and contribution across the complete measurement window.
caveats: Preseason attribution alone does not prove incremental demand; adjust for the store's category, cash and campaign calendar.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Use attribution-window gaps to detect delayed seasonal conversion
cards.summary: Compare mature attribution windows to understand reporting lag without calling the difference causal lift.
cards.use_when: Interpreting your ad platform reporting in late October and early November, and deciding whether weak pre-sale ROAS is real weakness or a lagged signal.
steps: Compare available short and longer click windows on consistent cohorts and revenue definitions.
Wait for the longer window to mature before estimating how much conversion is delayed.
Use the observed lag to inform pacing scenarios, with uncertainty around how this season differs.
Separate attribution maturation from incrementality; the same sale being credited later does not prove the ad caused it.
Reconcile with net sales, contribution and controlled tests where available.
caveats: Source percentage gaps and historical reattribution examples are case observations; current platform windows may differ.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Build a post-treatment window into pre-season spend measurement
cards.summary: Spend that runs before a sale produces measurable incremental lift after the test window ends, and this lift is much larger around Black Friday than in evergreen periods.
cards.use_when: Designing geo-holdout or incrementality experiments for your store, and deciding how long to measure after a test ends before calling it a loss.
steps: Understand post-treatment lift: after an incrementality experiment's treatment window closes and you return spend to normal, measured incremental revenue can continue to appear. Source (House) reports experiments ending 3+ weeks before Black Friday produced a 105% post-treatment lift, and close-to-Black-Friday experiments added 41% of incremental value after the treatment window.

For your own storefront: if you scale spend in a region before the sale and then pull back, do not close the experiment at the pullback date — extend the measurement window to capture delayed conversions the sale triggers.

Category context from the source: fashion/apparel showed 93% post-treatment lift; health/wellness/food/beverage (CPG) showed 30%. If you're in fashion, backfill more pre-spend than if you're in CPG (these are source-cited category figures, not universal).
Source's framing: holding back budget ahead of Black Friday is 'digging a deeper hole,' not saving dry powder — because the delayed effects are large.
Reconcile experiment conclusions against marginal, not blended, returns so you don't credit lift the experiment didn't cause.
caveats: These figures come from a specific incrementality platform's report and one presenter's portfolio; they are illustrative, not benchmarks for your category.
Incrementality tools and their measurement windows change; verify current methodology before committing budget.
Post-treatment effects can also reflect organic seasonality — the source itself flags the causal-measurement limits of observational data.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Back-spend into the sale to avoid shrinking your own funnel
cards.summary: Underspending before a sale reduces top-of-funnel reach exactly when you need it, making the sale-conversion spike smaller.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to pull back or maintain ad spend in the days before your Black Friday sale opens.
steps: Recognize the mechanism: pre-sale conversion rates dip because shoppers hold out for the known upcoming sale. Converting spend fell in the source's portfolio in early November.
Do not interpret that dip as a reason to cut spend. Cutting spend shrinks top-of-funnel awareness and traffic, so when the sale opens there's a smaller funnel to collapse into purchases.
A sale collapses the whole existing funnel — people who knew about the brand but hadn't bought — into a revenue peak, which is why every sale is followed by a slump.
Deliberately back-spend into the sale period so the funnel is bigger when it opens; the ROAS will look weak before the sale and strong during it.
Source's Q4 allocation recommendation is roughly doubling November spend relative to October while keeping meaningful September/October pre-spend — not a light warm-up plus an all-November bet.
In the source's own client data, stores spending $500K–2M in November spent ~1.76–1.8x their October spend; the source treats that as a reasonable pattern, not a rule.
caveats: The 1.76–1.8x multiplier and the 31–43% Q4 split are source-portfolio observations from specific spend brackets (November spend between $500K and $2M+).
Small brands with a smaller addressable audience may hit frequency limits faster — see the saturation card.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Scale to marginal contribution margin (CM3), not blended ROAS
cards.summary: Compare incremental contribution with incremental spend rather than relying only on blended CAC or ROAS.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to push or pull ad spend during a peak sale weekend in your store.
steps: Define pre-ad contribution and CM3 explicitly so product costs, fulfillment, fees and advertising are included once.
Estimate incremental new customers and contribution from a controlled or otherwise well-qualified spend change.
Marginal CAC is change in spend divided by incremental customers; average CAC can remain acceptable while the last spend increment loses money.
At constant cost mix, break-even revenue ROAS is 1 divided by the pre-ad contribution rate expressed as a decimal.
Stop or reassess when the next spend increment fails the contribution, cash or profit objective.
caveats: Observed day-to-day differences are not automatically causal marginal returns; changes in demand, mix and reporting lag can confound them.
A flattened attribution ratio does not prove a campaign is only harvesting demand.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Use revenue-spend elasticity to cut spend, never to scale it
cards.summary: Use observational spend/revenue elasticity only as a diagnostic, with explicit mathematical and causal limitations.
cards.use_when: Reviewing intraweek or intraday ad performance during a sale and deciding whether to cut spend on a channel or account.
steps: For positive spend and revenue with changed spend, compute log(revenue2/revenue1) divided by log(spend2/spend1).
Do not compute when spend is unchanged, and treat near-zero denominators as unstable. The value is not bounded between zero and two.
Investigate promotion timing, seasonality, pricing, stock and attribution before interpreting the association.
Use the source's spend-cut preference as a conservative hypothesis; correlation alone does not prove a cut will improve profit.
Triangulate with contribution and better-designed spend tests.
caveats: Smoothing does not remove confounding or establish causation.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Expect CPMs to spike and reach to fall during November — buy before the auction inflates
cards.summary: Auction pressure pushes CPMs up 25–50% during Black Friday, so November is a harvest period, not an acquisition period — you can only convert what you already built.
cards.use_when: Setting your media plan and reach assumptions for November and deciding when to buy audience-building impressions.
steps: Source data across ~$50–100M of ad spend: CPMs run 25–30% above October baseline starting around Nov 12, then spike higher through the weekend.

Triple Whale's 2025 Black Friday report cited in the source: Meta CPMs up ~50% period-on-period; Google up only ~10%. Meta CPA improved and ROAS improved (offsetting margin compression); Google CPA and ROAS both worsened.
Treat November as bottom/mid-funnel harvesting: you cannot meaningfully buy top-of-funnel audiences — you can only harvest what you already built.
Plan reach shortfall explicitly. If you spend the same budget at spike CPMs you reach fewer people; budget for lower reach or accept fewer impressions.
Build your top-of-funnel reach earlier (September/October) so it's available to convert when the sale opens.
Expect ad inventory growth of ~18% (2025) to compress in 2026, which makes price-per-ad increases likely — don't count on sub-2025 CPMs.
caveats: The 25–30% and 50% figures come from different source reports with different methodology, as the source itself notes. Treat as directional.
Platform pricing and inventory policies change; verify current data before locking budgets.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Exploit the post-Christmas CPM window (Q5) with a deliberate offer
cards.summary: CPMs drop massively between Dec 16–31, making it a cheap period to roll a fresh offer into if you have the inventory and creative prepared.
cards.use_when: Planning a post-Christmas promotion or deciding whether to extend a sale into the low-competition late-December window.
steps: Reserve a December offer (bundle, gift-with-purchase, clearance) to launch after Christmas, when auction pressure falls.

Expect CPMs to be lower than Black Friday, but note they may inflate modestly if your offer performs very well — source explains CPM is correlated with expected action rate on the landing page, so Meta charges more when your store converts well.
Have creative and landing pages pre-built for this window so you can launch without delay and capture the cheap inventory.
Use this period to move any remaining Grade C or slow inventory rather than discounting it inside Black Friday.
Reconcile the window against your P&L, since a Q5 offer on clearance stock will run at lower margins.
caveats: The source calls it 'Q5' but this is jargon, not a platform-defined period.
CPM direction and magnitude vary year to year; verify current auction conditions before committing.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Recognize that audience saturation is offer/creative fatigue, not reach exhaustion
cards.summary: Frequency barely rises during Black Friday, so declining response is usually fatigue on the offer or creative, not running out of people.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why an ad set or account stops responding mid-Black-Friday and deciding whether to rotate creative or expand audiences.
steps: Source portfolio data: baseline frequency 1.75, peaking at 1.96 during Black Friday, pulling back to 1.82 in Q5. The source says nobody really ran out of people.
When an account stops responding at peak, first check offer and creative fatigue, not audience size.
Only treat it as a reach problem if you under-spent into the period and built too small a funnel (see the funnel-flattening card).
Rotate creatives and refresh offers before broadening audiences, since the source suggests you usually have reach left.
For smaller brands, expect frequency to climb higher if you don't have a large audience pool — the source's data is from large brands.
caveats: The 1.75/1.96/1.82 figures are portfolio-level from large brands; small brands with narrow audiences may hit real reach limits.
Frequency thresholds for 'too high' differ by channel and audience — verify in your own account.
The source notes exhaustion can sometimes be an audience-reach issue if you didn't spend enough into the period.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Model base and stretch scenarios with pre-agreed unlock thresholds
cards.summary: Enter Black Friday with two budgets and clear efficiency/spend unlock rules so spend can push up or pull back without waiting for owner approval.
cards.use_when: Setting up your Black Friday pacing plan and delegating spend authority for the peak weekend.
steps: Build a base case and a stretch case, each with explicit efficiency gates (e.g. CM3 floor, marginal CAC ceiling, ROAS band).
Define the conditions under which the team is auto-authorized to move to the stretch case — the source calls these 'pre-agreed efficiency and spend unlocks.'
Define the conditions that trigger a pullback, so cuts don't require a live check-in either.

Treat the budget as a ceiling to be deployed based on incremental returns, not a target to be spent. Source is explicit: 'The goal's not to spend the budget.' This matters most for large retailers with a mandated spend figure.
Document the stretch target as a team goal — source says it gave the team something to work toward and prevented coasting on the base case.
Keep the pacing sheet updated daily (or intraday at very high spend levels) against the unlock thresholds.
caveats: Source admits people underspend pre-sale because conversion rates dip — the unlock structure is designed to counter that tendency.
Intraday/hourly pacing is not warranted for every account; source says it's overkill for many.
Not all teams have authority to run auto-unlocks — agree in advance on who approves.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Prepare Google Ads as a harvest platform, not a ramp platform
cards.summary: Google Ads needs structural preparation (asset, feed, and promotion updates) before Black Friday; scaling budgets in real time is usually the wrong move.
cards.use_when: Setting up Google Search, Shopping and PMax campaigns ahead of a Black Friday sale, and deciding whether to scale Google budget during the weekend.
steps: Update titles, descriptions and assets across search and PMax to be Black Friday-relevant and contextualized.
Roll over Merchant Center product feeds, set up promotion feeds, and add promotional assets and promotional titles to search and PMax.
Add discounted price lines so pricing is consistent across feeds and landing pages.
Expect these preparation steps to lift CTR and conversion rate versus competitors who skip them — the source treats this as the main Google lever, not budget pushes.

During the weekend, avoid cranking Google budget just because ROAS looks high. Source's Triple Whale citation: on Google, CPA worsened and ROAS worsened during the Black Friday weekend (period-on-period), and impression-to-purchase dropped — Google was less efficient, not more.
Source flags that Google ROAS often looks inflated because Meta traffic and branded searches are flowing in — that demand capture, not Google's own efficiency, drives the number.
Use paid incrementality checks (geo holdout) to distinguish Google-driven revenue from demand it simply captured.
caveats: Google interfaces and PMax features change; verify current asset and feed requirements before rolling over.
Triple Whale data cited is one large dataset; results vary by account.
Source's recommendation is not to eliminate Google spend, just to avoid blind budget scaling.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Employ cost-cap campaigns during Black Friday to find the marginal frontier
cards.summary: Cost caps are avoided year-round by Blue Sense, but used during Black Friday to learn how much volume the account can absorb before diminishing returns.
cards.use_when: Testing the maximum efficient spend level in a Meta account during a high-demand sale period.
steps: Understand the source's default position: Blue Sense avoids cost caps year-round, citing account volatility and high creative volume demands.
During Black Friday, run a limited set of cost-cap campaigns alongside maximize-volume campaigns.
Observe what the cost-cap campaigns spend to — this reveals the marginal frontier the account can absorb.
Use that read to inform how aggressively to push the maximize-volume campaigns.
Do not use cost caps as the primary scaling mechanism for the whole account; they are a diagnostic tool in this context.
caveats: The source is explicitly anti-cost-cap in normal periods, so this is a Black Friday-specific tactic.
Cost-cap mechanics and performance vary by account; test before expanding.
The source calls this a portfolio-level technique, not a universal rule.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Build an hourly-delayed attribution multiplier for intraday pacing
cards.summary: During Black Friday, spend peaks 5–7am but revenue peaks 7–11am, so early hourly ROAS must be adjusted with per-hour multipliers before you act on it.
cards.use_when: Running intraday media buying on Black Friday and interpreting early-morning ROAS to make push/pull decisions.
steps: Expect spend to peak in many accounts between 5:00 and 7:00am, while revenue peaks between 7:00 and 11:00am.
Do not compare 5am ROAS to the daily target directly — it will look artificially weak because that revenue attributes later in the day.
Build per-hour delayed attribution multipliers: the source gives an example of a 5am reading at ROAS 1 that should be treated as roughly ROAS 2 once reconciled.
Pull conversion rates by hour. The source says this has been a 'huge unlock' — it indicates ability to push spend in real time without relying on platform attribution, which lags.
Reconcile intraday spend decisions against the marginal/CM3 framework, not just hourly ROAS.
Only apply hourly pacing if spend volume is high enough to justify it — source says it's overkill for many accounts and only worth it at very high spend with rotating offers.
caveats: Hourly pacing is complex; the source warns you need to understand the delayed revenue mechanics before acting.
The 5am ROAS 1 -> ROAS 2 example is illustrative, not a fixed multiplier.
For large retailers with significant organic demand, hourly pacing may be driven by correlation rather than causation.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Choose profit play vs inventory play before setting CAC tolerance
cards.summary: Black Friday has two distinct strategic modes — maximize contribution profit or clear slow inventory — and the answer materially changes how hard you push spend and how you KPI the weekend.
cards.use_when: Deciding your Black Friday objective for a store with slow-moving or Grade C inventory, and setting the media team's CAC and KPI thresholds.
steps: Decide in advance which play you're running: profit play (maximize contribution profit by spending to the marginal frontier) or inventory/cash play (clear slow-moving inventory at whatever discount it takes).
Discount limits are set by margin and cash/stock — source notes you can only discount a product as much as its margin allows, and the natural candidates are Grade C inventory that hasn't moved.

If you're running an inventory play, authorize the media team to accept negative incremental contribution margin at the end of the weekend to sell through stock — otherwise they'll pull back autonomously.
If you want to do both, the source suggests a gift-with-purchase bundle with multiple tiers — it moves greasy inventory (as free gifts) while still maximizing margin on the paid products.

Understand the trade-off: the source states that straight 80% off greasy inventory is a purer inventory play than bundling it as free gifts onto good (non-discounted) products — one mode will be better than the other, depending on the goal.
Tell the media team which play is in force before the weekend, because it changes both the CAC tolerance and the KPI they're managed on.
caveats: Source is explicit that you cannot do both equally well — one play will always dominate.
The gift-with-purchase structure assumes you have inventory that's genuinely slow-moving and can be bundled without cannibalizing paid product.
Cash and margin constraints, not just strategy, determine what's feasible.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Pre-build backup offers and creative for trade-reactive Black Fridays
cards.summary: If you manage to trade/revenue targets and need to pivot offers mid-weekend, build the backup offers, landing pages, and ad creative in advance so you can switch on without production panic.
cards.use_when: Planning Black Friday operations for a store that reacts to real-time trade numbers rather than committing to one fixed offer.
steps: Identify in advance what the backup offers are — the source's examples: a gift-with-purchase, a 'TAF' (tell-a-friend / referral), free shipping, a bundle, or a deeper site-wide sale.
Build the landing pages and ad creative for each backup offer before Black Friday, and pre-load creative into ad accounts so it can be turned on instantly.
Define the trade trigger for each backup offer — the numbers that tell you to switch.
If the switch happens, redirect traffic to the new landing pages and turn on the pre-loaded creative rather than trying to edit hundreds of live assets in real time.
Accept that the pre-loaded creative may never go live — it's insurance, not waste.
caveats: The source says it is 'not super pro' on being reactive to trade, but acknowledges it if the business's revenue target requires it.
Pivoting offers across hundreds of live creatives in real time is very difficult and stressful — the whole point of pre-building is to avoid that.
Backup offer structures and ad account pre-loading capabilities may vary by platform; verify current features.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Forecast creative volume from peak ad spend, not from a fixed creative count
cards.summary: Black Friday creative volume should be back-propagated from peak daily spend divided by realistic per-ad spend ceilings, not from a target number of assets.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many ad creatives your store needs to produce for a high-spend Black Friday.
steps: Look at last year's November data: what did your highest-spending individual ad spend per day? The source's pulled data: highest observed was ~$12.5K/day in one AUD account; most evergreen ads spent $4–8.5K; realistic working ceiling is roughly $8–13K/day.
If you want a shortcut, the source's functional estimates: average evergreen ad ~$5K/day; realistic winner ceiling ~$10–12K/day.

For your peak spend day, divide peak budget by the working per-ad ceiling to estimate how many ads you need. Example from source: $150K peak / $10–12K per ad requires 12–18 ads that can hold that spend — not 12–18 ads total.
Include a diversity buffer: the source shows that the bottom 80% of ads still hold ~54% of spend — winners alone won't carry a large account.
Distinguish clearly between 'has 12–18 ads running' and 'has 12–18 ads that can each absorb $10K/day in spend.'
caveats: The $4–12.5K per-ad figures come from the source's portfolio in AUD; your ceiling depends on your account size, offer strength and market.
The '18% of spend held by top 3 ads' and related concentration figures are portfolio data from large brands; concentration is higher for smaller accounts.
Do not treat per-ad spend ceilings as fixed limits — they are observed working ranges, not hard platform caps.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Recognize that Pareto's principle does not apply to Black Friday creative concentration
cards.summary: Unlike evergreen periods, Black Friday spend is spread broadly across ads — the top 20% do not hold 80% of spend, so you need volume across the tail.
cards.use_when: Planning how many creatives to ship for a Black Friday campaign and whether you can rely on a small set of winners.
steps: Source finding: across the portfolio, the top single ad held ~7% of spend, top 3 held 17%, top 5 held 23%, top 10 held 33%, and top 20 held 46%. So the bottom 80% of ads still held ~54% of spend.
Abandon the assumption that the top 20% of ads will hold 80% of spend during Black Friday — it is not true across the source's portfolio.

Account size changes concentration: stores that spent under $250K in November had their top 20% of ads hold 53% of spend (then 44%, then 33% as size grew). Bigger accounts had more distribution across the tail.
Interpretation: individual ads have daily spend ceilings, so a large account naturally distributes spend more widely — plan creative volume accordingly.
Don't over-invest in perfecting the top few creatives; you need breadth because the tail does meaningful work.
caveats: These figures come from the source's portfolio of mostly large brands — smaller accounts may show higher concentration.
Concentration figures may shift year to year with platform changes and account structure.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Use the creative format mix from last year's Black Friday portfolio as a planning reference
cards.summary: A balanced creative format mix (offer statics, overlayed evergreen, creator/founder, VSL, early access) with roughly defined spend shares held up well across a large portfolio.
cards.use_when: Deciding what types of ad creative to produce for a Black Friday campaign, and what share of spend each should hold.
steps: Source's recommended allocation: offer static ~19% of spend; offer-overlay evergreen catalog ~18%; creator/founder ads at the highest share (with founder content optional, redistributed to others if unavailable); product/VSL top-of-funnel ads at a small share; and early access/VIP ads where applicable.

Understand why each format exists: catalog evergreen showed high ROAS in the data but high frequency too — it's bottom-of-funnel retargeting, so it naturally converts well but shouldn't be over-indexed.
Offer statics are the highest-volume format — keep them 'stupid simple': discount, end date, legible at thumbnail size.
Make three variants of the same offer: vary the people in the creative, the product, or the offer itself — the source says this alone can spin out 50 statics quickly.
Test legibility by shrinking the ad: if the sale discount is unreadable at thumbnail size, redo it. Also check that 9:16 feed placements don't cut off the offer.
Put the offer or deadline in the first line of copy, because copy truncates on story and some feed placements.
No single format wins outright — the source explicitly says you need diversity of concepts, not just formats.
caveats: The 19%/18% shares are the source's recommendation from portfolio data, not validated benchmarks for your store.
Bold terminology ('stupid simple') is the source's stylistic framing, not a strict rule.
Format performance varies substantially by category — fashion, for example, does not typically run VSLs.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Don't turn off evergreen campaigns for Black Friday — overlay them instead
cards.summary: Evergreen campaigns carry campaign-level conversion history, so turning them off resets learnings; overlay the Black Friday offer onto duplicates instead.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to pause evergreen campaigns during Black Friday and how to incorporate sale messaging into existing winners.
steps: Source: evergreen campaigns should hold ~50–60% of spend during Black Friday — the portfolio observed this share last year.
Duplicate your best-performing evergreen ads (including fatigued winners from a year ago) and badge them with the Black Friday offer.
Do not turn off the original evergreen ads when you run the overlayed version — the source says this is the single biggest mistake people make during Black Friday.

If you edit copy on evergreen ads to be Black Friday-specific, weigh the pros (more bottom-of-funnel messaging) against the cons (resetting the learning phase). The source treats this as a per-account decision, not a rule.
Ensure DPA catalog copy includes the sale messaging — the source cites a poll where 74% of cold brands had no written messaging in their catalog and only 3% included sale messaging.
Avoid pausing and restarting evergreen campaigns, which disrupts optimization learning.
caveats: The 50–60% of budget figure comes from the source's portfolio, not a universal rule.
Learning-phase behavior changes with platform updates — verify current treatment before making large changes.
Some ad platforms penalize significant-editing of live ads; the source acknowledges the trade-off rather than giving a clean answer.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Distinguish creative quality from offer and product effects during Black Friday
cards.summary: Because the offer is doing so much work during Black Friday, ROAS during this period cannot reliably tell you whether a creative is good.
cards.use_when: Reviewing Black Friday ad performance and trying to decide which creatives to retire or scale.
steps: Recognize the confound: a 50%-off best seller will show a great ROAS even with mediocre creative; a strong scroll-stopping ad on a full-price, slow-moving product may show poor ROAS.
During Black Friday, do not treat top-ROAS ads as automatically the best creative. Use creative metrics (CTR, CPC, scroll-stop rate) to diagnose quality instead of ROAS.

Where practical, judge creative at the ad set level rather than the ad level, because multi-touch optimization plus last-click attribution plus Meta's breakdown effect makes ad-level ROAS unreliable during this period.
This flips normal practice — the source notes that in evergreen periods it would be wrong to judge ads on CPC alone; Black Friday is the exception because ROAS becomes noisy.
Use this diagnostic framing in your post-Black Friday retro to decide which concepts to carry forward, rather than blindly cutting the lowest ROAS ads.
caveats: The source is explicit that this is a Black Friday-period exception — it does not endorse CPC-based creative judgment year-round.
CPA/CPC thresholds themselves may shift with auction dynamics; compare within the same period.
Ideal approach is holdout-based incrementality, but that is often impractical for individual creatives.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Scrape competitor Black Friday pages and ads for next year's planning
cards.summary: November is a strong scraping period because everyone is publishing their landing pages, offers and ads simultaneously — use it to build next year's data set.
cards.use_when: Running competitive research during Black Friday week to inform next year's Black Friday strategy for your store.
steps: Scrape competitors' Black Friday landing pages, offers, and ad creative during November while they're all live.
Record the number of distinct creative concepts each brand is running, not just total ad volume.

Source observation from a November scrape of fashion brands: higher-performing fashion brands ran more distinct core concepts (True Classic ~11, Ridge ~10, Threadheads ~9, Alo ~7, Gymshark ~6), while lower-performance-marketing peers ran fewer.

Note the counterexample: Skims shipped 429 unique visuals but only three core concepts — the source argues this is not advisable at large scale because you need concept breadth, not just visual volume.
Store the scraped set for next year's retrospective and creative planning, alongside your own account data.
Use it to sharpen your own concept count target — the source's takeaway is that diversity of concepts is what matters, not diversity of formats.
caveats: Brand names and concept counts are examples from one scrape of the source's fashion portfolio — not benchmarks for your category.
Scraping methodology and platform access change; verify what's permissible under platform terms before scraping.
Not all fashion brands follow the concept-volume pattern; the source itself flags Skims as an exception.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Design Black Friday statics for one-second offer legibility and brand recognition
cards.summary: There is no single correct Black Friday aesthetic — a static succeeds if the offer is legible in under a second and the brand still looks like itself.
cards.use_when: Producing Black Friday ad statics or PDP hero assets where you need the offer and the brand to be instantly clear.
steps: Test against two criteria: (1) can a viewer understand the offer in under one second, and (2) do they still recognize the brand despite the discount context?
Keep the offer simple — 'up to X% off' style statements that are clear at a glance.
Keep product and logo identifiable; the source uses examples where the discount is clear and the brand logo remains visible.
Check legibility at thumbnail size during production, and check that feed placements don't crop the offer (9:16 layouts).
Put the offer and deadline in the first line of ad copy, since it truncates on story and some feed placements.
Apply the same legibility test to your PDP and landing page hero — the source frames legibility in under a second as the core requirement, which transfers to store surfaces.
caveats: The one-second legibility criterion is a design principle from the source, not a tested conversion benchmark.
Brand aesthetic norms differ substantially by category — a distinctive 'common format' in one brand's category may look out of place elsewhere.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Judge Q4 creative at ad set level, not ad level
cards.summary: During Black Friday, ROAS is unreliable at ad level because of multi-touch optimization plus last-click attribution; evaluate creative at ad set level instead.
cards.use_when: Deciding which Q4/Black Friday creatives to scale, pause or refresh when ad-level ROAS looks noisy or contradictory across the account.
steps: Recognize that ROAS degrades during the Q4 window: you are running multi-touch optimization but reporting on last-click attribution, so ad-level numbers are even more broken than usual. The source treats this as a general rule that matters more at Black Friday.

Pull the account's historical CPC-vs-ROAS or spend-vs-ROAS correlation for prior periods. The source notes R-squared is very low and the data is muddy, meaning CPCs and core KPIs often do not track each other reliably.
Because of that, judge creative performance at the ad set level rather than the ad level during the sale window. Ad set level aggregates enough signal to survive the attribution noise.
Treat the ROAS number during Black Friday as directional rather than precise, and lean more heavily on the supplementary metrics (CPC, CPM, spend pacing, contribution margin) that remain more stable.
Flag that Meta's breakdown effect compounds the unreliability of ad-level ROAS, so don't make pause/scale calls on a single ad's ROAS reading.
Verify the current Meta reporting interface and attribution options before acting, since breakdown behavior and available windows change.
caveats: This is a source-specific recommendation, not a platform rule; the reliability gap still exists the rest of the year, it just worsens during the sale window.
Even ad set level numbers can be distorted if the account structure is unusual or spend is very concentrated.
LTV/CAC and contribution margin remain the underlying truth metrics when ROAS is unreliable.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Creative is a CPM lever — build volume and diversity to win the auction
cards.summary: Source data shows better creative quality, diversity and volume are qualitatively tied to lower CPMs, so treat creative as your main CPM control during the expensive Q4 window.
cards.use_when: Planning Q4 creative inventory or trying to control rising CPMs during the Black Friday auction when media is materially more expensive.
steps: Reframe the mental model: creative is a CPM lever, not a conversion lever. In Q4 your biggest controllable cost input is often how efficiently your creative wins auctions.

Look at your own account's historical relationship between creative volume/diversity and CPM. The source found a qualitative relationship in last year's Black Friday data: accounts with more diverse and higher-volume creative pushed CPMs down.
Hypothesize why: with more creative variety, you have more opportunities to win auctions and accrue more impressions, which likely explains the CPM benefit.

Set a creative volume target from forecast spend, not from a fixed number of ads. During the September planning window, estimate required creative volume for your target spend and check whether you have enough Facebook pages or ad accounts to support that volume.
Phase that inventory across the sale: before-launch/teaser/early-access, launch, mid-sale refresh, and final 24–48 hour scarcity/deadline messaging.
Recognize that in Q4 creative volume, not budget, becomes the binding constraint at higher spend levels.
caveats: The correlation is qualitative, not a controlled causal proof; the source itself attributes the relationship to higher impression volume winning more auctions.
Do not assume the same CPM benefit at any spend level; it is a directional pattern from a specific dataset.
Facebook page/account limits and Meta policies change; verify current platform rules before scaling page count.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Phase creative across the Black Friday window
cards.summary: Build Q4 creative as a scheduled sequence: teaser/early access to launch to mid-sale refresh to final scarcity, so creative matches the demand curve rather than running one static set.
cards.use_when: Planning and scheduling Q4 creative production and launches so the store isn't running the same assets from early November through Cyber Monday.
steps: Split your Q4 creative plan into phases: (1) before-launch teaser and early-access content, (2) launch content, (3) mid-sale refresh, (4) final 24–48 hour scarcity and deadline messaging.
Produce assets for each phase before the window starts; the source treats this as table stakes but stresses the production load falls on the brand.
During the November 17–December 2 peak, refresh creative on schedule based on the mid-sale refresh point and the final 24–48 hour deadline push, rather than reacting only when performance drops.
Use the phased structure to also prevent offer fatigue by rolling through multiple offers rather than one static offer across the whole window.
Lock offers before making creative, since you cannot produce launch/scarcity assets until you know the offer.
Coordinate the phase boundaries with your actual sale calendar (Black Friday, Cyber Monday, and the cheaper post-peak window) so the last phase lands inside the true deadline period.
caveats: The exact phase timing depends on your own sale calendar and offer ladder; the source gives the sequence, not fixed dates for each phase.
Creative production capacity is the limiter — if you can't produce all phases, prioritize launch and final 24–48 hour deadline assets.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Model November cohort LTV before setting CAC tolerance
cards.summary: November-acquired customers often repeat substantially worse than February cohorts, so check your own cohort data before carrying the same CAC allowance into Black Friday.
cards.use_when: Setting Q4 CAC targets, ad efficiency goals, or aggressive spend allowances during the Black Friday window.
steps: Pull 6-month repeat-rate cohort data for November-acquired customers versus a normal month (the source used February as the comparison) for the last two years.

In the source's 10-brand sample, the November cohort delivered an average 38.5% 6-month repeat lift versus 63% for February — roughly half — but two of the ten brands showed no difference at all. So this is a per-brand question, not an assumption.
If November customers are materially worse, tighten CAC tolerance for the Q4 window and expect lower 12-month LTV from those customers.
If there is no difference in your data, keep CAC tolerance unchanged; the source explicitly says nothing else in the plan needs to change in that case.

Where the difference is real, adjust efficiency targets on two fronts: (a) discount compression of gross profit, and (b) reduced lifetime value of the acquired cohort. The source describes the default CAC allowance as 'wrong twice' if both are ignored.
caveats: The 50%/63%/38.5% figures are an average across one specific client portfolio, not a benchmark for your store.
Two of the ten brands showed identical November/February behavior, so do not assume your November cohort is worse.
This depends on reliable cohort tracking; if you don't have it, treat the assumption as unverified.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Recompute break-even ROAS after discounting compresses gross margin
cards.summary: Calculate discounted contribution and break-even ROAS directly; the relationship is nonlinear rather than a universal exponential rule.
cards.use_when: Choosing a Black Friday discount depth or setting the ROAS/contribution-margin target that acquisition spend is measured against during the sale.
steps: Calculate net selling price after discount and subtract actual pre-ad variable costs.
Break-even revenue ROAS = net selling price / pre-ad contribution dollars; reserve additional margin for overhead and profit.
Example: $100 price with $50 costs has $50 contribution and 2x break-even ROAS. A 40% discount gives $60 revenue, $10 contribution and 6x break-even, assuming unchanged costs.
Recalculate percentage fees, returns and shipping where they change rather than holding every cost fixed.
Keep cohort repeat-value assumptions separate from first-order economics.
caveats: The source's 2x-to-4.5x example does not follow from those simple assumptions; compute the actual store model.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Scale on three-day rolling marginal returns, not daily averages
cards.summary: Write scaling rules that act on three-day rolling marginal contribution and require consecutive poor reads before cutting, so you don't overreact to noisy holiday days.
cards.use_when: Running day-to-day Q4 budget and bid decisions during the Black Friday/Cyber Monday peak, especially when daily numbers swing wildly.
steps: Write the scaling rules down before the window starts, so decisions during the sale follow a pre-committed plan instead of live emotion.
Use three-day rolling marginal averages as the default read, rather than day-over-day. Sometimes the source uses day-to-day based on total spend and how fast spend is moving in the pacing sheet.
Rule up: if marginal contribution margin is improving over the three-day rolling window, increase spend and scale.
Rule hold: if marginal returns are flat, do nothing.
Rule down: if there are two consecutive poor reads, decrease spend.
Do not read daily performance against an 8:00 a.m. morning target during the peak window; the source explicitly warns against this during Nov 17–Dec 2.
Apply the pacing sheet as the budget yardstick during the peak, since holiday hours distort daily comparisons.
caveats: Three-day rolling is a source-specific default; brands with very high or very low spend may need a different window.
Marginal returns — not averages — should drive spend decisions; do not spend if the marginal return isn't there.
The rules require a pacing sheet with hourly revenue and spend curves from prior years to be meaningful.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Build a Black Friday pacing sheet from prior-year hourly curves
cards.summary: Pull last year's hourly revenue and spend curves into a pacing sheet so budget decisions during the sale reference actual intraday patterns rather than flat daily targets.
cards.use_when: Preparing the operational budget-control tool for the Black Friday through Cyber Monday window, before committing spend schedules.
steps: Pull last year's hourly revenue and spend curves for the sale period; the source treats this as an early September task.
Build a pacing sheet that maps expected spend against expected revenue by time block, so you can see whether current spend is ahead or behind where it should be.
Use the pacing sheet as the primary budget yardstick during Nov 17–Dec 2 rather than fixed daily caps.
Attach the scaling rules to the pacing sheet — three-day rolling marginal contribution improvement, no action when flat, and decrease after two consecutive poor reads.
Plan an attribution multiplier into the sheet because early spend is understated and the Black Friday weekend is flattered by last-click reporting; the source treats this bias as significant.
Do not read daily performance against an 8:00 a.m. target during the peak; hourly and rolling reads are more informative.
caveats: Hourly curves from prior years may not transfer cleanly if your promotion timing or offer structure changes.
The sheet is only as useful as its attribution adjustment; without one, early spend will look worse and the peak will look better than reality.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Front-load preseason spend (roughly a third of Q4 budget in Sep–Oct)
cards.summary: Source data suggests 31–43% of the September-to-December budget should sit in September and October, so fund preseason rather than saving everything for the peak.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to allocate Q4 budget between preseason (September/October), the Black Friday/Cyber Monday peak, and the post-peak cheap window.
steps: Use the source's observed range — 31–43% of the September-to-December budget — as a starting point for preseason spend, and adjust based on your own sales calendar and offer ladder.

Fund preseason for concrete purposes: building creative delivery data before the peak, ramping Google spend early, dialing in offers, and having an offer ladder ready if you need to switch offers reactively during the sale.
Use the accumulation of delivery data to decide which creative to press into during the peak rather than launching it cold on Black Friday.
Be deliberate with early Google ramps; the source flags the need for care while increasing spend there.
Plan an offer ladder, not a single fixed Black Friday offer, so you can switch during the window in response to trade.
Model preseason as spend that enables the peak, not as separate branding spend — its payoff is peak-window efficiency.
caveats: The 31–43% range is an observation from the source's own data, not a universal target; brands with different seasonality will differ.
Over-investing preseason without enough creative to deliver it just inflates spend without building useful delivery data.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Apply an attribution multiplier to correct Q4 reporting bias
cards.summary: Q4 reporting understates early spend and flatters the Black Friday weekend; use historical click-window analysis to build an attribution multiplier rather than trusting raw numbers.
cards.use_when: Forecasting Q4 performance or judging whether a given spend level is working in the run-up to and during Black Friday.
steps: Recognize the structural bias before building any forecast: last-click reporting understates spend earlier in the window and flatters the Black Friday weekend itself.
In October, run the 7-day-click vs 1-day-click historical analysis to estimate how much you underspent last year and what attribution multiplier to apply to in-period performance.
Apply a post-treatment window adjustment to the numbers so early-window performance is judged on the same basis as the peak.
Use the adjusted reads when making scaling decisions — otherwise you will cut spend too early because the raw number looks worse than it is.
Treat this as an ongoing discussion during October, since the multiplier depends on how attribution behaves in your account.
Verify the current attribution window options in your ad platform before relying on any specific window setting.
caveats: The required multiplier is account-specific; there is no universal value.
Attribution windows and defaults change over time; confirm current settings before recomputing.
This corrects reporting bias, not economic reality — you still need the margin and LTV adjustments as separate corrections.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Reverse-engineer required creative volume from spend targets
cards.summary: To know whether a Q4 revenue and spend target is achievable, model required creative volume from the spend plan and flag when creative, not budget, is the constraint.
cards.use_when: Setting Q4 revenue and ad-spend targets, or deciding how much creative the brand must produce to support planned peak-level spend.
steps: Start from two inputs: your Q4 revenue expectations and your ad spend expectations. The source won't build the model without them — they are the necessary starting point.

Model required creative volume against that spend using your historical data. The source frames this as a data-driven estimate, not a guess, and gives the illustrative example that a specific target might imply 365 creatives.
If the required creative volume exceeds what you can produce, either reduce the spend target or increase production capacity and page/account capacity before the window.
Address the structural constraint directly: at higher spend levels, creative is the binding constraint, so adding budget without adding creative does not produce the target.
Score your offer against the target before the window: if you don't believe the offer can generate the outcome, say so and propose changes before everyone is committed.
Reconcile the offer, target and creative plan in the September/October planning cycle so production time is available.
caveats: The 365-creative figure is an illustrative example from a specific model, not a benchmark for your store.
The model depends on the reliability of your historical creative-to-spend relationship, which varies by brand.
Extra Facebook pages to support more creative volume are subject to current platform policy — verify before assuming this route is available.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Use the cheap post-peak window for a Q5 offer
cards.summary: From roughly December 16 the auction gets the cheapest it ever is, making it a window where a Q5 offer can capture demand at low CPMs after gifting pressure fades.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to run a post-Christmas Q5 promotion or whether to keep spending through early December's still-expensive window.
steps: Plan the calendar in three zones: the expensive peak window (Black Friday/Cyber Monday), early December (still expensive because gifting demand stays high around Dec 1–16), and the cheap window that begins around December 16.
Treat the cheap window as an opportunity: CPMs there are the lowest of the cycle, so incremental spend can be efficient.
If a Q5 offer is relevant to your catalog, workshop it in advance — the source suggests brands raise interest early so the offer, creative and messaging can be built before the window opens.
Don't pull spend out of early December thinking it's post-peak; gifting demand and pressure typically persist through mid-month.
Pair a Q5 offer with the cheapest CPMs to reach audiences you couldn't affordably reach during the peak.
Verify the exact cheap-window start against your own category's demand pattern; the source gives a heuristic date, not a guarantee.
caveats: The December 16 date is a source-provided heuristic; actual auction dynamics vary by category and year.
A Q5 offer only works if the catalog and margin support it; not every store should run one.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Don't carry last year's CPMs into this year's forecast
cards.summary: Use 2025 as a caution, not a baseline: the source expects higher CPMs into a weaker consumer, so plan Q4 forecasts around more expensive media and softer demand.
cards.use_when: Building Q4 revenue and spend forecasts, or setting efficiency and scaling expectations for the upcoming Black Friday.
steps: Treat the prior year's CPM levels as misleading baseline data rather than a forecast input. The source expects this year's CPMs to be materially higher and doubts they will return to last year's lows.
Combine the two factors explicitly in your forecast: higher media costs and a weaker consumer. The source frames going at higher CPMs into softer demand as the core planning risk.
Set lower efficiency expectations before the window rather than adjusting during it, since the scaling plan depends on hitting the marginal-returns thresholds.
Build the forecast from your own spend, offer and margin data, and treat the source's numbers as directional context rather than a benchmark.
Use scenario planning (a higher-CPM case and a softer-demand case) rather than a single point forecast, so the scaling rules have room to act.
caveats: This is the source's expectation, not a measured outcome; CPMs and consumer conditions vary by category and region.
No specific CPM increase percentage is given, so do not invent one.
Forecast inputs should still be validated against your own account's actual Q4 trends as the window develops.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Roll multiple offers instead of one static Black Friday offer
cards.summary: Rolling through several offers across the Q4 window prevents offer fatigue and preserves an offer ladder you can react with if the original trade underperforms.
cards.use_when: Designing the Black Friday through Cyber Monday promotion schedule and building the creative plan that depends on knowing the offer.
steps: Plan an offer ladder — a sequence of offers across the window — rather than a single fixed Black Friday promotion.
Map offers to the creative phases: teaser/early access, launch, mid-sale refresh, and final 24–48 hour scarcity/deadline messaging.
Lock the offers before producing creative, since you cannot make launch or scarcity assets without knowing the offer.
Build in flexibility so the offer can be switched reactively if trade underperforms expectations; that requires the ladder to exist in advance.
Use the offer ladder as an input to the CAC and break-even modeling, because discount depth changes required ROAS.
Test whether offer switching is worth the operational cost for your brand; not every promo calendar needs multiple changes.
caveats: Offer fatigue prevention is the source's rationale, not a measured result; the trade-off between freshness and operational complexity is brand-specific.
Switching offers late can require creative that isn't ready — build the assets before the window, not after the decision.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Judge spend on marginal returns, not average returns
cards.summary: Scale only where marginal returns are positive; do not spend just because the average ROAS or contribution margin still looks acceptable.
cards.use_when: Making incremental budget decisions during Q4, especially when deciding whether to keep pushing spend into the most expensive days.
steps: Separate marginal from average: an account can hold a healthy average ROAS while a new increment of spend loses money, so use marginal reads for the decision.
Use the three-day rolling marginal contribution margin as the primary signal; improve for three days, scale; flat, hold; two consecutive poor reads, decrease.
Refuse to spend where marginal returns aren't there, even if the account average is fine. The source is explicit: don't spend unless marginal returns are present.
Let the pacing sheet set the shape of the spend, and the marginal-returns rule set the size of the adjustments.
Apply the same marginal logic to individual campaign or ad set decisions at whatever aggregation level survives the attribution noise.
Revisit the marginal thresholds if the break-even ROAS has moved due to discount depth.
caveats: This is the source's recommendation, not a universal rule; some brands accept negative marginal returns during key sale days for strategic reasons, and that trade-off should be explicit.
Marginal reads require enough spend per period to be statistically meaningful; very small accounts may not get clean signals.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Stand up a separate November CAC allowance
cards.summary: Set a Q4-specific CAC target that reflects November cohort quality and discount compression, rather than carrying your normal allowance into Black Friday.
cards.use_when: Setting Q4 acquisition efficiency targets and deciding how much you can pay for a November customer.
steps: Start from the November cohort repeat behavior (see the cohort-LTV check) to decide whether November customers are worth materially less in your business.
Adjust the CAC allowance for discount compression, since gross profit per order falls while discount depth rises.
Model discount depth against your own margin and elasticity to decide where the CAC allowance should move further and what scaling potential remains. This requires knowing your offers.
If November customers behave like your normal-month customers, keep the CAC allowance unchanged; the source says everything else in the plan stays the same.
If November customers are materially worse, be conservative and lower the allowance — the source describes most default allowances as wrong twice when discount and LTV are both ignored.
Review the allowance as offers firm up, since it moves with the actual discount you decide to run.
caveats: The adjustment size is brand-specific; there is no universal percentage reduction to apply.
Elasticity assumptions may not hold; treat the modeled scaling potential as a hypothesis.
Requires both cohort data and gross margin visibility, which some brands won't have.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Treat Q4 attribution and LTV as reporting problems you must correct before forecasting
cards.summary: Q4 planning is only credible when you first correct reporting bias and cohort value, then model creative and spend against the corrected targets.
cards.use_when: Building the Q4 forecast and scaling plan end to end, and deciding which inputs you need from the business before modeling.
steps: Get two inputs from the business first: the offer (and offer ladder) and the revenue/spend expectations, even if roughly stated. Without these the model can't start.
Correct the reporting basis: apply an attribution multiplier derived from prior-year 7-day vs 1-day click analysis so early spend isn't understated and the peak isn't flattered.
Correct the customer-value basis: use November cohort repeat data to set a November-specific CAC allowance.
Correct the margin basis: model discount depth against gross margin to derive the true break-even ROAS for the window.
Then model required creative volume from the corrected spend target and check the scaling plan against the pacing sheet.
Present the reality back: if the offer can't support the target, say so and propose changes rather than accepting an unachievable plan.
caveats: This is a planning framework, not a guarantee of results; each correction depends on data quality you may not have.
Forecasts built on assumptions should be revisited as Q4 data accumulates.
cards.source_name: Black Friday 2026 Strategy_ Spend, Creative, Offers, Pacing.docx

cards.title: Budget Allocation Across Ad Channels (50/20/10/20 Model)
cards.summary: Ridge's actual paid-media mix splits spend 50% Meta, 20% Google/YouTube, 10% influencer and 20% tertiary channels, each fed only up to its 'perfect level of spend.'
cards.use_when: Deciding how to split a paid acquisition budget across channels for a DTC store, or auditing whether spend is concentrated in one platform.
steps: Set a baseline mix: roughly 50% Meta, 20% Google/YouTube (search ~5% and YouTube ~15% within that), 10% influencer/podcast, and 20% spread across tertiary channels (Snapchat, TikTok, Reddit, X, Pinterest, AppLovin, linear TV). This is Ridge's mix at nine-figure scale, not a universal law.
Keep tertiary channels small and run them at roughly $1,000–$10,000/day combined, letting them ebb and flow rather than giving each a dedicated buyer.

Apply the 'next best dollar' principle: keep spending on a channel until the next incremental dollar is better spent elsewhere, then find that new channel's perfect level of spend. Revisit continuously because the right mix shifts.
Note the mix is directional: Meta spend ranged from 50% to 75% across years, and Ridge expected partner ads possibly rising toward half of spend in Q4.
For pre-scale brands, the source's own advice is to skip paid entirely and build organic short-form skill first (claimed enough to reach ~$10M/year); treat that as a strong opinion, not a rule.
Verify current platform ad products and interfaces before setting up campaigns; formats and placements change.
caveats: These percentages describe one large brand's mix and depend on margins and category; they are not benchmarks for every store.
The claim that organic alone can reach $10M/year is Ridge's founder's opinion.
cards.source_name: E-Commerce Masterclass_ How to Build, Scale & Win in 2026.docx

cards.title: Cut Branded Search and Treat Google Shopping as Low-Incrementality
cards.summary: Ridge's incrementality holdouts found branded search is largely non-incremental and should be kept under ~1% of marketing spend, with Shopping also weak incrementally.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a paid search budget to free cash for creative or new channels, especially for a store with strong brand recognition.
steps: Separate paid search into branded and non-branded campaigns before judging performance.
Run an incrementality holdout on branded search: pause spend in a held-out geography or audience and measure whether total revenue moves.
If the holdout shows little revenue change, cut branded search to under ~1% of total marketing spend (Ridge's stated target) rather than optimizing its reported ROAS.
Treat Google Shopping skeptically when a store has strong brand awareness — many converters may be arriving anyway; test non-branded search selectively.
Consider that for a brand bigger than its category (e.g., more people search the brand than the generic term), winning generic category searches is harder and less incremental.
Repeat holdout testing periodically since incrementality shifts with awareness and competition.
Verify current Google Ads campaign structures and measurement options, as Google's tools change.
caveats: These findings come from Ridge's holdouts and may not transfer to brands with low awareness or little branded search volume.
Reported platform ROAS on branded search can look strong while contributing little incremental revenue.
cards.source_name: E-Commerce Masterclass_ How to Build, Scale & Win in 2026.docx

cards.title: Incrementality Holdout Testing to Validate Channel Spend
cards.summary: Geo-based holdout cells (e.g., one state withheld from a channel) reveal whether spend drives incremental revenue, useful once multiple channels are in play.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to keep, cut or expand spend on a channel such as Meta or a tertiary network, or diagnosing whether platform-reported conversions are real.
steps: Build test 'cells': withhold a channel's spend from a matched set of geographies (e.g., North Carolina exposed vs South Carolina held out) while keeping other marketing consistent.
Compare total business revenue between exposed and held-out cells to estimate incremental revenue the channel actually caused.
Use the result to answer whether to spend the next dollar on that channel versus elsewhere — the core 'next best dollar' decision.

Consider starting once you spend across multiple channels; the source suggests the need arises when you diversify (he cites figures around $15M–$50M as when brands typically adopt it, framed as an estimate, not a fixed threshold).
Note that Meta reportedly offers free incrementality tests because it is confident in its own results; use these but understand the source of the test.
Vendors in this space (e.g., Northbeam, Measured, Haus-style holdout tools) change offerings — verify current capabilities before committing.
caveats: Results depend on matched geographies and clean experimental design; simpler state-vs-state comparisons are a simplification of more rigorous methods.
Incrementality tooling costs money; small stores may lack the volume for reliable signal.
cards.source_name: E-Commerce Masterclass_ How to Build, Scale & Win in 2026.docx

cards.title: Spend ~1% of Budget on Measurement and Media Tools
cards.summary: Ridge's guideline is to allocate about 1% of the marketing budget to attribution, media-mix modeling and incrementality tools, on the logic that a 5% improvement pays for them.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much to invest in attribution, MMM or incrementality tooling versus putting all budget into media.
steps: Carve about 1% of total marketing budget for measurement tools (multi-touch attribution, media-mix modeling, incrementality/holdout testing).
Evaluate tool spend against a simple test: if the tools improve media effectiveness by roughly 5%, they pay for themselves.

Use MMM (mixed media modeling) tools to survey all channel spend and suggest reallocation (e.g., toward TV or Snapchat); it is an older but still-used approach and, per the source, is somewhat falling out of favor relative to incrementality.
Use multi-touch attribution with clean naming conventions so spend can be compared apples-to-apples across channels and creative units.

Right-size by stage: if a store is only running Meta profitably at scale, the source suggests skip expensive measurement and put the money into creative instead; adopt incrementality tooling once spend spans multiple channels.
Verify current vendor pricing and methodology, as these platforms evolve.
caveats: The 1% figure and the 5% payback are rules of thumb from one operator, not a calculation.
MMM and incrementality methods and vendor prominence change over time; do not treat any single tool as definitive.
cards.source_name: E-Commerce Masterclass_ How to Build, Scale & Win in 2026.docx

cards.title: Naming Convention and Creative Tagging System for Attribution
cards.summary: Tag every ad with concept, hook, thumb-stop and edit variables so attribution tools can compare creative units across platforms and find what to scale.
cards.use_when: Setting up or cleaning up ad naming conventions so paid creative tests produce comparable, actionable data across platforms.
steps: Define naming fields that describe an ad's actual units: concept/angle, hook, thumb-stop (opening image or frame), and edit variation, plus format (static vs video) if useful.
Keep other variables constant when testing a variable — e.g., run 10 different hooks with the same body and CTAs to isolate hook performance.
Structure tests as head-to-head comparisons (A/B/C...) of hooks so results can be read directly.
Load these tags into an MTA tool (Ridge uses Northbeam) so you can see, for example, that one thumb-stop performs better across all platforms and should be scaled.
Interpret the results in context: watch-time/time-to-third-second can indicate a strong thumb-stop, but if viewers watch too far (reaching the end card) it can signal the mid-video CTA is weak.
Use free ad libraries (e.g., Facebook Ads Library) and tools like Foreplay or Motion for competitive creative research; verify current interfaces before adopting.
Keep on-site CTA placement decisions separate: multiple CTAs within a video can raise on-site conversion even when view-through patterns look 'off.'
caveats: Richer tagging requires tooling and team discipline; small teams may start with simpler 3-field conventions (e.g., format, theme, hook).
Creative-analysis metrics are indicative, not definitive attribution.
cards.source_name: E-Commerce Masterclass_ How to Build, Scale & Win in 2026.docx

cards.title: Find the 'Next Best Dollar' Across All Channels
cards.summary: Rather than maximizing one channel, pursue the perfect level of spend on every channel by comparing where each marginal dollar earns the most.
cards.use_when: Allocating incremental budget across channels or deciding whether to open a new channel (e.g., linear TV, TikTok) for a scaling store.
steps: Treat every channel as having an optimal spend level; the job is to reach it, not to max out any one platform.
Before adding budget to the current channel, ask whether the next dollar is better spent elsewhere; if yes, move it.
Fund smaller 'tertiary' channels (Snapchat, TikTok, Reddit, X, Pinterest, AppLovin, linear TV) at modest levels — around $1,000–$10,000/day combined — and let them fluctuate with performance.
Recognize platform dependency risk: when one platform was 95% of a media budget, one algorithm shift could stall the business. Diversify deliberately.
Re-run the comparison regularly because channel efficiency and creative performance keep changing.
Use incrementality results rather than platform-reported metrics to judge whether a channel deserves the next dollar.
Confirm current channel ad products and buying interfaces before expanding, as these change frequently.
caveats: Optimal channel mixes are business-specific and shift over time; there is no fixed formula.
Diversifying poorly (weak ad products, fraud-prone display, PMAX-type blended buys) can waste money — the source warns PMAX especially can mask wasteful spend.
cards.source_name: E-Commerce Masterclass_ How to Build, Scale & Win in 2026.docx

cards.title: Build an Organic-to-Paid Creative Flywheel
cards.summary: Use organic short-form as the proving ground: post broadly, then push proven organic winners into paid (including partner/ASC campaigns).
cards.use_when: Sourcing ad creative for a new or scaling store, or deciding which creative to put paid spend behind.
steps: Publish lots of short-form organic content across platforms (Reels, Shorts, TikTok, Snapchat, Pinterest) before spending on ads.
Watch for organic winners — the source reports that 70% of its best paid ads are organic best-performers, and this is a specific brand's result, not a guarantee.
Take top-performing organic posts and run them as paid (e.g., Advantage+ / ASC campaigns) on a recurring weekly cadence to build a flywheel.
Create multiple owned or partner social accounts as creative testing ground; account follower count is reportedly irrelevant to ad performance.
Consider partner ads (running creative from two handles together) — the source expects Meta's algorithm to favor them and aimed for up to half of spend on partner ads in a peak period.
For high-AOV stores with too little purchase signal to test at scale, seed concepts organically and/or optimize to add-to-cart or page-view conversions to get more signal.
Verify current Meta/partner-ad setup steps, as the product changes.
caveats: The '70% of best ads are organic winners' figure is Ridge-specific.
The claim organic content alone can carry a brand to ~$10M is the founder's opinion and not a benchmark.
cards.source_name: E-Commerce Masterclass_ How to Build, Scale & Win in 2026.docx

cards.title: Feed Meta Volume and True Creative Contrast
cards.summary: Meta rewards radically different creative at high volume; incremental tweaks (color, angle) register as the 'same' ad to the algorithm.
cards.use_when: Scaling paid creative production and deciding how many and how different ads to launch.
steps: Produce at high volume: Ridge launches hundreds of ads weekly to find the occasional top performer; the source says a top ad may cap around $100k, so consistent winners require constant new creative.

Prioritize true contrast: test ads with entirely different concepts, casts (e.g., 'just guys' vs 'just girls'), selling points and pain points — the algorithm reportedly treats minor variations (background color, slight angle) as the same ad.
Invest most in the opening: thumb-stop and hook matter most because they reach new people; middle and end matter less.
Test hooks head-to-head with body and CTAs held constant to isolate what works.
Run multiple production sources simultaneously (in-house studio, agencies, UGC creators) rather than relying on one.
For early-stage brands, make your own ads first — the source argues consumer brands are 'marketing companies' that shouldn't outsource core creative and paid media.
Confirm current Meta ad-system behavior and creative best practices, since the algorithm changes.
caveats: High-volume creative production requires budget and team; smaller stores must adapt the principle to their capacity.
Claims about how the algorithm classifies creative are the operator's interpretation and subject to change.
cards.source_name: E-Commerce Masterclass_ How to Build, Scale & Win in 2026.docx

cards.title: Product Launch Criteria: CAC vs LTV Classification and Product-Mix Focus
cards.summary: Classify products as acquisition (CAC) versus retention/LTV drivers, and track revenue share from new categories to shift from a single-product brand to a multi-line business.
cards.use_when: Deciding which products to launch, how to classify them, and which metrics to watch for product-mix evolution.
steps: Classify each product by role: a 'CAC product' acquires new customers (high AOV, low repeat) while an 'LTV product' drives repeat purchase and category expansion with broader appeal.
Track the share of revenue coming from new product categories (not just the flagship) to gauge whether the brand is evolving beyond a single hero product.
Observe the Yeti pattern: coolers were the entry hero but water bottles became ~70% of revenue — using one product to acquire and others to expand.
Watch new-customer acquisition by product and by market (e.g., 'how many of the newest product did I acquire today, in each country') as a core metric.
When repeat purchase is structurally limited (one-and-done products like wallets), add adjacent products to create repurchase paths rather than pushing the same item repeatedly.
Set a target like returning-customer revenue share (the source aims for 50%) and treat it as a gold-standard metric for category expansion.
