steps: At $4K–$30K/month spend: keep content founder-led. The source argues production budget should be your time, not money — statics and founder-led iPhone videos can carry spend to $30K/month. Founder involvement also builds the internal standard for what good creative looks like so you can later train and KPI others.

At $30K–$100K/month: allocate 25% of media budget to production (e.g. $25K/month at $100K spend). The source deliberately calls this uncomfortable but argues most brands under-spend here and that's why they stall.
Above $100K/month: let production asymptote toward ~10% of media budget. At a 25% MER, 10% of media budget equals roughly 2.5% of total revenue.
Budgets at the 25% level are intended to fund UGC, partnership ads, a designer on statics (full-time international or part-time in-house) and possibly a low-cost agency supplement (e.g. VSLs).
caveats: Percentages are the source's recommended allocations, not industry benchmarks; validate against your own contribution margins.
The source presents the 25% mid-band as intentionally uncomfortable and notes it 'democratizes' at scale — treat as a directional target, not a hard rule.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Treat creative as a revenue driver, not a cost centre: the redistribution math
cards.summary: Model the efficiency gain from moving ad budget into production versus running too few ads, and avoid the failure mode of scaling a starved account.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to shift spend from distribution channels into creative production when the account has few active ads relative to spend.
steps: Check your active-ad count against spend. The source's case example: a brand spending $350K/month on Meta had only ~15 live ads, an extreme mismatch.
When active ads are too few, media buyers over-compensate with account mechanics (over-segmentation, 25 campaigns, cost caps) because creative is the actual bottleneck.

Build the reallocation case explicitly: the source proposed moving $10K/month from Meta to production, which with an agency would yield ~40 assets (mix of unique, hook-swaps and statics), nearly doubling active ads and likely unlocking ~5% efficiency.

Translate the efficiency gain two ways: a 5% efficiency improvement on $350K = ~$17.5K saved (drop $10K spend, net ~$7.5K better), or hold spend flat and gain incremental revenue at their ~3x return (~$40–50K/month extra).
Treat creative budget as comparable to reallocating between channels — a distribution decision, not purely a cost line.
If you keep allocating nothing to production, expect the account to fatigue back down: this source reports the example brand's performance decayed as its 60 ads fatigued and spend reallocated away.
caveats: All figures are from a single client example and are illustrative, not a promised result.
The source states the brand eventually parted ways with the agency; this is a cautionary case, not a controlled test.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Test creative volume cheaply with trial reels before ad manager
cards.summary: Post ad cutdowns as trial reels with the CTA removed to get view data and retention graphs, then only push the best hooks into the ad account.
cards.use_when: Choosing which hooks or early-cut creative to fund with paid spend, or iterating on a video before final production.
steps: Export the ad asset and cut off the end call-to-action, then post it as a trial reel on the brand or personal page. The source states this applied as of April 2026.
Use the two outputs: (1) comparative virality/view data across posts, and (2) retention graphs showing where viewers drop.
Read the retention graph to diagnose whether the hook, bridge or body is losing viewers, and iterate on the next shoot accordingly.
Run V1 as a trial reel while round two is still in production so feedback arrives within ~24 hours, before the final asset is finished.
For hook testing at volume: post ~20 hook variations as trial reels, identify the strongest, and push only ~5 into the ad account rather than spending media budget discovering the same thing.
caveats: The source explicitly flags this as a time-sensitive tactic that may change as algorithms change — verify current trial reel behavior before relying on it.
Trial reels measure organic virality and retention, not purchase conversion or ROAS.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Understand creative fatigue as spend capacity plus audience size
cards.summary: Every ad has a finite lifetime spend capacity; fatigue comes from either the asset going stale or the targeted audience being too small.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to push a winning ad harder, introduce replacements, or re-target a narrow persona.
steps: Model each ad's life: spend ramps (manually or via Meta distribution), hits a maximum daily spend limit, then decays and is eventually turned off or stops receiving spend. The area under that curve is the ad's total spend capacity.
Accept two premises: every ad has a total spend capacity, and every ad will fatigue and be turned off.

Choose a shape deliberately: squeeze spend hard for short-term sell-through (higher peak, faster falloff) versus hold at a lower daily budget so the ad lives 6 months instead of 6 weeks (portfolio management view).

Tie the choice to inventory and cash: if you must clear inventory this month, squeezing a winner to sell through may be right even at degraded MER; if inventory is tight or you're growing faster than your cash conversion cycle, let ads breathe for higher efficiency.

Diagnose fatigue cause: (1) the ad is stale or repeats visuals/concepts/audience of other creatives — this fatigues faster when value propositions repeat; (2) the persona is too small, so frequency rises and profitability falls.
For narrow personas, rotate creative within the audience and account for churn (e.g. marathon-training audiences continually refresh), but do not over-saturate.
caveats: The source notes agencies without business context tend to squeeze winners for a 30–90 day case study and short-term ROAS, damaging long-term account health.
Spend-capacity is a conceptual model, not a precise measurable figure.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Match persona breadth to spend capacity; go specific first, broad later
cards.summary: Narrow persona callouts cap daily spend capacity; broader audiences scale further but demand stronger creative — start specific, expand at scale.
cards.use_when: Choosing how specific the persona callout in an ad script should be, or deciding when to broaden targeting to scale spend.
steps: Recognize that narrower callouts cap daily spend: the source's example of 'e-commerce CFOs in Australia owning over $100M' is a pool of roughly 1,000–2,000 people — spending $10K/day would hit them absurdly often.
Broaden the callout to scale: 'e-commerce founders earning over $100K/year' is a much larger pool and supports far higher daily spend.
Exploit audience churn: people enter and exit a specific persona (e.g. new marathon entrants), so rotate creatives to reach new entrants at a sustainable frequency rather than oversaturating.
Prefer specific callouts at first because they force sharper, better creative that resonates; only move to broader audiences once you reach scale, even though broad audiences spend further.

For ecommerce application: a tight callout like 'runners chasing a sub-4 marathon' may only support a few hundred dollars/day, whereas a broader 'runners' angle supports much more — but the specific version often converts better per impression.
caveats: The source notes high-quality top-of-funnel unaware creative is very difficult and says most brands should not attempt it unless they are already a $50M+ brand.
Broad callouts do not automatically outperform; they require creative that resonates with more people.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Recover spend from fatiguing ads with four tactics
cards.summary: Iterate hooks, move ads to cost-cap campaigns, re-use post IDs in scaling campaigns, or translate formats to extract more spend from a decaying winner.
cards.use_when: Extending a winning ad's life before turning it off or replacing it.
steps: Iterate the asset: take a proven hero ad and rotate new hooks onto it to extract more spend from the same body.
Move the ad into a cost-cap campaign to force more spend through it — a short-term media-buying tactic that also accelerates fatigue.
Carry the creative into another campaign (e.g. a scaling campaign) using the post ID so existing engagement is retained; the source says this sometimes works but won't save the account.
Translate formats: video → static, VSSL → UGC, static → long-form-copy unaware static. This is a variation on iteration and often the most durable option.
Accept that once a creative has fatigued there is limited upside; these tactics squeeze the back end. The real answer is a portfolio of other well-performing ads to fall back on.
caveats: Duplicating adsets is named but the source does not recommend it, calling it a dated tactic.
Cost-cap moves and post-ID re-use are explicitly described as tactical, not business-changing.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Run portfolio management across ads, products and the balance sheet
cards.summary: Above ~$50K/month, treat media buying as risk diversification across ads and products, and reconcile P&L optimisation with balance-sheet/inventory reality.
cards.use_when: Setting media buying priorities when running a large ad account, especially if unsold inventory is accumulating or efficiency targets conflict with sell-through.
steps: Apply the 80/20 pattern deliberately: decide whether you want Pareto concentration to occur naturally in the account or introduce structure to avoid over-leverage on a few ads.
Apply the same logic to products so spend is not over-concentrated on a small number of SKUs.
Recognise agencies are KPI'd on efficiency and profit, so they optimise toward maximum profit — that can under-optimise the balance sheet.
Check for the failure case: a business showing $2M P&L profit but holding $3M in unsold inventory is effectively negative $1M in cash.
If stuck with unsold stock, restructure the account to sell it through, accepting lower efficiency and making creatives for that stock — the source calls this a hard pill but the way out.
Keep the media buyer across inventory position so spend decisions align with stock reality.
caveats: The $50K/month threshold is the source's stated point at which this becomes the media buyer's job.
Profit-vs-balance-sheet framing is the presenter's opinion about agency incentives, not a universal rule.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Budget creative effort across replication, iteration and net-new
cards.summary: Allocate roughly 50–60% to replicating winners, 20–30% to iterating underperformers, and 20–30% to net-new concepts — most brands over-weight net-new.
cards.use_when: Planning a monthly creative production calendar and deciding which types of assets to brief.
steps: Categorise every asset into one of three types, prioritised by leverage: (1) winning content replication — re-making winners via hook iterations or format translations; (2) iterative content — fixing underperformers via hook/format changes, new personas or new offers; (3) net-new concepts — entirely new formats, angles and ideas.
Apply the source's recommended split: ~50–60% winning replication, ~20–30% iteration, ~20–30% net-new. The exact split shifts with business context.
Do not skip net-new entirely (some brands run 0%) — everything fatigues, so a pipeline of new concepts is required to feed the top of the system.
Avoid over-weighting net-new: the source admits doing 80–90% net-new in his own organic content and reports replication held ~80% of views while net-new underperformed.
Re-post and re-make content that worked instead of only creating new: each re-run reaches a new audience and tends to perform similarly.
caveats: Percentages are the source's general recommendation and are explicitly context-dependent.
The 80% view-share observation is from the presenter's own organic content, not a controlled ecommerce test.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Brief creators with their past work plus the brief behind it
cards.summary: Creator output quality follows brief quality; assess a creator by comparing what they produced against the brief they were given.
cards.use_when: Sourcing and briefing UGC creators or agencies for ecommerce ad production.
steps: Ask for examples of past work — the source calls skipping this self-evidently wrong.
For each example, request the original brief that the creator was given, so you can compare output to brief one-for-one.
Read the comparison: if they produced something great from a terrible brief, you can give them broad strokes; if the brief was extremely detailed, match that level in your own brief.
Default to writing the highest-quality, most in-depth brief possible.
If a creator doesn't want to follow the script, ask for one scripted take and one natural take, then choose or run both.

Ensure the creator is native to the target region: the source reports Australian accents underperform in the US, native US accents are needed, and UK-to-AU translates decently — but native accents always outperform. The script can be identical; the creator must be local.
caveats: Region-accuracy claims are the presenter's reported observation, not a benchmarked study.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Build the creative production team by spend tier
cards.summary: Hire a video editor, static designer and creative strategist (plus creators) in a tiered structure matched to monthly ad spend.
cards.use_when: Planning creative production headcount and roles for an ecommerce ad account as spend scales.
steps: At $4–30K/month: founder creates content (iPhone quality is fine, natural feel matters), scripts are where leverage lives, run ~3 core concepts, and allocate 60–80% of budget to testing since there isn't enough spend to scale winners.
At $30–100K/month: two to three UGC creators, ~5–6 concepts, a testing and a scaling campaign, ~30–100 new creatives per month, and introduce partnership ads.

Above $100K/month: a full team — scripter, editor, designer, and 4–6 creators (may be part-time), at least 10% of budget to creative, 8–10 active concepts, 100+ new assets/month, plus a financial model tracking cost per asset by source and profit contribution per ad, and ROI per ad against production cost.

Hire the roles as: a video editor (ideally AI-native for more assets and synthetic footage), a static designer, and a creative strategist. Both editor and designer can be global, part-time contractors or full-time.

Source the strategist role from copywriters (strategy is mostly copywriting — scripts, static briefs, persona ideation), by poaching from another company, or by backfilling a designer/editor into the role (faster feedback loops).
Optionally pay the strategist a variable tied to ad spend for their creatives — the source cites ~3% of ad spend working well mid-size but becoming absurd at large scale (e.g. $80K/month).
caveats: Tier thresholds and headcount are the source's recommendations, not universal requirements.
The ~3% ad-spend incentive model is the source's observation; he explicitly notes it breaks at large scale.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Automate the middle of the creative process with AI, not the ends
cards.summary: Apply AI heavily to briefing and script writing and to production, but not to ideation or final analysis.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to insert LLM/AI tooling into your creative production workflow.
steps: Map the process: ideation → briefing → production → publishing → analysis → back to ideation.
Do not automate ideation: the source states LLMs output the meme, and no amount of context or scraping produces sufficiently differentiated ideas — a strategist must validate concepting.

Heavily automate briefing and script writing: build a Claude skill that walks through a ~20-question questionnaire (persona, concept, offer, long-form or not, stage of awareness) and outputs a script/brief that is ~99% done with a ~1% tweak.
Leverage AI in production: it speeds workflows, and the source reports VSSLs and static image ads can be ~90% AI-produced.
Use AI with caution in analysis: it does not naturally weight your metric hierarchy or account structure context; the source reports AI analysis often misleads core decisions.
Net rule: skip the outsides of the process (ideation, final analysis), maximise throughput in the middle (briefing, production).
caveats: The '99% done' and '90% AI' figures are the source's estimates, not measured outcomes.
Tool names and interfaces may change — verify current capabilities of your AI tooling.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Match persona callouts and creative to audience warmth and account scale
cards.summary: Use broad audience creative only if you can sustain it; start content-first and video-heavy, and match creative to the awareness stage.
cards.use_when: Setting the targeting and creative approach for a new or growing ecommerce brand.
steps: For a smaller founder: post organically every day before going paid. The source argues this is the right approach for 2026–27 not because organic outperforms paid, but because it forces you to get good at creative that compounds into ads.
Diagnose your creative using retention graphs, shares and saves — the same signals that tell you whether an ad holds attention.
Recognise top-of-funnel unaware advertising has a very high skill ceiling; the source says most shouldn't attempt it unless already a $50M+ brand.
Use specific persona callouts that force sharper creative first, and only broaden once you have the scale to justify it.
Be careful with DPAs: the source warns they are generally good but tend to over-spend and their ROAS is over-inflated.
caveats: The '$50M+ brand' qualifier is the source's opinion.
DPA over-spend is the presenter's observation, not a benchmark; test incrementality on your own account.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Google Ads structure: consolidation beats segmentation, unless commercial reality forces segmentation
cards.summary: Merge low-data campaigns into consolidated ones so the algorithm learns from more conversions, and only split out for commercial necessity (clearance, new arrivals).
cards.use_when: Restructuring an ecommerce Google Ads account that is fragmented into many campaigns with low conversion volumes.
steps: Understand the rule: campaigns learn in isolation — a campaign with 50 monthly conversions optimises from 50 data points, while a sibling with 10 optimises from 10 (ignore limited platform-level sharing for the model).
Expect the pattern: as conversion volume per campaign falls, ROAS tends to fall with it, usually causally.

Fix by consolidating: delete the low-volume campaigns and move their products and budget into the highest-conversion campaign so all conversions train one model (e.g. 90 conversions/month instead of 50+20+10).
Segment only when a commercial reality demands it — the source's examples: grade-C inventory you must burn or discount, and new arrivals that need shopping visibility for seasonality.
Key principle: be as consolidated as possible while injecting only the commercial realities that justify a split.
caveats: The 'consolidation beats segmentation' rule applies to Google Ads campaign structure as the source describes it; verify against your current account setup.
The 50/20/10 conversion example is illustrative, not a measured result.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Recognise Google spend as either over-spending or under-spending
cards.summary: Google sits bottom-of-funnel and captures existing demand at high ROAS, which leads to two opposite errors: pushing spend that isn't incremental, or refusing to scale when cold search demand exists.
cards.use_when: Auditing Google Ads spend levels and deciding whether to increase, hold or decrease budget.
steps: Overspend pattern: top-of-funnel demand is generated by Meta/TikTok/affiliates, and Google captures the bottom intent and claims high ROAS. Brands push spend up on Google even though it isn't incremental, and end up over-spending.

Underspend pattern: brands that believe Google is only bottom-funnel refuse to spend above ~$10K/month even while spending $4M/month on Meta — despite having scalable cold search demand in their category.
Decide which camp you are in and move spend accordingly.
Test incrementality rather than trusting platform ROAS alone — the source's own test was finding PMAX reported a 5 ROAS while backend revenue didn't move when budget doubled.
Use the platform's reported ROAS as a hypothesis, and hold-out or incrementality testing as the check.
caveats: The $10K/month and $4M/month figures are the source's example, not a threshold.
Incrementality testing methodology is not detailed here; treat the platform ROAS as unverified for causal claims.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Apply the five major Google Ads shifts when restructuring in 2026
cards.summary: Account for PMAX's ceiling, standard shopping's return, changed match-type definitions, AIMAX/demand gen, and DSA deprecation before rebuilding the account.
cards.use_when: Revisiting a Google Ads account built on older playbooks or when PMAX stops scaling.
steps: PMAX has hit its ceiling: early discounts in the auction created arbitrage, then everyone moved spend in and the advantage went away. There's no clear visibility into where spend goes, and scaling PMAX to $100–300K/month did not produce matching backend revenue in the source's tests.
Standard shopping is back: once PMAX scales far enough it shows diminishing returns, and layering standard shopping is required to keep growing cold new-customer acquisition.

Match types changed: exact match now matches on meaning, phrase match broadened, broad match stayed broad. SCAGs (single-keyword ad groups) is no longer recommended — the source says it stopped working around 2020.
AIMAX and demand gen have been introduced; DSAs are being deprecated.
Structure the account around these realities rather than 2022–23 playbooks, and expect the platform to ship changes every few months.
caveats: This reflects the source's 2026 view; verify current platform behaviour and product availability before acting.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Justify every campaign beyond one (justification-based account structure)
cards.summary: Build Google Ads accounts around one default consolidated campaign and require a commercial justification for each added campaign.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing the account structure for a store's Google Shopping/Search program and deciding whether to split into more campaigns.
steps: Treat one campaign as the theoretical default, acknowledge it is rarely realistic, and require heavy justification for every additional campaign layered on top.

Segment only for one of the four valid reasons: (1) brand vs non-brand search so brand placements don't share budget with cold acquisition, (2) geography when selling to multiple countries, (3) different margin or efficiency goals, (4) genuinely different product categories that learn toward different personas.

Split on margin specifically because Google bids on revenue, not profit: a 70% gross-margin collection and a 35% gross-margin collection cannot share one tROAS target, since the high-revenue, lower-margin collection will absorb the spend even when barely profitable at that target.
Use the office-chairs-vs-plants example as the test for category splits: if two products share a plausible use case but attract different buyer personas, segment so each learns in isolation.
When no justification applies, consolidate rather than segment to avoid reducing performance for the sake of complexity.
caveats: The source's '70% vs 35% margin' numbers are illustrative examples of the margin-segmentation principle, not a threshold formula.
The four justifications are the source's framework, not a universal rule.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Route 80-90% of ecommerce spend to Shopping, not Search
cards.summary: Ecommerce and retail accounts should put most spend into Shopping because pre-click information improves traffic quality.
cards.use_when: Deciding budget allocation between Shopping and Search campaigns for an ecommerce store.
steps: Aim for 80-90% of spend in Shopping for ecom/retail, reserving Search for additional volume once Shopping saturates.

Reason: Search ads show only a headline, an unread description and extensions — no image, price, variants or brand cues — so users click on faith and land on the wrong product, producing worse conversion rates.
Shopping listings show image, price, title, promos/reviews and competitor listings side by side, so the user pre-compares across ~6 listings and pre-selects the most relevant one before clicking.

Exception: ecommerce businesses with a B2B component often perform better on Search, because business buyers making bulk/supplier purchases distrust Shopping price listings and click Search ads instead.
caveats: The 80-90% figure is the source's rule of thumb, not a guaranteed optimum.
Shopping outperforms Search 'until you completely saturate the Shopping network' per the source.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Use single-topic ad groups (STAG) instead of SKAGs
cards.summary: Replace single-keyword ad groups with themed ad groups holding 10-20 related keywords and theme-tuned ads.
cards.use_when: Building or restructuring Search campaign ad groups for a store's keyword themes.
steps: Group 10-20 thematically related keywords per ad group (e.g. 'general plumbing', 'emergency plumbing', 'affordable plumbing' as separate themed groups).
Tune the ad copy in each group to that theme so it is contextually relevant to every keyword in the group.

Abandon SKAGs: responsive search ads have ~2,700 asset combinations and need ~250,000 impressions to properly test, which a single exact-match keyword can never deliver, keeping the ad in permanent learning.
Tie consolidation to scale: higher volume through the ad group/ad level is the only way for the campaign to exit learning.
Reject Google/Facebook advice by default, but treat consolidation of keywords as the minority of platform advice worth testing — the source reports it wins across all accounts they work on.
caveats: Responsive search ads are now the only ad type available in Search (per source at time of recording); verify current Google Ads interface.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Structure PMax asset groups by product type with matched listing groups
cards.summary: Build 3-20 PMax asset groups segmented by product type, each with its own customized listing group of at least 15 products.
cards.use_when: Setting up or fixing a Performance Max campaign for an ecommerce catalog.
steps: Default PMax creates one asset group — actively build multiple, remembering the asset group is the ad-unit equivalent (like a Meta ad) and the listing group is the feed-product bundle.

Customize the listing group inside each asset group so the products match the assets (a jeans asset group holds only jeans products); forgetting this lumps all products into every group and defeats the segmentation.
Segment by product type (furniture: chairs/tables/lighting/decor; hardware: hand tools/power tools/fasteners/accessories).
Ensure at least 15 products per asset group; never a single product (it may get starved of spend).
Enforce the rule as minimum 3 asset groups, maximum ~20 — past 20, most businesses lack the complexity to justify it, and simpler structures won repeatedly in the source's tests.
caveats: The 15-product floor and 3-20 range are source-stated heuristics, adjustable to catalog size.
The source ran tests up to ~200 hyper-segmented asset groups; simpler always won.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Diagnose why PMax segmentation is worth breaking consolidation
cards.summary: Use four concrete benefits to decide whether splitting PMax asset groups is justified for a store.
cards.use_when: Justifying or rejecting PMax asset-group segmentation for a specific product category set.
steps: Creative relevance (retargeting): segment so a user who viewed jeans is retargeted with jeans imagery/headlines across Display/YouTube, not random fashion products.
Cold creative relevance: PMax places cold on Display/YouTube; segmented feeds let it serve jeans to in-market-for-jeans users rather than the entire catalog to anyone interested in the brand.
Audience signals: set granular signals per asset group; per the source these are directional inputs for launching (not Meta-style targeting) and Google bypasses them once real conversion data exists.
Search themes: feed in actual historically converting search terms from your account rather than invented keywords; also signal-only, not targeting.
Performance visibility: segmentation lets you read which product types outperform (e.g. tops beating jeans seasonally) and reallocate.
caveats: Source ran PMax on 250+ accounts and consulted on ~400 ecom accounts; they report audience signals/search themes are near-irrelevant (1% at best) for mature accounts spending $30-100k+/month, mattering only at new launches. Treat as source opinion, not law.
Verify current Google Ads interface for brand/negative options, which change frequently.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Set brand exclusions (two ways) on PMax to stop pure retargeting
cards.summary: Always exclude branded traffic from PMax so the campaign cannot over-credit warm/repeat conversions.
cards.use_when: Configuring PMax campaigns and auditing whether brand traffic is inflating reported ROAS.
steps: Apply a brand list exclusion via campaign settings → brand exclusions → add new brand; Google indexes and finds branded terms, then apply the list.
Also add brand terms as negative keywords now that PMax supports them, and apply BOTH as fail-safes — brand list catches missed variations, negatives protect if the list fails.
Recognize that a PMax without brand exclusions is effectively a retargeting campaign.

Rank PMax levers by importance per the source: (1) GMC feed titles/descriptions/imagery (when PMax prioritizes Shopping), (2) brand exclusions, (3) asset & listing group structure plus copy, (4) bidding strategy, (5) audience signals and search themes.
caveats: Negative-keyword support in PMax is a relatively recent rollout; verify current availability in your account.
An unaudited account may still be the right call if the campaign is genuinely driving cold acquisition.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Run feed-only PMax to force Shopping placement and fix runaway spend
cards.summary: Delete asset groups to create a feed-only PMax that can only serve Shopping + Display retargeting, controlling misrouted spend.
cards.use_when: When PMax is over-spending on Gmail/YouTube or you want to force spend into Shopping placement.
steps: Delete the asset groups — only the listing group (GMC feed) remains, so PMax can only place on Shopping and Display remarketing (the old Smart Shopping behavior).
Turn OFF URL expansion in settings, or PMax scrapes/auto-builds URLs and asset groups itself.
Turn OFF automatically created assets, or PMax fabricates assets and defeats the feed-only constraint.

Use case from source: a client spending a couple hundred thousand/month on PMax saw clicks spike and ROAS drop ~20% as spend shifted to YouTube (2% → 10%) and Gmail cold (10%); going feed-only blocked those placements and fixed the issue.
caveats: Source notes Gmail 'clicks' count email opens, not outbound website clicks — inflated click volume is a signal to check placements.
Feed-only is a context-dependent nuance; the source does not prescribe it universally.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Move to tROAS for stability, then avoid the over-tightening trap
cards.summary: Start on max conversion value for data, roll into target ROAS for day-to-day reliability, and watch for the tROAS trap of throttling cold reach.
cards.use_when: Choosing and tuning a bidding strategy for a store's PMax/Shopping campaigns.
steps: Launch on max conversion value to accumulate data, then transition to target ROAS; the source says the average performance over the period is similar, but tROAS flattens week-to-week volatility.
Set the initial tROAS slightly below trailing ROAS (e.g. trailing ~420-430% → set ~400%).
If budget is capped, raising tROAS squeezes efficiency but shrinks the targetable audience toward warmer users — efficiency looks better while genuine new-customer acquisition falls.
Diagnose with a mental cold/warm pool: higher tROAS = smaller circle = warmer; scaling spend = larger circle = colder and less efficient.
Do not over-optimize tROAS to chase a headline number; the source says the lower, less 'impressive' tROAS was likely the better position.
caveats: Smart bidding requires sufficient conversion data; brand-new accounts with no data are forced onto manual bidding (verify current eligibility).
The stability-vs-performance trade is the source's account of observed platform behavior, not a guarantee.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Build a feeder strategy: cold funnel campaign feeding a high-tROAS retargeter
cards.summary: Run a very low-tROAS cold campaign to cheaply reach under-bid auctions, then convert that traffic with a high-tROAS campaign.
cards.use_when: When you need genuine cold acquisition in Google that PMax over-attributes on its own.
steps: Set up a cold campaign (standard Shopping, per source) at a very low tROAS (source example: 50%/0.5x) to reach the whole pool of users searching relevant terms — including the low-intent half almost no one bids on.
Set up a second campaign at high tROAS (source example: 600%) to retarget the warm pool that the first campaign fed.
Confirm the arbitrage premise: most high-tROAS bidders compete only for the high-intent half, so the low-intent auctions are cheap to win.

Expect the first campaign's in-platform attribution to look weak and the second to look strong; per source, PMax 'substantially overattributes' (~50%+ of conversions are repeat/warm) while standard Shopping underattributes because PMax takes the final click.
caveats: The 50%/600% figures are source examples, not recommended universal settings.
The source states ~50%+ PMax conversions being warm/repeat is their finding across agencies, presented as opinion, not a published benchmark.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Standard Shopping structures: top-sellers split, feeder, and labelizer
cards.summary: Three in-market Shopping structures plus when each is (and isn't) worth the complexity.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to organize standard Shopping campaigns for a store's catalog.
steps: Top-sellers split: put top sellers in one campaign and everything else in another, forcing ~80% of spend into the top 20% of products while keeping testing budget on the rest to roll up new winners. Only for non-fashion catalogs with a large SKU count; not for fashion and not for 5-10 product stores.
Feeder strategy: standard Shopping as the cold acquisition layer feeding a high-tROAS campaign (see feeder card).

Labelizer: split products into over-index / index / near-index / under-index / no-index tiers with custom labels, either manually (small catalogs) or via an automated labelizer script that re-tiers on 30-day rolling performance and assigns tier-appropriate bids/budgets.
Default to consolidation; apply the four justification variables (brand/non-brand, geography, margin/efficiency, category) before segmenting.
caveats: The source explicitly does not recommend labelizer for most businesses — it adds segmentation with limited upside unless you have thousands of SKUs.
Segment based on the four justification variables, not on arbitrary splits.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Run Search campaigns only for the right cases; use STAGs and front-load negatives
cards.summary: Search is secondary for most ecom, but essential with B2B — structure with topic ad groups and aggressive early negative-keyword policing.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest in Search and how to police it for a store.
steps: For 90% of ecom brands, put ~90% of focus into Shopping; add Search for additional volume after Shopping saturates.
Exception: ecom with a B2B component often performs better on Search (bulk/supplier buyers distrust Shopping price listings).
Use single-topic ad groups (themed keywords, theme-tuned ads) rather than SKAGs.

Front-load negative keywords in the first 30 days — highest-leverage window because the campaign goes broad; review weekly (or daily at high budget) then drop to weekly-ish, avoiding over-tweaking which resets learnings.
Maintain a universal account-level negative list inherited by every new campaign (job/careers/intern/hiring/salary terms, etc.); source suggests a pre-made list or building one with an LLM.
Always exclude brand on Search campaigns; typically use smart bidding (tROAS, max conversions).
caveats: Review cadence ('weekly', 'daily at high budget') is source guidance, not a fixed rule.
Confirm negative-keyword tooling and bidding eligibility in the current Google Ads interface.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Treat landing-page testing as the biggest Search lever
cards.summary: A/B test landing pages within ad groups over 30-60 days to raise conversion rate and unlock higher bids.
cards.use_when: Running acquisition on Google and looking to increase conversion rate and winning auctions.
steps: In an ad group/campaign, run two ads pointing to two different landing pages.
Monitor conversion rate over 30-60 days; keep the higher-converting landing page.
Rotate in a third landing-page test against the winner, turn off the loser, and repeat — compounding the account's average conversion rate.

Tie this to auction economics: Google is ultimately an auction of who can pay the most; 2x conversion rate lets you spend ~2x per click at the same return, and higher AOV squeezes more revenue from the same clicks.
Treat CPC as a vanity metric: across large datasets CPC and ROI show little relationship in the middle range (extremes aside), so don't optimize for lowest CPC.
Add AOV optimization alongside CVR for compounding leverage.
caveats: The 30-60 day test window and '2x CVR → 2x click budget' are the source's reasoning, not a measured guarantee.
The CPC-ROI relationship conclusion is the source's observation from its own account analyses.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Fix seven common Google Ads account hygiene mistakes
cards.summary: Audit and correct frequent account-level setup errors that waste budget or distort attribution.
cards.use_when: Auditing an ecommerce Google Ads account for structural errors before scaling.
steps: Do not use GA4 events as the primary conversion — the source reports a ~10-15% (sometimes higher) attribution gap versus direct snippet code; use the direct snippet for the primary conversion.
Never run just one asset group on PMax — enforce segmentation at the asset-group level.
Do not run broad match with maximize clicks — broad match requires a smart bidding strategy to work.
Disable Display in Search campaigns, especially for cold traffic.
Add branded negatives on cold campaigns plus general negatives on Search campaigns.
Turn off Google's auto-apply recommendations — they almost always act against your interest.

Apply a proper naming convention so anyone can read context: agency tag → region → campaign type (PMax/Shopping/Search) → audience (cold/brand/theta) → goal (usually dropped, since it's conversions 99% of the time).
caveats: The 10-15% GA4 attribution gap is the source's reported figure; verify against your own setup.
Some items (auto-apply behavior, broad match requirements) can change with platform updates — recheck the current interface.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Google Ads bidding: expansive vs restrictive strategies
cards.summary: Choose between expansive (Max Conversions/Max Conversion Value) and restrictive (tROAS/tCPA) bidding based on whether you need to test new audiences for scale or protect efficiency.
cards.use_when: Deciding on the account-level bidding strategy for a Google Search, Shopping or PMax campaign and diagnosing whether the current strategy is starving the campaign of new-audience tests.
steps: Classify each option: Max Conversions and Max Conversion Value are expansive because they can enter any auction within results constraints; tCPA and tROAS are restrictive because they only enter auctions where the efficiency target can be met. Confirm current interface labelling in Google Ads before changing.

Model the trade-off as a testing budget: the source's heuristic is that an expansive campaign allocates roughly a share of budget to adjacent, not-yet-proven tests (new keywords, audiences, placements, regions), while a restrictive campaign allocates close to zero. Treat this as an illustrative heuristic, not a measured figure.

Recognise that the effective testing budget of a restrictive strategy depends on how aggressive the target is versus actual performance: if you achieve 4x and target 4.5x, expect near-zero testing; if you achieve 5x and target 2x, the campaign behaves more like expansive.

Rotate between the two modes over extended periods rather than staying on tROAS permanently: long-term restrictive bidding silos the account into one audience and can create a negative feedback loop as conversion data ages.
For new accounts with no conversion history, expect to be forced onto Manual CPC or Maximize Clicks until data exists; treat these as temporary and move off them as soon as possible.
caveats: Smart bidding availability and naming change over time — verify the current interface and your account's eligibility.
The 'testing budget' percentages are the presenter's conceptual illustration, not measured platform mechanics.
Some accounts use Maximize Clicks deliberately in advanced arbitrage tests, but the source says this is rare (not in ~90% of accounts they manage).
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Prefer value-based bidding for ecommerce over lowest-CPA bidding
cards.summary: In ecommerce, optimising for Max Conversions pushes budget to the cheapest product; Max Conversion Value optimises towards margin mix instead.
cards.use_when: Setting or auditing the bidding objective for an ecommerce Google Ads account with a wide price range across products.
steps: Map the risk: a Max Conversions campaign targets the lowest cost per acquisition, so it will concentrate spend on low-price, easy-to-convert items (e.g. a $40 t-shirt) rather than high-value items (e.g. a $200 jumper) even when the higher-value item returns a better ROAS on that spend.

Work the illustrative comparison from the source: the t-shirt might acquire at ~$20 CPA at 2x ROAS while the jumper costs ~$60 to acquire at 3.5x ROAS; a CPA-optimised campaign still funnels budget to the t-shirt and the account loses the better return.

Switch ecommerce accounts to Max Conversion Value (value-based) in the large majority of cases so optimisation follows revenue rather than order count. The presenter recommends value roughly 90% of the time.
Use tROAS as the restrictive version of Max Conversion Value when you need to defend an efficiency floor, and Max Conversion Value when you need to find new converting audiences.
Review which products are absorbing spend after any objective change to confirm the mix matches your margin priorities.
caveats: This is the presenter's ecommerce-specific recommendation for established accounts; new accounts without conversion data may not have access to value-based smart bidding.
Value-based bidding requires accurate conversion values in tracking, so fix tracking before switching.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Detect and stop the tROAS death spiral
cards.summary: A tROAS target that stops being met shrinks targeting, reduces spend, starves the model of conversion data and accelerates decline — pull the target back aggressively and early.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing a Google Ads account where spend and conversions are gradually trailing off over weeks and campaigns appear to be dying.
steps: Plot cost and conversions on a weekly view across 90–180 days and look for a slow trailing-off trend rather than a sudden drop, which is the signature of the spiral.

Understand the mechanism: tROAS models primarily off the last 30–90 days of conversion data, so once conversions fall the sample size bias worsens targeting, which lowers conversions further and pushes you further from the target, so spend pulls back again.

When you see the spiral, pull the tROAS target back aggressively rather than in small steps — the source's observation is that the common failure is being too timid, after which the account keeps declining.
If you leave tROAS untouched while it is not being met, expect the campaign to keep narrowing and eventually stop driving meaningful volume.
Check for the trigger that started the decline — seasonality, a top product going out of stock, feed disapproval — and resolve it alongside the bidding change, or the spiral restarts.
Consider rotating to an expansive strategy for a period to rebuild conversion volume and re-widen the audience pool before returning to a restrictive target.
caveats: The 30–90 day modelling window is the source's characterisation of platform behaviour and should be verified against current documentation.
Aggressive target changes still destabilise campaigns; make one significant change and observe before layering more.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Merge campaign learnings with portfolio bidding strategies
cards.summary: Portfolio bid strategies let segmented campaigns share learning and let you apply max/min CPC caps on top of value-based bidding.
cards.use_when: You need tight campaign segmentation for reporting or structure but individual campaigns are too data-starved to learn well, or you want to cap expensive clicks in a high-CPC niche.
steps: Set up a portfolio bidding strategy at the account level and apply it across the relevant campaigns so they pool conversion learnings instead of learning in isolation.

Use it when your segmentation has fragmented conversion volume to the point where no single campaign can model effectively — the portfolio breaks down the silos without undoing your campaign structure.

Apply a max CPC floor/ceiling on top of a value-based or tROAS strategy when certain auctions are structurally unprofitable: the source's example is high-end furniture where $10–$30 clicks are never worth it regardless of intent.
Verify current feature availability before relying on portfolio strategies; access levels and the comparable SA3 feature have changed and are plan-dependent.

For Search campaigns specifically, look at the smart bidding exploration setting, which the source says allows the campaign to test outside the target in percentage bands and creates a middle ground between restrictive and expansive bidding. It is not available on PMax or Shopping — confirm in your account.
caveats: Feature availability differs by account type, spend level and platform release; check the live interface.
Pooling learnings means a bad performer can influence the whole portfolio, so monitor campaign-level results after applying it.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Change Google Ads budgets and strategies slowly, downward faster than upward
cards.summary: Increase Google budgets in roughly 20% increments; reductions can be faster, but large overnight increases or bidding changes cause instability.
cards.use_when: Scaling or cutting spend on a Google Ads campaign and deciding how large a single change to make.
steps: Increase Google budgets in ~20% steps rather than doubling overnight; the source reports this rule holds on Google and that large upward jumps are consistently a bad idea because Google is a more stable, consistent platform that responds to methodical changes.
Apply the same caution to bidding strategy changes: move slowly upward, and avoid introducing a new target CPA or tROAS overnight.
Reduce budgets faster when needed — the source reports that cutting budgets quickly generally causes little instability or performance drop-off, unlike increases.
On Meta and TikTok, you have more flexibility and can raise budgets faster than the Google 20% guideline.

Treat 'Limited by budget' status as an indicator, not proof: the source says they see it on nearly every account regardless of spend level, including campaigns spending $5,000–$10,000/day in small markets, so validate incremental opportunity with other evidence before scaling.
caveats: The 20% guideline is the source's rule of thumb for Google, not a platform-enforced limit.
Budget cuts can still harm campaigns that depend on stable delivery; monitor conversion volume after any large reduction.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Optimise Google Merchant Center titles from search term data
cards.summary: Product feed titles are the main lever for Shopping and PMax placement; build them from historically converting search terms rather than default product names.
cards.use_when: Improving Shopping or PMax performance by rewriting product feed titles, or auditing a feed where default variant names are being used.
steps: Recognise the default problem: feeds typically pull 'Nathan dress size 12' plus colour, with brand auto-appended. The brand name is meaningless if brand is excluded from campaigns, and the product name means nothing to shoppers who don't already know the product.
Push the brand to the end of the title, or omit it entirely if you're not a recognised brand. Keep the unique product name only where it adds meaning.

Pull the keywords you front-load from the search term report — identify which terms have actually converted historically on the account — then place the strongest converting descriptor first (e.g. 'formal dress' ahead of the product name).

Add as many relevant attributes as fit within the title length limit (colour, style, size, format) so the listing can surface for attribute-based queries such as 'blue dress' that it previously couldn't match.

For generic or CPG products, layer multiple validated keyword variations into one title: e.g. 'dissolvable creatine powder clear flavoured portable [brand]', maximising the surface area of terms the listing can match.
Roll title changes out slowly over time rather than swapping every title at once, and watch CTR, CPC and ROAS to check the changes are making a material difference.
caveats: There is no golden rule for title structure — the source offers a directional template, not a fixed formula.
Changing many titles simultaneously resets learning phases on campaigns; the source warns against a mass overnight rollout.
If feed changes do not move CTR, CPC or returns, test alternative keyword selections rather than assuming the template failed.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Spin variant listings to cover multiple keyword pools
cards.summary: When a product has multiple variants, each variant generates its own Shopping listing — use separate titles and creative per variant to target different keyword pools and audiences.
cards.use_when: Merchandising a multi-variant product (sizes, formats, pack sizes) in Google Shopping or PMax and looking to expand reach without duplicating landing pages.
steps: Confirm that each variant (e.g. 50g, 100g, 500g creatine) produces a separate feed listing depending on how the feed is configured.
Assign each variant a distinct title and image focused on a different validated keyword pool, so the set of listings collectively covers more search demand than a single listing could.
Accept that all variants route to the same product landing page — the differentiation happens at the listing/feed level, not the destination page.
Monitor each variant listing separately for CTR and conversion so you can identify which keyword pool is winning and shift title emphasis accordingly.
Combine this with title optimisation so the distinct pools are backed by search terms that have actually converted historically.
caveats: Behaviour depends on feed configuration and platform rules for variant grouping; verify how your feed currently splits listings.
Do not use variant spinoffs to create near-duplicate listings that violate feed policy — the differentiation must be genuine product variants.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Fix feed image aspect ratios and build contrast for click-through
cards.summary: Shopping images occupy most of the listing real estate, so match the platform's required aspect ratio and design for contrast against competing listings — not for maximum CTR on the wrong audience.
cards.use_when: Auditing product feed imagery for a Shopping or PMax campaign where CTR is weak or images are being auto-cropped.
steps: Override the feed with a supplementary feed using the platform's current preferred image ratio. The source reports fashion images often come through at 9x6 and get auto-cropped badly; they specify 4x5 as the ratio Google wants to receive. Verify the current requirement in Merchant Center documentation.

Treat the image as the analogue of an ad hook: the goal is to attract the right shopper, not every shopper. The source cites Eugene Schwartz's principle that a headline targets the right reader, not all readers.

Build visual contrast against the listings you actually compete with: if competitors all use white-background studio shots, keep your product photography but change the background colour so your listing stands out in the grid.
Do not optimise purely for click-through rate — higher CTR from mismatched browsers harms conversion; judge image changes on return metrics, not clicks alone.
Check the rest of the feed while you're there: descriptions and attributes should already be clean; if not, fix them as a one-time setup.
caveats: Aspect ratio and image requirements are platform policies that change; confirm the current standard rather than assuming 4x5 indefinitely.
The cited ratio and the '70% of listing real estate' figure are the source's observations, not verified current specifications.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Set up separate feeds per currency for international Shopping
cards.summary: Running multiple regions through a single-currency feed forces live currency conversion on the listing, which suppresses CTR and conversion.
cards.use_when: Selling to customers in more than one currency via Google Shopping and reviewing the feed structure.
steps: Check whether all regions run through one feed with one currency — the source reports this as a common audit finding.
Create separate feeds for each currency so listings display in the shopper's local currency instead of showing a live-converted price.

Fix this because converted listings display disclaimers like 'converted from AUD' plus tax, which signals an international store to the shopper and depresses both click-through and conversion — even when you are not actually an international store.
Pair the currency feed fix with the broader feed clean-up (titles, images, attributes) as part of a one-time setup rather than a recurring task.
caveats: Multi-currency feed configuration interacts with Merchant Center account and country settings; verify current setup requirements before restructuring.
Localised pricing has tax and legal implications that vary by market.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Sequence the 90-day Google Ads improvement rollout
cards.summary: Implement Google Ads fixes in a defined order: tracking, structure map, PMax checks, waste removal, assets, then feed changes slowly.
cards.use_when: Planning an account-wide Google Ads overhaul or onboarding a new ecommerce account with multiple issues to fix.
steps: Start with tracking: no J4 duplicate events, back-end conversions firing with enhanced conversions and auto-tagging on. Everything downstream depends on clean data.

Build a structure map: start from one campaign as the default and require a commercial reason for each additional campaign (e.g. splitting brand from non-brand), with consistent naming across the structure.

Run a PMax-specific check: asset groups split by product type, listing groups split out, brand exclusions on, audience signals present, tROAS not set absurdly high (which turns PMax into a retargeting campaign), and the correct bidding strategy per the expansive/restrictive logic.
Audit for wasted spend: kill campaigns that spend too little to matter and roll the budget up, negative-keyword unprofitable search terms, and turn off display on Search campaigns.
Health-check ad assets: sitelinks, call ads, and promos that aren't stale or outdated, and maximise assets in every campaign to increase ad real estate.
Finish with the feed check (titles, images) and roll changes out slowly, watching CTR, CPC and returns in real time to confirm material impact.
caveats: The order matters — feeding optimisations into broken tracking produces misleading decisions.
Feed and structure changes reset learning phases, so avoid batching all of them at once.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Run a 5-minute business-level diagnostic before touching Google Ads
cards.summary: Before troubleshooting Google, verify cross-channel spend mix, decompose the revenue equation, separate attributed from true business KPIs, and rule out seasonality.
cards.use_when: Revenue or efficiency has dipped and you are deciding whether the problem is even a Google Ads problem before diving into the account.
steps: Do a cross-channel check first: if Google is only 10% of ad spend, a revenue dip is far more likely a Meta issue; prioritise platform investigation by share of spend. The source reports that for most of their clients the majority of spend skews to Meta, so Meta is usually checked first.
Ask what changed outside Google: coming off a sale, a Meta creative refresh that immediately preceded the dip, an offer change, or anything else that could explain the drop.

Decompose the revenue equation: revenue = conversion rate × average order value × sessions. Identify which of the three moved. Falling conversion rate points to the website; falling sessions points to a traffic source losing click volume; falling AOV points to product mix or a changed upsell/cross-sell.

Separate true business KPIs (revenue, profit contribution) from attributed platform metrics, and reconcile them — an attribution error or conversion lag can make a platform look broken when the business is fine.
Check seasonality against your forecast before starting a long diagnostic; without forecasting, normal seasonal dips are mistaken for problems.
caveats: The 10% / 65-35 examples are illustrations of the prioritisation logic, not universal thresholds.
This step often resolves the issue — the source notes Google is typically the most consistent platform and rarely the cause when it is a minority of spend.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Complete three pre-checks before any Google Ads diagnosis
cards.summary: Check change history, extend the time horizon, and use conversions-by-conversion-time before concluding performance has genuinely declined.
cards.use_when: Starting an account diagnostic or about to make changes after noticed a performance dip.
steps: Check change history first — never audit or make changes straight after a series of changes. Review what you, teammates, or the client altered in the account before drawing conclusions.
Extend your time horizon rather than comparing two short windows; short windows invite small-sample-size errors. Zoom out relative to the account's conversion volume before acting.
Account for conversion latency: Google attributes a purchase back to the click date, not the purchase date, so the most recent 3–4 days always look terrible on default conversion columns.
Pull the custom column 'conversions by conversion time' to see conversions attributed to the day the customer actually purchased, giving a usable read on recent days.
Only then decide whether the dip is real, and avoid launching a full diagnostic over a latency artefact.
caveats: Conversion latency behaviour and available custom columns may change; verify current column options in the interface.
Even with conversion-time columns, very recent data remains incomplete — combine with forecasting for the last days of a period.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Drill from account to campaign to ad group to find the inflection point
cards.summary: Troubleshoot Google Ads by sorting campaigns by spend, plotting metrics on 90–180 day weekly views, and locating the exact date performance changed — then descend to the responsible campaign and ad group.
cards.use_when: A confirmed Google Ads performance decline needs to be traced to a specific campaign type, campaign and ad group.
steps: Work from the account overview over 90–180 days on weekly view, rotating through cost, conversions, conversion value, cost per conversion, ROAS and CTR to see what moved and when.

Go to the campaign tab and sort by cost descending. Focus on the top five campaigns by spend: a campaign holding ~10% of budget cannot materially move the account even with a 100% performance change, so deprioritise small campaigns.
Identify the inflection point — e.g. a specific date after which a metric started trailing off — and find which campaigns changed at that point.
Repeat at ad group level (or PMax asset groups) to isolate which element contributed to the metric change.
Determine which campaign type failed first, because failure modes differ: PMax, Shopping and Search each decline for different reasons.
Prioritise this because a small campaign's improvement is diluted further by Google's share of total media spend — a 5% Google-level impact can become single digits at business level.
caveats: The top-five-by-spend focus is a prioritisation heuristic, not a rule that small campaigns can never matter.
Sorting by spend assumes the largest campaigns carry the largest business impact, which is usually but not always true.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Diagnose PMax failures: warm/cold drift, disapprovals, tROAS narrowing, product bloat
cards.summary: PMax campaigns fail in four recurring ways — audience drift, feed disapprovals, tROAS-driven audience narrowing, and product/SKU churn resetting learning.
cards.use_when: Troubleshooting a declining Performance Max campaign in an ecommerce account.
steps: Check warm/cold drift: PMax can retarget existing customers even when labelled a cold campaign. Review the search term report and audience report; brand terms appearing or an existing-customer skew means brand exclusion is broken or tROAS is set too high, forcing retargeting.

Check feed disapprovals: in ecommerce, the source estimates 80–90% of PMax performance comes from Shopping, and Shopping performance comes from feed quality. Look for top-spending products that went out of stock, were turned off, or were disapproved, then verify in Merchant Center.

Check tROAS narrowing: raising tROAS does not create magic efficiency — it narrows targeting to buyers more likely to convert at the target, which skews warmer. Expect worse new-customer ROAS; the source says you can verify with third-party attribution (e.g. Triple Whale) or natively in Google Ads, and that a high-tROAS PMax typically shows much worse NC ROAS than the same campaign with a low tROAS.

Check product bloat and stock churn: rapidly adding SKUs floods the campaign and hurts learning. A product holding ~15% of campaign spend that goes out of stock for even a few days resets that product's learning and affects the whole campaign.
If stock volatility is chronic, restructure the account so a single unstable product cannot drag down the campaigns around it — the source's agency asks clients to flag this at onboarding.
caveats: The 80–90% Shopping share and 15%-of-spend example are source observations, not universal benchmarks.
NC ROAS measurement depends on your attribution tool's correctness.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Diagnose Search campaign failures: search terms, auctions, tROAS, display leakage
cards.summary: Search campaign declines typically trace to changed search term spend allocation, new auction competition, raised tROAS or unintended display spend.
cards.use_when: Troubleshooting a declining Google Search campaign where volume or efficiency has dropped.
steps: Compare the search term report before and after the inflection point, sorted by spend: check whether the terms absorbing spend and their efficiency materially changed. The source notes broad match plus smart bidding can produce wild shifts in search term allocation that cause the performance change.
If search terms look stable and performance per term is unchanged, move on to the next check rather than forcing a search term explanation.
Check auction insights before and after the dip: a new competitor entering the auction can raise CPCs or reduce your share of entries, lowering volume.
Verify tROAS has not been squeezed upward, which narrows targeting and shifts spend toward warmer audiences — same mechanism as PMax.
Confirm display is turned off on the search campaign so spend has not been silently allocated into display placements.
caveats: Auction insight metrics are directional; interpret alongside your own CPC and impression-share trends.
Negative keyword work and broad match settings interact with smart bidding — changes here can take time to stabilise.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Diagnose Shopping campaign failures through the feed first
cards.summary: Shopping failures closely mirror PMax mechanics minus audience drift; the dominant causes are feed and product availability issues.
cards.use_when: Troubleshooting a declining Google Shopping campaign in an ecommerce store.
steps: Check tROAS settings as for PMax — a raised target narrows audience and pulls spend warmer.
Check Merchant Center thoroughly: out-of-stock top products, recent title or description changes, and any feed errors or warnings. This is usually the most important check for Shopping.
Check whether too many products have been added to the campaign, which can impact learning as described in the PMax product bloat failure mode.
Check search partners: the source notes heavy spend flowing to search partners performing poorly is worth verifying, though they consider it less likely to be the root cause.
Remember that Shopping lacks the warm/cold retargeting dimension of PMax, so feed and product status take more of the diagnostic weight.
caveats: Feed changes reset learning, so correlate the timing of any recent feed edit with the start of the decline.
Search partner performance varies by account — verify with segment-level reporting before excluding.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Decompose campaign KPIs via submetric formulas for root cause analysis
cards.summary: Every campaign metric is a product of underlying metrics; drilling into the right submetric locates the true root cause instead of a symptom.
cards.use_when: Investigating why a specific campaign's revenue, ROAS, CPA or conversion volume moved, in order to find the actual root cause.
steps: Apply the core formulas: CPA = CPC ÷ conversion rate; clicks = impressions × click-through rate; attributed revenue = clicks × conversion rate × average order value.

Start with whether efficiency (ROAS/CPA) or volume (clicks) is the issue. If ROAS dropped while clicks held steady, drill into CPC and conversion rate. If click volume dropped, the cause is either impressions compressing (fewer auctions entered) or falling CTR (competitors' listings becoming more convincing).

When troubleshooting AOV, decompose it into new-customer AOV and returning-customer AOV, and identify which one dipped before looking at offers. Then look at units per transaction and average unit retail to find the mechanical cause within the affected segment.

Treat the deeper formula breakdowns as the goal: the source argues the more granular your metric understanding, the better your root cause analysis compared to operators who change offers without checking which AOV component actually moved.

Check the quality score components when CPCs move: add quality score, expected CTR, ad relevance and landing page experience as columns and see which changed after the inflection point. Ad relevance is usually a quick fix; expected CTR is driven by actual CTR; landing page experience often requires dev work and can take weeks or months to refresh.
caveats: Formula structures are stable, but which columns expose each component changes with the platform interface — verify column availability.
Landing page experience rescoring timing is unpredictable; the source reports real cases where the fix took weeks to months to register.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Use revenue equation to route ecommerce diagnosis
cards.summary: Revenue = conversion rate × AOV × sessions; identifying which lever moved tells you whether to look at the website, a traffic source, or product mix.
cards.use_when: A top-line revenue decline needs to be attributed to a store-side or media-side cause before choosing a fix.
steps: Compute the three components across the affected period and identify which one changed.
If conversion rate dropped, investigate the website: broken pages, changed product pages, checkout issues, or structural changes.
If sessions dropped, investigate traffic sources: find which platform lost click volume and why.
If AOV dropped, check both product portfolio prioritisation (e.g. Google Ads now pushing cheaper products) and website changes such as a modified upsell or cross-sell structure.
Rule out external causes (sales ending, creative refreshes on other platforms, offer changes) before attributing the change to Google Ads.
caveats: The equation treats the three components as independent; in practice they interact (e.g. traffic mix shifts change AOV).
Session and conversion data quality depends on tracking accuracy — fix tracking first.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Google Ads Diagnostic Tree: Top-Down Root Cause Analysis
cards.summary: A top-down order of investigation for diagnosing Google Ads performance declines, from business level down to the submetric.
cards.use_when: Paid search or Shopping performance has dipped and you must decide whether to act, what to change, and in what order before touching the account.
steps: Never start at the metric the client or dashboard flagged. Start at the business level and ask what materially changed: revenue, margin, offer, site. If business-level numbers are up, a 10% ROAS dip in your fifth-largest spender may not warrant investigation at all.

Move down one level at a time: channel level (did Meta, email or organic change, since a brand search campaign is largely dependent on Meta spend?), then campaign type, then specific campaign, then finally the submetric.
At each level ask 'why' before descending. Diagnose the metric (CPA up? volume down?) to route to the relevant submetric branch.

Only act once you can complete the sentence: 'This campaign is underperforming because [metric] dropped, driven by [submetric], caused by [trigger], which is the root cause.' If you cannot finish that sentence, do not touch the account.
This ordering is the source's asserted separator between strong and weak media buyers; treat it as a working heuristic rather than a proven performance benchmark.
caveats: Source is explicit that most 'broken' accounts are simply misread, so a cross-channel sanity check belongs before any in-platform change.
Requires access to business-level revenue and margin data, not just ad platform numbers.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Diagnosing Rising CPC: Three Causes and When It Actually Matters
cards.summary: CPC is treated as a vanity metric; diagnose quality score, new auction entrants, and premium auction entry before reacting.
cards.use_when: Cost per click has risen in Google Ads, Meta or TikTok and you need to decide whether it signals a real problem for store acquisition cost.
steps: Check CPA first, not CPC. The source's position is that CPCs are a vanity metric on Google, Meta and TikTok because they only matter at the extremes. Higher CPC with proportionally higher conversion rate keeps CPA flat and is acceptable; higher CPC with flat conversion rate is the problem case.

If CPC is the issue, test three explanations: (1) Quality score components deteriorated, with ad relevance and expected CTR being more actionable than landing page experience; (2) a new competitor entered the auction, verified by comparing Auction Insights before and after the dip point; (3) you moved to more premium auctions after changing tROAS or another bidding strategy.
For the premium-auction case, ask whether the higher-cost clicks are actually higher quality. If conversion rate has not risen to offset the CPC increase, the premium auctions are not paying off.
Adjust bidding strategy, creative or market coverage based on which cause you confirm rather than cutting spend reflexively.
caveats: Landing page experience is the hardest quality-score component to move: it depends on dev work and Google's re-crawl/re-score cycle, and the source reports cases taking weeks to months to turn around even after the site was fixed.
Google's quality score internals and re-crawl cadence are opaque and change; verify the current interface and behaviour before relying on any specific component.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Diagnosing Falling Conversion Rate: Tracking, Landing Page, Audience, Learning, Offer
cards.summary: A five-step check for conversion-rate declines, ordered from tracking errors to offer changes, that applies to platform and storefront conversion alike.
cards.use_when: Ad platform conversion rate or site conversion rate has dropped and you need to separate measurement artefacts from real storefront problems before rebuilding anything.
steps: Check tracking first: has the pixel or tag stopped firing, or are you reading a window shorter than the actual conversion lag? Conversion-by-time views exist for exactly this; a bad tracking setup makes conversion rate look broken when nothing on the platform changed.

Check whether the landing page materially changed: a different URL, a price change, a redirect, added upsells or cross-sells, or altered merchandising. The source calls this probably the number one real cause of conversion-rate declines.

Check whether the audience changed: read search term reports for new, non-converting terms, and review whether the bidding strategy change pushed you toward a different audience. Low congruency between query, ad and landing page depresses conversion.
Check whether the learning phase reset. Large structural account changes push Google Ads back into learning, during which it enters wrong auctions and drives poor traffic.
Check whether the offer changed: expired promo, removed discount, or an altered free-shipping threshold all depress conversion rate independently of ads.
caveats: Conversion lag means short-window reads systematically understate conversion rate; always compare like-for-like windows.
The source gives no numeric thresholds, so treat the ordering as a diagnostic sequence, not a ranked statistical model.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Diagnosing Volume Declines: Impressions, Impression Share and CTR
cards.summary: When efficiency holds but volume falls, trace it to clicks, then to impressions lost to budget versus bid, then to CTR.
cards.use_when: Google Ads revenue or spend has fallen while CPA is stable, and you need to decide whether to raise budget, raise bids, or change creative.
steps: Identify the branch: if efficiency (CPA/ROAS) is unchanged but volume is down, the problem is clicks. Clicks decompose into impressions and CTR.

For impressions, distinguish impression share lost to budget from impression share lost to rank using the platform's impression share columns. If you are hitting your daily budget cap, you are losing share to budget and simply need more spend.
