caveats: Platform defaults and definitions change frequently — verify current settings. This card reflects the presenter's audit observations and may not apply to every account.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Platform lift tests vs geo-lift tests: choosing your incrementality method
cards.summary: Compare in-platform lift experiments and geo-lift experiments on speed, cost, verifiability, and effort so you pick the right one for your paid media validation.
cards.use_when: You need to validate whether a paid channel (Meta, TikTok, Google, YouTube) is driving genuinely incremental purchases rather than just claiming credit for existing demand.
steps: Understand the in-platform lift test mechanism: the platform splits users individually into a treatment bucket (sees ads) and control bucket (no ads), then measures purchase behavior via pixel and computes incremental impact.
Know the in-platform lift pros: fast, can run continuously (Meta allows always-on runs), and works at individual user level so no country splitting is needed.
Know the in-platform lift cons: you rely entirely on the platform's data science and cannot verify their math or see raw data; it also depends on attribution being accurate.
Know geo-lift pros: you control the experimental design, own all the data, and can verify everything end-to-end.
Know geo-lift cons: slow to run, requires large spend to reach statistical significance, and requires holding variables constant across states and the test period.
Watch for minimum spend hurdles: the source notes TikTok (and similarly Google) may require roughly $200k spend before you can actually run the test; verify current platform minimums.
Source position: use both methods in one experiment design strategy rather than treating either as a silver bullet.

Ecommerce application: for a store deciding whether to keep or scale a channel, run a platform lift test when budget is limited and speed matters, and reserve geo-lift tests for high-revenue scenarios where you need verifiable causation.
caveats: Platform lift experiments cannot be independently verified — you trust the vendor's readout.
Geo-lift tests require large budgets and long timelines and are not easy to run.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Using causal impact / counterfactual modeling for retroactive channel analysis
cards.summary: Apply Google's open-source causal impact package to retrospectively estimate what revenue would have been without a channel intervention, using third-party confounding variables.
cards.use_when: You introduced a channel or campaign (e.g., YouTube, TikTok) at some point in the past and want a directional retrospective read on whether it actually drove revenue.
steps: Recognize the core problem: with no geo split you cannot prove causation, so you use a predictive model to build a counterfactual of what revenue would have been absent the intervention.
Identify predictive confounding variables for your daily revenue, such as ad spend, keyword seasonality, influencer spend, and inflation data.
Load those variables plus the intervention point into Google's open-source causal impact package (the source misspoke initially as 'causal inference').
Read the output as a predicted counterfactual revenue line versus actual revenue; the gap over the period is your directional incremental impact.
Apply the pack to real decisions: the source's example found an extra ~$10k revenue against $10k ad spend — roughly a 1x ROI — showing the channel was far less effective than assumed.
Use it as an add-on to your tooling to go back and analyze a past TikTok, YouTube, or similar launch.
Ecommerce application: before reallocating budget to a channel you launched during a strong season, run this analysis to avoid crediting the channel for what seasonality or spend already drove.
caveats: Causal impact is a predictive model using third-party variables, not true experimental proof — treat it as directional only.
It is Bayesian/statistical inference, not a substitute for a real geo-lift experiment when causation matters.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Why launch timing confuses channel results (Black Friday and Q4 era)
cards.summary: Brands wrongly credit a new channel for a strong period because they launched it during seasonality peaks without any measurement system.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to keep a channel you launched in October/November or during any peak season based on a good subsequent month.
steps: Identify the trap: introducing YouTube, TikTok, or another channel in October and then seeing a strong November leads many to assume the channel worked.
Ask how the uplift was actually measured — the source notes most cannot answer this; there is no test design, only correlation drawn from a good period.
Recognize that 'revenue went up after we launched' is not evidence the campaign caused it when seasonality is a strong confounding variable.
Demand a causal experimental design before treating the channel as a winner; without it, you may find your assumptions are wrong.

Ecommerce application: for a store planning a new channel launch, avoid launching it into peak season or, if you must, build the counterfactual model before drawing conclusions about its incremental value.
caveats: The source example is illustrative, not a quantified benchmark.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Setting up Conversions API (CAPI) on Meta for better tracking and optimization
cards.summary: Route purchase events server-side through Meta's Conversions API to bypass unreliable browser tracking and improve event matching and optimization.
cards.use_when: You are auditing or fixing Meta ad tracking for an ecommerce store and want to improve data quality feeding the ad platform.
steps: Install the Conversions API (CAPI) on Meta; the source says to make sure it is set up and working.
Understand the mechanism: instead of purchase events firing from the browser pixel, they fire on your own local server, which then reroutes them to Meta.
Know why it matters: this removes reliance on the browser, which is unreliable due to iOS changes, ad blockers, and privacy regulations.
Understand the matching benefit: CAPI passes back first-party data (email, phone number, customer ID), all hashed/privatized, which improves event match rates.
Use it for offline conversions: if someone buys in store using an email or phone, CAPI can link that purchase back to an ad served on the platform.
Accept the optimization payoff: better tracking means more data flowing into the platform, which improves ad optimization.
Ecommerce application: prioritize CAPI setup before scaling Meta spend, since poor tracking degrades optimization for every campaign you run.
caveats: Tool interfaces and setup steps change over time — verify current Meta CAPI setup instructions.
The source says brands doing $10-20M+/year should already have tracking configured, so this is more of a check than a from-scratch rebuild at that scale.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Avoid Shopify marketing/attribution reports for decisions
cards.summary: The source finds Shopify's marketing and attribution reports unreliable and recommends not using them for business decisions.
cards.use_when: You are setting up your measurement stack for an ecommerce store and deciding which data sources to trust for spend and revenue decisions.
steps: Do not rely on Shopify's marketing or attribution reports for decision-making; the source says it has rarely seen helpful data there.
Recognize this is fundamentally the same attribution problem you face elsewhere — the attribution models in Shopify are not reliable for understanding true impact.
Instead, build your decision dashboard on financial-based KPIs and platform data, not Shopify's attribution models.
Use G4 and Shopify only as needed; the source treats them as secondary or redundancy layers rather than primary decision dashboards.
Ecommerce application: when deciding budget shifts between channels, pull the numbers from your own incrementality testing and financial KPIs rather than the Shopify attribution report.
caveats: The source's assessment is as of May 2026 and reflects its own client experience — verify whether Shopify has updated its reporting.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Treat GA4 as a redundancy layer, not a daily decision dashboard
cards.summary: GA4 should collect data properly as a fallback, but should not drive day-to-day ecommerce decisions because it offers nothing you can't get from Shopify or the ad platforms.
cards.use_when: You are deciding what to actually open each day to make budget and campaign decisions for your store.
steps: Position GA4 as a redundancy layer: if your platform tracking breaks, GA4 gives quick directional insight as a fallback.
Ensure GA4 is set up properly — firing correctly, with campaigns segmented — so the fallback data has been collecting all along.
Do not use GA4 as your primary daily decision dashboard; the source says there is nothing in GA4 you cannot get from Shopify or the ad platforms.
Prioritize more important financial and incrementality metrics for indexing against your decisions instead.

Ecommerce application: for daily budget or scaling calls, work from new-customer revenue, acquisition CAC, and profit contribution dashboards; keep GA4 configured only so it is there when you need a backup read.
caveats: Source opinion as of May 2026; GA4 capabilities may change — verify before relying on this.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: One-day view attribution overattribution mistake
cards.summary: Running one-day view through all campaigns inflates reported ROAS with massive overattribution, so remove it to see reality.
cards.use_when: You are auditing Meta (or similar) campaign reporting and wondering why reported ROAS looks great but the business results disagree.
steps: Check whether one-day view attribution is enabled across all campaigns and being used in reporting.
Recognize this causes massive overattribution — the source cites 30-50% of reported ROAS coming from view-throughs.
Remove one-day view from reporting to get a more realistic read of what is actually occurring in the business.
Ecommerce application: before scaling budget on the strength of reported ROAS, strip view-through attribution and recalculate so your scaling decisions are based on real impact.
caveats: The 30-50% figure is the source's observation from audits, not a universal benchmark.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Account for Google's halo effect when judging ROAS
cards.summary: Google overattributes by taking credit for conversions that other platforms drove, so its ROAS should be reconsidered with skepticism.
cards.use_when: You are evaluating a PMax or Google campaign showing very high ROAS and deciding whether to increase spend.
steps: Understand the halo effect: Google's reported ROAS looks better than reality because it absorbs credit for what other platforms drove.
Do not conclude Google cannot acquire new customers — the source says you can profitably spend $100-200k/month on Google, but only if it is genuinely net incremental.

Stress-test the number: if a PMax campaign (even with brand excluded) shows 20x ROAS, skeptically consider putting an extra $1,000 in and checking whether you actually get $20,000 back in topline — likely you will not.
Treat Google's incrementality as usually overstated and account for the halo when reporting.
Ecommerce application: when deciding to scale Google spend for your store, validate with an incrementality test rather than trusting reported ROAS.
caveats: High Google ROAS is not proof of no incremental value — it means the reported figure overstates incremental impact.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Brand spend waste caused by over-prioritizing ROAS
cards.summary: Chasing ROAS as the north star leads accounts to leave brand search in, causing large waste even at 8-figure retailers.
cards.use_when: You are structuring paid search or campaign budgets and deciding whether to suppress brand terms.
steps: Recognize why brand waste happens: because ROAS is the north star metric, teams leave brand in to keep ROAS high.
Note the source sees this even in large 8-figure retailers, causing significant waste within the account.
Exclude brand where it is not genuinely incremental, and minimize brand search spend in your account structure.
Ecommerce application: in a store's paid search budget, separate brand and non-brand, and do not let brand conversions inflate the portfolio ROAS that justifies further spend.
caveats: Brand terms are not always non-incremental; the source's point is that ROAS-driven incentives cause over-investment in them.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Over-segmentation causes measurement fragmentation
cards.summary: Too many campaigns relative to business complexity and spend fragments data and makes decision-making convoluted.
cards.use_when: You are reviewing account structure and considering splitting campaigns further, or auditing why reporting is hard to interpret.
steps: Check whether your number of campaigns is disproportionate to your business complexity or spend level.
Understand the compounding effect: over-segmentation fragments data, which creates a measurement problem.
Recognize that with fragmented data, decision-making becomes very convoluted.
Consolidate campaigns to match business complexity and spend level to keep data readable.
Ecommerce application: for a store running many campaigns with modest budgets, simplify account structure so measurement and decisions stay clear rather than splitting further.
caveats: Over-segmentation is a judgment call; there is no fixed campaign count — assess against business complexity and spend.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Beware overattribution on low-spend tertiary channels
cards.summary: Small third-party channels like Snapchat, Pinterest, and Reddit show inflated ROAS because low spend defaults to reaching warm pixel audiences rather than driving new growth.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether a small tertiary channel's high ROAS justifies keeping or growing it.
steps: Identify the tertiary channels: Snapchat, Pinterest, Reddit, and similar channels with very low spend allocation.
Understand the mechanism: at low spend, the algorithm prioritizes the warm audience already hitting your site (with pixel) rather than new users.
Recognize the result: incredibly high reported ROAS on channels that are not actually driving new incremental growth.
Treat these high ROAS numbers with skepticism before crediting them for growth or scaling them.
Ecommerce application: for a store testing a small channel, measure new-customer impact or run an incrementality test rather than trusting the channel's reported ROAS.
caveats: The overattribution problem is driven by low spend, so larger budgets on these channels may behave differently and should be tested.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Stop existing-customer overspend that inflates metrics
cards.summary: Spending more on existing customers because ROAS looks good inflates all numbers and drives further misallocation.
cards.use_when: You are setting campaign objectives and budgets and need to decide whether to exclude existing customers.
steps: Look for budget increases justified by strong ROAS that are actually driven by existing-customer spend.
Recognize this inflates all the numbers and leads teams to increase budgets further based on misleading ROAS.
Exclude existing customers from top-of-funnel campaigns so results reflect acquisition.
Ecommerce application: in a store's prospecting campaigns, suppress past purchasers so reported returns reflect new-customer acquisition rather than repeat buyers who would have purchased anyway.
caveats: Excluding existing customers is specific to top-of-funnel campaigns; retention campaigns intentionally target them.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Top-funnel Meta objectives (traffic/reach) need a measurement system
cards.summary: Running traffic or reach campaigns on Meta without any measurement system means unmeasurable spend and false confidence drawn from correlation.
cards.use_when: You are considering traffic or reach campaigns for your store, or auditing whether existing ones are justified.
steps: Recognize that traffic/reach campaigns have no ROAS, which is why they are often run on assumed performance.
Understand the typical failure: almost no one running traffic campaigns has a way to actually measure their impact — they attribute revenue lift to correlation from agency reporting.
Evaluate the source's critique: running a traffic campaign at 3% of budget during Black Friday has essentially no measurable impact, and before/after correlation cannot prove it did.
Choose one path: if you run traffic or reach campaigns, fine, but have a measurement system (e.g., lift study or causal impact) in place to validate them.
Otherwise, do not run spend you cannot measure — the source's position is it is just wasting budget on something unvalidated.
Ecommerce application: for a store testing awareness-style objectives, predefine the lift test or counterfactual method before launching, not after.
caveats: This is the source's strong position that unmeasured top-funnel spend is not worth running; it does not forbid these objectives, it demands measurement.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: DPA overspend driven by attractive ROAS
cards.summary: Scaling dynamic product ads because ROAS looks good leads to non-incremental spend since DPAs sit at the bottom of funnel.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to increase DPA budget based on strong reported ROAS.
steps: Identify the pattern: DPAs show attractive ROAS, prompting people to spend more and more.
Recognize this is not actually incremental because DPAs sit at the bottom of the funnel and harvest existing demand.
Apply the same skepticism you use for brand and retargeting when reviewing DPA returns.
Ecommerce application: for a store scaling catalog/DPA campaigns, validate incrementality before raising budget rather than scaling purely on ROAS.
caveats: Bottom-funnel campaigns can still be valuable for conversion; the warning is against treating their ROAS as evidence of incremental growth.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Build a measurement and testing structure so every decision is validated
cards.summary: Without a testing/experimental design, you cannot validate whether anything is working, which the source considers a core scaling failure.
cards.use_when: You are setting up or auditing the measurement foundation for a store's paid media and need to decide what to test and how.
steps: Recognize the core diagnosis: most brands that fail to scale paid media have a measurement problem, not a paid media problem.
Understand the consequence: they optimize to numbers that do not match what is actually occurring in the business.
Establish a testing or experimental design before running any new initiative — if you cannot validate whether something works, the source argues it is not worth doing.
Connect this to the traffic/reach campaign problem: running something with no measurement system means you are just making assumptions.
Ecommerce application: for a store, define what outcome each new channel or campaign is meant to drive and the method (lift study, geo-lift, causal impact) that will validate it before spending.
caveats: The source's framing ('if you can't validate it, there's no point') is a strong position; smaller stores may still run low-cost exploratory spend.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Action items for $1-5M revenue stores: fix reporting basics
cards.summary: At $1-5M revenue, switch to 7-day click on Meta, tag COGS in Shopify, build a profit-focused dashboard, and exclude existing customers from top-of-funnel.
cards.use_when: You run an ecommerce store in the $1-5M revenue range and want the right baseline measurement actions.
steps: Switch to 7-day click reporting on Meta — the source says it correlates much better to acquisition metrics in the business.
Tag up Shopify cost of goods on all products so you get real-time visibility into gross margin.
Set up a dashboard giving a daily read on: acquisition new-customer profit contribution, new-customer revenue, new-customer orders, and blended CAC.
Exclude existing customers from top-of-funnel campaigns.
Minimize brand search spend.
Ecommerce application: implement these as the foundation for a store at this revenue level before layering in more advanced incrementality testing.
caveats: These are revenue-band heuristics from the source, not proven thresholds; apply based on your actual situation.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Action items for $5-20M revenue stores: layer in lift studies
cards.summary: At $5-20M revenue, add in-platform lift studies for top-funnel experimentation and use incremental attribution as a second validation layer beyond 7-day click.
cards.use_when: You run an ecommerce store in the $5-20M revenue range and have the basics in place, ready to add validation infrastructure.
steps: Retain all the $1-5M basics (7-day click, COGS tagging, profit dashboard, existing-customer exclusion, brand minimization).
Start layering in lift studies within the platforms.
Run top-funnel experimentation measured against those lift studies.
Use incremental attribution as a second validation layer beyond 7-day click reporting.
Ecommerce application: for a store at this scale, use lift studies to validate top-funnel spend that ROAS cannot measure, feeding incrementality factors back into reporting.
caveats: Revenue bands are source heuristics, not fixed rules; also note in-platform lift studies cannot be independently verified.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Action items for $20M+ revenue stores: geo-lift tests and incrementality factors
cards.summary: At $20M+, run geo-lift tests outside the platform and apply resulting incrementality factors to attributed ROAS numbers for a realistic view.
cards.use_when: You run an ecommerce store at $20M+ revenue with a complex channel and revenue capture mix and need verifiable incrementality measurement.
steps: Run geo-lift tests outside the platform for channels where you need verifiable causation.
Build a dashboard that pulls in omnichannel metrics from every revenue capture place, not just platform data.
Add one or two additional metrics on top of the baseline dashboard as your scale allows.

Apply incrementality factors: when a geo-lift gives an incremental return output, use it as a factor applied to in-platform attributed ROAS numbers to get a more realistic incremental view across campaigns and platforms.
Run consistent geo-lift tests at high frequency so you can derive incrementality factors across all channels and campaign types.
Ecommerce application: for a large store making big budget allocations, use these factors to correct platform ROAS before reallocating spend.
caveats: Requires very high frequency testing to build factors across all channels; geo-lift tests take significant time and spend.
Revenue bands are source heuristics.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Shift from ROAS to financial-based KPIs for scaling decisions
cards.summary: The source argues winning brands move toward financial-based KPIs and incrementality testing rather than optimizing to platform ROAS.
cards.use_when: You are setting the north-star metric for your store's paid media and deciding what to optimize.
steps: Identify the trap: optimizing to numbers that do not match what is actually occurring in the business, often ROAS inflated by view-throughs, brand, and bottom-funnel capture.
Understand the consequences chain: a measurement problem drives bad decision-making loops, and brands attribute credit to the wrong funnel stage.
Move toward financial-based KPIs (e.g., new-customer profit contribution, blended CAC, incremental return) rather than platform-reported ROAS as the north star.
Add incrementality tests at larger revenue levels to validate those financial KPIs.
At any level, prioritize cleaning up in-platform reporting as the first step.
Ecommerce application: for a store deciding where to scale, base the call on new-customer profit and CAC rather than a reported ROAS that may overattribute.
caveats: This is the source's strategic opinion, framed as where winning brands are headed in 2026-2027; the source also has a commercial interest in providing audits.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Calculate CAC and LTGP monthly as your two core operating metrics
cards.summary: Every DTC brand should compute cost to acquire a customer and constrained lifetime gross profit each month, then treat them as the fundamental diagnostic instead of ROAS.
cards.use_when: You need a single monthly scorecard to decide whether the store can profitably scale paid acquisition, cut spend, or fix retention.
steps: Compute CAC = total ad spend across all platforms in the period divided by new customers acquired in that same period. Pull new customers from your own order data, not from a platform summary.
Compute LTGP = gross profit from a customer over a fixed window, where gross profit means revenue minus cost of goods AND cost of delivery (shipping/fulfilment), not just revenue minus COGS.

Choose the window based on how often your category repeats: use first-purchase gross profit (a very short window) for repurchase-poor categories like furniture and homewares; extend to roughly 180 or 365 days for consumables, supplements and subscription models.

Pull the lifetime figure from a real cohort analysis (cohorts of customers by acquisition month, tracked forward to day 30/60/90/etc.), not from attributed revenue dashboards, daily returning-customer revenue, or a 'percent new customers' Shopify tile.

Record both numbers every month in one table so you can see the trend. When either CAC rises or LTGP falls, drill into that metric first rather than assuming it is a creative, seasonality or traffic problem.

Timestamp every structural change (new product, new channel, new agency, heavier discounting) and read it against the CAC and LTGP series to see whether the change improved the ratio, then double down or reverse.
caveats: Applying an assumed gross-margin percentage to cohort revenue is a workaround; the source says generating it from actual cost of goods is better.
Platform-attributed ROAS can stay stable while the real business declines, because view-through and over-crediting inflate it.
cards.source_name: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Read the LTGP:CAC bands and know what each one demands
cards.summary: LTGP:CAC below 1 is a death spiral, 1-2 needs extremely lean opex, 2-3 is the source's target scaling zone, and above 3 suggests underinvesting in acquisition.
cards.use_when: You are setting a paid-media budget or deciding whether to push spend harder, hold, or pull back on acquisition.
steps: Diagnose your current position: if LTGP is $100 and CAC is $120, the ratio is below 1 and you lose $20 on the first purchase. The source treats sub-1 as structurally dangerous unless retention is genuinely exceptional, which it calls very rare.

Recognise the 1-2 band as workable but tight: at $1 in and $1.50 out in gross profit, the 50 cents must cover operating expenses, so you need unusually lean opex or very large volume to produce a healthy net margin. The source says it is possible to run here with strong operations and retention, just uncommon.
Treat 2-3 as the zone where the source always suggests scaling and ramping budgets.
Treat above 3 as a signal you are leaving money on the table and should ramp harder.

Do not chase a fantasy ratio: LTGP is bounded by category structure. A low-ticket product (e.g. a $50 supplement) cannot deliver an arbitrary multiple, so benchmark against the best operators in your own category and set a realistic CAC target from there.
caveats: These bands are the presenter's heuristics for DTC ecommerce, not a universal law, and they assume ecommerce dynamics (weak consumer stickiness) rather than service or B2B models.
The bands assume LTGP is measured over the correct window for your repurchase frequency; comparing a 30-day LTGP to a 365-day CAC benchmark is meaningless.
cards.source_name: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Derive CAC from CPM, CTR and conversion rate to offset rising ad costs
cards.summary: CAC = CPC / conversion rate, and CPC = CTR x CPM, so annually rising CPMs can be offset by lifting click-through rate or conversion rate.
cards.use_when: Your CAC is climbing and you need to decide which lever — ad creative, PDP/landing page conversion, or media efficiency — to work on.
steps: Write out the chain: CAC = CPC / conversion rate and CPC = CTR x CPM, so CPM sits several layers beneath CAC via CPC.
Accept the structural premise the source states: platforms need to grow revenue every year, so CPMs will very likely be higher next year. Plan for it rather than treating it as a crisis.
Offset that lift by improving either CTR or conversion rate. If you lift one of them enough, you hold your profitability roughly flat year over year even as CPMs rise.

For ecommerce application: CTR improvements come from creative and offer framing in the ad, while conversion-rate improvements come from the PDP, landing page, offer clarity, pricing presentation and checkout. Assign the fix to the right surface rather than defaulting to 'creative'.

Set a discipline of compounding small improvements — the source frames it as improving about 1% a day on CTR and conversion. Operators who stay better than the majority keep feeling less CPM pressure and can push budget harder when competitors pull back.
Note that platform algorithm updates are designed to lift advertiser ROI so the platform can then raise CPMs; the platform does not hand you the surplus, so your own improvement is the offset.
caveats: This is a decomposition, not a prediction; conversion rate here means purchase conversion on your traffic, not lead conversion.
CTR and CPM interact with audience and placement; a CTR gain on cheap placements may not translate into cheaper CAC.
cards.source_name: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Split the P&L into first-time and returning customer views
cards.summary: Filter every P&L line by order-type tag to expose an acquisition loss that a combined, blended P&L hides behind returning-customer profit.
cards.use_when: Total profit still looks acceptable but you suspect new-customer acquisition has quietly turned loss-making, or before raising capital or debt.
steps: Tag orders in your commerce platform by first-time versus returning customer, then generate two full P&Ls by filtering every line item on that tag.

Read total profit contribution at the bottom of each. A brand can lose, illustratively, $50,000 a month on the first-time-customer P&L while making $300,000 on the returning-customer P&L, so the business looks profitable while acquisition is bleeding.
Track the trend in the first-time P&L specifically: the source's example is a client falling from +$20,000/month on first-time customers to -$70,000/month, invisible in the blended view.

Use this split when deciding whether returning revenue is genuinely subsidising acquisition or merely masking it. If returning profit is not covering the first-time loss, the model is fragile and any retention wobble becomes an existential event.
If a full split is impractical, use the unit-level LTGP:CAC ratio as the everyday proxy — the source says it tells you the same story at unit level that the P&L split tells you at volume level.

Pair the split with a cohort view of CAC month over month and new-customer volume month over month, since the pattern the source describes is CAC exploding and spend being cranked up to hold volume, after which CAC never recovers.
caveats: Requires reliable order-type tagging; mis-tagged orders corrupt both P&Ls.
The dollar figures cited are illustrative case examples from the presenter's audits, not benchmarks for your store.
cards.source_name: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Diagnose the death spiral from the two numbers, not from traffic, creative or seasonality
cards.summary: The spiralling CAC pattern — CAC rises, new customers fall, spend is increased to hold revenue, CAC rises again — is structural and should be diagnosed from the CAC and LTGP series first.
cards.use_when: Revenue or profitability has deteriorated for a quarter and leadership is blaming traffic, creative fatigue, seasonality or the macroeconomy.
steps: Trace the described loop: CAC creeps from, say, $50 to $60; at a fixed $100,000 budget you acquire fewer customers; revenue falls; with weak repeat purchasing you increase spend to hold revenue; the extra spend pushes CAC higher again, and it can end up double the prior level.

Before accepting any other explanation, pull CAC month over month alongside new-customer volume and revenue month over month. The signature is CAC breaking upward and spend being cranked up afterwards to maintain volume.

Reject the three default misdiagnoses the source names — that it is a traffic problem (just needs more spend or cheaper CPCs), a creative problem (creative drives targeting so it must be the ads), or a seasonality/macro problem. In the source's experience across 1,000+ audits, it is usually none of these.
Work backwards from LTGP and CAC to identify the actual constraint, then fix that constraint rather than adding spend on top of a broken unit economic.
Be aware that forcing scale through a bad LTGP with raised capital does not work; the source states that the ratio, not the funding, determines whether the business can scale.
caveats: The source acknowledges operating expenses can also sink brands, particularly smaller ones ($50k-$300k/month), often causing cash-constrained failure rather than a pure LTGP:CAC failure.
The audit volume and client scale cited are the presenter's own experience, not an independent study.
cards.source_name: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Rank your measurement methods by distance from base reality
cards.summary: Move up a hierarchy from expert opinion and platform ROAS to multi-regression, quasi-experiments and geo holdouts, because decisions are only as good as how closely the metric tracks reality.
cards.use_when: You need to decide how much to trust a platform-reported number before reallocating budget between channels or scaling spend.
steps: Place methods on the ladder: expert opinion plus anecdote at the bottom, then simple correlation (platform-attributed ROAS), then advanced correlation such as multi-regression or marketing mix modelling, then quasi-experiments such as difference-in-differences or regression discontinuity, then true experiments such as geo holdouts at the top.

Prefer the highest rung you can practically run for the decision at hand; the source's framing is that the highest-ROI activity in business is making the correct decision, which requires seeing reality as clearly as possible.

Sanity-check platform numbers by removing view-through conversions first. In the source's example, a reported ROAS that looked like ~20 collapsed to ~7 once view-throughs were stripped out, and dropped again when narrowed to a stricter attribution model.
Watch the de-inflated number over time rather than the topline: a de-inflated figure declining month over month is the early warning the topline hides.

Where you spend across multiple platforms, use experimental design (holdouts, quasi-experiments) to attribute contribution, because LTGP:CAC alone cannot tell you which platform drove the good or bad result.
Keep LTGP:CAC as the ultimate scorecard of business health even while using experiments to explain why it moved.
caveats: The source explicitly says avoiding all of this by simply watching LTGP:CAC is acceptable for many operators — the hierarchy is for platform-level attribution decisions.
The specific ROAS collapse figures are a single anonymised client example.
cards.source_name: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Match your CAC discipline to the retention structure of your category
cards.summary: Furniture and homewares should run on first-purchase gross profit with a deliberately flat CAC, while fashion and CPG can extend the LTGP window because repeat revenue genuinely accrues.
cards.use_when: You are setting the measurement window and CAC target for your category, or deciding whether to invest in retention or defend acquisition cost.
steps: Classify your category's repeat behaviour. The source cites day-365 gross-profit lift benchmarks of about 55% for fashion, about 110% for CPG and supplements, and near 0% for furniture and homewares.

For repurchase-poor categories (furniture, homewares), treat lifetime gross profit as effectively nonexistent and manage the business on first-purchase gross profit with a stable CAC. The source's operational guidance for these clients is to keep CAC flat over time.

For categories with genuine repeat behaviour (fashion, CPG, supplements, subscription), extend the LTGP window out to around 180-365 days and use cohort data to measure it, while still keeping CAC controlled.

Do not assume retention tactics can transform a low-lift category. The source argues the achievable LTGP band is largely structurally predetermined by industry and price point, and that executing many retention tactics will not move a number that the business model fixes.
Pick CAC benchmarks from the best operators in your specific industry rather than from cross-industry ratios, then aim to approach them.

Recognise the source's own estimate that roughly 80% of brands have weak lifetime gross profit contribution (often only 20-40% gross-profit lift by day 365), in which case CAC control is the primary lever.
caveats: The 55% / 110% / near-0% figures are the presenter's cited vertical benchmarks, not a universal measurement standard.
B2B has materially different repeat dynamics from D2C and is called out as a different game.
cards.source_name: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Use cohort analysis to read retention instead of surface retention metrics
cards.summary: Shopify-style cohort boxes, read forward in time, are the source's required method for measuring lifetime gross profit and retention rather than Klaviyo attributed revenue or daily returning-customer revenue.
cards.use_when: You want to measure retention properly to set your LTGP window and confirm whether recent acquisition cohorts are degrading.
steps: Open cohort analysis and read month zero as revenue from a customer on day one, then follow the same cohort forward to day 30, 60, 90 and beyond to see its cumulative value.

Reject the metrics the source explicitly disqualifies for this purpose: Klaviyo attributed revenue, returning-customer revenue measured daily or monthly, and the percentage-of-new-customers tile in Shopify.
Pull the column matching your chosen window (for example the day-90 column) and convert that revenue to gross profit using actual cost of goods where possible.
Compare that LTGP figure to the CAC recorded in the acquisition month for the same cohort to produce a windowed LTGP:CAC ratio per cohort.

Look across cohorts, not just in aggregate: the source's example is November cohorts being markedly worse than adjacent months because of product portfolio changes and margin compression from discounting, which drags the extended lifetime window down.

Use the cohort view to spot margin compression: even when CAC is stable month to month, first-purchase gross profit can swing from, illustratively, $70 to $40 depending on discounting and portfolio mix.
caveats: Native cohort reporting may not display gross profit, so the source builds a custom cohort analysis to get GP rather than revenue.
The illustrative $70/$40 and November-cohort examples are from anonymised client audits, not general benchmarks.
cards.source_name: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Three legitimate ways to fund a sub-1 LTGP:CAC — and who should not use them
cards.summary: Losses on first purchase can be funded by returning-customer profit, investor capital, or debt, but the source warns that capital- and debt-funded models demand an advanced operator.
cards.use_when: You are deliberately losing money on first purchase and must choose how the gap gets financed, or you are evaluating whether to take investment or debt to scale acquisition.
steps: Option one: fund it with repeat purchase. If returning-customer profit contribution reliably exceeds the first-time-customer loss, the business is profitable overall even while acquisition loses money. Verify with the two-P&L split rather than assuming.
Option two: raise capital. The source does not call this inherently bad and notes that many fast-scaling DTC brands used capital to drive content network effects and aggressive ad scaling.
Option three: use creditors/debt. The source's caution is that debt makes profitability visibility more complex, so it requires a dialled-in operator.

Screen yourself against the source's stated threshold: it would not work with a $6-7m revenue brand carrying investors or creditors, calling the risk profile enormous and saying it has rarely seen them do well. This is an opinion, not a rule.
Regardless of funding source, keep measuring LTGP:CAC monthly so the funding decision is based on the real acquisition economics rather than a blended P&L that looks fine.
caveats: The source's position on not serving $6-7m brands with investors or creditors is that presenter's own risk preference and agency policy, not a universal law.
None of these options fixes a structurally negative ratio; they only buy time to fix it.
cards.source_name: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Treat operating-expense creep as a separate cash-risk failure mode from the death spiral
cards.summary: Smaller brands can fail from over-invested operating expenses that compress margin, force debt for inventory, and end in a cash constraint rather than a ratio problem.
cards.use_when: You are setting opex and hiring plans for a smaller store (roughly $50k-$300k/month) and must protect working capital for inventory.
steps: Track whether margin is being compressed by opex growth, not just by CAC or COGS. The source's diagnosis of many small brands is that they overinvested in operating expenses while being poor capital allocators.

Model the downstream effect: compressed margin leaves less cash, which pushes you to take debt to purchase future inventory, which pressures the whole financial position and can end in failure from a cash constraint rather than a bad LTGP:CAC.
Before adding fixed cost, confirm your current LTGP:CAC can carry it. The source notes that a better ratio would have paid for the opex in these cases, so the ratio is still the root fix.
If your store sits in the low band of LTGP:CAC (1-2), apply extra scrutiny to every fixed-cost addition, because that band requires unusually lean operating expenses to produce acceptable net profit.
Distinguish this failure mode explicitly from the acquisition death spiral when diagnosing a declining store, so you apply the right corrective action.
caveats: This observation is drawn from the presenter's early-agency experience with roughly 300-400 SMB ecommerce brands over three years, not a controlled study.
The $50k-$300k/month band is the source's observed range for this pattern, not a hard threshold.
cards.source_name: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Treat first-purchase liquidity as the ecommerce norm, not the service-business norm
cards.summary: Unlike services where payback can stretch over months, consumer ecommerce brands should aim to be as profitable and liquid as possible on the first purchase because consumer stickiness is weak.
cards.use_when: You are setting payback expectations and acquisition targets, and deciding whether to accept a long first-purchase payback period.
steps: Stop importing service-business logic. The source notes agencies often break even around month 4-6 after acquisition costs because businesses repeat-transact for years; consumers are lucky to make a second purchase and rarer still a third.
Set the ecommerce default to near-breakeven or better on the first purchase, and treat anything materially below that as a risk position unless retention is genuinely exceptional.

If your LTGP:CAC is below 1, quantify the requirement precisely: applying an assumed percentage of cohort revenue to get gross profit and using an illustrative $100 LTGP against a $120 CAC gives a $20 first-purchase loss per customer.
If you must run a long payback, make it survivable with genuine measured repeat revenue rather than hoped-for retention — see the two-P&L split for verification.
Communicate the difference in expectation internally: this card is about purchase conversion and repeat purchasing, not sales close rate or lead conversion, which follow different payback logic.
caveats: The source's framing assumes D2C consumer behaviour; B2B and service models have different stickiness and payback tolerance.
The $100/$120 example is illustrative arithmetic, not an industry standard.
cards.source_name: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Use owned channels for returning revenue while accepting that new acquisition is rented
cards.summary: Email, SMS, community and brand reduce dependence on paid traffic for repeat revenue, but the source argues new-customer acquisition almost always involves renting attention.
cards.use_when: You are allocating effort between paid acquisition and list/community ownership, or pushback arises that paid should be abandoned in favour of owned channels.
steps: Classify your demand sources: renting is paying for traffic that disappears when payment stops; owning is assets you keep, such as an email list, an SMS list, or a community.
Direct owned-channel effort primarily at the LTGP side of the equation, since the source says list and community value largely sits under returning-customer revenue and drives repeat purchase.

Accept that new-customer acquisition remains rented in most forms. The source's reasoning: you acquire a customer first and only then hold first-party data to remarket to, and even large organic followings do not guarantee delivery of a post to that audience.
Do not adopt the dogma that you should never pay for attention. Keep improving owned assets while continuing to rent space to bring in new customers, then convert them into owned relationships.
Note the source's defence of the 'own your list' rhetoric as correct but incomplete — it is a large and worthwhile focus on the retention side, not a replacement for paid acquisition.
caveats: The source is explicitly arguing against the position that rising CPMs mean paid is dead and email is the answer.
Organic reach limitations are illustrated by the presenter's own account (roughly 50,000 followers getting far fewer views per post) — an anecdote, not a platform-wide measurement.
cards.source_name: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Timestamp and measure big structural changes against CAC and LTGP
cards.summary: Every major business change — new agency, new channel, new product launch, heavier ad volume — should be dated and then read back against the CAC and LTGP historical series to see if the ratio improved.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to repeat, roll back or expand an investment such as a product launch, a new ad platform, or a change in creative partner.
steps: Before making the change, record the current CAC and LTGP baseline and the date the change goes live.

After the change, compare the post-change values against the historical series. The source's example: a March product launch that raised LTGP — expected, because portfolio diversity increases cross-sell opportunity.
Ask explicitly whether the ratio improved, and then whether you can afford to repeat the action without putting the balance sheet at risk.
Double down and iterate in the direction of changes that demonstrably improved the ratio rather than judging them on gut feel or a single month's revenue.

Apply the same test to structural decisions such as introducing a new platform (e.g. Snapchat) or significantly increasing ad volume, since those consume capital and must earn their place on the ratio.

Avoid the failure pattern the source describes: a store whose monthly profit slid from, illustratively, $100,000 to $80,000 while nobody checked the first-time-customer P&L, which had swung from positive to deeply negative.
caveats: Requires sufficient data after each change to separate signal from normal variance; short windows may mislead.
The $100k/$80k and March-launch examples are from anonymised client work, not guaranteed outcomes.
cards.source_name: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Smoke test angle validation with static image ads
cards.summary: Use one product-on-white image with different text call-outs to cheaply identify which value prop or angle earns clicks before investing in video.
cards.use_when: New product launch or angle selection: you have a modest test budget and need to find which value proposition makes people click before spending on video production.
steps: Take the same product-on-white image and keep it identical across variants.
Create a white bar with bold text (a call-out) over the image, changing only the message: e.g. 'reduce anxiety', 'increase focus', 'stress release'.
Run all variants in one simple campaign and read which call-out earns the most clicks/engagement.
When one call-out clearly wins, expand that single angle into video rather than making video for all angles.

For the video, decide whether the person on screen should be a man or a woman; consider not showing a face and instead showing only hands, arms or body type so more viewers can see themselves using the product.
After the ad-level test, move scrutiny to the landing page; keep testing ad performance in-platform to compare image vs video and value prop vs value prop.
Repeat the loop: image test, then video, then add creators, colours and regions to get more granular as winners emerge.
caveats: The source presents this as his own starting method, not a validated universal rule.
CPC/CPM baselines differ by niche (he cites $15-$30 CPM as niche-dependent); judge clicks against your own account history, not the source's numbers.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Diagnose price before scaling spend
cards.summary: Read cheap front-end click and cart metrics first; if traffic is cost-effective and carts still abandon, the price or offer is the problem, not the ad.
cards.use_when: Early-stage acquisition: deciding whether to spend more budget or change pricing after a first test tranche.
steps: Check whether clicks and impressions are cost-effective against your own niche baseline (the source notes CPMs vary widely by audience; hitting middle-America moms is expensive).
If people click the ad, click through to the PDP, reach the cart and then abandon, treat it as a price/value-exchange signal and change the price.
If people buy with good unit economics, the price point is working; if they get far along and don't buy, split-test the price.
Treat price and product playfulness as the first thing to figure out with a small learning budget, before blaming creative.
caveats: The source frames this as his own sequencing; his $15-$30 CPM range is illustrative and niche-specific, not a benchmark.

At larger spend and stronger email/retention assets, a cheap cost-per-cart may be worth keeping even when the final sale doesn't happen — a judgment the source reserves for brands that can monetise the backend.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Tranches of cash: define what each test budget must uncover
cards.summary: Frame your ad spend as learning tranches — a $10k tranche and a $500 tranche both buy the same lessons, just at different speeds.
cards.use_when: Budget planning for a launch or a channel test: deciding how much to allocate and what questions the money must answer before it's gone.
steps: Before spending, write the question the tranche must answer: is my price right, which channel is most efficient, which product works, what messaging?
Accept that a small budget learns the same things as a large budget but takes longer; velocity is the only difference.
In the first quarter, set the total tranche you can afford and treat it as a bet you must make work (the source's own launch example was $75k-$100k).
Run the front-end metrics in parallel with price: are people clicking the ad, clicking through the PDP, reaching the end, buying?
If unit economics are good, keep going; if not, isolate whether the break is creative, traffic cost or price.
caveats: The source's Breeze figures ($75k-$100k first quarter, doubling month over month) are his brand's example, not a promise.
He notes brands that can't survive without first-purchase profitability face a harder road, particularly if the product isn't repeat-purchasable.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: CAC targets anchored to LTV, not a universal number
cards.summary: Set target CAC from known customer lifespan and repeat behaviour, and accept a loss on first acquisition only when the backend justifies it.
cards.use_when: Acquisition planning: deciding your target and ceiling CAC, and whether to run first-purchase-profitable or loss-leading campaigns.
steps: Estimate how long customers stay and how often they rebuy for your specific product class; the source's working CAC is $85-$90 with a ceiling around $120-$130 on bad months.
State that target internally so media buying can be judged against it rather than daily ROAS.
If your product has repeat purchase or product expansion, you can justify spending to break even or a small loss on the first order.
If your product is a one-off (his examples: rugs, a t-shirt), plan to be first-order profitable because you won't recover the loss.
During launch on a brand-new product, budget extra for market education — teaching the category that the product is legitimate and legal can be part of the CAC.
caveats: His $85-$90 target and $120-$130 ceiling are his brand's figures and depend on his LTV; do not copy them as benchmarks.
Loss-leading on first purchase requires confidence in retention and backend conversion; without that it is simply unprofitable spending.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Organise the ad account by story, not by funnel stage
cards.summary: Replace strict top/middle/bottom funnel segmentation with asset-and-angle folders that carry one consistent story from ad to landing page.
cards.use_when: Account structure decisions for paid social: how to name, group and route campaigns and how much to rely on audience segmentation.
steps: Accept that the old three-tier funnel — prospecting for new customers, a value-prop middle, a discount-retargeting bottom — is now muddier and less segmented in practice.

Stop forcing audience segmentation to control which ad a new customer sees; that control was needed when the platform couldn't be trusted to serve the right creative, and the source argues we are now in a 'trust the algorithm' era.
Instead, build folders around your stories and angles: e.g. a 'feel better tomorrow' group that contains every video, image and landing page version of that story.
Keep the story consistent from the landing page all the way through the ad assets inside each folder.
Invest the saved effort into telling more convincing stories and building more offers, since landing pages can now be built or adapted in a day with current tools (verify current tools' interfaces).
caveats: This is the source's read of platform direction and his own account practice, not a platform mandate; some accounts may still benefit from tighter segmentation.
His claim that creative now outweighs audience selection rests on a platform engineering article he references, not on a controlled test.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Creative as the new targeting
cards.summary: Build ads whose cast, setting and language mirror the region and identity of the audience you're buying, because narrative now does the targeting work.
cards.use_when: Creative direction and casting for paid social: choosing who appears in ads and which regional variants to produce.
steps: Identify the market you're buying and match the people in the ad to it: the source reports ads with people who look like they've lived in Florida perform better in Florida, and New York-styled creative performs better in New York.
Treat a creative as stackable bricks — hook, value prop, benefits, problem, solution — and rearrange them for each audience or product claim.
Test granularity: for example, three women stating three effects within the first few seconds versus founders on camera; the source reports far longer retention when the viewer sees themselves.
In the briefing, specify the placement, framing and length, plus examples of what is working and examples of what has failed, so creators know the boundaries without losing their own voice.
Archive and reuse: keep an organised drive of past winning assets because long libraries are now a competitive asset for remixing into new clips.
caveats: Regional-matching results are the source's own-reported observations, not published benchmarks.
Continuously refreshing the library matters because asset styles age quickly.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Design creative natively for each placement
cards.summary: Build and brief separate assets for 4x5 and 9x16 placements instead of letting a square ad with cut-off captions run everywhere.
cards.use_when: Ad production and briefing: fixing poor performance caused by mismatched aspect ratios and unreadable captions on Reels and Stories.
steps: Decide the placements in advance (the source focuses on Meta) and produce assets at the correct ratios — he names 4x5 and 9x16 — rather than one square that gets reused everywhere.
Check that captions and the focal point of the creative are visible instantly in the chosen ratio; square ads with words and dots in a story are a common, fixable mistake.
In the creator brief, state the placement and format explicitly (e.g. 'this is for Meta Reels, we need 9x16 or 4x5'), plus framing rules such as shooting in sunlight.
Build the fix into the workflow: return creator footage that is too close or has the product cut off on the right for reshooting rather than shipping it.
Sort every concept into an image version and a video version for each placement — the source calls this more work but necessary at serious spend.
caveats: The exact ratios and platform behaviours can change; verify current placement specs in the ad platform before briefing.
The source says small brands may not be able to obsess at this level initially; it prioritises placement hygiene at higher spend.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Make the media buyer a P&L-aware creative strategist
cards.summary: Collapse the pod into a media buyer who also owns creative strategy and sees the P&L, with designers and editors supporting them.
cards.use_when: Team design for paid acquisition: deciding the roles needed to run ads and what performance reporting the buyer should own.
steps: Restructure from separate pods (creative strategist, account manager, media buyer, junior buyer, designer) to one owner who is both media buyer and creative strategist, supported by a designer and creators.
Put that person in direct contact with whoever owns creative strategy on Slack so iterations, hooks and asset formats move in real time.
Give them visibility of the P&L and forecasting so their decisions account for the whole business, not just an ad-platform ROAS widget.
Expect a media buyer who believes they control performance mainly through account settings to be replaced by one who manages creative supply.
Consider using an outside expert for a short weekly check-in while someone internal learns the account — the source used this as a hedge and short-term training.
caveats: The source's example is an internal hire who had never run an ad and was given four weeks to self-teach, supported by an existing creative team — not a guarantee for every brand.
He also says a freelance media buyer at a high level now needs designers and editors around them; the lone button-pusher is the role at risk.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Run a weekly creative volume target tied to spend
cards.summary: Measure new assets launched and winners that attract spend, then staff against the volume the season and profitability require.
cards.use_when: Creative operations and resourcing: setting a weekly production target and deciding when to hire editors or creators.
steps: Set a weekly target in concepts, not just assets — the source's example is 10 concepts with 2 ads each, 20 total, as a successful week.
Track two numbers per week: how many new assets launched, and how many hit the success metric, which he defines as dollars spent on them.
Adjust the target for season: product drops, Q3/Q4 and summer versus Q1 change the required volume and the profitability target.
Use the target to size the team: if the target doubles in busy season, that tells you when to hire against it.
Do not produce assets for SKUs that can't be sold — if products are backordered, funnel that time and money elsewhere.
Keep roughly a 30-day runway of assets, planning monthly and rotating in drops, holidays and evergreen angles.
When introducing new ads, avoid flooding the account: adding 5-15 new ads while only two or three proven ads carry spend can skew the whole account, which often forces the team to kill the new ads.
caveats: The 10 concepts/20 ads figure is the source's own weekly benchmark for one brand; it shifts with season and product drops.
Too much volume can destabilise a profitable account — the source explicitly names the tension between 'more assets' and 'we're unprofitable, kill everything'.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Think about the funnel in numbers: 70/30 to 90/10
cards.summary: Split spend between proven winners and tests, moving from 70/30 toward 90/10 or 100/0 when company performance is weak.
cards.use_when: Allocating budget inside a paid social account: how much to keep on convictions and how much to reserve for new tests.
steps: Target roughly 70% of dollars on assets you have conviction in and 30% on things you are unsure about.
When overall company performance is bad, shift to 90/10 — the source says even 100/0 is defensible then.

Time tests against where your sales actually come from: the source notes his product gets more energy Friday-Sunday, so spending heavily Monday-Thursday risks wasting budget that would perform better on the weekend.

Let the ratio flex daily based on profitability and on the platform's allocation behaviour — if Meta shifts spend to a non-converting ad, turning it off can stop the account from spending, so the buyer has to push and pull budgets rather than letting the account run limp.
Make sure you keep testing while new people are coming in, or the account eventually runs out of fresh winners.
caveats: 70/30 and 90/10 are the source's heuristics, not calculated from a dataset or universal rule.
The right ratio depends on how much proven creative you already have and how tolerant your unit economics are.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Judge ads on multiple KPIs, not dashboard profit alone
cards.summary: Combine CAC, email/text capture and CPM to decide which ads to keep, and blend results across channels rather than killing an ad on one platform's ROAS.
cards.use_when: Ad reporting and optimisation: deciding whether to switch off an ad or channel that looks unprofitable on its own dashboard.
steps: Use CAC as the primary success metric for a customer.
Treat email or text capture as a legitimate secondary KPI: if an ad gets people to cart cheaply, the source keeps spending because the address is captured and the backend can convert later.

Look at CPM as a softer third indicator, particularly on awareness-heavy placements that don't produce the highest-quality traffic but do reach people; the source says a small brand probably shouldn't let this drive decisions yet, while a larger one can.
Blend channels into one pot: an ad source (his example: Apple Search Ads) may lose on CAC but win on email collection, and the company-level question is whether total channels hit the goal CAC.

Coordinate spend with the rest of the business: if email flows, a product drop or a discount programme will land in the next days, pull back ad spend rather than overspending on customers who would buy anyway.
caveats: The 20% subscriber take rate he cites is his brand's figure; relying on email capture assumes your own backend can convert those addresses.
The 'let it run past profitability' approach is explicitly something he says works at his scale, not a rule for brands without strong retention and flows.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Match site experience to customer history
cards.summary: Show first-time, returning and high-value visitors different SKUs and messages based on what they have already bought.
cards.use_when: Site merchandising and CRM: deciding what a visitor sees on arrival based on purchase history.
steps: For a visitor who has never bought, communicate the SKUs they should try first, chosen from historical repeatability data.
For a returning buyer, do not show the same products they already bought; present a welcome-back message and what to try next based on what they have tried.
Segment by lifetime value: the source says someone who spends over $500 with them should be treated very differently from someone who has never seen the brand.
Build the depth of this journey deliberately — the message and product set should change with the customer's stage, not just the acquisition campaign.
caveats: Requires purchase history and some data depth; the source's $500 threshold is his own brand's example.
Works best with products that have continuation or expansion paths; a single-SKU store has limited levers.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Fix the homepage for your SKU count
cards.summary: Low-SKU stores should make the landing page almost a one-product conversion page; high-SKU stores should lead with offer, then bundles, then categories.
cards.use_when: Homepage and landing page design: structuring the first screens of a store based on how many products you sell.
steps: For low-SKU stores, keep the landing page close to a landing page with a little brand story; the single product should be added to cart or checkout as fast as possible with minimal extra clicks.
For high-SKU stores, put the current offer or promoted campaign in the header area where it gets the most visibility.

Directly beneath that, show the highest-AOV bundles and packs — the source points to True Classic's pack structure as an example — acknowledging that raising the first-order value is the goal for every store.
Further down, introduce categories so shoppers with many SKUs can browse, plus reviews and feedback for individual items.
Do not overcomplicate the number of pages at the start.
caveats: The True Classic reference is the source's example of testing volume, not a guarantee your store will match it.
High-AOV merchandising assumes your economics and fulfilment can support larger pack sizes.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Replace blank white PDP first images with lifestyle imagery
cards.summary: A product page whose hero is a plain product on white wastes prime real estate that could carry lifestyle context and a strong headline.
cards.use_when: PDP optimisation: revising the first image and adjacent copy on a product page.
steps: Audit the first image on each product page; if it is a plain product on white, replace it with a lifestyle image, the product in use, or a dynamic shot.
Put the strongest benefit headlines next to the hero rather than a weak description of why someone would buy.
Use the first-image choice as a split test to see whether lifestyle context lifts performance versus the plain shot.
Pair the visual change with the strongest angle discovered in your smoke tests so the PDP matches the ad that brought the visitor.
caveats: The source allows product-on-white can be a useful A/B variant, but calls it a wasted default, not an absolute requirement in every category.
Marketplace conventions (mentioned for Amazon) can differ from DTC norms; match the channel the shopper expects.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Use clipping marketplaces to scale distribution cheaply
cards.summary: Buy fixed-budget clip campaigns from low-cost creators who post to their own pages, paying only for approved posts and capped at your budget even if clips go viral.
cards.use_when: Acquisition creative sourcing: testing a paid clipper model to add volume and impressions beyond your own accounts.
steps: Choose an offer and state a budget plus a target CPM (the source's example: $5,000 at an 85-cent to $1 target CPM — a figure to treat as illustrative, not a benchmark).
Provide the creative brief and assets you want used so the clippers post material consistent with your angles.
Use the marketplace's approval step: you don't pay until you approve a post.
Accept the cap: if a clip goes viral and would be worth far more at the target CPM, you still pay only the agreed budget.
Expect the audience to be random pages driving to your site, which means you need an organised backlog of briefs and assets to keep feeding the army.
Treat follower counts as irrelevant; the source's framing is that impressions and traffic back to the store are what matter.
caveats: He predicted the tactic would become widely known and CPMs could rise as large advertisers enter; verify current marketplace terms and pricing before committing.
The clip model relies on clippers not needing the physical product, which may not fit every category or legal/compliance context.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Set up a testing pipeline and organic posting habit
cards.summary: Run a repeating image-to-video test tree across value props, male/female presenters and regions, and keep posting organically because it supports the ad account.
cards.use_when: Standing up a paid social testing process and deciding whether organic posting is worth the time for an ecommerce brand.
steps: Start the tree with image smoke tests, expand winners into video, then add creators, colours and regions as you learn.

Alongside the paid tests, post organically on your channels; the source reports that when the brand stops uploading assets to social channels, ad account performance weakens, and that organic content often becomes top-performing paid creative because it doesn't feel like an ad.
If you don't yet have an ad account, post on every platform as a starting practice — the source suggests twice a day as a best-practice target.
Route learnings back to creators quickly: share what is working in real time, including failed formats to avoid.
Use the pipeline to answer micro questions — which value prop, which presenter type, which region — and let answers feed the next round of briefs.
caveats: The claim that organic activity improves the ad account is the source's reported observation, not a documented mechanism; the twice-a-day cadence is his suggested practice.
Ad platform behaviour and current posting tools change — verify current platform guidance before building the calendar.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Build an always-on creative bench and 30-day asset runway
cards.summary: Keep testing and producing even when you have winners, because the account is the lifeline of new customers and stopping is not an option.
cards.use_when: Creative and media planning over a month or quarter: keeping a rotating pipeline rather than scheduling one-off production bursts.
steps: Assume more creative is better than less: with nothing working you need more anyway, and once something works it tells you what more to make.
Plan in monthly cycles, rotating in drops, holidays and evergreen angles that historically perform, and keep launching those plus new tests.
Keep testing while new customers are coming in, so the account doesn't run out of fresh winners.
Maintain roughly a 30-day runway of assets: you can build many variants off what is working now, but only about a month's worth before trends shift and the assets become obsolete.
Watch for the account being lopsided: if only a couple of proven ads carry spend and every new ad misses, the account can destabilise and the team may have to pull back the new launches.
caveats: The 30-day runway is the source's rule of thumb, not a calculated optimum.
He also acknowledges days when nothing is taking budget and the right move is to pull back rather than force spend.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Brief editors and designers with references plus brand context
cards.summary: Untrained editors replicate a reference pixel-by-pixel; the editor you want understands the reference, your brand and how to improve on it.
cards.use_when: Creative production and outsourcing: writing briefs for external creative help who understand performance marketing.
steps: Recognise that performance-aware editors are scarce and that using a generic designer to add badges or sparkle produces incoherent ads.
Give references explicitly and state this is an example of the outcome you want, then supply what your brand stands for and the assets and value props involved.
Tell the editor they should adapt the reference to your brand rather than copy it word-for-word or pixel-by-pixel.
Include examples of things that are working and things that failed, while telling creators to keep their own voice because they know their audience.
Expect that your own idea of what you want becomes clearer once you receive a first version, so budget for a second or third revision rather than judging the initial brief.
Source talent where time zones align (the source works with editors in Canada and Latin America for this reason) and verify current rates and platforms.
caveats: The source says brand owners often can't communicate what they want until they see something — plan for iteration rather than expecting a perfect first cut.
Talent-market and time-zone specifics change; verify current arrangements.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Learn the ad account yourself before hiring out
cards.summary: Founders and leadership should run ads up to roughly $10k-$30k of spend so they can ask better questions and avoid paying management on top of test budget.
cards.use_when: Early paid acquisition: deciding whether to manage ads internally or hand them to an agency or freelancer.
steps: Run the account yourself at the start, up to about $10k-$30k in monthly spend, so you understand what the eventual manager is doing and can ask better questions.
At very low spend ($3k-$10k/month), weigh the management fee against test budget: paying someone thousands more may leave too little to learn with, so eat the work yourself.
Use current tools; the source argues they are sophisticated enough that you don't need heavy outside support.
If you do want help, hire someone for a short consult or a weekly look over your shoulder rather than a full retainer.
Insert an outside expert for a limited weekly audit while an internal person learns — the source used this as a hedge during a handover.
caveats: The $10k-$30k threshold is the source's rule of thumb, not a computed break-even.
At higher spend the internal creative-strategist model with a P&L-aware owner becomes more viable than founder operation.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Track daily burn, discount rate and high-value orders together
cards.summary: Understand your daily burn and your discount percent of sales so rising revenue doesn't hide shrinking margin.
cards.use_when: Finance and acquisition coordination: setting daily tracking and deciding when to pull ad spend or run promos.
steps: Track daily spend and return at the channel level each day — the source's team reviews spend and return hourly, Monday to Sunday.
Add discount as a percent of sales as a core metric and know your sweet spot; if sales rise while discount percent rises too, you may not be outrunning burn.
Track orders over $1,000 per day as an indicator of high-value customer activity.
Use discount dollars as a lever that trades off against ad spend: when media pulls back, promotions or discounts can fill the gap for those days.
Keep the marketing and finance forecast in the same conversation so spend changes are made with the daily cash position in mind.
caveats: Hourly, daily, always-on review reflects a brand at the source's scale; smaller brands may track less frequently but should still monitor burn and discount rate together.
The $1,000 order threshold is his brand's metric, not a universal target.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: PDP hero image: lifestyle over white-background product shot
cards.summary: Treat the first PDP image as a split-testable asset and favor lifestyle/in-use imagery over sterile white-background shots.
cards.use_when: Designing or A/B testing the lead image and above-the-fold layout on a product detail page.
steps: Audit your PDP hero images: if the first thing a shopper sees is a bare product on a white background, flag it for testing.
Build a lifestyle alternative that shows the product in use, on a person, or in its real context, and test it as the PDP first image against the current shot.
